Container ship sinks in Hormuz mine strike amid US-Iran naval clashes (VIDEOS)
A container ship sank after striking a mine in the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday, amid a wave of attacks on shipping in the region and stalled talks between the US and Iran. More than 20 oil tankers and other vessels have been attacked this month.
The Singapore-registered container ship GFS Pride caught fire and later sank, with all 21 crew members rescued, according to the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore.
Photos and videos shared on social media show smoke rising from the listing vessel and dozens of shipping containers floating in the water.
A second Singapore-registered vessel, the GFS Giselle, was struck the same day, sustaining hull damage. It managed to leave the area under its own power, with no injuries reported among the crew.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy said the GFS Pride, which was carrying more than 2,500 containers, sank while sailing along what it described as an “unauthorized and dangerous route.”
“Local vessels and fishermen must exercise the utmost safety when navigating this route so they do not collide with containers floating on the water,” the IRGC Navy said in a statement carried by Press TV.
BREAKING: Iran announces a large UAE-owned container ship carrying more than 2,500 containers hit a naval mine, exploded and sank this morning in the US-backed southern Omani corridor of the Strait of Hormuz. It is the first vessel sunk by a mine in the war. Initial reports indicate the cargo ship was carrying luxury perfumes and iPhones from Dubai.

Top Iranian negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf reiterated earlier this month that Iran would not reopen the vital waterway, which normally handles around a quarter of the world’s seaborne oil and LNG trade, until the US accepts Tehran’s terms. The conditions include lifting sanctions and releasing frozen Iranian funds.

Delhi Metro Rail Corporation announced the reopening of all metro stations after imposing temporary restrictions.
NEW DELHI: Delhi Metro Rail Corporation (DMRC) Wednesday informed Supreme Court that there was no curtailment or cancellation of metro services and no reduction in the number of train trips, with 272 trains operating on Oct 10.“A full complement of 4,157 train trips were conducted on Oct 10 as per schedule across the Metro network,” it said, adding that 258 stations, or 85% of the total number of stations, remained fully operational, accessible and functional for commuters.Following the Supreme Court’s Oct 9 order, which disapproved of a complete shutdown of metro services, Delhi Police reviewed its Oct 8 order for entry/exit closure of 57 of 303 metro stations in Delhi on Oct 10, the day of CJP protest, and applied its directive to 45 stations, DMRC said. It said metro services functioned normally except for closure of entry/exit points at 45 stations on Oct 10 and a total of 32 lakh commuters travelled on the network that day, as against approximately 58 lakh on a normal second Saturday.“Crucially, out of the 45 stations where entry/exit gates were regulated, 14 key interchange stations (including major transit hubs such as Rajiv Chowk, Kashmere Gate, Central Secretariat, Mandi House, Hauz Khas, Dilli Haat-INA and Netaji Subhash Place) continued to provide full and uninterrupted line-interchange facilities for commuters,” it said, adding that all stations were fully operational after 10 pm on Oct 10.
“At key sensitive stations, such as GTB Nagar and Vishwavidyalaya, DMRC did not impose a total prohibition on movement; rather, it implemented a measured and calibrated regulatory protocol to control incoming passenger flow while actively facilitating disembarking commuters,” it said.
On instructions from police, entry/exit to six metro stations—Patel Chowk, Janpath, Rajiv Chowk, Mandi House, Central Secretariat and Barakhamba Road—were closed from 6 am to 5 pm on Oct 12 to avoid untoward incidents as the police had said there was “likelihood of unruly mob movement towards sensitive locations”, DMRC said.In its Oct 9 order, SC had said, “We clarify that although there shall be no outright prohibition on the movement of metro trains, a prudent decision may be made to permit the operation of Metro trains and other rail services in a suitable and regulated manner.”

SC: Cops can’t seek digital footprints for roving probe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
00:51:16 UTC
09:51:16 KST

NEW DELHI: SC has said police cannot direct social media platforms under IT Act to share an accused’s digital footprints for periods well before the crime he is being probed for, in an order that is likely to become a precedent for protection of privacy, reports Dhananjay Mahapatra.“Information and Technology Act provisions cannot be misused by police to launch a roving and fishing inquiry by obtaining personal data of an accused in breach of right to privacy,” said SC quashing a Ghaziabad Police order asking ‘X’ to furnish digital footprints of journalist Abhishek Upadhyay since June 1 when he was accused of a road rage incident in Aug 18.Cops must apply principles of proportionality, says SCA bench of CJI Surya Kant and Justice Joymalya Bagchi said: “Police must apply the prin-ciples of proportionality while taking steps to investigate a crime and can resort to seeking digital footprints only after recording that alternative methods to obtain information about a crime has proved inadequate”. The court also kept in operation its interim order pro-tecting the journalist from arrest as long as he cooperated with the investigators.Upadhyay, through senior advocate Pradeep Rai, said he had carried out a journalistic investigation into theft of donations at Ayodhya Ram Temple and was first to publish a news article on his digital platform on June 7. The real intent behind the cooked-up FIR of Aug 18 was to seek information from June 1 to identify the sources who informed him about pilferage of donations by devotees, Rai argued.
Ghaziabad Police commissioner had informed the court that police searched for the petitioner for three days in connection with the road rage case, in which he is accused of hurling caste slurs at the complainant bike rider, and when he was untraceable, police sought details of digital footprint from ‘X’.
SC said the commissioner’s explanation and the order seeking digital footprint details appear to be at variance for the purpose of investigation of the road rage case.“Police can surely look for digital footprints if the crime was committed with long planning and conspiracy, but not in such cases where questions of privacy and right to act as a journalist are involved,” said the bench.Rai with advocate Anoop P Awasthi complained to the court that the journalist’s vehicle, which was seized after the FIR against him, has not been returned. The bench directed Ghaziabad Police to return the vehicle to the petitioner within two days.The bench cautioned Ghaziabad Police against using any of the private and personal information related to the petitioner it has obtained from ‘X’.

Unemployment rate remains at 4.7pc in September

09:50:22 KST

Australia's unemployment rate remained at 4.7 per cent in September, after August's jobless rate was revised upwards.
It means the national unemployment rate remains at its highest level in the post-COVID era, in seasonally adjusted terms.
An estimated 39,300 fewer Australians were in work last month, and the number of unemployed people increased by 8,900.
The proportion of people in work or actively looking for work also surprisingly fell to 66.8 per cent, from 67 per cent.
In trend terms, the national unemployment rate remained at 4.6 per cent.

Air Force May Buy Land for 120 New Sentinel ICBM Silos
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
00:46:59 UTC
09:46:59 KST

The Air Force may wind up buying land to build 120 new intercontinental ballistic missile silos as part of its revamped infrastructure approach for the new Sentinel ICBM.
The service revealed that and other new details about its Sentinel plans as it announced the start of an environmental impact analysis meant to supplement the program’s original review, which was completed in 2023.
The environmental impact statement released in March 2023 cleared a key procedural hurdle in the Air Force’s effort to replace the aging Minuteman III with the Sentinel across three bases in the western U.S.: F.E. Warren Air Force Base, Wyo.; Malmstrom Air Force Base, Mont.; and Minot Air Force Base, N.D. But much has changed since that EIS—in early 2024, critical cost and schedule overruns for Sentinel triggered a notice to Congress and a Pentagon review under the Nunn-McCurdy Act.
The program’s issues are not caused by the missile, but rather by the massive infrastructure and civil engineering work needed to build the systems it requires, officials say. The Air Force had hoped to reuse much of the infrastructure that supported Minuteman, but analysis showed much of it was too old or too expensive to upgrade.
Eventually, Pentagon leaders certified the Sentinel program to continue. But in an effort to control costs, Air Force officials decided in spring 2025 it would be more effective to build entirely new silos instead of reusing the old ones. There are 450 active Minuteman silos, which the Air Force plans to replace on a one-for-one basis.
At the time, a spokesperson told Air & Space Forces Magazine that the new silos would be “predominantly Air Force-owned real estate, which means reusing the existing missile sites but not the 55-year-old silos.”
A new website associated with the supplemental environmental impact analysis, launched Oct. 9, states that just over a quarter of the sites could be on land not currently owned by the Air Force, with the service considering:
- Acquisition of land and construction of up to 30 new launch silo sites around F.E. Warren
- Acquisition of land and construction of up to 30 new launch silo sites around Malmstrom
- Acquisition of land and construction of up to 60 new launch silo sites around Minot
Additionally, the service said it is evaluating old sites at Malmstrom formerly operated by the 564th Missile Squadron, now inactive, to reuse for up to 60 new launch silo sites.
The Air Force is planning to buy up to 12 acres per silo, according to the supplemental EIS website.
Launch Centers
Silos aren’t the only ICBM infrastructure getting a refresh in the Air Force’s latest plan for Sentinel.
Currently there are 45 missile alert facilities across the three bases where Airmen stay on watch 24/7. The original plan for Sentinel called for building new “launch centers” to command and control the ICBMs at 24 of those facilities and razing the rest.
The new EIS website states that the Air Force will reutilize Missile Alert Facility sites for Launch Centers “where feasible,” but at Minot specifically, officials are considering “construction of new launch center sites in previously undeveloped areas,” the website states. Each Launch Center would have a footprint of up to 16 acres.
Another new consideration is the construction of a “purpose-built Operations Group Facility” at Malmstrom.
Timeline
Now that the Air Force has announced its plans to craft a supplemental EIS, there is a 30-day public “scoping” period where federal, state, and local agencies, interested organizations, and members of the public can all provide comments on the proposed actions.
After that, the service will release a draft of its supplemental EIS, and there will be another window for public comments. The Air Force plans to release its draft by fall 2027.
A final supplemental EIS is scheduled for release in spring 2028, after which the Secretary of the Air Force can sign a Record of Decision, clearing the way for the acquisition of land and construction.
After that, it will be several more years before Sentinel is in the ground—the current Air Force estimate is for the new missile to reach initial operational capability by the early 2030s.
For now, though, the Air Force and contractor Northrop Grumman are already building a prototype silo for Sentinel at Northrop’s Promontory, Utah, facilities.

Ukraine’s war budget has $52 billion hole, and army needs $45 billion more on top
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
00:46:27 UTC
09:46:27 KST

Ukraine is seeking fresh funding for 2027 and says it is ready to deliver the reforms. Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi says Ukraine’s external budget financing need for 2027 exceeds $52 billion, with more than $32.6 billion still to be raised.
That money underwrites the basics of a country at war: the army, pensions, hospitals, and support for business, he notes. Defense and security alone will take almost 44 percent of GDP in the 2027 budget, and the gap comes as Russia keeps hammering the infrastructure that generates Ukraine’s own revenue.
“The defense capability of the country, the payment of pensions, the support of hospitals and business depend on these funds,” Koretskyi says.
The hole Russia keeps digging faster than Kyiv can fill it
Russia’s strikes widen the gap even as Kyiv tries to close it. Russia systematically attacks critical infrastructure, business, production and civilian sites, and the destruction and halted enterprises will leave tax revenues about $1.5 billion below forecast by the end of the year, he warns.
For instance, output of Ukraine's steel industry, one of the pillars of its wartime economy, fell 57.3% in August due to Russian strikes. This sector is Ukraine's second-largest foreign-currency earner, employing more than 70,000 people directly and another 250,000 in related industries, and paying close to $1 billion a year in taxes.
Beyond the budget itself, the off-budget needs of Ukraine’s Defense Forces for 2027 are estimated at $45 billion, or about 40 billion euros, a figure that sits on top of the $52 billion budget requirement, he says.
The reforms Kyiv must deliver to unlock the money
The money hinges on reforms Ukraine still has to deliver. In the next few days, the government is to approve all the decisions needed to continue financing.
“Ukraine continues to work on fulfilling its part of the commitments. This week, the government is expected to approve all the necessary decisions to ensure continued funding,” the Ukrainian prime minister says.
Meanwhile, the Parliament plans to consider the bills required under the support programs of the IMF, the World Bank and the EU.

US Space Force electromagnetic weapons played key role in Venezuela, Iran operations - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
00:37:39 UTC
09:37:39 KST

US Space Force electromagnetic weapons played a crucial role in US military operations in Venezuela and Iran, The Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday.
The WSJ was granted access to a US Space Force base in Colorado, where it was shown some of the Pentagon's space warfare capabilities, including systems designed to disrupt enemy satellites and detect threats to the US military.
Among the weapons demonstrated was Meadowlands, an offensive system that can jam enemy satellites and disrupt their communications.
According to the WSJ, these satellites are used for surveillance, communications, and navigation.
Meadowlands often operates alongside a defensive system known as Bounty Hunter, which scans the electromagnetic spectrum to detect and locate potential threats to US forces, the report explained. Commanders can then pinpoint the location of a specific threat and order a defensive strike.
Transportable jamming system used by US Space Force
The US Space Force has also accelerated the deployment of a newer jamming system known as the Remote Modular Terminal. The equipment can be packed into a container and transported to locations around the world, allowing US personnel to deploy electronic warfare capabilities quickly.
Over the past year, US Space Force soldiers, known as Guardians, have transported and deployed these systems to support US military operations in both Venezuela and Iran.
According to the WSJ, “In a sign of how important space systems are, Iran repeatedly targeted US space capabilities, including satellite communications terminals, to try to degrade those advantages.
“Satellites help the US detect missile launches, guide weapons, and get a clear picture of the battlefield,” taking high-resolution imagery from above.
Tech.-Sgt. Joshua Lomax, who helped counter threats during operations in Venezuela before being deployed to defend against threats from Iran, described the pressure of preparing for the missions.
“The threat is real,” Lomax told the WSJ.
He recalled having just 72 hours to pack the equipment in Venezuela, load it onto an aircraft, and depart for Iran.
“It was incredibly intense,” he told the WSJ. “Everybody was head on a swivel.”
Importance of electromagnetic waves in modern warfare
The US Space Force also highlighted the importance of electromagnetic waves, which travel at different wavelengths and frequencies and underpin many of the technologies used in modern warfare. These systems connect military assets ranging from submarines and drones to radar installations.
According to US Space Forces’ Combat Forces Command, led by Lt.-Gen. Greggory Gagnon, a key mission for the US is to dominate the electromagnetic spectrum.
“That thing you never see is incredibly important in warfare,” he said. “If we can dominate the spectrum, we can keep our systems, our satellites, our ships, our planes, all connected and working more effectively, but we can also disrupt the adversary’s ability to do it.”

US considers easing sanctions on shadow fleet vessels to cut freight rates, official says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
00:36:54 UTC
09:36:54 KST

The Trump administration is considering easing sanctions on so-called shadow fleet vessels that have transported oil and petroleum products from countries including Russia, Iran and Venezuela, in an effort to reduce record-high global freight rates, a US official said on Wednesday.
The discussions are happening days after President Donald Trump temporarily lifted sanctions on Russian diesel fuel, a move met with a torrent of criticism from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, European countries and some of Trump's fellow Republicans in the US Senate.
Both Zelenskiy and the US senators called that move a gift to Russian President Vladimir Putin that would provide Russia with revenue to keep funding its war in Ukraine.
The new talks center on the United States potentially allowing "legal oil" to flow on previously sanctioned vessels, the US official said. That means crude or petroleum products not sanctioned by Washington, rather than Russian and Iranian oil, which are under punitive measures.
The goal is to get more refined products and crude out of the Gulf, the official said.
US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said in a video to the World Petroleum Congress in Riyadh this week that the administration was talking about easing the sanctions on shadow fleet vessels in an effort to cut record freight rates that have cut into demand for US crude, according to Energy Aspects, a research group.
Bits of the talk were broadcast on social media, but Reuters was not able to obtain the full video or a transcript. The Department of Energy said it was not available.
Companies seeking to use the sanctioned vessels would have to apply to the US Treasury Department to use the vessels, the official said.
The Department of Energy said any move to relieve sanctions on the shadow fleet would not help Russia to move oil or oil products. The Treasury Department referred questions to the Department of Energy.
But Trump's push to move Russian diesel to global markets quickly could put pressure on the departments to allow shipment via the vessels.
The White House did not respond immediately to a request for comment.
High oil and fuel prices are a risk for Trump in the November 3 midterm elections in which Republicans are hoping to maintain control of both chambers of Congress. He lifted the sanctions on Russian diesel through April 7.
Tanker freight rates soar to record highs
Tanker freight rates have soared to record highs as the wars in Iran and Ukraine have stoked inflation and put US crude oil out of reach for Asian refiners, pushing them to seek alternatives from the Middle East and Latin America.
Energy Aspects said in a note to clients that easing the sanctions on the shadow fleet would not greatly impact freight rates but could allow more movement of oil in the Middle East.
Lifting the sanctions on the tankers that are mostly old and not well maintained is "unlikely to add meaningful mainstream fleet capacity overnight, especially as most tankers sanctioned over Russian or Venezuelan links have been actively trading over the past three months," it said in the note.
Easing the restrictions "could make a small number of additional tankers available for certain (Strait of) Hormuz shuttle runs," in the waterway between Iran and Oman.
Lifting the measures is unlikely to result in a broad easing of freight rates as ship insurers will still be bound by EU and UK regulations, maritime industry sources said.

Israel blocks Gaza base for Trump's Board of Peace as election nears, Guardian reports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
00:30:48 UTC
09:30:48 KST

Israel is blocking construction of a military outpost in the Gaza Strip intended to serve as a base for an international stabilization force operating under U.S. President Donald Trump's Board of Peace, The Guardian reported Wednesday, citing a person with direct knowledge of the project.
According to the British newspaper, the Board of Peace awarded its first Gaza construction contract in early August to Arkel International, a Louisiana-based company tasked with building a fortified compound for approximately 150 international troops.
More than two months later, construction has yet to begin because Israel has not authorized contractors or construction vehicles to enter the territory, the source said.
"Israel won't open the border," the source told The Guardian.
The newspaper said a Board of Peace spokesperson declined to comment, while the Israeli government and IDF did not respond to requests for comment.
A military base holding up Gaza reconstruction
The proposed compound would measure approximately 100 by 100 meters and be built on a site formerly used by the Gaza Humanitarian Foundation (GHF), the now-defunct aid distribution operation that delivered humanitarian supplies through private contractors.
The facility is intended to accommodate rotating deployments of 150 armed international troops, drawn from a larger contingent of approximately 500 personnel dispatched from Morocco and Kosovo, according to the report.
The troops would form part of the International Stabilization Force (ISF), a multinational security mission planned to operate in Gaza under the Board of Peace.
But the source warned that the absence of the military base is preventing the broader reconstruction program from moving forward.
Without the stabilization force on the ground, there would be no security arrangements to enable construction crews to enter, deliver equipment, install utilities or establish basic infrastructure, the source explained.
The delay therefore threatens far more than the construction of a single military facility. It could prevent the launch of the initial reconstruction projects planned for southern Gaza.
Is Israel's election behind the delay?
The source told The Guardian that officials involved in the Board of Peace believe Israel will allow construction to proceed after the country's October 27 election.
That assessment raises questions about whether Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government is reluctant to permit the start of Gaza reconstruction during the election campaign.
However, the report did not establish that electoral considerations were the reason Israeli authorities had withheld the necessary approvals.
The delay comes despite Israel having already approved the Board of Peace's entry into Gaza and the launch of a limited reconstruction initiative.
In July, Israel's security cabinet approved a pilot program to restore basic services in the territory, with the first stage expected to take place in Rafah, in southern Gaza.
The initiative is intended to lay the groundwork for a broader international effort to stabilize the territory and begin rebuilding infrastructure damaged during the war.
Countries expected to contribute troops to the stabilization force include Uganda, Morocco, Kosovo and Kazakhstan. Discussions have also been held with Albania, Vietnam and Georgia about possible participation.
Temporary housing and a Palestinian administration
Beyond the military outpost, the reconstruction initiative calls for temporary housing facilities in Rafah to accommodate Palestinian residents.
Under the reported plans, Palestinians seeking to move into the designated areas would undergo extensive security screening intended to prevent individuals affiliated with Hamas or connected to the terrorist organization from entering.
The pilot area would be the first in Gaza administered by the Palestinian technocratic body known as the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG).
The committee would operate with the backing of the international stabilization force, which is intended to provide security for the reconstruction effort and support the establishment of civilian administration.
The arrangements form part of Trump's broader postwar framework for Gaza, which places the Board of Peace at the center of efforts to stabilize and reconstruct the territory.
For now, however, the plan remains dependent on Israeli authorization to move the first contractors and equipment into Gaza.
According to the source cited by The Guardian, officials involved in the initiative expect that approval may come only after Israelis go to the polls on October 27, leaving the first phase of the reconstruction effort on hold.

WASHINGTON, October 15. /TASS/. US President Donald Trump has expressed confidence that Canada will eventually become part of the United States.
"They'll end up being the 51st state because it's the only way it works," he said at a campaign rally in Arizona ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.
"You know, we don't need them, but they need us," he said, adding that the United States has been losing up to $100 billion a year due to trade and economic relations with Canada. Ecuador to shore up electric system ahead of peak El Nino months: president
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
08:25:04 CST
09:25:04 KST

QUITO, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- Ecuador is set to shore up its electric system to ensure service during the critical months of the El Nino weather phenomenon, forecast to run from late November through February, President Daniel Noboa said Wednesday.
"We are facing a very harsh weather situation, especially along the coast, though highland areas are also being affected," Noboa said in an interview with Radio Centro in the central city of Ambato.
According to Noboa, adverse weather conditions have led to an increase in disruptions in electricity, with incidents climbing from an average of "20-odd" times per day in a normal year to between 60 and 70 currently.
The government has added more than 400 megawatts of electricity generation capacity by granting permits and providing support to the private sector, with the goal of strengthening the system's capacity, he said.
The announcement comes amid Ecuador's dry season, marked by a lack of rainfall in the southern part of the country, home to the reservoirs that supply the Paute Hydroelectric Complex of the National Interconnected System.
The complex is the country's largest hydroelectric system and supplies about 35 percent of national electricity demand.
Currently, large industries in Ecuador are facing up to 72 hours of power cuts a week due to the dry season, a measure intended to reduce consumption and ease pressure on the national electrical system.
In 2024, the country went through an unprecedented energy crisis, with power outages lasting up to 14 hours a day that affected households, businesses and industries.
Ecuador was hit with extreme weather from El Nino in 1982-1983 and 1997-1998, including torrential rains and flooding, particularly in the coastal region. ■

Costa Rica opens mega-prison as Bukele model embraced across Latin America
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
00:24:03 UTC
09:24:03 KST

Costa Rica opens mega-prison as Bukele model embraced across Latin America
President Laura Fernandez says mega-prison is part of ‘tough-on-crime model’ embraced by her government.
Costa Rica has announced the opening of a new mega-prison amid near-record homicide levels and growing organised crime, as countries across the region embrace police crackdowns that have proven popular but often weaken key civil liberties.
President Laura Fernandez opened the High-Containment Centre Against Organised Crime, or CACCO, on Wednesday. The prison will have capacity for 5,100 people, equivalent to about 20 percent of the country’s current prison population.
“The CACCO will force criminals to face a new model – a tough-on-crime model. Costa Rica will become a global benchmark for prison security,” Fernandez said during an inauguration ceremony.
Candidates across Latin America have embraced mega-prisons, seeking to replicate the policies of Nayib Bukele, the president of El Salvador, who has won widespread popularity through a campaign of mass arrests and the suspension of basic rights in the name of combating crime.
Costa Rica, long spared from high levels of violent crime compared with its neighbours, saw a record-setting 905 homicides in 2023, followed by 876 in 2024 and 873 in 2025.
Analysts say that is partly due to increased fighting between criminal groups over lucrative drug routes.
The first transfers to Costa Rica’s new mega-prison will take place at the end of October, with Justice Minister Gabriel Aguilar saying the facility will help the government reassert control over the prison system and diminish infiltration by organised crime.
Right-wing leaders in other Latin American countries have also sought to replicate the mega-prison model.
Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori, inaugurated in July, has announced plans to tour El Salvador’s Terrorism Confinement Centre (CECOT), in anticipation of creating a similar facility in her country. CECOT can hold about 40,000 people.
In Colombia, meanwhile, newly elected leader Abelardo de la Espriella campaigned for the presidency, in part, on a pledge to build 10 mega-prisons. He took office in August.
Brazil, the largest country in Latin America, is currently in the midst of its own presidential election, and right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro has advanced to the final round of the vote. His platform also includes building five mega-prisons, citing the Salvadoran model.
El Salvador first imposed a “state of exception” under Bukele in 2022, expanding police and military powers.
That emergency declaration has been credited with a sharp drop in that country’s homicides, but rights groups say it has led to severe rights abuses and has been weaponised against critics of the government.
The “state of exception” has also resulted in mass arrests and mass trials, with rulings delivered against hundreds of defendants at a time. Some defendants have been detained without charge.
While the Bukele administration frequently touts its success in dismantling the gangs, the government has continuously extended the state of exception since it was first imposed.
Critics have warned that conditions inside mega-prisons are often poor, with imprisoned people facing overcrowding, due process violations and alleged torture in facilities like CECOT.

Thousands of protesters have taken to the streets across Colombia to condemn Israel's genocidal war in Gaza and the government's decision to open an embassy in West Jerusalem, marking a major shift in the country's foreign policy.

====================================================================================================

Israel may be left out of global climate summit in Turkey amid security fears
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
00:22:43 UTC
09:22:43 KST

A total of 197 countries are expected to participate in the global climate summit in Turkey next month. Unfortunately, Israel will likely not be among them, due to a combination of security concerns and diplomatic isolation.
The Ministry of Environmental Protection said it had submitted a request to security officials on behalf of both the ministry and the Foreign Ministry, but noted: "At this stage, approval for the joint delegation's departure has not yet been granted. However, the matter is currently being reconsidered, and no final decision has been made."
'It's more of a political conference'
The summit is an annual gathering of countries that are parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change. This year's agenda will include a review of national emissions reduction targets and mark a decade since the Paris Agreement, aimed at limiting global warming, entered into force.
Asked how important Israeli participation is, Prof. Colin Price, head of Tel Aviv University's Climate Initiative, said: "It's more of a political conference, which is why it's important for us to be there, just as we participate in the United Nations even though we don't have much influence. But being there matters. This year, the situation is apparently different. The fact that the conference is being held in Turkey is preventing many people from attending.
The Ministry of Environmental Protection barely functions these days, so there's less interest. It's a combination of security concerns and a lack of interest on the government's part. So we won't be there, although there may be private-sector representatives.
"Scientists working and conducting research in the climate field don't feel that there's any boycott or that the current situation is affecting international cooperation, including conferences," he added. "I think there's much less politics at the scientific level. I served as a reviewer for one of the chapters of an Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) report."
At the same time, Price warned that the private sector could suffer from Israel's absence.
"There's no exposure, no networking and no investment. Four years ago, there were far more foreign investors in companies. I'm involved in a startup, and over the past year or two, investors have stopped responding. They simply don't answer our emails. There's much less foreign investment in climate tech [innovative technologies designed to address climate change]. If we don't attend the summit, we miss out on those connections and meetings."
Udi Avni, co-country director of Greenpeace Israel, also expressed concern over Israel's likely absence from the event.
"Against the backdrop of extreme climate events around the world, Israel's participation in the summit is essential," he said. "The absence of official representation harms the national interest and the Israeli public. If this were Eurovision, things would look and sound very different. The government should be doing everything in its power to demand that the host country guarantee the Israeli delegation's safety or ask the United Nations to relocate the summit. Turkey was chosen as the host nearly a year ago.
"Unlike Eurovision, the climate summit produces technical but important decisions on issues such as renewable energy transition targets, environmental regulations and funding for green technologies. These decisions directly affect the quality of life of all Israelis, the cost of living and the economy, national security and our ability to cope with the consequences of the climate crisis, including wildfires and drought."
Avni added that "the summit is also an opportunity to promote Israeli technologies and international cooperation that could help improve Israel's diplomatic standing by supporting key demands on the agenda, including a rapid, just and adequately funded transition away from fossil fuels, the development of an ambitious national roadmap for phasing out fossil fuels and support for the 'polluter pays' principle by taxing the windfall profits of energy corporations to finance climate compensation funds."
'Another blow to the environment'
Dr. Avner Gross, Head of the Climate Change Research Laboratory at Ben-Gurion University of the Negev, said: "The climate crisis is one of the greatest challenges facing humanity, and it will be with us from now on. To address it, we need the entire global community, including Israel. One way to have an impact and be part of the effort is to participate in the international climate summit, which nearly every country in the world attends. Israel's absence would signal a further withdrawal from the global dialogue, potentially harming the country academically and economically."
Mor Gilboa, CEO of Zalul, an Israeli environmental organization focused on protecting marine and freshwater ecosystems, said Israel's failure to attend the summit would be another blow to environmental and climate efforts in a region that urgently needs cooperation to better protect and manage the resources shared by Mediterranean countries.
"It is deeply regrettable that political tensions and security threats will likely prevent Israel from participating in the summit," Gilboa said. "The climate crisis will not wait for political circumstances to change. In reality, it continues to worsen and even adds further tensions to an already strained political situation."

US rejects recommendation for ICE body cams to be automatically activated
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
00:20:56 UTC
09:20:56 KST

US rejects recommendation for ICE body cams to be automatically activated
WASHINGTON – The Trump administration has rejected a government watchdog’s recommendation that US immigration officials should use technology that would automatically activate body-worn cameras when an officer pulls their weapon or sets off a car siren.
Automatic activation of body-worn cameras was one of a number of recommendations outlined in a report released on Oct 14 by the Government Accountability Office (GAO), an independent nonpartisan watchdog agency for Congress.
The recommendation comes as US agencies face mounting scrutiny over enforcement tactics used in an immigration crackdown that has included fatal shootings of two US citizens in Minneapolis, raising questions about officers’ accountability.
The GAO report said US Immigration and Customs Enforcement and US Customs and Border Protection “should improve body-worn camera programme management”, adding that CBP and ICE have not updated their programme plans since 2022 and 2024, respectively.
Covering the period from February 2025 until September 2026, the report recommended that ICE implement additional controls to make sure that cameras are activated.
“We maintain that additional controls, such as automated camera activation, would provide greater assurance that body-worn cameras meet ICE’s desired results for transparency, accountability, and public trust,” the GAO said in the report.
The Department of Homeland Security, of which ICE is a part, said in comments cited in the report that it did not agree with the recommendation, citing what it said were privacy and operational risks.
For ICE, automatic activation risked the possibility of inadvertent or false activations during routine movement, the DHS said in the report.
DHS also said in the report that inadvertent or false activations could result in the unauthorised recording of sensitive interactions with informants or victims, or the recording of bystanders engaged in free speech activities in areas where camera use is restricted.
ICE has been the face of President Donald Trump’s deportation drive, which he says aims to improve domestic security.
Rights advocates say the crackdown has violated due process and free speech rights and created an unsafe environment, particularly for ethnic minorities, who have raised concerns about racial profiling.
Responding to the GAO report’s publication, a DHS spokesperson said on Oct 14 ICE had acquired devices to equip all officers and agents with body cameras.
“Training required to equip individual officers remains ongoing and we expect to complete this training soon,” the spokesperson said. REUTERS

US rejects recommendation for ICE body cams to be automatically activated
WASHINGTON – The Trump administration has rejected a government watchdog’s recommendation that US immigration officials should use technology that would automatically activate body-worn cameras when an officer pulls their weapon or sets off a car siren.
Automatic activation of body-worn cameras was one of a number of recommendations outlined in a report released on Oct 14 by the Government Accountability Office (GAO), an independent nonpartisan watchdog agency for Congress.
The recommendation comes as US agencies face mounting scrutiny over enforcement tactics used in an immigration crackdown that has included fatal shootings of two US citizens in Minneapolis, raising questions about officers’ accountability.
The GAO report said US Immigration and Customs Enforcement and US Customs and Border Protection “should improve body-worn camera programme management”, adding that CBP and ICE have not updated their programme plans since 2022 and 2024, respectively.
Covering the period from February 2025 until September 2026, the report recommended that ICE implement additional controls to make sure that cameras are activated.
“We maintain that additional controls, such as automated camera activation, would provide greater assurance that body-worn cameras meet ICE’s desired results for transparency, accountability, and public trust,” the GAO said in the report.
The Department of Homeland Security, of which ICE is a part, said in comments cited in the report that it did not agree with the recommendation, citing what it said were privacy and operational risks.
For ICE, automatic activation risked the possibility of inadvertent or false activations during routine movement, the DHS said in the report.
DHS also said in the report that inadvertent or false activations could result in the unauthorised recording of sensitive interactions with informants or victims, or the recording of bystanders engaged in free speech activities in areas where camera use is restricted.
ICE has been the face of President Donald Trump’s deportation drive, which he says aims to improve domestic security.
Rights advocates say the crackdown has violated due process and free speech rights and created an unsafe environment, particularly for ethnic minorities, who have raised concerns about racial profiling.
Responding to the GAO report’s publication, a DHS spokesperson said on Oct 14 ICE had acquired devices to equip all officers and agents with body cameras.
“Training required to equip individual officers remains ongoing and we expect to complete this training soon,” the spokesperson said. REUTERS

Israel's largest Hasidic sect threatens to withhold 30,000 votes in election feud
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
00:18:54 UTC
09:18:54 KST

Less than two weeks before Israel's October 27 election, the country's largest Hasidic movement is threatening to withhold its support from United Torah Judaism (UTJ), potentially costing the ultra-Orthodox alliance some 30,000 votes as an internal power struggle threatens to spill over into the ballot box.
The Gur Hasidic movement, which traditionally holds the most senior position within the Hasidic Agudat Yisrael faction and its representation in the broader UTJ alliance, has yet to begin encouraging its followers to vote. The silence has drawn criticism from within the party, particularly as other ultra-Orthodox communities intensify their election campaigns.
In Hamodia, the newspaper affiliated with Gur, there has been no reference to the election and no public instruction from the movement's spiritual leader, Rabbi Yaakov Aryeh Alter, urging followers to support the party.
The absence is especially unusual so close to election day. In previous campaigns, calls to vote for UTJ were prominently featured in the newspaper weeks before Israelis went to the polls.
Initially, Gur officials dismissed the need for an early campaign, arguing that "the rebbe will tell people on election day whom to vote for, and they will listen."
But the continued silence now appears to reflect a deeper dispute over the balance of power within the ultra-Orthodox political alliance.
The split threatening 30,000 votes
The crisis began just hours before the deadline for submitting candidate lists, when lawmaker Meir Porush, representing the Shlomei Emunim faction, and Elyakim Stark, the representative of the Belz Hasidic movement, broke away from Agudat Yisrael.
The two established a separate party, Homat Torat Yisrael, while remaining within the broader United Torah Judaism electoral alliance.
The move effectively freed them from the authority of Agudat Yisrael's institutions, particularly its Council of Torah Sages, the senior rabbinical body that guides the party's decisions.
Porush and Stark occupy the fourth and sixth positions, respectively, on the joint UTJ candidate list.
In Gur, leaders are now considering withholding an official call for their followers to vote, a move that could reduce the number of seats won by the alliance and prevent Stark from entering the Knesset.
"Goldknopf will get in anyway. Our representative is number two on the list, so his seat is secure," a Gur source said, referring to Yitzhak Goldknopf, the movement's senior political representative.
Gur has approximately 30,000 eligible voters, whose support could translate into roughly one to one-and-a-half Knesset seats.
"If Gur gives its mandate or mandate and a half to the party, it will bring Elyakim Stark into the Knesset, even though he is not loyal to the council and has left Agudat Yisrael," the source added.
The calculation is straightforward: Gur's own representative is placed high enough on the list that his election is considered secure, while Stark, in sixth place, could lose his seat if the alliance wins fewer mandates.
Negotiations before election day
Gur representatives are currently engaged in negotiations aimed at securing an agreement on the distribution of positions within the alliance before the election.
If those negotiations fail, the movement could maintain its current position and refrain from encouraging its followers to vote, potentially depriving UTJ of tens of thousands of ballots.
Agudat Yisrael is seeking understandings with Degel HaTorah, the Lithuanian ultra-Orthodox faction that forms the other major component of UTJ, regarding the standing of Porush and Stark.
It is also demanding that Degel HaTorah refrain from negotiating separately with Homat Torat Yisrael in future elections until the breakaway faction returns to Agudat Yisrael and again accepts its organizational framework.
Agudat Yisrael did not respond to a request for comment.
Another concern within Gur is that a last-minute voting instruction from the rebbe could carry less weight among some followers than the traditional campaign appeals issued well in advance of election day.
Nevertheless, the prevailing expectation within the movement is that its leadership will ultimately instruct followers to vote for UTJ, whose ballot designation is the Hebrew letter gimel, as it has in previous elections.
Before that happens, however, Gur officials want an agreement on the allocation of political positions to prevent the dispute from continuing after the election.
The internal struggle has also been fueled by the leadership change within the Belz Hasidic movement.
The Belz rebbe appointed Stark, a powerful figure within the community, as its new representative on the UTJ list, replacing veteran lawmaker Yisrael Eichler.
Eichler has served in the Knesset almost continuously since 2003 and currently holds the position of deputy communications minister. He previously chaired the Knesset's Labor and Welfare Committee and served as a deputy Knesset speaker.
With election day approaching, the dispute has left one of Israel's most influential ultra-Orthodox voting blocs without its customary campaign instructions, while negotiations continue over whether its 30,000 voters will be mobilized to support the joint list.

To scale up air defense without straining the front, Ukraine enlists business. In under year nearly 100 companies have joined, their crews downing 60-plus targets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
00:17:23 UTC
09:17:23 KST

Ukraine is handing its factories the right to shoot back at the Russian drones hunting them. Nearly 100 companies have joined Ukraine’s experimental program that allows private enterprises to operate their own air defenses, granting them authority to conduct air defense operations and form their own crews, the Defense Ministry says.
Russian drones strike Ukrainian factories, warehouses and power sites so relentlessly that the state cannot shield every one, so the Defense Ministry is enlisting the businesses being hit to defend themselves.
The program has grown quickly, from 24 companies in April to 81 by mid-September and nearly 100 now, and its crews have already destroyed a substantial number of Russian aerial targets.
The companies range from operators of critical infrastructure to state and private firms across the economy. The project is carried out under a Cabinet resolution dated 19 November 2025, which mobilizes enterprise resources to support Ukraine’s defense against air threats.
Civilian crews that answer to the Air Force, not themselves
These teams do not fire into a shared sky on their own. About 50 air-defense groups have been formed and are operating under the relevant Air Force commands, and crews from six enterprises are already carrying out combat missions, the ministry says. The rest are training or finishing preparation before they join.
As of 14 October, the groups have downed more than 60 aerial targets, mostly Russian drones, using interceptor drones and automated turrets with heavy machine guns, according to the ministry. The Air Force command sets each group’s targets based on its weapons and tasks, and, jointly with the company, defines its sector, personnel, and equipment.
Who pays, and who pulls the trigger
The arrangement splits cost and control. Some weapons the enterprises buy with their own money, holding end-user status, while a company can also ask the Air Force to lend arms and ammunition from military stocks.
Private air defense is one layer of a multi-tiered shield, meant to protect industrial capacity, critical infrastructure and civilian staff from systematic drone attacks. The crews began combat work in 2026.

Mexican court closes case against official over 2023 detention centre fire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
00:08:58 UTC
09:08:58 KST

Mexican court closes case against official over 2023 detention centre fire
Victims’ groups, however, have denounced the ruling as ‘selective’ justice that exonerates a former government head.
A Mexican judge has closed the case against Francisco Garduno, former head of the country’s immigration agency, for crimes related to the 2023 fire at a Ciudad Juarez detention centre that killed 40 migrants and injured 30 others.
The incident was the deadliest event ever to occur at a Mexican immigration centre, and critics said it exposed the shortcomings and irregularities in the country’s detention system.
Garduno faced trial for the crimes of abuse of public office and dereliction of duty after footage from the fire showed guards had failed to respond to cries for help.
On Tuesday, Judge Victor Manlio Hernandez Calderon ruled that Garduno had fulfilled the court-mandated measures required to address the damage. But victims rejected that decision and announced they would appeal.
“Yesterday, corruption and the impunity of politicians protected by power won again,” the Foundation for Justice, one of the NGOs representing some of the victims, wrote on social media on Wednesday.
The victims have also compared the judge’s decision to close the criminal case to a de facto exoneration for Garduno.
In their view, the ruling “confirms that justice in Mexico is selective” and denies the victims “full reparations” and concrete guarantees that such an event will not be repeated.
Miguel Zenteno, one of the foundation’s lawyers, noted that the ruling is not yet final because it will be appealed and because another injunction is pending against the court-mandated reparations, which critics say failed to meet the standards for serious events.
On March 27, 2023, some 70 men were crammed into a locked dormitory with no ventilation and barely any water at the Ciudad Juarez immigration detention centre, on the border with El Paso, Texas.
As night fell, a small group set fire to some mattresses in protest, and within seconds, smoke engulfed the entire area.
Security cameras recorded the guards leaving the area despite cries for help. They made no attempt to open the gates of the dormitory. Only the women, held in another cell, were released. Most of the victims were Central Americans and Venezuelans.
Garduno, a former prison guard and current official at the Ministry of Education, led the National Migration Institute (INM) starting in 2019 and continued in the role until 2025 despite the fire.
The judge had previously ordered Garduno to compensate the families, provide them with free specialised medical care, issue a public apology, provide human rights training to migration personnel and guarantee that the events would not be repeated.
Zenteno acknowledged that the measures were implemented only partially because Garduno did not pay the damages as stipulated by the legal process.
Instead, Zenteno pointed out that the funds came from the INM, and the payments did not fully compensate the families. Furthermore, he added, the victims were not even informed how to access free medical services, and the apology “was a mere formality, not substantive”.
In addition to Garduno, prosecutors accused another former director of the institute of the same crimes.
Six immigration agents – including a military officer and a private security guard – and the two migrants accused of starting the fire are charged with homicide and assault. Most of the officials remain free pending trial.

Israeli prison guards have shot Palestinian detainees with rubber bullets in confined spaces, leaving one prisoner requiring surgery and another undergoing an operation for a fractured shin, Israeli daily Haaretz reported, citing medical records and inmate testimonies.
According to Physicians for Human Rights Israel and the Public Committee Against Torture in Israel, at least 21 shooting incidents have been documented across five Israeli prisons since October 2023.
Rights investigators noted that most cases occurred in late 2025 and the first half of 2026, often at point-blank range and without any preceding unrest or security disturbance.
The most severe incident occurred in June at Ketziot Prison in southern Israel.
Hospital records from Soroka Medical Centre confirmed that an inmate's organ was completely destroyed by rubber-coated ammunition, necessitating immediate surgical excision.
In formal legal testimony, the prisoner stated that guards initially kicked him during a strip search a week earlier before members of the prison service's specialised Masada unit discharged rubber rounds directly into his cell, striking his previously injured groin and knee before dragging him roughly 50 metres while bleeding heavily.
Systemic abuse
Further records from Ketziot revealed that another prisoner underwent emergency surgery in July after sustaining a fractured left shin from a rubber bullet.
A former detainee told Haaretz he was shot at close range in April and denied medical care for 15 days, receiving surgery only upon release.
Rights organisations confirmed that shootings occurred inside sleeping cells, exercise yards, and legal consultation waiting areas.
Although rights monitors formally petitioned authorities in August to prohibit the use of rubber and plastic ammunition in confined settings, the Israeli Prison Service rejected a blanket ban.
Meirav Ben Zeev, a lawyer with the Public Committee Against Torture in Israel, emphasised that detainees remain fearful of reporting abuse due to potential retaliation, noting that previous complaints failed to produce prosecutions.
Around 9,350 Palestinians, including 350 children and 90 women, remain incarcerated in Israeli facilities amid widespread reports of torture, starvation, and severe medical neglect.

“Every little boat here, every fisherman… is an act of resistance”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
00:00:00 UTC
09:00:00 KST

Meet Alexandre Anderson – a water defender from Brazil
For Alexandre Anderson de Souza and other artisanal fishers, Guanabara Bay in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, is a source of livelihood, identity and culture.
But pollution from multiple sources, including the oil and gas industry, industrial waste and untreated sewage has turned the bay into a sacrifice zone. Artisanal fishers face contaminated water, declining fish stocks, eroded mangrove, shrinking fishing areas and increasingly dangerous routes, while polluters profit without paying for the environmental degradation they cause.
Alexandre co-founded Associação Homens e Mulheres do Mar (Association of Men and Women of the Sea – AHOMAR), a network of artisanal fishers that has spent nearly two decades defending the bay and their traditional way of life from the impacts of oil and gas infrastructure. Several environmental human rights defenders (EHRDs) told Amnesty International that they feared for their safety, some facing intimidation and harassment.
Among them, Alexandre has been repeatedly threatened and has survived several attempts on his life. Here, he shares his story:
My name is Alexandre Anderson. I am 54 years old; I am a fisherman and I have been living and working in Guanabara Bay since 1997.
Artisanal fishing is not just a means of subsistence. It is our culture, a way of life.
In the 1990s, we felt that something was already changing in Guanabara Bay. Our elders say that when the first refinery started to work, the bay suffered a lot. There was a lot of oil around because it was next to two rivers and these rivers were used to illegally discharge sewage.
I’m not the oldest fisherman in the region, but the elders say that fish used to be abundant here, and they disappeared. It wasn’t a natural phenomenon, it was a phenomenon of man’s influence, an industrial phenomenon. Oil is not synonymous with wealth, it’s not synonymous with growth, it’s synonymous with destruction.
“No one warned us”
I remember that I used to sail, on a rudimentary boat… always built by us. With the disappearance of fish, we had to go further into the sea, and I had to buy an engine for the boat. The fish kept moving away, because the shore was increasingly polluted.
The fishermen were then forced to leave the region or change profession. Some say that this is environmental racism. Some say that this is a ‘sacrifice zone’. There has been no public communication… no consultation in our community. No one warned us. When we came to know about the industry, the infrastructure was already being built in the middle of the sea, or in the middle of a beach. (With growing industry presence) there was violence, physical violence, even personal violence against some leaders. Unfortunately, at dawn on 18 January 2000, there was a big (oil) leak in the water caused by an oil pipeline. This whole area was contaminated, and we were pushed away from artisanal fishing. We were pushed to leave everything that we understand – cultural, religious, traditional – and even leaving the place where we were raised, where we were born.
“We are successful in what we do because we work with the truth”
We revolted against everything that was happening and started to look for actions we could take. In 2003 we started to search for answers as a group, and we founded the Associação Homens e Mulheres do Mar (Association of Men and Women of the Sea – AHOMAR).
Soon after in 2009, through our monitoring efforts, we were able to remove two oil sites which were illegally occupying our space and contaminating our region. We are successful in what we do because we work with the truth and we do not work alone. We’re supported by many well-known organizations, such as Amnesty International and observers have even accompanied us to these sites.
In 2009, we lost a treasurer and our founder was shot. In 2012, we had two more deaths of artisanal fishers monitoring the bay. But we are resilient, history will remember us as a resistance and as heroes, and the oil giants will be remembered as destroyers and polluters.
… History will remember us as a resistance and as heroes,
… and the oil giants will be remembered as destroyers and polluters.
Alexandre Anderson
The killings came after sustained threats against Alexandre Anderson de Souza and other members of AHOMAR. The threats relate to complaints the group have made against the construction of a gas pipeline in the bay, and environmental damage that is threatening artisanal fishers’ livelihoods.
On 22 May 2009, the treasurer of AHOMAR, Paulo César dos Santos Souza, was beaten and shot in the head in front of his wife and children; the following year Márcio Amaro, a founding member of the association, was also shot dead in his house.
Both cases remain unresolved.
“We are resilient, but we didn’t ask for this”
Every little boat here, every artisanal fisher who still bravely wakes up early or arrives late from the sea, is an act of resistance. As long as there are boats like these, they cannot take over Guanabara Bay. Protecting artisanal fishing territories means ensuring that rivers and seas continue to be a source of life and dignity, and not just profit.
Guanabara Bay represents everything. It’s our livelihood and our struggle is against large companies. Sometimes we don’t have any more space to fish, it’s something we always tell them. We are not after money, we only want what is ours, we just want to fish in Guanabara Bay, it’s our right and they are taking away our rights.
We are resilient, but we didn’t ask for this. We must resist or we die. We transformed our tears into struggle. This revolt, this sadness that is part of our history, (but) we transformed it into action.
We transformed our tears into struggle.
This revolt, this sadness that is part of our history, (but) we transformed it into action.
Alexandre Anderson
The struggle in Guanabara Bay reflects a reality observed all over the world: fossil fuel and other extractive projects benefit a few at the expense of nearby individuals and groups. But it also tells the story of community power: artisanal fishers leading the fight for environmental and climate justice.
Their stories cannot be erased.

Florida can enforce state law barring young kids from social media, appeals court rules

Florida can enforce state law barring young kids from social media, appeals court rules
- Florida can enforce H.B. 3, a law barring under-14s from social media with addictive features, after the 11th Circuit said it does not breach free speech rights.
- Tech groups NetChoice and the CCIA, backed by Meta, TikTok and Snap, sued to block the law. NetChoice said it is “currently evaluating all of our options”.
- The court also sent Florida’s case against Snap back to state court. Florida says the law protects children’s mental health, while critics say it limits teens’ online speech.
AI generated
ATLANTA – A federal appeals court on Oct 14 allowed Florida to enforce a state law barring children under 14 from accessing social media platforms like Instagram, TikTok or Snapchat, rejecting tech industry groups’ claims that the law violates the US Constitution’s free speech protections.
In a unanimous ruling, a three-judge panel on the Atlanta-based 11th US Circuit Court of Appeals vacated a lower court’s preliminary injunction blocking the law, known as H.B. 3.
The court said the law does not regulate the content hosted by social media sites and therefore does not run afoul of the First Amendment.
“HB3 applies to platforms wholly without regard to the topics discussed or the ideas or messages conveyed on them,” wrote Circuit Judge Kevin Newsom, an appointee of President Donald Trump.
“Truth Social is just as likely as Instagram to be affected by HB3.”
Representatives for Florida Attorney-General James Uthmeier, who defended the law, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The law bars social media platforms that have so-called addictive features, which include things like video autoplay and infinite scroll, from allowing children under the age of 14 to create accounts.
Tech industry groups NetChoice and the Computer & Communications Industry Association, which count Meta Platforms, TikTok and Snap as members, had sued in 2024 to block the law.
In a statement after the ruling on Oct 14, Paul Taske, director of the NetChoice Litigation Center, said the group is “currently evaluating all of our options as we continue the fight to ensure Floridians’ rights to free expression online are protected, and parents remain in the driver’s seat when it comes to making decisions for their families”.
Snap sued
Florida was among the first of several states to pass a law regulating social media use for children amid a broader reckoning over the apps’ role in young people’s mental health.
After H.B. 3 took effect, Uthmeier sued Snapchat owner Snap in April 2025, accusing it of illegally employing features that addict children and opening accounts for children aged 13 and younger. S
nap said H.B. 3 and the lawsuit sought to restrict teens’ speech online in violation of the US Constitution.
A few months later, the judge overseeing the industry groups’ lawsuit granted their request for a preliminary injunction blocking the law’s enforcement, saying H.B. 3 was likely unconstitutional.
Uthmeier appealed that ruling to the 11th Circuit, and the court had stayed the injunction while it weighed the case.
Separately, a lower court overseeing Florida’s case against Snap had rejected the state’s request in August 2025 to order Snap to comply with H.B. 3, also finding the law likely violated constitutional rights.
But in a second ruling on Oct 14, the 11th Circuit vacated that decision and said the case should move forward in state court, not federal.
A representative for Snap declined to comment. REUTERS

Ukraine’s anti-corruption bodies, whose independence EU made condition for membership, have clawed back $5.1 million for state budget
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
23:37:35 UTC
08:37:35 KST

Ukraine’s anti-corruption agencies just clawed back millions for the state budget. The National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU), the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office (SAPO) and the State Property Fund have returned about $5.1 million to the state budget, the bureau says.
NABU and SAPO were created in 2015 after the Euromaidan revolution as independent bodies to fight high-level corruption, and their independence is a core condition for Ukraine's path to the EU. This recovery is the kind of concrete payoff that EU-backed reform was meant to produce.
Investigating one case, detectives and prosecutors found that the leadership of a regional branch of the State Property Fund had failed to act. Because of that inaction, the state risked losing millions of dollars.
To head off the loss, NABU and SAPO alerted the fund’s central leadership and gave it access to part of the investigation materials.
How the agencies turned a case into cash
The fix came from sharing what the investigation had uncovered. After working through the data, the State Property Fund took the necessary steps and secured the full budget amount, the bureau says.
NABU and SAPO continue to cooperate with other state bodies to protect the country’s economic interests and prevent corruption crimes, the bureau adds. The agencies framed the case as proof that enforcement, beyond investigation alone, can return money the state would otherwise lose.
Why these agencies matter beyond one case
The recovery lands at a fraught moment for the two institutions. Their independence has been under sustained pressure, and in July 2026 parliament briefly stripped it before mass protests and EU warnings forced a reversal.
In 2025, Brussels tied as much as 50 billion euros in aid and the pace of accession talks to the agencies’ autonomy, treating NABU and SAPO as pillars of the rule-of-law reforms Ukraine promised on its way into the bloc.

Russia is trying the Dobropillia road to the last big free cities of Donbas again, a year after it failed. This time it brought another army
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
23:36:52 UTC
08:36:52 KST

- Russian reinforcements are surging toward Dobropillia in eastern Ukraine's Donetsk Oblast
- The Russians have a plan: to fight through Dobropillia and open a path toward the free city of Kramatorsk
- Ukrainian forces aren't powerless to resist, but many of their own best troops are busy attacking elsewhere
The Russians are pouring troops into a key sector just southeast of the town of Dobropillia in eastern Ukraine's Donetsk Oblast, threatening to overwhelm Ukrainian defenses and march one settlement closer to Kramatorsk and Sloviansk, the last two big free cities in Donetsk.
But the Russians' push toward Dobropillia isn't without cost. Russian losses in this sector are "colossal," according to the mapper Playfra. And every soldier the Kremlin deploys along the Dobropillia axis is a soldier it can't deploy elsewhere.
And that may help explain why the Russians are falling back in two other key sectors. The Dobropillia axis is the Russians' clear priority. For the Ukrainians, that's an opportunity to attack elsewhere.
Dobropillia, a former mining town with a pre-war population of around 28,000, is now a fortress. It anchors Ukrainian positions along the T0514 highway threading north to Kramatorsk, 40 km away.
Russia has tried this road before. In August 2025, Russian troops pushed a salient toward the Dobropillia–Kramatorsk highway, and Ukrainian counterattacks cut it apart. By October that year, President Volodymyr Zelensky put Russian losses on the Dobropillia front at about 13,000.
For the Russians, there are several possible paths to Kramatorsk. But the southwest path along the T0514 is the likeliest to actually lead Russian troops to the city. There's a route into Kramatorsk from the southeast, but it's blocked by stubborn Ukrainian forces still clinging to positions in the ruins of Kostiantynivka. There's a northern route, too, but starting this spring the Ukrainian 3rd Army Corps rolled back 18 months of Russian gains along that route.
The Russian command clearly sees the road through Dobropillia for what it is: the best way forward for an army that's been struggling to complete its conquest of Donetsk, to say nothing of breaking through in other front-line oblasts.
And that's why the Russians are channeling fresh forces into the Dobropillia sector. Part of the 41st Combined Arms Army and units of its 90th Guards Tank Division are now fighting there, Ukrainian military analyst Kostiantyn Mashovets wrote on 9 October, and the Russian command keeps feeding fresh assault infantry into the sector through the village of Nove Shakhove despite heavy losses. The open-source account Unit Observer tracked the buildup as early as September.
Potentially tens of thousands of troops from those formations join the main forces of the 2nd and 51st Combined Arms Armies, according to Mashovets, as well as elements of the Russian naval infantry, facing the Ukrainian 1st Azov Corps and 19th Army Corps around Dobropillia.
The reinforcements give Russian commanders more options. Mashovets expects the 51st CAA to push south and southwest of Dobropillia and the 2nd CAA toward Raksha and Sviatohorivka, enveloping the town and cutting its supply routes from Bilozerske before any direct assault. The neighboring 8th CAA is fighting around Kostiantynivka. The Russians' immediate goal is "to maintain this offensive pressure from summer into the fall," Unit Observer wrote, setting conditions for a possible siege of Kramatorsk next year.
The outlook for the Ukrainian defenders of Dobropillia is "worsening," Playfra warned on 13 October.
The Russians have a seemingly infinite manpower pool here and a clear numerical advantage, which allows them to significantly increase the flow of infiltrators and, as such, the chance of some passing through Ukrainian defenses.
This leads to especially deep Russian infiltrations, which in turn slowly but surely destabilize the situation for the Ukrainians, which are progressively forced to abandon their most advanced positions.
Trending Now
The Ukrainians aren't without options, Playfra explained. They should double down on their current strategy of saturating the fields around Dobropillia with drones in a ring at least 2 to 3 km deep, forestalling large-scale Russian movements until the winter strips the leaves off the trees, depriving the Russians of their best cover from overhead surveillance. This could buy Dobropillia "much more time," Playfra predicted.
Mashovets sees the same deadline. If Dobropillia and neighboring Druzhkivka hold until mid-to-late December, he wrote, Russia's plan would have to be substantially rebuilt.
Help isn't coming
Just don't expect a lot of Ukrainian reinforcements along the Dobropillia axis. Many of Ukraine's best troops are busy attacking.
Taking advantage of the surge of Russian manpower in the direction of Dobropillia, Ukrainian forces have counterattacked where the Russians are weakest: in northern Donetsk Oblast and also in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, just south of Donetsk.
In months of carefully planned assaults supported by ground robots and intensive drone strikes, Ukrainian forces have liberated hundreds of square kilometers in northern Donetsk and Dnipropetrovsk. The Ukrainian 3rd Army Corps' Operation Vivaldi in northern Donetsk largely removed the immediate northern threat to Sloviansk and neighboring Kramatorsk.
But it didn't do anything to help in the direction of Dobropillia, where the Russians have many more troops, much more firepower, and—equally importantly—a singular focus: to open a road to the last free cities in Donetsk.
Ukraine’s 3rd Army Corps took the lessons of the failed 2023 counteroffensive into Operation Vivaldi. It fought small, and won.

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan has arrived in Azerbaijan's capital, Baku, ahead of the seventh summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia (CICA).
Hosted by Azerbaijan as the current CICA chair, the summit convenes representatives from member states, observer nations, and international organisations to bolster regional connectivity, digitalisation, and sustainable development.
The gathering is expected to adopt the Baku Declaration alongside a formal framework on occupational safety and health, whilst announcing Laos' accession as a new member.
Addressing the forum on Thursday, Fidan will stress the need for collective solutions based on consultation, consensus, mutual trust, and regional ownership to tackle global crises and geopolitical challenges, while calling for the preservation of UN-centred multilateral diplomacy.
Fidan is also scheduled to raise Israel's continuing genocide in Gaza, condemning illegal settlement expansions and severe restrictions on humanitarian aid to Palestinians.

Fidan will also champion deeper economic integration across Asia, highlighting Türkiye-backed infrastructure initiatives such as the Middle Corridor and the Development Road.
He will advocate aligning the Middle Corridor with China’s Belt and Road Initiative to consolidate transcontinental trade routes.
On emerging technologies, Fidan will urge a human-centred approach to artificial intelligence that safeguards digital sovereignty, whilst reaffirming Ankara's climate commitments as future host and president of COP31.
Established as a dialogue platform, CICA brings together 28 member states encompassing roughly 90 percent of Asia's landmass and more than half the global population.
Under its 2024–2026 chairmanship, Azerbaijan is spearheading efforts to accelerate CICA's transformation into a fully fledged international organisation.
Türkiye, a founding member that chaired CICA from 2010 to 2014, coordinates key institutional portfolios spanning military-political cooperation, counterterrorism, and trade.
