RIYADH/SANAA, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- Fighting between the Saudi-led coalition and Yemen's Houthi group continued on Wednesday, with both sides carrying out fresh attacks and the Houthis vowing to continue targeting airports and oil facilities in Saudi Arabia in the coming days.
In a statement posted on social media platform X, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Sarea said the group's forces targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh with a ballistic missile, claiming it was a "precise and direct" hit.
The announcement came hours after the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the Houthis toward Riyadh. Loud explosions were heard in the Saudi capital earlier in the day, while residents received aerial-threat alerts on mobile apps.
The Saudi Civil Defense said later in the day that one Arab resident was injured and a residential building and a vehicle sustained minor damage after debris from an intercepted ballistic missile launched by the Houthis fell in Riyadh.
Earlier in the day, Sarea claimed a large-scale missile and drone attack targeting Saudi energy giant Aramco in Dhahran in the Eastern Province, as well as King Khalid International Airport and an Aramco refinery in Riyadh. He said the operation was carried out in retaliation for Saudi strikes.
Sarea vowed that the group's attacks "deep inside Saudi Arabia" would continue in the coming days, targeting airports and oil facilities. He also renewed a warning to international airlines, civilians and employees to stay away from airports and oil facilities in Saudi Arabia that the group had designated as targets.
Houthi-run al-Masirah TV reported Wednesday that an unnamed Houthi military source advised Aramco shareholders to "dispose of their shares" to avoid potential losses in the coming days, without providing further details on the basis for the warning or whether it was linked to possible further Houthi attacks on Aramco.
Meanwhile, fighting and airstrikes continued across Yemen. Sarea said Wednesday evening on X that Saudi-led coalition forces had carried out 42 strikes using warplanes and missiles on what he described as civilian facilities in the capital Sanaa and the provinces of Taiz, Lahj, Marib and Amran, as well as Mayyun Island in the Bab al-Mandab Strait.
Majid Al-Nuzaili, spokesperson for Yemen's government forces, said in a statement that the forces had carried out 2,309 "precise and direct" attacks against Houthi positions using warplanes, drones, field artillery, rocket launchers and sniper units.
The spokesperson claimed the operations had neutralized about 1,250 Houthi fighters and destroyed or damaged more than 460 military vehicles and other equipment.
The Houthis, meanwhile, said they had fired three ballistic missiles at gatherings of government forces backed by the Saudi-led coalition in the Ras al-Arah and Al-Mudarabah areas of southern Lahj province, causing a large number of casualties and damage to several military vehicles.
The continued fighting drew fresh regional reactions. During a meeting with Saudi Crown Prince and Prime Minister Mohammed bin Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud in Riyadh on Wednesday, Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi condemned the attack targeting King Khalid International Airport and attacks on civilian and vital facilities in Saudi Arabia, describing them as a threat to regional security and stability.
Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Wednesday reaffirmed Pakistan's commitment to protecting Saudi Arabia's sovereignty, security and territorial integrity as well as its support for the kingdom's legitimate right to self-defense.
Yemen has been mired in conflict since late 2014, when the Houthis seized Sanaa and much of northern Yemen. A Saudi-led coalition intervened in 2015 in support of the internationally recognized Yemeni government. ■

China hopes that the agreement will help unify Libya's state institutions and lay the foundation for national elections and the completion of the political transition, said Sun Lei, China's deputy permanent representative to the United Nations.
At the same time, he said, whether the agreement can be truly implemented depends on whether it can gain broad support from all Libyan parties. In supporting Libya's political process, the international community must uphold the Libyan-led and Libyan-owned principle and avoid imposing external solutions.
The political deadlock must be broken as soon as possible, he told the Security Council.
"Libya's security situation is closely linked to its political process. Any new armed conflict could undermine hard-won mutual trust and render political efforts futile," he said.
Recently, attacks on energy facilities have continued in western Libya, and the resulting tensions are a cause for concern. The parties concerned should stop the attacks and refrain from taking any action that could lead to a deterioration of the situation, Sun said.
The unification of military and security institutions is crucial to maintaining a lasting ceasefire and is also an important condition for ensuring the smooth conduct of elections and the transfer of power. China supports the eastern and western sides in strengthening dialogue, building mutual trust, and accelerating the process, he said.
The international community, on the basis of respecting Libya's sovereignty and ownership, should provide greater support to the country in strengthening border management, combating transnational criminal networks, and curbing the illicit flow of weapons, he added.
Sun also called for efforts to improve economic governance and people's livelihoods in Libya.
The international community should call on all Libyan parties to fully implement the unified budget framework, strengthen fiscal transparency and independent oversight, and make greater efforts to support Libya in combating oil smuggling, to ensure that its oil revenues are used for national development and the well-being of its people. International partners should support Libyan authorities in improving public services and advancing development and reconstruction, to strengthen public confidence in national unity, stability and development, he said.
As a good friend of Libya, China stands ready to continue working with all parties and make greater efforts to help Libya achieve lasting peace and stability and enable its people to live and work in peace and contentment at an early date, Sun said. ■

SC: Tough PMLA bail conditions can't override accused's right
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
23:27:22 UTC
08:27:22 KST

NEW DELHI: SC has said that stringent bail conditions set under special laws such as PMLA cannot override rights granted by the Constitution, holding prolonged incarceration of an undertrial violates the fundamental right to speedy trial.A bench of Justices Aravind Kumar and Vipul M Pancholi said an accused could not be kept in custody till completion of trial and held that the accused was entitled to bail in case of delay in trial despite the stringent bail conditions under the anti-money laundering law.Section 45 of PMLA prescribes twin conditions for grant of bail.PMLA accused can't be in jail till trial ends, says SCThe PMLA section says no accused shall be released on bail unless the public prosecutor has been given an opportunity to oppose the application for such release, and the court is satisfied that there are reasonable grounds for believing that he is not guilty of such offence and that he is not likely to commit any offence while on bail. The second condition puts the onus on an accused to convince the court that he is not guilty.The bench, however, said, "The twin conditions under Section 45 of PMLA cannot override the constitutional safeguards under Article 21 of the Constitution, as has been held in the case of Manish Sisodia vs Directorate of Enforcement. Prolonged incarceration, if allowed to continue, will set at naught the constitutional safeguards extended to accused persons."
The court granted bail to an accused who was allegedly involved in money laundering of over Rs 6,210 crore. ED said the accused had created 62 shell companies, 34 people were made dummy directors and 20 companies were manned by his relatives who contributed to the offence. He was arrested in Dec 2024.Granting him relief, the bench said, "We are of the opinion that the culmination of the trial is a time-consuming process, since the trial court will have to go through documents running into thousands of pages and examine around 98 witnesses. The appellant must not be subjected to the rigours of custody as long as the trial is pending. Hence, the appellant must be released on bail, subject to furnishing of bail bonds to the satisfaction of the trial court and subject to such other terms and conditions as may be imposed by it."The bench admitted that economic offences were very serious as they impacted the financial fabric of the country but said the rights of accused too have to be protected."In a bail matter, especially in serious offences, the job of a court is to balance the rights of the state with those of the arrestee. In special laws such as PMLA, the conditions for granting bail are stringent, and the circumstances in which bail can be granted are rare, for the simple reason that economic offences of a large magnitude punch a hole through the financial fabric of the country, causing a top-down ripple effect into the entire ecosystem, resulting in large consequences for most of the population.
That is the justification for making the provisions of PMLA stringent. In the same breath, sight must not be lost of the fact that the institutions have a duty to expeditiously investigate the cases. Process must not be turned into a punishment unto itself," the court said.The bench referred to its earlier verdict in the Manish Sisodia case in which it was held that prolonged incarceration before being pronounced guilty of an offence should not be permitted to become punishment without trial, and keeping the appellant behind bars for an unlimited period of time in the hope of speedy completion of trial would deprive him of his fundamental right to liberty under Article 21 of the Constitution.

Lavrov to attend 7th CICA summit in Baku
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
23:14:25 UTC
08:14:25 KST

BAKU, October 15. /TASS/. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov will take part in the 7th Summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence-Building Measures in Asia (CICA) in Baku.
The top Russian diplomat arrives in Baku on Wednesday and has already held a meeting with his Chinese counterpart Wang Yi.
According to the Russian Foreign Ministry, the event will "address the further development of CICA, including its integration into the broader landscape of cross-platform cooperation across the Eurasian space."
"Discussions are expected to cover a wide range of practical cooperation areas on the CICA agenda, including the spheres overseen by Russia: support for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and the assurance of international information security," it said, adding that the participants will also exchange views on pressing international and regional issues.
One of the summit’s expected outcomes is the accession of Laos to the Conference as a full-fledged member, the ministry said.
The summit’s agenda is expected to focus on issues of ensuring the region’s sustainable development, strengthening connectivity across the broader continent, and addressing new challenges and threats, including in the area of international information security.
The summit is expected to yield a general policy declaration and a document on raising the standards of occupational safety.
CICA is a multilateral dialogue platform for addressing pressing regional issues and deepening cooperation among member states to build confidence in the military-political, economic and humanitarian spheres, as well as in addressing new challenges and threats. The initiative to establish this format was put forward by the then Kazakh President Nursultan Nazarbayev in 1992.
CICA has 28 member countries, namely Russia, Afghanistan, Azerbaijan, Bahrain, Bangladesh, Cambodia, China, Egypt, India, Iran, Iraq, Israel, Jordan, Kazakhstan, Kuwait, Kyrgyzstan, Mongolia, Pakistan, Palestine, Qatar, the Republic of Korea, Sri Lanka, Tajikistan, Thailand, Turkey, the United Arab Emirates, Uzbekistan, and Vietnam and 15 observers - Belarus, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, Saudi Arabia, the Philippines, Turkmenistan, the United States, Ukraine, Japan, the Arab League, the International Organization for Migration, the OSCE, and the Parliamentary Assembly of Turkic States.
The CICA Chair is elected for a two-year term, with the possibility of mandate extension. Kazakhstan held presidency in 2020-2024 and was succeeded by Azerbaijan in December 2024. The summits are held every four years.

North Korea test-fires submarine-launched cruise missiles amid rising tensions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
23:12:08 UTC
08:12:08 KST

North Korea test-fires submarine-launched cruise missiles amid rising tensions
North Korea test-fired two types of submarine-launched strategic cruise missiles on Wednesday, state media KCNA reported Thursday, saying the launches posed no threat to neighbouring countries. The tests follow heightened tensions with South Korea after a September 21 landmine explosion in the Demilitarised Zone injured three South Korean soldiers.
North Korea has test-fired two types of submarine-launched strategic cruise missiles, state news agency KCNA said Thursday.
The agency said the missiles were fired Wednesday into the East Sea, also known as the Sea of Japan, without "any adverse impact on the security of neighboring countries".
The reported launch came after weeks of mounting friction over a landmine explosion along the heavily fortified border between North and South Korea.
Three South Korean soldiers were injured in the September 21 blast in the Seoul-controlled area of the Demilitarised Zone (DMZ), with both countries testing upgraded missile technology in the aftermath.
The latest testing "aimed to examine the current mobilized posture of the underwater combat systems" and served as a Navy training exercise, KCNA said.
The tests showed the "high reliability, trustworthiness and ability of the war deterrents of the DPRK," the agency reported, referring to North Korea by the abbreviation of the country's official name.
Photos released by KCNA showed one missile blasting vertically out of the sea trailed by a thick plume of smoke. Another photo appeared to show a projectile erupting from the water at a 45-degree angle.
Read moreNorth Korea launches ballistic missile as tensions with Seoul grow over border mine blasts
Other images showed a missile flying horizontally over the sea, as well as a submarine traveling on the water's surface.
The North's ability to launch missiles from submarines at two different angles carries "tactical significance", Hong Min of the Korea Institute for National Unification told AFP, as the two launch methods serve different purposes.
"Vertical launches allow missiles to climb steeply before descending towards their targets, potentially extending their range," he said.
"Angled launches, on the other hand, allow missiles to fly at lower altitudes from the outset, making them harder for missile defence systems to detect and intercept."
North Korea has carried out several missile launches from submarines in recent years, although its sea-based launch capabilities remain unclear.
Cruise missiles tend to be jet-propelled and fly at a lower altitude than more sophisticated ballistic missiles, making them harder to detect and intercept.
Proven submarine-launched ballistic missile capability would take North Korea's arsenal to a new level, allowing deployment far beyond the Korean peninsula and a second-strike capability in the event of an attack.
North Korea has carried out multiple ballistic missile tests in October, most recently on Monday.
The two Koreas have engaged in a tit-for-tat series of missile tests this month, with both sides test-firing hypersonic weapons.
South Korea test-fired its first homegrown hypersonic missile last week, days after Pyongyang said it had launched an AI-assisted intermediate-range hypersonic missile.
Seoul and Pyongyang remain technically at war as the Korean conflict ended in 1953 with a truce rather than a peace treaty.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

Israel has yet to allow the construction of a military outpost for international troops in the Gaza Strip, The Guardian reported on Wednesday, citing a source familiar with the matter.

Arkel International, a Louisiana-based company, is expected to build the outpost, which would measure approximately 100 meters by 100 meters, at a site previously used by the Gaza Humanitarian Foundation project, The Guardian reported.

Board of Peace plans can't continue without initial outpost built
However, the source said the Board of Peace's larger plans cannot proceed without the initial construction project.
“You can’t get in without an International Stabilization Force (ISF). You can’t rebuild,” the source said, as quoted by The Guardian. “There’s no security. There’s no deliveries of construction equipment. You can’t even start putting utilities. You can’t start putting in basic life-support facilities, you know, because without the ISF you can’t go in.”
Despite the delays, the source said the Board of Peace believes the Israeli government will allow construction to proceed after the October 27 Israeli elections.

First Israeli ballots cast as diplomats vote abroad from New Zealand to New York
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
23:10:58 UTC
08:10:58 KST

Israeli diplomats have begun casting ballots abroad for the 26th Knesset more than a week before Israel's October 27, 2026 elections, N12 News reported on Thursday.
While Israeli citizens are generally ineligible to vote by absentee ballot, exceptions are made for Israeli diplomats and their family members, with the Foreign Ministry and Central Elections Committee (CEC) operating 101 polling stations at 99 Israeli diplomatic missions around the world.
According to N12, about 4,800 Israelis will use the program to vote abroad, and specific mission employees and government envoys are also eligible.
The first ballots were cast in Wellington, New Zealand, at 11:00 p.m. on Wednesday, Israel time, followed by Israel's newest mission in Suva, Fiji, at 12:00 Thursday.
The voting will continue westward, according to the report, until the final polling stations close in Los Angeles and San Farnciso on the West Coast of the United States at 6:00 a.m. on Friday.
The report noted that the program's largest polling station will be at Israel's New York Consulate, where 700 participants are expected to cast their votes.
Ballots to be transferred to Israel upon completion of program
Once cast and collected, the physical ballots will be transferred to Israel to be counted as a standard part of the upcoming elections, N12 reported.
The N12 report emphasized the logistical coordination required for the program, with the entire voting process lasting around 30 hours.
The physical polling stations and election materials had to be transported to their respective embassies and consulates ahead of time, and the CEC had to train local polling station teams to ensure a uniform and secure procedure in accordance with israeli election law.

moyo shirt jacket weaves korean hanbok silhouette with east african kitenge textile
the moyo shirt jacket brings together two distinct cultural aesthetics, reinterpreting the traditional korean hanbok's silhouette using kitenge, a signature east african textile.
[FEATURED]
HANBOK SILHOUETTES meet EAST AFRICAN KITENGE TEXTILES in MOYO
The MOYO shirt jacket, developed by design-focused social enterprise Jerrybag in collaboration with designer Hyunah Kim of ili studio, combines the structural silhouette of the Korean Hanbok with East African Kitenge textiles. Named after the Swahili word for ‘heart,’ the garment translates the layered construction, wrapping technique, and relaxed proportions of traditional Korean dress into a modern shirt jacket format.
The design pairs the understated geometry of the Hanbok with the high-contrast colors and dynamic patterns of Kitenge fabric, bridging Asian and African design languages. The familiar shirt jacket format serves as an accessible entry point for consumers in both regions to engage with cross-cultural aesthetic elements.
FROM KAMPALA TO SEOUL: SUSTAINABLE PRODUCTION AND DISTRIBUTION
Production of the MOYO jacket takes place in Kampala, Uganda, through a local women’s cooperative trained at Jerrybag’s Sustainable Design Center, an initiative established in 2024 via the KOICA Inclusive Business Program to support skill-building and entrepreneurship. Hyunah Kim, drawing from her experience living in Rwanda, developed the concept to explore shared design possibilities between Korea and East Africa. The shirt jacket is distributed through AFRO LOOM, a lifestyle design retail platform operating in Seoul and Kampala.

What is Starshield, SpaceX’s military version of Starlink?
- Ukraine says SpaceX limited “military-grade” Starlink, raising concern over battlefield drone and air defence support.
- Starlink is SpaceX’s civilian satellite internet service, with more than 11,000 satellites and about 13 million users worldwide.
- Starshield is the Pentagon’s military version, with secure communications, stronger encryption and separate terminals, but it still uses the Starlink satellite backbone.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – Ukraine said on Oct 14 that Elon Musk’s SpaceX had restricted “military-grade” Starlink services, hampering Ukrainian drone strike missions and air defences.
The complaint has drawn renewed attention to the distinction between Starlink, SpaceX’s commercial satellite internet service, and Starshield, a military version developed for the Pentagon. While Musk has said the two systems are separate, in many cases, they share the same underlying satellite technology.
“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government,” Musk said on Oct 14 in a post on X, adding that any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military or the president.
“Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company.”
What is Starlink?
Starlink, the main profit engine of SpaceX, is a satellite internet network of more than 11,000 satellites that beam broadband service directly to user terminals about the size of a folded newspaper. Its roughly 13 million subscribers range from households and hikers to shipping companies and major airlines.
Since launching its first Starlink satellites in 2019 aboard reusable SpaceX rockets, the company has built a vast low-Earth-orbit constellation that blankets much of the planet, delivering faster connections than traditional communications satellites, which typically operate much farther from Earth and in far smaller numbers.
Starlink gave Ukraine a critical communications advantage early in the war, reshaping how militaries operate on the battlefield. But Musk has restricted Starlink for certain military uses while highlighting Starshield, a more secure network developed for government and military missions.
What is Starshield?
Starshield is a SpaceX business unit that develops military and intelligence satellite systems for the Pentagon.
While its missions are separate from Starlink’s commercial broadband service, the distinction is not always clear-cut: Starshield’s secure communications services use enhanced encryption and dedicated terminals, but rely on the vast Starlink constellation as their backbone.
Starshield leverages the technology, engineering and operational experiences of Starlink, according to SpaceX. In addition to secure communications, the company says the militarised version can also provide users with Earth observation and the ability to integrate sensors or other payloads.
The Pentagon, Starshield’s largest customer, has spent billions of dollars on both Starlink and Starshield services. It has also bought dedicated Starshield satellites, including communications spacecraft for missile-warning missions and a spy constellation for the National Reconnaissance Office, Reuters reported in 2024.
Questions over the relationship between Starlink and Starshield have persisted since Russia threatened Western satellites supporting Ukraine in 2022. SpaceX unveiled Starshield later that year, but the secrecy surrounding national security space programmes has left the precise boundaries between the two systems opaque.
Those distinctions became a point of contention earlier in 2026 when the Pentagon clashed with SpaceX over higher prices for satellite services used by military drones during the Iran conflict, Reuters reported. SpaceX argued that some customers paying roughly US$5,000 (S$6,400) per terminal for Starlink should instead have been using a Starshield service costing about US$25,000 per terminal.
Britain has also adopted Starshield. Under that arrangement, the service uses the same satellite constellation, ground stations and terrestrial infrastructure as Starlink, but operates through dedicated terminals and separate network gateways, Britain’s Defence Ministry has told Reuters.
Other US partners are evaluating the system as well. New Zealand is doing a trial of Starshield to assess its usefulness for military operations, the New Zealand Defence Force previously told Reuters. REUTERS

Denmark pushes back as Trump touts Greenland oil and mineral deals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
23:03:10 UTC
08:03:10 KST

Denmark pushes back as Trump touts Greenland oil and mineral deals
Recent US-Greenland-Denmark agreement excludes mining or drilling rights while reinforcing Greenland’s sovereignty.
Denmark has demanded that US resource exploration in Greenland respect the island’s laws amid President Donald Trump’s claim that oil, gas and mineral extraction will soon begin there.
The Danish Foreign Ministry reaffirmed on Wednesday that last month’s agreement between Denmark, Greenland and the US did not alter the rules for extraction.
The agreement “does not grant investors from the US any preferential treatment” over investors from other NATO and EU countries when it comes to access to natural resources in Greenland, the ministry said.
In a post on Truth Social, US President Trump called the semi-autonomous Danish territory “our new and beautiful Greenland”.
“Massive Oil, Gas, and Mineral Exploration is getting ready to begin,” he wrote, without providing details.
What the deal covers
Trump, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenland’s Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen signed the 10-page agreement on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York on September 22, ending months of tensions over Trump’s threats to control Greenland.
The deal allows the US to “modernise and expand” its activities at the Pituffik Space Base, a remote US military installation in northwest Greenland.
It also paved the way for two new military bases and Trump’s “Golden Dome” missile defence system, while reaffirming Danish sovereignty and Greenlanders’ right to self-determination.
It did not allocate any rights for mining or drilling.
Greenland’s ban
Greenland banned uranium mining and all future oil exploration in 2021.
Its government is reviewing whether a Texas firm, Greenland Energy, can use permits that predate the ban.
The company said in August it planned to drill for oil in 2027 at an untested basin on Greenland’s east coast, although it lacked its own permit.
Danish security policy adviser Jacob Kaarsbo said Trump’s comments could signal that his desire to control Greenland remains unchanged.
“It is extremely dangerous to view this agreement between the Trump administration and Denmark as something that has altered Trump’s intentions,” he said.
Mikkel Olesen, a senior researcher at the Danish Institute for International Studies, told Al Jazeera that details regarding mining and exploration rights remained unclear and that information coming mostly from the US side should be taken “with a grain of salt”.
Richard Weitz, a fellow at the NATO Defense College in Rome, said Trump “backed down and settled for less” than he sought, but still “got pretty much everything he wanted, except formal annexation”.

Stopping Pip for ADHD or autism would not make big savings, says thinktank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
23:01:15 UTC
08:01:15 KST

Banning people with anxiety, ADHD or autism from claiming disability benefits would not deliver major financial savings and would probably make it harder for them to get or stay in a job and participate in society, a leading thinktank has warned.
The Resolution Foundation said any proposals to make certain mental health and neurodevelopmental conditions ineligible for personal independence payments (Pip) would be “crude changes” aimed at hitting unrealistic savings targets.
But it warned that Pip was “failing on several fronts” and called for a major overhaul to keep a lid on costs – currently rising at an “unsustainable” rate – and restore public trust in a benefit widely seen as unfair and dysfunctional.
About £4.4bn a year could be saved if Pip support was better targeted, it said. Cash support could be removed from an estimated one in six working-age Pip claimants (670,000) who report having no extra costs as a result of their disability.
However, it added that any reforms should proceed with caution because of the success of Pip in ensuring high numbers of disabled and ill people were able to participate in “economically valuable” activities, such as work, caring, training or volunteering, that they would not be able to do otherwise.
Official concern over Pip has soared in recent years, in part because of the rapidly rising number of claimants, particularly among young people, with much of that sharp increase linked to claims for mental health, ADHD and autism.
Spending on Pip in England and Wales has risen in real terms by 183% since it was introduced in 2014. This year the bill is expected to be £28bn, rising to £34bn by the end of the decade, according to official forecasts.
Attempts by the previous Labour administration under Keir Starmer to push through £5bn of crude savings to Pip collapsed last year amid a rebellion of backbench MPs. His successor, Andy Burnham, has said renewed attempts to reform benefits would not involve “crude cuts”.
Welfare officials, who are awaiting an official review of Pip by welfare minister Stephen Timms and the Milburn review of the youth jobs crisis, are understood to be considering proposals to exclude under-25s from the Pip system.
Pip has also found itself at the heart of culture war rows, with some, such as the Tory leader, Kemi Badenoch, arguing it should not be paid to claimants with so-called “mild” conditions that were not disabling or likely to incur higher daily living costs.
The Resolution Foundation said attempting to link Pip awards to particular conditions was simplistic and impractical as most claimants reported multiple conditions – often combining physical, mental and behavioural conditions.
Lindsay Judge, the thinktank’s research director, said: “Pip is a vital benefit for disabled people that enables them to participate in society and live fuller and more active lives. But the current system is failing on several fronts – claimants don’t trust it, awards don’t fully reflect the nature of disability today and spending is rising unsustainably.
“As well as continuing to provide cash awards to help with ongoing additional costs, a reformed Pip system should focus on supporting disabled people to participate in society. A system more attuned to people’s needs would also mean that around one in six current Pip recipients who don’t face significant limitations or additional costs because of their disability would no longer qualify for cash support.
“There is no perfect system of disability support, but one that better reflects the fact that people often have multiple and fluctuating conditions must target greater support and engagement where it’s needed, and avoid waste where it’s not.”
A Department for Work and Pensions spokesperson said: “Pip is awarded based on a functional assessment that determines how a condition impacts a person’s day-to-day needs. But as the Timms Review report made clear, Pip is no longer fit for purpose and the recommendations from its final report will lay the foundation for sustainable reform.”

ICE pushes back on report suggesting body cameras that automatically record
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
22:57:13 UTC
07:57:13 KST

ICE rejects recommendation for body cameras that automatically record
The immigration agency has rejected a report from a government watchdog, making suggestions for improved body camera policy.
Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), a United States agency that has taken a central role in President Donald Trump’s mass deportation campaign, has rejected a government report calling for its agents to wear body cameras that automatically activate.
On Wednesday, the Government Accountability Office, a nonpartisan agency that provides research to Congress, released a report recommending an update to ICE guidelines for camera usage.
It suggested that “automated camera activation” would be helpful in situations where “unexpected and unplanned incidents, unrelated to sensitive operations, result in use of force by or against personnel”.
“Given the important role of body-worn cameras in law enforcement activities, we maintain that additional controls are needed to help ensure that ICE personnel capture footage in accordance with policy,” the report said.
Automatic activation, it added, would address difficulties ICE agents face in manually turning on their cameras during enforcement operations.
But ICE has rejected the recommendation for automatic activation, which could be triggered by an agent pulling a gun or turning on a car siren. The agency cited privacy concerns.
But the Trump administration faces public pressure to improve transparency during its immigration raids.
Agents from ICE and other agencies such as Customs and Border Protection (CBP) have faced accusations of excessive force and civil liberties violations.
In January, two US citizens – Renee Good and Alex Pretti – were shot to death in separate shootings in Minneapolis, Minnesota, during immigration operations.
The New York Times estimated in July that immigration agents had opened fire on at least 25 people since the start of Trump’s second term. A CBS News review updated this week counts at least 30 shootings, with nine people killed and 13 others wounded.
ICE has often blamed such incidents on aggression against its agents, and it has argued that its officers have opened fire to defend themselves from danger.
But in several cases, that rationale has come under scrutiny.
Critics argued that video footage in Good’s fatal shooting disproved government statements alleging that she had weaponised her vehicle against agents. Her car, according to observers, appeared to be turning away from agents, not towards them.
In another case, ICE agent Christian Castro was accused of making false statements about a shooting that resulted in injury to Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis, a Venezuelan man living in Minneapolis.
Castro faces federal charges for allegedly lying about being attacked with a snow shovel and broom before the shooting, after video footage contradicted his account. Castro pleaded not guilty last month.
More recently, on October 8, immigration agents shot a man named Oscar Belgal in New York City while his five-year-old son was in the backseat of his car. ICE stated that Belgal appeared to be “going towards officers” in his car when they opened fire.
On Tuesday, a judge rejected the government’s effort to have Belgal deported.
Activists say better recording procedures for body camera footage could help clarify what happened in such incidents.
But the Trump administration has largely refused to implement reforms to ICE protocol.
Earlier this year, Democrats in Congress delayed funding for the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, on the basis that significant changes needed to be made to reduce incidents of excessive force.
The department said on Wednesday that automatically recording cameras could result in “the unauthorised recording of sensitive interactions with informants or victims”.
The agency added that all ICE offices had received body cameras as of August 5, but that training in their use was still ongoing and would be finished “soon”.

2026-10-14
22:45:00 UTC
07:45:00 KST

Musk suggests US govt behind any slowdown in Ukraine’s Starshield system
WASHINGTON – SpaceX boss Elon Musk said on Oct 14 that any disruptions reported by Ukraine in using the Starshield satellite communications system would be the responsibility of the US government, not his company.
“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” Musk said, referring to US President Donald Trump.
Musk drew a distinction between the Starshield system, which Ukraine relies on for battlefield communications, and the parallel Starlink civilian satellite system, which Ukraine also deploys but is not allowed to use for offensive operations. Both were designed by Musk’s SpaceX.
Musk was responding to a post on X by Ukraine’s former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov, who said that “Starlink connectivity at speeds of up to 160kmh is being restored”, but that “removing Starshield’s speed limit entirely is now critical for Ukraine’s defence”.
Fedorov then thanked Musk for his “continued support”.
Ukrainian defence officials have suggested Washington is behind slower speeds reported on some internet terminals that help the country’s military hit Russian-occupied territory and operate interceptor drones.
Ukraine has also accused the United States of helping Russia by failing to warn it of incoming missile strikes, with Kyiv hit by ballistic missiles for two nights in a row before air raid sirens could sound to warn people to take cover.
Opposition Democrats in the US Senate and House denounced the Trump Administration over the reported interrupted connections.
“Trump’s making a choice – and it directly aids Putin’s slaughter of Ukrainian civilians,” House Foreign Affairs Committee Democrats said in a post on X, describing restrictions as “unconscionable” while Ukraine faced an onslaught of Russian drones and missiles.
In the Senate’s Foreign Relations Committee, top Democrat Jeanne Shaheen said the “restrictions on Ukraine’s access to Starshield must stop immediately”, adding that “lives are at stake”.
Shaheen also said that the defence department is required to notify “Congress if it pauses or downgrades intelligence sharing with Ukraine”, and called on Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth to immediately provide that notification if there are changes.
Republican Senator Tom Tillis also voiced concern, posting on X: “Supporting Ukrainian sovereignty – or at the very least, allowing for it – should not be a grey area for the US government or for American corporations.”
Trump, facing key midterm elections in November, in which fuel prices are a major issue, has blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries for the squeeze on supplies and increase in prices at the pump.
A senior official in Kyiv confirmed that the United States had in recent days threatened to stop providing intelligence about Russian missile launches that Ukraine uses to thwart attacks.
Trump denied doing so on Oct 13. AFP

Australia is the monster that turns World Cup dreams to nightmares
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
22:37:28 UTC
07:37:28 KST

Fri, 18 Sept, 7:50 pm, Final score, Tigers 0, Raiders 6
analysis
Australia's dominance looms over the women's Rugby League World Cup
Almost a decade ago, the women's Rugby League World Cup final was the last day before everything changed.
Australia's cracking 23-16 win over New Zealand in 2017 didn't just deliver the team its first-ever World Cup final victory on home soil; it was the last major match before the women's game was transformed forever.
The following season, the interstate series moved under the NRL banner, the first NRLW season kicked off, and women's rugby league began to take giant strides.
A few players from that watershed moment are still around for this year's Rugby League World Cup, which begins tomorrow in Parramatta, when Australia plays Samoa.
Isabelle Kelly, Kezie Apps and Simaima Taufa are still wearing green and gold; Zahara Temara has switched to New Zealand and will play for the Kiwi Ferns in their tournament opener against Fiji on Sunday alongside Raecene McGregor and Apii Nicholls.
These six exist in a different world from the one they came from, one where the players are now faster, stronger, fitter and more skilful; where pathways have improved, and player numbers have exploded; and where the game has evolved to the point where this should be the last World Cup held simultaneously with the men's tournament because the product is strong enough to stand alone.
But the issue heading into the tournament is at the top end of the product, because Australia's dominance has become one of the growing pains the game must endure as everyone else tries to catch up.
Since that win in 2017, the Jillaroos have won 15 of 16 matches. They have not conceded more than two tries in a game since 2018.
In the last World Cup, they won their five matches by a cumulative scoreline of 312-12, including a 54-4 massacre of New Zealand in the final.
The last time they played England, they won 90-4, and those four points mark the only try they've conceded to a team other than New Zealand in their past 16 games.
They won the Pacific Championship last year, scoring 110 points and conceding just 12 across three matches, with the Kiwi Ferns copping a 40-8 belting in the final.
State of Origin regulars like Jesse Southwell and Abbi Church, both overlooked for the match against Samoa, can't make this team. A living legend like Ali Brigginshaw can't even make the squad.
The Jillaroos have nine players from this year's NRLW Dally M Team of the Year. In Tamika Upton, Olivia Kernick, Tarryn Aiken, Isabelle Kelly and Jess Sergis, they have the best player, forward, halfback and centres in the world.
They are, without question, the best women's rugby league team ever, and they are so much better than everyone else that anything less than a dominant run to the final and a thumping victory at Lang Park will feel like a departure from a predestined fate.
Other teams have improved. New Zealand, which handed Australia its sole loss in recent years in 2023 and went down by just six points in one game last year, has risen highest with the tide.
As the Warriors settle back into the NRLW, they could rise higher still, and their squad for this year's tournament should put them in contention for the final.
Samoa is another side that has improved and could still get better. The Fetu have benefited from the injection of diaspora players like Taliah Fuimaono, Evania Isa'ako and Amber Hall, plus fresh faces like Queensland Origin flyer Destiny Mino-Sinapati and reigning NRLW rookie of the year Mercedez Taulelei-Siala.
They are a vision of what is possible for the expansion of women's rugby league and beneficiaries of the improved pathways leading to the NRLW.
It will take time, because we are talking about change that can take a decade or more to become apparent, but the benefits are there for all to see in the men's game.
The women's game is on the same path; they're just not as far along. This is a brave, dangerous side with a real future, one which is easy to see unfolding before us.
One day a team like Samoa might be able to give the World Cup a real shake. But not these days.
The Samoans are currently 53.5-point underdogs against the Jillaroos in tomorrow night's match. They lost to them 60-0 in the corresponding clash last year.
Even that was nothing compared to the 90-4 belting England copped in Las Vegas last year, an eye-popping result that showed just how lopsided things had become.
The English will get a chance at revenge in Perth next week, and they're a much better side than the one that travelled to Nevada.
Roosters backrower Jasmin Strange is a welcome addition, and they have a core of NRLW players, including North Queensland's Fran Goldthorp, Canberra forward Hollie-Mae Dodd and clever Newcastle playmaker Georgia Roche.
If they can keep things respectable against the Jillaroos, that will be progress.
That gap can close as more top-level talent filters through the ranks, for England and everybody else.
But it will take time to run the Jillaroos down. And because the women's game is semi-professional, it's unlikely to happen as rapidly as it has in the men's game, meaning progress could take a decade or more.
Until then, there is no choice but to keep going.
Every nation will have a moment. Some will have more than one because there will be glories outside of absolute victory. Fiji will make its World Cup debut and Papua New Guinea will look to continue its steady progress of recent years.
A semi-final berth would be a major achievement for Samoa and a place in the final would be a shot in the arm for the game in England, so their group-stage clash is the pick of the early tournament matches.
The Kiwi Ferns will fancy their chances of an ambush should they meet Australia in the final, given the Jillaroos will have had a soft run in. They will point out that they are the one in 15-1, and perhaps they will be right.
But at the end lurks Australia, the monster at the end of the dream that turns it into a nightmare. And, just under a decade since the rest of history began, the truth of the pain it is about to inflict is simple.
This is the best collection of players ever assembled in women's rugby league, and if they are at any point over the next month beaten, it will be one of the biggest upsets the game has known.

Albania protests turn violent as protestors demand PM Rama's resignation

Albania protests turn violent as protestors demand PM Rama's resignation
Anti-government protests in Albania’s capital Tirana turned violent for a second consecutive night on Wednesday, leaving several government buildings damaged and at least one ablaze. Thousands demanded Prime Minister Edi Rama’s resignation and improved university conditions. Police fired tear gas and deployed water cannons as protesters smashed windows and attacked buildings.
Anti-government protests in Albania's capital left several official buildings badly damaged and at least one on fire on Wednesday as demonstrations spiralled into violence for a second straight night.
Protesters and riot police clashed in Tirana as thousands of demonstrators rallied for better university conditions and demanded Prime Minister Edi Rama's resignation.
Over several hours, police deployed water cannons and tear gas while demonstrators attacked government offices and shops in the city centre, smashed windows and set fire to multiple buildings.
Riot police repeatedly tried to push them back, even using tear gas, but the crowd showed little sign of dispersing.
As night fell, crowds continued to spread through the city, attacking government buildings.
In one incident, protesters smashed windows before setting a floor of the justice ministry building on fire.
Read moreAlbania's "Flamingo revolution": Trump-linked luxury resort plan triggers mass protests
Police chased protesters away before firefighters brought the blaze under control.
Throughout the day, demonstrators hurled paving stones and petrol bombs, set fire to bins and used street fencing to erect barricades.
Protesters also attacked the finance ministry, using fencing to smash windows and break down doors, with some briefly entering the building.
Pushed back by police, protesters moved towards the prime minister's office, where they threw stones at the building prompting police to use water cannon.
A tree near the building entrance briefly caught fire before firefighters extinguished it.
'Masked mob'
Interior minister Ervin Demo acknowledged the concerns of students but blamed the "malicious hands of outsiders" for the violence.
"To those currently setting fire to and destroying public and private property, I say: pull back before it is too late," he said.
"While individual accountability before the law may be delayed amidst the destructive frenzy of a masked mob, it will never forget."
Earlier, AFP saw two people climb over the education ministry wall and throw flares into the building.
Thick black smoke poured from a window shortly afterwards, before firefighters managed to put out the blaze.
Read moreKushner-backed luxury resort sparks outrage, dividing Albanian population
Local media reported that protesters had also attempted to storm a police station, smashing police cars and damaging the entrance before being chased away.
Several banks were attacked and many shopfronts were smashed in the city centre.
Police said late on Wednesday that 14 officers had been injured and 35 people had been detained. Six officers were injured and 16 people were arrested on Tuesday.
"Police are continuing to identify and detain individuals who have committed acts of violence and worn masks during the protest," a statement said.
Demonstrators originally gathered early on Tuesday to demand Rama's resignation and more support for students in the country, citing poor university conditions and high tuition fees.
For more than four months, anti-government protests have routinely drawn crowds in their thousands.
Originally sparked by a luxury tourism project linked to US President Donald Trump's family in the country's south, the demonstrations have occasionally flared into violence amid ongoing calls for Rama's resignation.
Police said officers had "faced constant violence" on Tuesday and were "pelted with stones, blunt objects, firecrackers and Molotov cocktails by groups of masked demonstrators".
The European Union, which the Balkan nation aspires to join, voiced concern over what it called the "violent escalation at the protest in Tirana".
It also called for a prompt investigation of allegations of excessive force by police and called "all sides to de-escalate the tension".
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

Lawyers for man shot by ICE in New York City say agent did not identify himself
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
22:30:42 UTC
07:30:42 KST

Lawyers for a man wounded by an immigration officer while driving with his young son in New York City said in a court filing Wednesday that the agent who shot him never identified himself before he ran up to the car, smashed one of its windows, then fired several shots into the vehicle.
The account by lawyers for Oscar Belgal contrasted sharply with the version of events outlined by Department of Homeland Security officials. They have said officers opened fire only after Belgal smashed his car into two government vehicles and “accelerated toward other officers”.
The Legal Aid Society, in a petition filed in Brooklyn federal court seeking Belgal’s release, said he had picked up his son from school and was stopped in front of a fire hydrant, looking for a parking spot, when “an anonymous, masked man” stormed up to the vehicle with his gun drawn, followed by other masked men with guns.
“The men did not identify themselves, show any documents or otherwise communicate with Oscar in any substantive way,” Belgal’s lawyers wrote. “Instead, without identifying himself, the first man struck and shattered Oscar’s window and began firing a pistol into Oscar’s car while his son cowered in the back seat. One of those bullets struck Oscar in the neck and he immediately began to bleed.”
New York City police security camera footage released by the department last week shows some of the encounter but doesn’t conclusively resolve the dispute about how the shooting happened.
The video shows a man wearing a sweatshirt and a red hat running up to the car with his gun pointed at Belgal, then immediately using the barrel of his gun to bash the driver’s side window. The window shatters on the second blow.
A second officer comes into view alongside the car and draws his gun. Belgal then pulls into the street, away from the two officers. The car pulls out of view of the camera, with the officer in the red hat in pursuit.
Whatever happened next didn’t appear on the NYPD’s security cameras, but the chase ended just a moment later, with Belgal’s damaged car resting against a concrete barrier with bullet holes in its windshield and a rear window.
Video from bystanders and NYPD body camera footage show that ICE officers handcuffed Belgal and tended to a gunshot wound to his neck as he sat on the pavement outside the car. NYPD officers took Belgal to a nearby hospital.
DHS didn’t comment Wednesday on the claims by Belgal’s lawyers, saying the incident remains under investigation. But DHS officials have maintained that ICE officers fired their weapons because they believed their lives were in danger.
Belgal’s lawyers said he didn’t learn the men were ICE officers until he awoke later in the hospital. They say he remains detained at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn, where he has yet to receive surgery to remove the bullet lodged in his neck. They also say he has lost sensation on the left side of his face and now has impaired hearing.
The Federal Bureau of Prisons, which manages the jail, didn’t immediately comment.

CBI said it is investigating into the roles of all persons involved
New Delhi: The Enforcement Directorate (ED) Wednesday said it has seized Indian assets worth Rs 2,033 crore belonging to Reliance Power Ltd (RPL), an entity of the Reliance Anil Ambani Group, under Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), for the alleged siphoning of assets worth an equivalent amount to tax havens of British Virgin Islands (BVI) and Cayman Islands.The attached assets include bank balances of RPL and its shareholding in Sasan Power Limited. "The Headquarter Investigation Unit has seized assets worth ₹2,032.81 crore in India belonging to RPL, which are equivalent to the foreign exchange held outside India in contravention of FEMA," ED said. ED has already attached assets worth thousands of crores of the Anil Ambani group, including his residences in Mumbai, in multiple money laundering cases involving over Rs 40,000 crore.ED said its investigation into findings of Sebi, pertaining to write-offs/provisions aggregating ₹2,101.46 crore made by RPL in its books of account, had revealed that "these write-offs were related to overseas investments and advances made to companies in the British Virgin Islands (BVI) and the Cayman Islands".In a statement released to BSE and NSE Tuesday, RPL said the ED order of seizure of assets "relates to foreign currency convertible bonds issued in 2006, i.e.
20 years ago, and the related overseas investment made in 2008, i.e. 18 years ago, in a subsidiary in Singapore with all applicable approvals. The seizure primarily pertains to the shares held by the company in its wholly owned subsidiary Sasan Power Ltd, which are already pledged in favour of Power Finance Corporation Ltd (a govt undertaking) under security arrangements for more than 10 years, as well as certain bank balances of the company".ED had conducted related searches in March and seized "several pieces of incriminating evidence", recording statements of several persons. "Investigation has revealed that Reliance Natural Resources Ltd (since merged with RPL) raised $300 million through foreign currency convertible bonds in 2006. Of this, $275 million was invested in its wholly owned Singapore subsidiary Reliance Natural Resources (Singapore) Pte Ltd (RNRL-S)."RNRL-S placed these funds on deposit with Deutsche Bank (Suisse) SA, Geneva. The deposits were used as collateral for loans extended to entities incorporated in the British Virgin Islands. The investigation found that the BVI entities were controlled and managed from India by the Reliance Anil Ambani Group (RAAG) through front persons, who acted as per the group's directions," ED said.
Further, the loan proceeds were utilised for varied purposes, including temporary round-tripping of funds to India through foreign entities based in Mauritius, the central agency said, adding that this was done to benefit the RAAG."The BVI entities failed to repay the loans extended by Deutsche Bank. As part of cover-up, documents were fabricated to show that RNRL-S and Indonesian subsidiaries of RPL had made advances to these BVI entities for apparently genuine business purposes. During investigation, it was found this documentation was backdated and prepared in order to project these transactions as genuine business transactions," ED said. Further investigation is in progress.

“Now leakers should be dealt with very, very strongly,” Trump told the crowd.
He then escalated his criticism, declaring: “The leakers are the scum of the earth.”
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced plans last week to livestream the execution, scheduled for December 3, with a military firing squad expected to carry out the sentence. The proposal has drawn criticism and sparked debate across the US.
Trump subsequently indicated that he would make the final decision on whether the execution would be broadcast and that the livestream could still be canceled.
Trump recounts sensitive information leaked
During his Arizona speech, Trump revisited his account of how sensitive information about Operation Midnight Hammer, the planned June 2025 attack on Iran’s nuclear program, reached the media before the mission was carried out.
According to Trump, the disclosure included the precise departure and arrival times of the American bombers.
“But they leaked that we were leaving at 12:07 from Missouri, and it was in the New York Times, CNN,” he said.
Trump said he subsequently contacted Gen. Dan Caine, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, to discuss the potential implications for the operation.
“I said, ‘General, that’s not good, is it?’” Trump recalled.
According to the president, Caine replied: “Not good, sir, but we can do it anyway.”
Trump said he nevertheless decided to change the timing of the mission.
“So I called off the raid,” he told the audience.
The decision, he claimed, was particularly disappointing to the pilots who had been preparing for the operation.
“You know the unhappiest people were the pilots. They were miserable,” he said.
Trump went on to explain that two days later, he decided the attack could proceed — using the same departure time that had previously been disclosed.
“All right, good. Now we can do the raid. Let’s leave it exactly the same time,” he recalled telling his team.
“We used the exact same time,” he added.
According to Trump’s account, returning to the original timing meant the Iranians would be less likely to anticipate the aircraft’s movements.
The president presented the episode as an example of the potential consequences of leaking operational military information and as justification for imposing exceptionally harsh penalties on those responsible.
He did not present new evidence identifying the alleged leakers or independently establishing the circumstances of the disclosures he described.
Trump says the US has eliminated numerous Iranian leaders
Later in the rally, Trump returned to another theme he has raised repeatedly in recent days, joking that the US may have eliminated so many members of Iran’s leadership that Washington is now struggling to determine whom it should negotiate with.
The president began by listing what he described as the destruction of Iran’s military capabilities.
“Their radar is gone. Their anti-aircraft is gone. Their leaders are gone,” Trump said.
“That’s one of the problems. I might have gone too far. I don’t know who the hell to deal with.”
Trump continued his account of the successive losses suffered by Iran’s leadership, claiming that American military operations had eliminated multiple generations of senior officials.
“Their first level leaders are gone. They picked the second level. Their second level leaders are gone. They picked the third level, half of them are gone.”
The comments were delivered in a joking, boastful tone, rather than as an expression of regret over the American campaign.
Trump also claimed that he had been asked to refrain from targeting additional Iranian leaders and had agreed.
“They made me promise not to take out anymore, and I did. I promised them,” he said, without specifying who had made the request.
The president then joked that the leadership losses had made the prospect of assuming power in Tehran particularly unattractive.
“But nobody wants to be the president of the Islamic Republic of Iran,” Trump said.
“We hear, we have conversations. We hear them. Who would like to be the president of Iran? Please raise your hand. No, I don’t want to be.”
Returning to the difficulty of identifying a negotiating counterpart, Trump repeated the joke.
“I probably went a little too far. I’m sorry, because I don’t know who the hell we’re dealing with anymore.”
Despite the seemingly apologetic language, the comments formed part of a broader speech in which Trump repeatedly celebrated the effectiveness of American military operations against Iran.
He also reiterated his argument that military action had been necessary to prevent Tehran from acquiring a nuclear weapon.
According to Trump, before the June 2025 attack, Iran had been just two weeks away from obtaining such a weapon — an assessment he presented as justification for ordering the strikes.
The president argued that the economic consequences of the confrontation, including higher gasoline prices, were a relatively small price to pay for preventing a nuclear-armed Iran.
Trump claims US control of Strait of Hormuz will bring fuel prices down
Trump also addressed the economic consequences of the continuing confrontation with Iran, asserting that the US had established control over the Strait of Hormuz and that more oil was now moving through the strategic waterway than before the conflict began.
He credited the US Navy and the American blockade, which he described as a “Wall of Steel,” for securing the waterway.
The president argued that the military operations had prevented Iran from threatening global security and suggested that energy prices would decline further once the confrontation ended.
“But that’s going to end very soon, and when that ends, your gasoline is going to go down to even lower than it was before,” Trump told supporters.
His comments came amid continuing tensions with Tehran and renewed American warnings against Iranian-backed forces in the region.

Ukraine accuses US of helping Russia as missiles hit Kyiv
Ukraine on Oct 14 accused the United States of helping Russia by failing to warn it of incoming missile strikes and hobbling Kyiv’s military response through changes to the Starlink system it uses on the battlefield.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called on US tech billionaire Elon Musk to restore Starlink, which Kyiv says has been slowed down.
“I hope that it’s a mistake, maybe huge technical problem,” Zelensky told UK journalist Piers Morgan. “I don’t know, but we are asking to do it, to switch (it) on.”
Former Ukrainian defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov later said that “Starlink’s operation at speeds up to 160kmh is being restored. Strike drones and interceptor drones should be able to fly again”.
Attacks in Strait of Hormuz reach highest level since start of Iran war
At least ten vessels have been attacked in or near the Strait of Hormuz since Oct 11, a high since war broke out between the United States, Israel and Iran, security data showed on Oct 14.
Four vessels were struck on Oct 13 and six on Oct 11 – the highest number of attacks in a single day since the start of the conflict – according to data from security firm Vanguard, the International Maritime Organization (IMO) and the British maritime agency UKMTO.
Two seafarers have been reported missing and a container ship reportedly sank as a result of recent attacks, according to the maritime sources.
Trump’s new press secretary Katie Zacharia faces scrutiny over credentials
The White House was facing mounting questions on Oct 14 over new press secretary Katie Zacharia’s legal credentials, after a faltering first day in the job when she gave an inconclusive answer about where she had passed the bar exam.
A US watchdog group filed a complaint with the State Bar of California, asking it to investigate whether President Donald Trump’s spokeswoman – the public face of the administration – had broken the law by repeatedly presenting herself as a lawyer without a licence.
Campaign for Accountability said Zacharia had described herself as a lawyer during television appearances and listed herself as general counsel of a California-based conservative nonprofit.
Nasdaq ends sharply lower as hot inflation data stirs rate-hike worries
Hotter-than-expected inflation data sent the Nasdaq to a sharply lower close on Oct 14, with worries about more interest rate hikes from the Federal Reserve pummelling shares of Oracle, CoreWeave and other AI stocks sensitive to higher borrowing costs.
Increased bets that the Fed will need more rate hikes to tame inflation dealt a sharp blow to some of the market’s biggest gainers of 2026. Oracle lost 8.8%, while AI-infrastructure firms CoreWeave and Nebius tumbled 15% and 10%, respectively.
Dell and Hewlett Packard Enterprise sank 11.4% and 8.2%, respectively, after Barclays downgraded the AI server makers to “equal-weight” from “overweight”.
PSG outgun embattled Man City in six-goal Champions League thriller
Paris Saint-Germain further soured the mood at the Etihad Stadium as Manchester City’s first home game since the guilty verdict on widespread flouting of Premier League financial rules ended in a 4-2 Champions League defeat on Oct 14.
The European champions turned on the style to strike three times inside the opening 35 minutes through Desire Doue, Ousmane Dembele and Vitinha.
But City stormed back in the second half as Erling Haaland scored twice either side of Maghnes Akliouche’s strike that briefly restored PSG’s three-goal cushion.

‘The Escape’ makes its debut, ‘Shalom’ enchants - review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
22:15:28 UTC
07:15:28 KST

The biggest news on Israeli TV this week is the premiere of "The Escape," the new, all-star series on Channel 12. Based on the opening episode, which can also be streamed on mako.co.il, it’s tense and suspenseful.
It’s also a cautionary tale about why authorities shouldn't look the other way when a cult leader gains too much power. It feels like a mix of The Handmaid’s Tale, "Shtisel," and one of the movies about the 1978 Jonestown massacre.
Keshet 12 produced the series, and Keshet International is set to distribute it internationally.
"The Escape" stars Ido Tako, who just won the Ophir Award for Best Supporting Actor for his performance in the movie Where To, as Yoel, a young man born into a sect that, despite a disclaimer, will remind many of the Lev Tahor cult.
Like that group, the cult in the series preaches an extreme version of ultra-Orthodox observance and has moved its members out of Israel and into the Colombian jungle. Yoel has grown up in this cult from a young age, but he is clearly unhappy there.
He sees other members of the group punished brutally for minuscule infractions, such as taking two slices of bread at a meal, and wants a different life for his son, Nachman. The child gazes at the stream by their compound and asks where it flows. When his father explains the concept of an ocean, he is fascinated, and it is obvious he has lived his whole life in this compound.
Yoel lives with the other men, although he is married to Feigi (Naya Beinstock, who appears in the movie Matchmaking 3). Men and women are strictly segregated, except when husbands and wives can “fulfill a commandment” together on the Sabbath.
Yoel does not seem impressed with the group’s leader (Mark Evanir), who talks about blessings and purity but rules with an iron hand. If the title didn’t give it away, Yoel and his family are planning a jailbreak.
Another major character is Carmeli (Yehuda Levi, who became a star over 20 years ago in Yossi & Jagger and has recently appeared in Trust No One and A Body that Works), a Mossad agent who, at the start of the series, is in a Colombian city.
There, he rescues an Israeli arrested on drug charges from a hospital. A complicated backstory involving his family in Israel is hinted at, and he seems to be the latest incarnation of the brave, workaholic, emotionally stunted covert operative we are used to seeing from so many dramas. But Levi’s charisma breathes new life into what might otherwise have been an overly formulaic character.
The series, which was filmed in Colombia, Georgia, and Israel, was created and written by Ariel Cohen for Keshet 12 alongside Yoav and Doron Paz, who also directed. The three collaborated on the movie The Golem, and the Paz brothers also made Plan A and Jeruzalem, the zombies-in-the-Old-City movie.
They carefully create a foreboding atmosphere and make you instantly root for Yoel and his family. In the coming weeks, we'll see what twists and turns "The Escape" has in store for us.
New 'Shalom' film tells story of Jerusalem biblical zoo rhinoceros
The touching movie Shalom, by Meital Zvieli, airs on KAN 11 on October 17 and will then be available on kan.org.il. It tells the story of Shalom, the beloved rhinoceros at Jerusalem’s biblical zoo (officially called the Tisch Family Zoological Gardens), but it's about so much more.
The movie uses the zookeepers’ relationships with the animals very effectively to symbolize the delicate reality of coexistence in the capital. It is beautiful in all the ways a movie can be: moving, wonderfully photographed, and using a simple device to tell a far more complex story.
Shalom came to the zoo just as the 1978 Camp David Accords were being signed. When the film opens, in the early 2020s, he’s tired. The Jews and Muslims on the staff are drawn together by their love for him and their desire to help him when his health begins to fail.
Some may remember the excellent children’s film shown in the Noah’s Ark exhibit at the zoo, and will recognize Rushdi Alyan (the main human protagonist in Shalom) and Gilad Moshe, two of the zookeepers who appear in it and are among the interviewees in both movies. They work together again in this new documentary, and it seems that, against all odds, their bond has grown stronger over the years.
Part of the movie covers the difficult period following the Hamas-led invasion and massacres in Israel on October 7, 2023, and shows how the animals are affected by the missiles fired near the zoo. As the Israel-Hamas War intensifies, Shalom becomes ill, and at the same time, many zookeepers are sent off to fight in Gaza. One of them quips, “The whole world keeps asking me, ‘Where’s Shalom?’”
For many years, I used to visit the zoo in Jerusalem every week with my son, who is on the autism spectrum. I know what it’s like to become attached to these animals and to find calm in this oasis of coexistence and harmony in a city, and a world, roiled by so many conflicts, so I could relate to every minute in this documentary.
But even if you don't share my deep connection to this place or respect for the people who run it, watching Shalom will still be an emotionally resonant experience. Hats off to Meital Zvieli for giving this unique, lovely part of Jerusalem the cinematic treatment it deserves.
New 'Cupertino' series running across Israeli TV providers
"Cupertino" is a new series from Robert and Michelle King, the husband-and-wife duo behind "The Good Wife" and "The Good Fight," and it’s currently running on Hot 3, Hot VOD, Next TV, Yes VOD, and Cellcom TV.
Fans of both shows, especially "The Good Wife," which set a new standard for witty, topical legal drama, have been looking forward to "Cupertino" because it aims to be a cross between "The Good Wife" and "Silicon Valley."
Unfortunately, though, based on the series pilot, which was released to the press, it brings to mind more the clunky, short-lived "BrainDead," a series by the Kings that tried to combine comedy, political humor, and sci-fi horror in a series that didn’t work in any of these genres.
On paper, the premise of "Cupertino" sounds great: Two recently fired lawyers who worked at Silicon Valley tech companies start their own law firm, specializing in defending wrongly terminated Davids against tech Goliaths. It also delves into issues raised by the development of AI.
Mike Colter, who was so good as the charismatic but scary drug lord Lemond Bishop on "The Good Wife," stars as Michael Price, a tech co-founder and lawyer who suddenly finds himself on the street when his partner decides not to share the wealth.
Colter is always good, but here he seems blander than I’ve ever seen him. Blandness is also a problem with his co-star, Rachel Keller as Olivia, a religious Christian lawyer at the same company, who is sexually harassed by her boss but decides to sue because the company’s AI avatar has been based on her.
The jokes and the plotting are painfully obvious much of the time, but I’ll try to keep an open mind and hope things pick up in subsequent episodes.

‘Waves’ captures thrill and tragedy of resistance at Prague radio station in ’68 - review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
22:14:55 UTC
07:14:55 KST

People talk about the concept of resistance to political authority in ways that are often very abstract, but it’s fascinating to see real resistance in practice. The movie Waves, which just opened in Israel, does just that, dramatizing a story of the very sophisticated political opposition to the Soviet Union at a Prague radio station from 1967-1968.
The movie, directed by Jirí Mádl, is based on true events and focuses on two brothers whose parents are dead, Tomás (Vojtech Vodochodský), who is in his 20s, and his teenage brother, Paja (Ondrej Stupka). Tomás is preoccupied with just putting food on the table, while Paja is involved in political activism against Russian control over Czechoslovakia.
Tomás discourages this activism, urging his brother to devote himself to his studies. But Paja is energized by what he hears on Czechoslovak Radio, the international news department, of which is helmed by Milan Weiner (Stanislav Majer), a brave and visionary news editor who inspires his staff and pushes the boundaries of what the station is permitted to report.
When Paja goes to a kind of audition-job interview there, Tomás follows to keep an eye on him.
In a very believable scene, Tomás gets a job as a technician because when a phone rings in the room where they are auditioning, he is the only one to pick it up and bring the message to the editors.
Tomás enjoys his work and respects Weiner and the staff, but is uneasy when government officials pressure him to become an informer. They threaten to take away Paja and put him into an orphanage if he doesn’t cooperate.
The bulk of the movie is about how Tomás manages to play it both ways, giving the secret police just a little information so they will issue warnings but will allow the station to continue functioning.
The situation weighs on Tomás, who is quiet and sensitive, and adds to his worries about his brother. In addition to the personal story of this concerned older brother and that of the ambitious, quirky staff of this rebel radio station, the movie details the events of the Prague Spring, leading up to the Soviet crackdown and invasion in 1968.
The film incorporates news footage seamlessly into the story, which is a beautiful illustration of what it looks like when the personal really does become political. And in a lower-tech era, the tricks they use to keep broadcasting are brilliant.
'A love letter to news radio and newspapers'
MUCH OF Waves is about the exhilaration of resisting, and how exciting it can be to give people the knowledge they need, which is being kept from them, to make their own decisions.
It’s a kind of love letter to news radio and newspapers, and it is set to a soundtrack of classic rock music, which the staff loves, as well as popular Czech songs from the same period.
The ensemble cast is excellent, and Vojtech Vodochodský makes you feel the tension of the untenable position he is forced into very effectively. Majer is suitably charming as the news editor and Tatiana Pauhofová is appealing as a tough translator who has a softer side.
As I watched, it was hard not to think of the Iranian protests in January, in which the government killed tens of thousands of protesters. Some people say that the Iranian people should bring down their oppressive regime on their own, with no outside help.
But Waves, which was the Czech Republic’s official Oscar submission in 2025, depicts a reality in which those who opposed the Soviet-influenced regime had a great many tools at their disposal, such as radio stations and opposition newspapers.
Yet they were still crushed by the reality of the tanks rolling in. It’s sobering to think that the characters in Waves had to live under this regime for another 21 years.
While Waves is entertaining on its own, as a historical drama, it may make you long for the day when there will be a Persian Spring in Iran that will bloom far longer than the one in Prague did.
