Istanbul's Yedikule Gate bears traces of Byzantine, Ottoman history
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
22:00:01 UTC
07:00:01 KST

Ali Osman Kaya and Halis Sunnetci
15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
Istanbul's historic Yedikule Gate, located along the southern section of the city's ancient land walls near the Sea of Marmara, bears traces of both the Byzantine and Ottoman periods through its surviving architecture and centuries of restoration work.
The gate, located near Yedikule Fortress and north of the Golden Gate, is featured in the ninth installment of Anadolu’s media series "Gates Opening onto the City's History."
Situated between Towers 11 and 12 of the land walls, the gate features a pointed arch built with two courses of brick and a restoration inscription dating to the reign of Ottoman Sultan Ahmed III.
Only the passageway through the main wall survives today, while a second passageway in the outer section of the walls has disappeared.
The gate and surrounding walls underwent repairs during the reigns of Ahmed III and Osman III, reflecting the structure's continued use during the Ottoman period.
Once connecting the area within the city walls to the surroundings of Yedikule, the gate remains an important part of Istanbul's Byzantine and Ottoman architectural heritage.
Kadir Pektas, a professor of art history at Istanbul Medeniyet University, told Anadolu that Yedikule Gate stands near the southern end of Istanbul's land walls, which extend toward the Sea of Marmara.
He said the gate served defensive purposes during the Byzantine period and was used for both defense and security during the Ottoman era.
"Today, only the section of the gate that opens onto the main, large walls—the arch—remains. The outer wall section has not survived to the present day," Pektas said.
He noted that 19th-century photographs suggest a second arched gateway once stood at the site, while archaeological research indicates that it may date to the Byzantine or Late Byzantine period.
Describing the surviving structure, Pektas said: "It is a pointed-arch gate, built of brick in two courses. In this respect, it bears all the hallmarks of the Ottoman style."
He also highlighted a restoration inscription above the arch dating to the reign of Ahmed III.
Two additional inscriptions along the walls, dating to the reigns of Ahmed III and Osman III, indicate extensive restoration work in the area during the 18th century, he said.
Pektas suggested that Yedikule Gate may have undergone more extensive restoration than other gateways in the city's walls because of its connection to the Yedikule Dungeons.
"It is a gate that leads directly to the Yedikule Dungeons and was also used during the Ottoman period. These successive repairs in the 18th century were likely related to access to the Yedikule Dungeons," he said.
He added that figurative reliefs once visible on the city-facing side of the gate have since disappeared.

Putin instructed the special services to tighten control over internet providers and IT companies in Russia
Kyiv • UNN
Putin ordered the special services to strengthen cooperation with providers, IT companies, and banks due to cyber threats. In the Russian Federation, 326 data breaches were recorded.
Russian dictator Vladimir Putin called on security forces to strengthen cooperation with internet providers, IT companies, and financial institutions due to an alleged increase in cyber threats. The Moscow Times reports this, citing the Kremlin, writes UNN.
Details
During a meeting on information security, Putin stated that Russia is facing "direct and hybrid external aggression" that threatens the economy, transport, logistics, and public administration.
To neutralize these threats, it is necessary to improve coordination between law enforcement agencies and special services and communications operators, financial organizations, internet companies, and other entities
Russia has become the world leader in data breaches
In addition to strengthening control, Putin instructed officials to modernize cybersecurity and expand monitoring of dependence on foreign digital platforms.
According to F6 analysts, 326 information leaks were recorded in Russia during 2025 and the first half of 2026, exposing 1.175 billion rows of personal data. This is almost twice as much as in a number of other regions of the world combined.
Despite these figures, Putin stated that Russia's digital sovereignty had been strengthened. At the same time, he did not mention the strikes by the Armed Forces of Ukraine on the data centers of "Yandex" and "Sberbank."

Russian authorities move to evict war refugees from temporary shelters south of Moscow. Many have nowhere else to go.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
21:58:57 UTC
06:58:57 KST

Russian authorities move to evict war refugees from temporary shelters south of Moscow. Many have nowhere else to go.
The Tula regional government has decided to evict residents from local temporary accommodation centers. Since 2022, the centers have housed refugees from Ukraine and Russia’s border communities. Many are single mothers with children, older people, or people who only recently escaped the fighting and have yet to find work and settle in. They cannot return home: The war continues where they lived, and many homes and even entire communities have been destroyed.
Journalists from the Bereg cooperative spoke with residents of one temporary accommodation center in the Tula region about how they became refugees and what they expect after eviction. Meduza is translating their report in full.
‘We’re all pleading with you not to throw us out on the street’
The parking lot outside a health resort in the Tula region is packed with cars bearing license plate codes rarely seen here. “180” and “181” designate the annexed Donetsk and Luhansk People’s Republics. The rarest code is “188.” Those plates were issued in the Kharkiv region during the six months in 2022 when Russia occupied part of the region.
Schoolchildren play on swings outside two buildings that were temporarily converted into a refugee accommodation center just two years ago. Pine trees surround the courtyard. Adults sit on benches under plastic canopies, smoking and talking.
These residents usually live in the neighboring complex, which has operated as a temporary accommodation center since 2022. In the summer, management moves them out and gives the better rooms to tourists and people attending forums held here. Those guests pay 8,000 rubles a night for the cheapest two-person cottage.
The refugees praise the accommodations. Their only complaint is the food: Cooking in the rooms is prohibited, and the cafeteria food is sometimes undercooked or spoiled.
In May 2026, the Tula regional government issued a decree requiring all refugees to leave temporary accommodation centers by September 1. Only a few categories of residents were exempt.
Residents say they were threatened with eviction by OMON riot police if they did not leave voluntarily. The refugees sought help from the regional Social Protection Ministry, the prosecutor’s office, and Tula Governor Dmitry Milyaev. Then they recorded a video appeal to Vladimir Putin.
Shortly after it was published, officers from Russia’s Federal Security Service came to the resort, residents told Bereg. “They searched all of us from top to bottom. They went through my entire phone. They asked: Who are the activists? Who are the traitors? Who do you support? How do you feel about the special military operation? What do you think of the president?” says one refugee, who asks not to be named.
Residents received perfunctory replies to their complaints about the eviction. But the deadline for leaving the resort was extended — first to October 1, then to October 15. In early October, the center’s management gathered the residents and told them there would be no further extensions.
The refugees have been unable to obtain any official documents explaining the grounds for their eviction. The prosecutor’s office had asked residents to supply those documents before it would look into the matter. Local officials said the residents were being evicted due to insufficient funding.
On October 4, the refugees recorded another video appeal to the president. About 70 people lined up in a clearing beneath the pines. The previous video had been filmed on the resort’s front steps, but this time, management asked them to ensure the center could not be identified in the footage.
Anna, 39, and Nataliya, who is about 50, address Putin on behalf of all the center’s residents. “Our communities are closed off and completely destroyed. We have nowhere to go back to,” Nataliya says. Her voice trembles slightly, and she breaks off midsentence. A dog barks nearby: Some residents managed to bring their pets out amid the shelling.
Nataliya continues the appeal. She says eviction will cost people both their housing and their temporary residence registration at the center. Without it, they will have trouble finding formal employment, enrolling their children in preschools and schools, and obtaining medical care.
Anna says refugees from the Kharkiv region will face particular hardship: They have neither official recognition as forcibly displaced people nor permanent residence registration in Russia. “We’re all pleading with you not to throw us out on the street,” she says as she finishes her appeal.
The participants disperse. Some recall that their previous video was mistaken for an AI-generated fake. I ask whether they believe the appeal will work. “We’ve already appealed to every authority there is!” one of them says in despair.
‘We supported the Russians so much — you wouldn’t believe it. But after living here for four years… It hurts that nobody wants us’
The resort currently houses 246 refugees. Roughly as many live in two neighboring temporary accommodation centers. All fled shelling in Russia’s border regions or destroyed towns and villages in the Donetsk, Luhansk, and Kharkiv regions. Some are still afraid to return home; many simply have no home to return to.
At the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the Russian army captured part of the Kharkiv region, including Izium, Kupiansk, and Vovchansk. But by September 2022, during Ukraine’s counteroffensive, Russian forces had retreated — or, as the center’s residents cautiously put it, “redeployed.”
The number of cases in Ukraine involving collaboration with Russian forces is growing: Even residents of formerly occupied territories who worked as cleaners or building attendants and agreed to cooperate with Russian authorities are going on trial. Some refugees at the Tula center say they worked as teachers or distributed humanitarian aid, then found themselves on lists of “collaborators” in Ukrainian Telegram channels.
Tatyana worked on the railroad for many years. “I worked the switchboard: They moved railcars back and forth. And we were basically working with the Russian military,” she says. When Ukrainian forces entered Kupiansk, Tatyana and her husband were attending a funeral in another city. After learning that Kupiansk was back under Ukrainian control, they fled to Russia with just the clothes they were wearing and their passports.
“We supported the Russians so much — you wouldn’t believe it. But after living here for four years… It’s not exactly disappointment, but it hurts. It hurts that nobody wants us. Wherever you go, they tell you, ‘You’re one of us.’ And then it turns out we’re not,” Tatyana says with a sigh.
The Tula regional authorities are promising to reimburse rental expenses for families with three or more children and refugees receiving old-age pensions. People living alone will receive up to 20,000 rubles, and families up to 30,000.
But to apply for the payments, refugees need a rental agreement. Finding a landlord willing to sign a formal lease, pay taxes on the rental income, and then wait while local authorities review the tenants’ application is not easy.
Residents say they know of cases in which assistance was denied without justification: “There’s simply no money in the budget.” Many residents are also older people living alone who have never rented a home themselves.
Anyone who moved into a temporary accommodation center after July 1, 2025, is ineligible for the payments. The refugees estimate that one in five residents falls into that category. Some arrived as recently as September 2026. They are now being asked to sign an agreement to leave the center by April 1, 2027.
Marina, 50, fled the town of Yampil in the Donetsk region with her husband, Sergei, and their 15-year-old daughter, Daryna. They spent three and a half years living in a dugout Sergei had built under a shed. Daryna suffered a mild concussion when a drone struck the shelter.
Marina did not want to leave for Ukrainian-held territory. “Yes, I speak Ukrainian, and so does my daughter. But I’m Russian. I wasn’t going to live there looking over my shoulder and letting people push me around. [In a country] where they send men off as cannon fodder,” she says.
The family did not escape the combat zone until February 2026 and arrived at the temporary accommodation center in April. Sergei now works at the neighboring hotel complex, while Marina is currently unable to work because of health problems. In six months in Russia, the family has saved just 35,000 rubles — not enough to rent a home or move elsewhere. They do not even have warm clothes.
Marina is angry at indifferent officials who “sneer” when they see her Ukrainian documents. She emphasizes that she and her parents are Russian, and that she was desperate to get to Russia. But so far, she has been unable to obtain any compensation. “It hurts to spend all those years hiding from the Nazis, lose your health, have your daughter miss out on her childhood — and end up like this,” she says with a sigh.
Residents are certain it will be hard to find a landlord willing to arrange temporary residence registration for them. Without permanent registration in their passports, they believe it will be almost impossible.
The refugees insist that when they moved in, they were promised they could stay until the war ended. Still, those whose homes were destroyed would like to leave — if they received compensation to rebuild.
‘They came to our homes and destroyed everything’
Temporary accommodation centers in other regions remain open. Residents of the Tula centers have already learned that some even have vacancies. But they need authorization from the regional administrations to move in and have not received it.
Refugees who have received Russian passports do not understand why they face contempt from officials, bureaucratic hurdles, and scrutiny from the security services in their new homeland, which claimed the places they lived as its own.
“They [the officials] say: We want you to integrate into the Russian Federation. When did the DPR and LPR become part of the Russian Federation? When Putin signed the law in 2022. So we’re already integrated! I understand that every country has its own laws, and I accept that. But people were desperate to come here. They were desperate to come home,” says a refugee from the Donetsk region.
Balloons are taped to the walls of Anna’s room. She fled Kupiansk. The family recently celebrated her daughter Rita’s 12th birthday, then her mother Irina’s 62nd. For both, it was their fourth birthday away from home.
The Russian army entered Kupiansk without a fight in the first days of the invasion. Anna lived near a bridge that was repeatedly shelled. The family spent all of March in the basement.
During that time, Anna developed anemia and thyroid problems — she was later diagnosed with hypothyroidism. Rita also began getting sick. Rumors were circulating in Kupiansk that Russia would not hold the city and fierce fighting would soon break out. In April 2022, the family decided to leave.
Anna says she was in such a hurry that she did not even take her daughter’s birth certificate, and Rita was so nervous at border control that she forgot her mother’s name. But the border guards let them through: The photo gallery on Anna’s phone was full of pictures of Rita, so the guards believed them.
The family spent the next eight months in Belgorod. Without residence registration, Anna and Irina could not get passports, and schools would not enroll Rita. Eventually, Anna found a job and met a colleague who helped them arrange temporary registration. Other refugees had to pay for it: At the time, six months of temporary registration in Belgorod cost 9,000 rubles, Anna says.
The family’s life was starting to improve, but in late 2022, a Ukrainian missile hit a neighboring house. “It sliced the roof clean off, like a knife through butter,” Anna says. After that, the family decided to move to Voronezh.
In 2023, Irina was diagnosed with breast cancer, and the family was offered a place at a temporary accommodation center in the Tula region. Anna’s brother Andrei and his family were already living at another center in Tula.
Anna says he stayed in Kupiansk until September 2022 and “left the city in a tank.” Andrei was at work across the river when the bridge connecting the two parts of the city was destroyed. Ukrainian forces entered the area where his wife and their 1-year-old child were still at home. Andrei did not want to leave his family behind, but Anna says the Russian soldiers insisted: “Do you want to live? Then come on, [get in].” In November, Andrei’s wife and child managed to leave, traveling through Ukraine and Europe to reach Russia.
Before the war, Anna and Andrei’s family had two houses in a neighborhood of detached homes. Both are now destroyed.
In Russia, Irina underwent two operations and needed care. Meanwhile, Rita was bullied at school, so Anna switched her to a paid online school. Anna left her job to care for her mother and raise her daughter. The family now lives entirely on Irina’s pension and a child benefit — just 34,000 rubles. Anna says almost half goes toward schooling.
They were barely getting by on that money until the Tula regional authorities decided to evict the refugees. Only Irina can stay at the resort: She has a Group II disability classification.
To keep his family, which now has a second child, from ending up on the street, Anna’s brother Andrei bought an apartment with a mortgage. He used the government’s maternity capital benefit for the down payment. Anna says there was no money left for furniture, and the family is sleeping on the floor for now. The terms of his loan prevent Andrei from registering his mother and sister at his apartment.
Anna now uses the printer she bought for Rita’s schoolwork to print letters, complaints, and applications to help refugees from the Kharkiv region who have spent four years in Russia without official recognition as forcibly displaced people or compensation for their destroyed homes.
“Social services say, ‘You’ve been sitting here for four years. You should’ve saved up for an apartment.’ They also say, ‘We started from scratch too!’ But we didn’t choose to be in this situation, having to start over from scratch. They came to our homes and destroyed everything!” Anna says angrily.
‘We’ve been here all this time, and we’ll go home and get killed’
Vera Nikolayevna, 72, moved to the center from the Kursk region. She is shy about speaking to journalists: She feels others have it worse and that she should not complain.
Her village is about 60 kilometers (37 miles) from the border. She says the “incredibly loud explosions” began in the first days of the war. But Vera Nikolayevna did not consider leaving until the summer of 2023, when, she says, Ukrainian saboteurs shot up a column of Russian troops 20 kilometers (12 miles) from her home. Bereg could not confirm this account.
Her 48-year-old daughter, Olga, lived in a neighboring village and immediately drove over to her mother’s house. They packed in a hurry. Later, Olga and Vera Nikolayevna told neighbors they could take their stock of canned food — they no longer expected to return.
Vera Nikolayevna and Olga have lived at the center ever since. Vera Nikolayevna’s room is tidy, with few possessions. Photographs of relatives hang on the wall above her bed — she has three daughters and three grandchildren.
In one photograph, a young man in military dress uniform adjusts a young woman’s blond curls. Vera Nikolayevna’s grandson serves in Astrakhan. He was recently sent on a temporary assignment near Kaluga to “shoot down drones.” She speaks proudly of him and Olga. Her daughter received a “medal for supporting the special military operation”: While working at a kindergarten near the border, she spent her evenings mending soldiers’ uniforms.
Vera Nikolayevna’s house has not been destroyed, but she has been back only once since leaving, in 2025. She decided to stay, but on the very first night, an explosion woke her. “It wasn’t just a bang — I can’t even describe it. I thought the roof was gone, that everything had been blown away. We sat there and couldn’t tell whether we were alive or dead. We didn’t turn on the lights. We didn’t breathe,” she says.
In the morning, she learned that Ukrainian forces had attacked a place where Russian soldiers were sheltering. The missiles left craters and damaged neighboring houses, and Vera Nikolayevna changed her mind about staying in the village. “There are explosions and gunfire, and drones are flying around. We’ve been here all this time, and we’ll go home and get killed,” she says.
Vera Nikolayevna receives a pension of 20,000 rubles. Olga works every other day and is paying off a loan. Despite Olga’s disability, the family is not entitled to stay at the center: She has a Group III classification, while only people with Group I or II classifications are allowed to remain.
Vera Nikolayevna calculates that even with rental assistance, she and her daughter will not have enough money to live on. “The main thing is for them to let us stay here,” she says. “At least until spring. Surely the special military operation will be over by spring?”
‘We just believed in Russia, believed the words “We don’t abandon our own”’
Wagner fighters took Alina, her mother Olga, and her father Nikolai out of Soledar, a city in the Bakhmut district of the Donetsk region. The fighters forbade the refugees from looking out the windows of the combat vehicle, which was covered in camouflage netting, so they would not see anything they were not meant to see.
By early January 2023, when the private military company entered the city, Soledar had suffered extensive damage. Alina had already spent six months sleeping on the floor in the hallway; the family cooked over fires in the courtyard. Her grandmother died of cardiac arrest around that time, and they buried her amid the shelling.
Ukrainian forces repeatedly offered to evacuate the family, but they refused. Nikolai turned 58 in 2022 and was still eligible for conscription. He had worked as a miner for almost his entire life, Alina’s mother was a senior laboratory technician, and Alina managed facilities at a company. The family loved their city, lived comfortably, and did not want to lose everything they had built up.
Olga, Alina, and Nikolai were waiting for Russian forces to arrive. “We just believed in Russia, believed the words ‘We don’t abandon our own.’ Those exact words,” Alina says.
Alina and her parents did not want to leave Soledar with the Wagner fighters either. The family even offered to sign a statement accepting responsibility for their own lives, but the fighters would not listen and would not let them leave the basement to collect belongings from home. Fortunately, Alina always carried a backpack with their documents, and they were allowed to take their cat, Maruska.
Alina and Olga both recall the soldiers’ assurances: “Don’t worry, everything will be fine. Russia will welcome you there and give you everything. A shower, clothes, shoes, passports — they’ll take care of everything.” The family left Soledar confident they would be welcomed in Russia.
Disappointment came quickly. In Pervomaisk, a city 35 kilometers (22 miles) from Soledar, the evacuees were given a sack of sugar and flour for food. In Torez, 80 kilometers (50 miles) from Soledar, the local authorities did not welcome the displaced people either. “And that’s when we realized: Nobody wants us,” Olga says.
Despite his years of work as a miner, Nikolai was awarded a 10,000-ruble pension in Russia. Alina found work at a café in Torez, while her parents went to the Vladimir region to earn money. Her father died there of cardiac arrest in 2024. Olga returned to her daughter.
By June 2025, the temporary accommodation center in Torez had closed, and the women moved to the Tula region. Both started working and saving money. Alina developed rheumatoid arthritis. In the DPR, she was given expensive steroid medication, but her supply is running out. To receive the medication in Russia, she needs to have her disability officially recognized, which requires medical examinations she must pay for.
The women are upset that Russia has not welcomed people it claims as its own. Alina has changed jobs several times, and at every workplace, colleagues called her “khokhlushka,” an anti-Ukrainian slur. Sometimes people she spoke with blamed her and all of Donbas for starting the war.
Alina hopes they will be allowed to stay at the center at least until spring so they have time to save enough to rent a home in the Tula region. If that does not happen, Alina and Olga plan to move to Svitlodarsk, a city 35 kilometers (22 miles) from Soledar. Svitlodarsk is being shelled, but rent there is cheap.
Alina and Olga take turns showing a video from an unidentified Ukrainian Telegram channel. It shows part of a residential building in Soledar collapsing after a strike. Their apartment was in that very building.
Olga cries. She does not have a single photograph of her loved ones left. In a choked voice, she says: “We understand that nobody wants us. They took our lives away. Our bodies are still here, but our lives are gone.”
* * *
On October 5, regional officials visited the center. They offered to let the refugees continue living there if they paid. They did not give exact prices but said food would cost 300 rubles a day.
The residents who spoke with Bereg fear that staying at the center will cost about as much as renting a home in the Tula region. They do not have that kind of money.

Ukraine accuses SpaceX of restricting Starlink access for military drones
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
00:56:44 EEST
06:56:44 KST

Ukraine has accused SpaceX of disrupting military drone operations through restrictions on Starlink satellite communications, as President Volodymyr Zelenskyy criticised Washington over its support for Kyiv. SpaceX chief executive Elon Musk denied responsibility for the restrictions, saying the US government controls the military satellite network and its operating limits.
Ukrainian military officials reported that terminals connected to Starshield, SpaceX's military communications service, began losing connectivity on Tuesday night when travelling above 160 kilometres per hour.
Add Helsinki Times as a preferred source on Google (opens Google in a new tab)
The restrictions affected Ukrainian attack drones and interceptors used to defend cities against Russian aerial assaults.
Presidential adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov said Ukrainian forces received no advance warning, resulting in disrupted missions.
"Our defence forces did not receive a warning about this limitation, and this led to the disruption of several missions," Beskrestnov wrote on Telegram.
A Ukrainian Defence Ministry source told Reuters that some military units experienced connection failures at speeds below the reported threshold.
Musk responded on X that the restrictions were not SpaceX's decision.
"Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," he wrote.
Ukraine's former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov reported on Wednesday evening that services had been partially restored. He called for the removal of all speed restrictions.
The disruption coincided with Russian missile and drone strikes against Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure.
Ukrainian authorities reported that approximately 600,000 people lost electricity following attacks on Kyiv, Kharkiv and surrounding areas.
Russia's Defence Ministry confirmed strikes against six power plants, while Zelenskyy said 30 energy facilities had suffered damage.
Six people were killed in Lutsk, western Ukraine, according to regional authorities. In Kyiv, officials reported two deaths and 21 injuries at a residential building struck during the bombardment.
Zelenskyy accused Russia of disregarding US President Donald Trump's proposed ceasefire on energy infrastructure.
Speaking to Piers Morgan during a visit to London, Zelenskyy also expressed frustration with Washington's approach to the war.
"It's painful when President Trump chooses one side, not our side," he said.
Asked whether he felt betrayed by Trump, Zelenskyy replied: "Really, yes," adding that the situation involved more than his personal feelings.
The Ukrainian president warned that restrictions on satellite communications would result in further casualties.
"This decision will bring a lot of human losses," he said.
Relations between Washington and Kyiv have deteriorated following Trump's decision to ease restrictions on Russian diesel purchases and his demands that Ukraine stop attacking Russian oil refineries.
The Financial Times reported, citing unnamed European officials, that Washington had threatened to restrict intelligence sharing unless Kyiv suspended those strikes.
Ukrainian officials also reported receiving no advance warnings from Western partners before Russian missile attacks for two consecutive days. Trump denied that Washington had stopped sharing intelligence.
Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski, whose government finances Ukrainian Starlink subscriptions, questioned Musk's involvement.
"Are you playing politics with your products again?" Sikorski wrote on X.
During Zelenskyy's visit to London, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham pledged continued military assistance, including £45 million in surface-to-air missiles, with £10 million earmarked for accelerated delivery.
Britain also committed to examining further sanctions against Russia and measures to accelerate weapons supplies.

Ebola detected in Kenya for the first time in history: one infected person has died
Kyiv • UNN
Kenya has confirmed its first two cases of Ebola: one patient has died, while the other has been isolated. In neighboring Congo, the outbreak has claimed the lives of nearly half of those infected.
Kenya has confirmed the first two cases of Ebola infection in the country's history. One of the patients died, while the other was placed in quarantine. Meanwhile, a large-scale outbreak of the disease is ongoing in neighboring Democratic Republic of the Congo. Finnish outlet Yle reports this, citing AFP, writes UNN.
Details
The first infected person was a man who lived in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. He died last week in Kenya. Later, doctors detected the virus in his close relative.
The second patient was isolated immediately after symptoms appeared. According to Kenya's Ministry of Health, no new cases of infection have been detected so far; however, specialists continue to identify everyone who may have been in contact with the infected people.
Almost half of those infected have died of Ebola in the Congo
The outbreak, which began in May 2026, has most severely affected the eastern regions of the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
According to local authorities, more than 9,000 cases of Ebola infection have already been confirmed in the country. Approximately half of those infected have died.
Cases of the disease have also been recorded in Uganda, which borders both the Congo and Kenya. At least two deaths are known to have occurred there.

The Armed Forces of Ukraine explained how restrictions on Starlink&apos;s operation are already affecting the performance of combat missions
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
00:49:09 EEST
06:49:09 KST

The Armed Forces of Ukraine explained how restrictions on Starlink's operation are already affecting the performance of combat missions
Kyiv • UNN
SpaceX has restricted the speed of Starshield terminals, causing drones to lose connection in flight. The Ministry of Defense has appealed to the United States, SpaceX, and NATO.
On the night of October 14, SpaceX imposed restrictions without warning on the Starshield military satellite communications system, causing Ukrainian drones to begin losing connectivity during flights. Some Ukrainian Armed Forces units have already had to cancel some combat missions. Defense Express reports this, citing sources in the military and Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense, UNN writes.
Details
According to the publication, SpaceX set a speed limit for Starshield terminals at 160 km/h. After this threshold is exceeded, the terminal loses connectivity. At the same time, the military is recording disruptions even at significantly lower speeds—approximately 72 to 161 km/h.
In particular, when drones fly at speeds of 110–120 km/h, the connection may disappear for 10–20 seconds. Although the drones continue moving, such interruptions significantly complicate controlling them.
The restrictions threaten attack drones and interceptors
The greatest problems arise with high-speed drones, in particular Middle Strike-type drones, which need to reach high speed immediately after launch. Due to the unstable connection, some aircraft may lose the ability to carry out their missions.
The restrictions have also affected interceptor drones. At the same time, the forced reduction in flight speed makes Ukrainian UAVs more vulnerable to Russian countermeasures.
According to a Defense Express source, on October 14 alone, one of the unmanned systems units was forced to cancel some missions because of problems with Starlink.
Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense confirmed to journalists that the restrictions had been introduced and said it was already in contact with the United States, SpaceX, and NATO partners. The American company has so far provided no official explanations for the reasons behind the changes.

HRW says 31 executed by eastern Libya authorities
Unknown

Breadcrumb
HRW says 31 executed by eastern Libya authorities
The NGO Human Rights Watch said Wednesday that military authorities in eastern Libya executed at least 31 people earlier this year, the first reported death sentences to be carried out in the country since 2010, according to the group.
Forces under the control of military leader Khalifa Haftar and his clan executed the people between late August and September 10 "following grossly unfair military trials", HRW said in a statement, adding another 50 people in detention were "at imminent risk of execution".
Libya has struggled to regain stability since former ruler Muammar Gaddafi was toppled and killed in 2011, and the country remains divided between the Haftars in the east and a UN-recognised government in the west.
Haftar's forces "are putting people to death after secret trials built on confessions allegedly extracted through torture, in courts that Libya's own Supreme Court has said should not be trying civilians", said Bassam Khawaja, HRW's deputy Middle East and North Africa director.
He called on the international community to pressure the military authorities to halt any future executions.
Khawaja said the country had gone more than 15 years without an execution, but the eastern authorities "shattered that moratorium in a matter of weeks".
"The lives of at least 50 more people now depend on whether Haftar's forces, and the governments that back them, choose to stop this," he added.
HRW said the detainees were being held in a prison about 100 kilometres east of Benghazi.
It is largely under military control and outside the jurisdiction of the judicial authorities, and is frequently accused of human rights violations, torture and ill-treatment.
The death penalty is still in force in Libya for the crimes of murder, terrorism and offences against state security, though in recent years sentences have not been carried out.

Ukraine deposits seeds in Norway's Arctic vault for 1st time since 2022
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:43:41 CST
06:43:41 KST

OSLO, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- Ukraine has deposited 773 seed samples in the Svalbard Global Seed Vault in Norway's Arctic archipelago, marking its first contribution to the facility since the Russia-Ukraine conflict broke out in 2022, the Norwegian government said Wednesday.
The deposit on Tuesday was part of an international effort that delivered more than 16,000 seed samples from 21 genebanks to the vault, according to a statement from Norway's Ministry of Agriculture and Food.
The latest Ukrainian deposit included samples of buckwheat and other crops, providing an additional safeguard for the country's agricultural genetic resources.
Norwegian Minister of Agriculture and Food Nils Kristen Sandtroen said the latest deposit demonstrated the importance of international cooperation in protecting global crop diversity.
Six international agricultural research genebanks under CGIAR contributed a total of 8,917 samples, while Italy's Council for Agricultural Research and Economics made its first deposit, including historic wheat and rice varieties.
Established by the Norwegian government in 2008, the Svalbard Global Seed Vault provides free long-term storage for backup copies of seed collections from genebanks around the world.
Located inside a mountain on the island of Spitsbergen, the vault now holds more than 1.4 million seed samples belonging to over 130 genebanks, making it the world's largest secure repository of cultivated crop diversity.
The facility is funded by the Norwegian government and operated in partnership with the Nordic Genetic Resource Center (NordGen) and the Global Crop Diversity Trust. ■

Archaeologists uncover 23 Roman-era graves in southern BiH
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:43:39 CST
06:43:39 KST

SARAJEVO, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- Archaeologists have uncovered 23 graves dating back to the fourth century at a Roman-era burial site near Livno in southern Bosnia and Herzegovina (BiH), shedding light on burial customs during the late Roman Empire, local news agency FENA reported on Wednesday.
The excavations at the Stitic site in Suhaca, near Livno, have unearthed rare intact ceramic vessels, glass fragments, jewelry, clothing accessories and a coin bearing the image of Roman Emperor Constantine I.
Archaeologist Marija Maric Bakovic, who participated in the excavations, said the site was the oldest cemetery in the Livno area to undergo systematic excavation, with graves preserved in their original positions.
The findings offer insight into burial customs and beliefs during the period. Ceramic vessels and coins were placed in graves as offerings, while some burials contained as many as three vessels. The significance of this practice remains unclear.
Researchers have also found evidence of earlier cremation practices, indicating a transition to the burial of uncremated bodies, as seen in the fourth-century graves at the site.
Further excavations are planned for next year. ■

====================================================================================================

Feature: Made-in-China toy ball finds place in Finland's beloved "baby box"
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:43:27 CST
06:43:27 KST

HELSINKI, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- Among the tiny clothes, blankets and other essentials packed into Finland's traditional "baby box" for newborns, a soft little ball makes its debut this year. The colorful ball decorated with pictures of animals and fruits has become part of a cherished Finnish welfare package.
Finland's Social Insurance Institution, known as Kela, announced Wednesday that it had begun distributing the 2026 maternity package, which for the first time includes a toy ball made in China.
The package contains 52 items, ranging from baby clothes and bedding to everyday necessities, following an increase in the maternity grant from 170 euros to 210 euros (189.62-234.24 U.S. dollars). Even the cardboard box itself can serve as a baby's first bed.
A SMALL BALL WITH A BIG ROLE
Ten centimeters in diameter, the ball is manufactured in China under license from U.S. toy brand Fisher-Price and imported by Finnish company Toyrock Group, according to Kela.
Priced at around two euros (2.23 dollars), the ball was selected through Kela's competitive public procurement process. According to Finnish news agency STT, Kela rated the winning product as having very high quality, citing its clear, appealing patterns and well-made seams.
The ball may be simple, but its usefulness grows with the child.
Heidi Virrasoja-Prami, marketing and communications coordinator at Toyrock, told STT that even very young babies could enjoy its colorful patterns and practice grasping its soft fabric surface. As they grow older, children can roll it, throw it, or play with their siblings. A rolling ball may even encourage a baby to start moving after it, she explained.
"The beauty of the ball is that it is a really long-lasting toy," Virrasoja-Prami said.
According to earlier procurement reports, Kela plans to purchase balls for approximately 30,000 maternity packages.
A TRADITION THAT SPANS GENERATIONS
Finland's maternity package has a history dating back nearly nine decades. First introduced in 1938 to support low-income mothers, the maternity grant was extended to all mothers in 1949. Over time, the package has become a beloved national tradition, symbolizing the country's commitment to giving every child a good start in life.
Families can choose between the maternity package and a cash grant, with the box remaining especially popular among first-time parents.
Its contents change each year to reflect evolving childcare needs and sustainability considerations. This year's edition also features a peach-colored, space-themed box design called "Imagining the Future."
According to Kela, the new ball is funded through the government's "Finland on the Move" program, which aims to encourage physical activity across all age groups.
Kela specialist Veera Petaja said the ball was intended to promote interaction between babies and parents and encourage them to be physically active together.
The package also reflects an emphasis on sustainability and reuse, encouraging families to give baby products a second life. "When your baby no longer needs the items in the maternity package, you can pass them on," Petaja said in Wednesday's announcement.
MADE-IN-CHINA PRODUCTS HELP NEW FINNISH PARENTS
The little ball is not the only Chinese-made item in this year's parent kit.
According to Kela's official product list, several other essentials, including baby clothes, insulated mittens and booties, and a snowsuit that doubles as a sleeping bag, are also manufactured in China.
Supplied by different companies, these products have found their way into the welfare package that Finnish families have treasured for generations.
As the newest baby boxes arrive at Finnish homes, the little ball made in China is ready for a new journey - from catching a newborn's attention to becoming a playmate as the child learns to grasp, roll and chase.
For Arja Saakslahti, an associate professor of physical education at the University of Jyvaskyla, the significance of adding a ball to the maternity package goes beyond encouraging physical activity.
In an article published on the university's website, she stressed that the simple toy also sends an important message to parents: spend time with their babies and encourage interaction through play.
Perhaps that is where the little ball's greatest value lies. Having traveled thousands of kilometers from China to Finland, it helps bring parents and children closer, adding moments of joy and connection to everyday family life. ■

Costa Rica opens mega-prison as organized crime fight intensifies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

06:41:17 KST

Costa Rica opens mega-prison as organized crime fight intensifies
SAN JOSE, Oct 14 - Costa Rica inaugurated a maximum-security prison on Wednesday as it stepped up its fight against organized crime after a surge in killings in what was long one of Latin America's safest countries.
President Laura Fernandez opened the High-Containment Center Against Organized Crime, or CACCO, a prison modeled on El Salvador's mega-prison and a key element of Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele's anti-gang crackdown. The facility near the capital of San Jose has a capacity for 5,100 inmates, roughly 20% of the nation's current prison population.
Costa Rica recorded an all-time high of 905 homicides in 2023, according to judicial data. Killings eased only slightly to 876 in 2024 and 873 in 2025, remaining well above earlier levels. Authorities have said most murders are linked to disputes among criminal groups over drug trafficking routes and local markets.
"The CACCO will force criminals to face a new model—a tough-on-crime model. Costa Rica will become a global benchmark for prison security," Fernandez said during the inauguration ceremony.
The president also announced a visit to El Salvador on Friday.
Bukele's crackdown is widely credited with sharply reducing gang violence in El Salvador, but rights groups say it has also brought mass arbitrary detentions, due process violations and an erosion of democratic safeguards.
Fernandez said the new prison's impact would depend in part on the judiciary securing more convictions. Her government has clashed with judicial authorities over crime policy and budget cuts, while judges and prosecutors have warned against pressure on democratic checks and balances.
Justice Minister Gabriel Aguilar has presented CACCO as part of a broader effort to reassert state control over the prison system, which he says has been infiltrated by organized crime. The first transfers to the prison will take place at the end of October.
Fernandez recently told Reuters that greater US security presence would help Costa Rica confront drug trafficking and organized crime, although current coordination remains focused on patrols, investigations and extradition efforts. REUTERS

Colombia opposition groups launch protest against de la Espriella’s cuts

Colombia opposition groups launch protest against de la Espriella’s cuts
Former left-wing President Gustavo Petro joined thousands of demonstrators in Bogota in a march against austerity, restored Israel ties.
A coalition of opposition parties, trade unions, indigenous groups and social movements has protested in Colombia against a series of economic and security policies advanced under right-wing President Abelardo de la Espriella.
Thousands marched in major cities including the capital Bogota on Wednesday, the first day of a nationwide campaign led by the country’s former left-wing President Gustavo Petro.
Under Petro, Colombia expanded access to public universities, increased the minimum wage and improved labour protections for workers.
Opposition groups say many of those reforms are now under threat, as de la Espriella’s government embraces cuts to government programmes.
Colombia’s Congress has until Tuesday to approve its 2027 fiscal year budget. But as part of the new administration’s austerity measures, allies of de la Espriella are advancing proposals to reduce government spending.
De la Espriella has also pledged to turn Colombia away from his predecessor’s left-wing leanings and towards more free-market policies aligned with those of United States President Donald Trump.
The government issued new rules for police ahead of the protests, handing expanded powers to law enforcement to more quickly deal with protesters who vandalise public property or disrupt access to essential services.
“The right to protest is respected, but there is no right to destroy, attack the security forces, assault others or sow chaos,” de la Espriella said in a social media statement announcing the decree.
He added that “violence, vandalism and blockades that trample on the rights of millions of citizens will not be tolerated”.
Indigenous communities and political groups in rural parts of the country sometimes block roads as part of their protests, with impediments to traffic sometimes lasting weeks.
But critics have pointed out that the protests this week have been largely peaceful.
Many chanted “It will fall”, a reference to the perceived failure of de la Espriella’s government.
A former defence lawyer and millionaire businessman, de la Espriella was a political newcomer when he ran for the presidency this year on a far-right ticket.
He was elected in a June runoff race by a narrow margin. He campaigned on a hardline platform to address crime, immigration and the economy, including proposals to expel millions of migrants from Colombia and shrink the size of the government.
De la Espriella also pledged to backtrack on reforms made under Petro, Colombia’s first left-wing president. He took office in August.
A former left-wing fighter-turned-politician, Petro took part in protests on Wednesday. He was not eligible for re-election in this year’s presidential race; Colombian law currently caps presidents at a single term.
He wrote on social media that the mobilisations were a wake-up call “two months into the start of a tyrannical and imposed government”.
Protesters also expressed concerns about cuts to labour protections and healthcare under the new administration.
“I feel like we have no guarantees and that the little we did obtain … we’re about to lose,” teacher Ester Guerra, 32, told the news outlet AFP in Bogota.
Some demonstrators also took issue with the new administration’s overtures towards Israel. Several carried Palestinian flags, in a sign of solidarity.
On Wednesday, de la Espriella’s government opened a Colombian embassy in Jerusalem, a controversial move as Israel and Palestine have both claimed parts of the city.
Petro had been a staunch supporter of Palestine and had cut relations with Israel over its genocidal war against Gaza. But de la Espriella has moved to restore the severed ties since taking office.
That struck protesters like Jimena Rodriguez, a 20-year-old student, as an effort to ignore accusations of Israeli abuses against Palestinians.
Several noted that de la Espriella’s actions towards Israel mirrored Trump’s, who moved the US embassy to Jerusalem during his first term in 2018.
President de la Espriella “just wants to hand the country over to the United States, to Israel,” Rodriguez said. “I feel dark times are coming.”

Sanctions are permanent, until Washington decides otherwise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
21:33:59 UTC
06:33:59 KST

Sanctions are permanent, until Washington decides otherwise
The agreement to supply Russian diesel fuel to the United States has made a considerable political impact, and it comes amid another escalation of the Ukraine conflict during which both sides have been exchanging large-scale missile and drone strikes.
Meanwhile, the European Union has approved its 22nd package of sanctions against Russia, while Washington has adopted another round of punitive measures under the so-called Hellish Sanctions Act.
Yet against this backdrop, the US Treasury has issued a general license authorizing transactions involving the sale, delivery, unloading and import of Russian diesel fuel until April 2027, which, at first glance, appears extraordinary.
In reality, however, such exemptions are a familiar feature of American sanctions policy as they illustrate a fundamental paradox of the US system: exceptionally severe restrictions coexist with considerable flexibility when Washington’s own interests are at stake.
On one hand, sanctions against Russia, particularly those targeting its energy sector, have become increasingly entrenched, and the latest legislation makes their removal considerably more difficult, adding to an extensive framework of federal laws, presidential orders and administrative regulations accumulated over recent years.
On the other hand, the American executive retains substantial powers to authorize exceptions, meaning even the harshest sanctions need not prevent transactions that Washington considers necessary.
The latest exemption is particularly revealing because the administration didn’t need to invoke the waiver provisions contained in the new legislation, given that Section 115 of the Lindsey Graham Act, for example, permits exemptions provided the administration submits a written justification to Congress, so instead, the Treasury employed a much simpler mechanism.
Last week, Bradley Smith, director of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), signed a general license permitting the diesel transactions. Formally, therefore, the decision was taken not by President Donald Trump, or even by the Treasury secretary, but by a specialized department within the department.
There’s nothing unusual about this procedure. Under the sanctions program targeting what Washington calls Russia’s “malicious activities,” more than 100 general licenses have been issued covering a wide range of transactions, meaning another license is hardly a sensation.
Nor should it be mistaken for the lifting of sanctions because general licenses typically have limited validity and can be revoked before their expiry and a change in the political climate, a shift in Washington’s priorities, or an influx of imported diesel into the American market could be sufficient grounds for withdrawing the exemption.
There are precedents for licenses remaining in force for years. During the improvement in US-Belarusian relations in the 2010s, several major Belarusian enterprises benefited from exemptions that effectively suspended certain restrictions, but when relations deteriorated again in the early 2020s, those licenses were withdrawn.
In other cases, licenses serve the entirely technical purpose of allowing companies to complete transactions or wind down existing operations without violating sanctions, which means the distinction between the political significance of the Russian diesel agreement and its legal substance is therefore essential.
No sanctions have been lifted and Washington has merely employed an established administrative mechanism that can be reversed at any moment.
Nevertheless, the episode demonstrates something important about American sanctions policy in that even as Congress seeks to make restrictions against Russia increasingly permanent, the executive branch retains considerable room for maneuver.
The US can impose unprecedented economic restrictions while simultaneously creating exceptions whenever its interests demand them.
The legal machinery is already in place, but what ultimately determines how it is used is political will.
This article was first published by Kommersant, and was translated and edited by the RT team

The Prime Minister of Armenia proposed exchanging territories with Azerbaijan to finally settle the long-running conflict
Kyiv • UNN
The Prime Minister of Armenia proposed an equal exchange of land to eliminate the enclaves. He also called for opening routes and abandoning claims.
Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan proposed that Azerbaijan carry out an equal exchange of territories to resolve the issue of enclaves and remove one of the obstacles to peace between the countries. He said this in his address, UNN reports.
Details
Under Pashinyan's proposal, the two states could exchange plots of land of equal size. This would eliminate enclaves—territories that belong to one country but are surrounded on all sides by another.
In addition, the Armenian prime minister called for transport routes and communications between the countries to be opened, as well as for a final renunciation of mutual territorial claims.
Why Armenia and Azerbaijan have been in conflict for decades
The main cause of the confrontation was Nagorno-Karabakh—an internationally recognized part of Azerbaijan that was predominantly populated by ethnic Armenians until the events of 2023. In the late 1980s, the dispute over the region escalated into an armed conflict and, after the collapse of the Soviet Union, into a full-scale war.
In the 1990s, Armenian forces established control over Nagorno-Karabakh and adjacent Azerbaijani districts. During the 2020 war, Azerbaijan regained a significant portion of these territories, and in September 2023 it restored control over all of Karabakh. After that, more than 100,000 ethnic Armenians left the region.
Despite the end of hostilities in Karabakh, disputes over borders, enclaves, and transport links remained between the states. Pashinyan proposes resolving these issues through a territorial exchange and mutual recognition of sovereignty.

Bars, clubs and restaurants will offer up to 100,000 jobs to young people not in employment, education or training (Neet) over the next three years in an effort to give them a first step on the ladder into work.
The move comes before the publication of a report on Neets by the former health secretary Alan Milburn, who has warned that the number of young people not in work or education in the UK could rise to 1.25 million over the next five years unless ministers intervene.
His full review into Britain’s crisis in youth unemployment, including recommendations to the government about how to tackle the crisis, is expected soon after the autumn budget on 28 October.
Working with the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP), hospitality businesses including the restaurant chains Wagamama, Nando’s and Burger King, the hotel chain Premier Inn and pub chains including Fuller’s and Mitchells & Butlers will offer Neets aged 18 to 24 placements of up to four weeks to gain “the skills and confidence needed to take their first step into work”.
The initiative, which will be launched by Andy Burnham during a visit to a hospitality venue on Thursday, comes after the DWP announced a similar scheme for retailers including Marks & Spencer, Asda, Pets at Home and the John Lewis Partnership last month.
The work and pensions secretary, Pat McFadden, said the scheme would help young people “get their first step on the ladder” and build their careers. “With the UK employment rate now the second highest in the G7, this will unlock 100,000 jobs and connect young people with employers ready to take them on and help them build a brighter future,” he said.
Lucy Powell, the education secretary, is expected to announce a review of school exclusion changes, after research showed that students who are persistently absent from school are nearly four times more likely to end up unemployed and not in education or training.
A consultation will gather views on measures to support students at risk of exclusion, improve integration into the classroom and help children stay engaged in the classroom.
Powell said: “Absence and exclusion are too often a path to disengagement, with increased risks of becoming Neet. Too many young people who fall out of education risk being permanently left on the sidelines of work and opportunity.”
Milburn has signalled that Britain’s benefits system should be overhauled, alongside measures to boost job support, training and apprenticeships. Ministers are understood to be considering sweeping changes to the welfare system, including scrapping a critical disability benefit for under-25s and replacing it with a multibillion-pound package of support to get into work.
Milburn has previously argued that a national apprenticeship readiness scheme should be introduced in England to close the gap for young people between leaving school and starting work.
The chancellor, John Healey, has indicated a readiness to curtail the government’s rising benefits bill, while McFadden has said there is a moral and economic case to shake up the welfare system, as the war in the Middle East rattles the public finances.
The Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, has made demands for cuts to welfare a central plank of her attacks on the government, telling Burnham in prime minister’s questions (PMQs) on Wednesday that he should cut welfare to fund higher defence spending.
But ministers will be wary of going head to head with Labour MPs, and will hope to avoid a repeat of the welfare rebellion that forced Keir Starmer and Rachel Reeves into an embarrassing and costly U-turn.

How the EU can protect the court from U.S. sanctions
The blocking statute allows the European Union to counter the effects of foreign sanctions on its territory. Halevy warned that the flow of goods into the Gaza Strip would drop by 50%, adding: "Hamas will try to blame Israel."

According to the statement, the decision to strike came after members of Hamas' security apparatus arrested the son of a merchant whose father had refused to comply with the terrorist organization's demands for extortion payments and taxes.
According to the IDF, reports received from merchants indicate that Hamas demands a cash payment of approximately 10,000 shekels for every truck entering the Gaza Strip. It also requires merchants to sell require merchants to sell about 30% of their merchandise in cash transactions, a measure designed to enable Hamas to seize the proceeds directly and thereby preserving its grip on power. 
Moreover, the practice directly violates the commitment made by merchants authorized to operate in Gaza to conduct payments exclusively through monitored bank transfers. Reports also indicate that the taxation system has recently been expanded to include secondary merchants and that Hamas intends to impose it even on drinking water supplies.
The merchants' strike directly undermines Israel's ability to meet its commitments. Under the ceasefire agreement, Israel is obligated to allow approximately 600 trucks into Gaza each day, divided roughly equally between international organizations and independent Gazan merchants. Because the private sector accounts for about 50% of all trucks entering the Gaza Strip each week, the strike is expected to reduce the daily flow by approximately 300 trucks, a drop of about 50%.
Three years into the war, Hamas remains standing, managing daily life for Gaza's residents and exerting significant influence over the entry of aid trucks. The IDF has acknowledged that it has so far failed to develop a system that would allow aid trucks to enter Gaza and reach residents without passing through Hamas' hands. There are concerns that the consequences of the strike — a de facto reduction in the flow of goods into Gaza — will intensify international criticism of Israel and further delegitimize its operations in the Gaza Strip.
In his letter, Halevy made clear that Hamas bears full responsibility and called on international officials to act immediately to prevent the terrorist organization from interfering with the mechanism for bringing aid and goods into Gaza and exploiting it to strengthen itself economically and militarily. Halevy also warned that Hamas would exploit the merchants' strike to spread false claims about shortages of goods and Israel's alleged failure to comply with the terms of the agreement.
Raids in the West Bank
Meanwhile, the IDF and Shin Bet security agency said they had uncovered cooperation between "charitable organizations" and terrorist groups in Judea and Samaria, the West Bank. During two targeted operations in Ramallah and Yatta, five terrorists who had collaborated with Hamas and the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (PFLP) were arrested. According to the IDF and Shin Bet, the "charitable organizations" served as offices for the terrorist groups.
Earlier this week, IDF and Shin Bet forces raided the offices of the Addameer charitable organization in Ramallah. During the operations, suspects were arrested and computers, documents and checkbooks bearing the logos of organizations designated as Hamas-affiliated funds were confiscated. The IDF said Addameer is financed by terrorist funds and operates to provide legal assistance to imprisoned PFLP terrorists. Some of the terrorists employed by the organization took part in the August 23, 2019, terrorist attack at the Dani Spring, in which Rina Shnerb was murdered.

The detainees and seized materials were transferred to security forces for further investigation. The organization served as an organizational and financial arm of Hamas, including transferring funds to the terrorist group and supporting the families of terrorists and prisoners. Turkey seizes control of opposition TV channel as Erdoğan tightens grip on media
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
21:24:05 UTC
06:24:05 KST

Turkish authorities raided the headquarters of Halk TV on Wednesday, one of the country's most popular television channels and among its last remaining independent media outlets. Citing an ongoing corruption investigation, authorities appointed a state trustee to take control of the channel. The dramatic raid interrupted its live broadcast and is seen as an escalation in President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan's efforts to suppress criticism and silence Turkey's free press.
The raid on Halk TV's headquarters in Istanbul began early Wednesday morning, with large numbers of police officers seen surrounding the building. The channel reported on its website that "hundreds of police officers" entered its offices while its journalists were barred from entering. The live broadcast was cut off at 6:30 a.m., after which the channel began airing prerecorded programs.
The Istanbul prosecutor's office said the raid and takeover of the channel's management were part of an investigation into its owner, Cafer Mahiroğlu, on suspicion of "bribery, bid rigging and laundering assets derived from criminal activity." Arrest warrants were issued for 17 suspects as part of the investigation, 11 of whom were detained. Authorities also announced that several companies linked to Mahiroğlu had been seized and that the Savings Deposit Insurance Fund (TMSF) had been appointed as trustee to manage them.
Mahiroğlu, who lives outside Turkey and was not in the country at the time of the raid, described it as "a dark day for Turkey." In a video he released, he accused authorities of "taking control of the public's access to information for political reasons." He dismissed the allegations against him as baseless and said seven members of his family had been arrested during the raid.
Özgür Özel, leader of the main opposition New Party (Yeni Parti, YEP), also strongly condemned the raid, calling it further evidence of Erdoğan's dictatorial rule.
"A dawn raid on a television channel, the appointment of a trustee — only dictators do such things," he wrote in a post on X. "Those who appointed trustees to take over local governments and trampled on the will of the people are now appointing a trustee to take control of Halk TV, a channel watched by millions. Because they are I-N-C-O-M-P-E-T-E-N-T and C-O-W-A-R-D-S!"
During Erdoğan's more than two decades of increasingly tight control over Turkey, press freedom in the country has been severely undermined. This year, Turkey ranked 163rd out of 180 countries in the World Press Freedom Index compiled by Reporters Without Borders. The organization says 90% of the country's national media outlets are under government control.
Halk TV is the fifth major media outlet in recent years to be placed under the control of a state-appointed trustee by Turkish authorities, in a move aimed at controlling its broadcasts and reporting and preventing criticism of Erdoğan's government.
State-appointed trustees have similarly been installed to run numerous local authorities as part of what is widely seen as a broader crackdown on the opposition. That campaign included the arrest last year of Istanbul Mayor Ekrem İmamoğlu, who was charged with corruption. İmamoğlu is considered Erdoğan's most prominent rival and the opposition's candidate in the next presidential election.
Several other mayors were also arrested, while mounting pressure on the opposition has prompted some opposition mayors to defect to Erdoğan's ruling Justice and Development Party (Adalet ve Kalkınma Partisi, AKP).
Erdoğan's crackdown continued this year when the judiciary, which is under his control, annulled the results of the 2023 internal party leadership election of the Republican People's Party (Cumhuriyet Halk Partisi, CHP) in May. The secular party, founded by modern Turkey's founding father, Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, had until then been the country's main opposition party.
The annulment led to Özel's removal as party leader and the reinstatement of former chairman Kemal Kılıçdaroğlu, who led the CHP to defeat against Erdoğan and his party in the 2023 elections but is now seen as an ally of the president.
The court ruling sparked unrest, and police even stormed the party's headquarters and forcibly removed Özel, around whom the opposition had rallied following Imamoglu's arrest.
Özel subsequently left the CHP and founded the New Party, which was joined by large numbers of lawmakers who defected alongside him. It is now the largest opposition faction in parliament.
Since being reinstated as CHP chairman by court order, Kılıçdaroğlu has expressed positions more closely aligned with Erdoğan's government. The raid on Halk TV came just days after he, too, criticized the channel's coverage and announced that he had filed a complaint against it with the media regulator.
Nevertheless, following the raid, Kılıçdaroğlu also joined the chorus of criticism, describing the move as an example of "systematic pressure" on opposition-affiliated media.
European officials also criticized the raid, although Europe's growing dependence on security cooperation with Turkey, a NATO member, means that, as in previous cases, the criticism is unlikely to be accompanied by concrete action.
Nacho Sánchez Amor, the European Parliament's rapporteur on Turkey, said Turkish authorities were "not happy with controlling 90% of media" and were seeking to extend their control to 100%.
"Amidst detentions of journalists & broad online censorship, freedom of media & expression will soon be just a memory," he warned.
