Yelena Morgunova, wife of Russian performance artist Pavel Krisevich, describes two arrests, threats against her family, and an ultimatum to leave Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
20:23:22 UTC
05:23:22 KST

Yelena Morgunova, wife of Russian performance artist Pavel Krisevich, describes two arrests, threats against her family, and an ultimatum to leave Russia
On October 10, protest artist Pavel Krisevich said his wife, Yelena Morgunova, had managed to leave Russia after a series of “back-to-back” arrests. Police detained Morgunova in the Ryazan region on August 28 after she returned to Russia for a brief visit with relatives. Krisevich and Morgunova had been living in France since late 2025 — they left on a humanitarian visa after the artist served two jail terms for administrative offenses. In an interview with Meduza, Morgunova spoke about her detention, life in a Paris squat, and her relationship with former Pussy Riot member Rita Flores, who recently admitted to cooperating with Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB).
Warning: This article contains profanity.
‘What if they gave you some assignment — to bring in explosives?’
— Where are you now?
— I’m in Europe now, on my way to Paris to join Pasha. The problem is, I can’t fly because Céline [Morgunova and Krisevich’s dog] has a short, brachycephalic snout, and there’s a risk that the pressure inside her skull could rise on a plane. So I’m taking trains.
It’s quite an experience. I used to think of France and Germany as some other planet. But when you travel like this, you see how close everything is.
— How are you feeling?
— I’m okay, in a sort of survival mode where you have to hold it together and can’t fall apart. I had to hold it together in the detention center. Then I got out, and right away I had to figure out where to stay, how to get [to France with the dog]. I still haven’t had a chance to settle anywhere.
— What are your plans now?
— We’ll apply for family reunification so I can get a [French] residence permit and permission to work [Morgunova previously had a French humanitarian visa, but it expired]. Then I’ll look for work so I have some money and can help my family. If I can’t see them, at least I can help them that way.
Unlike Pasha, I didn’t apply for asylum at first. I wanted to be able to visit my parents in Russia from time to time.
— Why did you have to go to Russia now?
— I wanted to visit my family. And everything sort of came together: I had nowhere to live in Paris. Maybe if I’d had somewhere to stay, I would’ve gone after the elections, once everyone had calmed down. But I was already emotionally exhausted, and I wanted a little break somewhere familiar. Besides, I had my own place in Moscow.
Pasha and I were living in really difficult conditions in France, in a squat — an abandoned office. Russian-speaking artists and other creative people occupied one part of the space. They’re wonderful people, and we’re friends. They’re helping us however they can now, even though they’re barely scraping by themselves. Our half was pretty cozy, and there was a kitchen. But it was still hard to live like that. We lived in a coatroom; we didn’t even have a window.
People from Arab countries occupied the other half. Many were just passing through and didn’t clean up after themselves. Someone might just pee in the hallway. That was a bit of a shock for me.
We thought it would be temporary, but it dragged on. We arrived in France on June 3 — I remember because it was my name day — and lived there for almost three months. The paperwork took longer than we’d expected. At first, we hoped they’d give us housing together, because France has a law against separating families. People advised us to try [to get housing together], because everything in France is so random — maybe they’d accommodate us.
And at first, they really did try to accommodate us; they asked us for more documents. But in the end, despite a pile of recommendation letters and all the required paperwork, they told us only Pasha could get temporary housing in a dormitory [for refugees], and that he’d be better off taking it.
He got housing. I stayed for a couple of weeks in the apartment of some people I knew who were on vacation, then went home [to Russia] to my mom.
I looked for work in France. But it’s almost impossible to get a work visa while you’re already in the country. It’s much easier for local companies to hire people who already have permission to work. That’s why I kept getting turned down. And when a job opportunity came up, I went to Russia. I thought I’d wait there and, if I got an offer, apply for a work visa. Then I’d return to France on that visa.
— When you flew to Russia, did you consider the possibility that you might be detained?
— I’d planned from the start to keep visiting Russia. All my social media accounts were private, I kept a pretty low public profile, and I didn’t take part in Pasha’s protests. I didn’t think I was at much risk — it seemed like there was a rule that, for the most part, they left people’s loved ones alone. Besides, after Pasha left Russia, I lived in Moscow for about another six months, and I had no problems.
When I arrived in Russia, they checked my passport at the border — everything was calm. I spent two days in Moscow. Then my aunt invited my mom and me to the Ryazan region to see my nieces and help her dig up potatoes. My mom, the dog, and I set off for Skopin. I wasn’t feeling well, but I decided to go even though I had a fever. We never made it there, though.
— How did they detain you?
— My mom and I were on the bus, almost in Skopin. Suddenly, the bus stopped and two police officers got on. They came over to us and said they were conducting some kind of operation: checking the passports of people who’d returned from “unfriendly” countries.
They took us off the bus, and we went to the local police station. At the station, they asked me, “Your husband wouldn’t happen to be a ‘foreign agent,’ would he?” I said, “‘Foreign [agent].’” They said, “Then we have to check your phone.”
I didn’t want to unlock my phone. I told my mom to prepare herself: I’d be spending time in jail [for an administrative offense]. They kept me at the station for a while. Then they took me to the station chief, and he asked, “Will you hand over the phone, or will you put up with what’s coming?” I said I’d put up with it.
Then they took me to court. The court record said I’d supposedly failed to show my passport. I thought maybe they’d mixed something up… I thought, great, maybe I’ll serve a jail term for an administrative offense and get out with my phone. Pasha had given me that phone and said, “Please don’t lose it or let anyone steal it.”
I didn’t admit guilt in court, but when they gave me the record, it said I had. I asked the judge’s assistant, “Why does it say that? I didn’t admit anything.” She said nothing.
I wrote that I agreed with the record. It was clear anyway that once they’d detained me, they weren’t just going to let me go [and I’d have to spend some time in jail for an administrative offense].
— Had you faced any administrative or criminal proceedings before?
— I faced administrative charges four times over rallies and pickets in 2020 — back when we still believed we could change something.
My first rally was over the “Network case.” But I’d never been held in a detention center. And I’d always passed every security check when applying for jobs.
— On what grounds did they detain you?
— They took us to the station because I’d “recently been in an ‘unfriendly’ country.” And once we were there, they arrested me for supposedly failing to show my passport, which wasn’t true. By then, my cold had given me a fever and a terrible headache. I could barely stand.
I signed the court record — I thought, who cares anymore, a lawyer isn’t going to come anyway, and there won’t be an appeal. I thought they’d take me to the detention center, I’d lie down, and I’d quietly serve out those days.
But they took me to another office. There were six FSB guys in plain clothes. Two were definitely from Moscow; the others were local, as far as I could tell. They all had different roles.
One was hysterical and aggressive, shouting, “Who do you think you are? I’m not going to address you politely; you haven’t earned it.” I told him I was used to being shouted at — I’d grown up with it — and it wouldn’t work on me. Then he started threatening my mom and my dog, who were still at the station. That really floored me, because I hadn’t expected anything like it. I’d been detained illegally before, too, but in Moscow they’d been more or less polite.
Actually, the interview with Rita [Flores] that I’d watched the day before helped me. She said they’d used her mom to pressure her, too. And the lawyer Dmitry Zakhvatov told her that the real threat was most likely criminal prosecution for “fake news,” rather than anything happening to her mom.
I don’t remember exactly how he threatened to kill the dog, but at one point I said, “Are you officers or animal abusers?” After that, he just kept saying they’d throw her out on the street and other dogs would tear her apart.
When they started threatening to arrest my mom too, put her in the next cell, and make me listen to her screams, I figured they were bluffing. So I always gave the same answer: I give you permission to take my phone for inspection; let’s write up the paperwork. I sounded like a broken record.
There was another FSB guy, apparently from Moscow — a real dandy with slicked-back hair. Tanned, with shiny skin. He was calm. And there was a young guy from Skopin who kept telling me, “I really feel sorry for your mom and your dog. But this is all your fault.” It went on for a long time, several rounds. They all took turns talking. “What if you’ve been recruited? What if they gave you some assignment — to bring in explosives?”
‘I knew that if this continued, I’d grab a pen off the desk and keep hitting my wrist with it so they’d think I was unstable’
— When were you detained the second time?
— When I got out of the detention center. It’s all in the same little courtyard: the detention center and the police station’s duty desk. They took me into an office with a giant DPR flag and a poster with cringey quotes from Dzerzhinsky: “Your clean criminal record isn’t your achievement — it’s our failure.”
An officer there said, “I think you take drugs.” I asked him where he thought I’d taken them, given that I’d been in the detention center. Never mind that I don’t take them at all. He said my pupils were dilated and my cheeks were red.
They called in witnesses to observe the procedure. In front of them, he asked whether I was refusing a medical examination. I kept saying they should let me see a lawyer first, because accusing me of taking drugs was serious. I was afraid that without a lawyer, they’d take me somewhere and anything could happen there.
He said, “Do you like it abroad? Your husband is a political prisoner.” I said, “My parents are here.” Then he started asking whether I supported my husband’s protests. I said, “Let’s not have these conversations. Only with a lawyer.”
I was shocked by what was happening, and I still had a fever… And this song kept running through my head: “If they’ve picked you up, take a deep breath… […] I don’t know anything. I’m a housewife, I listen to love songs.” I really love it. I kept saying I didn’t know anything and couldn’t remember anything.
— You told the Telegram channel No Future that you were arrested because you’re Pasha’s wife.
— Yes. They wanted to send me for a medical examination to check for drugs, and they wanted me to go without my phone. I got scared because I didn’t know where they’d take me or what they’d do there. Besides, I knew a lawyer was waiting just outside the door, and I asked them to let her in. Of course, they didn’t.
When I was sentenced again, instead of taking me to the detention center, they took me back to that office. There were two men there again: the “dandy” and, apparently, his boss. The boss said, “What’s your name?” And for me, the scariest and most unpleasant part was these conversations outside any formal legal procedure.
I said, “You don’t know my name? Ask your colleague.” He said, “I’m not asking my colleague. I’m asking you.” I introduced myself. He said:
— Do you know why you’re here?
— Explain it to me.
— Who’s your husband?
— My husband is Krisevich.
— And you’re here because you’re his wife. Do you like living this way?
And he asked, “Why do you look so sad? Did something happen? This will keep happening over and over, over and over.” I asked:
— What do you want?
— We want you to leave as quickly as your husband did. Understand?
— I understand. But I won’t be able to leave that quickly.
— How many days do you need?
And they gave me three days to leave.
— Do you think they were trying to figure out whether they could recruit you?
— I think they were testing the waters. That’s what the lawyer thinks.
— Your lawyer, Nataliya Tikhonova, said they suggested you “leave” Pasha. What exactly did they say?
— They said, “What do you need Pasha for? He got you into this. You’re here because of him; he ruined your life. You could be working in peace right now.” I think they were testing the waters, looking for a rift they could then use to put pressure on me.
Hi, I’m Katya.
I’ve been running Meduza’s crowdfunding since 2021. Today, supporting Meduza is a crime in Russia. You can be sent to prison just for donating. We’re still able to do our work thanks to thousands of our Russian readers who now live abroad. But even they’re no longer safe.
Imagine you’ve left Russia, but then your mom becomes seriously ill. It could be your last chance to see her, so of course you go home. At the border, you’re interrogated. Officers hack into your phone and search for any trace that you’ve donated to Meduza.
The Kremlin is counting on that fear, and it’s working. People are afraid to donate. I’m afraid for our supporters, because any one of them could end up in prison. And I’m afraid for Meduza. Without crowdfunding, we simply can’t continue. So if you live outside Russia and don’t have to worry that donating to Meduza could keep you from going home to your family, I’m asking for your help. Please support our work.
— Did you end up handing over your phone?
— [Even before the first arrest,] they interrogated me, and I kept giving the same answer. They took me to the detention center and said, “Be tougher on her.” I spent some time there, and then they called me back to their office.
I walked in, and my mom was already sitting there with [our dog] Céline. As I found out later, they’d pressured my mom too, insulted her, and so on.
Céline was trying to get to me. They started pressuring me again, and I kept giving the same answer again. The dog lunged toward me. And then my mom couldn’t take it anymore and started crying. That high-strung officer started pulling the leash out of my hands. I unclipped it from the harness. Then he started pulling on the harness: he pulled one way, I pulled the other. Céline pressed herself against me. I dug my fingernail into his hand so he’d let go — without thinking, it was just my reaction. And he said, “Keep digging your nails in, and you’ll go to prison under Article 318.”
My mom is very naive. They told her that if I gave them my phone password, I’d be out on Monday. I said, “Mom, that’s not going to happen.” And I watched her get up from her chair, walk over to them, and say, “Please don’t, please don’t.” I was afraid she’d have heart trouble or her blood pressure would [shoot up]…
And I gave them the phone password. They unlocked it. Then they let my mom and the dog go. But I also had a passcode on Telegram, which they hadn’t noticed.
I went back to the detention center. After a while, they called me in again and said, “Tell us the Telegram passcode.” I said, “I don’t remember; the stress has wiped my memory.” I didn’t have the strength to actively resist anymore, so I just started trying to trick them. I entered the wrong passcode several times. I don’t know how long all of this lasted.
They took me back to the detention center. Then they called me in again at night and said, “Do you know Nadya Tolokonnikova?” I said, “No.” They said, “You’re fucking lying. We hacked your Telegram.” They brought in my phone — and Telegram was open, with my messages with Nadya. So [Pavel] Durov’s security is really unreliable; he gets a thumbs-down from me.
When it was finally over, one of the FSB guys said, “Go get some sleep. If you want to get out early, ask for me.” It was Friday, and they didn’t work on weekends. And those days were the scariest for me — I was afraid they’d come back and these conversations would start again.
Sound carried really well in that place: you could hear everything happening in the hallway, every phone call, every word, every whisper. You’d jump at every sound. But I already had a plan. I knew that if they kept this up, I’d just grab a pen off the desk and keep hitting my wrist with it so they’d think I was unstable. Knowing I had a backup plan calmed me down.
The lawyer came on Saturday. We talked everything over and agreed to go public so this recruitment attempt, if that’s what it was, would stop. After that, they didn’t come back.
I also had a PTSD episode because they all addressed me with the informal “you.” My aunt sent me shampoo in the detention center, and I was reading the instructions, which said, “Your hair will shine,” using the informal “you.” I thought, damn, why is this shampoo talking to me like a cop?
— What else stands out from your time in detention?
— I remember that despite all of this, there were humane, kind people there, too. But I can’t go into more detail, because I don’t want anyone to get into trouble for acting like a human being.
I also remember my cellmate Lena, who I spent three days with. When I first arrived, they told me I was lucky: Lena wasn’t there. They said she threw fits and attacked people. They only put her in with me during my second jail term.
At first, I’d sometimes hear detention center officers walk past her cell and taunt her. For example, she was due to get out on August 20, but they’d tell her, “You’ll get out on the 30th,” and she’d start crying really hard.
She was in for violating court-ordered supervision, and before that, I think she’d been convicted of causing serious bodily injury and robbery. But most likely she’d just taken the blame for those crimes — she was a little crazy.
Once, I heard her crying again, and some friends had just sent me a pastry, so I said [to the guards], “Give it to Lena.” They did. The next day, I heard her refusing all food, saying she only wanted black bread. My aunt had sent me a care package then. I put together some things from it for her and said, “Give it to Lena,” and they did that, too. Then the next day, the guards came and said, “The chief says you need to be moved into a cell with Lena. There’s just one problem — she smells.”
Lena turned out to be an absolutely lovely woman. She’s about 57, and she told me her stories. Even though she’s a little crazy, she understood a lot of things better than other people. For example, she’d say we should give them [the guards] and their children the food they fed us, and see how they liked it.
She also told me why they didn’t pick on the others: the others had relatives who’d complain if something happened — but she was an orphan, and there was no one to stand up for her. I kept telling her she’d serve exactly as much time as the judge had ordered, and no one could change that.
When Lena and I were put in separate cells, I heard an officer come back and start tormenting her again, and she told him, “I’ll serve exactly as much time as the judge ordered.” I thought, “Oh, she learned that from me!”
Another time, I heard a different officer go into her cell and start speaking to her rudely: “When you go to the shower, you’ll be washing in your own piss.”
I told him, “If you keep mistreating her, I’ll file a complaint. She’s behaving herself, and you should too.” After that, they stopped.
I don’t understand that kind of humor. Maybe working there for a long time warps you somehow.
— How did your mom cope with all of this?
— It was really hard for her. In the detention center, I tried to tell her I was fine so she wouldn’t worry so much. But when they said I had to leave like that, it was hard. I’m an only child, and I never wanted to leave for good. We spent those three days together. Mostly we dealt with paperwork and arranged powers of attorney.
— So they got access to your phone and your messages. Do you think they could have learned anything from them?
— I think everyone had time to delete their messages with me, because Pasha found out I’d been detained.
— You mentioned Rita Flores. Do you think the security services’ interest in you could be connected to her recent interview?
— I don’t know how much it could have to do with the interview. They asked me about Nadya [Tolokonnikova], Rita, and [Marat] Gelman. Those were the people they were interested in.
— What did they ask?
— Whether I was in touch with Rita. And they asked about Nadya — she put Pasha in touch with Babel, which published his book. They asked where Pasha got his money — I laughed at that question. They asked about Gelman, how Pasha was connected to him [Pasha had stayed at his artist residency]. I told them things that were already public knowledge.
I think my detention was more likely connected to the elections — and to the fact that I went to Skopin. Apparently, the local FSB guys in Skopin are a bit unhinged. I even think that if I’d stayed in Moscow, maybe things would’ve been more civilized.
The Moscow FSB guys knew Pasha well. And they’d had time to prepare. They knew my father had had three strokes and wouldn’t survive finding out I’d been detained. They knew Rita’s and Nadya’s patronymics.
— Why do you connect your detention to the State Duma elections?
— I think it was some kind of preventive measure, because they let me go the day after the elections. They were playing it safe and doing what was expected of them — to show their bosses they’d done everything they could.
‘Even Artyom Kamardin asked in every letter from prison whether Pasha and Lena had left. But we didn’t want to leave’
— Do you believe what Rita Flores said in her interview?
— I do. We really were in touch when Pasha was detained, and she really did try to persuade us to leave. The only problem was that it was impossible to persuade Pasha.
But when Pasha was designated a “foreign agent,” we considered leaving as a backup plan — it’s just hard for “foreign agents” to comply with the law. We started looking into visa options even then. We just didn’t think it would become so urgent.
Pasha and I talked on the phone [when he was in prison], and I told him lots of our friends were advising us to leave. Even Artyom Kamardin asked his wife Sasha in every letter whether Pasha and Lena had left. Artyom was really worried something might happen to us. But we didn’t want to leave, because we had a more or less settled life.
Pasha had a job, too. He worked at a Yandex warehouse as a self-employed contractor. When all his shifts disappeared after the “foreign agent” designation and he couldn’t book new ones, his boss started looking into what had happened. It turned out Yandex’s head office had blocked him.
— In her interview, Rita Flores said she tried to drive a wedge between you and Pasha, and that she supposedly told you Pasha didn’t think about you at all.
— That happened. Pasha and I really did have a falling-out when he went to jail for a protest I’d asked him not to stage. We had a huge fight. I was hysterical, and Rita happened to message me then and ask, “How are you?”
I needed to get it off my chest, and I wrote to her that I was really hurt, because I had a new job and was struggling, and he’d gone to jail. Though of course he hadn’t planned on going to jail either. Anyway, I wrote all that to Rita, and she just supported me.
Maybe she wrote what she actually thought, but I figured she was just the kind of friend who always takes your side. And I didn’t make much of it. I just don’t believe anyone can drive Pasha and me apart.
Rita and I keep meaning to call each other, but it never works out. Either I’m busy or she is. I hope everything turns out okay for Rita.
— During your second jail term, did you expect them to let you leave?
— When I was getting out after the second jail term, I didn’t know what was waiting for me. Would there be more, or would they let me leave? At that point, they didn’t give me my phone back, and they took me to an office where there was an investigator.
He was like, “How’s it going?” I said, “Fine.” He said, “Well, in our line of work, the main thing is not to lose your optimism. What are your plans?” I said, “Well, as we agreed — I’ll leave.” And he was like, “Okay.” Then I knew that was it, they weren’t going to keep me there. When I left the detention center, they gave me my phone back.
— Why do you think they let you leave?
— I think it’s because they let Pasha leave. We do live in a very sexist society, after all. There were some really horrific stories recently involving Kynev and Morozov; apparently, they don’t get that brutal with women. I think, yes, it’s because I’m a woman. And if they didn’t put Pasha in prison, maybe they thought putting his wife in prison wasn’t something a real man would do.
— I take it you won’t be going back to Russia?
— Not anytime soon. It’s really hard. It feels like I’ve been torn away from my life in Russia. It breaks my heart that I can’t see my mom. But I’m trying not to fall apart and to set some new goals here.

Ghalibaf says US must be punished to accept Iran's demands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
20:19:50 UTC
05:19:50 KST

Speaking in a televised interview aired on Wednesday evening, Ghalibaf criticized Washington for violating the Islamabad Agreement. "Even if the United States accepts commitments in a signed document, this would not, by itself, prevent another attack on Iran."
He also noted that continuing the war and escalating tensions alone would not necessarily deter the adversary from making further threats. According to Ghalibaf, Iran’s strategy must combine military preparedness with negotiations to establish lasting deterrence.
Referring to Iran’s eight-year war with Iraq, Ghalibaf said that despite the costs and hardships of the conflict, Iran had established conditions that deterred attacks against the country for decades.
Ghalibaf stressed that military strength is not the only factor in deterrence, pointing to a broader range of domestic and regional capabilities.
He cited improvements in Iran’s firepower, offensive capabilities and air defenses as key military components, saying these capabilities had increased between the 12-day war and the most recent conflict. He also highlighted the capabilities of regional resistance groups, Iran’s strategic position overlooking the Strait of Hormuz, national unity, and economic and social resilience.
The parliament speaker said the goal was to make Iran strong enough that the United States and other regional and international actors could not achieve their objectives through military attacks.
Ghalibaf said Iran must be prepared to defend itself with full force when necessary while using diplomatic opportunities to consolidate military gains and protect national interests.
He argued that military victories should be translated into political and legal gains, while negotiations should provide Iran with the time and resources needed to strengthen its capabilities.
Ghalibaf emphasized that combining war and negotiations did not mean pursuing an endless war or engaging in permanent negotiations. Rather, he said, the objective was to compel the other side to accept Iran’s demands or, if it refused, acknowledge defeat and grant concessions that would allow Iran to strengthen its deterrence capabilities.
He concluded by stressing the need to maintain national unity and strengthen Iran’s military, economic and diplomatic capabilities. He said the country must use its existing resources to ease the economic pressures facing the public and turn current hardships into a more promising future.

Ultra-Orthodox extremists storm building housing IDF cybersecurity program that recruits Haredim
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
20:18:04 UTC
05:18:04 KST

Extremist ultra-Orthodox protesters attempted to storm an office building in Bnei Brak on Wednesday evening where soldiers serving in the IDF's Kodkod program, a specialized training track for software and cybersecurity personnel, are based. Police clashed with the protesters, and two suspects were arrested.
The soldiers participating in the program work on one of the building's floors. Although some protesters managed to enter the building, they apparently did not reach the soldiers. During confrontations with police, protesters were heard shouting "Nazis" at officers.
"Two rioters were arrested after attempting to break into an office building in Bnei Brak and were taken to the police station for questioning," police said in a statement. "Police forces are at the scene. The incident has ended."
The Kodkod program is a specialized technology initiative designed for ultra-Orthodox men aged 23 and older who are not eligible for combat service. The program, which has so far been considered successful, recruits hundreds of young ultra-Orthodox men each year into an adapted military service framework that does not require them to wear uniforms.
Organizations opposing ultra-Orthodox military enlistment have made the program a particular target precisely because it appeals to many young men and offers professional training that could benefit them in their future careers.
Opponents of the program have also succeeded in gaining the support of prominent ultra-Orthodox religious leaders. About a month ago, all members of Agudat Israel's Council of Torah Sages, including the leaders of the Gur, Belz, Vizhnitz and Sanz Hasidic movements, issued a strongly worded letter opposing the program.
"Recently, various tracks have been opened for members of faithful Jewry under the guise that soldiers in these units will serve without uniforms," they wrote. "From now on, no one should join any of the tracks intended for the ultra-Orthodox, without exception."
The Hasidic leaders also accused the programs of seeking to "change the character and spirit of the ultra-Orthodox community. Do not follow their path. Keep your feet from their ways," they urged.
Since its launch in 2023, the Kodkod program has expanded rapidly. It currently has approximately 1,000 soldiers, about 20% of whom are still undergoing training, and recruitment continues to increase.
The IDF estimates that participation will reach approximately 1,100 to 1,200 soldiers by the end of 2026, with hundreds of new recruits joining each year.

Yemeni army claims over 200 Houthis killed, injured in clashes in Taiz

Mohammed Sameai and Sahin Demir
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
The Yemeni army said Wednesday that more than 200 Houthi fighters were killed or injured in clashes in the southwestern province of Taiz.
The Taiz Military Axis said in a statement on US social media company X that fierce fighting continued throughout Wednesday on the Dhubab front west of Taiz and the Al-Aqrud and Al-Shaqab fronts to the south.
It said clashes, which began in the morning, intensified during the afternoon.
The statement said warplanes targeted a convoy of tanks and military vehicles belonging to the Houthis in the Ras al-Najd area of Al-Misrakh district.
Warplanes also carried out two airstrikes early Wednesday on Houthi positions near Sofitel Hill east of Taiz city
Two additional airstrikes targeted a tank and a military vehicle on the Dhubab front west of the city late Wednesday, it said.
The army said Houthi losses during the day included more than 200 fighters killed or wounded, one military vehicle destroyed, two tanks damaged, a drone that was downed and an armed convoy destroyed.
The figures could not be independently verified, and there was no comment from the Houthis.
The fighting comes amid the “Dawn of Yemen” military operation launched by Yemen’s internationally recognized government earlier this month to retake Houthi-held areas, including the national capital, Sanaa.
The offensive, backed by a Saudi-led coalition, has intensified fighting on several fronts, particularly in Taiz, where government forces and the Houthis have battled for control of strategic positions and supply routes.
Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthis seized Sanaa in 2014, forcing the internationally recognized government from the capital. A Saudi-led coalition intervened militarily in support of the government in 2015.

What is Starshield, SpaceX's military version of Starlink?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
20:15:58 UTC
05:15:58 KST

What is Starshield, SpaceX's military version of Starlink?
Elon Musk’s SpaceX restricted “military-grade” Starlink services overnight into Wednesday, hampering Ukrainian drone strike missions and air defenses, Ukraine reported. In response, Musk said that the US government was behind any slowdown in Ukraine's Starshield system.
The claims drew renewed attention to the distinction between Starlink – SpaceX’s commercial satellite internet service – and Starshield, a military version developed for the Pentagon. While Musk has said the two systems are separate, in many cases they share the same underlying satellite technology.
“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government,” Musk said on Wednesday in a post on X, adding that any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military or the president.
“Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company.”
What is starlink?
Starlink is a satellite internet network of more than 11,000 satellites that beam broadband service directly to user terminals about the size of a folded newspaper. Its roughly 13 million subscribers range from households and hikers to shipping companies and major airlines. It is the main profit engine of SpaceX.
Since launching its first Starlink satellites in 2019 aboard reusable SpaceX rockets, the company has built a vast low-Earth-orbit constellation that blankets much of the planet, delivering faster connections than traditional communications satellites, which typically operate much farther from Earth and in far smaller numbers.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Starlink gave Ukraine a critical communications advantage early in the war, reshaping how militaries operate on the battlefield. But Musk has restricted Starlink for certain military uses while highlighting Starshield, a more secure network developed for government and military missions.
What is Starshield?
Starshield is a SpaceX business unit that develops military and intelligence satellite systems for the Pentagon.
While its missions are separate from Starlink’s commercial broadband service, the distinction is not always clear-cut: Starshield’s secure communications services use enhanced encryption and dedicated terminals, but rely on the vast Starlink constellation as their backbone.
Watch moreStarlink restriction 'no surprise' after Musk condemned Ukraine strikes on Russian data centres
Starshield leverages the technology, engineering and operational experiences of Starlink, according to SpaceX. In addition to secure communications, the company says the militarised version can also provide users with Earth observation and the ability to integrate sensors or other payloads.
The Pentagon, Starshield’s largest customer, has spent billions of dollars on both Starlink and Starshield services. It has also bought dedicated Starshield satellites, including communications spacecraft for missile-warning missions and a spy constellation for the National Reconnaissance Office, Reuters reported in 2024.
Questions over the relationship between Starlink and Starshield have persisted since Russia threatened Western satellites supporting Ukraine in 2022. SpaceX unveiled Starshield later that year, but the secrecy surrounding national security space programmes has left the precise boundaries between the two systems opaque.
Those distinctions became a point of contention earlier this year when the Pentagon clashed with SpaceX over higher prices for satellite services used by military drones during the Iran conflict, Reuters reported. SpaceX argued that some customers paying roughly $5,000 per terminal for Starlink should instead have been using a Starshield service costing about $25,000 per terminal.
Britain has also adopted Starshield. Under that arrangement, the service uses the same satellite constellation, ground stations and terrestrial infrastructure as Starlink, but operates through dedicated terminals and separate network gateways, Britain’s defence ministry has told Reuters.
Other US partners are evaluating the system as well. New Zealand is doing a trial of Starshield to assess its usefulness for military operations, the New Zealand Defence Force previously told Reuters.
(FRANCE 24 with Reuters)

Elon Musk said on Wednesday, Oct. 14, that the US military – including US President Donald Trump himself, not SpaceX – decides speed limits on Ukraine’s military Starshield terminals.

“It is clear that the Russians are trying to exploit problems with Starlink’s operation in Ukraine, as interceptor drones rely significantly on this connection,” President Volodymyr Zelensky said in a statement on Wednesday, after meeting with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham in London.

Meanwhile, Ukraine’s former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov said Starlink’s connectivity at speeds of up to 160 kilometers per hour (100 miles per hour) is being restored. “Removing Starshield’s speed limit entirely is now critical for Ukraine’s defense,” he said in a post on X, thanking Musk for his “continued support.”
EU Disburses Another €2.86B to Cover Ukraine’s ‘Most Urgent Needs’ – Drones and Missiles
According to the latest estimates by Zelensky, Russia launched 124 drones overnight and another 145 during the day, with more than 40 Shaheds still in Ukraine’s airspace as he wrote.
UK fast-tracks missiles against jet-powered drones
Zelensky said he and Burnham agreed to speed up deliveries of British air defense systems to counter the jet-powered drones, which fly faster and higher than older Shahed models.
Earlier on Wednesday, The British government said it would accelerate deliveries of Lightweight Multirole Missiles (LMMs), under a £45 million (approximately $60 million) surface-to-air missile package, bringing forward £10 million (approximately $13 million) to meet Ukraine’s urgent winter needs.
“My message to the Ukrainian people could not be clearer, we are with you for as long as it takes, and we will go further and faster in our support to back your courageous fight for peace in Europe” Burnham said ahead of the meeting.
He has also tasked ministers with preparing new sanctions and further military and financial aid.
According to the BBC, Burnham greeted Zelensky at Downing Street with a military ceremonial guard – the first such honor for a foreign leader.
The visit followed a massive overnight strike in which Russia fired at least 39 missiles and 128 drones, cutting power to at least 600,000 people, according to Zelensky earlier in the day.
Questions over US intelligence sharing
The recent strains with Washington deepened after Ukraine received no early warning from Western partners about incoming Russian ballistic missiles for two nights in a row.
Zelensky said Kyiv’s systems detected the missiles only as they approached the capital.
Although NATO and EU, as well as Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said they had seen no sign that sharing had stopped, recent reports by other senior Ukrainian authorities appeared to suggest otherwise.
The lapse followed reports that Washington had threatened to cut intelligence sharing for Kyiv during roughly eight hours of talks in Miami on Friday, Oct. 9.
Reportedly, senior US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner warned Ukraine’s delegation that it could lose access to US intelligence if it kept striking Russian oil refineries.
Several US media separately reported that Trump’s administration also warned it could suspend the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) – a mechanism that enables European purchases of US weapons for Ukraine, the main channel for buying Patriot interceptors.
US Ambassador to NATO Matthew Whitaker denied the claims, saying that no change has been made.
On Oct. 9, Trump struck a diesel deal with Putin that eased US sanctions on Russian fuel, which 12 senators from both parties called “a betrayal of Ukraine” in a joint letter, urging the US President to rescind the diesel deal and enforce the new Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026.
Around the same time, Trump criticized Zelensky and said it was “time for Ukraine to get a new president.”
The US President then announced an energy truce on Oct. 11 that neither Kyiv nor Moscow confirmed, insisting the two sides agreed “because I said, ‘You agree.’”
Although Ukraine abided by the abrupt ceasefire announcement, Russia continued striking Ukraine nationwide. On Wednesday, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said that Trump’s energy truce was never defined, so Russia cannot be accused of breaking it.

Mark Rutte said that NATO has not detected preparations by Russia for an attack, but considers it a long-term threat. The Alliance is ready to respond to aggression.
NATO currently sees no signs that Russia is preparing for a direct attack on NATO countries, although Moscow remains a long-term threat to European security. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said this during a visit to Estonia, The Moscow Times reports, citing the secretary general's press conference, writes UNN.
Details
According to Rutte, Russia is currently not in the best position, and its hybrid attacks against European states indicate weakness rather than strength.
The secretary general stressed that the Alliance is not observing a buildup of Russian forces that could be used to invade NATO territory. At the same time, he assured that the allies would respond immediately if such preparations began.
NATO is ready to respond to any aggression
We will defend every inch of the territory of NATO countries, regardless of whether people live there or not, whether it is located near Paris, Tallinn, Washington, or Ottawa. We have all the necessary plans, and we are ready for this
He recalled that forward-deployed ground forces are already stationed along the Alliance's eastern flank. In addition, Supreme Allied Commander Europe Alexus Grynkewich previously warned that, in the event of an attack on any member state, the Alliance would destroy all forces involved in the aggression.
Rutte separately commented on Russia's hybrid operations in Europe. According to him, NATO has sufficient tools to counter sabotage and other threats, but not all retaliatory measures will be made public.
The secretary general explained that the Alliance's response would not necessarily be reciprocal. In some cases, the allies would respond symmetrically, while in others they would use different methods of counteraction without disclosing their details.

Spanish NGO halts Mediterranean rescue operations, citing fuel prices
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
20:10:15 UTC
05:10:15 KST

Spanish NGO halts Mediterranean rescue operations, citing fuel prices
SMH says it can no longer afford search-and-rescue work in one of the world’ss most dangerous migration routes.
A Spanish charity has postponed its next migrant rescue mission in the Central Mediterranean until next year due to rising fuel costs, underscoring the humanitarian impact of rising energy prices.
Salvamento Maritimo Humanitario (Humanitarian Maritime Rescue, or SMH) said on Wednesday that the doubling of fuel prices forced it to shift its activities to waters around Valencia, southeastern Spain.
The group, which operates a fishing vessel converted into a rescue ship, also launched a crowdfunding campaign to cover the extra costs.
The Central Mediterranean crossing from North Africa to Italy is one of the world’s most dangerous migration routes.
Many of those attempt the crossing on overcrowded, unsuitable boats from Libya’s coast, which has been a main transit point for migrants fleeing war and poverty in Africa and the Middle East.
A report released by the International Office for Migration said migrant sea crossings have dropped sharply since January this year.
The agency said about 60,000 migrants and refugees reached Europe by boat so far in 2026, down 39 percent from roughly 98,000 over the same period last year.
Despite the drop, at least 2,292 died or went missing attempting the crossing this year.
Spanish NGO Open Arms has said it scaled back its Central Mediterranean missions in recent years, also due to rising fuel costs as well as Italy’s policy of assigning rescue vessels ports in Northern Italy.
NGO ships from Spain typically sail for two to three days to reach their operating area, increasing costs and reducing time available for search-and-rescue work.
The Italian prime minister’s right-wing, anti-immigration government says humanitarian rescue attempts encourage migrants to make the crossing.

OpenAI employee who left for Apple took files about unreleased device, OpenAI alleges
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14

05:04:11 KST

An OpenAI employee who left the ChatGPT maker for Apple sent more than 100 files about an unreleased product to a personal account and later made a presentation about the unreleased product to senior Apple leadership, a new filing in the lawsuit between OpenAI and Apple alleges.
In a filing in US federal court in San Jose, California, OpenAI alleged that the presentation occurred months ago and that Apple is now developing its own AI products, citing the release of Apple's HomeView product this week.
"OpenAI is very concerned that its trade secret and confidential information is now circulating inside Apple, where Apple engineers can shape Apple’s upcoming products based on OpenAI’s confidential and innovative work," OpenAI said in its filing.
Apple said that it has policies and procedures in place to ensure new employees do not use confidential information from previous employers and that it has found no evidence to support OpenAI's allegations.
The document, filed on Tuesday, is part of an ongoing trade secret dispute that Apple filed earlier this year, in which it alleged that employees of the iPhone maker left and took confidential information to OpenAI's hardware division. OpenAI has denied those allegations.
US district court grants access to digital files from OpenAI
Earlier this week, US District Court Judge Edward Davila granted part of Apple's request to get early access to digital files from OpenAI in the suit.
Davila said Apple could gather data from some of its former employees' devices and sit three of them for depositions on a sped-up schedule, including the two defendants in the case, Chang Liu, a former senior system electrical engineer, and Tang Yew Tan, a former vice president of product design for iPhone and Apple Watch.
The case is likely to go to trial in October 2027, though OpenAI has said in court filings that it could be ready for trial as soon as June 2027.

Commissioner examining how Commonwealth could hold states, territories to account on child protection
The National Commissioner for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children and Young People, Sue-Anne Hunter, has given more details on the outcomes of her child protection roundtable in WA last month.
Media scrutiny of two high-profile child protection failures in the WA mining town of Port Hedland prompted her visit.
At the roundtable, Hunter heard directly from stakeholders and community members about the faults they saw in the state's child protection system.
She said it was "really clear" the systems "aren't working" and that families and communities needed to be "better supported".
"It's really clear we need a unified approach from the top down to help our kids, we need to support families better and communities surrounding them," she said.
The commissioner said there were two key asks to come out of the roundtable.
"One is a WA commissioner for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children and young people, and the other one was a peak body around child safety and families," she said.
Hunter is also planning a targeted review of the Pilbara's child protection system, looking at how it interacts with housing, police, health, education and the community.
"We need a whole-of-government approach on this; it's a whole-of-government failure," she said.
Hunter said too often Indigenous child safety was treated like a "cultural issue."
"This isn't an Aboriginal issue. This is an issue of government and their systems failing."
She said her team was also looking into what role the Commonwealth could play in holding states and territories accountable for child protection outcomes.

"You carve them out, protect the pensioners, and we will pass this legislation in a heartbeat."
The proposed legislation would save the government about $3 billion, which it wants to reallocate to the aged care sector, but a carve-out for pensioners would halve that to $1.5 billion.
Health Minister Mark Butler has vowed to re-introduce the exact same legislation today.
Shoebridge said the Greens would reject that.
You can take a look back at what happened in the story below by national health reporter Stephanie Dalzell.
Digital duty of care bill 'unsalvageable', Liberal frontbencher says
Liberal frontbencher James Paterson says the government's digital duty of care bill is "unsalvageable" despite the government's changes.
The communications minister will introduce Labor's digital duty of care bill to parliament today, which will require big tech companies to mitigate and protect under-18 users from harmful content on their platforms.
But Labor has removed the controversial ministerial discretion in the legislation and added protections for news content.
Speaking to News24, Paterson says the Coalition has a problem with the bill's intent and that it might censor some views online.
"We cannot support it because ultimately the problem here is not any one clause in the bill; it's the government's intent," Paterson says.
"Anika Wells, the communications minister, has made that very clear from the beginning when she said the problem the government was trying to solve is that people don't trust her."
Paterson vows to continue opposition to private health bill
Liberal frontbencher James Paterson has signalled the Coalition will stand firm in its opposition to Labor's bill to wind back the over-65 private health insurance rebate.
The Coalition teamed up with the crossbench yesterday to discharge the government's bill, effectively booting it from parliament.
But Labor has vowed to reintroduce the legislation today. It says it will save $3 billion over four years and redirect it to the aged care sector.
But Paterson has told News24 the Coalition won't stand down on its position.
"Unless the Greens buckle, that's the only issue. We are not for moving. The Liberal and National parties have led the fight every step of the way against these cruel cuts to older Australians. We will continue to fight them," Paterson says.
Senate will push digital duty of care to an inquiry, Greens say
Greens Senator Sarah Hanson-Young said the Senate will send the government's digital duty of care legislation to an inquiry today, with a report due back in November.
"That's important, I will be using that inquiry to kick the tyres on the government's proposed laws … and making sure it actually works," Hanson-Young said.
The digital duty of care legislation is due to be tabled in parliament today and Communications Minister Anika Wells is due to give a National Press Club address on the matter.
Labor has already scrapped ministerial powers to designate harms from the legislation, which will require big tech companies to mitigate risks to prevent harmful content on their platforms.
The Greens have been calling for harsher penalties than the government's proposed $109 million, saying fines should be a percentage of global revenue.
"There's no point having a duty of care on paper that can’t actually be enforced," Hanson-Young said.
NSW govt promises to protect businesses from federal trust changes if re-elected
The NSW government is pledging to shield small businesses from paying stamp duty if they switch from discretionary trusts to an alternative arrangement.
Labor introduced legislation to parliament yesterday, that if passed, would apply a minimum 30 per cent tax on discretionary trusts.
Businesses have raised concerns about being hit with stamp duty if they restructure to avoid the new tax.
But NSW Treasurer Daniel Mookhey says if the Minns government is re-elected next year, it'll make it clear that discretionary trusts which opt into the federal government's excluded election trust pathway are not considered a taxable event.
"The reason why we want to make this change is to send a very clear message to New South Wales small businesses that your state government is not intending to make a windfall gain at your expense," Mookhey says.

Neighborhood air pollution linked to slower brain development in early adolescence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
20:00:52 UTC
05:00:52 KST

An analysis of data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study found that preteens living in neighborhoods with high levels of fine particulate matter or ozone showed less neurocognitive maturation over two years than demographically similar peers in low-pollution areas. Compared with their peers, they showed smaller gains in cognitive task performance, less maturation of brain network organization, and less of the cortical thinning that normally occurs with development. The paper was published in Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience.
Adolescence is a period of rapid brain development during which the ability to maintain attention, process relevant information, and exercise cognitive control continues to improve. At the same time, the cerebral cortex undergoes major structural and functional changes, including cortical thinning and increasing specialization of communication between brain networks.
Air pollution has attracted growing concern as a possible environmental influence on these developmental processes. Fine particulate matter, or PM2.5, is especially concerning because its particles are smaller than red blood cells and can travel through the bloodstream, while some toxic components may reach the brain through the nasal cavity and the olfactory system. Ozone, a gas found in smog, may harm nerve cells through chronic oxidative stress, and inflammation in the brain has been proposed as another pathway by which pollutants could affect development.
Neuroimaging studies have linked exposure to PM2.5, ozone, and nitrogen oxides with differences in cortical thickness, brain volume, surface area, and functional connectivity in children and adolescents. However, the direction and meaning of these associations have been inconsistent, with some findings suggesting delayed maturation and others appearing to suggest more advanced developmental patterns. Few studies have also examined whether these brain differences are reflected in children’s thinking abilities.
One difficulty is that pollution exposure is closely intertwined with socioeconomic and neighborhood factors, making it challenging to determine whether observed brain differences are caused by pollutants themselves or by other characteristics of the environments in which children live.
Study author Omid Kardan of the University of Michigan and his colleagues set out to isolate the effects of exposure to high levels of PM2.5 and ozone in pre- and early adolescence on brain development and cognitive performance. They hypothesized that high exposure to either pollutant would be associated with slower neurocognitive maturation.
The researchers analyzed data from the ABCD Study, an ongoing longitudinal study of 11,868 children across 21 sites in the U.S. who were enrolled between the ages of 9 and 10.9. The analysis used data from the start of the study and from a follow-up two years later.
The data included resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) scans, which show how brain regions communicate, structural brain scans, and cognitive tasks measuring attention, working memory, inhibitory control, processing speed, memory, vocabulary, and reading. A total of 3,645 participants had usable data at both time points.
The researchers estimated each child’s exposure from modeled air pollution levels in the 1 km2 area around their primary residence at the start of the study. They used U.S. Environmental Protection Agency standards to define high exposure: an annual average above 9 µg/m³ for PM2.5 and a peak ozone level above 70 parts per billion. Low-exposure comparison groups were drawn from children living with less than 7 µg/m³ of PM2.5 or less than 60 parts per billion of ozone.
No participants met the threshold for high exposure to nitrogen dioxide, so that pollutant was not analyzed. The researchers also excluded 40 children who were exposed to high levels of both PM2.5 and ozone, to separate the effects of the two pollutants.
Because pollution exposure is tied to family income and neighborhood, the researchers compared each high-pollution group with a control group matched on household income, parental education, race and ethnicity, sex, and age. The final samples included 348 children with high PM2.5 exposure and 279 matched controls, and 355 children with high ozone exposure and 324 matched controls. The analyses also adjusted for factors including puberty, mental health symptoms, and neighborhood disadvantage.
The researchers combined three measures into a single index of neurocognitive maturation: cognitive task performance, average cortical thickness, and a measure of how closely the organization of a child’s brain networks resembled that of adults rather than infants. Cortical thinning is a normal part of brain maturation in this age range, so greater thinning indicates more maturation.
Children in the low-pollution control groups showed a statistically reliable increase on this maturation index over the two years, but children in the high-PM2.5 and high-ozone groups did not. In other words, the controls showed greater gains in cognitive performance, more maturation of brain network organization, and more cortical thinning than their peers in high-pollution areas. The differences were small, and they held up when the researchers accounted for exposure to the other pollutant.
“As healthy cognitive development is central to multiple domains of resilience and academic achievement, more effort should be directed toward reduction of these pollutants in residential and school areas,” study authors concluded.
The study contributes to the scientific knowledge about environmental factors affecting cognitive development. However, the study was observational, and the air pollution data were based on ambient air pollution in the 1 km2 area around each participant’s home, which may not fully reflect their actual exposure. Pollution was also measured only at the start of the study, so the data may not capture moves during the study or exposure earlier in life, including before birth.
In addition, the ozone measure was based on the highest level recorded in a year rather than the EPA’s standard calculation, which may have overstated how many children had high exposure. To create well-matched groups, the researchers also had to exclude 35 children with high PM2.5 exposure who had no demographically similar peers in low-pollution areas, which limits how representative the findings are.
The paper, “Neighborhood air pollution is associated with attenuated neurocognitive maturation over early adolescence,” was authored by Omid Kardan, Chacriya Sereeyothin, Kathryn E. Schertz, Mike Angstadt, Alexander S. Weigard, Marc G. Berman, Mary M. Heitzeg, and Monica D. Rosenberg.

Restrictions on the speed of the Starshield system are set by the U.S. president — Musk
Kyiv • UNN
Elon Musk said that Starshield is controlled by the U.S. government, and that the restrictions are set by the U.S. military and the president.
Billionaire Elon Musk stated that he does not determine the restrictions for SpaceX’s Starshield system used by Ukraine. According to him, the system is controlled by the U.S. government, while the final decision on limiting speed or use is made by the U.S. president, UNN writes.
Details
Former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov wrote on the social network X: "Connectivity via Starlink is currently being restored at speeds of up to 160 km/h. The complete lifting of the speed restriction in Starshield is currently of crucial importance for Ukraine’s defense. Thank you, Elon Musk. We hope for your continued support."

The use of Starlink is restricted to civilian or defensive purposes and cannot be used for offensive military actions, as that would be inappropriate for a commercial company," Musk wrote.
Additional information
Starshield is a division of SpaceX’s subsidiary "Starlink" that creates specialized satellites in low Earth orbit designed to provide military space capabilities for the United States and its allies.
The Starshield project was adapted from the global Starlink communications network, but has additional capabilities, such as target tracking, optical and radio reconnaissance, as well as early warning of missile attacks.

Ukraine’s “Ptashka,” Who Survived Russian Captivity, Receives First Lord Ashcroft Award for Courage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
19:54:19 UTC
04:54:19 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine’s “Ptashka,” Who Survived Russian Captivity, Receives First Lord Ashcroft Award for Courage
Ukrainian servicewoman and former Russian prisoner of war Kateryna Polishchuk, widely known by her call sign “Ptashka” (Birdie), has become the first recipient of the Lord Ashcroft Award for Courage , presented during the Warsaw Security Forum in Poland.
The recognition was announced by Ukraine's Ministry of Foreign Affairs on October 13.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Polishchuk, who gained widespread recognition for her role in defending Mariupol's Azovstal steel plant during Russia's siege of the city in 2022, received the award in recognition of her courage and continued service to Ukraine.
At the age of 21, she worked as a volunteer paramedic at Azovstal, providing medical assistance to wounded Ukrainian defenders under constant Russian bombardment. She was subsequently captured by Russian forces and spent four months in captivity before returning to Ukraine and resuming her frontline service.
During her participation in the Warsaw Security Forum, Polishchuk addressed Russia's war crimes, the treatment of Ukrainian prisoners of war, attacks on civilian cities, Ukrainian-Polish relations, and the importance of continued European involvement in supporting Ukraine.
She also warned European countries about the threat posed by Russia and emphasized the need for a coordinated response to its actions.
“I received an award for exceptional courage. I consider this award not a personal recognition, but an acknowledgment of the courage and strength of every man and woman who defends the world against Russia,” Polishchuk wrote.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha praised Polishchuk's resilience, describing her experience as a reflection of the determination demonstrated by Ukrainian defenders throughout Russia's full-scale invasion.
“Russia tried to break Kateryna, but failed. Her story embodies the strength of spirit of Ukrainians who continue fighting for freedom despite Russian crimes. Kateryna's call sign is Ptashka. Russia tried to put her in a cage, but could not. Because Ptashka proved stronger than Russia. And if Ptashka endured, Ukraine will endure too,” Sybiha said.
The foreign minister also drew attention to the continued detention of Ukrainian soldiers captured during the defense of Mariupol. According to him, more than 700 defenders of Azovstal remain in Russian captivity, with Ukrainian authorities continuing to pursue their release through prisoner exchanges.
Sybiha also condemned Russia's treatment of Ukrainian prisoners of war, particularly members of the Azov Brigade, and recalled the killing of at least 53 Ukrainian POWs at the Olenivka detention facility.
He stressed that those responsible must be held accountable regardless of how much time passes.
“The reason for this particular treatment is the unbreakable spirit of our warriors. They embody true Ukrainian courage. That is why the Russians are trying to break them. And that is why we must make every effort to bring them home,” the minister added.
Highlighting the broader scale of alleged Russian violations of international humanitarian law, Sybiha cited United Nations findings indicating that more than 95% of Ukrainian prisoners of war had experienced torture, while nearly all released detainees returned home severely weakened by starvation.
According to the figures cited by the minister, one Ukrainian serviceman lost 77 kilograms during five months in Russian captivity. The UN has also documented 129 executions of Ukrainian prisoners of war and 48 deaths in captivity.
Sybiha further stated that Russia holds Ukrainian detainees at more than 300 locations to which the International Committee of the Red Cross has been denied access.
As of July 2026, at least 38 Ukrainian prisoners of war from the Azov Brigade who survived the 2022 explosion at the Olenivka detention facility have been convicted or are facing prosecution in Russia, the Media Initiative for Human Rights (MIHR) reported on July 28, marking the fourth anniversary of the attack.

Popular Irish novelist Sally Rooney to withdraw books from UK market over Palestine Action support
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
19:53:49 UTC
04:53:49 KST

Aysu Bicer
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
Popular Irish novelist Sally Rooney has agreed with her publisher to withdraw her books from sale in the United Kingdom, citing legal concerns over her public support for Palestine Action, which was banned as a terrorist organization in July 2025.
Rooney, whose works include Normal People and Conversations With Friends, said her support for the group meant she could no longer receive royalties from UK sales.
“In July 2025, the direct-action protest group Palestine Action was proscribed as a terrorist organisation in the UK. The following month, I wrote an opinion piece expressing my intention to go on supporting Palestine Action, which is not a proscribed or otherwise prohibited group here in the Republic of Ireland," Rooney said in a statement provided to The Guardian.
“As a result, the fulfilment of contracts to publish my work in the UK could now constitute a serious criminal offence. After a process of consultation and deliberation, and with my full agreement, my publisher Faber has therefore determined that it can no longer supply my work within the UK. I have made every effort to be honest with the public about my beliefs and intentions, and I am wholly prepared to accept the consequences,” she added.
After the group was banned, Rooney said she intended to use proceeds from her book sales to support Palestine Action. She later cancelled a trip to the UK to collect an award, citing fears of arrest.
Under Section 15 of the UK's Terrorism Act, it is an offense to provide money or other property while knowing or having reasonable cause to suspect that it will or may be used for the purposes of terrorism. The offense carries a maximum prison sentence of 14 years.
Faber said the legislation had prevented it from transferring UK earnings to Rooney.
“Current legislation in the UK has led to circumstances where Faber cannot pass on UK earnings to Sally Rooney for her work. To sell a writer’s work and not be able to pass on earnings is an unconscionable situation for a publisher,” the publisher said.
Surge in terrorism-related arrests in UK
Rooney's books have achieved significant commercial success in the UK. Normal People has sold more than 1 million copies, while Conversations With Friends and Beautiful World, Where Are You have each sold more than 500,000 copies.
Both Normal People and Conversations With Friends were adapted for television by the BBC.
Terrorism-related arrests in the UK have surged by 1,553% to a record high, with the vast majority linked to support for Palestine Action, according to new Home Office figures.
A total of 3,867 arrests were made for terrorism-related activity in the year ending June 2026, up from 234 in the previous 12-month period.
Of these, 3,630 arrests — around 94% — were linked to support for Palestine Action following the group’s proscription.
The Labour government, then led by Keir Starmer, banned Palestine Action under terrorism legislation in July 2025, making it the first direct-action group to be banned under the Terrorism Act in British history.

Yemen urges UN, Security Council to act urgently to lift Houthi siege of Taiz

Omer Asur Cuhadar and Rania Abushamala
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
Yemen on Wednesday called on the UN and its Security Council to take urgent steps to lift the Houthi siege of the southwestern city of Taiz, warning of severe humanitarian consequences from the Houthis’ escalation.
Foreign and Expatriates Minister Afrah al-Zouba made the appeal in a letter addressed to the UN secretary-general, the Security Council president, the UN high commissioner for human rights, the president of the International Committee of the Red Cross, and the UN under-secretary-general for humanitarian affairs.
According to Yemen’s official Saba news agency, the letter highlighted the “serious deterioration of humanitarian conditions in Taiz province due to the escalation by the terrorist Houthi militias.”
Al-Zouba warned that the latest escalation and tightening of the siege on Taiz and surrounding villages threatens a humanitarian catastrophe affecting more than 4 million people, including residents trapped inside the city and people displaced from affected districts such as al-Shamayatayn, al-Mawasit and Jabal Habashi.
She called for direct international pressure to immediately lift the siege, open all access routes into Taiz to civilians and supply chains, and ensure sustained, unhindered access to food, fuel, and drinking water.
The foreign minister also urged stronger monitoring, documentation, and accountability mechanisms to preserve evidence of violations, hold perpetrators accountable, and prevent impunity.
She called for a clear international position against practices that deprive civilians of basic means of survival or use their humanitarian needs to exert pressure or impose a fait accompli.
‘Direct threat to civilian lives’
Al-Zouba reaffirmed the government’s commitment to cooperating with the UN, its specialized agencies, humanitarian and human rights groups, and regional and international partners.
She said the government would provide relevant information and facilitate humanitarian response efforts to ease suffering, protect civilians, and ensure that aid reaches those in need.
The situation in Taiz “poses a direct threat to civilian lives, dignity and basic rights, requiring an urgent international response that goes beyond expressions of concern,” she said.
She urged practical measures to end the siege, restore essential supplies, protect civilian facilities, and prevent the humanitarian crisis from worsening.
Yemeni human rights and humanitarian groups say the Houthis have closed most roads leading to government-controlled areas of the province.
They accuse the group of besieging the city since the conflict erupted in 2015 and blocking aid convoys from reaching residents and people affected by the war. The Houthis deny those accusations.
Earlier Wednesday, Yemeni Prime Minister Shaya al-Zindani said continued Houthi attacks on civilians and the siege of Taiz constitute a “war crime that is not subject to a statute of limitations,” stressing that those responsible would not escape punishment and accountability.

US lifts sanctions on Venezuela’s top legislator

US lifts sanctions on Venezuela’s top legislator
Jorge Rodriguez has been removed from OFAC’s sanctions list in latest US push for oil control and bilateral diplomacy.
The United States Department of the Treasury has lifted sanctions on the head of Venezuela’s National Assembly, Jorge Rodriguez, brother of the country’s interim President, Delcy Rodriguez.
The move by US Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) comes amid major US-Venezuela energy pacts and other talks with the Latin American country’s government.
The delisting notice was posted on the federal agency’s website on Wednesday, officially removing Jorge Rodriguez’s name from OFAC’s Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) blacklist.
The top lawmaker in the country, Jorge Rodriguez has held the position of National Assembly president since 2021. He was reappointed in January, weeks after the abduction of former President Nicolas Maduro by the US government. He served as vice president under Venezuela’s late President Hugo Chavez, among other posts.
Jorge and Delcy Rodriguez had been sanctioned under US President Donald Trump’s first administration due to their ministerial roles under Maduro, who now faces several federal charges, including a sweeping superseding indictment adding torture to his other alleged crimes.
In 2018, the State Department said that Jorge Rodriguez was given prominent government positions by Maduro “to help him maintain power and solidify his authoritarian rule”.
A source familiar with the matter told Al Jazeera that the decision to lift sanctions on Jorge Rodriguez is part of Washington’s wider diplomatic recognition of the interim Venezuelan government, and Trump’s three-phase plan for Venezuela’s stabilisation and political transition.
During a press briefing at the US State Department on Friday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters that the next round of negotiations on Venezuela’s future was scheduled to begin on Wednesday. He also urged all Venezuelan opposition factions to join US-backed political talks with the interim president.
Earlier this year, the US Treasury dropped sanctions against Delcy Rodriguez and later lifted the restrictions on Venezuela’s central bank and its state-owned national airline, signalling Washington’s pivot from economic warfare to backroom bargaining. She has largely complied with Trump’s demands for Caracas to open up its energy industry to American companies.
As interim president, Delcy Rodriguez has promised to hold elections – including in her recent remarks at the United Nations General Assembly – but no firm date has been set. Opposition leader and Nobel Peace Prize winner Maria Corina Machado has demanded they take place by July.
Jorge Rodriguez has shepherded several major reforms through the ruling party-controlled legislature since his sister took power, including a law that facilitated the entry of more foreign oil companies, a similar law for the mining sector and an effort to allow private investment for the country’s battered power grid.
Since Maduro’s ouster, Caracas and Washington have cut a deal giving the US access to 17 Venezuelan oil fields, while international energy firms have separately committed to expanding projects in the Latin American country. In August, Trump announced a plan to secure direct US access to a large share of Venezuela’s vast oil to refill the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve.

SpaceX chief Elon Musk says the version of Starlink that Ukraine’s military uses, StarShield, is owned and controlled by the US government rather than by his company. His claims come amid a storm over Ukrainian reports that a speed cut had broken their frontline operations.
Ukraine’s drones and air defenses rely on Starlink to steer and strike, so a limit on the network hits combat directly. Musk’s answer shifts the decision and the blame from SpaceX to the US government and, ultimately, to the president.

The exchange that forced Musk to answer

The faster package Ukraine cannot do without
The ordinary Starlink Mini mounted on drones is capped at about 160 km/h, which is too slow for some missions, so faster flight requires access to the military version, StarShield, Ukrainska Pravda notes. Ukraine has used StarShield since 2024.
