As Ukraine struggles with Starlink and US satellite data, Europe has no quick fix
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
19:00:57 UTC
04:00:57 KST

As Ukraine struggles with Starlink and US satellite data, Europe has no quick fix
KYIV - As Ukraine reported problems with Starlink satellite internet terminals and US data that warns of Russian ballistic missile attacks, Kyiv also faced the harsh reality that its European allies cannot offer any ready-made alternatives.
Ukrainian officials said on Oct 14 the functioning of Starlink’s military-grade service Starshield had been interrupted when terminals were moving at high speed, hampering Ukrainian drones for attack missions and air defence.
Separately, President Volodymyr Zelensky said that, for the second night running, Ukraine had received no warning from its partners of a Russian ballistic missile attack on Kyiv.
The reasons for the difficulties were not immediately clear but followed another souring of relations between US President Donald Trump and Ukraine, after Trump announced a deal to waive sanctions on Russian diesel and called for Zelensky to be replaced.
Trump said on Oct 13 that the United States was still sharing intelligence with Ukraine. Elon Musk and his SpaceX company had no immediate comment on Ukraine’s assertions.
European countries have voiced strong support for Ukraine and Zelensky. But the problems with vital data highlighted that Ukraine and Europe depend heavily on US systems for both low-orbit satellite communications — provided by SpaceX via Starlink — and space-based infrared sensing that feeds into early-warning systems.
A US satellite constellation called the Space-Based Infrared System provides early missile warnings.
“That is fairly unique and … what basically that can detect is the heat generated by missiles as they're launched,” said Marc DeVore, an associate fellow at think tank Chatham House. “There is nothing equivalent in Europe.”
No simple Starlink swap for Ukraine, Europe
As for Starlink, Europe does not have a ready-made alternative that Ukrainian soldiers could attach to their drones, although European governments and companies are working on long-term options.
Shares in European satellite operator Eutelsat soared on Oct 14 following news of Ukraine’s difficulties with Starshield, fuelled by investor bets that European providers could benefit from growing strains between Washington and Kyiv.
But Christian Freiherr von der Ropp, an independent satellite consultant, said Eutelsat’s OneWeb network was not well suited to wartime use.
“Its current constellation remains rooted in an outdated architecture and technology conceived a decade ago, without any evolution of its underlying design,” he said.
“Capacity and performance constraints, combined with the cost, weight, bulk and power consumption of its user terminals, limit its suitability for frontline applications.”
A spokesperson for Eutelsat told Reuters that the company continued to provide connectivity services in Ukraine through its low Earth orbit and geostationary orbit networks with its partners. It declined to comment further “given the sensitive nature of the situation.”
Von der Ropp also said switching networks would require replacing thousands of terminals, as Starlink and Starshield terminals use proprietary technology and could not simply connect to OneWeb.
Bohdan Sas, co-founder of Ukrainian defence technology startup Buntar Aerospace, said the sudden interruption to Starshield services “highlights to almost every end user both in Ukraine and abroad you can’t rely solely on one solution that can be switched off.”
“You need to have some kind of sovereign capabilities,” he added, so that “you are not subject to somebody’s mood today.”
Fears of over-reliance on US defence technology have grown in Europe in recent years, as Trump has threatened to quit the NATO military alliance just as European leaders see Russia posing the greatest threat to the continent in decades.
European Defence Commissioner Andrius Kubilius said at a conference hosted by Politico in Brussels on Wednesday that the continent was “quite dependent on American space capabilities.”
“The answer to that situation is to develop our own capabilities,” he added, mentioning the European Union’s planned satellite constellation IRIS² and urging European countries to work together to avoid frustration.
But that project is years from becoming operational even if everything goes according to plan, causing frustration among European government officials. Germany is developing its own military satellite constellation. REUTERS

US Congresswoman Jayapal slams India's purge of 133 million people from voter rolls, backs protests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
19:00:53 UTC
04:00:53 KST

US Congresswoman Pramila Jayapal has slammed India's removal of over 133 million people — roughly equivalent to the population of Mexico — from electoral rolls via the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) process, equating it to US voting rights challenges under the Republic administration and affirming support for non-violent Indian protests demanding free and fair elections.
"I am deeply concerned about the actions of the Indian government to purge 130 million people from the voting rolls. This appears to be a similar playbook to what the Trump administration is doing here at home to undermine voting rights in a democracy," Jayapal wrote on X on Wednesday.
Jayapal was comparing the situation to 2026 US administration’s efforts to audit state voter rolls for non-citizens, which courts have blocked in several cases over concerns about privacy violations and potential disenfranchisement of eligible voters.
The Indian-American House representative expressed her support for youth activists and opposition parties who are demanding the resignation of India's chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, who they say has manipulated voter rolls to benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling right-wing party.
"Protecting democracies everywhere is essential work, and the Indian people — like the American people — deserve free and fair elections. Non-violent resistance movements are essential in these moments and I stand with the Indian people who are engaging in non-violent protests to counter anti-democratic efforts in India," Jayapal added.
India's Election Commission claims the deletions as targeting dead voters, permanently shifted residents, and untraceable individuals to clean up rolls, but critics including opposition parties and many media reports say the deletion has disproportionately impacted Muslims and other groups who are less supportive of Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
'Basic targets were the Muslims'
Widespread protests have erupted across Indian cities against the exercise, with calls for the chief election commissioner's resignation and Supreme Court involvement, amid claims some living citizens were removed despite opportunities to re-enroll.
In northern West Bengal state for example, over 9.1 million voters—more than 10 per cent of the electorate—were removed from rolls by April 2026. Despite appeals by 2.7 million people, they remain excluded.
In Nandigram area of the state, an analysis revealed that Muslims made up 95 per cent of voter roll deletions in certain lists, despite accounting for only 25 per cent of the electorate.
Non-Muslims, who constitute roughly 75 percent of the population, accounted for just 4.5 percent of deletions, according to data sourced from India’s election commission.
The electoral list revision, which began last year, has led to more than 133 million names being removed from voter rolls, according to media reports. Critics say the exercise has disproportionately affected minorities, particularly Muslims.
According to The Hindu newspaper, Muslims, who make up 13.6 per cent of voters on the draft electoral roll in the capital, New Delhi, accounted for 20.3 per cent of those flagged for "logical discrepancies" and 30 percent of those flagged under five categories indicative of family size by the Election Commissionr's ERONET software.
In northern Bihar state, which didn’t have "logical discrepancy" checks, Muslims accounted for 18.4 percent of deleted electors, in line with their 17.7 percent share in population, the newspaper reported on Wednesday.
Recent investigative reports indicate that BJP agents attempted the mass deletion of Muslim voters from electoral rolls during a statewide revision exercise in India's eastern Odisha state.
Reports across Indian states including Uttar Pradesh, Gujarat, and Madhya Pradesh detail systematic efforts to disenfranchise Muslim voters through targeted voter list deletions, registration hurdles, and discriminatory labelling.
In interview with India Today, former chief election commissioner S Y Quraishi argued that the scale and execution of voter deletions showed bad faith, stating, "Basic targets were the Muslims, and potentially all non-BJP voters."
India arrests 'cockroach' movement members
Meanwhile, two leaders of India's youth-led movement Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), led by founder Abhijeet Dipke, were remanded in custody for five days, as police clamp down on protests against the election commission.
Delhi Police said CJP leaders Ashutosh Ranka, 30, and Saurav Das, 27, were taken into custody for their "alleged repeated attempts to disturb public peace and violate the law".
Parliamentary opposition leader Rahul Gandhi, from the Congress party, backed the protest leaders.
Rights advocates and critics say Modi's right-wing government has eroded democratic freedoms during more than a decade in power, citing pressure on journalists, civil society groups and political opponents — allegations the government rejects.
Human Rights Watch said on Wednesday the Indian government must uphold the right of citizens to protest peacefully.
"The Modi government should stop throwing young protesters in jail and instead engage with them to address concerns over the right to vote and fairness of elections," it said in a statement.
Home Minister Amit Shah, Modi's powerful right-hand man, has dismissed the protests as localised and accused Gandhi of pursuing an "action plan to protect infiltrators".
"The people of India are not going to fall for your deception," he said, predicting a "resounding majority" for government in the next general election, due in 2029.

Saving Lives on the Front Line: Kyiv Post’s Jason Smart Hits €1M Milestone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
19:00:00 UTC
04:00:00 KST

Along the roads leading into Ukraine’s front lines, safety is measured in sheer speed. Routes that were quiet thoroughfares months ago are now tunneled under makeshift anti-drone netting, where Ukrainian troops must floor the accelerator to outrun Russian FPV operators actively hunting any moving target. Between regular visits, familiar landmarks vanish: cozy roadside cafes where soldiers once shared coffee are flattened into rubble, and bridges are wiped off the map.
In a battlespace where Russian electronic countermeasures shift constantly and transport vehicles are destroyed daily, off-the-shelf military gear often fails to keep troops alive. Bridging that lethal gap, an emergency pipeline spearheaded by Kyiv Post special correspondent Jason Jay Smart and security analyst Sergej Sumlenny has surpassed €1 million. This effort pooled contributions from 8,585 international donors to rush nearly 2,000 custom-engineered drones, replacement vehicles, and electronic warfare systems directly to combat brigades.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Built Around What Soldiers Need
“We don’t come with a product,” Sumlenny explains. “Instead, we come with the question, what do you need?”
For the German security analyst, rapid frontline adaptation has rendered cookie-cutter tech supplies ineffective. Traditional military supply chains relied on mass-issuing standardized hardware, but the electronic battlefield moves too quickly for a one-size-fits-all approach. A commercial drone that flies reliably in one sector can be rendered completely useless ten miles away by localized Russian jamming.
Russian forces lean heavily on centralized, mass-produced systems, whereas Sumlenny works backward from a Ukrainian unit’s immediate tactical dilemma. His team engineers drones tailored to distinct radio horizons, flight ranges, and payload weights. Rather than shipping boxes through backline depots, Sumlenny personally delivers the systems to combat zones, running immediate field tests and modifying components based on pilot feedback.
Such constant presence has put him on speed dial for frontline commanders whose survival depends on solving unexpected equipment crises in real time.
This direct lifeline proved critical when soldiers from the 93rd Mechanized Brigade contacted Sumlenny after Russian strikes destroyed both of their transport vehicles. With available campaign funds exhausted, Sumlenny initially had to tell the unit he could not help. Then, while they were still on the phone, an unexpected donation from a supporter, in Germany, flashed across his phone’s screen.
“Oh, actually we have money now,” Sumlenny recalled telling the relieved soldiers.
Thousands of Donors Saving Ukrainian Lives
Behind these shipments are thousands of individual donors, largely drawn from Smart’s YouTube audience across the United States, Europe, Australia, and dozens of other nations.
“The soldiers are incredibly appreciative of all the support they receive,” Smart said, reflecting on his visits to frontline positions.
Sumlenny regularly relays donors’ personal messages to the troops, explaining that teachers, veterans, retirees, and families thousands of miles away are personally backing their survival.
Assistance has reached key fighting formations, including the 1st Azov National Guard Corps, the 4th Rubizh National Guard Brigade, the 47th, 67th, and 93rd Mechanized Brigades, the 225th Assault Regiment, and the 501st Marine Battalion. In many cases, the Ukrainian soldiers have recorded video messages, thanking donors, which were later broadcast on Smart’s YouTube channel.
                                
                                    
                                
                                
                                Night behind truck with Ukranian flag: In Kharkiv - with the 225th Assault Regiment. 
                            
Among them, fighters from the Rubizh Brigade thanked contributors after receiving 200 drones, while the 67th Mechanized Brigade’s air-defense unit credited the online community with supplying 22 interceptor drones.
According to Smart, who hosts the largest English-language YouTube channel focused on the inner workings of the Putin regime, reaching his goal of €1 million raised to support Ukraine’s soldiers - more than military medals or other recognitions - is his greatest source of pride from the past four years.
“I am profoundly thankful to all the people who watch the channel and chose to contribute, for keeping abreast of the existential fight in which Ukraine is heroically engaged. The struggle for Ukraine’s future does not stop at its borders; it is one that touches the lives of all of us,” said Smart.
“If the Putin Regime is not crushed now,” continued the American, “we can expect greater wars that will undoubtedly spiral into incalculable costs for countries around the world, especially in the West. By standing with Ukraine today, we are making the world a better place for future generations. This is the fight of our lives.”  
                                
                                    
                                
                                
                                Standing in front of some drones being delivered: In Sloviansk with the 501st Marine Battalion. 
                            
Recognition From Ukraine’s Military Leadership
Beyond his public analysis and fundraising, Smart, who first moved to Ukraine in 2015 at the invitation of the Director of the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU), has collaborated closely with Ukraine’s defense and security apparatus. Formal decorations have followed from the nation’s senior command, including the Armed Forces’ Medal of Merit, the Medal of Valor in Service to the Military, Third Class, and a medal from the Department of State Protection of Ukraine (ODU), the agency tasked with safeguarding the president and top state officials.
                                
                                    
                                
                                
                                Jason in front of Pyaterka: Ukrainian-occupied Kursk, Russia 
                            
Defense Intelligence Chief Kyrylo Budanov issued an official citation recognizing Smart’s sustained assistance in achieving military intelligence objectives. While still Ukraine’s top military commander, General Valeriy Zaluzhny conferred a commendation for his contributions. Separately, the Center for Strategic Communications and Information Security formally acknowledged his work in countering Russian state disinformation.
                                
                                    
                                
                                
                                Jason in armored personnel carrier: At the zero line entering Ukrainian-occupied Russia. 
                            
Urgent Winter Appeal
Following Russian strikes on October 13 and 14 that damaged all three of Kyiv’s municipal heat and power plants, the initiative launched a €25,000 drive to supply frontline units with portable power stations, drones, and medical gear before winter.
Building on contributions from 8,585 international donors, this upcoming push focuses on rushing critical equipment to combat units facing freezing temperatures and ongoing grid disruptions.
Smart noted that supporters can contribute directly to frontline deliveries through the initiative’s PayPal link. Contributors donating over €100 are eligible to receive a commemorative military patch produced in Ukraine.

Lithuania freezes the assets of Russian oligarchs Fridman and Usmanov

The government added that Latvia and Estonia are also imposing national sanctions on Fridman and Usmanov, and that on September 24, 2026, these individuals were placed on the list of foreigners banned from entering Lithuania for a five-year period.
As a reminder
EU diplomats reported that representatives of the member states had agreed to remove the two billionaires from the sanctions list concerning Russia and extend the sanctions against the remaining 3,000 individuals and legal entities for another three years.

EU Disburses Another €2.86B to Cover Ukraine’s ‘Most Urgent Needs’ – Drones and Missiles

18:59:40 UTC
03:59:40 KST

The European Union (EU) has disbursed another €2.86 billion ($3.1 billion) to Ukraine for air defense, particularly drones and missiles, as the country nears its fifth winter of Russia’s aggression.
The European Commission confirmed the payment on Wednesday, Oct. 14, made under the defense component of the €90 billion (approx. $100 billion) Ukraine Support Loan. The funds will also cover radars, electronic warfare systems and ammunition.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Amid intensified Russian attacks on our cities and critical infrastructure, this support is vital,” Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said in a statement on Telegram.
“More drones, air defense systems, missiles, and ammunition mean stronger protection for our people and greater capabilities for our defenders on the front line,” he added, noting that Kyiv is working with European partners to secure the rest of the defense funding without further delays.
Funds arrive as Russia escalates its air campaign
The disbursement follows one of Russia’s heaviest strikes on Ukraine’s energy system this autumn.
Overnight on Oct. 13-14, Ukraine’s Defense Forces recorded roughly 39 missiles and 128 launched by Russia, which left at least 600,000 people without power according to President Volodymyr Zelensky.
“As Russia stalls on the frontlines, it continues to escalate its aerial attacks – cruelly targeting Ukrainian civilians and infrastructure,” President of the European Commission Ursula von Der Leyen said.
Russian Strikes Destroy Epicentr K’s Last Major Logistics Hub
The defense payments are expected to reach Ukraine in the upcoming weeks.
What remains for 2026
Ukraine still has €29.64 billion (roughly $33 billion) in EU financial support available for the rest of the year, according to the Commission.
That includes €25.24 billion ($28 billion) under the Ukraine Support Loan, split between €12.54 billion (approx. $14 billion) for Ukraine’s defense industry and €12.7 billion (about $14 billion) in budget support, plus €4.4 billion (about $5 billion) left under the earlier Ukraine Facility.
Budget payments depend on Kyiv meeting conditions set out in the Ukraine Plan and a memorandum of understanding with the EU.
Ukraine had received €1.2 billion (roughly $1.3 billion) just a week earlier, on Oct. 7, bringing total funding received under the program to nearly €13 billion ($14.5 billion) according to Koretskyi.
Mid-September, Koretskyi warned Ukraine risks losing a substantial amount of $29.5 billion in planned international financing if the parliament misses deadlines for required legislation.
The government has moved its deadline for 42 required decisions to Oct. 15 as it prepares for winter pressure on the budget.
According to the European Commission, the Ukraine Support Loan was adopted in February 2026, and it provides up to €90 billion (approx. $100 billion) over 2026-27, with an indicative €60 billion ($67 billion) for defense and €30 billion ($33 billion) for the budget.
The Council approved this year’s allocation on April 23 after Ukraine submitted its financing strategy.
Since 2022, the EU and its member states have provided €231.5 billion ($258 billion) in total support to Ukraine, including €3.8 billion ($4.2 billion) from proceeds of immobilized Russian assets.

Its 15-member crew was safely evacuated to the Port of Varna, with five receiving medical assistance.

The human toll has also grown, with 28 of the 37 reported maritime fatalities recorded in 2026 alone, the association said.
The changing nature of the conflict is reshaping the Black Sea into a "multilayered security environment," said Murat Ersavci, a retired ambassador and director of the International Studies Center at the Economic Policy Research Foundation of Türkiye.
He said in a recent assessment for the foundation that the boundary between trade and security was becoming increasingly blurred, adding that a ship's destination, flag, and links to particular companies and sanctions regimes are also becoming part of the security equation.
Ersavci called for a comprehensive maritime security arrangement to ensure safe, predictable commercial navigation, distinguish civilian vessels from military targets, and coordinate efforts among littoral states to protect energy and food shipments.
Canan Tercan, a foreign policy expert at Istanbul Aydin University, warned that the Black Sea risked mirroring the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz, where prolonged disruptions have jolted global markets and driven up insurance costs.
Meanwhile, Tercan warned that bringing outside warships into the basin could trigger a wider conflict. "Navigational safety must be secured through an international non-combat agreement, not through naval forces." ■

-- Iran has offered to mediate. Foreign Minister Seyed Abbas Araghchi told his Saudi counterpart Sunday that Tehran was ready to assist in launching Saudi-Houthis talks toward a political solution.
Iran's stance reflects both influence and limits. Though Tehran has long-standing ties with the Houthis, analysts say the group pursues its own agenda rather than taking orders. Abdul-Ghani Al-Iryani, a senior researcher at the Sana'a Center for Strategic Studies, told Xinhua the Houthis were signaling to Riyadh that they act in their own interests.
"Iran does not need to control every Houthi decision to benefit from its influence," Yemeni political analyst Muqbil Naji noted. "By offering mediation, Tehran can turn that influence into diplomatic leverage while keeping itself at a distance from direct involvement."
Al Jazeera, citing political analyst Negar Mortazavi, said Iran was seeking to link the Houthi-Saudi conflict to a broader deal with the United States, with Tehran's political objective being "an informal non-aggression arrangement between Iran and its allies on one side and the United States and its regional partners on the other."
-- Israel, meanwhile, has reportedly sought a military opening. Israeli newspaper Haaretz reported Monday that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu sought Saudi approval, through U.S. mediation, for Israel to join operations against the Houthis, a proposal Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman rejected.
Citing sources, the report said Israel believed such cooperation could strengthen ties with Riyadh and advance normalization. Saudi authorities have not commented publicly.
Riyadh insists that normalization with Israel remains tied to resolving the Palestinian issue. The reported overture highlights the gap between shared security concerns and political alignment, analysts say.
"A shared threat can create common interests, but it cannot erase political barriers," Naji said. "Israel may see the crisis as an opening toward Riyadh, while Saudi Arabia has to weigh the wider political cost."
-- Türkiye and Pakistan have taken a third path via the Mecca Alliance for Defense. On Oct. 5, the three members agreed to deploy agreed forces and capabilities to Saudi Arabia in response to Houthi strikes.
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan reaffirmed Ankara's support for Riyadh Tuesday, while Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif reiterated Islamabad's support for Saudi Arabia's right to self-defense Wednesday.
How far those commitments will go remains unclear. Reports have alleged Pakistani participation in strikes against Houthi targets, but Islamabad has denied its jets conducted cross-border operations. Türkiye, meanwhile, is expected to focus largely on defense technology and technical support, while any overseas troop deployment requires parliamentary authorization.
Analysts say Turkish and Pakistani capabilities could strengthen Saudi air and missile defenses and counter-drone systems without drawing either country deep into the conflict. The alliance thus lets Ankara and Islamabad demonstrate solidarity with Riyadh while limiting their exposure to another open-ended Yemen campaign.
-- Washington perhaps harbors the most difficult calculation. U.S. President Donald Trump said Tuesday that the Houthis were "behaving very badly" and accused them of seeking to drive up oil prices ahead of U.S. midterm elections, highlighting Washington's concern that the confrontation could ripple into global energy markets.
The Trump administration faces pressure to back a key regional partner, but another direct campaign carries uncertain costs after past U.S. military action failed to eliminate Houthi long-range strike capabilities.
Analysts see little U.S. appetite for a prolonged confrontation, yet warn that continued attacks on critical Saudi infrastructure could narrow Washington's room for restraint.
"Washington would prefer to contain the crisis rather than inherit it," Naji said. "But that calculation becomes harder to sustain if the conflict begins imposing greater costs on Saudi security, oil markets or U.S. interests." ■

Roundup: German economic recovery slows in Q3 as inflation pressures mount
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
02:58:31 CST
03:58:31 KST

BERLIN, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- Germany's economy got back to a recovery path after stronger-than-expected growth in the first half of the year, but appears to have lost momentum again in the third quarter, the government said in an assessment released Wednesday.
In its monthly report, the Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy said the recovery likely slowed temporarily in the third quarter, dragged down by sluggish industrial activity, weaker exports and subdued domestic demand.
It pointed to fading demand for energy-intensive goods, which had supported industrial output and exports earlier in the year, as well as inland shipping disruptions caused by low water levels over the summer.
Citing the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis) data, the ministry said industrial rebounded 2 percent in August after a 1.2-percent decline in July, driven largely by a surge in construction output that partly reflected the completion of a major energy infrastructure project.
New industrial orders, meanwhile, plunged 10.6 percent month-on-month in August, largely due to a sharp drop in large-scale contracts for transport equipment including ships and military vehicles after an exceptionally strong July.
Such orders have been a major source of volatility in German industrial demand and output as Berlin has ramped up debt-funded spending on infrastructure and defense this year, giving much of the industry a significant boost.
Business surveys have also pointed to an overall industrial recovery. After contracting for much of the past three years, Germany's manufacturing Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) rose back above the 50-point threshold separating expansion from contraction this year, standing at 53.9 in September, slightly down from August's 51-month high of 54.3.
However, the ministry cautioned that underlying industrial demand remained weak. Excluding large-scale contracts, "the downward trend since spring had not been reversed," it said.
The German Chamber of Commerce and Industry (DIHK) echoed concerns over the lack of a broad-based recovery. Jupp Zenzen, an economic expert at the chamber, said much of this year's industrial momentum had come from defense spending, while manufacturing orders had stagnated for months once large-scale contracts were excluded.
"Broadly, economic momentum is lacking," Zenzen said, calling for structural reforms to boost Germany's industrial competitiveness.
Meanwhile, Germany's exporters are facing renewed pressure after a strong first half of the year, when shipments were boosted in part by front-loaded demand linked to the Middle East conflict. Exports fell for a second straight month in August, according to Destatis.
Citing surveys by the Munich-based ifo Institute, the ministry said weakening expectations in key sectors, including the auto industry, and shipping disruptions caused by low water levels on inland waterways were likely to weigh on exports, pointing to slower third-quarter growth.
Adding to the woes of a fragile recovery, a surge in energy prices has fueled renewed inflationary pressures, straining households and businesses further.
Destatis data released Tuesday showed Germany's inflation rate climbed to 3.3 percent in September, the highest level in nearly three years, from 2.9 percent in August and 2.8 percent in July.
Energy prices jumped 14.9 percent year-on-year in September, their sharpest increase since February 2023, as higher fuel and heating oil costs pushed up consumer prices.
The Economy Ministry warned that consumer prices were expected to keep rising into winter, mainly due to persistently high energy costs. It also noted signs that businesses were increasingly passing higher costs on to consumers.
To ease the burden, the government introduced temporary fuel tax cuts on Oct. 1, aimed at lowering petrol and diesel prices by around 17 euro cents (0.19 U.S. dollars) per liter through the end of the year. The move is expected to shave around 0.1 percentage points off inflation in the fourth quarter, the ministry said.
Berlin also plans to introduce a temporary fuel price cap by January 2027, as part of broader efforts to shield households and businesses from high energy costs.
Despite these measures, the government's autumn economic forecast, released last week, projected that inflation would accelerate from 2.2 percent in 2025 to 2.7 percent this year, before rising further to 3 percent in 2027, largely driven by surging energy prices.
Persistently high corporate insolvencies remain another concern for Germany's recovery.
Citing the latest figures from the Halle Institute for Economic Research (IWH), the ministry said insolvencies rose 9.2 percent month-on-month in September to 1,666, up 13.4 percent from a year earlier. In the third quarter, insolvencies hit their second-highest quarterly level since 2005, it said. ■

News Analysis: Houthi attacks expose Saudi air defense limits, highlight need for regional security mechanism
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
02:58:14 CST
03:58:14 KST

CAIRO, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- Recent Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia have renewed focus on the limits of Saudi air defense systems and underscored the need for a regional security mechanism, observers have said.
SAUDI AIR DEFENSE BREACHED
Saudi Arabia operates advanced air defense systems, including U.S.-made Patriot and Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) systems. Yet even sophisticated defenses face operational and economic constraints when confronting repeated attacks by the Houthis involving mixed missile and drone threats.
The challenges stem partly from the kingdom's vast territory and the wide range of potential targets, from civilian infrastructure to key economic facilities, analysts note. Defending against multiple threats from different directions places heavy demands on surveillance networks, command systems and interceptor supplies, said Egyptian military expert Samir Ragheb.
Ragheb explained that low-flying drones and cruise missiles are hard to detect early, while ballistic missiles pose a different challenge: their speed and flight trajectories allow them to ascend to extreme altitudes, sometimes beyond the atmosphere, before descending rapidly, leaving air defenses with a narrow response window.
He estimated a ballistic missile could reach Riyadh from Yemen in roughly seven minutes, underscoring the critical need for early warning, rapid coordination and timely interception.
The use of relatively inexpensive drones against costly air defense systems also presents an economic challenge during prolonged attacks, the expert said, noting interceptors are expensive and stocks are finite, making it harder to match defensive responses to different types and scales of threat.
Ragheb said integrated command systems, layered long- and short-range defenses, and improved surveillance and early-warning could help Saudi Arabia use its capabilities more efficiently. Cost-effective counter-drone systems would also ease pressure on expensive interceptors, he added.
REGIONAL SECURITY MECHANISM NEEDED
The challenges have added urgency to regional security efforts. Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Türkiye signed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement on Aug. 7, under which an attack on one member is seen as an attack on all.
The three countries on Oct. 5 agreed to provide agreed forces and capabilities and facilitate their rapid deployment in Saudi Arabia in response to intensified Houthi strikes on Riyadh. Yet no details on specific forces, systems, or timelines were disclosed.
Meanwhile, Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty said in a Bloomberg TV interview on Tuesday that Cairo would respond positively to Saudi requests and seriously consider joining the pact.
"Countries participating in the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement are likely to deploy air defense systems and fighter aircraft in Saudi Arabia as integral components of the kingdom's defensive network," Ragheb said.
Egyptian researcher on Arab and international affairs Mostafa Amin said closer security cooperation should be assessed not only by military capabilities but also by its contribution to regional stability.
Amin said Saudi Arabia could improve its ability to detect and intercept aerial threats while channeling closer regional cooperation into a stabilizing force.
"The two tasks are closely connected but require different approaches. Better sensors, layered defenses and more efficient use of interceptors can reduce the vulnerability of critical facilities, while regional consultations and diplomatic engagement can help limit the risk of further escalation," Amin said.
"Lasting security will depend both on adapting to evolving military threats and on whether regional powers can turn their growing cooperation into effective mechanisms for preventing conflict," he concluded. ■

UNITED NATIONS, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- The Security Council on Wednesday adopted a resolution to renew the sanctions regime on Haiti for another year.
Resolution 2831 extends the sanctions regime, which includes an arms embargo, travel ban and assets freeze measures, for one year from the date of the adoption of the resolution.
It reaffirms the Security Council's decision that UN member states shall take appropriate steps to prevent the illicit trafficking and diversion of arms and related materiel in Haiti.
The resolution calls on member states that transfer firearms, ammunition and related materiel to relevant Haitian authorities, either by sale or donation, to support those authorities in strengthening physical security, stockpile management, and post-delivery controls to mitigate the risk of diversion.
It calls on the Haitian authorities to strengthen their weapons and ammunition management and to reinforce border and customs controls.
In addition, it confirms that the multinational Gang Suppression Force (GSF) in Haiti should support the Haitian National Police and the Haitian armed forces to record and dispose of illicit arms, ammunition and other materiel, seized as part of offensive operations or in the course of carrying out its mandate.
It further calls on the GSF to report any diversion of weapons and ammunition, including through loss and theft, to the Panel of Experts that assists the Sanctions Committee.
The resolution also extends the mandate of the Panel of Experts for a period of 13 months from its date of adoption.
It requests the panel to provide an interim report to the Security Council by March 28, 2027, and a final report no later than Sept. 1, 2027.
Resolution 2831 was adopted with 14 votes in favor among the 15 Security Council members. Russia abstained.
The Security Council introduced sanctions against Haiti in October 2022. ■

The experts love to say that Americans don’t vote based on foreign policy, but it doesn’t take much digging to conclude that isn’t always true.
Sure, U.S. voters are probably thinking primarily about domestic issues when they go to the polls, but there have been a number of big elections in which war has undoubtedly been a major factor.
The Iraq War was the definitive issue of the 2008 Democratic primary, when then-Senator Barack Obama (who opposed the war) beat then-Senator Hillary Clinton, who voted for it. In 2016, Trump generated support by railing against “endless wars” and calling the U.S. invasion of Iraq “a big, fat mistake.” Most recently, Kamala Harris’s refusal to oppose the Gaza genocide helped seal her 2024 loss.
It’s hard to believe that foreign policy won’t be a major factor in November’s midterms, as Trump’s disastrous war on Iran continues to spin out of control with no discernible signs of an exit strategy.
At the beginning of the summer, it seemed that the administration was on the verge of securing an agreement, but its inability to restore the Strait of Hormuz to its pre-war status simply generated a series of botched negotiations and idle threats.
Americans are enduring astronomical gas prices, but they’re also seeing another “Forever War” potentially take shape, and although the Trump team has sought to censor details on the war, news about the scope of the conflict has inevitably trickled out.
A recent Congressional Research Service report reveals that 81 U.S. military aircrafts have been destroyed or damaged in the war. The Intercept’s Nick Turse points out that the Pentagon quietly raised its official count of U.S. casualties to 21, a full six months after Maj. Sorffly Davius died while “conducting operations” at Camp Buehring in Kuwait. According to estimates by Moody’s Analytics’ chief economist Mark Zandi, the war has cost U.S. consumers $265 billion so far, which is roughly $2,000 for every household.
An extensive Drop Site News investigation into the February 28 attack on a Minjab school revealed that at least 156 people were killed, 120 of them children.
“Why is [Trump] saying Iran may have bombed their own people when we can see the wreckage of Raytheon cruise missiles in the photos that we obtained that were taken from under the rubble?,” journalist Jeremy Scahill, who led the report, told NPR. “There were two direct hits on a school filled with children and teachers. It’s not that there hasn’t been reporting on this. It’s that reporting has not been translated into a very robust, aggressive investigation of what I would say is one of the worst single war crimes committed by the United States since Vietnam.”
Polling shows that war was unpopular with the U.S. population from the beginning, but recent surveys show that approval has continued to plummet. According to the Pew Research Center, just 34% of Americans believe that attacking Iran was the right decision, down from 38% in March. That shift has come entirely from Republican voters. 63% of them now believe it was the right call, compared to 69% who believed that in March.
This reality has forced some Republicans, like Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers and Ohio Sen. Jon Husted, to walk a tightrope between calling for an end to the war and remaining loyal to the President.
“The war can no longer be treated solely as a matter of executive decisions and geopolitical calculations,” writes political scientist Brian Hudson. “Responsibility extends beyond the White House to lawmakers who have supported its continuation, remained silent, or used party unity as a substitute for public debate. Accountability is no longer simply an external demand imposed on the party; it has become an internal issue affecting its credibility and cohesion.”
It’s also become an issue that Democrats can pin on the opposition party.
“It’s less Iran in particular than it is this notion of never-ending conflict and war in the Middle East, which Americans are so done with,” declared Rep. Jason Crow, who is demanding answers on a U.S. airstrike that killed at least 5 people attending a wedding in Iran. “It is very salient.”
This week, Democratic challenger Troy Jackson hammered GOP Senator Susan Collins (D-ME) on the issue during a debate, pointing out that the longtime incumbent voted for the war multiple times, despite currently expressing a desire for it to end.
“The reason why our fuel prices is going through the roof, and the way our — the reason why our electricity costs are going through the roof is because the cost of fuel, cost of oil is so high, because she wouldn’t stop President Trump with the Iran war,” he told the crowd.
Conservative W. James Antle III, Executive Editor of The Washington Examiner Magazine, writes that Republicans were always expected to lose some seats as an extension of being in power, but that anger over the war could sustain a massive electoral shellacking.
“Thanks to the Iran war and its fallout, there is a potential for a midterm election more like 2006. Twenty years ago, as Cook Political Report’s Amy Walter pointed out earlier this year, we had an unpopular president waging an unpopular war while Republican congressional incumbents were beset by assorted scandals,” he writes in Responsible Statecraft. “Today, the public has even less patience for the current war than in 2006.”
The reality is that the GOP is headed for a potential disaster in a few weeks, thanks in no small part to Trump’s terrible war.

NIH appears to shut down comments on science peer-review rule change ahead of schedule

03:55:23 KST

Members of the public who tried to submit their views on a proposed change to the National Institutes of Health’s grant funding system say they found themselves locked out after the system shut down ahead of schedule.
The proposed change has been criticized as potentially reducing transparency. It seeks to revise how grant application scores—averaged measures of a research project's predicted outcomes—are communicated to both funding applicants and NIH program officers.
Under the change, applications would be sorted into three broad categories of merit, while their overall score, as determined by a panel of experts, would remain a secret. Some researchers have said this could open up the grant approval process to undue political influence.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Ahead of any rule change, the NIH invited members of the public to have their voices heard by submitting comments through a website portal, which opened in August. On a version of the site soliciting comments stored on the Wayback Machine, the deadline is shown as “11:59:59 P.M. EST [sic]” on October 13. The system for sending in comments appeared to shut down hours early, however, with several scientists posting on social media that when they tried to submit comments ahead of that time, they were unable to do so. Speaking to Scientific American, Joshua Weitz, a biology professor at the University of Maryland, says he attempted to access the site before the midnight deadline and could not.
The proposal marks the latest attempt by the Trump administration to have greater influence over federal science grants. Floated earlier this year, a separate bid to have political appointees—rather than independent expert panels—decide grant recipients garnered significant backlash. That earlier proposal was put on hold until at least December after Congress rejected the change.
The NIH did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Spain’s Socialists widen lead in state poll as housing dominates election debate

2026-10-14
18:54:35 UTC
03:54:35 KST

Alyssa McMurtry
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
Spain’s ruling Socialists widened their lead over the conservative opposition in a state poll released Wednesday, contrasting with other surveys that favor the right ahead of a snap election dominated by the housing crisis.
The Center for Sociological Research (CIS) put Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s party at 34%, nearly 12 percentage points ahead of the Popular Party (PP), compared with a 5.5-point lead last month.
The Socialists gained three points while the PP fell to 22.2%. Far-right Vox remained third with 17.1%, followed by the Socialists’ coalition partner Sumar at 6.1% and left-wing Podemos at 3.1%.
Together, the three left-wing parties would receive around 43% of the vote, roughly four points more than the PP and Vox combined.
The survey comes amid public anger over the eviction of Maricarmen Abascal, an 87-year-old woman forced out of the home she had rented for seven decades who died two weeks later.
Her case sparked protests and encampments in Madrid and other cities, intensifying demands for action over housing costs and evictions.
Sanchez announced the Nov. 29 election after parliament rejected two government housing decrees.
Spain’s largest unions, CCOO and UGT, have also called a general strike for Nov. 11 to demand better wages and affordable housing, two days before the official election campaign begins.
Wednesday’s survey underscored the scale of concern, with a record 55.7% naming housing among Spain’s main problems, far ahead of immigration and the economy.
Anomalous poll
However, the CIS findings contrast sharply with other polls suggesting the conservatives and far right could win enough seats to govern together.
A 40db survey for El Pais and Cadena SER conducted after the election announcement gave the PP and Vox a combined lead of about 15 points over the Socialists, Sumar, and Podemos.
Public broadcaster RTVE’s polling average likewise projected a comfortable parliamentary majority for the PP and Vox, with a combined 202 seats in the 350-seat lower house.
The divergence is not new. An El Pais analysis of 44 elections since 2018 found that CIS surveys overestimated support for the left in 43 of them.
Its final poll before the 2023 general election came close to the Socialists’ actual vote share, but incorrectly predicted they would finish ahead of the PP.
The latest CIS survey was based on 5,025 interviews done in early October.

In Ukraine, civilian casualties were already rising. Restrictions on Starlink will only worsen the death toll
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
18:54:34 UTC
03:54:34 KST

In Ukraine the situation was already jittery enough. Donald Trump has been inventing ceasefires and buying Russian diesel to shore up his flagging popularity, while a sinister new wave of faster, jet-powered drones are breaking through Kyiv’s stretched air defences. Casualties are rising as the weather turns.
Overnight, Russia bombed three power plants that supply Kyiv, aiming to cut off heating and electricity to the city. According to the president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, for a second night in a row no warning came from Ukraine’s western allies of the incoming ballistic missiles – and so no air raid alert was issued.
Then, on Tuesday night, and without warning, Ukraine’s military found that Elon Musk’s Starlink mobile internet system, on which it heavily relies, had stopped working on its drones flying faster than 160km/h (100mph).
Or at least that was the official limit: in practice, drones flying over 80km/h could no longer communicate.
The immediate assumption in Kyiv is that the White House is once again trying to bully Ukraine into accepting an unattractive deal with Russia.
However, on Tuesday Trump did say that no intelligence-sharing had been paused, and similar comments were made by Mark Rutte, the secretary general of Nato on Wednesday. It is possible the lack of ballistic warning is coincidental.
Even Serhii Beskrestnov, Zelenskyy’s high-profile military technology adviser, has expressed public doubts about whether the US had paused the sharing of missile detection. “Friends, this is not the first time that the launch of an S-400 has not been detected,” he posted on Monday. “We should not jump to conclusions.”
However, there has now been an absence of incoming warnings for two days in a row. The second of these was in tandem with the unexpected throttling of Starlink, a system supplied by Musk with the approval of the US military.
So it is hardly reassuring against the backdrop of White House threats, which have emerged every time a flailing Trump has tried to end the war in Ukraine.
The last time Trump paused intelligence-sharing – which is, in effect, valuable information about Russian positions and movements – was in March 2025, shortly after Zelenskyy’s infamous dusting down in the Oval Office.
“You don’t have the cards,” Trump said, as he took another away. Ukraine rapidly lost a chunk of territory it had occupied in Russia’s Kursk region before sharing was restored.
A confirmed pause this time would mark a serious breach when Ukraine is more than holding off its larger neighbour on the frontline, even as the situation on the home front is worsening.
Russia has bombed two bridges in Kyiv, gas stations, city centre buildings and out-of-town warehouses, showing little restraint as it aims to harm Ukrainian civilians while it struggles to win the conventional war.
The effect of a more permanent halt to Starlink for Ukrainian drones or anything military that moves faster than 50mph is a little more complex. Starlink is how Ukraine directs many of its mid-strike (or mid-range) drones accurately towards their targets into occupied areas behind enemy lines, critical for helping the defenders maintain the rough balance on the front.
Yet, ironically, Starlink is not used for the long-range missions that target the Russian oil refineries about which Trump is so concerned, because it has long been disabled by the company inside Russia’s internationally recognised borders.
“There’s no meaningful effect on deep-strike operations,” one Ukrainian soldier said, while conceding there could be as much as a 30-fold drop in mid-strike operations because the alternatives are 30 times more expensive. Commanders are “replanning everything”, the soldier added, and aiming to find ways to carry on missions using different technologies and techniques.
Starlink is also, more importantly – as Beskrestnov emphasised on Wednesday – used by air-defence interceptors in the most effective system to down Russia’s deadly new jet-powered Shahed drones. These are at least twice as fast as traditional piston-engined Shaheds, and Ukraine’s rate of interception had dropped to 60% in September, before recovering to 75% according to the country’s air force.
The reality, then, is that the Starlink manoeuvre may not have much impact on oil prices, and only a limited effect on Ukraine’s frontline position, while putting the country’s civilians in greater danger.
As the Ukrainian human rights activist Oleksandra Matviichuk put it: “Without that protection, Russian drones will strike residential buildings, hospitals and schools like targets in a shooting gallery.”
Meanwhile, diplomatically, the situation is more finely poised. It was already the case that the Trump White House had proved to be a difficult and unreliable partner. What Zelenskyy, on a visit to London on Wednesday, needs from the likes of the UK prime minster, Andy Burnham, is pressure on the US to ensure the Starlink pause and whatever is happening with intelligence-sharing does not metastasise into a deeper crisis.

French President Emmanuel Macron believes the students waging three weeks of protests that have closed many schools have "legitimate" grievances but are also being "exploited" by political forces, a government spokesperson has said.
The leader, who is in his final six months of office, has asked the government to come up with "concrete responses" to the unrest by high school pupils within weeks, spokesperson Maud Bregeon told reporters on Wednesday.
She spoke following Macron's weekly meeting with his cabinet, a day after nationwide solidarity demonstrations showed significant support for the students.
The interior ministry said 161,500 people turned out for Tuesday's demonstrations held in Paris and other cities. Unions organising the rallies put the figure at 480,000.
Some violent scenes erupted on the sidelines of marches in Paris and Lyon, with police firing tear gas in response.
In his cabinet meeting, Macron "stressed that young people have legitimate concerns, but said these are being exploited for political purposes and turned into urban violence", Bregeon said.
With French presidential elections due in April and May next year, some opposition parties have seized upon the demonstrations.
Jean-Luc Melenchon, the presidential candidate for the far-left France Unbowed (LFI) party, participated in one of the Paris protests.
The far-right National Rally (RN) party of Marine Le Pen, leading opinion polls, has voiced support for police deployed to the demonstrations and blamed students for violent episodes.
Alleged police brutality
Students, unions, rights groups and parents have accused the police of brutality against the students, with some of the young protesters maimed.
The family of one 15-year-old high school student who lost his hand when a police stun grenade exploded on Wednesday said they had started legal action to demand an "impartial" investigation.
One of the family's lawyers, Bertrand Wattez, said the boy, Evan, denied the police account, relayed by prosecutors, that he had tried to pick up the grenade when it went off on October 5. He also denied taking part in the student protests in his city of Lens.
The lawyer said that Evan not only lost his left hand as a result of the blast but also several fingers on his right hand.
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said on Wednesday that 248 students had been injured during the protests, "most often in cases of urban violence".
A total of 937 police officers had also been injured, as had 149 members of teaching staff, Lecornu told a parliamentary question session.
The premier alleged that the student movement had been "instrumentalised by the allies of France Unbowed... for electoral reasons".
8,000 arrests
The justice ministry said that nearly 8,000 people had been arrested since the protests started in late September.
It said a total of 7,950 people were apprehended, 85 per cent of them minors, with charges laid against 2,735 of them. Twenty-six people were remanded in custody.
In another violent incident, a 16-year-old student was blinded in an eye during a September 30 protest outside his school in the western city of Tours. His family blamed the police.
Late Tuesday, the prosecutor for Tours said the officer involved had been charged with aggravated battery.
Police have opened internal investigations into 36 allegations of officer violence against demonstrators, according to the interior ministry.
Late Wednesday, the police union Alliance said it had lodged a lawsuit against the government for "putting lives in danger" over what it termed "contradictory orders" given to officers deployed in the protests.
A statement said that officers felt "betrayed" by their political leaders because of their "unclear instructions" and what they said were public expressions of "empathy towards the rioters".
French authorities have expressed hope that the student protest movement would ease in coming days because of two weeks of school holidays that start at the weekend.
The government said 2,000 of 3,000 substitute teachers promised for 114 of the country's worst-affected schools had already taken up their positions.
Education Minister Edouard Geffray told parliament that a third of France's 3,700 lycees, high schools for students aged 15 to 18, had been strongly impacted by the protests, with another third impacted to a limited degree.

Instead it was Netanyahu’s policies over several years that had “increased the dangers posed by terrorist organisations in Gaza”, it said.
Bar resigned in June 2025, saying at the time that “all the systems collapsed” in the security agency and that Shin Bet “failed to sound the alarm”.
But Bar said he was resigning to take responsibility as head of the organisation and insists he did warn Netanyahu before Oct 7 of potential threats linked to Hamas.
Bar is seeking three million shekels (around S$1.2 million) in damages from Netanyahu.
Bar said he telephoned the prime minister’s military secretary as soon as signs of a possible attack came up but that he did not have Netanyahu’s direct number.
“Ronen, are you serious?” Netanyahu responded in a statement issued by his Likud party on Oct 14.
“You had my number on the red line and could have called me immediately, as all security chiefs do.”
“How many lives could we have saved if only you had called in time?” he asked.
Hamas stormed into Israel with pickup trucks and paragliders and opened fire at sites including a music festival. The attack resulted in the deaths of 1,221 people, according to an AFP tally from official Israeli figures, with militants also dragging 251 hostages into Gaza, 44 of them already dead.

One interviewee in the film said: "After October 7, everyone kept saying, 'There are no innocent people in Gaza.'
"This notion spread throughout the army, and suddenly we are toppling entire buildings. It wasn't even an issue."
The Israeli Defense Forces (IDF) have released a statement on their website, calling NAZA a "manipulative depiction of reality"
The statement also says the filmmakers did not accede to the IDF's request they submit any allegations to them for examination and response before the documentary was published.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has threatened to strip Abraham and Sozr of their citizenship and pursue defamation charges.
The filmmakers have been unable to return to Israel and are residing in the UK.
It took Abraham and Sozr three years to gather the NAZA interviews and research from more than 100 confidential sources.
"We've made sure that every major claim in the film has multiple sources, in some cases more than a dozen sources who are backing up that claim," Abraham told the ABC.
"So, we feel very confident about the truth of what the soldiers are saying in the film."
What is NAZA?
NAZA is an Israeli military acronym for collateral damage, or, according to one interviewee, the number of civilians likely to die from a strike.
"We say 15 NAZA. We don't say 15 people killed and certainly not that 15 children and women will be killed. We say 15 NAZA."
Another interviewee asserts that Israeli forces work off "NAZA maps" that allow them to see potential civilian bombing victims.
"Twenty NAZA became the benchmark. We'd take down lower ranks in Hamas without a second thought. They were official orders," he said.
Another interviewee said he was part of a strike that involved the approval to kill 500 civilians "for one human target".
"The targets are like a video game because everything is done remotely," he said.
Many consider themselves "cogs" in a machine, stuttering or falling silent when Abraham pushes them to recognise the numbers as human lives.
"One soldier in the film says, 'No matter what we do, they deserve it,'" Abraham says.
"There's something about when so many people in society normalise this violence. Soldiers talk about it in the film, that [the dehumanisation] becomes like the water you swim in."
What is Lavender?
NAZA interviewees explain how the IDF uses an AI system called Lavender to process huge amounts of surveillance data to identify bombing targets.
Every building in Gaza is numbered, and every storey in every building is accounted for.
Targets for large-scale attacks are identified via the Lavender algorithm.
One interviewee said Lavender had earmarked up to 70,000 phone numbers.
"Every such phone that we located, we could bomb," he said.
But he said Lavender "made a lot of mistakes".
"It once marked an 80-year-old woman. They bombed her house with her entire family in it. This bothered the intelligence community on a professional level," he said.
"The intelligence officer said he was willing to risk being wrong 15 per cent of the time."
Where's Daddy?
A section of NAZA titled Where's Daddy? details the military "consensus" to use surveillance data to target private homes at night.
"There is a serial number for every private home in Gaza … 'Where's Daddy' is a mechanism of alerting us when an operative comes home. We'd spy on the family to know when the father comes home," one interviewee said.
"I hack into the phone of a 12-year-old girl. If a girl says, 'Mummy, when are you returning home? Daddy just came back', that's a message that would alert the system because it contains the words 'return' and 'daddy.'"
"You hack into her phone and then kill her."
Another interviewee said: "We would use the phones of family members to hear them in their homes before bombing it.
"I'd hear the final moments of a person's life."
One man described searching for photos of a Palestinian man's house in his phone's photo gallery to find bombing access points. Instead, he found a selfie of the man with his two daughters, smiling on his balcony.
"The IDF bombed that place, but he had already left his apartment and only forgot his phone there. The two girls were there … I saw that these were little girls between three and six years old," the interviewee said.
"I remember I heard a woman crying and screaming on the phone that her daughter's body was burning. The daughter was still alive, she was begging someone to come save her."
The man confirmed the girls died. He was unsure what happened to their father.
Loss of 'international legitimacy'
Some interviewees corroborate UN reports, including those related to the forced displacement of civilians.
"At one point the army decided to flatten entire areas … inside my unit the destruction was viewed as strategic," an interviewee said.
"The goal was to try and destroy as much as we can before we lose international legitimacy. We 'cleaned' it — you wouldn't even believe there was ever civilisation there.
"I sat in meetings with senior officials talking about moving the whole population from northern Gaza to the south with no intention of allowing them to return. We would burn every house we entered. Every house. It didn't matter. We wanted to make sure they wouldn't return."
Loading...
An interviewee said Palestinian civilians were killed if they crossed into an unmarked zone the IDF had claimed.
"No-one was ever armed. Whoever you decided to kill was considered a terrorist … we never collected the bodies. The dogs eat them," he said.
Another corroborates UN reports of Israeli snipers shooting Palestinians lining up for food distribution.
Towards the end of the documentary, an interviewee tries to reconcile his view of what the Nazis did with his own actions.
"I thought they were just pure evil, but today I understand it. I understand how a man can blow a place up and go home to his degree in clinical psychology. I still see those Nazis as evil, but what does that mean I am?" he says.
Abraham says his aspirations for NAZA extend beyond Palestine and Israel.
"It's helpful to understand the mechanisms that allow individuals to participate in such crimes because they are universal mechanisms," he says.
"It's not an evil that is only rooted in something connected to Israel or the Israeli society — it's something that has occurred and will re-occur throughout history.
"We should try to understand how human beings can do this to other human beings, because that is one of the ways in which we can hopefully prevent or minimise the chance that these things will happen again."
What is Israel's response?
Netanyahu has called for the prosecution of the 24 interviewees in NAZA, who he has accused of spinning "a false, misleading and biased narrative".
Abraham said the reaction would have a chilling effect on journalism.
"[For] Netanyahu … it's about making sure that there will be no more Israeli soldiers and officers who do this again, who will speak out about what they've seen," he said.
After NAZA's Venice premiere, the Israeli government promoted a film titled Naza: The Real Story, which mimics the rooftop interviews of Abraham and Sozr's documentary and claims Israel has "the most moral army in the world".
"It's a bit frustrating. They're free to make any film they want, but it's misleading because they made it the same title and the same on the rooftops and it's clear they're trying to mislead audiences into thinking that the film that they've made is our film," Abraham said.
"Listen to the testimonies of the soldiers in our film, and you're free to listen to the more spokesperson version of that and make up your mind which sounds more credible and which testimonies match what we've seen on the ground in Gaza more.
"To me, I think the answer is quite obvious."
NAZA will open in select Australian cinemas from October 15 before being released in totality for free via The Guardian's website in late November.
No Israeli cinemas have agreed to show it.
Abraham says it would be an exaggeration to say "the society is beginning to reconcile or reckon with what has happened in Gaza", but that among the denials and death threats the filmmakers have received, he has seen "small cracks" of anger and outrage.
"I'm not naive," he says.
"I know the overwhelming majority reaction is going to be hostile, but I'm hopeful that these small cracks in the walls of denial will perhaps widen a little bit more."

Yusuf Alioglu and Rania Abushamala

Yemen’s Houthi group said Wednesday that it had hit the main airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh with a ballistic missile.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group’s forces struck King Khalid International Airport “with a ballistic missile, scoring a precise and direct hit.”
Saree did not specify when the attack took place or provide details of possible casualties or damage.
The announcement follows 10 attacks on five Saudi airports on Oct. 5-11 that killed 20 people and injured hundreds, while causing property damage and disrupting flights, according to an Anadolu tally based on official statements.

It remained unclear whether Wednesday’s Houthi announcement referred to an earlier attack or a new operation.
The developments come amid continued military escalation between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis since July, including attacks on civilian aviation facilities and energy infrastructure.
Saudi Arabia has led a military coalition supporting Yemen’s government against the Houthis since 2015. The group has controlled the capital Sanaa and several provinces since 2014.

ParaMatildas hunt more Australian football history at World Cup
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
18:43:42 UTC
03:43:42 KST

ParaMatildas out to defend IFCPF World Cup title in Atlanta
In short:
The ParaMatildas are looking to defend their IFCPF World Cup title in Atlanta after winning the 2024 tournament.
The Pararoos are also searching for a breakthrough top-10 finish in the men's competition.
What's next?
The ParaMatildas will begin their group stage against Ireland on Saturday morning, with the Pararoos getting underway against Brazil on Friday.
The ParaMatildas begin the 2026 IFCPF World Cup in uncharted territory for an Australian football team.
At the 2024 tournament in Spain, the side broke through as the nation's first-ever winner of a round ball World Cup.
Now, the players are aiming to become the first Australian team to successfully defend a world title.
It has been a rapid ascent for the side, only officially launched in 2022, but coach Charlotte Ercil said her players were comfortable with added expectation.
"I think it adds a little bit of pressure, but it's exciting at the same time," Ercil told ABC Sport.
"But we always prepare like every game, including our first group game, is the World Cup final."
The ParaMatildas, and their male counterparts, the Pararoos, play football designed for athletes with cerebral palsy, acquired brain injury and symptoms of stroke.
The sport features smaller fields and goals as well as shorter halves than in the mainstream game and does not include the offside rule.
This month's tournament in the US city of Atlanta will be just the third instalment of the Women's World Cup and the first edition to be held outside Spain, while the Pararoos are hopeful of a best-ever finish in the concurrently running men's competition.
In the brief international history of the women's game, Australia and the US have emerged as its two great powers, with the ParaMatildas going down to the stars and stripes in the final of the 2022 tournament before exacting revenge in the 2024 decider.
Getting one over the Americans in their own backyard looms as the ultimate test for the ParaMatildas, and Australia central defender Eloise Northam does not doubt the hosts' motivation to reclaim their crown.
"I feel like they definitely are plotting against us," Northam told ABC Sport.
"I think that's what we were doing back in like the second World Cup — we were ready to take on the US and take their championship away from them."
The ParaMatildas are also wary of the sport's expanding talent pool. The growth of the global game means that teams and tactics are evolving rapidly, while players with newly acquired brain injuries are constantly welcomed into the fold.
Australia will face Ireland, the Netherlands and newcomers Colombia during the group stage.
"Every year or every time we interact with or play against any country, there are always changes and improvements, which is good for the game; it means it's growing," coach Ercil said.
Throw in lingering summer temperatures as well as the possibility of severe thunderstorms, and the ParaMatildas are taking nothing for granted in the American south.
The Pararoos, meanwhile, are bullish on progressing from a difficult group featuring Brazil, Spain and Chile.
The Australian squad for the tournament comes with bucketloads of experience, with 11 of the 14 players selected having previous World Cup experience.
One of those returning athletes is Taj Lynch, who believed his side was now well placed for a breakthrough top-10 finish.
"I feel confident in the players we're taking across; a lot of us have been there before," Lynch told ABC Sport.
"We've learned a lot, we've got a lot of things wrong, but we've grown, and we've improved.
"We're not a team of boys playing against men anymore. I think we're finally starting to be a team of men who can take on the best teams in the world."
Captaining the Pararoos in Atlanta is Australian football legend David Barber.
The veteran debuted for Australia in 1999, and will overtake Andorra's Ildefons Lima as the male player with the longest international football career when he steps out for the Pararoos' tournament opener against Brazil.

Florence’s ‘Maricarmen’: 94-year-old faces losing her home of 60 years as rent nearly triples
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
18:43:01 UTC
03:43:01 KST

The elderly widow, almost blind and using a walking frame still does not know about the eviction; her daughter says her story echoes Maricarmen, a symbol of Spain's fight for housing.
A 94-year-old woman in Florence faces losing the home she has lived in for more than 60 years after her landlord said her rent would rise from €450 to €1,200 a month.
Franca’s contract expires in February, and her family says she will not be able to afford to renew it on the new terms. Her case closely echoes that of María del Carmen Abascal, known as Maricarmen, the 87-year-old who became a symbol of the fight for housing in Spain after a steep rent rise led to her eviction in Madrid. She died in hospital a few days later.
"My mother gets a minimum pension and my father’s survivor’s pension. If she had to pay €1,200 in rent, she would be left with practically nothing to live on, not even enough to eat," her daughter told Corriere Fiorentino (source in Italian).
She has asked not to be named because she has not yet been able to bring herself to tell her mother.
The 70-square-metre flat has been Franca’s home since the early 1960s. She lived there with her husband, and her daughter was born there. According to her daughter, it is the only place her mother feels truly at home, filled with photos of her grandchildren, paintings of Florence’s narrow streets and mementoes from her daughter’s wedding.
The building contains several flats, all owned by the same landlord. It was once home mainly to Florentine families, many of whom had lived there for generations, but the tenants have changed over the years.
As far as her daughter knows, the flats are not being turned into holiday lets and remain ordinary residential tenancies. She believes, however, that the new management wants to squeeze far higher returns from the properties.
"They phoned me to tell me they would not renew the contract for my mother," she told the newspaper. "The contract was renewed every two years. They let me know that, for her to stay there, the rent would have to go up to €1,200 a month. But how can you ask for that kind of money from a 94-year-old pensioner?"
The family accepts that the rent cannot stay the same forever, and her daughter says she would help cover an increase so her mother could spend her final years at home.
"We could manage a small increase, I could help her out. But going from €450 to €1,200 is something else altogether. It is an impossible amount. And what pains me is that there was not even any chance to open a proper negotiation, to try to meet halfway."
She has since turned to the tenants’ union Sunia for help.
Franca’s case comes amid a wider squeeze on tenants in Tuscany, where 2,427 eviction orders were issued in 2025. Florence accounts for around 35% of all enforcement requests filed in the region.
