Ukraine’s Warships Join Forces With Britain’s Powerful HMS Dauntless in Major Naval Drills
Five Ukrainian Navy minehunters completed a seven-day training exercise off the southern coast of England, conducting live-fire drills, underwater mine disposal operations, and coordinated maneuvers alongside the British Royal Navy destroyer HMS Dauntless.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the Royal Navy on October 12, the training marked the final phase of Exercise Lion Protector, a multinational military exercise organized by the UK-led Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF) to strengthen maritime security and protect critical infrastructure across northern Europe.
The Ukrainian vessels—Henichesk, Mariupol, Melitopol, Chernihiv, and Cherkasy—are currently stationed in Portsmouth as part of Britain’s ongoing military assistance to Ukraine.
Training operations took place in waters near Dorset, Hampshire, and the Isle of Wight, where Ukrainian crews practiced naval gunnery, formation sailing, and the detection and neutralization of underwater explosives.
One of the principal components involved the SeaFox mine-disposal system, a remotely operated underwater vehicle designed to identify and destroy naval mines.
The system uses sonar and onboard cameras to examine suspected explosive devices. Its mine-disposal variant carries an explosive charge, allowing operators to destroy identified threats remotely through a fiber-optic control connection.
The Ukrainian minehunters Chernihiv and Cherkasy conducted live SeaFox operations, successfully destroying simulated mine threats through controlled underwater explosions.
The exercise concluded in the eastern Solent, where all five Ukrainian vessels sailed in close formation with HMS Dauntless, a Type 45 air-defense destroyer. The maneuver tested the Ukrainian crews' ability to coordinate movements and operate safely alongside a significantly larger warship.
The naval training formed the fifth and final stage of Lion Protector, which ran from August through October 2026 and involved forces from the 10-member Joint Expeditionary Force. The training also supports Ukraine’s preparations for future mine-clearance operations in the Black Sea.
Earlier, Ukraine considered deploying its UK-based minehunters to help clear naval mines from the Strait of Hormuz as part of a potential British-French-led operation. The proposal emerged as Ukraine’s warships remained unable to enter the Black Sea due to restrictions under the Montreux Convention.

The IDA Türkiye Defense and Aviation Industrial Cooperation Days summit kicked off in Ankara on Wednesday, gathering global sector representatives to facilitate industry partnerships.
The event was organized by the Ostim Defense and Aviation Cluster (OSSA), with support from the Turkish National Defense Ministry and the Defense Industries Agency (SSB). Anadolu serves as its global communications partner.
Ibrahim Yarsan, chair of OSSA, said at the event’s opening that the event has been rebranded since its 2013 launch to reflect its expanding global mission.
He said the cluster currently includes 359 firms, most of them small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) that form the key supply chain powering major defense firms.
“This event is not just a trade show but a business development gathering,” he said, noting that IDA has facilitated over 8,000 one-on-one business meetings over the years.
“We’re taking it to the next phase, with the first step being IDA Spain,” he added. “We want Turkish firms to work more closely with Spanish firms and we have a key collaboration that began in Valencia, where we will hold the event next year.”
Orhan Aydin, chair of the Ostim Organized Industrial Region, said that Türkiye’s successful domestic defense production model is now being adapted to civilian sectors.
Aydin said that enforcing domestic contribution requirements similar to the SSB’s model enhanced Turkish industries’ capabilities to produce homegrown light rail vehicles, metro cars and high-speed trains with the participation of defense contractors such as Aselsan.
Seyit Ardic, president of the Ankara Chamber of Industry, said that the technological know-how gained through innovations in artificial intelligence (AI), autonomous systems and advanced materials can be brought to the civilian economy to improve efficiency.
“We must look at the success of Turkish defense and benefit from the technological and efficiency gains it brought across the entire industrial sector,” he said.
He suggested establishing a healthcare industries directorate to transfer strategic know-how gained in the defense sector to help accelerate domestic production in healthcare.
He added that efforts are underway to integrate more firms from the machinery, electronics and software sectors into high-value defense projects.
Gursel Baran, president of the Ankara Chamber of Commerce, said that Türkiye’s defense industry reached a domestic content rate of 80% as of this year, while defense and aerospace exports rose from $248 million in 2002 to $11 billion as of August 2026.
He noted that some 4,000 firms active in the sector manage over 1,400 ongoing projects and employ 100,000 workers, while annual research and development (R&D) spending in the sector reached $3.5 billion.
“A technology developed in the defense industry is used in many fields, ranging from automotive to healthcare, from communications to energy, and from transportation to space exploration,” he said. “Defense industry investments are also invested in the country’s scientific knowledge, production capacity, skilled workforce, and economic future.”
The IDA Türkiye 2026 summit will conclude on Friday.

UN peacekeeping chief says talks on future of Lebanon mission must begin soon

Unknown Publisher

UN peacekeeping chief says talks on future of Lebanon mission must begin soon
BEIRUT, Oct 14 - UN peacekeeping chief Jean-Pierre Lacroix on Wednesday urged the UN Security Council to begin negotiations on the future of peacekeepers deployed in Lebanon, as Beirut campaigns for an extension to the mandate set to expire at the end of this year.
A UN peacekeeping force known as UNIFIL has been deployed in southern Lebanon since 1978 but the Security Council last year ordered the mission to begin withdrawing at the end of 2026.
Since a new war erupted in March between Israel and Iran-backed Lebanese armed group Hezbollah, the Lebanese government has campaigned for an extension to UNIFIL's mandate, citing its role in monitoring hostilities and facilitating aid deliveries to villages in Israeli-occupied zones.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres earlier this year presented proposals for a continued uniformed UN presence in Lebanon but no action has been taken yet, Lacroix told Reuters in Beirut.
"These proposals are on the table of the Security Council. There has been no movement in the Security Council until now, but I believe that the negotiations will begin ... shortly, in earnest," he said.
"I think it would be better to have a decision soon rather than later, right? Because that would clarify also the horizon for us, certainly from the more limited point of view of our own planning," he said.
FORCES OPERATE HOTLINE TO EASE TENSIONS
Diplomats say the US is not supportive of an extended mandate for UNIFIL, but Lacroix said it was important to focus on Lebanon’s request and that negotiations at the Security Council could yield a constructive outcome.
Some 7,500 UNIFIL peacekeepers are still deployed at about 50 positions in southern Lebanon, which would be expected to be handed over to Lebanese army troops if no new UN force is agreed.
But since most of those posts lie in territory now occupied by the Israeli military, it remains unclear how Lebanese soldiers could deploy to take over the positions.
Lacroix said that clarity on whether a new UN force would deploy to southern Lebanon would help UNIFIL make sure it does not "leave those positions prematurely before we know what could come next".
In addition to facilitating aid deliveries and monitoring hostilities, the force operates a hotline to ease any tensions between the Lebanese and Israeli militaries.
Lacroix said the deconfliction role was particularly crucial given the presence of Israeli troops in a self-declared security zone deep in Lebanese territory.
He said that Israeli and Lebanese troops in the same geographic area presented "the risk of escalation, the risk of incidents getting out of control" and that "there is a need for a third party to de-escalate". REUTERS

Microplastics are linked to inflammation—scientists might have finally worked out why
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
18:02:43 UTC
03:02:43 KST

Microplastics are a source of extreme concern for health: the presence of these tiny pieces of plastic has been linked to heart attacks, stroke, dementia and brain tumors. But what drives these associations is unclear. Now a study published in Nature offers a tantalizing clue: microplastics interact with water, generating highly reactive molecules.
When microplastics come into contact with water, the water near their surface can become chemically active, generating highly reactive species that can modify nearby substances, including biologically important molecules.
As plastics wear down to microscopic sizes, their surface-to-volume ratio increases dramatically. For example, when a credit card is fragmented into particles some 10 microns in diameter, there is a more than 200-fold increase in its surface area, says Wei Min, a chemist at Columbia University and one of the senior authors of the study. As a result, any chemical activity is amplified.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Min and his colleagues examined various microplastics—including polystyrene, polyethylene, polyvinyl chloride, polypropylene and polyethylene terephthalate. Plastic surfaces are hydrophobic, meaning they repel water, Min says. Thus, water molecules cannot form the hydrogen bonds they maintain in liquid form. That changes molecular arrangements, and, in turn, the change influences the local electrical environment and chemical reactivity.
The presumed chemical inertness of bulk plastics overlooks the toxicity of their fragmented microscale forms. “For microplastics, this is especially important because fragmentation creates enormous amounts of new surface area,” Min says.
In past research, microplastics have been shown to cause inflammation, oxidative stress and decreased mitochondrial activity. The new study provides a possible mechanism for this, showing that plastic-water interfaces can perturb proteins, cell membranes, and more.
How this might contribute to damage in living tissues in humans is still unclear, Min says. “Ultimately, we hope to connect fundamental interfacial chemistry with quantitative measurements of biological effects, which would help us better understand potential health risks,” he adds.
Martin Wagner, a toxicologist and a biologist at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology, who was not involved in the new work, says the study’s findings are exciting. The paper gives scientists a new way to look at the effects of plastic pollution, Wagner says. “It implies microplastics themselves are a source of oxidative species ... and oxidative stress is not a secondary effect of exposure.”

Lisa Cook lawyer doubts Trump committee's fairness as president calls her 'automatic no vote'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
18:02:17 UTC
03:02:17 KST

An attorney for Lisa Cook voiced strong doubts that President Donald Trump's committee investigating mortgage fraud allegations against the Federal Reserve governor would be fair and objective.
The lawyer, Abbe Lowell, said the committee is plagued by issues that undermine the appearance of the Fed's independence, including "demonstrably biased members" and "unspecified additional allegations" against Cook.
Those and other issues "would have to be addressed before a hearing could occur" in the probe, Lowell wrote in a letter sent Tuesday to Will Scharf, Trump's aide and counsel.
No such hearing could take place until at least December, weeks later than the initially scheduled date, Lowell insisted.
The letter came three days after Trump slammed Cook as "dishonest" and griped that she was an "automatic no vote" — apparently referring to her opposition to cutting interest rates, which the president strongly desires.
Cook last voted to cut rates in December 2025, siding with the majority. The Fed unanimously voted to raise rates after its most recent meeting in September.
"She shouldn't be in an important position," Trump said of Cook in those remarks to reporters after returning from a rally in Tennessee on Saturday.
White House spokesman Matthew Middleton said in response to Lowell's letter that Trump "is performing his constitutional duty in evaluating Lisa Cook's conduct and eligibility to continue serving as a governor on the Federal Reserve."
"The Constitution charges the President with ensuring that the laws are faithfully executed and that the conduct of members of the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System is above reproach," Middleton said in a statement.
An in-person hearing at the White House is currently scheduled for Nov. 5, according to Trump's Oct. 7 presidential memo establishing the "committee of inquiry" into Cook.
Cook's lawyers did not immediately rule out participating in that hearing, and in fact said the Fed governor "welcomes the opportunity to present the facts so she can clear her name," despite their concerns.
But in Tuesday's letter, Lowell said Cook cannot attend a hearing on Nov. 5 because she "will be executing her official duties as Governor at financial and monetary policy meetings in Europe."
After that, Cook will immediately start preparing for the next meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee in early December, Lowell said.
The White House did not immediately respond when asked by CNBC if the scheduled hearing would be moved in light of Cook's alleged scheduling conflicts.
Lowell also said he needs time to speak with Cook about issues raised by the White House's most recent correspondence, as well as to prepare her for any possible hearing, "which, because of her being in Asia on Federal Reserve duties, cannot be done until she returns."
"With all of that (and court hearings I have scheduled in November), the earliest date for any hearing would need to be in December following the FOMC meeting," Lowell wrote Scharf.
Trump established the three-member committee two months after reviving his long-running effort to fire Cook, an appointee of former President Joe Biden, from the central bank's board of governors.
The Supreme Court in late June blocked Trump's first attempt to remove Cook, ruling that she was not given sufficient due process under federal law. But that decision did not stop Trump from trying again.
Middleton said in his statement, "The President is going beyond what the Supreme Court required by offering Lisa Cook an in-person hearing that will be conducted in a fair and open process."
But Lowell wrote Tuesday, "We have significant concerns regarding the objectivity and fitness of the committee," which comprises three executive branch officials, including top Trump economic aide Kevin Hassett.
Hassett "already has publicly insinuated that the President has 'cause' to fire Governor Cook," Lowell noted, citing the economic advisor's comments from August 2025.
Hassett in those remarks also accused Cook of "making a partisan stance contrary to the independence of the Fed" by refusing to step aside while a Justice Department investigation played out into the mortgage fraud allegations, which Cook denies.
The comments suggest Hassett has already prejudged the case, Lowell told Scharf, "surely belying your assertion that the 'hearing' as proposed would be 'substantive and fair.'"
"A hearing with demonstrably biased members, unspecified additional allegations, and an unclear schedule for the disclosure of any additional evidence – with no explanation for why it was not previously produced – is not a process that respects the appearance or history of independence," Lowell wrote.

====================================================================================================

How war with Iran is influencing Israeli, US elections - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
18:00:55 UTC
03:00:55 KST

Many and varied are the reasons so many people are looking forward to October 28, the day after Israel’s elections, and November 4, the day after the US midterms.
One reason is that election campaigns do not exactly bring out the best in people, and the end of the campaigns in both countries will put an end to bitter partisan rhetoric that only deepens the divides and fuels antagonism.
Campaigns are not great unifiers, and both countries could use more unity. If that is too much to ask, then a little less divisiveness would also be welcome.
Another reason is that war and elections do not go well together. When the two overlap, it becomes difficult to tell what is driving what: Are electoral considerations shaping military decisions, or are battlefield developments shaping the elections?
Sometimes, both.
The first question is particularly pertinent in Israel, where any military action taken now, justified or not, will be viewed through the prism of the campaign. If Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu launches an attack against Iran because of steps it is taking or contemplating, a significant part of the country will inevitably see it as an attempt to sway the vote.
Netanyahu pushed Trump to resume strikes on Iran before elections
Consider Israel’s bombing of Iraq’s nuclear reactor in 1981, just over three weeks before that year’s election. The operation was successful, but Labor leader Shimon Peres accused prime minister Menachem Begin of timing it to boost Likud’s electoral prospects. Its proximity to the vote cast a political shadow over an extremely consequential military decision.
Conflicting reports of discussions between Netanyahu and US President Donald Trump illustrate the problem.
On Tuesday, Channel 12 reported that Netanyahu had repeatedly urged Trump to renew attacks on Iran before Israel’s October 27 election and the US midterms a week later. According to the report, Netanyahu cited concerning Iranian nuclear developments, while American officials came away with the impression that he wanted action before the elections.
The Prime Minister’s Office denied that Netanyahu was seeking to start a war before the vote. Netanyahu reportedly told Israeli security chiefs that Trump, not he, had initiated the discussion about renewed fighting before the elections.
A Maariv report over the weekend presented another version: Washington had pressed Israel to strike Iran alone, leaving Israel to assume the political risks of an operation that could have negative consequences for Trump ahead of the midterms.
According to that report, American officials believed Israel would be interested in striking before its own election. The report also said Washington had since backed away from the proposal.
Who was pushing whom? For what reason? And why before the elections?
The reports do not provide a settled answer. They do, however, show how thoroughly the electoral calendar has become entangled with discussion of military action.
There is another layer. Channel 12 reported that Israeli security officials saw no change in the intelligence assessment of Iran that would justify a joint operation in the coming two to three weeks. The same report said IDF Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir warned that renewed fighting could postpone the Israeli elections.
That possibility adds fuel to an already combustible debate. Netanyahu’s opponents have long warned that he might initiate a major military campaign to delay the vote.
And the problem is not confined to Iran.
On Tuesday, Netanyahu visited the seam line in the West Bank and warned that Israel’s enemies were thinking of testing it before the elections. He said the military was prepared for various scenarios, including Palestinian security forces turning their weapons against Israel.
That is a serious threat, one the military needs to prepare for regardless of the date. But when the prime minister explicitly links a security warning to the approaching elections, the political interpretations quickly follow.
Is he deterring an attack? Demonstrating his security credentials? Preparing the public for military action?
Those possibilities are not mutually exclusive. That is precisely what makes the mix so difficult to sort out.
Then there is a question often lost in the argument: Would an Israeli-initiated military operation necessarily help Netanyahu?
Danger comes when every security decision is viewed as a campaign maneuver
If it were successful, it could reinforce one of his strongest electoral assets: his record of confronting Iran. But if it went badly, brought Israeli casualties or dragged the country into another prolonged conflict, the political effect could be very different.
Starting a military operation doesn’t guarantee an electoral dividend. Its outcome matters, as does whether the public believes it was necessary.
Still, until the vote is behind us, any major operation will face an additional question alongside the military ones: Why now?
That question is legitimate. The danger comes when suspicion overshadows everything else, and when every security decision or warning is seen as a campaign maneuver. Israel’s enemies do not suspend their activities because Israelis are going to the polls. On the contrary, they sometimes step up their activities.
A government must remain able to respond, but it must also be able to explain why a response is necessary now.
Then there is the other direction of influence: military action designed to affect an election – an overriding concern now in the US.
Trump has said he will not resume attacks on Iran before the November 3 midterms, ostensibly to avoid shocks to the oil market. The last thing he needs before Americans vote is a sharp rise in gasoline prices.
Iran understands that vulnerability as well.
Reuters reported Wednesday, citing two senior Iranian officials, that Iran was deploying new tactics to target ships sailing through the Strait of Hormuz, seeking to keep oil prices high and influence the US election.
The Iranians would plainly welcome a Republican drubbing and Democratic control of Congress, hoping that a strengthened opposition would make it more difficult for Trump to pursue the war against them.
According to Reuters, Iranian officials are explicitly linking pressure on shipping to the American electoral calendar. The aim is to have developments in the Gulf felt at the American gasoline pump, and then at the ballot box.
Which brings us back to those eagerly awaited mornings after the elections.
October 28 and November 4 will not remove politics from decisions about war. Nor will they resolve the threats posed by Iran or Israel’s other enemies.
They will, however, remove the immediate electoral deadline that now hangs over those decisions and over every interpretation of them.
Until then, voters need to keep two questions in mind: Is military action necessary, and is it happening now because an election is approaching?
The answer could be both, but in the heat of an election campaign and amid heightened regional tensions, the two become difficult to untangle.

====================================================================================================

Psilocybin, LSD, and 2C-B leave different fingerprints on the brain, new study suggests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
18:00:28 UTC
03:00:28 KST

A new study in rats suggests that three classic psychedelics, psilocybin, LSD, and 2C-B, produce distinct patterns of brain energy use, both immediately and a week after a single dose. The findings, published in Nature Communications, challenge the common practice of treating these drugs as interchangeable, though the authors stress that any implications for treating specific mental health conditions remain speculative.
Scientists classify psilocybin, LSD, and 2C-B as serotonergic psychedelics because they all bind to the serotonin 2A receptor, a specific protein on the surface of brain cells whose activation is linked to the altered states psychedelics produce. Because they share this primary target, these drugs are often grouped together as potential treatments for mental health conditions like depression and anxiety.
But their chemical structures differ, and they interact with other brain receptors in distinct ways. A 2023 review argued that while these drugs all stimulate the serotonin 2A receptor, their varying interactions with other biological targets could allow them to affect the brain quite differently.
To map these effects, researchers often track how the brain consumes energy. Brain cells use glucose, a simple sugar, for fuel, so measuring where glucose goes can reveal which brain areas are highly active and which are quiet. A 1997 study in humans used this technique, called positron emission tomography or PET, to show that psilocybin increased activity in the frontal cortex.
The research team was led by Mikael Palner, an associate professor at the University of Southern Denmark and head of the Palner Lab, alongside first author Frederik Gudmundsen, now a postdoctoral researcher at Aarhus University Hospital. “This was the idea of Frederik Gudmundsen, who was a PhD student in my lab at the time,” Palner told PsyPost. “After discussing it back and forth a lot and seeing that many papers and researchers were combining these psychedelic drugs into one bucket we knew we had to test the hypothesis, that serotonergic psychedelics are not just one drug class, but quite distinct drugs.”
The researchers wanted to see if psilocybin, LSD, and 2C-B produce similar or different metabolic patterns over time. They focused specifically on two interconnected webs of brain regions. The first is a network linking the outer layer of the brain to deep structures that regulate movement, habits, and compulsive behaviors. The second is a system spanning memory and emotion centers that is involved in fear and anxiety.
Understanding how different drugs alter these networks could provide a biological map for matching specific psychedelics to specific psychiatric disorders. In related work, a study covered by PsyPost in 2026 found that a single dose of psilocybin reduced depression-like behavior in rats for up to 12 weeks, alongside lasting increases in the excitability of prefrontal brain cells.
To test the effects of the three drugs, the researchers divided 48 rats into four groups of 12. Three groups received a single injection of either psilocybin, LSD, or 2C-B, while the fourth group received a saline injection as a control. The researchers gave the rats doses of psilocybin (1 milligram per kilogram), LSD (0.3), and 2C-B (3). In a separate group of nine rats, they confirmed that these doses occupied 51 to 70 percent of serotonin 2A receptors, a level associated with intense psychedelic effects in humans.
Finding the right dose to mimic the human experience yielded an unexpected result. “We compared three different drugs that are often used in humans: LSD, 2C-B and psilocybin,” Palner explained. “One thing was a big surprise and that is how much LSD we need to give a rat per body weight compared to a human.”
Scaled up by body weight, the rat dose would equal about 200 times a typical human dose. “The dose of LSD is 0.3 mg/kg in the rat; in a 70 kg human that’s 21 mg LSD (a regular dose is 0.1 mg),” he continued. “We don’t know why, but the rat has several protective mechanisms towards neurotoxins that may play a role.”
“The dose issue above is a common flaw in animal research with psychedelics and other neuropharmacological drugs for that matter,” Palner added. “One can’t just extrapolate the dose per kg and give the same to a rodent. We need to measure target effects and estimate the correct dose to translate between rodents and humans.”
Each rat underwent three PET scans: a baseline scan before receiving any drugs, an acute scan shortly after the injection, and a long-term scan one week later. During each scan, the rats were injected with the radioactive glucose tracer and allowed to remain awake in their cages for 45 minutes while their brains absorbed the fuel.
Afterward, they were temporarily anesthetized and placed in a PET scanner for 35 minutes to image the tracer’s distribution. The researchers also examined how strongly activity levels in pairs of brain regions tended to rise and fall together across the rats in each group, a rough indicator of how those regions work together.
Because all three psychedelics reduced overall glucose tracer uptake across the brain, which the authors suspect may partly reflect reduced blood flow, the researchers mathematically adjusted the data to look at relative changes. They calculated how much glucose each specific brain region absorbed compared to the rest of the brain. This adjustment allowed them to spot localized spikes or drops in activity relative to the animal’s global brain metabolism.
The acute scans showed that each drug produced a distinct metabolic signature. Psilocybin led to a relative increase in energy use in the dorsal striatum, a deep brain structure involved in habit formation, as well as in the insula, an area linked to emotional processing and bodily awareness. Unlike the 1997 human study, the researchers found no psilocybin-related changes in frontal regions in rats, and a possible strengthening of the link between two frontal areas did not hold up after statistical correction.
In contrast, LSD was associated with widespread decreases in metabolism across the outer layer of the brain, alongside increased activity in the midbrain and emotional centers like the amygdala and hypothalamus. 2C-B shared some features with LSD, including decreased frontal cortex activity and increased activity in midbrain areas that produce dopamine, a chemical messenger linked to reward and motivation, but its midbrain increase was larger and formed a distinct hotspot in a whole-brain analysis. 2C-B and psilocybin both increased activity in the insula.
A week after the single injection, the immediate spikes and drops had mostly faded, but some distinct network changes remained. Psilocybin left a lasting trace of increased metabolism in the insula and strengthened the link between activity in the insula and the prefrontal cortex, the only such network change in the study that held up after statistical correction. Psilocybin and LSD, but not 2C-B, also showed modest lasting decreases across several cortical, limbic, and midbrain areas.
For LSD, most acute metabolic changes had faded by one week, and a possible change in coordination between the cortex and the striatum did not hold up after statistical correction. The drug 2C-B left lasting effects primarily in dopamine-producing midbrain regions, without the sustained cortical effects seen with the other two drugs.
The authors offer what they describe as purely speculative ideas about therapeutic matching. Given their effects on the insula, psilocybin and 2C-B might suit disorders involving anxiety or disturbed bodily awareness; psilocybin’s tentative effects on links involving the orbitofrontal cortex, a frontal region, might make it suited to impulse-control conditions such as obsessive-compulsive disorder; and LSD’s effects on circuits linking the midbrain and striatum might suit substance use disorders. Overall, the results point to drug-specific brain responses rather than a single, universal psychedelic effect.
“Understand that just because one psychedelic drug is reported to do something to your mental health, it’s not necessary that others do the same,” Palner emphasized. “I think with the increased focus and ease of legislation this will be really important to understand.”
“I hope this is taken further and we will see that the right drug is given to the right patients,” he continued. “Whether it’s LSD or psilocybin for depression or anxiety. We need to do the comparison at some point.”
In earlier work, Palner’s lab found that repeated low doses of psilocybin made rats more resilient to stress and reduced compulsive behavior. “We are especially interested in dose reduction and finding the right drug, as our prior experiments with psilocybin microdosing were also interesting,” Palner noted.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. Because the measurements were relative to each brain’s overall average, an apparent increase in one region could partly reflect decreases elsewhere. Each drug’s effects were also measured against the same rats’ own baseline scans; the paper does not report statistical tests comparing the drugs directly with one another. And the drugs occupied somewhat different shares of serotonin 2A receptors (51 to 70 percent), so some differences could reflect intensity rather than drug identity.
The study was also small, with 11 or 12 rats per group, and most of the network changes did not survive correction for multiple comparisons. “This is a small study, yet still significant, meaning that the distinct effects are quite robust, otherwise they would drown in noise,” Palner noted. “With rodent work we must balance ethics and significance and justify how many subjects we included.”
Finally, the study was conducted in healthy rats, and no behavior was measured, meaning the links to specific mental health conditions cannot be directly tested here. The emotional and psychological experiences of a psychedelic trip cannot be measured in animals, so the behavioral impact of these metabolic changes remains a topic for future study.
“This was a huge team effort and so many talented young researchers were involved,” Palner said. “I really want to thank them for their time in my lab and wish them all the best in their next adventure.”
Palner disclosed owning shares in Compass Pathways and ATAI, companies developing psychedelic treatments.
The study, “Serotonergic psychedelics induce distinct patterns of metabolic activity and covariance within biologically informed rat brain networks,” was authored by Frederik Gudmundsen, Julia Czurylo, Daniel R. Rijsketic, Camilla Trang Vo, Janika Fortunato, Naja S. Jessen, Sophie Woodruff, Christina Baun, Matthias M. Herth, Vladimir Shalgunov, Boris D. Heifets, Patrick M. Fisher, and Mikael Palner.

This strange sea animal is on menus, but it is disappearing from our reefs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

Sea cucumbers can live 100 years, but may not survive our hunger
The alien-looking sea cucumber is a delicacy eaten in soups or consumed for its perceived health and libido benefits.
But a boom in demand since the 1980s has led to overfishing and population collapses in parts of the world, including the Pacific.
Entire species are disappearing from remote Australian reefs, with illegal fishing pointed to as a key culprit.
And there are now concerns that regulators for Australia's legal sea cucumber fisheries are underestimating how long it takes fished stocks to recover.
A new "first-of-its-kind" genetic study, published in iScience, indicates at least one sought-after sea cucumber species lives longer than we thought.
Study lead author and molecular ecologist Sven Uthicke, from the Australian Institute of Marine Science, said the black teatfish (Holothuria whitmaei) could reach 100 years of age.
It was assumed the species, found in Australia's tropical waters but less so in other Pacific countries, only lived five to 20 years in the wild.
Dr Uthicke said the finding meant fishery management needed to revise whether current catch limits were sustainable.
"They're currently assuming that these animals are replaced, basically, 10 times more than they are likely to be,"
he said.
The age a marine species reaches is a major factor for calculating a fishery's environmental sustainability.
Dr Uthicke said the sustainable catch limit for black teatfish and similar species might be lower than we thought.
What are sea cucumbers?
Sea cucumbers are part of a large group of "spiny skin" animals that includes starfish and sea urchins.
Colours and patterns of their leathery skin range from plain browns to vibrant reds and yellows.
Sometimes they have alien-like mouth tendrils, which are actually modified "feet".
Sea cucumbers are believed to benefit the health of coral and seagrass meadows.
"We don't necessarily understand all the ecological services that sea cucumbers provide, but we do know that they are very important in aerating sediment," CSIRO marine ecologist John Keesing said.
Much is still unknown about these weird animals, with few studies into basic biology like how long they can live.
How old do sea cucumbers get?
In the new study, Dr Uthicke revisited a no-fishing zone near Lizard Island in the Great Barrier Reef 24 years after another study he did into the growth rates of black teatfish.
He was surprised to find 31 out of the 76 sea cucumbers from his earlier fieldwork in 2000.
"I'm pretty sure a few of those were over 50, 60 years old,"
Dr Uthicke said.
"We still don't know how fast they grow because the individuals in my study basically did not grow at all over the entire 25 years … and we didn't find any small ones."
As the research was only conducted in one location, Dr Uthicke said other locations and species could be looked at.
But, he said, regulators could use the current findings to manage stocks more conservatively.
Black teatfish stocks have previously collapsed at the Great Barrier Reef and Zenadh Kes (Torres Strait).
As black teatfish are considered globally endangered, the federal environment department has to sign off on any fishing regimes occurring in Australia.
The species is not caught in the regulated Western Australia or Northern Territory sea cucumber fisheries, but it is caught in Queensland fisheries.
A Queensland Department of Primary Industries spokesperson said a recent stock assessment for black teatfish indicated the species was being fished at sustainable levels.
"Future stock assessments will consider all new, relevant information."
An Australian Fisheries Management Authority spokesperson said the new research would be considered when advice was developed for future management settings in the Torres Strait.
They said a past CSIRO survey in 2019–20 found the black teatfish had significantly recovered from historic overfishing and was safe to be fished under a strict harvest strategy.
"Black teatfish is an important source of income supporting livelihoods and the traditional way of life in the Torres Strait," the spokesperson said.
"Torres Strait Islanders have exclusive access rights to black teatfish, which is estimated to be worth over half a million dollars to the local economy."
How much do sea cucumbers sell for?
Dried sea cucumbers can go for hundreds of dollars per kilogram in domestic markets like Hong Kong.
A similar price bracket to other high-end produce like Wagyu beef and foie gras.
Sea cucumbers move slowly, so they are easy to pluck from the water by the basket-load.
Once caught, a sea cucumber is gutted, cooked, salted and dried.
"There's very few other animals that eat them," Dr Keesing said.
"That's the reason why they don't bother hiding themselves too much."
This vulnerability is thought to have led to local extinctions at remote Australian reefs.
Where sea cucumbers are disappearing already
A study led by Dr Keesing last year suggested the golden sandfish (Holothuria lessoni), which was once common at Ashmore Reef, has gone locally extinct, with overfishing the most likely cause.
The reef is located about 200km from Indonesia and 300km from the Kimberley region of Australia.
"Reefs like Ashmore Reef to the north are now sort of fished out so they're [illegal fishermen] looking further south," Dr Keesing said.
At the next reef down, Scott Reef, black teatfish and white teatfish (Holothuria fuscogilva) have reportedly collapsed.
Illegal fishermen have been intercepted as far south as Rowley Shoals, islands west of Broome, in recent years by federal authorities.
Another study earlier this year suggested the white teatfish was no longer in Rowley Shoals and three other species, including the black teatfish, were close to dropping under a critical population threshold for remaining viable.
"That level of fishing just over quite short a period of time has had a very significant impact on those populations," Dr Keesing, one of the authors, said.
"If that can be prevented by greater surveillance, greater consequences for being intercepted, then those populations should recover.
"If that's just allowed to continue … then potentially you could have the Rowley Shoals in the same state as Ashmore Reef."

Chalmers and Frydenberg have more in common than they like to admit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

analysis
From GST to trusts, reform is almost impossible in this fraught political climate
Jim Chalmers and Josh Frydenberg have more in common than they like to admit.
The two former (and perhaps future) rivals are both sharp media performers. Both are highly energetic and ambitious. Both have also had complicated relationships with their respective prime ministers.
And this week both have been reminded of the difficulty of pursuing policy reform.
In the case of Frydenberg, it was the mere suggestion of revisiting the GST as part of broader reform to make the tax system more efficient.
"We need a considered but ambitious national debate about lifting the GST and removing some exemptions, with a significant portion of that additional revenue to fund a major reduction in income tax," he wrote in his memoir, A Grateful Son.
It's hardly an original or radical idea, having been floated over the years by everyone from the Liberal luminaries who brought the GST to life, John Howard and Peter Costello, to corporate leaders such as Matt Comyn and David Thodey, and economists Richard Holden and Saul Eslake.
But Frydenberg's attempt to revive the debate was shot down instantly by Angus Taylor.
"We will not be raising the GST in the middle of a cost-of-living crisis," the opposition leader told Insiders. "We won't be raising taxes," he declared more broadly, which suggests the Coalition will instead seek to fund its growing list of expensive promises through spending cuts alone.
Not that Frydenberg is deterred. His book, and various media interviews this week weighing a potential political comeback, have received a mixed response among Liberal MPs in a party room that has shifted to the right since he was last there.
But the former treasurer is upbeat about the broader public reception. If anything, he's even more energised. And after planting the flag on the GST, Frydenberg isn't walking away from his argument about the need to tackle difficult reform.
Chalmers's difficult week
As for Jim Chalmers, reminders have been coming thick and fast, ever since the May budget, of how bruising reform can be.
After months of blowback over negative gearing and capital gains tax changes that weren't taken to an election, now it's trusts.
Labor is confident it will ultimately win the support of the Greens to impose a 30 per cent minimum tax on discretionary trusts, but fears this could be an even tougher fight than the earlier tax battles, particularly when small business is already angry over a separate matter — the Tax Office decision to ban credit card payments.
The week became even more difficult for Chalmers after the prime minister appeared to suggest he'd been sidelined.
After trying to settle the nerves of anxious Labor backbenchers in Tuesday's caucus meeting, the prime minister then appeared on stage at an Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (ACCI) dinner to claim credit for fixing the Tax Office problem.
"Andrew did text me last Thursday morning," Albanese said, referring to ACCI chief executive Andrew McKellar. "By Friday morning we had an announcement."
The comment not only created the impression Chalmers had been overruled, but it also suggested government positions could be quickly influenced by an industry group text message.
Chalmers, clearly, couldn't let that sit.
He then revealed he had in fact spoken to the prime minister a day earlier. "On the Wednesday I had discussions with the PM. We agreed it would be appropriate to find a better way through."
In other words, it was a joint decision taken between the two of them before the text message from Andrew McKellar.
Loading
Labor MPs divided on 'rift'
By Question Time yesterday, the prime minister was denying any rift, describing the decision as unanimous.
Tension between a prime minister and treasurer is nothing unusual, as Josh Frydenberg can attest. When it's publicly on show, that's a problem.
The opposition made the most of it, stirring both the prime minister and treasurer in parliament. Labor MPs, meanwhile, were divided.
Some reckon Chalmers should have seen the Tax Office troubles coming earlier. Others reckon it was a bit rich for Albanese to pass the buck after over-egging the benefits of removing credit card surcharges with a social media post suggesting "your morning coffee could be cheaper".
Either way, it's in the interests of neither to appear at odds.
Ultimately, Albanese and Chalmers agree on the big stuff. They both know the government is facing challenges. Both are confident Labor will be in a stronger position this time next year. And both agree sticking with the budget tax changes is the only course.
But delivering reform is proving more difficult by the day.
Late yesterday, the Coalition and Greens joined forces in the Senate to deliver a blow to the government on another front. They've sent Labor back to the drawing board on its plan to remove the more generous private health insurance rebate for over-65s.
That's another $3 billion savings measure up in the air.
As both Chalmers and Frydenberg would surely agree, there's no easy path to repairing the budget.
David Speers is national political lead and host of Insiders, which airs on ABC TV at 9am on Sunday or on iview.

Investing bonanza as younger Australians lean on AI advice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

AI, crypto and ETFs see record number of Australians investing outside of superannuation
In short:
The stock exchange operator says market participation is at a record high among Australians.
An ASX survey found 54 per cent of Australian adults hold investments outside their super and primary home.
What's next?
The ASX estimates 950,000 Australians who do not currently invest plan to start within the next 12 months.
A record 11.5 million Australian adults now hold investments outside their superannuation and their main home, a new survey by the stock exchange operator finds.
The ASX Australian Investor Study 2026 has revealed an estimated 2.5 million Australians have joined the investor population since 2020.
Investors, the survey showed, now represent 54 per cent of the adult population.
"Australia is a nation of investors," ASX chief executive Anthony Attia said.
Who are Australian investors?
Most investors were middle-income earners and middle-aged, with a median gross income of $110,000 and an average age of 46.
Younger people, aged 18–29, made up 21 per cent of investors.
For the first time, the ASX survey looked at how investors were using AI tools for investment information and advice.
The bourse said investors continued to use professional advisers, brokers, online investment platforms, family and friends, social media, podcasts and other digital sources.
It found AI uptake was strongest among younger investors, used by 14 per cent of investors aged 18 to 29.
Mr Attia said Australia's public participation in share trading was among the highest in developed markets.
The survey, which polled roughly 4,500 people in January and February this year, found shares were the most widely held assets, followed by residential property, exchange-traded funds (ETFs), term deposits and cryptocurrency.
"What is particularly encouraging is the next generation of investors entering the market,"
Mr Attia said.
"Almost 1 million more Australians are looking to start investing.
"The rapid growth of ETFs, with ownership more than doubling since 2020, shows how innovation is opening new opportunities for investors."
ETF boom as money pours into stocks
Since the ASX survey, money has continued to increasingly flow into ETFs.
Data from investment firm Betashares showed the Australian ETF industry experienced $7 billion in cash flowing in during September after monthly inflows surpassed $7 billion for the first time in August.
The industry hit a record $388 billion in assets under management.
Recent tax changes appear to be behind the enthusiasm for stocks in general, but ETFs in particular.
The government announced in the May budget that it planned to replace the current 50 per cent capital gains tax (CGT) discount with a discount based on the actual rate of inflation.
It also said it would introduce a minimum 30 per cent tax on gains from July 1, 2027.
Forager Funds chief investment officer Steve Johnson said ETFs were popular under the new settings as net gains and losses were contained inside the investment, so a surge in an individual company that might attract capital gains tax could be offset by another loss-making stock.
Betashares agreed investors had paid more attention to the relative tax effectiveness of index-based investment strategies and ETFs following the CGT changes.
The firm also said the continued fall in Australian house prices was giving investors more reason to look at other asset classes like shares, bonds and commodities.
Global X ETFs senior strategist Marc Jocum said the scale of investing over the past quarter had been "significant".
"Australian ETFs have just delivered a record $21 billion quarter, demonstrating that they are becoming a core building block in Australian portfolios," Mr Jocum said.
"Investors are no longer using ETFs for one purpose.
"They are using them to build the foundations of their portfolios, access opportunities around the world and create more diversified sources of growth and income."
Regulator watching market evolution
As more Australians turn to investing, more are exposed to digital assets including cryptocurrencies.
Corporate watchdog ASIC is looking to firm up the regulation of digital assets, today beginning consultation on guidance and standards to accompany new laws which commence on April 8, 2027.
ASIC wants digital asset platforms (DAPs) and tokenised custody platforms (TCPs) to hold an Australian financial services licence, provide customer disclosure documents and platform rules, and comply with asset holding standards, transactional and settlement standards, and net tangible asset requirements where relevant.
ASIC commissioner Alan Kirkland said that ASIC's proposal recognised the rapid evolution of global markets and "the increasing role of digital assets and tokenisation, including in traditional parts of the financial system".
"Our approach is based on the principle of 'same activity, same risk, same regulatory outcome' to align Australia with the approach of comparable overseas jurisdictions."
'Investors in waiting'
ASIC's job is only likely to get bigger with the pool of investors projected to keep expanding.
The ASX survey found an estimated 950,000 Australians who do not currently invest plan to start within the next 12 months.
Women, the survey showed, represented 61 per cent of this group.
Australians aged 18 to 29 accounted for almost four in 10 "investors in waiting".
The ASX said demand for financial advice was also increasing, with knowledge listed as the number one barrier to entering the market.

Where should Canadian Jews go? Where is the Promised Land? - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

A recent article in the Canadian newspaper The Globe and Mail by Marsha Lederman, titled “The Promised Land,” deals with Jewish Canadian concerns over the marked increase in antisemitism in Canada, particularly after October 7.
Anti-Jewish experiences have included the intimidation of Jewish students at all educational levels, harassment at Jewish events, physical assaults, arson attacks on Jewish businesses, and drive-by shootings at synagogues.
Very recently, a mass shooting on Yom Kippur at a small synagogue in Belleville, Ontario, was only prevented because of the presence of an armed police officer, a fixture at all synagogues and Jewish facilities in Canada. The shooter died, and the officer suffered serious wounds.
Lederman’s focus is a program called Lech L’Tulsa, initiated by the Jewish community of Tulsa, Oklahoma, to attract Canadian Jews to the city. It includes some financial help for those making the move. A description of the program also appeared in a December 2025 issue of the National Post, another Canadian newspaper.
Lederman points out that antisemitism is common in the US, as well as in Canada, and many American universities and cities are hostile environments for Jews. However, she also refers to “pockets of respite,” such as Tulsa and Florida, and this made me realize how little the Jewish world has changed over the centuries.
For much of the Middle Ages, and well into the Renaissance, the uppermost question for European Jews was, where to flee? Where could they be safe?
It is not a coincidence that the legend of the Wandering Jew, a Jew said to have taunted Jesus on the way to the Crucifixion, and was then condemned to wander the Earth until the Second Coming, originated in the 13th century.
England has the dubious honor of having been the first European country to expel all of its Jews, in 1290. The first blood libel also originated in England, in 1144. Other countries followed suit: France on three occasions (1182, 1306, and 1394), and Spain in 1492.
Germany was different because German unification did not happen until 1871. Until then, Germany was a patchwork of small kingdoms, principalities, duchies, and free cities. Jews expelled from one place could find sanctuary in a friendlier territory nearby.
For example, Glikl, the Yiddish memoirs of a late 17th-century Jewish woman, edited by Chava Turniansky and published in English in 2019, describes how the Jews of Hamburg were periodically banished from the city, but they could live in nearby Altona, which was under the more welcoming jurisdiction of the King of Denmark.
Similarly, Jews were banned from living in the city of Nuremberg, in Bavaria, for hundreds of years, but they could do business there, then return every evening to their homes in the nearby town of Fürth. In fact, Jews benefited from the first German railroad, a six-kilometer line built in 1835 to join Nuremberg and Fürth.
Moving toward the Promised Land
Lederman's article was interesting and timely, but I was surprised there was no mention of Israel. While it is true, as she notes, that Canada and the US share a common language and culture, Canada and Israel are a closer match when it comes to social support in areas like health and education, not to mention, for Jews, history, and religion.
She does mention that her maternal grandparents obtained visas to go to British Mandate Palestine, but did not go and were murdered in Treblinka.
However, many of the Jews who had to go did, and are still going. In fact, about half of the more than 7.5 million Jews living in Israel today are either immigrants or descendants of immigrants, most from either the post-war DP camps of Europe, the Arab/Muslim world, or the former Soviet Union.
A small but steadily increasing stream of immigrants has also arrived from North America. The Israel Central Bureau of Statistics indicates that about 16,000 Canadians have made aliyah since the establishment of the state in 1948.
Israel’s Aliyah and Integration Ministry reported that 440 Canadian Jews moved to Israel from September 2025 to September 2026. Another 1,000 Canadian Jews have opened new aliyah files. This is a formal process, including an interview with a representative of the Jewish Agency and the submission of documents, including birth certificates and marriage records.
While the Tulsa initiative has received a significant number of inquiries from Canadians, the number of families who have actually made the move so far is quite small, according to an article in The Forward by Benyamin Cohen.
It quotes Jewish Canadian journalist Jesse Brown: “There’s a sadness,” he said about the Jewish exodus from Canada. “I’m not enthused or compelled by what I see as a ‘re-shtetling.’”
The Canadian Jewish population, about 400,000, is almost as large as that of France, the third largest Jewish community in the world. Antisemitism is a serious problem there as well. This year, 4,000 French Jews made aliyah, about 10 times the Canadian number.
A 2026 Canadian survey cited by Lederman indicates that one quarter of Canadian Jews are planning to leave Canada or are thinking seriously about it, and there are no signs that the antisemitism experienced by Canadian Jews is abating. While I don’t think we will see a stampede of Jews leaving Canada, I do think the numbers leaving will gradually increase.
As in the French example, Israel will be their primary destination. After all, in the final analysis, it turns out that America is not the Promised Land.
The writer, a Fellow of the Royal Society of Canada, is a retired professor at the University of Waterloo, Ontario, Canada.

What to Know About Pope Leo's Lung Cancer Diagnosis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
17:58:24 UTC
02:58:24 KST

After discovering a nodule in Pope Leo XIV's lung, surgeons at Gemelli Hospital in Rome performed surgery on Tuesday that revealed the Pope has cancer.
Dr. Stefano Margaritora, professor of thoracic surgery at the Catholic University of Sacred Heart, led the team that operated on the Pope at Gemelli, which has long provided care for Popes. The surgery was prompted after the Pope’s medical team, led by Dr. Luigi Carbone, found a suspicious nodule and performed tests that suggested it could be cancerous, according to a statement released by the Vatican. During the 90-minute operation, Margaritora removed the lower lobe of the Pope’s right lung, and further testing of the tissue confirmed adenocarcinoma.
What is lung adenocarcinoma?
Lung adenocarcinoma is the most common type of lung cancer worldwide, accounting for 40% to 45% of lung cancer cases globally. Adenocarcinomas belong to a broader category of lung cancers known as non-small cell lung cancer, which tend to grow more slowly and spread less quickly to other parts of the body. Detecting adenocarcinomas early can help keep them from progressing to advanced disease.
How is lung cancer detected?
Current recommendations in the U.S. and most of the world advise low-dose CT scans to screen for lung cancer in high-risk people only: those 50 years or older who have smoked heavily in the past or who currently smoke. Many non-smokers are diagnosed with lung cancer when they get a chest CT for another reason, such as after an accident or other injury. Some advocacy and patient groups are pushing for expanded screening among those at higher risk so that more people can benefit from early detection, including those who are younger and may have been exposed to other factors that can increase lung cancer risk, like radon in the environment. “The best chance to cure lung cancer is when it’s Stage 1 and very early,” says Dr. David Jones, chief or thoracic surgery at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, who was not involved in the Pope’s care. “That’s what screening can help with.”
The Pope's smoking history is not publicly known, but lung adenocarcinoma occurs in both smokers and non-smokers, says Jones. “Lung adenocarcinoma is by far the most common type of lung cancer in non-smokers,” he says.
Why did surgeons remove part of the Pope’s lung?
Surgeons decided to remove part of the Pope’s lung “to ensure a radical resection,” according to the Vatican statement. That means doctors wanted to be sure they removed any tissue that might be cancerous, giving the Pope the strongest chance of avoiding any recurrence of disease.
How long will the Pope be hospitalized?
The Pope woke up from surgical anesthesia without any complications, and requested dinner while conversing with Vatican staff. He will be observed as additional tests are performed on his removed cancer tissue to guide doctors on what treatments might be needed next. The Vatican anticipates the Pope will remain at Gemelli for one week.
What are the treatments for lung adenocarcinoma?
The Pope’s treatment options depend on what additional tests on his tumor reveal. For some patients with Stage 1 cancer that has not spread to the lymph nodes, surgery and monitoring for recurrence may be sufficient, says Jones.
If the cancer is more advanced, a number of relatively new options for lung cancer are available, including targeted therapies designed to specifically attack certain mutations in cancer cells, or immunotherapy, which activates the immune system into destroying cancer cells. “The innovation in treatments for lung cancer have been profound,” says Karen Knudsen, CEO of the Parker Institute. Adenocarcinomas tend to have high numbers of mutations, which make them good targets for the immune system to recognize as foreign. That also makes them promising targets for checkpoint inhibitors, a new category of cancer therapy that releases the brakes on immune cells and allows them to better detect and destroy cancer cells. “Our knowledge base is improving, and there are better outcomes for non-small cell lung cancer because of immunotherapy,” says Knudsen.
Some patients can rely on targeted therapies alone and avoid chemotherapy, says Jones, while others may need chemo with immunotherapy, depending on how much of the cancer surgeons were able to remove and whether the cancer had spread to the lymph nodes.
Will Pope Leo be able to resume his papal duties?
The Vatican reports that prior to the surgery, the Pope was active, playing tennis and taking regular walks, and with the range of treatment options now available to treat his cancer, experts believe he should be able to return to his daily activities. “Advances in treatments all point to better prognosis and quality of life for patients with lung cancer,” says Jones. “And given his history of physical activity, even after removing one lobe of his lung, he should be able to do what he wants to do with very little limitation.”

Palantir, London mayor end legal battle over AI deal with metropolitan police
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
17:57:23 UTC
02:57:23 KST

Aysu Bicer
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
US technology company Palantir and London Mayor Sadiq Khan’s office have withdrawn allegations against each other in a legal dispute over a £50 million ($65 million) police technology contract, heading off a High Court trial scheduled for January.
Palantir sued the Mayor’s Office for Policing and Crime (MOPAC) in June after Khan intervened to block a proposed two-year contract for the Metropolitan Police to use artificial intelligence to process intelligence in criminal investigations.
The system, known as unified operational analytics (UOA), was intended for use by Scotland Yard.
Khan’s intervention followed concerns about the company’s work with the Israeli military and the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown. The mayor previously said Londoners wanted public money to go to companies that “share the values of our city.”
Palantir’s UK and Europe head, Louis Mosley, accused Khan of politicizing procurement, saying he was “putting politics above public safety.”
In a joint statement Wednesday, Palantir and MOPAC said the May 2026 decision to block the contract “was not based on Palantir’s values or ethics or any wider reporting about the company.”
MOPAC said media coverage of a statement by the mayor’s spokesperson before the decision could have created the impression that an assessment of Palantir’s values had influenced the decision.
It added that its assessment was based on its statutory responsibilities and relevant legal requirements concerning procurement, governance, affordability and value for money.
Khan said he was proud that leading software companies chose London as their home, and that Palantir contributed to jobs and investment in the capital.
The agreement comes one month after former Labour Party deputy leader Tom Watson was hired as a full-time lobbyist by Palantir. The company had raised concerns that excluding it from public contracts over objections to its leadership’s values could undermine its ability to operate in the UK.
Palantir also faces opposition to retaining its £330 million National Health Service medical data contract, amid calls from some members of the public and lawmakers for it to be replaced.
A new procurement process for the police contract is underway. MOPAC has agreed to treat Palantir “fairly and equally” if it submits a bid, although it is not obliged to award the contract to the company.

TIRANA — Student demonstrations in Tirana spiraled out of control Wednesday as protesters clashed with police for over 10 hours, setting buildings on fire, entering government institutions and looting.
While Albania has seen daily protests since the end of May over opposition to a Jared Kushner-linked resort in the south of the country, on Tuesday, students took to the streets over conditions in universities and dorms, the cost of living, and grievances over governance.
“The right to peaceful protest is a foundation of democracy and the state’s obligation to guarantee it. But violence cannot be a means of expressing dissatisfaction, nor should the use of force by the police exceed the limits of the law and proportionality,” President Bajram Begaj said in a public statement Wednesday. Advertisement
Starting outside the Ministry of Education on Wednesday morning, masked individuals threw stones, paving slabs, bottles and improvised pyrotechnics at the institution. They ripped up metal railings from the side of the road and used them to batter the iron gates of the building. After several hours, police with batons, tear gas guns, water cannons, and riot gear moved in, forcibly removing protesters and citizens from the vicinity.
Over the following hours, the situation escalated further as protestors set fire to benches, trees, and several buildings. They breached the Ministry of Education, the Ministry of Justice, and the Ministry of Finance, damaged several private businesses and billboards, then moved to the main boulevard and encircled the prime minister’s office. They later broke into shopping centers and banks.
Economy Minister Delina Ibrahimaj condemned the “burning and destruction of institutional premises,” calling them “unacceptable acts.”

On Tuesday evening, one young man had his legs broken and required emergency surgery following an altercation with police.

The U.S. Embassy in Tirana warned its citizens to be vigilant and avoid areas impacted by the protest, noting that it could spread. Explosions and sirens continue to be heard throughout the city center on Wednesday evening.
Meanwhile, the delegation of the European Union to Albania stated it has taken note of allegations of excessive violence by police against protestors and journalists and expects the police to prioritize full investigations. The EU delegation also called for de-escalation from both sides.

As Ukrinform previously reported, as of the morning of October 14, Russia's large-scale attack on Ukraine's energy infrastructure had caused new power outages in Kyiv and seven regions. In some regions, scheduled outages of up to two groups were being implemented.

Judge blocks US sanctions on rights groups helping ICC Gaza war crimes inquiry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
17:53:58 UTC
02:53:58 KST

A US federal judge has temporarily blocked the Trump administration from placing sanctions on two US-based human rights groups for working to help the international criminal court’s (ICC) investigations into war crimes in Gaza.
In a 30-page order issued on Tuesday, Jesse M Furman, a judge at the US district court for the southern district of New York, granted a preliminary injunction to the two groups, Democracy for the Arab World Now (Dawn) and Taxpayer Alliance Against Genocide (Taag).
The two organizations sued the Trump administration this summer, challenging an executive order issued in February 2025 that imposed sanctions against the ICC.
The order warned the US government would “impose tangible and significant consequences” on people involved in investigations that Washington said threatened the national security of the US or its allies, including Israel.
The order came after the ICC issued arrest warrants for the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, and his former defense minister Yoav Gallant, accusing them of war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza. Both men have rejected accusations against them, and the US government also opposed the court’s decision to issue the warrants.
In his opinion, Furman noted that last year two law professors brought a separate lawsuit challenging the 2025 executive order, and that the court had held that the order “violated those plaintiffs’ first amendment rights because it constituted a content-based regulation of their speech-based activities and did not survive strict scrutiny”.
Furman said that this lawsuit brought by Dawn and Taag – groups he described as “American advocacy organizations” – raised a “substantially similar challenge”. He wrote that the groups were challenging the 2025 order on “both statutory and constitutional grounds, re-upping many of the arguments made in the earlier cases”.
Dawn and Taag are rights groups that had worked to gather information for the ICC as it investigated allegations of war crimes against Palestinians.
“The court concludes that the 2025 order likely violates plaintiffs’ first amendment rights because it constitutes a content-based regulation of their speech-based activities and cannot survive strict scrutiny,” Furman wrote.
However, the judge stopped short of declaring the executive order “facially unconstitutional” and rejected the groups’ request to “enjoin the president and to enter a ‘universal’ injunction barring enforcement of the 2025 order against anyone”.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment from the Guardian on the ruling.
A spokesperson for the US state department said in a statement to the Guardian that “we do not comment on pending litigation” but added: “The Trump administration has been clear: the ICC poses an intolerable threat to US sovereignty.”
Joseph Pace, a lawyer for Dawn and Taag, described Tuesday’s decision as “a victory for the first amendment and an important step in unraveling the ICC sanctions regime”.
And in a statement, Omar Shakir, Dawn’s executive director, said: “Today, a US federal court has put the brakes in a major way on the Trump administration’s efforts to shield from justice the Israeli officials who have perpetrated a genocide and their US backers.”
Dawn also said that it would “immediately resume” its advocacy with the ICC “to prosecute Israeli and American perpetrators of grave crimes”.
The ruling comes just days after the US imposed financial sanctions on the ICC.

Israeli Bedouin infiltrated IDF as spy for Gaza terror group linked to Bibas murders
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
17:52:14 UTC
02:52:14 KST

The Beersheba District Court on Wednesday sentenced Shahadeh Abu Alqian, a resident of an unrecognized Bedouin community in the Negev, to 24 1/2 years in prison after he was convicted under a plea agreement of assisting the enemy in wartime, terrorism offenses and weapons violations. Abu Alqian acted on behalf of a terrorist organization based in the Gaza Strip and even enlisted in the Israel Defense Forces on his handlers' instructions to gather intelligence. He also stole a weapon from an IDF soldier and later transferred weapons to the West Bank for the terrorist organization.
According to the amended indictment filed by attorney Hofit Kantrowitz of the Southern District Attorney's Office, Abu Alqian decided in 2019 to take revenge against Israel and harm its security after an administrative demolition order was issued for his father's home. In September of that year, he stole an M4 assault rifle, a magazine and a laser sight from an IDF soldier in the Yatir area, then buried them near his home.
Beginning in 2021, Abu Alqian contacted terrorist operatives in the Gaza Strip through social media and Telegram, expressed support for the struggle against Israel and sought to join Hamas' military wing. He later began operating on behalf of the terrorist organization Kataib al-Mujahideen, providing his handlers with information and photographs of IDF bases, train stations, government-owned companies and shopping centers. He also reported on the movements of soldiers and helicopters near his home.
In March 2022, an operative from the terrorist organization known as "Abu Suleiman" contacted him and asked to purchase weapons. Abu Alqian offered to sell him the rifle he had stolen from the IDF and insisted on delivering the weapons directly to the West Bank. In May 2022, he recruited his cousin to help him, and the two loaded an M4 rifle, thousands of rounds of ammunition and five hand grenades into a vehicle and drove to the West Bank. There, they left the weapons in a hiding place for the terrorist organization.
At the same time, acting on his handler's instructions, Abu Alqian enlisted in the IDF on May 22, 2022, intending to gather information from within the military about Bedouin soldiers, army bases and military positions and pass it to the terrorist organization. About eight days after enlisting, he was arrested by Israeli security forces, thwarting his activities.
In December 2025, Abu Alqian was convicted after admitting to the charges in an amended indictment as part of a plea agreement. The offenses included assisting the enemy in wartime, active membership in a terrorist organization, aggravated theft, weapons offenses involving carrying and transporting firearms and handling weapons for terrorist purposes.
During sentencing arguments, prosecutors sought a lengthy prison term, a suspended sentence and a substantial fine. They also emphasized the severity of Abu Alqian's ties to Mujahideen Brigades, which was involved in the murder of members of the Bibas family during the war that began with Hamas' October 7, 2023, attack on Israel.
A three-judge panel consisting of Daniel Ben Tolila, Tal Lahiani Shoham and Yoav Atar sentenced Abu Alqian to 24 1/2 years in prison, a suspended sentence and a fine of 25,000 shekels.
Kantrowitz, who prosecuted the case, said after the hearing: "This is an exceptionally serious case in which an Israeli citizen chose to act against his country, maintain ties with a terrorist organization and even enlist in the IDF on behalf of a terrorist organization, with the aim of gathering information from within the military and harming national security.
"It is worth noting that, alongside the criminal proceedings, the defendant's details were also forwarded to the interior minister for consideration of revoking his citizenship. The sentence reflects the severity of his actions, the harm to national security and the need for significant deterrence," she added.
"The prosecution will continue to pursue the full extent of the law against those who choose to act on behalf of and assist terrorist organizations, endangering the security of the state, its soldiers and its citizens."

"Israel restricts its flight crew from certain countries, including Indonesia based only on their citizenship. This practice is contrary to the non-discriminatory principle and the spirit of international aviation facilitation," said Yvonne.
Israel ordered an Ethiopian Airlines flight bound for Tel Aviv to turn back because one of its pilots was Indonesian, Israel’s Channel 12 reported Monday.
The aircraft was about an hour into its flight from Addis Ababa and still in Ethiopian airspace when the order was issued
Channel 12 said the pilot's nationality had been flagged to Israeli intelligence and airport authorities, prompting security officials and the Transportation Ministry to bar the flight from landing.
The plane returned to Addis Ababa, where the pilot was replaced, before departing again and landing in Tel Aviv.
Ethiopian Airlines described the incident as a mistake, saying it had been unaware that the pilot was barred from operating flights to Israel, according to the report.
Channel 12 also said Israeli authorities had instructed foreign airlines not to assign crew members from certain countries without diplomatic relations with Israel to flights bound for the country – namely from Afghanistan, Algeria, Indonesia, Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Niger, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Somalia, and Venezuela.
The incident comes after an attempted hijacking on Sept. 30 of a FlyDubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv.

Ukraine's Third Army Corps, together with its attached units, has retaken another 101 square kilometers during the fourth stage of Operation Vivaldi on the Lyman sector in Donetsk Oblast, the corps announced on Oct. 14.
Ukraine liberated the villages of Zelena Dolyna, Lypove, and Kolodiazi, while Russia lost about 3,000 of its soldiers in the fourth stage of the operation, the corps reported on Telegram.
"The enemy was unable to cut the key logistics artery of our group in the Donbas. We thwarted the offensive of the group 'Zapad' and forced it to transfer part of the units of the 1st Tank Army, which weakened the pressure on Kupiansk-Vuzlovyi," corps commander Brig. Gen. Andrii Biletskyi said.

The fight for the heart of the so-called Donbas fortress belt — Sloviansk, Kramatorsk, Druzhkivka, and Kostiantynivka — is crucial going into the winter months, when Russia will look to maximize its foothold in urban areas to prepare for a 2027 offensive campaign.

Russia has been increasingly deploying jet-powered drones that are faster and more difficult to intercept than older Shahed models, posing a new threat as Ukraine braces for massive strikes against energy infrastructure in winter.
Of the 45-million-pound package, the U.K. will expedite the delivery of 10 million pounds ($13 million) worth of LMMs to meet the most urgent winter needs.

The U.K. further reiterated that it stands by its plans to ban maritime services for Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG) exports.

The EU plans to ban Russian LNG imports by January 2027 but has failed to agree on a full ban on maritime services, with Greece securing a carve-out for Russian LNG exports to non-EU countries.
