Germany puts Ukrainian on trial over Nord Stream sabotage
Ukrainian citizen Serhii Kuznetsov went to trial in Hamburg on Oct. 14 on suspicion of involvement in the sabotage of the Nord Stream pipelines.
A series of explosions rocked the controversial Nord Stream 1 and 2 pipelines in September 2022, destroying three out of four key gas pipelines linking Russia and Germany via the Baltic Sea.
Kuznetsov, a former soldier, was accused of leading the sabotage group, involving six other people. German investigators claim that he commanded the yacht "Andromeda," from which a team of divers allegedly carried out the attack against the pipelines.
On the first day of the trial, prosecutors accused Kuznetsov of being an accomplice to war crimes by committing an attack against civilian infrastructure.
Kuznetsov and Kyiv have denied any involvement in the sabotage.
The trial — the first held in connection with the Nord Stream sabotage — is expected to run until February.
Kuznietsov was arrested in August 2025 near the Italian town of Rimini under a European arrest warrant before being extradited to Germany.
Another Ukrainian suspect, Volodymyr Zhuravliov, was detained in Croatia in August 2026 and awaits extradition. Zhuravliov was first detained in Poland in September 2025, but a Polish court refused to extradite him to Germany and instead released him a month later.
The Nord Stream 2 pipeline, which never became operational, had long been a flashpoint in European energy politics.
Even before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, critics said it deepened Germany's dependence on Russian gas and undermined European energy security.

Teresa Elena Frontadoin Washington
Bank of America, the second-largest US bank, failed to promptly report hundreds of millions of dollars in suspicious transactions bearing signs of Chinese money-laundering networks, US regulators said on Tuesday, announcing more than US$1.21 billion in penalties for broader anti-money-laundering and sanctions failures.
The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, or FinCEN, said the activity included large wire transfers to counterparties in China, repeated credit-card purchases at major retailers and shipping companies, and payments towards cards held by third parties without an apparent commercial purpose.
Most of the suspected network activity involved a group of customers purporting to operate in logistics or electronics, according to a consent order. The agency said their transaction patterns were inconsistent with legitimate commercial activity for those businesses.
The China-related findings form part of a wider enforcement action against the bank. FinCEN imposed a US$1.2 billion penalty, against which it will credit a US$750 million payment to the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC).

Pope's cancer prognosis may depend on these factors, doctors say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
17:47:04 UTC
02:47:04 KST

Pope Leo's lung cancer prognosis could depend on these factors, doctors say
Pope Leo XIV was recovering Wednesday, a day after having a lobe of his right lung removed and confirming a diagnosis of lung cancer.
Leo had blood tests and a chest X-ray that showed a "normal post-operative course," the Holy See Press Office said. "The values are within the expected range for the type of procedure performed."
The surgery removed what the pope and Vatican described as a localized nodular lesion.
"Those types of lesions can actually be removed and even cured just by surgery alone," CBS News chief medical correspondent Dr. Jon LaPook said.
But the Vatican has not shared the stage of cancer, or whether it has spread, which would help determine if Leo needs further treatment.
Here's what multiple doctors, who are not involved in the pope's treatment, told CBS News about his possible prognosis.
What type of cancer does Leo have?
Leo was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, a common type of non-small cell lung cancer, doctors say.
"It's very common and also generally a very good prognosis when found early on," Dr. Kalvin Lung, a thoracic surgeon at the Northwestern Medicine Canning Thoracic Institute, told CBS News 24/7 on Tuesday.
The surgery Leo underwent "is also something we commonly do, and it's a very successful surgery and people can recover very quickly from it," Lung said.
What stage is the cancer?
The Vatican has not said what stage the cancer is. "They may not know yet," LaPook said Wednesday morning.
But the information that has been provided suggests the cancer may have been caught early.
"The fact that he can have a successful surgery so quickly is all a very good prognosticators of probably an early-stage lung cancer," Lung said.
If there had been evidence that the cancer had spread elsewhere in the body, Leo may have had treatment before the surgery like chemotherapy or immunological therapy, LaPook said.
"But the fact they went right in and tried to take it all out might say to you, well, they think maybe that's it," he said.
If that is the case, Leo likely would not need further treatment, Lung and LaPook said.
Is there lymph node involvement?
If the cancer spread to the lymph nodes, which filter fluid in the body, that would change the prognosis and possible treatment plan, doctors said.
"Sometimes it looks like on all the tests beforehand that it's just localized, and it turns out the lymph nodes are involved," LaPook said.
Further testing would determine the treatment, he said.
"There are all these special tests you do. Look at the genetic makeup of it. Are there any special markers? Are there any special things on it that are driving it to multiply?" LaPook said.
What is the recovery?
Doctors have said the recovery from the surgery is typically a few weeks. Leo is expected to stay at the hospital for a week, according to the Vatican.
The pope's recovery was "proceeding as expected," the Holy See Press Office said Wednesday.
"The Holy Father has carried out respiratory physiotherapy and has begun walking around his room," they said. "He has resumed a regular diet, having both breakfast and lunch."
Leo may have some pain from the surgery "for the first couple of days up to the first one to two weeks," Lung said.
"I think he'll be back to doing what he wants to do around three to four weeks," said Dr. David Jones, chief of thoracic surgery at the Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center. "Maybe a little slower, but he'll be fine."

====================================================================================================

How Azerbaijan is building its next chapter in tourism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
17:45:25 UTC
02:45:25 KST

Florian Sengstschmid, CEO of the Azerbaijan Tourism Board, tells the Travel and Tourism Summit how direct flights, regional investment and a 2030 plan are shaping the country’s future.
Florian Sengstschmid first set foot in Baku in 2001. After a career working in destinations around the world, the Austrian-born CEO of the Azerbaijan Tourism Board might be hard to surprise. Yet he says the country still has surprises in store.
A crossroads with European roots
Sengstschmid believes the South Caucasus is underrated. Its countries are often lumped together under a post-Soviet label, he says, without their individual histories and cultures being fully understood.
Azerbaijan sits where Europe meets Asia, and he points to a European thread that few visitors expect. Bridges built by the Siemens brothers can still be crossed. German heritage villages such as Helenendorf remain. Across the country, a mosque, a church and a synagogue sit side by side. With its distinctive red-tiled roofs, the country’s largest Jewish settlement is believed to have been the only entirely Jewish settlement outside Israel and the United States, as well as the world’s last surviving shtetl.That mix of cultures and faiths, he says, is part of everyday life in Azerbaijan.
He also sees the regional peace process, including the initial deal signed in Washington in August 2025, opening the door to multi-country journeys. That could make the South Caucasus easier to visit for long-haul travellers and raise the region’s profile.
A city that knows how to host
Just days before the summit, Baku hosted a Formula 1 weekend that drew more than 17,000 international visitors, alongside the Azerbaijan Investment Forum. Hospitality, Sengstschmid says, is deeply rooted in the country’s culture, with visitors treated as guests.
Baku’s profile has grown since Eurovision in 2011, and COP29 in 2024 tested its capacity further.
“Who can host a COP can host any other meeting and conference,” he said.
Beyond the capital
Still, Sengstschmid urges visitors not to stop in Baku.
Along the Silk Road lie side valleys, ancient heritage villages and the UNESCO-listed town of Shaki, set in the Greater Caucasus and known for its Khan palaces. There is also a wine route, while wellness cluster includes unique natural resources such as naftalan oil, which has been used for skin treatments for centuries.
The country spans a vast range of climate zones, from desert landscapes to peaks reaching 4,000 metres.
Winter tourism is another focus. A five-year partnership with the International Ski and Snowboard Federation (FIS) will bring races and World Cups to Azerbaijan, including FIS World Cup finals in freestyle moguls and dual moguls in the mountains of Shahdag in March.
Connectivity is improving too. Baku airport holds a five-star Skytrax rating, while Azerbaijan Airlines is taking delivery of new aircraft this year. From 8 May 2027, the carrier will fly four times a week between Brussels and Baku.
Entry is also straightforward. For major events such as F1, a passport and a valid ticket are enough, while other travellers can use the e-visa system, with standard processing within three days and urgent visas issued within three hours.
“Connectivity and accessibility are the key bottlenecks in tourism,” Sengstschmid said.
Building tourism with the people who live there
Behind the growth sits a new state program running to 2030. It aims to stimulate demand through incentives for charter airlines, new routes and tour operators. On the supply side, it encourages quality, green-built accommodation in the regions and supports micro and small entrepreneurs. It also asks transport, customs and other parts of the visitor journey to pull together.
Sengstschmid says protecting local life comes first. He cites Basgal, a mountain village on the Silk Road and a historic centre of silk printing that had been largely abandoned.
After investment in infrastructure, families returned. Today, the village has small tea houses and food stalls, while women practise traditional silk printing. Visitors can experience the village’s traditions alongside the people who live there.
In 2025, tourism contributed 7 billion manat, around €3.5 billion, or 5.4% of GDP. The target is 12 billion manat by 2030. Sengstschmid says the plan centres on longer stays and greater economic impact, with visitor numbers, currently just under three million, rising only modestly.
A village that feels like a secret
Asked to share a secret, he chose Sim, a village in the south of the country that he describes as a fairytale.
Moss covers the old wooden buildings and their balconies, water runs through the village, waterfalls tumble nearby and a UNESCO-listed forest begins at its edge. It feels like a jungle, he says, yet you are in Azerbaijan.
Asked to sum up the country in three words, he did not hesitate: real, warm and uplifting.
Warm, because of its people. Real, because he believes development has left much of the country genuine and intact. And uplifting, because Azerbaijan still has new things to show him.
For someone who first set foot in Baku in 2001, still being surprised 25 years later may be the strongest endorsement of all.

​World's oldest shipwreck found off Turkey's coast, archaeologists say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
17:44:53 UTC
02:44:53 KST

World's oldest shipwreck found off Turkey, archaeologists say: "Time capsule at the bottom of the sea"
Archaeologists have discovered the world's oldest shipwreck off the coast of Turkey, dating it to between 4,400 and 4,700 years old.
The structure of the ship has not survived the nearly five millennia underwater, but its contents of clay jars have been preserved surprisingly well, with some still containing traces of what they transported over 4,000 years ago.
The archaeologists who found the vessel said that it was a nearly 33-foot-long trade ship transporting goods across the Mediterranean Sea and originated somewhere on the eastern Mediterranean coast.
The wreck dates back to the same time period as when the Pyramids of Giza were being built, and will "offer insights into ancient trading connections and the everyday lives of seafarers," according to Turkey's Culture and Tourism Minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy.
"The shipwreck is a time capsule at the bottom of the sea," Hakan Öniz, an associate professor at Turkey's Akdeniz University who oversaw the expedition to uncover the ship, told CBS News' partner network BBC News.
Alongside the 30 ceramic storage jars in the wreckage, called amphorae, three stone anchors were also discovered.
Öniz told CBS News that when his team first found the wreck four years ago, the amphorae only appeared to be a century or two old.
"However, we later became excited when we saw the same amphora forms in a publication on Egyptian archaeology and returned to the site," Öniz said. "Indeed, they were similar to those found at the Giza pyramids in Egypt. We were incredibly excited."
The design of these amphorae — with two handles, a flat base and a ridge in the middle — was distinctive to pottery from that period of history.
Karin Sowada, an archaeologist at Australia's Macquarie University, examined the pots after they were brought to the surface. She told the BBC that there was still a viscous, glossy residue inside some of the amphorae.
"I looked inside and nearly fainted. I could not believe how much [residue] was visible. It wasn't just like spots … a lot of this material was still remaining," she said.
Analysis of the clay used to make the jars suggests that they were produced in workshops in the Middle East's Jordan Valley, located along Jordan's border with Israel and the West Bank.
"It appears the vessel sank while transporting olive oil or wine from that region westward — perhaps to Troy or to the Minoan civilization in Crete," Öniz told CBS News.
Similar examples of amphorae have also been found in Egypt, Troy and Crete, according to Ersoy.
Öniz told the BBC that when he was diving for the wreck, his first thoughts were on the lives of the many people connected to the ship.
"We are the first humans who [have] touched these objects after 5,000 years," he said.
"We are always thinking of the sailors ... the producers of the amphora and the person who carried the amphora on their shoulders to the ship, and the women who were waiting for their husbands, and they unfortunately couldn't go back."
The discovery has taken the record of the world's oldest shipwreck from the previous holder in the Aegean Sea located near Greece, which was dated to 4,200 years ago.

Attacks in Strait of Hormuz reach highest level since start of war: Security data
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
17:43:29 UTC
02:43:29 KST

Attacks in Strait of Hormuz reach highest level since start of Iran war: Security data
LONDON - At least ten vessels have been attacked in or near the Strait of Hormuz since Oct 11, a high since war broke out between the United States, Israel and Iran, security data showed on Oct 14.
Four vessels were struck on Oct 13 and six on Oct 11 – the highest number of attacks in a single day since the start of the conflict – according to data from security firm Vanguard, the International Maritime Organization (IMO) and the British maritime agency UKMTO.
Two seafarers have been reported missing and a container ship reportedly sank as a result of recent attacks, according to the maritime sources.
Merchant vessels transiting the vital passage were first targeted by Iran in March in retaliation for US-Israeli strikes on its territory, and Tehran has continued to strike vessels passing through the strait via routes it has not approved.
The attacks have disrupted shipping through the strait, which is normally one of the busiest routes for exporting oil and other commodities from Gulf countries.
Twenty-three attacks have been recorded since the start of October, almost double the average monthly number of incidents since the start of the war.
The United States said on Oct 10 that it had struck a cargo vessel as part of its embargo on Iranian ports, but the incident was not listed by the IMO.
The recent uptick in energy exports, which almost returned to pre-war levels at the start of October but have since fallen back, may be behind the latest increase in attacks, according to Vanguard analyst Barun Gupta.
“Gulf oil flows have been recovering, with traffic through Hormuz recently returning to around 80 per cent of pre-war levels despite the conflict.
“Increasing the tempo of attacks therefore gives Tehran a way of demonstrating that it can still disrupt that recovery and impose costs on commercial shipping and global energy markets,” Gupta told AFP on Oct 14.
He said Trump’s promise last week not to launch further attacks on Iran before the midterm elections in the US could also be a factor, giving Tehran “a perceived window to increase pressure with a lower immediate risk of US military escalation”.
Some 24 seafarers have died as a result of incidents in the area near the Strait of Hormuz since the start of the conflict, according to the IMO. AFP

From first to 22nd: How world’s former №1 plunged in global broadband rankings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

17:43:14 UTC

From first to 22nd: How world’s former №1 plunged in global broadband rankings
South Korea's fixed broadband speed has plunged to 22nd place, once ranked first in the world, according to an analysis by Seattle-based network intelligence platform Ookla, AJU Press reports.
Ookla, which tracks internet speeds worldwide, said South Korea's median fixed broadband download speed stood at 251.33 Mbps in August, ranking 22nd among 149 countries, behind Viet Nam in eighth place and Thailand in ninth.
Singapore topped the ranking at 462.50 Mbps, followed by the United Arab Emirates (UAE) at 382.40 Mbps.
By city, Seoul ranked 34th, behind Bangkok in sixth place and Ho Chi Minh City in 14th. Valparaíso, Chile, topped the ranking at 416.81 Mbps, followed by Abu Dhabi in the UAE at 408.67 Mbps.
But South Korea's mobile internet download speed remained high, ranking sixth globally at 250.56 Mbps.
Ookla compiles its rankings from data collected when users visit websites or apps and tap the "go" button. However, results may be skewed if more users repeatedly click the button when their connections feel slow or unstable. Critics also say that differences in subscription plans and access environments across countries make the rankings unreliable for direct comparisons.

Return to war with Iran after US midterm elections may be increasingly likely - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
17:40:12 UTC
02:40:12 KST

A return to war between the United States and Iran is far from a certainty, and an ongoing tense standoff is still the most likely scenario, but there is no question that the chances of renewed conflict between Washington and Tehran will jump after America’s midterm elections on November 3.
Many have misinterpreted Iran’s latest additional moves to better defend the Pickaxe Mountain nuclear facility as a sign that the Islamic Republic is possibly trying to rush out to a nuclear weapon.
The Jerusalem Post has confirmed that Iran has no significant active nuclear operations currently at Pickaxe Mountain and that Israeli concerns there are more about the future.
The Post was also told by numerous sources that it is unclear that even American mega bunker busters such as the 30,000-pound Massive Ordnance Penetrator bomb could fully penetrate the Pickaxe Mountain nuclear facility – even prior to any of the recent new defenses.
Iran may be trying to deter US, Israeli ground operations
In that sense, the new defenses are likely an attempt to deter the US and Israel from staging a ground operation at the mountain.
The US staged a successful temporary ground operation in Iran at the height of the war in early 2026 to rescue shot-down pilots, and Israel staged a ground operation to destroy a major underground Iranian-built Syrian nuclear facility in Masyaf, Syria, in September 2024.
Iran wants to convince both Washington and Jerusalem that pulling off such an operation at Pickaxe Mountain would be much harder, more costly, and therefore not worth the risk.
In that sense, all of Iran’s efforts currently show it is preparing for war in the near future and will try to strike America and its allies’ weak underbellies: energy facilities, slow and large ships, and other economically damaging targets.
Despite constant warnings from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz, there is still little inclination from Iran to get caught up in another war with Israel.
Iran’s regime saw that Israel’s war-fighting was more merciless than America’s in the sense of targeting top Iranian officials and that Jerusalem was more ready to continue attacking Iran indefinitely as compared to Washington, which was worried about a drawn-out conflict.
In that sense, all of the warnings about Iran seeking to pick a fight with Israel are mostly about lower-grade hostilities, such as attempting terror attacks against Israelis, or Jews globally, or small targeted attacks on Israel which would fall short of requiring a massive Israeli response.
Iranian threats potentially intended to force US concessions
Such Iranian threats against Israel are more about forcing the US into making concessions out of fears that an Iranian attack, which would bring Israel back into the war, would lead to Washington losing control and creating greater regional instability.
In August, the US’s military power achieved a shift vs Iran in which the harm to the West’s economy was regularly reduced while the harm to Iran’s economy continually worsened.
All of this led US President Donald Trump to bet that Iran would blink before the US midterm elections. In that scenario, he could declare victory leading into those elections and potentially even regain some of the nuclear concessions ceded earlier, in the summer.
Trump’s error was projecting Western rationalism onto the IRGC and religious fanatics running Iran, who believe their regime is aided by divine messianic currents.
The president and his team have alternated between proclaiming that a deal with Iran is imminent after the midterm elections and threatening a return to full war with the regime after the midterms.
Iran believes that when Trump’s Republican Party loses the midterms, he will make more concessions to extract himself from this otherwise potentially endless conflict, which appears to sap his popularity daily.
And if Trump does not give in after the midterm elections, the Islamic Republic may escalate to cause enough chaos to bring him back to those concessions.
None of this is a grand strategy in which Iran could badly hurt the US or Israel in any deep or strategic way.
Iran has more ballistic missiles left over, around 1,600, than the US and Israel expected in April, but the number is so much lower than the around 6,000 it had expected to reach by now. Further, its future production has been slowed by about as much as 90%.
Most importantly, the regime cannot fire more than a few dozen rockets in a day vs the several hundred it was able to fire daily in early 2026.
Iran’s preparations are therefore more about either deterring the US from launching a new massive attack, being better prepared to outlast such an attack if it happens, or carrying out a limited Iranian offensive to try to get some more concessions from the US.
For months, America’s midterms have been viewed as a turning point in the conflict.
Developments in recent weeks suggest that turning point could mean more conflict. The whole world will be watching closely after November 3.

The ministers asserted that the delay would “once again deprive Palestinians of the opportunity to vote and will further erode public confidence in democratic institutions.”
They additionally highlighted the importance of the elections in light of Abbas and the PA’s earlier commitments to reform, accountability, and democratic renewal.

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14

02:39:58 KST

Hezbollah has exploited the European Union’s failure to designate its political wing as a terrorist organization to launder money raised through human trafficking in South America and Africa, according to a new analysis published by the Jerusalem Center for Security and Foreign Affairs (JCFA).
Ella Rosenberg, a senior research fellow at the JCFA and a member of the Dvorah Forum, argued in her analysis that the EU’s failure to designate Hezbollah’s political wing has allowed the Iran-backed group to operate more freely in its fundraising activities.
She said the distinction between Hezbollah’s political and military wings has enabled proceeds from human trafficking in Latin America, Africa, and the Middle East to be laundered through front companies, charitable organizations, and trade networks in Europe.
Hezbollah's documented fundraising through crime
Although Hezbollah, as an Iranian proxy, receives much of its weaponry and resources from Tehran, it also maintains a documented criminal network that relies heavily on human trafficking to finance its activities.
Although Lebanon criminalized human trafficking in 2011 under Law 164, enforcement has frequently been undermined by state corruption and Hezbollah’s influence, Rosenberg argued. The law covers the sexual exploitation of women, yet reports dating back to 2016 have highlighted prostitution rings allegedly operated in cooperation with Hezbollah-affiliated officials.
The terrorist organization has reportedly protected these rings, using its influence to prevent state security agencies from intervening in their illicit activities in exchange for an unknown share of the profits.
According to Rosenberg, the protection money generated by the sex trafficking rings was reportedly directed toward Hezbollah’s social welfare programs and used to cover the living expenses of terrorists killed in action.
Outside Lebanon, Hezbollah-affiliated logistical hubs have become deeply entwined with human traffickers, she continued. In Latin America, particularly Argentina, Brazil, and Paraguay, cartel members have reportedly supported Hezbollah operatives.
Victims trapped in debt bondage are coerced into forced labor or illicit activities to repay exorbitant transit fees charged by Hezbollah-aligned facilitators. Reports also indicate significant cooperation with violent drug cartels, including Los Zetas, generating substantial proceeds that are subsequently laundered through trade-based mechanisms.
Questions over the origins of Hezbollah's funds
In West and Central Africa, Hezbollah has a “deep financial footprint,” Rosenberg wrote. Hezbollah operatives are said to systematically exploit both the Lebanese diaspora living in the region and local populations.
Rosenberg also described Hezbollah’s alleged involvement in trafficking blood diamonds and narcotics across Africa. The group can reportedly organize bulk-cash smuggling operations and use schemes involving real estate and vehicles to facilitate transactions that leave little trace and transfer funds to Beirut while circumventing sanctions.
The origins of Hezbollah’s funding have come under increased scrutiny in recent weeks after reports that the group received $200 million from Iran to support people displaced by its war with Israel. The US State Department dismissed the initial report as a fabrication. However, days after Reuters reported on the alleged transfer, Hezbollah announced financial assistance of up to $14,000 for displaced families.
The origins of the funds have seemingly caused some confusion in Beirut. Lebanese MP Fouad Makhzoumi said that there were “serious questions about the sources of these funds, how they were brought into Lebanon, and how they were transported and distributed outside official financial frameworks.”
“Assisting our affected people is a national duty, but their suffering cannot serve as a cover for parallel financial systems or a pretext for circumventing Lebanese laws…,” he said.
“There can be no sovereignty for a state that does not monopolize arms nor assert its authority over the movement of money. Nor can we accept a state within a state, neither militarily nor financially. Lebanon needs one state, one legitimate weapon, and a law applied to all without exception.”

Fire damages Starlink ground station in Bulgaria that is used in part by the Ukrainian military
Unknown

2026-10-14
17:38:54 UTC
02:38:54 KST

An unidentified group set fire to Starlink satellite communications antennas in Bulgaria. Ivaylo Mirchev, a local lawmaker from the Yes, Bulgaria! party, was the first to report the incident.
Mirchev said 11 of the site’s 17 Starlink antennas were damaged at the facility, which is located near the Bulgarian capital, Sofia. On his Facebook page, Mirchev published a video of the fire. The footage shows a facility resembling a Starlink ground station — a key piece of terrestrial infrastructure that links satellites in orbit with the internet network.
It is unclear exactly when the fire was set. The first post about the incident was published on the evening of Oct. 12.
Mirchev said two unidentified people set the station on fire. He accused Bulgarian authorities of keeping quiet about the incident.
“It is obvious that these antennas were not chosen as a target by chance, because they provide the main communications link with the satellites. In late September, similar Starlink antennas were also attacked in Poland. How did the Polish state respond? It informed citizens and the public and took swift action.”
The exact location of the incident was not initially disclosed. Mirchev said only that the fire occurred at a “secret facility” near Sofia. Surveillance footage he posted shows a distinctive antenna and a sign reading “Plana Earth Station.”
The site appears to be the Plana satellite communications station, located south of Sofia. Satellite imagery reviewed by The Insider shows spherical structures at the site characteristic of Starlink ground stations.
Bulgaria’s parliament held a hearing about the incident on Oct. 14. Prime Minister Rumen Radev confirmed the incident and said an investigation was underway, though he declined to comment on the details.
Plamen Tonchev, head of Bulgaria’s State Agency for National Security, said the Starlink antenna site had been scheduled for expansion and that part of the fencing had therefore been removed. That appears to have made it easier for the perpetrators to gain access to the facility.
The station also provides service used by the Ukrainian military.
It remains unclear who was behind the fire. Mirchev suggested Russian intelligence services could have been responsible, though there is currently no evidence to support that claim.
A similar incident occurred in Poland in late September. Two suspects in that arson attack were detained in Germany earlier this week. Polish authorities have said they suspect Russian intelligence services of organizing the attack.

====================================================================================================

'Office' is actually having a scarcity problem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
17:35:44 UTC
02:35:44 KST

A version of this article first appeared in the CNBC Property Play newsletter with Diana Olick. Property Play covers new and evolving opportunities for the real estate investor, from individuals to venture capitalists, private equity funds, family offices, institutional investors and large public companies. Sign up to receive future editions, straight to your inbox.
Barely a few years after what some saw as a pandemic-driven collapse of the U.S. office market, the sector is roaring back to health at an unexpectedly fast clip. That speedy recovery is resulting in a shortage, especially of premium space.
The office market posted its fifth consecutive quarter of positive net absorption, with occupiers adding 6 million square feet in the third quarter of this year, according to a new report from JLL. And employers are expanding, with signed leases now averaging a 13% increase in footprint. Just two years ago, the main theme in office was downsizing.
This all comes at a time when supply is falling — and falling faster than demand is recovering. Just 3.5 million square feet of new office space was delivered in the third quarter, which matches the near-record low supply seen in the second quarter. At the same time, 9.6 million square feet was removed through either conversions or redevelopments. The inventory of office space nationally has lost 45 million square feet since the end of 2023.
There is currently just 23 million square feet of new office space under construction, and with demand for premium office surging, this new space is becoming increasingly scarce. JLL deems it a "flight to scarcity." As a result, rents are finally rising.
Effective rents for first-generation trophy space are now up more than 20% compared with the third quarter of 2025. The lack of available trophy space is now pushing more occupiers to second-generation space. In turn, rents for that sector are up 10% annually.
"Office, which is having a real renaissance right now. … If you own, if you bought that 18, 24 months ago, you've done incredibly well in office in San Francisco and New York," said Willy Walker, CEO of Walker & Dunlop, a commercial real estate finance and advisory firm, on CNBC's "Closing Bell Overtime."
There are, as always, stronger local drivers to different metropolitan markets. Tech is leading the way with the highest net absorption in San Francisco and Austin. Sun Belt markets have also seen strong demand, with gateway area leasing volume up 13% from a year ago. Smaller, tertiary markets have come back to roughly 95% of their 2019 leasing volume.
With supply shrinking and demand rising, construction should be picking up, but it's not.
"Now is the perfect time to be putting a shovel in the ground, except no one's going to do it," said Walker, noting that this year office construction is at about 9% of its normal annual supply. "It's a perfect time to start projects to be delivered in the next two or three years. The problem with it is back to equity capital. You're not finding the equity capital going towards it right now, and as a result of it, we will be in a supply-constrained market, which, what will that do? It'll push rents up."

Kiarostami’s “Where Is the Friend’s House?” selected for Tokyo festival
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
17:35:35 UTC
02:35:35 KST

Kiarostami’s “Where Is the Friend’s House?” selected for Tokyo festival
TEHRAN- The 1987 Iranian film “Where Is the Friend’s House?” by the late acclaimed filmmaker Abbas Kiarostami will be screened at the 39th Tokyo International Film Festival in Japan as part of a special program celebrating films cherished by legendary Japanese director Akira Kurosawa.
Produced by the Institute for the Intellectual Development of Children and Young Adults (Kanoon), the film is scheduled to screen on October 26 at TOHO Cinemas Chanter in Tokyo, according to Kanoon’s public relations and international affairs department.
The film will be presented alongside three other works in the program “Akira Kurosawa’s Favorite Films”: Charlie Chaplin’s “The Circus” (1928), and Kurosawa’s own films “Sanshiro Sugata” (1943) and “Ikiru” (1952).
The special program brings together works associated with Kurosawa’s cinematic legacy, placing Kiarostami’s landmark Iranian film in conversation with major works from the history of world cinema.
“Where Is the Friend’s House?” follows Ahmad, a schoolboy who discovers that he has accidentally taken home his classmate’s notebook. Determined to return it before his friend faces punishment for failing to complete his homework, Ahmad sets out to find the boy’s house in a neighboring village. His search becomes a journey through rural Iranian life, exploring childhood, responsibility, kindness and the challenges children encounter in a world governed by adult rules.
With its understated storytelling, naturalistic performances and close attention to everyday life, the film became one of the defining works of Kiarostami’s career and helped introduce Iranian cinema to wider international audiences. It also established themes that would recur throughout the director’s work, including the moral complexity of ordinary decisions and the relationship between children and adults.
The film has won several awards since its release, including the Bronze Leopard at the Locarno International Film Festival in Switzerland and the Critics' Prize at the Sao Paulo International Film Festival, and the Pasinetti Award at the Venice Film Festival.
“Where Is the Friend’s House?” is one of Kiarostami’s landmark works and the first installment of his Koker trilogy, which also includes “And Life Goes On” (1992) and “Through the Olive Trees” (1994).
The film has been screened at numerous international film festivals and cinematheques over the decades and continues to feature in retrospectives and programs dedicated to world cinema.
Kiarostami was a film director, screenwriter, poet, photographer, and film producer. An active filmmaker from 1970, he was involved in the production of over 40 films, including shorts and documentaries. He attained critical acclaim for directing “Close-Up” (1990), “The Wind Will Carry Us” (1999), and “Taste of Cherry” (1997). In later works, “Certified Copy” (2010) and “Like Someone in Love” (2012), he filmed for the first time outside Iran: in Italy and Japan, respectively.
He was part of a generation of filmmakers in the Iranian New Wave, a Persian cinema movement that started in the late 1960s and emphasized the use of poetic dialogue and allegorical storytelling dealing with philosophical issues. He is known for his use of Persian poetry in the dialogue, titles, and themes of his films. His films also contain a notable degree of ambiguity, an unusual mixture of simplicity and complexity, and often a mix of fictional and documentary elements. The concepts of change and continuity, in addition to the themes of life and death, play a major role in Kiarostami's works.
Kiarostami, the winner of the Palme d’Or at the Cannes Film Festival in 1997 for his “Taste of Cherry”, died of cancer on July 5, 2016 at the age of 76.
The screening in Tokyo offers another opportunity for international audiences, including younger generations of filmgoers, to discover Kiarostami’s work and revisit a film that remains an enduring reference point in Iranian cinema.
The 39th Tokyo International Film Festival will run from October 26 to November 4 under the theme “Connecting — Cinema Connects Us to the World Beyond.” The festival will present more than 200 films across its various sections, with screenings and related events taking place in Tokyo’s Hibiya, Yurakucho, Marunouchi and Ginza areas.

Merck CEO tells CNBC he expects breakthrough cancer vaccine will become faster to make
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
17:33:57 UTC
02:33:57 KST

Merck CEO Rob Davis told CNBC on Wednesday that he expects the company's breakthrough cancer vaccine with Moderna to get faster to manufacture over time.
Shortening the current six-week timeline could potentially help the companies reach more patients.
"We are going to drive for improvement, but right now the focus really is, let's make sure we have the supply ready, we have the market ready to bring this important innovation to the market, and then we'll talk about how do we accelerate," he told CNBC in an exclusive interview. "But I do think over time you're going to see that timeline shortened."
The personalized cancer vaccine turnaround spans from sequencing a patient's tumor to delivering it to the hospital. Merck and Moderna's vaccine is designed to target the specific mutations in each individual patient's tumor rather than using a one-size-fits-all approach, which makes it complicated to produce.
The idea is to train the immune system to recognize and kill those unique cancer markers and then pair that response with Merck's blockbuster immunotherapy Keytruda, which aims to help the body attack the cancer more effectively.
Davis acknowledged that manufacturing the vaccine is a "complex system," but said Merck and Moderna have the process "down to a very tight science."
"I'm actually very confident that we're not going to have complexities in getting this to patients in a very timely fashion," he added. "We're doing it in our clinicals, and I only see improvement going forward."
His comments come after the two companies in August released positive initial data from a late-stage trial on the shot in combination with Keytruda in melanoma patients. Davis said the company is also examining the vaccine in trials across other tumors, including non-small cell lung cancer, types of bladder cancer and renal cell carcinoma.
"You like to talk that maybe you can start moving toward talking about a cure," he said. "We're not there yet, but we're moving in a direction with technology that's really unprecedented."
Merck's new R&D facility
Davis spoke to CNBC after Merck earlier Wednesday officially opened its new 120,000-square-foot research facility, which it has named Advance, in its West Point, Pennsylvania, campus. Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro joined Merck executives and other government officials for a ribbon-cutting ceremony to celebrate the launch of the facility, which features highly automated robotic systems and advanced digital AI capabilities.
Merck says the facility is designed to streamline the analysis of biological samples from the company's ongoing drug programs and improve its research and development.
The opening of the new facility comes as Merck prepares for the upcoming loss of exclusivity of Keytruda, which is one of the world's top-selling drugs and is widely viewed as the backbone of modern cancer treatment. Keytruda's core U.S. compound patent expires in December 2028, while secondary patents extend protection into 2029 and beyond.
Merck has implemented a multi-layered strategy to turn the Keytruda transition into what it views as a manageable "hill" rather than a sharp revenue cliff. That includes accelerating internal research and also funneling $65 billion in external acquisitions and licensing agreements over the five years to build its pipeline of next-generation medicines.
The pharmaceutical giant is also developing new forms of Keytruda and combination regimens that it can transition patients onto and protect the drug's revenue even after key patents expire before 2030.
The Food and Drug Administration in September 2025 approved the subcutaneous form of Keytruda, which is considered a more convenient version because it is administered under the skin in minutes. The standard form of the drug is an intravenous infusion that takes around 30 minutes.
But Merck is facing a legal battle over the newer version in some European markets, raising questions about the market size for the drug.
A Dutch court issued an injunction earlier this month blocking Merck from selling, stocking or manufacturing subcutaneous Keytruda across eight European countries: Belgium, Denmark, France, Ireland, Italy, Sweden, Switzerland and the Netherlands. That followed a patent infringement suit brought by the biotech company Halozyme Therapeutics over its own subcutaneous drug delivery platform.
Merck has said it strongly disagrees with the rulings and plans to appeal. Patients can still receive the original form of Keytruda in Europe while the patent dispute unfolds.
Still, Halozyme has also sued Merck for patent infringement in the U.S., alleging the subcutaneous formulation of Keytruda infringes 15 patents that the biotech has filed since 2011.
Meanwhile, Merck is focused on rolling out a slate of new drugs. That includes Winrevair, a treatment for a rare, life-threatening lung disease that was approved in 2024 and acquired a few years earlier through its $11.5 billion acquisition of Acceleron.
Another closely watched launch is Merck's cholesterol-lowering pill Lipfendra, which was approved by the FDA last month.

Ex-UK army chef jailed for ‘terror’-related offence

Ex-UK army chef jailed for ‘terror’-related offence
The former British Army member harboured ‘extreme right-wing’ views and was ordering explosives components, say police.
A British court has handed a former army chef a nearly four-year jail term for possessing weapons for “terrorist purposes”.
Mark Broadhurst, 28, was given the sentence on Wednesday at Sheffield Crown Court in England, two years after police uncovered online messages in which he expressed racist views and an intention to sell homemade firearms to right-wing groups.
Police found a stockpile of weapons at Broadhurst’s home address when they took him into custody in September 2024, including knives and crossbows, black powder, ammunition, air pistols and what officials described as “an improvised homemade cannon”.
The former British Army member was also found to be part of an online chat group with three other men who last year were jailed for planning to carry out a “terrorist” attack at mosques or synagogues as part of what they believed to be a coming “race war”.
Frank Ferguson, head of the special crime division of the UK’s public prosecution agency, the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS), said Broadhurst was “clearly interested in violence and developing weapons that had the ability to cause untold harm to innocent people”.
Detective Chief Superintendent James Dunkerley, who heads “counterterror” policing in the northeastern region, said Broadhurst was found to be harbouring an “extreme right-wing mindset” and was “proactively ordering components to make explosives”.
Broadhurst pleaded guilty to firearm possession and possessing an explosive under suspicious circumstances, but denied they were for “terrorism” purposes. A judge, however, ruled that Broadhurst’s offences were connected to “terrorism”.
His conviction comes against a backdrop of rising racial tensions and hate crimes in the UK, with marginalised communities increasingly targeted.
British police in July arrested 12 people in connection with an “extreme right-wing terrorism threat” targeting an Islamic gathering in eastern England.
Six months earlier, UK prosecutors said they were handling the highest number of hate crime cases referred by police in its history.

UN envoy says Libya's political progress 'milestone,’ significant challenges remain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
17:30:37 UTC
02:30:37 KST

Merve Aydogan
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
The UN's special envoy for Libya said Wednesday that the Smaller Convening Agreement signed in Tripoli marks a break in the country's prolonged political deadlock, but warned that disinformation and rejection of dialogue by some parties continue to threaten progress.
Hanna Tetteh, who also heads the UN Support Mission in Libya (UNSMIL), told the Security Council that "since my last briefing, we have seen encouraging progress on the UNSMIL-facilitated political process."
She said the parties to the Smaller Convening Agreement signed it on Aug. 30 after four months of deliberations, and that it "has received broad support from national and international actors."
Tetteh stressed that elections cannot be separated from wider institutional problems, including the fragmentation of the judiciary.
"The electoral process cannot be isolated from wider institutional challenges which impact the holding of elections, including the fragmentation of the judiciary," she said.
On security, she described the situation as "fragile" but welcomed "positive steps toward enhanced military cooperation between Eastern and Western military and security institutions."
Drawing attention to southern Libya, she said that "strengthening state presence, improving border management, as well as addressing local grievances related to access to services, can contribute positively to stability in these areas."
Tetteh warned of a continuing wave of "misinformation, disinformation, hate speech and incitement" targeting refugees, migrants, humanitarian actors and UN personnel in Libya.
"Legitimate public concerns regarding migration must be addressed through responsible policy, dialogue and verified information, not through hate speech, intimidation or violence," she said.
She cautioned that the continued rejection by some parties to engage constructively, together with inflammatory rhetoric, risks "hardening political positions, eroding willingness to compromise, and seeking to justify unilateral actions that would undermine the political process or lead to violence."
Calling on the council to back the parties with "positive incentives and guarantees," Tetteh said that "the council should hold spoilers accountable."
"I appeal to this council to urge all parties to move forward quickly given the political, economic and security fragility of the situation in Libya and its impact on the overall stability of the region," she said.
Tetteh also said that "the path to a stable, unified, and prosperous Libya remains long, but our destination remains within reach."

Smart use of Hormuz Strait
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Smart use of Hormuz Strait
The Iran newspaper analyzed the increasingly complex regional environment and argued that careful strategic judgment is essential. According to the paper, the convergence of multiple crises, including the Gaza war, tensions in the Red Sea and the Bab al-Mandab Strait, the Iran-Israel rivalry, the US military presence, and competition among regional powers, has made security in West Asia more fragile than ever. One of the clearest examples of this fragile balance is the Strait of Hormuz.
The geopolitical value of the strait for Iran lies primarily in its deterrent capability. Although a complete closure of the waterway has long been discussed in strategic circles, such a move could trigger broad international consensus against Iran, increase the legitimacy of intervention by external powers, and diminish Iran's geopolitical capital. Consequently, the paper suggested that in the event of escalating tensions, Iran is more likely to rely on limited, gradual, and reversible measures rather than fully employing this strategic tool.
Sharq: Iran at the Trump-Putin table
Shargh discussed the reported agreement between Putin and Trump regarding diesel fuel. Although details of the conversation between the two presidents have not yet been released, questions remain over whether they also reached understandings concerning Iran. For Tehran, the issue is sensitive. On one hand, Iran considers Russia a strategic partner; on the other, it sees that same partner, only hours after discussing regional developments with the Iranian president, sitting down with the US president and reaching an agreement. The visible outcome of the call was an announced deal for supplying Russian diesel fuel to US and global markets. For Putin, the agreement represents both an economic and political achievement. For Trump, it provides an opportunity to demonstrate to voters, ahead of the Congressional midterm elections, that he is taking steps to reduce living costs and curb rising fuel prices. In Tehran, however, the issue goes beyond diesel fuel. What raises concern is the timing of the agreement amid continuing tensions between Iran and the United States and uncertainty about the political content of the conversation between the two leaders.
Kayhan: Trump trapped in an Iranian quagmire
Kayhan wrote about Trump's inability to escape a predicament created by Iran. The economic situation of ordinary Americans continues to deteriorate under the shadow of the war with Iran. It also cited the Hebrew-language newspaper Calcalist as reporting a decline in America's financial strength. The impact of the Iran conflict is weighing heavily on US Congressional midterm elections. Analysts allegedly believe voters may punish Trump and his Republican supporters by backing Democrats in the Nov. 3 elections. Proposals such as keeping the Strait of Hormuz open, distributing financial assistance to citizens, and reaching a diesel agreement with Putin are among the measures Trump is pursuing to avoid electoral defeat.
Siasat-e-Rooz: Iran's new initiative to end the Yemen war
Siasat-e-Rooz highlighted Iran's announcement that it is prepared to facilitate dialogue between Yemen and Saudi Arabia. As fighting between Saudi Arabia and Yemen intensifies, and while Western countries and Israel are accused of fueling the conflict in an effort to regionalize it, Iran says it is ready to help create conditions for negotiations between the two sides. Tehran has consistently sought to play a constructive role in regional security. Although Iran itself is currently engaged in confrontation with the United States and Israel, it maintains that it remains committed to responsible regional behavior and is actively pursuing a political solution to the Yemen crisis. Analysts believe that ending regional conflicts and including a halt to Yemeni attacks in any future agreement involving Iran could reduce pressure on Riyadh.
Ettelaat: How would China benefit or suffer from Iran-US war?
Ettelaat published an interview with Morteza Firouzi, a professor of international relations, comparing Russian and Chinese positions regarding the Iran war. Firouzi argued that China gains little economically from such a war. Unlike Russia, which he believes would benefit from confrontation between Iran and the United States, China would suffer economically. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz, he said, would also be detrimental to Beijing. China is currently drawing on its energy reserves and therefore faces economic challenges. He added that both Russia and China understand that the United States has focused much of its strategic planning on moving beyond the Middle East and concentrating on China. Washington has strengthened political and military cooperation with countries such as Japan, South Korea, and Australia in preparation for long-term competition with Beijing. From China's perspective, Firouzi argued, it is preferable for the United States to remain deeply engaged in Middle Eastern crises rather than redirect its full attention toward China. Therefore, while a conflict harms China economically, continued US involvement in the Middle East could provide strategic advantages for Beijing.

The Guardian view on Trump’s deal with Putin: grim and grubby, but not gamechanging | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
17:30:08 UTC
02:30:08 KST

When Donald Trump pledged to end the war in Ukraine within 24 hours of re-entering the White House last year, no one with any depth of insight into the conflict believed him. But Mr Trump took his own words seriously enough to feel the lack of a ceasefire as an affront to his self-image as a master dealmaker. After a period when it seemed that Kyiv’s European allies had steered the US president away from pro‑Kremlin partisanship, he has reverted to the grotesque view that Ukrainian capitulation is a necessary precondition for peace.
These are the perilous circumstances in which President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met Andy Burnham on Wednesday in Downing Street. In recent days, the US president has called for a change of government in Ukraine. He claimed that a partial ceasefire had been agreed, while Russia escalated its bombardments. According to Mr Zelenskyy, the latest missile strikes have come without the intelligence warnings from the US that have, in the past, facilitated self-defence. There have been reports of Ukrainian soldiers losing access to the Starlink satellite network, controlled by Elon Musk, the US tech oligarch. This raises suspicion of coordinated pressure to tip the scales in Russia’s favour after many months when Mr Putin’s forces have failed to deliver significant advances and his country’s economy has been suffering from the effect of Ukrainian missile and drone counterstrikes.
Mr Trump is unhappy with Ukraine targeting Russian oil refineries. He claims that this is the cause of high energy prices afflicting American consumers and threatening Republican prospects in next month’s midterm elections. The domestic imperative to keep pump prices down led Mr Trump to do a grubby deal to import diesel from Russia, in flagrant breach of international sanctions.
The real driver of global energy prices is not Ukraine defending itself from Russian attack, but Mr Trump’s failing war against Iran. However, the US president is incapable of admitting any fault. Blaming Mr Zelenskyy enables him to deny his own culpability and, with malevolent encouragement from Mr Putin, to revive the preposterous notion that Ukrainian intransigence rather than Russian aggression is the reason why his promise to broker a peace deal remains unfulfilled.
Disrupting Mr Trump’s pro-Russian delusions is not easy, but it has been done before. It is not a gratifying diplomatic task to indulge the monstrous vanity of the US president by trying to impress upon him a view of his country’s national interest, that Mr Putin is not an ally of his country or his personal friend, which is self-evident to any rational observer.
Mr Burnham rightly resists invitations to denounce the US president in public. He recognises that Ukraine’s cause and, by extension, also the cause of European democracy more widely, is better served by making the case in private. The best response to Mr Trump’s perfidy is for Mr Zelenskyy’s friends to reaffirm their support, as Mr Burnham has done, thereby signalling that Ukraine will not be beaten by deals between the Kremlin and the White House.
Russia is failing to achieve its war aims because the invasion was conceived in delusional hatred for the very idea of independent Ukrainian nationhood, which routinely underestimates that country’s will to resist. That is a flaw in Mr Putin’s plans that no amount of collusion with Mr Trump can fix.

Three Russian artistic gymnasts — Angelina Melnikova, Viktoria Listunova, and Anna Kalmykova — have been denied visas to the Netherlands ahead of the Oct. 17-25 World Championships, the Russian Gymnastics Federation said on Telegram earlier today. Two have publicly backed Russian government policies, while a third is believed to have ties to Rosgvardiya, Russia’s National Guard, a separate internal-security force that reports directly to Vladimir Putin.
The federation said the three leading Russian gymnasts were denied visas four days before the start of the competition in Rotterdam, where the first team qualification spots for the 2028 Olympics will be awarded. It quoted the reason given for the refusals:
“One or more Schengen-area member states consider the athletes a threat to their international relations.”
Russian Sports Minister Mikhail Degtyarev said the Russian Olympic Committee would appeal to the International Olympic Committee and World Gymnastics, the sport’s international governing body, demanding that the Rotterdam event be stripped of its Olympic qualifying status.
Kyiv has accused all three gymnasts of either supporting Russia’s full-scale invasion or having links to Russian security institutions.
In Melnikova’s case, in 2025 Ukraine’s Ministry of Youth and Sports called for the 2020 Olympic champion to be stripped of her neutral status, saying she had posted photos featuring the letter Z, a symbol widely used in support of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. The ministry also said she held “charity” training sessions for the children of Russian occupation forces and helped raise money for the daughter of a Russian serviceman.
Ukrainian authorities also noted that Melnikova represents CSKA, a sports club subordinate to Russia’s Ministry of Defense, which they said means she has a contractual relationship with the Russian Armed Forces. In addition, in 2025 Melnikova ran for a seat on the Voronezh City Duma as a candidate for the ruling United Russia party.
Viktoria Listunova took part in a March 2022 rally-concert attended by Vladimir Putin shortly after the start of the full-scale invasion. The event marked what the Kremlin calls the “anniversary of Crimea’s reunification with Russia” (its euphemism for the illegal invasion and subsequent annexation of the Ukrainian peninsula in 2014). Listunova appeared at the event wearing a jacket emblazoned with the letter Z; she was 16 at the time. According to Ukraine’s Sports Ministry, she also raised money for the family of a Russian serviceman killed in the war.
According to Ukraine’s Sports Ministry, Anna Kalmykova competes for Moscow’s Dynamo club and is under contract with Rosgvardiya, whose units have taken part in the invasion and occupation of Ukraine.
Other Russian gymnasts from both the women’s and men’s teams also applied for Dutch visas. The Russian Gymnastics Federation said three of the six Russian women — Alyona Glotova, Lyudmila Roshchina, and Milana Kayumova — were granted entry documents by the Netherlands. Elizaveta Us, who was listed as an additional reserve, also received a visa.
Five of the six male gymnasts who applied received visas as well. The federation said 47 of the 61 members of Russia’s delegation were granted permission to travel to the world championships in Rotterdam.

Weekly German newspaper Die Zeit said it will use every legal means available after a Hamburg court ordered it to hand over interview recordings, a step journalist groups condemned as an assault on press freedom.
Prosecutors and officers from the Hamburg State Criminal Police Office visited Die Zeit’s offices on Monday and threatened a search of the editorial rooms. The Hamburg Regional Court had issued a warrant covering audio recordings of an interview on a high-profile kidnapping case. The editor who did the interviews handed over the files, sealed, to avoid an immediate search.
Die Zeit editors-in-chief Giovanni di Lorenzo and Jochen Wegner said protecting sources is essential for media that report independently. “As part of press freedom, the protection of sources, which is of vital importance for independent media, is particularly indispensable. That is why we will use every legal means available to defend ourselves,” they said in a statement.
Mika Beuster, chairman of the German Journalists’ Association (DJV), criticized the authorities’ approach. “At the start of Hamburg Press Freedom Week, the attitude shown by the authorities raises serious questions about the protection of journalistic work,” he said. Beuster added that journalistic conversations must not be turned into tools for criminal investigations.
Reporters Without Borders called the move a serious attack on press freedom. The trade union known as Ver.di demanded the immediate return of the seized material, saying research material is not a depot for evidence for the judiciary and that such coercion undermines editorial secrecy.
Alleged kidnapping
A court spokesperson said the recordings concern conversations done roughly two weeks after the alleged kidnapping of Christina Block’s two children from Denmark on New Year’s Eve 2023-2024. The interviews involved the children’s father, Stephan Hensel, his wife Astrid Have, and the children. The court argued the files could hold evidentiary value in the trial of Block and six co-defendants, potentially illuminating events not yet examined in the main hearing.

Thousands of filed seized
In a recent television interview, Hanning rejected any role in the alleged kidnapping or related accusations. About 2,000 confidential BND files seized during searches of Hanning’s premises in September 2025 led to a separate inquiry and his arrest. He was taken into custody this Oct. 7. Federal prosecutors accuse Hanning of obtaining and using the classified documents in his private consulting work, including for a foreign intelligence service, and of maintaining intensive contact with another foreign intelligence official. They charged him with espionage, researching state secrets, and attempted treason. His lawyer rejected the accusations, saying Hanning is being unjustly prosecuted.

Strikes on three combined heat and power plants did not cause a total blackout in Kyiv: what to expect in winter
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
20:27:53 EEST
02:27:53 KST

Strikes on three combined heat and power plants did not cause a total blackout in Kyiv: what to expect in winter
Kyiv • UNN
An expert explained why the attacks did not leave Kyiv without electricity and what determines the duration of repairs. Disruptions to heating are possible in winter.
Russian forces are attempting to damage Kyiv’s energy infrastructure, including combined heat and power plants and substations that ensure the transmission of electricity. Energy expert Mykhailo Honchar told a UNN journalist more about how critical the damage to all three of the capital’s CHP plants is and whether prolonged outages should already be expected.
Why Kyiv was not left without electricity after the strikes on the CHP plants
According to the expert, Russia is attempting to carry out comprehensive strikes on energy facilities, seeking to disrupt the city’s electricity and heat supplies simultaneously. However, he notes that the enemy has not carried out such attacks for the first time; in particular, attempts to destroy the energy system began as early as 2022.
In such massive combined attacks, the calculation is always that “that’s it—now we’ll strike once and for all,” but that is not how it turns out. Of course, we have more damage, but the situation here depends on how quickly our repair crews respond
In addition, Mykhailo Honchar emphasizes that the mere fact of a strike on one energy facility does not automatically mean that the entire city will be de-energized. The consequences depend on the facility that was hit and the nature of the damage. Kyiv is the largest electricity consumer in Ukraine.
Kyiv has an energy deficit in terms of the generation available within the city. The issue of the energy deficit was finally resolved with the commissioning, at the end of 2015, of the 750 kV Rivne Nuclear Power Plant–Kyivska substation transmission line. Together with the power flow from the Khmelnytskyi Nuclear Power Plant, this made it possible to balance the needs of Ukraine’s largest electricity consumer—Kyiv and the Kyiv metropolitan area
In addition, according to the expert, Russian attacks are aimed not only at the city’s combined heat and power plants, but also at Ukrenergo substations through which electricity flows from nuclear power plants toward the capital; damage to such facilities complicates the supply of electricity and forces energy workers to change its transmission schemes. At the same time, the extensive structure of the energy system makes it possible to create alternative routes, although this does not rule out disruptions in the operation of the grid.
The enemy’s main efforts are aimed not only at striking Kyiv’s CHP plants. This is specifically intended to make it impossible to generate heat for city residents. Other strikes target substations that carry power from nuclear power plants toward Kyiv. These strikes have periodically been effective, but as we can see, although the situation is problematic, they have not achieved the expected result—namely, leaving Kyiv in darkness
Why restoring electricity and heat supplies may take different amounts of time
Mykhailo Honchar explained that the duration of repairs after shelling depends on exactly what equipment was damaged and whether a replacement is available. The availability of backup equipment and the security conditions under which repair crews can begin work are also important.
It varies greatly. It depends on what you have to replace. Figuratively speaking, it is one thing when you need to replace severed wires—this can be done quickly; but if, for example, a transformer has been hit, then it takes a long time. It also depends on whether backup equipment is available and where it is located. So it is impossible to say exactly how long it will take. Each case is separate
Moreover, Russian forces may carry out repeated strikes on the same facilities, forcing repair crews to take additional risks into account.
Before repair crews begin repair work, the State Emergency Service must inspect the area to determine whether any dangerous objects remain in the affected zone. In addition, we see that they have already done this many times: a subsequent strike follows the first impact. Therefore, unlike before—even last year—when repairs began immediately after the impact and the fire was extinguished, if there was one, the process is now being slowed down for security reasons
Also, due to the specific features of the city’s power grid, the consequences of attacks may differ even in neighboring districts of the city, Mykhailo Honchar noted. He explained that this is related to the configuration of the distribution network, its technical condition, and the ability to redistribute the load. This leads to the uneven application of outage schedules.
The networks are operating in an abnormal mode. Therefore, one district may be without electricity for half a day or even a full day, while somewhere else things may be more or less normal — the power was switched off for several hours, and that’s it. There is no malicious intent here whatsoever. You never know what will be hit and where, how long restoration will take, or how to set up a bypass route if the direct one is not functioning
Does Kyiv face a prolonged lack of heat in winter?
Strikes on all three of the city’s main combined heat and power plants pose risks to getting through the heating season, since the primary purpose of these facilities is heat production. At the same time, damage to them does not mean that all residents of the capital will necessarily be left without heating. According to the expert, the city has boiler houses to which consumers can be reconnected if necessary, although the feasibility of such a solution depends on the specific district and the condition of the infrastructure.
A combined heat and power plant, that is, a cogeneration plant, has the primary task of generating heat. Electricity is produced in parallel, and that is task number two. The enemy’s main efforts are aimed at making heat generation impossible. Heat and heating are not yet needed now, so the enemy is working with the winter outlook in mind
In addition, the expert recalled that in winter, after the combined heat and power plants were hit, some districts of Kyiv also experienced heating problems, but in some cases heat supply was restored by reconnecting buildings to boiler houses. According to him, this shows that even significant damage does not always mean that restoring heat by the next heating season is impossible.
Let’s recall how we dealt with the situation in January–February this year, when they also hit all these combined heat and power plants and there was no heat supply. Yes, entire districts of the capital were left without heat. I remember someone writing in a closed chat: "That’s it, we probably won’t be able to repair anything, even by the start of the next heating season." But imagine our surprise when heat supply was restored literally in just under three weeks. It turned out that they had reconnected them to a boiler house
However, Mykhailo Honchar believes that residents of the capital should nevertheless prepare for possible disruptions, but should not draw conclusions about an inevitable large-scale blackout after every enemy attack.
Hoping for the best, we need to be prepared for the worst-case scenario. I think that, with the experience of the past four winters, our people are more prepared than usual. At the same time, when you look out at night and see that the lights have gone out somewhere in the building opposite, and someone immediately writes falsely on a Telegram channel that Kyiv is experiencing a blackout, this is stoking passions and operating as the enemy’s useful idiot
Thus, strikes on Kyiv’s combined heat and power plants and substations may complicate the operation of the energy system and cause localized disruptions to electricity and heat supplies. At the same time, the further development of the situation will depend on the extent of the damage, security conditions, and the speed of repairs. The expert urges people to prepare for possible difficulties, while assessing the situation based on verified information.

It stressed that all measures and decisions to change the legal and historical status of Jerusalem are “null and void and have no legal effect.”
It said that “opening an embassy to Israel in occupied Jerusalem violates international legitimacy resolutions, particularly UN Security Council Resolutions 476 and 478.”
The two resolutions that were adopted in 1980 affirm the illegality and invalidity of Israeli measures intended to alter the character and legal status of Jerusalem, amid Israel’s enactment of a law annexing East Jerusalem.
The ministry said Colombia’s move also “undermines the international consensus on the city’s legal status and infringes on the Palestinian people’s inalienable rights.”
It warned that the step encourages Israel to continue its “colonial policies and attempts to impose illegal realities on the ground.”
READ: Colombia opens embassy in West Jerusalem despite city’s disputed international status
In addition to Colombia, the US, Guatemala, Honduras, Kosovo, Papua New Guinea, Paraguay, Fiji, Nauru and Somalia’s breakaway region have moved their embassies to West Jerusalem or opened embassies in the city, a move that runs counter to international resolutions concerning the status of Jerusalem.
The Palestinian Foreign Ministry urged Colombia to comply with international law and respect relevant UN resolutions, calling on it to “reverse this step to preserve prospects for achieving a just and comprehensive peace.”
Earlier Wednesday, Colombia opened the embassy in West Jerusalem. The move follows the restoration of its diplomatic relations with Israel in August, after Colombia severed ties with Tel Aviv in May 2024 under a previous government.
Jerusalem remains at the heart of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict and is widely regarded as one of its most sensitive issues.

Europe risks becoming mere tourist attraction – Polish FM
Europe risks becoming little more than a tourist attraction unless it dramatically expands its military capabilities, Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski has warned, calling for an increasingly confrontational stance against Russia and refusing to return its frozen assets.
Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum on Tuesday, Sikorski argued that Europe must translate its economic power into military strength to avoid being sidelined as the US, China, and Russia compete for global influence.
”What’s at stake is not whether we will be occupied,” referring to speculation of a Russian invasion, which Moscow has dismissed as nonsense. The main question, according to Sikorski, is Europe’s “status in the global division of power.”
“The triumvirate that divides the world into spheres of influence” will either be composed of the US, China, and Russia, while Europe serves as “suppliers of data and tourist attractions,” or Europe will be the “third leg” of the group instead of Russia, he said.
Sikorski called for a more assertive military posture toward Russia, including the creation of a European army that Russia would never attack.
Moscow has denied that it has any intention of attacking Europe, warning that the continent’s accelerating military buildup could instead provoke a direct confrontation. Russian officials have cautioned that the conflict could be “very short” and potentially nuclear.
The Polish foreign minister also rejected the idea of returning Russia’s frozen sovereign assets, declaring that Moscow will recover the assets “over our dead bodies.”
Around $300 billion in Russian central bank reserves have been frozen by Western countries since the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022. The EU has already begun channeling proceeds generated by the assets to Kiev but has stopped short of confiscating the principal, amid legal and financial concerns.
Belgium – which hosts Euroclear, the clearinghouse that holds most of the frozen assets in the EU – has resisted outright confiscation. Officials warn that doing so could undermine confidence in Europe’s financial system and send “a very bad signal to other countries worldwide” that hold assets in the EU.
Russia has denounced the proposals to seize the assets as outright theft, warning that doing so would trigger legal action and retaliation against Western assets in Russia.
