A fatwa (a legal ruling on a point of Islamic law) against buying olive products from settlers was issued by the grand mufti of Jerusalem and the Palestinian Territories and head of the Supreme Fatwa Council, Sheikh Muhammad Ahmad Hussein, in response to the rise of settler attacks on the olive industry.
The legal ruling was given on Tuesday in response to escalating settler violence, specifically against olive trees this harvest season, Hussein’s office published.
“The basic principle is the prohibition of buying something stolen, because its seller does not own it, nor does he have the right to dispose of it; Buying it encourages theft, cooperates in sin and aggression, and endorses wrongdoing,” Hussein said.
“The sin is magnified if buying stolen goods encourages the enemies to seize the lands of the Palestinians, plunder their resources, and displace their people from them.”
Based on this ruling, the Grand Mufti insisted it was forbidden to purchase olive products “stolen from Palestinian trees and sold by settlers, due to the great evils involved.”
Olives are the backbone of Palestinian agriculture
“Among these evils is that it empowers the usurping occupier of our land, which necessitates concerted official and popular efforts to reject the sale and purchase of usurped and stolen goods,” he said.
His ruling came weeks after Israeli military bulldozers allegedly bulldozed olive groves near Ramallah.
Though the IDF has not issued a statement on the alleged destruction of the groves, the military has previously cited the need to clear land of olive trees to prevent security threats or ambushes on troops.
The olive harvest usually begins in the first week of October. Olives are the backbone of Palestinian agriculture, a sector that accounts for around 8% of GDP and more than 60,000 jobs, according to the Palestinian Authority’s Agriculture Ministry.
It has also reported that more than 45,000 trees, including more than 26,000 olive trees, were cut down or damaged across the West Bank during the first half of 2026.
The National has also reported that Palestinian farmers have been killed in recent weeks by extremist settlers, including an individual named by the Palestinian Health Ministry as 44-year-old Ali Hassan Yusor al-Bazzari.
Notably, the official account for the Palestinian Authority deleted an AI-generated video showing multiple Israeli bulldozers destroying an olive grove, and the images have been shared widely across pro-Palestinian social media accounts.

Kenya’s health ministry confirms second Ebola case

Kenya’s Health Ministry confirms second Ebola case
A relative of the first case, 39-year-old man’s infection raises concerns of a cross-border spread.
Kenya has reported a second Ebola infection, about a week after confirming its first-ever case of the disease when a citizen who had been living in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) travelled to Kenya and died two days later at a Nairobi hospital.
The second patient, a 39-year-old man who is a close family member of the first case, fell ill on Tuesday and was already in quarantine when he came down with symptoms of fever, fatigue and joint pain, the Ministry of Health said in a statement Wednesday.
‘Leave Uganda out’
Last week’s case raised concerns about deficiencies in border screening systems in the region after the patient drove from the DRC to Uganda and flew to Nairobi from there.
Given the closure of the border between the DRC and Uganda since May because of the outbreak of the virus, it is not clear how he was able to enter the country.
Alan Kasujja, executive director of the Ugandan government’s media centre, questioned how Kenya allowed the man to enter via its airport.
“Leave Uganda out of this conversation. We don’t have Ebola here,” he wrote on X.
When asked how the patient was able to travel through three countries undetected, Kenya’s Director-General for Health Patrick Amoth said last week that a meeting was scheduled with officials from the DRC and Uganda and the Africa CDC to investigate.
Stepped-up response
Kenya has intensified its national response to the disease since the country recorded the first case. At the time, Kenya traced everyone who came in contact with the patient and reported at least 57 people, with 10 immediately quarantined, Health Minister Aden Duale told journalists on October 7.
Kenya is the fourth country to record a case linked to the Ebola epidemic in the DRC, the second-largest on record globally with more than 9,000 cases and more than 4,000 deaths.
Uganda reported 20 cases and two deaths earlier in the year but was declared Ebola-free in August. A doctor who returned to France in June from the DRC tested positive, but there was no further spread of the virus.
Ebola spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of infected people, whether living or dead. The disease can cause fever, vomiting, diarrhoea and, in severe cases, internal and external bleeding.
The second patient is currently at a designated treatment centre, where he is receiving the appropriate care, the Health Ministry said. It will continue to share information on his progress, the ministry added.

Senior Ukrainian officials accused the United States on Wednesday of imposing restrictions on Kyiv's ability to use the Starlink satellite network, owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX, for military operations in its defense against Russia's invasion. Musk and his company have not commented on the allegations, which come amid intense pressure from U.S. President Donald Trump, a close ally of Musk, on Kyiv to halt its attacks on oil facilities deep inside Russia. Musk allowed Ukrainian forces to use Starlink's internet satellites in the early days of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Since then, the communications and navigation capabilities they provide have become critical on the battlefield.
Starlink is also considered more resistant to electronic jamming, making it useful for drone attacks carried out by Kyiv, particularly in Russian-held areas of eastern and southern Ukraine. According to Reuters, Ukrainian drones do not use Starlink when entering Russian territory, relying instead on other communications systems.
But senior Ukrainian officials now say restrictions on military use of Starlink are severely hampering Ukrainian operations, particularly along the front lines. The New York Times reported that officials in Kyiv were stunned by the restrictions.
Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov, an adviser to President Volodymyr Zelensky, said Wednesday morning that no advance warning was given before the restrictions were imposed, disrupting several "missions."
According to Beskrestnov, the restrictions cut off access to the military version of the service at speeds exceeding 160 kilometers per hour (100 mph). He added that Starlink is also crucial to air defense systems Kyiv is using to intercept the fast jet-powered drones Russia has begun deploying in attacks on Ukrainian cities in recent months. These faster drones are more difficult to intercept.
Beskrestnov suggested the move was deliberate. "It is clear that this action cannot be a coincidence and is related to the current political situation," he said.
Ukraine's military said the restrictions had also caused disconnections during drone flights at lower speeds of 110 to 120 kilometers per hour (68 to 75 mph).
"The drones kept moving, but these interruptions made them harder to control," said the 7th Rapid Response Corps, a Ukrainian air force unit operating in the country's southeast.
A source in Ukraine's Defense Ministry also told Reuters that the restrictions significantly complicate logistics and the operation of several types of drones.
The Starlink restrictions come alongside allegations made in recent days by Zelensky and his aides that Kyiv had, on several occasions, failed to receive advance warnings from Western allies about Russian missile attacks.
Western intelligence is also critical to Kyiv's preparations for such attacks, and no warnings were issued in the Ukrainian capital on either of the past two nights when Russian missiles were launched toward the city.
According to the Ukrainian air force, Russia launched another 39 ballistic and cruise missiles overnight Tuesday into Wednesday, along with 128 drones. Only four missiles and 115 drones were intercepted.
At least four people were killed and about 20 others wounded in the overnight attack on Kyiv. Two other civilians were killed in the Dnipropetrovsk region and a third was killed in the Zaporizhzhia region.
"A Russian ballistic missile attack on Kyiv. Once again, no early warning from our partners," Zelensky said Wednesday morning.
A U.S. official told Agence France-Presse that Washington "has not changed its policy on intel-sharing" with Ukraine. However, a senior official in Kyiv told the news agency that the United States had threatened to suspend intelligence assistance unless Ukraine stopped attacking Russian oil refineries.
According to the Ukrainian official, Washington had in fact failed to warn Kyiv about ballistic missile launches on two occasions.
"And on top of that they've throttled Starlink speeds," the Ukrainian official said on condition of anonymity. "It's obvious they [the United States] are helping Russia for some reason."
Trump has demanded that Ukraine halt its attacks on Russian oil refineries, arguing that they have caused a surge in global diesel prices. Experts, however, say the war in Iran is the main reason for the increase, which is hurting Republicans' chances of retaining control of Congress in the U.S. midterm elections.
After stunning Kyiv and its European allies by lifting sanctions on Russia late last week to allow it to export diesel to global markets, Trump also announced an "energy ceasefire" on Sunday, supposedly with the agreement of both sides. In reality, however, no such agreement had been reached.
Zelensky revealed Tuesday that Ukraine had indeed suspended its attacks on Russian oil facilities for two days, but said Russia had continued attacking energy facilities in Ukraine throughout that period.
He said the latest overnight strikes also targeted Ukrainian energy infrastructure, particularly in the Kyiv and Kharkiv regions, leaving 600,000 people without electricity.
"We ask America and everyone in the world who does not close their eyes to reality to react and react harshly. Russia missed the opportunity for de-escalation and clearly chose to continue its insane war of destruction," Zelenskyy said following the overnight Russian attack.
Zelenskyy called on Trump to renew pressure on Moscow, invoking the approach of former Republican President Ronald Reagan. "Peace can only come through strength, and we ask America to remember this principle of Reagan's," he said.

The “big man” gibe refers to a public dispute on social media between Musk, Sikorski and United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio in 2025, when the SpaceX boss told Sikorski to “be quiet, small man” on his X platform.
Starlink is a sensitive topic between Sikorski and Musk. The two previously clashed over the technology after the trillionaire said Ukraine’s “entire frontline could collapse” if he switched off Starlink.
Following the dispute in 2025, Musk said “no matter how much I disagree with the Ukraine policy, Starlink will never turn off its terminals.”
At the time he added, “We would never do such a thing or use it as a bargaining chip.”
‘Cannot be a coincidence’
The slowdown comes after Russian ballistic missiles struck Kyiv for the second night in a row, killing at least nine people and damaging electricity and heating infrastructure. Zelenskyy said Ukraine did not receive its usual warnings from Western allies for a second day, without specifying which partners.
Sources have told Reuters and other media that the US has threatened to cut off intelligence for early warning of missile strikes on Ukraine, pressing Kyiv to suspend attacks on Russian oil refineries.
Trump said on Tuesday the US has not stopped sharing intelligence.
Beskrestnov warned that the slowdown “cannot be a coincidence” after Trump struck a deal with President Vladimir Putin to import Russian diesel – despite international sanctions to isolate Moscow.
Speaking to AFP, another Ukrainian official accused Washington of throttling Starlink and helping Russia.
On Saturday, Trump suggested Zelenskyy had not done enough to end the war with Russia, blaming him for high diesel prices in the US.
Last week, Trump lifted sanctions on Russian diesel under pressure to curb fuel prices that have soared since the US war with Iran began as the midterms rapidly approach. He told Kyiv to stop attacking Russian refineries and urged Ukrainians to replace Zelenskyy.
“It’s painful when President Trump chooses one side, not our side,” Zelenskyy said in the interview with Morgan.
The Ukrainian leader explained he was fine with Trump being in the middle between Ukraine and Russia, but “if you are in the middle, you have to stay in the middle.”

Families of Iran's terror victims call on Pakistan to act against militants
TEHRAN — Families representing Iran's 23,000 victims of terrorism have sent an open letter to the government of Pakistan urging decisive action against terrorist groups operating along the southeastern border, following a recent escalation of attacks in Sistan and Baluchestan Province.
The letter, issued Tuesday by the Habilian Foundation, which represents families of terror victims in Iran, specifically names the Takfiri group Jaish al-Adl, now operating under the title People's Strugglers Front. It accuses the group of exploiting border conditions to move freely into Pakistan, reside and find shelter in some areas.
Such a sustained pattern, the families wrote, could not occur without the knowledge of some local and central officials in Pakistan, citing Pakistani media reports and interviews with members of the groups.
The letter frames the issue not only as political and human rights concern but as a matter of legal obligations. It cites the Island of Palmas arbitration of 1928 and the International Court of Justice ruling in the Corfu Channel case of 1949 on the duty of states not to knowingly allow their territory to be used against the rights of other states.
It also invokes U.N. Security Council Resolution 1373 (2001), adopted under Chapter VII and binding on all members under Article 25 of the U.N. Charter, which requires states to refrain from supporting terrorists, deny them safe haven, prevent use of territory against other states, bring perpetrators to justice and ensure effective border controls, as well as to exchange operational information and cooperate bilaterally. It further cites Resolution 1566 (2004) on full cooperation with victim states and the principle of extradite or prosecute.
The families also refer to the General Assembly's 1970 Friendly Relations Declaration, its 1994 Declaration on Measures to Eliminate Terrorism and its 2006 Global Counter-Terrorism Strategy, while distinguishing those instruments from binding Council decisions.
On bilateral frameworks, the letter cites the 1960 Iran-Pakistan border administration agreement, the 1960 extradition treaty noted in the April 24, 2024 joint statement, and that statement's pledges on cooperation against terrorism, hostage-taking and kidnapping.
The families, acknowledging these are duties of due diligence rather than absolute guarantees, say the continued, open movement of militants is incompatible with any reasonable standard of care. They call on Islamabad to dismantle safe havens, secure the border, share intelligence, prosecute or, where treaty conditions are met, extradite suspects, establish a joint security and judicial mechanism, issue a formal written response, and create a permanent channel to receive documents from victims' families and inform them of proceedings.
The letter stresses that Iran-Pakistan ties have been uniquely fraternal since Pakistan's independence and warns that terrorists seek to undermine that bond.

Access to Public Lands Should Unite All Americans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
17:00:26 UTC
02:00:26 KST

Experiencing wild, open, and natural spaces is part of what it means to me to be American, and I know I'm not alone in that belief.
Our shared connection to nature crosses geography, generations, and political beliefs. From a neighborhood trail to a national park or a stretch of open desert, the outdoors gives us places to come together, find perspective, and experience something larger than ourselves.
At a time of growing loneliness, division, and stress, being outside can improve physical and mental well-being, strengthen community, and reconnect us with one another. For millions of Americans, public lands make that possible.
But the places that sustain that connection are under growing pressure due to decisions made by elected leaders. That is why, as we head into this year’s midterm election, voters must ask every candidate a simple question: How will you protect our public lands?
The answer will help determine what we leave future generations.
Consider Bears Ears National Monument in Utah. A presidential proclamation issued this summer reduced the monument’s boundaries from roughly 1.36 million acres to about 131,000, removing monument protections from more than 90% of the landscape. Bears Ears is a living cultural landscape and sacred ancestral homeland of deep significance to Tribal Nations.
Similar decisions are unfolding across the country. Congress rolled back protections for the Boundary Waters, opening the door to mining in its headwaters. The Trump Administration is also considering transferring a parcel of Yosemite National Park to a private developer. Pristine roadless backcountry may also be opened to development and extraction. These decisions will have lasting consequences.
There is room for honest debate about how public lands should be managed. Recreation, conservation, grazing, timber, energy development, and local economies all deserve consideration. Responsible stewardship requires balancing those interests while protecting the places that generations of Americans have worked to preserve.
That debate matters because public lands are not only a conservation legacy—they are also an economic engine.
Outdoor recreation generates $1.3 trillion in economic output and supports 5.2 million American jobs. Communities and businesses across the country depend on the forests, rivers, trails, parks, and open spaces that draw people outdoors.
The meaning runs deep. Public lands are among the few places in American life that connect all of us. The rock climber in Yosemite and the hunter in Montana may not share the same politics, but they share a stake in keeping these places healthy, accessible, and protected. Public lands remind us that our common ground is more than an idea—they’re real places beneath our feet.
The decisions made today will outlast this administration and this Congress. Once public lands are permanently altered, fragmented, or developed, there’s no going back.
One of the best ways to protect these places is to help connect more people to experience them. People protect what they know. They fight for places that become part of their lives. The future of our public lands will be decided by whether Americans still believe they are worth protecting, and whether we elect leaders who believe it too.
As candidates ask for our vote, we should ask where they stand. Look at the choices they have made. Look at the policies they support and listen carefully to their answers. For generations, Americans of every political persuasion have chosen to safeguard extraordinary places for everyone who would come after them. The forests, rivers, and mountains we enjoy today exist because of those choices.
Now, the choice is ours.
We can treat public lands as another political issue, or we can recognize them for what they are: places that make us healthier, bring us together, and connect us to something larger than ourselves.
This November, we must elect leaders who believe that public lands are worth protecting.

She defended the decision to invite City even as the prime minister came under fire for his own contacts with the club, telling the Guardian it had played a vital role in helping build infrastructure in her city.
“If a football club has broken the rules, a football club should be punished for breaking the rules, and that is pretty clear in an independent process,” she said.
“I think what can also be true at the same time though, if you ask residents in east Manchester, have they benefited from a new library, a new leisure centre, a new sixth-form college, infrastructure investment, the job opportunities that come from them being a good employment charter signee and an early adopter of the real living wage – then they will have felt that benefit.”

The revelation comes as Burnham faced pressure over his relationship with City’s owners during his time as mayor of Greater Manchester. The prime minister was forced to clarify on Wednesday that he had two additional dinners with the club chair, Khaldoon al-Mubarak, at the Etihad Stadium, having previously declared those only as matchday hospitality.
Speaking at PMQs, Burnham said no one from the club had raised the Premier League charges with him.
Craig’s defence of the club came as her mayoral authority published details of Burnham’s contacts with City officials when he was mayor.
The release showed the prime minister had attended a formal meeting with al-Mubarak, chatted to him in the stands at a player’s testimonial game and was accompanied by staff from the club on official overseas visits.
But the Sun newspaper revealed later on Monday that Burnham had twice attended a pre-match dinner with the chair, which was declared in now-deleted council paperwork. No 10 said it was routine for the records to be deleted when a new mayor was in place.
Burnham’s initial response to the findings against City had drawn criticism after he said he would be “really concerned” if its Abu Dhabi owners sold the club in the wake of the Premier League findings, calling them a “huge partner in the building of modern Manchester”.
As the prime minister came under fire for his comments, Downing Street clarified that he believed where wrongdoing had been established, those responsible should face the consequences.
City attended the trade delegation alongside several other northern sports and leisure organisations, including Lancashire cricket club and Visit Lake District. While in India, the football club took part in an event in Delhi promoting British tourism.
The Great North – a coalition of mayors from the north of England which organised the India event – said its aim was “to shine a spotlight on the great tourism products across the north of England”.
The Greater Manchester mayoral authority said on Tuesday that representatives of Greater Manchester sporting clubs would “routinely join business delegations” on international visits during Burnham’s time as mayor.
Burnham’s defence of City and its owners has focused attention not only on his links to the club but on how reliant he was on investment from Abu Dhabi to power Manchester’s strong growth rates when he was mayor.
Other senior politicians on this week’s trade delegation include Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, Douglas Alexander, the Scotland secretary, and Angela Eagle, the environment secretary.
Reynolds took part in a Premier League event on Tuesday, where he met schoolchildren being taught by British-trained coaches. He denied afterwards that the charges against City had tainted the league’s reputation. It is otherwise one of Britain’s most successful cultural exports.
“The brand of the Premier League – one of the UK’s most important brands … that is incredibly powerful,” he said.
Asked whether it was appropriate for City to have been invited, given the charges it faced, he said: “That’s a Greater Manchester issue, and obviously they are a major participant in the economy in Greater Manchester.
“I understand the interest – the relationship between Manchester and Manchester City – but in terms of the allegations, their appeal, that is a football matter.”

Can math stay human in the age of AI?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
17:00:00 UTC
02:00:00 KST

Can math stay human in the age of AI?
When AI companies value competition over collaboration, we may lose out on understanding
“Exponentially exploding,” mathematician Thomas Bloom told me by phone, describing the flood of new results in his field. Little did he know that hours later, OpenAI was going to post 722 mathematical manuscripts an unreleased AI model had produced.
The firehose of new work lends new urgency to the question: How is AI changing mathematical discovery? In their race for headline-grabbing breakthroughs, AI companies typically do not disclose their methods and data. That competition among AI companies threatens to overwhelm human collaboration and understanding.
This tension had been playing out in miniature on a website Bloom runs that tracks progress on more than 1,000 problems originally posed and collected by Paul Erdős, one of the 20th century’s most prolific mathematicians. Here, people used to collaborate to discuss open problems, or ones for which the best solution either hasn’t been found or isn’t known to the greater math community. But increasingly, visitors were competing to close open problems with AI proofs that they often didn’t understand. Bloom, a mathematician at the University of Manchester in England, doesn’t want to spend his days refereeing AI-generated work. So, soon after we spoke, and before he knew that OpenAI would be announcing its latest results, Bloom posted that he’d no longer tag problems as open or solved, and he also closed comments.
It’s definitely exciting that AI can tackle so many open problems so quickly. But can it help mathematicians understand the answers and build on them?
Just two days after OpenAI’s deluge of results, the peer-reviewed edition of a Google DeepMind study became public. First reported in a preprint earlier this year, it offers an inside look at how one AI system tackles open math problems. The system called AlphaProof Nexus solved 9 Erdős problems and made a number of other interesting mathematical advances, researchers report October 8 in Science.
The report includes a detailed description of how the results were obtained. Plus, human mathematicians vetted many of the proofs. That’s “quite different” from how OpenAI and Anthropic are handling their math results, Bloom says.
“The ultimate objective of any AI for math research,” says research scientist and study co-author Swarat Chaudhuri of Google DeepMind in London, should be “to advance mathematics as done by human mathematicians.”
A look inside an AI math machine
In the recently published study Chaudhuri and his colleagues tested different configurations of their system. To tackle a collection of 353 open Erdős problems, they used multiple agents powered by the Gemini language model. These could call on AlphaProof, an AI model specially trained to do math, and the inspiration for the name of the overall system, for difficult steps. The agents also relied on Lean, math software that identifies steps that remain unproven, to check their logic. The agents shared their work, circulating promising proof attempts and discarding ones that weren’t going well.
The team also tested a simpler setup on the nine problems the full system solved. Independent Gemini agents worked through proofs using Lean’s feedback, without sharing attempts or consulting AlphaProof. That setup solved all nine, too. It was cheaper—using fewer computing resources—than the full system on easy problems and more expensive on the two toughest ones. The team did not establish whether the simpler setup would solve any of the problems the full system had missed.
The fact that the simpler setup could solve the same nine problems as the full system surprised Chaudhuri. It suggests that increasingly capable language models can tackle research mathematics with relatively simple checking tools.
But computer-checking comes with a caveat. Lean checks only the statement it’s given, as it is written in its code. And a mathematical statement may be incorrectly translated to or from Lean code. An October 6 preprint shows why this translation matters. In the paper, the researchers pinpoint mismatches between parts of OpenAI’s written Navier–Stokes proof and its Lean counterpart. The mismatches do not mean the written proof is wrong, the team writes, but they note that a valid Lean proof does not automatically validate an AI-generated math paper.
That’s why the vetting human mathematicians did for the DeepMind publication is so important. “The human mathematician has to really think through the problem and set goals for the system,” Chaudhuri says. And even if the system failed to finish a proof, its checked steps helped mathematicians focus on the remaining gaps. “Math is ultimately a human art,” Chaudhuri says. “The system enhances the human user’s insights, and the human user is able to guide the system with new ideas.”
With math ability comes responsibility
The mathematical results that the AlphaProof Nexus system achieved are “not really at the top level of importance,” says Bloom, who wasn’t involved with the work. But that underscores the team’s more measured approach. Google DeepMind, he says, is “trying to be more responsible with the science,” while companies like OpenAI are using math to showcase their software. OpenAI’s papers and accompanying Lean proofs were entirely AI-generated, leaving it up to the math community to work out what’s useful or useless.
OpenAI says they worked with an independent advisory group to develop best practices on how to share their AI math results. But that group has said their advice was to not test unreleased AI models on advanced math, guidance the company clearly ignored.
The company’s fast-moving, competitive approach continues to alienate mathematicians such as Bryna Kra of Northwestern University in Evanston, Ill. She says the company made some improvements in their efforts to cite past literature. And she’s excited about AI’s potential to solve important problems in math. But there is widespread concern, she says, that AI models have accessed people’s unpublished work. “We had a healthy, collaborative, sharing culture that is being destroyed,” she says. “Now, people are wary of sharing their ideas.”
Not all mathematicians feel this way about AI. The technology is “making math more accessible,” says Andrew Turner, who wonders why a small group of mathematicians should get to decide how we solve problems. Turner, who studied math and physics and is Now CTO of the company Plasma AI, based in New York City thinks “math is becoming engineering.” And doing math with machines will allow people to “answer questions previously unfathomable.”
A few days after Bloom shut down the competition on his website, Plasma AI announced a new website to track progress on Erdős problems. They will welcome AI results.
Bloom doesn’t see math as a Silicon Valley–esque move-fast-and-break-things competition. I agree, and hope that curious people will continue to explore problems they care about, with AI helping rather than taking over. At the end of his post announcing the changes to his website, Bloom wrote something that makes me tear up every time I read it. I hope everyone, even the most enthusiastic AI users, can find the time for this type of work: “Be confused, be stuck, be inspired. Find a messy proof, then find a better one,” he wrote. “Get tired, get hungry, get into a flow state. Argue, laugh, give up, drink some coffee and attack it again. Be human. Let your brain be open.”

Israel has signed an agreement with the U.S. Department of War to buy 12 Boeing AH-64E Apache attack helicopters, the newest version of the Apache, with deliveries scheduled to begin early in the next decade, the Israel Ministry of Defense said on Oct. 14.
The ministry’s director general, Maj. Gen. (res.) Amir Baram, instructed Israel’s defense mission in the United States to sign the deal after the Israeli government approved it on Wednesday. The ministry did not disclose the value of the agreement or a specific delivery date, saying only that the helicopters are due at the start of the next decade.
The order is well below the package Washington cleared earlier this year. On Jan. 30, the U.S. State Department approved a possible sale of 30 AH-64E helicopters to Israel, together with 70 engines, Longbow fire-control radars and targeting sights, at an estimated cost of $3.8 billion. A Foreign Military Sales approval sets a ceiling, and buyers often sign for fewer aircraft than the notification covers.
Israeli officials said the agreement was tailored with U.S. counterparts to fit Israel’s needs, and both the defense minister and the ministry’s director general pointed to obstacles that had to be cleared to finish it.
“The execution of the Apache agreement was made possible thanks to creative solutions we developed together with our American partners, without compromising operational needs,” Baram said.
Neither official explained what those challenges were or whether Israel plans to order more of the 30 helicopters approved by Washington. Baram said the ministry will keep working to sign further agreements covering platforms and munitions as well as interceptors.
“The Israeli defense establishment invested considerable effort and acted with determination to overcome the challenges and complete this agreement,” said Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz.
The new helicopters are meant to replace the oldest part of the Israeli Air Force’s Apache force. Israel flies a mix of AH-64A Peten and AH-64D Saraf helicopters, and its 48-strong fleet includes 26 A-models that are up to 39 years old. Israeli Apaches have flown heavily since the war with Hamas began in October 2023, including strikes in Gaza and Lebanon and interceptions of drones.
The AH-64E, also known as the Apache Guardian, has more powerful engines and improved sensors and avionics over earlier models. It can also control drones from the cockpit and receive their video feeds, a feature the U.S. Army uses to pair Apaches with unmanned scouts.
Boeing Israel President Maj. Gen. (res.) Ido Nehushtan said the Apache deal follows Israel’s earlier selection of Boeing’s KC-46A aerial refueling tanker and its decision to buy a second squadron of F-15IA fighters.

Can Trump Strip Ilhan Omar of Her Citizenship? Here's How the Process Works
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:57:47 UTC
01:57:47 KST

In a highly unusual step, federal agents this week aggressively intensified their investigations into Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar of Minnesota, weeks before she stands for reelection in her home district.
The Department of Justice on Tuesday subpoenaed relatives of Omar’s family members, including her sister Sahra Noor, according to The New York Times. The grand jury subpoenas were issued shortly after a raid of the lawmaker’s residence in Washington, D.C. on Monday.
The judicial search warrant, which is under seal, was executed by Homeland Security Investigations, the investigative branch of Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Although the Department of Justice did not provide any more details of the investigation, multiple outlets, citing anonymous sources, reported that the search stemmed from Omar’s immigration paperwork, which was filled out by her late father when she was a child.
Prior to the investigation, multiple Trump Administration officials have accused Omar of immigration fraud without presenting any evidence. In a podcast interview in March, Vice President JD Vance said the White House was exploring “legal remedies” to her alleged immigration fraud. Last month, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the investigation into Omar was “ongoing” and dismissed efforts to frame the case as political retribution.
“If we actually move a case forward, it’s not a political case. It's actually a case because they did things wrong,” Mullin said during the interview with right-wing podcaster Benny Johnson.
Omar, who has long denied the allegations, condemned the raid on her home as “political intimidation” and said she will “not be silenced.”
President Trump, along with many MAGA Republicans, has repeatedly floated the idea of revoking Omar’s citizenship, a process also known as denaturalization, and deporting her.
But legal and immigration experts tell TIME that denaturalizing a U.S. citizen is a rare and difficult process, one that requires federal authorities to clear a high bar in front of a federal judge. Here’s what to know about how the process works.
How does denaturalization work?
Stripping someone of their citizenship is a more arduous legal process than most other immigration efforts that involve the courts. Deportation proceedings, for instance, are initiated by ICE agents under the Department of Homeland Security and are then approved by immigration judges who are hired and work within the Department of Justice. The denaturalization process, on the other hand, must be approved by an independent federal judge, who evaluates the request by a higher standard.
All denaturalization efforts begin at DOJ. In order to revoke a naturalized person’s citizenship, a DOJ lawyer must decide whether to file a civil or a criminal petition in court. Yuripzy Morgan, an attorney and host of Free Range National podcase, said a civil complaint does not have a statute of limitation, whereas a criminal complaint has a statute of limitation of 10 years and must clear a much higher legal bar.
“For civil denaturalization, the government has to show that there is clear, convincing, and unequivocal evidence that the person in question obtained their naturalization either illegally, or they willfully misrepresented a material fact, ” Morgan says. She stressed that simply having an error in an immigration document doesn't mean that a judge is going to approve stripping a person of their citizenship.
For a criminal denaturalization conviction, the federal government must show “proof beyond a reasonable doubt” that the individual knowingly obtained citizenship through fraud, which is the highest legal standard of proof required to secure a criminal conviction. In 2017, the Supreme Court unanimously ruled in Maslenjak v. United States that only an illegal act that played a role in a person’s citizenship application could lead to criminal denaturalization, further narrowing down the scope of such efforts.
Omar’s father filled out and submitted her citizenship application on her behalf when she was 17. It is unclear what evidence, if any, the federal government has to show that anything in the application was fraudulent, or that Omar or her father intentionally misrepresented anything in that application.
Andrew Arthur, a former immigration judge and a resident fellow at the Center for Immigration Studies, pointed out that even after someone gets denaturalized, a deportation is not guaranteed. The person would still be able to retain their previous legal immigration status until a final order of removal is issued to the person by ICE.
“If they had a green card before they naturalized, even after they get denaturalized, they are going to have a green card,” Arthur says.
How did Rep. Omar get naturalized as a U.S. citizen?
According to Omar’s House biography, Omar and her family fled her home country Somalia when she was eight. The family eventually sought asylum in the United States in 1995. She told The New York Times that she became a U.S. citizen in 2000 when she was 17.
At the time Omar went through the process, federal law allowed immigrants under the age of 18 to get naturalized as U.S. citizens if both of their parents had become U.S. citizens. The law was eventually replaced by a new law in 2001, which only requires one parent to become a citizen for the children to be naturalized.
At the center of this investigation is whether Omar’s father, Nur Omar Mohamed, lied about her age in immigration documents so she could be eligible to derive citizenship through him, according to The Washington Post, which cited two unnamed sources.
According to Arthur, the former immigration judge, if Omar was 18 at the time of the naturalization application, she may have been able to apply for her citizenship on her own after having a valid green card for five years.
The allegations regarding Omar’s citizenship gained attention among conservative activists and commentators starting in 2019, when Omar became a member of Congress. Shortly after her election, Omar’s staff sought to change her official birth year in public records from 1981 to 1982, according to multiple outlets.
How often does the U.S. government strip people of their citizenship?
Despite the renewed push from the second Trump administration, denaturalization remains an exceedingly rare legal process. According to the Migration Policy Institute, a Washington, D.C.-based think tank, an average of 11 denaturalization cases were filed per year between 1990 and 2017.
Denaturalization efforts have increased in Trump’s second term. The DOJ has announced efforts to strip at least 108 people of their citizenship in 2026. That is still considerably smaller than the hundreds of thousands of people whom the U.S. government grants citizenship to through naturalization every year.

US carriers dare not approach Hormuz, we are waiting to sink them
TEHRAN – The commander of the Islamic Revolution Guards Corps Navy says American warships have withdrawn to hundreds of kilometers from the Strait of Hormuz out of vulnerability, warning that Iranian forces are counting the moments for them to come within range.
Rear Admiral Ali Ozmaei said in remarks published Tuesday that the United States Navy, despite its advanced hardware, no longer dares to approach Iranian waters.
"Today, by God's grace and with our naval combatants, we are standing against the vicious enemies," Ozmaei said. "The US Army has turned into a fuel smuggler and its fleet has become useless because it is vulnerable and does not dare to come close to Iran."
The commander said Iran has turned its tactical weaknesses into strengths and challenged Washington to test who really controls the world's most critical energy chokepoint.
"If the Americans want to see whether the Strait of Hormuz is open or closed, let them enter the field to see who controls it," he said.
According to Ozmaei, even the United States' 13-billion-dollar aircraft carrier has been rendered ineffective and is now operating about 700 kilometers away from the Strait because it fears being hit.
"We are waiting for the American warships to approach the entrance of the Strait of Hormuz to sink them; we are counting down moment by moment for this to happen," he said.
Ozmaei said Iran has so far publicized only one or two examples of its punishment of violating vessels, noting that the US and its regional partners of imposing a media blackout to hide the fact that offending ships are being disciplined.
"We showed only two samples of the punishment of offending ships," he said, adding that Iranian forces act without compromise against violators.
The commander stressed that the Strait of Hormuz and the Persian Gulf are under the control of the IRGC Navy, while the Sea of Oman is controlled by the Islamic Republic Army, meaning that any blockade now lies beyond the Sea of Oman, in the Arabian Sea.
"The IRGC Navy conducts smart control of the Strait of Hormuz," Ozmaei explained. Vessels bound to or departing from Iran are issued permits through a hierarchy and transit only through the Iranian waterway, he said.
Addressing the Iranian public, he said naval combatants are in the field alongside the people and deal firmly with offenders.
"We can establish economic, political and military security with our neighbors. We do not need the Americans. They are after plundering the wealth of the people of the region," he said. "Today the American army has been humiliated and reduced to misery."
Ozmaei added that Iran's position is stronger than in the early days of the imposed war, and that its fighters are more prepared today than yesterday.
His remarks coincided with two fresh maritime incidents reported Tuesday in and around the Strait.
In the morning, the IRGC Navy's public relations department announced that a violating container ship carrying more than 2,500 containers, which had attempted to transit the Strait of Hormuz through an unauthorized and dangerous route, struck a naval mine in the southern waters of the Strait, exploded and caught massive fire before sinking.
Local vessels and fishermen were advised to navigate with maximum caution to avoid colliding with floating containers, the statement said.
At noon on the same day, the Islamic Republic Army Navy reported that a violating oil tanker, which had switched off its tracking systems and was trying to pass through a prohibited zone east of the Strait of Hormuz, suffered damage and fire and was detected by Army surveillance teams.
Announcing a new formation and deployment of operational units east of the Strait of Hormuz and in the Arabian Sea and Sea of Oman areas, the Army Navy said it maintains full, round-the-clock surveillance over all enemy activities and vessel traffic.
It advised all vessels to strictly refrain from switching off their electronic equipment in violation of international law and to coordinate with the Armed Forces of the Islamic Republic of Iran for safe passage.

What are Iran and Russia's mounting hybrid attacks on Europe?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:55:52 UTC
01:55:52 KST

Iran and Russia-linked hybrid attacks in Europe are mounting, U.K. spy chief says. Here's a look at recent incidents.
London — The head of Britain's top domestic spy agency MI5, Sir Ken McCallum, painted a dark picture Tuesday of the changing national security threats facing the U.K. and the world.
"We have entered a new era of national security, requiring a new response," he said in his annual threat update at MI5 headquarters in London. "Those who mean the U.K. harm aren't attacking things government owns or controls. They're aiming at people, businesses, communities."
McCallum said that among state threats, "Russia remains aggressor number one," while intelligence analysts have also seen a "major shift" in "Iranian ambitions to come at harder targets."
Both countries, he said, have adopted more and evolving "hybrid tactics" as they target everything from air force bases to synagogues across the U.K. and Europe. Below is a look at some of the incidents that fit that description over the last year alone.
Iran
Iran has used and continues "using criminal proxies to try to intimidate oppositionists, Iranian media organizations, and Israeli sites," McCallum said.
But as the U.S. war with Iran nears the eight month mark, analysts have also seen the Iranian regime, "like Russia, attempting to expand their hybrid campaign," he said, leading to more than 50 arrests in the U.K. over the last year alone.
"Sadly, much of this aggression has been aimed at British Jewish communities," McCallum said, speaking of incidents this year that included "a wave of arson and sabotage incidents targeting Jewish communities in the U.K. and other European nations," but also acts targeting "harder targets, like military sites."
Many of these attacks were claimed by a group calling itself Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya (HAYI), or the Islamic Movement of the Companions of the Right, which U.K. authorities have sanctioned and said is tied directly to the elite Quds Force of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, which Britain considers a terrorist organization.
A CBS News investigation in March found the group appeared to have links to Iran, and a member said it would "keep threatening U.S. and Israeli interests worldwide until we've avenged every child in Gaza, Iran, Lebanon, and the resistance nations … We urge people to stay away from Zionist and American interests and individuals to keep themselves safe."
These Iran-linked attacks include:
- Liège, Belgium: March 9. An explosive device detonated at a synagogue, causing no casualties. Attack claimed by HAYI.
- Rotterdam, The Netherlands: March 13. The firebombing of a synagogue. Attack claimed by HAYI. Dutch authorities say they're investigating Iranian links to the incident.
- Amsterdam, The Netherlands: March 14. A device detonated outside a Jewish school. Attack claimed by HAYI.
- Golders Green, London: March 23. Four ambulances belonging to a Jewish volunteer ambulance service set on fire. Attack claimed by HAYI.
- Antwerp, Belgium: March 24. A car set on fire in a Jewish quarter of the city. Attack claimed by HAYI.
- Paris, France: March 28. 17-year-old allegedly tries to place an explosive device at the Bank of America headquarters. French authorities suspect HAYI was behind the attack, though the link was not confirmed.
- Nijkerk, The Netherlands: April 4. A device detonated outside the premises of a group called Christians For Israel. Attack claimed by HAYI.
- Finchley, London: April 15. Molotov cocktails and a brick thrown at Finchley Reform Synagogue. Attack claimed by HAYI.
- Park Royal, London: April 15. An attempted arson attack against Persian-language news outlet Iran International. Responsibility for the incident was never claimed. In March 2024, a journalist for the channel, Pouria Zeraati, was stabbed outside his home in London. According to The Guardian, counterterrorism police and security services in Britain believed the Iranian regime used criminal proxies to carry out the attack.
- Hendon, London: April 17. Attempted arson at the former premises of charity Jewish Futures. Attack claimed by HAYI.
- Harrow, London: April 18–19. A suspected arson attack at a synagogue in Harrow, then a bottle containing accelerant was thrown at the Kenton United Synagogue a day later. Attack claimed by HAYI.
- Golders Green, London: April 29. Two Hasidic Jewish men stabbed in the north of the capital. Attack claimed by HAYI.
- RAF Fairford, England: Sept. 27. Suspected plot involving British base used by U.S. bombers to strike Iran. Gasoline was found in vehicles, but no viable explosives. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the incident was "almost certainly" directed by Iran.
- Manchester, England: Oct. 2. Two Iranian nationals are charged with terrorism offenses following an alleged plot targeting a Jewish community in the northern city of Manchester.
Russia
For now, Russia remains the biggest threat to security, according to the U.K. spy chief's Tuesday briefing.
"The Russian military and intelligence services are once again escalating their attempts at hybrid warfare," McCallum said, adding that Moscow was "being careful to stay below the NATO Article 5 threshold" with its actions, which would trigger the alliance's collective defense principle.
"It'd be foolish for them to cross" that line, he said, and so far Russia "is using tactics that stop short — though sometimes not much short — of conventional conflict."
Incidents linked to Russia this year include:
- Off Vaindloo Island, Estonia: March 19. Russian SU-30 fighter allegedly violates Estonian airspace – NATO scrambles aircraft in response.
- Hutthurm, Germany: March. Authorities thwarted a Russian-ordered assassination attempt targeting the head of a Germany defense company, according to Die Zeit.
- Norwegian waters, near the U.K.: Reported April 9. The U.K. and Norway deployed military vessels to deter Russian submarines found to have lingered for over a month from attacking undersea cables. Over the last few years there have been several incidents of alleged Russian sabotage of such cables.
- Labege, France: June 1. Molotov cocktails thrown at a drone factory that supplies the French and Ukrainian armed forces. French authorities are investigating Russian links, according to Le Monde.
- Leipzig, Germany: Aug. 4. An explosive-laden drone is found near cargo facilities and Ukrainian aircraft. German authorities explicitly attributed the incident to Russia.
- Skarzysko-Kamienna, Poland: August. Fire at a WB Electronics factory that produces drones and other military components. EBU reports that authorities believe Russia used "low-level operatives" to carry out the attack, but authorities do not identify those responsible.
- Tallinn, Estonia: Aug. 15. Arson attack on Milrem Robotics, a defense company that supplies robotic military vehicles to Ukraine. Estonian authorities attributed the attack to Russia in late September.
- Swindon, England: Sept. 9. Joshua Cammidge charged over allegedly sharing locations of drone factories with people linked to Russian military intelligence and offering to carry out sabotage attacks.
- Wola Krobowska, Poland: Sept. 23. Arson attack on a Starlink satellite ground station, which Poland officially blames on Russia in October.
- Lithuania, September. Drone carrying explosive device crossed Belarusian border is shot down by NATO aircraft. Italian defense minister says it "most probably" came from Russia.
- Denmark: Oct. 7. A Danish intelligence official says Russia attempted acts of sabotage against defense industry companies supplying Ukraine over summer.

Could AI ‘change the stakes’ in the development of bioweapons?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:54:43 UTC
01:54:43 KST

Could AI ‘change the stakes’ in the development of bioweapons?
Experts say the technology could help terrorists and nation states with production but that significant hurdles remain
In his annual speech on threats to the nation, Sir Ken McCallum, the head of the UK’s intelligence service, MI5, warned that AI had the potential to “change the stakes” on existing and even new bioweapons. Here we look at how AI might help in the development of bioweapons and the hurdles that remain.
How could AI help people make bioweapons?
It depends on who wants to make them. One risk is the rogue, unskilled bad actor or terrorist group that works from a garage laboratory. AI chatbots could help them skill up, by compiling relevant information, planning experiments and troubleshooting problems. It’s likely the work would focus on using existing pathogens and toxins.
The other risk comes from well-resourced organisations and nation states that have plenty of skilled scientists, high containment laboratories and all of the equipment and reagents needed to work on bioweapons safely. AI tools could help researchers identify genetic tweaks to make existing pathogens more lethal, for example. This is the more immediate concern, according to Dr Filippa Lentzos, a reader in science and international security at King’s College London. “Here, AI does not remove the need for expertise, it amplifies expertise that is already there,” she says.
A more distant risk comes from highly skilled groups using AI to design completely new pathogens and toxins that are resistant to drugs or have no antidotes.
Have people tried using AI to make bioweapons?
Last year, police in India uncovered a suspected bioterrorism plot in which a doctor and several others drew on AI chatbot queries and AI-driven search, allegedly to help them make ricin, a deadly toxin, using kitchen tools. It is unclear whether the AI’s responses helped, but other accounts suggest the tools can provide relevant and dangerous information.
The AI company Anthropic raised further concerns in September when it reported five cases of scientists in unnamed countries trying to use its Claude chatbot for what may have been dangerous work on viruses or toxins. One red flag, the company said, was that after being blocked, the scientists found workarounds.
In one case, Anthropic said researchers used the chatbot to plan experiments that would introduce mutations in a highly pathogenic bird flu virus to make it adapt and spread more easily in mammals. The work, and the other cases, could signify attempts to make pathogens more dangerous, but such studies are also done in legitimate labs to help researchers spot future pandemics and develop vaccines and drugs to treat disease.
What else has raised concerns?
A flurry of studies has shown how AI tools can provide potentially dangerous information on bioweapons. In a recent exercise at MIT, non-science students were asked if they could get an AI chatbot to help them unleash a pandemic. Within an hour, the chatbots listed four potential pandemic pathogens, explained how to make them from synthetic DNA, and supplied names of DNA synthesis companies that were unlikely to screen their orders. It is easier said than done, however.
In another case, the Stanford University researcher Dr David Relman described how an AI explained how to modify a pathogen to make it resistant to treatment. Another scientist revealed that an AI chatbot had explained how to use a weather balloon to release biological weapons from the sky.
The dual-use nature of biological research can make it hard to distinguish valuable work that could protect health from attempts to develop bioweapons. In 2025, scientists at Los Alamos National Laboratory trained an AI to predict how exceptionally potent neurotoxins from marine snails latch on to human cells, work that could help in the development of antidotes. But the US government became concerned when Chinese researchers drew on the work to develop their own tool to design new toxins. The Chinese researchers said the work was aimed solely at developing drugs.
In April, scientists raised further concerns when they made the first viruses designed by AI. The viruses are a particular type that only invade bacteria, and the work could lead to new medicines, but experts warned that it raised “urgent biosafety and biosecurity questions”.
What hurdles make it difficult?
Most work on bioweapons is beyond the reach of unskilled groups: as well as being highly technical, it is extremely dangerous. While AI chatbots might be prompted to give information on bioweapons, a list of instructions is not enough. “Information is only one part of the problem,” says Lentzos. “Tacit expertise, access to biological materials and equipment, experimental validation, scale-up and delivery all remain substantial barriers.”
Sonia Ben Ouagrham-Gormley, the deputy director of the biodefense programme at George Mason University in Virginia says tacit knowledge – the unwritten knowhow that an AI is unlikely to help with – has been key in the success of historical state-run bioweapons programmes.
Prof Martin Pačesa at the University of Zurich said access to material was critical. “Any graduate physicist could sketch up plans for a potentially more effective nuclear bomb, but where is he going to get a lump of uranium from? Same for bioweapons. If you have access to material and facilities capable of producing them, then AI is not going to make too much difference if you want to do harm.”
What extra measures are needed?
Some AI companies are taking steps to prevent people from using their tools to develop bioweapons, but the majority are not announcing what, if anything, they are doing, says Prof Tom Inglesby, director of the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security. “We have no formal government policies in place in any country yet to protect against this kind of misuse,” he says.
He wants formal independent evaluations of new AI models before they are released, with any dangers eliminated before the models are made public. And high-risk biological data, such as information on how pathogens might spread more easily, should be restricted. Meanwhile, companies that make genetic material for researchers must screen orders to ensure they are not for the creation of novel, highly dangerous viruses. Some screening already happens, but it is largely voluntary, and can be sidestepped if researchers use AI to design new, harmful genetic sequences that companies are not checking for.

Poland considers reinstating conscription

Poland considers reinstating conscription
Poland is mulling reintroducing compulsory military service that was abolished in 2009, Deputy Defense Minister Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka has said. Her comments came shortly after an opinion poll indicated that over a half of Poles under 24 were against the reinstatement of conscription.
In an interview with RMF FM radio station on Wednesday, Sobkowiak-Czarnecka revealed that “discussions at the Ministry of National Defense today cover all possible scenarios.” The official said that she personally is a proponent of universal conscription modelled after the Israeli draft system, where both men and women are called up for service.
Sobkowiak-Czarnecka argued that the pool of volunteers should first be exhausted before moving toward the reinstatement of the draft. The Polish deputy defense minister acknowledged, however, that she has “colleagues who are absolutely opposed” to the idea of compulsory military service.
Earlier on Wednesday, RMF FM reported that a recent Opinia24 poll indicated that 46% of respondents were in favor of reintroducing conscription, while 38% were against, with the other 16% undecided. The share of those opposing the draft rises to 53% in the 18-24 cohort. Following the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022, Warsaw has announced plans to expand its military from the current 220,000 personnel to 500,000, including 200,000 reservists, by 2039.
Speaking at a press conference on the sidelines of the Warsaw Security Forum on Tuesday, Polish Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz called on the European Union to shift to “war-mode” military production.
In recent years, Poland has emerged as one of the most rapidly militarizing EU nations, with its military spending reaching around 4.7% of its GDP. The country has also been one of Kiev’s staunchest backers in its conflict with Moscow, providing Ukraine with weapons, including artillery systems, tanks, armored vehicles, warplanes, and ammunition. Some estimates place Poland in first place among all other Western countries in terms of the volume of assistance provided relative to its own GDP. Poland has also served as a key logistical hub for Ukraine-bound arms shipments from other countries.
Neighboring Germany has emerged as Ukraine’s top backer in Europe in absolute terms, according to the Kiel Institute for the World Economy. The German government is likewise aiming to increase the number of active-duty troops to more than 260,000 by 2035, backed by 200,000 reservists. In recent months, several politicians in Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s ruling coalition have floated the idea of reinstating conscription.
A new military service system introduced in early 2026 requires all 18-year-old men to register for potential service. While enlistment remains voluntary for now, parliament can activate compulsory service if recruitment targets are not met or the security situation deteriorates.
The new model has sparked nationwide student protests, with an estimated 45,000 demonstrators taking to the streets in some 100 cities and towns late last month.
Both Poland and Germany have justified their respective military buildups by claiming that Russia is harboring aggressive plans against NATO member states. Moscow has repeatedly dismissed these allegations as “nonsense” and even suggested providing written guarantees that it has no such plans.
President Vladimir Putin has accused
European NATO member states of openly preparing for war with Russia while using bogus claims. Moscow has also repeatedly warned Western nations against supplying ever more sophisticated weaponry to Ukraine, saying that the bloc is becoming increasingly involved in the conflict with Russia, with potentially dire ramifications.

U.S. special ops test drone laser for longer mortar shots
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:53:16 UTC
01:53:16 KST

- A PDW C100 drone carrying a Leonardo DRS STAG-5 laser designator guided mortar engagements beyond standard 120 mm mortar range at Dugway, Utah.
- The Iron Sting validation event, run for U.S. Army Special Operations Command, tested the accuracy and range of new precision mortar munitions.
A small Performance Drone Works quadcopter carrying a Leonardo DRS laser designator guided precision mortar rounds onto targets beyond the normal maximum range of a 120 mm mortar during a recent test for U.S. Army special operations forces at Dugway, Utah, Leonardo DRS said on Oct. 14.
The company said its STAG-5 electro-optical and infrared gimbal with a built-in laser target designator flew on PDW’s C100 drone during the Iron Sting Precision Mortar Validation Event at the White Sage Mortar Range. Repeated engagements were completed at ranges beyond the standard maximum for a smoothbore 120 mm mortar, according to Leonardo DRS, though the company did not give the distances, the number of rounds fired or how close they landed to their targets.
The event was run by the Capability Development and Innovation office, previously known as the Irregular Warfare Technical Support Directorate, for U.S. Army Special Operations Command. Organizers tested the safety, accuracy and extended-range performance of new precision mortar munitions, and let operators try the technology in realistic scenarios.
Leonardo DRS did not name the munitions used. The event shares its name with Iron Sting, a 120 mm mortar round made by Israel’s Elbit Systems that combines GPS and semi-active laser guidance and has been used in combat by the Israel Defense Forces since 2023.
A laser designator marks a target with a coded beam, and a laser-guided munition steers itself onto the spot where that beam reflects. Putting the designator on a drone lets the observer stay well away from the target while still lighting it up, and lets a mortar team engage targets that its crews cannot see.
“The STAG-5 is designed to provide operators with precise, reliable ISR and targeting capabilities that can enhance mission effectiveness across a wide range of operational environments,” said Jerry Hathaway, senior vice president and general manager of the Electro-Optical Infrared Systems business at Leonardo DRS.
Leonardo DRS says the gimbal pairs its laser with day and night cameras so operators can find a target, mark it, confirm the strike and watch the mission from a safer distance.
The C100 is already in U.S. Army service. In September 2024 the service selected PDW’s C100 and Anduril’s Ghost X for its Company-Level Small Uncrewed Aircraft System program, which puts reconnaissance and target acquisition drones in the hands of maneuver companies in brigade combat teams. The rucksack-portable quadcopter can carry about 6.8 kg (15 pounds) of payload and fly for up to 74 minutes.

The World Bank has announced $93 million in new funding to strengthen the Ebola response in the African region as the Democratic Republic of Congo battles to contain the current outbreak, according to a statement Wednesday.
The statement said $80 million would strengthen disease surveillance, laboratory capacity, clinical case management, infection prevention and control, and community engagement in affected areas in Congo.
“Health emergencies don’t wait and neither did we,” said World Bank Division Director for Congo Albert Zeufack.
The number of confirmed Ebola cases in Congo has reached 9,066, including 4,381 deaths, since the outbreak declaration in May, according to the latest Health Ministry update.
The epidemic has affected seven provinces: Haut-Uele, Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Bas-Uele, Tshopo and South-Ubangi.
Financing will also help sustain maternal and child health services in Ituri, the epicenter of the disease, so that the outbreak does not increase risks for women and newborns.
It will also help protect livelihoods in affected communities and enable children to continue attending school safely, according to the statement.
Across the region, $13 million in additional financing would strengthen emergency preparedness, response and resilience in 11 regional countries through the Health Emergency Preparedness, Response and Resilience program, said the bank.
In May, after the Ebola outbreak was declared in Congo and Uganda, the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) warned that 10 African countries were at high risk of the outbreak, including South Sudan, Rwanda, Kenya, Zambia, the Central African Republic, Tanzania, Ethiopia, Angola, the Republic of the Congo and Burundi.
While Uganda has been declared Ebola-free, Kenya last week reported its first imported case from Congo.
The World Bank Group has committed $426.6 million to the overall Ebola emergency response to date, through a combination of existing and new grant and concessional financing.

SBU detains 18-year-old suspected FSB agent in Kyiv over attempt to activate 148 Starlink terminals for Russia
Ukraine's Security Service (SBU) has detained an 18-year-old man in Kyiv suspected of working for Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB). According to investigators, he attempted to register 148 Starlink terminals for use by Russian forces.
The SBU reported that the terminals were intended to support the planning of Russian military operations in the Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia regions. Ukrainian security officers say they prevented the devices from being activated.
According to the investigation, the suspect is a former student at a Kyiv college, where he trained to become a welder. After completing his studies, he began looking for ways to earn quick money through Telegram channels.
He was allegedly contacted by an FSB officer who offered him money in exchange for cooperation.
Within days of being recruited, the suspect registered 15 Starlink terminals using the passport details of relatives and acquaintances. He then prepared personal information belonging to other individuals to register another 133 devices.
SBU officers detained the suspect near a post office, where he allegedly planned to activate another batch of terminals.
The 15 previously registered Starlink terminals, whose details had already been sent to his Russian handler via a messaging app, were also blocked.
The suspect remains in custody without the possibility of bail. If convicted, he faces life imprisonment and confiscation of property.
The case adds to a growing number of incidents in which Russia allegedly recruits Ukrainians to carry out assignments on Moscow's behalf, including a recent case on Oct. 12, when Ukrainian authorities detained a 19-year-old suspected of plotting a bomb attack on a bus carrying soldiers in Rivne.
According to the SBU, the suspect had also been recruited through Telegram channels offering quick money.
On Oct. 6, the SBU reported arresting a suspected collaborator in Kyiv who allegedly helped Russia establish repeater stations for its drones and gather intelligence on targets in the capital.
In August, the SBU detained a suspected Russian agent in Kharkiv Oblast who allegedly registered 27 Starlink terminals for Russian forces.

New UK sanctions powers will enable action against supporters of illegal Israeli settlements
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:51:25 UTC
01:51:25 KST

The UK is expanding its sanctions powers to freeze assets and target entities enabling illegal Israeli settlements, obstructing humanitarian aid or unlawfully holding prisoners.
The statutory instrument introducing the global human rights and international humanitarian law sanctions adds three new grounds to the 2020 regime: serious violations of international humanitarian law, obstruction of humanitarian assistance and serious violations of the right to liberty and security of person.
Unlawful settlement activity will be captured through a breach of international humanitarian law, including the Geneva convention on occupation.
The Israeli government closed the UK consulate last week in protest, forcing the it to withdraw 21 diplomats and downgrade the consulate to the status of a mission. But the Israeli punishment does not appear to have deterred the UK government.
The proposed new powers also extend government reach beyond direct perpetrators of wrongdoing to those who facilitate, incite, promote or support qualifying conduct, provide it with finance, goods or technology, conceal evidence of it or benefit from it.
Banks and commercial entities could also fall within this remit as designation only requires reasonable grounds to suspect involvement.
The proposed sanctions measures include asset freezes and prohibitions on making funds or economic resources available, travel bans and director disqualifications.
A new urgent procedure will allow ministers to mirror designations already made by the EU, US, Canada or Australia for up to 112 days while a specific separate UK case is prepared.
The new global sanctions regime will come into force on Thursday but will need endorsement by MPs and peers within 28 days.
The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, is pushing through the measures at speed because the Israeli government has vowed to press ahead with an E1 settlement containing 1,234 homes in the West Bank – a development that many observers say would sever a contiguous, viable Palestinian state, so making the so-called two-state solution to the Palestinian-Israeli conflict near impossible.
The E1 bids close on 19 October but the Israel Land Authority has confirmed that the tender box will not be opened, nor the bids considered, before 19 November, which is after the Israeli election on 27 October.
The British Palestinian Project said the Israeli deferral “does not remove the need to deter commitments being made now, since bidders and their backers commit on 19 October, contracts could still be signed before a new Israeli government is formed”.
The project welcomed the addition of the right to liberty and security of person in the new laws, saying it opens a route to sanctions for serious arbitrary or unlawful detention, including of Palestinian children, and of those responsible for or enabling it. Save the Children estimated in November 2023 that 10,000 Palestinian children had passed through Israeli military detention over the preceding 20 years.
A UN 2026 report on children and armed conflict verified that 981 Palestinian children were detained by Israeli forces in 2025 and 180 of them remained in administrative detention without charge or trial at the year’s end.
The UK has already applied sanctions designations for restrictions on humanitarian aid in Sudan and South Sudan but this is the first time this general power is being applied as part of a new worldwide regime including Israel.
Refusing permits or blocking convoys will be sufficient grounds to apply sanctions, without requiring the obstruction to constitute a formal breach of international humanitarian law – thereby lowering the threshold for action.
Separate work is under way by UK officials in conjunction with European partners on how to outlaw British trade with unlawful Israeli settlements.
