MODA notifies supermarkets to bolster cybersecurity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:42:33 UTC
01:42:33 KST

The Ministry of Digital Affairs (MODA) yesterday said it had notified the nation’s largest supermarket chains to inspect their Internet of Things (IoT) devices and install firmware updates to address security vulnerabilities, after a cyberattack earlier this week caused about 150 supermarkets in France to incur substantial food losses.
The incident involving Internet-connected refrigeration systems — which resulted in fridges and freezers heating up to 50°C, spoiling food and triggering fires — was one of the main subjects discussed at the legislature’s Transportation Committee meeting yesterday.
Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Legislator Hsu Chih-chieh (許智傑) said Taiwan has an extremely high density of convenience stores and supermarkets, so people’s lives would be hugely disrupted if similar attacks happen in Taiwan.
Photo: Reuters
The ministry should address the issue and prevent hackers from launching cyberattacks on Taiwan’s critical infrastructure using IoT, he added.
Minister of Digital Affairs Lin Yi-ching (林宜敬) said many companies began linking their internal systems to public Internet networks when IoT became a trend about a decade ago, but they overlooked the importance of cybersecurity protection.
“The global trend in the corporate world is disconnecting the internal networks from the Internet unless it is absolutely necessary. They only need to connect to the Intranet and monitor access to internal systems by establishing a whitelist,” Lin said.
Administration for Cybersecurity Director-General Tsai Fu-lung (蔡福隆) said the firmware of the French supermarkets’ refrigeration system was outdated and its vulnerabilities has not been addressed for a long time, so hackers had the opportunity to tamper with the temperature setting.
“After the incident, we quickly notified the supermarket chains around the nation through the Taiwan Computer Emergency Response Team/Coordination Center to examine IoT devices and update firmware,” Tsai said.
Meanwhile, DPP Legislator Lin Chun-hsien (林俊憲) highlighted the national security risks posed by the use of eSIMs, which many Taiwanese travelers purchase when they travel overseas.
A Taiwan’s Consumers’ Foundation survey found that 72 percent of 172 eSIMs purchased from the market have Internet traffic routed through China or Hong Kong, rather than the countries users are traveling in, he said.
This means that the content transmitted through these eSIMs are subject to regulation and surveillance under Hong Kong’s National Security Law or China’s Cybersecurity Law, he added.
The minister said the market is inundated with cheap, but unsafe eSIM cards routed through Chinese telecoms — such as China Mobile — as their massive consumer base gives them greater bargaining power when negotiating profit-sharing arrangements for international roaming services.
The government can regulate eSIMs sold through domestic e-commerce platforms such as momo and PChome, but lacks jurisdiction over those purchased from overseas Web sites, he said.
To reduce the risks associated with cheap foreign SIM cards, the Ministry of Digital Affairs and the National Communications Commission, in collaboration with Taiwan’s three major telecom operators, require customers to purchase domestic eSIMs online using real-name authentication, he added.

Parents on limiting their kids’ social media and AI use
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:42:32 UTC
01:42:32 KST

When it comes to their kids, many parents don’t trust tech companies any more.
Social media companies have spent the better part of the last decade arguing that their platforms are safe for teens, but quite a few parents aren’t convinced. They, along with a growing number of regulators, have increasingly accused companies like Meta of designing products that are addictive to younger users.
AI firm OpenAI, thrust into the public consciousness much more recently than Meta, has had to defend against dozens of lawsuits alleging chatbot ChatGPT lacks safety guardrails. Now, workers at the world’s leading AI firms have warned that their employers prioritize competing with each other over building their models safely.
Photo: AP
Both the AI and social media companies have denied the claims, and introduced additional safety measures such as parent-linked teen accounts.
Still, for many parents, lawsuits and public accusations have been enough to change their minds about whether to allow their children to use both social media and AI.
Parents were asked whether their perspective on their children’s use of social media or AI has changed in the last year and whether they plan to let their kids use either technology. The vast majority of those who responded said they no longer wanted their children to use social media, and many of them said they also try to steer their children away from AI.
“They are the most precious thing in my life,” Caroline Gray Ford, a 42-year-old parent from Cambridge, UK. “So why would I ever turn them over to a bunch of tech companies whose sole motivation is to profit from their time and harvest their data?”
TECH WORKER TORN BETWEEN TWO WORLDS
I work in tech, specifically in the AI sphere, and honestly I worry about the future that’s going to be there for my kids. Not in a doomsayer way, but, being realistic, the world is going to be a very different place when they grow up. I’m torn between two worlds — the world I work in, and that supports their upbringing, and the knowledge that the very work is destroying their future — whether that be on an economic or environmental level.
Do I feel the need to encourage them to use AI? Yes. Do I want to? No. On the flipside, social media is out. They can use WhatsApp to connect and build real-world relationships. But otherwise no good can come of it.
— Andy, 43, London, UK
THE MOM WARY OF SOCIAL MEDIA AND AI
The recent major lawsuits against Meta, along with decisions by non-US governments to limit social media use for under-16s, have enabled me to have meaningful conversations with my daughter about the real risks of social media use for her age group. She still asks to use these products, but I remind her of the decisions we’ve made, together, to wait until she’s older before she can use them.
My 11-year-old is not permitted to use social media on her own. As for AI chatbots, she may occasionally use them if they show up on a Google search when we are looking up a topic, but I encourage her to check the validity of anything AI-generated. She’s very aware of AI hallucinations, and hates AI images. She will actually call me or her older sister out if we accidentally share an AI-generated image.
Our family is very eco-conscious — we’re aware that AI uses massive amounts of water and energy, so we try to avoid AI apps as a family, if there are other options at our disposal to obtain information.
— Kate, 47, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania
TECHNOLOGY IN SCHOOLS
My perspective has become significantly more cautious.
As a parent and someone who works in AI, I’m increasingly concerned about the gap between the way these technologies are marketed and the risks they can pose to children. I want my daughter to grow up understanding and using technology, including AI, but I don’t think children should be treated as unwitting test subjects for products whose effects on their learning, development and wellbeing are not yet fully understood.
What’s particularly concerning is how early these tools are being introduced through schools, often with little meaningful parental involvement or choice. I’m increasingly questioning whether companies are prioritizing children’s interests or engagement and profit, and whether schools and local authorities are doing enough to scrutinize the technology they’re putting in front of children.
I don’t think children are being adequately educated about how to use these tools safely or critically. There’s a huge difference between teaching children how to use technology and simply putting devices and apps in front of them.
But I also think the responsibility shouldn’t fall solely on parents. Schools and local authorities need to ensure that children are being taught digital literacy and critical thinking alongside the introduction of these tools.
— Anonymous, Scottish borders
VIDEO GAME SKEPTIC
I have been skeptical about social media and AI since the beginning. I see in my 12-year-old son the obsessive grip that social media has on him. I include videogaming here, as it comes with YouTube influencers, and interaction with others on Discord servers. It is shaping his childhood and worldview in a way that I don’t like. I’m particularly concerned about digital media crowding out IRL activities that help him grow as a person and understand the world – like reading, exploring, playing with other kids face-to-face ...
My son has been given a Chromebook at school (no choice given to parents), and has a laptop for gaming, with time limits. Managing his screen time is a cat-and-mouse game that everyone hates at home. He has found ways of circumventing restrictions as only a creative child can. He is unable to control his impulse to go on his devices – that’s difficult enough for adults, let alone a child. The lack of guardrails and regulation of children’s access to digital technology means that millions of individual households have to manage and set the rules themselves. It’s stressful and poisons the atmosphere at home.
— Anonymous, Madrid

F1 to return to Africa in ‘early 2030s’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:42:31 UTC
01:42:31 KST

Rwanda is to host Africa’s first Formula One Grand Prix since 1993 in “the early 2030s” after the circuit on Tuesday announced a decade-long deal with the country.
The East African nation has been chasing a Grand Prix race for years, having already used soccer, basketball and other sports to enhance its image and attract investment.
Rwandan President Paul Kagame had formally announced the bid when the nation hosted a gathering of the FIA, the governing body of the sport, in December 2024.
Photo: AFP
The last time an F1 race was held in Africa was the 33rd South African Grand Prix near Johannesburg in 1993, one year before apartheid formally ended there with democratic, multiracial elections.
The first African Grand Prix in Rwanda would take place “once a new purpose-built circuit in Bugesera, Rwanda, has been completed,” F1 said in a statement.
“Today is a landmark moment for Formula One,” F1 president Stefano Domenicali added. “With Rwanda joining the calendar from the next decade, our sport will race in every inhabited continent, bringing the world championship closer than ever to fans around the globe.”
A landlocked country still widely associated with a horrific genocide in 1994, Rwanda has used sports to revamp its image, attract tourists and impress investors with its organizational efficiency.
It has spent lavishly on soccer sponsorship deals with clubs including Arsenal and Paris Saint-Germain, partnered with the NBA to be the main hub of its African basketball league, and hosted last year’s cycling world championships.
“This partnership is long overdue, but it is a success and a milestone for the entire continent, especially for African fans,” Kagame said.
Seven-time world champion Lewis Hamilton has long called for an African stop on the F1 circuit, backing Rwanda’s plans in 2024 and calling the country “one of my favorite places.”
South Africa had also been bidding to host an F1 race, and its sports minister last week said it should not be ruled out.
“Remember though that one country, Italy, has had two F1s a year, and some react like a continent of 55 countries can only get one,” South African Minister of Sports, Arts and Culture Gayton McKenzie wrote on X on Thursday last week.
He said that “SA will get F1, even before 2030.”

ASML struggles with chip tool demand
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:42:31 UTC
01:42:31 KST

ASML Holding NV yesterday warned that soaring artificial intelligence (AI) spending meant that it faces a potential supply shortfall with its chipmaking machines in the next two years, even as it boosted its own sales forecast for this year.
“We are investigating ways to increase capacity for 2028 beyond the 30 percent increase we previously communicated,” ASML chief executive officer Christophe Fouquet said in a statement on the Dutch company’s results.
“Customers are asking us every single day to get more tools,” he said in a separate video.
Photo: Bloomberg
Robust customer demand prompted ASML to slightly raise its full-year sales forecast, predicting annual sales of between 44 billion euros and 45 billion euros (US$49 billion and US$50 billion). The low end of the range was previously 43 billion euros.
ASML, Europe’s biggest tech firm by market value, said in July that it plans to boost capacity by 30 percent next year for its second-most advanced tool, the low numerical-aperture extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography machine, which would take its annual shipment target to about 85 units.
The chip-gear maker’s customers have boosted their equipment demand forecasts based on the “size and duration of AI-related investments,” Fouquet said.
Some customers “are expressing an interest in placing orders with us for 2029 and even 2030,” he said.
ASML is the only company that makes the cutting-edge lithography machines used to produce semiconductors for the data centers powering the AI boom. Its outlook offers an indication of investment plans by chipmakers such as Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (台積電), Samsung Electronics Co and Intel Corp as spending on AI infrastructure surges.
The company is working to ship tools faster to customers by reducing the cycle time, or the period between starting production in its clean rooms and shipping a completed machine. It began construction on its second industrial campus in the Netherlands, the first phase of which is set to be completed in 2029.
Net sales in the July-to-September quarter rose to 11.66 billion euros, ASML said. That compares with the average analyst estimate of 11.7 billion euros, data compiled by Bloomberg showed.
Net profit came in at 5 billion euros in the quarter, compared with 2.1 billion euros in the same period last year, ASML said.
The company sold 17 EUV machines in the quarter while revenue from the service and upgrades of machines already installed at customers’ sites increased 19 percent as chipmakers looked to be more productive.
“Against the backdrop of an overall 36 percent increase of 2026 in comparison to 2025, you see that that is largely driven by EUV,” ASML chief financial officer Roger Dassen said in a video accompanying the results. “So the EUV business grows over 45 percent this year.”
South Korea remained ASML’s largest market for new system tools in the third quarter, followed by Taiwan and China. China is expected to account for about 20 percent of ASML’s total revenue this year.

The Taiwan Creative Content Agency (TAICCA) has signed an agreement with South Korean producer B.A. Entertainment, saying international partnerships and pooled resources are key to bringing Taiwanese content to global markets, the agency said Wednesday.
The partnership will focus on talent development, financing, co-productions and international distribution, according to an agency statement.
TAICCA Chairperson Sue Wang (王時思) and B.A. Entertainment CEO Jang Won-seok signed the memorandum of understanding Monday during the Busan International Film Festival and its accompanying Asian Contents & Film Market (ACFM).
Photo: CNA
Wang said international partnerships and pooled resources were central to expanding the global reach of Taiwanese content. Jang praised Taiwan’s creative capabilities and said he hoped the partnership would produce work that can compete internationally, the statement said.
B.A. Entertainment is known for “The Roundup” franchise and “The Gangster, the Cop, the Devil.” Participating Taiwanese companies include 1 Production Film Co., whose credits include “Detention” (返校) and “Monga” (艋舺), and Money Entertainment Investment Co., Ltd., according to TAICCA.
The statement did not disclose financial commitments, an implementation timetable or specific productions under the agreement.
After the signing, TAICCA held a “Taiwan Night” reception attended by more than 500 film industry professionals and buyers, the agency said.
Guests included representatives of South Korea’s CJ ENM and Barunson E&A, the production company behind “Parasite,” as well as film festivals, markets and distributors from Europe, the U.S. and Asia.
The reception featured footage from Taiwanese films and series and joint projects presented at the festival and market, offering opportunities for promotion and business meetings.
Taiwan’s pavilion at the ACFM showcased 235 works, with more than 100 companies and nearly 60 industry representatives taking part, TAICCA said.
Taiwanese participants also joined pitching, publishing and co-production programs and won two awards Tuesday.
“Uncle” (阿叔), a film project directed by Yen Hao- hsuan (顏皓軒) and produced by Patrick Mao Huang (黃茂昌), won the CathayPlay Award at the Asian Project Market.
Taiwanese audiovisual technology company imCore received the InnoAsia Most Promising Startup Award, according to the agency.

WBC outfielder Fairchild to visit Taiwan next month
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:42:29 UTC
01:42:29 KST

Taiwanese-American outfielder Stuart Fairchild, who hit two home runs for Taiwan at this year’s World Baseball Classic (WBC), is to visit the country next month, his representatives said on Tuesday.
His agency, GSI Agency, wrote on Instagram that the trip would give Fairchild an opportunity to experience the enthusiasm of Taiwanese fans in person.
It did not give dates or an itinerary, saying further details would follow.
Photo: Reuters
“From game-changing moments on the diamond to the incredible energy from the stands, STU has always appreciated the unwavering love and support from fans across Taiwan,” the agency wrote.
The 30-year-old, affectionately known to Taiwanese fans as “Feizai,” played for Taiwan at the WBC in March. His mother moved to the US from Taiwan when she was 12.
He hit a grand slam against the Czech Republic and a two-run homer against South Korea, helping Taiwan win both games at the Tokyo Dome.
Fairchild finished the tournament batting .250 with two home runs, six RBIs and three stolen bases, making him one of Taiwan’s leading offensive contributors, although the team were eliminated in the group stage.
Fairchild is also scheduled to receive an Employment Gold Card at a public ceremony next month, under plans announced by the National Development Council in August.
Council Deputy Minister Peng Li-pei at the time said that Fairchild’s application had been approved and that the council and the Ministry of Sports were arranging the presentation.
The card combines an open work permit, resident visa, Alien Resident Certificate and re-entry permit, giving eligible foreign professionals more flexibility to work and live in Taiwan.
A Seattle native, Fairchild made his MLB debut with the Arizona Diamondbacks in 2021. He has since played for the Seattle Mariners, San Francisco Giants, Cincinnati Reds, Atlanta Braves and Cleveland Guardians.
In six major-league seasons, he has played 292 games, batting .221 with 18 home runs, 69 RBIs and 27 stolen bases, according to MLB’s database.
This season, Fairchild appeared in 14 games for Cleveland and one for Seattle, finishing with three hits in 19 at-bats, a .158 batting average, one RBI and two stolen bases.

Advocate urges protection for persecuted activists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:42:29 UTC
01:42:29 KST

Taiwanese democracy advocate Lee Ming-che (李明哲) on Tuesday met with the European Parliament, calling for greater protection for human rights advocates, follow-up action on resolutions concerning Hong Kong and deeper cooperation between Taiwan and Europe in the face of China’s transnational repression.
A delegation led by Lee met with European Parliament members Bernard Guetta and Engin Eroglu, joined by Representative to the EU and Belgium Hsieh Chih-wei (謝志偉), the New School for Democracy said in a statement last week.
Lee thanked the European Parliament for its solidarity when he was detained in China for five years.
Photo courtesy of the New School for Democracy via CNA
Transnational repression not only targets advocates, but also often involves threats against their family members, deterring persecuted people from speaking out, he said.
Lee said that while he was detained, China threatened his wife with concerns about his safety, and demanded that she stop speaking out and cut off contact with the Taiwanese government and civil society groups.
Family members of other people detained in China have reached out to him for help since he returned to Taiwan, he said.
They fear that speaking out or seeking help from the Taiwanese government could impact their loved ones’ safety, Lee said, adding that threats to loved ones’ safety silence people, cover up the truth and leave advocates isolated.
He called on democratic countries to provide state protection and work with non-governmental organizations to ensure that people facing threats can safely seek help and continue participating in public affairs.
Guetta and Eroglu drew parallels between the cross-strait situation and Russia and Ukraine, asking about Taiwan’s assistance to Ukraine and how the nation is resisting Chinese repression and infiltration.
Taiwan’s resistance is visible and invisible, Taiwanese human rights advocate Hsiao I-ming (蕭逸民) said.
For example, China exploits criminal cases and manipulates information to deepen distrust of the government and divide Taiwanese society, Hsiao said.
Supporting and protecting victims, and fostering a society built on mutual assistance and trust are part of the everyday work of defending democracy, he said.
Lee uses the Internet to introduce Chinese to Taiwan’s democratic experience and built a network to support the families of Chinese political prisoners, Hsiao said, citing it as an example of resistance that goes unseen.
This cross-border exchange of democratic ideas and mutual support helps people facing political persecution, he said.
China’s threats against Taiwan do not only involve the military, but also directly impact people’s freedom and democratic rights, he said, adding that judicial reform, protecting victims and advocating for human rights are all part of resisting authoritarianism.

A Pacific pivot ahead for Taiwan?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:42:25 UTC
01:42:25 KST

On Aug. 31 when Minister of Foreign Affairs Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍) joined the Pacific Islands Forum leaders’ meeting in Koror, Palau — invited as a development partner, a status the forum has extended to Taiwan since the early 1990s — Chinese Special Envoy for Pacific Island Countries Affairs Qian Bo (錢波) promised “consequences.” Less than two weeks earlier, China had advised its citizens against travel to Palau, reprising the tourism embargo it imposed in 2017 after Palau reaffirmed ties with Taiwan. Five of the forum’s 18 leaders also stayed home, and Kiribati sent its former ambassador to Beijing to lead its delegation.
The Pacific islands have long occupied an outsized role in Taipei’s foreign policy, and Taiwan continues to be an important part of the region’s fabric. Historically, Taiwan’s engagement has largely been a fight for recognition, but now, as geopolitics descends on the region, stakes are raised for everyone. This is true not only for Taiwan’s place in the Pacific, but also for what sort of diplomatic community the Pacific states want to create for themselves, what sort of partnerships they seek to build, and how they view exercising Pacific sovereignty. When Beijing threatens a host government over its guest list, it claims a veto over Pacific institutions.
While recent history has been grim — in July, Papua New Guinea ordered Taiwan’s office closed without consulting Taipei, which followed the loss of Solomon Islands, Kiribati and Nauru as allies since 2019 — but not all is lost. The partners that Taiwan has kept sit in some of the most strategic waters of the Asia-Pacific region, most importantly Palau, where this year’s drama unfolded, but also the Marshall Islands whose vast exclusive economic zone lies along the routes that connect Hawaii, Guam and Australia.
From Washington’s perspective, Palau is now more important than any time since World War II. A recent US budget request includes US$384.6 million for port improvements, while US Marines are stationed on Peleliu where an imperial Japanese airfield is being overhauled, and Washington has helped Palau establish a Maritime Joint Operations Center. Japan has similarly expanded its own maritime and infrastructure work in Palau, and the Philippines is interested in building closer ties with its neighbor. All this benefits from the physical and social infrastructure Taiwan has built over decades.
Together these countries — Taiwan, the Philippines, Palau, the US and Japan — largely encircle the Philippine Sea, a location of increasing People’s Republic of China (PRC) presence and potentially common geography for these partners to focus cooperation, and the link between the First and Second Island Chains of the Western Pacific.
Taiwan brings expertise this region needs. Every nation around the Philippine Sea faces some version of the same PRC coercion playbook: illegal fishing, research vessels conducting surveys that the law of the sea largely permits, influence operations aimed at local elites and economic punishment calibrated to small economies’ dependence on tourism. Taiwan has faced the full-scale version of this strategy the longest. The National Security Bureau logged more than 2.3 million pieces of disinformation and more than 45,000 inauthentic accounts in a single year. Its Whole-of-Society Defense Resilience Committee, created in 2024, ties civil mobilization, stockpiling, infrastructure protection, medical capacity and communications security into exercises that run across multiple cities. Palau, Guam and the Northern Marianas face the same pressures with a fraction of the analytic and institutional capacity. When the Chinese research icebreaker Ji Di (極地) loitered in Palau’s exclusive economic zone without authorization in May, Palau’s available response was a diplomatic note.
At sea, the region’s smaller states hold purview over vast waters, but they lack the capacity to patrol, while larger states hold means without jurisdiction. Palau has donated patrol craft and too few mariners to crew them. Taiwan, with a capable coast guard and one of the Pacific’s largest distant-water fishing fleets, sits on both sides of the illegal fishing problem, which argues for bringing it inside regional monitoring, where its fleet’s conduct becomes a shared responsibility. Precedent exists in Taiwan’s participation as a fishing entity in the Western and Central Pacific Fisheries Commission, which manages the world’s largest tuna fishery, and the same logic could apply to Palau’s Maritime Joint Operations Center, where partners could post liaison officers to pool data on illegal fishing, research-vessel movements and vessels loitering over undersea cables.
Expanding Taiwan’s space with these neighbors requires no government to change its recognition policy, and Manila has shown how. In April last year, the Philippines lifted most restrictions on officials traveling to Taiwan for trade and economic missions, and in August last year Lin led a trade delegation to Manila in a private capacity. Last month, when Beijing protested Taipei’s plan for a second office in Cebu, the Philippine Department of Foreign Affairs answered that its “one China” policy does not preclude economic, cultural and functional cooperation with Taiwan.
Three steps would move the region forward: The Pacific Islands Forum should convert Palau’s open door into standing practice, so development partners’ attendance stops depending on each host’s tolerance for Beijing’s displeasure. The US, Japan and the Philippines, as they deepen trilateral ties, should bring Palau — as well as Micronesia and the Marshall Islands — into their maritime cooperation initiatives, and build channels on illegal fishing, cable security and disaster response that Taiwan can join from the start. Governments that encourage Pacific states to engage with Taipei should agree in advance on how they would offset the coercion that follows, with tourism promotion, air connectivity and budget support ready before the next coercive tactic or set of “gray zone” activities lands.
The Pacific architecture emerging during today’s geopolitical flux will be built by whoever shows up with something to contribute. For Taiwan, the place to start is close to home: the region surrounding the Philippine Sea, where it can build working channels with Palau, the Philippines, Japan and the US on the waters they share. Taiwan’s story in the broader region is not over — a Pacific that keeps Taiwan at the table will have more with which to build.
Michael Schiffer is a distinguished senior fellow (non-resident) at the Sasakawa Peace Foundation USA, and has served as assistant administrator for Asia at the US Agency for International Development, US deputy assistant secretary of defense for East Asia, and as a congressional staffer. Brian Harding is a senior fellow (non-resident) at the foundation. He previously led programming on Southeast Asia and the Pacific at the US Institute for Peace, and has worked at the Center for Strategic and International Studies and the Center for American Progress, and served in the Office of the US Secretary of Defense as country director for Asian and Pacific security affairs.

On Oct. 10, 1911, gunfire in Wuchang (武昌) shattered the stillness of late-Qing China. What began as a regional uprising quickly ignited a chain reaction across the empire, toppling a dynastic order that had endured for more than two millennia and ushering in one of Asia’s first republics — the Republic of China (ROC). From that moment, the 10th day of the 10th month became a date of epochal significance, not merely in Chinese history, but in the broader arc of Asia’s encounter with modernity. Yet today, as Taiwan marks Double Ten National Day, the holiday’s meaning has undergone a transformation

What hope does Taiwan have? Quite a bit more, in fact, than Shuster lets on. Shuster points to genuine problems. The first Donald Trump administration had a mostly positive record on Taiwan policy. Head of MI5 warns Iran targeting UK
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:42:22 UTC
01:42:22 KST

Iran is trying to hit military sites in Britain and the suspected plot to attack a US-run military air base last month was “not unique,” the head of the MI5 spy agency said on Tuesday, as he warned that Tehran and Moscow are expanding their attacks against the UK.
Ken McCallum, who leads the UK’s domestic security service, said that Tehran is seeking to intensify its attacks in Britain beyond the traditional targets of Iranians opposed to the country’s Islamic authorities.
That has included arson and sabotage attacks on Jewish sites that Britain says were carried out by Iranian proxies.
Photo: Reuters
Another “major shift this year has been Iranian ambitions to come at harder targets, like military sites,” McCallum said.
The incident at Royal Air Force (RAF) Fairford “is not unique. There have been other examples, not just in the UK but around the world,” he said.
His comments came as Iran summoned British Ambassador to Iran Hugo Shorter to warn it could “seriously reconsider” bilateral relations unless the UK provides evidence linking Tehran to the alleged plot.
Tehran told the ambassador it was protesting what it called Britain’s “irresponsible and destructive approach.”
“The British government must provide documents and evidence supporting its accusations against Iran,” the Iranian Ministry of Foreign Affairs said, according to the Islamic Republic of Iran Broadcasting.
McCallum delivered his annual speech outlining major threats to the UK as counterterror detectives investigate a suspected terror plot against the US-run base in western England, which has been used to bomb Iran during this year’s war.
Scores of residents were evacuated from their homes near the base on Sept. 27 as armed police officers and army bomb-disposal experts swarmed the rural area.
Police later said they had found a quantity of an accelerant — gasoline — in three vans at the site, but no explosives.
Seven men in their 20s have been arrested and released on bail under investigation.
In all, more than 50 people have been arrested over Iran-linked plots in the past year, McCallum said.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham on Monday said that the apparent plot was “almost certainly” directed by Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Corp (IRGC).
Iran has denied involvement, although it has previously said that it considers any base used to attack its territory a legitimate target.
The US pulled its bombers from RAF Fairford after the incident and the administration of US President Donald Trump said it believed the base faced Iranian threats intended to kill as many US troops and destroy as many US planes as possible.
Iran has so far used low-level criminal proxies who lack the capacity to mount a sophisticated large-scale attack, McCallum said.
However, the IRGC has shown stronger capabilities in countries closer to Iran, “so it would be foolish for a person in a role like mine to discount the possibility,” he added.
McCallum said that the UK faces a “new era of national security,” with a generational shift equivalent to the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks against the US.
The myriad threats to national security now range from “arson, sabotage, cyberattacks, coercion, violence” to “what online algorithms are feeding your teenagers in their bedrooms,” he said.
McCallum said his agency’s work countering state threats — chiefly from Russia, Iran and China — has quadrupled in the past decade, while Russia and Iran are escalating hybrid warfare campaigns against the UK and other European countries.
Russia has been linked to attacks including an attempt to use an explosives-laden drone at Germany’s Leipzig airport and is “using tactics that stop short — though sometimes not much short — of conventional conflict,” he said.

Musk’s Terafab plan poses no short-term threat to TSMC: Analyst
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:42:22 UTC
01:42:22 KST

Elon Musk’s reported plan to build a massive semiconductor fabrication complex in Texas will have no impact on Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC, 台積電) in the short to medium term, as such a project would take five to 10 years to materialize, a veteran semiconductor analyst said yesterday.
Speaking to reporters on the sidelines of a forum in Taipei, Kirk Yang (楊應超), chairman and CEO of Kirkland Capital LLC and a former foreign brokerage analyst, said building a leading-edge chip foundry is highly complex.
Even for TSMC, the world’s largest contract chipmaker, constructing and ramping up a new fab takes several years, Yang said.
Photo: CNA
If Musk, who leads companies including Tesla Inc and SpaceX, succeeds in building a chip fab, it will likely be five to 10 years before it becomes operational, Yang said, adding that the project poses “absolutely no impact” on TSMC in the short or medium term.
Musk plans to build “Terafab,” a massive vertically integrated semiconductor manufacturing and artificial intelligence (AI) computing complex in Grimes County, Texas, according to recent media reports.
Yang said many multinational companies had attempted to enter semiconductor manufacturing in the past, but failed because of the industry’s high technological barriers and enormous capital requirements.
He cited IBM Corp’s semiconductor business, where he previously worked, as an example, noting that it was ultimately sold to GlobalFoundries Inc.
Still, Yang said he remains confident in Musk’s long-term ability to execute the project, citing the billionaire entrepreneur’s strong execution record at Tesla and SpaceX, whose businesses span electric vehicles, autonomous driving, robotics, energy storage, AI, satellite communications and space exploration.
The global chip shortage during the COVID-19 pandemic, coupled with US-China trade tensions, has strengthened US companies’ desire to vertically integrate their supply chains, covering chip design, manufacturing and advanced packaging, he said.
Musk’s initial plan to invest about US$3 billion in a pilot fab is likely to involve US partners such as Intel Corp, as Washington still hopes domestic companies will play a leading role in semiconductor manufacturing, he added.
Looking further ahead, Yang said TSMC could benefit if Musk follows through on his proposed sublease model and allows the company to provide technical consulting services or lease space at the facility.
“Intel will sooner or later become a competitor to TSMC. That’s unlikely in the short term, but five or 10 years from now, it’s hard to say,” Yang said. “It wouldn’t be a bad thing for TSMC to get closer to Intel, as the two sides could gain a better understanding of each other.”
TSMC closed unchanged at NT$2,490 in Taipei yesterday after reaching a high of NT$2,535, as investors took profits ahead of the chipmaker’s earnings conference today.

Lai pledges net zero transition support
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:42:22 UTC
01:42:22 KST

Companies’ ability to cut emissions would affect their future orders and Taiwan’s industrial competitiveness, President William Lai (賴清德) said yesterday, pledging financial and policy support for their transition.
Increasingly stringent emissions requirements in international supply chains mean businesses need to build net zero goals into their operating decisions, Lai said at the Energy Taiwan and Net-Zero Taiwan exhibitions in Taipei.
“The ability to cut carbon affects future orders and directly influences the international competitiveness of Taiwan’s industries,” he said.
Photo: Lin Ching-hua, Taipei Times
To support that transition, the government will use carbon fee revenue to help industries go green and fund technological innovation, Lai said, adding that Taiwan has completed its first round of carbon fee declarations and payments, putting a price on emissions.
Other measures included the Taiwan Green Growth Fund, which seeks to attract private investment for net zero industries, and plans to invest an additional NT$100 billion (US$3.12 billion) over eight years to help micro, small and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs) pursue digital and net zero transitions, Lai said.
He reiterated Taiwan’s targets of cutting greenhouse gas emissions by 28 percent and 38 percent by 2030 and 2035 respectively compared with 2005 levels.
Reliable power supplies are also essential as artificial intelligence (AI) drives up electricity demand, he said.
Taiwan’s renewable energy capacity has risen from 4.7 gigawatts (GW) in 2016 to 25GW, and its cumulative offshore wind capacity ranks fifth in the world, Lai said, adding that the government would continue developing a mix of renewable sources, energy storage, energy conservation and grid resilience.
Taiwan External Trade Development Council Chairman Huang Chih-fang (黃志芳) linked energy supply to the pace of technological change.
“As AI changes our world, energy will determine how far the transformation can go,” Huang said, emphasizing that no single technology could meet the challenge alone.
Lucas Lin (林雍堯), chairperson of SEMI’s Green Energy and Sustainability Alliance, said companies needed to translate customers’ renewable energy commitments into everyday production and supply chain decisions, making the net zero transition a source of industrial upgrading and competitiveness.
The exhibitions, organized by the council and the alliance, feature more than 400 companies and run through tomorrow in Hall 1 of the Taipei Nangang Exhibition Center.
Displays cover renewable energy, energy storage, energy efficiency, carbon management and green finance, offering businesses technologies and services for reducing emissions.

Sanctions imposed by China’s Taiwan Affairs Office (TAO) on a firm owned by Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Legislator Puma Shen’s (沈伯洋) father are an egregious attempt to pressure Taiwanese society and interfere with Taiwan’s democratic elections, the Mainland Affairs Council (MAC) said yesterday.
Hong Kong’s Ta Kung Pao (大公報) and Wen Wei Po (文匯報) on Tuesday reported that VWAY Co — a company owned by Shen’s father, Shen Tu-cheng (沈土城) — was still earning money in China after Sicuens International Co (兆億), also owned by Shen Tu-cheng, was sanctioned in June last year.
VWAY trade totaled about US$700,000 in about 10 months through March, reported the newspapers, which are owned by the Hong Kong Liaison Office.
Photo: Gan Meng-lin, Taipei Times
The latest sanction, imposed by the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) on VWAY, follows the same pattern as last year, the MAC said.
Targeted reporting is published by Hong Kong media, then the TAO issues an official sanction announcement, the council said.
During elections in Taiwan, the CCP collaborates with media to manipulate public opinion, label specific political camps and candidates, and exert economic pressure, the MAC said, adding that they are clear and egregious attempts to coerce Taiwanese society and interfere with its elections.
The government will do everything it can to protect the legitimate rights and interests of Taiwanese citizens and businesses, and will resolutely defend Taiwan’s free and democratic system, it said.
TAO spokesman Chen Binhua (陳斌華) told a news conference yesterday that China in June last year sanctioned Sicuens International, but Shen Tu-cheng allegedly continued doing business with Chinese companies through VWAY.
China has also sanctioned VWAY Co, banning it from doing any business or cooperating with organizations in China, Chen said.
Puma Shen, the DPP’s candidate for Taipei mayor, earlier yesterday told reporters that the reports are recycled claims from 2024 that he has addressed many times.
His family does business with Ecuador, but it is portrayed as operating in China, he said, adding that people would see through the attempt to revive old rumors.
Puma Shen said he has already been sanctioned and placed on a Chinese wanted list, while Chinese authorities have hired Hong Kong residents to monitor him.
“I will wait and see what else they can dish out,” he added.
Taipei residents are choosing their next mayor and the TAO should understand that such tactics would not earn the trust of Taiwanese, including Taipei residents, Puma Shen’s campaign team said.
The DPP legislative caucus said that the same script — Hong Kong media releasing reports orchestrated by the CCP — played out last year.
Whoever speaks loudest in defense of Taiwan becomes the primary target and this attack is clearly aimed at Puma Shen, the caucus said, adding that no democratic country would allow a foreign state to interfere in its elections.
Voters will see through these tactics, it said.

SOCCER
English clubs in danger: IFR
English soccer clubs are “dangerously exposed” to financial risk, the country’s Independent Football Regulator (IFR) said in a report released on Tuesday, after finding that 94 percent of clubs in the top five divisions were operating at a loss. The regulator, established last year, proposed stronger cost controls and contingency planning as part of a six-point plan to improve the financial sustainability of the English game. Its draft State of the Game report, which is to undergo an eight-week public consultation before a final version is published, found nearly two-thirds of English Football League and National League clubs were “technically insolvent” and increasingly dependent on cash injections from owners. “While some of our clubs are among the richest and most competitive in the world, others are standing on the edge of financial disaster... A significant number of clubs have told us they would not survive if their owners walked away,” IFR chair David Kogan said.
ATHLETICS
Runner Korir suspended
Kenyan marathon runner Ronald Kipkoech Korir has been provisionally suspended for using a prohibited substance, the Athletics Integrity Unit (AIU) said on Tuesday. Korir, 35, finished fourth behind winner Eliud Kipchoge in the 2023 Berlin Marathon and his time of 2 hours, 4 minutes, 22 seconds placed him in the elite bracket of marathon performers. An athlete is provisionally suspended while his case is investigated. More than 140 Kenyan athletes, including current women’s marathon world record holder Ruth Chepngetich, have been suspended or banned by the AIU since 2017.

Indian ‘cockroach’ leaders jailed over banned protests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:42:16 UTC
01:42:16 KST

Two leaders of India’s youth-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) yesterday were remanded in custody for five days, as police increased efforts to clamp down on protests against the nation’s election commission.
CJP activists and opposition parties have defied a security crackdown to demand the resignation of India’s top election commissioner, accusing the poll body of manipulating voter rolls to benefit Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling party.
The commission, which oversees voting in the world’s most populous nation, has denied any wrongdoing.
Photo: AP
Delhi Police said CJP leaders Ashutosh Ranka, 30, and Saurav Das, 27, were taken into custody for their “alleged repeated attempts to disturb public peace and violate the law.”
At the end of the five-day remand period, they could have their detention extended, be granted bail or be released.
On Tuesday, the pair jumped security barricades to wave the national flag at Jantar Mantar, a decades-old protest site that police have barred people from using.
“Their alleged attempts to instigate others through social media to engage in similar unlawful activities were also taken into consideration,” police said.
Congress Party leader Rahul Gandhi backed the men, who were detained after entering the site.
Jantar Mantar, in the heart of the capital, has been sealed off for days with yellow metal barricades and guarded by security personnel.
Delhi Police on Monday said that they had removed the site from its list of designated protest venues.
“Waving the Tricolour at Jantar Mantar in a peaceful protest is not a crime,” Gandhi said on social media, referring to the Indian flag. “Jailing youth for it is an act of cowardice.”
The Congress and CJP have protested over the voter roll revision.
Gandhi yesterday said that “all protests are one.”
“Different banners, one cause,” he said.
CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke praised the men, saying they “knew they could be thrown behind bars,” but went ahead to wave the national flag.
“They’ve shown the entire country that the only way to stand up to a bully like Modi is to never bow down, no matter the consequences,” he said on social media.

Chinese in US accused of poisoning
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:42:16 UTC
01:42:16 KST

A University of Wyoming microbiology graduate student from China has been arrested on accusations she poisoned the tea of a colleague who had pending patents and with whom she did not get along, then tried to flee the country after police questioned her.
Wang Aili, 32, was arrested on Tuesday last week at Los Angeles International Airport, where prosecutors allege she sought to return to China.
With her were laptops, electronic storage devices and documents now in the possession of police, who allege Wang was seen on surveillance video rummaging through the desk of the victim who specialized in technology for disease treatment — research similar to work she had done in China.
Photo: AP
Wang remained jailed without bail on Tuesday in Los Angeles.
She allegedly bought a chemical, acrylamide, over eBay, and it was first detected when the alleged victim’s wife and others tested water from the coffee maker he used to brew tea.
US officials for years have accused China of stealing intellectual property from US universities.
Mark Gomelsky, the microbiology professor overseeing both graduate students, said that the accusations left him reeling.
He was uncertain if the victim would fully recover, Gomelsky said.
“It’s been disheartening, to say the least, to see that one of your student’s life is in jeopardy and another student may be responsible for that,” he told reporters. “That was one of the worst shocks in my professional career.”
Wang had no attorney listed in court documents.
The police investigation began after the victim — identified in court documents as “K.T.” — began experiencing symptoms, and his wife and others allegedly isolated the chemical in the coffee maker water.
The victim and campus police set up surveillance cameras in the office space he shared with Wang at the university in Laramie.
Wang allegedly was recorded on Sept. 27 going through K.T’s desk.
On Oct. 1, she was recorded “taking photos and manipulating notebooks” on his desk, as well as rinsing out his mug with a liquid from her own mug, a University of Wyoming campus police officer’s affidavit said.
Wang and the alleged victim, who did not share research areas, did not get along, the affidavit said.
During an interview by campus police on Oct. 5, Wang allegedly said she “had not used acrylamide in years.”
A day later she was taken into custody in Los Angeles while in possession of “multiple laptops, multiple portable external digital storage devices, related accessories, physical records and written materials,” according to a request by Wyoming prosecutors to “significantly increase” her US$200,000 bond upon extradition.
Wang had no reason to go through the desk of the other student whose federally funded, patent-pending research involved “new technology for cancer, neurological and genetic disease treatment,” the affidavit said.
Wang “was reportedly working on similar research in China before coming to the US,” it said.
Gomelsky described the alleged victim as a highly successful student from Vietnam.
Wang failed her first attempt to defend her dissertation and became envious of her colleague’s success in discovering how to deliver RNA to human cells using bacteria, Gomelsky told reporters.
The alleged victim began experiencing extreme tiredness, inability to sleep and other unexplained symptoms soon after attending a prestigious conference in August, Gomelsky said.
K.T. also noticed a strange taste in the tea that he made with a small coffee maker on his desk, Gomelsky said.
When he washed the coffee maker, the taste would go away, Gomelsky said.
Suspecting someone in their shared office could be poisoning the graduate student, he said that a chemistry professor tested the water and identified acrylamide.
Wang faces a felony aggravated assault and battery charge in Wyoming punishable by up to 10 years in prison and a US$10,000 fine.

Lawmakers still disagree on pension hikes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:42:15 UTC
01:42:15 KST

The legislature’s Social Welfare and Environmental Hygiene Committee yesterday referred proposed amendments to the National Pension Act (國民年金法) to cross-party negotiations amid disagreements on how much to raise pension benefits.
While ruling and opposition party lawmakers agreed that pension benefits should be reviewed every two years, they remained divided over how much monthly benefits should be increased.
The Executive Yuan’s proposed amendments call for raising monthly pension benefits for seniors, family survivors and indigenous peoples to NT$5,000 and disability benefits to NT$6,715, while requiring that pension benefits be reviewed every two years, down from the current four-year requirement.
Photo: CNA
The Cabinet’s proposal would also require adjustments to be announced immediately if the consumer price index rises by 3 percent or more since the previous adjustment.
The committee reviewed the bill on March 19 and July 22, but failed to reach a consensus, with Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT), Democratic Progressive Party and Taiwan People’s Party (TPP) legislators proposing different benefit hikes.
The proposed senior pensions ranged from NT$6,000 to NT$8,000, up from NT$3,500, while proposed disability pensions ranged from NT$8,000 to NT$12,000, up from NT$4,700.
The Executive Yuan’s proposal would increase pensions by 23.5 percent, aligned with adjustments to six major social welfare allowances, including farmers’ pensions, Deputy Minister of Health and Welfare Lu Chien-te (呂建德) told reporters after the meeting.
While lawmakers’ desire to secure better benefits is understandable, raising pensions independently of other social welfare programs could raise concerns about fairness, Lu said.
KMT legislators Tu Chuan-chi (涂權吉) and Liao Wei-hsiang (廖偉翔) supported the party’s proposal, saying that international developments such as Russia’s invasion of Ukraine have fueled severe inflation in the past few years.
The benefits of the nation’s economic growth should be shared by everyone, they said, calling for more frequent pension reviews and higher benefits to support disadvantaged groups.
TPP Legislator Chiu Hui-ju (邱慧洳) said pensions should not just be reviewed every two years, but adjusted every two years.
KMT Legislator and committee convener Chen Ching-hui (陳菁徽) said the committee had completed its review and referred the unresolved provisions to cross-party negotiations.

Minister warns EU over dependence on China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:42:10 UTC
01:42:10 KST

Minister of Foreign Affairs Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍) on Tuesday promoted the “Taiwan model” in a speech at the Warsaw Security Forum in Poland, presenting Taiwan as a high-tech powerhouse and a trusted partner in Europe’s reindustrialization and warning the EU about dependence on China.
Dependence on Chinese suppliers poses a risk to the bloc’s freedom, he said, ahead of an EU summit in Brussels where trade with Beijing is to be high on the agenda.
The bloc’s leaders are to discuss China as the first point of their summit starting today as Brussels attempts to reduce the bloc’s trade deficit and mitigate what many see as the risks of becoming overdependent on Beijing in sensitive sectors.
Photo: CNA
Reindustrialization and rearmament are shared goals for Taiwan and Europe amid rising threats from authoritarian regimes in Russia and China, Lin said.
Russia’s war in Ukraine has exposed the dangers of Europe’s dependence on an authoritarian energy supplier, he said.
“What is happening in Ukraine is shaping the security of Warsaw, of Berlin, of Paris — and, indeed, of Taipei. In an interconnected world, the front lines of freedom are no longer separated by geographical landscape,” he said.
With the rise of artificial intelligence (AI), the world is undergoing the fastest technological transformation in modern history, Lin said.
“Europe, like many others, cannot tackle these challenges alone. This is where Taiwan comes in,” he said. “Taiwan sits at the center of the world’s most cutting-edge supply chains. We make the overwhelming majority of the most advanced semiconductors. We are a global powerhouse in electronics and precision manufacturing. We produce the very hardware on which AI runs.”
“Our strengths are not a threat to Europe’s; they are complementary to them,” he added.
While Europe leads in industrial machinery, automotive engineering, chemicals and design, “Taiwan brings the chips, the components, and the manufacturing ecosystem that can turn European ambition into finished, competitive products,” Lin said.
Beyond technological know-how, Taiwan is also a partner Europe can trust, he said.
By contrast, the alternative “China model” is one that “does not play by the rules of the world trading system. It relies on massive state subsidies and unfair, nonmarket practices to undercut and overwhelm European competitors,” he said.
“Its aim is not mutual benefit; it is dominance — to make Europe dependent and to control European markets, and ultimately, reduce a continent to the status of an economic dependency,” Lin said.
“Because China’s authoritarian ideology is fundamentally incompatible with Europe’s democracy, dependence on China is not merely an economic risk — it’s a threat to European freedom and sovereignty itself,” he added.
A Europe controlled through its supply chains would be a Europe that had surrendered part of its liberty, Lin said.
While Taiwanese foreign ministers previously rarely visited Europe due to Beijing’s objections, Lin has gone several times since he assumed his position more than two years ago, including to Poland.
This is the second consecutive year Lin has attended the annual forum.
The forum, one of Europe’s major security conferences, focuses on strengthening transatlantic cooperation and addressing security and defense challenges in Central and Eastern Europe.
Europe has its own disputes with Beijing, over trade imbalances and its criticism of what it sees as Chinese support for Russia.

Democratic Progressive Party Legislator Chiu Chih-wei (邱志偉) yesterday urged tighter agricultural import regulations after kiwifruit with false country-of-origin labels were allegedly spotted at Taipei’s First Fruit and Vegetables Wholesale Market.
Chiu made the comments during a meeting with Ministry of Agriculture officials at the legislature, saying his office received credible claims that one of the capital city’s biggest wholesale venues was selling fruits bearing labels that read “produce of CWA.”
The International Organization for Standardization does not recognize CWA as a valid country code and images of kiwifruit packaging bearing the three-letter code has sparked rampant speculation on the Internet that “China’s western area” was the source of the produce.
Photo: Yang Yuan-ting, Taipei Times
Minister of Agriculture Chen Junne-jih (陳駿季) said CWA is an invalid country code and that he did not know which country produced the fruits.
CN is the correct country code for agricultural products from China, he said, adding that the ministry would ask the Food and Drugs Administration to assist in investigating the fruits’ origins.
Taiwan is largely dependent on foreign imports for kiwifruit and imported 28,501 tonnes of it from January to last month, trade records show.
New Zealand is the nation’s largest supplier of kiwifruit, accounting for 26,565 tonnes of imports over the January-to-September period. Italy was a distant second at 1,223 tonnes and China at third place with 695 tonnes.
However, China has doubled its kiwifruit exports to Taiwan compared with a year earlier.
Taiwanese strongly distrust the safety of Chinese produce despite its sizeable market share, as health authorities have repeatedly found agricultural chemical residues exceeding the safety limit in fruits and vegetables from the country.

Tehran municipality accused of ‘overstep’ after launching welfare projects
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:41:42 UTC
01:41:42 KST

Tehran municipality accused of ‘overstep’ after launching welfare projects
Tehran’s municipality has launched new welfare initiatives to combat inflation, drawing intense scrutiny over funding sources, institutional overlap, and transparency.
Tehran municipality has launched a series of welfare initiatives to help residents cope with soaring living costs, but the measures have raised questions about their financing and effectiveness, as well as whether the local authority is taking on responsibilities better handled by Iran’s national government.
The local authority has launched four projects it says are aimed at protecting citizens, including a housing project, freezes on the prices of 12 basic goods, and a maternity package.
Questions have been raised about how they will be funded and whether the municipality is overstepping its traditional functions.
In Iran, municipalities are responsible for local services and urban management, while the national government oversees broader economic policy, including efforts to control inflation.
Iranian law does give municipalities some responsibilites beyond conventional urban services, but Article 55 of Iran’s Municipal Law does call for municipalities to provide for public food markets, make certain essential goods more affordable, and provide social welfare facilities and low-cost housing.
The dispute is therefore less about whether Tehran municipality can provide the services, and more about their scale and financing.
The municipality’s price-freezing initiative, dubbed the “Zero Inflation” project, has been the most controversial. It comes as year-on-year inflation reached nearly 90 percent last month, while annual food inflation hit 108.8 percent.
Doubts have been raised about how the project will be funded and its effectiveness. Others believe that the measures could fuel inequality between the capital and other cities.
They are viewed as steps to address the huge economic challenges faced by Tehran residents, worsened since the United States and Israel launched a war on Iran on February 28.
Tehran Mayor Alireza Zakani said the municipality had recently guaranteed prices ranging between 5 percent and 50 percent below market rates for the next six months.
Yousef Akandeh, a political activist, told Al Jazeera that freezing the prices of some goods or providing free services will not reduce inflation to zero alone.
“Even if we assume that the Tehran municipality succeeded in stabilising the prices of 12 basic goods, what about the rise in rents, medicines, transportation prices, and the rest of living expenses,” Akandeh asked.
Real steps to tackle inflation, Akandeh said, would have to begin with controlling liquidity growth and monetary discipline, which he said are nearly impossible amid the ongoing war.
The municipality has also introduced a maternity support programme offering mothers of children born this year monthly credits worth up to 40 million rials ($15) for two years for each newborn.
Akandeh raised the issue of institutional overlap, noting that a similar national scheme already exists.
“The government implements a similar package and provides monthly financial amounts for all newborns across the country and not just in Tehran, and if the municipality’s package is independent of it, the Tehrani family may benefit from the national and municipal programme simultaneously,” Akandeh said.
Receiving support from both programmes would not, in itself, indicate wrongdoing. But critics are instead raising the question of whether it is an appropriate use of Tehran’s municipal resources, particularly when the city faces competing spending demands.
Amir Dabiri Mehr, a former adviser in the Tehran municipality, told Al Jazeera that although supporting the homeless falls under the municipality’s social responsibilities, the problem lies in a lack of transparency. The municipality is funded by taxes and building density licences.
“The people have the right to know what the municipality spends within the framework of its original tasks, and in tasks it has chosen for itself, and where it gets its resources from?” Dabiri Mehr said.
The municipality-affiliated Hamshahri newspaper said that the “Zero Inflation” project is not funded by municipal budget subsidies, but through direct purchases from producers and reducing commercial profit margins in council-run stores.
The biggest crisis facing Tehran’s residents is housing, which is the national government’s responsibility, Mehr said. Food and living expenses are the national government’s responsibility.
“If the goal is to solve the people’s problems, it seems that the biggest problem facing the residents of Tehran today is the housing crisis, and this dilemma cannot be solved by building an apartment building consisting of a few residential units,” he said.
Al Jazeera attempted to contact the Tehran municipality for comment but received no response.
Tehran Mayor Zakani has, however, defended the financing arrangements, telling a local newspaper, Hamshahri, that the Zero Inflation initiative would not rely on direct subsidies from the municipal budget, but instead on purchasing goods directly from producers and reducing commercial profit margins in city-run stores.
Zakani also said that the programme would draw on municipal resources, bank financing, and partnerships.

Yemen separatist leader calls for mobilisation against Houthis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:41:38 UTC
01:41:38 KST

Breadcrumb
Exiled Yemen separatist leader calls for mobilisation against Houthis
Thousands of people have attended demonstrations across southern Yemen in response to a call from exiled separatist leader Aidarous al-Zubaidi for a "popular mobilisation" to halt the ongoing Houthi advance.
In his first address since fleeing the country in January, the head of the Southern Transitional Council on Tuesday called on southern Yemenis to join the Saudi-backed government's efforts to turn the tide of the war.
Videos published by pro-separatist media showed mass protests in several cities - including Aden, Mukalla, Seiyun and Al-Ghaydah - which coincided with the anniversary of the 14 October revolution, the South Yemeni rebellion against British rule in 1963.
Some demonstrators were seen waving Emirati flags and carrying portraits of UAE President Mohammed bin Zayed in an expression of support for the STC's main foreign backer.
"We declare the general mobilisation to defend the south and its national liberation project, and to continue the national defence battle against the Houthi militias and their Iranian expansionist project," Zubaidi said in his televised statement.
He stopped short of issuing a specific call but urged southern Yemenis to "prepare to meet the call to defend our homeland … against the invading Houthi militia".
Yemen's internationally recognised Saudi-backed government has suffered major setbacks since its war with the Houthis resumed last month.
Since September, the Iran-backed Houthis seized control of the Red Sea coast and encircled Taiz, Yemen's third-largest city and a major government stronghold. It has also mounted dozens of attacks on Saudi Arabia, including a strike on Riyadh airport over the weekend that killed 13 people and wounded hundreds.
Political analyst Mohammed al-Qadhi said the timing of Zubaidi's address was significant, coinciding with the 14 October revolution and the Houthis' gains on the battlefield, which are "significantly altering the balance of power" in the country.
"The STC wants to demonstrate that it remains an important and influential force in the south and should play a key role both militarily and in any future political settlement," he told The New Arab.
UAE backing
Zubaidi condemned the Houthi attacks on the kingdom but called on Riyadh to support the STC's ambitions for south Yemen's independence.
Saudi Arabia has fiercely opposed separatism in southern Yemen and in January launched a decisive military intervention against the STC and other UAE-backed militias.
The operation resulted in the dissolution of the STC inside Yemen and Saudi-backed groups asserting control over the south. Zubaidi was charged with treason by the Yemeni government and he fled the country as a result. He is thought to have been living in Abu Dhabi for the past nine months.
"Zubaidi’s intervention is primarily about political leverage," Andreas Krieg, senior security studies lecturer at King's College London, told The New Arab.
"He is telling Riyadh that southern forces are prepared to fight the Houthis, but not simply to restore a Saudi-backed Yemeni state that has spent the past year dismantling their political project. He is effectively presenting southern independence as the price of military cooperation."
The Saudi intervention has also curtailed Abu Dhabi's influence in Yemen, with the Emirati military withdrawing from the country and its surrogates being brought into closer alignment with Riyadh.
"Abu Dhabi wants to recover influence without again assuming responsibility for Yemen's war," said Krieg.
"What we are witnessing is an attempt to turn Saudi Arabia's deteriorating military position into Emirati political leverage."

Sally Rooney books can’t be sold in UK amid Palestine Action ban, publisher says
The Irish writer is a supporter of the activists, who have been put on the same ‘terrorist’ blacklist as militants like Hamas and Hezbollah
Irish author Sally Rooney can no longer sell her books in the UK because of her support for the activist group Palestine Action, her publisher Faber said on Wednesday.
Rooney has previously expressed her support for the group, which was banned as a “terrorist” organisation by the UK government in July 2025. It is not banned in Ireland, where Rooney lives.
The proscription, which the organisation is appealing against, puts Palestine Action on the same blacklist as militant groups Hamas and Hezbollah, making it illegal in the UK to be part of, support or finance it.
“Current legislation in the UK has led to circumstances where Faber cannot pass on UK earnings to Sally Rooney for her work. To sell a writer’s work and not be able to pass on earnings is an unconscionable situation for a publisher,” Faber said in a statement on its website.

Middle East oil exports plunge as attacks disrupt Hormuz shipping
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:41:01 UTC
01:41:01 KST

Crude oil and petroleum exports from the Middle East sharply dropped over the past week as attacks on commercial vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz have intensified.
Maritime transit in the region has suffered drastically since the US and Israel’s attacks on Iran on February 28, followed by Tehran’s effective closure of the vital waterway and a subsequent American naval blockade.
Attacks on commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz reached a new peak this year over the past week.
At least 14 incidents of attacks, attempted strikes and obstructions were recorded in and around the Strait of Hormuz on October 5–12, while six ships were attacked on Monday alone, according to the UK Maritime Trade Operations and global maritime security sources.
Commercial vessel traffic via the strategic chokepoint fell to its lowest since July 22, affecting outward energy flows.
Oil, petroleum and liquefied natural gas (LNG) exports from the Middle East plummeted in the wake of the war, and while there have been signs of partial recovery, intensifying security risks sparked concerns.
Houthi militia increased their attacks on Saudi Arabia, threatening transit through the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean.
Vessel transits through Bab al-Mandab, Hormuz hit new low
Middle Eastern crude oil, petroleum and liquid chemical exports, including shipments from the Gulf of Oman and the Red Sea, fell from 21.1 million barrels per day on October 8 to 6.7 million barrels on October 11, 10.4 million barrels on Monday and 8.3 million barrels on Tuesday, according to Kpler.
The weekly average of 17 million barrels remained below the pre-war volume of around 23.3 million barrels per day.
Only six commercial ships were able to transit the Strait of Hormuz on Monday, while previously 32 ships passed through on October 8, 24 on October 9, 11 on October 10 and 12 on October 11.
Meanwhile, vessel transit through the Bab al-Mandab Strait also dropped, with 35 vessels passing through on October 8, 39 on October 10, 46 on October 11 and 32 on Monday.
The attempts by the Houthis to establish a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia to seize control of the Bab el-Mandeb corridor added a new volatile dimension to the wider conflict.
Large-scale supply disruptions across both the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandab Strait could pressure global energy supplies and market stability even further, analysts say.

Behlul Cetinkaya and Emir Yildirim
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
Turkish and Nigerian officials offered Islamic finance as a resilient solution to global economic volatility at the fifth AlBaraka Summit in London.
The summit kicked off on Tuesday, gathering global Islamic finance leaders to discuss ethical principles, regulatory frameworks and technological and financial opportunities in the sector. Anadolu serves as its global communications partner.
The second day of the event saw Türkiye Wealth Fund (TWF) CEO Salim Arda Ermut emphasize that the centuries of geopolitical instability Türkiye has navigated have equipped the country with unique experience to help the global economy weather today's challenges.
“As regional issues become global, our experiences become increasingly more important to adapt to new challenges,” he said. “Finance should support production, encourage entrepreneurs, and add value to society and the economy — we, the TWF, deem Islamic finance as a key component of our long-term strategy.”
Ermut stated that integrating Islamic banking into global markets would help generate value rather than wealth through interest, with its interest-free and ethics-focused approach at the system’s core.
He noted that Islamic banking will be key to bringing about $500 billion worth of private, “under-the-mattress gold,” back into the Turkish economy.
He stated that the newly established Istanbul Financial Center (IFC) is a financial bridge connecting Europe, Asia, the Middle East and Africa, and it will employ 50,000 workers once operational to serve as a hub of the global Islamic economy.
“We need the new generation and new human capital to embrace this idea and we’re working to build this based on our experiences here in Türkiye, with new departments in universities,” he said.
Doris Uzoka-Anite, Nigerian budget and economic planning minister, stated that financial systems designed for Muslims meet the requirements of the broader global economy.
She stated that Nigeria’s national sukuk framework helped fund major public infrastructure projects, noting that tangible wealth is what matters when it comes to the true measure of any financial system and how it contributes to a nation’s real economy.
The second day of the summit also featured a keynote address on financial ethics by Muhammad Taqi Usmani, chair of the Accounting and Auditing Organization for Islamic Financial Institutions (AAOIFI).
Industry leaders also participated in panel discussions on the Islamic economy, digital transformation and ethical policies to serve Muslim consumers worldwide.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:36:43 UTC
01:36:43 KST

Merve Aydogan
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
The UN Security Council on Wednesday adopted a resolution renewing the sanctions regime on Haiti for one year, including an arms embargo, a travel ban and an assets freeze.
The draft resolution passed with 14 votes, while Russia abstained.
The text also extends the mandate of the Panel of Experts assisting the Haiti sanctions committee for 13 months.
US Deputy Permanent Representative Jennifer Locetta said the decision sent a strong message of support for Haitians.
"Today’s vote is yet another unwavering signal that the international community stands with the people of Haiti," said Locetta.
She said the arms embargo does not apply to the sale, supply or transfer of arms or related materiel, or to related assistance and training, for the Haitian government when intended to further peace and security objectives.
Panama's UN envoy Eloy Alfaro de Alba said the international community’s responsibility does not end with the adoption of the resolution. He stressed that the crisis has many facets and requires sustained attention from the council and member states.
Haiti has been grappling with gang violence and political instability for years, and the sanctions regime is one of the tools the council uses to address the crisis.

Ukraine accuses US of helping Russia as missiles hit Kyiv
LONDON - Ukraine on Oct 14 accused the United States of helping Russia by failing to warn it of incoming missile strikes and hobbling Kyiv’s military response through changes to the Starlink system it uses on the battlefield.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called on US tech billionaire Elon Musk to restore Starlink, which Kyiv says has been slowed down.
“I hope that it’s a mistake, maybe huge technical problem,” Zelensky told UK journalist Piers Morgan. “I don’t know, but we are asking to do it, to switch (it) on.”
Former Ukrainian defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov later said that “Starlink’s operation at speeds up to 160kmh is being restored. Strike drones and interceptor drones should be able to fly again”.
Musk said any disruption was the responsibility of the US government, not his SpaceX company.
He drew a disctinction between the Starshield system, which Ukraine relies on for battlefield communications, and the parallel Starlink civilian satellite system, which Ukraine also deploys but is not allowed to use for offensive operations.
“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” Musk said, referring to US President Donald Trump.
Zelensky replied in the affirmative when asked if he felt “betrayed” after US President Donald Trump announced a diesel-supply deal with heavily sanctioned Moscow.
“It’s painful when President Trump chooses one side, not our side,” he said. “I think his advisors are wrong. I don’t know who is pushing him not to the right side. This is not (the) right side of history,”
Zelensky had framed the lack of warnings from allies about a wave of powerful strikes the night of Oct 13 and early Oct 14 as “completely unjust”, and accused Russia of wilfully flouting a supposed “energy ceasefire” announced unilaterally by Trump.
A senior official in Kyiv confirmed that the United States had in recent days threatened to stop providing intelligence about Russian missile launches that Ukraine uses to thwart attacks. Trump denied doing so on Oct 13.
Defence officials also suggested Washington was behind slower speeds reported on some Starlink internet terminals which help Ukraine’s military hit Russian-occupied territory and operate interceptor drones.
“It’s obvious they (the United States) are helping Russia for some reason,” the senior official told AFP.
Zelensky adviser Sergiy Beskrestnov said the attacks and Starlink restrictions were more than a coincidence.
“Through their actions, our partners are depriving us of one of the few chances we have to defend the country against jet-powered Shahed drones,” he wrote on Telegram.
Close contact
In Moscow, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Russia was watching for any sign that Washington’s backing for Ukraine may have shifted.
“We are carefully noting all this. It is too early to draw any systemic conclusions,” he told reporters.
President Vladimir Putin’s special envoy on economic cooperation, Kirill Dmitriev, meanwhile said the first contracts on providing diesel to the United States would be signed in the coming days.
“We are in close, hourly contact with the American side, and everything is moving very quickly,” he added.
Trump, facing crunch mid-term elections in November, has blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries for the squeeze on fuel supplies and increase in prices at the pump.

‘Disrespect’
