“Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States,” said Zelensky, accusing Moscow of squandering a chance to ease hostilities.
The lack of warning has been reported only rarely during the conflict and Ukrainian officials have previously suggested the Russian military’s use of hard-to-detect missiles or potential technical issues could be to blame.
Fifteen people were killed around the country in the latest round of strikes, while significant damage to energy facilities and equipment knocked out power to swathes of Kyiv.

Fossil overlooked for 100 years ID'd as new dinosaur species
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:35:10 UTC
01:35:10 KST

New dinosaur species, a T. rex cousin that "would have chased us," identified from fossil found 100 years ago
London — A previously unknown species of dinosaur — a "long-clawed predator the size of a tiger" and a cousin of the Tyrannosaurus rex — has been identified from a fossil originally found 100 years ago, but which remained hidden away in a British museum until recently.
The species has been named Invictibellatrix amberina, and it belongs to a group of two-legged carnivores known as megaraptorans according to an article published in the Royal Society Open Science research journal.
Megaraptorans were closely related to the group of dinosaurs T. rex originated from, the tyrannosaurs. Unlike T. rex, however, scientists say Invictibellatrix did not attack prey with its mouth, but with its long arms and giant curved claws.
Researchers believe the dinosaur would have been between 10 and 13 feet long and almost 5 feet tall. Its body would have had feathers, and it would have hunted smaller dinosaurs, lizards and mammals.
The fossil that led to the discovery sat in a drawer at the Natural History Museum in London for nearly 100 years, having first been obtained by the vaunted institution in 1924.
Dr. Cassius Morrison of University College London, the lead author of the article that announced the discovery, called it a "real mystery that the fossil was overlooked for so long."
Morrison wrote that while Invictibellatrix "was not the apex predator of its time," it would have been a formidable threat to humans if they had coexisted with the species — even "more dangerous than a T. rex."
"We would have been perfectly sized prey, about a third of their body weight," he said. "They definitely would have chased us. A T. rex would not have bothered, as we would have been too small."
The fossil itself is a chunk of the back of a skull. It was one of 1,000 specimens originally discovered by Reginald Walter Tooley on the Isle of Wight, off the south coast of England, and it was then acquired by the Natural History Museum.
Invictibellatrix lived during the Early Cretaceous period, around 120 million years ago, and is one of the smallest and earliest known members of the megaraptoran group.
To understand Invictibellatrix, researchers first took a CT scan of the fossil to create a 3D model of that part of its skull. The results were compared with the skulls of other two-legged meat-eating dinosaurs, such as tyrannosaurs, spinosaurs and raptors. A number of unique features led researchers to conclude they had discovered a new species.
Invictibellatrix is Latin for "unconquered female warrior" and amberina refers to the amber found in the rocks where the fossil was discovered. The researchers said by naming the dinosaur Invictibellatrix, they wanted to "give hope and strength to all those who are bullied, discriminated, victimized, and oppressed that tomorrow will be theirs and not to give up in the face of such odds."

China records highest trade surplus in nearly 2 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:34:47 UTC
01:34:47 KST

Ali Canberk Ozbugutu, Burhan Sansarlioglu and Emir Yildirim
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
China’s trade surplus hit its highest level since January 2025 at $133.5 billion in September, according to China’s customs authority (GACC).
Chinese exports rose 36.3% year-on-year to $447.1 billion, and imports jumped 31% to $313.6 billion.
Wang Jun, spokesperson and vice president of the Chinese customs authority, said in a recent statement that strong global demand for artificial intelligence (AI) and electrical infrastructure boosted demand for chips and components, driving exports.
Chinese exports to the US surged 39.5%, while exports to the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) jumped 52.2% and those to EU countries rose 25.2%.
Imports have been on the rise since the beginning of the year due to rising global energy and raw material prices.
Having posted a trade surplus of $938.1 billion in the first nine months of the year, China is expected to run a record surplus again this year after reaching a record of $1.19 trillion in 2025.
China’s consumer price index (CPI) rose 0.9% year-on-year last month, moderately accelerating on a monthly basis but falling short of expectations, which signaled that domestic consumption remains weak.
China’s producer price index (PPI) rose 5% year-on-year in September, its fastest rise since June 2022, above the 3.8% estimate.
Chinese economic policymakers may have to implement additional policy support to achieve both short- and long-term growth targets, analysts say.
Lynn Song, chief economist for China at ING Group, told Anadolu that core trade ties are expected to remain stable through the end of the year, ensuring the year’s growth driver continues to operate.
He stated that Chinese exports to the US continued to recover as the trade agreement remains in effect.
“China's exports have evolved significantly over the past decade, both by product breakdown and by destination,” he said. “As China moves up the value-added ladder, its fastest-growing exports increasingly include higher-margin goods, while low-end manufacturing is moving elsewhere in the region.”
Song stated that imports rose 27.5% year-on-year over the first three quarters, reaching $2.43 trillion. “Compared with early-year expectations, imports have been the biggest surprise this year,” he said.
“Technology products remained the main driver of import growth, suggesting China continues to spend in the ongoing tech race,” he noted.
“Yet the subsequent pickup in exports in recent months has set China up to build on last year's record-breaking $1.2 trillion trade surplus this year,” he added.

Govt approves Finance Ministry bill on asset taxation rules, abuse prevention in line with EU standards
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
19:32:25 EEST
01:32:25 KST

The Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine has approved a draft law developed by the Ministry of Finance regarding the implementation of taxation rules in the event of the transfer of assets outside Ukraine, the general anti-tax avoidance rule, and rules for addressing the effects of hybrid mismatches in accordance with Council Directive (EU) 2016/1164 (ATAD), according to a Wednesday announcement on the Ministry of Finance's website.
The registration of the draft law with the Verkhovna Rada is a structural milestone of the EFF program with the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
The document aims to protect the national corporate income tax system from tax evasion, tax base erosion, and the shifting of profits to jurisdictions with lower tax rates. Along with the draft law on the implementation of these provisions.
The agency notes that the draft law provides for the introduction of a mechanism to tax the appreciation in the value of assets ("exit tax") in the event that assets are transferred outside Ukraine, if the state loses the right to tax them. The rule applies to corporate income tax payers, including non-residents with permanent establishments; however, it does not apply to the temporary (up to 12 months) transfer of assets as part of financing, collateral, or liquidity management transactions, nor to transfers between a taxpayer and a subsidiary if Ukraine does not lose its right to tax those assets.
The document also introduces a general anti-abuse rule (GAAR), under which transactions without valid commercial reasons, carried out for tax benefits in violation of the Tax Code, will not be recognized as abusive. The burden of proof will rest with the tax authority, and audits and the consideration of objections will be carried out by a specially established Commission comprising representatives of the Ministry of Finance and experts from the taxpayer.
Rules are also being introduced to address the consequences of hybrid mismatches, reverse hybrid mismatches, and tax residency mismatches arising from differences in the tax treatment of instruments or entities across different jurisdictions.
The new rules will take effect on the date the law is published and will come into force on January 1, 2028, following its adoption by Parliament. Administration will be carried out within the framework of existing reporting requirements without the introduction of separate tax returns.
The document has not yet been registered with the Verkhovna Rada.

It’s not all about strikes against Russia — why U.S. intelligence is important for Ukraine
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
19:31:00 EEST

It’s not all about strikes against Russia — why U.S. intelligence is important for Ukraine
Kyiv • UNN
U.S. intelligence is critically important for Ukraine’s air defense and strikes. An expert called its provision and the sale of weapons levers of pressure on Trump.
American intelligence is needed by Ukraine both to defend against Russian missiles and to strike military targets on enemy territory. Over the past few days, Ukraine has not received warnings about the enemy preparing missile attacks. Will the United States put Ukraine in an intelligence “vice” and what other levers of pressure does Trump have — UNN journalists discussed these issues with Oleksii Buriachenko, president of the International Institute for Security Studies.
Why American intelligence is important for Ukraine
According to the expert, American satellite intelligence helps Ukraine detect missile threats and use weapons that operate according to U.S. communications standards. In the expert’s view, this concerns not only American systems but also some weapons supplied by other NATO countries. At the same time, European states have their own capabilities, particularly France and the United Kingdom, but they do not cover the full range of U.S. capabilities.
We use U.S. satellite intelligence in two areas: both for defense and for moving the war onto the territory of the aggressor state. That is why it is critical for us to be able to detect missile launches in time and accordingly configure air defense systems for our own protection
Oleksii Buriachenko also emphasized that European partners are already partially compensating for the need for intelligence, but there is currently no full replacement for American capabilities. Therefore, if the transfer of information to Ukraine is halted, it will have to adapt to new conditions.
The issue is not compensation, but the fact that we work simultaneously with American satellite intelligence and with our European partners. However, the specific nature of NATO and American weaponry is that it is primarily designed to work with American satellite intelligence. Therefore, as of now, Ukraine will not be able to emerge from this situation without losses if the United States really decides to stop providing us with satellite intelligence
Can Trump use intelligence as an instrument of pressure
The political scientist recalled that Donald Trump had previously restricted Ukraine’s access to American intelligence for several days. According to him, at that time it was more difficult for Ukrainian air defense systems to respond to massive Russian attacks. However, in his assessment, the current situation is different because Ukraine has partially diversified its sources of intelligence information.
If we are talking about the current situation, we have no confirmed information that Trump is doing this or will do so. At least in the public sphere, he clearly stated that the United States continues to provide intelligence to Ukraine. In other words, there is no delay. The military says that this delay may be related to the fact that Russia has modified its missiles for the S-400, which had already caused us problems
Oleksii Buriachenko also believes that the domestic political situation in the United States may influence the American president’s decisions regarding Ukraine. However, in the political scientist’s view, the possibility of restricting the transfer of intelligence and the sale of American weapons nevertheless remains one of Washington’s instruments of influence.
Elections are the main reason behind this entire story. The configuration may turn out completely differently. If major criticism of Trump in the public sphere over the diesel deal gains momentum, he may, on the contrary, do something else beneficial for Ukraine. But the opposite may also happen: if Trump decides to force through the terms he agreed on with the Russian Federation, he may resolve this issue by putting pressure on Ukraine. He has instruments of pressure — intelligence and the sale of American weapons
In addition, the expert noted that Ukraine’s dependence on U.S. permits for the sale of American weapons remains a separate problem, even if those weapons were purchased by third countries. He emphasized that without official authorization from Washington, Ukraine will not be able to buy such equipment from other states, and therefore called preserving access to intelligence and the ability to purchase American weapons important tactical objectives for Ukraine.
For Ukraine, it is important now that, under any circumstances, it retain access to intelligence and the ability to purchase American weapons. The United States and President Trump have their own political and economic goals. Sometimes they coincide with ours, and sometimes they do not

Nobel laureate Navi Pillay slams Trump, predicts Netanyahu's arrest and rejects Goebbels comparison
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:30:54 UTC
01:30:54 KST

Navi Pillay, the South African jurist awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize, sharply criticized U.S. President Donald Trump on Wednesday over new sanctions imposed by his administration on the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague. In an interview with AFP, Pillay, 85, said the sanctions were illegal and that the timing of their announcement, just hours after news of her Nobel Prize win, was no coincidence. She claimed the move was retaliation for the prestigious award not going to the American president.
Asked what message she would like to convey to Trump, Pillay replied: "Call in your legal advisors to explain to you what international law is and why you must not interfere in the affairs of an independent international court." She said the sanctions against the court were illegal and intended to undermine its independence and ability to carry out its duties.
Last Friday, just hours after Pillay was announced as the Nobel Peace Prize winner, the United States announced unprecedented sanctions against the ICC. Unlike previous sanctions targeting the court's judges and prosecutors, the latest measures are directed at the institution as a whole, with the aim of disrupting its day-to-day operations.
The sanctions are expected to disrupt the court's technological infrastructure, banking services and ability to conduct international transactions. The U.S. administration has granted a six-month transition period to give companies providing services to the court time to prepare to end their dealings with it.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio also made clear that the administration intends to dismantle the court "brick by brick," citing its opposition to the ICC's authority to prosecute citizens and leaders of countries that are not parties to the court.
The U.S. administration is particularly angered by the court's decision to issue an arrest warrant for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity during the war in the Gaza Strip. Both Israel and the United States reject the ICC's jurisdiction over Israel, which is not a member of the court.
Pillay accused Washington of hypocrisy, pointing to the differing responses of U.S. administrations to the court's decisions. She noted that previous administrations had welcomed the arrest warrant issued against Russian President Vladimir Putin over suspected war crimes in Ukraine, yet when the court takes action against an Israeli leader, the United States seeks to paralyze its operations.
"This is selective, it is a double standard and it is unacceptable," she said.
'I was offended by the comparison to Goebbels'
Pillay also addressed the harsh reactions in Israel to her Nobel Prize win. The South African jurist previously chaired the The Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including East Jerusalem, and Israel, which concluded last year that Israel was committing genocide in the Gaza Strip. Israel strongly rejected the commission's findings, describing the investigation as biased and politically motivated.
Following the announcement of her win, Netanyahu attacked Pillay, calling her "prejudiced." The Foreign Ministry also issued an unusually harsh condemnation, arguing that her selection legitimized hatred and prejudice against Israel.
The ministry said that if there were a prize for "lies, hatred, and blood libels," Pillay would be among the leading contenders. It added that her role in the "politically motivated demonization of Israel and promotion of the genoLIE" reflected her views.
The statement ended with an extraordinary remark: "Now that the Nobel commission has rewarded the biggest lie of the 21st century, Joseph Goebbels is certainly applauding from hell."
"I find these remarks deeply hurtful and offensive," Pillay told AFP.
Addressing the comparison to Goebbels, the Nazi propaganda minister, she said: "Goebbels had blood on his hands. He was responsible for the deaths of thousands of people. Not just Jews, but also people whose skin color is like mine."
Despite her criticism of Netanyahu, Pillay acknowledged that the current political climate offers little willingness to pursue his arrest so that he can stand trial before the ICC. Nevertheless, she expressed confidence that it would eventually happen.
"Throughout my life, I have seen people overcome obstacles, and that is why I am convinced it will eventually happen," she said.
Pillay, who was born in South Africa during the apartheid era, previously served as the U.N. high commissioner for human rights and a judge at the International Criminal Court., said she was still struggling to come to terms with winning the prestigious award.
She said she initially found the news difficult to believe, partly because relatively few women have received the prize over the years.
"They award their prizes to very few women — a glaring inequality that has persisted until now," she said.
At 85, Pillay is also aware that her ability to continue traveling around the world and advocating for international law is more limited than in the past. "I think my age will slow me down a little. I can no longer be as active as I used to be," she acknowledged. She recalled visiting 79 countries during her tenure as U.N. high commissioner for human rights.
Nevertheless, she has already begun considering how to use the prize money, totaling 12 million Swedish kronor, equivalent to approximately 1.1 million euros.
Pillay said she was consulting various people about how best to use the money to advance social causes and suggested that some of it could be invested in her native South Africa. "Africa is suffering. South Africa is suffering. It is very difficult to raise funds there," she said.
Pillay noted that the University of KwaZulu-Natal has established a unit named after her and said she intends to begin discussions with university officials about the possibility of supporting its work. "I believe in educating children and young people," she concluded.
Pillay was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in recognition of her decades of work promoting human rights and international law. In explaining its decision, the Norwegian Nobel Committee highlighted her contributions to the fight against war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide, as well as her role in strengthening the international justice system at a time when it faces growing political pressure.

Michael Kotlikoff, the president of Cornell University, has spoken to the New York Times about sexual assault allegations at the school, acknowledging for the first time that he knew a student had reported being sexually assaulted in November 2024, but did not follow up with the Jane Doe involved in the months after learning about the alleged assault.
He also revealed that he did not know she had dropped out of Cornell until she filed a lawsuit last month.
Kotlikoff addressed his administration’s handling of the 2024 allegations as the university faces mounting scrutiny and calls for his resignation.
“The fact that Jane Doe experienced what she experienced at Cornell is something that I am personally sorry for,” Kotlikoff said in the interview, his first since the woman filed her civil lawsuit last month. “And I think this entire campus is sorry that occurred.
“I’ve heard enough from the community that there is a loss of trust,” he added. “People are angry. I understand that anger.”
Last month, a former student, identified in court documents by the pseudonym “Jane Doe”, filed a civil lawsuit against multiple parties, including the university, accusing seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity of sexually assaulting her at a party at their fraternity house on campus in October 2024. All of the men named in the lawsuit have denied wrongdoing, and none have been criminally charged.
The woman reported the incident to the Cornell University police department in November 2024. According to records obtained by the New York Times, after an internal investigation at Cornell, two of the men were expelled, two were suspended, and another, who had already graduated, was barred from campus. The remaining men received lighter punishments, which included an order to not contact Jane Doe, and to write “reflection papers”.
At the time, the Tompkins county district attorney declined to bring charges against the men, saying that there was not sufficient evidence.
The district attorney has since said that he would reopen his office’s investigation, and Kathy Hochul, the New York governor, said she was appointing Letitia James, the state’s attorney general, as special prosecutor to investigate the claims.
Kotlikoff called the allegations “deeply disturbing” in a statement earlier this month, and said he welcomed Hochul’s decision to appoint James to the case.
During the 90-minute interview, he was asked to respond to the criticisms that his administration had failed to respond to the former student’s allegations until she filed a lawsuit.
Kotlikoff pointed to a presidential taskforce that was established to examine sexual assault on campus.
He added, “I do think it’s important to understand we have more information now than we had at that time. We’ve learned some more information that has come out around how this process unfolded.”
Cornell’s faculty senate is expected to hold a rare vote of no confidence in the president later this month, according to reports.
In the interview, Kotlikoff also said that he had not been aware that the former student had left the school.
“I do think there’s an argument for what you said, which is that if in fact a student has withdrawn because she feels unsafe at the outcome of the” university’s administrative review process “or there’s specific concerns around individuals – you know that there were no-contact orders for those individuals – I think that’s something that leadership should be made aware of. I would agree with that.”
On Tuesday, after the interview, Kotlikoff announced that Cornell would suspend parties at fraternity houses for the remainder of the academic year. The university also said it planned to add experienced sexual assault investigators to work with its police force in response.
A newly formed special committee of the Cornell University Board of Trustees also announced that it had retained Sally Yates, who was a deputy attorney general in the Obama administration, to “lead a comprehensive independent review of how the university prevents and responds to sexual harassment, sexual assault and related misconduct on campus”.

Stunning video captures a whole year of our sun’s chaotic corona
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:29:19 UTC
01:29:19 KST

We’re usually not supposed to look directly at the sun except during the glorious totality of a solar eclipse. But NASA’s PUNCH mission has been staring unblinkingly at our star since June 2025. PUNCH, short for Polarimeter to Unify the Corona and Heliosphere, avoids frying its optics via a sunlight-blocking coronagraph that creates a permanent personal eclipse for its Narrow Field Imager. Now, in a video revealing PUNCH’s newly processed data, you can see a year of the sun’s dancing corona, too—without risking your retinas.
The solar corona is the topmost layer of the sun’s atmosphere. Curiously, it’s much hotter than the layers beneath it by millions of degrees Fahrenheit. And it’s suffused with protons and electrons streaming away from the sun; these atomic building blocks can’t coalesce into atoms because of all that heat, but that leaves them free to become almost perfect electrical conductors, according to PUNCH principal investigator Craig DeForest.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Electricity and magnetism are linked, so that near-perfect electrical conductivity means the outflowing protons and electrons spiral along the sun’s magnetic field lines as they traverse the corona. Sunlight shimmering off the electrons makes magnetic field lines visible in the video as bright golden rays interspersed with explosive coronal mass ejections (huge bursts of magnetized plasma erupting from the sun). The overall visual effect is like a cosmic variant of the wacky inflatable tube people outside used car dealerships.
The sunlit electrons tell us about “the amount of particles in the corona and the shape of the magnetic field,” says Alfred de Wijn, a research engineer who studies the sun at the National Science Foundation’s High Altitude Observatory and is unaffiliated with the PUNCH mission. “We can see that the corona is constantly changing as a result of the solar wind—a stream of charged particles—and coronal mass ejections.”
Behind the sun’s glowing corona, background stars slide from left to right, including several familiar constellations: Leo passes behind the sun in August (around three to four minutes into the video) and part of Sagittarius is visible in November (around 6:20 to 7:20). Venus and Mercury also make several appearances as large, bright white dots crossing from either side.
Several comets also pass through PUNCH’s field of view. The comet C/2025 R3 (PanSTARRS), a far-flung traveler from the outskirts of the solar system, passed very close to the sun on April 19, 2026, and makes a spectacular appearance in the video at 11:09.
PUNCH is composed of four separate spacecraft precisely aligned and calibrated as they orbit Earth over the poles, staying in constant view of the sun. The video is “a triumph,” DeForest says, because it shows how the mission’s instrument responsible for imaging the corona, the Narrow Field Imager, overcame an unexpected problem. When PUNCH initially opened its eyes, Earthshine (sunlight reflecting off Earth) bounced into its sensors and overwhelmed the delicate signal from the corona. At first, “you couldn’t see a darn thing,” DeForest says, but thanks to some clever image processing that treated each image as a four-million-dimensional vector, the research team was able to remove the bright, flickering Earthshine and recover the entire year’s worth of coronal data, creating the new video.
“This is not some distant, abstract system we’re looking at,” DeForest adds, pointing out that PUNCH’s spacecraft pass over us every sunset no matter where we are on the globe. “We live on the Earth, but our neighborhood is the inner solar system. Being able to see this invisible part of our environment is profound.”

It’s leaf-peeping season. Has this year’s extreme weather hurt fall foliage?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:29:12 UTC
01:29:12 KST

Leaf-peeping season is swinging into high gear. Yet after months of record-shattering extreme heat, wildfires and perhaps the strongest El Niño in living memory, will fall foliage also fall victim to the weather?
The good news, experts say, is leaves always change color in some way because of seasonal shifts in sunlight. But extreme weather conditions, such as droughts, heavy rainfall or heat, can affect the timeline of the color change—and scientists are still trying to understand exactly how and why.
“Day length is the primary driver of leaf change; that doesn’t change year to year,” says Andy Finton, a conservation ecologist at the Nature Conservancy in Massachusetts. “There’s always going to be fall color. It’s just going to vary depending on climate trends and weather conditions.”
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
When summer turns to fall, trees get less sunlight, and they slowly stop photosynthesizing to conserve water and nutrients for the winter. At the same time, many trees suck up chlorophyll from their leaves, revealing yellow shades. (Chlorophyll creates the green pigment in leaves and holds lots of valuable nutrients.) Some trees, such as maples, also produce new, red pigments called anthocyanins in the fall that protect them as they’re absorbing nutrients.
This whole process is designed to conserve as much chlorophyll as possible, says Christy Rollinson, a forest ecologist at the Morton Arboretum in Illinois. “Green is really expensive—not just in my wallet but in the tree’s wallet as well,” she says. “All of these different colors are related to the tree trying to protect the green.”
As the climate warms, it can cause trees to extend their growing season, and warm evenings don’t trap fall colors in the leaves as well as colder ones, meaning later and less vibrant changes to foliage. Extreme weather events, such as drought or heavy rainfall, also stress trees and can trigger them to rapidly protect themselves by more rapidly pulling in the chlorophyll from their leaves, dulling fall colors.
Just as leaves that fall from different trees have distinct shapes and hues of crimson or gold, tree species vary in how susceptible they are to weather. Sugar maples, a “superstar” of New England leaf peeping, are extremely sensitive to temperature and precipitation, Finton says. Oak trees, on the other hand, are more tolerant. But there’s a lot that scientists still don’t understand about how different trees are affected.
A question Rollinson is curious about is how much of the changing of trees’ leaves is related to temperature versus sunlight—and what fall foliage might reveal about the overall health of a given tree and its ecosystem.
The effect of wildfires on foliage are also little understood, says William Keeton, a forest ecologist at the University of Vermont. Early research suggests that smoke from these disasters can blow onto trees across the country and coat leaves, blocking sunlight and interfering with photosynthesis.
This year the Midwest has seen a vast variety of weather conditions, from extreme heat to massive tornadoes to heavy rainfall, so it’s difficult to know how the trees there will react, Rollinson says.
“Normally I’m able to make some general statements about the health of trees going into the fall, but I think there’s a huge variation because each tree will respond to those stressors a little bit differently,” she says.
In New England, meanwhile, the summer saw extreme heat and some drought. But because, so far, this fall has been “cooler, crisper and clearer,” Finton says, the leaves are coming in right on time, and he expects a relatively typical foliage season.
Most of the northern U.S. is seeing peak foliage colors this week. The mid-Atlantic and Midwest regions can expect the best leaf peeping in the second half of October.

UN migration agency says over 4,400 child migrants died worldwide since 2014
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:29:00 UTC
01:29:00 KST

Beyza Binnur Dönmez
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
At least 4,414 children died during migration journeys worldwide between 2014 and 2025, but the actual toll is "likely much higher," the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said Wednesday.
The UN agency said in a new report that its Missing Migrants Project recorded nearly 81,000 migrant deaths and disappearances during the period, with 44,862 cases, or 55.5%, lacking information on age.
That suggests an unknown number of child deaths remain unidentified in official statistics.
On the Central Mediterranean route, the agency said children represented 19% of arrivals in Italy and Malta in 2024 but only 2% of recorded deaths, highlighting significant data gaps.
"Every child who dies on a migration journey deserves to be counted, yet too many are missing from the data," said Stuart Campo, IOM's chief strategy officer for data, insight and policy. "We cannot protect children from dangers we cannot see."
The report found that records from medical examiners and law enforcement accounted for just 18% of documented migrant deaths.
IOM urged governments to improve documentation of migrant deaths, systematically record victims' ages and strengthen information sharing among authorities and humanitarian organizations while protecting personal data.

Around half of customers of electronics retailer Comfy have begun visiting physical stores less frequently and prefer quick in-store collection after checking products online, changing their offline shopping habits despite prolonged adaptation to wartime conditions amid continuing attacks, the company’s press service has said.
“Some 51% of customers visit shopping malls and physical stores less frequently: 27% avoid shopping malls, another 21% visit only when necessary, and 3% have stopped going to physical stores altogether,” Comfy said, citing its survey.
Half of respondents in this group opt to collect their orders from stores, one-third use delivery by postal operators, and 15% order courier delivery.

Demand for physical stores is particularly evident in frontline regions. According to the survey, 60% of respondents in frontline cities would like to retain access to physical stores alongside online shopping, even if the stores operate in a limited capacity, the retailer said.
The survey found that 27% of respondents are moving all their shopping online, relying on reviews and product assessments, while only 16% still prefer the traditional in-store experience of seeing and examining a product and consulting a salesperson.
As of September 2026, Comfy operated 115 stores in 56 Ukrainian cities, including eight in Dnipro. The company reported revenue of UAH 55.8 billion in 2025, up 17% from 2024.
According to YouControl, Comfy Trade LLC is wholly owned by Cyprus-based Comfy Holdings Limited. Its ultimate beneficial owners are Stanislav Ronis and Svitlana Hutsul.

Ahmed Touizi elected Morocco's new parliament speaker
Unknown

2026-10-14

Breadcrumb
Ahmed Touizi elected Morocco's new parliament speaker
Morocco on Tuesday appointed a new parliament speaker following last September’s parliamentary elections.
Ahmed Touizi, from the Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM), which won the largest number of seats in the elections, was elected by a majority of MPs and replaces former speaker Rachid Talbi Alami.
He secured 220 votes in the 395-seat House of Representatives.
He defeated opposition Justice and Development Party (PJD) candidate Driss Azami Al Idrissi, who received 59 votes. A total of 369 ballots were cast, including 60 invalid votes.
Touizi was the candidate of Morocco's newly formed governing coalition, led by Prime Minister Fatima Zahra Mansouri.
Under Article 52 of the House of Representatives' internal regulations, the speaker is elected by secret ballot and must secure an absolute majority of the chamber's members in the first round.
The opposition PJD, which has an Islamist orientation, nominated its parliamentary group leader, Driss Azami Al Idrissi, in what it described as a symbolic challenge intended to introduce competition into the speaker's election.
The party acknowledged that its candidate had little prospect of winning, given the parliamentary majority backing Touizi.
PAM formally selected Touizi as its candidate on Tuesday morning following a meeting of its expanded political bureau committee and parliamentary representatives.
He was chosen from a shortlist that included former Justice Minister Abdellatif Ouahbi and Higher Education Minister Azzedine El Midaoui.
Meanwhile, the National Rally of Independents (RNI), which finished second in September's election, abstained from voting after being excluded from the new governing coalition announced by Mansouri on Monday.
The ruling coalition brings together PAM, the Istiqlal Party, the Socialist Union of Popular Forces (USFP) and the Party of Progress and Socialism (PPS).
The RNI, which led the previous government under former Prime Minister Aziz Akhannouch, has moved into opposition.
While Morocco’s 23 September elections significantly reshaped the distribution of parliamentary seats and its political landscape, they were marked by apathy, particularly from younger voters disillusioned with the political system.
Voter turnout was only 38.2%. While Morocco is officially a constitutional monarchy, the king still wields significantly more power than elected representatives and the country is often described as an autocracy with a façade of democratic politics.

Why are portions of prepared meals getting smaller in Russia? Rising costs may be only part of the answer.
Portion sizes for prepared food in Russia fell by 10.3% over the past year to 266 grams (about 9.4 ounces), according to calculations by the analytics company Ntec, as cited by Kommersant.
Prepared food remains the fastest-growing category in grocery retail. Retail stores account for about a quarter of the prepared food market, and that share could reach 40% by 2030, according to Stanislav Bogdanov, chairman of the Association of Retail Companies.
Profit margins in the category are very low, however. Retailers have to invest in central kitchens, packaging, and logistics, while 14% of products are written off because of their short shelf life.
Production costs are rising, but producers are finding it harder to pass them on to consumers. Intense competition and weakening demand are forcing them to hold down prices. As a result, producers are choosing to reduce portion sizes, experts said.
Smaller portions may reflect both shrinkflation and changing demand, the experts said. Russians buying prepared food have increasingly been choosing small snacks such as onigiri, sandwiches, and hot dogs. In the first half of 2026, sales of these snacks rose by 48% in value, while sales of main dishes and salads grew more slowly — by 16% and 14%, respectively.

Mexico's president signs decree to protect minors from harmful online content
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

01:21:18 KST

Mariam Ashalem De Andres
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum signed a decree Wednesday to regulate digital platforms and protect children and adolescents from harmful online content, warning that platforms could face legal sanctions if they fail to make progress.
“If no progress is made, it would become a law,” Sheinbaum said at a news conference, adding that legislation would include penalties for the platforms.
She said digital platforms agreed to the measures and requested one month to prepare their systems for implementation.
Presidential legal adviser Maria Luisa Alcalde Lujan said she met representatives of Meta, TikTok, Google, Microsoft and other digital platforms to discuss the decree, and highlighted their willingness to adhere to the measure.
The decree bans platforms from exposing minors to content promoting sexual violence, suicide, self-harm, eating disorders, bullying and other harmful material.
They will be required to immediately identify and remove accounts and content that promote or generate violent behavior, classify content according to age groups and verify the ages of users.
Platforms must alert authorities to content that threatens life, while a 24-hour contact point will support investigations.
The Ministry of Public Education and the Ministry of Health will make the Linea de la Vida, or Lifeline, hotline available to provide psychological support. Authorities will also provide a guide on emotional awareness.
The announcement follows a meeting between government officials and representatives of major technology companies, although additional details on the decree's enforcement mechanisms were not provided.

The veteran British broadcaster Sir Trevor Phillips had some strong words of advice for his CBS News colleagues when facing off against critics who question the editorial integrity of the network: “Why don’t you just fuck off and let us do our jobs?”
Phillips made his blunt suggestion during a contentious meeting of the network’s London bureau on Tuesday, during which the foreign editor, Shayndi Raice, went on a lengthy tirade criticizing unnamed staffers for suggesting that editorial oversight amounted to “interference” and informing colleagues that disobeying editors would be insubordination and “legal grounds for firing”.
Phillips’s decision to join CBS was announced in June. It came after its billionaire owner, David Ellison, installed the opinion journalist and broadcast newcomer Bari Weiss as editor-in-chief in a move that shook staff.
The Guardian, which first reported the Tuesday meeting, reviewed an audio recording of the contentious session that rattled staffers. A CBS News spokesperson and Phillips declined to comment on the meeting.
Phillips spoke up initially to defend Raice, saying that the message she was delivering was common sense. “I’m genuinely surprised that you had to say anything that you just said in the last 15 minutes,” he said during the meeting. “It just seems to be axiomatic in any organization … I did want to say that I’m kind of surprised that in an organization of this vintage and capability, with the clever people I’ve met around here, that any of this actually has to be said.”
He then turned to outside opinion about CBS, telling colleagues that he faced criticism after it was announced he was leaving his perch at Sky News to serve as the network’s senior global affairs correspondent. Phillips is also a contributor to CBS’s flagship news show 60 Minutes, and voiced a short piece on Sunday on protests in Europe. Since CBS parent Paramount Global was acquired by Ellison’s Skydance Media in the summer of 2025, the company’s leadership has faced accusations of tilting the editorial scales in a more conservative-friendly direction.
“I could spend the next hour telling you the number of people when it was announced that I was coming here, the number of people who told me for all of the reasons you just explained, why this is the end of my career and how I was going to destroy everything that I’ve ever created, and all of that bollocks,” Phillips said.
He continued: “I think we’re in a new game now, actually, where we are now players as journalists. And what people are constantly trying to do is to knock us off – to frighten us, essentially, into doing this or doing that. It puts a premium on two things – one is our objectivity, and two: having each other’s backs. I think the worst thing that can happen now is if we start to go about telling people, ‘Well, I would have done this if the higher-ups hadn’t told me to do that.’ That’s exactly what everybody wants us to get into the game of. That’s how we become vulnerable. That’s how we start adjusting our copy according to somebody else’s lines outside of here … I think what you said is really, really important, but it points me in the direction of us having the mentality – forgive my French here – of telling everybody, ‘Why don’t you just fuck off and let us do our jobs?’”

Draft EU summit conclusions reveal what leaders will and will not say on Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:20:40 UTC
01:20:40 KST

Draft EU summit conclusions reveal what leaders will and will not say on Ukraine
A red carpet and European Union (EU) flags in the Europa building ahead of a European Council meeting in Brussels, Belgium, on Thursday, Oct. 23, 2025. (Simon Wohlfahrt/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Editor's Note: Following publication, the Kyiv Independent received the revised draft conclusions, which set out a less ambitious position on Ukraine's bid for EU membership. Read the story here.
BRUSSELS, Belgium — Leaders of the EU's 27 member states have a Ukraine-packed agenda when they meet in Brussels Oct. 15-16, according to the latest draft conclusions of the upcoming meeting seen by the Kyiv Independent.
The 25-page document contains six-and-a-half pages of comments specifically on Ukraine, three-and-a-half pages on defense and security, where Ukraine features prominently, and a page on the future of enlargement.
Those hoping for a long list of decisions from the European Council will be left disappointed, as the document mostly consists of leaders noting developments since they last met in June and issuing calls for what should happen next.
But some of those calls can lead to concrete outcomes further down the line.
For example, the draft conclusions say that the European Council "calls for the swift and effective implementation of the measures concerning Russian ex-combatants, and for further (sanctions) measures."
A visa ban for Russian soldiers was pushed for in the bloc's previous sanctions package, but ultimately fell through after France and Italy railed against it.
Since Russia's drone attack on Leipzig, Germany, the conversation has shifted, and EU diplomats from three countries said France had begun to budge when foreign ministers met in Luxembourg on Oct. 12.
Finland also upped the pressure by issuing a letter arguing against issuing visas to Russians and outlining five key demands.
The draft conclusions signal that concrete action is due to land soon.
In a similar vein, the Council conclusions state that it "underlines the EU's readiness to step up its engagement" on "diplomatic efforts to bring Russia's war of aggression to an end."
The week before, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen's right-hand man discussed peace with the U.S., NATO, and Ukraine.
But those talks were overshadowed by U.S. President Donald Trump's announcement of a likely-illegal diesel deal with Russia — a development that the conclusions note with "regret."
Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha told journalists on Oct. 12 that the U.S.' approach shows that "Europe should take its future in its own hands, speak with one voice, and restore peace," and the conclusions' readiness to do so suggests that the EU agrees.
Shouting into the wind
On other topics, the draft conclusions expose the EU's seeming inability to tackle Ukraine's most pressing issues.
With Kyiv being pummeled by ever more jet-powered drones and ballistic missiles, the call for "further intensified efforts and coordination to strengthen Ukraine's air and missile defense capabilities, the resilience of its critical infrastructure, and its energy system," rings especially hollow.
Similarly, the call for "immediate restoration of safe passage for grain cargo ships in the Black Sea," after weeks of Russian blockade, and the sinking of ships — which has also led to the loss of life — reads as weak in the absence of any accompanying measures.
However, the European Council "stresses the need to prevent grain stolen by Russia from temporarily occupied Ukrainian territories from being exported via the EU," read the conclusions, which suggests support may be gathering for a Russian grain transit ban, as proposed by Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania the week before.
Likewise, support may be brewing for future EU action to prevent Russia's re-entry into international sports and cultural events, which the conclusions say should not be allowed to happen, three days after EU Sports Commissioner Glenn Micallef met with EU foreign ministers for the first time to discuss the issue.
The result of Micallef's meeting was the EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, announcing that her team "will put forward proposals on how to sustain Russia's isolation in global sports."
And in the meantime, some countries take unilateral action, such as the Netherlands, which has denied visas to Russians due to compete at an international gymnastics event in Rotterdam, even as the world body for gymnastics has again allowed Russian and Belarusian athletes to compete under their own flag.
Other mentions in the conclusions can be seen as messages to other allies of Ukraine, in Europe and beyond.
That the EU "strongly condemns the deployment of North Korean military forces in the war against Ukraine" is a useful reminder to South Korea of what is at stake for them, just as relations between Kyiv and Seoul reach a new low.
And the renewed call for "international partners to swiftly step up their support to help meet Ukraine's pressing financing and military needs," likewise points to the fact that since the EU adopted its 90 billion euro loan ($100 billion) for Ukraine in April, third countries appear to have slowed down on their own contributions to Kyiv.
read also
Conspicuously absent: Russia's immobilized assets
One word missing from the draft conclusions: "assets." This is despite a renewed push from various directions to revive discussions about how to use 200 billion euros ($224 billion) of immobilized Russian wealth to directly support Ukraine.
Four EU countries reopened the topic with an open letter in August, and it came up prominently during the Oct. 12 meeting of foreign ministers.
Sybiha spoke about the idea to journalists, published an opinion piece the same day with news website Politico, and had strong support from his Swedish colleague Maria Stenergard, who even brought along visual aids for the discussion.
But the lack of a mention is because the EU is still by no means united on what approach to take.
Belgian newspaper De Morgen reported on Oct. 13 that President Volodymyr Zelensky wants to meet with Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever bilaterally around the EU leaders' summit, which he will also attend on Oct. 16.
De Wever led resistance to the use of Russian assets in December 2025, the last time it was seriously discussed, and as the vast majority of immobilized Russian government assets are in Belgium, a solution that does not work for De Wever will go nowhere.
read also
In response to a question from the Kyiv Independent about the Russian assets, Kallas said "I think this discussion will continue because eventually it is about sharing the risks between member states."
"It is important that it is not off the table. We are thinking about different tools to fill that financing gap," Kallas said.
Alternative options do exist: Russian assets could be invested more profitably to create new funds for Ukraine, as suggested by a plan called the Windfall Optimization Loan Framework, or the EU could simply agree to create new loans.
What is clear is that the topic is not set to disappear just yet, with one senior EU official telling the Kyiv Independent they expect it to dominate EU leaders' December meeting.
read also
Don't forget the future
The October meeting of EU leaders was supposed to have the future of EU enlargement as a main topic, to which end the European Commission issued proposals for consideration on Oct. 6.
Instead, with a new multi-year budget to discuss, energy prices, migration issues, the Middle East, and all the other Ukraine topics on the agenda, enlargement risks being overshadowed, and it only accounts for one page in the 25-page Council conclusions draft.
Even so, that one page contains a potentially big shift, if the conclusions are adopted as written.
"The European Council ... looks forward to the opening of all the other clusters as soon as possible, in line with the merit-based approach," read the draft conclusions.
What looks like an innocuous enough sentence takes on new meaning when one has in mind the last leaders' meeting in July, in which Hungary lobbied hard to remove the words "as soon as possible" because it wanted Ukraine to pass a law bolstering the rights of its Hungarian-speaking minority first.
Ukraine passed that law on Oct. 12, unlocked two further enlargement clusters on Oct. 13, and may have no further obstacles to overcome.
France and Poland were expected in some quarters to make it difficult to unlock the remaining cluster covering agriculture due to fears of Ukrainian competition, but they publicly ruled this out on Oct. 13.
A high-ranking EU official and a European minister told the Kyiv Independent that they expect the last two clusters to open in December 2026, as several EU countries must follow their own political procedures at home to give a formal green light.
For example, Slovenia needs to vote on the decision through its parliament, even if the vote itself is not expected to cause any problems, and has never done so for Ukraine so far.
But that does not mean Ukraine has nothing still to do.
Both for the EU's financial support to be greenlighted, and for Ukraine to join the bloc one day, the Council conclusions "recall the importance of Ukraine continuing its reform efforts and upholding the rule of law."

New York Seeks to Ban Horse-Drawn Carriages
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
19:20:15 EEST
01:20:15 KST

New York Seeks to Ban Horse-Drawn Carriages
Kyiv • UNN
Mayor Zohran Mamdani supported banning horse-drawn carriages in New York starting in June 2028. The Council may vote on the bill on October 22.
Mayor Zoran Mamdani and the speaker of the New York City Council have agreed to ban horse-drawn carriage rides in the city, a popular tourist attraction that has drawn widespread criticism, UNN reports, citing The Guardian.
Details
Mamdani agreed to support a bill backed by Julie Menin, the speaker of the New York City Council, that bans the operation of horse-drawn carriages starting in June 2028, Politico reported on Tuesday. The City Council is expected to vote on the legislation next week.
"The horse-carriage industry is coming to an end in New York City. Our administration will ensure that workers and owners are protected, and that the horses are safe," Mamdani wrote on X on Tuesday.
A person familiar with City Hall confirmed that an agreement had been reached.
Although carriage rides are ubiquitous in Central Park, animal advocates have long raised concerns about the treatment of the horses. Since 2020, several horses have died, at times collapsing during carriage rides.
The push for a ban intensified over the summer after 18-year-old tourist Romanch Mahajan died after being thrown from a carriage.
In a statement, Menin said that horse-drawn carriages had "become a growing public-safety concern."
"We can honor our city's traditions while recognizing that it is time to move forward in the interests of public safety, protecting workers and strengthening the economic vitality of our city," Menin said.
A spokesperson for Menin said that the City Council speaker would bring the bill to a vote on October 22.
In addition
Despite broad support for a ban on horse-drawn carriages, officials have struggled to advance the legislation because the Transport Workers Union of Greater New York, which represents carriage drivers, has raised concerns about the drivers' livelihoods.
Mamdani had previously indicated that he would support a bill banning horse-drawn carriages; however, he expressed concerns about the bill as drafted because it contained insufficient protections for carriage workers.
A copy of the bill sent to The Guardian contains language requiring the city to create a workforce-transition program providing carriage drivers with counseling and referrals to other jobs in the private and public sectors.
The bill also requires the city to "consider" creating a compensation program for carriage owners based on the value of their businesses.
John Samuelsen, the international president of the Transport Workers Union, told Politico that the bill does not provide "significant economic relief for workers."
"This is shameful political opportunism, and Zoran should not simply go along with it, especially when the livelihoods of immigrant families are being destroyed," Samuelsen said. "This entire situation is reprehensible."
It is unclear whether Mamdani plans to sign the bill in its current form or whether additional changes will be made.
Sneha Chowdhury, a spokesperson for City Hall, said in a statement: "We are working closely with the City Council, union partners, carriage drivers, animal-protection advocates and community leaders to ensure a just transition that protects workers while ending the use of horse-drawn carriages in Central Park once and for all."
The bill also requires the city to introduce a program to help drivers humanely relinquish their horses—prohibiting them from selling the horses, transporting them for slaughter or selling them for use in horse-drawn carriage operations elsewhere.

To unlock Britain’s innovation potential, Labour needs to think outside the box | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:19:16 UTC
01:19:16 KST

Gordon Brown wants Britain to invent, invest in and own the future (British households would be £5,000 richer if we were more innovative. Let’s unleash our talents, 9 October). But invent what, and for whom? His hunt for “lost Einsteins” rests on a narrow vision: a lone genius invents, commercialisation scales, the problem is solved.
That may suit a cancer drug, but not the wicked problems of our time – social care, education, climate – which demand not silver bullets but new technologies and practices for collaboration, distributed ownership and collective innovation.
The current struggle to retrofit governance, accountability and benefit on to AI exposes the fiction of genius-engineered “solutions”. Nor do trillion-dollar companies make every household £5,000 richer. They concentrate short-term gain in a narrow founder-investor class; the rest of us carry the work and cost of long-term cleanup.
It’s a vicious cycle: the government worries about big tech yet incentivises more of it, competing with Silicon Valley by doing the same – just not quite as well. My organisation is a community interest company with an asset lock, built for competitive innovation in the public interest.
Labour created this structure in 2005 to enable a new generation of public-good companies, but innovation policy has yet to back it. UK Research and Innovation is closed to us: we aren’t a research organisation. Innovate UK now deems our community interest company ineligible for a knowledge transfer partnership, despite previous success with the University of Edinburgh. The Advanced Research and Invention Agency backs lone inventors. The Seed Enterprise Investment Scheme and the Enterprise Investment Scheme reward only uncapped shareholder returns.
Much is made of Palantir and the NHS, yet current policy doesn’t let a competitive British alternative emerge: one that tackles systemic data problems while letting trusts and communities retain ownership and agency. With funding, that is five years away, not a fantasy. If the government wants innovation that tackles the hardest problems, benefits all citizens, and competes globally, it must look beyond the models it rewards today.
Kate Fleming
Director, IDEMS
Gordon Brown’s analysis of Britain’s innovation ecosystem is largely correct. We do have world-class universities, rigorous research and a track record of discovery, and he’s right to highlight the gap between these strengths and their commercial returns. It’s no doubt a defining challenge of our time.
But there’s one word conspicuously absent from his argument: creativity. In making the case for innovation, Brown has fallen for a common trap, defaulting to a vision of research and development (R&D) that begins and ends with Stem (science, technology, engineering and mathematics). This vision leaves no place for the creative advantage that in many cases makes true innovation possible.
The UK’s creative industries contribute £145bn to the economy annually, growing at four times the national rate. Research by the Creative Industries Policy and Evidence Centre shows that nearly two-thirds of creative micro-firms have engaged in R&D in the past three years, outstripping every other industrial strategy priority sector. Brown might be surprised to learn that the UK university producing the most student startups is actually University of the Arts London (UAL).
UAL startups are using lateral thinking to develop biodegradable alternatives to plastic, building tools that decarbonise supply chains, pioneering food waste fermentation technology, and creating new materials from agricultural byproducts that could transform the construction industry.
They are engaging in real-world R&D to solve major global problems that transcend the creative sector, yet as creative businesses with arts graduates at the helm, they are consistently excluded from the narrative and the wider policy framing.
If we are serious about innovation driving good growth, we cannot afford a definition that excludes one of our most dynamic, inventive and internationally competitive sectors. Unlocking Britain’s full innovation potential means recognising that creativity and science are partners, not opposites.
Jenny Haigh
Head of policy for creative economy, University of the Arts London

An uplifting article by Phineas Harper about plans for self-build houses by Lewisham council in London (Free land for those who will build social homes on it. Is this the radical solution to the UK’s housing problem?, 8 October).
The original 1970s Lewisham self-build scheme that he mentions, using methods developed by the German architect Walter Segal, was proposed by a friend of mine, Brian Richardson, who was a Lewisham council architect at the time.
Brian persuaded the local authority to offer people on the council house waiting list the materials to build their own homes, with advice from him. They had no building skills, but they worked evenings and weekends, and built homes and a community.
Brian often said that the most successful outcome was the changes to the builders themselves in terms of pride and self-confidence.
Just search for “Walter’s Way Lewisham” online for contemporary and more recent videos and the views of the builders themselves.
John Banks
Ledbury, Herefordshire
Phineas Harper is right to highlight Lewisham council’s proposals to make publicly owned land available for community-led social housing. From a valuation perspective, the most interesting aspect to me is viability. Land value is often a significant barrier to delivering social housing, particularly on smaller sites that can involve almost as much time, effort and cost as larger schemes, and are therefore difficult for developers and housing associations to justify taking on.
This will not replace established affordable housing delivery, and there will still be challenges around building costs, funding, planning and delivery. But it could provide a practical way to unlock smaller, community-led schemes.
Sometimes improving viability is not about increasing development value, but reducing the cost of the land itself. I will be interested to see whether other local authorities follow suit.
Jonathan Pearson
RICS registered valuer, Residentially Chartered Surveyors

The problem with living in a rich man’s world | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:19:01 UTC
01:19:01 KST

The idea that the departure of the super-rich is a problem ignores a historical fact (Apparent exodus of super-rich suggests UK is no longer billionaires’ playground, 7 October). Capitalism works better without them. The most successful countries today are states where redistributive taxation has empowered the working masses and provided a better and more stable market for business people.
How do today’s complaining uber-rich explain the postwar decades, when the top rate of income tax was commonly 80% or 90%, and yet the period is known as a golden age of capitalism? Then Margaret Thatcher lowered the top rate to 60% and the country tilted into a massive recession. The rich get to a point where they simply become wealth extractors, using their money to buy assets and raising the cost of them for the rest of us – housing being a good example today.
A good story from 1969 comes from a music writer who was embedded in the Rolling Stones’ tour of America. Earwigging the band talking about becoming tax exiles, if not on main street, then maybe in France, he hears Charlie Watts (a non-songwriter, so less affluent) say that he rather likes his land and his house and his horses, and he wouldn’t want to leave. Isn’t that rich enough for most of us? It’s appropriate that John Maynard Keynes is now on stage in the West End. People might remember what he said about the dangers of wealth disparity and the bubbles of speculation that they bring.
David Redshaw
Saltdean, East Sussex
Your report (‘I reside in Monaco’: billionaire said to have quit UK over potential wealth tax had already left, 7 October) exposes something far more troubling than billionaires fleeing Britain: the extraordinary power of the super-rich to hold an entire country hostage to the threat of their departure.
Ordinary working people cannot relocate their tax obligations to Monaco. They pay their taxes, fund public services and shoulder the consequences of a system increasingly tilted towards those who need its protection least. Yet we are expected to tremble at the prospect of billionaires taking their fortunes elsewhere. Why? Wealth does not exist in a vacuum. It is built on a society’s workers, infrastructure, institutions and opportunities.
If the wealthiest can enjoy the fruits of that society while escaping their fair share of its responsibilities, the scandal is not that they leave. It is that successive governments have allowed them to make the rules. A country that cannot afford to lose its billionaires should ask itself why it can apparently afford to impoverish everyone else.
Fernando Quintana
London

Nigeria elected to UN Human Rights Council seat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:17:48 UTC
01:17:48 KST

Kabir Adeniyi
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
Nigeria has been elected to the United Nations Human Rights Council for a three-year term beginning in January, the government said Wednesday.
Nigeria was among 15 countries elected to the 47-member council for the 2027–2029 term during Tuesday’s vote in New York.
The country received 172 out of 181 votes, placing third among the four African countries elected. Zambia received 177 votes, Ghana 173 and Burundi 160, according to the results.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs thanked UN member states for supporting Nigeria’s candidacy and reaffirmed the country’s commitment to international cooperation, dialogue and the promotion of human rights.
“Nigeria’s election reflects international confidence in its commitment to advancing human rights and improving human rights conditions across the world,” Foreign Affairs spokesperson Oluwafemi Adeniyi said in part.
The government said Nigeria looked forward to working with other council members to strengthen global efforts to protect fundamental freedoms and uphold human dignity and justice.
The Human Rights Council, based in Geneva, is the UN body responsible for promoting and protecting human rights worldwide. It addresses alleged violations, makes recommendations to member states and conducts the Universal Periodic Review, through which the human rights records of all UN member states are assessed.
The council has 47 members elected by the General Assembly, with seats allocated among regional groups. Members serve three-year terms and are expected to uphold high standards in the promotion and protection of human rights.
Nigeria’s term will begin Jan. 1 and run through Dec. 31, 2029.

Spanish NGO postpones Mediterranean rescue mission over fuel costs
MADRID, Oct 14 - Spanish humanitarian rescue charity SMH has postponed its next mission in the central Mediterranean until 2027 due to soaring fuel costs, the group said on Wednesday, highlighting the financial pressures facing humanitarian efforts along one of the world's deadliest migration routes.
SMH, which operates the Aita Mari, a former fishing vessel converted into a rescue ship in 2017, said on X the doubling of fuel prices had forced it to suspend operations in the central Mediterranean and shift activities to waters around Spain's Valencia coast, and the islands of Mallorca and Menorca.
It also launched a crowdfunding campaign to cover the extra costs.
The central Mediterranean crossing from North Africa to Italy and southern France is one of the world's most dangerous migrant routes, used by migrants from Africa and the Middle East seeking to reach Europe, often in overcrowded or unseaworthy boats.
Spanish NGO Open Arms said it had also scaled back its central Mediterranean missions in recent years because of rising fuel costs and Italy's policy of assigning rescue vessels ports in northern Italy. The practice can require ships to sail for two or three days from their operating area, increasing costs and reducing time available for search-and-rescue work.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's right-wing, anti-immigration government has repeatedly argued that humanitarian rescue vessels encourage migrants to attempt the crossing. REUTERS

Moscow names Kyiv, Kharkiv power plants as targets
Russia’s Defense Ministry said that its forces used ground-based precision weapons and long-range attack drones against energy and communications facilities it claimed were serving Ukraine’s military and defense industry.
The ministry listed the Darnytsia CHP-4 and CHP-5 combined heat and power plants in Kyiv, as well as CHP-6, the Trypillia thermal power plant and a major electrical substation in Kyiv region.

Zelensky Says He Feels Betrayed By the US, Warns Ukraine Is Losing America as Partner
According to Ukraine’s Air Force, Russia launched 39 missiles and 128 drones in the attack, which began at 6 p.m. local time. Air defenses downed four missiles and 115 drones.

How the truce claim unfolded
Following a telephone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Friday, Oct. 9, Trump announced that the US struck a diesel arrangement with the Kremlin.
Shortly after, the US Treasury Department issued a license authorizing the sale and import of Russian diesel through April 7, 2027.
On Sunday, Oct. 11, Trump announced that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to stop striking each other’s energy infrastructure, without an official response from neither Ukraine nor Russia.

NYC moves to ban Central Park horse carriages after 150 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:14:00 UTC
01:14:00 KST

New York City lawmakers are preparing to ban horse-drawn carriages from Central Park, potentially ending a 150-year tourism tradition amid longstanding animal welfare concerns and renewed scrutiny following the death of a teenage tourist last spring.
The City Council is expected to approve a bill next week that would end the rides by 2028. Three consecutive mayors had called for an end to the carriage rides because of safety concerns, only to have lawmakers yank back the reins.
A spokesperson for Julie Menin, the council speaker, confirmed the incoming vote and said the proposal had enough support to pass. Mayor Zohran Mamdani's office said he had reached a deal with the speaker on the legislation.
"The horse carriage industry is coming to an end in New York City,” Mamdani said in a social media post.
The latest push for a ban started in June, when 18-year-old Romanch Mahajan, visiting the city from India, died after jumping from a runaway horse carriage during a ride with family members. His death, which appeared to be the first fatality in a horse carriage accident since they were introduced in Central Park, reignited the debate over whether carriages, a romantic throwback to the city's past, have a place in a modern metropolis.
Mahajan's family has appeared at City Hall, in person and through videoconference calls from India, begging the city to finally end the rides.
"We are shattered, our whole family shattered. The pain does not go away,” his father, Deepak Mahajan, told city council members via a videocall during a hearing for the bill last summer, saying his son leapt from the carriage to try and help his mother, who was flung from her seat, after the horse bolted. "Every morning we wake up and think of nothing but the loss of our son.”
For decades, animal welfare activists and other critics have decried the carriage industry, arguing horses shouldn't be hauling tourists around busy streets and Central Park while having to navigate bustling traffic and gawking passersby. In the past, horses have collapsed, gotten startled and run off, hitting cars or other objects, with each accident resulting in fresh calls for a ban.
"The tragic and preventable death of 18-year-old Romanch Mahajan made clear that the status quo is no longer acceptable. Horse-drawn carriages have long been part of New York City’s history, but in an increasingly busy Central Park, this tradition has become a growing public safety liability,” Menin said in a statement.
The industry and its supporters have long cast the rides as a way for visitors to experience the New York they know from classic movies and television.
Fred Astaire and Cyd Charisse danced into one of the carriages in "The Band Wagon.” Robert Redford and Jane Fonda rode one in "Barefoot in the Park.” Macaulay Culkin escaped bandits in a carriage in "Home Alone 2: Lost in New York.”
"Taking a horse and carriage ride in New York City is one of the most iconic things to do in New York City and people from all over the world know about us and travel to New York to go to a carriage ride in New York,” Conor McHugh, a longtime carriage driver, told the Council earlier this year.
Efforts to close down the industry have been met with pushback from unions and influential supporters, often resulting in tiresome political fights that have seen mayors throw up their hands over nagging worries about putting carriage drivers out of work and what to do with the horses if they can no longer work.
Transport Workers Union International President John Samuelsen said the Council's bill has "no meaningful economic relief for workers” and that Menin "used the tragic death of a tourist to contrive a public safety crisis.”
"This is disgraceful political opportunism, and Zohran should not simply go along with it, particularly when immigrant families’ livelihoods are being destroyed. This entire situation is reprehensible,” he said in a statement.
The proposal as written would require the mayor's office to develop a workforce transition plan for drivers, and includes a measure that would allow the city to consider some kind of compensation for industry workers. Carriage owners could not sell their horses off for slaughter, according to the bill's language, which requires that horses be disposed of in a "humane manner.”
"I think we have a civic responsibility to ensure that we are not leaving anybody out to dry,” Mamdani told reporters Wednesday.
The mayor's predecessor, Eric Adams, called for ending the industry during the waning days of his administration, but the proposal went nowhere. The mayor before that, Bill de Blasio, had pledged to eliminate the rides on day one of his administration but abandoned the crusade after heavy opposition from unions and a media blitz involving actor Liam Neeson.
Over the years, the city has placed various safety regulations around the industry, including a requirement that the horses get at least five weeks of vacation a year outside of city limits with daily access to a pasture. The horses are inspected by a veterinarian twice a year, and the maximum age they can work at is 26, according to city regulations. And they don't work when it is hotter than 89 degrees.
