`123456’ password used in massive Danish CPR data breach
At least three accounts at the company linked to a major breach of Denmark’s CPR register reportedly used the password “123456”, including an administrator account.
At least three user accounts at the Funen-based IT company Pays used the password “123456” when hackers gained access to Denmark’s CPR register, Politiken reports.
One of them was the company’s administrator account.
The breach exposed information linked to around 8.8 million CPR numbers. The CPR system is Denmark’s central civil registration database and contains personal information on people living or previously registered in Denmark.
The newspaper Politiken reviewed data from the breach that the hacker allegedly used to gain access to the system.
Jens Myrup Pedersen, professor at Aarhus University’s Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, described the company’s password security as “hopeless”.
“There is really no security, it is an open door. A password like ‘123456’ is one of the very first things you would guess if you took a list of common passwords,” he told Politiken.
“I find it hard to see that you could have worse security. It was a matter of time before things went wrong.”
Pays ApS, based in Odense, confirmed to TV 2 on Friday that it was the company whose access had been compromised.
“We can confirm that we are the company that has been subjected to an attack where our legal access to search for information in the CPR system has been abused,” managing director and owner Sophie Laursen said in an email to TV 2.
The hacker had access to the CPR register from 10 September for a total of 21 days and 17 hours.
An anonymous hacker told Politiken on Thursday that they were behind the attack and claimed gaining access had not been particularly difficult.
According to the hacker, access was initially obtained using a leaked password belonging to a former employee of a small Danish company. The hacker then allegedly created two computer programs to retrieve information from the CPR system and store it externally.
The hacker told Politiken that there were no plans to sell or publish the information.
Private companies and associations can be granted access to information in Denmark’s CPR register when they have a legitimate need, for example to obtain address information about customers or members.
According to Denmark’s Central Business Register, Pays ApS had two employees as of July 2026.
One in four Danish driving penalty points linked to mobile phone use
Danish motorists received almost 21,000 penalty points for using handheld mobile phones while driving last year – the highest number in four years.
Mobile phones are playing a growing role in traffic offences in Denmark.
In 2025, motorists received 20,910 penalty points on their driving licences for using a handheld mobile phone behind the wheel, according to figures from the police case management system POLSAS.
That means mobile phone use accounted for roughly one in every four of the 84,056 penalty points issued for traffic offences during the year.
The number of mobile-related penalty points increased by 7.5 percent compared with 2024 and reached its highest level in four years.
On average, police issued 57 penalty points every day for handheld mobile phone use.
Britta Bjerregaard, claims director at insurance company Alm. Brand, described the development as deeply concerning.
“Most people know full well that the phone should stay put while driving. Still, it can be tempting to just answer a call, reply to a message, or change the song,” she said.
“Traffic does not pause while you look at the screen.”
89 metres without watching the road
The Danish Road Safety Council considers inattention one of the major risks on Danish roads, with mobile phones posing a particular problem.
“The mobile phone takes an incredible amount of attention if you use it behind the wheel,” deputy director Karina Petersen said.
“If you look at the screen for four seconds at country road speed, you are driving 89 metres blind.”
However, Petersen cautioned that the increase in recorded offences does not necessarily mean that more drivers are using their phones.
The rise could also reflect more police checks or improved camera equipment used for traffic enforcement.
What are the rules in Denmark?
Using a handheld mobile phone while driving in Denmark results in a DKK 1,500 fine and a penalty point on your driving licence. An additional DKK 1,000 contribution to the Victims’ Fund is also charged.
The rule applies even when the car is stationary in traffic or waiting at a red light.
Drivers may briefly operate a phone if it is securely mounted, and using a vehicle’s built-in screen is also permitted.
The ban on handheld mobile phone use also applies to cyclists, electric scooter users and drivers of other motorised vehicles.

Hacker retained access to Danish CPR register for nearly 22 days before breach was discovered
An unauthorized user had access to Denmark’s national Civil Registration System (CPR) for nearly 22 days before authorities discovered the security breach, according to documents obtained by TV 2.
The access began September 10 and was stopped October 2, lasting 21 days and 17 hours.
However, preliminary investigations suggest the unauthorized activity ended September 20, approximately 10 days after it began, according to a report submitted by the CPR office to the Danish Data Protection Agency.
The Ministry of Research, Education and Digitalization announced Monday that personal information belonging to approximately 8.8 million people had been exposed, including names, addresses and CPR identification numbers.
The breach occurred through a small Danish company with legitimate access to the register.
According to DR, the company is based on Funen and shares ownership and an address with a larger business. Its identity has not been publicly confirmed.
Authorities discovered the incident after receiving an unusually large invoice for searches conducted through the company’s account.
Approximately 14 million CPR searches had been made using its access credentials.
“The number far exceeds the company’s customer base, and the company has indicated that they did not perform the lookups themselves,” the CPR office stated in its report.
Private companies and organizations can pay to access certain CPR information.
Research, Education and Digitalization Minister Christina Egelund of the Moderates party acknowledged that security measures had been inadequate.
She has requested a security review of the register following the breach.
The company had not responded to DR’s requests for comment as of Friday morning.
Sardine sales surge in Copenhagen as social media skincare trend gains popularity
Canned sardines are selling rapidly across Denmark, particularly around Copenhagen, as supermarkets report rising demand and occasional shortages.
Four major grocery retailers, Coop, Salling Group, Nemlig.com and Dagrofa, confirmed significant sales increases to TV 2 Kosmopol.
Coop, which operates 365, SuperBrugsen, Brugsen and Kvickly, reported a 170 percent increase in sardine sales in Denmark’s Capital Region between June and September 2026 compared with the same period last year.
Nationwide, Coop’s sales rose 163.5 percent.
Jacob Herbst Lassen, Coop Denmark’s press manager, said the sudden popularity has left some shelves with fewer products while purchasing teams work to replenish supplies.
Salling Group also reported pressure on availability, although spokesperson Alma Lyhne Kristensen said the company remained adequately stocked overall.
Online supermarket Nemlig.com said Greater Copenhagen and North Zealand accounted for 75 percent of its sardine sales.
Dagrofa, which operates Meny and Spar stores, reported that sales in the capital area had more than doubled compared with last year.
The surge may be connected to the social media trend “eat your skincare,” which promotes foods believed to benefit skin health.
Sardines have attracted attention for their omega-3 fatty acids, collagen and protein.
However, dermatologist and researcher Cæcilie Johansen cautioned that evidence linking sardine consumption directly to healthier skin remains limited.
She said some studies suggest omega-3 fatty acids may help with eczema, but the research involved large quantities.
Johansen emphasized that avoiding smoking, limiting alcohol and using sunscreen are more important measures for protecting skin health.
Denmark resumes citizenship and immigration cases after criminal records error
Denmark’s Ministry of Immigration and Integration has resumed processing citizenship applications that were suspended because of errors in the country’s Central Criminal Register.
The ministry announced the decision in a press release after the National Police concluded that the errors had only a very limited impact on the register.
Immigration authorities have also been instructed to restart affected cases involving permanent residence permits and family reunification, according to an update from the Danish Immigration Service.
The applications had been placed on hold September 7 while authorities investigated the problem.
The errors became public in early September when National Police Commissioner Lasse Boje informed politicians at Christiansborg, the seat of Denmark’s parliament, that some criminal records had been deleted incorrectly.
Authorities had discovered the problem in June.
The National Police said further investigations would determine whether the errors had affected decisions made by other public authorities.
If problems are identified, police will work with the relevant authorities to determine how those cases should be handled.
The errors also disrupted the issuance of child protection certificates, which are background checks used to identify certain criminal convictions relevant to working with children.
Applications for these certificates were temporarily suspended while police reviewed the affected records.
The National Police reopened applications September 18.
During its review, police restored 43 decisions that had been removed from the Criminal Register earlier than they should have been.
Those decisions were relevant to child protection certificates.
The ministry has not specified how many citizenship, permanent residence or family reunification applications were affected by the suspension.
Danish court rejects detention request for two Kosovo prison officers accused of assault
Two prison officers from Kosovo accused of assaulting an inmate at Copenhagen’s Vestre Prison will remain free while police investigate the allegations.
Denmark’s Eastern High Court rejected prosecutors’ request to hold the two men in pretrial detention Friday afternoon.
The decision upheld a ruling by Copenhagen City Court on Wednesday, which found insufficient grounds to detain them.
Both courts concluded there was no significant reason to believe the men would flee Denmark before a possible criminal trial.
The officers, aged 29 and 24, are undergoing training in Denmark ahead of assignments at Gjilan prison in Kosovo, which Denmark is renting to house prisoners.
According to police allegations, the two officers assaulted an inmate inside a cell at Vestre Prison around 4 p.m. Monday.
The inmate was allegedly pushed onto a bed before being punched in the face and body.
Police arrested the officers Tuesday morning, and prosecutors requested their detention the following day.
Both men deny using violence against the inmate.
During Wednesday’s hearing, a Copenhagen City Court judge found reasonable grounds to suspect the officers had committed the alleged assault.
However, the judge ruled that detention was unnecessary because both men reside in Denmark and are employed by Danmarks Fængsler, the Danish Prison and Probation Service.
Prosecutors challenged that decision, but the Eastern High Court reached the same conclusion Friday.
The investigation remains ongoing, and no decision has been made on whether the officers will face trial.
Once police complete their investigation, prosecutors will determine whether there is sufficient evidence to bring criminal charges before a court.

Government unveils security-focused budget proposal
The Danish government has presented a proposed budget for 2027 that prioritizes national security, with more money allocated to defence amid an increasingly tense international security situation.
The proposal, titled “A stronger defence of Denmark – a strengthened Denmark to defend”, was presented by Finance Minister Peter Hummelgaard of the Social Democrats (S) at the Ministry of Finance on Friday morning.
The government wants to ensure that defence spending reaches 3.5 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) by 2030.
Hummelgaard said the proposal reflected the need to make “hard priorities” in response to the current security situation. He also described the Danish economy as being “in top shape”.
“The government’s proposal for the finance bill shows that we take responsibility upon ourselves, and that we lead the way in working for a greener, freer, and more equal Denmark,” Hummelgaard said.
Pia Olsen Dyhr of the Socialist People’s Party (SF), the minister for economic and interior affairs, also highlighted the security situation.
“We do not solve all the challenges we have in Denmark with this finance bill. But we are well on our way,” she said at the press conference.
“I also think everyone must remember that we are in an escalated security policy situation,” Olsen Dyhr said.
Much of the proposed budget had already been announced, either in the government’s policy platform or through statements by ministers in recent weeks.
The proposal allocates 1.2 billion DKK to children’s services and education in 2027, including Denmark’s public primary and lower secondary schools, known as folkeskole.
It also sets aside a total of 10.1 billion DKK in 2030 for tax cuts. These include abolishing the intermediate income tax and the top-top tax, as well as reducing corporation tax.
“We are simplifying the tax system,” said Taxation and Growth Minister Jakob Engel-Schmidt of the Moderates (M).
The tax measures will be negotiated separately as part of a tax reform. While the budget proposal includes tax cuts, the government also plans to freeze several tax thresholds, which would increase the tax burden for some taxpayers as incomes rise.
The liberal think tank Cepos estimates that the government’s various plans will result in a net tax cut of 2.2 billion DKK in 2030.
Business and Competitiveness Minister Martin Lidegaard of the Danish Social Liberal Party (R) highlighted investment in young people and education.
“We are significantly strengthening knowledge, general education, and formal education in Denmark, from ABC to PhD. It is good for the individual young person, but it is also good for Denmark’s future,” Lidegaard said.
Unlike in recent years, when the government’s fiscal room for manoeuvre helped fund much of its budget plans, this proposal includes several measures to find additional savings.
These include cuts to the Danish student grant (SU), savings on senior pension payments, a proposed tax on cruise ships and further reductions in state administration costs.
The government must now negotiate with other parties in the Danish Parliament, the Folketing, to secure a majority for the 2027 budget.
The proposal includes a negotiating reserve of 500 million DKK annually from 2027 to 2030, which other parties can seek to use to fund their own priorities.
Business groups warn 200 DKK cruise passenger tax could drive tourists away
Two Danish business organizations are warning that a proposed tax of 200 DKK per cruise passenger could lead cruise ships to skip Danish ports, reducing tourism revenue for cities and smaller destinations.
Dansk Industri (DI), the Confederation of Danish Industry, and Dansk Erhverv, a business organization representing companies across several sectors, are responding to the government’s proposal to introduce the tax from 2028.
“A cruise tax at this level will hit both the major cities and rural districts,” said Lars Bertolt Winther, head of tourism, culture and experiences at DI, in a press release.
Jesper Kronborg, industry director for transport at Dansk Erhverv, also criticized the proposal.
“In Dansk Erhverv’s view, it is a bad proposal, or at least a proposal that requires a very thorough analysis,” he said in a press release.
The government expects the tax to generate an additional 300 million DKK in annual revenue from 2028.
The aim is to make cruise tourism contribute more toward the costs associated with ships, including pollution, noise and congestion.
Figures from Statistics Denmark show that 1.1 million cruise passengers visited Denmark in 2025. The number of cruise ships calling at Danish ports increased by 16% compared with the previous year.
Copenhagen, Aarhus, Skagen and Rønne on the island of Bornholm are the country’s main cruise destinations. Together, they account for more than 98% of cruise passengers.
DI and Dansk Erhverv argue that cruise visitors generate local revenue through port fees and spending at shops and other businesses.
Both organizations point to Iceland, where a similar tax was introduced before being reduced.
“Following the introduction of a high passenger tax, bookings dropped significantly, especially to the smaller ports, and the tax was subsequently lowered to limit the damaging effects,” Winther said.
“There is no reason to believe that Denmark does not risk the same,” he added.
According to the industry organization Danske Havne, which represents Danish ports, Iceland now charges 85 DKK per cruise passenger, while Greenland charges 50 DKK.
Tine Kirk, director of Danske Havne, described the proposed Danish tax of 200 DKK as “unreasonably high.”
“The cruise ships can very easily opt out of Denmark. We fear that the shipping companies will either bypass Denmark completely or concentrate their port calls in the largest cities,” she said in a written comment.
Drop in exports to the US drags down Danish exports
Danish exports fell by 3.3 percent in August, driven in part by a decline in goods exports to the United States, according to Statistics Denmark.
Total exports of goods and services amounted to 194 billion DKK in August, down 3.3 percent from July. Goods exports fell by 6.2 percent, while services exports rose by 0.7 percent.
Søren Kristensen, chief economist at AL Sydbank, described the overall decline as “worryingly large”.
“But it is part of the story that a large part of the decline is concentrated around the US, where we also see fluctuations from month to month,” he wrote in a comment.
Exports of goods and services to both the US and the United Kingdom fell in August. Total exports to the US amounted to 31.7 billion DKK, down 2.8 billion DKK from July.
Goods exports to the US fell by 3.3 billion DKK, while services exports rose slightly.
Kristensen said fluctuations in the prices of products such as medicines sold by Danish companies in the US could partly explain the decline. He therefore cautioned against drawing too negative a conclusion from the latest figures alone.
The August decline followed an increase in exports in July. Overall, Danish exports of goods and services rose by nearly 19 billion DKK, or more than 10 percent, between August 2025 and August 2026.
According to Kristensen, Danish exports have so far held up despite geopolitical unrest, higher energy prices and rising interest rates.
Still, the August figures are bad news for the Danish economy when viewed in isolation.
“However, it will take several months of this development before we become worried,” Kristensen wrote.
Hacker claims simple password allowed access to 8.8 million Danish CPR numbers
An anonymous hacker has claimed responsibility for accessing nearly 8.8 million Danish CPR numbers, telling newspaper Politiken that a weak password made the breach possible.
CPR numbers are personal identification numbers used in Denmark’s national Civil Registration System to identify residents and access public services.
The hacker told Politiken that the breach occurred on September 11 through a small Danish company with access to the CPR register.
According to the hacker, a leaked password belonging to a former employee allowed entry into the system. The password was reportedly “123456.”
After gaining access, the hacker said they created two computer programs to retrieve CPR information and store it outside the system.
The person’s identity has not been made public, and their account has not been independently confirmed.
The hacker told Politiken they had no plans to sell or publish the personal identification numbers and were “really shocked” by the security weaknesses they encountered.
To describe the situation, the hacker compared it to someone leaving dangerous material unattended.
“Someone leaves a suitcase with 10 kilos of plutonium unattended at a train station. Then a homeless person steals it,” the hacker said.
“Yes, of course you shouldn’t steal other people’s suitcases. But you also shouldn’t leave nuclear material at a train station.”
The hacker provided Politiken with a file containing the CPR numbers.
The newspaper forwarded the file to Emil Hørning, an IT security expert at Danish cybersecurity company Defend Denmark.
Hørning said the hacker’s account appeared credible and that the described method was plausible.
Politiken conducted its interview with the hacker in English through an encrypted communication service.
Danish government proposes tighter senior pension rules to save 800 million DKK annually
The Danish government wants to change how workers qualify for senior pensions, potentially saving 800 million DKK annually by 2030, according to Jyllands-Posten.
Currently, people whose health limits their ability to work to 15 hours a week or less can receive a senior pension up to six years before reaching the state retirement age.
Their work capacity is assessed against their most recent job. Under the proposal, applicants would instead be assessed against all types of employment.
The Finance Ministry estimates savings of 200 million DKK in 2028, rising to 800 million DKK in 2030.
The proposal has divided political parties and organizations.
Anders Vistisen of DF, Dansk Folkeparti, the Danish People’s Party, said his party would oppose the changes.
“We are not going to cut for the worn-out,” he told Jyllands-Posten, citing Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen’s promises of more dignified retirement.
Ældre Sagen, Denmark’s senior citizens’ advocacy organization, also criticized the proposal.
Deputy Director Michael Teit Nielsen warned that applicants could face longer assessments to determine whether they could work in another profession.
However, Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry, Denmark’s main employers’ association, welcomed the proposal.
Deputy CEO Søren Kryhlmand said assessing workers against the entire labor market would allow those capable of other jobs to remain employed.
The government also plans to increase the separate Arne early retirement pension by approximately 3,000 DKK monthly. Its current maximum is 15,650 DKK per month.
Changing the senior pension scheme, introduced in 2019, requires agreement among the parties behind it before a general election.
Finance Minister Peter Hummelgaard is scheduled to present the budget proposal today.

Three Danish films shortlisted for Europe’s Oscars
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:00:39 UTC
23:00:39 KST

Three Danish films have been shortlisted for the European Film Awards, often described as Europe’s equivalent of the Oscars.
The films are the dramas Kvinde ukendt by May el-Toukhy and Gæsten by Mads Mengel, and Sine Plambech’s documentary Rescue, the Danish Film Institute announced on Instagram.
A total of 45 films have been shortlisted in the fiction category.
May el-Toukhy’s Kvinde ukendt has already received international recognition. The drama was selected for the Venice Film Festival in September, where it won the main prize, the Golden Lion. Its lead actress, Mathilde Arcel, was named best actress.
The film has also been selected as Denmark’s entry for the Academy Awards in the Best International Feature Film category.
Set during the liberation of Denmark in May 1945, the drama follows a woman who has worked as a maid in the home of an elderly, respected widower she is now preparing to marry. She struggles to hide the fact that she has had a relationship with a German soldier.
Mads Mengel’s Gæsten has also attracted international attention. In July, the film received two awards at the Karlovy Vary International Film Festival in the Czech Republic.
It won the Special Jury Prize in the festival’s main competition, known as the Crystal Globe Competition, while Mengel was named best director.
The film follows Karl and Emilie, a couple preparing to host a naming ceremony for their son. Their plans are disrupted when an uninvited guest arrives: Karl’s mother, played by Trine Dyrholm, with whom he has not spoken for years.
The third Danish film on the shortlist is Rescue, a documentary by anthropologist Sine Plambech. It had its world premiere at the Toronto International Film Festival in September.
The documentary follows people fleeing across the Mediterranean and examines how the European Union’s border policies affect the lives and conditions of refugees.
Rescue is one of 15 films shortlisted in the documentary category.
Producers, distributors and other rights holders can submit films for consideration by the European Film Academy. The academy’s board and invited European experts then select films for the shortlist.
Members of the academy, which includes professionals from across the European film industry, watch the shortlisted films and vote to determine the final nominations. They vote again to select the winners once the nominations have been announced.
The final nominations will be announced on November 14. The awards ceremony will take place in Athens, the Greek capital, on January 16.

Liberal Alliance wants mindset interview for citizenship applicant
A debate in Denmark over a proposed law granting citizenship to 2,055 people has centered on whether the applicants have been checked well enough for anti-democratic opinions.
Liberal Alliance, a political party in Denmark, carried out its own check of the people listed in the citizenship bill. During this review, the party found a woman who had repeatedly praised Hamas and former Hamas leaders Yahya Sinwar and Ismail Haniyeh.
Following the discovery, Liberal Alliance wants the woman called in for an interview with Indfødsretsudvalget, the Naturalization Committee of the Danish parliament.
Alex Vanopslagh, the leader of Liberal Alliance, spoke about the matter to the Danish newspaper Politiken.
“As we see it, it just emphasizes the need to wait to grant more citizenships until a proper screening model is in place, so that we can specifically catch some types who, based on what we can see so far, appear strongly anti-democratic,” he told the newspaper.
Every six months, a new bill is introduced in Folketinget, the Danish parliament, to give people Danish citizenship. This happens after an application process that is often long and detailed. This process was also followed under the previous coalition government in Denmark.
The most recent round of citizenships was scheduled at the same time a parliamentary election was called in the spring. Because of the election, the bill that included citizenship for the 2,055 people was delayed.
The delay gave momentum to demands from opposition parties. They argued that officials must carry out a more thorough review of the people on the list to find out if any of them hold anti-democratic views. Socialdemokratiet, the Danish Social Democratic Party, supported this demand as well.
However, the new government decided to present the citizenship bill before a new screening system was ready. This choice led to a larger debate during the opening of the Danish parliament.
During that debate, Rasmus Stoklund, the political spokesperson for Socialdemokratiet, said that if opposition parties found a person on the bill who had anti-democratic views, they could inform the Naturalization Committee. Liberal Alliance has now acted on that suggestion.
Politiken also spoke with the woman identified by the party. She denied that she supports Hamas or any killings.
“I do not support anyone who kills anyone. Because I do not like anyone killing anyone, regardless of whether they are Israeli, Russian or anything else,” the woman told the newspaper.
She stated that she is ready to attend an interview with the committee to explain her position.
Other political parties have reacted differently to the proposal. Dansk Folkeparti, the Danish People’s Party, supports calling the woman in for an interview.
However, Enhedslisten, the Danish left-wing Red-Green Alliance party, strongly opposes the idea.
“It is deeply concerning that Liberal Alliance now to such an extent wants to begin exercising thought control,” Peder Hvelplund, the citizenship spokesperson for Enhedslisten, told Politiken.

Denmark’s minister for homeland security and emergency preparedness, Lisbeth Bech-Nielsen, says there is a clear need to talk with members of the Danish parliament about how to protect the country against cyberattacks.
Bech-Nielsen belongs to SF (Socialistisk Folkeparti), the Socialist People’s Party, which is a left-wing and green political party in Denmark. She spoke about the situation to the Danish broadcaster TV 2.
“The serious threat assessment and recent events are the reason why I have summoned the parties to a discussion of what initiatives can be set in motion,” she said.

The minister said it is still too early to draw final conclusions about the latest incident, but noted that “the authorities are investigating” it.

Kirsten Schwalbe becomes Denmark’s oldest person ever at 112
A woman from Struer has set a national longevity record, reaching 112 years and 218 days on Wednesday and surpassing the previous record held by Karla Lindholm Jensen.
Schwalbe also joins the list of Europe’s 10 oldest living people. The world’s oldest living person is Britain’s Ethel Caterham, who is 117.
The previous Danish record holder, Karla Lindholm Jensen from Herning, died in 2020.
Ahead of the milestone, Jyllands-Posten attempted to interview Schwalbe, but she needed a day of rest. Instead, the newspaper spoke with two of her three daughters.
Her daughter Hanne Jensen, 86, described how her mother sometimes struggles to understand that her children are now elderly themselves.
“She knows well enough that we are getting older, but she forgets that we can no longer withstand everything,” Jensen told the newspaper.
Schwalbe was born in Salling in 1914, just months before World War I began, and grew up alongside nine siblings.
She married her first husband in 1938, and the couple had three children.
Despite her age, Schwalbe continues to live in her own home in Struer.
Her life has previously been documented by regional broadcaster TV Midtvest in the television series “Kirstens vilde år,” which airs on TV 2.
Schwalbe has attributed her longevity partly to genetics. Four of her nine siblings also lived beyond 100, she told Berlingske in 2024.
She has also emphasized the importance of maintaining a positive outlook, previously telling TV Midtvest that a person’s mood plays an important role in living a long life.
Government party proposes mandatory helmets for e-bike riders
Rising numbers of serious traffic injuries have prompted Moderaterne, the Moderates, to call for stricter safety rules for people using electric bicycles.
Sten Larsen, the party’s health spokesperson, told regional broadcaster TV2 Østjylland that helmets should become a legal requirement for e-bike riders.
“E-bikes are both heavier and faster than regular bicycles,” Larsen said.
He pointed to an increase in serious injuries and deaths involving electric bicycles as justification for the proposal.
Currently, Denmark does not require helmets for ordinary bicycles or standard e-bikes, whose motors provide assistance at speeds of up to 25 kilometers per hour.
However, helmets are already mandatory for speed pedelecs, which can provide motor assistance up to 45 kilometers per hour.
According to the Danish Road Directorate, 200 e-bike riders were injured in traffic accidents in 2025, including 133 who suffered serious injuries. Another 11 riders died.
The number of seriously injured e-bike riders was the highest recorded in six years.
Larsen wants to discuss the proposed legislation with Transport Minister Signe Munk of Socialistisk Folkeparti, the Socialist People’s Party.
Ritzau sought a comment from Munk, but her ministry said she was unavailable.
Cyklistforbundet, the Danish Cyclists’ Federation, opposes making helmets compulsory, arguing that such a measure could discourage cycling.
“Our purpose is to get more people to cycle. So every measure that pulls in the opposite direction, we will oppose. But we warmly recommend that people use a bicycle helmet,” federation chair Jens Peter Hansen told TV2 Østjylland.
The proposal would introduce a helmet requirement for standard e-bikes, bringing their rules closer to those already applying to faster electric bicycles.

Denmark should maintain its current foreign aid budget but change where the money goes, according to Jacob Jensen, foreign affairs spokesperson for Venstre, Denmark’s Liberal Party.
Jensen told Ritzau that his party wants to continue spending 0.7 percent of gross national income on development aid annually.
However, he wants more funding directed toward four or five North African countries facing migration pressures toward Europe.
The money would come from aid currently allocated to regions including the Caribbean, South America and Southeast Asia.
Jensen argued that providing education and employment opportunities could discourage young people from attempting dangerous Mediterranean crossings.

Jensen wants to discuss revising Denmark’s development strategy with Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen of the Moderates party.
The government’s proposed aid priorities for 2027 through 2030 already include measures to reduce irregular migration.
Before the general election, Venstre proposed cutting development aid to 0.5 percent of national income to free approximately 6.5 billion DKK for welfare.

Greenland moves closer to restoring former time zone and ending daylight saving time
Greenland’s three governing parties have agreed to support a proposal that would move the territory back to UTC-3 in 2028, reversing a decision made just a few years ago.
The parties, which hold a majority in Inatsisartut, Greenland’s parliament, announced their position during a debate Tuesday, according to Sermitsiaq.
The proposal would also abolish daylight saving time starting next year.
“We have decided that we should return to UTC-3 on the basis of the many people who have submitted a consultation response,” the governing parties said.
In 2022, Greenland’s parliament approved a move from UTC-3 to UTC-2 to balance the time difference with Europe and the United States. The change took effect in March 2023.
However, the decision has remained controversial, with 4,142 residents signing a petition calling for the previous time zone to return.
Opposition parties Naleraq and Siumut proposed reversing the change in May. The government initially opposed the move but supported ending daylight saving time.
Despite the government’s changed position, Greenlandic leader Jens-Frederik Nielsen of Demokraatit, the Democrats party, warned about potential consequences.
He said the change would increase the time difference with Europe by one hour in winter and two hours in summer.
Nielsen argued that reduced overlap with Danish medical specialists could lead to longer patient waiting times.
He also warned of higher costs for businesses, weaker flight connections with Europe and financial expenses associated with changing the time zone.
The proposal is scheduled for a final parliamentary vote October 21.

Greenland cancels 39.8 million DKK in benefit repayment claims
Greenland’s government has cancelled repayment claims totaling 39.8 million DKK against more than 19,000 residents who received excessive employment benefits because of government IT errors.
Naalakkersuisut, Greenland’s government, announced Saturday that recipients would not have to return the overpayments from the Suila-tapit program.
Suila-tapit is an employment tax allowance of up to 1,313 DKK a month for workers earning between 70,000 and 500,000 DKK annually.
The program was introduced on January 1, 2025, to encourage employment and reduce economic inequality.
Errors in the Greenlandic Self-Government’s IT systems caused some residents to receive excessive payments during 2025. The government initially demanded that the money be repaid.
“Some citizens were paid too much without having done anything wrong themselves, and that responsibility does not lie with the individual citizen,” Finance Minister Aqqaluaq B. Egede of Inuit Ataqatigiit said.
Residents who have already repaid the money will receive refunds.
“We cannot turn back time, but we can take responsibility and ensure that citizens do not have to pay for the mistakes made in the system,” Egede said.
The repayment demands had faced public opposition. A large demonstration was planned in Nuuk on Saturday but was cancelled shortly after the government announced it would withdraw the claims.

Denmark’s Motor Register has been unavailable for almost 24 hours after authorities detected irregularities following a weekend update.
The Danish Motor Agency, which operates the register, temporarily suspended access after identifying the problem.
“At the present time, we cannot say more about the actual error in the Motor Register,” Deputy Director Claus Holm said in a written statement.

The Motor Register contains information about all vehicles registered in Denmark. It is used for tasks including registering new vehicles and transferring ownership when cars are bought or sold.

Copenhagen has far more municipal savings per resident than poorer municipalities
Danish municipalities differ significantly in how much readily available money they hold, according to an analysis by CEPOS, a Danish liberal think tank.
Copenhagen Municipality has the largest liquid holdings per resident, with savings equivalent to 31,685 DKK for each person.
At the other end of the ranking are Hjørring, Sorø, Thisted, Lolland and Aalborg municipalities. Their liquid holdings range from 3,127 DKK to 4,354 DKK per resident.
Liquid holdings can be viewed as municipal savings that have not been allocated to a specific purpose. Municipalities typically use the money to manage ongoing incoming and outgoing payments.
CEPOS said municipalities must always maintain a certain level of liquidity to cover their regular financial obligations.
Local authorities may also build up savings to finance future projects.
More than 500 marine mammals stranded along Danish coasts in 2025
A total of 538 marine mammals were recorded as stranded along Denmark’s coasts in 2025, according to a report from the Danish Environmental Protection Agency’s emergency service for stranded marine mammals.
The animals included 363 harbor seals, 38 grey seals and 137 harbor porpoises.
Most were found dead. Of the harbor seals, 310 were dead when discovered, while 136 of the 137 harbor porpoises were found dead.
The report identified disease, parasites, injuries and weakness as possible reasons for the strandings.
One animal from each of the three groups was recorded as having stranded after becoming caught unintentionally in fishing nets.
More unusual marine mammals were also found along the Danish coastline during 2025. These included a humpback whale and a striped dolphin.
Ambulances get deer whistles to avoid hitting animals
Ambulances and emergency medical vehicles in the North Denmark Region will be equipped with wildlife whistles to reduce the risk of collisions with animals.
The small plastic whistles are mounted outside vehicles and produce a high-frequency sound when air passes through them. The sound is intended to frighten animals away from the road.
“Unfortunately, we have a number of collisions with animals when we drive with emergency signals in forests and natural areas,” the region’s Prehospital Services wrote on Facebook.
“It is dangerous for the people in the car, it delays the driving, and is dangerous for the animals.”
The decision comes as Denmark faces a possible record year for deer collisions.
Dyrenes Beskyttelse, Denmark’s largest animal welfare organization, recorded 8,739 deer collisions during the first nine months of 2026. That compares with 7,994 during the same period in 2025.
The previous annual record was 11,870 collisions in 2025.
The risk of encountering deer is particularly high during autumn and around sunrise and sunset.
However, it remains unclear whether wildlife whistles effectively keep animals away from roads.
Two insurance companies previously gave the devices to motorists as part of separate trials. According to FDM, Denmark’s main car owners’ association, the companies could not reach a clear conclusion about whether the whistles reduced collisions.

Apartment prices in Copenhagen fell for the second consecutive month in September, while prices in Aarhus rose sharply.
The average sales price for owner-occupied apartments in Copenhagen Municipality declined by 1.0 percent from August to September, according to housing platform Boligsiden. Prices fell by 0.5 percent the previous month.

“Supply has grown significantly in 2026, and now we see a price drop partly as a consequence of more options and lower demand among buyers,” she said.

In Aarhus Municipality, apartment prices rose by 3.7 percent in September, the third-largest monthly increase since records began in 2011.

Prices in Aarhus have increased by 23.3 percent over the past year. Nordea housing economist Lise Nytoft Bergmann called the development “extraordinary” but warned that prices would eventually reach a limit.
Nationwide apartment prices were unchanged in September. Prices for houses and holiday homes increased by 0.3 percent overall.
Suspected hacker says AI created program used in Danish CPR breach
The suspected hacker behind the theft of nearly 8.75 million Danish CPR numbers says artificial intelligence created the computer program used in the attack.
“Any AI model launched within the past year or so would be able to do it,” the anonymous person told Danish newspaper Politiken.
Two experts reviewed the program, which contains more than 40,000 characters, and concluded that its code was generated by artificial intelligence, Politiken reported.
Danish authorities disclosed last week that unauthorized people accessed names, addresses and CPR numbers during approximately 10 days in September. CPR numbers are Denmark’s personal identification numbers.
The suspected hacker said the program accessed the national CPR register through a website operated by Odense-based company Pays ApS. Login details were allegedly obtained from a former employee’s leaked password.
Politiken reported that at least three Pays accounts used “123456” as their password, including the administrator account. Pays confirmed to Danish broadcaster TV 2 that it was the compromised company.
The suspected hacker denied having advanced technical skills. An error in the AI-generated code reportedly caused the program to search for people born in 1877 instead of 1977. Consequently, data for people born in 1977 was absent from material shared with Politiken.
The person said they did not intend to sell or publish the information. Pays’ director did not respond to Politiken’s inquiries about the company’s security.

Museums and animal parks are the most popular attractions among Danes planning activities during the autumn holiday.
One in five people spending the holiday in Denmark plans to visit a museum or animal park, according to a Norstat survey conducted for Dansk Erhverv, the Danish Chamber of Commerce and a major business association.
Historical attractions, amusement parks and water parks follow on the list of preferred activities.

Number of disability pensioners under 40 falls for first time since 2020
The number of people under age 40 receiving disability pensions in Denmark has fallen for the first time in more than six years, according to figures from the Jobindsats.dk employment database.
In September, 43,229 people in the age group received disability pensions, 98 fewer than in August. It was the first monthly decline since early 2020.
Jesper Brask Fischer, head of welfare at pension company PFA, said it was too early to celebrate.
“The number of young people on disability pension is far higher than just a few years ago, and the development underlines the need for a strong effort toward prevention and early assistance,” he said.
The number of disability pension recipients under 40 has increased from 29,000 to more than 43,000 over the past decade. PFA has previously identified a possible connection between poor mental health and the increase.
Across all age groups, the number of disability pension recipients has declined for two consecutive months for the first time since late summer 2021.
Denmark had 261,418 disability pension recipients in September, down 487 from August.
Fischer said further consecutive declines could indicate that fewer people are entering the disability pension system. For now, however, he described the figures as only a cautious positive sign after years of significant growth.
Renovating all public concrete shelters could cost up to 3 billion DKK
Renovating Denmark’s 1,694 public concrete trench shelters and preparing them for use could cost between 2 billion and 3 billion DKK.
Public Security and Emergency Preparedness Minister Lisbeth Bech-Nielsen of the Socialist People’s Party provided the estimate in a response to the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament, according to construction trade publication Licitationen.
The estimate remains highly uncertain and requires further assessment.
Renovating only the 831 shelters that already meet basic requirements and could be opened during an immediate emergency would cost between 500 million and 1 billion DKK.
Most of the shelters require treatment for mold and pests because they have not been used for many years, the parliamentary response said.
The Ministry of Public Security and Emergency Preparedness began inspecting Denmark’s shelter capacity and condition in May 2025. The review of concrete trench shelters is complete, while inspections of reinforced shelters are expected to continue until 2027.
Concrete trench shelters are public facilities intended for people away from home, including road users and residents of buildings without shelters.
Most Danish shelter spaces are in reinforced rooms inside residential and other buildings. Denmark also has supplementary shelters that offer some protection but do not meet full shelter requirements.
A 2024 inventory found about 3.4 million shelter spaces nationwide. Concrete trench shelters accounted for 113,018 of them.

Two Danish Armed Forces aircraft flew over several parts of Denmark Monday to mark the 100th anniversary of Air Force Squadron 721.
A Hercules B-537 transport aircraft and a Challenger C-215 passenger aircraft participated in the flight, which also served as a training exercise for their crews.
Squadron 721 was established in 1926 and is Denmark’s oldest operational air force squadron. According to the Air Transport Wing, the Danish Armed Forces unit responsible for military air transport, it is also among the world’s oldest squadrons still in operation.

The Challenger is used for passenger transport and has carried members of Denmark’s royal family and government.
The Hercules can transport up to 20 tons of cargo. For Monday’s flight, it was decorated with a winged dolphin, the symbol used on the squadron’s crest.
Squadron 721 regularly participates in international operations. One of its aircraft is stationed in Kangerlussuaq, Greenland, for about 10 days each month.
District heating prices set to rise for thousands of Danish customers
Thousands of district heating customers in Denmark face higher bills in 2027, with 10 companies so far announcing price increases, TV 2 reported.
Most of the announced increases range from six to 10 percent.
Tue Patursson, a building specialist at the homeowner knowledge center Bolius, said the increases reflect higher energy prices.
“Since district heating plants depend on biofuel, gas, oil and electricity, one must expect that the price will also rise for district heating across the board,” he told TV 2.
Customers in Præstø in South Zealand face a 40 percent increase next year. The local district heating company had lowered its prices during the previous two years.
Præstø Fjernvarme is converting its production to electricity but has been affected by insufficient capacity in the power grid.

Danish inflation rises to 2.2 percent as fuel prices increase
Denmark’s annual inflation rate rose to 2.2 percent in September, up 0.2 percentage points from August, Statistics Denmark reported Monday.
Higher fuel costs were the main reason for the increase, with transportation prices contributing significantly to inflation between August and September.
Mette Hørdum Larsen, chief economist at Lederne, an organization representing managers and executives, said similar developments were visible in neighboring countries.
“But in fact, the rising energy prices do not become quite as visible in Danish inflation because the electricity tax has largely been removed this year and next year,” she wrote in a commentary.
Lower prices for holiday home rentals, package holidays and food helped offset the increase.
Larsen said there was no reason for serious concern because inflation remained close to the two percent level generally associated with stable prices. She added that there were no signs that higher energy costs were spreading throughout the economy.
Søren Kristensen, chief economist at Danish bank AL Sydbank, reached a similar conclusion.
However, he said the reduced electricity tax was concealing a significant rise in underlying inflation during recent months.
“In fact, in recent quarters there has been a decline in purchasing power for the Danes because precisely during that period prices have run faster than wages,” Kristensen wrote.

Danish business emergency network grows to 223 members
The number of companies and organizations in Virksomhedsberedskabet, Denmark’s business emergency preparedness network, has risen from 63 to 223 in just over 10 months.
Together, its members represent about 350,000 private-sector employees.
The network coordinates resources from private companies so they can help maintain essential services during serious crises.
“It is about having this conversation about what one already has on the shelves, and how it can actually be repurposed for a crisis and support critical infrastructure,” director Maja Broløs said.
Fitness centers could provide shelter, baby stores could supply essential products and department stores could make their buildings available. Companies participating in the network include SATS Denmark, BabySam and IKEA.
Virksomhedsberedskabet is part of a broader effort to strengthen Denmark’s emergency preparedness. In February, the government launched a total defence preparedness initiative and allocated 1.2 billion DKK to the area.
Broløs said more members would be needed to respond effectively to a nationwide crisis.
“If it is a major regional crisis, we are in a pretty good position. But if it is nationwide, then those are completely different numbers we need to reach,” she said.
The network aims to exceed 1,000 members by 2029. By 2028, it plans to be capable of mobilizing members’ resources nationwide within six hours.

DTU Aqua, the National Institute of Aquatic Resources at the Technical University of Denmark, will establish 40 fish nurseries and spawning grounds near Bornholm over the next five years.

`123456’ password used in massive Danish CPR data breach
At least three accounts at the company linked to a major breach of Denmark’s CPR register reportedly used the password “123456”, including an administrator account.
At least three user accounts at the Funen-based IT company Pays used the password “123456” when hackers gained access to Denmark’s CPR register, Politiken reports.
One of them was the company’s administrator account.
The breach exposed information linked to around 8.8 million CPR numbers. The CPR system is Denmark’s central civil registration database and contains personal information on people living or previously registered in Denmark.
The newspaper Politiken reviewed data from the breach that the hacker allegedly used to gain access to the system.
Jens Myrup Pedersen, professor at Aarhus University’s Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, described the company’s password security as “hopeless”.
“There is really no security, it is an open door. A password like ‘123456’ is one of the very first things you would guess if you took a list of common passwords,” he told Politiken.
“I find it hard to see that you could have worse security. It was a matter of time before things went wrong.”
Pays ApS, based in Odense, confirmed to TV 2 on Friday that it was the company whose access had been compromised.
“We can confirm that we are the company that has been subjected to an attack where our legal access to search for information in the CPR system has been abused,” managing director and owner Sophie Laursen said in an email to TV 2.
The hacker had access to the CPR register from 10 September for a total of 21 days and 17 hours.
An anonymous hacker told Politiken on Thursday that they were behind the attack and claimed gaining access had not been particularly difficult.
According to the hacker, access was initially obtained using a leaked password belonging to a former employee of a small Danish company. The hacker then allegedly created two computer programs to retrieve information from the CPR system and store it externally.
The hacker told Politiken that there were no plans to sell or publish the information.
Private companies and associations can be granted access to information in Denmark’s CPR register when they have a legitimate need, for example to obtain address information about customers or members.
According to Denmark’s Central Business Register, Pays ApS had two employees as of July 2026.
One in four Danish driving penalty points linked to mobile phone use
Danish motorists received almost 21,000 penalty points for using handheld mobile phones while driving last year – the highest number in four years.
Mobile phones are playing a growing role in traffic offences in Denmark.
In 2025, motorists received 20,910 penalty points on their driving licences for using a handheld mobile phone behind the wheel, according to figures from the police case management system POLSAS.
That means mobile phone use accounted for roughly one in every four of the 84,056 penalty points issued for traffic offences during the year.
The number of mobile-related penalty points increased by 7.5 percent compared with 2024 and reached its highest level in four years.
On average, police issued 57 penalty points every day for handheld mobile phone use.
Britta Bjerregaard, claims director at insurance company Alm. Brand, described the development as deeply concerning.
“Most people know full well that the phone should stay put while driving. Still, it can be tempting to just answer a call, reply to a message, or change the song,” she said.
“Traffic does not pause while you look at the screen.”
89 metres without watching the road
The Danish Road Safety Council considers inattention one of the major risks on Danish roads, with mobile phones posing a particular problem.
“The mobile phone takes an incredible amount of attention if you use it behind the wheel,” deputy director Karina Petersen said.
“If you look at the screen for four seconds at country road speed, you are driving 89 metres blind.”
However, Petersen cautioned that the increase in recorded offences does not necessarily mean that more drivers are using their phones.
The rise could also reflect more police checks or improved camera equipment used for traffic enforcement.
What are the rules in Denmark?
Using a handheld mobile phone while driving in Denmark results in a DKK 1,500 fine and a penalty point on your driving licence. An additional DKK 1,000 contribution to the Victims’ Fund is also charged.
The rule applies even when the car is stationary in traffic or waiting at a red light.
Drivers may briefly operate a phone if it is securely mounted, and using a vehicle’s built-in screen is also permitted.
The ban on handheld mobile phone use also applies to cyclists, electric scooter users and drivers of other motorised vehicles.

Hacker retained access to Danish CPR register for nearly 22 days before breach was discovered
An unauthorized user had access to Denmark’s national Civil Registration System (CPR) for nearly 22 days before authorities discovered the security breach, according to documents obtained by TV 2.
The access began September 10 and was stopped October 2, lasting 21 days and 17 hours.
However, preliminary investigations suggest the unauthorized activity ended September 20, approximately 10 days after it began, according to a report submitted by the CPR office to the Danish Data Protection Agency.
The Ministry of Research, Education and Digitalization announced Monday that personal information belonging to approximately 8.8 million people had been exposed, including names, addresses and CPR identification numbers.

Approximately 14 million CPR searches had been made using its access credentials.
“The number far exceeds the company’s customer base, and the company has indicated that they did not perform the lookups themselves,” the CPR office stated in its report.
Private companies and organizations can pay to access certain CPR information.
Research, Education and Digitalization Minister Christina Egelund of the Moderates party acknowledged that security measures had been inadequate.
She has requested a security review of the register following the breach.

The Danish government has presented a proposed budget for 2027 that prioritizes national security, with more money allocated to defence amid an increasingly tense international security situation.
The proposal, titled “A stronger defence of Denmark – a strengthened Denmark to defend”, was presented by Finance Minister Peter Hummelgaard of the Social Democrats (S) at the Ministry of Finance on Friday morning.

Two Danish business organizations are warning that a proposed tax of 200 DKK per cruise passenger could lead cruise ships to skip Danish ports, reducing tourism revenue for cities and smaller destinations.

The aim is to make cruise tourism contribute more toward the costs associated with ships, including pollution, noise and congestion.

DI and Dansk Erhverv argue that cruise visitors generate local revenue through port fees and spending at shops and other businesses.
Both organizations point to Iceland, where a similar tax was introduced before being reduced.

“There is no reason to believe that Denmark does not risk the same,” he added.

Tine Kirk, director of Danske Havne, described the proposed Danish tax of 200 DKK as “unreasonably high.”
“The cruise ships can very easily opt out of Denmark. We fear that the shipping companies will either bypass Denmark completely or concentrate their port calls in the largest cities,” she said in a written comment.

Hacker claims simple password allowed access to 8.8 million Danish CPR numbers
An anonymous hacker has claimed responsibility for accessing nearly 8.8 million Danish CPR numbers, telling newspaper Politiken that a weak password made the breach possible.
CPR numbers are personal identification numbers used in Denmark’s national Civil Registration System to identify residents and access public services.
The hacker told Politiken that the breach occurred on September 11 through a small Danish company with access to the CPR register.
According to the hacker, a leaked password belonging to a former employee allowed entry into the system. The password was reportedly “123456.”

The hacker provided Politiken with a file containing the CPR numbers.
The newspaper forwarded the file to Emil Hørning, an IT security expert at Danish cybersecurity company Defend Denmark.
Hørning said the hacker’s account appeared credible and that the described method was plausible.

Danish government proposes tighter senior pension rules to save 800 million DKK annually
The Danish government wants to change how workers qualify for senior pensions, potentially saving 800 million DKK annually by 2030, according to Jyllands-Posten.
Currently, people whose health limits their ability to work to 15 hours a week or less can receive a senior pension up to six years before reaching the state retirement age.
Their work capacity is assessed against their most recent job. Under the proposal, applicants would instead be assessed against all types of employment.
The Finance Ministry estimates savings of 200 million DKK in 2028, rising to 800 million DKK in 2030.
The proposal has divided political parties and organizations.
Anders Vistisen of DF, Dansk Folkeparti, the Danish People’s Party, said his party would oppose the changes.
“We are not going to cut for the worn-out,” he told Jyllands-Posten, citing Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen’s promises of more dignified retirement.
Ældre Sagen, Denmark’s senior citizens’ advocacy organization, also criticized the proposal.
Deputy Director Michael Teit Nielsen warned that applicants could face longer assessments to determine whether they could work in another profession.
However, Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry, Denmark’s main employers’ association, welcomed the proposal.
Deputy CEO Søren Kryhlmand said assessing workers against the entire labor market would allow those capable of other jobs to remain employed.
The government also plans to increase the separate Arne early retirement pension by approximately 3,000 DKK monthly. Its current maximum is 15,650 DKK per month.
Changing the senior pension scheme, introduced in 2019, requires agreement among the parties behind it before a general election.
Finance Minister Peter Hummelgaard is scheduled to present the budget proposal today.

These include cuts to the Danish student grant (SU), savings on senior pension payments, a proposed tax on cruise ships and further reductions in state administration costs.
The government must now negotiate with other parties in the Danish Parliament, the Folketing, to secure a majority for the 2027 budget.
The proposal includes a negotiating reserve of 500 million DKK annually from 2027 to 2030, which other parties can seek to use to fund their own priorities.

Iron Dome architect behind new counter swarm system
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:00:15 BST
23:00:15 KST

A defence technology company founded in Washington and Israel has unveiled what it describes as the world’s first native counter swarm defence system, designed from the outset to engage large numbers of drones at once instead of picking off one target at a time, according to the company.
Skapion said the system has been designed by its founding architect, General (retired) Pini Yungman, who was the architect of Iron Dome and formerly general manager of Rafael’s air and missile defence division. It is built around what the company calls a native many-to-many architecture, allowing multiple interceptors to engage multiple targets at the same time.
The company said the mobile, fully kinetic system is designed to engage more than one hundred targets simultaneously with an interception rate above 97 per cent, at a significantly lower cost per interception than conventional air defence. A vertical launch arrangement gives 360 degree coverage, and the company said it is designed for deployment from ground, airborne and maritime platforms.
Ido Bar-On, co-founder and chief executive, said: “The next generation of threats cannot be defeated by simply stacking yesterday’s air-defense solutions. A swarm is not just a larger number of discrete drones. It changes the dynamics of the engagement, the number of simultaneous decisions, the speed at which they must be made and the economies of every interception. Native Counter-Swarm means designing the entire system from day one for simultaneous mass engagement.”
Most air defence systems were developed to engage single targets or small numbers of them, which creates capacity and cost constraints against simultaneous mass attack. Skapion cited the wars in Ukraine and Iran, where it said legacy air defence is being saturated by swarms built to exhaust the defender’s magazines and budgets.
A Shahed type one-way attack drone costs tens of thousands of dollars. The interceptors fired at it can cost hundreds of thousands or more, and the magazine on any launcher is finite, so an attacker who can generate enough cheap airframes wins on arithmetic even when every shot is defeated. Bringing the cost per interception down, and the number of simultaneous engagements up, is what several companies on both sides of the Atlantic are now chasing.
At the centre of the Skapion system is an AI command and control architecture that fuses data from the company’s own sensors or from third party systems, evaluates and prioritises threats, allocates interceptors and manages engagements in real time. The company said it can run with full end-to-end autonomy or with a single human operator in the loop, depending on customer policy, and that the open, sensor-agnostic design allows integration with existing command and control and other counter-drone systems.

Happiness, not awe, may be the better emotional lever for openness to diversity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:00:14 UTC
23:00:14 KST

Feeling happy might do more to open people’s minds to social diversity than experiencing a sense of awe. New research published in the International Journal of Psychology indicates that a brief burst of joy leads to more positive attitudes toward inclusion, while awe has little effect. The findings challenge the expectation that awe would outperform other positive emotions in fostering acceptance of others.
Awe is an emotional response typically triggered by perceiving something vast and extraordinary that challenges a person’s usual understanding of the world, like a starry night sky or a towering mountain range. This feeling tends to diminish attention to oneself and make people view their surroundings as interconnected and meaningful.
Because awe encourages people to feel part of something larger than themselves, researchers have wondered whether it could help foster more positive attitudes toward diversity. The research, led by Jens Agerström, a professor of psychology at Linnaeus University, set out to test whether experiencing awe could encourage greater openness toward different social groups.
“Previous research has shown that people who are exposed to awe-inducing stimuli (e.g., vast and beautiful landscapes, moon landings) are more likely to act more prosocially (e.g., help another person),” Agerström told PsyPost. “We wanted to extend the research literature by examining whether awe can also make people more diversity oriented by, for instance, expressing more positive attitudes toward ethnic minority groups.”
Prior work provided reason to think awe might bridge social divides. For instance, a 2015 study found that awe shifts attention away from the self and promotes generosity: in one experiment, adults who watched an awe-inducing nature clip gave away more raffle tickets than those who watched a happiness-inducing one. Building on this, an experiment covered by PsyPost in 2023 found that experiencing awe, rather than joy, made children more likely to donate to members of an outgroup.
Happiness served as the comparison. Like awe, it is a positive emotion that tends to broaden people’s outlook and encourage helping and cooperation, which made it a solid benchmark. But the researchers expected awe to come out ahead, because awe is more strongly tied to a sense of a smaller self and a connection to others. Happiness also has a more mixed record: a 1994 study found that happy moods can lead people to rely more heavily on social stereotypes.
To test this, the researchers recruited 3,196 adults through the online research platform Prolific. The participants, who averaged about 40 years old, were randomly assigned to one of three groups, and each group watched a 28-second video designed to evoke a specific emotional response.
The awe group viewed majestic images of the universe, vast landscapes, and the Apollo 11 moon landing accompanied by sweeping music. The happiness group watched cheerful scenes of children playing and birthday parties paired with joyful music. A third, neutral control group saw everyday images of people studying or taking a coffee break with ambient background noise.
Immediately after watching the clips, the participants completed three questionnaires assessing their orientation toward diversity. The first survey measured general attitudes toward diversity, asking respondents if they value getting to know people from different racial or cultural backgrounds. The second survey measured diversity fatigue, which captures feelings of weariness or annoyance toward societal inclusion efforts. The third survey assessed social dominance orientation, which captures how much a person believes some social groups are simply inferior to others and that inequality between groups is acceptable.
The researchers found that the awe video did not measurably change how participants answered the surveys. On all three measures, the awe group’s responses did not differ statistically from those of the neutral control group.
Happiness, on the other hand, consistently shifted responses in a more inclusive direction. The neutral group’s average diversity attitude score was about 4.6 on a 6-point scale, and the happiness group scored about 0.08 points higher. The happiness group also scored 0.10 points lower on diversity fatigue (neutral group average: about 2.1 on a 5-point scale) and 0.15 points lower on preference for group hierarchy (neutral group average: about 2.4 on a 6-point scale).
When the two emotions were compared directly, the happiness group reported more positive attitudes toward diversity than the awe group and showed a slightly lower preference for social hierarchy, a difference that fell just short of statistical significance. The two groups did not differ reliably in diversity fatigue. The results held when the researchers excluded participants who finished unusually quickly or slowly and when they accounted for age and gender.
These shifts are small, but the authors note they emerged after a 28-second video and on measures thought to be fairly stable. The researchers suggest that happiness may promote social bonding, cooperation, and concern for others, which could carry over into more welcoming attitudes, though the study did not test this explanation.
“Brief inductions of awe do not seem to make people more diversity oriented,” Agerström noted. “Somewhat unexpectedly we found that happiness, which we used as a contrasting emotion, resulted in more positive diversity-related attitudes. Perhaps most interestingly, happiness seems to reduce social dominance, an individual difference characteristic capturing preferences for inequality and discrimination.”
The team’s biggest surprise, Agerström said, was “that happiness seems to triumph over awe when it comes to diversity.”
The lack of an effect for awe is in tension with research covered by PsyPost in 2025, which found that evoking awe through science fiction increased people’s identification with all of humanity. However, that earlier study measured a broad sense of global connection rather than specific attitudes toward demographic diversity and social equality.
“The main takeaway is that even a brief experience of happiness can make people more positive toward diversity and reduce diversity fatigue and social dominance orientation. Interestingly, the researchers did not find similar effects for awe,” said Ewa Palikot of the Institute of Psychology at the Polish Academy of Sciences, who was not involved in the study. “Like the authors, I expected awe to have a positive effect on attitudes toward diversity, especially since previous research suggests that awe can make people feel more connected to others and encourage prosocial behavior.”
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. The study relied on a very short video clip to spark emotion. A 28-second video can easily lift a person’s mood, but it might not be intense enough to trigger the profound, transformative sense of awe that comes from standing at the edge of the Grand Canyon. It is possible that a stronger, real-world experience of awe would yield different results.
The researchers note, however, that in a pretest with 125 people, the awe video produced about as much awe as the happiness video produced happiness, so a weaker emotional jolt does not obviously explain the difference. The main study itself did not check how participants felt after watching.
The researchers offer a few possible explanations for why awe fell short. Awe is a complex emotion, and although their awe video produced very little fear, it did produce some surprise, which the authors suggest could prompt a disorienting search for order rather than curiosity and openness. It is also possible the video did not create the “small self” feeling thought to drive awe’s social benefits, something the study did not measure.
“The size of the observed effects of happiness was small and it is important to examine whether happiness has the potential to shape diversity-oriented behavior in real-world settings,” Agerström said. “For example, can a more joyful workplace reduce prejudice?”
Palikot cautioned against generalizing the experimental findings to everyday life. “It is important to remember that these findings do not mean that happier people are necessarily more open to diversity in everyday life,” she told PsyPost. “The researchers looked at how a brief feeling of happiness affected people’s reported attitudes right after watching a video. We still don’t know how long these effects last or whether they influence people’s actual behavior.”
The participants in this study also started out with relatively low preferences for social hierarchy, which left less room for their scores to drop, although the happiness effect still emerged.
“As is always the case, findings need to be replicated before strong conclusions are drawn,” Agerström emphasized. “Also, other awe-inducing methods (than those we tested) may have the potential to increase diversity. Future research needs to look into this.”
Looking ahead, Agerström said the team’s long-term plan is “to unobtrusively study effects of awe and happiness on diversity behavior.” Unobtrusive studies observe what people actually do without making the measured behavior obvious, which can reduce the pull to give socially desirable answers.
“From a cross-cultural perspective, I would be curious to see whether happiness and awe have similar effects across cultures,” Palikot said. “Previous research shows that happiness and positive emotions are not viewed in the same way in different cultural contexts. For example, in some East Asian cultures, emotional balance is more valued, and strong positive emotions like happiness can also be associated with negative consequences. This does not necessarily mean that these emotions have different effects on social attitudes, but I think it would be interesting to explore.”
The study, “Happiness, Not Awe, Makes People More Diversity-Oriented,” was authored by Jens Agerström, Magnus Carlsson, and Towe Nilsson.
