4,700-year-old amphorae discovered near Türkiye's Kekova Island
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:23:05 UTC
22:23:05 KST

Ozcan Yildirim and Halis Sunnetci
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
Culture and Tourism Minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy announced on Wednesday that underwater excavations near Kekova Island in Türkiye's southern Antalya province uncovered amphorae dating back 4,700 years.
Ersoy shared details of the discovery on social media, describing the site as the world's oldest shipwreck.
"In the Blue Homeland, we are bringing to light the traces of the world's oldest shipwreck," he said.
The ancient vessels, believed to have transported olive oil or wine, provide evidence of maritime trade and cultural exchange across the Eastern Mediterranean, according to Ersoy.
Clay analyses suggest the amphorae may have been produced in workshops in the Jordan Valley, while similar examples discovered in Egypt, Troy and Crete point to extensive ancient maritime trade networks, he said.
Ersoy highlighted one amphora featuring nine distinct markings and two holes in its body.
The vessel, believed to have been used as a churn for making cheese or butter, could offer clues about whether ancient seafarers produced food during long voyages, he added.
The minister said Türkiye would continue uncovering Anatolia's maritime history while preserving underwater cultural heritage for future generations.

European Defense Commissioner Andrius Kubilius urged EU countries to keep defense spending high in the EU's next long-term budget — or face delays in the bloc's military ramp up.
"Please support the next [multi-annual financial framework] defense lines," he said, speaking at POLITICO's European Resilience Summit. Otherwise, he added, "we shall have less possibilities to build the defense systems we need to have, or to build our infrastructure in space. That's very clear."
His comments come as EU leaders are set meet Thursday to discuss the EU's next long-term budget from 2028 to 2034. Over the weekend, the Council of the EU's Irish presidency proposed cutting the Commission's original proposal by around 8% to appease a German-led camp demanding major cuts. The cuts overwhelmingly affect EU-wide priorities such as competitiveness, defense and foreign aid.

Lavrov arrives in Azerbaijan to participate in CICA summit

BAKU, October 14. /TASS/. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov arrived in Azerbaijan to take part in the Conference on Interaction and Confidence-Building Measures in Asia (CICA).
His plane landed in the country’s capital Baku, a TASS correspondent reported.
The Russian Foreign Ministry said the event will focus on further development of the organization. Besides, the participants will exchange opinions on pressing international and regional issues.
CICA is an inter-governmental forum for resolving key regional problems and developing cooperation between member states.
CICA has 28 member countries: Azerbaijan, Afghanistan, Bahrain, Bangladesh, Cambodia, China, Egypt, India, Iran, Iraq, Israel, Jordan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Kuwait, South Korea, Sri Lanka Mongolia, Pakistan, Palestine, Qatar, Russia, Tajikistan, Thailand, Turkey, United Arab Emirates, Uzbekistan and Vietnam.
Belarus, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, Saudi Arabia, Turkmenistan, Ukraine, the United States, the Philippines, and Japan, as well as the UN, the Arab League, OSCE (Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe) and the Parliamentary Assembly of Turkic-Speaking Countries have observer status.

Iran says container ship sank after striking naval mine in Strait of Hormuz
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:21:28 UTC
22:21:28 KST

Mohammad Sio and Ikram Kouachi
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy said Wednesday that a ship carrying more than 2,500 containers sank after striking a naval mine while attempting to cross the Strait of Hormuz through “an unauthorized” route.
In a statement carried by Iranian state broadcaster IRIB, the IRGC Navy said the vessel struck a mine and caught fire while attempting to navigate “a dangerous and unauthorized” passage through the strategic waterway.
The ship sank in waters south of the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday morning after the fire intensified, the statement said.
The IRGC Navy urged local vessels and fishermen to exercise extreme caution when navigating the area, warning that containers from the sunken ship were floating on the water's surface.
The statement did not identify the vessel, its flag or operator, or provide details on the fate of its crew.
String of maritime incidents
The reported sinking came amid a series of maritime incidents in the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran has imposed restrictions on commercial shipping, including designated transit routes and requirements for prior authorization from the IRGC Navy.
The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) reported on Wednesday two incidents from the previous day in which container ships were struck by unidentified projectiles in the Strait of Hormuz.
It said in a statement that a 50,000-ton vessel conducting an inbound transit, was struck at 1640UTC, while the other, a 19,000-ton vessel conducting an outbound transit, was hit at 1700UTC.
Both vessels reported minor damage and no casualties and were able to continue their passages, according to the agency.
Earlier this week, the IRGC Navy reported that several oil tankers had struck naval mines or come under attack while attempting to navigate unauthorized routes through the waterway.
Since April, Iran has imposed restrictions on maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, including designated transit routes and a requirement for prior coordination with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy.
On May 30, Tehran announced that vessels passing through the strait would be required to obtain prior authorization from the IRGC Navy, warning that transit without permission would constitute a “security threat.”
The developments come amid continued tensions between Iran and the US over navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s most important strategic routes for energy and commodity supplies and a key issue in negotiations between the two sides.
The war began with US and Israeli attacks on Iran on Feb. 28, before a ceasefire was reached in April. Clashes between Washington and Tehran later resumed as negotiations stalled despite the two sides signing a framework agreement in June.

Planned capacity of 12,000 interceptors a year, under 100 seconds to target: US firm pitches a low-cost drone killer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:21:17 UTC
22:21:17 KST

US defense-tech company CHAOS Industries introduced its Vespid interceptor family in Washington on 12 October, as the Association of the US Army (AUSA) annual meeting opened there, the company announced. CHAOS pitches the drones as low-cost defense against small and mid-size drones and one-way attack munitions. The company expects initial production capacity of 12,000 interceptors a year, expandable to 50,000 as demand grows.
The pitch lands as Russia moves its strike drones to jet power. Russia has stopped building the Geran-3, an earlier jet model, and makes about 3,000 faster Geran-4s and Geran-5s a month, Ukraine’s military intelligence (HUR) told Militarnyi in August. In mid-September, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said two Ukrainian companies had passed combat tests with interceptors against such drones, while 67 were still working on them. Ukrainian defense outlet Defense Express measured the new US drones against exactly that threat.
One to carry, one to launch in batches
The Mk 1 made its first public appearance on 12 October aboard a Forterra MESA autonomous ground vehicle, Army Recognition reported. It fires from tubes on launchers such as the 10-round ISS Aerospace HAL10. It takes midcourse guidance from CHAOS radars or external command systems, then an AI-assisted infrared seeker handles the final approach, the company says. An electric ducted fan rather than a jet engine drives it, which CHAOS says cuts cost and logistics compared with turbojet interceptors.
The smaller Mk 0 is man-portable and needs no operator input once fired, its product page says. Both are rated to reach a target in under 100 seconds, with a listed range of 10+ km. Defense Express called that range a serious weakness that more launchers around a city could offset.
Most drone interceptors ram or explode. This Ukrainian one just throws a net—six shots to a module
CHAOS lists cruise speeds of 100 m/s (360 km/h) for the Mk 0 and 150 m/s (540 km/h) for the Mk 1. Defense Express said those speeds may be enough to intercept the Geran-4 and Geran-5, which it puts at 340 km/h and 450–600 km/h.
Ukrainian makers say their interceptors already down jet Gerans
Wild Hornets’ Sting interceptors downed several of the slower jet-powered Geran-3s in November 2025. An unnamed Wild Hornets representative told NV, in an interview published on 22 September, that the company’s new interceptor had destroyed about ten Geran-4s and several Geran-5s in limited use. The company plans mass production within a month of finishing combat tests.
On 12 October, former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov said he and Pavlo Yelizarov, commander of Lasar’s Group, had created a new interceptor with troops and engineers. He said it downed two Geran-5s headed for Kyiv.
Crews from Lasar’s Group, which Fedorov has called a National Guard special unit, flew those combat tests, he said. Separately, Fedorov reported in August that a Ukrainian jet interceptor with a top speed above 600 km/h had entered combat testing.

NATO may eventually have to shoot down missiles over western Ukraine – former Polish security chief

NATO may eventually have to shoot down missiles over western Ukraine – former Polish security chief
Former Head of Poland’s National Security Bureau Stanisław Koziej said this in an interview with Ukrinform, answering a question about whether NATO countries would eventually be able to agree on shooting down missiles over western Ukraine.
According to Koziej, he has been proposing for the past two or three years that NATO establish what is known as an advanced missile defense zone, which would provide for the interception of at least dual-purpose missiles, including those capable of carrying nuclear warheads.
Koziej acknowledged that reaching consensus within the Alliance on such an initiative would be difficult. At the same time, he believes that further escalation of Russian aggression and an increase in the number of aerial incidents could force NATO to take this step.
Koziej separately emphasized the need to deepen security cooperation between Poland and Ukraine.
“We need to be as close to each other as possible. We should put political and emotional disputes aside as soon as possible and move toward pragmatic cooperation in the security sphere, especially along the border,” he said.
According to the former head of Poland’s National Security Bureau, the two countries need to exchange information about drones and missiles in order to respond to threats in advance. He also stressed the importance of ensuring an uninterrupted supply of aid to Ukraine and urged that historical disputes not be allowed to obstruct efforts to address urgent security issues.
Koziej described Russian disinformation as one of the problems that Poland currently finds most difficult to counter. At the same time, he said Poland is beginning to pool efforts in this area, including by establishing a special center to counter disinformation.
He expressed hope that the center’s work would help develop a strategy to protect society from Russian manipulation aimed at exacerbating divisions between Poles and Ukrainians.
As Ukrinform reported, unidentified debris was found on a beach in Karwia, Pomeranian Voivodeship, Poland. Preliminary findings indicate that it may be drone debris, but the type of object has not yet been established.

Masterpieces ranging from Mondrian to Warhol are among 200 artworks owned by Peter Simon, the British entrepreneur and founder of high-street fashion brand Monsoon.

Finnish cities pushing for mandatory school attendance law
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:18:17 EEST
22:18:17 KST

Helsinki and five other Finnish cities are calling for stricter laws on homeschooling.
According to Helsinki Mayor Daniel Sazonov (NCP), homeschooling should only be allowed in exceptional cases, for example for health reasons.
In practice, the cities are proposing that in-school attendance should be compulsory.
"Going to school is much more than just learning defined academic content, it is also a social process," Sazonov said.
Attending school is also a tool for integration, according to the mayor.
"In Helsinki, many pupils speak a language other than Finnish or Swedish as their mother tongue; it is also essential from an integration perspective that they are at school and part of the school community," he said.
Homeschooling is not a widespread phenomenon in the capital. Just over 200 children in Helsinki were being home-schooled this year, accounting for about 0.4 percent of all pupils. The number has increased in recent years, however.
A total of around 1,000 children in Finland are home-schooled, with many choosing the option for health or wellbeing reasons.
Last week, the Helsinki City Council decided to tighten supervision of homeschooled pupils.
Supervision abilities limited
But according to Sazonov, the jurisdiction of municipalities regarding homeschooling is limited.
Not all home-school instructors have accepted more active supervision, Sazonov said.
He noted that there have been no major problems with homeschooling in Helsinki. However, he did point to concerns raised by the Finnish Security and Intelligence Service (Supo) that homeschooling can carry the risk of promoting radicalisation.
Supo's national security review suggested that homeschooling could, over time, heighten security risks linked to social fragmentation. Its report warns that isolated educational settings may enable the spread of extremist ideologies, including radical Islamist or far-right teachings.
Helsinki University terrorism researcher Leena Malkki noted that Finland should not close its eyes to these concerns.
"Finland is a society built on trust. Supervision, and even support, is not always the strictest when it comes to home schooling," she said.
Tampere is among the cities calling for educational law change. But according to Tampere Deputy Mayor for cultural services, Anne-Mari Jussila, radicalisation risks are not the reason.
"I would prefer to see children among their peers at school, learning together with other children," she said.
Tampere currently has about 50 home-school pupils.
Jussila emphasised that radicalisation is not a problem in Tampere, even though it may be a problem elsewhere.
Newspaper Helsingin Sanomat on Tuesday queried parliamentary groups regarding homeschooling.
Left Alliance leader Minja Koskela told HS that Finland needs to introduce mandatory school attendance, arguing every child has the right to education.
Some Swedes have moved to the Åland Islands, attracted by the option of homeschooling.

Iran targets Starlink as ‘tool of war’ with hints of more internet curbs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:17:34 UTC
22:17:34 KST

Iran targets Starlink as ‘tool of war’ with hints of more internet curbs
One official claims satellite internet could erode online governance in Iran amid war with the US and Israel.
Tehran, Iran – Iranian authorities have pledged to continue a crackdown against satellite internet service Starlink, along with further restrictions on the global internet as the US-Israel war on Iran continues.
Elon Musk’s Starlink, which is free of the heavy filtering and restrictions imposed by Tehran, is outlawed in Iran on national security grounds. The use of satellite-based internet services and the distribution of Starlink terminals are subject to fines and imprisonment.
It is one of the many measures imposed by Iranian authorities since the United States and Israel launched strikes on the country on February 28, leading to a prolonged and economically punishing war between the countries.
Iran’s 90 million people have undergone two lengthy state-imposed global internet shutdowns in 2026 – for three weeks during nationwide protests in January and for 88 days at the start of the ongoing war.
Mohammad Amin Aghamiri, secretary of the Supreme National Cyberspace Council, described Starlink as a “tool of war” for enemies.
“It is a tool used for command and control by the enemy, for espionage and information gathering,” he said. “We have several systems for cutting off Starlink satellite terminals.”
He did not elaborate on what measures or devices were being used to block Starlink, but one was deployed during the January protests and authorities were prepared to share the technology with aligned countries.
Iran is among several countries that have banned or restricted Starlink due to national security concerns.
It has set baseline sentences of between six months and two years for using or possessing Starlink. Importing and distributing the devices carry jail terms of up to five years. If paired with national security or espionage charges, individuals can even face the death penalty.
Aghamiri has called on Iranians to use domestic platforms, supported by what the authorities call the National Information Network. He also backed a tiered-access model, which envisages protected international access for selected groups – such as traders, researchers and journalists – during periods of internet restrictions.
A Tehran-based internet and telecommunications expert, speaking on condition of anonymity, told Al Jazeera that Iranian authorities use a combination of measures to block Starlink connections.
This includes the use of multiple jammers with different configurations to disrupt services, along with spoofed GPS locations to slow new devices being set up. They can also identify Starlink-associated internet protocols if they connect to local applications and services.
Authorities also try to physically intercept terminals using patrols and drone searches, or raid locations selling the terminals.
In June, Israeli politician Naftali Bennett claimed that Israel had smuggled tens of thousands of Starlink devices into Iran when he was prime minister, between 2021 and 2022, to aid antigovernment protesters.
Since 2023, Iran has also pursued the matter at the International Telecommunication Union’s Radio Regulations Board, trying to pressure the US and Norway, which plays a role in the satellite network’s regulatory filings, to halt transmissions.
On October 4, Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs summoned the Norwegian ambassador in Tehran to protest against what it described as a failure to act over unauthorised Starlink operations.
During a governance meeting at the end of September, Deputy Technology Minister Mohammad Hafez Hakami had warned authorities that Starlink could signify “the last nail in the coffin of the [cyberspace] governance” of Iran if it becomes prevalent, due to the unfettered internet access it provides.
He pointed out that the government blocked the messaging app Telegram after the cost-of-living protests in 2017-18, but had to resort to a weeklong internet shutdown for the first time during the nationwide protests in 2019. WhatsApp and Instagram were blocked after the 2022-23 protests, which preceded the near-total shutdown during the January 2026 protests.
“If this trend continues, in the next crisis we will have to cut electricity, because Starlink, as a new tool of evading state governance, is fundamentally not even dependent on our network,” Hakami said.
Starlink has allowed Iranians to send out videos of the protests abroad since 2022 despite state restrictions. Tens of thousands of terminals are believed to have been smuggled into the country since, but exact figures are unknown.
Due to the risk of a state crackdown, limited availability and financial costs, most people still have no access to Starlink and must rely on Iran’s domestic internet, which blocks most international services and thousands of websites. US sanctions and banking restrictions further impede Iranians’ access to global services.
To circumvent the many roadblocks, most Iranians use virtual private networks (VPNs) and other methods that grant access to the free internet. But those tools can reduce connection speeds, prove costly or provide unsafe connections that jeopardise user data, and become harder to come by during periods of state-imposed internet blackout.
According to the authorities, more restrictions were possible in the future if the war intensifies, after a relative decrease in violence since the June memorandum of understanding, which eventually lapsed without a permanent ceasefire, between the US and Iran.
Government spokesperson Fatemeh Mohajerani told a news conference on Tuesday that state bodies were deliberately disrupting the internet ostensibly to protect people and national assets from cyberattacks.
“It is obvious that due to the importance of our databases and internet-based services, decision-making bodies are sometimes forced to bring down internet speeds,” she said. “We don’t deny this issue.”
The authorities claim that they have considered removing restrictions on some platforms, although no action has been taken yet.
State-linked media late on Tuesday released a policy and governance framework document that the cyberspace council’s Aghamiri said has been under consideration for nearly two years but remained confidential due to security concerns.
The document offered no timeline for reopening any platform, and media reports said implementation had been halted by wars and protests.
The document says Google Play and WhatsApp could potentially be unblocked, while YouTube and Telegram would have to negotiate with Iran and accept certain conditions determined by the authorities to be unblocked. Such steps by the social media giants are considered extremely unlikely.

In Confronting China, The West Needs Partners in Southeast Asia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:17:00 UTC
22:17:00 KST

Leaders from across Southeast Asia will be meeting in Manila on November 10 for the upcoming ASEAN summit. This is the same date on which the China-U.S. trade truce was set to expire. While the September 24 summit between Presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump has widely been characterized as “heavy on pomp and light on substance,” it did deliver one tangible benefit: more time. The extension of the trade truce offers Washington a modicum of breathing room. With that extra time, engaging leaders at the ASEAN summit should be top of the U.S. priority list.
Meanwhile, Europe is signaling a greater willingness to confront China’s unsustainable trading practices. The limits of this relationship must be managed, so that Western countries can reindustrialize and regain market share. However, that effort should not come at the cost of compromising economic partnerships with countries in Asia.
Since 2020, ASEAN and China have been each other’s largest trading partner. Furthermore, Southeast Asian countries have come to rely heavily on China as a provider of intermediate goods. Economic partners in Asia are restrained in their options; for them, some form of relationship with Beijing remains unavoidable. Thus, as the West seeks to shift its relationship with Beijing, it must not do so at the cost of Southeast Asian countries who are willing to cooperate toward a fairer global trade picture.
The U.S. and European position is valid. China is fully integrated into the global economy, and continues to be a manufacturing powerhouse. Problematically, however, Beijing seems to have abandoned its attempts at fixing its domestic consumption issues, as it also looks ahead to an impending demographic crisis. While the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) may outwardly project that it can sustain a globally competitive manufacturing sector, analysis of its economic outlook reflects that Beijing is far more restrained in the kind of development it can pursue. Crucially, however, China’s massive trade imbalance is likely a symptom of internal factors, and not a concerted policy objective.
The CCP’s legitimacy continues to be derived, in large part, from its ability to guarantee domestic economic prosperity. As such, the regime’s targeted growth rates can be observed as a political goal, with overarching implications for the economy. In past years, to achieve a consistent 5 percent growth rate, Beijing has leveraged subsidies and targeted sectoral investments, while growing its exports. The net effect of these policies has resulted in a competition crisis marked by diminishing returns amongst different industries, which is further compounded by the problem of weak domestic consumption. A less ambitious growth target this year, coupled with Xi’s call for “high-quality growth,” signals that there is pressure to restructure aspects of the economy.
Further, in the context of both global and regional trade, Beijing itself has shown an unwillingness to keep trade relationships entirely separate from its political ambitions. A study of China’s relationship with trading partners, published in 2020, has revealed a trend of politicization over time. Researchers considered the case of China-U.S. trade, and their findings were intriguing: “A positive shock to America’s exports to China leads to persistently worse relations with China… It stands to reason that Chinese officials genuinely do feel that China’s relations with the U.S. worsen when the U.S. increases its exports to China.”
Trade activities themselves are not necessarily immune from political effect, and Chinese officials are sensitive to greater market penetration by foreign countries. In effect, this also demonstrates Beijing’s unwillingness to work toward a balanced trading relationship, and its preference for exporting more than it consumes, unless it is importing energy and commodities.
Southeast Asian countries have no choice but to confront this reality. Despite Beijing’s territorial claims in the South China Sea, China’s neighboring states continue to seek agreement on economic issues where it is possible. Interdependence runs deep, as evidenced by China’s $296 billion trade surplus with ASEAN in 2025. There is simply no other option for Southeast Asian countries seeking to move up the global value chain.
This does not mean that these countries are unaware of Beijing’s coercion, or that they are not responding. Yet, with few international options, they are exposed to Beijing’s attempts at intertwining foreign aid with its regional ambitions. To that end, while simultaneously increasing its trade surpluses, China has also created parallel institutions such as the Belt and Road Initiative, the Silk Road Fund, and the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, which have been used as leverage to reward countries that support its political objectives.
It is a fundamentally positive development that the West is looking to take a stronger stance against China’s global trading practices, in pursuit of a more balanced relationship. This position opens the door to Western reindustrialization and stimulates a push for innovation, while harboring high domestic political support within democracies. However, both Washington and Brussels must not lose sight of the constrained position of Southeast Asian countries, which rely on Chinese intermediate goods to develop and rise within the global value chain. A plan to confront Beijing without subsequent outreach toward these same countries will sacrifice national imperatives for willing partners; and those are hard to come by.
For Brussels, an alternative would be its accession to the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP), with the goal of stimulating market access between the West and its Southeast Asian partners. For Washington, the fact that it has become ASEAN’s largest export market is a positive step, but subsequent policies should seek to displace China as the supplier of intermediate goods without punishing Southeast Asian countries seeking to develop away from Beijing.

FIFA is expected to propose distributing more than $6 billion back into football between 2027 and 2030, more than double the amount previously earmarked for the period, The Athletic reported Wednesday.
Under the proposal, each of FIFA's 211 member associations would receive $25 million over the four-year cycle, up from a planned $10 million, while each of the six continental confederations would receive $99 million.

Infantino is seeking reelection at the FIFA Congress in Rabat, Morocco, next March.

Ukrainians blast SpaceX limits on Starlink
Elon Musk’s SpaceX has disrupted Ukrainian drone missions by abruptly restricting the military’s high-speed access to the Starlink satellite network, according to officials in Kiev and frontline commanders. The complaints come as US President Donald Trump has ramped up pressure on Vladimir Zelensky to stop strikes on Russian oil refineries and hold a long-overdue presidential election.
The development was reported on Wednesday by Sergey Beskrestnov, Zelensky’s technology adviser, who claimed that SpaceX had imposed a speed limit of 100 miles per hour (160 km/h) on Starshield, its military-grade satellite communications service, without informing Kiev in advance. 
“Our defense forces were not notified of this restriction, and it has resulted in the disruption of several missions,” he wrote, adding that the move was clearly connected to the “current political situation.”
Later, he added that the curbs imposed on long-range missions are only part of the problem, as the restrictions also impact Ukraine’s interceptor drones, rendering them less potent in tackling Russia’s own strike UAVs.
The disruption was corroborated by four Ukrainian frontline sources cited by Ukrainskaya Pravda. According to the article, one commander provided footage showing two drones losing connectivity above cloud cover and becoming unable to complete their mission.
Ukraine’s 7th Air Assault Corps also confirmed serious operational problems, noting that satellite connections were dropping for 10–20 seconds at speeds of just 110–120 km/h, well below the reported 160 km/h limit. It also warned that slower-flying drones become more vulnerable to Russian air defenses, while aircraft used in mid-range strikes against Russian logistics could become impossible to launch or operate effectively.
Sergey Sternenko, a Ukrainian activist and former Defense Ministry adviser, suggested that SpaceX had acted at the request of the Trump administration. Neither Washington nor Musk has commented on the reports.
Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski also weighed in, addressing Musk directly. “Hey, Elon Musk, big man, are you playing politics with your products again?” he wrote on X. Poland spends approximately $50 million annually on Starlink services supporting Ukraine, and Sikorski had previously threatened to reconsider those payments after SpaceX announced roaming restrictions affecting Polish customers, a decision which was later rolled back.
Meanwhile, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Russia had no independent information about the reported restrictions but argued that “it would be better if remarkable technologies such as Starlink were not used for military purposes at all.”
Starlink has become a cornerstone of Ukraine’s military communications since the escalation of its conflict with Russia in 2022, with Kiev’s forces relying on the network for reconnaissance, logistics, and drone control. However, SpaceX has refused to enable the service for strikes deep inside Russia, with Musk reportedly believing that doing so would escalate the conflict.
The reported disruption comes as Trump has ramped up pressure on Kiev to stop attacking Russian oil refineries – something Zelensky said he was ready to agree to on the condition that Moscow stops targeting Ukraine’s energy infrastructure. The US president has also eased restrictions on Russian diesel exports following talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin, triggering Zelensky’s pushback.
Musk echoed Trump’s criticism of the strikes, writing on X that “Zelensky has gone too far.”
The Trump-Zelensky feud also turned personal, with the US president suggesting that Ukraine needs “a new president.” The Ukrainian leader’s presidential term ended in 2024, and he has refused to call a new election, citing martial law. Russia has since declared him “illegitimate,” arguing that his dubious status is a major obstacle to signing a binding peace deal.

Commandos build underground hospital near Glasgow
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:13:47 BST
22:13:47 KST

Commando engineers have dug and built an underground field hospital near Glasgow so that surgeons can resuscitate and operate on casualties below ground, in a trial drawing directly on how Ukrainian medics have been forced to work, according to the Royal Navy.
Soldiers of 24 Commando Royal Engineers spent six days building the facility at Barnsford Bridge, excavating around 243 cubic metres of rock and soil to create a space twenty metres square, about the size of one and a half tennis courts. Medical specialists from the Special Operations Surgical Team and the Commando Forward Surgical Group then used it to resuscitate and operate on simulated casualties during Exercise Strike Warrior in south west Scotland.
Chief Petty Officer Ellie Walls of the Commando Forward Surgical Group set out why the work is being done at all. “As an organisation we see the need to develop our ability to build, survive, work and live in these spaces as medics now are not always protected by the Red Cross and can be routinely targeted,” she said.
“We can look at the lessons learnt from Ukraine and other medical uses of the subterranean space but we have to start experiencing the issues for ourselves to really understand and work through the problem. When looking at using the subterranean space, we have to evaluate if the risks from being below ground outweigh the risks from being above ground.”
She added: “However, our demands can be quite specific, we have to take into account the needs of the casualty and ensuring the environment does not negatively impact their outcome.”
Lieutenant Michael Mathers, Access Troop Commander of 54 Commando Squadron, whose troops were given the task, said: “By designing, constructing, and handing over this facility, our troops gained first-hand experience of the realities of modern peer-on-peer conflict, where survivability, protection, and concealment are critical to success.
“Beyond delivering a unique capability, the project provided invaluable engineering training across multiple trades, challenging our soldiers to develop new skills and adapt established techniques to a novel environment.
“Equally important, it highlighted where we must continue to innovate, ensuring lessons identified are refined, shared, and integrated in future designs and shared across UK Commando Force and the Corps of Royal Engineers.”
Putting a clinical environment into what amounts to a hole in the ground threw up problems a tented field hospital never has to solve as soil contaminants, bacteria and pests all bear on whether a patient survives, and once it was handed over the medical teams worked out how to allocate power, how to move casualties through the compartments according to their injuries and how to move around at all.
Surgical teams are used to light, air circulation, plumbing, electricity and the room to move and resupply, none of which a trench offers, and the effect of working without them on the clinicians themselves came under examination too. “Whilst it has given us some answers it has generated a lot of questions and thoughts,” CPO Walls said.
“If we can prepare our equipment and people to work in such areas, we give our patients a better chance of survival.”
The Navy described the facility as a prototype, part of an effort to develop, trial and standardise subterranean facilities for use across the UK Commando Force and the Corps of Royal Engineers, with the intention of taking the concept through to full operational capability.
Small attack drones and loitering munitions have made the ground behind the front line as dangerous as the front itself, and both sides have pushed stabilisation points, casualty collection and surgery underground into cellars, dugouts and bunkers.

Iran and US on brink of war as Russian mediation falters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:13:33 UTC
22:13:33 KST

Breadcrumb
Iran and US on brink of all-out war as Russia fails to break diplomatic deadlock
Diplomatic efforts to ease tensions between Iran and the United States remain deadlocked despite continued exchanges of messages and mediation attempts, raising fears of a renewed military confrontation as both sides step up their threats and preparations.
Qatar and Pakistan have continued efforts to bring Tehran and Washington back to the negotiating table, but little progress has been made as tensions escalate in the Strait of Hormuz, where Iranian attacks on vessels attempting to use non-Iranian shipping routes have increased.
The diplomatic stalemate comes amid growing US threats and reports of a possible Israeli attack on Iran ahead of Israel's parliamentary elections on 27 October.
Iran, meanwhile, has placed its military on heightened alert, conducting new missile tests in recent days and threatening to unveil additional weapons.
Tehran has also warned Washington and regional governments that another round of war could trigger retaliation across a wider geographical area, including potential ground incursions.
The renewed fighting between Yemen's Houthi movement and Saudi Arabia has further complicated the regional situation, with observers linking the escalation to the wider confrontation between Iran and the US and Israel.
Russia's mediation efforts falter
Russia entered the diplomatic efforts around a week ago, with the Kremlin announcing that President Vladimir Putin had conveyed Tehran's proposals for ending the war with the United States to US President Donald Trump.
According to Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov, Putin discussed his forthcoming telephone conversation with Trump during a meeting with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian in Turkmenistan last week, on the sidelines of a summit of Commonwealth of Independent States leaders.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei said on Monday that Pezeshkian had clearly outlined Tehran's position to Putin, including its seven-day proposal for resolving the conflict and other issues surrounding the negotiations.
However, Baghaei stopped short of describing Russia as a formal mediator.
"Technically speaking, in the strict sense of the word, Pakistan and Qatar are still playing the role of actual mediators between Iran and the United States," he said.
He added that Tehran welcomed diplomatic efforts by friendly countries, noting that consultations with Moscow on the nuclear issue and other matters were longstanding.
Iranian analyst Ali Gholhaki told The New Arab that Russian diplomacy was proceeding with "weak and lacklustre steps".
He argued that Moscow was attempting to link efforts to resolve the Iran-US conflict with negotiations over the Russia-Ukraine war, hoping that both disputes could be addressed simultaneously.
This, he suggested, explained Russia's more active diplomatic involvement.
Gholhaki said Iran had demonstrated flexibility, but warned that the current regional military positioning suggested another war was considerably more likely than a diplomatic settlement.
He said a new wave of military escalation could erupt at any moment, although Washington appeared reluctant to become embroiled in a full-scale war before the US congressional midterm elections in November.
According to Gholhaki, the Trump administration would prefer to postpone any expansion of the military confrontation until after the vote.
What could another Iran-US war look like?
Iranian military analyst Mehdi Bakhtiari told TNA that another war was a strong possibility, although he expected any confrontation to be relatively short and extremely intense.
He argued that Washington might attempt another military campaign to secure concessions from Tehran and overcome the strategic difficulties it had encountered in its confrontation with Iran.
Bakhtiari said the US and Israel had already fought two wars against Iran, inflicting substantial damage and losses but failing, in his assessment, to achieve their strategic objectives.
Instead, he argued, they had encountered new challenges, particularly the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz and the resulting rise in global energy and fuel prices.
He suggested that another military campaign could differ significantly from previous confrontations, with attacks potentially concentrating on Iranian nuclear facilities and the country's southern regions.
A central objective, he said, would likely be securing the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.
Bakhtiari also warned that Iran had prepared new military strategies for such a scenario.
These could include intensified attacks on US naval vessels, particularly destroyers, following incidents in recent weeks in which Iranian forces had fired towards American warships.
He also raised the possibility of Iranian attacks against a larger number of US military bases across the region, particularly in the United Arab Emirates.
According to Bakhtiari, Iranian military planners believe that targeting US interests in the UAE could significantly increase the costs of further escalation for Washington.
He said Iran's military establishment had spent recent weeks rebuilding its missile and air defence capabilities in preparation for a potential confrontation at sea.
Bakhtiari added that both Iran's political elite and wider public increasingly regarded another round of fighting as likely.
Deep divisions over terms for peace
Masoud Foroughi, former editor-in-chief of the conservative Iranian newspaper Farhikhtegan, said the approaching US and Israeli elections were closely connected to calculations about the military confrontation with Iran.
Speaking to TNA, he argued that the war had not ended in the conventional sense but had instead changed its form and geographical scope.
From Tehran's perspective, he said, the conflict would end only when Washington accepted that military force could not fundamentally alter Iran's political system or its behaviour.
Washington, by contrast, was seeking what he described as Iran's complete surrender, whether through military pressure or diplomacy.
Foroughi said the gap between the two sides' demands was so wide that negotiations under current conditions were unlikely to bridge it.
He compared the situation to two parties standing 50 kilometres apart without any means of communication, arguing that even a distance of one kilometre would be too great for them to hear one another.
As a result, he said, the outcome would continue to depend largely on developments on the ground and each side's political, economic and social ability to withstand pressure.
Foroughi argued that the increasingly aggressive rhetoric from Washington and Tehran was intended to influence each other's strategic calculations.
Regardless of whether Trump intended to launch another direct military campaign before the November elections, he said, the administration was seeking to maintain sufficient pressure to force Iran to reconsider its position.
He concluded that diplomacy would only become effective when the costs of continuing the war became sufficiently high to compel Washington to halt its military campaign.

Ethiopian government forces reached the border with Eritrea on October 13 during a counteroffensive against rebels in the Tigray region, heightening the risk of a new armed conflict between the two countries.
Reuters reported this, citing six sources, including a diplomat, a conflict expert and people in contact with local residents.
According to the news agency, the Ethiopian army reached Zalambessa, a border town with a population of about 15,000 previously controlled by Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) rebels.

Amid the escalating tensions, the UN Security Council was scheduled to hold closed consultations on the conflict in the Horn of Africa on October 13.

According to local residents, Eritrean troops moved from Zalambessa through Adigrat toward Edaga Hamus. Witnesses reported convoys of dozens of trucks carrying troops and heavy weapons. However, the BBC could not independently verify these accounts.

One source of tension remains Ethiopia’s ambition to regain access to the Red Sea, which it lost when Eritrea gained independence in 1993. Eritrean authorities view Addis Ababa’s statements on the issue as a threat to the country’s sovereignty.

The Kiev regime’s harsh statements directed at US President Donald Trump will not help Vladimir Zelensky and will not contribute to accelerating a peaceful settlement: "The [negotiation] style of the Kiev regime’s representatives is well known to us and to the whole world. I don’t think spatting with the US president will help the Kiev regime in any way. At this point, it’s unlikely anything can help it. But the fact that this spatting does not contribute to accelerated progress toward a peaceful settlement is unequivocal."
Possibility of bilateral, trilateral meetings in China
A trilateral meeting in China between Russian President Vladimir Putin, US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping would be highly beneficial, but it remains unclear whether the leaders’ schedules will coincide: "There is a shared view that it would be good to hold such a meeting. But we do not yet know how well the leaders’ schedules align, and we do not yet know what the agenda for such a meeting might be. However, there is a shared understanding that it would be highly beneficial."
Nuclear arsenals are unlikely to feature on the agenda of such a meeting, should one take place: "Nuclear arsenals are not an appropriate topic to bring up."
Moscow respects Beijing’s position that China’s nuclear arsenal is currently incomparable to those of Moscow and Washington: "You know that our Chinese friends believe their nuclear potential is currently incomparable to the nuclear capabilities of Russia and the United States; they believe there is no subject for discussion. That is China’s position, and we respect it. Therefore, it is unlikely that this issue could be discussed in a trilateral format,"
A meeting between Russian President Vladimir Putin and his US counterpart Donald Trump has not yet been agreed upon, but if they happen to be at the same venue during the APEC summit in China: "No, not yet. But if they happen to be together in China, then, of course, one can assume that such a meeting will be discussed."
Reports on slowdown of Starlink for Ukrainian army
There has been no official statement from the US on the slowdown of the Starlink service for the Ukrainian armed forces, so it is too early to jump to conclusions: "How do we know this? This is just completely scattered information. ‘What if…’ Indeed, there is a lot of information suggesting that there are some restrictions on the provision of intelligence and early warning information about our missile launches. But, on the other hand, there have also been statements from Washington that the assistance is continuing."
"We need to wait for some more or less specific information here,"
"We don’t know what the US has done. How can we speculate about what it can or cannot do? We haven’t heard any official statements from representatives of [Elon] Musk’s company [which owns the service], nor have we heard any official statements from representatives of the Kiev regime on this matter."
"We’ve heard statements from [US President Donald] Trump that aid is continuing. Let’s analyze the information as it comes in and not rush to conclusions."
On Ukrainian settlement
Asked if Moscow had taken part in the consultations, the Kremlin spokesman answered in the negative.
Russia did not participate in consultations on a package agreement on resolving the Ukraine conflict, allegedly prepared by Washington, and so far has no plans to take part in any trilateral talks on the issue: "We don’t expect them at the moment. You know that the president said: after Ukraine tried to disrupt our elections, we will think about when to resume trilateral talks."
Moscow will decide whether to resume trilateral consultations on the Ukrainian settlement with Kiev and Washington at a later date and strictly in accordance with Russia’s national interests: "We will do so strictly in accordance with our national interests.".

Colombia opens embassy in West Jerusalem, defying global opposition

Colombia has opened an embassy in West Jerusalem, becoming the 10th country to establish an embassy in the contested city despite widespread international opposition to moves recognising it as Israel’s capital.
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar, Colombian Foreign Minister Omar Bula Escobar, and Moshe Lion, mayor of West Jerusalem, attended the opening ceremony on Wednesday, according to the Israeli foreign ministry.
Lion said Colombia had become the 10th country to relocate its embassy to West Jerusalem.
The move follows the restoration of diplomatic relations between the two countries in August 2026, after Colombia severed ties with Israel in May 2024 under its previous government.
Jerusalem remains at the heart of Israel’s dispossession of Palestinians and subsequent occupation of Palestinian lands and is widely regarded as one of its most sensitive issues.
While Israel claims the entire city as its capital, Palestinians view East Jerusalem, occupied by Israel since 1967, as the capital of a future Palestinian state, in line with longstanding international consensus and UN resolutions.
Israel illegally annexed East Jerusalem in 1980, a move that has not been recognised internationally.
In Resolution 478, adopted in August 1980, the UN Security Council rejected Israel’s measures seeking to alter the character and status of Jerusalem and called on countries with diplomatic missions in the city to withdraw them.
Most countries maintain their embassies in Tel Aviv or surrounding areas rather than Jerusalem, reflecting the city’s contested status and the international position that its final status should be resolved through negotiations.
The US, Guatemala, Honduras, Kosovo, Paraguay, Papua New Guinea, Fiji, Nauru, and Somaliland, which Israel alone recognises, are the only ones with embassies in West Jerusalem.

Uber has begun a trial of autonomous vehicles on the streets of Manchester as it looks to bring robotaxis to cities around the UK.

Uber said it was “excited to take this first step toward making this technology accessible to people across the UK”.
In social media posts, Verne said it had “started our autonomous vehicle testing in Manchester”, while Pony said there were “plans to bring robotaxis to the city” and that testing was under way.
The tests involve the company mapping the streets of the city in north-west England with a safety driver behind the wheel and no passengers.
Limited passenger services started last month in London, but with a safety driver in the front seat of cars supplied by Wayve under Transport for London’s licensing rules for private hire vehicles.

A critical report from London assembly’s transport committee this week called for the government to devolve authority over autonomous taxi services.
It said there was “considerable uncertainty about many of the claimed benefits of autonomous passenger vehicles”, and fears over the impact on public transport and congestion, as well as safeguarding and accessibility for disabled passengers.
There has been no official application to launch passenger services in Manchester so far.
A spokesperson for Transport for Greater Manchester said it wanted the city’s taxis to be the safest in the country.
“New technologies play an increasingly important role in the growth of our city region,” they said. “But they need to be introduced responsibly, safely and with real thought about what it means for our residents.
“Although no applications have been made to operate driverless taxis in the Greater Manchester, we’re aware of potential interest from companies to do so.
“Safety will always be our top priority, and we will need strong assurances that no vehicles will operate on our roads that pose any risk to residents.”
Uber said it expected to offering robotaxi trips in as many as 15 cities worldwide by the end of 2026, mainly in the US and the Middle East.

Turkish authorities appointed a government trustee to run pro-opposition broadcaster Halk TV, prosecutors said on Wednesday as police raided its Istanbul office, extending a crackdown on the opposition and prompting fresh concerns over media freedom.
The Istanbul Chief Prosecutor's Office said its financial crimes unit had conducted an investigation into Halk TV Chairman Cafer Mahiroglu over "bribery, tender-rigging, and laundering of assets derived from crime."
Prosecutors ordered the detention of 17 people, including Mahiroglu, and 11 have been detained, the statement said, with firms linked to Mahiroglu seized and the Savings Deposit Insurance Fund (TMSF) appointed as trustee.
Mahiroglu is currently outside Turkey and being sought by the authorities.
The channel's live broadcast was cut at 6:30 a.m. (0330 GMT), after which pre-recorded material began airing. "Hundreds of police" were inside, and entry into the premises was not being permitted, it said on its website. A Halk TV programmer said negotiations with the trustee delegation to continue broadcasts had yielded no results.
The move comes days after Kemal Kilicdaroglu, the court-appointed chairman of Turkey's former main opposition Republican People's Party (CHP), publicly criticized Halk TV and Mahiroglu over its coverage. He said the CHP had complained to Turkey's RTUK television watchdog but no action was taken.
Kilicdaroglu lost the CHP leadership to Ozgur Ozel in 2023, but was reinstated by a court ruling in May amid an unprecedented legal crackdown on the opposition. He has refused to call new party elections, while his rhetoric has become more aligned with the government.
The CHP later criticized Wednesday's raid on Halk TV as a "shameful" example of "systematic pressure" on opposition media.
The European Parliament's Turkey rapporteur Nacho Sanchez Amor criticized the move on X/Twitter, saying that the government was "not happy with controlling 90% of media" and was "aiming for the 100%."
"Amidst detentions of journalists & broad online censorship, freedom of media & expression will soon be just a memory."
Crackdown on press freedom
Wednesday's move makes Halk TV the fifth major Turkish news outlet to have a trustee appointed, following similar legal decisions for Flash TV, Eko Turk, Haberturk and Tele1.
Authorities have appointed trustees in recent years to take over many municipalities, previously seizing those run by pro-Kurdish opposition mayors in southeastern Turkey and more recently major municipalities - including Istanbul and its districts - won by the opposition, prompting some mayors to join President Tayyip Erdogan's ruling AK Party.
Rights groups and Western countries have criticized the government over its use of the judiciary, its record on rights, and its crackdown on press freedom in recent years as it establishes tighter control over mainstream media. Several opposition or independent outlets have experienced access bans, fines, and other restrictions.
The government says Turkey's judiciary is independent. It has not commented publicly on the latest moves against Halk TV.
Opposition head decries Turkish authorities as 'impotent, cowards'
Ozel, who now leads the main opposition New Party, condemned Wednesday's move, as did the pro-Kurdish opposition DEM Party.
"Dawn raid on a television channel, appointing a trustee — only dictators would do such a thing," Ozel said on X. "Those who appoint trustees to municipalities and trample the people's will have now appointed a trustee to Halk TV, watched by millions. Because THEY ARE IMPOTENT AND COWARDS!"
The raid on Halk TV came as Erdogan's biggest political rival, jailed Istanbul Mayor Ekrem Imamoglu, was expected to start his defense on Wednesday in a sweeping corruption trial of more than 400 defendants linked to the Istanbul municipality.
"On such a day, a trustee was appointed to Halk TV, one of the most-watched news channels in Turkey," Turkish Journalists' Union Chairman Gokhan Durmus told Reuters, adding Turkey was facing another "dark chapter" in terms of freedom of press and expression.
"It remains unclear what the fate of our 200 colleagues working inside (Halk TV) and its editorial line will be from now on."

From Protest to Procedure
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:10:56 EEST
22:10:56 KST

Oleksandr Larin, Founder of ‘Idealist Media’ platform, General Secretary of the Basketball Federation of Ukraine (2011-2015), Deputy Minister of Sport of Ukraine (2010)
Recently Ms. Stella Zakharova, Olympic champion and Vice President of the Ukrainian Gymnastics Federation submitted a report to the Gymnastics Ethics Foundation, the body responsible for ethical and disciplinary matters within the World Gymnastics system. The report is based on documented actions by Russian gymnastics structures in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine. It was prepared not as a political declaration, but as a legal case: facts, documents, federation rules, procedure, and a request that the competent body provide an assessment.
At first glance, this is a story about gymnastics. To me, it is much more than that. It tests whether Ukraine is capable of moving from the model of “we object your decision” to a different one: “here are your rules, here are the actions of your member — explain whether the two are consistent.” And it brings us back to a broader question: why has Ukraine still not built a systematic legal mechanism for protecting its interests in international sport?
Several years ago, we already proposed a different approach: not to wait for an unfavorable decision and not to start looking for lawyers after the problem has already emerged, but to work proactively — through statutes, regulations, disciplinary procedures, the rights of national federations, and, when necessary, the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS).
In 2023, after the Ms.Olga Kharlan case, Mr.Taras Samborskyi said it directly: the rules of international federations must be worked with before a conflict, not after one. In December of that same year, the NGO Sports Context presented the Office of the President and the Ministry of Youth and Sports(Ministry) with a concept for reforming the system: the state should stop merely reacting to consequences and instead create mechanisms that function regardless of who happens to occupy the minister’s office.
The problem was visible, and an alternative was proposed, but it never became a system. That is why the principle we proposed to the state of Ukraine is now being implemented, together with the lawyers and experts of Sports Context, in our work with Ms.Stella Zakharova. There is a concrete case, a procedure, and eventually there shodw be a result.
The State and International Sport Use Different Tools
The state operates through diplomacy, political statements, sanctions, intergovernmental relations, and decisions by public authorities. International sport operates through its own statutes, disciplinary codes, ethical rules, appeals procedures, membership rules, and dispute-resolution mechanisms.
Even if Ukraine is one hundred percent right politically, an international federation is not legally obligated to act the way we demand. A minister of Youth and Sports can make a statement, the Foreign Ministry can send a diplomatic note, partners can support Ukraine — but in the end, the federation will open its own statute. If we do not speak the language of that statute, political legitimacy risks remaining nothing more than a statement.
A Different Strategy Could Have Been Chosen Earlier
After the start of the full-scale invasion, the focus on the political and diplomatic isolation of Russian sport was logical and produced results. But over time, the limitations of that strategy became clear: “neutral status,” the return of Russian athletes, and the gradual rollback of restrictions. And each time, Ukraine was reacting to a decision that had already been made.
Mr.Matvii Bidnyi has been part of the leadership of the Ministry of Youth and Sports since 2020 — long enough to see the weak points of the existing strategy and to hear an alternative. That alternative existed: move from a reactive model to a systemic one — work through law, procedures, the internal mechanisms of international federations, and support Ukrainian national federations as full-fledged actors in international sport.
That transition never happened. First, an international institution makes a decision; then Ukraine looks for a way to stop it, change it, or appeal it. At this point, the problem is no longer a single decision. It is the architecture of the policy itself.
The Difference Between Protest and a Legal Problem
A political statement can be ignored. A properly framed legal question is much harder to ignore.
“Do not allow Russian athletes to compete because Russia is waging a war” is a strong moral and political position, but it still leaves a federation room to choose. A very different question is: “Do the actions of your member comply with your own rules?” At that point, the federation no longer has to be persuaded to support Ukraine; it has to explain how it applies its own rules.
That is the logic behind Ms.Zakharova’s case: not “support us,” but “here is the fact, here is the document, here is the action of your member, here is the relevant rule — now provide an answer.” Political volume is replaced by a legally structured contradiction.
And This Is Where Sports Context Has to Be Mentioned
The evidentiary and strategic architecture of this case is being developed with the participation of experts from the NGO Sports Context — the same organization that previously proposed this kind of work to the Ministry.
In January 2025, as head of the NGO, I signed a memorandum of cooperation with Mr.Matvii Bidnyi. We saw it as an opportunity to move from conversations about reform to joint professional work. A permanent mechanism for that cooperation never took shape.
We were ready to cooperate, but not to serve as expert decoration, not to endorse decisions that had already been made, and not to participate in a process where an expert is expected to agree rather than maintain an independent position. We were ready to work on changing the rules. That model turned out not to be needed.
The work moved outside the Ministry. We are now implementing the same approach directly within sport. Ms.Stella Zakharova’s case is one example — and, at the same time, an experiment: political reaction after a problem emerges versus a legal sequence of fact, evidence, rule, and procedure.
What a “Legal Approach” Means in Practice
First, the fact is established. The evidence is verified. The applicable rule is identified, along with the competent body, the applicant’s procedural standing, and the relevant procedure. Only then does political and diplomatic support come into play.
If a Russian sports structure is operating in occupied Ukrainian territory, the first question should not be, “What statement will the Ministry make?” It should be: what rule may have been violated, who has standing to submit a complaint, to which body, within what deadline, under what standard of proof, and with what documents?
That is when politics strengthens the law instead of replacing it.
The State Should Not Do the Federation’s Job
This should be part of the state’s sports infrastructure. Today, we see two extremes: either the state treats federations as if they were its own administrative departments, or it suddenly remembers the autonomy of sport and says, “that is your problem.” Both approaches are wrong.
The state should not draft an appeal to an international federation on behalf of a national federation. It should provide access to sports lawyers, an evidence base, systematic monitoring, diplomatic support, and, where necessary, funding for complex international proceedings. Its role is not to manage the federation, but to strengthen its capacity.
The responsibility of the relevant minister is not to produce the best statement after the latest decision by World Gymnastics, the IOC, or another international federation. It is to make sure the system is working before that decision is made.
Developments should be monitored continuously, documents should be collected, and a legal team should immediately determine whether there is a potential violation, whether a procedure exists, who has standing, and what further action is available. A national federation should not have to start from scratch every single time.
That is exactly what we proposed. So the question is not whether the minister knew about another approach. He did: there were meetings, proposals, a concept, and even a memorandum of cooperation.
Why did this approach never become part of state sports policy?
What Such a System Should Actually Do
It should monitor not only the eligibility of Russian athletes, but deeper processes as well: which Russian sports federations incorporate organizations from occupied territories into their structures; where Crimea, Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia, or Kherson regions appear in official Russian sports documents; who participates in competitions; who is included on judging lists; which regional organizations are recognized; which appointments are made; and what changes are introduced into statutes.
Every fact should pass through a legal filter: what is legally significant here, what rule may have been violated, which body has jurisdiction, and what procedure is available? That is what professional policy looks like.
We are Not Saying the Ministry and the NOC Did Nothing
There were statements, diplomatic efforts, and legal steps. The question is why they never became a permanent system. Why does law usually appear only after a crisis? Why is there no unified evidence infrastructure? Why are Ukrainean national sports federations so often left alone with the problem? Why were the experts who proposed such a model several years ago never integrated into a permanent mechanism?
Against that background, Ms.Zakharova’s case is particularly revealing: a concrete legal process is now being prepared with the same expert team whose potential for systematic cooperation the Ministry failed to recognize.
The NOC Could Also Play a Different Role
The National Olympic Committee of Ukraine can be an important institution precisely because it is not a government body, yet it operates inside the international Olympic movement. It could accumulate legal practice across sport federations, maintain expertise in international procedures, and create an early-response mechanism. But the Ukrainean NOC should not turn into a second Ministry. Its strength lies in its autonomy.
A Strong Sport Federation Is a Resource, Not a Problem
The state does not need a weak sport federation that is easy to control. It needs a strong one — one that knows its rights, has the necessary expertise, and is capable of acting within its international federation.
A government official often has no procedural standing there, while a national federation does. A minister can send a letter; a federation, under certain conditions, can initiate a procedure. That is why sports autonomy is not a threat to the state, but an additional channel for protecting the national interest.
The Most Important Part of Ms.Zakharova’s Story Is Still Ahead
I do not know what decision the GEF will make, and no one has the right to guarantee the outcome: legal results are not announced in advance.
But already today, a small team of athletes, lawyers, and experts is doing what we proposed several years ago should become part of a state system: gathering evidence, verifying facts, identifying rules, determining procedures, working with a person inside the sports system who has the appropriate standing, and building a legal case instead of merely creating a media event. To a significant extent, this is happening outside the state system.
So my question to the Ministry — and personally to Mr.Matvii Bidnyi — is not whether they support Ms.Stella Zakharova’s report. That is secondary. The real question is why an expert resource capable of building cases like this never became part of the system for protecting Ukrainian sports interests, especially when this very approach had been proposed to the Ministry in advance.
From Asking for Support to Becoming a Legal Actor
Ukraine has already learned how to explain to international sport why its decisions are unfair. The next step is to learn how to work with the system itself: its statutes, regulations, procedures, competencies, disciplinary bodies, and CAS.
And to move from the position:
“Support us because we are right”
to another:
“Here is the fact. Here is the evidence. Here is your rule. Here is the procedure you created. Now apply your own rules.”
To me, that is what real agency means.
For the Ukrainian state, the principle is simple: do not manage sport in place of sports institutions; create the conditions in which those institutions are capable of professionally defending both their own rights and Ukraine’s national interests.
This is the logic we have been advancing for several years at Sports Context. The Ministry had the opportunity to use this expertise; at one point, we even formalized our cooperation, but no lasting working relationship emerged. The expertise did not disappear. It simply began to be implemented directly through actors within sport.
After the Ms.Stella Zakharova case, I would leave two questions.
First: what is more effective for the state — to control an independent expert community, to distance itself from it, or to learn how to use it as a normal part of a modern sports ecosystem?
And second: if the approach we proposed to the Ministry several years ago is now beginning to work without the Ministry, perhaps it is finally time to look not at who proposed it, but at the approach itself.

WASHINGTON – UVision unveiled new launch and ISR integrations at the Association of the United States Army (AUSA) Annual Meeting & Exposition in Washington, DC, expanding its portfolio beyond loitering munitions with a networked sensor-to-effect architecture built around its CORTEX mission-management system.
The company displayed an eight-canister launcher for the Hero120 alongside new airborne intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) links designed to tie sensing and strike nodes into a single operational loop.
The Multi-Canister Launcher, shown in an eight-round configuration, is designed for remote operation and can be deployed on mobile, fixed, or containerized platforms across land and maritime environments. Itzik Huber, general manager of UVision, told Defense & Tech by The Jerusalem Post at AUSA that the containerized solution can hold up to 20 Hero-120 or Hero-400 loitering munitions.
Integrated with CORTEX, the launcher operates as part of a distributed network connecting surveillance assets, decision tools, and precision-strike capabilities.
At the exhibition, UVision promoted persistent border defense as one application with launch nodes positioned along extended border areas and tied into CORTEX with ISR platforms, enabling continuous monitoring and rapid response across multiple sectors.
“We have changed the concept to a multi-layer, multi-solution instead of a single solution for a single soldier,” Huber said, explaining that one soldier can now strike several targets rather than just one.
At the exhibition, the company also demonstrated an expanded sensing layer through the integration of Wayland Autonomy’s IRIS airborne ISR payload with Tactical CORTEX.
IRIS is a compact, platform-agnostic airborne ISR payload that provides wide-area surveillance and onboard target generation, including in GPS-denied environments, allowing UVision to fuse airborne sensing with its growing portfolio of launchers and effectors across the Hero, Viper, and Peregrine families.
“It’s not just about having more effects in the field. It’s about having them where you need them, when you need them, and giving forces the flexibility to use the right capability for the mission,” said Dr. Ran Gozali, CEO of UVision. “That’s what we’re focused on: bringing sensing, mission management, and a broader range of effects together in a way that gives forces more options and greater operational flexibility.”
Expanding global footprint
Headquartered in Emek Hefer, UVision has a strong foothold in Israel, India, and the United States, where it is continuing to expand its footprint. The company’s Hero-120 is supporting the army’s Lethal Unmanned Systems program, and Hero-90 is participating in the Low Altitude Stalking and Strike Ordnance effort. The company is also building out domestic manufacturing, integration, and training capacity as it moves toward a more comprehensive mission-solutions role.
The war in Ukraine has forced European governments, that for years have neglected their defenses, to recognize that major conflict on the continent remains a reality. That has led European nations to accelerate their investment in autonomous weapons and unmanned systems.
And the wars that have been raging in Europe and the Middle East have fundamentally altered battlefield requirements. Huber argued that autonomy and artificial intelligence will be among the most consequential technologies shaping future conflicts.
"AI and autonomy will be more influential on future battlefields," he said.
And with that, UVision sees a future battlefield built around layered, networked capabilities rather than single platforms. According to Huber, "It's a different way of thinking. It's a more complex, holistic solution."
