NAD and CDS want capability delivered faster as DSEI 27 launched
The National Armaments Director and the Chief of the Defence Staff urge faster capability delivery, greater innovation, and improved readiness.
- Rupert Pearce and Chief of the Defence Staff (CDS) Air Chief Marshal Sir Richard Knighton have jointly launched DSEI UK 2027, under the theme Delivering the Integrated Force.
- National Armaments Director Rupert Pearce has warned the UK and its allies have until “the end of 2030, at best, to deter and be ready to fight”.
- DSEI UK, the flagship biennial defence exhibition, is expected to attract 65,000 visitors and up to 1,700 exhibiting companies to ExCeL London in September 2027.
National Armaments Director Rupert Pearce, and Air Chief Marshal Sir Richard Knighton KCB, Chief of the Defence Staff, have jointly launched DSEI UK 2027: Delivering the Integrated Force.
Mr Pearce, who is responsible for defence acquisition and industrial capability, warned that the UK and its allies have just over four years to prepare for conflict.
Rupert Pearce, National Armaments Director, said:
  This is the time for us to focus on accelerated delivery. We have until the end of 2030, at best, to deter and be ready to fight. DSEI UK is a perfect time for the different stakeholders to come together and to figure out how we can do this together at pace.
Setting out his approach to building up the UK’s defences by creating “an innovation engine which horizon scans for new technologies and capabilities, advances them and matures them”.
Mr Pearce explained:
  We need to build our core capabilities in a way which allows them to be infused with future innovation.
That is the perfect discussion to have at DSEI UK with all the stakeholders together: military, industry, procurement agencies, innovators and the finance community… If we get that right at DSEI UK we will position the UK Armed Forces in a vanguard of being the most innovative armed forces in the world.
CDS and Mr Pearce have issued a clear challenge to the defence sector, across UK and allied nations, as plans for DSEI UK 2027 were unveiled.
CDS, the most senior UK military officer, explained that the UK and its allies were in a race with potential hostile states to gain the battlespace advantage as tensions rise across the globe. Speaking about plans for the event, CDS warned of the need for nations to prepare at speed.
Sir Richard said:
  Fundamentally this is a race, we have to be faster and better than our adversaries. That is going to happen if we can bring together industry, science and technology and the war fighters as well as those responsible for acquisitions and that is what DSEI does.
DSEI UK is the flagship, biennial defence event that is expecting 65,000 visitors and sees up to 1,700 companies showcase developed and in-service capability to the global defence market of military buyers.
DSEI UK 2027 takes place from 7–10 September 2027 at ExCeL London.

Lufthansa to become new TAP shareholder, says Portuguese government
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:22:39 UTC
21:22:39 KST

Portugal has chosen Lufthansa to buy a 44.9% stake in TAP, completing the first phase of the airline’s privatisation. The deal still needs regulatory approval.
The Portuguese government announced after Wednesday's cabinet meeting that German carrier Lufthansa had been chosen to buy a 44.9% stake in TAP as part of the Portuguese airline’s privatisation.
"The government is successfully bringing to a close the first phase of the privatisation of our national airline. A process conducted with strict respect for competition, a stringent approach to negotiations and complete transparency vis-à-vis the Portuguese public," Portuguese prime minister Luís Montenegro said.
The prime minister then announced that, after assessing the bids, the government had opted for the Lufthansa Group, "whose financial offer is 16% higher than the rival proposal and carries a lower degree of uncertainty."
The transaction will bring in "€1.201 billion in this first phase" and the state will retain a majority stake of 50.1% in the company. "Lufthansa will be responsible for executive and operational management," he said.
"This is an offer that gives the airline a total valuation of €2.552 billion. A figure far above the independent valuations put forward a few years ago or even just a few months ago," he added.
Montenegro also stressed the "ambitious strategy" in the aviation sector, particularly when it comes to airport infrastructure.
As a result, "we are ensuring the growth of TAP, the growth of the fleet, the growth in passenger numbers, the growth in destinations and routes, and also the growth in investment, not only in TAP but across the entire aeronautics sector in Portugal," he said.
The proposal will support further investments, including €500 million to set up a new pilot training school in Tancos, an innovation centre in Aveiro and a corporate services centre, in addition to the already announced investment by Lufthansa Technik in Santa Maria da Feira.
Montenegro also pointed to plans to create jobs. "We are envisaging 3,000 associated jobs linked to TAP's projected growth and a total of 5,500 direct and indirect jobs across all these investment initiatives in our country."
Miguel Pinto Luz, minister for infrastructure and housing, set out the offer in detail, highlighting plans to expand the fleet to 117 aircraft by 2035 and 130 after 2035. Up to eight Airbus A350-900s are also due to be transferred to TAP from 2030 onwards.
The proposal also includes investment in Francisco Sá Carneiro Airport, the strategic base for the entire operation, as well as in Faro Airport and the airports in Portugal’s autonomous regions.
At the end of September, Air France-KLM and Lufthansa submitted their respective final bids to acquire 44.9% of the Portuguese airline's share capital, according to Parpública, the company that manages state holdings.
A further 5% of the company’s shares are reserved for employees. However, under the decree-law on TAP's privatisation, published in August and cited by Lusa, the chosen private investor — in this case Lufthansa — may also buy any shares not bought by employees. The state will retain the remaining 50.1%.
According to Portugal's business press, TAP posted a loss of €99.2 million in the first half of 2026, 40% higher than a year earlier.
The finance minister, Joaquim Miranda Sarmento, said last week that the privatisation process would only be concluded in 18 to 24 months, in 2028, after approval from the European Commission.

An Israeli security official assessed Wednesday that Israel is unlikely to launch a preemptive strike against Iran before the elections. At the same time, Israeli authorities have heightened their alert level amid concerns that Tehran or its proxies could attempt to interfere with the vote by launching an attack.
Israel has conveyed warnings that if Iran "makes a mistake," it will face an unprecedented Israeli strike.
An Israeli official said that, as in the past, everything depends on what U.S. President Donald Trump wants. Without his approval, Israel would be unable to attack Iran. For now, Trump appears to remain undecided and is weighing his options.
"There is an understanding that without a U.S. ground operation, there is no chance of achieving anything different or new," another Israeli official said. "Repeating more of the same before the U.S. elections would be a political disaster for Trump.
"We also have to consider the possibility of a miscalculation. The Iranians could believe Israel is about to attack and try to strike first."
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu appeared to lend some support to those assessments. Asked in an interview with Army Radio about the possibility of a preemptive strike on Tehran before the elections, Netanyahu said, "I don't think the timing is convenient for us."
Overnight, Trump threatened another major attack on Iran amid growing tensions in the Strait of Hormuz.
"Wait till you see what we do to Iran. We're going to we're going to do a number. Wait till you see," the U.S. president said during a campaign rally in Alaska.
His remarks came after he said last week that he would not launch another attack on Iran before the U.S. midterm elections on November 3.
On Tuesday, Netanyahu toured the seam zone along the West Bank in Samaria, where he again warned of a possible "turning of the guns," referring to a scenario in which Palestinian security personnel turn their weapons against Israeli forces.
"Our enemies are thinking about testing us in the days leading up to the elections," he said. "I warn them that we are prepared for every scenario, including what is known as 'turning of the guns.'"
Recently, IDF Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir warned senior U.S. administration and military officials that an escalation with Iran could lead to the postponement of Israel's elections, scheduled for October 27.
During those discussions, Zamir raised serious concerns about the political and security consequences of another direct confrontation with the Islamic Republic.
According to a source familiar with the discussions, Zamir warned that a military escalation at this stage could force Israel to postpone its general elections.

Pope's cancer diagnosis leaves Catholics questioning what comes next
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:22:17 BST
21:22:17 KST

Pope's cancer diagnosis leaves Catholics questioning what comes next
- Published
Vatican transparency about papal health has come a long way from the secrecy of the past.
But that does not mean Catholics were prepared for such seismic news about cancer and removal of a large section of Pope Leo XIV's lung - even after he announced on Sunday that doctors had discovered a nodule.
On Tuesday, the 71-year-old was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma following 90-minute surgery to remove a lower lobe of his right lung.
Part of the shock has, of course, been because there had been few signs until now that concern was needed about any imminent risks to the Pope's health.
A member of the Order of St Augustine, a saint who placed great importance on developing good habits, the Pope is known to place great importance in good habits, including when it comes to health and fitness, such as weekly games of tennis.
Now, with so many unknowns about the pontiff's prognosis and what treatment he might need, questions swirl around what may have to change in his routine, and for how long.
Certainly, given the dangers surrounding air travel soon after lung surgery, and the high altitude of some of the stops involved, a November trip to South America – including to Peru, the country Pope Leo called home for more than 20 years – may be in doubt.
His predecessor, Francis, once wrote that he had started his papacy thinking he might only have a few years in the role, having already suffered health complications throughout his life.
As such, it was clear that he was intent on making waves quickly and implementing what some saw as fairly radical change in the Church at a swift pace.
While Pope Leo's papacy has undoubtedly started in what appears to be a comparatively measured way, he has still grown quickly into being a powerful, uncompromising and compassionate moral voice on the world stage.
His messaging in opposition to war, in support of the dignity of migrants and on the dangers of AI in particular has stood out in its clarity.
To some extent, he has already done what many Catholics had feared was barely possible, in starting to bring closer together different factions of a Church that had seemed somewhat divided.
Noticeably, both progressive and traditionalist followers often talking of him as a voice that reflects their own.
But even after successful surgery, and with no details yet about what happens now, speculation has already begun as to whether a cancer diagnosis will mean an evident shift in Pope Leo's pace in implementing changes he sees as necessary.
On the other hand any dramatic moves, such as on doctrine, would certainly feel out of character for a Pope who for nearly a year and a half has shown himself to be measured, thoughtful and discerning, as well as having a focus on stability.

Louvre boss warns of closure risk without major renovations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:21:41 UTC
21:21:41 KST

Louvre boss warns of closure risk unless museum is 'repaired, updated and transformed'
The world's most-visited museum "will eventually have to close its doors to the public" unless the French state steps in to finance a major overhaul, Louvre director Christophe Leribault told Le Figaro on Wednesday, in the latest dire warning about the creaking institution hit by a string of scandals including water leaks, ticket frauds and a high-profile jewel heist.
The Louvre museum risks having to close its doors to the public unless lawmakers approve a major overhaul of the creaking and over-capacity institution, its head told a French newspaper on Wednesday.
Speaking to Le Figaro, Christophe Leribault said that the museum intended to tap private sources of funding for its transformation, but that a major injection of public money would need to be approved after national elections next year.
"Whoever forms the next government must keep in mind that if the Louvre is not repaired, updated and transformed, it will very quickly fall behind and will eventually have to close its doors to the public. That would be a disaster," he said.
Successive minority governments in France have struggled for years to pass annual budgets and current Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu is struggling to rein in public spending to reduce the country's vast deficit.
Leribault was appointed in February in the aftermath of an embarrassing October 19 heist last year which saw a gang of thieves raid the Louvre to steal crown jewels worth an estimated $100 million.
Read moreThe Louvre heist: Security flaws and deeper cracks at France’s top museum
He has made tackling the problems highlighted by the theft a priority, with the rollout of an 83-million-euro security masterplan "moving forward at speed", he told AFP ahead of the one-year anniversary of the crime.
Measures include creating a new head of security position, upgrading the security camera network – which was found to have old cameras and major gaps – as well as improved surveillance around the perimeter and at access points.
No 'miracle' solution
Leribault argued that long-term improvements could only be made as part of the larger overhaul he has planned for the institution, which welcomed around nine million visitors last year.
"The operations needed to secure the museum require work on the historic building and its infrastructure," he wrote.
"There is no easy, miracle 'surface' solution. Everything is interconnected, everything is linked," he added.
The world's most-visited museum is widely seen as facing structural problems from its old plumbing, badly insulated galleries and cramped public areas.
The extent of the work and the cost have become extremely political, with President Emmanuel Macron championing a 600-million-euro overhaul that would include a new entrance.
Trade unions criticised Macron and Leribault's predecessor, Laurence des Cars, for prioritising grandiose plans for an architectural overhaul instead of more modest changes that would improve the visitor experience.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

====================================================================================================

Guinea-Bissau denies it has approved controversial vaccine trial in newborns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:21:16 UTC
21:21:16 KST

Guinea-Bissau has not approved the controversial hepatitis B study in newborns that would be funded by the US government and private partners, the African country’s minister of health said on Tuesday.
The study, which would not investigate the safety or effectiveness of vaccines but would instead track “nonspecific” health outcomes like overall mortality or neurodevelopmental conditions, has been championed by Robert F Kennedy Jr, secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and a longtime anti-vaccine activist.
Members of a Danish research ethics committee were informed that officials in Guinea-Bissau had approved an updated design of the study, which influenced some committee members’ votes to proceed with the trial last week.
But the health ministry never agreed to or authorized the trial, said Quinhin Nantote in Portuguese at a press briefing, where he referred to the study as “tests”.
“The ministry did not authorize the tests under the terms presented in the publications currently in circulation,” the health minister said. He said officials in Guinea-Bissau were “surprised” to see media reports that the country had given approval to the study.
“Any scientific research initiative involving human beings, particularly children, must strictly comply with applicable national legislation, international ethical principles, competent evaluation and approval mechanisms,” Nantote said.
He spoke after convening an emergency meeting in Guinea-Bissau with the Bandim Health Project, the local ethics committee, the National Institute of Public Health (Inasa) and the Expanded Vaccination Program (PAV).
The Bandim Health Project is run by the Danish researchers Peter Aaby and Christine Stabell Benn, whose decades of research have been called into question in the past year.
The claims made in nearly all of their papers are “highly misleading”, said Charlotte Strøm, a Danish researcher who has co-authored research showing that Aaby, Stabell Benn, and their co-authors had no significant findings in 24 out of 25 studies and that they’ve chosen not to publish research that may not support their viewpoints.
“When researchers operate like this and abandon proper methodological rigor, they literally decide on the results themselves, and that is not science,” Strøm said, calling it “problematic, questionable [and] unethical”.
She added: “I believe there is serious cause for concern.”
Kennedy has repeatedly praised their work, which he says shows that after vaccination, “you can have mass injuries, and catastrophic injuries, and they’re hiding in plain sight”.
Aaby, Stabell Benn and Frederik Schaltz-Buchholzer did not respond by press time to the Guardian’s questions about why the Danish ethics committee members were told the trial had been approved by local authorities and why it could not be held in Denmark.
In Denmark, infants born to hepatitis B-negative parents do not receive the shot, there is widespread testing for and low incidence of the virus, and the robust healthcare system can track health outcomes and provide timely and comprehensive medical care – making it an ideal location for such a study.
“It’s completely unethical that this trial is even proposed,” because a safe and effective vaccine has been available for decades, said BK Titanji, a researcher at Emory University.
It’s “reassuring” to see Guinea-Bissau pushing back on the trial, Titanji said, adding: “A study like this one needs the highest level of ethical scrutiny. You are going to be conducting a study on the most vulnerable population, which is newborn babies, in a country that is resource-constrained.”
When Titanji recently applied for approval of a collaborative study in Cameroon, she had to include extensive documentation in her application – and it was a survey, not medical research on human subjects, she said. “I can’t come to Emory’s [institutional review board] and just be like: ‘I got permission from Cameroon.’ I have to provide the document.”
The researchers should release these documents and an updated protocol showing how the study would be conducted, she said.
Experts have decried the African experiment as “horribly unethical and cruel”, “neocolonialist” and “damaging”.
“For the government of Guinea-Bissau to stand up against the United States and Denmark exploiting its children is no small statement,” said Colette Delawalla, a researcher and founder and CEO of the non-profit Stand Up for Science. “We absolutely must respect their sovereignty as a nation.”
It would cost approximately $13,200 to buy enough vaccines through Unicef and Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, to immunize all newborns in Guinea-Bissau each year, Delawalla pointed out.
Everyone involved should work together to ensure that every baby in Guinea-Bissau receives the birth dose of the hepatitis B vaccination, she added. “This is not muddy water: we can use Black babies to further pseudoscience or we can save children’s lives with a 20-cent shot.”
It is unclear whether the US plans to move forward with the study, even after reporting indicated that the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has again set aside $1.6m for funding for the trial this year, to be matched by private funding from the Pershing Square Foundation and the Bluebell Foundation.
“The study has not been approved,” the HHS told Reuters in a statement. The agency has not responded to the Guardian’s questions about the trial.
At least four members of the Danish committee resigned after approval for the trial was fast-tracked. The rules of the committee had to be changed because randomized controlled trials were outside of its purview. When committee members requested more information about the Guinea-Bissau approval, no further details were provided.
The study would enroll 14,000 newborns in Guinea-Bissau, half of whom would be vaccinated at birth and half of whom would be denied the immunization for the first six weeks of life. Hepatitis B is widespread in the country, and infection in children can have serious lifelong effects.
Guinea-Bissau, which currently has a transitional military government following a coup in November, requested in January a team of experts from the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) to help evaluate the study. In the meantime, Nantote said at the time, it was “canceled or suspended”.
Other officials in Guinea-Bissau also pushed back on the research. “It’s not going to happen, period,” the foreign minister, João Bernardo Vieira, said in February.
The World Health Organization (WHO) has offered support in rolling out the hepatitis B vaccine at birth to all newborns in Guinea-Bissau. “WHO stands ready to support Guinea‑Bissau as it considers its way forward and in accelerating the introduction of the birth dose and strengthening implementation,” the organization said in a February statement pushing back on the trial.

====================================================================================================

Tunisian journalists fear jail again as freedoms erode
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:20:49 UTC
21:20:49 KST

Tunisian journalists fear jail again as freedoms erode
TUNIS, Oct 14 - Journalists in Tunisia who enjoyed a burst of press freedom after the 2011 Arab Spring are once again looking over their shoulders in the knowledge their work may land them in prison.
The 2011 overthrow of autocrat Zine El-Abidine Ben Ali unshackled Tunisia's media, but a decade later President Kais Saied's seizure of sweeping powers began eroding those gains.
Now, independent media face a full-on crackdown, rights groups say, and Tunisia has tumbled more than 50 places in the past five years to 137th in Reporters Without Borders' press freedom index.
"We are living in a grey area, as if we were in a shifting minefield, and we pay the price every day," said Aymen Rezgui, editor-in-chief of independent outlet Nawaat, reflecting on how at least limits were clear pre-2011 versus current uncertainty.
Around him, in a small garden in Tunis, about half a dozen colleagues sit smoking, trading jokes and discussing investigations they plan to publish on subjects ranging from the quality of drinking water to conditions of prisons.
They know that any of the stories could lead to prosecution.
Some 20 journalists face criminal charges over their reporting or social media posts, with four already imprisoned, according to Zied Dabbar, head of the National Syndicate of Tunisian Journalists, who called the situation unprecedented.
Saied has said he is not a dictator and that journalists are free to criticize authorities and frequently do.
Authorities say prosecutions are impartial judicial matters and that no one is above the law.
The Tunisian prime minister's press office did not respond to requests for comment.
Rezgui said Nawaat regularly receives threats — anonymously or from government supporters on social media branding him a traitor — over reporting on issues ranging from prisons to power cuts and water shortages.
The outlet has also faced judicial restrictions, including a government order suspending activities for a month last year.
Many other journalists report similar pressures.
Last month, Mohamed Yousfi, editor-in-chief of independent news website Al-Qatiba, was arrested on his way to a private radio station for a live programme. A judge has charged him with illicit enrichment, which he says is a fabrication.
Other jailed journalists and media figures include prominent broadcasters Mourad Zeghidi and Borhen Bsaies, who were first convicted of spreading false news and insulting the president, and later of tax evasion. They deny the charges and say they have been framed.
SOME CHOOSE EXILE
For some, leaving Tunisia has become the only option to avoid a similar fate, despite the personal cost.
In December 2025, Khaoula Boukrim, founder of independent website Tumedia and a prominent critic of the president, left for France fearing imminent arrest.
Months later, she was sentenced in absentia to four years in prison over writings critical of the judiciary and a system of governance she described as authoritarian.
Journalist Haythem Mekki has also left Tunisia after receiving a prison sentence following public comments he made denouncing conditions in a hospital morgue.
Saied’s supporters say such cases have nothing to do with freedom of expression.
Press freedom groups argue, however, that prosecutions are increasingly being used to intimidate and silence critical voices.
Beyond prosecutions, journalists are frequently prevented by police from working in public and are sometimes detained for hours, the journalists' syndicate says.
Most ministries no longer have press offices, while several international correspondents have been denied accreditation, further restricting independent coverage.
Political and critical programmes have disappeared from many private radio stations. State media has increasingly marginalised dissenting voices, the syndicate says, though the TAP state news agency remains a rare exception, continuing to cover protests, opposition activities and civil society initiatives.
The pressure reverberates beyond newsrooms.
A photograph of Zied Heni, a radio journalist sentenced earlier this year to a year in prison after criticising a judicial ruling, hangs in the living room of his Tunis home.
His wife, Thouraya Zouari, said she and their three daughters have struggled to cope with his detention.
"We cannot accept that Zied is in prison," she said. "We are living through a nightmare."
But she said that the family was determined to carry on the struggle for freedom of expression in his absence.
"He has instilled in his daughters the resolve not to remain silent in the face of injustice and oppression," she said of the daughters who still criticise Saied on social media and take part in street protests. REUTERS

Russia Could Test NATO Regardless of How War in Ukraine Ends, Estonian Defense Minister Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:19:30 UTC
21:19:30 KST

- Category
- World
Russia Could Test NATO Regardless of How War in Ukraine Ends, Estonian Defense Minister Says
Russia is likely to test the security of a NATO member state regardless of how its war against Ukraine ends, Estonian Defense Minister Martin Herem warned, suggesting that Moscow could seek to undermine the Alliance by exploiting divisions between its members.
In an interview with European Pravda published on October 13, Herem said Russia would begin strengthening its military capabilities as soon as the war in Ukraine came to an end, potentially creating conditions for further aggression against European countries.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the Estonian defense minister, the threat would persist regardless of whether Ukraine successfully liberated its occupied territories or the conflict ended with a freeze in hostilities.
“If I take into account the attitude of the Russian state [towards its neighbours], and if I look at what they are producing right now for military purposes, then I think when they stop here [in Ukraine]—it doesn't matter how, whether you kick them out beyond the border, or the war is frozen. And given their attitude, they will definitely test somebody,” Herem said.
While acknowledging the possibility of Russian aggression against Estonia, Herem emphasized that Moscow could choose another country, including neighboring Latvia, as its next target.
He argued that Russia's primary objective would not necessarily be territorial occupation but rather the expansion of its political influence through actions designed to weaken trust within targeted countries and among NATO allies.
“Whether their first attack will be against Estonia, I'm not sure. It could be Latvia or somewhere else. What they want to achieve is influence. They need power… They need to harm us and make us distrust each other, both in Estonia and among the Allies.,” he explained.
Herem suggested that Russia could deliberately provoke a confrontation with NATO to undermine the Alliance's unity, potentially conducting operations either below the threshold for invoking Article 5 or through actions that trigger the collective defense provision.
He also warned that Russia could exploit divisions within NATO even if the Alliance successfully defended itself under Article 5. He argued that a costly military victory could trigger criticism among member states over their failure to prevent the conflict, allowing Moscow to propose a return to normal relations and gradually expand its influence over the Alliance.
Asked whether future Russian attacks could be prevented, Herem expressed skepticism about the effectiveness of deterrence alone, arguing that NATO countries must prioritize military preparedness.
“I'm not sure if we can deter the mad person. But what we have to do is to prepare. And that's the only thing. We have to prepare very seriously [for an attack] and if we do that, we may prevent it. We have to be ready,” the minister stated.
Herem's warning comes as NATO continues developing its military strategy to counter a potential Russian attack, drawing on lessons from Ukraine's experience defending against Moscow's invasion.
According to The Wall Street Journal on October 12, NATO's Supreme Allied Commander Europe, General Alexus Grynkewich, presented a new defense strategy known as the “Theory of Victory” during the Warsaw Security Forum. Its classified version had been finalized three months earlier.
The strategy focuses on stopping an initial Russian offensive, preventing further advances, and systematically weakening attacking forces. Drawing on Ukraine's battlefield experience, it also emphasizes what Grynkewich called “affordable mass,” prioritizing relatively inexpensive drones to complement NATO's advanced weapons systems and strengthen the Alliance's defensive capabilities.

Russia Scrambles to Hide Its Strategic Bombers From Ukrainian Drones, Builds 16 Giant Shelters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:19:10 UTC
21:19:10 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Scrambles to Hide Its Strategic Bombers From Ukrainian Drones, Builds 16 Giant Shelters
Russia is building 16 massive aircraft shelters at its Engels-2 air base in the Saratov region in an apparent effort to conceal and protect its strategic bombers from Ukrainian drone strikes. The construction follows repeated Ukrainian attacks on the facility, which houses Tu-160 and Tu-95MS bombers used to launch cruise missiles against Ukraine.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Defence Blog on October 13, satellite imagery published by open-source intelligence group AviVector shows that Russia has nearly completed the steel frameworks for the first three shelters.
Images captured by Airbus Defence and Space on October 12 reveal three large structures standing on newly constructed concrete platforms, each connected to the airfield by paved taxiways.
Construction began in early September, when AviVector first identified preparations for the 16-shelter project.
Each shelter measures approximately 63 by 63 meters (207 by 207 feet), with walls reaching 7 meters (23 feet) and a maximum height of around 17 meters (56 feet).
The structures are large enough to accommodate Russia’s Tu-160 supersonic strategic bombers, which measure approximately 54 meters in length, as well as the smaller Tu-95MS aircraft.
Satellite imagery also shows earth barriers behind the shelters, apparently designed to redirect engine exhaust. Their positioning suggests that Russian bombers could start their engines inside the structures before taxiing directly onto the airfield.
The project could significantly change how Russia conceals its strategic aviation assets at Engels-2, where bombers have traditionally remained exposed on open parking areas.
The new shelters would make it more difficult for satellite surveillance to determine which aircraft are stationed at the base while potentially offering protection against Ukrainian drone strikes and debris.
However, the structures currently consist only of steel frameworks, and their ability to withstand attacks will depend on the materials used for their walls and roofs.
Engels-2, located approximately 600 kilometers (370 miles) from the Ukrainian front line, is one of Russia’s primary strategic aviation bases and has repeatedly been targeted by Ukrainian long-range drones since December 2022.
In July 2026, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) had destroyed a Tu-95 strategic bomber at Engels. Satellite imagery released afterward appeared to confirm the aircraft’s destruction.
Another Tu-95 was damaged during an August 28 drone strike conducted by the SBU’s Alpha unit.
The Tu-95 is no longer in production, meaning Russia cannot replace destroyed aircraft with newly manufactured bombers of the same type.

World’s oldest shipwreck off Turkey: 4,700-year-old amphorae discovered
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:18:12 UTC
21:18:12 KST

The shipwreck found near Antalya’s Kekova Island, dated to roughly 4,400–4,700 years ago, sheds light on maritime trade in the eastern Mediterranean.
Underwater excavations carried out off the island of Kekova in Antalya have brought to light amphorae dating back around 4,400–4,700 years. The finds, which are said to belong to a wreck from the Early Bronze Age, are expected to shed light on Anatolia's maritime history and trade links in the Eastern Mediterranean.
Turkey's Minister of Culture and Tourism Mehmet Nuri Ersoy, in a post on his social media account, underlined the importance of the ancient vases recovered during the excavations, saying: "In our 'Blue Homeland', we are bringing to light traces of the world's oldest shipwreck."
Clay analyses carried out on the amphorae, which are thought to have been used to transport olive oil or wine, indicate that the jars were probably produced in workshops in the Jordan Valley. The discovery of similar examples in Egypt, Troy and Crete reveals traces of trade and cultural interaction between different regions.
Ersoy stated that they would continue to illuminate Anatolia's maritime history with new findings and to preserve the underwater cultural heritage for future generations. The minister also congratulated Associate Professor Hakan Öniz, who's leading the scientific excavations, and the team involved in the work.
How was the wreck off Kekova found?
Amphora samples taken from the remains of a wreck identified off the island of Kekova during underwater surveys carried out in previous years by Akdeniz University showed that the ship may date back to the Early Bronze Age.
Acting on permits from the Ministry of Culture and Tourism, excavations in the area began in 2026 under the leadership of the Antalya Museum Directorate.
The fact that similar vessels have been found near the pyramids of Giza, Saqqara and Abusir in Egypt, as well as in Troy and Crete, suggests that the cargo carried by the wreck may have been linked to an extensive trade network. Researchers believe that the ship set sail from a port on the Levantine coast and headed towards Troy or Crete.
An amphora marked with nine signs sheds light on sailors' lives
One of the amphorae found in the excavations stands out with two holes in its body and nine distinct marks on it. Initial examinations suggest that the jar may have been a churning amphora used in the production of cheese or butter.
This possibility raises the prospect that sailors of the period may have carried goats on long voyages, milked them on board and produced their own dairy products. The finds therefore contribute not only to research into the transport of commercial goods, but also to studies on the everyday conditions of sea journeys and eating habits.

U.S. Marine Corps orders SAFE MULE loaders
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:15:00 UTC
21:15:00 KST

- The U.S. Marine Corps awarded SAFE Structure Designs a contract worth more than $10 million for an initial, low-quantity order of SAFE MULE loaders.
- The tracked loader lifts a loaded 10,000-pound 463L pallet from the ground and is light enough to fly inside a V-22 Osprey.
The U.S. Marine Corps is buying a small tracked cargo loader that can pick a fully loaded 4,500 kg (10,000-pound) air cargo pallet off the ground and still fit inside an MV-22 Osprey, under a contract worth more than $10 million to Las Vegas-based S.A.F.E. Structure Designs.
The company announced the award for its SAFE MULE expeditionary logistics platform on Oct. 13 in a press release, describing it as an initial, low-quantity order that includes operator training and ongoing technical support. SAFE did not say how many vehicles the U.S. Marine Corps is buying, which command placed the order, or when deliveries will begin, and it said talks are underway on a larger purchase expected in 2027, subject to final requirements, funding and procurement decisions.
The machine is built around the 463L pallet, the standard aluminum cargo pallet U.S. military aircraft use to move supplies. A loaded 463L tops out at about 10,000 pounds, and the SAFE MULE is designed to lift one from the ground onto its own deck and drive away with it, a job that at most forward sites would otherwise call for a forklift and a separate truck or a large aircraft loader that may not be available.
“The engineering challenge was to deliver substantial lifting capability without creating a machine too heavy to travel with the force it supports,” said Johnny Buscema, president and CEO of SAFE Structure Designs.
According to the company, the loader is light enough to ride inside a V-22 and can also be carried in the aft ramp position of a U.S. Air Force C-17 transport. Its adjustable cargo deck has built-in rollers so pallets can slide straight across to an aircraft floor or a truck bed, while rubber tracks let it move loads across unimproved ground where wheeled forklifts struggle.
A 2024 company technical sheet described an earlier configuration that weighed roughly 2,950 to 3,080 kg (6,500 to 6,800 pounds), was operated remotely by a single person and could work in mud, water or snow up to 61 cm (24 inches) deep. The same document listed a scissor deck able to raise more than 10,000 pounds to 165 cm (65 inches) and a towing capacity of over 10,000 pounds.
The version going to the U.S. Marine Corps uses non-radio-frequency controls, so it can be operated without a wireless control link. SAFE said that matters around ammunition and ordnance, where units limit radio emissions near explosives, though handling specific loads still depends on military safety rules and approvals.
SAFE announced in March 2026 that it had finished research and development on the SAFE MULE and moved it into production, presenting it as a platform for U.S. Navy, U.S. Marine Corps and U.S. Air Force logistics. The company’s other work includes aircraft maintenance stands and specialized military support equipment.

Ukraine is facing a funding shortfall for 2027, and the European Union is trying to raise additional funds for the country during meetings of the International Monetary Fund and finance ministers of the Group of Seven (G7), taking place this week in Bangkok. European Commissioner for Economy Valdis Dombrovskis said this, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
Details

However, despite the additional €45 billion ($50 billion) promised by the EU for 2027, Ukraine’s needs will be significantly higher, so the EU is making efforts to raise funds from countries such as Norway, Switzerland, Canada, Japan, and the United Kingdom.

"From the very beginning, we have emphasized that the European Union aims to cover approximately two-thirds of Ukraine’s financial needs, and we expect the rest to be covered by other partners," he said.
To buy time to secure contributions from other parties, the EU plans to accelerate the allocation of the €45 billion earmarked for Ukraine as early as next year; however, the situation is complicated by the fact that the EU is still determining the exact amount of funds Ukraine will need next year.

Iranian delegation attending WHO RC73
TEHRAN – An Iranian delegation led by Ali Jafarian, a senior advisor to the health minister, is participating in the 73rd session of the WHO Regional Committee for Eastern Mediterranean (RC73), being held from October 13 to 15 in Cairo, Egypt.
The event has brought together health ministers and high-level delegates from the 22 countries and territories to set regional health priorities and guide WHO work with member states.
The Iranian official is scheduled to deliver a speech focusing on different health issues such as the impacts of sanctions and wars on the health system, the supply chain of medical items and equipment, the health ministry’s website reported.
Strengthening preparedness and response to public health emergencies, expanding technical and regional cooperation, and benefiting from the capacity of WHO to support the priorities of national health systems are among the issues to be discussed by the Iranian delegation. Jafarian is also planned to hold meetings with health officials from the Eastern Mediterranean office and the region.
The opening ceremony celebrated outstanding contributions to health in the Region. The State of Kuwait Prize for the Control of Cancer, Cardiovascular Diseases and Diabetes in the Eastern Mediterranean Region was presented to three laureates from Iran, Egypt, and the United Arab Emirates.
Amir-Ali Hamidieh, an Iranian professor at Tehran University of Medical Sciences, grabbed the prize for his pioneering work in paediatric haematology, oncology and stem cell transplantation.
A distinguished physician, academic and pioneer in paediatric haematology, oncology and stem cell transplantation, Hamidieh earned his M.D. from Islamic Azad University, Tehran, and pursued postgraduate training in paediatrics and paediatric haematology/ oncology at Shahid Beheshti University of Medical Sciences. He later completed advanced fellowships in haematopoietic stem cell transplantation at The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center and Baylor College of Medicine in Texas, United States of America.
Hamidieh currently serves as Professor of Pediatric Hematology/ Oncology and Stem Cell Transplantation at Tehran University of Medical Sciences, where he also directs the Pediatric Cell and Gene Therapy Research Center.
He is the founder of the Iranian paediatric stem cell transplantation programme and the national stem cell donor network, which established the country’s first human leukocyte antigen (HLA) registry.
He chairs the National Council for Development of Stem Cell Sciences and Technologies under the Vice-Presidency for Science and Technology and is a member of the executive boards of the Asia-Pacific Blood and Marrow Transplantation Group and the Iranian Food and Drug Administration.
His leadership has enabled the development of seven paediatric transplant centres across the Islamic Republic of Iran and the successful completion of more than 2100 paediatric stem cell transplants.
 
Hamidieh has authored more than 100 peer-reviewed articles on research spanning regenerative medicine, gene therapy, immunodeficiencies and paediatric cancers.
He has also led clinical innovations in CAR-T cell therapy and photopheresis across many countries. Through his academic leadership, clinical excellence and commitment to equitable care, Hamidieh has significantly advanced the field of paediatric stem cell transplantation in Iran and the broader Eastern Mediterranean Region.
RC73 at a critical time for health
The opening of RC73 comes at a critical time for health in the Region. Protracted and escalating emergencies continue to disrupt health systems, putting millions of lives at risk, at a time when countries are contending with disease outbreaks, persistent inequities, a growing burden of noncommunicable diseases and mounting financial pressures.
In his opening remarks, Adham Rashad Ismail, Officer-in-Charge of the WHO Regional Office for the Eastern Mediterranean, highlighted the immense humanitarian and financial pressures facing the Region.
The official reaffirmed WHO’s commitment to sustaining essential health services and supporting countries through ongoing crises: “WHO must continue to support populations affected by conflict and crisis, protect essential health services and advocate for uninterrupted humanitarian access and funding. The people relying on health services in Afghanistan, the Gaza Strip, Sudan, Yemen and elsewhere cannot bear the consequences of shrinking resources.”
With the opening ceremony concluded, member states will discuss the Annual Report of the Regional Director 2025/2026, which provides a regional stock take of health progress, persistent challenges and WHO’s work with countries over the past year, helping to identify areas where progress needs to be sustained or accelerated.
The Committee will discuss two technical papers, “Advancing health financing for stronger financial protection in the Eastern Mediterranean Region: pathways to equity and resilience” which focuses on ways to build equity and resilience in health care funding and enhance financial protection for populations across the Region, and “A multi-disease elimination architecture for communicable diseases in the Eastern Mediterranean Region” which outlines joint strategies to tackle and eliminate multiple communicable diseases simultaneously.
Discussions will also cover health emergencies and polio eradication, and a panel on artificial intelligence for health will explore the opportunities presented by rapidly evolving technologies.
Member States will hold a regional consultation on the draft Program Budget 2028–2029 and review governance matters and resolutions and decisions of regional interest adopted by the World Health Assembly and WHO Executive Board.
The discussions and decisions taken at RC73 will guide collective action across the Eastern Mediterranean Region, from protecting health amid emergencies and completing the last mile of polio eradication to strengthening health financing, accelerating disease elimination and preparing health systems for the future.

Laser vision correction: can the surgery be performed before pregnancy, and what is important to know about the procedure
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:12:57 EEST
21:12:57 KST

Laser vision correction: can the surgery be performed before pregnancy, and what is important to know about the procedure
Kyiv • UNN
Planning a pregnancy is not a contraindication to laser vision correction, but the surgery is postponed during pregnancy and breastfeeding. A comprehensive examination is required before the procedure.
Laser vision correction is surrounded by a number of myths; however, in reality, the possibility of performing a safe and effective procedure depends on several important factors. An ophthalmologist, medical director and scientific consultant at the German Eye Clinic, Professor Oksana Vitovska, told UNN journalist more about who laser vision correction is actually suitable for, whether it can be performed before pregnancy, and what examinations are necessary before the procedure.
Laser Vision Correction and Pregnancy
One of the most common myths is that women who have not yet given birth or are planning a pregnancy cannot undergo laser vision correction. According to the doctor, planning to have children in itself is not a contraindication to the procedure.
The fact that a woman has not yet given birth or is planning a pregnancy in the future is not a contraindication to laser vision correction. The operation does not affect reproductive function, does not prevent a future pregnancy, and in itself is not a reason to change the method of delivery
According to the ophthalmologist, this myth may have arisen from another recommendation—not to perform laser vision correction directly during pregnancy, because of the changes that occur in a woman’s body during this period.
During pregnancy, hormonal levels, water balance, and the condition of the tear film change. Refraction, curvature, thickness, and other characteristics of the cornea may temporarily change. This matters for refractive surgery, where highly accurate measurements are important. That is why the operation is postponed during pregnancy. A cautious approach is also used during lactation. It is advisable to wait until hormonal levels, refraction, and the condition of the ocular surface have stabilized. But this is a temporary restriction, not a ban on correction for women planning to have children
At the same time, according to the doctor, temporary changes in vision during pregnancy are possible; however, they may be related not to a previous operation but to natural changes in the body.
In most cases, pregnancy after successful laser vision correction does not “cancel” its result. During pregnancy, some women may experience temporary changes in refraction. This can happen regardless of whether laser vision correction was performed previously. After childbirth and the completion of hormonal changes, refraction often returns to its previous state. At the same time, laser vision correction does not stop natural processes in the eye. Therefore, it is important to undergo surgery when refraction is stable
That is why, before surgery, doctors consider not only the current prescription but also whether vision has remained stable over a certain period; if vision is still changing, they may suggest waiting before proceeding with the intervention.
Does Age Matter?
Another common question is whether there is an age after which laser vision correction is no longer performed. Oksana Vitovska explained that there is no universal upper age limit; however, age does affect the choice of treatment method.
The usual lower age limit is considered to be 18, but what matters more than the number in one’s passport is the stability of refraction. If myopia continues to progress in a young person, it is advisable to postpone the operation
At the same time, another factor may emerge with age, to which doctors will pay attention.
After the age of 40–45, it is not so much the possibility of performing laser vision correction that changes as its strategy. At this age, presbyopia develops—the natural decline in accommodation. A laser can provide good distance vision, but it does not stop age-related changes in the lens and accommodative apparatus. For example, a person with mild myopia may be able to read up close without glasses. After full correction of myopia, they may see well at a distance but require reading glasses. This is not a complication of the operation, but a manifestation of presbyopia, which myopia had previously partially compensated for
Therefore, if there are already age-related changes in the lens or an incipient cataract, laser corneal correction may be technically possible, but it is not always strategically optimal.
In such cases, a doctor may suggest another refractive approach. Therefore, it is more appropriate to ask not “Am I too old to undergo laser surgery?” but “Which vision-correction method would be optimal for my eye at my age?”
Thus, age alone does not determine whether the procedure can be performed. Instead, a comprehensive evaluation enables the doctor to determine which correction option is appropriate in a particular case.
What examinations are needed before laser vision correction
According to Oksana Vitovska, preoperative diagnostics largely determine the safety, predictability, and quality of the outcome, so determining visual acuity and the number of diopters alone is not enough.
The doctor must answer three main questions: Is the cornea healthy, can its shape be safely changed, and which correction method best corresponds to the specific characteristics of the eye
And in order for the doctor to determine this accurately, the patient must undergo the following procedures:
"- Refraction and visual acuity. The current optical error and its stability are assessed; examinations are performed under cycloplegia.
- Corneal topography and tomography. The shape of the anterior and posterior surfaces, symmetry, and other parameters important for detecting keratoconus and other ectasias are examined.
- Pachymetry. The thickness of the cornea and its distribution are determined, and the future biomechanical reserve after the planned correction is also assessed.
- Ocular surface. The tear film, the presence of dry eye, and meibomian gland dysfunction are assessed. If necessary, these conditions are treated first.
- Anterior and posterior segments of the eye. The cornea, anterior chamber, lens, intraocular pressure, retina, and optic nerve are assessed.
- Additional examinations. Where indicated, OCT, a detailed examination of the retinal periphery, aberrometry, and other tests are performed," explained Oksana Vitovska.
In addition, the doctor says, a personalized approach plays a special role in modern refractive surgery. This means that when planning the procedure, not only standard vision parameters but also as many individual characteristics of the specific eye as possible are taken into account. Modern AI-based technologies assess all the parameters of the eye, rather than just the cornea; they make it possible to create a digital model of the patient’s eye, select the optimal correction plan, and predict its outcome.
Modern refractive surgery is increasingly moving from the simple principle of "removing diopters" toward personalized modeling of the optical system of a specific eye. That is why the quality of preoperative diagnostics is of fundamental importance. At our clinic, before surgery, the InnovEyes Sightmap platform conducts a comprehensive examination of the eye and creates its individual three-dimensional digital model — a kind of digital optical twin. Based on these data, a personalized laser-correction profile is automatically created
What else is important to know about laser vision correction
The doctor also draws attention to myths directly related to how the laser works.
Myth 1: "The laser burns the cornea".
"Modern laser systems model the shape of the cornea with high precision. This involves a controlled change in a microscopic volume of tissue, not "burning" the eye," the expert says.
Myth 2: "It will be impossible to operate on cataracts after laser vision correction"
"Cataract surgery can be performed. It is important to inform the ophthalmologist about the previous refractive surgery, as this is taken into account when calculating the intraocular lens," the professor noted
Myth 3: "A high prescription automatically means that laser correction is impossible"
"The degree of myopia is only one of the parameters. The shape and thickness of the cornea, the extent of the required correction, biomechanical risk, and other characteristics of the eye are important. For some patients, another technology may be more suitable," Oksana Vitovska emphasized.

Tehran, Doha explore partnership opportunities in ICT sector
TEHRAN – Information and Communication Technology (ICT) Minister Sattar Hashemi and Qatar’s ambassador in Iran Saad bin Abdullah Al-Mohammad Al-Sharif have underlined the need to expand cooperation between the two countries in the ICT sector.
The officials met in Tehran on Wednesday, discussing ways to develop joint efforts in the field of ICT, particularly digital technologies, Mehr news agency reported.
The talk also focused on Iran and Qatar collaborations in international organizations and specialized forums, including the interaction of the two nations within the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) and the ITU Plenipotentiary Conference.
Regarding the role of ITU in shaping global policies and standards within the ICT sector, coordination and interaction among member states can provide a favorable basis for pursuing shared perspectives and interests, as well as strengthening international cooperation.
The next ITU Plenipotentiary Conference (PP-26) is set to take place from November 9 to 27 November in Doha, Qatar. Held every four years, the conference brings together member states to make decisions on strategic and financial direction, future activities, elect leadership, and adopt resolutions that shape global telecommunications and Internet policy for the next four years.
Expanding ICT ties with neighboring nations on the agenda
On the sidelines of the first session of the UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance, convened by the UN General Assembly in Geneva on July 6 and 7, the head of the Information Technology Organization of Iran, Mohammad-Mohsen Sadr, has held separate meetings with Iraqi, Pakistani, and Omani officials to discuss ways to enhance collaboration between Iran and these countries in the ICT sector.
Holding a meeting with Iraqi Minister of Communications Mustafa Jabbar Sanad, the two sides highlighted the role of information technology and artificial intelligence in helping to address energy imbalances, developing smart infrastructure, enhancing productivity in the energy sector, and fostering cooperation in e-government and data transit. They also discussed expanding cooperation in digital transformation, exchanging technical expertise, and implementing joint projects.
The Iranian official met Shaza Fatima Khawaja, the Pakistani Minister for IT and Telecommunications, as well. During the meeting, both parties explored avenues to enhance cooperation between Iran and Pakistan in the fields of information technology, e-government, artificial intelligence, digital economy, cybersecurity, and the development of the innovation ecosystem.
In his X account, Sadr described the meeting with the Omani official as a constructive one, which particularly focused on e-government, artificial intelligence, digital economy, communication infrastructure, and expanding technological interactions between the two countries.
The two countries have high capacities to deepen digital cooperation and develop joint initiatives in the future of the digital economy, he added.
AI governance is the set of rules, standards, and oversight practices that determine how artificial intelligence systems are built, deployed, and held accountable, and in July 2026, it moved onto the world stage.
The official said a workshop on Artificial Intelligence and the Government Digital Ecosystem held on July 7 at the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) headquarters in Geneva was very well received by the participants; it included his speech and the talks of other representatives from UNDESA’s E-Government Assessment Branch and the ITU Development Sector, as well as university professors.
The UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance was the world’s first intergovernmental platform where every government and stakeholder group sat at the same table to align on AI oversight.
It is a direct product of the Global Digital Compact, the digital cooperation framework adopted in September 2024.
 
The Dialogue brought together all 193 UN member states alongside the private sector, civil society, academia, and the technical community. It received the first annual report of the UN Independent International Scientific Panel on Artificial Intelligence, giving member states a shared evidence base.
Crucially, the forum adopts no binding resolutions or regulations. It is a place to exchange best practices and build common approaches, and it ran alongside the World Summit on the Information Society (WSIS) Forum 2026 and the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) AI for Good Global Summit in the same week. A second session is scheduled for New York in May 2027.

British energy giant sells Nigerian gas business

British energy giant sells Nigerian gas business
British energy giant Shell has agreed to sell its domestic gas distribution business in Nigeria, further reshaping its operations in the West African country amid unresolved legal battles over oil pollution.
The company announced on Tuesday that Vaaris Energy, a privately owned Nigerian firm, will acquire its entire interest in Shell Nigeria Gas Group. Financial terms were not disclosed, and the transaction requires regulatory approvals. Operations will continue under Shell until completion.
Established in 1998, the business supplies more than 130 industrial and commercial customers through around 170 kilometers of pipelines across Ogun, Abia, and Rivers states. Shell said the sale would simplify its portfolio and concentrate investment where it has competitive strengths.
“We believe this agreement provides a much stronger platform for the business’ next chapter under new ownership,” Shell’s chair in Nigeria, Elohor Aiboni, said. The deal covers gas distribution rather than production or exports. Shell will retain its deepwater oil and gas operations and its interest in Nigeria LNG.
The company, active in Nigeria since 1937, completed the sale of its onshore subsidiary, Shell Petroleum Development Company of Nigeria (SPDC), to the Renaissance consortium in March 2025. The agreement announced in 2024 provided for payments of up to $2.4 billion.
Shell’s operations in Africa’s most populous nation have been marked by long-running disputes over oil pollution. Residents of Ogale and Bille in the Niger Delta are seeking compensation and cleanup over spills they say devastated their land and waterways.
In September, the UK High Court allowed Bille claimants to argue that Shell was responsible for all oil pollution in their region from 2011-2013, including damage not traced to individual spills. Trial is scheduled for May 2027. A 2011 UN assessment found benzene in wells in Nisisioken Ogale at more than 900 times World Health Organization guidelines and estimated that restoring Ogoniland could take 25 to 30 years. Shell disputes the claims, blaming most pollution in the case on oil theft, sabotage, and illegal refining.
French oil major TotalEnergies has also faced criticism from Nigerian communities and activists over oil spills and environmental damage. Its planned withdrawal from onshore oil operations suffered a setback in September 2025 when regulators revoked approval for an $860 million asset sale to Chappal Energies over unmet financial commitments, before the company signed a replacement agreement with Vaaris in January this year.

Third Corps forces carried out the attacks using combined arms tactics with dismounted and mounted infantry working in tandem with drone swarms, first to infiltrate to Russian positions and then to cut them off from supply and isolate them, before systematically mopping them up, Biletsky said.
“[T]he key to the operation was speed. We did not give the enemy time to replace his losses or to construct a viable defense. The disoriented commanders of the enemy made mistake after mistake,” Biletsky stated.
Overall, throughout Vivaldi operation, 3rd Corps forces returned Ukrainian control to “more than” 16 towns and villages and 277 km² (120 square miles) of Ukrainian territory, and inflicted total enemy losses of at least 8,000 troops, Biletsky said. Kyiv Post review of battle reports and OSINT trackers found battle lines in the Lyman sector generally consistent with Biletsky’s statements.
Accounts in 3rd Corps internal unit feeds reviewed by Kyiv Post found multiple reports of accumulating Russian casualties mostly to drone strike. Neither Russia nor Ukraine publish their own actual casualty counts.
“Vivaldi has demonstrated that an offensive is possible with outnumbered forces using asymmetric tactics. It is possible to, simultaneously, maintain an effective defense in other sectors,” Biletsky said.
In an evaluation generally shared by Ukrainian military analysts, Biletsky said that his 3rd Corps troops, by gaining ground and defeating defending Russian troops in positions east of Lyman, had scored an operational success by pushing Kremlin forces away from the logistically critical Slovyansk-Kramatorsk highway, thereby ensuring defenses in both those cities – named by Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin as top objectives for Russian conquest – would stay well-supplied.
A parallel offensive led primarily by Ukrainian air assault infantry and paratrooper units has since mid-summer used similar drone + infiltrating-infantry tactics to turn back Russian assaults further south in the Donetsk region, to the east of the cities of Slovyansk and Kramatorsk.
Together those successes made Ukrainian aggregate terrain gains in September 2026 slightly greater than Russia’s for the first time since June 2025.
Ukraine’s Slovyansk-Kramatorsk counter-offensive is still ongoing
Biletsky, in closing comments, suggested a possible follow-up to the Vivaldi Operation was being planned, saying, “At the very least there is still Wagner and Bach.”
Russia’s Defense Ministry during the Lyman/Vivaldi operation has steadfastly insisted Kremlin forces are holding their ground, and, in some places, advancing.
Russian milbloggers – even vehemently pro-Moscow content-creators, in contrast – have warned for weeks of a worsening situation and Russian forces under heavy pressure from Ukrainian drone swarms and infantry assaults.
Popular milblogger Mikhail Zvinchuk (450,000+ followers), in an Oct. 6 post on the Lyman battles, said Russian defenses were unable to stop infiltrating iUkrainian infantry, and that Ukrainian drone strikes were preventing Russian troops from digging in.
“The enemy has numerical superiority and a significant advantage in drones,” Zvinchuk wrote.

In the Wednesday announcement, 3rd Corps named combat units participating in the Vivlaldi operation, many of which were among the most combat-experienced in the entire AFU.
Among 3rd Corps units involved in the offensive, Biletsky said, were the 3rd Assault Brigade, the 60th Separate Mechanized Brigade, the 125th Separate Territorial Defense Brigade, the 3rd Separate Reconnaissance Battalion, the 25th Separate Anti-Tank Battalion, and the 21st Separate Special Operations Battalion “Kraken,” a unit raised in Kharkiv at the start of Russia’s second invasion of Ukraine, in February 2022, from retired commando civilians at the time, who volunteered to return to service to fight Russia.
The 3rd Assault Brigade, a regular army unit raised in Kyiv originally as untrained militia on the first day of Russia’s second invasion, is widely considered one of the AFU’s most effective fighting outfits and an early proponent of closely coordinated infantry-drone tactics.
Reinforcements attached to the 3rd Corps included the 66th Separate Mechanized Brigade, the 3rd Border Detachment, the 10th “Dozor” Mobile Border Detachment, and commando groups from the 8th Special Operations Forces Regiment, Biletsky said.
Along with Kyiv’s 3rd Assault, four units participating in the Vivaldi offensive – the 3rd Reconnaissance, the 21st Kraken, the 10th Dozor, and the 8th Special Operations – are long-established, veteran infantry outfits with excellent fighting records, specializing in infiltration, raiding, and behind-the-lines operations supported by drones, Kyiv Post research found.
Biletsky named the National Guard’s “Lasar’s Group,” the special operations battalion from the regular army’s K-2 Regiment, and unmanned air vehicle (UAV) units from the Special Operations Center A as the drone units giving the Vivaldi operation air support. All three are long-established, crack flying outfits with average pilots having flown hundreds of combat sorties and experienced operators thousands.
The K-2 Regiment, formally known in the AFU as the 20th Separate Brigade Unmanned Systems K-2 (Ukrainian: 20-та окрема бригада безпілотних систем «К-2») was raised in 2017 as a squad of drone enthusiasts. According to AFU lore, it probably was one of the first military units in history to employ civilian MAVIC drones in a war and then modify them for combat purposes.
K-2 was, reportedly, the first AFU unit to convert a commercial drone into a bomber jury-rigged to drop grenades, and to employ 24/7 small drone presence with a “cab rank” of strike drones ready to attack over a battlefield target. In 2025, according to a unit statement, K-2 became the world’s first military unit to field a dedicated Unmanned Ground Vehicle (UGV) sub-unit.

DOE unveils global real-time dust source monitoring system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:09:37 UTC
21:09:37 KST

DOE unveils global real-time dust source monitoring system
TEHRAN – The Department of Environment (DOE) has unveiled a global real-time monitoring system designed to identify and track dust hotspots around the world.
The system also enables the analysis of dust patterns, the identification of populations at risk, more effective resource allocation, and the implementation of preventive measures to mitigate the impacts of dust storms.
The system comprises 13 stages organized into three main parts, including setting and initial analyses, identification and refinement of hotspots, and management analysis, IRNA quoted the head of Iran’s National Headquarters for Dust Storm Policy and Coordination, Behzad Raygani, as saying.
The official made the remarks on Tuesday while addressing the 24th meeting of the National Headquarters for Dust Storm Policy and Coordination. During the meeting, a decision-support system for managing dust storms was also unveiled in Khuzestan province.
“The system is described as global because it can generate reports on different regions around the world. Users can select their area of interest in the first section and specify a monitoring period, ranging from seasonal intervals to custom time frames. This feature enables more precise tracking of changes over time,” Raygani said.
Given that remote sensing analyses are subject to errors, a specific step has been incorporated for masking and eliminating errors and areas that do not generate dust, he added.
The second section focuses on identifying and refining dust hotspots. It includes extracting barren land areas, refining the identified hotspots, and generating the required outputs.
The third section makes it possible to examine wind conditions and analyze whether a dust event has originated from a specific source or not, he added.
The system also generates reports on populations exposed to dust and determines the timing, intensity, and location of the phenomenon within a specific region. It can provide reports on exposed populations at both provincial and urban scales.
In places where there are wetlands, the system also enables the estimation of the water volume needed to maintain moisture and prevent dust generation.
For her part, the head of the DOE, Shina Ansari, underlined the importance of boosting environmental diplomacy with neighboring countries, developing regional cooperation to curb sand and dust-storm sources, as well as monitoring the effectiveness of measures taken to address dust phenomena.
Referring to the global dust hotspot monitoring system and the decision-support system for managing dust storms launched in Khuzestan province, Ansari said the global system operates based on ground-based monitoring stations providing data on the location and severity of dust hotspots, affected people, and tracking the changes in the dust centers. The system enables real-time monitoring of dust at the national level, while utilizing global systems as well.
The second system, launched in Khuzestan province, helps make sound and timely decisions in response to dust events. Through enhancing collaboration and coordination among different organizations, the system helps accelerate interaction among the relevant agencies, she noted.
The system represents a strategic step towards strengthening governance capacity for dust storm management; an approach that has to be proactive, coordinated, and highly effective, she stressed.
To make the best use of these two systems, the training of the users must be put on the agenda, she further noted.
UNDP-backed assessment prioritizes 30 SDS hotspots in Iran
A national assessment supported by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) has identified and prioritized 30 critical domestic source areas for sand and dust storms (SDS) in Iran, providing an evidence base for targeted measures to reduce risks to communities, infrastructure and vulnerable ecosystems.
Sand and dust storms are an increasingly serious environmental and development challenge in Iran, affecting public health and livelihoods, damaging infrastructure and putting additional pressure on fragile ecosystems. More than 25 provinces are affected to varying degrees, highlighting the need to shift from responding to individual storms toward prevention, preparedness and long-term resilience.
Since 2023, UNDP has been working with Iran’s DOE and the National Secretariat for Policy Making and Coordination of Management for the Sand and Dust Storms Phenomenon to support this transition.
The national assessment combines data on SDS hazard intensity, ecological vulnerability and the exposure of populations and critical infrastructure. By bringing together environmental information with data on settlements, roads, railways and agricultural areas, the assessment identifies locations where vulnerable landscapes and exposed communities overlap.
The findings provide an evidence base for directing resources to areas where interventions can have the greatest impact, ranging from vegetation restoration and soil stabilization to wetland protection and measures to safeguard infrastructure and communities.
The assessment found that 20 percent of Iran’s territory falls within high- or very-high-risk SDS categories, underscoring the importance of targeted and preventive action.
“Sand and dust storms do not respect borders. Over the past three years, our partnership with UNDP has demonstrated what collective action can achieve, advancing mitigation and adaptation
Measures across four provinces and strengthening resilience to their impacts,” Raygani said.
At the same time, Iran is strengthening its capacity to anticipate and manage SDS events. With support from UNDP, forecasting and early-warning capabilities have been enhanced through fixed and portable monitoring systems. Technical work has also laid the foundation for a national and regional real-time SDS monitoring application.
The initiative extends from national systems to landscapes and local communities. Technical assessments in Khuzestan, Ilam, Yazd and Semnan have incorporated SDS considerations into biodiversity and landscape planning across approximately 47,000 hectares, linking SDS mitigation with ecosystem conservation and future investment decisions.
In Semnan’s Touran landscape, the integrated approach combines vegetation restoration, more efficient water use and improved grazing management with efforts to protect one of Iran’s most important biodiversity areas. SDS mitigation measures have also been implemented across 270 hectares of the Touran Protected Area, an important habitat for the endangered Asiatic cheetah.
Provincial capacity assessments in Ilam and Khuzestan have resulted in new action plans, clearer institutional responsibilities and stronger SDS working groups, helping translate national priorities into coordinated action at the local level. These efforts form part of a broader national shift toward proactive SDS management.

IEA warns global gasoil market tightness to extend into 2027
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
20:09:27 CST
21:09:27 KST

PARIS, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- Tightness in the global gasoil market is expected to extend into 2027 amid prolonged supply disruptions and escalating attacks on energy infrastructure in the Middle East, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said Wednesday.
In its October Oil Market Report, the IEA said global diesel exports fell by 700,000 barrels per day (700 kb/d) year on year in September, as prolonged supply disruptions led to counter-seasonal stock draws ahead of autumn refinery maintenance and peak winter demand.
Although global gasoil prices have eased from record highs of more than 200 U.S. dollars per barrel in September, benchmark prices remain nearly twice the level of crude oil prices and almost double their own pre-crisis levels.
The IEA warned that record gasoil prices were already having widespread economic consequences, raising the cost of goods and affecting real incomes, economic activity and inflation.
The IEA said the gasoil market balance is expected to remain tight well into 2027, depending on a recovery in product supplies from the Middle East. It added that without such a recovery, further demand reductions may be needed to balance the market, potentially at a high economic cost.
Global oil demand is forecast to fall by 2.5 million barrels per day (mb/d) year on year in the fourth quarter of 2026 and by an average of 2.6 mb/d over the full year. A partial recovery of 2 mb/d in 2027 is expected to leave global oil consumption 620 kb/d, or 0.6 percent below 2025 levels, it said.
Global oil supply is projected to decline by an average of 5.8 mb/d to 100.7 mb/d in 2026, before rebounding by 7.7 mb/d in 2027. However, renewed attacks in the Gulf are threatening to undermine the recovery, the IEA said.
A recovery in Middle Eastern oil supply was well underway in September, with Gulf crude oil exports approaching pre-war levels. However, escalating attacks on regional energy infrastructure and tanker traffic are threatening further gains, the IEA said, adding that Brent crude futures have risen by 13 percent since the beginning of September to around 107 dollars per barrel.
In the absence of a resolution to conflicts in the Middle East, oil markets may experience more turmoil in the months ahead before any eventual surplus emerges in 2027, the IEA said. ■
