WHO calls for urgent health action across the Eastern Mediterranean
The head of the World Health Organization (WHO) has called for promoting, providing and protecting health in the Eastern Mediterranean region, home to some of the world’s top humanitarian crises such as Sudan, Yemen and the Occupied Palestinian Territory.
Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus was speaking on Wednesday to health leaders and senior officials attending the WHO regional committee meeting underway in Cairo, Egypt.
“Over the past year, Member States have continued to advance the health and wellbeing of their people, often under the most difficult circumstances,” he said in remarks on the annual report for the region, which spans 22 countries and territories.
He highlighted numerous achievements, including strengthened response to noncommunicable diseases – such as cardiovascular disease, cancer and diabetes –which account for roughly two thirds of all deaths in the region, with more than 2.8 million lives lost every year.
Millions displaced, healthcare attacked
Yet, the report was also a reminder that the Eastern Mediterranean continues to face a multitude of challenges.
“This region remains the epicentre of global humanitarian need, with more than 117 million people in need of humanitarian assistance,” he said. It is also home to some of the world’s largest displacement crises.
“Conflict continues to affect millions of people across several countries and territories,” he said.
“We continue to see an appalling number of attacks on healthcare and climate-related shocks continue to place additional pressure on already fragile health systems.”
These developments are unfolding amid a sharp fall in international funding for both healthcare and humanitarian operations and increasing fiscal constraints at the national level.
“At the very moment when needs are increasing, resources are declining,” he said.
Investment and preparation
Tedros urged leaders to continue measures that promote health, such as reducing tobacco use and other risk factors for noncommunicable diseases and ensuring that all children are vaccinated.
Governments should also continue to invest in strong, equitable and resilient health systems and in health workers.
“Make every primary healthcare facility a place where a woman can receive quality care during pregnancy, where every newborn and child can get a healthy start in life and where hypertension, diabetes and cancer can be detected and managed early,” he said.
The WHO chief called for protecting health by strengthening preparedness, security and resilience.
“The threats facing this region are evolving,” he warned, noting that conflicts and outbreaks continue while climate risks continue to grow.
“Preparedness cannot be an afterthought. Preparedness saves lives before emergencies begin,” he said, underlining the need for continued investment in surveillance, laboratories, emergency workforces, resilient health facilities and supply chains.

On Monday afternoon, peacekeepers from MINUSCA’s Zambian contingent and Central African Armed Forces (FACA) personnel patrolled the main roads in and around Birao. Patrols are also being reinforced in Am-Dafock and several surrounding localities.

Established in 2020, the Forum of Mayors connects city, national and global actors to share local solutions for implementing the UN Sustainable Development Goals.
Their commitments cover six areas:
- Efficient, safe, green and accessible transportation
- More green spaces, biodiversity protection, and lower pollution and emissions
- Inclusive, participatory planning and climate resilience
- Affordable, secure, climate-resilient housing for vulnerable people
- Protecting cultural and natural heritage for responsible tourism
- Using culture, creativity, innovation and ethical AI to improve urban services and civic participation
The mayors noted that across all areas, fiscal constraints, fragmented governance and limited local capacity hinder implementation and urged States and international organizations to strengthen the legal, institutional, policy and financial frameworks needed to address the issue.
The head of the UN Economic Commission for Europe (UNECE), which organises the forum, explained why cities must be at the heart of decision-making.
“Cities are where people experience the major challenges of our time most directly – from housing and access to essential services to mobility, climate impacts, inequality and disaster risks. But, cities are also where solutions are being developed every day,” she said.

DR Congo: Cholera cases spike amid fight against Ebola
The cholera epidemic continues to spread in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), where more than 125,000 suspected cases and 3,644 suspected deaths were recorded between January 2025 and the end of September 2026, the World Health Organization (WHO) warned on Wednesday.
Key points
- While the country is battling Ebola in the restive east, cholera is gaining ground in several regions, fueled by a lack of access to clean water and sanitation infrastructure
- Since the beginning of 2026, more than 51,412 suspected cholera cases, including 1,487 deaths, have been reported in 21 provinces: WHO
- Health authorities recorded 2,932 suspected cases and 86 deaths from 21 to 28 September, compared to 2,506 cases and 62 deaths the previous week
- Cholera is a severe diarrhoeal disease that can be fatal within hours if not treated
- Quick access to treatment is crucial and access to safe water, basic sanitation and hygiene is essential to prevent cholera
Regions hit hardest
The provinces of South Kivu, North Kivu and Haut-Katanga account for nearly 60 per cent of reported suspected cases.
Transmission remains high in provinces where cholera is endemic.
During the latest surveillance period, four new health zones were affected, three in Tshuapa province and one in South Kivu.
Security, logistics challenges
However, response operations are facing security and logistical challenges.
In the east of the country, insecurity restricts medical teams’ access to certain areas, particularly Kibua and Masisi. The remoteness of villages from healthcare facilities also delays treatment, increasing the risk of death, WHO warned.
Environmental conditions are also exacerbating the situation.
The use of well water and rainfall, which can carry contaminated water to sources used by households, promotes the transmission of the disease.
To reduce the risk of contamination, response teams are preparing to install four water chlorination sites in the most affected areas of North Kivu and, in Tanganyika, plans are underway to disinfect nearly 4,000 households and 5,900 latrines.
Cross-border vaccine campaign
Preparations for an oral vaccination campaign are also continuing in the islands along the Congo River corridor.
DRC and the Republic of Congo are developing a joint cross-border vaccination plan.
In South Kivu, reactive vaccination campaigns are continuing in the Mulungu and Shabunda health zones, alongside community awareness activities.
Ebola: 9,000 cases
This increase in cholera comes as DRC faces an Ebola epidemic that is severely straining the country’s health capacity.
According to the latest WHO data published on Tuesday, 9,066 cases and 4,381 deaths have been recorded in seven provinces and 65 health zones, representing a case fatality rate of 48.3 per cent. The report also indicates 2,389 recoveries.
In DRC, the response continues with the support of the WHO and its partners. In the Haut-Uele province, the Ebola treatment centre in Isiro has been expanded to accommodate more patients, while preserving essential health services at the city’s main general referral hospital.
WHO also delivered an additional tonne of medical supplies to bolster operations on the ground.
Uganda, Kenya affected
The outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo strain of the Ebola virus, has also raised concerns in neighbouring countries.
After reporting 20 cases and two deaths, Uganda was declared Ebola-free in August.
Last week, Kenya confirmed in Nairobi the death of a Kenyan national infected with the virus after traveling from the DRC via Uganda.
This is the first imported case reported by the country in connection with this outbreak, with media reports indicating a possible second Ebola case.

Colombia: UN independent experts call for Ecopetrol to provide reparations to victims of armed conflict
UN independent experts welcomed on Wednesday a recent landmark corporate accountability ruling involving the Ecopetrol oil company by Colombia’s Special Jurisdiction for Peace, calling for reparations for victims.
The Jurisdiction for Peace (JEP) ruling related to the Macro-Case 08, which recognises the responsibility of several State agents and a director of the State-owned company for their involvement in acts related to serious human rights violations, war crimes and crimes against humanity committed during the armed conflict in Barrancabermeja, Colombia’s oil capital.
“The JEP’s decision represents a significant step forward for truth, justice and accountability regarding the impacts of corporate activities in conflict-affected contexts,” the experts said. “It also opens an unprecedented opportunity to place victims at the centre of reparation and restoration efforts.”
The experts welcomed the cooperation provided by Ecopetrol during the proceedings and encouraged the company to deepen that commitment through ongoing dialogue and concrete actions for reparation and restoration aimed at the affected individuals and communities.
Companies must respect human rights
“Companies have a responsibility to respect human rights and to participate in redressing the negative impacts they have caused or contributed to, in accordance with the United Nations Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights,” they noted.
The experts urged Ecopetrol to continue engaging in good faith in a constructive dialogue with the victims and their representative organisations, adopting a restorative approach that allows for the identification of the harms suffered, expectations for reparations and the measures necessary to help restore the rights violated.
“Victims should not be mere observers of the reparation processes, they must be active participants in their design and implementation,” they said. “Effective reparations require meaningful participation, acknowledgment of harm and a sustained commitment to restoring rights and rebuilding trust.”
State’s duty to protect
As the majority shareholder of Ecopetrol, the experts highlighted the role of the Colombian State in this process.
“When it comes to State-owned enterprises, business responsibilities to respect human rights converge with the State’s duty to protect such rights,” they said.
“Colombian authorities must ensure the company participates fully in efforts towards truth, justice, reparations and guarantees of non-repetition and that this process effectively contributes to strengthening public trust in institutions,” the experts said.
The independent experts, who are appointed by the Human Rights Council, are not UN staff and do not receive a salary, reiterated the call by the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights for sufficient funding of Colombia’s comprehensive peace system, which includes the JEP and the Unit for the Search for Missing Persons.
“We stand ready and willing to support the Government of Colombia and Ecopetrol in this process, in order to strengthen corporate accountability in contexts of transitional justice and to build sustainable peace,” they concluded.

Health workers tackle taboos over drinking with new AI tool

Health workers tackle taboos over drinking with new AI tool
A new AI-powered hub for health professionals aims to help identify alcohol-related risks and launch discussions with patients, including the link between drinking and cancer, the World Health Organization (WHO) announced on Wednesday.
“Alcohol harm isn’t abstract,” said Dr. Carina Ferreira-Borges, the WHO Europe regional adviser on alcohol. “It can be heart and liver disease. It can be a baby exposed to alcohol before birth. It can be anxiety and depression. It can be a woman who develops breast cancer without ever being told alcohol was a risk.”
The launch highlighted the widespread lack of awareness about alcohol-related health risks.
‘Not an awkward extra’
“We know screening and brief interventions work, but only if health professionals feel able to use them” she continued.
“A doctor or nurse with a few minutes between patients can now ask the hub’s AI assistant how to ask about alcohol consumption and get an answer based on WHO evidence. That makes conversations about alcohol a normal part of care, not an awkward extra.”
Only 15 per cent of people surveyed in 14 European Union countries know that alcohol can cause breast cancer, WHO said, adding that it actually causes at least seven types of cancer as well as cardiovascular and liver disease.
“Alcohol is so deeply embedded in our cultures and social lives that even doctors and nurses can feel uncomfortable asking patients about it, particularly when the patient has come in for something seemingly unrelated,” said Dr. Ferreira-Borges. “Add time pressures, limited training and uncertainty about how to approach the subject without sounding judgemental and you have a major missed opportunity for prevention.”
Prevention opportunities
To address this gap, WHO Europe has launched its new alcohol screening and brief interventions hub, which brings together evidence, guidance and practical tools to help health professionals discuss alcohol-related risks.
Health workers can begin with a 10-question screening test to assess a patient’s alcohol-related risk then use the hub’s AI assistant to prepare for a conversation or find relevant guidance.
“The science is evolving and keeping up with the evidence on alcohol and its links to more than 200 diseases and health conditions is not always straightforward,” Dr. Ferreira-Borges noted.
Catching links
Alcohol is among the least frequently discussed behavioural risk factors in healthcare, WHO noted, and is raised less often than smoking, physical activity or diet.
Many health professionals have been trained to recognise the symptoms associated with heavy drinking, “but not necessarily to understand and communicate the risks associated with more routine consumption”, Dr. Ferreira-Borges continued.
“Say they have a patient with high blood pressure or mental health issues, alcohol rarely comes up, even though it can play an important role.”

Haiti sanctions renewed: Starving the gangs of bullets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Haiti sanctions renewed: Starving the gangs of bullets
Haiti is living through one of the world’s most acute security crises.
Armed gangs control large parts of the capital, Port-au-Prince, and are pushing into rural areas, terrorising communities, killing people, committing rape and other sexual assaults, kidnapping for ransom and extorting individuals and businesses.
About 1.5 million people, roughly 12 per cent of the population, have been forced from their homes.
Haiti makes no guns or ammunition of its own, yet the gangs never seem to run out.
On Wednesday, the UN Security Council renewed sanctions meant to change that by targeting people considered responsible for or involved in activities threatening Haiti’s peace, security and stability.
What are the sanctions?
Created in 2022 by the Security Council, the Haiti sanctions committee has three main enforcement tools at its disposal: an arms embargo, a travel ban and an asset freeze.
The embargo targets weapons and ammunition reaching armed groups. The travel ban and freeze apply to named people and entities who contribute to the Caribbean island nation’s insecurity and gang violence.
Nine individuals and two groups are currently sanctioned by the council.
Why are they needed?
The human cost of gang violence in Haiti is stark.
More than 3,000 people were killed and over 1,500 injured between October last year and April this year.
A UN partner reported treating over 2,400 survivors of sexual violence in Port-au-Prince between January and May. Most were women and girls and 16 per cent were minors. Cases involving children as young as eight were also reported.
Children are also being recruited by gangs.
How are the sanctions enforced?
Mostly by governments, at ports, borders and banks.
Haitian authorities have recently intercepted several illicit shipments at ports.
United States authorities have also intercepted firearms and ammunition destined for Haiti and pursued trafficking investigations.
The UN Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) supports regional efforts to counter trafficking.
Is it working?
Haiti does not manufacture firearms or ammunition, but according to the figures released by the UN human rights office last year, there are an estimated between 270,000 and 500,000 illegal weapons in circulation.
The arms embargo is violated “on a regular basis” according to the panel of experts on Haiti, an independent fact-finding body established by the Security Council, which gathers evidence and analyses information related to sanctions violations.
These independent experts have travelled to Port-au-Prince and Cap-Haïtien in Haiti, Santo Domingo in the neighbouring Dominican Republic and Miami in the US to meet government officials, police, financial institutions, civil society representatives and people affected by gang violence.
Some of the gang’s bullets come from national stockpiles, and police do not centrally track what they seize, so some weapons are unaccounted for or diverted by corrupt officers.
The asset freeze has fared worse, the panel said. Only two sanctioned individuals’ accounts were reported frozen, with meagre sums, because banks acted slowly and the targets moved money or hid it under third parties’ names.
The panel found no attempts to break the travel ban, but warned that fraudulent passports could help sanctioned people travel under false names.
What do the experts say?
The independent panel’s message is that “targeting gang leaders without addressing the networks that sustain them will inevitably fall short.”
It points to political, economic and security figures who back gangs and says many gang leaders beyond those on the sanctions list meet the criteria.
What happens next?
Gangs have continued their deadly expansion despite the sanctions already in place, a clear indication that enforcement matters.
At Wednesday’s meeting, speakers from some of the Security Council’s 15 Member States re-emphasised the need to disrupt gang financing, close loopholes and hold the networks supporting armed groups accountable.
The council extended the work of its sanctions committee by 13 months.
Haiti welcomed the renewal while warning that sanctions alone cannot restore security.
For Haitians living with gang violence, what matters is whether work of the sanctions committee and the efforts made by the Haitian Government and countries in the region translate into safer neighbourhoods, fewer weapons in criminal hands and greater freedom to travel, work and reach essential services.

Artist of the month: Steph Huang
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:58:56 UTC
20:58:56 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – When picking up a bottle of olive oil at the supermarket, few consumers consider the complex geographic landscapes and global capital networks it crossed before reaching the table.
For London-based Taiwanese artist Steph Huang (黃麗音), food serves as a primary lens through which to dissect the globalized economy and contemporary labor systems. Following prestigious accolades including top honors at the Taipei Art Awards in 2022 and the Mark Tanner Sculpture Award in 2023, alongside exhibitions at Tate Britain and Perrotin, this year marks another career pinnacle for the 1990-born artist.
In October, Huang teams up with curator Liao Chuan-ya (廖釧雅) for her solo exhibition, "The Glittering Grove," at TKG+ gallery in Taipei. Meanwhile, a British iteration of her signature project, "Lili Deli," debuted at Frieze London.
As the featured artist of the month, Huang reflected on her creative path, tracing global food systems from memories in Taiwan to the olive groves of southern Spain.
Huang’s practice frequently centers on micro-objects from everyday life. In "Grafting," presented at Art Basel Hong Kong, she layered mangoes, shoji screens, and Taiwan’s colonial histories to explore family memory and identity.
In "The Glittering Grove," her field research shifted to olive groves and industrial assembly lines in southern Spain. Huang explained that while both projects started with specific agricultural products, olive oil operates on a planetary scale that shapes our fundamental relationship with food and nature.
Immersing herself in Spanish olive orchards, Huang witnessed the stark realities of agricultural economics firsthand. She was surprised by how small a fraction of the market price actually returns to the farmers for their fruit.
She said that while advertisements promote ultra-processed foods, fresh produce rarely receives such attention because it carries no brand and generates no outsized profit margins. The remote, off-grid experience also reshaped her personal outlook, leading her to realize that much of the modern convenience people pursue is not strictly necessary.
Inside the exhibition space, visitors hear the subtle sounds of olive harvesting, while wallpaper featuring field photographs of fallen olives and branches frames the room.
Blown glass plays a crucial role in Huang’s material vocabulary, where its delicate, translucent, and fluid quality contrasts sharply with mass-produced olive oil. Huang explained that the fragility of blown glass serves as a metaphor for the vulnerability of the global food system.
For Huang, using readymades is an act of assemblage rather than a desire to provoke. She said that readymades carry their own history and weight, allowing her to utilize their material forms and textures to reveal hidden social relations.
By highlighting discarded olives and branches, Huang elevates systemic remnants into visual focal points. Unharvested pods, fish bones, fallen figs, discarded shells, and old shoji screens have all taken center stage in her recent work as part of an effort to subvert conventional perspectives and flip hierarchical relationships.
"The Glittering Grove" observes that while an olive's economic value shifts across production stages, the fruit itself remains unchanged while the surrounding institutional framework transforms.
When asked if this mirrors the market fate of artworks, Huang offered a candid view on the dual reality of art.
She explained that while a piece accumulates layers of commercial value and class signifiers upon entering art fairs and collections, art ultimately exists for the public to engage with, criticize, and view. She added that when standing in front of a work with friends, the discussion revolves around personal affinity rather than market value.
Huang’s cross-cultural experience living in London sharpens her view of global supply chains. She attributed her curiosity about food systems to her Taiwanese background, saying that being an outsider makes it natural to question local dining habits and cultural traditions.
Looking ahead, Huang remains eager to explore new media, including an upcoming project incorporating a collection of vintage ties. Through poetic assemblages, Huang translates global capital into tangible form, encouraging viewers to look at everyday items on supermarket shelves with a renewed sense of awareness.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The upgraded Hai Lung submarine will be the focus of joint sea-air anti-submarine warfare exercises in waters southwest of the country from Oct. 28 to Nov. 27.
The Navy’s surface fleet and 256th Submarine Squadron will conduct the exercises in three phases, per Liberty Times. The surface fleet’s portion will involve joint sea-air anti-submarine operations, with Air Force P-3C anti-submarine aircraft and Navy S-70C(M) anti-submarine helicopters also taking part.
The Hai Lung has completed a combat system upgrade and test-fired a US-made MK-48 heavyweight torpedo. Its sister submarine, the Hai Hu, is undergoing a separate combat system upgrade at a shipyard.
The upgrade gave the Hai Lung a new combat management system designed to improve target tracking and its ability to engage multiple targets simultaneously, Liberty Times reported. The submarine can also fire US-made MK-48 Mod 6 Advanced Technology heavyweight torpedoes and submarine-launched Harpoon anti-ship missiles.
Military sources said the exercises are strategically important for securing the southwest maritime corridor. Waters are deep and have complex currents, making them a key area for submarine operations and a potential route for Chinese submarines seeking to pass through the First Island Chain and enter the Pacific Ocean.
Frequent exercises in the area allow surface ships and submarines to practice defensive tactics under realistic conditions and build a database of local underwater conditions, according to Liberty Times. This knowledge could help Taiwan improve its underwater warfare capabilities and deter Chinese submarines from infiltrating nearby waters or imposing a maritime blockade, the sources said.
The exercises will also test coordination among naval and air force units, which must share information to detect and track underwater threats. During the drills, the Hai Lung is expected to serve as a simulated adversary or a key component of underwater defense scenarios involving P-3C aircraft, S-70C helicopters, and Navy surface vessels.

The new facility is located near Millerovo in Russia’s Rostov Region, at coordinates 48.995968, 40.286255.

About six weeks passed between the start of site preparation and the appearance of the main elements of the launch infrastructure.

Ukrainian long-range strikes have repeatedly targeted Tsymbulova.
In September, Ukrainian drones hit some of the bunkers and damaged hangars at the site. Satellite images also showed signs of detonations and debris from destroyed drones in the area where they were prepared for launch.
Following another strike on October 1, storage areas and launch infrastructure at the site were again damaged.

Researchers use genome sequencing to study tuberculosis transmissions in Kaohsiung
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:58:27 UTC
20:58:27 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Researchers have used whole-genome sequencing to trace how tuberculosis bacteria spreads in Kaohsiung and understand the role of older adults in the chain of transmission.
“As many countries face rapidly ageing populations, reading the genetic code of TB bacteria can show us where the disease is really spreading and help us act earlier,” said Lin Hsien-ho (林先和), a co-corresponding author of the study and the director of the Institute of Epidemiology and Preventive Medicine at National Taiwan University.
In a study published in The Lancet Microbe, researchers read the complete genomes of tuberculosis bacteria collected from close to 4,000 patients diagnosed over five years in Kaohsiung and compared the samples to identify links between infections.
Taiwan recorded 5,742 tuberculosis cases last year, the lowest number on record, but more than half of the patients were aged 65 or older, according to data from the health ministry. The study sheds light on the role older adults may play in transmission, suggesting they are not only vulnerable to the disease but may also contribute to its spread.
“We often think of older people with tuberculosis as patients who need treatment, not as part of the chain of transmission,” Lin said. “Our results suggest they may be both.”
The researchers found that adults aged 65 and older accounted for about four in 10 patients whose samples were genetically linked to those from at least one other patient, suggesting relatively recent transmissions.
The study also identified distinct patterns of transmission among different strains of tuberculosis bacteria. One strain spread readily in rural and mountainous areas but did not reach urban areas, where another group of strains predominated.
“Combining bacterial DNA with information about patients and where they live can reveal where tuberculosis is spreading and which groups of people need closer attention,” according to a press release.

Royal Caribbean cruise passenger who went overboard rescued after she spent 20 hours at sea, Greek coast guard says
A woman who allegedly jumped off a cruise ship into the Ionian Sea was rescued over the weekend after 20 hours in the water, the Greek coast guard said.
The incident occurred early on Friday when the Royal Caribbean Cruises ship Odyssey of the Seas was sailing southwest of the island of Zakynthos, the coast guard said.
The 44-year-old Salvadorian woman subsequently told her rescuers she had jumped because "she wanted to disembark," a coast guard spokesperson told AFP.
"She was 20 hours at sea," the officer said.
After an alert went out early on Friday, two coast guard boats and a navy helicopter were dispatched to the area and other nearby ships were rerouted.
The Odyssey of the Seas also joined the search, the officer said.
 A passing freighter eventually located the woman, fully conscious, in a life ring early on Saturday and she was picked up by a Greek coast guard patrol boat.
A video released by the coast guard shows a crew throwing a rope to a woman floating inside an orange life ring in the water in the dark.
She was taken to the port of Katakolo and then to hospital in the nearby city of Pyrgos for health tests that include a psychiatric evaluation ordered by a local prosecutor, the officer said.
According to Royal Caribbean, Odyssey of the Seas is 1,138 feet long and can accommodate 4,198 guests. The ship offers seasonal cruises to the Greek Isles.
Last year, a man jumped off a Royal Caribbean cruise ship near the Port of San Juan — allegedly to avoid paying off more than $16,000 in gambling debt to the cruise line. Jey Gonzalez-Diaz jumped into the water as the ship disembarked, during U.S. Customs and Border Protection inspection, according to a criminal complaint. He was then brought to shore by someone passing by on a jet ski, and later charged with attempting to avoid monetary reporting requirements when traveling into the U.S.

A state-funded school renovation project in Helsinki has become the centre of a labour exploitation scandal involving unpaid wages, false employment records and a subcontractor allegedly managed from an Estonian prison by a man convicted of involvement in organised crime.
Finland's Construction Union (Rakennusliitto) identified the suspected violations at the Valteri Ruskis school in Ruskeasuo, which serves children and young people requiring special educational support.
Add Helsinki Times as a preferred source on Google (opens Google in a new tab)
The union said its investigation uncovered 30 workers classified as self-employed despite working under conditions resembling regular employment. Several foreign workers received wages below collective agreement rates, while the authorities had not properly verified the right of some workers to work in Finland.
State property agency Senaatti Properties commissioned the renovation, with Mirlux Oy acting as the main contractor. The allegations concern subcontractors Varatek Oy and Kore Metal Oy.
According to the union, Varatek registered 36 people to work at the site, although only three were its direct employees. Others worked through an invoicing service, raising concerns that the company had disguised employment relationships to avoid labour obligations.
The union also identified unpaid overtime and Sunday work allowances. Some workers received trainee-level wages despite working extended hours.
Finnish newspaper Helsingin Sanomat reported that three employees worked 122 hours across 13 days within a two-week period. Union calculations indicated that each had lost nearly €1,500 in wages.
The investigation also found that up to 12 workers had not undergone proper checks of their right to work in Finland. Most workers came from outside the European Union, particularly Ukraine. Some Ukrainian nationals had been incorrectly registered as Finnish citizens.
Rakennusliitto placed Varatek under a union boycott on Tuesday after the company allegedly failed to resolve the wage disputes.
Toni Malmström, senior expert at the union, criticised the oversight failures, warning that companies violating labour agreements gain an unfair advantage over employers following the rules.
The union said such practices also threaten Finnish construction workers amid continued unemployment in the sector.

Cornell scientists identify rare human genetic disorder in two unusually long-legged cats
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:56:22 UTC
20:56:22 KST

Cornell scientists identify rare human genetic disorder in two unusually long-legged cats
- Date:
- October 14, 2026
- Source:
- Cornell University
- Summary:
- Two unusually long-legged cats have helped scientists uncover the first genetically confirmed cases of Marfan syndrome in domestic felines. Researchers at Cornell University discovered that the brothers carried two altered copies of a gene linked to the rare connective tissue disorder, which can affect the eyes, heart, and blood vessels. Surprisingly, the cats survived into adulthood because their genetic mutation still allowed some normal function.
- Share:
Two brothers named Gary and Shaggy have helped Cornell University researchers make a rare genetic discovery. In a study published in Scientific Reports, scientists reported the first molecular characterization of Marfan syndrome in domestic cats, a condition primarily recognized in humans.
Gary and Shaggy first stood out as kittens because of their unusually long limbs. As they grew older, veterinarians also identified abnormalities in their eye structures and an enlarged aorta, the body's main artery. Together, these symptoms suggested Marfan syndrome, an inherited condition that weakens connective tissues throughout the body. The disorder affects approximately 1 in 4,000 people, but these brothers represented the first known documented feline cases.
"The findings provide a foundation for improved veterinary diagnostics," said senior author Dr. Jacquelyn Evans, assistant professor in the College of Veterinary Medicine and at the Baker Institute for Animal Health. "It can help veterinarians recognize similar cases in the future and may help develop genetic tests."
Scientists Uncover a Surprising Genetic Twist
To determine what caused the brothers' unusual symptoms, researchers from multiple disciplines conducted thorough medical examinations and analyzed their DNA. Their investigation identified changes in a gene called FBN1, which provides instructions for producing fibrillin-1. This protein is essential for healthy connective tissue, helping support structures throughout the body, including blood vessels, bones, ligaments, skin, and eyes.
Genetic testing revealed that Gary and Shaggy each had two altered copies of FBN1, having inherited one from each parent. This was especially notable because, in humans, a mutation in just one copy of the gene can be enough to cause Marfan syndrome. Having two altered copies is exceptionally uncommon and can severely disrupt the production of normal fibrillin-1.
Yet the brothers' genetic changes had an unexpected effect. Further analysis showed that their particular variant did not completely disable the gene. Instead, it interfered with how the gene's instructions were processed while still allowing some normal activity to continue. That remaining function helps explain why Gary and Shaggy were able to survive into adulthood, even though carrying two copies of such a mutation could otherwise have resulted in a much more severe form of the disorder.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Cornell University. Original written by Teresa Griffin. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Shawna R. Cook, Jessica J. Hayward, Soon Hon Cheong, Linda Impe, Ian R. Porter, Brian Lamendola, Gavin R. Hitchener, Urs Giger, Philip R. Fox, Jacquelyn M. Evans, Bart J. G. Broeckx. A homozygous hypomorphic FBN1 splice region variant in domestic cats with Marfan syndrome. Scientific Reports, 2026; DOI: 10.1038/s41598-026-70702-3

Wie Maroš Šefčovič der Durchbruch im Handel mit China gelang
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:56:11 UTC
20:56:11 KST

Wie Maroš Šefčovič der Durchbruch im Handel mit China gelang
Europas Handelskommissar hat ein erstes Zugeständnis aus Peking errungen. Nun muss er die EU-Spitzenpolitiker davon überzeugen, dass der Dialog noch mehr bewirken kann.
Als Maroš Šefčovič im Juli den EU-Botschaftern seine Strategie für den Umgang mit China vorstellte, richtete er eine Warnung an die Regierungen, die auf strengere Handelsmaßnahmen gegen Peking drängten.
„Manchmal ist es sogar populär, einen Handelskrieg zu beginnen, aber es ist sehr schwierig, ihn zu beenden“, erinnerte sich der EU-Handelskommissar später in einem Interview mit POLITICO.
Drei Monate später ist Šefčovič ein erster Durchbruch gelungen: Letzte Woche wurde in Peking eine Vereinbarung erzielt, die Importe chinesischer Hybridautos drastisch zu reduzieren. Dieser symbolische Erfolg ist ein kleiner Schritt zur Stabilisierung der Handelsbeziehungen, die nach Ansicht Brüssels einen gefährlichen Wendepunkt erreicht haben.
Für Šefčovič, der im vergangenen Jahr mit Donald Trump einen Zollwaffenstillstand ausgehandelt hatte, deutet die Vereinbarung darauf hin, dass sich seine Strategie des Engagements, gestützt durch die Androhung härterer Handelsmaßnahmen, allmählich auszuzahlen beginnt.
Šefčovič hatte sich bei einem Treffen mit dem chinesischen Handelsminister Wang Wentao Ende Juni in Brüssel darauf geeinigt, den Handelsdialog aufzunehmen.
Der slowakische Kommissar hoffte, wenn er sich zuerst auf den Automobilsektor konzentrieren würde – einem Bereich, in dem die EU als einer der wenigen großen Märkte, die chinesischen Herstellern noch offenstehen, über Einfluss verfügt – einen vertrauensbildenden Erfolg zu erzielen. Erst später will er sich den schwierigeren Fragen zuwenden: den kritischen Rohstoffen bis hin zu Chinas enormen industriellen Überkapazitäten.
Gleichzeitig bemühte er sich darum, die europäischen Regierungen parallel hinter einer Initiative zur Stärkung der Handelsschutzmaßnahmen der EU zu vereinen. Šefčovič untermauerte seine Verhandlungsposition mit der Androhung härterer Maßnahmen, um das Handelsdefizit der EU gegenüber China in Höhe von einer Milliarde Euro pro Tag zu senken.
Der Hybrid-Deal ist jedoch nur der erste Schritt in einem weitaus größeren Wettstreit.
Advertisement
Die Staats- und Regierungschefs der EU treffen sich am Donnerstag in Brüssel, um Bilanz zu ziehen. Sie müssen abwägen, ob sie die Forderungen nach aggressiveren Maßnahmen zum Schutz der europäischen Industrie durchziehen.
Das Treffen wird zeigen, ob ein Kommissar, der seine Karriere darauf aufgebaut hat, Kompromisse mit schwierigen Partnern zu finden, die Unterstützung Europas für eine Strategie aufrechterhalten kann, deren Erfolg alles andere als sicher ist.
„Man hat es mit demselben Partner am Verhandlungstisch zu tun“, sagte Šefčovič im August in einem Interview mit POLITICO über die Risiken eines Handelskriegs. „Wenn man das also vermeiden kann, wäre das viel besser.“
Marktmacht
Šefčovičs erster Schritt bestand darin, sich auf einen Bereich zu konzentrieren, in dem Europa noch Einfluss hat: den Zugang zu seinem Markt mit 450 Millionen Menschen.
Chinas Hersteller haben sich zu globalen Kraftzentren entwickelt, kämpfen jedoch mit einer schwachen Nachfrage im Inland. Ein anhaltender Einbruch auf dem Immobilienmarkt belastet den Privatkonsum, während der gnadenlose Wettbewerb Preiskämpfe ausgelöst hat. Die Inlandsverkäufe von Pkw gingen im September gegenüber dem Vorjahr um 28 Prozent zurück.
Dadurch gewinnen die Märkte in Übersee zunehmend an Bedeutung. Da die USA chinesische Importe ausschließen, bleibt Europa einer der lukrativsten Märkte, der chinesischen Herstellern noch offensteht.
Advertisement
Šefčovič setzte darauf, dass Peking lieber Exportbeschränkungen akzeptieren würde, als den Zugang zum europäischen Markt gänzlich zu riskieren.
Er richtete sein Augenmerk auf den Automobilsektor, in dem chinesische Hersteller sehr schnell Fuß gefasst haben. Im Jahr 2024 hatten chinesische Autohersteller einen Anteil von lediglich 2 Prozent sowohl am europäischen Hybrid- als auch am Plug-in-Hybrid-Markt; bis zur ersten Hälfte des Jahres 2026 waren die jeweiligen Anteile laut Branchenzahlen auf 14 Prozent beziehungsweise 25 Prozent gestiegen.
Die Kommission bereitete sich darauf vor, die Einfuhr von Hybridfahrzeugen auch ohne ein Abkommen zu beschränken. Eine Verhandlungslösung bot Šefčovič jedoch auch einen politischen Mehrwert: den Beweis, dass der Dialog mit Peking zu greifbaren Ergebnissen führen kann.
Die Verhandlungen verliefen intensiv, wie eine mit den Gesprächen vertraute Person auf chinesischer Seite berichtete.
„Es war sehr, sehr hart“, sagte die Person, die anonym bleiben wollte, um offen über die hinter verschlossenen Türen stattfindenden Verhandlungen zu sprechen. „Beide Seiten hatten seit langem keine solche Intensität mehr erlebt. Keine Sommerpause, keine Feiertage. Sie arbeiteten rund um die Uhr, sogar noch ein oder zwei Tage vor Šefčovičs Reise nach Peking.“
Während Brüssel den Dialog suchte, wollte es Peking gleichzeitig davon überzeugen, dass es bereit sei, härtere Maßnahmen zu ergreifen, sollten die Verhandlungen scheitern.
Advertisement
Šefčovič hatte zuvor Pläne für ein neues „Diversifizierungsinstrument“ angekündigt, das Unternehmen in kritischen Sektoren dazu verpflichten würde, wesentliche Vorleistungen von mindestens drei Lieferanten zu beziehen – ein Schritt, um Chinas Fähigkeit einzuschränken, Europas Abhängigkeit von seinen kritischen Rohstoffen auszunutzen.
Dann, nur drei Tage vor Šefčovičs Reise nach Peking, erhöhten Frankreich und Deutschland den Druck.
Präsident Emmanuel Macron und Bundeskanzler Friedrich Merz forderten eine wirkungsvolle neue Handelswaffe, die es Brüssel ermöglichen würde, Ländern, denen unlautere Wettbewerbsvorteile vorgeworfen werden, innerhalb weniger Tage den Zugang zum europäischen Markt zu beschränken – oder sogar ganz zu sperren.
Der Vorschlag nannte China zwar nicht ausdrücklich, doch Peking war das offensichtliche Ziel.
Den Zusammenhalt wahren
Mehreren Diplomaten zufolge werden die EU-Staats- und Regierungschefs die Einigung voraussichtlich begrüßen, die Kommission jedoch gleichzeitig dazu drängen, rasch zu handeln, um die Handelsschutzmaßnahmen der Union zu stärken. Die in Peking erzielte Einigung hat Zeit gewonnen, aber noch nicht geklärt, wie weit Brüssel gehen sollte, falls die chinesischen Exporte weiter steigen oder die Verhandlungen ins Stocken geraten.
„Wir verlieren Tausende von Arbeitsplätzen in der Industrie; Olivenöl und Eiscreme werden das Kernproblem nicht lösen“, sagte ein EU-Diplomat, nachdem Šefčovič die Botschafter am Sonntag informiert hatte, und bezog sich dabei auf die gemeldeten Ergebnisse der Gespräche.
Advertisement
Ein hochrangiger deutscher Beamter begrüßte das Abkommen von Peking als einen ersten Schritt in die richtige Richtung. „Es ist ein positives Zeichen – das natürlich das Problem des Handelsdefizits mit China nicht vollständig löst“, sagte der Beamte.
Doch Berlins Unterstützung für eine härtere Linie könnte sich als kurzlebig erweisen.
Alicia García-Herrero, Senior Fellow beim Thinktank Bruegel, argumentierte, dass Pekings Zugeständnisse darauf ausgelegt gewesen seien, Berlin zu beschwichtigen, angesichts der Bedeutung der Automobilindustrie für die deutsche Wirtschaft.
„Ich hoffe nur, dass Merz nicht von dem Brief abrückt, den er an die Kommission geschickt hat“, sagte sie. Da der deutsche Bundeskanzler im eigenen Land politisch geschwächt ist, befürchtet García-Herrero, dass er zögern könnte, eine langwierige Konfrontation zu riskieren: „Ich mache mir Sorgen, dass Merz diesen schnellen Erfolg nutzen und sich aus dem Staub machen wird.“
Damit steht Šefčovič vor einem Balanceakt: Er muss die EU-Regierungen bei der Fortsetzung des Engagements mit China an Bord halten und gleichzeitig die glaubwürdige Drohung mit härteren Maßnahmen aufrechterhalten, falls die Gespräche scheitern sollten.
„Ich gehe davon aus, dass [die Staats- und Regierungschefs] der Kommission grünes Licht geben werden, weitere handelspolitische Schutzmaßnahmen voranzutreiben. China könnte dies als Verrat auffassen. Sollte das der Fall sein, könnten wir sehr schnell wieder in einen Konflikt geraten“, sagte Noah Barkin, Senior Advisor im China-Team der Rhodium Group.
Advertisement
Der bevorstehende Kampf
Für Šefčovič besteht die Herausforderung nun darin, einen begrenzten Durchbruch bei den Autos in eine umfassendere Neuausrichtung des Handels mit China umzumünzen – und Europa gleichzeitig Zeit zu verschaffen, seine Abwehrmaßnahmen zu stärken, falls die Verhandlungen scheitern sollten.
„Es spricht einiges dafür, China das anzutun, was China Europa jahrelang angetan hat – Peking in Dialogen und Verfahren zu verzetteln, während Europa seine Instrumente bereitstellt. Aber die EU muss die Zeit, die diese Gespräche bieten, voll ausschöpfen“, sagte Barkin von Rhodium.
Der Handelskommissar wird voraussichtlich im Januar ein Videogespräch mit Wang führen, bevor sich die beiden im kommenden März erneut treffen. Diese Gespräche werden zeigen, ob Peking bereit ist, weitere Zugeständnisse in Sektoren zu machen, in denen die europäische Industrie zunehmend in die Defensive gerät, darunter die Chemieindustrie.
Eine weitere Priorität sind kritische Rohstoffe, bei denen China zugestimmt hat, weiterhin Ausfuhrlizenzen für Seltene Erden zu erteilen. Pekings Kontrolle über deren Versorgung verschafft dem Land erheblichen Einfluss auf europäische Hersteller, was die Grenzen von Šefčovičs Verhandlungsposition deutlich macht.
Die Kommission bereitet zudem zwei Vorschläge für Dezember vor: das Diversifizierungsinstrument, das darauf abzielt, die Abhängigkeit von chinesischen Lieferungen zu verringern, und einen Mechanismus zum Schutz europäischer Industrien und Regionen vor Vergeltungsmaßnahmen.
Das Ausmaß der Herausforderung ist gewaltig: Chinesische Importe von Hybridautos beliefen sich im ersten Halbjahr 2026 auf 6,7 Milliarden Euro, während das Handelsdefizit zwischen der EU und China im vergangenen Jahr bei 360 Milliarden Euro lag. Das Abkommen verschafft den europäischen Automobilherstellern zwar eine gewisse Erleichterung, trägt aber kaum dazu bei, das zugrunde liegende Ungleichgewicht zu beheben.
Advertisement
Brüssel hofft, dass die Schutzmaßnahmen für Hybridfahrzeuge als Blaupause für den Schutz anderer Branchen dienen können, die mit einem Anstieg chinesischer Importe konfrontiert sind.
„Wir hören auf unsere Industrie. Dazu gehören die chemische Industrie, die Windkraftbranche und die Möbelindustrie. Wir wissen, wo es zu einem Anstieg kommt, und wir wissen, was uns im Hinblick auf unsere Deindustrialisierung am härtesten trifft“, sagte ein hochrangiger Kommissionsbeamter am Montag.
Šefčovič räumte in seinem Interview im August die Grenzen des Dialogs ein und warnte, dass Verhandlungen ohne greifbare Fortschritte immer schwieriger aufrechtzuerhalten seien.
„Es wäre sehr wichtig, zurückzukommen und zu sagen, dass das Problem anerkannt wird und es bereits einige Pilotprojekte gibt, die wir testen wollen, um zu sehen, ob sie funktionieren“, sagte er.
„Aber wenn einfach nichts geschieht, dann wird es für uns natürlich viel schwieriger sein, nur über diese Themen zu sprechen.“
Jordyn Dahl in Brüssel und Hans von der Burchard in Berlin haben zu diesem Artikel beigetragen.

Uvision shows remote kamikaze drone launcher at AUSA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:54:37 UTC
20:54:37 KST

- Uvision is showing an eight-canister HERO 120 launcher at AUSA 2026, designed for remote operation in mobile, fixed and containerized configurations.
- The HERO 120 is already on contract with the U.S. Army under a Lethal Unmanned Systems deal worth up to $982 million.
Israeli loitering munition maker Uvision is showing an eight-canister launcher for its HERO 120 at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting in Washington, pitching the remotely operated system as a way to spread strike capacity across land and maritime platforms and tie it to the company’s AI-enabled CORTEX mission management software.
The Multi-Canister Launcher holds up to eight HERO 120 loitering munitions and is designed for remote operation, according to the company’s Oct. 13 announcement. Uvision says it can be fielded in mobile, fixed and containerized configurations, and that CORTEX, which the company describes as an AI-enabled battle intelligence and mission management system, links the launcher with sensors and decision-makers in what it calls a sensor-to-effect network.
Loitering munitions, often called kamikaze drones, can circle over an area while an operator searches for a target and then dive onto it with a warhead. The HERO 120 is a mid-range design aimed at armored vehicles and other high-value targets, combining reconnaissance and strike in one airframe with a built-in camera that lets the operator abort an attack and re-engage.
Uvision singled out border defense as one use for the multi-canister setup, with launch nodes spread across long stretches of border in mobile and fixed positions and connected through CORTEX to surveillance assets, so that a threat spotted in one sector can be answered from the nearest launcher. The company did not name any customer that has ordered the launcher or say whether it is being offered to the U.S. Army.
At the same show, Uvision is demonstrating Wayland Autonomy’s IRIS airborne surveillance payload running with Tactical CORTEX, a version of the software for forward units. The company says the pairing adds wide-area surveillance and onboard target generation, including in areas where GPS signals are jammed or unavailable.
“It’s not just about having more effects in the field. It’s about having them where you need them, when you need them, and giving forces the flexibility to use the right capability for the mission,” said Dr. Ran Gozali, CEO of Uvision.
The HERO 120 already has a foothold in the U.S. Army, and in October 2025 the service awarded Mistral Inc. and Uvision a multi-year contract worth up to $982 million under the Lethal Unmanned Systems program to buy, field, train on and sustain the weapon, with Mistral as prime contractor and Uvision as design authority. Production systems passed their first lot acceptance tests in August 2026, and the companies then received an additional order worth more than $50 million to increase the number of HERO 120 systems and support equipment going to soldiers.
The smaller HERO 90 supports the U.S. Army’s Low Altitude Stalking and Strike Ordnance effort, known as LASSO, which tests soldier-portable, tube-launched loitering munitions for infantry units. The U.S. Marine Corps fitted HERO 120 munitions on one of its Long-Range Unmanned Surface Vessels in 2023, an early example of the maritime launch role Uvision now advertises for the multi-canister launcher.
Beyond the HERO line, Uvision markets the VIPER encapsulated multi-mission systems and the PEREGRINE tactical kinetic systems, and says CORTEX is meant to manage effectors across all three families.

US dollar’s rally pauses as markets brace for inflation report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:52:53 UTC
20:52:53 KST

Ali Canberk Ozbugutu, Burhan Sansarlioglu, and Emir Yildirim
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
The US Dollar Index paused its upward rally and traded flat on Wednesday, ahead of the key US inflation data expected to shape the Federal Reserve’s future policy roadmap.
The US dollar closed Tuesday after a 0.4% decline to 102.2, while retreating slightly from a recent peak of 102.6 that was its highest since April 2025.
The index stood relatively flat at 102.2 as of 1100GMT, as currency markets are bracing for the inflation report.
The US headline inflation is expected to rise 3.4% on an annual basis to a range between 3.6-3.7%, while core consumer inflation is expected to rise from 2.4% to 2.5%.
The Fed’s hawkish expectations could rise with higher-than-expected inflation, while money markets expect the bank to maintain rates this month with an 80% probability and to hike rates in December with a 92% likelihood.
New York Fed President John Williams’ remarks cooled the dollar’s immediate momentum after he said further tightening after a singular rate hike this year will likely be unwarranted, noting that the disinflationary factors remain and that the US inflation will decline next year.
The US dollar is expected to sustain its broader dominance over other currencies due to deep structural weaknesses and political turmoil pressuring the euro, analysts say.
Jane Foley, senior foreign exchange strategist at Rabobank, told Anadolu that the US’ strong economic growth allowed markets to overlook the country’s fiscal deficit but similar fiscal indiscipline is currently pressuring the euro.
“The same is not true for France — in both late 2024 and 2025, tough budget negotiations in France led to government instability and an underperformance of French government debt. By the end of last year, the 10-year Oat-Bund yield spread was trading at levels significantly wider than those in early 2024, before President Macron called a snap election,” she said.
Foley stated that the European economy showed some resilience but other factors continue to weaken the currency.
“Factors such as the region’s energy importer status, concerns about hybrid Russian warfare and political worries concerning growing far-right support in both Germany and France are likely undermining the EUR,” she said.
“These worries are reflecting kindly on the USD, given its safe haven status. We expect the dollar index to remain well supported in the coming months,” she added.
Kit Juckes, head of foreign exchange strategy at Societe Generale, told Anadolu that the Middle East conflict beginning in late February drove the US dollar’s rise from its lowest levels since 2022.
“The US is a major energy producer now and higher oil prices, as well increased global uncertainty, are dollar supportive,” he said.
He noted that the developments in artificial intelligence (AI) supported the American economy’s growth than other countries, which was evident when growth forecasts for the US were upwardly revised in the first quarter.
He mentioned that the reshaping of monetary policy expectations after the Fed’s Jackson Hole summit also supported the dollar, as Fed chair Kevin Warsh emerged “not afraid” to raise rates.
“The shift in market pricing of Fed Funds since then, has taken the dollar to current levels,” he said. “The fourth (factor driving up the US dollar) has been the rise in global bond yields, which has caused concern about the European bond market and underpinned the dollar.”
“Now, the question is, with a peak level of rates at 4.7% priced into the market, whether that will prove excessive — the key to expectations about where rates will peak, will be sensitive to tomorrow’s US CPI data, where the market expects core CPI inflation to rise from 2.4%, and headline inflation to increase from 3.4% to 3.6%. Further near-term dollar strength may be predicated on a higher-than-expected inflation print, or increased strain in global bond markets,” he added.

Thousands of sources about Golden Horde and Kazakh Khanate found in Eastern countries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Thousands of sources about Golden Horde and Kazakh Khanate found in Eastern countries
Thousands of works and historical sources related to Kazakhstan’s ancient history, the Golden Horde, and the Kazakh Khanate were discovered in the archives of Eastern countries, director general of the Suleimenov Institute of Oriental Studies Duken Masimkhanuly announced at an international conference in Almaty, Qazinform News Agency reports.
Addressing the international scientific and practical conference “Historical, cultural, political and economic relations between Kazakhstan and the Eastern countries: History, Present and Development Trends,” he highlighted the importance of studying Kazakhstan’s historical, cultural, and economic ties with Eastern countries.
He emphasized, after gaining its independence, Kazakhstan began establishing diplomatic relations with Western and Eastern countries, creating a need for systematic academic research in both directions. One of the Institute’s key tasks has been to search foreign archives for historical sources related to Kazakhstan and introduce them into scholarly circulation.
He also highlighted studying the history, culture, languages and religions of Eastern countries, as well as their socio-political and economic development, is not just a matter of academic interest; it is an important task linked to our strategic interests.
“During two and a half centuries of the colonial period, we lost part of our historical memory. Eastern sources can help us rediscover information about our forgotten language and civilization,” he said.
The scientist added work at the archives of the Eastern countries helped discover substantial materials shedding light on various periods of Kazakhstan’s history. In particular, the point at issue is thousands of studies and historical sources related to ancient times, the Middle Ages, the Golden Horde and the Kazakh Khanate.
Duken Masimkhanuly said thirty years is a significant milestone. This conference will show the public the achievements Kazakhstan has made over three decades of studying the East, as well as the discoveries and findings that have emerged from this work.
The conference also focuses on Kazakhstan’s political, economic and cultural cooperation with Eastern countries, regional security issues, and interaction within international organizations.
Special attention is being paid to the historical significance of the Great Silk Road, the religious landscape of Central Asia, and integration processes among Turkic-speaking states.
A presentation of the photo album book Ordaly otyz jyl dated to the 30th anniversary of the Suleimenov Institute of Oriental Studies and a collection of conference papers will be held as part of the conference.
Besides, an exhibition of scientific publications has also been organized.
It should be noted, a Kazakh-language edition of French historian Marie Favereau’s book Altyn Orda. Dala imperiasy älemdı qalai özgerttı (Golden Horde. How the steppe empire changed the world) was presented in Almaty.

French journalist Natacha Polony joins growing field of 2027 presidential hopefuls
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:51:48 UTC
20:51:48 KST

She is stepping away from her role as an observer to make herself "useful" to her country, denouncing a France mired in "chaos", amid a debt crisis, "tragic" unrest in secondary schools and a "total lack of prospects."
The list of candidates for the 2027 French presidential election continues to grow.
Speaking on France Inter radio on Wednesday, Natacha Polony, a 51-year-old journalist and essayist, announced that she would run for president, saying she wanted to "shake up the political landscape."
'The situation leaves me no choice'
Former editor-in-chief of Marianne magazine, Polony denounced what she describes as France's "complete loss of standing".
She advocates economic, energy and food sovereignty and calls for a reindustrialisation policy to "revive economic activity" and "bring money into the state's coffers."
In a video posted on her social media accounts shortly after her radio appearance, the newly announced candidate outlined her vision of a more sovereign France.
"A nation that no longer produces what it needs is no longer truly free to fund our schools and hospitals, preserve our social model, create skilled jobs and prepare for artificial intelligence," Polony said.
"We must produce...We must produce at home, on our own terms," she insisted.
A decision months in the making
At the end of August she launched her movement "Nous sommes la France" aimed at "all those orphaned by politics", saying she wanted to bring together "those who no longer feel represented by the current political options."
Speaking on France Inter, Natacha Polony claimed that her movement had 60,000 members who wanted to "fight against France's decline".
Often described as a "sovereigntist", she rejects the label, calling it the system's "favourite anathema".
In late September, during a heated televised debate with French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot, Polony accused him of seeing France as a "small country".
In her view, under Emmanuel Macron, Paris "fantasises" about European unity and seeks "at all costs" to be "Europe's star pupil", even if that means sacrificing the country's "vital" interests.
She points in particular to the cancellation of the Franco-German fighter jet project, as well as decisions she considers detrimental to French interests regarding European preference in the defence sector, while Germany continues to favour purchasing American weapons systems.
Crowded field of candidates
Besides Natacha Polony, nearly 30 public figures have already announced their candidacy or are being tipped to run in the 2027 presidential race.
Among the main contenders are Marine Le Pen of the National Rally (RN), Jean-Luc Mélenchon, leader of La France insoumise, and former prime ministers Édouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal.
On the centre-left, Raphael Glucksmann, who won the first round of the social-democratic primary, hopes to position himself as an alternative to Jean-Luc Mélenchon's radical left.
Meanwhile, former Socialist president François Hollande, Dominique de Villepin, a former prime minister under Jacques Chirac, and Bruno Le Maire, who served as economy minister from 2017 to 2024, have yet to reveal whether they intend to run.
The list remains provisional: to officially stand in the first round of the presidential election, scheduled for 18 April 2027, candidates must secure at least 500 sponsorships from elected officials.

French navy chief sees no threat to US catapult supply for future carrier
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

French navy chief sees no threat to US catapult supply for future carrier
PARIS, Oct 14 - The US has not yet decided whether to abandon the electromagnetic launch system for aircraft carriers, France's navy chief said on Wednesday, two months after President Donald Trump ordered the US Navy to drop the technology that France has chosen for its next carrier.
Trump ordered the Navy in August to revert to the older steam-powered catapults, calling the electromagnetic system unreliable. The move raised doubts over the future supply of the technology, which is used for launching jet fighters from the ships.
"The American decision has not yet been taken," Admiral Christophe Cluzel, chief of France’s naval staff, told a parliamentary hearing. "I do not see our contract threatened."
The US Embassy in France did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The situation highlights France's reliance on US technology for the vital component of its next-generation aircraft carrier, the France Libre, due to replace the ageing Charles de Gaulle around 2038. European dependence on US defence technology has come under growing scrutiny as the continent seeks greater strategic autonomy.
Cluzel added that he had a meeting scheduled with his American counterpart next week, and that he thought the topic would be discussed.
The Admiral was answering a question from a member of parliament about the dependency of the French aircraft carrier, a key part of its nuclear deterrence, on an American technology, and the possibility that it could be left without supply if the US turned to steam catapults.
"It’s a dependency that within the framework of the programme was accepted and considered to be under control", the navy chief said. He added that France would buy a substantial stock of spare parts from the beginning of the programme. Naval Group is leading the construction of the carrier.
However, Cluzel also said that a study was planned to examine France’s capacity to design such catapults, its potential costs and delivery times, with conclusions expected in 2028.
"I think we would be able to do it, but on timelines that go far beyond the service-entry horizon of the France Libre, and at a unit cost that would obviously be considerably higher", he said. REUTERS

EXPLAINER - Why is a 1988 privacy law before the US Supreme Court?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:49:55 UTC
20:49:55 KST

- US Supreme Court is set to hear arguments in a case on whether subscribers to non-video services qualify for protection under a 1988 federal video privacy law
-  Dispute arose after a sports newsletter subscriber accused Paramount of sharing his video-viewing history with Facebook through an online tracking tool
-  Expected later this year, a ruling could determine who can sue over the sharing of viewing data, with implications for digital publishers, streaming platforms and targeted advertising
The US Supreme Court will hear arguments on Wednesday in a case that could determine how far a nearly 40-year-old federal privacy law extends to users of modern websites, streaming platforms and other digital services.
The case, Salazar v. Paramount Global, centers on the Video Privacy Protection Act (VPPA), a 1988 law originally designed to prevent video rental stores from disclosing customers’ viewing histories.
At issue is whether people who subscribe to a company’s non-video services, such as email newsletters, are protected when that company shares information about the videos they watch online.
The outcome could affect how media and technology companies collect and share viewing data, potentially exposing them to lawsuits over practices commonly used in targeted advertising. 
What is the case about?
The dispute began in 2022 when Michael Salazar filed a proposed class-action lawsuit against Paramount Global, the owner of 247Sports, a website covering US college sports and recruitment.
Salazar subscribed to a free newsletter from the website and watched videos while logged into his Facebook account.
He alleged that Paramount used a tracking tool known as the Facebook Pixel to send information about his viewing activity to the US social media platform without his consent.
The information allegedly included the titles and web addresses of videos he watched, along with his Facebook identification number, which could be used to identify him.
Pixel is a small piece of computer code that websites can install to collect information about visitors’ activities and share it with advertising platforms.
Such tools are widely used to measure advertising performance, track user behavior, and deliver targeted advertisements.
Salazar argued that disclosing his viewing history violated the VPPA, which restricts video providers from sharing personally identifiable information about their customers without consent.
Paramount disputed his interpretation of the law, arguing that subscribing to a sports newsletter did not make him a protected consumer of audiovisual services.
A federal district court in Tennessee dismissed his lawsuit, and the US Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit upheld that ruling in April 2025.
The appeals court concluded that the law protects people who rent, purchase or subscribe to audiovisual products or services, not everyone who subscribes to an unrelated offering from a company that also provides videos.
Federal appeals courts in New York and Chicago had previously adopted broader interpretations of the law in separate cases, creating a legal disagreement that prompted the Supreme Court to intervene. 
Why does a 1988 law matter today?
Congress enacted the VPPA after the video rental history of Robert Bork, a Supreme Court nominee, was obtained and publicized during his controversial 1987 confirmation process.
The episode raised concerns that viewing records could expose sensitive information about people’s political beliefs, religious interests and personal lives.
The resulting law prohibited video providers from knowingly disclosing information identifying customers and the specific videos they requested or obtained, subject to certain exceptions.
It also allowed individuals to sue over violations and seek damages of at least $2,500, along with potential punitive damages and legal costs.
Although Congress amended the law in 2013 to update consent requirements for electronic services, much of its original language remains unchanged.
The statute still refers to “video tape service providers,” even as video consumption has shifted from physical rental stores to websites, streaming platforms and mobile applications.
That shift has created disputes over whether modern online users qualify for protections originally written for people renting or purchasing videotapes. 
What are the competing arguments?
Salazar argues that the law’s definition of a consumer includes anyone subscribing to goods or services from a video provider, regardless of whether the subscription itself involves videos.
His lawyers maintain that Congress could have explicitly limited the definition to audiovisual services but did not do so.
Paramount argues that the law must be read in its original context, which was to protect customers engaged in video-related transactions.
Under its interpretation, subscribing to an unrelated service does not establish the customer relationship necessary to bring a privacy claim.
The case has attracted attention from privacy advocates and major technology and media organizations.
The Electronic Privacy Information Center and other privacy experts support Salazar’s broader interpretation, warning that a narrower definition could leave users’ viewing histories vulnerable when companies bundle video content with newsletters and other digital services.
Meta Platforms, which owns Facebook, and several media and business organizations have filed briefs supporting Paramount.
Industry groups argue that expanding the law could expose websites to substantial financial liability and undermine advertising-supported business models.
News organizations have also warned that a broader interpretation could discourage the use of free video content or force changes to digital advertising and analytics practices. 
What could the Supreme Court decide?
A ruling favoring Salazar could allow more website users to bring lawsuits over disclosures of their viewing histories, even when their subscriptions are not specifically for video content.
A ruling favoring Paramount would reinforce a narrower interpretation, limiting protection to consumers who have a qualifying relationship involving audiovisual goods or services.
However, the case does not directly ask the justices to decide whether tracking tools themselves are unlawful or whether Paramount ultimately violated the VPPA.
Those questions involve separate legal requirements, including whether the information disclosed identifies viewers and their video activity.
The Supreme Court’s decision could nevertheless establish an important boundary for privacy protections in an online environment where written content, video, advertising and data collection are increasingly interconnected.
A ruling is expected before the court’s current term concludes in 2027.

‘A big responsibility’: Clifton Suspension Bridge master hails £7.6m renovation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:46:23 UTC
20:46:23 KST

The job does not give the holder age-old perks such as the right to drive sheep across the great structure, but the title “bridge master” does have a certain ring to it.
“I don’t tend to say I’m the bridge master when I’m at a party,” said Tristan Ralph, the current holder of the title. “But people do seem to know and bring it up. It’s a job less ordinary, isn’t it? It’s a Victorian sounding title and people are really, really interested.”
There is, however, nothing ceremonial about the title. Ralph is in charge of maintaining and running the Clifton Suspension Bridge, a UK feat of engineering, without any public money.
“It does feel a big responsibility,” said Ralph. “When the chairman of the trustees rang to say we’d like you to do it, you suddenly feel the pressure. It’s so famous and people in Bristol, quite rightly, are proud and almost possessive of it. Bristolians think: ‘It’s our bridge.’”
The bridge master – and the not-for-profit charity the Clifton Suspension Bridge Trust – have the task of maintaining the bridge “in perpetuity”. “I’m a temporary custodian,” Ralph said. “When I’m finished, I have to make sure it is handed on in just [as] good a condition or better than I inherited it.”
Ralph, a bridge engineer by profession, was speaking to mark the conclusion of a large refurbishment project that has taken two and a half years and involved hand-painting more than 4,000 original iron chain links and installing an energy-efficient lighting system. It has cost about £7.5m. “It’s been a big job,” he said. “But it’s come pretty much bang on budget, which is rare these days.”
That is important because, to many visitors’ surprise, the bridge does not receive public funding. “The upkeep of the bridge, the running of it, the salary costs and everything are all paid only by our toll money,” said Ralph. “People think that we might get something from local or central government. But, no, it’s just the toll money.”
Motorised vehicles – including motorcycles – pay £1 to cross the bridge. There is no charge for pedestrians, cyclists or horse riders. As well as being a beautiful structure, it is also a vital part of Bristol and North Somerset’s transport system.
Ralph said: “It draws the tourists in. We get visitors from hundreds of countries every year but primarily, it’s still a vital piece of local infrastructure. If the bridge wasn’t here, the difference it would make to Bristol traffic would be incredible. We average over 8,000 vehicles a day still. Maintaining it as a transport link is utterly vital.”
The end of the refurbishment does not mean Ralph can rest on his laurels and spend more time hobnobbing with members of the Bridge Owners Forum.
“In a few years, we’ll need to paint the underside of the bridge. The under-bridge gantry unit itself will be replaced over the coming years. So there’s always something. We need to keep on top of things. It’s like your house or your car. If you just ignore it, don’t do things for a couple of years, they start breaking down.”
As in most walks of life, the climate emergency is a challenge Ralph and the trust are having to face. “We were monitoring the bridge daily in the summer with the very hot weather. And maybe if the bridge was being designed today, there would be a little bit more robustness around wind.”
The prevailing south-west wind is not usually a problem and the bridge rarely has to close but if it blows directly through the Avon Gorge it can be more difficult. “We need to keep an eye at both the magnitude of any wind events but also their frequency,” Ralph said.
The engineer admires the bridge’s designers, including Isambard Kingdom Brunel. “It’s remarkably advanced for its time.”
And there is no sign that its days are numbered, largely because the Victorians did not skimp. Ralph said: “There are three layers of chains. The original Brunel design only had two, but because it went from a timber design to a cast-iron deck, they upped it to three.
“There’s a little bit of comfort in there. Today there might be pressure to say, well, can you keep it to two, but in Victorian times they did like to add a little bit of meat on the bones.
“It doesn’t have a finite life. There’s no end date in our plans. We all just keep it going in the highest standards as we can. It’s in really good condition as long as we keep doing what we need to do, keep our attention on it and don’t let things drift. Forever is a long time but there’s no reason why we have any need to worry at the moment.”
