French viewers shocked by Israeli soldiers’ accounts of Gaza in ‘NAZA’ documentary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:31:41 UTC
20:31:41 KST

French viewers who attended screenings of “NAZA,” a documentary exposing Israel’s killing of civilians in Gaza, said they were shocked by Israeli soldiers’ accounts that reduced Palestinian victims to numbers rather than recognizing them as human beings.
Produced by British newspaper The Guardian and directed by Oscar-winning filmmaker Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, the documentary was screened in French cinemas on Oct. 12-13.
The film drew considerable interest in Paris on its opening day, with most tickets sold.
French viewers who watched “NAZA” at two cinemas in the capital shared their reactions with Anadolu. 
‘I think the filmmakers are very courageous’
A French viewer, Kenzi, said the documentary explained the meaning of NAZA, a term referring to civilian casualties, and left him deeply shocked.
He said Israeli soldiers repeatedly discussed numbers and calculations, almost all of which represented people killed in Gaza.
“We know what is happening, we talk about it, we see it, but not to this extent. And here, it was really shocking to see Israeli soldiers talking about it. Sometimes you could sense regret, sometimes not so much. They spoke quite coldly. So, it really disturbed me. And, I think it was very well made. It went by very quickly,” he said.
Noting that the soldiers compared their actions in Gaza to a video game, Kenzi said: “They talk about artificial intelligence to identify people to kill. At a certain point, you see that they no longer measure the number of people they are going to kill, the collateral damage, the NAZAs.”
He said the soldiers frequently referred to a “system.”
“It seemed as though they had been brainwashed and made to believe that they were on the right side, until they realized for themselves that what they were doing was vile,” he said.
Kenzi recalled the soldiers repeatedly saying they “just wanted to eliminate the enemy.”
“They clearly said that the enemy was children aged 3 to 6, women who had done nothing to deserve this. Often, they wanted to eliminate an enemy leader, and in the end, they killed his entire family except that person,” he said.
Praising the Israeli directors, he added: “I think the filmmakers are very courageous to have initiated a project like this.” 
‘It affected everyone in the theater’
Iona, a 23-year-old French viewer, said: “I think the film is extremely important. It is extremely important to have this perspective because we often hear testimonies from victims, but here we have testimonies from the attackers, who put the situation into concrete words.”
She said the documentary could help people understand what was happening and stand on the right side of history, adding that the language used and the questions asked deeply affected her.
“He was not afraid to use the word ‘genocide.’ He asked directly whether it was genocide, and they said yes,” she said, referring to the interviewer.
Iona said she found it shocking that the soldiers did not regard the victims as people.
She also highlighted scenes showing people living normally in Tel Aviv while people in Gaza were dying.
“Everything was extremely striking,” she said.
Emphasizing the importance of making such films and allowing everyone to speak, she added: “There was everyone in the theater — young people, older people. You could see that it affected everyone in the theater. There was silence at the end. It was extremely moving.”
She urged people to watch the documentary, ending her remarks with: “Free Palestine.” 
‘Reducing human beings to numbers shocked me the most’
Adam, a 27-year-old French viewer, said the documentary left him speechless throughout.
“I was aware of the history and the political issues behind it, of the massacre and genocide taking place in Palestine,” he said.
But hearing testimony from people within the system was still shocking, he added, saying it gave concrete substance to the atrocities.
“Overall, I think the documentary is very well made and presented, because it raises several questions, particularly about the dehumanization of victims through the term NAZA.
Ultimately, the victims, the ‘collateral damage,’ as they like to call them, become nothing more than numbers. Reducing human beings to numbers was what shocked me the most,” he said.
Adam said the massacre in Palestine did not begin in October 2023 and praised the directors’ courage despite pressure from the Israeli government.
‘An interviewer who recognized the disastrous situation in Gaza’
Another French viewer, Yacine, said the repeated emphasis on numbers was among the documentary’s most striking elements.
“They had an interviewer who appeared objective, who had some distance and recognized the disastrous situation unfolding in Palestine and Gaza,” he said, referring to Abraham.
By contrast, he said, the soldiers interviewed appeared conditioned by war.
“There is a real contrast between the images we saw of Tel Aviv, where people seem safe and appear to lead fairly peaceful daily lives, and the images of Gaza at the end of the film, which embody war and destruction themselves,” he said.
“When you see the images, you get the impression that there is almost no life left. People are surviving.”

She Remains a Stranger: Motherhood, memory and the loss of home
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:31:09 UTC
20:31:09 KST

Breadcrumb
Rasha Hilwi's She Remains a Stranger: On motherhood, inherited exile and the meaning of home
In the opening pages of her recently published literary memoir Dhalat Gharibeh (She Remains a Stranger), Palestinian author, storyteller and journalist Rasha Hilwi offers a lexicographical meditation on the word ghurba.
"Ever since I crossed those seas, I’ve tried to translate the word ghurba into other languages. I came to the same conclusion as others before me: some things cannot be translated.
Ghurba derives from the root gharaba.
Ghurba (noun). The verbal noun of gharuba.
“His ghurba lasted long”: his separation from his homeland and family lasted a long time.
Ghurba is nawā or being far away.
“He lived for a long time in ghurba”: he lived for a long time in lands of displacement.
“I found him in a state of ghurba”: he was found in loneliness and desolation.
“The loss of loved ones is itself a ghurba”: whoever loses someone dear becomes like a stranger among people, even if they have never left their homeland."
Published in July 2026 by the Berlin-based Arabic bookshop and publisher Khan Al Janub, She Remains a Stranger is an intimate autobiographical narrative about motherhood, Palestine, and what it means to inhabit several forms of ghurba all at once.
For Hilwi, the impulse to write this book was an old one. But it was motherhood, and the estrangement born of it, that ultimately gave form to the story.
"Before motherhood, writing about culture was a major part of my life. Then motherhood came and severed me from that world. This is characteristic of how motherhood functions more generally: It imposes a particular kind of isolation, separating you not only from your former self, but also from the outside world," Hilwi tells The New Arab.
"But more than that, motherhood put me face to face with so much I had left unresolved: my relationship with myself, with places, with my family’s heritage, and that of my ancestors. It forced me to deal with feelings of pain, loss and, above all, ghurba," she adds.
Together with the realisation that she was battling postpartum depression, this confrontation set Hilwi on a journey of healing.
So, in 2022, she returned to her most familiar form of expression: writing.
She began chronicling her life as a new mother of twins in Amsterdam, far from her first home, Palestine, and the coastal city of Akka, where she grew up.
Writing became a way of making sense of it all.
"It shielded me from a heaviness I hadn’t yet realised I was carrying," she asserts.
Hilwi writes of the weight she was carrying, which was never hers alone. It comprised the histories of the women who had moulded her, particularly her mother and grandmother, and all they had passed down to her.
It was an inheritance imbued with both pain and love.
She also writes of the weight of becoming a mother abroad: of her attempts to root her children in a heritage that is geographically remote yet intimately present.
Sometimes, this means something as ordinary as encouraging them to enjoy her familiar spreads of labneh, za’atar and olive oil on their Amsterdam dining table.
At other times, it means insisting they pronounce helwe properly with the Arabic ‘ḥ’ rather than the ‘h’ of a foreign accent.
As Hilwi navigates everyday life, the book's bigger question begins to take shape. What can a mother give her children of a home they have not known as she has?
But just as writing offered Hilwi a way through this question, the devastation unfolding in Gaza rendered the very act of writing meaningless.
For Hilwi, motherhood made the distance between Amsterdam and Gaza unbearable.
She found herself comparing her children’s safety against the reality of Palestinian mothers struggling to keep theirs alive, or "how one child could be playing on an actual slide while another slides down the wall of a destroyed house in Gaza."
Yet, with time, Hilwi realised she could not abandon writing. However modest, it was a contribution she could make, "a small piece in a much larger mosaic through which Palestinians continue to affirm their continued existence, whether in academia, theatre, cinema, literature, or elsewhere."
Making a home from fragments
Hilwi’s She Remains a Stranger contributes to that mosaic, her act of remembering offering some relief from a deepening sense of ghurba.
As she takes the readers with her through the daily rhythms of motherhood in Amsterdam, Hilwi journeys back through memory, revisiting the life she once shared with her family in Palestine, from Haifa, where her grandparents rebuilt their lives after being forcibly displaced from their village of Iqrit in the Upper Galilee in 1948, to Akka, her hometown, where she was born and raised.
As a third-generation Nakba woman, she imagines the life that might have been. She writes of a ghurba that did not begin with her departure from Palestine to Berlin, or her subsequent move to Amsterdam.
It is a ghurba that was already part of her inheritance.
"There is a ghurba that I know: that of Palestinians in their own country, in their own cities, especially those who stayed. I am one of them. I did not witness the Nakba, but I have lived with its direct impact on my grandparents, who became strangers on their own land, constantly reminded by an entire system that they were strangers and refugees in their own country."
But if ghurba can be inherited without ever leaving home, what happens when one does leave? This question also runs through Hilwi’s account of her journey from Akka to Berlin, a city she sought out in search of a life she had been denied.
"I did not go to Berlin for Berlin. I went for Arab Berlin, a city that had taken in so many of our people because of our catastrophes."
There, she found glimpses of the life she might have known in Akka had the Nakba never happened. Surrounded by friends from Beirut and Cairo, she could eat Syrian food, attend an Egyptian show, or listen to Lebanese music.
In Berlin, she found a home assembled from fragments of other homes, brought together by people whose different journeys had directed them to the same city.
"There was still alienation, of course, much of it arising simply from being in a new city, with a new language and a new way of life. Despite all that, Berlin gave me a sense of home. I needed it because I had been denied that in my own hometown. Israel had taken that right from me."
But finding something of home elsewhere did not mean that Hilwi’s ghurba disappeared. When she eventually moved from Berlin to Amsterdam, to be with her husband and raise her family, it followed her, taking on new meanings.
"It was in Amsterdam that motherhood truly put me face to face with all these forms of estrangement: from Palestine, from the experience of creating a life in two new cities; and from the heritage I was carrying."
With time, however, Hilwi came to see that her ghurba was not necessarily something to overcome, but something to understand.
"I don’t think there will ever be a moment when I stop feeling estranged. Ghurba will always accompany me, and perhaps that is important because it gives rise to questions as well as a constant search for meaning."
As it acknowledges the persistence of ghurba, Hilwi’s text is equally concerned with the life that remains possible after rupture, whether after motherhood, displacement or the devastation of genocide.
For Hilwi, this possibility materialised in motherhood, which offered "a sense of home" and, as she writes in the book, became "the vital force that stirs the muscle of imagination."
For her, motherhood was not only another site of estrangement, but a way of imagining life beyond it. And storytelling, in turn, became Hilwi’s way of insisting on that life’s continuation.
"The fact that we are still able to tell the story, that the story continues to be told, is itself an answer to genocide."
A Dutch Translation of She Remains a Stranger, titled Ze blijft een vreemde and translated by Djuke Poppinga, is scheduled for publication in November 2026 by Uitgeverij Jurgen Maas in Amsterdam.
The book excerpt featured at the beginning of this article was translated from Arabic by Nourhan Tewfik.

Bank of America Fined $1.21B Over AML Failures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:29:00 UTC
20:29:00 KST

Reported by
U.S. authorities imposed more than $1.21 billion in penalties on Bank of America on Tuesday over failures in its anti-money laundering controls and apparent violations of U.S. sanctions, in what the Treasury Department called the third-largest enforcement penalty in its history.
The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) assessed a $1.2 billion penalty, saying the bank failed to adequately detect and report financial activity involving priority national-security and illicit-finance risks, including Chinese money-laundering networks and activity along the U.S. southwestern border. Regulators said Bank of America failed to report more than $5 billion in suspicious transactions, including more than $1 billion linked to such priority risks.
As part of the FinCEN resolution, Bank of America admitted to willfully violating the Bank Secrecy Act, including by failing to maintain an adequate anti-money laundering program, conduct required due diligence on correspondent accounts for foreign banks, and file suspicious activity reports. The bank must also use an independent third party to identify and report suspicious activity its systems previously missed.
Separately, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) imposed a $750 million penalty — the largest in the regulator’s history. That amount is credited toward FinCEN’s $1.2 billion penalty rather than added to it. The OCC said the bank’s compliance program remained “deficient and ineffective” despite a 2024 cease-and-desist order and that weaknesses in transaction monitoring caused late suspicious activity reports involving billions of dollars.
The Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) also reached an $11.66 million settlement with the bank over 475 apparent violations of sanctions programs targeting Russia, Belarus, Iran, Myanmar, Somalia, narcotics trafficking and global terrorism. OFAC cited payments involving blocked banks, failures to properly prioritize sanctions alerts and delays in updating watchlists.
Bank of America said it worked with regulators to resolve the cases and was addressing the deficiencies.
“Financial crime compliance is serious, and we are responsible for getting it right,” a spokesperson said, adding that the bank has invested billions of dollars in technology and assigned thousands of employees to combat financial crime. The bank said its remediation work is well advanced and that it remains committed to completing the measures required by regulators.

Hundreds of generators, mobile boiler houses and backup power plants: Klitschko spoke about how Kyiv will get through the most difficult winter
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:28:32 EEST
20:28:32 KST

Hundreds of generators, mobile boiler houses and backup power plants: Klitschko spoke about how Kyiv will get through the most difficult winter
Kyiv • UNN
Kyiv has prepared nearly 700 generators, 70 mobile boiler houses and three diesel power plants. The capital's hospitals have 480 generators.
Kyiv’s city authorities have prepared hundreds of generators, mobile boiler units, and other backup power sources to ensure the operation of critical infrastructure. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko stated this from the parliamentary rostrum after being invited to the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine on October 14, reports UNN.
Details
The mayor said that throughout the full-scale war, the capital had been increasing the number of backup power sources intended to ensure the operation of critical infrastructure in the event of possible prolonged power outages.
In particular, nearly 700 generators of various capacities and 70 mobile boiler units have been prepared for heat and water supply facilities. In addition, three diesel power plants have already been built in the capital, and a backup water intake has been arranged.
Currently, Kyivvodokanal has 103 generators. At the same time, the utility is awaiting additional high-capacity generator systems being manufactured abroad for Kyiv
According to him, the mayor’s office paid particular attention to providing residential buildings with backup power. Under the city’s energy resilience programs, more than 6,000 pieces of equipment have been purchased for residential buildings, including generators, inverters, and batteries.
Ensuring the provision of hospitals and educational institutions
According to the mayor, all educational institutions in the capital are equipped with generators of various capacities. Among them are 285 high-capacity generators.
In the medical sector, additional capabilities are also being created to enable institutions to operate autonomously in the event of disruptions to centralized electricity, water, and heat supplies. In particular, hospitals in the capital currently have 480 generators
He added that their own wells for water supply had already been installed at 15 medical institutions, while six more are under construction.
In addition, eleven hospitals have autonomous heating supplied by their own boiler houses. By the end of 2026, the city authorities plan to increase the number of such medical institutions to 21
Klitschko emphasized that these measures are aimed at maintaining the operation of vital institutions even if centralized networks are damaged.
We remind you
A little earlier, the Kyiv City State Administration explained how preparations for winter are progressing at medical institutions.

Nearly 200 high schools across France were expected to remain closed on Wednesday amid continuing student blockades, as the government promised proposals to improve university admissions.
Education Minister Edouard Geffray told French broadcaster BFMTV that 96 percent of high schools were open, with no disruptions reported in three-quarters of the country’s departments. His remarks came a day after the fifth round of nationwide protests.
Several schools remained blockaded in Paris, including Voltaire, Helene-Boucher and the Balzac school complex. Balzac’s administration suspended in-person classes, citing difficulties accessing the site and safety concerns.
Geffray said Higher Education Minister Philippe Baptiste would submit proposals to improve Parcoursup, France’s university admissions platform, to the prime minister by the end of October.
He said he was open to “adjustments, possibly substantial ones”, while questioning what would replace the platform if it were abolished.
According to Geffray, fewer than 20 percent of the 90,000 contributions submitted through a government platform collecting students’ complaints concerned Parcoursup.
He ruled out immediate changes to the baccalaureate, France’s school-leaving examination, saying: “I’m not going to change the baccalaureate six months before a presidential election; we need to stop constantly reforming.”
Students demand investment
Student representatives are scheduled to meet Geffray and Baptiste on Thursday afternoon as they press for €10 billion ($11 billion) in investment.
Pierre Sourzat, president of the organisation Les Lyceens!, told Franceinfo that students expected concrete measures after receiving “only crumbs”.
Although protest organisers have not called for a sixth round of demonstrations on Thursday, the Union of High School Students urged demonstrators to maintain their blockades.
Union President Ryad Rani and other student representatives also called for participation in a “yellow vest” demonstration scheduled for Saturday.
Meanwhile, classes resumed at Kleber High School in Strasbourg, where clashes between students and police had occurred in recent weeks.

Ukraine Cancels Drone Missions as Starlink Restrictions Disrupt Battlefield Communications
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:27:36 UTC
20:27:36 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Cancels Drone Missions as Starlink Restrictions Disrupt Battlefield Communications
Ukrainian forces have been forced to cancel drone missions after new restrictions on SpaceX’s Starlink satellite communications disrupted connections during flight, with some unmanned aircraft losing contact for up to 20 seconds at speeds as low as 110–120 km/h.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to hromadske on October 14, Ukraine’s 7th Air Assault Corps confirmed that its units operating in the Huliaipole sector of the Zaporizhzhia region began experiencing connectivity problems overnight. The disruptions affected Starshield, the military-oriented satellite communications service used to control drones in flight.
Military personnel reported that connections could disappear for 10–20 seconds when drones reached speeds of approximately 110–120 km/h. Although the aircraft continued flying, the interruptions made remote control more difficult and increased the risk of losing them during operations.
The restrictions also create additional risks for Ukrainian drone operators. Reducing flight speeds to maintain connectivity makes unmanned aircraft easier targets for Russian forces, while faster drones may be unable to complete their missions under the new conditions.
The 7th Air Assault Corps warned that the problem is particularly serious for medium-range strike drones, which must accelerate rapidly during launch. Unstable communications at those speeds could prevent certain aircraft from taking off successfully or carrying out their intended missions.
The operational consequences have already emerged. According to the corps, one Ukrainian drone unit operating in the Huliaipole sector was forced to cancel several missions on October 14 because of the connectivity disruptions.
Separately, a source within Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense told hromadske that overnight testing identified restrictions preventing Starshield from functioning at speeds exceeding 160 km/h.
The source said the limitations were complicating military logistics, unmanned systems operations, and medium-range strike missions. Ukraine’s Defense Ministry is investigating what caused the restrictions.
Earlier, sources in Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense told UNITED24 Media that overnight testing had identified new restrictions affecting StarShield terminals moving at speeds above approximately 160 km/h.
The reported restrictions came a day after SpaceX owner Elon Musk publicly supported US President Donald Trump’s criticism of Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries. Musk wrote on X that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had gone too far.

Ukrainian forces have made a confirmed advance in the Sumy region while disrupting a series of Russian offensive operations across several other sectors of the front, according to the Institute for the Study of War’s (ISW) October 13 assessment.
Geolocated footage published on October 12 shows Ukrainian troops advancing southeast of Yunakivka, northeast of Sumy, confirming recent gains in the area.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
ISW also found no evidence of meaningful Russian progress in several sectors where Moscow continued offensive operations over the previous two days.
In northern Kharkiv region, Russian forces continued attacks on October 12 and 13 without making confirmed gains. Near Kupiansk, Russian troops were also reported to be using Ukrainian civilians as human shields while withdrawing, an action that would violate international humanitarian law.
Russian sources separately claimed attacks southeast of Borova, but ISW found no evidence that those operations resulted in territorial advances.
The same pattern was visible farther south. Russian forces attacked Lyman and areas north of the city toward Kolodiazi, but Ukrainian counterattacks prevented them from consolidating new positions.

Russian assaults around Kostiantynivka also failed to produce confirmed gains. Moscow’s forces attacked inside the city, west of it, and southwest of Druzhkivka on October 12 and 13, but ISW recorded no advances. Farther west, Russian troops attempted additional infiltration south of Dobropillia, prompting Ukrainian strikes against positions around Matiashove and Svitlle.
On the Oleksandrivka axis, Russian forces continued offensive operations without confirmed success as Ukrainian troops counterattacked toward Fedorivka.
Russian attacks around Huliaipole on October 11 and 12 similarly failed to produce verified territorial gains.
Earlier, Ukrainian forces regained control of another 101 square kilometers (39 square miles) of territory and liberated three villages in the Donetsk region, bringing the total area recovered during Operation Vivaldi to 277 square kilometers (107 square miles).
Ukraine’s Third Army Corps commander Brigadier General Andrii Biletskyi reported that Ukrainian forces had restored full control over 16 settlements during the four-stage operation.
Biletskyi said Russian forces suffered approximately 3,000 personnel losses during the latest phase, raising their estimated total losses throughout the operation to 8,000. These figures have not been independently verified.

Ukraine says it frees more territory in Donetsk region counteroffensive
KYIV, Oct 14 - Ukraine has freed 16 villages from Russian forces in the eastern Donetsk region in its latest counteroffensive, a senior commander said on Wednesday, part of what he called a major frontline pushback amid increased Russian air attacks elsewhere.
Kyiv's Third Army Corps has waged an operation, announced last month, to dislodge Russian troops north of the strategic city of Sloviansk, one of the two main bastions in Ukraine's so-called "fortress belt" anchoring its eastern defences.
Brig. Gen. Andrii Biletskyi said recent Ukrainian assaults had liberated three more villages in the area of the counteroffensive - some 30 km (19 miles) north of Sloviansk - bringing the total of freed territory to 277 square kilometres (107 square miles) and the number of settlements to 16.
Russia, whose pace of battlefield gains has slowed this year, has demanded that Ukraine cede the 20 percent of the Donetsk region it still controls before it stops fighting.
"The Kremlin's plan to seize the Donetsk and Luhansk regions will not be implemented in the foreseeable future," Biletskyi said in a video address. Donetsk and Luhansk, which Russia almost entirely occupies, make up Ukraine's mineral-rich Donbas.
The highly publicised operation, dubbed "Vivaldi", comes as Ukrainian forces aim to seize the ground initiative from Russia in the fifth year of fighting, in part by embracing technology and new tactics.
Russia regularly reports seizing frontline villages. Reuters could not immediately verify the battlefield reports.

Aramco executives' offices damaged in Houthi attack, regional officials say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:24:58 UTC
20:24:58 KST

An overnight Houthi strike damaged executive offices at Saudi oil giant Aramco's headquarters in Dhahran, two regional officials told The Associated Press on Wednesday, as fresh explosions shook Riyadh and the Iran-backed rebels intensified their missile and drone campaign against Saudi Arabia.
The reported damage to one of the kingdom's most important economic institutions came amid renewed attacks on airports, military installations and oil infrastructure, raising concerns about Saudi Arabia's ability to withstand sustained strikes and the potential consequences for global energy markets.
Residents of Riyadh reported hearing additional explosions Wednesday. The Saudi-led military coalition fighting the Houthis said its air defenses had intercepted cruise missiles, ballistic missiles and drones targeting the capital, as well as a ballistic missile aimed at Dhahran and a cruise missile targeting Al-Kharj.
Dhahran is home to Aramco's headquarters, while Al-Kharj houses Prince Sultan Air Base and Saudi Arabia's state-owned Military Industries Corporation.
The attacks have increased pressure on US President Donald Trump, who has said he is considering whether American forces should join Saudi strikes against the Houthis.
Saudi officials have reported repeated attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh over the past week, with strikes killing at least 18 people and injuring more than 300.
The Houthis described the latest attacks as retaliation for what they called Saudi aggression against Sanaa, Yemen's rebel-held capital, and other areas under their control.
Russia and China involved in ceasefire efforts
Despite the escalation, diplomatic efforts to halt the fighting are underway.
Mohamed al-Bukhaiti, a senior member of the Houthis' political bureau, told AP that Oman had attempted to bring the warring sides back to negotiations, while Russia and China had also pursued contacts through Iran.
"We're welcoming any mediation that leads to an end of the war and the blockade between Sanaa and Riyadh," al-Bukhaiti said.
"We're ready for a comprehensive end of the war and the blockade from both sides, not just a temporary ceasefire."
The Houthis nevertheless continued threatening Saudi airports and oil installations.
The attacks have severely disrupted air travel across the kingdom. More than 3,000 flights scheduled to depart from Saudi airports over the past week were canceled or listed as not operating, according to aviation analytics firm Cirium.
The campaign has also highlighted the Houthis' ability to inflict significant disruption despite Saudi Arabia's advanced Western-supplied air defenses.
Saudi air defenses under growing pressure
Saudi Arabia, one of the world's largest purchasers of American weapons, has sought additional military support from allies as it confronts daily missile and drone attacks across a vast territory.
Regional officials have warned that the kingdom is running low on missile interceptors, while military analysts say completely preventing Houthi strikes is virtually impossible.
Saudi Arabia covers an area approximately three times the size of Texas, and Houthi weapons are capable of reaching targets more than 1,600 kilometers, or 1,000 miles, away. Some missiles can also change course during flight, complicating interception efforts.
Even successful interceptions can cause casualties and damage on the ground.
Saudi Arabia's Civil Defense said debris from two intercepted Houthi ballistic missiles fell on residential neighborhoods in Riyadh overnight, injuring four people, including a child, and damaging 15 homes.
The escalating attacks have revived concerns about the vulnerability of Saudi Arabia's oil infrastructure and transportation networks, with repeated strikes threatening facilities central to the kingdom's economy.
Saudi strikes intensify inside Yemen
Saudi Arabia has responded with its own military operations against Houthi-controlled areas of Yemen, supporting the country's internationally recognized government.
The latest confrontation erupted after the Houthis accused Saudi Arabia of attacking an airport in Sanaa, reigniting tensions over the longstanding Saudi blockade of rebel-held territory.
The Houthis subsequently announced their own blockade against Saudi Arabia, while the Saudi-led coalition launched a major military offensive approximately a week and a half ago.
On Wednesday, the Houthi-run Health Ministry said two people had been killed and two wounded in a Saudi airstrike Tuesday on an oil facility in the Ras Isa port area of Hodeida province.
The Saudi-led coalition also struck an oil facility in Sanaa.
Ahmed Nagi, a senior Yemen analyst at the International Crisis Group, said the attacks on fuel storage facilities in Houthi-held areas represented a new phase in the conflict.
He warned that a prolonged war of attrition could significantly weaken the Houthis' military capabilities.
"The Houthis are betting on pressure, while the Saudis are betting on time," Nagi said.
"The Houthis are trying to strike critical infrastructure in Saudi Arabia to raise the cost of continued military intervention and support for the Yemeni government."
Humanitarian crisis deepens
The renewed fighting has also threatened to plunge Yemen deeper into the civil war that devastated the country before four years of relative calm.
The International Committee of the Red Cross reported an unprecedented increase in people suffering weapons-related injuries along Yemen's front lines, particularly in Marib, Taiz and areas near the Red Sea.
Hospitals are struggling to cope with the surge in casualties, with increasingly frequent incidents involving large numbers of wounded patients.
The World Food Program also warned that it could no longer reach more than 600,000 people dependent on humanitarian assistance in the besieged city of Taiz.
With Saudi Arabia and the Houthis continuing to exchange strikes, the diplomatic efforts involving Oman, Russia and China have yet to produce a breakthrough, leaving both the kingdom's critical infrastructure and Yemen's civilian population exposed to further escalation.

European Commission allocates nearly €2.9 bln more to Ukraine for drones, air defense and missiles
According to Ukrinform, this is said in a press release published on the Commission’s website.
“As Russia stalls on the frontlines, it continues to escalate its aerial attacks - cruelly targeting Ukrainian civilians and infrastructure. Europe's steadfast support matters more than ever to help Ukraine protect its skies and save lives. With today's €2.86 billion disbursement, we keep addressing Ukraine's most urgent operational needs, including drones and missiles vital to its defence,” Ursula von der Leyen, President of the European Commission, said.
The Ukraine Support Loan totals €90 billion for 2026–2027, including €60 billion for defence needs and development of Ukraine’s defence‑industrial base, and €30 billion for budget support.
During 2026, €28.3 billion is expected to be directed to support Ukraine’s defence industrial capacity. The Commission said further disbursements under the 2026 defence leg of the instrument will continue in the coming weeks.
By the end of 2026, Ukraine will still have access to €29.64 billion available in EU financial assistance. This includes €25.24 billion under the Ukraine Support Loan (with €12.54 billion for defence‑industry support and €12.7 billion for budget financing) and €4.4 billion in remaining budget support under the initial Ukraine Facility.
In total, more than €17 billion is earmarked to ensure the stability of Ukraine’s budget for the remaining months of 2026. Disbursement depends on meeting conditions set out in the Ukraine Plan and the Memorandum of Understanding.
As reported, since 2022 the European Union and its Member States have provided €231.5 billion in assistance to Ukraine, including €3.8 billion from the proceeds of immobilised Russian assets.
In February 2026, the European Parliament and the Council adopted Regulation (EU) 2026/467, establishing the Ukraine Support Loan. The Regulation provides for up to €90 billion in support to Ukraine. The support is designed to strengthen Ukraine’s defence capabilities and ensure the uninterrupted functioning of the state, delivery of essential public services and economic resilience amid Russia’s aggression.

China-EU consensus on vehicle trade to stabilize industry expectations: CAAM
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
19:23:12 CST
20:23:12 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- The consensus reached between China and the European Union (EU) on hybrid and electric vehicle trade will help stabilize industry expectations on both sides and ensure the smooth operation of automotive industrial and supply chains, the China Association of Automobile Manufacturers (CAAM) said on Wednesday.
The consensus follows intensive bilateral talks under the China-EU trade and investment consultation mechanism, guided by the principles of mutual respect and equal consultation, the CAAM said in a statement.
As major global economies and automotive markets, China and the EU have strong industrial complementarity and broad scope for cooperation, the association said.
Managing differences and properly addressing trade frictions through institutionalized consultations, replacing confrontation with dialogue and resolving disputes through cooperation, are a rational choice that serves the fundamental interests of both sides, the CAAM noted.
Escalating trade tensions would raise business costs, disrupt normal market order and harm consumers, while hindering the automotive industry's transformation and upgrading, the CAAM said.
Regarding hybrid vehicles, the two sides emphasized and confirmed three basic principles: respect for facts, non-discrimination and compliance with World Trade Organization rules.
On electric vehicles, China and the EU achieved a "soft landing" in the EU's anti-subsidy case in January this year, with the bloc issuing a general guidance document on price undertakings. The EU will continue to advance relevant procedures concerning price undertakings by companies involved in the case, as well as other review procedures.
The consensus will provide a more predictable environment for automotive companies to pursue trade and investment cooperation and help safeguard the shared interests of industry players and consumers on both sides, the CAAM said.
The association said it would continue to promote industry dialogue and coordination, support China and the EU in working together under their trade and investment consultation mechanism to implement the consensus and properly resolve differences, and jointly uphold a fair, open and non-discriminatory international trading environment. ■

PHNOM PENH, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- Cambodia saw a 16.4-percent rise in revenue from the exports of bananas, mangoes, and longans during the first nine months of 2026, driven by strong Chinese demand and preferential tariff agreements.
The Southeast Asian nation generated 312.17 million U.S. dollars from the exports of these commodities during the January-September period this year, up from the 268 million dollars recorded during the same period last year, a Ministry of Commerce report showed on Wednesday.
The report detailed varying performances across the three major fruit categories. Banana exports climbed 35.7 percent to 180.33 million dollars, and mangoes ticked up 0.12 percent to 108.25 million dollars. Conversely, longan revenues fell 12.6 percent to 23.59 million dollars.

"I believe the fruit industry is poised for double-digit annual growth, provided Cambodia continues expanding local processing facilities such as drying and juice manufacturing to buffer against seasonal price shifts," he told Xinhua. ■

====================================================================================================

China Focus: "China Hotline" helps foreigners plug into people-centered governance
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
19:22:48 CST
20:22:48 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- After "China Travel" draws global travelers to its capital, China is offering the world another way in: the "China Hotline," a 12345 service that lets foreign nationals make their voices heard and help improve the city they reside in.
The service is part of a broader reform that began in Beijing in 2019, when the city, home to over 20 million residents, launched a "swift response to public complaints" initiative. The goal is to address concerns promptly and resolve everyday challenges efficiently. More than 60 hotline services have been integrated into a single number, 12345, which now serves as the main channel for residents to report issues.
Operating 24/7, the hotline is staffed by over 1,700 operators who work in shifts to take calls and handle requests covering nearly every aspect of urban life, including transportation, housing, education, healthcare, employment and business services. Foreign visitors and residents in Beijing are covered by the service, where they are treated not as outsiders but as part of the city.
Official data shows the Chinese capital has handled about 200 million public appeals in just over seven years, with resolution and satisfaction rates both exceeding 97 percent.
"The experience of Beijing's citizen service system offered valuable lessons for Athens in advancing people-centered urban governance and building a city that listens to its citizens and responds to their concerns," said Georgios K. Giannaros, first deputy mayor of Athens, Greece, during the 2026 Beijing Forum on Swift Response to Public Complaints.
The two-day event, which opened Monday, brought together more than 3,200 participants from over 70 countries and regions to explore new paths for modernizing urban governance, a challenge shared across the world.
OPEN HOTLINE
Marie, an expat living in Beijing, once hit a snag when signing up for a water show on the Grand Canal in Tongzhou District: the online registration form on WeChat only accepted Chinese mainland resident ID cards, leaving no way to enter foreign passport details.
After Marie raised the issue through the 12345 hotline, the case was assigned to Tongzhou authorities, who activated a fast-track mechanism for requests involving foreign nationals. Working with the platform operator and its technical team, they upgraded the registration system within just one working day, adding a field for passports and other foreign ID documents.
The 12345 hotline's foreign-related services are not only efficient, but also expanding in both scope and capacity.
"Foreign callers have all kinds of requests, with visa and entry-exit policies and work permit applications among the most common inquiries," said Wang Dongbo, an English-language operator on the hotline, adding that whether they live in Beijing or are just visiting briefly, foreigners who run into trouble can call 12345, and someone will see the matter through.
"Besides our dedicated English lines, calls in other languages are transferred to the multilingual service center at Beijing Foreign Studies University, where volunteers join in on a three-way call," said Shan Qiang with the Beijing Citizen Hotline Service Center. The hotline now provides round-the-clock services in eight foreign languages.
Beyond the hotline, Beijing has rolled out "12345 Online," a digital platform offering the same service. Meanwhile, a multi-dimensional support network for foreigners is taking shape in the Chinese capital.
The network spans "GO BEIJING" -- a one-stop service platform for overseas visitors -- the English edition of Beijing's official public services app, the International Web Portal of Beijing and airport service points, responding to their needs at every stage, from pre-trip planning and entry, to life in Beijing.
"In the governance logic of China's capital, where every complaint gets a response, the 'people' in 'the people's voices are heard' now include foreigners living in Beijing," said Zhang Yi, director of the institute for capital governance at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences.
SHARED GOVERNANCE
Being heard is only part of the story. Traik Souhail from Morocco spends almost every weekend studying at Beijing Library in Tongzhou District. He noticed that seat-hogging was a common problem here. "Public resources shouldn't sit idle or go to waste. Every seat should go to someone who actually needs it," he said.
In August last year, he submitted a proposal through "12345 Online," suggesting the library set a 30-minute limit on unoccupied seats to stop long-term seat-hogging.
After verifying the situation, the library moved quickly to address this issue. It posted notices in Chinese and English urging readers to use the library respectfully and refrain from hogging seats, stepped up manual patrols, and promptly cleared unattended items from seats, bringing order back to its reading areas.
Li Wenzhao, a professor at the School of Public Administration and Policy, Renmin University of China, said Beijing's "swift response to public complaints" has transformed the traditional top-down model of urban governance into a collaborative, multi-stakeholder approach. It is equally open to foreign residents, encouraging them to take ownership and bring international perspectives, experience and expertise into the capital's governance.
"Cities become more beautiful through openness, which is also essential to a world-class, harmonious and livable capital," he said.
"Anyone who lives in this city has a channel to voice concerns and take part in governance. The hotline not only bridges language barriers but also opens a path for diverse groups to integrate into urban governance," said Yao Lei, director of the Beijing Citizen Hotline Service Center.
CHINESE SOLUTION
In June, more than 20 young scholars from leading think tanks across Latin America visited the 12345 hotline call center in Beijing.
"Over 20 million appeals a year. That's incredible!" Chilean scholar Maria Fernanda Garredon said after seeing the full call-handling process for herself. "If residents didn't find it effective, they wouldn't call. Such a high volume shows that once you get through, your concerns are heard and solutions are found."
In recent years, the center has hosted nearly 2,500 foreign visitors from more than 120 countries, including the United States, Belarus and Thailand. Belarusian delegations have visited three times to learn from the hotline's experience, and the country plans to draw on Beijing's 12345 model to set up its own hotline.
"When you set foot on Chinese soil, see firsthand how institutions operate and learn how ordinary people get their problems solved, you come to understand that China is truly committed to improving people's livelihoods and tackling real problems," said Salvadoran scholar Juan Gilberto Contreras Gomez.
"There is a global phenomenon unfolding in Western countries, developing countries and elsewhere. People don't feel that governments respond to their needs or their immediate problems -- mainly services and quality of life," said Omar Razzaz, a senior fellow at Harvard Kennedy School and former prime minister of Jordan. He has been actively promoting Beijing's "swift response to public complaints" reform at various international events.
Razzaz called the 12345 citizen hotline "a model of efficient and balanced governance," noting that it represents a deep integration of technological empowerment and institutional innovation. "I've seen elements of it in different countries. But the way it worked here was quite impressive, and I felt like China should share that experience," he added. ■

====================================================================================================

Feature: AI reshapes global labor market, opens new paths to entrepreneurship
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
19:22:46 CST
20:22:46 KST

by Xinhua writer Liu Yang
BANGKOK, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- Artificial intelligence (AI) is unlikely to transform the labor market merely through mass job displacement. Instead, it is reshaping the skills employers seek, expanding what individual workers can do and opening new pathways to entrepreneurship, participants at the 2026 Annual Meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank Group said.
Describing the AI wave as a "slow-moving tsunami," IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva warned that around 40 percent of jobs worldwide could be affected by AI over time -- either augmented, downgraded, or eliminated.
Divya Kirti, senior economist in the IMF's Asia and Pacific Department, also cited research showing that hiring demand has fallen by about 10 percent in jobs where AI is more useful.
"But the bigger story is that we also see that employers do still want people in these jobs, even as AI has gotten much better. What has happened is that employers have started thinking about workers differently, and they now want workers that can use AI to do more," Kirti said.
The shift points to a labor market where the debate is less about whether machines can replace humans, and more about how people can work alongside AI systems.
During the meetings, one concept that took center stage was "Small AI" -- practical, affordable AI designed for specific tasks and local needs, including tools that can work on basic devices, with limited connectivity, and in local languages.
World Bank Group President Ajay Banga outlined several potential applications of Small AI in agriculture and healthcare at a flagship event. He described how an illiterate woman farmer in India could use a basic 3G phone to identify crop diseases simply by pointing the device at the back of a leaf and pressing a button.
In Indonesia, he added, healthcare workers at primary care centers could use AI tools to conduct preliminary patient assessments before referring cases for remote consultation with doctors.
Thailand's Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister Ekniti Nitithanprapas also introduced a simple AI assistant called Nokrasip, or Whispering Birds in Thai.
Embedded in the mobile wallet applications already used by merchants to access government subsidies, the tool acts like a business advisor, helping nearly 1 million small merchants to manage stocks and work out profits, he said.
Such tools may seem distant from cutting-edge AI industries, yet they illustrate another way the technology could transform employment: rather than replacing the jobs of nurses, farmers or small-business owners, it could give them access to capabilities once available mainly to large institutions.
Participants therefore stressed the need to lower the cost of AI adoption and make tools more accessible to small and medium-sized enterprises, startups and universities.
For developing economies in particular, they said, Small AI that can run on ordinary smartphones and function with limited internet connectivity could help broaden access to the benefits of the technology.
In addition to overhauling traditional occupations, AI is also giving rise to new forms of employment. Singaporean President Tharman Shanmugaratnam said that AI is going to blur the distinction between employee and entrepreneur, pointing to the emergence of the One-Person Company (OPC) as a new form of employment.
An OPC begins with a single founder and can gradually bring in additional people as the business grows. The model is already emerging in both developed and developing economies, he said.
Hailing the OPC as a new growth area in the labor market, Shanmugaratnam said that the government should encourage its development.
"If you look at Zhejiang Province in China, they now have a service alliance for OPCs providing a range of such services, including AI models, sources of energy, and some professional services," he said.
Still, access to technology alone will not determine who benefits from AI. Skills and training will be crucial as job requirements evolve.
Ximena Lincolao, Chile's Minister of Science, Technology, Knowledge and Innovation, called for a shift away from the traditional view of education as a sequential process in which people study first and enter the workforce afterward.
Vocational training, apprenticeships and higher education need to be more closely connected, she said, while workers must continue updating their skills throughout their careers.
No one could yet tell precisely how many jobs AI will create or eliminate. But the emerging picture suggests that the advantages of the AI era may not be tied to any single profession.
Ultimately, the challenge is not for humans to compete with machines, but to learn how to harness the technology while preserving the qualities that remain essential to human work: judgment, creativity, communication and responsibility.
As Georgieva put it in her closing remarks in a discussion, "Get AI to do all the stuff we don't want to do and let us enjoy the things we love to do. High productivity, high standard of living, but also the dignity of being socially viable." ■

Yemen's Houthis claim large-scale missile, drone attack on Saudi airport, oil facilities

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14

20:22:37 KST

SANAA, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- Yemen's Houthi group said Wednesday it had launched a large-scale missile and drone attack targeting an airport and oil facilities in Saudi Arabia, vowing to continue strikes against Saudi targets in the coming days.
In a statement broadcast by Houthi-run al-Masirah TV, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Sarea said the group targeted Saudi energy giant Aramco in Dhahran in the Eastern Province, as well as King Khalid International Airport and an Aramco refinery in Riyadh.
According to Sarea, the operation involved "a large number of ballistic and cruise missiles and drones," which accurately hit their targets, causing damage and fires.
The Houthi spokesperson said the operation was carried out in retaliation for Saudi Arabia-led strikes on the Houthi-held capital of Sanaa and other areas under the group's control. He said Saudi-led forces had carried out 2,281 air and missile strikes since the latest escalation began.
Sarea vowed that the group's attacks "deep inside Saudi Arabia" would continue in the coming days, targeting airports and oil facilities. He also renewed a warning to international airlines, civilians and employees to stay away from airports and oil facilities in Saudi Arabia that the group had designated as targets.
The Houthi claim came after the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said it intercepted six Houthi missiles and three drones heading towards Saudi Arabia on Tuesday. An Aramco administrative building in Dhahran was targeted Tuesday evening, sparking a limited fire, while debris from two cruise missiles intercepted over Riyadh injured four people and damaged 15 homes, Saudi authorities said Wednesday.
The latest Houthi operations followed a series of Saudi-led coalition strikes on Tuesday targeting the Yemen Petroleum Company's Al-Sabaha fuel storage and distribution facility west of Sanaa, as well as fuel facilities in the Red Sea province of Hodeidah.
Cross-border hostilities have intensified sharply in recent days. A Houthi attack on a passenger terminal at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Saturday killed 12 people and injured 309 others, according to the Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation. The Saudi-led coalition subsequently vowed a firm response to the attack.
Yemen has been mired in conflict since late 2014, when the Houthis seized Sanaa and much of northern Yemen. A Saudi-led coalition intervened in 2015 in support of the internationally recognized Yemeni government. Major hostilities had largely subsided following a UN-brokered truce in 2022, before the latest fighting led to a sharp escalation in ground battles and cross-border missile, drone and air attacks. ■

Russia seeks to strip Dutch event of Olympic status over gymnast ban
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:22:35 UTC
20:22:35 KST

Russia seeks to strip Dutch event of Olympic status over gymnast ban
Russia will seek to strip an upcoming gymnastics championship in the Netherlands of its Olympic qualifying status after the Dutch authorities denied visas to three of its top athletes, Sports Minister Mikhail Degtyarev announced.
The Netherlands refused entry visas to Angelina Melnikova, Viktoria Listunova, and Anna Kalmykova, the Russian Gymnastics Federation (RGF) revealed on Tuesday, barring them from the World Artistic Gymnastics Championships in Rotterdam in three days, a qualifying event for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. According to the RGF, official refusal notices said “one or more Schengen member states” considered the athletes “a threat to their international relations.”
In a statement later that day, Degtyarev said the Russian Olympic Committee (ROC) will demand that the International Olympic Committee (IOC) and World Gymnastics revoke Rotterdam’s Olympic qualifying status over “discrimination” and violations of equal competition rules.
“The politically motivated refusal by the Netherlands to issue visas to the leaders of Russia’s artistic gymnastics team once again shows that Europe is no place for high-performance sport,” Degtyarev said, warning: “Today, Europeans have disregarded the decisions of international organizations and denied Russians visas, tomorrow they will refuse entry to someone else.”
Only four gymnasts from the Russian squad have so far obtained visas; five others are still awaiting decisions.
Melnikova was set to defend her women’s all-around world title after winning gold at last year’s championships in Jakarta. She also won all-around gold at this year’s European Championships in Zagreb. Listunova won Olympic team gold alongside Melnikova at the Tokyo Games, where she was Russia’s youngest gymnast at just 16. Kalmykova, 18, is among the youngest members of the squad. She helped Russia win the team title in Zagreb and claimed individual all-around silver.
Missing Rotterdam will hurt the trio’s chances of reaching the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics but won’t rule them out. The championships are the first stage of the qualification process, with individual berths still available through later World Cup events and continental championships in 2027 and 2028.
‘Inhumane’: Visa snub sparks outrage
The move drew criticism from Russian athletes and sports officials. The RGF called it “direct discrimination against Russian athletes” and a “a flagrant violation of the principle of equal conditions for Olympic qualification.” RGF Vice President Nikita Nagorny called the situation “disgusting.”
Two-time Olympic gymnastics champion Lidia Ivanova accused the Dutch of deliberately sidelining Russia’s strongest competitors.
“With this decision, they are demonstrating their weakness,” she told Match TV. “They did this knowing full well that they were denying visas to top Russian gymnasts... It’s sheer nastiness.”
Olympic speed skating champion Svetlana Zhurova also accused the Dutch of shutting out strong rivals, telling RT that politicizing sports is destroying it.
Reacting on social media, Melnikova said she “felt like crying” and called the actions “inhumane.”
“If they keep mixing sport with politics to such an extent, it will become a complete nightmare,” she said, posting a team photograph with the caption: “This is what the Netherlands considers a threat to international relations.”
Western bans and Russian medals
Russian and Belarusian athletes were excluded from numerous international competitions following the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in February 2022, after an IOC recommendation and bans imposed by individual federations. Earlier this year, the IOC provisionally lifted its suspension of the Russian Olympic Committee, opening the way for a broader return. Several federations, including World Gymnastics, have since eased their restrictions.
The shift has met resistance in the EU, a strong supporter of Ukraine. Nine member states, including the Netherlands, urged Brussels in an open letter to cut funding for international sporting bodies that readmit Russian and Belarusian athletes. On Monday, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas promised proposals to “sustain Russia’s isolation in global sports.”
Russia has called the bans on its athletes politically motivated and “cowardly.” Despite the restrictions, Russian athletes have continued to win titles wherever they are allowed to compete.
Last week, Inal Tasoev won gold in the men’s over-100 kg division at the 2026 World Judo Championships in Baku. In August, Russian artistic swimmers swept all three golds awarded on the opening day of the World Junior Aquatics Championships in Budapest. In July, Pavel Graudyn won the men’s individual saber title at the World Fencing Championships in Hong Kong, and Russian junior figure skaters swept all four disciplines at an ISU Junior Grand Prix event in China in August, returning after a four-year ban.

Exhibition of pioneering Hong Kong school for national talent in early 1940s opens

Exhibition of pioneering Hong Kong school for national talent in early 1940s opens
Showcase of Ta Teh Institute and its legacy will be presented at Hong Kong Museum of History from Wednesday to February 15 next year
A new exhibition about a pioneering school that nurtured talent for the country has opened at a Hong Kong history museum as part of the government’s efforts to promote national education, with many exhibits shown in the city for the first time.
“National Development and Achievements Series: Cultivation and Renewal – The Education Legacy of Hong Kong’s Ta Teh Institute”, a free exhibition presented by the Leisure and Cultural Services Department, will run at the Hong Kong Museum of History in Tsim Sha Tsui from Wednesday to February 15 next year.
Ta Teh Institute was a liberal arts university established in Tuen Mun in 1946 during the Chinese Civil War. It was the second university to be established in the city after the University of Hong Kong. The institute closed down in 1949.

====================================================================================================

Syria accuses Israel of arming Druze militias in Suweida
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:21:01 UTC
20:21:01 KST

Breadcrumb
Syria says Israel funding Druze militias to fuel chaos
Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani has accused Israel of supplying weapons and financial support to armed militias in the southern province of Suweida, alleging that Israel is seeking to destabilise Syria and undermine its sovereignty.
Speaking at a press conference in Damascus on Tuesday, al-Shaibani said Israel was supporting armed groups operating outside the authority of the Syrian state, amid continuing tensions over the future of the predominantly Druze province.
"Israel supports armed militias operating outside the law in the city of Sweida, providing them with weapons and funding to pursue an agenda of chaos in the region," he said, according to Syria's official SANA news agency.
The accusations come amid mounting concerns over Israel's involvement in southern Syria, where Israeli forces have expanded their military presence since the overthrow of Bashar al-Assad in December 2024.
Al-Shaibani accused Israel of pursuing a wider campaign to destabilise the country through attacks on infrastructure, the occupation of additional Syrian territory and the displacement and detention of Syrian civilians.
He said the fate of dozens of Syrians detained by Israeli forces remained unknown, calling on the international community to intervene and prevent further escalation.
Suweida has remained largely outside central government control following deadly clashes in July 2025 involving Druze armed factions, Bedouin groups and Syrian government forces.
The violence, which included abuses against Druze civilians by government-linked fighters, deepened mistrust between Damascus and sections of the Druze community.
Israel subsequently launched airstrikes against Syrian government positions, including targets in Damascus, claiming that its intervention was necessary to protect Syria's Druze minority.
However, Israeli involvement has also raised concerns about efforts to encourage the fragmentation of Syria by supporting armed groups opposed to the central government.
Much of Suweida is now controlled by factions associated with Druze religious leader Sheikh Hikmat al-Hijri, who has openly advocated separating the province from Damascus and establishing an independent Druze entity under Israeli protection.
In January, al-Hijri told Israeli newspaper Yedioth Ahronoth that his movement considered itself closely aligned with Israel and viewed the country as a guarantor of its political future.
"We see ourselves as an inseparable part of the existence of the State of Israel. This relationship is international and of critical importance," he said.
He also called for Syria's partition, arguing that independent or autonomous territories represented a possible future for the country.
In August, al-Hijri went further, declaring during a gathering in Suwayda that his supporters were an "integral part of the State of Israel" and shared its ideology.
His position has nevertheless faced opposition from other Druze religious figures, activists and armed factions who reject Israeli intervention and support maintaining Suwayda within a unified Syrian state.
The New Arab has previously reported on allegations that Israel has provided financial and military assistance to Druze militias operating in Suweida, including the Military Council, an armed faction associated with al-Hijri.
According to a Washington Post investigation published in December 2025, Israeli officials acknowledged providing support to Druze armed groups through the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF).
The report detailed financial transfers, weapons supplies and military assistance, including an alleged payment of $24,000 to help establish the Military Council.
It also described cooperation involving military training and the provision of weapons, including anti-tank missiles, to strengthen Druze factions opposed to Damascus.
The allegations have added to concerns that Israel is seeking to cultivate armed allies in southern Syria as part of a broader effort to prevent the re-establishment of strong central government authority.
Israel has repeatedly demanded the demilitarisation of southern Syria and opposed the deployment of Syrian government forces near its borders, while continuing military operations inside Syrian territory.
Following Assad's overthrow, Israeli forces seized the UN-monitored buffer zone established under the 1974 disengagement agreement and expanded their presence beyond positions occupied before December 2024.
Israel has occupied most of Syria's Golan Heights since 1967, an occupation not recognised by the international community.
Despite the tensions, Damascus and Israel have engaged in several rounds of US-mediated negotiations aimed at establishing new security arrangements along their shared frontier.
In August, Syrian and Israeli delegations met in Jordan under American mediation to discuss Israeli military operations, the detention of Syrian civilians and the possibility of withdrawing Israeli forces to positions held before Assad's overthrow.
Al-Shaibani called for Israel to return to the 1974 disengagement agreement and allow the United Nations Disengagement Observer Force to carry out its responsibilities.
He also urged Israel to engage seriously in the US-sponsored negotiations, reiterating Damascus's commitment to reaching an agreement that respects Syrian sovereignty and territorial integrity.
The Syrian foreign minister's latest accusations come as the government of President Ahmed al-Sharaa continues efforts to consolidate its authority across the country, with Suwayda remaining one of the principal areas outside Damascus's control.

2026-10-14

Update: Russian soldier arrested, suspected of killing 5 Ukrainian soldiers, 1 civilian in Kharkiv Oblast
Editor's Note: This story has been updated to include the most recent developments.
A Russian soldier suspected of killing five Ukrainian soldiers and one civilian was arrested in Kharkiv on Oct. 14, the Kharkiv Regional Prosecutor's Office reported.
Previously, Ukrainian media reported that a Russian prisoner of war (POW) escaped from captivity and killed five Ukrainian service members in Kharkiv Oblast on Oct. 13. Prosecutors confirmed that an investigation was underway and authorities were searching for the attacker.
The detained suspect is a 36-year-old Russian citizen from St. Petersburg serving in the Second Battalion of Russia's 1009th motorized rifle regiment, the Kharkiv Regional Prosecutor's Office said after the arrest.
According to the prosecutor's office, investigators believe the suspect may have been involved in Russian sabotage and reconnaissance operations. The report did not identify the individual as a POW, but said he was wearing civilian clothes at the time of his capture.
Investigators also believe the man may have shot and killed a civilian in addition to the murders of five Ukrainian soldiers.
The suspect is alleged to have seen a man fishing in the village of Tsyrkuny, some 16 kilometers (10 miles) from the Russian border, and shot him for fear of exposure. An autopsy revealed a gunshot wound to the head, the prosecutor's office said.
The gunman then made his way to the village of Momotove, outside the regional capital, where he allegedly shot and killed five members of the Ukrainian military. The suspect was eventually arrested in Kharkiv.
Earlier on Oct. 14, multiple media outlets reported that five Ukrainian military personnel had been murdered in Kharkiv Oblast the previous day.
Around 4:00 p.m., a man in civilian clothing approached a building housing members of the 72nd Separate Mechanized Brigade, opened fire, and first killed one Ukrainian service member, before entering the house and killing four others, according to Glavkom.
A source in the military command in the Kharkiv region told BBC Ukraine that the suspected attacker was a Russian prisoner of war.
The Regional Prosecutor's Office confirmed an investigation was underway, but did not identify any suspects as Russian POWs.
The prosecutor's office said investigators were examining several possible motives, including whether the attacker may have been linked to a Russian sabotage and reconnaissance group.
The brigade shared a statement, saying that "On October 13, a tragic event occurred in the territory of Kharkiv region, as a result of which servicemen of the 72nd separate mechanized brigade named after the Black Zaporozhians died."
"According to preliminary information, persons who are likely citizens of the Russian Federation may have been involved in the incident," it added.
In total, the shooting lasted for about two hours, Glavkom said, while BBC Ukraine added that residents called the local police station at 04:20 p.m. about the incident. Another service member was injured in a neighboring village, according to Glavkom.
Glavkom said that two servicemen of the Russian armed forces fled captivity in Kharkiv Oblast.
During the search for the suspect, BBC Ukraine reported that the attacker was a man with a height of 160-170 cm, a lean physique, with dark hair and a unkempt beard, wearing dark blue jeans, a long-sleeved black jacket, and a grey backpack, and carrying a machine gun.
On Oct. 6, Ukraine's Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War said that Ukraine took 858 more Russian servicemen into captivity than Ukrainians were taken into Russian captivity, an average 107 per month.
Since mid-2023, the group said, Ukraine has taken more prisoners than Russia. The Ukrainian military provides bonuses for taking Russian soldiers as prisoners, as each Russian soldier might be an opportunity to exchange Ukrainian service members or civilians in Russian captivity, it added.
Ukraine and Russia exchange prisoners of war, one of the few remaining areas of direct humanitarian cooperation between the two countries amid Russia's full-scale invasion.
Ukraine and Russia have also continued repatriating the bodies of fallen soldiers despite a broader diplomatic process that has largely stalled.

Ukraine accuses SpaceX of crippling drone missions as ties with US worsen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:20:47 UTC
20:20:47 KST

Ukraine says SpaceX hampers drones for attack and defence, as US ties fray
KYIV - Ukraine said Elon Musk’s SpaceX had limited its satellite services on Oct 14, hampering Ukrainian drones for attack missions and air defences, as relations between Kyiv and Washington have taken a sharp turn for the worse.
Russia rained more missiles and drones down on Ukrainian cities, knocking out electricity for hundreds of thousands of people in attacks President Volodymyr Zelensky called “ostentatious disrespect” to Donald Trump’s call for an energy ceasefire.
The US president publicly turned on Zelensky in recent days after abruptly lifting sanctions on Russian diesel last week, under political pressure to lower fuel prices that have soared since he launched a war against Iran. He has called on Kyiv to halt attacks on Russian refineries, and said Ukrainians should replace their wartime leader.
“It’s painful when President Trump chooses one side, not our side,” Zelensky told Piers Morgan Uncensored. He said that he was OK with Trump being in the middle of Ukraine and Russia, but added: “If you are in the middle, you have to stay in the middle.”
Asked about the restriction on the military version of SpaceX’s Starlink services in Ukraine, Zelensky said: “It’s a big mistake ... this decision will bring a lot of human losses.” He did not say who was responsible.
Trump announced at the weekend that Ukraine and Russia both agreed to halt attacks on energy targets, although neither side confirmed this and the past two days have seen intensive Russian bombing, including of Ukrainian power stations.
After a night of bombardment of the capital Kyiv, Russian strikes continued throughout the day on Oct 14 with six people killed in the western city of Lutsk, where the regional governor said a warehouse and a residential building were hit.
Ukraine, for its part, continued long-range strikes on Russia, hitting Russia’s biggest data centre, although it says it is holding back from hitting energy targets for now to show respect for Trump.
No warning before Starlink cuts
Ukrainian military officials said Musk’s SpaceX had without warning started to interrupt functioning of its military-grade terminals when they are moving at high speed.
Kyiv installs SpaceX receptors in many of its drones as part of their onboard guidance systems. The terminals operate across Ukraine, including in territory held by Russian forces.
“Our defence forces did not receive a warning about this limitation, and this led to the disruption of several missions,” presidential adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov wrote on Telegram, saying the restriction affected StarShield, SpaceX’s military and intelligence service.
The speed cutoff hampers Ukraine’s ability to conduct strikes on Russian targets inside Ukraine, or to defend itself from Russian drones using its own interceptor drones, according to a defence ministry source and another military source.
Beskrestnov said SpaceX had imposed a speed limit of 160kmh. The defence ministry source told Reuters military units had reported guidance systems losing their connections at speeds of less than half that.
SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The defence ministry source said Ukraine was in contact with the company as well as the US government and NATO to seek clarification over the sudden limitations.
The suggestion that Musk’s company had limited Ukrainian military capabilities drew a sharp response from Poland, which pays for Ukrainian Starlink subscriptions on Kyiv’s behalf.
“Hey, @elonmusk, big man, are you playing politics with your products again?” Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski asked Musk on X. “As your European customers, we are watching you.”
There was no immediate response from Musk, who in the past has called Sikorski a “small man”.
Shares in European satellite operator Eutelsat, which is seen as Europe’s best shot at taking on Starlink, jumped on Wednesday as some investors bet that European providers could benefit from growing strains between Washington and Kyiv.
Musk is a close political ally of Trump, and the suggestion that SpaceX might limit Ukrainian capabilities reinforced wider Ukrainian concerns that Washington could withhold battlefield support to compel its one-time ally to make concessions.
Sources have told Reuters and other media that the US has threatened to cut off intelligence for early warning of missile strikes on Ukraine, to press Kyiv to suspend attacks on Russian oil refineries.
No warning ahead of missiles
Rescue workers in Kyiv were stretchering the injured from the wreckage of a blasted-out residential building overnight, while firefighters battled a huge blaze in the darkness. Officials said 2 people were killed and 21 wounded at the site.
Some 600,000 people were left without power as Russian missiles careened into power stations during hours of attacks that primarily targeted Kyiv and Kharkiv, Ukraine’s second-largest city.
Russia’s defence ministry confirmed it had struck four power plants in and around Kyiv and two in Kharkiv, among other targets. Zelensky said 30 energy facilities were damaged.
Ukrainian officials said late on Oct 13 they had received no warnings from Western partners for a second day before Russian missiles hit the capital. Trump had insisted on Oct 13 that Washington was still sharing intelligence.
Zelensky cast the latest Russian attacks as a deliberate snub to Trump’s declaration of a ceasefire on energy targets.
“Russia does not consider the American President’s statements strong,” Zelensky wrote on X. “The strike was entirely deliberate and demonstrative in its scale – Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States.”
Zelensky has said Ukraine is willing to observe an energy ceasefire and has not targeted Russian refineries since Trump announced it, but will not continue to hold back if Russia ignores the purported truce. The Kremlin said on Oct 13 that contacts were continuing about an energy truce.
Ukraine reported downing just 4 out of 39 Russian missiles, reflecting Kyiv’s weakened air defences against fast-moving ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones amid a shortage of weapons. REUTERS
