Scandal surrounding the Director of the NABU: witness reveals details of the 2008 case involving Kryvonos’s vote-buying and deception of contractors
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:19:38 EEST
20:19:38 KST

Scandal surrounding the Director of the NABU: witness reveals details of the 2008 case involving Kryvonos’s vote-buying and deception of contractors
Kyiv • UNN
Serhii Kutsenko accused Semen Kryvonos of organizing voter bribery and failing to pay contractors in 2008. The court found Kryvonos guilty, but he was amnestied.
The current head of the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU), Semen Kryvonos, has found himself at the center of a public scandal over testimony concerning his activities in 2008. Serhii Kutsenko, the owner of an advertising agency, spoke about the current official’s involvement in organizing a voter-bribery system, nonpayment to partners, and manipulation of court proceedings. This is reported by "Fakty".
According to the witness, in the spring of 2008 he worked with Kryvonos, who acted as a client on behalf of the Yulia Tymoshenko Bloc (BYuT). The task was to recruit up to 8,000 people from leading universities in the capital (Kyiv Polytechnic Institute, Kyiv National Economic University, National Aviation University, and National University of Life and Environmental Sciences of Ukraine) to create a campaign network.
The scheme involved three stages of funding:
First tranche (30%): collection of voters’ personal data (full name, telephone number, address).
Second tranche: payment before voting.
Third tranche: financial remuneration for confirmed voting.
Kutsenko said that, fearing wiretapping, coordination meetings were held exclusively in parks near the universities. When it became clear that the campaigning was turning into direct vote-buying, Kutsenko’s agency refused to participate any further.
The witness says that his agency refused to become involved in black vote-buying schemes and left Kryvonos’s operation after the first legal stage. Because of this withdrawal, Semen Kryvonos, who personally handed out money to contractors, underpaid the company by about 6,000 US dollars. According to Kutsenko’s testimony, after the project was shut down, Kryvonos’s team disappeared, leaving about 10 other contractors unpaid as well.
The witness alleged that Kryvonos manipulated the registration of paternity over a child in order to avoid a prison sentence in a criminal case, which he later renounced after a DNA test.
"That is neither humane nor manly. If you declared yourself the father, then keep your word. But as it turned out, you used a small child solely to cover your own backside," Serhii Kutsenko remarked.
The witness expressed surprise at Kryvonos’s appointment to a leadership position at NABU, given his past background. He noted that Kryvonos’s pathologically condescending attitude toward people, failure to fulfill obligations, and readiness to break the law for his own benefit were personally obvious to him as far back as 2008.
For reference The Holosiivskyi District Court of Kyiv found Semen Kryvonos guilty of committing a crime under Part 3 of Article 157 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine (voter bribery). However, in 2009 the official avoided actual punishment by registering paternity and submitting to the court a document confirming that he had a minor child dependent on him. Just eight days later, the court applied an amnesty to Kryvonos. Subsequently, in 2018–2019, the same Holosiivskyi court, following a lawsuit filed by Kryvonos and based on the results of a DNA examination, officially annulled the record of his paternity with respect to that child.

Estonian defence minister: "Russia could attack NATO. I'm not sure if we can deter the mad person"
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:19:00 EEST
20:19:00 KST

Estonian defence minister: "Russia could attack NATO. I'm not sure if we can deter the mad person"
Martin Herem is Estonia’s new minister of defence, having taken office less than a month ago. His predecessor, Hanno Pevkur, was forced to resign amid a scandal over arms procurement for Ukraine.
Herem is not a politician, but a career officer in the military.
And the new minister isn’t just any officer.
He is a full general, holding the highest military rank. Herem served as Commander of the Estonian Defence Forces from 2018 to 2022, and in that capacity he witnessed the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. In this interview, he also acknowledges that he has been on the front line in Ukraine.
While in Kyiv, General Herem met with the editor of European Pravda to discuss this, as well as his expectations regarding Russia’s next attack, including whether Russia might attack NATO.
European Pravda is the first non-Estonian media outlet to interview Martin Herem since his appointment as defence minister.
"Prevent a Russian attack? I'm not sure if we can deter the mad person"
Ukrainians are used to saying that Ukraine will definitely not be the last country that is attacked by Russia. Do you believe that as well?
If I take into account the attitude of the Russian state [towards its neighbours], and if I look at what they are producing right now for military purposes, then I think when they stop here [in Ukraine] – it doesn't matter how, whether you kick them out beyond the border, or the war is frozen – then every day they will start collecting military fat. And given their attitude, they will definitely test somebody.
Whether their first attack will be against Estonia, I'm not sure. It could be Latvia or somewhere else.
What they want to achieve is influence. They need power.
For that they don't need to occupy us, for example, Estonia.
They need to harm us and make us distrust each other, both in Estonia and among the Allies.
And if we have any nasty, ugly aggression, and Russians are gathering along the border, then we don’t want to see it again. And then we may choose the Russia-proposed solution.
That's exactly what they want: influence and instability.
You referred to Estonia and Latvia as examples, I believe, because both are in NATO. Does that mean that you expect an attack on NATO?
They may do it against NATO just to break NATO.
Acting below [the threshold of] Article Five, you mean?
Below Article Five, or under Article Five.
Because when Article Five is invoked, and we win this conflict but the victory is too ugly, then many will start blaming NATO and each other. And that’s the moment when the Russians will offer their solution: "Let's talk, let's do business as usual," and so on. And once we are under Russian influence, we go down.
I grew up in the Soviet Union, I have some understanding about this.
And Estonia has a history which teaches that Russia always attacks.
For the last thousand years, yes.
Can you see any way of preventing those attacks from happening?
I'm not sure if we can deter the mad person. But what we have to do is to prepare. And that's the only thing.
We have to prepare very seriously [for an attack] and if we do that, we may prevent it.
We have to be ready.
What are some practical ways in which small countries can prepare to contain the aggression?
First, our own self-defence capability must be very, very strong.
We must be ready to fight like Ukraine – on the front line and in the rear. And also to be able to eliminate all the threats coming from the enemy's depth, which means we need to develop our own deep strike [long-range] capability as well.
And we cannot do it on our own. We need our allies. Usually Estonia is seen as a country without strategic depth. I say we have a strategic depth. All of Europe is our rear.
That’s why we have to pay special attention to the sea. And again, it's not aggressive, it's not blocking the Baltic Sea or anything. It's ensuring the sea lines of communication at any given time. And that's what we’re doing right now together with our allies.
"In July 2022, I was in Estonian uniform on the front line in Ukraine"
Estonia is one of the countries active in the JEF (Joint Expeditionary Force).
JEF is a tool within NATO – it's not additional to NATO. JEF could make us faster to provide some support, but it still must follow the NATO plan. So it's nothing additional. It’s not an alternative – it's a small NATO inside NATO.
Does Ukraine have a place in the JEF?
I'm too young a minister to have any experience of discussions about Ukraine joining JEF, but I would say, if Ukraine has aspirations or a plan to join JEF, Estonia will definitely support it.
Let’s talk about Ukraine’s role in helping Estonia and NATO to deter threats and defend itself. You've just signed a drone deal. What are some practical ways to implement it?
The drone deal brings us not just technology, but experience.
And it's not just about how to operate an interceptor drone. It's about how to build our system of air defence or our system of fortifications, our counter-drone system. You have a lot of knowledge, a lot of data which we must adapt and bring to Estonia.
So it's not just the technology, and not even just the experience – it's about the knowledge.
How does it work in practical terms?
It could work in many ways. One of them is that we must come here to Ukraine and learn on the ground. Also, we must bring Ukrainian experts to Estonia to get advice on how we are building our defence line. That includes not just the fortifications or positions, but also sensors, energy, communications, all the necessary counter-drone assets and so on.
To be honest, it’s also about how we prepare our rear area – hospitals, local municipalities, police stations, energy, everything – against whatever air threat, be it an Iskander ballistic missile, a cruise missile, or hundreds of Shahed-type drones.
You mentioned that you could come here. Do you expect Estonian, i.e. NATO, military personnel in Ukraine during the war?
To be honest, we have been visiting since 2022.
I was here for the first time in July 2022 – I came here to learn. At that time, I was Commander of the Estonian Defence Forces.
How does that fit with statements that NATO military personnel are not in Ukraine?
In July 2022, I was in Estonian uniform on the front line, and the front line then was a few kilometres from Kharkiv. I was there in uniform.
The difference is that we do not operate here. We learn. So we don't take up weapons, we don't operate the radar or whatever. But we visit.
And this is not a threat to Russia at all.
But it is, because you bring what you’ve learned back to Estonia.
Estonia will never use this knowledge unless Russia crosses our border.
We have no plan to cross the border and attack Russia. We have no such plan and never have had. But if they come, then we will use everything we have learned from Ukraine.
"Russian hybrid attacks aim to keep conflicts warm"
Russia is not that active in conventional attacks against Estonia, but in the hybrid domain they are. Would you agree?
In the conventional domain, I don't think we should expect anything active from Russia as long as they are tied down here in Ukraine. But actually, with conventional power, sometimes you don't have to use it.
It's enough to show it.
It’s like my fist. (The general shows his fist.) Threatening with a fist is also something. Because if you show it, then one day you may use it. And since Russia is showing it, like they do today against us, that’s also part of conventional power.
How are they showing it?
They're building the Leningrad Military Region, for example. They're building new units. They are producing tanks, artillery, ammunition, aircraft, everything, behind our border.
Why are they doing this? They know NATO has no plan to cross the border. We have no plan to attack.
Then why are they building fortifications and new military bases behind the border of Finland? Why did they create this Leningrad Military Region and so on?
They’re doing it to threaten us, and maybe to prepare.
And what about hybrid threats?
Referring to hybrid operations, we used to talk about sabotage, cyber operations, information operations, whatever.
But in general, hybrid actions serve to prepare the conditions and the environment, keeping the conflict warm.
Because if you want to use conventional power, you need to explain to your own nation and to third countries that you had a problem with Estonia, or with the West. You need a kind of justification for your actions.
And no one will know later that it was you who caused the sabotage. The people in Russia only see that "we had a problem with them and we had to solve it". Now, [Russian] Foreign Minister [Sergei] Lavrov has said very clearly: everybody supporting Ukraine will be punished by us. He said it one or two months ago, and now we see their actions.
But all these hybrid actions just cause harm – it hurts – but it's not a threat to our being, our existence.
Isn’t it? People in Estonia expect NATO to protect them against hybrid threats, and it doesn’t. This could also diminish public trust in the Alliance.
There are no good solutions, no good response, to this problem.
However, if you look at what the Russians have done during the last few months, for example – that armed drone in Germany [that attacked the airport], or when they set fire [to a military production base] in Estonia – what was our response? The Germans increased their support to Ukraine. Estonia decided to support Ukraine through PURL with another €10 million.
Next week we will have a meeting in Tallinn to discuss what kind of support we will send to Ukraine next year – and that will be more than €100 million just from Estonia.
These are actually the responses to all these acts, sabotage and so on. We say to Russia: you can try, but we will not stop.
And one more element of our response is the public disclosure of Russian actions.
If there is something burning, blowing up or falling down, and the Russian special services are behind it, then we must say that openly and attribute it to them as fast as possible. If Russia is not the cause and it's just criminal activity, then okay. But if the Russians are behind it, we must attribute it to them immediately.
"I would like to see Ukraine win this war"
How do you see Ukraine’s role in the future security architecture of Europe?
First, Ukraine has experience. And not just experience in fighting. You’ve learned how to stop this aggressor which is a threat to us as well. And your experience can contribute to European security.
Secondly, I think Ukraine must be an equal member of this security system. It doesn't matter whether we talk about the EU or NATO or whatever. Whether it would be full membership or some kind of association – that's up to Ukrainians and NATO. But if you asked me, I would say: why not full membership?
Is NATO ready to accept Ukraine as a full member?
I don’t know how we [Estonia] joined NATO – whether it was our success, or a miracle, or just a lucky moment.
I can tell you why. It’s because Russia was weak.
Russia was weak. And maybe not everyone realised what they were doing when they agreed to take us into NATO. I don't know.
But if we are in NATO, my question is:
Why wouldn't Ukraine join NATO then? What is the difference?
The only difference is that you have an active war going on right now. But when the war is over, frozen, whatever – why not?
For example, Estonia doesn't even have an official border with Russia. We are not at war, but still, we don't have an agreed border, and that’s also a little bit shaky.
So, it's up to the politicians, but first of all it’s up to the Ukrainian nation and then the other 32 Allied nations to decide.
As you mentioned, because Russia is stuck in Ukraine, they cannot attack you. They don’t dare to cross the border of Estonia, Latvia, Finland – anywhere. Doesn't that mean that to some degree, some Western allies may have an interest in keeping Russia stuck in Ukraine as long as possible?
I've been asked this many, many times. We may say yes, that's possible. But I say honestly: even if stopping the war here is risky for us because then the threat against us will grow, thinking like that goes against our values.
If we forget our values – freedom, democracy, whatever we want to achieve – then we will very soon lose everything.
That's why we should not abandon Ukraine. That's why we have to support Ukraine as much as possible – not to keep the war here, but to support Ukraine to win the war.
If somebody says "Maybe we should just keep the war boiling here, so it doesn’t come to us," that’s definitely not my aim or objective. I would like to see Ukraine win this war. That's my understanding.
Do you believe this is how other allies see it as well?
Maybe I'm too naive, but it's hard to believe that Latvians, Finns, Lithuanians or Poles have this kind of plan to keep Russia fighting here and to let Ukraine suffer. Maybe I'm too naive, but I say: I don't believe that. Because all of us – Finns, Latvians, Lithuanians – see Ukraine as our alter ego. And we don't want Ukraine to suffer. Definitely not.
Otherwise we would not spend so much money and resources or pay that much attention to this.
Sergiy Sydorenko
European Pravda

Mamata Banerjee slammed the BJP-led Centre over the arrest of Cockroach Janata Party leaders.
NEW DELHI: West Bengal chief minister Mamata Banerjee has rallied behind the arrested Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) leaders, accusing the BJP-led Centre of trying to suppress democratic rights and silence young people.In a message posted on X on Wednesday, Banerjee condemned the arrests of Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das, who were sent to judicial custody, and assured young people of her support. “Your Didi is with you - today and forever!” she wrote.
The arrests came amid opposition protests in Delhi over alleged electoral irregularities and demands for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar.
Why the CJP leaders were arrested
Delhi Police detained CJP leaders Ashutosh Ranka, Saurav Das and Ajinkya Shinde on Tuesday. They were accused of allegedly entering the Jantar Mantar area without authorisation and violating peace bonds signed earlier by Ranka and Das.The area was recently denotified as a designated venue for demonstrations. Police alleged that the three leaders breached barricades, entered the restricted area, raised slogans demanding Kumar's resignation and displayed the National Flag.Shinde was granted bail, while Das and Ranka were sent to five days of judicial custody after being produced before an executive magistrate on Wednesday morning.
They were subsequently lodged in Tihar Jail.
Mamata calls arrests an attempt to silence youth
Condemning the police action, Banerjee said the fight for democratic rights had continued across generations and called on people to stand together to protect them.“We, and many generations before us, have fought strongly for our democratic rights. We must continue to do so. I strongly condemn the arrest of Ashutosh and Saurav of the CJP. These moments are about us all, pledging and standing up to fight unitedly to protect our great democracy,” she wrote on X.Banerjee described the arrests as an “attempt to intimidate and silence an entire generation” and said people must not give up their constitutional rights.“This is unacceptable. We must never surrender our constitutional rights. This murdering of democracy is happening in many parts of the country. At this moment, 14,000 of our people in Bengal are facing the brunt of police and political atrocities,” she claimed.
The Trinamool Congress leader had also joined opposition protests in Delhi demanding Kumar's resignation. She backed the agitation initiated by the CJP and supported by the INDIA bloc, which has raised allegations of “vote chori” (vote theft) and electoral roll manipulation linked to the Election Commission's Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise.“A government that has forgotten that 'it is of the people, by the people, for the people' is nearing its end. To the millions of young people I say: Your Didi is with you - today and forever! Let us stand together and save our Mother India. Jai Hind! Vande Mataram! Joy Bangla!” Banerjee wrote.
Opposition leaders join criticism of Delhi Police
Abhishek Banerjee, the Diamond Harbour MP from the Mamata-led TMC faction, also criticised the arrests, accusing the BJP of targeting people for displaying the national flag.
“The so-called biggest nationalists are now arresting Indians for unfurling and waving the Tricolour in their own country, an act which, according to the Union Government, constitutes a breach of peace. Welcome to the @ BJP4India's new Pakistanified Bharat,” he wrote on X.Other leaders from the faction, including Derek O'Brien and Mahua Moitra, also criticised the police action.Several opposition figures have voiced concern over the arrests, including Lok Sabha Leader of Opposition Rahul Gandhi, former Tamil Nadu chief minister and DMK leader MK Stalin, AAP leader and former Delhi chief minister Arvind Kejriwal, CPI general secretary D Raja, NCP MP Supriya Sule and Shiv Sena (UBT) MLA Aditya Thackeray.

Russia says ‘great deal of noise’ present in media regarding Ukraine peace proposals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:17:45 UTC
20:17:45 KST

Burç Eruygur
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
The Kremlin said on Wednesday that there is a “great deal of noise” present in the media concerning peace proposals to end the ongoing Russia-Ukraine war, calling much of it “fabrication.” 
Speaking at a press briefing, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov commented on a story by The Washington Post published on Monday, which, citing an unnamed US official, reported on a joint peace proposal under development by the US and Europe. 
“There is a great deal of noise in the press about all this right now, and much of that noise does not correspond to reality – it is pure fabrication,” Peskov said. 
Peskov claimed that European countries were doing everything possible to continue the over-four-year war, as the US makes efforts to end it. 
He said work to resolve the Ukraine war is proceeding in a discreet manner and will continue to do so, adding that it is premature to make conclusions about a change in Washington’s approach to military support for Kyiv. 
Peskov denied there were agreed-upon international meetings on the war on the agenda, and declined to comment on media reports about a possible visit by FBI Director Cash Patel to Russia. 
“Overall, of course, it would be better if brilliant technologies like Starlink were not used for military purposes at all,” Peskov said, concerning remarks from earlier Wednesday by a freelance adviser to Zelenskyy, who said speed restrictions were implemented on Starlink satellites in Ukraine. 
Earlier Wednesday, Serhii Beskrestnov said on Telegram that SpaceX implemented speed restrictions for Starlink terminals without notification, limiting speed to 100 miles per hour. 
Neither US officials nor SpaceX have commented on the statement. 
Peskov further said that work surrounding an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine announced by US President Donald Trump on Sunday is ongoing, while also questioning the specifics of the Trump-proposed halt. 
"And what was announced? What are the parameters of the energy truce, and what does it entail? Were any specific details provided?" Peskov said. 
The spokesman also spoke about artificial intelligence, arguing that some countries were weaponizing it and that it is necessary to be prepared for the challenges brought by these technologies.

Vehicles travel along a road in Riyadh as black smoke billows from a fire at a nearby oil facility in this file photo from October 3, 2026. (AP File Photo)
Yemen’s Houthis said on Oct. 14 they had targeted facilities belonging to Saudi Aramco, after Saudi officials reported a strike on a building in an area housing the energy giant’s operations center.
Powerful explosions meanwhile rattled the Saudi capital, as the coalition fighting the Houthis said it had intercepted a missile fired by the Iran-backed group towards Riyadh.
Saudi Arabia, the world’s top crude oil exporter, has in recent days come under sustained attack in a dramatic escalation in the war with the Houthis.

Dhahran is home to Aramco’s headquarters, a vast complex comprising numerous buildings and residential compounds.
According to two company employees who spoke to AFP on condition of anonymity, a tower in the headquarters was hit overnight.
“Top three floors have gone,” said one of the employees.

Lawyers at Start of Nord Stream Trial Argue Bombing May Not Have Been a Crime
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:17:00 UTC
20:17:00 KST

Lawyers for a Ukrainian ex-military officer accused of leading the bombing of Russia's Nord Stream pipeline in September 2022 argued at the start of his trial in Germany on Wednesday that "an aggressor's infrastructure" may have been a lawful target.
Serhii Kuznetsov is accused of leading a group of Ukrainian agents including divers and an explosives expert that blew up Russia's largest gas pipeline to Europe in one of the biggest infrastructure sabotage operations of modern times.
The case provides the first opportunity for a public hearing of evidence gathered during a years-long investigation, which has been diplomatically and politically awkward for a German government that remains staunchly supportive of Ukraine despite the investigative trail linking Kyiv to the bombing.
Moving to have the case dismissed, Kuznetsov's lawyer Nicola Canestrini argued that the pipeline — which provided half of Germany's imports of natural gas before Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine — was a "Russian weapon."
"Is it unlawful to destroy an aggressor's infrastructure without harming any human beings?" Canestrini asked.
Right to remain silent
Prosecutors have alleged that Kuznetsov, who was arrested under an international warrant in Italy last year, worked with members of the Ukrainian military to plan the clandestine operation on behalf of unidentified Ukrainian state entities.
Kuznetsov, 50, who prior to Wednesday was referred to publicly only as Serhii K. under German legal rules, has denied any involvement in the blasts that ruptured the 1,200-kilometer (750-mile)-long Baltic Sea pipeline.
Wearing a grey suit and with a shaved head, he exercised his right to remain silent in court but did not cover his face. His lawyers said he could not mount a proper defense because he was obliged to withhold Ukrainian state secrets.
The government in Kyiv has also denied any involvement, a sensitive point in its relations with Germany, Ukraine's largest European supplier of military aid. Russia said on Monday it expected a "just verdict" that would reveal the names of the perpetrators and those who ordered the operation.
Kuznetsov's legal team had tried reaching out to Ukraine for information that might assist the defense but heard nothing, according to another defense lawyer, Jes Meyer-Lohkamp.
Attacking civilian targets is considered a war crime
German prosecutors say the actions Kuznetsov is accused of — attacking civilian targets and causing explosions that destroyed infrastructure and damaged public services — would amount to a war crime.
Kuznetsov is the only person on trial, but Croatian authorities have arrested another man, identified as Vladimir Z., who prosecutors believe was one of the divers.
The explosion of Nord Stream sealed the end of Germany's longstanding dependence on Russian natural gas, although Moscow had already cut supplies over Berlin's support for European sanctions following Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
Nord Stream's supply had been due to double with the opening of a twin pipeline, Nord Stream 2, already built, but Berlin canceled approval to open it just prior to Russia's invasion.
Plumes of methane gas
The trial, expected to continue into February next year, could have domestic political implications.
Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), leading in opinion polls for more than a year, has called for an end to military aid for Ukraine and a restoration of energy ties with Moscow.
Although German state parliaments have no role in foreign policy, the AfD filed a motion in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt on Wednesday calling for an end to support for Ukraine, noting the "historical parallel" with the start of the trial.
The Nord Stream system, lying at a depth of 80 to 110 meters under the Baltic and built by Russian gas concern Gazprom to supply up to 110 billion cubic meters of gas to Germany, was formerly at the core of economic ties between the two countries.
The Sept. 26, 2022, blasts that ruptured three of the four concrete-coated steel pipelines created a giant whirlpool at sea as huge plumes of methane gas rose into the atmosphere.
Prosecutors allege that Kuznetsov traveled to Germany through Poland some three weeks before the attack, using a forged Ukrainian passport. He and his group then used a sailboat hired in the northern German city of Rostock to reach an area close to the Danish island of Bornholm, where they rigged specialized military-grade explosives to the sea floor.
The weekly Der Spiegel magazine and ZDF public television have previously reported that five men and one woman were on the rented yacht Andromeda, which left Rostock on Sept. 6 and returned on Sept. 23, 2022.

Iran steps up Hormuz surveillance: Attacks soar, oil flows crash again
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:16:21 UTC
20:16:21 KST

Iran steps up Hormuz surveillance: Attacks soar, oil flows crash again
Ships in the Strait of Hormuz have been experiencing the worst spate of attacks since the start of the US-Israel war on Iran.
Iran’s military said it has expanded its surveillance of the Strait of Hormuz by deploying new units to target ships, amid a desperate tussle between Tehran and Washington to control the waterway, among the world’s most important passages for energy transport.
With the United States naval blockade of Iran’s southern ports in place and sanctions tightening, Tehran has repeatedly said it will pursue military and diplomatic efforts to put pressure on Washington to submit to its demands regarding reopening the strait.
Tehran’s latest announcement coincides with a surge in attacks in the waterway and a fall in oil transit after crude flows had risen back to pre-war levels in September.
Chris Featherstone, a political scientist at the University of York in the United Kingdom, told Al Jazeera the increased attacks and their impact on energy flows demonstrate the fragility of the strait as a key pathway for oil exports.
So, what’s going on and who controls the Strait of Hormuz now?
Here’s what we know:
What has Iran said about expanding its presence in Hormuz?
The navy said these units would maintain “real time surveillance of enemy activities and maritime traffic in the region”.
It also warned vessels not to switch off their transponders and urged them to coordinate with Iranian armed forces for safe passage through the area.
Separately, an Iranian official told the Reuters news agency that Tehran had started using different offensive tactics against vessels it considered in violation of its restrictions about 10 days ago, adding that this had led to an increase in attacks on such ships.
The strategy includes a change in the type as well as the pace of attacks, with one goal being to influence the outcome of the November midterm elections in the US, according to the official.
Attacks in Hormuz rise to record levels
Ships in the Strait of Hormuz have been experiencing the worst spate of attacks since the start of the US and Israel’s war on Iran in late February.
According to maritime tracking firm Kpler, 10 tankers were struck in the strait between September 28 and October 4, followed by another strike on October 5.
The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) centre has separately recorded 15 other attacks between October 6 and October 14, with 11 of them occurring in just the past four days. They include a container ship and a tanker hit by unknown projectiles in the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday, UKMTO said.
Iran maintains that its attacks and restrictions in the waterway are a matter of national security and self-defence in response to the US-Israel war. Iranian authorities have also signalled they intend to disrupt a US-assisted shuttle system that has enabled more energy exports through the strait during the war.
In its latest report on Sunday, the US Navy-led Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC) noted that the threat to merchant shipping in the Strait of Hormuz remained “severe”, the second-highest level.
Attacks by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), “attempted attacks, and/or harassment activity persisted including UAV overflight, targeted surveillance of merchant shipping, and occasional VHF hailing,” JMIC said.
UAV stands for unmanned aerial vehicle, or drone, while VHF hailing refers to Iranian forces using standard marine radio to verbally contact, track, and intimidate passing merchant ships on international communication channels.
How have attacks affected oil flows?
Before the US-Israel war on Iran began on February 28, the Strait of Hormuz typically handled about 125 large commercial vessels a day and shipments through it accounted for about 20 percent of global crude and liquefied natural gas supplies.
In retaliation for the US-Israeli attacks, Iran effectively closed the strait and has stepped up attacks on vessels trying to break its regulations. Meanwhile, Washington has also maintained a blockade on Iranian ports.
In September, however, Gulf oil flows through Hormuz, excluding Iran, recovered to more than 81 percent of pre-war levels, while crude exports from the wider Middle East exceeded pre-war levels on 14 days during the month, Kpler reported. Shepherded by the US Navy, more and more oil tankers had started passing through.
The Iranian threat meant ship crew were being paid hefty bonuses, insurance rates remained very high, and some analysts suspect that Gulf nations may also have been paying off Iran to allow tankers to transit. This means that while more oil was being exported from the region, crude prices remained high.
But the surge in Iranian attacks in recent days has changed the equation. According to Kpler, only 2.9 million barrels of oil were carried through the waterway on October 11, the lowest level this month. As recently as October 8, nearly 20.8 million barrels of oil passed through the strait. The pre-war average was 17.1 million barrels a day.
Oil prices continued to climb on Wednesday morning, with Brent crude futures gaining 89 cents, or 0.8 percent, to $106.58 a barrel as of 00:30 GMT. Brent futures had closed at $105.69 a barrel on Tuesday, while West Texas Intermediate settled at $94.14.
What is the US saying?
On Wednesday, a US military official confirmed to Reuters that Iran had changed tactics in the Strait of Hormuz in one significant way.
The official noted that after Washington destroyed much of Iran’s radar capabilities, the IRGC had started using unarmed spotters in small boats to identify potential targets, including US naval vessels.
The US military determined that Iranian spotters were operating from dhows, calling in targets to the IRGC, the official said, adding that US forces confronted one such vessel, told its occupants to abandon ship and then destroyed it.
US Central Command (CENTCOM) has also rejected assertions by the commander of the IRGC that Tehran controls the Strait of Hormuz and would sink approaching US warships.
“IRGC’s navy commander has no navy. American forces and regional partners clearly control the Strait of Hormuz,” CENTCOM said on X.
The military command added that US forces assisted Gulf partners to ship more than 19 million barrels of crude oil through the strategic chokepoint on Monday.
So, who controls Hormuz?
Since Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz after the war began, the US Navy has reportedly opened up a route so Gulf states can export oil and other commodities amid the energy crisis caused by Iran’s attacks on ships.
On Sunday night, Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, claimed that US Central Command, with the assistance of the United Arab Emirates military, was using smaller vessels to transfer oil to larger tankers.
He said this US shuttle system was an explicit target for Tehran, and that Iran has been striking five or six participating vessels nightly for weeks.
“You are smuggling, but the strait is under Iran’s control, and we manage it,” he asserted.
This appeared to be a taunt aimed at US President Donald Trump, who has hailed energy exports at times reaching pre-war levels over recent weeks.
Iran has claimed that the US accepted some of its seven conditions for the full reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and for ending the war, but that Washington’s response was “insufficient”. Tehran insists that a deal will only materialise when all its demands are met.
“The Trump administration has not moved to engage with continued negotiations, and hasn’t sought further help from potential interlocutors, such as Qatar and Pakistan,” Chris Featherstone, the University of York political scientist, said.
“For Iran, they may be seeing this as a point to increase pressure on the Trump administration.”
But he noted that the strait is not under Iranian control, and that Tehran’s attacks only attempt to show that Washington does not control the waterway either.
“As such, US allies will increase pressure for the Trump administration to bring more stability to the region, or show a path towards achieving greater stability,” he added.

Iranian deputy foreign minister arrives in Beirut
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:15:23 UTC
20:15:23 KST

Ikrame Imane Kouachi
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Saeed Khatibzadeh and an accompanying diplomatic delegation arrived at Beirut International Airport on Wednesday, Iran’s ISNA news agency reported.

World Standards Day at MAHAK means accountability in supporting children
TEHRAN - On the occasion of World Standards Day, October 14, MAHAK carried out a series of initiatives to move the concept of “standards” beyond technical and organizational requirements and connect it with the quality of treatment, safety, transparency, accountability, and the quality of life of children with cancer.
At MAHAK, standards are not limited to obtaining certificates or complying with a set of guidelines. When a child’s health and life are at stake, standards mean making treatment decisions based on scientific evidence and up-to-date protocols, identifying and managing risks, addressing the medical, psychological, and social needs of children and their families, ensuring transparency in the management of resources, and continuously working to improve the quality of services.
Initiatives
To mark World Standards Day, MAHAK’s Public Relations and International Communications Department launched a 360-degree campaign centered on the question, “What Do Standards Mean at MAHAK?” The campaign brought together a range of communication, content, and organizational initiatives aimed at explaining the role of standards in the quality of MAHAK’s treatment and support services.
One of the campaign’s main activities was the production and publication of a photo-video titled “What Do Standards Mean at MAHAK?” The content followed a child’s experience throughout the treatment journey and highlighted the standards encountered at different stages of care. The video was shared across MAHAK’s social media platforms.
A campaign was also launched through the MAHAK App to raise funds for the chemotherapy treatment of children supported by MAHAK. The initiative aimed to connect the concept of standards with access to treatment and the resources that directly contribute to the quality and safety of care.
In the area of international affairs, MAHAK also continued efforts to update its international standards and certifications, including those related to SGS and IPMA, through formal correspondence and follow-up with the relevant organizations.
As part of the media outreach, news content was prepared for publication in two national and domestic English-language media outlets, helping communicate MAHAK’s approach to standards and its related initiatives to a wider audience.
Together, these activities reflect MAHAK’s view that standards are not a final destination, but an ongoing process of measurement, learning, improvement, and advancing quality.

Preparing for winter: a home checklist to help retain heat and prepare for outages
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:11:29 EEST
20:11:29 KST

Preparing for winter: a home checklist to help retain heat and prepare for outages
Kyiv • UNN
These tips will help retain heat, check the heating system and electrical wiring, and prepare supplies of water, food, and medicine. Fire safety is also highlighted separately.
Against the backdrop of Russia’s aggressive attacks on Ukraine’s energy system, people are trying more actively than last year to prepare for winter, both in cities and in towns. All the more so because domestic and foreign politicians and experts unanimously warn that the winter of 2026–2027 could prove to be the harshest and most difficult in the entire history of our country.
UNN has compiled a practical checklist for residents of apartments and private houses that will help reduce heat loss in advance, make sure equipment is in working order, arrange a water supply, and plan what to do in case of power outages.
How to insulate windows and doors to avoid losing heat
It is worth starting with the simplest things: check whether there are drafts coming through the windows, balcony doors, or entrance doors. Worn-out seals should be replaced, gaps around frames should be sealed, and the fittings adjusted if necessary.
You can take thick-fabric curtains out of the closet or buy some. They help reduce the feeling of cold near the window and eliminate small drafts. However, they should be positioned so that the fabric does not cover the radiators. First, such an artificial barrier between the room and the radiator will inevitably prevent the room from warming up. Second, there is a risk that at some point the curtain could begin to smolder from the high temperatures and cause a fire.
Likewise, radiators should not be blocked by furniture or decorative screens, so as not to impede the distribution of heat throughout the room.
If you live in a private house, in addition to the windows and doors, you should обязательно inspect the roof and take care of insulating the attic. Without this, even continuous gas or stove heating will not create a feeling of warmth in the home, because heat losses will be enormous.
At the same time, you should not resort to the opposite extreme of completely blocking ventilation openings for the sake of warmth. Even in winter, rooms need to be aired, especially if condensation forms on the glass or mold appears. If the house is heated with firewood or food is prepared on a stove powered by a gas cylinder, properly functioning ventilation is an essential condition for safe living. Neglecting safety could ultimately end tragically for all the home's residents, who risk fatal carbon monoxide poisoning.
Why heating should be checked before the first frosts
Residents of apartments with centralized heating should inspect radiators, valves, and pipe connections. Traces of rust, moisture, or leaks are reasons to contact the building manager or a plumber.
Owners of gas boilers need to arrange maintenance in advance: checking the boiler, ventilation, and flue systems to ensure they are working properly. If the house has a stove or fireplace, its structure should be checked for cracks before the season begins, the chimney cleaned, and the dampers and doors checked to make sure they function properly.
A separate issue for apartment buildings is preparing the common property. Through the homeowners’ association or management company, it is worth finding out whether the heating substation has been inspected, pipes in the basement insulated, windows in the entrance stairwell glazed, and doors made to close tightly.
How to prepare the electrical system and backup lighting for the winter months
Before winter, it is also worth inspecting accessible sockets, switches, and cables. Hot sockets or a burning smell are good reasons to call an electrician.
In case of power outages, it is advisable to have flashlights, spare batteries, charged power banks, and cables for phones at home. You should ask your provider whether the internet will work without electricity and how to power the router.
If finances allow, you can purchase a power station. It should be selected according to the power requirements of the appliances you plan to connect. Such equipment must not be covered, placed near heat sources, used with damaged cables, or connected to the home electrical system with a homemade cable featuring two plugs. You should also avoid buying a power station "second-hand," from questionable sellers, or on Chinese marketplaces. In such cases, there is a possibility of encountering an uncertified, damaged, or defective product.
Water and food supplies in case of a blackout
One of the most important aspects of preparing for winter (especially in a city) is storing water. The guideline for an adult is about three liters of drinking water and 10–12 liters of utility water per day. It is advisable to calculate a minimum reserve for at least three days, taking into account children, pets, and the needs of people requiring care.
For storing drinking water, clean, tightly sealed food-grade containers are suitable. Utility water for hygiene and flushing the toilet can be kept in other large bottles or buckets, or the bathtub can be filled with it.
Among food products, it is better to choose those that can be stored for a long time without refrigeration and do not require heat treatment (boiling or frying): canned goods, crispbreads, nuts, dried fruit, ready-made cereals, or other long-storage products. Before arranging these supplies on the shelves of a kitchen cabinet, it is worth checking the expiration dates once again and placing a manual can opener nearby.
How to live in a home without heating and not freeze
In case the heat goes out, you should prepare thermal underwear, warm socks, several layers of clothing, blankets, and sleeping bags. For temporary accommodation, you can choose one room with the fewest drafts and close the doors to other rooms: one small room is easier to heat than a multi-room apartment or private house.
It is strictly forbidden to heat a room with a gas stove or oven, or to use barbecues and charcoal indoors. A generator must also not be started in an apartment, building entrance, garage, or on a balcony: it should be used only outdoors, at least six meters away from doors and windows, in accordance with the manufacturer's instructions.
In addition, it is important to know and understand from the outset that prolonged cooling of a home is especially dangerous for young children, older people, and people with chronic diseases. If the temperature in the residence becomes critically low, you should consider in advance moving to a heated building or the nearest Point of Invincibility.
How to ensure fire safety and prepare a first-aid kit in winter
Before the season begins, it is advisable to check the smoke detector, and in homes with gas or stove heating or other combustion appliances, install a carbon monoxide detector. Carbon monoxide has no smell, so it is impossible to detect its presence without a special device. The fire extinguisher must be in working order and easily accessible.
You should also review your home first-aid kit: check the expiration dates of medicines, replenish first-aid supplies, and stock up on medications that must be taken regularly, in accordance with the doctor's prescriptions.
It is also useful to keep a small bag with the most essential items ready in case of a temporary evacuation.
General advice is to keep some cash in small denominations in case of disruptions to communications and payment services. For pets, provide food, water, and a carrier.
Reminder
Previously, UNN reported on what you should have at home to get through power outages.

The family of a man killed by a tiger at a wildlife park in the UK have spoken about their “severe distress” at the circulation of online media after Donald Trump reposted a video of the incident.
William Chapman, 23, was mauled to death after entering an enclosure at Yorkshire Wildlife Park, near Doncaster, on Saturday.
His family described him as “bright, warm and engaging” and suffering from severe mental illness. They said online footage being shared was “deeply offensive” and causing them “severe distress”.
One of those to circulate footage was the US president who posted a video clip of the tiger attack to 13 million followers on his Truth Social platform on Tuesday.
The clip showed the tiger biting and clawing Chapman as he was sitting in the enclosure. At one point he wags his finger at the animal.
Trump signed the footage with: “Don’t ever mess with nature! President DJT.” It did not show Chapman being killed.
Later the president posted an AI-generated video of himself grinning and having fun by chasing and play fighting with the tiger. It is accompanied by the song The Lion Sleeps Tonight by The Tokens. It features Trump copying the pointing gesture made by Chapman and ends with him and the tiger hugging.
Will Travers, the executive president of the Born Free Foundation, said the AI post was “not only incredibly insensitive”, but also reckless.
“It increases the risk to the lives of humans and captive wild animals,” he said. “Such images and videos can encourage individuals to seek out direct, unrealistic and high-risk contact with captive wild animals.”
Relatives of Chapman, in a statement released on Tuesday evening, said: “The family are utterly devastated by their loss and are struggling to come to terms with what has happened. The publication and circulation of deeply offensive media content is causing them severe distress at an exceptionally vulnerable time. We ask people to stop doing this.
“The family are hopeful that the relevant authorities will do their upmost to get to the bottom of why our amazing son did what he did.”
The statement continued: “William was a bright, warm and engaging young man whom his family dearly loved – and William loved them back. Sadly, William suffered from significant mental illness over a number of years and was consequently prescribed strong medication.
“It will be for the coroner to decide what part this played in his death.
“We would ask everybody to respect that process.”
As a child, Chapman appeared in ITV’s 2009 comedy drama May Contain Nuts and in BBC Learning’s True Stories series, according to IMDb.
He previously attended Jackie Palmer stage school in High Wycombe, Buckinghamshire, which paid tribute on Facebook and posted a picture of Chapman as a child student.
The school said it was “deeply saddened” by Chapman’s death, adding: “We loved watching William grow, both as a person and as a performer. It was a privilege to be part of his journey and he will be remembered with great fondness by everyone who had the pleasure of knowing him.
“William will be truly missed, and he will always hold a special place in our hearts. Rest in peace, William.”
The wildlife park has said the Amur (Siberian) tiger called Altai, who was in the enclosure, will not be euthanised. The park has remained closed since the weekend and Doncaster city council, which is responsible for licensing the park, said it had started a health and safety investigation.
An inquest is due to open into the death at Doncaster coroner’s court on Thursday morning.

Melike Pala
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
The European Commission on Wednesday disbursed €2.86 billion ($3.2 billion) to Ukraine to fund drones, air defense systems, missiles, and other urgent military needs amid continued attacks.
The funding was provided under the defense component of the EU's €90 billion Ukraine Support Loan, the EU Commission said in a statement.
The money will be used to procure drones, air defense systems, missiles, radars, electronic warfare systems, and ammunition.
"As Russia stalls on the frontlines, it continues to escalate its aerial attacks - cruelly targeting Ukrainian civilians and infrastructure. Europe's steadfast support matters more than ever to help Ukraine protect its skies and save lives," European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said.
The €90 billion loan package for 2026-2027 includes €60 billion earmarked for defense and €30 billion for budgetary assistance.
The commission said €28.3 billion was planned for disbursement in 2026 to strengthen Ukraine's defense industrial capacity, with further payments under the defense component expected in the coming weeks.
It added that Ukraine still had €29.64 billion in financial support available for the remainder of 2026.
Of that amount, €25.24 billion is available under the Ukraine Support Loan, including €12.54 billion for defense industrial capacity and €12.7 billion in budget support.
Since 2022, the EU and its member states have provided €231.5 billion in overall support to Ukraine, including €3.8 billion generated from proceeds of immobilized Russian assets, according to the commission.

Tsui Hark at Lumière Festival: ‘We don't know where the future will bring us’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:10:58 UTC
20:10:58 KST

"We all know that the thing about humanity is that we always fear being replaced by something." Euronews Culture sits down with legendary Hong Kong filmmaker Tsui Hark during this year's Lumière Film Festival.
Anyone who is a fan of Hong Kong cinema and martial arts films will immediately recognise the name Tsui Hark.
He is one of the key figures in Hong Kong’s New Wave, responsible for reinventing the martial arts genre. As a writer, producer and director, he boosted the careers of many like Chow Yun-fat, Jet Lee and even John Woo. And until last year with the box office success of Ne Zha 2, the 75-year-old director’s film The Battle at Lake Changjin was the highest-grossing Chinese film of all time.
Four of his films - the period romantic comedy Shanghai Blues (1984), the groundbreaking action-comedy Peking Opera Blues (1986), the martial arts epic Once Upon a Time in China (1991) and the action thriller Time And Tide (2000) - are being honoured and screened at this year’s Lumière Film Festival.
Euronews Culture sat down with the legendary filmmaker after the Lumière ceremony during which directors are celebrated with a golden plaque on Rue du Premier Film, beside the Institut Lumière, to talk about the festival, his work, and the challenges we face.
Euronews Culture: How does it feel having your plaque on the Lumière wall now?
Tsui Hark: I feel very dreamy, as a matter of fact! (Laughs) You know, I suddenly realized that I’ve come to the place where motion pictures started, at their beginning. I never thought that I would come to a place like this, where you suddenly go back to the original motion picture. It becomes a very surreal thing. You come to a place where your career was started by someone that you don't know, but they [the Lumière brothers] are the source of your creativity and everything. I feel very blessed, being given the task of making movies.
During your stay at the festival, several of your films are being screened, including restored versions of Shanghai Blues and Peking Opera Blues. How does it feel seeing these films on a big screen once more?
It’s strange with the films I've made 40 years ago! (Laughs) For me, it's like it's very far, far away, and suddenly they come back again. It makes you feel like the time never passed. You go to a theater showing your film that you made 40 years ago, and people still like it. It's a wonderful feeling.
You are known for your work in action films and martial arts, but there’s a focus in the selection of films screened at the festival on comedy and romance. In your opinion and experience, where does the cinematic language of action and comedy intersect?
I actually think of myself as a comedy person than an action director, but everything happened in 1979. I worked in a television, and I was given a job to make a costume action drama [The Butterfly Murders]. I was given an assignment to do an action film, and since then, I have been associated with action genre for so many years. But for me, it’s a bit weird!
Throughout your films, you’ve always managed to balance action and the epic scale and scope of your stories with very emotional and personal considerations. It’s not an easy balance to get right when it comes to big productions... I suppose my question is: What's your secret?
There's no secret at all! It all depends on my take on something I really like. When I was a kid, when I watched this kind of genre, I felt very exhilarated when looking at life. When I have a chance to make a movie, I go in that direction - a direction based on how I identify with the people inside the world, especially in epic or costume dramas.
I’m very serious when it comes to making people identify and associate themselves with the story I’m telling. The quality of humanity in the characters and the story is a major concern of the material. I always try to make the story understandable and relatable for everyone. You see, many think about movies as being for a certain age or people. I feel like movies should be for audiences of all ages and hopefully for people of all cultures - not just our culture that we're so familiar with. I hope that movies, culture, and art can be shared by everyone.
Have you noticed a certain sensitivity that European audiences have towards your films?
Actually, I have no idea what's going on! (Laughs) Sometimes I go to a place and they will say “I've seen your movie” and I'm quite surprised. The first time I was in Cannes, and they said, “Oh, I've seen your movie”, I was very shocked. I made the movie elsewhere and it was shown to a different kind of audience, but still, they understood and accepted the film. For me, it’s a form of encouragement and it gives me energy to make movies that can be shared by all people and bring cultures together.
Considering the breadth of your career and your filmography, are there any genres that you would like to explore that you haven’t had the chance to? I ask, because you made a horror-comedy in 1980, We’re Going To Eat You, and I can’t deny I’d love to see another horror film from you...
Oh, yes! Exactly! Horror is a genre I always want to explore, because I feel horror is not just about making people scared but about making people feel a different kind of energy. I've seen a lot of horror films, and I feel like they are often very negative about human beings and humanity. That’s why I feel like I’d like to try something different in this genre.
Speaking of negativity, many are expressing fears nowadays about the future of cinema and the arts in general, especially with the push towards artificial intelligence. Is that something that worries you?
It’s a very up-to-date question you’ve asked. We all know that the thing about humanity is that we always fear being replaced by something. The fear that we are being replaced comes from everywhere. In relationships, career, economy... Or even our own idea of freedom. This is always a threat, and we don't know where the future will bring us.
The fear and the danger of losing everything is everywhere, and human beings tend to be neglectful of the weakness of our nature. We neglect the power of destruction created by us and at the same time, the power of destruction created by nature. In our era, we have faced a lot of crises – from virus, science, technology, and war. We have no solution for it so far. Humans are a weak species when it comes to solving problems like that.
The more we go through every test we encounter on the path of our survival, we realise that we actually have no solutions. Simply because we are the destructive element in nature. I hope that it's not true. Hopefully I'm mistaken in that respect, and that we bring some good things in life.
You know, at my age, I always feel like there’s not a long time to worry about the future... But I hope that things will not get worse. I want to be optimistic, but there is strong evidence of negative things happening. Since World War II, everybody tried to avoid that happening again, but it's happening. Non-stop happening. I don't know what is the best solution for all these problems...
I certainly don't.
No one has. I know we’re getting deep and we can’t get too philosophical about what we’re going to do. The world is very chaotic, but I do think that at least something we can do is to make everybody look at a good aspect of humanity and remind ourselves to enjoy life and human creativity. And cinema is a good place to start.
Peking Opera Blues makes its French cinema debut on 21 October in a restored 4K version.
The Lumière Film Festival runs in Lyon through 18 October.

Iraq's shadow economy grows as billions evade oversight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:08:00 UTC
20:08:00 KST

Breadcrumb
Iraq's shadow economy grows as billions evade oversight
Iraq's shadow economy is expanding as millions of workers and businesses operate outside formal government oversight, depriving the state of revenue and complicating efforts to reduce its dependence on oil.
Informal activity ranges from unregistered small businesses and undocumented employment to tax and customs evasion.
Officials and analysts also warn that some financial channels outside formal oversight can be exploited for smuggling, corruption and money laundering.
The issue has taken on greater importance as Baghdad seeks to increase non-oil revenues and strengthen public finances.
Finance Ministry figures show Iraq collected about 8.74 trillion dinars in non-oil revenues during the first seven months of 2026.
That accounted for around 22% of total public revenues of 39.09 trillion dinars, compared with about 30.36 trillion dinars from oil.
The scale of Iraq's informal economy is particularly visible in the labour market.
OECD figures based on Iraq's 2021 labour force survey showed about 5.73 million people were in informal employment, representing 66.6% of the country's workforce.
About 4.72 million of them worked in the informal sector, while the rest held informal jobs within formally registered organisations.
The figures do not measure the total financial value of the shadow economy, but indicate how deeply informal employment is embedded in Iraq's labour market.
The government established a committee in 2023 to examine the issue, with a mandate covering tax reform, improved data collection and the relationship between tax evasion and money laundering.
The Central Bank, Integrity Commission and anti-money laundering authorities were among the bodies involved.
Iraq has also tightened oversight of foreign-currency transactions in recent years, including through new systems monitoring bank transfers and dollar flows.
Concerns over corruption and illicit finance
Anti-corruption specialist Saeed Yassin said the government needed to look beyond bringing small businesses into the tax system.
He said authorities should investigate networks that benefited from keeping economic activity outside formal scrutiny and examine the origins of funds entering markets without clear financial records.
Yassin said particular attention should be paid to so-called economic offices and their possible involvement in government contracts, border crossings, imports and trade.
Some parts of the informal economy could also be used to disguise proceeds from corruption, smuggling or money laundering through front companies and transactions whose real value was difficult to verify, he said.
Previous audits have exposed schemes involving hundreds of millions of dollars channelled through fraudulent transactions involving banks, exchange companies and other intermediaries.
He called for stronger systems to track financial flows, identify the real owners of companies, scrutinise high-risk contracts and link government databases.
Iraqi MP Youssef al-Kallabi said the scale of unregulated economic activity was weakening government efforts to raise non-oil revenues.
He said administrative and financial loopholes meant the state was failing to collect some revenues it was entitled to receive.
Parliament had previously proposed more than 16 measures to increase non-oil income, he said, but some had not been implemented.
Kallabi said exemptions and some government decisions had also disadvantaged legitimate private-sector companies while allowing well-connected economic groups to benefit from unequal conditions.
The wider problem comes as Iraq's government pursues a renewed anti-corruption drive aimed at recovering public funds and strengthening oversight.
A shortage of reliable data made it harder for the government to estimate how much revenue it should be collecting and to assess whether reforms were working, he added.
Economist Ziad al-Hashemi said many small and medium-sized businesses remained informal because operating outside the official system was cheaper and easier.
Complicated bureaucracy, weak public services and limited access to bank financing reduced the incentives to register formally, he said.
But remaining outside the system also restricted companies' ability to obtain loans, attract investment and expand into larger businesses.
Iraq's long dependence on cash and parallel-market currency trading has also helped sustain a highly informal financial system outside conventional banking channels.
Hashemi said reforms should make formal registration economically worthwhile.
He called for lower start-up costs, simpler procedures, easier access to bank finance and stronger legal and social protection.
The challenge, he said, was to make joining the formal economy an opportunity for businesses to grow rather than simply another tax and administrative burden.

Yunus Turk, Emir Yildirim
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
Türkiye’s exports to the EU rose 3.9% year-on-year to $81.5 billion in the first nine months of the year, according to the Turkish Exporters’ Assembly (TIM).
Türkiye’s total exports increased 5.2% to $210.9 billion over the same period, while exports to the 27 EU member states rose by nearly $3.1 billion.
Germany was Türkiye’s top European market, with Turkish exports rising 4.2% to $15.4 billion, followed by Italy with $9.6 billion, Spain with $8.3 billion and France with $7.9 billion.
Other leading export destinations included Romania and the Netherlands, with nearly $5.5 billion each, and Poland with $4.8 billion, contributing to the broader trend in which Turkish exports rose in 17 EU member states while declining in 10.
Türkiye’s total exports to its top four European markets — Germany, Italy, Spain and France — reached $41.2 billion in January-September.
The auto sector was the main driver of growth, with exports to the EU rising 4.8% to $22.9 billion, followed by the chemicals and chemical products sector with $10.2 billion and the ready-to-wear apparel sector with $7.3 billion.
The largest increase in exports to the EU came from the auto sector, up by nearly $1.1 billion, followed by the ferrous and non-ferrous metals sector with a $1 billion increase and the electrical and electronics sector with a rise of $489.3 million, the data showed.
The Turkish provinces of Istanbul, Kocaeli, Bursa, Ankara and Izmir contributed most to exports to the EU in January-September, accounting for a total of $60.9 billion.
Exports from Istanbul to the EU reached $29 billion, followed by the northwestern provinces of Kocaeli and Bursa with $11.4 billion and $9.4 billion, respectively. Exports from Ankara totaled $5.6 billion, while the western province of Izmir exported $5.4 billion to the bloc.

Scientists may have overlooked a hidden Alzheimer's culprit for decades
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:06:19 UTC
20:06:19 KST

Scientists may have overlooked a hidden Alzheimer's culprit for decades
A long-overlooked peptide once thought harmless could be a hidden contributor to Alzheimer's disease, challenging decades of research and opening new possibilities for treatment.
- Date:
- October 14, 2026
- Source:
- University of California - Santa Cruz
- Summary:
- For decades, scientists have focused on amyloid beta as a major culprit behind Alzheimer’s disease, spending billions of dollars developing treatments that have often delivered disappointing results. Now, researchers at UC Santa Cruz are drawing attention to a largely overlooked peptide called P3 that could also play a role in the disease. Previously believed to be harmless, P3 can form harmful-looking protein clumps even faster than amyloid beta and may also damage brain cells.
- Share:
For decades, researchers have invested billions of dollars in Alzheimer's treatments designed to target amyloid beta, a peptide that forms harmful deposits in the brain. But a biochemist at the University of California, Santa Cruz, believes scientists may have overlooked another potential contributor to the disease: a smaller, closely related peptide that was long considered harmless.
In a new commentary published in ChemBioChem, UC Santa Cruz professor Jevgenij Raskatov highlights research suggesting that this lesser-known peptide, called P3, can form microscopic clumps and threadlike structures known as fibrils. Evidence also suggests that P3 may interact with amyloid beta (Aβ), potentially influencing how it accumulates in the brain and how toxic it becomes. These findings raise the possibility that P3 contributes to the nerve cell damage associated with Alzheimer's disease.
"The P3 peptide is, most likely, not the innocent bystander it was commonly thought to be. There's still more research to be done. But this could turn Alzheimer's research on its head," said Raskatov, whose laboratory investigates amyloid peptides in hopes of identifying ways to prevent their harmful effects and develop better Alzheimer's treatments. "P3 is a distinct aggregating peptide that is itself potentially neurotoxic and may be contributing to Alzheimer's disease."
Why Alzheimer's Treatments Have Had Limited Success
Alzheimer's is the most widespread neurodegenerative disease, affecting approximately 35 million people worldwide and generating annual costs exceeding $800 billion. The number of people living with the condition is expected to double by 2050.
Despite decades of intensive research, developing effective treatments has proved extraordinarily difficult. More than 400 clinical trials have investigated potential Alzheimer's drugs, with most focusing on amyloid beta. Many of these efforts have failed, while others have produced only modest benefits. Some treatments have also been associated with serious complications, including brain hemorrhages and strokes.
Amyloid beta originates from a much larger protein embedded in cell membranes called the Amyloid Precursor Protein (APP). Two enzymes, β-secretase and γ-secretase, cut this protein in sequence, releasing amyloid beta peptides of different lengths.
Researchers have concentrated particularly on two versions, Aβ40 and Aβ42, which contain 40 and 42 amino acids, respectively. Aβ42 has attracted the greatest attention because it is especially prone to sticking together and forming toxic aggregates. As a result, it has remained a central target of Alzheimer's drug development for decades.
Existing medications, including cholinesterase inhibitors and N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor antagonists, can temporarily ease certain symptoms but do not stop the disease from progressing. More recently, antibody treatments such as Lecanemab and Donanemab have been approved to help remove amyloid beta from the brain.
However, Raskatov argues that the benefits achieved so far remain limited, underscoring the need to investigate other biological processes involved in Alzheimer's.
"Progress has been extremely slow, and the current state of the art in Alzheimer's therapy leaves much to be desired," he said. "We need fundamentally new approaches to the problem."
The Overlooked Peptide That May Also Damage Brain Cells
Unlike amyloid beta, P3 forms when Amyloid Precursor Protein is processed through a different sequence of molecular cuts. In this pathway, an enzyme called α-secretase acts first, followed by γ-secretase.
Raskatov has proposed calling this peptide "Amyloid α," or Aα, to better distinguish it from amyloid beta and reflect its ability to form aggregates.
For years, scientists largely assumed that P3 was incapable of forming amyloid deposits, was not toxic to cells, and would remain soluble in water. Under that interpretation, the peptide would simply dissolve rather than accumulate in the brain.
These assumptions were never adequately verified, according to Raskatov. Nevertheless, they helped establish the view that P3 was unlikely to matter in Alzheimer's disease, leaving it largely absent from research efforts.
Raskatov, a specialist in peptide chemistry, and researchers in his laboratory decided to test those long-standing beliefs.
Over the past five years, the team has published three major studies demonstrating that P3 can form amyloid deposits at least as readily as amyloid beta. In fact, their experiments showed that P3 produces these aggregates more rapidly.
The researchers also found evidence that P3 itself may be harmful to neurons, although its toxicity appears lower than that of amyloid beta.
According to Raskatov, an independent research group in the United Kingdom has confirmed and expanded upon his team's findings. Other laboratories are now beginning to investigate how P3 and amyloid beta interact, including whether their relationship affects the accumulation and toxicity of these peptides.
Together, the results challenge the long-held assumption that P3 is biologically harmless and irrelevant to Alzheimer's. However, further research is needed to establish whether and how it contributes to the disease in patients.
Challenging Decades of Alzheimer's Research
For much of the past several decades, amyloid beta has dominated scientific explanations of Alzheimer's disease. David Teplow, an emeritus professor of neurology at UCLA and a prominent Alzheimer's researcher, said the peptide has long been regarded as a central cause of the condition.
But an independent evaluation of Raskatov's research led Teplow to conclude that scientists are beginning to reconsider this narrow focus.
"This reevaluation has far-reaching consequences for both basic science and clinical research into the causes and treatment of Alzheimer's disease," said Teplow, a founding editorial board member of the Journal of Molecular Neuroscience and the American Journal of Neurodegenerative Disease, as well as editor-in-chief of Progress in Molecular Biology and Translational Science.
Raskatov has also encountered a troubling problem while examining how other scientists have interpreted his team's discoveries.
He identified at least four papers published in respected, peer-reviewed journals that cited his laboratory's research as evidence that P3 was harmless and unable to form amyloid deposits. Yet his team's experiments had demonstrated precisely the opposite.
"This is exactly the opposite of what we have actually shown," Raskatov said. "We remain in the dark on how this sort of grand confusion may have come about. Clearly, there is more work ahead of us."
The emerging evidence suggests that understanding Alzheimer's may require looking beyond amyloid beta alone. By examining P3 and its interactions with other amyloid peptides, researchers hope to gain a more complete picture of the processes that damage brain cells and potentially identify new directions for treatment.

Journal Reference:
- Jevgenij A. Raskatov. Amyloid Alpha: The Neglected Cousin of Amyloid Beta. ChemBioChem, 2026; 27 (5) DOI: 10.1002/cbic.202500912

UK government apologises for past burials of stillborn babies in mass graves
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:05:44 UTC
20:05:44 KST

The health secretary, Yvette Cooper, has issued a “profound apology” for the “unthinkable pain” caused to parents whose stillborn babies were buried in mass graves.
Parents spent decades not knowing where their babies were buried, owing to a practice in which stillborn babies were taken from mothers at hospital and buried in communal graves.
Over several decades between the 1930s and the early 1980s, many bereaved parents who lost babies in NHS hospitals were given no say in what would happen to their remains and no information about where they had been taken.
More than 1,000 stillborn babies were interred in Wirral, at Frankby, Plymyard and Landican cemeteries, between 1935 and 1981. Another mass burial ground in Royton, Oldham, is believed to hold more than 270 babies.
Gina Jacobs, from Wirral, whose son Robert was stillborn in 1969, did not know where he had been buried for 53 years. She has been among those campaigning for recognition from the government.
Speaking in the House of Commons during a baby loss awareness debate, Cooper said: “On behalf of the government, I want to issue a profound apology to them.”
She added: “I have issued that apology to Gina today, but to so many more like Gina who have sought answers over many years, I’m sorry for the unthinkable pain caused by those historic practices, because what happened to those parents should never have happened and we need to ensure it can never happen again.”
Jacobs told ITV News: “It didn’t kind of sink in at first. I’ve wanted this, I’ve campaigned for this, I’ve begged for this, anyone who would listen, for four years now, and to actually have it said to me by the minister herself.
“To me it’s like a lottery win because I have wanted this,” she added. “This brings dignity and respect to these babies, because they never got it at the time. And it brings it even to our missing babies.”
In July, Liverpool city council passed a motion calling on the government to apologise in parliament to families affected by the practice.
The motion, which was passed unanimously by all parties, said: “The historical handling of stillborn babies by public authorities was a cruel violation of human dignity that has caused decades of unresolved trauma, grief and anger for families across Liverpool.”
In response to the government apology, the Liverpool councillor Kris Brown, who put forward the motion, said: “The government’s words of apology will go a long way. For many, just acknowledging that it happened will bring a sense of closure and justice.
“However, this can’t just be words simply etched into Hansard. I hope that the secretary of state, along with the prime minister, issues a written apology and sets out a national framework on how families affected by the scandal can get support.”
The council has urged the government to set aside national funding to retrieve burial records and has called for a comprehensive review into the mass burials, which took place under many successive governments.
Brown welcomed the apology but said: “There is still far more to do for full justice.”
