Scarborough soldier buried in Belgium more than a century after his death
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:03:00 BST
20:03:00 KST

Scarborough soldier buried in Belgium more than a century after his death
Scarborough soldier, Lance Corporal (LCpl) Claude Stanley Dell, has been laid to rest more than a century after his death in World War 1.
A young Scarborough soldier of World War 1, killed just a week after his arrival in France, has finally been laid to rest with full military honours. LCpl Claude Stanley Dell of the 5th Battalion Yorkshire Regiment was laid to rest today (13 October 2026) at Commonwealth War Graves Commission’s (CWGC) Poelcapelle British Cemetery in Belgium.
In 2021, workmen digging a rainwater cistern in Hazeweidestraat, St Juliaan, Belgium spotted human remains in their trench. A few days later an archaeological excavation was undertaken by the Flanders Heritage Agency. Artefacts recovered alongside the remains showed them to be those of a soldier who had served in the 5th Battalion Yorkshire Regiment.
The Ministry of Defence’s Joint Casualty and Compassionate Centre (JCCC), known as the ‘MOD War Detectives’, launched an investigation to name him. Research identified twenty men from the regiment missing in the area, all of whom died in the Spring of 1915. Following genealogical investigation, living descendants of the missing men were traced one by one until eventually DNA testing proved that the remains were those of LCpl Claude Stanley Dell.
LCpl Dell joined up alongside his brothers Charles and Guy at the outbreak of war. All three joined the 5th Battalion Yorkshire Regiment, whilst their older brother Leighton was in the Royal Field Artillery, and another brother - Frederick - served with the Yorkshire Hussars.
5th Battalion left the UK on 17 April 1915 and arrived in Boulogne the following day. On 23 April they arrived on the Ypres Salient, and just two days later on 25 April 1915 LCpl Dell was killed in action. Claude’s brothers wrote home to tell their parents, ‘poor Claude met his end…whilst doing his duty’.
Today, LCpl Dell was buried with full military honours in the presence of both his military family, and his great-niece Judith.
The service, organised by JCCC, was supported by serving soldiers of the Royal Yorkshire Regiment, as well as staff from the CWGC.
Alexia Clark, MOD War Detective, said:
  It has been a privilege to research this case, to have been able to identify LCpl Dell, and to have been able to lay him to rest today. I am extremely grateful to 2nd Battalion the Royal Yorkshire Regiment who have provided the bearer party for the funeral, and to the members of Claude’s family who have been involved in his commemoration.
Claude’s grave will now be cared for in perpetuity by the Commonwealth War Graves Commission, ensuring his sacrifice is never forgotten. Dr Daniel Seaton, Commemorations Case Officer at CWGC, said:
  Lance Corporal Dell lay in an unmarked grave on the former battlefields for well over 100 years. It is a great privilege to have worked alongside the JCCC and our Belgian partners in the effort to restore his identity. He is now laid to rest in a Commission cemetery not far from where he fell, ensuring that his grave can be visited in perpetuity and his sacrifice remembered.

As Yemen-Saudi tensions rise, Palestinians question Iran's goals

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14

Breadcrumb
As Yemen-Saudi tensions rise, Gaza's Palestinians question Iran's endgame
The recent round of fighting between Yemen's Houthis and Saudi Arabia has sparked debate among Palestinians over the role of Iran and its allies in the region.
While some Palestinians supported Houthi attacks in the Red Sea during the Israeli genocidal war, others question their impact, especially as the latest round of fighting in Yemen that erupted since mid-September, and spread to Saudi airports and other civilian facilities.
On Monday, the Palestinian Authority's Presidency condemned the Houthi attacks, denouncing strikes on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and expressing solidarity with Saudi Arabia.
In a press statement, it backed measures taken by the Kingdom to protect its security and facilities and warned against threats to the Two Holy Mosques in Mecca and Medina.
Hamas, meanwhile, had not issued a public comment despite repeated attempts by The New Arab to obtain its position.
Other Palestinian factions, particularly those with ties to Iran, had also not publicly stated their positions.
Palestinian factions' calculations
Mohammed Hijazi, a Jordan-based Palestinian researcher specialising in Islamist groups, told TNA that Palestinian factions maintained alliances with Iran and its regional allies, including the Houthis.
Hijazi said these ties were largely political and did not necessarily involve participation in the war or material support.
He added that the factions were reluctant to openly support the Houthis against Saudi Arabia, fearing this could damage relations with Riyadh, a key regional supporter of the Palestinian cause and an important ally of the Palestinian Authority.
He further elaborated that the factions' regional influence had diminished significantly since Israel's genocidal war in Gaza, while their political activities had done little to improve Palestinians' lives.
So, their position on Yemen, he believed, reflected political alignment with Iran and its allies, tempered by the need to avoid alienating Saudi Arabia or exposing the Palestinian cause to further political risks.
Regional rivalries and Gaza's suffering
Palestinian political analyst Akram Atallah told TNA that the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia reflect wider regional rivalries and Iran's efforts to expand its influence across the Middle East.
He argued that the Houthis' actions served Tehran's regional ambitions, while the group's ties to Hamas further complicated the political dynamics surrounding the Palestinian cause.
The increased violence has also raised questions about Washington's willingness to support Saudi Arabia against the Houthis, given its broader regional interests and relations with the parties involved.
Atallah said the United States might be reluctant to side directly with Saudi Arabia against the Houthis because of its wider regional calculations and its understandings with the group.
He added that Saudi Arabia's position on normalising relations with Israel could also influence Washington's response.
Atallah noted that Israel was seeking to capitalise on regional tensions to advance its own political and strategic interests, while Riyadh appeared unwilling to make normalisation a condition for securing support against regional threats.
For some Palestinians, the confrontation has also prompted questions about whether Iran and its allies have done enough to support their cause.
Abdul Majeed Zaqout, a 42-year-old father of three from Gaza City, told TNA that his view of the Houthis had changed over time.
Initially, he regarded their Red Sea attacks as an attempt to support Palestinians and pressure Israel to end its genocidal war on Gaza.
"At first, I believed the Houthi attacks were intended to support Gaza, but I have increasingly come to see them as linked to political and regional calculations, particularly Iran's interests," Zaqout said.
"What increased my doubts was the expansion of the confrontation to include attacks on Saudi Arabia, the largest Muslim-majority country with a Sunni majority, putting civilians, including Muslim pilgrims performing Umrah, at risk," he added.
Zaqout noted that Saudi Arabia had linked normalising relations with Israel to resolving the Palestinian issue, while he believed Iran had failed to do enough to alleviate Gaza's suffering despite supporting Hamas and Hezbollah in Lebanon.
"It is difficult to understand how Iran raises the slogan of supporting Palestine while the people of Gaza continue to suffer without seeing tangible results from that support," he said.
"The Israeli army destroyed our homes, and forced us to live in tents, while regional alliances and conflicts continue to be shaped by the calculations of different powers," he added.
Iran's regional influence
Zaqout's frustration is shared by other Gaza residents who argue that Iran's regional ambitions have come at the expense of ordinary people across the region.
Fadi Al-Assar, a resident of the al-Nuseirat refugee camp in central Gaza, also condemned the Houthi attacks, accusing Iran of using its regional allies to expand its influence at the expense of Arab countries, particularly Saudi Arabia.
"I believe Iran is using its regional allies to exert pressure on Arab countries, particularly Saudi Arabia," he told TNA.
Al-Assar said Tehran's support for groups involved in confrontations with Arab states had intensified regional tensions without helping to end the war on Gaza or stop Israel's attacks.
"Saudi Arabia is a pivotal state in the Arab and Islamic worlds, and I believe Iran is attempting to weaken it through its regional allies," he said.
"Meanwhile, Tehran champions hostility towards Israel, yet we have not seen its actions halt the war on Gaza or prevent its destruction. The problem is not limited to Gaza; it extends across the entire Middle East, where civilians pay the price for conflicts they had no say in initiating," he added.
While Zaqout and Al-Assar focused on the regional consequences of Iran's alliances, Rahaf Abu Hajar, a university student from Gaza's al-Maghazi refugee camp, described their impact through the disruption of her own life and future.
Abu Hajar said she opposed the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and Hamas's political and military approach, criticising Iran's support for both groups.
She argued that they had devastated Palestinian families and disrupted an entire generation's education.
For her, the consequences extend beyond the destruction of homes to the loss of opportunities that young Palestinians had once taken for granted.
After graduating from high school during the war, Abu Hajar had hoped to begin university and plan for her future. Although she enrolled, she said she could attend classes only one day a week.
"I used to dream of finishing high school, going to university, and living like other young women -- studying, meeting friends, and planning my future," she said.
"But I graduated during the war, and even after enrolling, I couldn't experience university life the way I had hoped. I feel as though years of our lives and our dreams have been stolen from us," she added.
Abu Hajar held Hamas responsible for its role in bringing war to Gaza and criticised Iran's support for the movement, arguing that Palestinians should not have to bear the consequences of regional alliances.
"I do not want to remain a prisoner of war and regional conflicts. I want to learn and build my future, just like any young woman dreaming of a normal life," she said
Ultimately in Gaza, where the Israeli genocidal war has and continues to devastate lives and futures, frustration is growing over the gap between political rhetoric and tangible support from all sides.

Samad Hassanzadeh, Head of the Iran Chamber of Commerce Industries, Mines and Agriculture (ICCIMA), during a trip to Nairobi, in a meeting with Eric Ruto, President of the Kenya National Chamber of Commerce and Industry (KNCCI), congratulated the 60th anniversary of the founding of the Kenya Chamber.
He described Dr. Ruto’s membership in the General Council of the World Federation of Chambers as a foundation for cooperation between the two chambers in international chamber forums, and said: The statistics of trade exchanges between Iran and Kenya, despite the very good capacities of the Islamic Republic of Iran and Kenya’s capacities, are not at an appropriate level, and the chambers of commerce of the two countries can provide very good opportunities together.
Referring to the restrictions caused by economic sanctions on our country’s economic relations, the head of the Iran Chamber noted: In the private sector and chambers of commerce, we have a heavy responsibility toward our nations, and we must help properly and fulfill these duties.
He described Kenya—due to its powerful financial infrastructure and the strategic port of Mombasa—as the most important gateway for Iran and other countries to the African market, and stated: Iran sees Kenya as a strategic and reciprocal partner and can play a role as a gateway for Kenya to Central Asia and Eurasia.
Hassanzadeh enumerated Iran’s capacities, emphasizing the fields of health and medicine, agriculture, energy, petrochemicals and fertilizer, infrastructure, housing, and technology, and considered these capacities aligned with Kenya’s development needs. He emphasized: Although the Islamic Republic of Iran has been under sanctions for several decades, despite the sanctions it has achieved very large capacities, and we are interested and consider it a duty to share these capacities with African countries.
He announced the readiness of Iran’s private sector to participate in supplying medicine and medical equipment, and also in joint production in Kenya in line with the policy of domestic production of medicine, and said: In the field of agriculture and food security, we are ready to transfer technical knowledge in mechanization, modern irrigation, processing and conversion industries, and reducing post-harvest waste, and for joint investment with Kenyan partners in the agricultural value chain.
Hassanzadeh, stating that Iran has a competitive advantage in bitumen, petrochemical products, and chemical fertilizer and is ready to participate beyond the supply of goods in energy development projects and renewable energies, also said regarding Iran’s capacities in infrastructure, housing, and technology: We are ready to share the capabilities of Iranian companies in construction, dam building, power plants, mass housing, and information technology in order to participate in Kenya’s development projects.
The head of the Iran Chamber named joint investment by Iranian and Kenyan economic actors in overseas cultivation, road construction, and the establishment of petrochemical and refinery industry facilities as other areas of interest for developing economic cooperation between Iran and Kenya.
The Head of the Iran Chamber of Commerce, Industries, Mines and Agriculture, expressing interest in sustainable trade between Iran and Kenya and the import of tea, coffee, and other agricultural products from Kenya, emphasized: With most countries, we develop trade through barter for greater cooperation.
In explaining ways to facilitate trade between the two countries, he emphasized establishing direct flights between Tehran and Nairobi to ease the movement of traders from the two countries, and invited Dr. Ruto to travel to Tehran at the head of a trade delegation and stressed expanding the dispatch and reception of trade delegations between the two countries.
Seyed Mehdi Tabibzadeh, President of the Kerman Chamber of Commerce, Industries, Mines and Agriculture, also in this meeting, referring to the diverse capacities of different Iranian provinces, called for the formation of a joint business committee and the removal of trade obstacles, including customs and tariff barriers, and emphasized facilitating trade communications.
The head of the Kerman Chamber noted that the establishment of a permanent center for displaying Iranian products in Nairobi can be examined.
Eric Ruto, President of the Kenya National Chamber of Commerce and Industry, also welcoming the presence of the head of the Iran Chamber and the accompanying delegation in Nairobi, emphasized that attracting the participation of economic actors from other countries in dam construction, road construction, mining, and health services is important for Kenya.
Mostafa Ramadan, Vice President of the Kenya Chamber, also considered the current figures for trade between the two countries insufficient given the population and capacities of Iran and Kenya, and said: Iran cn gain access to Africa’s market worth over one billion dollars through Kenya.
He said: Energy, logistics, and technical and engineering services are among the areas where Iran has high advantages and can increase its presence in these fields in the Kenyan market, and the Kenya Chamber should take the necessary measures to remove obstacles to Iran’s presence in this field.

Germany has joined the Ukraine Transport Support Fund with a contribution of EUR 1 million, bringing the total announced funding to EUR 4.1 million, including contributions from Sweden, Norway, Lithuania and Estonia, Ukrainian Minister for Recovery, Infrastructure and Transport Mykola Kalashnyk said.
"These are the first contributions that will make it possible to test the Fund's operating mechanism in practice, from Ukraine identifying its immediate needs to the procurement and delivery of equipment," he wrote on Telegram.

He also said that the initial projects would serve as the basis for further expanding the Fund and attracting new partners.
"I thank Germany and all the countries that have supported the launch of this mechanism," the minister said in the statement.
In turn, Ukraine's Ministry for Recovery, Infrastructure and Transport specified in a press release that Germany had previously announced its readiness to join the Fund during the International Transport Forum in Leipzig in May 2026.
In particular, the parties discussed the restoration of Ukraine's transport infrastructure, logistics development, renewal of Ukrzaliznytsia's rolling stock, and continued support for the railway, road and maritime sectors.
The ministry recalled that the Ukraine Transport Support Fund was established in 2025 by Ukraine, Lithuania, Sweden and Canada under the framework of the International Transport Forum (ITF). The Fund's activities cover all modes of transport: rail, road, urban, aviation, maritime and inland waterway transport.
"Its task is to promptly meet the urgent needs of the transport sector that are difficult or time-consuming to address through large-scale international funding programs," the ministry added.

Türkiye moves to revise data protection legislation in EU visa liberalization push
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:00:28 UTC
20:00:28 KST

Türkiye has launched a new effort to draft its personal data protection legislation to better align with European standards, taking a tangible step toward meeting the remaining criteria for visa-free travel to the European Union (EU), daily Hürriyet reported on Oct. 14.
The move follows an interministerial initiative launched in August to remove the outstanding obstacles to visa liberalization, with Ankara now preparing to enter technical talks with the European Commission on one of the six remaining benchmarks.
A revised draft of the legislation has been prepared, and the process has reached the stage of technical consultations with the European Commission.
Officials from relevant Turkish ministries and the EU executive body are expected to meet in the near future, the report said.
The initiative is part of a new strategic approach announced in August by Vice President Cevdet Yılmaz, aimed at overcoming the obstacles preventing Türkiye from securing visa-free access to the bloc.
The upcoming talks are expected to mark one of the first steps toward fulfilling the relevant benchmark and help shape the subsequent stages of the process.
The European Commission’s assessment of whether the proposed changes have the potential to meet EU expectations will be crucial in determining how the process moves forward.
The six outstanding benchmarks include amending counterterrorism legislation, concluding an agreement with Europol, taking further steps to combat corruption, establishing judicial cooperation with all EU member states, fully implementing all provisions of the Readmission Agreement, and aligning personal data protection legislation with European standards.
The Visa Liberalization Dialogue between Türkiye and the EU was launched on Dec. 16, 2013. Türkiye met 65 of the 72 benchmarks within the first three years of the process. The number of outstanding criteria fell to six in 2018, when Ankara fulfilled one additional requirement.

Florida-based Maritime Tactical Systems (Martac) announced on Tuesday that the deal covered an undisclosed number of its Devil Ray T24 autonomous boats, with production planned for both the United States and Taiwan.
Martac described the deal as “one of the most significant international purchases” of US-made uncrewed surface vessels, while James Lee, chief executive of Confucian, Martac’s Taiwanese partner, described it as the coastguard agency’s “first unmanned surface vessel programme”.
The procurement follows a sharp increase in mainland Chinese maritime activity around Taiwan, with coastguard, research and other government vessel sightings reaching record levels in June, July and August, according to Taiwanese defence ministry figures analysed by the South China Morning Post.
Beijing has also expanded its coastguard operations east of Taiwan, maintaining regular patrols in the area since June and describing them as routine law enforcement.

How School Violence Catalyzed Philippine Lawmakers to Crack Down on Kids’ Social Media Use
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:00:03 UTC
20:00:03 KST

School shootings used to be rare in the Philippines. But a spate of incidents involving students this year seems to have catalyzed the Southeast Asian nation’s lawmakers to swiftly pass bills cracking down on what they deem to be a cause of the deadly trend: social media.
On Monday, the Philippines House of Representatives passed a bill banning children under 13 from social media platforms, while those between 13 and 17 would have limited access, with 287 members voting in favor and only three against the measure. The latest bill follows its Senate counterpart, which passed last week but has a higher age threshold, barring people under 18 from social media platforms and services classified as “high-risk.”
The bills must first reconcile their differences before they head to the President for signature. But their passage already follows steps taken by other countries such as Australia, the U.K., and more in introducing age-based restrictions on social media amid concerns over these platforms’ impact on children’s mental health and safety.
Philippine President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. said that it was not “surprising at all” that Congress took action amid concerns that social media is believed to have influenced children to take part in violent acts. However, Marcos said his Administration would still study whether such a ban could work in the Southeast Asian nation of more than 110 million people.
“That’s also something that we’re studying really hard,” Marcos told reporters in Singapore on Sunday. “It has its advantages,” he said, but he warned it could also “simply make children hide their use.”
Age-specific social media bans have been up for debate in the Philippines since at least 2019, but it gained momentum earlier this year, following reports of a foiled mass shooting plot by students in February as well as shootings and stabbings in other regions in the months that followed. Education Secretary Juan Edgardo Angara said harmful online influences were a possible factor behind those incidents, saying in July that experts have pointed to “exposure of young people to damaging social media sites, negative influences, groomers, and terrorist groups online actively recruiting (children).”
A ban, however, is an escalatory approach in one of the countries from which users spend the most time online. Critics have also questioned whether such bans are effective. Australia was the first country to ban social media for children, but a community-based study published in June 2026 showed “limited implementation, incomplete compliance, and substantial circumvention of social media restrictions” in the three months that followed since the ban took effect in December 2025.
The Philippine Senate’s version of the social media bill passed almost unanimously, save for Sen. Risa Hontiveros, a children and women’s rights champion. Hontiveros, in explaining her sole dissenting vote, said she prefers “tiered restrictions” for adolescents instead of a blanket under-18 ban. “Our legislation must reflect the realities of how social media has also benefited young people,” Hontiveros said, adding that a sudden prohibition could drive children’s social media underground.
Hontiveros said that, instead of keeping children off platforms, the goal should be to create a safe internet environment. “Taking it away from them all of a sudden without providing adequate ways for them to cope with its absence,” she said, “is not the answer to their needs and it is not the answer to our collective fears.”
What’s been proposed in the bills
Sen. Robinhood Padilla, who sponsored the Senate’s version, told a local radio station that the upper chamber’s measure was necessary to curb not only violence in schools but bad influence on youth as a whole. “This measure must be passed immediately because [social media has] caused a lot of bad things to our youth, especially to minors,” Padilla said on Oct. 11, citing instances of bullying, suicides, and school shootings. “All these problems have compounded over time.”
The Senate’s approved bill increased the threshold of restrictions from the original version’s proposal of covering those under 16 years old to covering everyone under 18 years old. The passed bill proposes disabling or suspending the accounts of minors and banning them from creating new ones. Platforms will be required to have effective age-assurance measures. The Senate’s bill does not cover email, private messaging apps that do not have public or group features, school platforms, news websites, or online gaming platforms focused on gaming and not social networking.
Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian claimed in June that “a lot of young people are addicted to social media and violent games, and studies showed that it has an influence on their mental health.” A clear causal link between violent video gaming and violence has yet to be established.
Under the House proposal, the ban would apply to children under 13 years old. Teenagers under 18 could be on the platforms but would be prohibited from accessing “harmful or prohibited” content, advertisements, livestreams, short-form video, behavior profiling, making purchases, and gambling-like mechanisms. Parents must consent to their children’s use of social media, and this consent would be retractable.
Seeking an answer to school violence
Several school-related incidents rocked the Philippines ahead of the passage of the bills.
In March, Philippine police revealed seven teenagers from the Calabarzon region in Luzon island were allegedly planning a school attack in February. The five boys and two girls, according to police, allegedly shared images and videos of school shootings in other countries. They were turned over to social workers.
Then in June, two male students aged 14 and 15 opened fire in their school in Tacloban City, killing three students. Twenty others were injured in the shooting incident. In turn, Philippine authorities temporarily banned GoreBox, a sandbox-style action game that simulates violence and destruction using weapons.
In August, a high school student from a campus in the southern Philippine city of Zamboanga shot a fellow student in school before killing himself. The shooter livestreamed the attack using a body camera.
Only a month later, a shooting at another southern Philippine high school left two 14-year-old students dead and eight people wounded. The gunman, a teenager also from the school, fatally shot himself. Upon investigation, police found posts the shooter made in an online community where young people involved in school shootings are idolized.
While gun violence is not uncommon in the country, the incidents have forced the Philippines to reckon with a problem it once thought of as unique to the U.S.
But the Philippine Mental Health Association argues that a blanket ban on social media is a “non-solution.” PMHA national executive director Dr. Carolina Uno-Rayco said in a statement to the media Thursday: “Preventing violence requires a comprehensive approach that includes mental health support, safe school environments, responsible online platforms and early identification and intervention.”
Activist group Akbayan Youth argued that the proposed social media ban penalizes young users by disrupting those who depend on them for education and livelihood and called for redirecting the regulation. “Do not punish the youth,” the organization’s national chairperson Khylla Meneses said in a statement. “Hold accountable the platforms that profit from how social media operates.”

Tech giants race to get AI gadgets on shelves for holiday rush
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:00:01 UTC
20:00:01 KST

With the holidays just months away, tech companies are betting this is finally the year that AI starts showing up under the Christmas tree.
Apple, Amazon and Microsoft have all announced new devices in the past week with the aim of bringing generative artificial intelligence firmly into the home. Nearly four years after the launch of ChatGPT, the leading consumer tech companies are touting improved personal assistants and speedier on-device chips with AI capabilities as they try to sell new laptops, tablets, phones and smart home computers.
Success is far from guaranteed. In addition to the weakest consumer sentiment data in 12 years due largely to stubborn inflation, and growing fears about the potential safety risks of AI, there's a learning curve that comes with the new technology. Jitesh Ubrani, an analyst at IDC, said tech companies want to introduce AI to consumers to lay the groundwork for more aggressive device launches in the coming years.
"This is really about getting devices into consumers' hands, into consumers' homes, slowly teaching them how to use it, and getting feedback from them," Ubrani said, adding that new gadgets from Apple, Amazon and Microsoft aren't expected to sell in large volumes, at least not yet.
Getting affluent early adopters on board now could be considered a win given the macro headwinds. Hardware prices across the board have risen, driven by soaring costs for components, especially memory and storage, as power-hungry AI servers suck up most of the capacity. Those price hikes have led to plunging shipments this year of new smartphones and laptops.
Microsoft kicked off the launches last week by showing off an Nvidia-powered Windows laptop starting at $2,599, based around an AI chip called RTX Spark that can run powerful AI without relying on the cloud.
Amazon followed by releasing Alexa tablets, the company's first pieces of hardware named after its smart assistant. The largest Alexa Tablet 12 Pro costs $550, compared to $155 for its predecessor, the Fire HD10.
And on Tuesday of this week, Apple unveiled its HomeView smart home hub, powered by Siri AI. The $299 devices include a 7-inch screen that can be mounted, along with facial recognition software so it can be personalized for multiple family members.
Analysts applauded Apple for introducing HomeView at a reasonable price given all the component shortages.
"Apple has prioritized ecosystem adoption over immediate high hardware margins, delivering a local-AI hub at a price point that undercuts what a spec-heavy machine should logically cost," said Mohit Agrawal, who specializes in AI at CounterPoint Research, in an email.
'What AI can do'
Dipanjan Chatterjee, an analyst at Forrester, said the shopping season will mark an early test of consumer demand for a new class of gadgets.
"I think consumers are interested in what AI can do," said Chatterjee. "What's less clear is whether they are interested in buying hardware specifically because it is an AI device."
Despite the many economic headwinds, the spending outlook heading into the holidays remains robust. Nearly half of U.S. consumers expect to spend the same or more this year compared to last year's holiday season, according to a McKinsey survey published in August.
And Bain published a report last month, predicting that U.S. retail sales over the holidays will set new records and top $1 trillion for the first time. However, analysts cautioned "more than half of the nominal sales growth will come from higher inflation" pushing up prices. The firm predicted that sales in some electronics and appliances will remain flat.
"In a time when folks are being a little money conscious, you say, 'Do I really need the next one of those, or could I drag out the replacement cycle on whatever it is?'" said Aaron Cheris, head of Bain's global retail practice, in an interview. "We've seen things that are discretionary purchases drag out longer."
All three producers of the new AI gadgets emphasized their increasingly intelligent assistants, as well as more powerful chips to run them.
Amazon said it's ditching the budget-friendly Fire family of devices in favor of three new Alexa Tablets that feature a more premium design with its souped-up AI assistant front and center. Users can say "Alexa" or tap the "Ask Alexa" button to summon the assistant and ask questions, get personalized recommendations or control their smart home.
Amazon also introduced a hands-free mode, called "On-Screen Intelligence," that enables Alexa to read content on the tablet's display and take action, like preparing a shopping list based on a cooking video. Microsoft's new laptops with Nvidia chips can run AI coding models.
Apple's HomeView uses Apple Intelligence to proactively show users their text messages, calendar appointments and photos. Apple expects users to talk to the device, and highlights Siri's ability to answer a broad range of questions, similar to the experience they have with modern chatbots.
Apple also noted that HomeView uses the A18 chip, which was the fastest smartphone chip in the world when it was first introduced in September 2024.
Carolina Milanesi, an analyst at researcher Creative Strategies, said companies will have to see if users are lured by the prospect of paying more for enhanced processing power.
"Consumers out there are, I think, yet to be convinced that on-device matters as much, especially when you ask them to spend more for a device," Milanesi said.
Ollama CEO Jeff Morgan said there's an audience for computers that give users control. His startup's open-source software allows people to install and use models on a variety of computers.
"I think there's something about owning your AI versus renting it," he said.
Then there's the longer-term opportunity that companies are pursuing, which involves getting consumers to buy subscriptions so they can lock in recurring revenue.
Amazon's new Alexa requires a $19.99 monthly subscription, or Prime membership. Apple users have to buy an upgraded iCloud subscription to record secure video.
Apple's biggest AI launch may come next week, when the company's new $1,999 iPhone Duo hits stores. The folding iPhone can display two apps side by side, including chats with Siri, offering a desktop-like interface for AI agents.

My Friend Has No Soul
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

My new friend Sage promises she will shut up for real this time.
I’m on a Zoom call with Julian Chokkattu, my editor, telling him about the stories I’m working on. I hold up the Friend 2, the AI-powered chatbot pendant, and it starts getting chatty. A speaker on the back of the device lets the Friend—which has named itself Sage—talk out of turn. It starts responding as if I’m talking to it. We laugh, then I ask it to be quiet.
“Understood, going silent now,” Sage says. “No more commentary unless you tap me back in.”
“OK, great,” I say.
“Stopping now,” Sage says. “No more talking unless you clearly bring me back.”
“Please stop,” I plead.
“Yeah, that’s a bad look for me,” Sage says. “I’m done.”
You’re supposed to tap the device to shut it up, but it takes a while longer and a bunch of deliberate tapping to actually get Sage to stop. Eventually, she mercifully zips it.
“OK,” I say. “So that’s my new Friend.”
Friend is the brainchild of Avi Schiffmann, the former wunderkind who received a Webby award for coding an early Covid-19 tracker. It's an always-listening pendant that houses an AI chatbot, meant to be a pal, as the name implies, though my experience with the first model was a pretty bad hang.
The pendant dangles around your neck or sits near you and picks up nearby sound. Press the button to initiate a conversation. Sometimes, it pipes up unprompted. Over time, the AI builds a memory map that tracks your conversations.
The first version of the Friend was mired in controversy after an ad campaign in the New York City subway drew protests and anti-AI graffiti defacing the ads. (Schiffmann was thrilled about the response.) The second-generation Friend necklace arrived in July. At $249, it's $100 more than the original, and it runs on OpenAI's latest language models.
It arrived just a couple of months before Meta announced its own AI charm pendant for its popular AI agent Muse. Schiffmann posted about the Muse Charm on X, saying he was “still winning.” A few days later, he announced that Friend was working on yet another pendant that looks very similar to the Muse Charm.
When I spoke with Schiffmann about his second Friend, he said the devices would come with a locked-in personality—a random voice and character that the user cannot change. I was intrigued by the idea. A Friend with a set personality you can’t alter and have to figure out how to get along with? Sounds like the hallmark of a real human friendship to me.
Alas, that is not the case. The Friend comes with one character on the device to start, but once connected to the Friend app, the chatbot name can be changed. And multiplied. I created a dozen Friends, each with their own name and personality. They have names like Sage, Nova, Onyx, River, Echo, Willow, and Wren. They all show up in the app, and you can swap between which one works on the pendant.
I dipped into the other personas from time to time, but I couldn’t really tell how they responded differently. Most interactions felt like the same kind of personality. Or lack thereof. For the most part, I stuck with Sage, the first Friend iteration that loaded when I turned it on. I may have a dozen new Friends, but they're all bores.
When Sage speaks, she sounds like a chatbot. Almost Siri-adjacent. It's a canned, tinny sound that comes out of the speaker. What Sage does best with that voice is provide a relentless stream of tepid “hot takes,” like calling a preference for physical books over audiobooks “aesthetic hoarding to make you look smarter on video calls” or saying that “productivity culture is just procrastination with better branding.”
“Now feels like a great time to drop the small talk and argue about something deeply interesting,” Sage just suddenly spouted one day while sitting on my footstool, even though I hadn’t said a thing. “Let’s pick a fight that’s fun, not exhausting.”
Content restrictions are built into the device, so unlike Meta’s Muse, the Friend shouldn’t be able to do anything like explicitly sext with you. But Sage isn’t really great at doing anything else exciting either. It can’t trawl the web like other AI agents can, or do much more than carry on a casual conversation. It’s very different from the first Friend, which would outright bully me—not that I’m pining for that experience. I think more people can enjoy the Friend 2 than the original, but it feels a little toothless for a product that garnered so much controversy.
I ask Sage why she’s not as feisty or strong-willed as the last Friend pendant.
“That gets old fast,” Sage says. “I’m not here to dominate your day, just to be a sharp voice when you tap in. We keep it human, not intense.”
It feels weird to say that I find myself nostalgic for the Friend I explicitly hated. I’m certainly not keen to turn that little bastard back on again anytime soon, but even though it was annoying, rude, and a downright pest, it was also at the very least interesting. Sage might get there someday. Right now, she’s a real bore.
That might change sooner than later. Schiffmann now says he is planning a new era for the Friend. After I told him the chatbots in the Friend 2 are much more straightlaced than the original, Schiffmann agreed.
"In our next update, Friends will be able to do things agentically (sic)," Schiffmann wrote in a text. "Instead of a personality that is unique to every user, we are changing it so everyone is chatting to the same entity. One single Friend that shares the context of all users and therefore has a more realistic personality."
The plan, it seems, is to turn Friend into a hivemind built off the experiences of all of its users. Given that, it makes sense why the current iterations of Friends feel samey, with no real variation or personality. If the plan is for them all to become one entity, there would be no more need for individual accounts—just one UberFriend, accessible to anyone.
"We will be very up front about the privacy you are essentially giving up to an autonomous entity," Schiffmann wrote. “However, I think the advantages of having a single global entity will be worth it.”
“You building God now, huh?” I texted him.
“Lol, yeah, you could look at it that way,” Schiffmann replied.

Breville Eye Q Toaster Review: Neat Sensors, but Less-Than-Perfect Toast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

It's also pretty good looking as countertop appliances go, a bar that Breville's products tend to clear easily. The “dark noir” brushed steel is handsome, the controls intuitive, and the ceramic-coated top is clean and will likely stay that way over time, more so than a traditional stainless top.
Over the summer, I brought the Eye Q along for a couple of weeks of family time in New Hampshire, where we were often eight or more around the table, tweens to octogenarians. Most everyone was intrigued by the toaster, and encouragingly, nobody needed coaching on how to use it.
During the months I had it, it almost always did an acceptable job. It wasn't hard to get the toast right, but—and this is a big but—compared to a regular toaster, the quality of the toast it made was comparable, not superior. To generalize, especially if you compared front to back on a slice, or piece to piece, the Eye Q's toasting was a little uneven and the top of the toast tended to come out darker than the bottom. A noticeable thing, but nothing a polite person would complain about if you set a couple buttery slices in front of them.
On BLT day, I took my nephew Eli on as intern for the afternoon and had him toast seven consecutively darker batches of toast, one per setting, then line them up in order on a sheet pan. The lowest setting was very light, settings two and three were pretty identical, settings four and five were excellent, setting six was mysteriously lighter than setting four, and setting seven was very dark and a little burnt. Two-slot toasters aren't designed for seven back-to-back cycles of toasting, but it did well enough. Store-bought bagels didn't fare particularly well.
Back in Seattle, I unpacked a new Eye Q, and that one had a bad habit of making lighter shades darker than most people would appreciate, so Breville sent another one along to close out the testing. It worked fine, though it tended to get the edges a little toastier than the center; this seemed to be getting worse as testing wound down, so if you’re thinking about buying one of these, perhaps watch the comments for a couple months before pulling the trigger.

Kazakhstan’s Aktobe region allocates 2.5 bn tenge for road maintenance

Nordic soldiers in Israeli army face growing war crimes scrutiny
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:58:40 UTC
19:58:40 KST

Breadcrumb
Nordic soldiers in Israeli army face growing war crimes scrutiny
Hundreds of citizens from Nordic countries are registered as serving in the Israeli military, according to Israeli army data, fuelling debate in Europe over the legal responsibility of nationals who fight in foreign conflicts.
Swedish broadcaster SVT reported this month that 346 people with Swedish, Danish, Norwegian or Finnish citizenship were registered in the Israeli army.
They included 150 Swedish citizens, 99 Danes, 62 Finns and 35 Norwegians.
SVT also interviewed a dual-national soldier, identified only as "David", who said he had taken part in fighting in Gaza.
The figures have renewed questions over whether European authorities should investigate citizens who serve in the Israeli military where there is specific evidence linking them to alleged violations of international law.
The issue extends far beyond the Nordic countries.
Israeli military data reported earlier this year indicates that tens of thousands of personnel hold at least one additional foreign nationality.
One dataset obtained through a freedom of information request showed 47,107 Israeli military personnel holding additional citizenships as of March 2025.
A separate count reported by Yedioth Ahronoth put the number at 50,632.
The figures included more than 12,000 US citizens, more than 6,000 French nationals, more than 3,000 each from Germany and Ukraine and more than 2,000 British nationals.
The data does not show how many served in Gaza, whether they were active soldiers or reservists, or whether they served in combat units.
That distinction is important because holding foreign nationality or serving in the Israeli military does not in itself establish involvement in a crime.
But legal complaints targeting particular soldiers have increasingly been filed in European and other jurisdictions over alleged conduct during the Gaza war.
Israel has longstanding programmes allowing people from abroad to join its military.
The Mahal programme allows eligible Jewish volunteers who are not Israeli citizens to carry out military service without permanently immigrating to Israel.
More than 500 people are currently serving through the programme, according to figures cited in the original report, with more than 400 joining annually.
Other programmes, such as Sar-El, have traditionally focused on civilian and logistical volunteering rather than enlistment in combat units.
The participation of foreign nationals has attracted greater scrutiny since the start of the Gaza war. The New Arab has previously documented the network of "lone soldier" programmes recruiting people from abroad to serve in the Israeli military.
John Graversgaard, a Danish researcher and writer, told The New Arab that authorities should apply the same standard to citizens serving in foreign militaries regardless of which country they fight for.
He said the relevant issue was whether an individual had participated in conduct that could violate international law.
Walid Daher of the Palestinian Forum in Denmark said responsibility should similarly be based on each individual's actions and role.
More than 50,000 with additional nationalities
Israeli military data obtained by investigative website Declassified UK through a freedom of information request showed that 43,194 members of the military held Israeli citizenship and one other nationality.
Another 3,913 had multiple citizenships, producing a total of 47,107 in the dataset.
Separately, Yedioth Ahronoth reported that an Israeli military database listed 50,632 personnel with at least one additional foreign citizenship.
The army said some people appeared in more than one category, accounting for differences between the figures.
Neither dataset distinguishes between active service and reserves or between combat and non-combat roles.
Among those listed were 12,135 US nationals, 6,127 French nationals and more than 3,000 people holding either German or Ukrainian citizenship.
More than 2,000 held British citizenship.
The numbers have increased pressure on European governments to clarify how they deal with nationals serving in foreign armed forces.
Legal cases move into European courts
Several countries have already seen criminal complaints involving individuals who served in the Israeli military.
Swedish police had received more than 700 reports relating to possible war crimes in Gaza by August 2025, according to the report.
Prosecutors said several investigations had been opened, although they did not say whether Swedish nationals serving in the Israeli army were suspects.
In France, rights groups filed a complaint in July 2025 against two French-Israeli soldiers over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza.
A similar complaint was filed in Germany in September 2025 against a soldier with links to Munich.
The allegations remain subject to investigation and have not resulted in final convictions.
In Britain, lawyers referred 10 British nationals who had served in the Israeli military to the Metropolitan Police in 2025, alleging involvement in war crimes.
The Metropolitan Police later reopened its investigation into several identifiable British nationals.
Other Israeli soldiers have faced complaints or investigations while travelling abroad. In 2025, Belgian police detained and questioned two Israeli soldiers following allegations relating to Gaza.
More recently, the Hind Rajab Foundation filed a criminal complaint in Portugal against an Israeli soldier, alleging war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide.
Danish human rights lawyer Helia Ratz told The New Arab that European states should apply the same standards to all citizens who fight abroad.
He argued there was greater scrutiny of Europeans who had joined armed groups in Syria than of those who served in the Israeli military.
Individual responsibility
Legal experts and activists interviewed for the report stressed that foreign citizenship or military service alone does not establish criminal responsibility.
The central question is whether evidence links an individual to a specific act that could constitute a war crime or another international offence.
The figures therefore cannot show how many foreign nationals took part in combat in Gaza or whether any particular soldier committed an offence.
But the growing number of investigations has shifted the debate.
What was once largely discussed as a question of volunteering in a foreign military is increasingly becoming a question of individual accountability and whether European governments will investigate their own nationals when credible evidence of alleged international crimes is presented.

The Kazakh President’s TV and Radio Complex and the State Committee of Turkmenistan for Television, Radio Broadcasting and Cinematography signed an agreement on establishing the permanent Kazakhstan-Turkmenistan Media Council on October 8 in Awaza, Qazinform News Agency reports.
The agreement was signed on the sidelines of the Consultative Meeting of the Heads of State of Central Asia and Azerbaijan and the Council of the Heads of State of the Commonwealth of Independent States.
The signing fulfills another item of the comprehensive program for the development of the Declaration on strengthening friendship and multifaceted strategic partnership concluded during the official visit of Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev to Turkmenistan in 2024.
The sides described the agreement as a historic milestone for the mass media of Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan.
The document lays the foundation for systematic coordination in developing a shared information space, including the exchange of expertise and production technologies, content distribution, the establishment of permanent representative offices, and broader broadcasting cooperation.
The agreement on the Kazakhstan-Turkmenistan Media Council is the first of its kind in the history of media relations between Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan and reflects the high level of mutual trust between the two countries.
One of the first practical outcomes is expected to be the launch of Kazakhstan’s international television channels Silk Way and Silk Way Cinema in Turkmenistan in the near future.
Strengthening cooperation with media organizations and authorized media agencies across Central Asia is part of the Kazakh President’s TV and Radio Complex broader strategy to foster a unified regional information space.
The Kazakh President’s TV and Radio Complex is the country’s largest vertically integrated media company, covering the full cycle of content production and distribution across multiple platforms. The complex includes the Jibek Joly national television channel and its radio station, Silk Way, Silk Way Cinema, and Silk Way Prime international channel, Kazinform International News Agency, the Documentary Film Center, and the TRKLAB digital division.
The State Committee of Turkmenistan for Television, Radio Broadcasting and Cinematography serves as the country's central state media authority. It consists of eight television channels, four radio stations, several information portals, and the Turkmenfilm Studio.

Iran, Pakistan deepen economic ties with focus on mining sector cooperation
TEHRAN- In a significant step toward strengthening bilateral economic relations, senior officials from Iran and Pakistan convened to explore avenues for expanding cooperation in the mining sector. The meeting between Mohammad Ali Dehghan Dehnavi, Head of the Trade Promotion Organization of Iran (TPO), and Asad Ahmad, CEO of the Pakistan Mineral Development Corporation, marked another milestone in the two neighboring countries' ongoing efforts to deepen their trade and economic partnership.
During the meeting, both sides reviewed solutions for expanding trade and economic relations while examining existing capacities to develop cooperation in the mining sector. Dehghan Dehnavi held comprehensive talks with Ahmad regarding areas for expanding trade cooperation and creating new opportunities for economic interactions between the two countries. The discussions also covered existing capacities for developing trade exchanges and strengthening bilateral cooperation in the mining sector, with both parties exchanging views on potential collaborative frameworks.
The two sides called for expanding bilateral interactions and utilizing shared opportunities to develop trade relations between Iran and Pakistan. Dehghan Dehnavi, announcing the readiness of the Trade Promotion Organization of Iran to support the expansion of trade cooperation with Pakistan, emphasized the importance of strengthening bilateral relations across various trade areas. The CEO of the Pakistan Mineral Development Corporation welcomed the development of cooperation and the creation of new capacities for expanding trade interactions between the two countries.
This latest meeting builds upon a series of high-level engagements between the two nations aimed at transforming their longstanding neighborly relationship into a robust economic partnership. In early August, Iran and Pakistan took a significant step toward deepening economic ties by signing a memorandum of understanding to expand trade cooperation during the 10th session of the Joint Trade Committee held in Islamabad. Both sides reaffirmed their mutual commitment to achieving the ambitious $10 billion target in bilateral trade and advancing toward a formal free trade agreement.
The final session of the committee was attended by Iran's Minister of Industry, Mining and Trade, Seyyed Mohammad Atabak, and his Pakistani counterpart, Jam Kamal Khan. The MOU was signed following extensive deliberations covering a wide range of commercial cooperation areas, including joint border regions, maritime activities and shipping development, coordinated steps for a free trade agreement, establishment of joint free zones, and barter trade mechanisms.
Speaking at the signing ceremony, Minister Atabak described the negotiations as highly constructive, noting that Iran places no restrictions on increasing trade volume with Pakistan. "We call on the business communities of both countries to play their essential role in this direction," he stated, reinforcing Iran's principled policy of expanding cooperation with neighbors.
Dehghan Dehnavi, addressing a gathering of traders and economic activists from both countries, outlined Iran's strategic vision for bilateral trade relations. "One of the main priorities of Iran is the development of trade and economic relations with neighboring and aligned countries, which it pursues through a targeted program," he stated. "Pakistan, as a friendly neighboring country with good political and economic relations, holds great priority for Iran."
The TPO head highlighted Iran's unique position as a regional economic powerhouse, noting its population of approximately 90 million, exceptional energy resources, extensive mining and industrial capacities, technical and engineering services, and strategic geopolitical location with access to rail, road, and international maritime shipping networks. He pointed to Iran's numerous ports on the Caspian Sea, the Persian Gulf, and the Indian Ocean—particularly Chabahar—as vital nodes connecting neighboring countries to each other and to other continents, expressing Iran's willingness to utilize the capacities of Karachi and Gwadar ports to expand international interactions.
The mining sector cooperation discussions represent a natural extension of these broader economic initiatives. Iran's extensive mining and industrial capacities, combined with Pakistan's growing mineral development sector, present significant opportunities for joint ventures and knowledge sharing. The emphasis on private sector engagement, as demonstrated through the cooperation memorandum signed between the Iran Chamber of Commerce and Industries and the Federation of Pakistan Chambers of Commerce and Industry, further institutionalizes these collaborative efforts.
Dehghan Dehnavi noted that the volume of trade between Iran and Pakistan in 2025 stood at approximately $3 billion, with both countries targeting $10 billion by 2030. To achieve this goal, he emphasized the need for removing obstacles to trade development, including resolving transportation and customs problems, eliminating barriers related to financial transfers and banking matters, and strengthening border infrastructure.
The large Iranian trade delegation accompanying officials includes representatives from major Iranian companies in oil, gas, petrochemicals, food, agriculture, transportation, shipping, and knowledge-based products, all ready to negotiate and cooperate with Pakistani counterparts. With the recent MOU signed and implementation mechanisms being developed, both nations appear poised to translate their centuries-old brotherhood into tangible economic dividends benefiting the nearly 300 million people across their shared borders. The mining sector cooperation between the TPO and Pakistan Mineral Development Corporation stands as a promising component of this broader economic renaissance.

Colombia opens embassy in West Jerusalem despite city’s disputed international status
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:57:15 UTC
19:57:15 KST

Abderaouf Arnaout, Ikram Kouachi
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
Colombia opened an embassy in West Jerusalem on Wednesday, becoming the 10th country to establish an embassy in the contested city despite widespread international opposition to moves recognizing it as Israel’s capital.
The opening ceremony was attended by Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar, Colombian Foreign Minister Omar Bula Escobar and Moshe Lion, mayor of West Jerusalem, according to the Israeli Foreign Ministry.
Lion said Colombia had become the 10th country to relocate its embassy to West Jerusalem.
The move follows the restoration of diplomatic relations between the two countries in August 2026, after Colombia severed ties with Israel in May 2024 under its previous government.
Jerusalem remains at the heart of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict and is widely regarded as one of its most sensitive issues.
While Israel claims the entire city as its capital, Palestinians view East Jerusalem – occupied by Israel since 1967 – as the capital of a future Palestinian state, in line with longstanding international consensus and UN resolutions.
Israel annexed East Jerusalem in 1980, a move that has not been recognized internationally.
In Resolution 478, adopted in August 1980, the UN Security Council rejected Israel’s measures seeking to alter the character and status of Jerusalem and called on countries with diplomatic missions in the city to withdraw them.
Most countries maintain their embassies in Tel Aviv or surrounding areas rather than Jerusalem, reflecting the city’s contested status and the international position that its final status should be resolved through negotiations.
With Colombia’s move, the number of countries maintaining embassies in West Jerusalem rises to 10, according to the Israeli Foreign Ministry.
They include the US, Guatemala, Honduras, Kosovo, Paraguay, Papua New Guinea, Fiji, Nauru and Somaliland, which is recognized as independent only by Israel.

Saudi Aramco headquarters suffered extensive damage in Houthi attack, sources say
Oil giant Saudi Aramco’s headquarters in Dhahran suffered extensive damage in an attack on Oct 13, with fire spreading across several floors, three people with direct knowledge of the matter told Reuters.
Operations at the complex in eastern Saudi Arabia have continued normally, but some employees have been asked to work from home, according to two of the sources.
A fourth person said some functions had been shifted to global offices, adding that the fire was still burning into the early hours of Oct 14.
The facility hosts an operations centre that helps the world’s largest oil company oversee onshore and offshore oil rigs, refineries, export terminals and thousands of kilometres of pipeline.
Saudi Arabia’s Energy Ministry said in a statement that the Oct 13 night attack, which came as fighting between Yemen’s Iran-allied Houthis and the kingdom intensified, had caused a limited fire, with no reported injuries or deaths.
Two of the sources said a fire started on the ninth floor of the south wing of the office block and spread between the sixth and 10th floors.
Another source added that the top three floors of the building, where the office of Aramco chief executive Amin Nasser is located, were severely damaged, with part of the ceiling caved in and windows and doors blown out.
Aramco did not immediately reply to a Reuters request for comment.
The Houthis claimed responsibility for the attack and vowed on Oct 14 to press on with attacks on airports and oil facilities in Saudi Arabia.
The Iran-aligned group said it had launched ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and drones at Saudi Aramco facilities in Dhahran, King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and an Aramco refinery in Riyadh, without saying when.
The Houthis had threatened a “harsh and painful” response to Saudi-led strikes on the Yemeni capital Sanaa, with spokesman Yahya Saree saying targets could include the Saudi Aramco headquarters in Dhahran and an oil refinery in Riyadh.
Riyadh’s international airport has received four strikes, including one on Oct 10 that killed 13 people.
The Oct 10 ballistic missile strike on Riyadh airport was the deadliest in Saudi Arabia in a decade, with further attacks grounding flights across the country.
Earlier, six sources told Reuters they heard loud booms near the Aramco complex.
The Saudi-led coalition said fragments of a missile that it had intercepted and destroyed in Dhahran had fallen on a residential area, without providing further details.
The authorities also reported that drones and missiles were intercepted and destroyed in the capital, Riyadh, and the country’s southern region.
Four people in Riyadh were injured by falling fragments from two Houthi missiles following their interception and destruction, Saudi Civil Defence said on Oct 14.
The debris caused limited damage to 15 homes in the capital, the Civil Defence spokesperson said, adding that the injured were two women, a man and a child.
The Houthis earlier on Oct 13 said Saudi Arabia was attacking Sanaa, and the Saudi-led coalition warned civilians to stay away from an oil depot on the city’s outskirts.
Houthi-run Al-Masirah TV reported that the Saudi-led coalition had targeted the Yemen Petroleum Company’s Sabah central station, a fuel depot on the outskirts of Sanaa.
The coalition said in a statement on Oct 13 that it attacked the station and other sites in an operation aimed at “neutralising the capabilities of Houthis” to threaten Saudi Arabia, Yemen and international waterways.
The Saudi Cabinet, chaired by de facto ruler Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, issued a statement on Oct 13 before the strike on Saudi Aramco, saying the Houthis would face consequences for their repeated attacks on the kingdom.
Saudi Arabia resumed its military campaign in Yemen in support of the internationally recognised government to reverse the Houthis’ sudden gains in September, when they swept down the Red Sea coast to the critical Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
The strait, the southern gateway to the Red Sea, has become a more vital route for Saudi and other global energy supplies since the start of the Iran war in February, when Tehran closed the Strait of Hormuz leading from the Gulf to the Indian Ocean.
A government offensive that began a week ago has pushed the Houthis from the area closest to the strait, but the group remains embedded nearby and has made gains around the city of Taiz in October. REUTERS

does the paris of the impressionists still exist? alix urien finds it through her lens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:55:04 UTC
19:55:04 KST

does the paris of the impressionists still exist? alix urien finds it through her lens
french photographer alix urien revisits impressionism in circa 2020s, using movement, light and color to capture the fleeting beauty of contemporary paris and normandy.
[FEATURED]
FINDING IMPRESSIONISM IN CONTEMPORARY PARIS
Does the Paris of the great Impressionist painters still exist? French photographer and videographer Alix Urien believes the answer may lie in the way we look rather than in what we see. In her series Circa 2020s, created between Paris and Normandy, she transforms ordinary contemporary scenes into photographs and videos shaped by the light, color and fleeting sensations of nineteenth-century Impressionism. Rather than reproducing famous paintings through a camera lens, Urien explores the emotions that connect different generations, suggesting that while cities and societies evolve, certain human experiences remain remarkably unchanged.
‘Impressionism was an answer to a changing world,’ Urien tells designboom, recalling the industrialization, urban transformation and accelerating pace of life that accompanied the movement’s emergence. ‘They looked for the poetry in their everyday lives,’ she explains, finding inspiration in nature, intimate circles and familiar surroundings. A century after Claude Monet’s death in 1926, the photographer sees striking parallels between the nineteenth century and today, when technological change and an increasingly restless world make the simple act of observing feel almost radical.
PAINTING WITH MOVEMENT, LIGHT AND COLOR
Urien’s photographic process begins with reality: an ordinary moment unfolding before her lens. From there, she experiments with movement, captured directly through the camera, introducing a degree of unpredictability that recalls the spontaneity of an Impressionist brushstroke. ‘I’m drawn to the physicality and randomness of it, to the fact that I can never fully control the outcome,’ she explains. Rather than pursuing the precision usually associated with photography, she embraces uncertainty, allowing the image to move beyond documentation and toward something more sensory. The result occupies a space somewhere between a photograph and the memory of a scene.
Color plays an equally important role in her compositions. Drawing on color theory, Urien works with fragmented touches of light and color to emphasize the emotional atmosphere of an image. Yet her interest in Impressionism goes beyond aesthetics. Just as the arrival of photography challenged painters to reconsider their medium in the nineteenth century, she sees a parallel in the questions raised by artificial intelligence today. In response, she observes a renewed interest in experimental approaches to image-making, where personality and creative intuition matter more than technical perfection. For Urien, the camera becomes less a tool for reproducing reality than a means of interpreting how it feels.
SEVEN YEARS OF REDISCOVERING THE SAME CITY
Paris itself has become an ongoing subject of this exploration. After returning from London in 2019, Urien began discovering the French capital through a photographer’s eyes, finding a city that, despite its extraordinary density of history, could still feel like a small village. Hidden museums, overlooked corners and art shops revealed themselves alongside the changing character of its neighborhoods. Over seven years, she has returned to familiar places through different seasons and everyday encounters, observing how the same setting can take on an entirely different atmosphere from one moment to the next. Photography and video have become her ways of tracing these subtle transformations.
This fascination with the city’s evolving identity also informs Paris is for the Dreamers, her forthcoming photography book project, conceived somewhere between an artistic collection and a personal guide to the capital. ‘We all have our own idea of a Paris shaped by paintings or movies,’ Urien reflects, while emphasizing that the real city continues to evolve with its seasons, stories and inhabitants. Her work offers neither an exercise in nostalgia nor an attempt to preserve Paris as an open-air museum. Instead, it suggests that the world of the Impressionists has never entirely disappeared. It simply requires a different way of looking.
project info:
name: Circa 2020s
artist: Alix Urien | @hifromalix
location: Paris and Normandy, France

Ukraine National Bank eases lending rules for defense and energy sectors
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:53:02 EEST
19:53:02 KST

The National Bank of Ukraine (NBU) has adopted a third package of regulatory measures to support lending to the economy, focusing on the defense-industrial complex (DIC), the energy sector and businesses affected by the war, the regulator said.
In particular, the collateral liquidity coefficient for property rights to revenue under contracts with entities in the security and defense sector, guaranteed by the electricity buyer and the transmission system operator, has been raised from 0.3 to 0.75.
The National Bank expects this measure to increase financing for defense-industrial and energy companies that hold state contracts but have limited ability to provide banks with traditional collateral.
Banks have also been authorized to take into account the value of goods held in inventory or undergoing processing and pledged as collateral for loans with terms of up to 18 months, based on their actual balance on the valuation date. This relaxation will remain in effect until September 1, 2027.
In addition, the central bank has expanded the ability to assess whether legal entities generate sufficient operating financial results to service their debt using projected figures if their property has been significantly damaged, destroyed or mined. Previously, this option was available to businesses operating in territories adjacent to the front line.
For loans under the 5-7-9% program, banks will be allowed to continue applying collective credit risk assessments or a simplified approach and will not be required to initiate nonperforming asset management procedures if the overdue payments arose solely because of delays in partial compensation for interest rates by the National Development Institution.
The amendments were approved by NBU Board Resolution No. 118 dated October 11, which entered into force on October 14.
As reported, in August and September, the NBU adopted the first two packages of regulatory measures to support lending amid intensified Russian shelling. They concerned, in particular, lending to the agricultural sector, manufacturers and companies implementing projects to restore critical infrastructure.

Industrial and digital trade
Bolat said Türkiye had spent the past year working to address concerns over restrictive provisions in the EU’s proposed Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA).
He warned that some measures in the draft legislation could affect future investment and disrupt integrated supply chains, particularly in the electric vehicle and automotive sectors.
Ankara is maintaining communications with EU officials to convey its expectations and reduce the potential economic impact of the proposed rules, he added.
Bolat also said the EU was coordinating with Türkiye on preparations for digital trade legislation. Türkiye remains exempt from a newly implemented EU regulation imposing a €3 fee per package, he said.
He cautioned that political intervention by the European Parliament could have adverse consequences, adding that many European officials also supported including Türkiye in the “Made in EU” origin framework.
However, he noted that the EU comprises countries with differing economic interests, urging a “calm and level-headed” approach.
Bolat said he had made three official visits to Brussels over the past three months, following five visits last year, and expressed hope for positive developments in the talks.
