Israel seeks urgent NIS 1b. purchase of Apache helicopters, diverting Arab sector funds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:35:13 UTC
19:35:13 KST

Israel’s Defense Ministry confirmed Wednesday that it has purchased 12 Apache attack helicopters from Boeing. Ministry Director General Maj.-Gen. (res.) Amir Baram instructed the ministry’s delegation in Washington to sign the agreement with the Pentagon.
“The helicopters, scheduled for delivery at the beginning of the next decade, are of the Echo variant, the newest and most advanced model of the helicopter,” the Defense Ministry said.
“The procurement of the Apache helicopters is a critical step in the IDF’s force buildup, one that will strengthen its operational capabilities against a wide range of threats and contribute to the security of the State of Israel in the years to come,” Defense Minister Israel Katz said.
“The Israeli defense establishment invested considerable effort and acted with determination to overcome the challenges and complete this agreement out of a deep understanding of its importance in ensuring the IDF’s strength and readiness for future challenges,” he noted.
“I thank our partners in the US administration and the Pentagon for their steadfast commitment to Israel’s security, and for the cooperation and flexibility that made this agreement possible. Thank you to all those involved, led by Baram, for their professional and dedicated work, and for the perseverance that led to the completion of this important procurement,” Katz said.
“The execution of the Apache agreement was made possible thanks to creative solutions we developed together with our American partners, without compromising operational needs,” Baram said.
“This professional work with the US administration reflects the depth of our strategic relationship and the mutual commitment to Israel’s security.
“The Defense Ministry will continue to work at full pace to sign additional critical agreements, including the acquisition of additional platforms, munitions, interceptors, and more. This is to ensure immediate readiness for any scenario, alongside the implementation of the decade-long force buildup plan as part of the Defense Ministry’s strategy in the face of emerging challenges,” he added.
“Boeing has been a trusted partner of Israel’s in building and advancing the country’s national defense capabilities since its earliest days, and we are proud to continue serving as a leading supplier of fighter aircraft, helicopters, munitions and other equipment in the future,” Boeing Israel President Maj.-Gen. (res.) Ido Nehushtan said.
“The IDF’s selection of the Apache Echo, following its selection of the world’s most advanced refueling aircraft, the KC-46A, and the decision to procure a second squadron of the world’s most advanced fighter jets, the F-15IA, is compelling proof of its proven operational capabilities on the battlefield and its continued relevance in addressing evolving threats and future operational challenges.
“Boeing will work in close cooperation with the Government of Israel to provide the Israel Air Force with the world’s most advanced and capable attack helicopters,” Nehushtan added. He served as IAF chief from 2008 until 2012 before leaving the military.
Arab sector funding diverted to Apache purchase
The government was preparing to allocate NIS 3.5 billion on Wednesday for urgent defense procurement, including a roughly NIS 1 billion deal to purchase Apache helicopters, The Jerusalem Post confirmed earlier on Wednesday.
The Finance Ministry told the Post that close to NIS 1 billion used for the Apache helicopter purchase would be diverted from funds earmarked for a five-year plan to develop Israel’s Arab sector. The remaining NIS 68 million would come from the 2026 state budget.
Government ministers were asked to approve the purchase via an urgent telephone vote, according to Israeli media.
The decision comes two weeks before the elections, a period during which the government must generally exercise restraint and avoid actions that are not particularly urgent.
A legal opinion attached to the government decision reportedly raised two main concerns: creating a situation in which the incoming government is faced with an irreversible situation, as well as risking prioritization of party interests over the public interest.
However, the document added that after examining the necessity and urgency of the decision to advance the procurement, bringing forward the procurement would be necessary for security reasons.
Shir Perets contributed to this report.

Russia Targets All Three of Kyiv’s Heat and Power Plants in Massive Missile Attack
Russian forces targeted all three of Kyiv’s combined heat and power plants in a large-scale missile attack on October 14, also striking critical energy infrastructure in Kharkiv and the surrounding region, according to Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi.
The Ukrainian prime minister said Russian ballistic missiles had specifically targeted energy facilities in Kyiv, Kharkiv, and the Kharkiv region, while additional strikes hit critical infrastructure in the Kyiv region responsible for supplying electricity to the capital and central parts of Ukraine.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“All three of the city's combined heat and power plants were attacked in the capital. The enemy also struck critical facilities in the Kyiv region that provide electricity to the capital and central regions,” Koretskyi stated.
Following the overnight strikes, emergency responders and energy workers were deployed to the affected sites, where firefighting operations and debris removal remained underway.
According to Koretskyi, repair crews had already begun initial restoration efforts at the damaged energy facilities as authorities worked to address the consequences of the attacks.
“Energy workers and rescuers have been working at the sites of the overnight attack since early morning. Firefighting and debris removal operations are ongoing. Specialists have already begun urgent restoration work at the targeted facilities,” the prime minister said.
During the overnight attack, Russian forces launched 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 drones, leaving at least 600,000 people without electricity. Ukrainian monitoring channels also reported an unprecedented barrage of approximately 25 Zircon missiles targeting Kyiv and the surrounding region.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed on October 14 that Russian strikes had damaged energy facilities and critical infrastructure in Kyiv, the Kyiv region, and Kharkiv, resulting in extensive power outages.
Zelenskyy described the assault as a deliberate attack on energy infrastructure that was supposed to be protected under the energy ceasefire announced by US President Donald Trump. He also characterized the scale of the strikes as an unusually direct challenge to Washington.
The latest attacks followed a two-day period during which Ukraine had refrained from striking Russian oil refineries and other energy facilities in response to Trump's announcement of the proposed ceasefire.
Despite Ukraine's decision to suspend such operations, Russian forces continued targeting Ukrainian energy infrastructure and other critical facilities, with attacks affecting 19 regions across the country during those two days, according to Zelenskyy.

Ukrainian Partisans Target Power Grid Feeding Russian Kh-101 Missile Components Factory
Unknown

19:35:00 KST

- Category

Ukrainian Partisans Target Power Grid Feeding Russian Kh-101 Missile Components Factory
Ukrainian partisan movement ATESH has claimed responsibility for sabotaging a critical electrical substation in Azov, Russia’s Rostov region, disrupting the power supply to a defense manufacturing facility involved in producing guidance systems and other components for Russian missiles.
According to ATESH on October 14, its agents carried out an explosion at a substation supplying electricity to the Azov Optical-Mechanical Plant, a facility that forms part of Russia’s Tactical Missiles Corporation.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The partisan movement said the operation disrupted the plant’s electricity supply, forcing key production workshops to suspend operations and affecting the manufacture of components used in Russian precision-guided weapons.
The Azov Optical-Mechanical Plant reportedly produces several specialized systems for Russia’s missile industry, including the Otblesk navigation lidar and flight automation units for Kh-101 cruise missiles.
The facility also manufactures radar homing heads, onboard thermal imaging equipment, and control systems used in R-37M, Kh-35U, and Kh-59/Kh-69 missiles, as well as ballistic missile systems, according to ATESH. The movement emphasized that these components play a critical role in the production of modern Russian missile systems, making the facility an important part of the country's defense-industrial supply chain.
Following the reported sabotage, the plant lost its stable electricity supply, leaving workshops responsible for assembling complex electronics, optical-mechanical equipment, and missile guidance systems without power.
ATESH claimed that the resulting emergency shutdown interrupted the facility's ongoing production cycle and disrupted deliveries of critical components intended for hundreds of Russian missiles.
In a separate attack overnight on October 14, Ukrainian drones struck a major data center operated by state-owned Sberbank in Balakovo, Saratov region. A nearby transport terminal was also reportedly targeted, while fires were recorded at several locations across the city's industrial district.
Ukrainian defense manufacturer Fire Point confirmed the strike on Sberbank's data center in an October 14 statement, also referencing earlier Ukrainian drone attacks against facilities operated by Russian technology company Yandex.

Germany to introduce sugar tax on soft drinks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:33:10 UTC
19:33:10 KST

Ayhan Şimşek
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
Germany’s governing coalition has agreed to introduce a tax on sugar-sweetened beverages starting July 1, 2027, resolving differences that had delayed the measure, the Finance Ministry confirmed.
Drinks with at least 5 grams of sugar per 100 milliliters will face a levy of 26 cents per liter, rising to 32 cents per liter for those with 8 grams or more, according to a draft obtained by German media outlet RND. The Cabinet is expected to endorse the plan on Wednesday.
Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil of the center-left SPD aims to raise revenue for the federal budget while encouraging manufacturers to reduce sugar content and offer healthier products. Officials project the tax will generate about €690 million ($773 million) in 2027 and €925 million ($1.04 billion) in 2028.
The Chancellery blocked Klingbeil’s earlier proposal at the start of the month, according to public broadcaster ARD. Chancellor Friedrich Merz faced pressure from his conservative CDU party after several state-level party officials argued that the levy amounted to state intervention and would impose unnecessary costs on consumers.
The measure comes as Germans consume far more sugar than the World Health Organization recommends. The WHO advises people of a healthy weight to limit sugar intake to no more than 50 grams a day, and preferably less than 25 grams, or about six teaspoons. Men in Germany consume an average of 78 grams a day and women 61 grams. When other sources of sugar are included, daily intake can reach 100 grams.

Ukraine warns of “a new type of humanitarian crisis” as Russia aims at its biggest cities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:32:37 UTC
19:32:37 KST

Ukraine is drafting crisis scenarios for November to March as Russian strikes target the country’s biggest cities, Head of the Presidential Office Kyrylo Budanov said on 13 October after chairing a meeting with donor-country diplomats and humanitarian organizations. His deputy Iryna Vereshchuk warned the same day that this winter may bring a new type of humanitarian crisis. She asked donors to be ready with fast extra funding.
Russia has struck Ukraine’s grid deep into winter before: last February, it launched more than 500 missiles and drones as temperatures fell below −20°C. Strikes have continued despite a US-announced energy truce Moscow has not confirmed. Kyiv now wants donors ready to pay for the humanitarian fallout in advance.
Crisis scenarios for November to March
The core task is clear crisis scenarios and synchronized response plans for that period, Budanov wrote. The government is building a baseline threat scenario through the State Emergency Service, while the military and intelligence will provide a risk assessment.
“The available resource must be concentrated where people will have the hardest time,” Budanov wrote.
Ukraine, he added, must hold its rear as reliably as the Defense Forces hold the front line.
What officials mean by a new type of crisis
A war of rear areas is underway, Vereshchuk wrote. Russia is changing tactics in an attempt to deepen the humanitarian crisis, especially in Kyiv, Kharkiv, Odesa, and Dnipro, she added.
Vereshchuk did not define what makes the crisis new, but she tied her warning to the big cities.
“This winter, it is the big cities that may become the testing ground of our national resilience,” she wrote.
Humanitarian organizations must adapt their plans to protect and support civilians, Vereshchuk wrote. Donors, she said, must be ready to provide additional crisis-response funding quickly.
The capital lags behind
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote on 13 October that even border and frontline oblasts were ahead of Kyiv on resilience plans as of mid-October. Even single hits by Shahed attack drones can cut power and water across much of the capital, he noted. He also began consultations on urgent security and management steps to fix the situation in the city.
Three days after Washington announced an energy ceasefire, Russia fires 39 ballistic missiles at Ukraine’s grid
Russia carried out more than 200 strikes on Ukraine’s power generation and transmission in the week to 11 October, Zelenskyy said. Overnight on 14 October, Russia fired 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 drones at energy and critical infrastructure. The barrage left at least 600,000 people without power, Zelenskyy said.

Colombia opens embassy in Jerusalem, marking dramatic diplomatic turnaround after Petro era
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:31:24 UTC
19:31:24 KST

Colombia inaugurated its new embassy in central Jerusalem on Wednesday, marking a major diplomatic shift following years of strained relations with Israel under former President Gustavo Petro. The ceremony was attended by Colombian Foreign Minister Omar Bula Escobar, Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar, Jerusalem Mayor Moshe Lion and Colombia's newly appointed ambassador to Israel, Tania Gilinski.
Gilinski assumed the position after three years without a Colombian ambassador in Israel, a period marked by Petro's criticism of Israel and its military campaign in Gaza. Her appointment followed the election of President Abelardo de la Espriella, who moved to restore diplomatic relations and strengthen cooperation between the two countries. 
The embassy is located in the historic Salameh Building on Rabbi Akiva Street in Jerusalem. The three-story building was constructed in the 1920s by Arab Christian businessman Constantine Salameh. In the early 1930s, it housed a well-known guesthouse called Goldschmidt House. During Wednesday's ceremony, the two foreign ministers affixed a mezuzah to the building's entrance.
Colombian Foreign Minister Bula Escobar described the opening as a new chapter in relations between the countries, emphasizing Colombia's commitment to restoring political dialogue and expanding their strategic partnership.
"We are renewing relations with greater strength, rebuilding our strategic partnership and reinforcing Colombia's presence in Israel," he said. "Relations between our countries should never have been damaged."
The minister noted that Colombia and Israel had maintained diplomatic relations for nearly seven decades, developing cooperation in trade, security, technology and other fields. He said the new embassy represented a tangible commitment to rebuilding ties that should never have been interrupted.
"Israel is a strategic partner. It always has been, and from now on it will be even more so," he said.
Bula Escobar highlighted security as a central priority, noting that Colombia faces threats from terrorism, drug trafficking and transnational organized crime. Addressing those challenges, he said, required strong national capabilities and international cooperation.
He also outlined plans to expand trade and develop partnerships linking universities, research institutions and businesses, particularly in artificial intelligence applications for export and public services.
"Today, with the opening of our embassy in Jerusalem, we are taking a decisive step toward strengthening relations between our countries," he said.
‘The 10th embassy in Jerusalem’
Foreign Minister Sa'ar welcomed the Colombian delegation and urged Jerusalem Mayor Moshe Lion to accelerate construction of additional office space to accommodate more foreign embassies.
"We are going to bring more embassies to Jerusalem," Sa'ar said. Turning to Gilinski, he added: "You've secured the best real estate in Jerusalem."
Sa'ar described the ceremony as a historic diplomatic achievement and emphasized the longstanding relationship between Israel and Colombia.
"Colombia is a sister nation and a strategic partner of Israel," he said. "The roots of our alliance run deep in history. Both countries share values of freedom, democracy and the pursuit of peace and security."
He pledged continued Israeli assistance to Colombia in addressing its security and humanitarian challenges, recalling that Israel had previously dispatched a delegation of 80 rescue and medical personnel following a devastating earthquake in the South American country.
"You can always count on us, on Israel, in good times and in challenging times," Sa'ar said.
The foreign minister also highlighted the growing number of diplomatic missions in Jerusalem.
"This is the 10th embassy in Jerusalem. When I took office, there were only five, and that number has doubled in two years. This is a major diplomatic achievement," he said.
Sa'ar argued that establishing embassies in Jerusalem represented both recognition of Israel's capital and acknowledgment of the city's historical significance to the Jewish people.
He said he would continue working to persuade additional countries to relocate their embassies.
"The 11th embassy, that of Congo, is on its way, and there will be more," Sa'ar said. "I know which country will be the 12th, but I can't reveal that."
‘Together, we can build something great’
Colombia's new ambassador, Tania Gilinski, said the relationship between the two countries had endured despite the severe deterioration in diplomatic ties during Petro's presidency.
She noted that Colombian businesspeople had continued working with Israeli partners and that young Israelis had continued traveling to Colombia, reflecting enduring connections between the countries.
"Colombia's new president immediately announced the restoration of relations with Israel and the relocation of Colombia's embassy to Jerusalem," Gilinski said.
She emphasized that both countries faced common challenges, particularly crime and terrorism, and expressed optimism about expanding their partnership.
"Colombia is committed to its alliance with Israel. We are two countries whose peoples are fighting crime, terrorism and the forces that divide us," she said. "Together, we can build something great."
Gilinski concluded with a tribute to her new diplomatic posting: "Jerusalem is a city of miracles, and Israel is a land of wonders."

UK watchdog probes US drug pricing deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:31:20 UTC
19:31:20 KST

Boxes of medication are seen on the shelves of the Keencare pharmacy, a member of the Green Light Group, on September 19, 2024 in London, England. | Leon Neal/Getty Images
LONDON — Britain’s public spending watchdog is probing the cost of Donald Trump’s drug pricing deal with the U.K., after six parliamentary committee chairs called for an investigation.
“I recognize that there is significant parliamentary interest in the arrangement, and I have therefore instructed my team to make preliminary enquiries about this matter,” the head of the National Audit Office (NAO), Gareth Davies, said in his response to lawmakers’ concerns.
The six committee chairs sent a letter to the NAO last month, urging the spending watchdog to investigate how much the U.K.-U.S. drug pricing deal will cost taxpayers and whether it offers value for money.
Advertisement
The deal saw the U.K. commit to doubling its spending on innovative medicines by 2035 from 0.3% to 0.6% of its GDP, in exchange for three years of tariff-free access to the U.S. market.
The government has said the deal will cost £1 billion over the current spending review period, with no additional funding to be announced in the budget this year. However, officials have refused to disclose the deal's full cost, arguing that doing so could harm international relations and commercial interests.
“Without a comprehensive impact assessment covering future years, parliament and the public are unable to fully understand the long-term implications of the agreement for NHS budgets and wider public expenditure,” the lawmakers wrote.
The letter was signed by Health and Social Care Committee Chair Layla Moran; Science, Innovation and Technology Committee Chair Chi Onwurah; Business and Trade Committee Chair Liam Byrne; Northern Ireland Affairs Committee Chair Tonia Antoniazzi; Scottish Affairs Committee Chair Patricia Ferguson; and Welsh Affairs Committee Chair Ruth Jones.
“I understand that there has been limited parliamentary scrutiny of the arrangement itself, and the government has no plans to publish the details of how the costs and benefits have been modelled,” Davies wrote in response.
Davies said that he would follow up with the committee chairs, once the NAO completes its initial enquiries.

NATO chief says US-Ukraine intelligence sharing has not stopped

Melike Pala
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said Wednesday that intelligence sharing between the US and Ukraine has not stopped, citing remarks by US President Donald Trump.
Speaking at a joint press conference with Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal in Tallinn, Rutte said Trump had made clear that intelligence sharing was continuing.
“I think the president was very clear yesterday when he had a short moment with the media leaving the White House for a campaign event, when he said intelligence sharing has not stopped,” Rutte said.
His remarks came in response to a question about whether he had spoken with Trump following reports that SpaceX had reduced Starlink speeds for Ukrainian users.
“With winter coming, and with Russia’s aggression unrelenting, allies need to do more, especially in support of air defense,” he said, adding that Russia’s actions would not weaken the alliance’s resolve.
“(Russian President Vladimir) Putin is trying to weaken our resolve and stop our support for Ukraine, but Russia is failing. It is failing on the battlefield in Ukraine, and we will not be intimidated,” Rutte said, describing Russia’s alleged hybrid activities as a sign of “weakness.”
He said NATO had prepared for Russian hybrid and cyber threats and had the necessary response options, although not all responses would be made public.
Asked whether Russia might consider attacking a NATO member state, Rutte said the alliance saw no imminent threat to its territory.
He said NATO would defend its members but stressed that the alliance remained strictly defensive.
“We will never ever mount an attack towards anyone else because that is not in our interest,” Rutte stressed.

MOSCOW, Oct 14 - Russian President Vladimir Putin will discuss cybersecurity with top officials on Wednesday, the Kremlin said, describing it as an increasingly pressing issue but denying the meeting was prompted by a spate of Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian data centres.
"Artificial intelligence technologies bring many benefits and advantages, boosting efficiency. But at the same time, of course, attempts by various states to weaponize these new technologies... pose threats to entire sectors of any country's economy," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters.
"Naturally, we are no exception, and we must be prepared for these challenges. That is why the president is holding this meeting today."

"No, this is a much more systemic meeting. It is not connected to those specific, isolated attacks," he said.

JackRabbit MG Cargo Bike Review (2026): Compact and Powerful
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

Petite, lightweight, and kind of kicky for a cargo bike. Can fit in a car’s back seat. Fat tires provide stability. Cushy bike seat is comfortable for long rides. So many accessories. Surprising 500-pound payload.
TIRED
Fast braking requires a firm hand. Range is middling. Battery indicator sneaks up on you. Not as petite as other JackRabbits. Technically a scooter, not an ebike.
I am not an obvious target customer for a cargo ebike, as I neither have kids to tote nor a large space for bike parking. But the new JackRabbit MG Cargo is so tiny, it doesn't conjure the dully utilitarian, heedlessly bulky nature that's common to other cargo ebike models. In fact, when I tested the wee, plucky ebike, I found its fat tires and tiny wheelbase make it feel more like a speedy urban dirt bike than anything else.
But despite being a relative lightweight (55 pounds) and petite enough to fit in the back seat of my old Montero, the MG sports a 750-watt motor that can haul nine times the bike's weight uphill. I even threw a grill onto a bike trailer to test this claim, which held up.
Note that likeall JackRabbits WIRED testers have reviewed, the MG is less an ebike than a scooter that looks and acts like an ebike: Instead of pedals, you get pedal-like footrests, plus a throttle. This means when the battery runs out, the bike stops moving. Also, the listed 48-mile range drops considerably when you ride at top speed or haul a large load. Nonetheless, the MG may have converted me to the pannier class.
After testing this MG for a couple of months, I no longer use my car when I need groceries, even when I'm taking a longer trek to the Grocery Outlet for discount steaks or salmon. The same is true when I want to haul a slushie machine across Portland’s steep mid-city ridge to a friend's house for cheeky weekday margaritas. By not acting like a cargo bike, the MG has convinced me to haul cargo on a bike.
Zippy Little Devil
Photograph: Matthew Korfhage
“How exactly is this a cargo bike?” my editor asked when I showed her a photo of the MG Cargo after it arrived. She wasn't asking out of wonderment. As mentioned, the MG flat-out looks less like a bike you'd use to haul stuff and more like a dirt bike.
JackRabbit is known for making lightweight, zippy, fun little scooter hybrids that physically resemble BMX trick bikes. I loved the easy mobility and high-speed capability of JackRabbit's equally powerful XG Pro (8/10, WIRED Recommends) when I tested that model last year. I'd worried that the MG Cargo—18 pounds heavier and nearly a foot longer than the XG—would compromise too much on these virtues. I needn't have worried. As I quickly learned, the pleasantly peppy MG rides like an off-road bike when you're not hauling a big load.
Its three throttle speeds max out at about 20 mph, 15 mph, and 7 mph, respectively. The lowest speed is manageable for a sidewalk, while the fastest hits top speed within about 50 feet on flat ground, unless you've got some weight behind (or on) you. The MG advertises a range of 48 miles, though I'll assume this requires being a lighter rider who is gentle on the throttle. As a man north of 200 pounds with an admittedly heavy throttle thumb, I only made it to about 25 miles, even with minimal cargo. Because the bike's battery indicator shows up as at least half-full for the vast majority of this range, you'll need to test and learn your personal range when doing so is not mission-critical.
Note that because JackRabbits don't have working pedals, the bikes exist in an interesting technical gray area in some states in terms of their classification. Specifically, one could debate whether they're really a Class 2 ebike that can ride on bike lanes and trails. Given the MG's maximum speed of 20 mph—aside from an honor-system 24-mph jailbreak speed you can unlock for off-road riding—it mostly looks and quacks like a Class 2 ebike. In my experience, it's also treated as such.
The MG also offers nice customization options for accessorizing. It's easy to add a couple of rear pannier bags to the rear mounting rack or side racks ($75) on each side, offering enough capacity for most small grocery trips or beach excursions without adding much bulk. You could also opt for a rear basket.
Photograph: Matthew Korfhage
While I can't quite stow the MG as easily as other JackRabbit models, it's still small enough that I can slide it into my back seat—as long as I uncork the front handlebars and turn its front wheel backward. (Some sources refer to the MG as “foldable,” but this isn't strictly true: it just has a quick-release wheel and an easily removed handlebar.)
Which is to say, even without the cargo component, I could like the MG just as a fun little commuter, especially with the welcome addition of a cushy Kinekt active-suspension seat post that provides some added give for longer rides.
The Little Cargo Ebike That Could
Despite its petite size, the MG performs well as a true cargo hauler that you could use to move trailers full of groceries or the more precious cargo of your own children. I didn't borrow any kids to test rear child trailers or JackRabbit's mini-me rear seat and handlebar set ($175). But I did use the MG's preinstalled Burley trailer hitch to haul a box containing a 150-pound grill up a hill with a 7 percent grade. While the MG didn't get to full speed on the ascent, it pulled the grill and my 200-plus-pound self surprisingly well.
The MG's stability and cornering capabilities also fared better than I expected, given its short base. Cargo bikes tend to lengthen their frame to add stability and make room for riders to pedal comfortably while carrying loads on the front or the back. The MG Cargo's stability mostly comes from its cushy fat tires, largely thanks to the clever design of the larger front tire, which both adds stability up front on rugged terrain and lowers the center of gravity where cargo hangs. The lack of pedaling also naturally removes some wobble.
You will make compromises, though: Cornering can be jumpy, leading to the occasional overcorrection. The range also drops considerably with heavy carries, given that you can't add your own pedal power. Braking is fast but does require a good grip, especially with larger loads downhill.
For the Occasional Hauler
The MG Cargo lives in an interesting middle ground between commuter and cargo ebike. If I were primarily using it to transport children or work gear, I'd probably opt for a bulkier hauler or the Specialized Global Haul ST, WIRED's top-pick electric cargo bike that offers a more reliable long range.
The best use cases for the MG Cargo are as a fun recreational ebike that stows easily into your back seat or as a multipurpose commuter with built-in storage that saves its rider from needing to wear a backpack. In either case, the cargo capabilities function as bonus features as opposed to being the main draw.
It's less a workhorse than a hobby pony: I've slipped books and a blanket into a pannier so I can read at the park, and I've spontaneously brought home six-packs from the brewery a couple of miles down the road. When I grocery shop using the MG Cargo, I'm spared the bother of tightly packed parking lots that make me angry before I reach the aisles. I zip in, I unlock the panniers, pop in my groceries, and zip right back out. In this way, the MG Cargo also doubles as the cheapest therapist I know.
Matthew Korfhage was a staff writer on WIRED’s Reviews team, where he focused on coffee, home, and home office technology. He also covered food, drink, business, technology, and culture for more than a decade at USA Today Network, The Virginian-Pilot, and his hometown newspaper in Portland, Oregon. His reporting has ... The Politics of Solar Energy Are Getting Weird, Mean, and a Little MAGA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

A mysteriously named political action committee has started running ads reminding voters in Colorado about that time GOP representative Lauren Boebert of Colorado and her date were caught on camera in 2023 getting handsy during a performance of the musical Beetlejuice.
That same PAC is producing a spot hitting Anthony Constantino, a Trumpist congressional candidate in upstate New York, because someone used his sticker-printing company to briefly make stickers that read, “Kill the Police.”
Attack ads are everywhere in the last month ahead of November’s election. But these spots are a little different. The semi-anonymous PAC that’s funding and making the ads, the Invest in Tomorrow Coalition, is a pro-solar-energy outfit. It’s funded in part by crypto billionaire Chris Larsen and run by a team of New York City political operatives.
“Playing hardball politics, that's what our opponents do, right, in oil and gas? And I just think the solar industry has been—I don't know how to describe it—a little too nice,” says Larsen, the cofounder of the blockchain finance firm Ripple and a major backer of the Invest in Tomorrow Coalition.
Green groups don’t usually act like this, with knives out, ready to stab opponents between the ribs. They tend to make appeals based on scientific consensus, or fears of what will happen to a warming planet without collective action. They’re also traditionally Democratic, but a few high-profile members of the MAGA movement are now speaking up for solar too. Texas, the home of the fossil fuel business, has quickly become a solar powerhouse. There are some signs that the Trump administration’s across-the-board opposition to solar may be starting to crack, at least a little, after years of slashing greentech subsidies and throwing up one roadblock after another to clean power projects.
Some of Larsen’s natural allies in the renewables field aren’t too happy about the PAC’s efforts, arguing that they’re alienating the decisionmakers they need most. But the politics of energy, especially solar energy, are changing.
Larsen’s PAC is devoting $15 million to go after seven of the more prominent opponents of renewable energy in this year’s congressional elections. That’s on top of roughly $5 million they’ve already spent in the primaries, cutting ads against Republican representatives Ralph Norman of South Carolina (whom the PAC called a “MAGA traitor”), Andy Ogles of Tennessee (“He doesn’t even bother going to work”), and Chip Roy (“chosen the side of powerful pedophiles”) of Texas. A PAC that received funding from Invest in Tomorrow has also gone after one Democrat, Rhode Island governor Dan McKee. All four lost their primary races.
In Roy’s case, the Invest in Tomorrow Coalition spent almost $1.5 million to stop his run for Texas attorney general. Most of the money went to ads on right-wing platforms like Truth Social and Rumble. The word “solar” was never mentioned.
“Don't talk about renewables. Don't talk about climate,” says Chris Coffey, the chief executive of the consultancy Tusk Strategies, which is running the PAC. “Pick the best issue that we can pick. And in a Republican primary, we should savage this guy for not being MAGA enough.”
Roy received a 100 percent rating from Heritage Action, the political arm of the Trumpist think tank. Coffey said he got some pushback from a few Democratic operatives, who were concerned that replacements for Roy and other PAC targets might not be any less extreme—on climate or any other issue. Without their far-right track record, the argument went, those replacements might even be stronger candidates in the general election.
“Who fucking cares? Who cares? Like, it can't be worse,” Coffey, a veteran of New York City mayor Michael Bloomberg’s City Hall, says in response. “At least we'll have extracted some payback.”
The PAC is currently putting $2 million into ads blasting GOP representative Victoria Spartz of Indiana as allegedly corrupt; it’s aiming to target Texas Republican Brandon Herrera for his “abolish old people” jokes and his plan to get rid of Social Security. Then there is the $1.5 million ad campaign about Boebert and the Beetlejuice incident. “If Lauren Boebert can’t be trusted in a room full of kids, then she can’t be trusted in the halls of Congress,” the commercial’s narrator says.
Other special-interest organizations have been running this playbook for decades. Groups supporting labor and opposing gun regulations regularly try to make examples of politicians who oppose their agenda. Green groups haven’t been as aggressive historically. That’s a problem, says Steph Bosh, the board chair of the Community Clean Energy Coalition. While her group has raised nearly $2 million to promote their favored hyperlocal candidates this cycle—and the League of Conservation Voters’ affiliated super PAC is spending another $50 million—Bosh says she appreciates that someone else is taking a less friendly approach.
“As a broad renewable energy industry, we need to be loved, respected, and feared,” Bosh adds. “We need to have a carrot, and we need to have a stick.”
James Carville, the Democratic pundit and former campaign manager, doubts the stick is big enough. “Twenty million—what the fuck do you think the carbon industry spends in a year?” he recently said to the Washington Monthly.
Roy, for his part, insisted that the PAC’s spending had played “zero role” in his race (while his campaign staff put out statements denouncing the “radical California Marxists trying to buy Texas elections”). Ralph Norman, his fellow solar target, warned about the “elite” taking out “the $1 million attack ad against me,” while Ogles complained, “they literally are trying to make an example out of me.”
“They were the difference maker,” Chris Burger, a Republican political consultant in Tennessee, says of the pro-solar group. “I don't think Charlie [Hatcher, Ogles’ primary opponent] wins if the PAC doesn't come in with $2 million.”
The Trump White House and its allies in Congress have been beyond hostile to renewables, which they believe to be intermittent sources of energy, and dominated by China. The administration has done everything it can to promote the production of oil, gas, and coal, while kneecapping renewable alternatives, from tying green projects in bureaucratic knots to pulling billions of dollars’ worth of solar subsidies and paying companies billions more to stop offshore wind farm construction. Then the Trump team tried to get other countries to adopt similar attitudes. “If you don’t get away from the green energy scam, your country is going to fail,” the president told the United Nations General Assembly last year.
But the Trumpists have been slightly less hostile to solar than to offshore wind farms, which, according to the president, cause cancer, “kill all your birds,” and drive whales “crazy.”
“While wind is dead, solar is merely in the ICU,” Richard Goldberg, a former member of the administration's National Energy Dominance Council, tells WIRED.
That has provided a small but real opening to promote solar to the America First set, especially with energy prices spiking at home, the war in Iran pushing up oil prices around the world, and the spread of AI data centers creating a borderline-insatiable need for more power.
In February, the American Clean Power Association launched a campaign to do just that, releasing a poll from former Trump campaign manager Kellyanne Conway’s consulting company showing that 75 percent of MAGA voters in key states supported the idea of adding more solar energy to the national mix. According to an internal memo reviewed by Politico, soon to follow were “paid media partnerships with podcasts like the Katie Miller Pod” (hosted by the former DOGE spokesperson, who is married to White House deputy chief of staff for policy Stephen Miller) as well as “advertorials and sponsorships with right-of-center publications.”
Katie Miller, once a consultant for Elon Musk, a renewable energy advocate, has repeatedly pushed for solar on social media since then. “Over 70 percent of the new utility-scale capacity went into states won by President Trump,” reads one of her posts. “Electricity generation is a national security issue—not a partisan one.” (Miller, who did not respond to requests to comment for this story, has previously denied receiving any funding from the clean power group.)
There’s also the data center issue. China hasn’t had problems powering its data centers, thanks in part to its widespread deployment of renewables—315 gigawatts of solar added to the grid last year, about six times more than the United States added from all sources combined. The US is in an entirely different situation. MAGA-minded promoters of solar are trying to leverage that gap to make a Trumpy argument for renewable energy. Concerns about the climate are out; fears about losing the AI race to China are in.
T1 Energy, which bills itself as one of the few truly all-American solar manufacturing companies, has hired Checkmate Government Relations, a lobbying firm led by Donald Trump Jr.’s old hunting buddy, and Tower Strategy, helmed by a former CIA operations officer, Rick De La Torre, to press its case in the administration. These lobbyists have tried to make the case that the administration’s beef isn’t with solar in general; it’s with Chinese solar. They’ve done it in the kind of pec-flexing language that’s become MAGA’s stock-in-trade.
“American-made, utility-scale solar is one of the few technologies that can be deployed at the speed and scale required” for data centers, De La Torre posted on LinkedIn. “China knows this. That is why it continues to flood markets, compress margins, and keep U.S. manufacturers on the defensive. Undercut. Outscale. Outlast.”
“Washington has a choice. Treat solar manufacturing as a strategic industry, the way we now treat semiconductors and critical minerals,” he added. Or only claim “to compete with Beijing.”
There are some indications that the argument may be gaining traction. In August, the Trump administration added a new 15 percent tariff and price floors on foreign-made solar components. T1’s CEO hailed it as a victory for domestic supply chains and manufacturing. More recently, negotiations in Congress are continuing on a bipartisan permitting reform bill that would, among many other things, make it easier for solar providers to plug into the electric grid.
Which led some solar executives to question whether it’s smart for the group to beat up on Republicans, right as a few of them seem to be creeping in solar’s direction.
“We’ve been hard at work speaking to Republicans about why supporting solar and batteries helps with energy abundance and affordability. And we’ve been successful. If this [Invest in Tomorrow Coalition] becomes about going after Republicans and turns solar back into a partisan issue, that would be an epic blunder,” says Russell Gold, T1’s executive vice president for strategic communications.
Tom Matzzie, the chief executive of solar company CleanChoice Energy, is serving as executive chair of the Invest in Tomorrow Coalition PAC. Cofounders include Peter Davidson, CEO of the investment firm Aligned Climate Capital, and Michael Brune, former executive director of the Sierra Club. But it’s Larsen who supplied the lion’s share of the early money for the PAC—$6 million of the initial $7 million or so it had raised through August 31, according to federal election commission records.
He’s had an uneven record of political giving, of late. Earlier this year, Larsen spent $3.5 million to support congressional candidate Alex Bores, who was targeted by the AI industry and lost his race. Larsen’s company, Ripple Labs, has donated nearly $100 million to Fairshake, the pro-crypto PAC, which racked up electoral successes in 2024 but just lost a major fight when its preferred bill to regulate cryptocurrencies died in the Senate.
The willingness to go on the attack isn’t the only way that Larsen’s PAC differs from others in the green movement. Not that long ago, renewable advocates talked about an “energy transition” away from old, dirty fossil fuels and toward newer, cleaner ones. Larsen is suggesting instead to red-district politicians that they embrace the idea of fossil and renewable energy sources existing side-by-side, even as the PAC he funds throws haymakers at solar’s enemies.
“You could be pro oil and gas and pro solar,” he says.

Ministry urges next government to tackle transport tax reform without delay
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:29:25 EEST
19:29:25 KST

The Ministry of Transport and Communications is urging the incoming government to implement a reform of transport taxation, warning in a new statement that further delay is no longer an option.
Transport tax revenues are set to fall sharply over the next decade as vehicles become increasingly battery-powered. The ministry also points to mounting pressure to raise transport taxation given the state of public finances.
Olli-Pekka Rantala, Head of Department at the Ministry of Transport and Communications, says current emission-based taxation is working as intended, but that very success is eroding the funding base.
The ministry’s statement follows a similar one issued by the Ministry of Finance last week.
1. Vehicle tax overhaul likely as electric car numbers grow
To secure sufficient funding for basic road maintenance, the ministry proposes linking vehicle tax to road maintenance costs. Currently, a significant portion of vehicle tax is based on a car's carbon dioxide emissions, while the state also levies a seperate fuel tax on vehicles that do not run on petrol.
"It is likely that taxation of electric vehicles would become stricter as a result. In that case, it will be essential to ensure through other means that road traffic emissions are reduced in line with Finland's international commitments," Rantala says.
Under the ministry's policy, tax revenue collected from transport should continue to cover at least the costs and nuisances caused by it.
The finer details of any tax changes, Rantala notes, will need to be worked out together with the Ministry of Finance.
2. Emission targets remain non-negotiable
Even if the focus of vehicle taxation shifts, the ministry stresses that emission targets must still be met through a broad set of tools — including transport emissions trading, energy taxation, distribution obligations and other EU legislation.
The EU's new road transport emissions trading system (ETS2), takes effect in 2028 and will impact fuel prices, according to Rantala.
The ministry also ties the shift away from fossil fuels directly to national security.
"It is also a security measure. Giving up fossil fuels strengthens Finland's strategic independence, since we won't be dependent on oil imports," Rantala says.
3. Congestion charges and even road tolls could be introduced
With public finances under strain, the ministry has also been exploring new ways to fund major road and rail projects — including new user fees and cost-sharing arrangements among those who benefit from them.
This approach, they argue, would help guide the selection of economically efficient projects. In practice, this could mean collecting separate user fees from those who use a major new road or railway line.
The ministry also wants regional congestion charges introduced in large urban areas, with revenue from such charges planned and agreed jointly with the cities concerned.
4. Maintaining existing infrastructure remains top priority
The ministry's statement also flags the poor condition of Finland's road and rail network. With funding already insufficient to repair anything beyond the busiest routes, the backlog of repairs — now at 4.3 billion euros including railways — is set to keep growing.
Sabina Lindström, Head of Department at the Ministry of Transport and Communications, says maintaining existing infrastructure — basic road upkeep in particular — remains the top priority.
Without confirmed funding, the current savings trajectory will have to tighten further, with direct consequences for provisional and lower-tier roads.
"In practice, this means that we can maintain these busiest routes, but unfortunately, all those that fall into a lower category will continue to receive too little maintenance," Lindström says.
Some in the public debate have occasionally floated the idea of stripping asphalt from roads in poor condition and converting them to gravel. Lindström says this offers little relief.
"Removing the surface is already part of the solution, and it's done every year. Unfortunately, it doesn't solve the problem. It's costly in itself, and maintaining a gravel road isn't cheap either. It's done on an appropriate scale," Lindström says.

Yemen: Sanaa fuel crisis erupts after Saudi-led coalition strike
A fuel crisis has hit Yemen's Houthi-controlled capital Sanaa after the Saudi-led coalition warned civilians to leave a major oil storage facility before carrying out strikes.
The coalition issued an evacuation warning for the Yemen Petroleum Company's al-Sabaha central station on the western outskirts of the capital.
The warning prompted residents and drivers to rush to petrol stations amid fears that attacks on fuel infrastructure could lead to shortages.
Al-Sabaha is one of the Yemen Petroleum Company's main storage sites in Sanaa and is believed to hold at least 200,000 litres of fuel.
The facility, which contains four main storage tanks, plays an important role in supplying the capital and surrounding areas.
The New Arab witnessed queues forming at petrol stations across Sanaa, with congestion forcing some to temporarily stop serving vehicles.
Residents said they feared shortages of petrol, diesel and cooking gas at a time when household finances are already under severe pressure.
Mohammed Abdul-Qawi said he went to secure cooking gas for his family because he was concerned supplies could disappear if the crisis worsened.
Truck driver Ali Jaber said a fuel shortage could leave him without an income.
"My livelihood and my family's livelihood depend on the vehicle I work with," he told The New Arab.
Transport workers are particularly vulnerable because thousands of families rely on income from trucks, taxis, buses and other vehicles.
Farmers could also be affected because diesel is widely used to pump water from wells and irrigate agricultural land.
Commercial electricity generators, which many residents depend on for power, could also face disruption or higher operating costs if fuel becomes scarce.
The tensions escalated further when Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree warned employees and civilians to leave areas near Saudi Aramco facilities.
He said the group's forces could target Aramco sites in Saudi Arabia if the coalition struck the facility in Sanaa.
Saree named Aramco's facilities in Dammam, King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and the company's Riyadh refinery among possible targets.
He also renewed warnings to airlines, airports, passengers and workers at Saudi aviation facilities.
The Saudi-led coalition subsequently carried out strikes on the Yemen Petroleum Company facility in Sanaa.
Strikes were also reported at Ras Isa oil port in Hodeidah province.
Ras Isa is one of three main Red Sea ports in Hodeidah used by the Houthi authorities to receive imported fuel.
The latest escalation follows months of renewed confrontation between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed government, including a new offensive around Sanaa and growing military activity across Yemen.
The Houthis have also threatened shipping in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab as the conflict has widened.
In July, the group announced what it described as a maritime embargo against Saudi Arabia, threatening further escalation in response to coalition attacks.

Australian researchers develop eye tests to detect early signs of dementia
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
18:28:16 CST
19:28:16 KST

SYDNEY, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- Researchers in Australia have developed new visual tests that could help detect early signs of dementia associated with Parkinson's disease, potentially enabling earlier diagnosis.
The researchers at Australia's University of Queensland (UQ) led the development of the tests to detect early signs of dementia in Lewy body disease, which includes Parkinson's disease and dementia with Lewy bodies, according to a UQ statement released on Wednesday.
Lewy body disease is the second most common form of degenerative dementia and occurs when Lewy bodies, abnormal clumps of a protein called alpha-synuclein, build up in the brain's nerve cells and interfere with how they work.
Difficulty processing visual information is an early feature of Lewy body disease and can appear before other obvious symptoms, said neurologist Professor Peter Nestor from UQ's Queensland Brain Institute, who led the development of the tests.
The researchers examined two visual pathways: one involved in recognizing what we are looking at, and the other in processing where something is located.
The study, published in the Journal of Neurology, examined visual processing across the full spectrum of Lewy body disease, including in people with Parkinson's disease who were not experiencing any cognitive symptoms, as well as people with Alzheimer's disease.
Results showed that visual problems were worse for those with Lewy body disease than Alzheimer's disease, with the two conditions affecting visual processing pathways differently. Visual hallucinations, a common symptom of Lewy body disease, were also closely linked to visual processing difficulties, the study showed.
Nestor said the new tests can detect the very earliest signs of emerging dementia in Lewy body disease, including in some people with Parkinson's disease who were not yet aware of their visual processing difficulties. ■

Rajnath Singh highlighted the centuries-old close ties between India and Southeast Asia.
Defence minister Rajnath Singh said on Wednesday that “India seeks an Indo-Pacific where all countries — large and small — make their own choices, protect their interests and pursue development in peace” and called for building trust, respecting each other’s sovereignty, following international law and keeping channels of dialogue open to tackle both emerging and conventional “borderless challenges”.Addressing the maiden Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) - India Defence Think Tank Forum at Manohar Parrikar Institute for Defence Studies and Analyses, the minister asserted that India and ASEAN share a clear interest in peace, stability, prosperity and an open and inclusive Indo-Pacific. He emphasised that India’s Act East policy and the vision of SAGAR (Security and Growth for All in the Region) and MAHASAGAR (Mutual and Holistic Advancement for Security and Growth Across Regions) advocate for an open and multipolar cooperation, and the nation aligns them through ASEAN-led mechanisms that are central to its Indo-Pacific vision.On defence industrial cooperation, Rajnath asserted that India is ready to explore cooperation with ASEAN partners in areas such as patrol vessels, radars, air-defence systems, helicopters, drones and other technologies, according to each country’s needs and priorities. He said the ‘Aatmanirbhar Bharat’ initiative focuses on building stronger domestic capabilities, but self-reliance does not mean working in isolation.
It can create opportunities for trusted partners to design, build, maintain and improve equipment together, he said. Underlining the importance of co-development, co-production, maintenance, repair and overhaul, training and long-term technical support, he said these arrangements can build local skills, support industry and make supply chains more reliable.Rajnath noted that the region is witnessing rapid changes in the face of growing strategic competition and pressure and uncertainty created at times through actions at sea, in addition to threats such as terrorism, cybercrime, piracy, trafficking, illegal fishing, climate-related disasters and risks to vital supply chains. No country alone can address these challenges, he said. Rajnath underlined the need to discuss differences early and peacefully, before they become disputes, and pitched for a regional order where countries work together without being forced to choose sides. “India believes that security is strengthened when countries build capacity together, respect international law and maintain trust through dialogue,” he said.He highlighted the centuries-old close ties between India and Southeast Asia rooted in shared history, culture, trade and ideas, reiterating that the Act East Policy is a long-term commitment to working with the region as an equal partner.Rajnath said that keeping the Indian Ocean and waters of Southeast Asia safe is a shared responsibility as they are part of one connected maritime space, crucial for trade, energy, people and essential goods. He stressed that as 2026 has been designated as ASEAN-India Year of Maritime Cooperation, it is an opportunity to turn shared interest into practical action. “We should improve the sharing of maritime information, strengthen cooperation among our navies and coast guards, and build the ability to respond together to emergencies.
We should also work against piracy, trafficking, illegal fishing and other threats, in accordance with international law,” he said.Terming defence technology as another crucial area, Rajnath pointed out that AI, drones, cyber capabilities and space-based systems are becoming increasingly important, with recent conflicts demonstrating that relatively low-cost drones can challenge expensive defence systems. He underscored the need to respond with practical, affordable and adaptable solutions.“India believes that innovation should not remain limited to a few large organisations. Start-ups, universities, research institutions and smaller companies can all contribute. India’s initiatives like Innovations for Defence Excellence (iDEX) and Technology Development Fund (TDF) have created a way to collaborate with innovators for our defence needs,” he said.

====================================================================================================

Convicted Belgian Cocaine Boss Poured Millions Into Luxury Dubai Properties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:27:00 UTC
19:27:00 KST

Convicted Belgian Cocaine Boss Poured Millions Into Luxury Dubai Properties
A Belgian drug lord spent millions of dollars investing in luxury real estate in Dubai. Belgian authorities successfully extradited him today, but it’s unclear what has happened to the profits he reaped from his property ventures in the emirate.
Banner:
Geraint Tellem/Robert Harding RF/robertharding via AFP
|
The Dubai skyline.
Based in the Netherlands, Ingrid Gercama joined OCCRP in 2025 as an investigative editor. Before joining OCCRP, she worked as a freelance investigative journalist reporting on crime, the environment, and politics. Her work has been published in more than fifteen countries, with bylines in major outlets including The Guardian and Süddeutsche Zeitung.
Ingrid has uncovered the illegal smuggling of tropical birds to the EU, reported on the operations of Balkan organized crime groups in the Netherlands and Belgium, revealed fraud with EU funds in Romania, and covered anti-corruption protests in Serbia and Georgia. Her cross-border investigations have contributed to law enforcement actions and she has won multiple awards.
Prior to becoming a journalist, Ingrid worked as an applied anthropologist in Ebola outbreaks in Africa, as well as in humanitarian aid and research. She studied cultural anthropology at the University of Amsterdam and holds a master’s degree in international development studies.
Belgian drug lord Nasserdine Tarrahi, who has been convicted of drug-related offenses in three separate cases, was extradited from Dubai to Belgium on October 14, the Antwerp prosecutor’s office confirmed to OCCRP and De Tijd.
Tarrahi, 38, was a senior figure in the “Turtles,” a Belgian-Moroccan gang that specialized in retrieving South American cocaine from containers passing through the port of Antwerp. Later in his career he fled to Dubai, where he continued to run drug trafficking operations from the Emirati city-state, according to the most recent court verdict against him, issued in May.
But although Belgian justice has finally caught up with him, authorities have struggled to confiscate the proceeds of his crimes, which a court in Antwerp estimated could amount to 5 million euros ($5.5 million). They only managed to find the equivalent of around $20,000 in cash, plus an assortment of exercise equipment crammed into an apartment in Antwerp he used as a base for drug trafficking.
Now, OCCRP and its partners in Belgium have learned that Tarrahi had stashed substantial assets abroad: He purchased six luxury properties in Dubai between 2019 and 2021, investing the equivalent of $6.2 million, according to property data obtained by OCCRP.
Although he has sold all the properties since then, the findings suggest he was able to move a significant amount of wealth into Dubai unbeknownst to authorities — and even profit from his real estate deals. Three of his properties were purchased for a total of $3.8 million and sold for $6.6 million three years later. (The sales price of the others is not known.)
About the Data
This story draws on several datasets and leaks obtained by OCCRP and partners about property ownership in Dubai, including our Dubai Unlocked project, a scrape of the Dubai Land Department, and financial data of facilities management firms in Dubai.
He was even able to gain permanent residency in Dubai based on his property holdings — with a visa issued barely a year after he was convicted in Belgium of trafficking drugs from his Dubai home base, OCCRP has learned.
Tarrahi’s lawyer did not respond to a request for comment. Under Belgian law, Tarrahi has the right to appeal the verdict of the Antwerp court when he arrives back on Belgian soil.
Dubai’s General Directorate of Residency and Foreigners Affairs and the UAE’s Ministry of Interior did not respond to requests for comment from OCCRP.
Credit: Elien Melis/Sky Vision/Port of Antwerp-Bruges
The port of Antwerp, where the "Turtles" were active.
Known for financial secrecy and low taxes, Dubai is where many of the world’s rich and powerful go to spend money they are unable to use elsewhere. A 2024 collaborative investigation by OCCRP and partners, Dubai Unlocked, mapped some 800,000 Dubai properties and found that many were owned by sanctioned politicians, alleged criminals, and or public officials and family.
Since then, the United Arab Emirates has passed a new anti-money laundering law that authorities promise will ease cross-border collaboration. The Belgian Justice Ministry says Dubai has been cooperative with a new drive to extradite criminals, but experts say it’s still unclear if the UAE is serious about targeting illicit wealth within its borders.
“Investigative reporting has repeatedly identified Dubai properties linked to individuals implicated in major corruption scandals … yet public information remains limited on whether UAE authorities investigated the potential laundering of illicit proceeds through those properties, and with what results,” said Hugh Jorgensen, the Corrupt Money Flows program lead at Transparency International.
A New Life in Dubai
The desert city is where Tarrahi chose to build a new life after the “Turtles” gang became embroiled in a war with a group of Dutch rivals, sparking a wave of shootings and gangland assassinations across the two countries. (The war between the two groups later served as inspiration for a wildly popular Belgian action film, “Gangsta.”)
It is unclear exactly when he relocated to Dubai, but immigration records obtained by OCCRP show that Tarrahi has visited the Emirates numerous times over the course of the last two decades. He was issued seven UAE visas between 2010 and 2020, according to data from the Federal Authority for Identity, Citizenship, Customs & Port Security, a UAE government agency responsible for citizenship and residency.
In 2013, in the midst of the “Turtles” gang war, Tarrahi was convicted by an Antwerp court of “jointly committed drug-related offenses.” The verdict was upheld by an appeal court the following year. He was sentenced to two years in prison, with one year suspended. (He spent around five months in pre-trial detention after his initial arrest in 2009, but reporters could not determine if he ever completed the sentence.)
But his criminal conviction didn’t stop him from gaining legal status in Dubai: He was granted a short-term residency visa in 2020 and was able to renew it two years later. In February 2023 the UAE granted him a ten-year visa as a property owner.
He undoubtedly qualified: Between 2019 and 2021, Tarrahi purchased six properties in Dubai for a total of $6.2 million, according to leaked real estate data obtained by OCCRP.
Three of them were flats in the Grand Bleu Tower, a luxury skyscraper with interiors by star fashion designer Elie Saab. As of September 2026, he had sold them all, but documents show that he was being charged service fees for one of the units as recently as the first quarter of 2026.
He also purchased a unit at one of the Bluewaters Residences buildings, on the luxury man-made Bluewaters Island, in December 2019. He paid 5.8 million dirhams ($1.6 million) for the three-bedroom unit, and sold it for 15 million dirhams (over $4 million) just over four years later, according to leaked property data. A tenancy contract shows that he earned the equivalent of around $177,000 renting the apartment out for a year.
Credit: Emmanuel Catteau / Hans Lucas / Hans Lucas via AFP
The Dubai Hills Estate luxury residences under construction in 2019. Nasserdine Tarrahi purchased a property there in 2021.
In March 2021, Tarrahi bought a property in Dubai Hills Estate, a gated community advertised as the “green heart of Dubai,” for the equivalent of $1.3 million. (He sold it later that year).
Just a month later, he acquired a unit in the Marina Vista Tower — a beachfront high-rise with sweeping skyline views and an outdoor swimming pool — for another $1.3 million. The apartment is no longer in Tarrahi’s possession, according to Dubai Land Department data, but it’s unclear when it was sold.
Not long after this property investment spree, Tarrahi was convicted again in Belgium for his involvement with another drug trafficking group, known as the Mixers. In February 2022, he was sentenced in absentia to 5 years for co-perpetration of cocaine trafficking, bribery of a police officer, forgery, money laundering, and participation in a criminal organization.
The Antwerp prosecutor's office declined to comment on whether Belgian authorities at the time asked Dubai to arrest Tarrahi for this conviction.
Still, he continued to run his drug businesses from his Dubai base and give orders to associates in Belgium, according to the verdict in the third drug case against him, issued by an Antwerp court in May.
To communicate, they relied on the encrypted messaging service Sky ECC. Investigators found that Tarrahi used the same passwords across various accounts: "dubai123" and "flapdrol," which means “fool” in Dutch slang.
From Dubai, he also used cameras to monitor activities at an apartment in Antwerp used by his associates to store and repackage cocaine before sending it on to end buyers. He could even open and close the gates and garage doors remotely.
When police searched the property in June 2023, they found 12 bricks of cocaine and a shopping bag with two firearms inside a parked Mazda car. Another 30 cocaine bricks were found hidden in a secret compartment in a Fiat on the premises.
They also found 30,000 euros’ worth of exercise equipment, like kettlebells, boxing gloves, and a treadmill. These, along with 16,000 Swiss francs (around $17,000) and another approximately 2,000 euros in bank funds, were itemized in the court’s verdict as assets seized from Tarrahi.
The Antwerp prosecutor’s office declined to comment on whether the court had been aware of Tarrahi’s six Dubai apartments, but the court’s judgement made no mention of the property. A spokesperson for the federal office responsible for seizures in the Belgian justice system confirmed that there have been no seizures of real estate in Dubai.
A New Era of Cooperation?
Belgian Justice Minister Annelies Verlinden has made it a priority to dismantle overseas safe havens for criminals, a push that has seen 22 people extradited from the UAE since she took office in February 2025, including Tarrahi.
A spokesperson for her cabinet told De Tijd that the Justice Ministry is now in talks with Dubai authorities on how they can work together to ensure the seizure of criminal proceeds.
“Building on the success of the extraditions, the aim is to implement a similarly successful collaboration regarding the confiscation of criminal proceeds,” the spokesperson said.
The new UAE anti-money laundering law enacted last year is expected to make it easier to confiscate assets sought by foreign states, since the Emirates will no longer require a separate local investigation before cooperating with asset-freezing and confiscation orders from abroad.
But although the law improves the framework for asset recovery, “assets must first be identified before they can be seized, and a number of policy gaps continue to hinder this process” said Jorgensen of Transparency International.
For example, he said most real estate developers in the UAE are still not covered by anti-money-laundering obligations.
“This means that a criminal or corrupt person can purchase a property or housing project through a developer without the developer being required to conduct any due diligence checks.”
Jodi Vittori, a professor at Georgetown University who studies corruption and illicit finance, said enforcement could also be hindered by a lack of transparency in the autocratic UAE.
“There are theoretical rules and procedures, but at the end of the day, if the person is important enough or has the right connections, they don’t apply, because there's no rule of law, there's no accountability, there's no transparency,” she said

Finland has begun distributing its 2026 maternity package, known as the baby box, with 52 products instead of last year's 38, following an increase in the state maternity grant from €170 to €210.

Add Helsinki Times as a preferred source on Google (opens Google in a new tab)
Parents eligible for the maternity grant have the option of receiving the package or taking a one-off payment of €210.
The latest package contains clothing, blankets, a sleeping bag, muslin cloths, a book, nail scissors and a toothbrush. Condoms and personal lubricant have also returned after their removal from the previous edition.
The increase in products follows the government's decision to raise the maternity grant by €40 at the beginning of 2026.
Kela specialist Veera Petäjä said the additional funding had allowed the agency to expand the package while maintaining its focus on quality, safety and long-term use.
The package also includes a soft ball funded through the government's "Finland on the Move" programme, which promotes physical activity across different age groups.
The initiative forms part of Prime Minister Petteri Orpo's government programme, adopted in 2023.
The ball features illustrations of animals and fruit, including English words such as "grapes" and "orange". Kela says the ball is intended to encourage interaction between babies and parents through play.
The 2026 package also features a new design by Finnish illustrator Eveliina Muotkavaara, titled Kuvitellaan tulevaa, meaning "Imagining the future".
The design uses a peach-coloured space theme intended to represent families' hopes for their children's future.
The cardboard box itself also serves as a sleeping space for newborn babies, continuing a feature associated with Finland's maternity package.
Kela selects the contents using product safety standards, durability requirements and feedback from families.
Finland introduced its maternity package in 1938, establishing a system that has become a recognised part of the country's support for families with newborn children.
The contents change annually, although the introduction date depends on when stocks of the previous package run out.

Ebola death toll surpasses 4,400
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:25:14 UTC
19:25:14 KST

Ebola death toll surpasses 4,400
The death toll from an Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has surpassed 4,400, with more than 9,100 infections recorded since the epidemic began, the country’s Health Ministry reported on Tuesday.
According to its latest figures, 4,410 people have died out of 9,144 confirmed cases, putting the fatality rate at 48.2%. The majority of new cases were reported in Ituri Province, which remains the epicenter of the outbreak, accounting for nearly three-quarters of all infections. Sixty-five health zones across seven provinces have been affected.
The outbreak was officially declared on May 15 and involves the Bundibugyo strain of the Ebola virus for which there are currently no approved vaccines or targeted treatments available.
The epidemic has also spread beyond DR Congo, with Kenya confirming its first-ever Ebola case last week after a man who had lived in DR Congo for seven years died in a Nairobi hospital. The patient had traveled through Uganda before arriving in Kenya on October 3. Kenyan authorities have identified 28 contacts and are tracing another 27 passengers and crew members from his flight.
Earlier this month, Congolese Health Minister Roger Samuel Kamba said the outbreak had passed its peak, citing a decline in new infections and fewer areas reporting active transmission. However, the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) cautioned that the epidemic was not yet under control, warning that insecurity in affected areas had disrupted surveillance.
The DR Congo’s mineral-rich east has been plagued by decades of violence, with dozens of armed groups, including M23, fighting Congolese government forces for power and control of resources such as gold and coltan. Clashes escalated in early 2025, leaving thousands dead and resulting in large-scale displacement, according to UN agencies. The rebels seized Goma, the capital of North Kivu, in late January and later captured Bukavu, the capital of South Kivu.
Ceasefire efforts have repeatedly faltered, including Qatar-facilitated talks in Doha. In February 2026, the parties agreed on arrangements for a ceasefire monitoring mechanism, a step welcomed by the African Union. Congolese authorities have long accused Rwanda of supporting the militants, allegations backed by a UN panel of experts. Kigali has denied the claims.
The accusations have strained Rwanda’s relations with Western partners, including Belgium. In March 2025, Kigali severed diplomatic ties with Brussels, accusing it of harboring “neo-colonial delusions” and interfering in the conflict. The two countries, however, restored diplomatic relations in September 2026.
In December 2025, Congolese President Felix Tshisekedi and his Rwandan counterpart, Paul Kagame, ratified a US-brokered agreement committing Kigali to withdraw its forces from the border and end alleged support for M23, while Kinshasa pledged to curb militias hostile to Rwanda. US President Donald Trump has said the pact, which includes calls for a joint security mechanism, gives Washington rights to local mineral wealth. The fighting has continued despite Trump’s claims that he ended the decades-long conflict.
The impact of the outbreak on the region’s humanitarian situation was also raised at the UN Security Council on Tuesday. Russia’s Deputy Ambassador Anna Evstigneeva warned that the Ebola epidemic was exacerbating an already severe humanitarian crisis in eastern DR Congo, where fighting between government forces and armed groups continues.
Russia has provided diagnostic assistance to the countries affected by the outbreak. On October 7, the Russian Foreign Ministry reported a new shipment of Russian-made diagnostic kits to Uganda, sufficient for 7,000 tests. The delivery followed a September training program in Russia for ten Ugandan health specialists on infection prevention and control.
