How Germany is training medical staff to fight Ebola
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:25:06 UTC
19:25:06 KST

With 9,000 infections and 4,000 deaths, Ebola continues to spread in eastern DR Congo. German experts are training local healthcare workers to treat patients safely and contain the virus.
Just two days ago, Louise Gotze was in the Ugandan city of Entebbe with her team, sharing her knowledge with around 30 doctors and nurses. She spoke to healthcare professionals about how to care for Ebola patients without becoming infected themselves.
"These training sessions are absolutely essential to ensure that staff do not become infected and that they know how to work safely when they are in the red zone, meaning the area where patients are being treated," Gotze told Euronews.
Around 200 healthcare workers are currently known to have become infected as a result of their work.
According to Charité doctor Maximilian Gertler, between 800 and 1,000 patients are currently infected or receiving treatment at medical facilities in the Ituri and North Kivu regions.
Gotze has travelled to the Ebola crisis region seven times this year to train local healthcare professionals. In Berlin, she works as an intensive care nurse in the special isolation unit at Charité hospital. Another trip is being planned.
The ultimate goal is to establish a network of trained healthcare professionals across East Africa who can, in turn, pass on their knowledge to others.
How the international community is fighting Ebola
Germany is sending teams to several countries, including the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Kenya and Uganda, as the virus does not stop at national borders.
"We are currently training a group of around 120 doctors from the partner states of the East African Community," explained epidemiologist Gertler from Berlin's Charité hospital.
"Graduates of our programme from the Democratic Republic of the Congo have also started conducting training sessions themselves in Kinshasa to prepare for the possibility of cases emerging in the capital."
Epidemiologist Maximilian Gertler confirmed that the situation in the Democratic Republic of the Congo is still not under control.
The number of infections has now risen to 9,000, with 4,000 deaths reported. According to Gertler, the fatality rate in this outbreak stands at 50%.
Simulation in Berlin: How Ebola patients are treated
He stands in front of a tent containing a height-adjustable hospital bed and other equipment needed to treat Ebola patients. But here in Berlin, in the courtyard of the Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development, there is no real patient.
Instead, a mannequin is being used to demonstrate how people with Ebola are examined and treated in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
Germany's Development Minister Reem Alabali-Radovan and the Secretary-General of the East African Community, Stephen Patrick Mbundi, are also present.
The climatic conditions in the country, which lies close to the equator, make the work more difficult. Protective clothing can only be worn safely for around 45 to 60 minutes.
More than 10,000 protective suits are used every day and must then be burned to prevent contamination. Only protective goggles, rubber boots and aprons made from more durable materials last longer.
Plastic walls with openings for arms also offer a solution.
"An innovative concept that the WHO and its partners have increasingly developed in recent years involves fitting the walls of these often tent-like structures in treatment facilities with transparent screens. This allows staff to care for and monitor patients without the need for protective equipment," Gertler explained.
Behind these walls, healthcare workers do not need to wear full protective gear and can still monitor the condition of several patients at the same time.
"This can significantly reduce the number of staff who need to remain in protective clothing continuously," Gertler said.
€21 million for protective equipment and training
Since the Ebola outbreak began in June, Germany's Development Ministry has increased its support by €21 million, including funding for protective equipment.
Germany's commitment is important for global health, according to Development Minister Reem Alabali-Radovan (SPD).
"We cannot prevent outbreaks of infectious diseases and pandemics unless we take active measures. That means it remains important that we continue to invest in global health," Alabali-Radovan said.
The outbreak in eastern DR Congo has already spread to other countries. Kenya has so far recorded one death, while Uganda has reported several dozen infections.
"Ebola has broken out in regions that are also affected by crises and conflicts. This means medical staff sometimes have to treat patients under life-threatening conditions, if they are even able to reach the affected areas," Alabali-Radovan stressed.
"We are trying to take the necessary measures to ensure that the outbreak does not spread across the entire region," Ambassador Stephen Patrick Mbundi, Secretary-General of the East African Community, said.
Gertler explained that the international campaign to prevent the further spread of the Ebola virus focuses on patient isolation and treatment, as well as public awareness.
According to Gertler, trust in "all kinds of state institutions" is relatively low in the "civil war-torn region". The population is not accustomed to a functioning healthcare system. Every year, 50,000 people die from infectious diseases such as malaria, cholera and measles. Some people are sceptical about the increased focus on Ebola, as fewer people have died from the virus so far.
"Awareness-raising is needed within communities, and these efforts must reach the people," Gertler stressed.
Alabali-Radovan thanked German personnel for their efforts and called for continued international cooperation to contain the outbreak.
Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo
The Ebola outbreak began in the Democratic Republic of the Congo in mid-May this year. By July, the number of confirmed cases had already exceeded 2,000, with 754 deaths reported. The total number of infections has now risen to more than 9,000, and according to WHO figures, the virus has killed over 4,000 people.
Some 2,269 people have survived Ebola. The outbreak is considered the most severe and fastest-growing in the country's history.
In May 2026, the World Health Organization declared a public health emergency of international concern.
During an international aid operation, two US citizens became infected and were brought to Germany for treatment in specialised isolation units.
Both doctors were later discharged in good health. According to the Robert Koch Institute (RKI), whether an infected person recovers depends "to a large extent on how good the medical treatment is."
There are still no approved vaccines against the Ebola Bundibugyo virus, although one vaccine candidate is currently undergoing testing.

Japan’s prime minister said on Oct. 14 that she probably spends “three or four more hours” than her male predecessors tackling household duties on top of her already packed daily schedule.
“In the morning, I bathe, fix breakfast and then wash dishes, not to mention apply makeup,” Sanae Takaichi, elected last year as Japan’s first woman premier, told parliament.
“I feel like I’m spending three or four more hours than male prime ministers doing these things.”
A self-described workaholic, Takaichi has previously said she slept just two to four hours a night and sometimes scheduled 3 a.m. staff meetings.

Discussions about Takaichi’s time management came up when a ruling coalition member asked her about the marathon hours Japanese prime ministers customarily spend attending parliamentary sessions.
Takaichi said in a post on X in July that she was “getting consumed until dawn with poring over documents brought home from work and those related to parliamentary questioning.”
“I do enjoy reading these piles of documents at midnight that I took home,” she said on Oct. 14.
“But it is difficult for me to squeeze out time to buckle down and think with a clear head” about “the future direction of this country or my grand vision for it,” she said.

English and Welsh water firms could be forced to return £107m via lower bills
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:21:05 UTC
19:21:05 KST

Thames Water, Yorkshire Water and other providers could be forced to cut tens of millions of pounds from household bills after the regulator said they had missed performance targets.
Customer bills at Yorkshire Water could fall by £27 on average, while those at Thames could decrease by £7, according to estimates by Ofwat, the regulator of the privatised industry in England and Wales.
The water industry has faced growing criticism in recent years amid rising bills, scrutiny over sewage pollution, high levels of debt and underinvestment in ageing infrastructure.
As water customers cannot switch away from their provider if it underperforms, Ofwat instead has an “outcome delivery incentive” (ODI) system of automatic payments or penalties based on agreed targets.
Yorkshire and Thames will have to return £75.1m and £45.8m, respectively, after missing targets in 2025-26, Ofwat said. The payments will add to the financial pressures on the companies, although Thames has been allowed to delay some of the penalties by a year.
Yorkshire is among the companies subject to enhanced monitoring by Ofwat over its financial resilience, while the government is considering whether to bring Thames Water under public control after years-long negotiations to reduce its crippling debts.
The other companies that must return money to customers include: Dŵr Cymru (or Welsh Water), at £16.7m; South West Water, at £16m; and United Utilities in north-west England, at £13.4m.
However, some companies will receive a reward payment because they met their targets – covered by higher bills.
Severn Trent, which serves the Midlands, south-west England and parts of Wales, and Northumbrian Water are in line to receive an extra £41.8m and £35.9m respectively, Ofwat said.
Northumbrian customers’ bills could rise by an average of £21, the regulator said. Severn Trent customers could pay £8 more per year.
Overall, the industry is expected to cut its bills by a net £240m for failures during 2025-26. Of this, £107m is expected to be returned to customers via lower bills in 2027-28.
Ofwat said at this stage the figures were still at the draft stage and not every household would receive the same change. Bills are “affected by a range of factors and the effect will vary by company and customer type”, the regulator said.
It will make its final decision on the payments by 15 December, which will take effect on bills from 1 April 2027.
Ofwat recently announced that water companies could increase annual tariffs by an extra £3.4bn, on top of the 36% average rise agreed over five years to 2030. Customer bills are rising to pay for long-overdue investments to fix leaking pipes and treatment works, as well as to pay for new assets such as reservoirs.
Andy Burnham last month said the government would pave the way for public ownership of water firms and promised a 10-year path to a “very different water system in the UK”.
The comments suggested the prime minister might opt for a temporary nationalisation of debt-laden Thames Water as the government seeks to make a decision on a £10bn rescue takeover put forward by lenders for the UK’s biggest water supplier.
Ofwat’s announcement came after Burnham said customers must not be “treated as a blank cheque” and after the regulator said in August it planned to allow yet more bill increases on top of those already agreed.
A government spokesperson said: “This government won’t allow customers to be treated as a blank cheque, and we are committed to protecting households from cost-of-living pressures. We will always challenge water companies where they seek to pass unnecessary costs on to households.
“We will deliver a strengthened water bill that puts people first, ensuring affordable access to clean water, driving down pollution, and strengthening public control.”
A Yorkshire Water spokesperson said: “We recognise that our performance last year fell short of the standards we and our customers expect in some areas, and we remain focused on improving.
“We are already delivering Yorkshire’s largest ever environmental investment programme and with the help of over 1,000 new colleagues, we’ve completed improvements at almost 300 locations across the county.”
A Thames Water spokesperson said: “To help smooth customer bills, Ofwat has agreed to defer the timing of some ODI penalties by one year. This does not remove or reduce the penalties. Customers still receive the full benefit, and Thames Water does not gain financially. We recognise these penalties reflect areas where our performance fell short. The deferral will prevent sharp year-on-year bill movements, which research shows our customers want us to avoid.”

Stalin later clarified that the movement was spontaneous, in response to reporters repeatedly asking whether the talks were over.Vijay revived the gesture in the assembly in June, mimicking Stalin as DMK legislators challenged the TVK government.The confrontation escalated over allegations of political opportunism and party funds, with Vijay accusing the DMK of collecting money in the name of party funds and saying his government would not loot public money.The remarks triggered a walkout by DMK legislators amid sloganeering in the House.

EU's methane rules face two-year delay, sparking environmental backlash
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:18:58 UTC
19:18:58 KST

Environmentalists warn that delaying EU methane rules will do little to lower energy prices, accusing Brussels of using energy security and competitiveness to justify weakening the Green Deal.
The European Commission proposed on Wednesday a one-year delay for importers to show compliance with EU methane rules, giving companies until May 2029 to prove that their supplies meet equivalent EU standards.
The proposal follows pressure from industry and governments concerned about compliance costs and energy security, but falls short of calls from some EU countries for a three-year delay.
Environmental groups condemned the move, arguing that the methane rules pose no threat to Europe's energy security and that the current supply crisis stems instead from the US-Israeli war against Iran, which has disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
Under the Commission proposal, importers of oil, gas and coal from outside the EU have more time to comply with the bloc’s methane rules. Originally, importers were expected to demonstrate by January 2027 that their suppliers had systems in place to monitor and report methane emissions equivalent to those required under EU law.
Under the proposed changes, the requirement would start applying in 2028, with the first report and proof of compliance due by 31 May 2029, covering supplies from the previous year.
EU governments and industry have pushed for a delay amid turmoil in energy markets, while climate campaigners accuse Brussels of weakening a recently adopted law without tackling the underlying causes of the crisis.
EU countries adopted methane rules in May 2024, introducing requirements to measure, report and verify emissions from the energy sector as part of efforts to curb one of the most potent greenhouse gases.
But the latest energy crisis, which has driven up prices and threatened diesel and gas supplies, has fuelled concerns that the rules could aggravate shortages.
French President Emmanuel Macron recently joined industry calls to delay the requirements, which were due to take effect in early 2027.
"It is also important not to weaken European production capacities while preparing for long-term supply difficulties," Macron said in a letter to the Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.
The United States, the EU's largest supplier of liquefied natural gas (LNG), has also repeatedly complained about the impact of the rules on American energy companies.
Suspending penalties
The Commission had already offered significant flexibility, including a three-year suspension of certain penalties, in a concession to industry. But it had stopped short of formally postponing the compliance deadline.
The EU methane law requires fossil fuel importers to provide information on emissions associated with production.
In practice, importers may need to collect reliable data from producers operating thousands of kilometres away, at the other end of a complex supply chain.
Importers argue that they still face legal uncertainty despite the proposed suspension of penalties, and have called for more time and clearer obligations.
Environmental groups, however, warn that even a limited delay could pave the way for further concessions, while doing little to improve Europe's energy security.
They also argue that reopening the legislation risks penalising companies and producing countries that have already invested in monitoring and reporting systems, while undermining confidence in EU rules.
Jack Corscadden, senior Campaigner at Environmental Investigation Agency, said there was no demonstrable link between the implementation of the EU methane rules and the current energy supply challenges.
“After a summer of record-breaking heatwaves and wildfires, the Commission is failing European citizens by delaying this vital piece of climate legislation to appease fossil fuel producers and exporters," Corscadden said.
Esther Bollendorff, fossil free program manager at the NGO Climate Action Network Europe, said that delaying the EU methane rules made no economic or strategic sense.
"At a time of yet another energy price crisis and tensions on the gas market, methane mitigation could unlock over 40 billion cubic meters of gas from the EU’s main fossil fuel suppliers - more than half the volume of US LNG imported by the EU in 2025," Bollendorff said.
The Commission's proposal still requires approval from the European Parliament and EU governments. It is set to be discussed by EU leaders at a summit in Brussels on Thursday, alongside broader concerns about European competitiveness and soaring energy prices.

Rolex and gold were for US and not Trump, Swiss trade chief says

“It’s a gift to the American people – it’s duly registered at the White House, and if all things go well, it will end up in a presidential library,” she said. “It’s a private-sector initiative, but I feel confident that they have kept within the margins of the law.”

Lawmakers filed criminal complaints seeking a probe for possible bribery, and a parliamentary report on the matter is expected in due course.

The unusual appeal to Trump in 2025 followed the imposition of 39% tariffs. Budliger was a key player behind the scenes to secure an accord that capped levies at 15%.
“The US has respected that deal,” Budliger said. “We want to have certainty, we want to have calmer waters.”
Talks are still ongoing to secure a more permanent legally binding agreement, she said.
“Sticking to being calm and cool-headed and seeing how we can make this relationship win-win has helped us to then get to a 15-all-in per cent deal,” she said. BLOOMBERG

Scientists discover how harmful “zombie cells” hide from the immune system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:17:58 UTC
19:17:58 KST

Scientists discover how harmful “zombie cells” hide from the immune system
Cedars-Sinai identified a protein that may allow harmful “zombie cells” to evade the immune system and accumulate as we age.
- Date:
- October 14, 2026
- Source:
- Cedars-Sinai Medical Center
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered a protein that may help harmful aging cells hide from the immune system, allowing them to accumulate and fuel age-related health problems. Blocking the protein in mice reduced these cells and inflammation while improving blood sugar regulation and strength, offering a promising new direction for anti-aging research.
- Share:
Researchers led by Cedars-Sinai Health Sciences University have discovered a protein that may allow harmful aging cells to escape detection by the immune system. By helping these cells remain in the body instead of being cleared away, the protein could contribute to their accumulation and the development of health problems associated with aging.
The discovery, published in Cell Metabolism, identifies PD-L2 as a potential target for therapies aimed at eliminating harmful aging cells. Scientists also believe the protein could serve as a blood marker, providing a way to detect and monitor these cells.
"Our findings suggest that PD-L2 may help aging cells stay in the body when they would normally be removed by the immune system," said Selim Chaib, PhD, research assistant professor of Medicine at Cedars-Sinai and first and co-corresponding author of the study.
How Harmful Aging Cells Escape the Immune System
As cells age or become damaged, some enter a state known as senescence. These cells stop dividing but remain alive, lingering in tissues rather than disappearing. Over time, they can accumulate and release substances that trigger inflammation and disrupt the normal activity of surrounding cells.
The buildup of these senescent cells has been associated with a range of health problems that become more common with age. Understanding why they persist, particularly when the immune system would normally remove them, could help scientists develop new ways to reduce their harmful effects.
The researchers found that PD-L2 may play an important role in this process by helping aging cells avoid immune clearance.
Blocking PD-L2 Reduces Aging Cells in Mice
To investigate the protein's role, scientists conducted experiments in laboratory mice in which PD-L2 was either removed or blocked. Both approaches reduced the accumulation of senescent cells and lowered levels of the inflammatory substances they release.
The benefits extended beyond changes at the cellular level. Mice with reduced PD-L2 activity also showed improvements in their ability to process sugar and demonstrated greater grip strength, suggesting that targeting the protein could influence physical functions affected by aging.
The team also examined human cells and tissues. They discovered that senescent human cells produced more PD-L2 than younger cells and that levels of the protein rose with age in certain human tissues. These findings suggest the mechanism observed in mice may also be relevant to human aging.
A Potential New Target for Age-Related Diseases
The results raise the possibility that blocking PD-L2 could help the immune system recognize and eliminate harmful aging cells, potentially reducing some of the health problems associated with their buildup.
"If we can find a way to block this protein, we may be able to help the immune system get rid of these cells and potentially improve health problems linked with aging," said James Kirkland, MD, PhD, director of the Center for Advanced Gerotherapeutics and senior author of the study.
Although the findings are promising, more research is needed before the approach can be considered for treating people. Future studies will investigate whether blocking PD-L2 is safe and can deliver meaningful health benefits in humans. Researchers also hope to clarify how the protein contributes to diseases associated with aging.
Additional Cedars-Sinai researchers who contributed to the study include Larissa Langhi Prata, Masayoshi Suda, Andres Sola, Jia Nie, Hyungsoo Kim, Tamar Pirtskhalava, Nino Giorgadze, Nicolas Musi, Ze'ev Ronai, and Tamara Tchkonia.

The trial of a Ukrainian citizen accused of organizing the sabotage of the Nord Stream gas pipelines in September 2022 is set to begin in Germany on October 14.
Reuters reports this.
According to German prosecutors, Serhii K. (Serhii Kuznetsov) led a group of Ukrainians that included divers and an explosives expert.
Investigators believe the group planned and carried out the sabotage operation on the orders of unidentified Ukrainian state agencies, planting explosive devices on the pipelines near the Danish island of Bornholm in the Baltic Sea.

The trial is expected to be the first opportunity to examine the evidence gathered during the years-long investigation publicly.

Meanwhile, Croatian authorities have arrested another man, Volodymyr Zhuravliov. German prosecutors believe he was one of the divers involved in the operation to sabotage the Nord Stream gas pipelines.
On September 18, the County Court in the Croatian city of Pula approved extraditing the Ukrainian national to Germany.
Germany submitted two requests to Croatia to extradite Zhuravliov under European arrest warrants issued in June 2024 and August 2026.
Zhuravliov and his defense team argued that the requests should be rejected, citing a ruling by the Warsaw District Court, which refused Germany’s extradition request in October 2025. At the time, the Polish court questioned whether German law applied to the explosions in international waters and stated that the case should be considered in the context of Russian aggression.

Ukrainian Ex-Officer Stands Trial in Germany Over Nord Stream Bombing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:17:05 UTC
19:17:05 KST

Lawyers for a Ukrainian ex-military officer accused of leading the bombing of Russia's Nord Stream pipeline in September 2022 argued at the start of his trial in Germany on Wednesday that "an aggressor's infrastructure" may have been a lawful target.
Serhii Kuznetsov is accused of leading a group of Ukrainian agents including divers and an explosives expert that blew up Russia's largest gas pipeline to Europe in one of the biggest infrastructure sabotage operations of modern times.
The case provides the first opportunity for a public hearing of evidence gathered during a years-long investigation, which has been diplomatically and politically awkward for a German government that remains staunchly supportive of Ukraine despite the investigative trail linking Kyiv to the bombing.
Moving to have the case dismissed, Kuznetsov's lawyer Nicola Canestrini argued that the pipeline — which provided half of Germany's imports of natural gas before Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine — was a "Russian weapon."
"Is it unlawful to destroy an aggressor's infrastructure without harming any human beings?" Canestrini asked.
Right to remain silent
Prosecutors have alleged that Kuznetsov, who was arrested under an international warrant in Italy last year, worked with members of the Ukrainian military to plan the clandestine operation on behalf of unidentified Ukrainian state entities.
Kuznetsov, 50, who prior to Wednesday was referred to publicly only as Serhii K. under German legal rules, has denied any involvement in the blasts that ruptured the 1,200-kilometer (750-mile)-long Baltic Sea pipeline.
Wearing a grey suit and with a shaved head, he exercised his right to remain silent in court but did not cover his face. His lawyers said he could not mount a proper defense because he was obliged to withhold Ukrainian state secrets.
The government in Kyiv has also denied any involvement, a sensitive point in its relations with Germany, Ukraine's largest European supplier of military aid. Russia said on Monday it expected a "just verdict" that would reveal the names of the perpetrators and those who ordered the operation.
Kuznetsov's legal team had tried reaching out to Ukraine for information that might assist the defense but heard nothing, according to another defense lawyer, Jes Meyer-Lohkamp.
Attacking civilian targets is considered a war crime
German prosecutors say the actions Kuznetsov is accused of — attacking civilian targets and causing explosions that destroyed infrastructure and damaged public services — would amount to a war crime.
Kuznetsov is the only person on trial, but Croatian authorities have arrested another man, identified as Vladimir Z., who prosecutors believe was one of the divers.
The explosion of Nord Stream sealed the end of Germany's longstanding dependence on Russian natural gas, although Moscow had already cut supplies over Berlin's support for European sanctions following Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
Nord Stream's supply had been due to double with the opening of a twin pipeline, Nord Stream 2, already built, but Berlin canceled approval to open it just prior to Russia's invasion.
Plumes of methane gas
The trial, expected to continue into February next year, could have domestic political implications.
Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), leading in opinion polls for more than a year, has called for an end to military aid for Ukraine and a restoration of energy ties with Moscow.
Although German state parliaments have no role in foreign policy, the AfD filed a motion in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt on Wednesday calling for an end to support for Ukraine, noting the "historical parallel" with the start of the trial.
The Nord Stream system, lying at a depth of 80 to 110 meters under the Baltic and built by Russian gas concern Gazprom to supply up to 110 billion cubic meters of gas to Germany, was formerly at the core of economic ties between the two countries.
The Sept. 26, 2022, blasts that ruptured three of the four concrete-coated steel pipelines created a giant whirlpool at sea as huge plumes of methane gas rose into the atmosphere.
Prosecutors allege that Kuznetsov traveled to Germany through Poland some three weeks before the attack, using a forged Ukrainian passport. He and his group then used a sailboat hired in the northern German city of Rostock to reach an area close to the Danish island of Bornholm, where they rigged specialized military-grade explosives to the sea floor.
The weekly Der Spiegel magazine and ZDF public television have previously reported that five men and one woman were on the rented yacht Andromeda, which left Rostock on Sept. 6 and returned on Sept. 23, 2022.

Indonesia wildfires choke Singapore, force East Timor schools shut
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:16:00 UTC
19:16:00 KST

Air pollution in parts of Singapore reached "very high" levels Wednesday while East Timor closed schools, as haze from Indonesian forest fires triggered a regional crisis.
The blazes in Indonesia have burned through hundreds of thousands of hectares of forest and plantations on Borneo and Sumatra islands, sickened local residents and sent thick haze across the region.
Air pollution in western Singapore on Wednesday hit "very high" – the country's top level – the National Environment Agency said.
It recorded levels of tiny particulates capable of penetrating the bloodstream and lungs, known as PM2.5, at 288 micrograms per cubic meter, vastly exceeding the World Health Organization's recommended average annual exposure of 5 micrograms.
Indonesia regularly battles wildfires during the dry season, but has seen stronger-than-usual blazes this year as a powerful El Nino cycle brings drought.
Experts also point to slash-and-burn land-clearing practices that have changed the naturally fire-resistant landscape of Sumatra and Borneo.
The haze has drifted into neighboring Singapore, Malaysia and East Timor, which said it would shut schools nationwide for three days from Thursday, and as far afield as the Philippines.
The closures in East Timor were necessary "as a preventive measure to protect the health of students, teachers and other members of the educational community, given current air quality conditions", the government said.
It urged families to keep children indoors and to use "respiratory protection" if going outside.
Singapore rolled out subsidies for haze-related medical treatment from Monday, a measure last activated in 2015 when similar blazes in Indonesia cloaked Southeast Asia in toxic smoke for weeks.
The city-state has also begun distributing N95 masks to eligible residents when pollution reaches very unhealthy levels.
Singapore's National Trades Union Congress said Monday that public transport workers and delivery riders could receive free N95 masks, but AFP found uptake was slow.
"It's a little bit uncomfortable to wear a mask, and some orders we have to walk around blocks, or park outside," a delivery rider, who gave his name only as Daniel, told AFP.
"With the mask, I will have to breathe heavier," the 27-year-old said.
Ong Kwang Wei, 57, who has asthma, said he wore an N95 mask outdoors and carried his inhaler and medication with him at all times.
He was accompanying his 88-year-old mother – also masked – for a health check-up after a recent bout of flu.
"Once the flu kicks in my asthma is exacerbated ... I get breathless, I cough, I get phlegm, so I need to use my inhaler," Ong said.
In Indonesia, tens of thousands of people have sought treatment for respiratory illness linked to haze from fires burning in Borneo, South Sumatra and Papua regions.
On Sumatra island, a fire razed nearly 300 homes, forcing hundreds of people to evacuate, an official said Tuesday.
Residents first spotted the fire approaching their village in Bangka Belitung province Saturday and tried to put it out themselves with portable water pumps.
But the fire continued to smoulder underground in peatland and when the wind shifted, the flames moved toward their homes.
The local disaster agency said nearly 1,000 people fled the village.
"My house is gone," Leni, a 55-year-old villager now staying at a shelter with her family, told AFP.
"There's nothing left. I could only save myself and take my kids with me ... I panicked and didn't have the time to grab anything," said Leni, who like many Indonesians has one name.
President Prabowo Subianto on Monday ordered the government to mobilize maximum efforts, with officials saying more than 60,000 personnel had been deployed to combat fires on the ground.
But efforts so far, including cloud seeding and water-bombing, have had limited success.

EU proposes delaying methane obligations amid pressure on energy importers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:15:59 UTC
19:15:59 KST

Melike Pala
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
The European Commission proposed Wednesday postponing by one year the implementation of certain provisions of the EU Methane Regulation concerning fossil fuel importers, aiming to ease cost pressures on European industry amid rising energy prices.
The proposed amendment would delay monitoring, reporting, and verification obligations for importers of natural gas, oil, and coal, as well as reporting requirements related to methane intensity for both importers and EU producers, according to a statement.
The bloc said the move comes as the conflict in the Middle East puts additional pressure on global energy markets, driving up energy prices and potentially reducing the availability of gas and oil.
"This is driving up energy prices and may cause reduced availability of gas and oil, hampering the EU's competitiveness and security of supply," the statement said.
The proposed one-year postponement is intended to prevent additional pressure on the security of imported fossil fuel supplies while giving companies and national administrations more time to prepare for compliance with the regulation.
The proposal will now be submitted to the European Parliament and the European Council for consideration and adoption.
The EU Methane Regulation, adopted in 2024, is the world's first comprehensive legislation addressing methane emissions associated with imports of oil, natural gas, and coal.
The regulation covers domestic production, transportation, and processing, as well as imports, and introduces progressively stricter requirements to improve transparency and reduce methane emissions.
The commission stressed that the proposed amendment would not affect the regulation's overall ambition, integrity, or scope, reaffirming the bloc's commitment to reducing methane emissions.

Are US, Israel racing to deploy space-based lasers or orbital weapons first? - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:15:29 UTC
19:15:29 KST

In September, two consecutive top US military officials made public, for the first time, that America has offensive weapons already deployed in space.
That the US, China, and Russia have anti-satellite weapons available is no secret and has been assumed in recent years, with China unofficially demonstrating old space weapons in 2007, and Russia and China both demonstrating newer weapons since 2021.
But a public declaration by the US set off speculation about whether the deployed weapons are focused on the area of: either directed-energy weapons such as lasers; or kinetic anti-satellite weapons such as missiles; or platforms for disrupting or disabling satellites’ activity without actually destroying them, which is also known as rendezvous and proximity operations (RPOs).
A fourth method could be nuclear, but it is assumed that this was not the focus of the US announcement since the terrible consequences in space would impact the attacker as much as the defender.
In April, Unit 9900 officer Lt. Col. “S” and space-war expert Tal Inbar discussed Israel's efforts to defend its space assets against adversaries.
Also, on June 24, with the Post noting that Russia, China, and Iran have all worked on ways to attack, damage, jam, or drag satellites in space, IDF Brig. Gen. Yael Grossman responded, “There are threats from space. We work with the Defense Ministry with a lot of power; with the broader defense establishment, we can all bring forward achievements.”
Developments in space vehicles
Regarding the US announcement, so far those space experts who are commenting are leaning toward category 3 of RPO.
This is especially true for deploying RPOs, which can fight off other RPOs.
The reason is that RPOs have existed in one form or another since the US used multiple space vehicles to repair one another in the 1960s. In that sense, the largest jump was developing the technology and tactics for sending one space vehicle or satellite to match the orbit of another.
Once a country makes that major scientific jump, adding on a robot arm to attack or an additional system to jam is just a matter of time and energy.
Another reason RPOs may be favored would be to avoid the debris problem caused by using kinetic anti-satellite weapons, such as missiles.
The US has said it is hoping to make major advancements in stationing anti-missile physical interceptors in space that can protect satellites by 2028.
Despite all this focus on RPOs for the US, China, and Russia, Israel has expressed keen interest regarding space weapons in relation to lasers.
On June 29, Defense Minister Israel Katz told a briefing of military reporters that Israel is developing space lasers to carry out attacks above the Earth.
This was an expansion and more specific version of a statement which Katz made earlier in June, when he committed Israel to becoming the leading player with space attack capabilities.
“One of the central goals which the prime minister and I set is that we are recruiting the best minds,” since “as of today, no country has the ability to mount attacks in space. We must be the leading country in the world with this capability,” said Katz.
The defense minister continued, “If we achieve this, it will ensure the advantage of deterrence, of the ability to attack, destroy, and all of the other matters, versus our enemies with large resources.”
Lasers to be used to defend Israeli assets
But Monday was the first time that Katz specifically mentioned space lasers.
Israel is already a leading country in developing Iron Beam as a land-based space laser, and during a visit to Elbit earlier in the summer, The Jerusalem Post saw and heard about work on presumed future fighter-jet-based lasers.
Overall, it seemed clear that Katz on June 29 was referring to Iran.
This is especially true since during the 2026 war, Israel struck multiple Iranian space war-related facilities, including facilities working on developing capabilities to attack satellites in space.
It was unclear if he indirectly also wanted to deter Russia and China from assisting Iran in this and other spheres.
According to foreign reports, lasers might be able to destroy enemy satellites and also burn up any debris that an attack in space by other means might cause.
Some have already speculated that Israel could destroy enemy space satellites using the Arrow 3 missile system, given that it already strikes ballistic missiles in space.
Yet, due to the same issue that Russia and China already fell into regarding debris, many countries are working on other techniques, such as paralyzing, damaging, jamming, dragging, or using lasers against satellites in space.
While some Israeli officials have hinted at such efforts, Katz’s public statements on June 29 were the clearest one to date by a senior Israeli official.
Why the US's first focus is on RPOs
In contrast, if Iran or other enemies advanced past Israel in space, they could attack Israeli satellites and reduce its surveillance capabilities.
After all of this, why then do most experts believe that the US's first and current focus is on RPOs, and not lasers?
It is not that the US and the other countries with space programs are not working on developing space lasers. They are.
Also, Israel’s success with developing the Iron Beam for actual deployments as a ground laser has spurred other countries forward in the more general laser defense area.
But lasers in space or on aircraft are still a distant solution, as they involve a series of more complex physics and engineering problems, which invariably will take longer to solve than RPOs.
RPOs are thereby an immediate answer to help deter enemies from attacking, since they can be used to attack enemy satellites, as well as providing defense against other countries’ potential RPO attacks.
If enemies have existing and immediate weapons to attack an object, such as a satellite, the US and other countries, potentially even including Israel, are likely to focus on immediate solutions, with the focus on space lasers being a longer-term goal.
In that sense, the US statement in September was about immediately deterring China and Russia from attacking American satellites.
In contrast, Katz’s June statement was less about immediate attack, defense, or deterrence.
Rather, it was more about either bragging to the Israeli public about a future distant achievement, or psychological warfare against Iran to the extent that the Islamic Republic might believe it can work with Moscow and Beijing to go after Israel’s satellite advantage.

Trump blamed Islam for France's protests. Students want teachers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:15:28 UTC
19:15:28 KST

Breadcrumb
France's students demand better schools as Trump turns protests into an Islam debate
At a demonstration in Paris’s 13th arrondissement on 10 October, high school students sang the national anthem and chanted "Macron démission." Their placards read "Nous avons besoin de plus de professeurs," "We need more teachers." Some urged others to stay calm and not to run, warning that this was what the CRS, France’s riot police, wanted. Before long, officers moved in to disperse the crowd.
For three students aged 16 to 18 from the 13th and 19th arrondissements, interviewed that day, the problems are concrete: overcrowded classrooms, no computer room, a shortage of teachers in their final year, and a canteen so packed that they have about 10 minutes to eat.
Meals must be booked in advance, and many end up buying food elsewhere. One week, they said, food had cost them €170. All three asked not to be named because of tensions around the protests.
When they sat their exams, the students said, they were sent to other sites, in rooms so stifling that some left for the toilets just to breathe. They took their concerns to a meeting at another high school with school leaders and officials, but the answers were disappointing.
Some issues were passed on to other authorities, including the education authority and Valérie Pécresse’s regional council, and the agreed changes won't take effect until next year. The students want them now.
On 6 October, as demonstrations spread across France, US President Donald Trump offered a different explanation.
"This isn’t about schools, this is about Islam wanting to take over a once great Country!" he wrote on Truth Social.
The students reject that. The protests have nothing to do with religion or immigration, they said. High school students come from every background, and there should be no shortcuts. None of them wanted their origins or religion mentioned. They wanted, they said, to be judged on what they were saying.
The movement began in September in disadvantaged suburbs of Paris and has since spread across the country.
More than 250,000 people took part in protests nationwide, according to the Interior Ministry, while organisers put the figure at 450,000.
'They tend to infantilise us'
A 23-year-old Arab medical student of North African heritage from Seine-Saint-Denis, the department north of Paris where the movement has deep roots, described classrooms not built for more than 30 pupils, broken furniture, and rooms that are hard to bear in winter. He asked to remain anonymous because of upcoming exams.
"Instead of trying to understand our difficulties and find solutions, they tend to infantilise us," he said. "We are capable of identifying the problems in our schools and saying what needs to change."
He is used to Trump’s provocations, he said, and pays them little attention. "What he said has, as usual, nothing to do with reality," he said, adding that he saw it as political point-scoring ahead of the US midterm elections.
What worries him more is that young people from immigrant families have their grievances read through assumptions about their identity, rather than their experience. "Our demands risk being reduced to questions of origin or religion," he said.
Many young people, he said, refuse to speak to channels such as CNews and BFMTV, which they see as portraying people from immigrant backgrounds in racist and Islamophobic terms.
"We want the media to talk about why we are mobilising, rather than turning our demands into a debate about our identity," the young student added.
A 21-year-old woman who went to school in Seine-Saint-Denis before moving to a Paris high school, and who also asked not to be named, said the protesters’ demands were legitimate.
She was stunned, she said, that students asking for better conditions had been met with violence. As for Trump, she said, "he should keep quiet."
The crackdown has been heavy. More than 1,800 people are being prosecuted over alleged offences linked to the unrest, including 1,483 minors, according to the Justice Ministry.
Inequality built into the system
The staffing crisis is national. According to the Education Ministry’s statistics directorate, DEPP, 9.8 percent of teaching hours in public secondary schools went undelivered in 2024–2025: 7.5 percent because absent teachers were not replaced, and 2.3 percent because schools were closed.
In Seine-Saint-Denis, two-thirds of schools had unfilled teaching positions, according to a union survey cited by Reuters.
Louise Paternoster, a representative of the CGT education union in the department, told Reuters the area did not receive resources to match its needs.
"In a period of budgetary restraint, it is more difficult to reduce inequalities," said Clémence Cardon-Quint, a professor at Paul-Valéry University Montpellier who studies education funding.
The problems start long before high school. A primary school teacher in her fifties, who asked not to be named, said her biggest challenge was supporting pupils with autism, ADHD and dyslexia.
"Inclusion is a very good thing, but we need the resources to welcome these children properly," she said.
Teachers sometimes have to make or buy materials themselves, which multiplies preparation time, and other children get less attention.
"Unfortunately, the die is very often cast as early as the first year of primary school," she said. A child who struggles to read needs help from speech therapists or psychologists, or support through France’s disability service, the MDPH, and that depends on families pushing for it. Some children, she said, reach secondary school without the level they need.
A concession, not a solution
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu acknowledged that young people’s anger did not come out of nowhere, while condemning violence and accusing outside groups of exploiting the protests. Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot rejected Trump’s reading, saying France should tell its own story.
On 8 October, Education Minister Édouard Geffray announced that around 3,000 qualified teachers who had not yet started work would be sent to schools facing staffing shortages.
It was a stopgap, not 3,000 new permanent posts. Student unions welcomed it as a first victory but vowed to keep mobilising.
Student unions have called a new national day of protest for 17 October. Asked about Trump’s claim that the protests were about Islam, the primary school teacher did not hesitate.
"It’s completely absurd and has absolutely nothing to do with it."

Iran executes monarchist accused of supporting Israel, Reza Pahlavi

Iran executed mountaineer and musician Ali Sina Mostafavi, 38, on Wednesday, according to state sources, continuing the Islamic Republic’s use of executions as punishment against protesters. The judiciary said he carried out armed attacks during the six-week war with Israel and the United States earlier this year, supported exiled Crown Prince Reza Pahlavi, and maintained links with Israel.
Mostafavi, from Bam in Kerman province, was executed after the Supreme Court upheld a death sentence handed down by a Revolutionary Court in Kerman, the judiciary-affiliated Mizan news agency reported.
Human rights groups had warned less than 24 hours earlier that he had been moved to solitary confinement and his family summoned for a final visit. Pahlavi’s communications team then issued an urgent appeal, saying he had been tortured into confessing and convicted in a sham trial.
Mizan said Mostafavi carried out a series of shootings in Kerman during the war, which Iranian authorities call the Ramadan War. It said he opened fire in Azadi Square on March 24, wounding a civilian and a young girl. On April 21, it said, he fired at conscript soldiers and passing vehicles, injuring several people. It also accused him of two failed shooting attempts targeting police on the Kerman-Mahan road.
Authorities said a search of his hideout turned up a scoped Brno rifle, two shotguns, 246 rounds of ammunition and 30 Molotov cocktails.
The judiciary also said Mostafavi sent photographs and videos of sites struck during the war to Persian-language opposition media abroad. It said he expressed willingness to carry out an operation at Kerman airport. According to the authorities, messages on his phone included exchanges with Persian-language broadcasters and messages to Israel’s official Persian-language account.
Mizan said he took part in the nationwide protests that began in December 2025 and continued into January, and sent footage of the unrest to media outside Iran.
The judiciary said the case was heard with a defense lawyer present. It said the conviction rested on investigative findings, security reports, and Mostafavi’s confessions. The public account did not include the defense’s arguments or independently verifiable evidence. Iranian authorities have not released evidence that he acted under the direction of Pahlavi or Israeli officials, while human rights groups have raised concerns about his treatment in detention and the circumstances of his conviction.
'A political prisoner and young athlete'
Pahlavi’s team described him as “a political prisoner and young athlete” in “immediate danger of execution.” The account said in Persian that he was a patriotic mountaineer and alleged his conviction followed “forced confessions under torture” and a “show trial.”
The League for the Defense of Human Rights in Iran said armed security officers arrested Mostafavi at his home in the early hours of April 25. The group alleged he was beaten during the arrest.
Branch 1 of the Kerman Revolutionary Court, presided over by Judge Hadi Aghaei, sentenced him to death on charges including moharebeh, or waging war against God, acting against national security, and gathering and colluding. Branch 41 of the Supreme Court upheld the sentence on September 28, according to human rights reports.
On Tuesday, rights groups reported his transfer to solitary confinement at Kerman prison.
Iran sees sharp rise in the use of the death penalty
Before his arrest, Mostafavi was an experienced mountaineer. IranWire and Human Rights for Sports said he climbed Island Peak in Nepal and attempted Ama Dablam, reaching about 6,600 meters. Records in Kerman mountaineering club archives show he joined a 2016 expedition to Alam-Kuh, one of Iran’s highest mountains. Human rights reports also describe him as a musician.
The execution follows a sharp rise in the use of the death penalty against people accused of involvement in the January protests, opposition activity and war-related security offenses.
On Tuesday, Amnesty International condemned the executions of five men between September 30 and October 5 who had been convicted in connection with the January uprising. “The arbitrary executions of these five young men serves as another chilling reminder of how the Iranian authorities weaponize the death penalty to render the cost of dissent so high that it terrorizes the population into silence,” said Diana Eltahawy, the group’s deputy regional director for the Middle East and North Africa.

Marrakech Airshow showcases building blocks of Israel-Morocco defense ties - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:15:10 UTC
19:15:10 KST

The recent Marrakech Airshow showed that Israel and Morocco are moving toward closer defense ties. Israel’s Defense Ministry said last week that Israel has opened a national pavilion at the show and that the ministry had led an Israeli delegation to Morocco to participate.
“This marks Israel's first official participation in the defense exhibition held in Morocco since the signing of the Abraham Accords, and the first time the Israel Ministry of Defense (IMOD) International Defense Cooperation Directorate (SIBAT) has opened an Israeli national pavilion and headed a delegation of Israeli defense industries at the show,” the ministry said.
Eight Israeli companies came with the delegation, including ASIO Technologies, Orbit Communication Systems, SHILAT Optronics, UVision Air, and XTEND Systems. Israel’s big three defense giants, Rafael Advanced Defense Systems, Elbit Systems and Israel Aerospace Industries, were also present.
This was an important opportunity for Israel’s large companies as well as the smaller and midsize ones to showcase various systems. The ministry highlighted “advanced, combat-proven technologies at the show, including loitering munitions, AI-powered robotic systems, autonomous navigation capabilities for UAVs, laser guidance for FPV drones, satellite communications, and more.”
The ministry is seeking greater defense cooperation with countries abroad. This includes numerous Israeli companies taking part in AUSA this week.
It also includes the recent major Israeli defense deal with Greece for Achilles Shield. In that deal, valued at around €3 billion, Israel will help Greece build a multi-layered air defense array based on Israeli systems. These systems include David’s Sling and Spyder, made by Rafael, as well as the Barak system, made by IAI.
As such, a trend is clear. Israeli ties with Morocco are not just about Morocco but part of a larger story of Israeli ties with Greece and the US. Morocco is seeking to acquire several Israeli defense systems, and reports indicate it has already acquired several. For instance, we reported in January 2026 that Morocco had deployed IAI’s Barak air defense system.
The Economist also reported last year that Morocco was producing drones in cooperation with an Israeli company. “Morocco is Africa’s new military tech hub,” an op-ed at The Jerusalem Post said in April.
Israeli-Moroccan friendship goes back years
The building blocks of Israel-Morocco relations include a friendship going back years. Morocco is part of the Abraham Accords. A small number of Israeli troops joined a US-backed exercise called Africa Lion in Morocco in 2025. Calcalist reported on October 12 that “Moroccan Military Industry (MMI) will begin delivering armored vehicle turrets to the Moroccan army in March 2027, the company's general manager said on the sidelines of the Marrakech Air Show.”
The report added that “sources at the air show and earlier media reporting have said MMI is closely linked to Israel's Elbit Systems and uses its technology. MMI itself told Reuters it is a Moroccan defense company, a characterization that leaves the precise nature of the relationship with Elbit unaddressed on the record.” A separate report at Calcalist also said that Morocco was interested in IAI’s Lora missile.
The Lora missile has been around for years. Back in 2020, IAI said that a “complex trial included two scenarios to test and demonstrate LORA’s advanced capabilities. The first scenario involved a short-range launch to 90 km and the second to a long range of 400 km.” The German Navy completed a successful dual operational firing trial with IAI's Naval Lora ballistic missile, IAI said in September.
On October 12, Morocco World News also noted: “Morocco and Israel are holding advanced talks over the possible integration of the Israeli David’s Sling air defense system into the Royal Moroccan Armed Forces, according to the German defense publication Europäische Sicherheit & Technik (ES&T).”
Several reports from the Marrakech show highlighted Morocco's search for more advanced defense equipment. For instance, Le360 reported that Morocco’s MMI unveiled a system called Spear, an “autonomous mortar system designed for light combat vehicles.”
The same site highlighted Israel’s pavilion at the air show. Le360 also noted that an Israeli officer “held a one-on-one meeting with the commander of the Royal Air Force. The two officials discussed strengthening strategic ties and continuing cooperation between the two air forces, according to reports.” The goal of these reports is to illustrate growing Israel-Morocco cooperation.
Morocco has been welcoming of Israel cooperation
The air show was a key part of publicly showcasing Israel-Morocco cooperation. At a time when Israel has sometimes faced challenges abroad and controversy, Morocco has been welcoming. It has been more welcoming than France, for instance. Morocco’s drive to increase its capabilities, especially in air defenses and precision fire, is important. It would knit Morocco into a regional defense architecture that brings together countries with advanced systems. These could include Israeli systems that are being sold in Europe, such as to Greece.
As such, one could imagine a link between Morocco, Greece, Israel, and other countries that share various advanced systems. This would also position Morocco as an advanced, capable military power at the head of the Mediterranean. This matters because Morocco and Algeria are rivals, and Algeria is hostile to Israel. A recent UAE-Algeria diplomatic crisis also adds to the complexity. Libya, divided by civil war, also plays a role.
With so much at stake in today's regional shifts from the Horn of Africa to the Sahel, Morocco-Israel ties likely matter more than ever. The recent air show symbolized these ties and showcased practical military technology.

Shas chairman MK Arye Deri said on Wednesday that his party would not join or support Israel’s next government unless legislation regulating the military service status of haredi (ultra-Orthodox) yeshiva students is passed, drawing criticism from opposition leaders as the October 27 election approaches.
Deri made the remarks in an interview with the haredi news outlet Kikar HaShabbat, making the passage of a draft law a condition for Shas’s participation in any future coalition, regardless of who forms the government.
“There will be no government in Israel with Shas’s support or participation unless the status of yeshiva students is regulated,” Deri said.
The declaration places the contentious issue of haredi military enlistment at the center of coalition negotiations even before Israelis head to the polls, with parties sharply divided over whether yeshiva students should continue receiving exemptions from IDF service.
Amid Shas and United Torah Judaism’s longstanding partnership in Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition, they have faced recent criticism over their stance regarding haredi conscription in light of the IDF’s severe manpower deficiency.
The haredi parties encouraged Netanyahu’s coalition to advance legislation that critics argued would not increase haredi enlistment during the government’s term.
They also boycotted coalition voting, stating that they would not cooperate with Netanyahu’s coalition until there was progress on the contentious legislation they had been pushing for.
In March, IDF Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir said the military could soon collapse if no solution was found for the manpower shortage.
Opposition bloc leaders condemn Deri's statements
Opposition leaders in the bloc seeking to replace Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in the upcoming elections condemned Deri’s statements, sharply criticized the premier’s partnership with the haredi parties, and warned of the IDF’s enlistment crisis.
Former prime minister Naftali Bennett, who leads the B’Yachad party, said that “Netanyahu will continue funding draft dodgers, and in return, Deri will give him the reins of power, all at the expense of those who serve.”
“The IDF chief of staff is raising 10 red flags over the army’s collapse, while Deri, a member of the Security Cabinet, tells him: ‘We intend to continue down the same path and institutionalize draft evasion,’” Bennett added.
“A vote for Netanyahu, [Finance Minister Bezalel] Smotrich, or Deri is a vote for draft evasion, 150 days of reserve duty a year, and billions of shekels every year transferred from the pockets of those who serve to those who evade service,” he said.
Leader of the Yisrael Beytenu party MK Avigdor Liberman noted that Deri had “admitted in his own words that he will agree to forming a government only if his puppet, Netanyahu, agrees to permanently exempt all haredim from military service.
“What does this mean in practice? Voting for the draft-dodgers’ government led by Bibi [Netanyahu] and Deri means an even greater burden on those who serve, hundreds more days of reserve duty, and further extensions of mandatory service for active-duty soldiers,” he said.

Ohio's working-class voters rethink support for Trump and the Republican Party
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:11:05 UTC
19:11:05 KST

Ohio's working-class voters rethink support for Trump and the Republican Party
WARREN, Ohio, Oct 14 - A decade after Republican Donald Trump peeled away working-class and union voters who had long been a cornerstone of Democratic support in Ohio, Democrats and labor leaders see an opening to win back some of them in the November 3 US elections.
Now midway through his second term, the president's magic appears to be losing at least some of its luster with blue-collar men and women as rising prices, the Iran war and concerns about his rhetoric prompt some voters to reconsider their support.
The state's reputation as a leading swing state began to fade in 2016 when Trump won strong support from working-class voters who felt their economic concerns were being heard, helping turn Ohio into a reliably Republican state.
Almost overnight, Ohio became rock-solid Republican. Ohio voted for the eventual winner in 14 straight presidential elections from 1964 until 2020 when Democrat Joe Biden won nationally but Ohio backed Trump.
A shift in Ohio toward Democrats could matter in elections that will help determine whether Republicans retain control of Congress during Trump's final two years in office or hand new leverage to Democrats over his agenda.
The stakes are high in Ohio, where Republicans are defending a US Senate seat and the governor's office. Two House races are rated "toss-ups." One, in northwestern Ohio, has long been held by a Democrat and the other, in northeastern Ohio, is Republican-held.
Trump is not on the ballot this time but has told supporters to act as if he is. It remains to be seen whether that could end up helping or hindering Republicans running in tough races.
Republican Senator Jon Husted is in a tight competition with Democratic former Senator Sherrod Brown, while Democrat Amy Acton is challenging Republican Vivek Ramaswamy for an open governor's seat.
Trump campaigned with Husted and Ramaswamy in Youngstown on Monday to try to energize the Republican base.
'GOD KNOWS WE DIDN'T VOTE FOR THIS'
Paul Ringold, a 48-year-old steel hauler and pastor of the mostly Black congregation at the Shalom Church of God and Christ in the city of Warren, embodies the uncertainty that Democrats hope could help them make inroads with working-class voters.
Ringold voted for Trump for president in 2016, Democrat Joe Biden in 2020 and Trump again in 2024, but said he remains undecided about whom to support for the US Senate, governor and other offices this year.
"I'm in the wilderness trying to find a place," he said.
Ringold said rising fuel and food prices and Trump's combative style have left him questioning some of the choices made by a president he once strongly supported.
"God knows we didn't vote for this," he said of inflation.
Like several voters interviewed by Reuters, Ringold also cited Trump's rhetoric. "I wish he would just tone down that rhetoric ... that old New York in-your-face 'I got you sucker'" persona, he said.
EARLY TURNOUT FAVORS DEMOCRATS
In early voting that began in Ohio last week, Democrats appeared to be more motivated than Republicans.
In Trumbull County, home to the city of Warren and many blue-collar jobs, a strong turnout during the first three days brought 1,224 Democrats to the polls, 559 Republicans and 453 with no known political affiliation, according to county data.
Paul Sracic, an Ohio-based senior fellow with the right-of-center Hudson Institute, said "working-class voters, if they are moving at all away from Trump, Brown is a safe landing spot for them" because of the former senator's populist record.
"Trump has done a good job of basically focusing on social issues with our guys," said Jose Arroyo, a United Steelworkers official who engages in contract negotiations and labor relations for the sprawling labor union.
Trump "seemed to latch on sort of to the dissatisfaction of where the working man has gone. Pensions go away. Plants close. Livelihoods they've always known disappear."
The problem, he said, is that focusing primarily on hot-button social issues ignores advancing policies that would "improve the lives of working people" and actually turn them into law.
The 50,000 manufacturing jobs in 1990 in the Youngstown-Warren area fell to about 20,000 in 2026, according to the US Bureau of Labor Statistics.
In recent years, the Mahoning Valley, long a powerhouse of the steel and automotive industries, has attracted a few new manufacturing plants. Arroyo said the Iran war has boosted domestic oil industry exploration, creating more demand for equipment made of steel. But he acknowledged that the war had also brought higher consumer prices.
NLRB 'DISMANTLING'
When Trump began his second term in January 2025, he promptly fired two Democratic officials at the National Labor Relations Board and left the agency without the quorum required to take actions. That paralysis lasted for nearly a year.
Ohio AFL-CIO President Tim Burga cited what he called Trump's "dismantling" of the NLRB as having hindered union organizing efforts and made it harder to contest unfair labor practices and secure work contracts with companies.
"We were on a path for the first time in my lifetime, under the Biden administration, for having a national industrial policy," Burga said, but the Trump administration rolled much of it back. Biden and Congress enacted programs to spur investment in such industries as clean energy and semiconductors.
Trump's trade battles with Canada also were unhelpful to labor, he said.
OHIO VOTERS REMAIN DIVIDED
Bill Callahan, 75, a self-described Democrat from Cortland, said some relatives who once backed Trump "are traveling back" toward Democrats because "they don't like (politicians) taking money out of their pockets."
A part-time warehouse worker from Cortland after a career at General Electric, he said he considered voting for Trump in 2016 but was put off by ethical concerns.
Others interviewed by Reuters said higher prices were not enough to change their vote.
Joe Scarabino, who co-owns a bait-and-tackle business with his wife Kathryn near Cortland, said the couple responded to higher fuel costs by raising delivery charges rather than product prices, thus having an impact on fewer customers and small business owners.
"We believe our Christian values are more than gas prices," he said. The couple declined to say who they support.
Retired coal-fired power plant worker Chuck Burns, 67, of Wellsville, credited Trump with reducing illegal immigration and boosting the value of his retirement investments. "He's done a good job ... he's got balls," Burns said.
Burns praised Trump's immigration restrictions at the southern border and said his retirement savings have increased in value since Biden left office.
Asked what issues worry him in this election season, Burns said, "It's just that Democrats – it's unbelievable some of the stuff that they want to do."
Asked to explain, Burns raised transgender issues. "Those poor people, they feel that way, that's fine, that's their business," he said. "They (Democrats) don't need to incorporate our young kids into that stuff." REUTERS

Nvidia, worth $5.5tn, donates $250m to UK for AI safety research
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:10:37 UTC
19:10:37 KST

The $5.5tn (£4.1tn) US chipmaker Nvidia is donating $250m worth of computing power to the UK to support AI safety research.
The donation from the world’s most valuable company comes as the UK government confirmed its AI Security Institute (AISI), which tests advance AI models, will be able to examine cutting-edge technology developed by companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic and Google before they are released.
Nvidia said the donation, which spans five years, would “support agentic safety and security research across the UK”.
Safety concerns about AI agents – highly capable computer programs that are able to design and perform sequences of tasks autonomously – have risen since the summer, when OpenAI confirmed that a “swarm” of agents had attacked Hugging Face, a tech startup.
Nvidia did not reference AISI in its statement but said most of the money would “support the wider UK AI safety and security research community”, with a proportion of the cash going to the British Open-Ended Learning and Discovery Lab, the Science of Fundamental AI Research Lab – run by the Edinburgh, Cambridge, Oxford and University College London universities – and Imperial College London.
The computing power will be delivered via UK-based datacentres using Nvidia chips.
“The UK brings world-class scientific rigour to this essential engineering challenge,” said Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s chief executive. “With this $250m commitment, Nvidia will put accelerated computing in the hands of UK researchers to develop, test and strengthen safeguards for increasingly powerful AI.”
Kanishka Narayan, the UK’s AI minister, said the announcement was a “vote of confidence in our world-leading strength and expertise in AI research”.
On Monday Narayan confirmed that AISI was conducting tests on US-developed AI models before they are released, after reports that the White House had restricted access.
The AI minister also warned that the UK faces agentic attacks similar to the one carried out by OpenAI agents on Australia’s healthcare system this year.
“It seems likely, if not inevitable, that our own cyber defences will be breached,” said Narayan.
Anthropic, the developer of the Claude chatbot, warned of a new AI safety threat on Monday after it published a blogpost stating its models could soon become self-replicating. They find ways to infiltrate internet-connected devices such as smart ovens and lawnmowers, the company said.
Under such a scenario the models could power themselves without datacentres, and instead could use a “botnet” of interconnected devices, Anthropic said, adding that the world should prepare for a future where such botnets were here to stay.
“A replicator like this would be challenging to shut down since there’s no centralised point to shut off,” Anthropic’s researchers wrote.
