China Focus: Drones rise over grassland the Red Army once crossed
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
17:36:30 CST
18:36:30 KST

A drone is seen in operation during an earthquake relief drill held in Tiebu Town of Ruoergai County, southwest China's Sichuan Province, May 12, 2026. (Xinhua)
CHENGDU, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- When Ngorcog was a child growing up on the vast grasslands of Sichuan Province in southwest China, she never imagined that barley and fruit would one day "fall from the sky."
For the young Tibetan woman, cargo transport used to rely on horses and yaks, and later, trucks. Today, the 25-year-old has a new role: pilot of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs).
"Learning to fly drones was difficult at first, but it was also fascinating," she said. Drone logistics services are becoming increasingly common in the Aba Tibetan and Qiang Autonomous Prefecture, where Ngorcog lives.
Ngorcog is from Baxi Town in Ruoergai County of Sichuan. In September 1935, during the Long March, the Central Committee of the Communist Party of China held the Baxi Meeting there, establishing the strategic policy of continuing northward.
The site of the meeting, Banyu Monastery, remains a place of regular worship for Ngorcog, who practices Tibetan Buddhism. In Tibetan culture, the sky holds special significance, with the mythical Garuda bird symbolizing good fortune.
Ngorcog's first encounter with drones came during her university years, when she and her classmates used one to take graduation photos.
"I felt both excited and nervous during takeoff," she recalled. "When the lens rose to the sky, offering a bird's-eye view of the surrounding world, the familiar scenery instantly looked different. My horizon was completely opened, and that sense of vastness was hard to describe in words."
However, it was not until after graduating in 2024 that she began professional training. Originally a music student, she decided to apply for drone training after seeing a recruitment notice from Ruoergai General Aviation Culture and Tourism Co., Ltd.
This company is the first low-altitude economy enterprise in Aba, a plateau region with an average altitude between 3,500 and 4,000 meters, and Ruoergai is China's first pilot county for the low-altitude economy on high-altitude plateaus.
Ngorcog was sent to a training and certification base in Jiande, east China's Zhejiang Province. "The hardest part was flying the 8-shaped route," she said. Three months later, she obtained her pilot license.
Her parents, both farmers, live 90 kilometers from her workplace. Having never seen a drone before, they were curious about their daughter's new job.
"They asked me if I could use the drone to spray pesticides on their vegetable plots," she said with a smile.
More than 90 years ago, the Red Army crossed the grasslands of Ruoergai and surrounding areas. In his book "The Long March: The Untold Story," American journalist and author Harrison Salisbury described the area as "untouched for 3,000 years." Filled with swamps, extreme cold and low oxygen, the treacherous terrain claimed the lives of many soldiers.
In recent years, Ruoergai has developed its low-altitude economy. So far, its low-altitude airspace covers 9,119 square kilometers, making it one of the largest contiguous low-altitude coordinated airspaces in China.
Located on a high-altitude plateau, Ruoergai is prone to extreme weather such as blizzards, and some areas face high risks of geological disasters. When roads are cut off by ice, snow or landslides, making them impassable for people and vehicles, drones can take off quickly to deliver urgent medicines, food and warm clothing to isolated areas.
In May this year, Aba held an earthquake relief drill in Ruoergai. The drill simulated a magnitude 6.6 earthquake that severed roads, paralyzed communications, and turned some villages into "isolated islands." During the exercise, compound-wing UAVs conducted aerial reconnaissance of the disaster area and airdropped first-aid kits, drinking water and communication equipment to the "stranded" zones, effectively addressing the communication and access challenges.
"When a sudden disaster occurs on the Ruoergai grassland, drones can fly immediately to areas inaccessible to vehicles, conduct reconnaissance and deliver emergency supplies," said Huang Peifeng, deputy head of Ruoergai County.
Meanwhile, Ruoergai is gradually incorporating drones into the monitoring and patrolling of grassland ecology and wetlands.
Including Ngorcog, the company established last year now has four local Tibetan female pilots who have successfully obtained licenses to operate medium-sized drones and officially started their jobs. Their main duties include aerial photography for tourism and resource data collection.
As a national strategic emerging industry, the low-altitude economy is rapidly gaining momentum. The Civil Aviation Administration of China predicts that the market size of China's low-altitude economy is set to exceed 3.5 trillion yuan (around 522 billion U.S. dollars) by 2035.
According to a report on education and industrial talent development in China's low-altitude economy this year, the shortage of core positions in the sector will reach 1.82 million in the next five years, with demand for technical roles surging by over 320 percent.
To enhance local children's understanding of drones, the company offers study tour courses.
According to Tsewang Lhamo with the Ruoergai General Aviation Culture and Tourism Co., Ltd., the company has collaborated with local schools for over a year, hosting 500 to 600 students. The curriculum includes aviation lectures, VR experiences, model aircraft making and drone soccer.
"Few people on the grassland had ever encountered drones before," Tsewang Lhamo said. "The children were very interested. I thought they might be afraid of the VR flying experience, but they weren't. During the lessons, they didn't even want class to end."
"Children here rarely have access to cutting-edge technologies. These drone study tours sow the seeds of the low-altitude economy on the grassland. The curiosity in their eyes is precious, and it shows us the unique potential of these grassland children," said Yang Rong, a teacher at a primary school in the Ruoergai county seat.
Tsewang Lhamo is also preparing to take her pilot license exam.
"I hope to master another skill," she said. "In the future, drones will be used in more places across the grassland." ■
Ngorcog (1st R) instructs trainees during a flight simulator training session in Ruoergai County, southwest China's Sichuan Province, July 15, 2026. (Xinhua)
A drone photo taken on Sept. 3, 2026 shows a monument to martyrs of the Red Army in Baxi Town of Ruoergai County, southwest China's Sichuan Province. (Xinhua)

Palestinian children’s rights lawyer Khaled Quzmar receives Amnesty Human Rights Award 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:36:17 UTC
18:36:17 KST

BERLIN, 13 October 2026 – This year’s Human Rights Award of Amnesty International Germany goes to the Palestinian lawyer Khaled Quzmar, in recognition of his longstanding commitment to defending the rights of children in the illegally occupied Palestinian territory. The award carries a prize of €20,000.
An internationally recognised expert on children’s rights, Khaled Quzmar has played a crucial role in exposing structural and systematic human rights abuses against Palestinian children and in placing demands for accountability and justice at the heart of public debate. He has documented human rights violations in the Gaza Strip and the West Bank, including East Jerusalem for UN bodies and international courts, and has enabled countless children and their families to access legal assistance and psychosocial support.
Because of his work, Quzmar, who is based in Ramallah, has been subjected to considerable pressure, repression and smear campaigns by the Israeli authorities. Such instances include being summoned by Israel’s internal intelligence service, Shin Bet, and threatened with a lengthy prison sentence. As long-serving Director General of the human rights organisation Defense for Children International – Palestine (DCI-P), he was forced to dissolve the organisation in spring 2026, after more than 35 years, in the face of sustained harassment by the Israeli authorities. Since June 2026, he has served as Executive Director of the organisation Palestinian Center for Child Rights (PCCR).
Julia Duchrow, Secretary General of Amnesty International Germany, said: “For almost 40 years, Khaled Quzmar has worked tirelessly and against all odds to give a voice to the most vulnerable group in Palestinian society: its children. Their devastating living conditions are the direct consequence of structural human rights abuses and systematic oppression, which have intensified significantly in recent years. This state of affairs is depriving entire generations of a future. Allies of the Israeli government, including the United States and Germany, have contributed to this situation. They not only turn a blind eye to serious human rights abuses against Palestinians but facilitate them through arms deliveries. This must come to an end. Palestinian children need immediate and the fullest possible protection.”
Structural human rights abuses and systematic discrimination
For decades, Palestinian children have been subjected to grave human rights abuses as a result of Israel’s unlawful occupation and cruel system of apartheid against all Palestinians. Since the massive escalation of violence in October 2023 and the beginning of the genocide against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip, their situation has deteriorated dramatically.
“What is often portrayed as a humanitarian crisis is the result of political decisions by the Israeli government that are systematically destroying these children’s lives. This is not only about the lack of humanitarian aid for children across the unlawfully occupied Palestinian territory; it is about their right to life and physical integrity, to freedom and security, to education, health and housing – and ultimately about whether these human rights apply to Palestinian children at all,” said Julia Duchrow.
In the Gaza Strip, the Israeli military has killed at least 20,000 children since October 2023, and more than 17,000 have lost their families. Tens of thousands of children are living with severe injuries, hunger and disease, amid destroyed infrastructure and without access to basic services, schools and education. In the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, children are affected by state-backed settler violence and displacement – with schools and infrastructure also being systematically destroyed there.
Repression of Palestinian civil society
Human rights defenders and human rights organisations in the Occupied Palestinian Territory face constant repression by the Israeli authorities and military. In October 2021, Israel designated the DCI-P – the organisation for which Khaled Quzmar had worked for many years – as a terrorist organisation, along with five other Palestinian civil society organisations, without providing any substantiated evidence. Amnesty International, the United Nations and numerous civil society organisations strongly criticised the designation. The German government and many other EU partners have also rejected Israel’s designation. Since the current ruling coalition took office – and particularly since 7 October 2023 – staff members of some organisations have increasingly been subjected to intimidation, smear campaigns, interrogation, arbitrary detention, imprisonment and ill-treatment, with some offices also being raided.
Amnesty International Germany’s Human Rights Award
Every two years, Amnesty International Germany honours individuals and organisations working for human rights under difficult conditions with its Human Rights Award. The award aims to recognise, support and protect their work and to raise public awareness of it. It carries a prize of €20,000. 2026 marks the 13th time the Amnesty Human Rights Award will have been presented. Previous recipients include Eren Keskin (Türkiye), Svetlana Gannushkina (Russia), Alice Nkom (Cameroon), Henri Tiphagne (India) and the Colombian organization Federation of Santander Fishers for Tourism and Environment (FEDESPAN).

Türkiye moves to speed fund repayments
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:35:47 UTC
18:35:47 KST

Parliament’s Plan and Budget Committee discusses a bill setting out rules for the liquidation of 131 investment funds and repayments to affected investors. (AA Photo)
Türkiye aims to complete the liquidation of 49 more investment funds by the weekend, after 43,643 investors received 6.4 billion Turkish Liras in payments last week.
The Communications Directorate announced the target after an Oct. 13 Fund Board meeting chaired by Vice President Cevdet Yılmaz.
Ziraat Bank made the payments to investors in funds managed by A1, Bulls and Pardus. The remaining liquidation involves 34.1 billion liras in assets.
Completion would bring cash payments and asset transfers across the three companies’ 66 funds to 40.5 billion liras, covering 45,745 investors.
The board aims to complete interim payments for another 65 funds swiftly once legislation governing the process is enacted, the directorate said.
The nine-article bill, submitted on Oct. 9, was on the agenda of parliament’s Plan and Budget Committee on Oct. 14.
The wider liquidation covers 131 funds run by seven portfolio managers and more than 455,000 investors.
Ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) lawmaker Ersan Aksu, one of the bill’s sponsors, said no Treasury or budget funds would be used.
Payments would come from each fund’s assets and money recovered from those responsible for losses.
The bill would allow interim payments of up to 1 million liras per eligible investor, based on cash paid into the fund minus withdrawals, without inflation adjustment. These would be deducted from final payments.
Investors with less than 1 million liras in net investments could receive that amount in full if sufficient cash is available.
Where cash is insufficient, the Capital Markets Board (SPK) could prioritize those with the lowest net investments.
Where fund assets fall short, final settlement calculations would adjust cash inflows and outflows up to the liquidation date using the average change in consumer and domestic producer price indices.
The bill would also allow the Savings Deposit Insurance Fund (TMSF) to sell assets placed under its trusteeship before trials conclude.
Aksu said the affected funds accounted for 7.7 percent of total fund assets and that the problems posed no systemic risk.
Opposition lawmakers called for closer scrutiny, saying the bill’s impact assessment lacked sufficient information.
Separately, Central Bank Governor Fatih Karahan said measures to contain risks spreading from funds under trading restrictions had limited the impact on the financial system.
In Bangkok on Oct. 14, he outlined increased repo funding, eased borrowing and collateral conditions and accelerated purchases of securities linked to the Turkish Lira Overnight Reference Rate.
The bank also raised the credit growth cap for small and medium-sized businesses from 4.5 percent to 5 percent.
Karahan said fund outflows had not significantly weakened residents’ preference for lira-denominated assets.

The reports have prompted renewed attention to possible cross-border risks, although the cause of the laboratory worker’s death has not been confirmed.

Far-right Colombian government opens embassy to Israel in Jerusalem
Colombia on Wednesday officially opened its embassy in Jerusalem, joining a small group of countries including the United States in taking the symbolic step of backing Israeli sovereignty in the contested holy city.
The vast majority of countries keep their embassies to Israel in Tel Aviv on the grounds that Jerusalemis under occupation and the status should be resolved through a diplomatic process.
"This is an important date for the State of Israel. It's also an important date for the city of Jerusalem," Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said during a ceremony while signing the Colombian embassy's guest book.
Colombia's new hard-right president, Abelardo de la Espriella, in July announced that he would move his country's embassy to occupied Jerusalem, a sharp shift from his leftist predecessor who criticised Israel over its genocida of Gaza.
President Donald Trump shattered international consensus in 2018 during his first term by moving the US embassy to Jerusalem, which is home to Israel's parliament, prime minister and most other major governmental institutions.
Since Trump's move, only a handful of small, US-aligned countries have followed suit: Fiji, Guatemala, Honduras, Papua New Guinea and Paraguay.
Kosovo and Somaliland, which are not member-states of the United Nations, have also opened what they consider their embassies in Jerusalem.
Argentine President Javier Milei, another right-wing Latin American who is an outspoken supporter of Israel, has promised to move his country's embassy to Jerusalem.
Israel occupied east Jerusalem and annexed it in 1967, in a move not recognised by the vast majority of the international community or international law.
In August, Colombia's new hard-right government recognised Israel's claim over the Golan Heights, which it seized from Syria in 1967. The US was until then the only country to recognise Israel's annexation of the territory in 1981.
The United Nations and the rest of the world maintain that the plateau is Syrian territory under Israeli military occupation.

Trump’s Phantom Ceasefires Are a National Security Problem

On Sunday, Oct. 11, at 10:16 a.m., President Donald Trump announced on social media an immediate ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine covering attacks on energy infrastructure. He asserted that both parties had agreed. In the same post he issued an unmistakable warning: “Do not break it!”
Within half an hour of Trump’s announcement, a senior Ukrainian official told the press that Kyiv had no information about the purported agreement. Within the same hour, Zelensky’s own response was public: the announcement “was news for me.” He added that Ukraine would agree to a ceasefire if Russia did the same.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Exactly 59 minutes after Trump announced the purported ceasefire, Russia attacked Kharkiv’s CHP-5 power plant.
The alleged ceasefire was over.
Crickets from the White House.
Second time in a month
This was the second time in one month that the president issued a false claim about a negotiated ceasefire.
On Sept. 14, Trump declared: “Ukraine has agreed not to hit Russian Energy Targets. Russia has agreed to do likewise!”
Yet a senior Ukrainian official made it clear that they had not heard of such a ceasefire. Zelensky expressed willingness to reciprocate if Russia halted its attacks, while saying Kyiv awaited details. Meanwhile, Russia continued to target Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.
There are several possible explanations for President Trump’s repeated misrepresentations about ceasefires to the world:
Moscow, Washington vs. Kyiv: Can Trump Force Ukraine to Capitulate?
Does any of this matter?
Yes, and it is a matter of national security.
Repeatedly announcing ceasefires that have not been established is a grave failure of presidential responsibility. Such statements can shape military calculations, diplomatic decisions, financial markets, and the expectations of civilians whose lives depend on whether the bombing will actually stop.
When a president declares that both parties have agreed, he places American credibility behind that assertion. If the agreement does not exist, he undermines trust in future American commitments, creates confusion about who has promised what, and risks allowing continued aggression to disappear beneath a headline proclaiming peace.
Congressional leaders have a duty to call immediate hearings, establish what the president knew, identify who supplied his information, and determine what corrective action is required. Whether the explanation is deliberate deception, gross negligence, confusion, or something else, announcing an international agreement without establishing the consent of its participants raises serious questions about the president’s competence to oversee American foreign policy.
Congress must treat this as a matter of national security and demand an explanation. A president’s words about war and peace carry the authority of the United States; they cannot be excused as a salesman’s harmless exaggeration.
In the meantime, the world must respond advisedly to such claims by President Trump. “Fool me once, shame on you. Fool me twice, shame on me.”

Lockheed gets $117M for Apache radar-hunting sensors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:32:34 UTC
18:32:34 KST

- The U.S. Army awarded Lockheed Martin a $117.1 million contract to support the Apache’s second-generation radar frequency interferometer through October 2031.
- Lockheed Martin is already developing a Generation 3 replacement sensor for the Apache fleet under a contract awarded in October 2024.
The U.S. Army has awarded Lockheed Martin a $117.1 million contract to keep supporting the second-generation radar frequency interferometer on its Apache attack helicopters, a passive sensor that lets crews find and pinpoint enemy radars without giving away their own position.
The Department of War contract announcement describes an indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity deal that mixes cost-no-fee, cost-plus-fixed-fee and firm-fixed-price terms for “post-production support services” on the Generation II system, with work running through Oct. 12, 2031. Lockheed Martin’s Owego, New York, business received the award after the Army solicited only one bid, and both work locations and funding will be set as individual orders are placed under the contract.
Known in military designation as the AN/APR-48B, the system listens for radar emissions on the battlefield rather than transmitting its own signal. It detects, identifies and locates enemy radars and then ranks them by priority for attack, while also cueing the Apache’s fire-control radar and warning the crew of radar-guided anti-aircraft threats. The same unit serves as the controller for the helicopter’s integrated survivability equipment, which ties it to the aircraft’s self-protection suite as well as its targeting.
Owego has supplied this family of sensors for decades. The first-generation AN/APR-48A flew on Apache Longbow helicopters in Desert Storm, Operation Iraqi Freedom and Operation Enduring Freedom, and the modernized second-generation version followed on the AH-64E Apache Guardian, the current production model flown by the U.S. Army.
The Generation II sensor also equips foreign Apache fleets, with Lockheed Martin delivering units to the United Kingdom, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and South Korea through Foreign Military Sales alongside those built for the U.S. Army.
Production of the current version has been winding down. An earlier $60.5 million award for AN/APR-48B production and related services scheduled work in Owego through Oct. 31, 2026, which places the new support contract right at the point where the Army shifts from buying the sensor to sustaining the fleet already in service.
A successor is already in development. In October 2024 the Army’s Apache program office hired Lockheed Martin to develop a Generation 3 radar frequency interferometer and radar warning receiver, promising better sensor performance in a smaller and lighter package built around a radio frequency system on a chip, and the new sensor is set to replace all Gen 2 systems across the Apache fleet.
That timeline explains the length of the new deal, since Generation II sensors will need spares, repairs and engineering support for as long as they remain on Apaches waiting for the upgrade. Neither the Army nor Lockheed Martin has said when Generation 3 will enter production or how quickly it will reach operational units.

As the US and China race ahead in AI, France carves its own path with Nvidia’s help
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:31:49 UTC
18:31:49 KST

Nvidia bets almost $10 billion in Europe as Paris pushes for AI sovereignty.
American Artificial intelligence giant Nvidia is spending big in France with a string of new investments in its technology and health companies, showing how Paris is safeguarding its technological sovereignty amid the AI race between China and the United States.
On Tuesday, Nvidia announced planned investments in medical booking website Doctolib, robotics company Genesis AI, chemicals and materials company Entalpic and enterprise software company Pigment.
The company says it brings its investments to Europe to nearly $10 billion (€9 bn) to the continent’s technology ecosystem.
Nvidia’s investments in France show how the country’s push, driven in particular by President Emmanuel Macron, to lead in technology has grown since the AI Action Summit in February 2025 and the ‘Choose France’ summits.
But AI sovereignty, which the European Commission defines as “Europe's ability to act independently in the digital world by developing and controlling key technologies,” depends heavily on infrastructure, which is currently being built in Western France.
The French AI structures
Taiwan’s Foxconn and French computing firm Bull announced in June they would partner to build powerful AI computers in Europe to power the continent's fast-growing network of AI factories, the large-scale computing centres that form the backbone of artificial intelligence infrastructure.
Foxconn initially manufactures or tests the components in its facilities in Czechia before final assembly, rack integration and validation take place at the newly opened Angers plant in Western France.
Foxconn will provide the AI factory infrastructure while Nvidia provides the latest AI chips.
Additionally, from 2028, Bull will manufacture systems based on the powerful NVIDIA Vera Rubin Ultra NVL72 rack-scale AI supercomputer in Angers.
Nvidia’s CEO and founder Jensen Huang said at Davos in January that AI is "exciting for Europe" because of its "incredibly strong manufacturing base" for building AI infrastructure.
Huang described this as Europe's moment to "leapfrog" the software era and also called robotics a "once-in-a-lifetime opportunity" for the continent.
The CEO describes AI as a five-layer cake that includes energy, chips, infrastructure, data centre servers and the AI models and applications.
“Nvidia is trying to help everyone across that cake, all the layers, work together and progress together,” Nat Ives, Nvidia’s director of enterprise for Benelux, France & Nordics, told Euronews Next in June.
He said that “comes home to roost in France in particular,” as France has nuclear renewable power, which is cheaper and more sustainable, as well as having the French multinational electric utility company EDF, which is owned by the French government.
The open weight debate
Another key announcement from Nvidia was its commitment to open-weight AI models, which means the numerical parameters are publicly released and allow anyone to download, run and modify them.
The race over open-weight AI, in which a model's parameters can be downloaded and run by anyone, has taken on a geopolitical edge.
Chinese developers have set the pace, while many American companies, such as OpenAI, keep their most capable systems closed. Meanwhile, the debate over safety has grown since AI agents have been found to go rogue and hack websites.
Nvidia said its own open models, called Nemotron, are now in production at French organisations that need “sovereign, trustworthy data”.
The company announced a big deployment in government. The workplace software platform called Twake.ai, built by French companies Linagora and Docaposte, has been chosen as the only officially recommended “sovereign” digital workplace for more than 2,500 French public organisations.
Here, sovereign will mean the data stays under French and European control rather than with foreign tech giants.
Additionally, in banking, a company called SBS is launching a platform that lets banks run AI tools, including AI agents that can carry out tasks on their own, inside their own systems. NVIDIA is working with SBS on the project.
It is not Nvidia’s first open-weight venture in France. In March, it partnered with French AI champion Mistral, which introduced its open-weight Mistral Large 4 in private preview last week.
France appears to be betting that sovereignty does not mean building everything alone, but rather with key partners across continents. With cheaper energy and its abundance of talent, it could forge its own path as China and the US battle it out.

She brought Israeli agriculture to the world; October 7 changed everything
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:31:18 UTC
18:31:18 KST

For years, Danielle Abraham worked to bring Israel's agricultural expertise and innovation to countries struggling with water shortages, food insecurity and harsh climate conditions. After October 7, that mission took a new direction. Instead of taking Israeli expertise abroad, she sought to bring it home and put it to work for farmers whose livelihoods had been devastated.
Just days after the Hamas attack, Abraham launched ReGrow Israel, an initiative aimed at rebuilding farms and agricultural infrastructure in communities near the Gaza border. Initially, she envisioned it as a consulting service for farmers, with a team of experts assessing their needs and developing long-term recovery plans. But the reality on the ground was far more urgent. Farmers had been left without tractors, equipment or the infrastructure needed to resume operations. Before planning for the years ahead, they needed help getting their farms running again.
What began as an emergency response in southern Israel has since expanded to farms and communities affected by the war in the north. The initiative supports farmers by providing equipment, restoring infrastructure and bringing in professional expertise and technology, while also working to strengthen Israeli agriculture over the long term.
For this work, Abraham will receive the Nefesh B'Nefesh Sylvan Adams Bonei Zion Prize at a ceremony this coming Sunday, marking Aliyah Day. The event will be broadcast live on ynet. Now in its 12th year, the award recognizes immigrants from English-speaking countries who have made exceptional contributions to Israeli society across a range of fields. Abraham was selected in the Global Impact category.
Abraham's journey began more than 15 years ago in a lecture hall in London. An Oxford University music graduate working at Britain's Home Office, she was 23 when she attended a lecture by Israeli agronomist Yitzhak Abt. Abt, who had helped establish Israel's international agricultural assistance program through MASHAV, the Foreign Ministry's Agency for International Development Cooperation, spoke about immigrating to Israel from South Africa and his work advancing agriculture in Israel and developing countries.
When Abraham returned home from the lecture, she told her family: "When I grow up, I want to be him." The encounter changed the course of her life. Abraham left her job, sold her car and immigrated to Israel in 2010.
Israel was not entirely unfamiliar to her. She had visited during summer vacations as a child and had relatives living in the country. She grew up in a Zionist household, was active in a Zionist youth movement and had visited Israel at 16. At Oxford, she led a Jewish student society and defended Israel in public debates. Still, leaving a sought-after job in London to begin life as a new immigrant in Israel was a leap into the unknown.
'Just for a year'
When Abraham accepted a position at Israel's Foreign Ministry, she had not yet fully committed to building her life in the country. She told everyone back home that she was coming for just one year. "Only after six months did I start saying I was thinking about making aliyah," she recalled. "My family and friends said, 'We knew from the moment you got on the plane.'"
Her parents, she said, never told her what to do and supported whatever decision she made. But there was one moment when they realized she was not coming back. "When I bought a piano for my home, they said, 'Now that you have that, you're not coming back.'"
One of her first challenges in Israel was the language. She would write down unfamiliar words she heard and send text messages to a friend asking what they meant. On weekends, she went to the beach with vocabulary lists from her Hebrew classes and memorized them. She also taped the lists to cabinets in her office. "My vocabulary was mostly agriculture and developing countries," she recalled. "I couldn't order food in a restaurant, but I could talk about irrigation."
At the Foreign Ministry, Abraham joined MASHAV and later served as a senior policy adviser, representing Israel at the United Nations, the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) and the German Development Bank. In many ways, she had fulfilled the ambition sparked by Abt's lecture: using Israeli expertise to solve real-world problems around the globe.
In 2017, she began leading Volcani International Partnerships, an organization that draws on Israeli agricultural knowledge and innovation to address challenges such as food security, water scarcity and farming in difficult climate conditions. Agriculture, she explained, is one of the fields in which Israel is a world leader, combining the Zionist vision with practical benefits.
Bringing the expertise home
After October 7, Abraham decided to use the experience, experts and international connections she had accumulated to help Israeli farmers. "When the extent of the destruction in the Gaza border communities became clear, I saw that some countries facing similar situations turn to outside assistance," she said. "I told everyone, 'We have everything right here: researchers, agronomists, innovation and high-tech. We just need to bring it all together.'"
ReGrow Israel began by providing emergency assistance to farmers in communities near Gaza, including replacing agricultural equipment and repairing damaged infrastructure. The initiative later expanded to farms and communities affected by the war in northern Israel.
Since its establishment, it has raised tens of millions of dollars to help rebuild Israeli agriculture. But Abraham said the goal was not simply to repair what was destroyed. She wanted to use the recovery process to build a stronger, more advanced and more resilient agricultural sector.
For Abraham, agriculture is more than an economic industry. It is closely tied to Israel's food security, the livelihoods of residents in outlying regions and the ability to sustain communities along the country's borders. "If agriculture isn't strong there, we won't have communities on the border," she said. Yet she believes Israel still does not sufficiently recognize agriculture as a strategic asset. "I still don't see enough effort being made to use it to strengthen Israel, both at home and abroad."
Despite everything October 7 changed in her life and work, Abraham has no doubts about her decision to immigrate. "Of course," she replied when asked whether she would choose Israel again. "You have to be a little crazy to live here, but you have to believe."
Looking back at the young woman who arrived alone in 2010, barely speaking Hebrew, Abraham sees a quality she is still trying to preserve. "I see a brave young woman with a kind of naivety that's important today. Everything was possible. I wasn't willing to take no for an answer," she said. "That's the spirit I try to hold on to, even as reality changes. We need people with big visions and hope, who make decisions that aren't crazy but are a little courageous, and who start with small things."
Alongside Abraham, several other immigrants will receive the Nefesh B'Nefesh Sylvan Adams Bonei Zion Prize. Naomi Stuchiner, founder of Beit Issie Shapiro, will receive the award in the Community and Non-Profit category; Dr. Philip Klipstein, a senior researcher in science and technology, will be honored in the Science and Medicine category; Rabbanit Chana Henkin, founder and dean of Nishmat, the Jeanie Schottenstein Center for Advanced Torah Study for Women, will receive the Education award; and Ami Baran, president of the Israel Athletics Association and CEO of the Israel Softball Association, will be recognized in the Culture, Arts and Sports category.
Professor Marta Weinstock-Rosin, a neuropharmacologist who developed Exelon, a drug used to treat Alzheimer's disease, will receive the Lifetime Achievement Award. Barak Swarttz, a content creator and founder of GRIT for Good, will receive the Young Leadership Award, while former ambassador Ron Dermer, who served as Israel's ambassador to the United States and strategic affairs minister, will receive a special recognition award.
For Abraham, the honor provides a platform not only for her work but also for Israeli agriculture and for immigrants seeking to find their place in the country. She said she still feels like "a little girl from London who made a small effort." To her, the message behind the award is simple: "You can come here and make a contribution, whether big or small."

Austrian court grants former property tycoon Benko's request for house arrest
VIENNA, Oct 14 - An Austrian court on Wednesday granted former property tycoon Rene Benko's request to be released from prison to house arrest with an ankle monitor after he served two-thirds of a 30-month sentence for insolvency fraud.
Benko, 49, will now move from prison in his home city of Innsbruck to a roughly 60-square-metre (650-square-foot) apartment that his lawyer Norbert Wess has said has been rented for him in the city so he can better prepare for a fraud trial next month. Benko denies all wrongdoing.
Benko has been convicted of insolvency-related fraud in the two cases brought to trial so far stemming from a sprawling investigation into the collapse of the Signa property group he founded. The second conviction resulted in a suspended sentence.
He remains a suspect in the continuing investigation into a range of potential crimes including fraud, with prosecutors estimating the total harm caused by Benko and other suspects at €1.5 billion ($1.7 billion). His first two trials dealt with sums in the hundreds of thousands of euros.
At its peak, Signa controlled all or part of luxury properties including five-star hotels in Venice and Vienna and the Chrysler Building in New York, as well as high-end department-store chains such as Britain's Selfridges and Switzerland's Globus. Benko became a self-made billionaire.
"It was ordered that investigative detention be continued as electronically monitored house arrest," the court in Innsbruck said in a statement issued after the closed-door hearing on Wednesday, adding that conditions attached included having no contact with anyone related to Signa.
The next trial Benko faces is for aggravated fraud and insolvency-related fraud, with prosecutors accusing him of making a false guarantee causing harm of €5 million. The trial is due to be held in Innsbruck next month. REUTERS

Men Can’t Stop Faking How Much They Know About AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

Say you’re a guy who reads WIRED—you know a thing or two about artificial intelligence. You recognize the names of well-known people developing AI, like OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. But do you know who Mira Murati is? What about Susan Milner? Craig Dalton?
In a new survey of more than 5,400 Americans, 73 percent of male respondents told Harvard researchers they knew who Altman was. A little over half—53 percent—said they knew of Murati, Milner, and Dalton.
There’s one problem. Murati is a real person: she’s the former CTO of OpenAI and the current CEO of Thinking Machine Labs. Milner and Dalton, on the other hand, do not exist.
Compared to women, “we're seeing that men are more optimistic and more confident” across the board when it comes to AI, Harvard Kennedy School’s Shorenstein Center executive director Laura Manley tells WIRED. Sometimes, that veers into overconfidence—like claiming to recognize fictional AI executives. (For context, 40 percent of women claimed to know who Milner and Dalton were; 38 percent said they recognized Murati.)
While Manley notes that men are more overconfident in general when surveyed, the report, published on Wednesday, digs into what the confidence gap on AI looks like, as well as the repercussions of gendered divides.
Researchers found that men use AI more frequently and are, on average, better able to correctly answer factual questions about AI. But men and women answer questions incorrectly at around the same rate. The discrepancy is based on how often women said they weren’t sure of an answer—an average of 3.3 questions out of 12 compared to 2.3 questions for men.
Researchers wondered if this predilection toward certainty colors coverage of AI. Across a year of media coverage, men were named in headlines about AI more than 14 times as often as women. Because top AI executives skew heavily male, researchers decided to reexamine coverage, looking solely at people who were quoted as subject experts. Three-quarters of these experts were men—a higher proportion than the actual AI talent pool, which is roughly 29 percent women.
“Maybe there should be more women prominently featured as experts or given the platform to express: not sure,” Manley says.
Besides intellectual bluster, Americans were generally in agreement that AI was freaking them out—men and women both rated “concern” as their top emotional response. However, female respondents were more concerned, fearful, and worried than their male counterparts. Men, meanwhile, rated every positive feeling—including curiosity, enthusiasm, and excitement—higher than women did.
In the current discourse, “there's so much confidence in either doom or abundance,” Manley says. “It just drowns out all of the voices that should be saying ‘not sure.’” There are many unanswered questions on proper uses for and the future of AI. One gender is simply less likely to acknowledge such uncertainty.
“We have to be able to be able to say ‘not sure’ more often,” Manley says.

In Odesa, nine members of Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Center notification groups were convicted of abducting and torturing men

12:29:18 EEST
18:29:18 KST

In Odesa, nine members of Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Center notification groups were convicted of abducting and torturing men
Kyiv • UNN
The court convicted nine military and civilian members of Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Center groups of abducting and torturing men. Six received actual prison sentences.
In Odesa, nine employees of the Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Centers were convicted of unlawful deprivation of liberty, kidnapping, and torture. Among those convicted were military personnel and civilians involved in mobilization activities. This was reported by the Office of the Prosecutor General, UNN reports.
Details
According to the available information, the court handed down the guilty verdicts in September–October 2026.
"Prosecutors from the Odesa Specialized Prosecutor's Office in the Defense Sphere of the Southern Region proved that in April–May 2026, they unlawfully detained men on the city's streets, forcibly put them into vehicles, and took them to the Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Centers. During the detentions, the victims were beaten, exposed to tear gas, threatened, and humiliated. The men were also forced to provide personal data and information about other persons of conscription age. In one case, the victim was threatened with sexual violence; in another, a man lost consciousness after tear gas was used. In addition, during the forcible transportation of one of the men, a convicted person took UAH 5,200 from his wallet," the Prosecutor General's post says.
According to the available data, all nine men pleaded guilty and entered into plea agreements, which were approved by the court.
"The punishment depended on each person's role in the crimes. Six of those convicted were sentenced to actual imprisonment. The harshest sentence was 7 years and 1 month in prison. Two others were each sentenced to 2 years of restriction of service, with 10% of their monetary allowance deducted and transferred to state revenue, while one was sentenced to 5 years in prison with a 2-year probation period. Four of those convicted were also prohibited for three years from holding positions in district Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Centers and from participating in mobilization activities," the post says.
The actions of those convicted were qualified under Part 1 of Article 28, Part 2 of Article 146, and Part 3 of Article 127 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine. One of them was additionally convicted of robbery committed under martial law (Part 4 of Article 186 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine).
The trial of two more defendants is currently ongoing.
Reminder
Law enforcement officers reported suspicion to three heads of district Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Centers—one incumbent and one former official in Zakarpattia, and one former official in Bukovyna. According to the investigation, from December 2025 to February 2026, the officials entered information on at least 857 fictitiously mobilized persons into the "Oberih" system, artificially inflating the reported performance of mobilization plans.

New Starlink restrictions disrupt Ukrainian drone missions. Kyiv adviser says move is tied to “political situation”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:29:07 UTC
18:29:07 KST

Ukraine’s presidential adviser Serhii Beskrestnov said SpaceX had imposed a 100 mph (160 km/h) speed limit on its military Starshield service overnight into 14 October, disrupting several missions without warning Ukraine’s defense forces.
Ukraine’s forces use Starlink-connected drones to strike Russian positions and logistics, including targets behind the front line. Unlike earlier restrictions introduced at Kyiv’s request to stop Russian forces from exploiting Starlink, the latest change reportedly targets the military Starshield service and was imposed without warning Ukraine’s military.
What the new restriction covers
Beskrestnov wrote that the restriction applies to the “military package” of Starshield services. He said the move “obviously cannot be a coincidence” and was connected with the “current political situation,” but did not explain what he meant.
Activist Serhii Sternenko, a former adviser to Ukraine’s defense minister, reported that connections began disappearing at speeds above 160 km/h. He suggested SpaceX had acted at the Trump administration’s request but provided no evidence. Starlink does not work inside Russia, and the drones hitting Russia’s oil industry use other means of communication, Reuters noted. Sternenko added that the ordinary satellite terminals were still working.
Later on 14 October, Sternenko wrote that, according to military reports, restrictions had been tightened further, with connections starting to drop at 60–70 km/h. Beskrestnov later warned that the restriction also hits Starlink-linked interceptor drones, which he called Ukraine’s most effective current defense against jet-powered Shaheds.
Front-line units report dropped connections
Ukraine’s 7th Rapid Reaction Corps confirmed the disruptions in a statement to Reuters. The corps’ press service told Novynarnia that its units on the Huliaipole front began experiencing problems overnight. The corps said the change affected drones controlled through Starlink in flight and concerned Starshield’s data-transmission speed, which it said had previously been unrestricted.
The corps said connections could disappear for 10–20 seconds at movement speeds of 110–120 km/h, complicating drone control. Flying slower creates its own risk, it said, because “slower targets become more vulnerable to being hit by the enemy.”
Some high-speed drones, particularly mid-range strike models, must reach high speed quickly, the corps said. An unstable connection “will make it impossible to launch such aircraft or use them as intended.” Since the start of the day, one unmanned systems unit on the Huliaipole front had to cancel some missions because of connection problems, the corps said.
Earlier limits came at Kyiv’s request
In late January, SpaceX began restricting Starlink in Ukraine at Kyiv’s request after Russian forces started mounting terminals on strike drones. After Russian drones struck a passenger train in Kharkiv Oblast on 27 January, Beskrestnov, then an adviser to the defense minister, suggested one of them may have been controlled via Starlink. In early February, Ukraine introduced a whitelist under which only registered terminals could continue operating. Beskrestnov called the earlier countermeasures “temporary” and “emergency.”
SpaceX had not publicly commented on the restriction, and Ukraine’s Defense Ministry was looking into its cause, Radio Svoboda reported. Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski asked Elon Musk on X whether he was “playing politics with your products again,” adding: “As your European customers, we are watching you.”

Russia-India relations remain unchanged amid global turmoil — foreign minister

Türkiye-EU Customs Union talks advance ‘case-by-case’ as bilateral trade hits $233B: Turkish trade minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:28:01 UTC
18:28:01 KST

Şerife Çetin, Ata Ufuk Şeker
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
Türkiye-EU Customs Union talks to amend the agreement are progressing on a “case-by-case basis” to include areas such as e-commerce, public procurement, investments and agricultural products, the Turkish trade minister said.
Omer Bolat told reporters during his visit to Brussels that maintaining economic ties is just as important for the EU as it is for Türkiye, highlighting bilateral trade between Türkiye and the bloc, which has surged elevenfold over the past three decades to reach a record $233 billion.
He said the bilateral analysis had been completed, referring to the new Turkish public procurement law passed in late July, and that technical discussions with European counterparts were underway.
He noted that while the EU Council has yet to officially mandate the European Commission to launch Customs Union modernization talks due to the positions of certain member states, technical negotiations have begun.
“We’re making progress on a case-by-case basis since the relevant issues have come up and authorities of the European Commission are conducting negotiations with us,” he said.
Bolat also said intensive work has been underway for the past year to address the EU’s restrictive regulations proposed under the draft Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA).
The official warned that certain provisions in the draft could affect future investments and disrupt integrated supply chains, particularly in the electric vehicle (EV) and automotive sectors.
He also confirmed that communications were ongoing to convey Türkiye’s expectations and mitigate the potential economic impact of the proposed industrial regulations.
Bolat said the EU was coordinating with Türkiye in its legislative preparations on digital trade, as the country remains exempt from a newly implemented EU regulation imposing a fee of €3 ($3.36) per package.
He said political involvement by the European Parliament could have adverse effects, noting that many European officials also believe Türkiye should be included in the “Made in EU” origin framework. However, he added that the EU is ultimately a complex entity made up of diverse countries with differing economic interests, emphasizing the need to remain “calm and level-headed” on the matter.
Bolat added that he held intensive contacts in Brussels, making three official visits in the last three months following five visits last year, and said he expected positive developments from the talks.

3 Hong Kong taxi drivers banned for 3 months under demerit points system
In a first, transport chief reveals number of taxi drivers disqualified since points system took effect two years ago
Secretary for Transport and Logistics Mable Chan said on Wednesday that since the mechanism took effect in September 2024, 229 taxi drivers had incurred demerit points as of October 2, with 125 cases involving a refusal to accept a hire.
In a reply to a question from lawmaker Chris Ip Ngo-tung, Chan said the three drivers had been disqualified for three months after incurring 15 demerit points or more on the Taxi-Driver-Offence points system - the first time authorities revealed this figure.
Under the system, taxi drivers will receive three, five or 10 demerit points for each of the 11 types of misconduct and can be disqualified from driving a taxi for three months if they accumulate 15 points or more within two years. Repeat offenders face a six-month suspension.

renewed 1983 bathhouse in japan preserves tilework and curved interiors
shizunoyu fukushima is a renovation project that transforms enmeiyu, a public bathhouse designed by architect yoshiji takehara in 1983, into a bathing facility exclusively for men.
[FEATURED]
MABI ARCHITECTS preserves former bathhouse’s curves and tiles
MABI ARCHITECTS renovates Enmeiyu, a public bathhouse designed by Yoshiji Takehara in 1983, into Shizunoyu Fukushima, a bathing facility exclusively for men. The project retains elements of the original architecture while introducing new functions and spaces for relaxation and socializing.
The renovation preserves the building’s curved forms and distinctive tilework, which reflect its history. As many existing tiles as possible remain in the washing area, maintaining a connection to the former bathhouse. New facilities include a cold plunge pool, sauna, outdoor bathing area, indoor relaxation space, and bar counter, integrated alongside the original materials and spatial features.
Shizunoyu Fukushima brings new uses to neighborhood bathhouse
By combining retained architectural details with new uses, the project by MABI ARCHITECTS Studio carries forward the bathhouse’s role as a place for informal encounters and conversation. Shizunoyu Fukushima continues the former Enmeiyu’s connection to the local community, creating a setting where visitors can gather and interact across generations.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Finance Minister Chuang Tsui-yun (莊翠雲) said Wednesday that doubling Taiwan's planned NT$10,000 (US$315) cash payout to NT$20,000 would require government borrowing, as most of the recent tax revenue increase went to local governments under a revised revenue allocation law.
During a Legislative Yuan Finance Committee session, KMT Legislator Lin Te-fu (林德福) said tax revenue in the first eight months of this year was NT$600 billion higher than in the same period last year, per Mirror Media. He called on the ministry to explain the basis for its borrowing estimates.
Chuang said national tax revenue rose by about NT$700 billion in the first nine months of this year compared with the same period in 2025, per Rti. However, the central government accounted for only NT$250 billion of the increase, while local governments received NT$450 billion.
The minister said the central government has allocated NT$235.7 billion in its proposed 2027 general budget to provide NT$10,000 to each eligible recipient, citing strong economic growth and rising tax revenue driven by the AI industry. She said increasing the payout to NT$20,000 would cost more than NT$470 billion and require government borrowing to cover the shortfall.
Chuang said local governments received most of the additional tax revenue partly because amendments to the Act Governing the Allocation of Government Revenues and Expenditures directed 95.5% of business tax revenue to local governments, Rti reported.
Lin also questioned why the payout was included in the general budget, suggesting the move was intended to coincide with an election year and pressure the Legislative Yuan into approving the spending, Mirror Media reported. Chuang said the NT$10,000 payout was included in the budget after careful fiscal assessment, without increasing net borrowing or affecting other government programs.
Chuang said the government hoped recipients could receive the money before Lunar New Year, but that would depend on the Legislative Yuan passing the 2027 general budget by Jan. 5 and President Lai Ching-te (賴清德) promulgating it by Jan. 20, according to Rti. If those deadlines are met, the ministry could complete the necessary system preparations in time to distribute the payments before the holiday, she said.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Tesla CEO Elon Musk’s reported plan to build a semiconductor fabrication plant is unlikely to affect TSMC in the short to medium term, Kirkland Capital Chair Yang Ying-chao (楊應超) said Wednesday.
Speaking on the sidelines of a forum, Yang said building a chip fab is difficult and could take five to 10 years to materialize, even for an experienced company, per CNA. Musk reportedly plans to invest about NT$96.6 billion (US$3 billion) in an experimental fab dubbed Terafab.
Yang said many multinational companies have failed to enter chip manufacturing, citing IBM’s semiconductor division, which was eventually sold to GlobalFoundries. However, he said he is confident in Musk’s execution, citing his track record at Tesla and SpaceX.
Yang said chip shortages during the COVID-19 pandemic and escalating US-China trade tensions have strengthened US companies’ push for vertical supply chain integration. Companies are seeking to manage everything from integrated circuit design and manufacturing to packaging in-house, he explained.
US companies, including Intel, could be major partners in Musk’s project, Yang said, adding that Washington wants domestic companies to lead semiconductor manufacturing. He said TSMC could also benefit if Musk follows through on plans to sublease fab space or technical consulting.
Yang said closer cooperation could help TSMC gain a better understanding of Intel, which he believes could become a competitor, although that prospect remains unlikely in the short term.

Russia Arrests Japanese Journalist on Suspicion of Spying
Unknown

Russia said on Tuesday it had detained a Japanese journalist on suspicion of espionage and accused Tokyo of using media correspondents to gather intelligence, marking a new low in bilateral relations that have deteriorated sharply in recent months.
Russia's Foreign Ministry identified the journalist as Yuki Imai and the FSB security agency said he worked for the Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper, which is a regional newspaper for Japan's northern island.
He was detained in the far eastern Sakhalin region the day before he planned to leave the country, the FSB said without specifying the date. It accused him of collecting and storing information on Russia's defense capabilities for intelligence purposes that it said could be used against Russian security.
The Hokkaido Shimbun did not confirm the journalist's identity, saying only that it was still confirming details and that the reporter's safety was its top priority.
Japanese Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said on Wednesday that Tokyo had asked Russian authorities for information and called for fair treatment and humanitarian consideration for the national.
Kihara stopped short of condemning Moscow, saying only that Tokyo would take appropriate action.
Japanese Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said on Wednesday that Tokyo had asked Russian authorities for information and called for fair treatment and humanitarian consideration for the national.
Japan summons Russian ambassador
A senior official of the Japanese Foreign Ministry later summoned the Russian ambassador to Japan and lodged a protest for detaining the Japanese national and unilaterally issuing statements regarding the matter without providing an explanation to Tokyo, the ministry said in a statement.
The director-general of the Foreign Ministry's European Affairs Bureau, Kimitake Nakamura, also asked the ambassador, Nikolay Nozdrev, to set up an opportunity swiftly to meet the detained journalist, the ministry said.
In a Russian state TV video report, three masked men in black uniforms handcuffed a man lying on the ground as a voice off camera said he was suspected of spying.
The video showed the man being accompanied by two FSB servicemen onto a plane, then in a cage in a Moscow court, which ordered him detained for nearly two months.
It is the most high-profile detainment of a foreign journalist since the 2023 detention of Wall Street Journal reporter Evan Gershkovich.
Gershkovich, who says his arrest was a carefully planned FSB sting, was found guilty of espionage by a Russian court, sentenced to 16 years and then freed in an East-West prisoner swap in August 2024.
Long-running tensions
The case adds to long-running tensions between Russia and Japan, which have yet to sign a formal World War II peace treaty due to a territorial dispute over the Kuril Islands, known in Japan as the Northern Territories.
Those tensions heightened when Japan joined Western sanctions against Moscow over the war in Ukraine, with Russia regarding Japan as an "unfriendly" country. But business ties remain with Japan a purchaser of Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG).
Then in August, Russian President Vladimir Putin visited one of the disputed islands, causing an uproar in Japan. On Tuesday, a delegation from a Chinese province visited the same island, in what appeared to signal closer coordination between Moscow and Beijing in their criticism of Tokyo.
Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova said on Tuesday that Japan had refused to consider Moscow's concerns about what she called Tokyo's "remilitarization." She criticized Japan's alleged use of accredited journalists in Russia to gather information that could undermine Russian security.
"We have to note that what has occurred will become an additional factor clouding the atmosphere of Russian-Japanese relations," Zakharova said.
Asked whether improving relations between Russia and the U.S. and Japan's purchases of LNG from Russia made it difficult for Tokyo to take countermeasures, Kihara said: "It is true that there are many issues between Japan and Russia.
"From Japan's perspective, despite the difficult situation in Japan-Russia relations, Japan has taken resolute measures based on its position. At the same time, Russia is a neighboring country to Japan, and communication is necessary to resolve these issues."

U.S. Navy taps HII for $56M AUKUS submarine design work
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:24:16 UTC
18:24:16 KST

- The U.S. Navy awarded Newport News Shipbuilding $56.2 million for AUKUS submarine engineering and design work, funded entirely by foreign partners.
- HII said its engineers will help design SSN-AUKUS, with an option that could raise the contract’s value to $91.1 million.
The U.S. Navy has awarded Huntington Ingalls Industries’ Newport News Shipbuilding a $56.2 million contract for engineering and design work on nuclear-powered submarines for America’s AUKUS partners, with foreign partner funds covering the full cost of the deal.
The Department of War contract announcement describes a cost-plus-fixed-fee deal covering engineering and technical support, along with design agent and design transfer activities for nuclear submarine capabilities and their sustainment. The work falls under Foreign Military Sales, the government-to-government channel Washington uses to sell defense equipment and services abroad, and an option, if exercised, would lift the total value to $91.1 million.
While the Pentagon notice leaves the foreign customer unnamed, HII filled in the gap on Oct. 13, saying in a company release that the award supports the trilateral Australia, United Kingdom and United States partnership known as AUKUS.
Signed in 2021, AUKUS is meant to give Australia a fleet of conventionally armed, nuclear-powered attack submarines. Canberra plans to acquire at least eight boats, including three to five Virginia-class submarines bought from the United States in the 2030s, followed by a new class designed with Britain and known as SSN-AUKUS.
According to HII, Newport News will keep supporting both the United Kingdom and Australia under the contract through technology insertion and engineering, as well as supply chain and workforce development. The award also funds an effort called United States Industry Support, under which Newport News engineers and designers will help design the SSN-AUKUS boat that Britain and Australia will build.
“Our longstanding nuclear experience at NNS directly benefits the AUKUS mission to support shared security objectives,” said Bryan Caccavale, Newport News Shipbuilding vice president of program management.
In submarine programs, the design agent is the yard responsible for a class’s technical design and for keeping it current over the boats’ service lives. Design transfer is the handover of that technical knowledge to another builder or navy, which Australia needs before it can maintain and eventually build nuclear submarines of its own.
Newport News will carry out 88% of the work at its Virginia shipyard, with the remaining 12% taking place at unspecified foreign locations. Work is scheduled to finish in September 2027, or in September 2028 if the option is exercised.
The contract carries no U.S. funding, and $19.1 million in foreign partner funds was obligated at the time of award without expiring at the end of the current fiscal year. Naval Sea Systems Command awarded the contract without competition, citing a statute that applies when only one responsible source can meet the requirement.
Newport News is one of only two American shipyards that build nuclear-powered submarines. It builds the bows, sterns and other modules for both the Virginia and Columbia classes, while General Dynamics Electric Boat in Groton, Connecticut, builds the central reactor section.
Electric Boat received a comparable award in April, a $196 million contract that Rep. Joe Courtney described as the first awarded by the U.S. Navy for AUKUS work. That deal used the same wording on engineering, design agent and design transfer support, and its options could raise its value to more than $930 million through April 2031.
On the Australian side, HII’s local operations won a 2025 contract to run the Australian Submarine Supplier Qualification Pilot Program, worth an initial A$9.6 million, which vets Australian companies for entry into the U.S. submarine supply chain.
Australia has pledged $3 billion to the U.S. submarine industrial base, paid in installments, and had delivered $2 billion of that amount as of April 23, according to Courtney.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has ordered the security establishment and the country’s attorney-general to identify and prosecute soldiers and officers interviewed in the investigative documentary "NAZA" about Israel’s mass killings of civilians in Gaza, Israeli media reported Monday.
In a letter to army Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir, Shin Bet chief David Zini and Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara, Netanyahu accused those who participated in the documentary of committing "serious information security offenses and criminal defamation” and causing harm to "Israel’s diplomatic and security interests,” according to Haaretz newspaper.
The award-winning documentary examines Israel’s use of artificial intelligence and automated surveillance systems in targeted killings and military operations during its genocidal war in Gaza.
The film’s title, "NAZA," refers to an acronym used by Israeli military intelligence to denote the number of civilians expected to be killed in an airstrike.
During the war, the Israeli army has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and injured over 175,000 others since October 2023 in a brutal offensive that has left the entire enclave in ruins.
Netanyahu claimed that the film has presented a "false, misleading and biased narrative” that defames Israel and its military and damages the country’s international standing.
"There is concern that those involved in the defamatory film committed serious criminal offenses by exposing highly classified information and creating a breach in the information security of a highly sensitive intelligence unit,” he said in the letter.
The film, based on testimony from 24 Israeli soldiers and intelligence personnel, won the Special Jury Prize at the Venice Film Festival last month.
Following the award, Israeli Culture Minister Miki Zohar asked the Interior Ministry to consider revoking the citizenship of the film’s creators, describing the documentary as "vile” and accusing them of "treason.”
Zamir separately ordered Military Intelligence, the Military Advocate General’s Corps and the Israeli Air Force to identify the soldiers featured in the film and determine whether they were active-duty troops, career officers or reservists, according to Haaretz.
During discussions on the issue, Military Advocate General Itai Offir said that there would be no legal basis for criminal prosecution unless participants were found to have committed information-security violations or disclosed classified material.
He said disciplinary or command measures could, however, be taken if military orders were violated.
The Israeli army claimed that the documentary’s portrayal of its targeting procedures in Gaza contained "substantial factual errors.”
The Guardian, which produced the documentary, defended the film, saying the process used to assess the credibility of the testimonies was "rigorous” and included classified documents, verification of specific strikes and corroboration from additional confidential sources.
The newspaper said it had interviewed more than 100 people familiar with Israeli military systems used during the war in Gaza, including senior commanders involved in authorizing strikes.
In November 2024, the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant over war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza.
The International Court of Justice (ICJ), the U.N.’s principal judicial organ, is also hearing a case brought by South Africa and joined by several countries accusing Israel of genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.
