US Embassy in Israel issues safety warning about unexploded ordnances after school trip explosion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:21:20 UTC
18:21:20 KST

The US Embassy in Israel issued a safety warning to American citizens on Tuesday about unexploded ordnance and munitions found across extensive areas of Israel, the West Bank, and the Gaza Strip, a day after a teenager was killed and 24 people were injured in an explosion during a school trip in northern Israel.
The warning followed the death of Elazar Yair Wilensky, who was killed when unexploded Hezbollah ammunition detonated during the school trip.
In its statement, the embassy warned that the danger was particularly great near border areas and that, in many cases, the locations of unexploded ordnance are unmarked, and the devices may be difficult to identify.
"Rain, flooding, agricultural work, and construction activities frequently bring buried munitions to the surface, making them more unstable," the embassy said.
The embassy stressed that unexploded ordnance can come in various shapes and sizes, including artillery shells, mortar bombs, rockets, grenades, landmines, and cluster munitions.
It warned particularly about small, round cluster bomblets, which may resemble balls or toys and attract children's attention.
"Assume that any unidentified object is dangerous," the statement said.
Embassy emphasizes three-step safety rule: Recognize, retreat, report
The embassy emphasized a three-step safety rule in its guidelines: recognize, retreat, and report.
Anyone who identifies a suspicious object should stop immediately and avoid approaching it to investigate. Instead, they should carefully retreat along the same route they used to reach the area, keep others away, particularly children, and report the object to Israel Police by calling 100.
The embassy also warned against physically touching unexploded ordnance, throwing objects at it, or using mobile phones and two-way radios nearby.
It further recommended against collecting ammunition casings, shell fragments, or war souvenirs, even if the items have reportedly been neutralized and are considered safe.
The embassy urged the public to avoid entering areas marked as minefields or contaminated by unexploded ordnance, and to remain on paved roads and familiar trails when hiking outside urban areas.
It also called on parents to explain to children that they must never touch unidentified metal objects and should immediately report any such discoveries to an adult.
In addition, the embassy recommended identifying the location of the nearest protected space, using Home Front Command warning applications, and keeping up to date with security guidance issued by the US State Department.

====================================================================================================

From Saddam Hussein to Israel: How Iran's wars have divided a nation - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:21:16 UTC
18:21:16 KST

On September 22, 1980, as Iraqi warplanes bombed Iranian airfields and Saddam Hussein's tanks crossed the Iranian border, Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini appeared remarkably unconcerned by what was unfolding in the fledgling Islamic Republic.
Iraq’s attack, he told the Iranian people, was little more than “a thief throwing a stone” before running away. There was no reason to panic, he insisted, and certainly no reason to believe that Iran had entered a major war. The country's armed forces were perfectly capable of dealing with the threat.
History, of course, would prove him spectacularly wrong as the war dragged on for eight long years and left an estimated half a million people dead.
Saddam's invasion brought together a deeply fractured Iranian nation
However, for all the destruction that followed, Saddam's invasion also achieved something that the Islamic Republic, barely a year and a half old, could scarcely have accomplished on its own. It brought together a deeply fractured Iranian nation, many of whose people had little affection for Khomeini or the clerical establishment that had seized power in Tehran.
Nearly half a century later, with Iran engaging twice in the space of one year against Israel and the United States, the question of how Iranians respond to an external enemy has returned to the fore. And while Iran's leaders have spent much of the past year insisting that the country stands united behind them, the events unfolding inside Iran tell a considerably more complicated story.
When Saddam launched his invasion, Iran was still struggling to come to terms with the revolution that had overthrown Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi in February 1979. The revolutionary government had barely established control over the country, while competing political factions were fighting for influence, and the military, once among the most powerful in the Middle East, had been weakened by purges of officers associated with the former monarchy.
There was unrest in the provinces and among different ethnic groups, opposition to clerical rule was growing, and the new Islamic Republic was still engaged in the bloody business of eliminating its political rivals.
From Baghdad, Hussein believed he had found his moment to strike and take, among other things, the Shatt al-Arab waterway and its key oil installations.
The Iraqi dictator calculated that Iran's internal turmoil would make a swift military victory possible, particularly if he could exploit the country's ethnic divisions. Hussein hoped that the Sunni-majority Arab population of Khuzestan, the oil-rich Iranian province bordering Iraq, would welcome his troops as liberators against their Shi’a oppressors.. He was very much mistaken.
Rather than embracing the invading Iraqi army, many Iranian Arabs joined their compatriots in defending their homeland. Political opponents of Khomeini, including supporters of the ousted monarchy, similarly recognized that whatever their differences with the new government, the country's territorial integrity was at stake. Crown Prince Reza Pahlavi, a trained fighter pilot and son of the exiled Shah, even extended an offer to his country’s new rulers to return and fight for Iran.
Iranian patriotism, it turned out, extended considerably further than loyalty to the Islamic Republic.
"We are ready to send all our children to battle the thugs,” Khomeini stated just days after the invasion.
For Khomeini, the war provided an opportunity to harness that patriotism and place the defense of the nation at the center of his revolutionary government's struggle for survival. As the fighting dragged on, the regime more and more associated resistance to the Iraqis and Hussein with support for the Islamic Republic itself, while the demands of wartime offered further opportunities to silence domestic opposition and consolidate clerical rule. This was also the period of massive expansion in the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps - originally formed to safeguard the revolution domestically.
By the time the guns finally stopped in August 1988, the Islamic Republic had survived its greatest external challenge and emerged with a far stronger grip on power than it had possessed when Iraqi troops first crossed the border.
If the 1980-88 war, however, was relatively successful in its ability to get Iranians to “rally around the flag,” the wars of 2025 and 2026 proved more difficult for the Iranian regime to succeed in garnering nationalist fervor.
Unlike Iraq, American and Israeli military campaigns were conducted from the air
Unlike Saddam's invasion, which involved Iraqi ground forces attempting to capture and occupy Iranian territory, the American and Israeli military campaigns were conducted overwhelmingly from the air, targeting nuclear facilities, missile installations, military infrastructure, and senior figures within the Islamic Republic's security establishment.
Neither the US nor Israel attempted a comparable occupation of Iranian territory, and both countries repeatedly presented their military operations as directed against the regime and the threat posed by its military capabilities, rather than against the Iranian people themselves.
The reaction this time around, from Iranians, was very different.
There were, of course, civilian casualties, and considerable anger at the attacks, including among Iranians who have little sympathy for the government. The bombing of one's country by foreign powers is hardly a straightforward proposition, regardless of how deeply one despises those who govern it.
But Iran in 2026 is also a country that has endured almost five decades of Islamic Republic rule, successive waves of protests, deteriorating economic conditions, and increasingly brutal attempts by the authorities to suppress opposition.
The nationwide uprising that began in December 2025, and the massacres that followed in January, which left an estimated 40,000 people killed in two days, added another devastating chapter to that history. Security forces sought to crush demonstrations that had spread across the country, leaving families mourning their dead and an already profound divide between the population and the political establishment even deeper.
It is against this background that Iranians' response is even more powerful.
During Iraq’s invasion, Iranians from across the political spectrum rallied to defend their country against a foreign army. In 2026, footage emerging from inside Iran has shown people thanking the leaders of the very countries carrying out strikes against the Islamic Republic.
Graffiti appealing directly to US President Donald Trump and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu began appearing during the January uprising, including messages pleading with them to intervene as protesters faced the security forces. Following the American and Israeli military operations, other messages went considerably further, thanking Trump and Netanyahu for their actions.
In Karaj, west of Tehran, graffiti reading "We love you BB," a reference to Netanyahu, appeared on a wall, while videos circulated by Iran International showed Iranians expressing gratitude toward both leaders.
The sight of Iranians publicly thanking an Israeli prime minister and an American president for military action against targets inside their own country would have been almost inconceivable during the Iran-Iraq War.
Such expressions are not representative of the entire population, but the fact they are seen and they are there is crucial in understanding the standing of the Islamic Republic currently. Many Iranians oppose foreign military intervention, including those who are bitterly opposed to the Islamic Republic, and the continued appearance of pro-government rallies (however falsified their attendance numbers) demonstrates that the authorities retain a constituency prepared to mobilize in their support.
Nevertheless, the messages of gratitude, particularly those directed toward Netanyahu, offer an astonishing illustration of how far relations between sections of Iranian society and their rulers have deteriorated.
The Islamic Republic, meanwhile, sought to portray the wars as further proof of the country's enduring national unity.
Following the Twelve-Day War in June 2025, senior military and political officials repeatedly praised the solidarity of the Iranian people, with IRGC spokesman Brigadier-General Ali Mohammad Naeini declaring that Israel had encountered the "ironclad unity of the Iranian people."
Similar declarations accompanied the renewed conflict in 2026. In September, IRGC Aerospace Force commander Brigadier-General Majid Mousavi praised the nightly pro-government gatherings, describing them as a demonstration of the Iranian people's commitment to defending their country's identity, independence, and very existence, while urging continued support for the Islamic Republic and its armed forces. Later that month, President Masoud Pezeshkian accused the US and Israel of attempting to sow divisions within Iranian society, insisting that the country was experiencing "unprecedented unity and cohesion."
Such language would have been familiar to Khomeini, who spent much of the Iran-Iraq War portraying the sacrifices of ordinary Iranians as evidence of the nation's commitment to the revolution. But to proclaim national unity is one thing. Demonstrating that the population remains united behind those making the proclamations is quite another.
An incident in Tehran last Friday evening provided a particularly interesting example.
Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei, one of the Islamic Republic's most recognizable diplomatic voices throughout the conflict, was booed by members of an audience attending a performance of Arash, an orchestral theatrical production based on the legendary Iranian archer who sacrificed himself to protect his homeland.
According to footage circulated by Iranian media, Baghaei had taken a microphone to address the audience when some spectators began booing him.
Arash occupies a special place in Iranian mythology, a patriotic figure immersed in the defense of the nation's territorial integrity. That a senior representative of the Islamic Republic should encounter such a hostile reception at a production celebrating one of Iran's most enduring national heroes speaks to the complicated relationship between Iranian national identity and the clerical government that claims to represent it.
It also lets us see into a small window of the current feelings of the Iranian people compared to 1980.
Hussein invaded an Iran was still coming to terms with the upheaval of revolution
Saddam Hussein invaded a country that was bitterly divided, politically unstable, and still coming to terms with the upheaval of revolution. His expectation that those divisions would make Iran easy prey proved disastrous, as Iranians who disagreed profoundly about their country's future nevertheless found common cause in defending its borders.
Khomeini was able to capitalize on that national resistance, using the war to strengthen the very political system whose future had appeared so uncertain when the fighting began.
The Islamic Republic's present leadership has sought to draw upon much the same sentiment, invoking the nationalistic language of sacrifice, sovereignty, and resistance, while insisting that the nation stands firmly behind its armed forces. For those who know Iranians, love of their homeland is one thing that can bring them together.
But the Iran of 2026 is a very different country from the one Saddam invaded. Its people have lived under the Islamic Republic for almost half a century, and for a substantial section of the population, the government itself has become inseparable from the grievances that have repeatedly brought Iranians onto the streets.
Forty-six years ago, Saddam discovered that Iranians were prepared to put aside their differences to defend their country, allowing Khomeini to transform a war for national survival into a foundation for the Islamic Republic's consolidation. Today, the same government continues to invoke the patriotism of the Iranian people, but after decades of repression, revolution, and economic uncertainty, it can no longer assume that those who love their country are still loyal to those who rule it.

High Court hears petition demanding protection for lawyers from courthouse harassment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:20:52 UTC
18:20:52 KST

High Court justices questioned Wednesday whether the Courts Administration’s instructions adequately protect lawyers from courthouse harassment, pressing for clearer rules on conduct that guards should halt and how those rules are communicated to the public.
The case concerns lawyers representing Palestinians and human rights groups who say right-wing activists follow them through the Supreme Court’s corridors, film them at close range, and accuse them of supporting terrorism. The petitioners argue that preventing physical attacks alone is insufficient: Lawyers must be able to prepare for hearings, consult privately with clients, and represent them without intimidation.
Justices Dafna Barak-Erez, Gila Canfy-Steinitz, and Yechiel Kasher examined possible protections, including clearly defined areas where lawyers could work without interference. No ruling was delivered during the hearing, and a decision is due to be sent to the parties.
Guards instructed to intervene against harassment, humiliation, intimidation of lawyers
The Court’s Administration rejected the claim that its protection policy warrants judicial intervention. In an updated response submitted ahead of the hearing, it said security preparations had been strengthened, and guards were explicitly instructed to intervene against the filming aimed at harassing, humiliating, or intimidating lawyers.
During Wednesday’s hearing, state attorney Hadas Eran condemned interference with lawyers and said that courthouses were not places for demonstrations. She maintained that the instructions were implemented through training and briefings, with guards exercising judgment according to the circumstances.
The justices questioned whether that approach provided guards with sufficiently concrete guidance.
When Eran referred to a summary of a June 2023 meeting as the written basis for the instructions, Barak-Erez questioned whether it amounted to a comprehensive set of rules and asked when further work on instructions would be completed.
“These are very general instructions,” Canfy-Steinitz said, questioning whether they told a guard what to do in a particular situation.
Barak-Erez also asked how many people had been removed from courthouses over the past year for disturbing public order. Eran said she would have to obtain the figure, but the discussion exposed a further question: how visitors could be expected to comply with restrictions that were not clearly published. Barak-Erez used the example of a distance limit on filming, asking how someone would know they had breached an unwritten rule.
Filed in 2024 by the Public Committee Against Torture in Israel, HaMoked, Gisha, Yesh Din, and Physicians for Human Rights Israel, the petition challenges the policy of the Courts Administration and its director, Judge Tzachi Uziel.
No proposal was adopted during the hearing
The organizations, represented by attorneys Michael Sfard and Einat Gayer, proposed confining protests to a designated area inside the courthouse. Sfard argued that lawyers should not have to retreat to a separate room to work undisturbed.
The justices explored whether clearer protections for lawyers’ personal space would suffice or whether part of the lobby should be designated free of filming and harassment. They also questioned the scope of guards’ legal powers. No proposal was adopted during the hearing.
In a written update filed ahead of Wednesday’s hearing, the petitioners described confrontations during hearings concerning humanitarian aid to Gaza, prison conditions, punitive home demolitions, and other contested policies.
The update identified activists from Im Tirtzu in several incidents and argued that repeated involvement by the same individuals calls for measures to prevent further harassment.
Among the most serious allegations is an incident from March 30, 2026, during a hearing over displaced Palestinians’ return to refugee camps in the northern West Bank. According to the petitioners, an activist followed lawyers after they left the courtroom while the justices examined classified material, then violently pushed Association for Civil Rights in Israel (ACRI) attorney Oded Feller as he tried to enter another courtroom.
The filing said footage was provided to the court’s chief secretary and the incident was brought to the panel’s attention. Feller submitted an affidavit supporting the account.
The petitioners also described an October 29, 2025, hearing concerning Red Cross visits to detention facilities, after which a court security officer escorted lawyers and association staff out of the building. They said that the group had to crouch behind bushes while awaiting transportation to avoid attracting the hostile crowd.
These incidents, they argued, demonstrate the inadequacy of a policy that leaves lawyers retreating while those harassing them remain free to move around.
The dispute followed complaints dating back to 2020. Instructions developed after the June 2023 meeting with Sfard treated intrusion into lawyers’ personal space, curses, and incitement to violence as disturbances requiring intervention. The administration subsequently said guards had been instructed to maintain a three-meter distance to protect lawyers’ personal space.
Its December 2024 response defended the balance between lawyers’ safety, freedom of expression, and public access, and it pointed to a Bar Association room available for private work.
In an update submitted on Sunday, the administration cited additional training, advance planning for sensitive hearings, and inspections that it said found no departures from instructions. An internal directive clarifying responsibilities and coordination remains under review.
That update also cited a December 2025 Supreme Court decision permitting advance restrictions on courtroom attendance where serious disruption is reasonably anticipated, alongside live-streaming or screening in another courtroom.
Wednesday’s hearing ended with the practical questions unresolved: whether the existing instructions provide sufficient protection, whether clearer written rules are needed, and whether parts of the courthouse should be set aside to allow lawyers to work without interference.

Yemen hospitals overwhelmed by surge in war casualties, Red Cross warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:20:38 UTC
18:20:38 KST

Yemen fighting overwhelms hospitals, cuts aid to 800,000 people: Relief agencies
GENEVA – Hospitals across Yemen are struggling to cope with a sharp rise in war casualties, while intensified fighting along multiple front lines has cut off aid to around 800,000 people, humanitarian agencies said on Oct 14.
Front-line hospitals in areas including Marib, Taiz and Yemen’s Red Sea coast were seeing unprecedented numbers of weapon-wounded patients, with some facilities admitting more than 700 casualties in a single week, according to the Red Cross.
More than 200,000 people have been displaced from their homes since fighting in the country began in recent weeks, sparked by renewed fighting between the Iran-backed Houthi group and Saudi-backed government forces in Yemen, according to the United Nations’ International Organization for Migration.
“Trauma care staff are under enormous pressure,” ICRC health coordinator Feras Abusamra said in a statement.
Only a small proportion of Yemen’s functioning health facilities are capable of providing comprehensive trauma care, he said, while hospitals face large numbers of wounded people amid shortages of surgical supplies, anaesthesia, oxygen and medicines.
Yemen’s health services, battered by more than a decade of conflict, economic crisis, displacement and disease outbreaks, may have limited capacity to absorb a new surge in mass casualties if fighting intensifies further, the ICRC warned.
The fighting has also cut off life-saving humanitarian assistance for 800,000 people in Taiz – Yemen’s third-largest city, which currently hosts the largest number of people fleeing the fighting – and other areas impacted by the conflict, the UN World Food Programme said on Oct 14.
Some districts are now inaccessible because of fighting and road closures, the WFP said, adding that wheat flour stocks are nearly exhausted and remaining food in local markets may last only a short time.
“This is the kind of situation that can rapidly spiral into a humanitarian catastrophe if assistance cannot move safely and reach those who need it most,” said El-Khidir Daloum, WFP Representative and Country Director in Yemen, in a statement. REUTERS

Only a small proportion of Yemen’s functioning health facilities are capable of providing comprehensive trauma care, he said, while hospitals face large numbers of wounded people amid shortages of surgical supplies, anaesthesia, oxygen and medicines.
Yemen’s health services, battered by more than a decade of conflict, economic crisis, displacement and disease outbreaks, may have limited capacity to absorb a new surge in mass casualties if fighting intensifies further, the ICRC warned.
The fighting has also cut off life-saving humanitarian assistance for 800,000 people in Taiz – Yemen’s third-largest city, which currently hosts the largest number of people fleeing the fighting – and other areas impacted by the conflict, the UN World Food Programme said on Oct 14.
Some districts are now inaccessible because of fighting and road closures, the WFP said, adding that wheat flour stocks are nearly exhausted and remaining food in local markets may last only a short time.
“This is the kind of situation that can rapidly spiral into a humanitarian catastrophe if assistance cannot move safely and reach those who need it most,” said El-Khidir Daloum, WFP Representative and Country Director in Yemen, in a statement. REUTERS

Golan also framed the debate over national unity as a question of accountability for the October 7, 2023 Hamas massacre and the government's conduct during the ensuing war. "And now they want us to give him another four years," Golan said. "Four more years of destruction, corruption and abandonment. Four more years that would endanger Israel's very future as a Jewish and democratic state."

Ukraine Says SpaceX Limits Starlink Operations, Disrupting Military
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:17:29 UTC
18:17:29 KST

Ukraine accused Elon Musk's SpaceX on Wednesday of limiting Starlink services, crippling its drones, as Russian missiles knocked out power stations in attacks President Volodymyr Zelensky called "ostentatious disrespect" to Donald Trump.
Kyiv's relationship with Washington has taken a sharp turn for the worse since U.S. President Trump abruptly lifted sanctions on Russian diesel last week and publicly turned on Zelensky.
Trump, under political pressure to lower fuel prices that have soared since he launched a war against Iran, has called on Kyiv to halt attacks on Russian refineries, and said Ukrainians should replace their wartime leader.
The U.S. president also announced that Ukraine and Russia had both agreed to halt attacks on energy targets, although neither side confirmed this and the past two days have seen intensive Russian bombing, including of Ukrainian power stations.
No warning before Starlink cuts
Ukrainian military officials said Musk's SpaceX had without warning interrupted functioning of military-grade Starlink terminals moving at high speed, effectively preventing Kyiv from using them as onboard guides for drones.
"Our defense forces did not receive a warning about this limitation, and this led to the disruption of several missions," presidential adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov wrote on Telegram.
The apparent suggestion that Musk's company might limit Ukrainian military capabilities drew a sharp response from Poland, which pays for Ukrainian Starlink subscriptions on Kyiv's behalf.
"Hey, @elonmusk, big man, are you playing politics with your products again?" Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski asked Musk on X. "As your European customers, we are watching you."
There was no immediate response from Musk, who in the past has called Sikorski a "small man." SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment outside of U.S. business hours.
Musk is a close political ally of Trump, and the suggestion that SpaceX might limit Ukrainian capabilities reinforced wider Ukrainian concerns that Washington could withhold battlefield support to compel its onetime ally to make concessions.
Sources have told Reuters and other news organizations that the U.S. has threatened to cut off intelligence for early warning of missile strikes on Ukraine, to press Kyiv to suspend attacks on Russian oil refineries.
No warning ahead of missiles
Rescue workers in Kyiv were stretchering the injured from the wreckage of a blasted-out residential building overnight, while firefighters battled a huge blaze in the darkness. Officials said 2 people were killed and 21 wounded at the site.
Some 600,000 people were left without power as Russian missiles careened into power stations during hours of attacks that primarily targeted Kyiv and Kharkiv, Ukraine's second-largest city. Russia's Defense Ministry confirmed it had struck four power plants in and around Kyiv and two in Kharkiv, among other targets. Zelenskiy said more than 30 power stations were damaged.
Ukrainian officials said late on Tuesday they had received no warnings from Western partners for a second day before the massive Russian attacks on the capital. Trump had insisted on Tuesday that Washington was still sharing intelligence.
Zelensky cast the latest attacks as a deliberate snub to Trump's declaration of a ceasefire on energy targets.
"Russia does not consider the American President's statements strong," Zelensky wrote on X. "The strike was entirely deliberate and demonstrative in its scale – Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States."
Zelensky has said Ukraine is willing to observe an energy ceasefire and has not targeted Russian refineries since Trump announced it, but will not continue to hold back if Russia ignores the purported truce. The Kremlin said on Tuesday that contacts were continuing about an energy truce.
Ukraine reported downing just four out of 39 Russian missiles, reflecting Kyiv's weakened air defenses against fast-moving ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones amid a shortage of weapons.
Starlink does not work inside Russia, and Ukrainian drones hitting Russia's oil industry use other means of communication, but Ukraine uses Musk's system to guide drones over its own territory, including parts of Ukraine occupied by Russia.
"According to our observations, during flights, the connection could drop for 10-20 seconds at speeds of just 110-120 km/h [68-75 mph]. The drones kept moving, but these interruptions made them harder to control," Ukraine's 7th Rapid Reaction Corps, deployed in the southeast, said in a statement to Reuters.
A source in Ukraine's Defense Ministry said the limitations significantly complicate logistics and some drone operations.
Since being turned on over Ukraine in the early days of Russia's invasion in 2022, Starlink has been the lifeblood of Ukrainian battlefield communications.
Its resistance to electronic signal jamming has made it a crucial tool for flying long-range attack drones and drones used to drop supplies to frontline troops.

Italian premier says Trump's Russian diesel deal 'very risky'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:17:02 UTC
18:17:02 KST

Melike Pala
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni on Wednesday described US President Donald Trump's agreement on Russian diesel as a "very risky" decision, ANSA news agency reported.
Speaking in the Senate ahead of the European Council summit, Meloni, who was considered a "Trump whisperer" before they fell out, said the surge in fuel prices was primarily driven by the war in Iran rather than Ukraine, questioning the rationale behind the US decision.
"Therefore, the outcome of this decision is uncertain, while the risks are clear: legitimization for Moscow," Meloni said, highlighting the potential risks of "additional revenues to finance its war and a weakening of Western sanctions leverage."
She said the agreement could send "contradictory" signals at a time when Western countries, including the US, have been seeking to pressure Russian President Vladimir Putin to negotiate an end to the war in Ukraine, which continues since 2022.
The Italian premier also called for a stronger European role in efforts to end the war, urging EU member states to appoint an authoritative representative with a mandate from all 27 countries to ensure Europe has a unified voice in negotiations.
"We must ensure that Europe does not stand idly by," Meloni stressed.
She criticized the possibility of France, Germany and the UK pursuing diplomatic initiatives through the so-called E3 format without a collective EU mandate, saying any such efforts should be conducted on behalf of all member states.
Trump has urged Russia and Ukraine not to strike each other's energy sites, and last week announced that Moscow will supply diesel to global markets in an effort to lower fuel prices. His administration also temporarily lifted US sanctions on Russian fuel.
 
- EU budget priorities
Meloni identified high energy prices as the main challenge facing the Italian economy and business competitiveness, calling for a coordinated and rapid European response.
She reiterated Rome's position on the next EU budget, saying Italy would not accept an agreement that comes at the expense of the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), fisheries or cohesion funding.
Acknowledging the objective set by the bloc to reach an agreement by the end of the year, she said Italy would not support a deal simply to meet a deadline.
"We will only sign an agreement when it is right for Italy," Meloni said.

Kazakhstan’s camel milk may hit shelves in China and Middle East stores
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:16:20 UTC

Kazakhstan’s camel milk may hit shelves in China and Middle East stores
Kazakhstan approved a new national standard for pasteurized camel milk to help domestic producers expand exports to China, the Middle East, and Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) countries, Qazinform News Agency reports.
Deputy director general of the Kazakh Institute of Standardization and Metrology Alexander Razzarenov told a briefing at the Central Communications Service.
According to him, Kazakhstan has long had a standard for saumal (fresh mare's milk). This year, a separate standard for pasteurized camel milk was developed based on scientific research.
He noted that laboratory tests showed Kazakh camel milk products outperform comparable products from trading partners in terms of quality. As a result, the new standard introduces stricter quality requirements, which are expected to strengthen the competitiveness of Kazakh producers in international markets.
Camel milk is widely used in Kazakhstan to produce the traditional fermented beverage shubat. Pasteurized camel milk is also used in the production of ice cream, jams, and coffee-based drinks, including the popular “camelccino,” a camel-milk version of cappuccino.
The Ministry of Trade and Integration said that the national pasteurized camel milk standard was approved on September 11, 2026, and will come into effect on November 1. The document establishes unified requirements for the quality, safety, labeling, packaging, transportation, and storage of pasteurized camel milk.
To note, Kazakh dried kumys and horse meat adapted to foreign market requirements.

As Ebola spreads in eastern DR Congo, mothers and children shun vital care
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:16:02 UTC
18:16:02 KST

As Ebola spreads in eastern DR Congo, mothers and children shun vital care
- Fear of Ebola in eastern DR Congo is stopping women and children from using healthcare, leading to more home births, delayed treatment and rising maternal deaths.
- UN figures show maternal deaths in Ituri rose nearly 70% from May to July, while hospital deliveries and obstetric care have fallen sharply.
- Misinformation and fear of Ebola treatment centres are also cutting childhood vaccinations and paediatric visits, risking bigger health problems for years.
AI generated
BUTEMBO, Democratic Republic of Congo – The fear of Ebola is keeping women and children from seeking healthcare in eastern Congo, health workers and aid agencies say, contributing to soaring maternal deaths and falling childhood immunisation rates that could strain the system for years to come.
Health workers say that misplaced anxiety about contact with Ebola is the primary reason women are forgoing crucial prenatal care and opting to give birth at home, and dying more often in the event of complications.
There is still limited data available but figures for Ituri province are raising alarm. United Nations figures show that maternal deaths in Ituri province soared nearly 70% between May and July compared with a year earlier, a troubling indicator of the impact of the Ebola outbreak – currently Congo’s worst on record – on the primary healthcare system.
Steep international aid cuts have also led to shortages of some life-saving medications.
In eastern Butembo city, nurses at the Masiki healthcare centre told Reuters that births have fallen sharply at their maternity ward since the Ebola outbreak was declared in May. Just one mother was resting with her newborn during a recent visit, among rows of empty beds.
“They think the medicines we give them contain the Ebola virus,” head nurse Liliane Adronga told Reuters – highlighting just one of many unfounded suspicions circulating about the virus and healthcare.
She described how women often avoided seeking care until it was too late, recalling a recent case where a woman was believed to have lost her baby while suffering from untreated malaria.
The UN Population Fund has reported a more than 30% drop in hospital deliveries and 50% drop in treatment for obstetric complications for the May to July period since the outbreak began.
Children missing routine vaccines
The Ebola outbreak has spread across seven provinces, infecting more than 8,000 people and killing over 4,000. Officials say it is far from being contained, although infections have slowed in parts of the country.
Routine data collection is a growing challenge but aid agencies say data for the first three months of the outbreak shows a sharp fall in routine childhood vaccinations and paediatric visits.
The United Nations Children’s Fund warned in August that routine vaccinations fell by more than half across Ebola hot spots in Ituri between April and June. In Mongbwalu, first-dose measles vaccinations declined by 69%. “We should be concerned not only about the direct impact of Ebola, but also its indirect effects on health, nutrition, child protection and insecurity,” said Raoul Kamadjeu, a public health emergencies expert at UNICEF. “The longer an epidemic persists, the greater the risks.”
Congo has long struggled with recurring measles outbreaks, for example, with tens of thousands of cases recorded every year, and 126,000 cases so far in 2026, according to data by its health ministry. UNICEF says that health facilities administered 23,000 fewer routine vaccine doses in May and June than in April.
Misinformation, superstition adding to concerns
For some parents, concerns about Ebola overshadowed the benefits of vaccination. “We didn’t want to bring our children to health facilities for fear of being referred to an Ebola treatment centre. Because once you end up there, you can die,” said Masika Furaha, a mother of three in Butembo. She did in the end have her youngest child vaccinated after seeing that children who received the shots remained healthy.
Mupenzi Mumbere, a paediatrician in Butembo, said misinformation is contributing to the fears among parents with sometimes tragic consequences. He described an episode in which a mother burst into tears when he referred her son to the main hospital for an X-ray because she believed staff would take him and kill him with Ebola. Many parents first try self-medication or seek help from traditional healers before eventually turning to hospitals, he said, often with devastating consequences.
“That’s when I realised how great the misunderstanding was,” said Mumbere. “In the worst cases, children arrive in such poor condition that there is little left to do but watch them die.” REUTERS

Business association Delovaya Rossiya proposes partially scrapping simplified tax system, taxing Russians’ passive income
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:16:00 UTC
18:16:00 KST

Business association Delovaya Rossiya proposes partially scrapping simplified tax system, taxing Russians’ passive income
The business association Delovaya Rossiya has drafted proposals to overhaul the Russian economy, the Russian business news outlet RBC reported. Some of the proposed measures would significantly tighten conditions for small and medium-sized businesses, while others target citizens’ passive income.
The draft document, which RBC reviewed, includes 52 proposals covering a wide range of topics. Among other things, the organization proposes the following:
- Eliminate the tax regime known as the “Income” version of the simplified tax system (USN), which carries a 6% rate. The Bell explains that this would mean “primarily an increase in the tax base for entrepreneurs who earn income through their own skilled labor.”
- Lower the threshold for applying VAT under the auto-USN regime from 60 million to 20 million rubles (matching the current threshold for the “standard” USN).
- Eliminate the patent-based tax system, which The Bell says is widely used by microbusinesses.
- Introduce social security contributions for citizens whose income mainly comes from interest or dividends.
- Introduce an inheritance and gift tax on amounts exceeding 50 million rubles.
- Restrict imports of “strategic innovative products.”
The Bell calls the proposal “a blow to small business” and says it “looks very bad” for medium-sized businesses too.

Tesla’s Roadster 2 Is Late—and Entering a Different EV World
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:15:00 UTC
18:15:00 KST

Almost nine years ago, a tanned, relatively well-rested-looking CEO named Elon Musk announced that his electric car company would make a new sports car, the Tesla Roadster 2. It would be “the fastest sports car ever made, period,” Musk said on stage in 2017. “The point of doing this is to give a hardcore smackdown to gasoline cars.” Lights flashed, and the red prototype did a few speedy laps behind him.
Times have changed. Musk is the leading donor to a political party that last year nixed buying incentives for electric vehicles and last month adjusted fuel-economy standards to make it easier for automakers to skip making EVs altogether. Musk has said he’s not even in the business of making cars anymore, instructing investors to think of Tesla as a robotics and autonomy company. On Thursday night, Tesla will host what it has billed as its last unveiling event for a human-driven vehicle. Six years after it was supposed to roll into driveways, the Roadster 2 is finally here. Tesla is slated to start deliveries next year.
“EVs exist today in a massively different environment than when the Roadster was introduced,” says Ed Kim, president of AutoPacific, an automotive research firm. When Tesla announced the car back in 2017, electrics were “toys for early adopters,” he says. By 2020, other automakers saw Tesla’s sky-high valuations and lawmakers’ plans to transition vehicles to batteries and made big electric promises, investing heavily in the shift. China began to dominate EV-making. Now, after the Trump administration reversed the US’s course on the powertrain, EV sales are shrinking, not growing.
Still, lots more options are available now. In 2017, research firm Cox Automotive says, US customers had 15 EVs to choose from; today, that number has jumped to nearly 90. Potential EV buyers are more likely to be normies, and so their needs are more practical. “People are looking for range, performance, charging ability, resale value,” says Stephanie Valdez Streaty, director of Industry Insights at Cox.
What success looks like for the Roadster, then, is a bit complicated. It’s a hypercar targeted squarely at, well, non-normies—people who like to show off and go very, very fast. Some of them want that signature gasoline-engine power and roar. That’s why some luxury automakers have taken pains to reproduce the sound of a V-8 without one present. And it’s why others—Porsche and Ferrari among them—have said they’ll keep developing gas engines. Lamborghini said earlier this year it would shelve electrics altogether. Even Bugatti’s CEO, who founded his own electric hypercar company, said he expects loud ICE cars to become a status symbol among the wealthiest car buyers.
“EVs in this space really have to wow the shopper with a lot more than practical things,” says Kim. “Great range, really quiet, charging at home—none of that matters.” In 2017, Tesla said the car would start at $200,000; reservation holders put down $50,000 deposits.
In 2017, Musk promised a then-record-breaking sub-2-second 0-to-60 acceleration time. Now that a handful of other production cars have broken that barrier, Tesla will have to meet a high bar. One option: Musk has suggested several times over the years that the new Roadster will fly, and reports suggest that the automaker will get help from Musk’s rocket company SpaceX. (In 2018, SpaceX used its Falcon Heavy rocket to launch the first Roadster into space.)
Going that fast “is not terribly comfortable," says Shea Burns, a partner in the automotive and industrial practice at AlixPartners. “The laws of physics are catching up with them, outside of the rocket piece.” It would be an interesting way for an EV-maker to exit human driving.

Cat-Like Whiskers Help Tiny Drones Fly in the Dark
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:15:00 UTC
18:15:00 KST

After a disaster like a landslide, an earthquake, or a major fire, rescue workers have to locate survivors as soon as possible, and they are increasingly using drones for this critical task—especially ultra-compact drones that can fit into the crevices of a collapsed structure. There are, however, some serious limitations to the technology.
Weighing less than a stick of butter, ultra-compact drones don’t have as much compute or power capacity as larger models, and this restricts the power of their sensors. That means if a building is filled with smoke or the disaster happens at night, the drone’s cameras and lidar will cease to function. Even a clear pane of glass can be an obstacle the drone might not sense.
Now, a research team at Delft University of Technology in the Netherlands—drawing inspiration from the whiskers of nocturnal animals—has developed a lightweight, tactile sensor for drones to navigate even when they can’t “see.” Some nocturnal animals, like mice and to some extent cats, can explore their surroundings using just the sensations of the environment around them on their whiskers, enabling them to move without vision. The research team wondered whether drones could do the same.
In the world of drone development, tactile navigation is a novel concept that comes with its own challenges. “For tactile sensing to work on drones, it needs to be lightweight, low-latency, and low-power,” Salwa Hamaza, a professor at Delft University of Technology, explained in a press release. Luckily, nature already did some of that innovating.
The “whiskers” Hamaza and her team crafted for the drone consist of delicate wires made of nickel-titanium, each measuring 0.4 millimeters in diameter—about the thickness of four sheets of paper. The antennae, however, were longer than the drone itself. To a palm-sized drone, the researchers attached two whiskers, each nearly 8 inches long with three small pressure sensors at the base. These can assess the bending of the wires, from which the drone estimates its distance from and position in relation to nearby barriers. All calculations necessary for this navigation are processed by a microcontroller onboard the drone, without relying on an external computer.
It may not sound too complicated, but even determining the angle at which to mount the wires was a challenge. Animals that navigate via whisker generally do not fly. Having a long protrusion, even if very light and delicate, can make the drone unstable. When moving along a wall, the researchers saw that resistance from the whisker could cause the drone to rotate and crash.
The researchers compared a total of 72 flights, testing six different angles at three different speeds. The drone flew without major incident when the whiskers were mounted at 30 degrees, 45 degrees, and 60 degrees. Of these, the 45-degree angle was adopted because it resulted in the least deviation in the drone’s orientation. They also took into account the fact that a 60-degree angle reduces the forward sensing range.
The researchers also encountered several hurdles in processing the information taken in by the whiskers. One was distinguishing between actual contact signals and disturbances caused by the drone itself, such as vibrations from the propellers. Even when filtering this noise out, about 38 percent of the drone’s detections were false positives.
The issue seemed to be drift, a phenomenon where sensor readings gradually shift over time. The research team, therefore, developed a correction algorithm that continuously estimates the trend of drifts over time—based on sensor readings when the drone is not touching anything—while in flight. When combined with the filter, false positives reportedly dropped to 0 percent.
These tests were largely done in an environment with three transparent walls arranged in a row. Whenever the tactile sensor touched a wall surface, the drone flew parallel to the wall, maintaining a distance of 60 to 100 millimeters from the surface until it reached the edge. The drone was even able to navigate when the wall was at an angle to it, something a drone with laser sensors would not be able to do.
However, in a real-world situation—like the rubble of a disaster—obstacles are not so neatly arranged. Even in your average room, a drone following a wall could easily get stuck in a corner or overlook barriers to the side. The researchers, therefore, encoded an exploration method that prioritizes moving through unexplored areas by probabilistically estimating the shape of walls. Using this method, the drone successfully found a 2.5-foot-wide exit in a small room with glass walls in 90 percent of tests.
And there is room for improvement, figuratively and literally, given that this touch system only uses a small fraction of the drone’s 192 KB of memory. “We wanted to show that touch does not have to come at the cost of size or computational power,” Chao-Shan Ye, a doctoral student at Delft University of Technology, added in the press release. “Our entire tactile perception pipeline runs onboard using just 34 KB of memory, allowing a tiny drone to sense and respond to its environment in real time.”
This story originally appeared on WIRED Japan and has been translated from Japanese.

Raytheon wins $8B deal for nuclear command terminals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:14:33 UTC
18:14:33 KST

- The U.S. Air Force awarded Raytheon an $8 billion ceiling contract to modernize and restart production of strategic communications terminals for nuclear command and control.
- The sole-source contract runs through October 2036, with $800,000 obligated at award, and work in Marlborough, Massachusetts, and Largo, Florida.
The U.S. Air Force has awarded Raytheon a contract worth up to $8 billion to modernize and restart production of the satellite communications terminals that link the president and military commanders to U.S. nuclear forces, the U.S. Department of War announced on Oct. 13.
The indefinite-delivery, indefinite-quantity contract covers development work to modernize the Air Force Nuclear Weapons Center’s strategic communications terminals, services to restart their production, and technical studies. Raytheon received the contract without competition and will do the work in Marlborough, Massachusetts, and Largo, Florida, through Oct. 12, 2036. The U.S. Air Force put only $800,000 of fiscal 2026 research and development money on the contract at award, with the rest to be ordered over the next decade as needed. The announcement did not say which terminals will be built or how many.
The terminals are part of the U.S. nuclear command, control and communications network, known as NC3, which lets national leaders pass orders to bombers, missile crews and command posts under any conditions, including during a nuclear conflict. The Air Force Nuclear Weapons Center’s Strategic Communications Division at Hanscom Air Force Base, Massachusetts, which awarded the contract, buys and sustains that equipment.
Raytheon’s main work for the division is the Family of Advanced Beyond Line-of-Sight Terminals, or FAB-T, which connects ground command posts and aircraft to the military’s most protected communications satellites, the Advanced Extremely High Frequency constellation and the older Milstar. FAB-T is built to keep working through jamming and nuclear effects, and it carries presidential voice conferences, warnings of incoming attacks and emergency action messages, the coded orders used to launch nuclear weapons. Raytheon took over the program from Boeing in 2014, and the original plan called for 61 ground and 23 airborne terminals.
The company has steadily added to that work. In 2023 the U.S. Air Force awarded Raytheon $625 million for Force Element Terminals, the FAB-T version fitted to B-52 bombers and other aircraft, and in March the service raised the ceiling on a separate Raytheon contract for Advanced Extremely High Frequency terminals by $2 billion, to nearly $3 billion. The new $8 billion ceiling is the largest award yet for the company’s strategic communications terminals, and the reference to restarting production suggests the U.S. Air Force expects to buy more terminals after earlier production runs ended.
The U.S. Air Force is modernizing most parts of the nuclear triad at the same time, including the B-21 Raider bomber, the Sentinel intercontinental ballistic missile and the Long Range Standoff cruise missile, all of which will need communications links that can survive an attack.

IMF chief urges urgent fiscal action as global economic resilience reaches limits
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:14:11 UTC
18:14:11 KST

Mücahithan Avcıoğlu
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva on Wednesday urged governments to urgently strengthen public finances, warning that the global economy’s resilience to repeated shocks is reaching its limits.
Speaking at a press briefing during the IMF-World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok, Georgieva said energy and fiscal buffers were being depleted, while persistent inflation and rising interest rates were adding to debt-servicing pressures.
Global growth is projected at about 3.1% in 2026, unchanged from April’s forecast but below last year’s 3.4%, she said.
The outlook reflects opposing forces, with the Middle East war disrupting energy supplies while demand linked to artificial intelligence supports economic activity.
Economies integrated into AI supply chains, including Thailand, Malaysia, South Korea and Singapore, were generally performing better, along with energy exporters unaffected by wars.
Low-income countries and fragile states, particularly energy importers excluded from the technology boom, faced the greatest pressures. 
Rising borrowing costs intensify debt pressures
Georgieva said government bond yields in advanced economies had risen to multidecade highs, reflecting inflation, investment demand, expectations of stronger AI-driven growth and fiscal weaknesses.
Higher benchmark yields were increasing borrowing costs for emerging markets even where their risk premiums remained stable, she said, warning that elevated financing costs were likely to persist.
Debt-servicing costs in low-income countries had increased from 6% of government revenues a decade ago to 14%, she added.
Georgieva urged governments to raise revenues, rationalize spending and improve public financial management. Assistance to offset rising food and energy costs should be temporary and targeted at vulnerable people while preserving price signals.
Central banks should remain focused on price stability, with the strongest case for tightening in economies where inflation exceeds targets and activity remains robust.
On global imbalances, she called on China to boost domestic consumption, the US to increase savings and reduce deficits, and Europe to strengthen investment.
US economic growth alone would not deliver the required fiscal adjustment quickly enough, making additional measures necessary, she said.
Georgieva also warned that disappointing near-term AI returns could trigger a disorderly market correction, while AI-enabled cyberattacks posed risks to financial stability.

Ministry proposes congestion charges and higher electric car taxes

12:11:03 EEST
18:11:03 KST

Finland's Ministry of Transport and Communications has proposed introducing congestion charges in major cities and increasing taxes on electric vehicles as part of a transport funding reform intended for the next government.
The proposals form part of recommendations prepared by ministry officials ahead of the 2027 parliamentary elections. They also include ending state subsidies for regional flights and increasing funding for road and railway maintenance.
Add Helsinki Times as a preferred source on Google (opens Google in a new tab)
The ministry argues that Finland must reform transport taxation as the growing number of electric vehicles reduces government revenue from petrol and diesel.
Government figures project annual transport tax revenue to fall to €2.7 billion by 2035, down from €4.9 billion in 2018.
The ministry proposes linking vehicle taxation more closely to road maintenance costs rather than carbon dioxide emissions. Such a change would increase the tax burden on electric vehicle owners, who currently benefit from lower emissions-based taxation.
Officials also want revenue from vehicle taxes directed towards maintaining Finland's transport infrastructure.
The ministry proposes congestion charges in the Helsinki metropolitan area and potentially Tampere, where drivers would pay to use certain roads during periods of heavy traffic.
The ministry argues that the charges would reduce traffic congestion and emissions while generating funding for urban transport improvements.
Officials also propose examining tolls and other user charges to finance individual road and railway projects.
The recommendations prioritise maintaining existing infrastructure over constructing new transport links.
Finland's road and railway network faces a maintenance backlog estimated at approximately €4.3 billion.
Sabina Lindström, a ministry department director, warned that insufficient funding would leave less frequently used roads without adequate maintenance.
The ministry also recommends ending government purchases of regional air services, introduced during the Covid-19 pandemic.
The state currently spends €20,2 million annually subsidising regional flights, while state-owned airport operator Finavia incurs another €20 million in annual losses associated with the airport network.
Officials argue that maintaining airports with limited passenger traffic diverts resources from investments at larger airports.
The ministry also wants to preserve Finland's renewable fuel blending requirements and other transport emissions policies, despite proposals to ease fuel costs.
Its recommendations are civil servants' policy proposals rather than government decisions. Any changes to vehicle taxation, congestion charges or regional aviation funding would require political approval and further preparation.

Morocco’s first female PM secures coalition deal

Morocco’s first female PM secures coalition deal
Morocco’s election-winning Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM) has agreed to form a government with three other parties, securing a parliamentary majority for the country’s first female prime minister, Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri. The new coalition excludes outgoing premier Aziz Akhannouch’s party.
The liberal-centrist party will govern alongside the nationalist Istiqlal Party, the Socialist Union of Popular Forces, and the Party of Progress and Socialism, according to a joint statement issued on Monday. The group holds 207 of the lower house’s 395 seats, above the 198 required for a majority.
The agreement followed two rounds of consultations led by Mansouri, the statement said. The parties pledged a “strong political government” committed to a shared reform agenda, including stronger rights and freedoms, social justice, and reducing regional inequalities. They said they would propose ministerial candidates “who are competent, politically astute, honest, and upright” and prepare a government program as “quickly as possible.”
The government replaces the previous three-party alliance, which was led by Akhannouch’s National Rally of Independents (RNI) alongside PAM and Istiqlal for a five-year term beginning in 2021. Before the September 23 election, PAM and RNI reportedly clashed over the recruitment of elected officials and traded blame over policy shortcomings, including a failure to curb rising food prices.
King Mohammed VI appointed Mansouri, a former housing minister and Marrakech mayor, on September 29 after PAM won 97 seats in the vote. RNI finished second with 66, followed by Istiqlal with 65. Turnout fell to about 38%, compared with around 50% in 2021.
The constitution requires the king to appoint the premier from the party winning the most parliamentary seats. The monarch retains sweeping powers over defense and foreign policy.
The new government will oversee preparations for Morocco to co-host the 2030 FIFA World Cup with Spain and Portugal. It faces demands for jobs and better education and healthcare, grievances that fueled deadly youth-led protests last year and July’s mass migrant crossing into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta.

The turret will be part of an air defense system capable of achieving a target destruction probability of over 90%, it said.

"Its [the system's] key feature is the ability to provide early detection and select the most cost-effective and suitable interception method. All combat operations of the anti-drone system will be automated, and the human operator will only need to make the decision to engage aerial targets. Arkodim is currently testing the system's components. According to the developer's estimates, the probability of a successful hit will exceed 90%," the CUST stated. The Center also specified that, in addition to turrets, the system will include a pre-guidance tower and an interceptor drone equipped with an onboard terminal guidance system to engage enemy UAVs at a range of several kilometers.

Bank of England and IMF bosses warn of cyber threat to trust in financial system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:07:59 UTC
18:07:59 KST

The heads of the Bank of England and the International Monetary Fund have issued a stark warning that rising cyber-attacks risk undermining trust in the financial system.
Speaking on a panel about online fraud at the IMF and World Bank meetings in Bangkok, the governor of the Bank of England, Andrew Bailey, pointed to alarming headlines about self-replicating AI agents hijacking personal devices, and the French supermarket hack that heated fridges up to 50C.
“If you try to say what’s at the heart of this debate about AI – for me, it’s about trust in technology and it’s about human control to achieve that trust in technology,” he said.
Pointing to the key importance of technology in underpinning today’s financial system, he added: “If we don’t have trust in money, we don’t operate as a society.”
Echoing his concerns, the IMF’s managing director, Kristalina Georgieva, said the toll of cyber-fraud was now so great that people could decide to opt out of the formal financial system altogether.
“I was born and grew up on the other side of the iron curtain,” the Bulgarian economist said. “We didn’t trust the system. What did we do? I would have my dollars in a shoebox under my bed.
“And I worry, today, that unless we figure out how to get ahead of this curve, given the speed, the scale and the cost of fraud growing up, we may end up with lots of people with shoeboxes under their beds.”
She said this threat was particularly acute for people on the fringes of the financial system. “Imagine what would happen if trust disappears or is eroded to a point that people no more have the courage to be included,” she said.
Her comments followed a warning from the IMF on Tuesday that the possibility of a big cyber-attack was one of the factors raising the global financial stability threat level to “elevated”, alongside higher borrowing costs and the risk of an AI share price crash.
Bailey stressed that fraud was now frequently committed via social media platforms and apps, not just traditional financial channels – and urged big tech to take responsibility.
He contrasted today’s environment with the legal status in the UK of outlets such as newspapers, which are responsible for the veracity of everything they publish.
Instead, the governor said: “We’ve moved into quite an extreme position of, well, these platforms are open to everybody and there’s no real liability to the provision of the platform to what’s on it. Guess what? Everything’s on it. You know, the good, the bad and the incredibly ugly and downright criminal and terrible.”
He added: “I don’t go around pointing the finger at people and saying: ‘You’re bad.’ What I have said is: ‘Look, there is responsibility all around.’ And we need to evolve to a world where everybody understands this responsibility, and everybody is then a part of addressing the problem.”
He added: “We must get the social media companies involved because a lot of this fraud is transmitted through those channels.”
Bailey called for the same tools that are being used by cybercriminals to be put to work protecting the financial system. “I’m going to use a sporting metaphor: this technology is arming the offence but it can also arm the defence, and it must do.”
The panel event at which the pair were speaking was to launch a new set of international principles for avoiding cyber-fraud in financial institutions, called the Bangkok blueprint.

Dilara Hamit
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
Relatives of Tupac Shakur described the lasting emotional damage caused by his 1996 murder after a Nevada court sentenced Duane “Keffe D” Davis to 40 years to life in prison for orchestrating the fatal shooting.
Davis, 63, was sentenced Tuesday to two consecutive terms of 20 years to life, one for first-degree murder and another for the use of a deadly weapon.
Tupac’s sister Sekyiwa Shakur and brother Maurice “Mopreme” Shakur delivered victim-impact statements during the hearing, recalling the rapper as a generous brother and an artist committed to social change.
“The loss of Tupac crippled my family emotionally,” Sekyiwa told the court.
“He dedicated his career to the advancement of his people, he was gently kind to women and children, he fed anyone he knew that didn’t have, he was truly my shining star,” she added.
Mopreme focused on the future his brother was denied.
“Pac didn’t have a chance to have kids, he didn’t have a chance to see his nieces and nephews grow up,” he said. “All Pac got was a death sentence.”
Clark County District Attorney Steve Wolfson said the sentence represented a long-delayed measure of accountability.
“Today, justice has been served for Tupac Shakur and his loved ones,” Wolfson said in a statement.
“While no amount of time in prison can bring Tupac back, we hope this sentencing brings some measure of closure and peace to his family after nearly 30 years. This case is a reminder that no matter how much time passes, our commitment to seeking justice never wavers.”
District Judge Carli Kierny also addressed the consequences of the killing before imposing the sentence.
“You don’t get to take a man from his family, you don’t get to take his very life, his whole future from him, and just walk away from it,” Kierny said. “Especially when that man is Tupac Shakur.”
She said the world had never forgotten the rapper or his death.
Davis did not deliver an extensive statement before sentencing. He told the judge that he intended to appeal, while his lawyer, Michael Sanft, also confirmed plans to challenge both the conviction and sentence.
A jury convicted Davis on Aug. 31 of first-degree murder with the use of a deadly weapon. Prosecutors did not accuse him of firing the fatal shots but argued that he organized the retaliatory attack under Nevada’s accomplice-liability law.
Tupac was shot on Sept. 7, 1996, while riding in a car near the Las Vegas Strip and died six days later at the age of 25.
Prosecutors said the attack followed a fight at a Las Vegas casino involving Tupac, members of his entourage and Davis’ nephew. Davis was the only person ever criminally charged in the case.
No prominent musicians or other entertainment figures had issued widely verified public statements about the sentence by Wednesday, with the clearest reactions coming from Tupac’s relatives, the presiding judge and Nevada prosecutors.

Rostec claims its 30mm anti-drone gun beats Western rivals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:06:18 UTC
18:06:18 KST

- Rostec says its 30 mm ZAK-30 Tsitadel anti-drone gun competes with Rheinmetall’s Skynex and the U.S. Phalanx and C-RAM on the world market.
- The system fires programmable shrapnel shells guided by radar and electro-optical sensors and has been used in the war in Ukraine, Rostec says.
Russian state defense conglomerate Rostec is pitching its new 30 mm ZAK-30 “Tsitadel” anti-drone gun as a direct competitor to Western systems such as Germany’s Skynex and the U.S.-made Phalanx, saying its combat use has shown advantages in automation, cost per shot, and effectiveness on the world market.
Rostec made the claim in a statement this week, arguing that each of the Western systems has drawbacks Tsitadel avoids. The company said Germany’s Skynex, which fires 35 mm AHEAD programmable rounds, produces a powerful cloud of fragments but is heavier and more expensive because of its larger caliber. It said the American Phalanx and its land-based version, the Counter-Rocket, Artillery and Mortar system known as C-RAM, fire at very high rates from 20 mm Vulcan Gatling guns but do not use programmable “smart” rounds, so they burn through more ammunition for each target.
Tsitadel fires 30 mm shells packed with shrapnel and fitted with a remotely set fuze. The system’s computer works out the best point on the drone’s flight path to detonate each shell, so the round bursts just ahead of the target and showers it with fragments, which Rostec says means fewer shells are needed per kill than with ordinary rounds. The gun finds and tracks targets with both radar and an electro-optical sensor that works in visible light and infrared, and Rostec says the process from detection to engagement is highly automated.
“The Russian programmable 30 mm shrapnel round creates a deadly cloud of fragments right in front of the drone. When fighting drones, economics are extremely important,” Russian military commentator Dmitry Kornev told the newspaper Izvestia.
Kornev also said Tsitadel’s accuracy and effectiveness put it far ahead of older systems such as Germany’s Gepard. Ukraine has used Gepard self-propelled anti-aircraft guns, supplied by Germany since 2022, as one of its main weapons against Russian Shahed-type attack drones.
Rostec first unveiled Tsitadel in May at a security forum near Moscow, describing it as a system for protecting fixed sites such as plants, depots and energy facilities from both multicopter and fixed-wing drones around the clock. Russian media have reported that the gun module appears to be based on the BM-30-D Spitsa weapon station with the 2A42 cannon used on Russian infantry fighting vehicles, and that the system can hit fixed-wing drones at up to about 1 km (0.6 miles) and small multicopters at up to about 800 meters (2,600 feet). Russian industry sources have also said a mobile version mounted on Ural trucks is planned. At the time of the unveiling, Rostec said the system had already been tested in real combat conditions during the war in Ukraine.
The Western systems Tsitadel is being compared with have their own combat records. Germany has supplied Skynex to Ukraine to protect key sites from Russian drones and cruise missiles, while the U.S. Navy has used Phalanx aboard warships and C-RAM has defended U.S. bases in Iraq and Afghanistan against rockets and mortars.

China’s exports surge amid AI-driven demand
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:05:17 UTC
18:05:17 KST

China’s exports surge amid AI-driven demand
Exports grew by 36.3 percent in September, the biggest leap since the COVID-19 pandemic.
China’s exports surged by more than one-third in September, a boost to the world’s second-largest economy as it faces slowing growth.
Exports grew by 36.3 percent last month year-on-year to reach $447.18bn, accelerating from a 25 percent gain in August, government figures released on Wednesday show.
The leap marked the biggest monthly rise in exports since 2021, when China’s trade figures were skewed by the effects of the COVID-19 pandemic and stringent lockdowns.
Tech-related trade led the growth, with semiconductor exports surging more than 108 percent and shipments of automatic data processing machines jumping nearly 55 percent.
Imports increased 31 percent year-on-year, up from 28.2 percent in August, according to the figures from the General Administration of Customs.
“High-tech demand, supported by the global and domestic AI upcycle, remained the key driver, while China’s pricing and supply-chain competitiveness in other major export categories also helped sustain the momentum,” Taylor Wang, an economist at HSBC in Hong Kong, said in a note to clients.
China’s total exports in the first nine months of the year rose 21.3 percent to $3.37 trillion, while imports gained 27.5 percent to $2.43 trillion.
The gap between exports and imports in the first three quarters gave China a trade surplus of $938.1bn.
The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) was China’s biggest export market by a wide margin, with exports rising more than 52 percent in September to $81.7bn.
Exports to the European Union rose 25.3 percent in September to $60.15bn, while shipments to the United States jumped 39.6 percent to $47.88bn.
After decades of relying on state-led investment and exports to power its economy, China is striving to find new avenues for growth amid a falling population, deflating property market, and weak domestic consumption, which contributes far less to gross domestic product (GDP) than in advanced economies.
China’s economy is expected to grow 4.5 percent in 2026, according to the International Monetary Fund’s latest growth outlook, which would be the slowest expansion since 1990, excluding the outlier years of the COVID pandemic.
“The strong export growth should keep China’s growth on track to achieve its growth target of 4.5-5 percent for 2026,” Lynn Song, chief economist for Greater China at ING, told Al Jazeera.
“Nonetheless, growth remains quite unbalanced, with domestic data quite soft in comparison,” Song said.
“It will be important to rebalance growth over the medium term if China is to achieve its longterm growth targets.”

The Maldives Plans to Offer Residency to the World’s Ultra Rich – And Create Islands From Scratch to Do It
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:05:00 UTC
18:05:00 KST

Nearly half of its population of just over half a million people are packed into the capital city of Malé, a small island that is only two square kilometers in size.
The government has spent recent years expanding existing islands and building brand new ones to ease overcrowding. There are plans to connect one future artificial island city, Ras Malé, to the capital via an undersea tunnel featuring what the president’s office has called a “railway on which tourists can observe the underwater beauty.”
Tourism has followed the same path. Since 2019, developers have begun opening up artificial island complexes that host a mix of hotels, shops, and entertainment at a scale impossible on smaller, naturally occurring islands. 
But with the exception of a handful of leasehold villas built on some resorts, existing developments have left little room for foreigners to call the Maldives home – until now. 
Some Maldivian politicians are trying to push back. In July, opposition lawmaker Ahmed Shamheed filed a resolution calling for the Maldives Pearl Residence program to be immediately suspended and to disclose all related agreements. (His resolution was rejected by parliament in August.) 
The lawmaker also fears SEZs like Project Ayla could effectively become miniature states within a state.
“Money laundering, terrorism financing, and what they do with banks set up there, we don’t know any of this. We have very few resources in the Maldives. We’re talking about billionaires, and we wouldn’t know if the world’s big mafia gangs come and operate there,” Shamheed told reporters.
“And this is just one city — apparently many such cities are to come.”
Azza Mohamed, a governance manager at Transparency International’s Maldives chapter, said the SEZ push is raising fears authorities could recreate the same sort of permissive conditions that led to a massive corruption scandal a dozen years ago. 
That scandal, investigated by OCCRP, saw senior politicians improperly lease islands to tourism developers in 2014 and 2015, while pocketing tens of millions of dollars in proceeds.
Avoiding a similar fate “would require full transparency over beneficial ownership, genuinely independent oversight of procurement and approvals, and enforcement systems that can trace, freeze, and recover illicit funds, including across borders,” Mohamed said.
Meanwhile, precisely who is financing Project Ayla is unknown. 
The project is being developed by the local entity Crystal Holdings Private Limited, which holds the SEZ permit, and the Dubai-based BluRock Group, both of whose underlying investors, equity partners, and ultimate beneficial owners are not made available to the public. 
Crystal Holdings and BluRock did not respond to reporters’ requests for comment.
‘Sovereign Portfolios’
The new residency by investment program will be developed and implemented by the Maldives government and Henley & Partners — a passport brokerage firm that has left behind a string of scandals in other island states.

Explosions reported in Saudi capital after Houthi attack near Aramco HQ

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
