How Israel’s ‘Yellow Line’ is reshaping southern Lebanon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
07:38:09 UTC
16:38:09 KST

How Israel’s ‘Yellow Line’ is reshaping southern Lebanon
Demolished homes, shifting military lines, stalled withdrawals leave Lebanese uncertain if they can return.
Beirut, Lebanon – Ali is from Khiam, a Lebanese village on the southern border with Israel, but for the last few months he has rented a house in Hasbaiyya, about a half-hour drive away to the northeast. He is one of tens of thousands of Lebanese who have been displaced from their homes in villages throughout the south of the country.
“Southerners are living a tragedy,” Ali, who did not wish to give his full name, told Al Jazeera. “This is all from flawed tragedies and failed politics.”
Despite a framework agreement between Lebanon and Israel signed in June – with the objective of securing Israel’s phased withdrawal from Lebanon – Israel has continued to occupy large parts of its neighbour’s south, where it has systematically demolished homes and infrastructure in dozens of villages.
Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz has previously said that his country’s troops will not be withdrawn from Lebanon, suggesting an extended occupation similar to the last Israeli occupation, which lasted 22 years.
‘Hard boundary’
The Lebanese Shia group Hezbollah fired rockets at Israel on March 2, for the first time in more than a year. The Iranian-backed group said the attack was a response to daily Israeli violations of the November 2024 ceasefire and the assassination two days prior of Iran’s Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, at the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran.
Israel responded by intensifying its war on Lebanon for a second time in under two years. Israeli attacks, as well as its reinvasion of southern Lebanon, displaced more than 1.2 million people. Since then, Beirut has entered into US-brokered direct negotiations with the Israeli government, despite the objections of Hezbollah, which has fought Israel since October 2023. The group traces its origins in the 1980s to resistance against Israeli occupation of Lebanese territory.
Yet the Lebanese government continued with the discussions, which eventually resulted in the framework agreement. One element of the agreement was the establishment of “pilot zones”, from which Israel would withdraw and be replaced by the Lebanese Armed Forces, who would then disarm any Hezbollah forces in the area.
Israel currently occupies a zone stretching up to 10 kilometres (6.2 miles) deep into southern Lebanon. Behind the “Yellow Line” that marks the end of that occupation zone, Israel continues to detonate homes. Israel uses the same “Yellow Line” term to refer to the areas it controls in Gaza.
“Israel’s primary goals were to empty, depopulate, and make those dozens of frontline villages and towns uninhabitable, and we’ve seen that now with the satellite imagery,” Mohamad Bazzi, a New York-based political analyst originally from Bint Jbeil in southern Lebanon, told Al Jazeera. “It was a way of applying that Gaza model to Lebanon.”
Around 50 frontline villages, including places like Khiam and Bint Jbeil, have been destroyed.
“Unlike previous occupations, the Israeli goal this time has been to empty those towns and villages of their residents, push them out, destroy as much of the housing and infrastructure as possible, and to make it extremely difficult if not impossible for people to return to their homes,” he said, adding that most of the destruction of the towns had occurred since April, despite several announcements of ceasefires.
“[The Yellow Line] is treated as a hard boundary, both in terms of troop presence and the controlled demolition of villages, which continues unabated despite the ceasefire,” Ahmad Baydoun, a Lebanese architect and open-source researcher based in the Netherlands, told Al Jazeera. “It is as if the ceasefire applies to the rest of Lebanon but not to this territory.”
On the northern side of the Yellow Line, residents have returned to devastated villages, including a couple of towns included in the “pilot zone” programme.
One of those towns is Froun, which the Israeli military destroyed via air and drone strikes, but which its troops did not enter.
“We were surprised that it was [included as a] pilot zone,” Hasan Bazzi, the president of Froun’s municipal office, told Al Jazeera.
Lines of all colours
The Yellow Line is not the only coloured line used in Lebanon to reference military demarcations. The Blue Line was established in 2000 in the wake of the end of Israel’s years-long occupation of southern Lebanon, with Israeli forces withdrawing behind it.
And there are now discussions in Israel about creating a “Grey Line”. Reports indicate that this line could extend 4 kilometres (2.5 miles) into Lebanese territory. The area behind the Grey Line would remain uninhabited, effectively serving as a buffer zone for Israel, which would not allow Lebanese civilians to rebuild their homes in the area.
“Part of the Israeli strategy here with the Grey Line, Blue Line, Yellow Line is to sow confusion and to hide or obfuscate the reality of what Israel has done on the ground [which is] to depopulate this vast Lebanese territory and to make it uninhabitable,” Bazzi, the analyst, said. “In the end, it doesn’t really matter what the definitions of these lines are because they are often shifting. We’ve seen that play out in Gaza, and the bottom line is Israel is illegally occupying and has illegally destroyed and ethnically cleansed a huge part of southern Lebanon, and the world sat silent while that happened for the most part.”
But even within the area on the Israeli-controlled side of the Yellow Line, some villagers remain, reflecting Israeli attempts to play on Lebanon’s sectarian divides. The majority of the population of southern Lebanon is Shia Muslim, but officials from non-Shia areas have said that they have received warnings not to host displaced people in their towns. Even those allowed to stay do not live in total freedom.
“The villages Israel has allowed to remain inhabited inside the Yellow Line are largely Christian and Sunni,” Baydoun explained. “But being allowed to stay is not the same as being free to live. In Kfarchouba, municipal workers were abducted while pumping the village’s water, and the mayor himself was detained. Even in Deir Mimas, a village outside the Yellow Line, the Lebanese army set up a post so farmers could reach their olive groves, and Israeli tanks came to the entrance of the village to confront it.”
Baydoun described the new reality of southern Lebanon as the “West Bankification of those who remained”, referring to Israel’s occupation of the West Bank.
“Residents are permitted to exist on their land but not to use it freely,” he said. “Access to fields depends on checkpoints, coordination and the mood of a patrol. Municipal officials are detained and questioned at will. It is a model of control that does not need to empty a village to govern it.”
Permanence of displacement
Analysts believe the occupation of southern Lebanon could extend into the foreseeable future. The Lebanese government has promised to erect prefabricated homes in some areas, but it may struggle to provide state services like water, electricity and sewage disposal to areas where infrastructure has been widely damaged or destroyed.
Even if the Israelis were to withdraw, much of the border area lies in complete ruin, collections of dust, rubble and ash lying where homes and agricultural lands once prospered.
“There are some towns where it might be possible to return with significant work, but in the 50 or so frontline towns or villages, I don’t think it will be possible in the short or medium term,” Bazzi said.
The subject is an open wound for many southerners, forced to continue their lives elsewhere while their homes and lands lie in ruins and under occupation. For them, Israel’s military occupation is reshaping southern Lebanon for the next generation.
“Khiam is destroyed, there’s nothing, it’s uninhabitable for the next 10, 15, 20 years,” Ali, the displaced man from Khiam, said. “They returned us to the Stone Age.”

Pope's AI adviser warns Australia's copyright changes risk 'new form of colonialism'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
07:36:56 UTC
16:36:56 KST

Pope's AI adviser warns Australia's copyright changes risk 'new form of colonialism'
In short:
The AI adviser to Pope Leo has praised Australia for taking a considered approach to tech companies.
Father Paolo Benanti warned Australia that changes to copyright laws to allow AI training would be risky.
He says tech companies openly court religious leaders to protect their business interests.
Australia risks reviving a "new form of colonialism" if it allows AI companies to train on copyrighted work without permission and send profits offshore, an influential AI adviser to the Vatican has warned.
Asked about Australia's consideration of copyright changes to attract AI training, Father Paolo Benanti compared the risk with Europe's history of taking resources from other countries and profiting from them elsewhere.
"You go, you take resources, and you monetise it outside the place where the resources [were]," he said.
He said Australian writing could become another resource used by foreign companies, with the money and tax revenue ending up overseas.
"Is it … a new form of colonialism from foreign power that could … exploit from the resources and monetise it outside of the place where they are taken?" he asked.
"So is this fair? Is this something that will produce real richness or pay back to Australia? I don't know."
Those were questions he said he would ask before voting on such a change.
Last month, the ABC reported that the attorney-general's department was quietly consulting on changes that would mean AI companies could train on copyrighted content unless its owner had opted out.
In June Attorney-General Michelle Rowland told 7.30: "This government has repeatedly said that there are no plans to weaken copyright protections when it comes to AI."
Earlier this week, the federal parliament's AI committee took the unusual step of pre-empting its own process to write a letter that urged reforms to pave the way for AI training.
Father Benanti praised Australia's efforts to regulate social media and AI when he met Prime Minister Anthony Albanese last week, and told 7.30 other countries should follow Australia's lead in reining in tech companies with policies like the teen social media ban.
On his visit to Australia as a guest of the Italian embassy, he described the country as being at the "foremost frontier" and defended it against aspersions about the effectiveness of laws like the social media minimum age.
He said the essential democratic principle was that "no-one should be above the law".
That included overseas social media companies, which he said could rely on protections in their home countries to avoid other governments' rules.
He said Australia's first steps were important, and hoped other countries would follow.
Working together would give governments more power to make technology companies comply with the rules in countries where they wanted to do business, he said.
'We need a brain helmet'
Father Benanti studied engineering before becoming a Franciscan friar and a professor specialising in the ethics of technology. He advised Pope Francis on artificial intelligence and now advises his successor, Pope Leo.
In May, Pope Leo presented his first encyclical, Magnifica Humanitas, a major papal letter sharing his teachings about humanity in the age of AI.
The landmark document made global headlines for criticising autonomous weapons as well as algorithms that could deny people access to health care, employment or security.
Father Benanti said the encyclical resonated beyond the Catholic Church's followers because it addressed moral questions they were already asking about how technology could change their lives.
"Human dignity is the core,"
he said.
He said its appeal came from keeping those questions open for public debate and allowing society to shape how AI was governed.
Father Benanti's concerns about AI extend to the emotional attachments people can form with the technology.
He is concerned that companies exploit loneliness and romantic attachment to their products to make money from people's emotions.
"Those are not neutral things, but are things that are designed by someone," he said.
The question, he said, was whether these products could operate without laws to protect the most vulnerable people.
Asked about protecting children, he compared minors' adoption of AI and smartphones to his experience with riding motorised scooters as a child.
When he was old enough he was given a small vehicle rather than a powerful model that could kill him.
He said smartphones put the same device in the hands of children and adults, without being tailored to children's capabilities.
"Probably we need a brain helmet," he said.
Business vs faith
Father Benanti said he believed tech companies had been courting religious leaders to attempt to protect their business interests.
He has been part of meetings with leaders of top tech companies held at company locations, rather than at the Vatican.
Their purpose, he said, "was not because they would like to talk about faith".
"There are politicians, there are religious leaders, there are scientists and things like that," he said.
"They don't want to have leaders against them that can move the people.
"So it's a matter of business-oriented interest."
Father Benanti said these leaders tried to persuade them of their own beliefs; that their work was bringing humanity close to an extraordinary moment in history, and even raising the possibility AI could be conscious.
Asked whether he found the pitch compelling, his answer was blunt.
"Not at all."

Will South China Sea’s code of conduct remain elusive as deadline looms?
The proposed code can only succeed if it sets clear rules to prevent clashes at sea rather than to resolve territorial claims, analysts say
5-MIN READ5-MIN
 Listen
Ushar Danielein Kuala Lumpur
A long-awaited code of conduct (COC) for the South China Sea risks becoming a toothless agreement, analysts have warned, as Beijing and Southeast Asian nations scramble to hammer out a deal by the end of 2026.
More than three decades since it was mooted, the proposed pact has remained gridlocked over how to balance competing territorial claims among China and four rival claimant states – Malaysia, Vietnam, Brunei and the Philippines.
Maritime experts speaking at a conference in Kuala Lumpur this week agreed that the code was not meant to settle sovereignty disputes and were divided on whether it could keep the peace.
“If anything involves clarifying maritime rights, not only China but also the Philippines and Vietnam will not accept a binding COC,” Ding Duo, a researcher at China’s National Institute for South China Sea Studies, told This Week in Asia on the sidelines of the Maritime Institute of Malaysia’s 9th South China Sea Conference on Tuesday.

Russia fired 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 attack drones and loitering munitions at Ukraine’s energy and critical infrastructure overnight into Oct. 14, knocking out power to at least 600,000 people days after President Donald Trump announced a halt to strikes on energy facilities, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
Zelenskyy said that the attack targeted Kyiv, the surrounding Kyiv region and Kharkiv, and damaged equipment at 26 facilities in Ukraine’s power system and four in the oil and gas sector. He warned that outages could spread further and said there were dead and injured, without giving numbers. Repair crews, power company staff and the State Emergency Service were working to restore supply on Wednesday morning.
Zelenskyy described the ballistic missile salvo as aimed specifically at the energy infrastructure covered by the ceasefire Trump announced on Truth Social on Oct. 11, and called the scale of the strike deliberate and demonstrative.
“Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States,” said Zelenskyy.
Moscow never confirmed accepting Trump’s energy ceasefire, and its scope remained disputed after the announcement, with a White House official telling Axios that the proposal initially covered oil refineries, while power plants and electricity grids might follow later. Zelenskyy told Fox News on Oct. 12 that Ukraine had held off on striking Russian energy facilities after the announcement, while Russia kept hitting Ukrainian gas and power sites. Ukraine’s charge d’affaires in Washington, Denys Sienik, said Russia had struck electricity generation and transmission facilities more than 200 times in the week before the announcement.
“Russia has squandered the opportunity for de-escalation and has clearly chosen to continue its insane war of annihilation,” said Zelenskyy.
Ballistic missiles are the hardest part of a Russian strike package for Ukraine to stop, because they fly too fast and too high for most of the country’s air defenses, and Ukraine relies mainly on U.S.-made Patriot systems to intercept them. Zelenskyy asked Washington and other partners for additional packages of Patriot interceptors, saying no country should be left alone against Russia.
He also called on Trump to impose strong sanctions on Russia under the sanctions law sponsored by Sen. Lindsey Graham, which Trump signed on Sept. 18 and which gives the president authority to raise tariffs and restrict Russian energy trade, with key measures due to take effect by Oct. 18.
“We ask President Trump to impose STRONG sanctions on Russia, especially since the Lindsey Graham bill, which was recently passed and signed into law, authorizes and regulates such measures,” said Zelenskyy.
The strike followed Trump’s Oct. 9 announcement of a deal to release Russian diesel onto U.S. and world markets, starting with 300,000 tons immediately and 500,000 tons in November, after the Treasury waived diesel sanctions until April 2027. Critics in Congress have said the arrangement gives Moscow additional revenue for the war. The White House had not responded publicly to the overnight strike by Wednesday morning, and Russia’s Defense Ministry had not commented on its targets.

After &quot;Yandex&quot; — &quot;Sberbank&quot;: Ukraine attacked one of Russia’s largest data centers

After "Yandex" — "Sberbank": Ukraine attacked one of Russia’s largest data centers
Kyiv • UNN
Ukraine’s Defense Forces attacked Sberbank’s mega data center and the Balakovo Metallurgical Plant in Russia’s Saratov region.
During the night of October 14, Ukraine’s Defense Forces struck the Russian Sberbank’s megadata center in the city of Balakovo, Saratov region, Russia, with drones. The attack was confirmed by the Ukrainian defense company Fire Point, reports UNN.
Well, you didn’t think it would be limited to just Yandex, did you? Sberbank, take up the baton!
Video: Telegram / supernova_plus
A massive drone attack on Balakovo continued during the night of October 14. Local residents reported dozens of explosions, after which fires broke out in the city’s industrial districts.
According to OSINT analysts from the Exilenova+ Telegram channel, one of the facilities attacked was Sberbank’s megadata center—a large-scale complex designed to store and process information and ensure the operation of banking IT systems and digital services.
The project is estimated to cost 122.2 billion rubles. The complex is designed for approximately 3,000 server racks and up to 120,000 servers, while its electrical capacity may reach 82 MW. Once construction is completed, it is expected to become one of the largest data centers in Russia.
Photo: Telegram / Exilenova+
Construction of the data center is still ongoing, although some parts of the complex may already have been commissioned. In addition to servicing banking infrastructure, its capacity was intended to host services of the Russian state digital platform GosTech.
Fire Point also reported that the MZ Balakovo steel mill was hit during the Defense Forces’ nighttime attack. The MZ Balakovo steel mill specializes in the production of steel and rolled metal products, including rebar and long products. The enterprise has its own steelmaking facilities, and its production capacity exceeds one million tons of products per year.
Photo: Telegram / firepointofficial
The attack was also confirmed by Roman Busargin, the governor of the Saratov region. According to him, several residential buildings were damaged and a woman was killed. At the same time, the Russian official stated that all of the city’s infrastructure facilities were allegedly operating normally. He did not comment on the reported damage to Sberbank’s megadata center.
Previously
Earlier, Ukraine’s Defense Forces carried out a series of strikes on Russian Yandex data centers in the Ryazan and Kaluga regions, as well as in Vladimir. According to Fire Point, after the attack on the last of the three facilities, all three of the company’s supercomputers became unavailable.
The strikes caused disruptions in the operation of Russian internet services, while the operations of companies using the Yandex Cloud infrastructure were put at risk.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy previously explained the strikes on Russian data centers as a reciprocal response to Russia’s attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure.

America’s broken promises, Iran’s resolve, and the dangerous game over the Strait of Hormuz
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
07:32:50 UTC
16:32:50 KST

The latest diplomatic deadlock over the Strait of Hormuz exposes the central problem in the US–Iran confrontation: Washington wants concessions from Iran, but Tehran is demanding clear commitments, credible guarantees, and an end to what it sees as a pattern of pressure, shifting demands, and broken trust.
On 11th October 11, 2026, Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, described the US response to Iran’s seven conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz as insufficient. Tehran says Washington has accepted some conditions while leaving others unclear. The two sides also disagree over the sequence of implementation, particularly whether Iran’s nuclear programme should be addressed at the outset or whether the immediate priority should be restoring maritime security and resolving the conflict. Qatar has served as an intermediary in the negotiations. These are not minor technical disagreements; they go to the heart of whether either side believes the other will honour an agreement.
This is precisely why Washington’s assurances are no longer enough for Tehran.
From Iran’s perspective, what is the value of another diplomatic promise if the terms remain ambiguous, the demands keep changing, or military pressure continues while negotiations are supposedly underway? A country cannot be expected to make consequential strategic concessions merely because a powerful adversary says that an agreement is possible.
Credibility must be demonstrated through specific commitments, verifiable implementation, and guarantees that cannot be casually discarded when political circumstances change.
The core issue is not simply whether the Strait will reopen. It is whether the United States expects Iran to negotiate as an equal party with legitimate security concerns or to negotiate under pressure until it accepts Washington’s preferred terms.
For years, Washington has relied on sanctions, military deployments, diplomatic leverage, and the threat of escalation to influence Iran’s decisions. The United States may regard these measures as instruments of national security. Tehran, however, sees them as evidence that negotiations can become another arena of coercion. That perception cannot be dismissed if Washington genuinely wants a durable settlement.
You cannot demand trust while refusing to address the reasons that trust has collapsed. You cannot preach diplomacy while making the other side fear that concessions today may become vulnerabilities tomorrow.
Iran’s refusal to accept an inadequate response is therefore a declaration that negotiations must have substance.
Tehran is signalling that it will not automatically exchange strategic leverage for vague assurances. Whether one agrees with Iran’s policies or not, the underlying principle is straightforward: an agreement must contain obligations for both parties, not concessions for one side and discretion for the other.
Iran is also demonstrating strategic confidence. It has not accepted the proposition that American military and economic power automatically entitle Washington to dictate the outcome. Its position is that its security, sovereignty, and national interests must be addressed before a settlement can be considered credible. That confidence does not guarantee Iran will prevail in every confrontation, nor does it remove the considerable economic and military risks it faces. But it does show that pressure alone has not produced the diplomatic outcome Washington seeks.
READ: Iran’s IRGC Navy threatens to sink US warships approaching Strait of Hormuz
The Strait of Hormuz: where the real leverage lies
The Strait of Hormuz is not an ordinary shipping lane. Before the current conflict, approximately one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas flows passed through this strategic chokepoint. Prolonged disruption can affect crude prices, shipping insurance, transport costs, inflation, and the economies of countries far removed from the battlefield. Reuters coverage of the Hormuz negotiations
That reality gives this confrontation consequences well beyond Washington and Tehran. Energy-importing nations, particularly those already vulnerable to higher fuel prices, have every reason to demand a serious diplomatic solution.
But there is an important distinction: leverage is not the same as victory. Restrictions on maritime traffic can impose costs on the United States and its partners, but they can also hurt Iran, neighbouring countries, commercial shipping, and ordinary people worldwide. The strongest diplomatic outcome would be one that converts this dangerous leverage into enforceable security arrangements rather than allowing the global economy to remain hostage to an escalating confrontation.
Washington must therefore decide whether its objective is a sustainable agreement or the appearance of having forced Iran to submit. Those are two very different outcomes.
Israel’s role: Strategic pressure or child’s play?
Israel cannot be separated from this crisis. The war began with US and Israeli strikes against Iran on 28th February 2026, according to Reuters reporting. The resulting confrontation has made the question of security guarantees central to Tehran’s calculations.
From Tehran’s standpoint, there is little reason to trust a diplomatic process if military escalation remains a possibility while negotiations continue. Iran can reasonably ask whether any agreement reached with Washington would survive a change in strategy, renewed attacks, or pressure from regional allies.
And this is where Israel’s approach deserves sharp scrutiny.
If Israeli leaders believe that repeated military strikes, threats, and pressure can permanently resolve a strategic conflict with a major regional adversary, that assumption risks becoming a dangerous political fantasy. Tactical military operations are not the same as a durable political settlement. Destroying infrastructure does not automatically eliminate political resistance, and demonstrating military capability does not guarantee that an opponent will accept the victor’s preferred terms.
Calling such a strategy “child’s play” is a forceful political criticism of an approach that mistakes coercion for resolution. Serious statecraft requires more than threats, military posturing, and the expectation that an adversary will eventually surrender its interests.
Israel has its own security concerns, including Iran’s nuclear programme and regional military capabilities. Those concerns cannot simply be wished away. But neither can they justify an endless cycle in which military escalation creates new grievances, new threats, and new obstacles to diplomacy.
If Washington and Israel want a more secure Middle East, they must recognise that security cannot be built indefinitely on the assumption that Iran will eventually break under pressure.
READ: Iranian attacks target 6 ships near Strait of Hormuz in 1 day, highest since war with US began
The United States must confront the crisis of credibility
The deeper problem is credibility. Critics of US foreign policy point to past disputes over international agreements, sanctions, and the use of military force as reasons to question whether American commitments will endure. Such criticisms must be examined case by case, rather than treating every allegation of betrayal as automatically proven. Nevertheless, the present deadlock demonstrates that assurances alone are insufficient when the parties disagree over obligations, sequencing, and the risk of renewed conflict.
Washington cannot expect Iran to accept an agreement whose key provisions remain unclear. Nor can it expect Tehran to treat negotiations as insulated from military threats when the conflict itself has repeatedly undermined diplomatic progress.
If the United States genuinely wants to demonstrate that its word carries weight, it should put forward explicit commitments, establish a verifiable timetable, clarify the reciprocal obligations of both parties, and identify mechanisms for resolving alleged violations. These measures would not require Washington to abandon its security interests. They would require it to show that diplomacy is more than a temporary instrument for extracting concessions.
The same standard must apply to Iran. Tehran must also make its obligations clear, address legitimate maritime-security concerns, and recognise that a durable settlement requires protections for commercial navigation and regional stability. An agreement cannot endure if either side treats compliance as optional.
The final message
Iran is telling Washington that the age of expecting automatic concessions in exchange for ambiguous promises is over. Whether Tehran can sustain its position under continued economic and military pressure is a separate question. But the current impasse makes one fact clear: neither power has yet established the trust necessary for a lasting settlement.
The United States has enormous military, financial, and diplomatic resources. But power has limits. Sanctions cannot manufacture trust. Threats cannot guarantee political submission. Military superiority cannot, by itself, produce a legitimate and lasting peace.
Iran, for its part, must understand that national strength is measured not only by resistance but also by the ability to turn bargaining power into concrete, sustainable gains. Its confidence will matter most if it can secure enforceable commitments while avoiding a wider war that damages its own people and the wider region.
Israel, too, must confront the limits of a strategy built primarily around military pressure. No country can bomb its way to permanent regional stability while ignoring the political conditions that sustain conflict.
The world does not need another round of declarations, threats, and theatrical diplomacy. It needs commitments that can be verified, obligations that apply to everyone, and a settlement that cannot be discarded the moment political calculations change.
If Washington wants Iran to trust its word, it must prove that word is worth trusting. If Israel wants lasting security, it must recognise that perpetual escalation is not a substitute for political resolution. And if Iran wants its strategic strength to translate into lasting success, it must use its leverage to pursue a settlement that protects its sovereignty without sacrificing regional stability.
The Strait of Hormuz is the immediate flashpoint. Trust is the underlying crisis. Until that crisis is addressed honestly, every new proposal risks becoming another exchange of demands, another missed opportunity, and another warning that the costs of failed diplomacy will be paid by millions of people who never chose this confrontation.

Ex-DRC President Kabila’s alliance with M23 rebels: Why it matters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
07:32:24 UTC
16:32:24 KST

Ex-DRC President Kabila’s alliance with M23 rebels: Why it matters
Kabila’s move confirms numerous accusations from the government in Kinshasa of his ties to armed rebels.
Former President Joseph Kabila of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has officially allied with armed rebel groups, raising fears of further escalation of an ongoing conflict in the country’s east that has already killed thousands.
Kabila on Monday launched a new political-military coalition to replace the M23-AFC alliance, which is fighting government forces and controls swaths of territory.
The new movement will “put an end to tyranny by any means necessary, including the use of force”, coalition spokesperson Claude Ibalanky said, in what appeared to be a chilling threat to the government in Kinshasa.
It comes precisely a year after Kabila was sentenced to death by a military court for alleged links to the rebel groups.
The M23 crisis has racked the mineral-rich eastern DRC for nearly 15 years. The United Nations says more than 7.8 million people are displaced while 28 million people face food shortages. An untold number have died.
The United States and UN accuse Rwanda of backing M23. Kigali denies it.
Here’s what we know:
What’s been announced?
Kabila introduced the new alliance, the Front pour la Refondation de la Nation (FRN), from his residence in Goma, confirming the DRC government’s accusations.
The former president said he will lead the alliance.
Corneille Nangaa, a Kabila ally who served as a former elections commissioner before leaving government to launch the Congo River Alliance (AFC), will serve as deputy, alongside Bertrand Bisimwa, an M23 spokesman.
Freddy Kaniki, a medical doctor and senior M23 health official, will serve as secretary-general, while Sultani Makenga of the M23 will be the army chief of the alliance.
Who is Kabila?
Kabila, 55, is the son of former President Laurent Kabila.
He took office as a 29-year-old back in 2001 after his father was assassinated. He previously served as army chief and fought in the two Congo civil wars, when Rwanda backed rebel groups against longtime Congolese leader Mobutu Sese Seko.
Kabila’s term, which officially ended in 2016, was marked by rights violations and corruption. He illegally delayed elections until 2018, citing voter registration challenges, and left office in 2019.
Before he stepped down, Kabila is believed to have signed a power-sharing deal with opposition candidate and election winner, current President Felix Tshisekedi. Kabila’s allies were initially installed throughout the cabinet after the deal, but in 2020, Tshisekedi began removing them, as their truce collapsed on a bitter note.
Tshisekedi’s government also launched corruption investigations against Kabila, forcing him into self-imposed exile in South Africa in 2023.
Why has Kabila joined the rebel alliance?
The former president’s latest move is unsurprising; Kinshasa has long alleged his ties to the M23-AFC alliance.
Amid intensifying M23-AFC offensives last year, Kabila wrote a scathing opinion piece in South Africa’s Sunday Times, accusing Tshisekedi of mishandling the conflict and proposing a “12-point plan” to restore peace. Reports also emerged of Kabila’s sighting in the eastern rebel-held Goma, where he owns homes.
Last October, a military court in Kinshasa sentenced Kabila to death on charges of treason, war crimes, and other major offences for alleged collaboration with Rwanda and M23-AFC.
In April, Washington imposed sanctions on Kabila, alleging that he funded rebel groups.
What does M23-AFC want?
Eastern DRC has been engulfed in violence for more than 30 years, and multiple groups have been fighting to dominate the region. The roots of the crisis go back to the 1994 genocide in neighbouring Rwanda, the alleged harbouring of Hutu fighter groups in the DRC in its aftermath, Kigali’s determination to fight them, and deep-rooted tribalism.
The March 23 Movement (M23) emerged in 2012 from the remnants of Congolese Tutsi fighter groups that fought in the Second Congo War. It claims to be fighting for the rights of minority Congolese Tutsis and seeks to unseat the government in Kinshasa.
M23 first took Goma and other towns in the east in 2012 offensives; however, its fighters were pushed back by a special UN force fighting alongside the FARDC – the Congolese military.
In 2022, amid Tshisekedi’s fallout with Kabila, M23 resurfaced with renewed force, allegedly backed by more than 4,000 Rwandan soldiers. Kigali has long accused successive governments in Kinshasa of supporting the DRC-based Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR) armed group, which includes Hutu genocidaires.
In 2023, as the M23 seized several towns and the Congolese army fell back, Nangaa, the then-elections commissioner, also fell out with Tshisekedi – reportedly over his move to run in elections. He then went into exile, formed the AFC, and allied with M23 as its political arm.
In early 2024, AFC-M23 launched lightning offensives that saw it sweep across vast swaths of the east, rapidly seizing territory. Goma fell again to the AFC-M23 in January 2025, following heavy battles that killed nearly 3,000 civilians.
The rebels, who have been accused of civilian massacres, currently hold North and South Kivu, where Kabila is from, including their capitals Goma and Bukavu, as well as border crossings with Rwanda and Uganda. Kampala has also been accused of supporting M23.
What does this mean for the conflict?
Al Jazeera’s Alain Uaykani reported that Congolese are worried the conflict could escalate again, and that a number of soldiers could defect to serve their former boss.
There are also fears that ongoing peace talks could collapse. In June 2025, DRC and Rwanda signed a US-led peace agreement.
In a separate process mediated by Qatar, the DRC and M23-AFC also signed the Doha Framework last November and were meant to meet this month.
But the changes may not end the agreements between the DRC and Rwanda, as Kigali will likely want to continue with the US-led talks, Bram Verelst of the Institute for Security Studies told Al Jazeera.
The real threat, he warned, lies to the Doha process.
“We are likely to see a hardening of Kinshasa’s position toward the rebel movement and Kabila, including efforts to isolate Kabila and FRN regionally,” Verelst noted.
“What this means for the conflict on the ground will depend on the capacity of Kabila to take control over the rebellion and to build and expand alliances beyond North and South Kivu,” he added.

Iran shifts to step up attacks on shipping before US vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
07:32:22 UTC
16:32:22 KST

Breadcrumb
Iran shifting tactics to step up attacks on shipping before US vote
Iran is deploying new tactics to target ships sailing through the Strait of Hormuz as it seeks to keep oil prices high and influence the US midterm elections, two senior Iranian officials told Reuters.
Tehran has tried to exert control over the Strait of Hormuz since the US and Israel launched a war against Iran on 28 February. It has restricted passage through the waterway, which carried about a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas trade before the war, in an effort to gain leverage over Washington.
Its threats and attacks have severely curtailed traffic through the strait, driving up oil prices, though some oil has continued to transit.
The two officials declined to provide details of the new strategy, but one said that Iran had started using different offensive tactics against vessels it considered in violation of its restrictions about 10 days ago, adding that this had led to an increase in attacks on such ships.
The strategy included a change in the type as well as the pace of attacks, with one goal being to influence the outcome of the US vote, they said.
"The aim is to frustrate efforts by the United States and its allies to bring down global oil prices," one of the two officials said.
The decision to adopt the new strategy had been taken at the highest levels of Iran’s leadership and was fully coordinated across the country’s ruling system, the officials said.
Iran using spotters
A US military official, speaking on condition of anonymity, confirmed that Iran had changed tactics in one significant way: after the US destroyed much of Iran’s radar capabilities, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) had started using unarmed spotters in small boats to identify potential targets, including US naval vessels, the official said.
Last week, in a previously unreported incident, the US military determined that Iranian spotters were operating from a dhow, calling in targets to the IRGC, the official said. US forces confronted the vessel, told its occupants to abandon ship and then destroyed it. There were no casualties, the US official said.
Unwilling to risk its remaining fast boats, Iran had been unable to prevent a ramp-up in oil exports through the strait, the official said, particularly after US strikes devastated its navy.
The war—and its $3 billion monthly price tag—has become a key issue on the US campaign trail for November's midterm elections, which will decide control of Congress.
US President Donald Trump has been weighing next steps against Iran, but has said he will not attack again before the vote.
The US has meanwhile been pressing its own naval blockade of Iranian ports and extending sanctions as it tries to pile economic pressure on Tehran to reach a deal to end the conflict.
The standoff over Hormuz has left global energy markets exposed to further disruption, with the threat of attacks and high shipping and insurance costs complicating efforts to restore normal traffic.
In recent days, attacks on commercial ships still sailing through the strait have surged to their highest level since the war began, according to independent data.
There have been at least five incidents in the past 48 hours involving tankers and other commercial ships around the Hormuz area, including drone strikes, according to data analysis from maritime security sources and incidents reported to British navy-affiliated agency United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO).
That approximately mirrored the rate of attacks on October 3-5, pointing to a new escalation, according to data from the UN shipping agency, the International Maritime Organisation.
"There is a tempo increase in strikes, which looks deliberate," one maritime security source said.
Attacks over an expanded area
As part of the new strategy, Tehran will also expand the geographical scope of its operations beyond the Strait of Hormuz to the Gulf of Oman and waters further afield, the officials said.
Analysis by maritime security sources based on attacks reported to UKMTO and maritime security companies in the region suggest this may already be happening. They show Iran targeting ships in areas beyond the Strait of Hormuz, including waters off the coast of Qatar and the United Arab Emirates, in recent days.
The second Iranian official added that Tehran would not allow Trump to bring down oil prices before the November elections.
"Just when they think they are getting close to the point where prices will fall, we will push them away from it. This is a game of chess,” the second official said. "Such vessels would be safe nowhere, even outside the Strait of Hormuz."
The Pentagon and Iran's Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Both Iranian officials said Tehran is moving towards a situation in which no vessel violating its restrictions would be able to pass through the strait. "It will be complete closure soon," one of the officials said.
In its latest report on Sunday, the US Navy-led Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC) said the threat to merchant shipping in the Strait of Hormuz remained "severe", the second-highest level.
"IRGC attacks, attempted attacks, and/or harassment activity persisted including UAV overflight, targeted surveillance of merchant shipping, and occasional VHF hailing," JMIC said.

Why Sri Lanka’s Rajapaksas are being investigated for corruption and crimes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Why Sri Lanka’s Rajapaksas are being investigated for corruption and crimes
Several members and allies of the once-powerful dynasty, including wife of former President Mahinda Rajapaksa, are under arrest.
Colombo, Sri Lanka – A court in the Sri Lankan capital has extended the custody of the wife of Sri Lanka’s powerful former President Mahinda Rajapaksa, who was arrested last week over allegations that her charity misused donations collected for a children’s hospital.
The October 7 arrest of Shiranthi Rajapaksa, 73, dealt a huge blow to the once powerful family that ruled Sri Lanka for nearly two decades until they were overthrown in a youth-led uprising in 2022.
A month before Shiranthi’s arrest, her 40-year-old parliamentarian son Namal Rajapaksa, who is also the national organiser of the Rajapaksa-controlled Sri Lanka Podujana Peramuna (SLPP) party, was arrested over bribery charges. He remains in custody.
Here’s all you need to know:
Who are the Rajapaksas?
The family, based in the stronghold of Hambantota district in southern Sri Lanka, counts Mahinda, 80, as its charismatic patriarch.
Elected prime minister in 2004 and president the next year, Mahinda is adored by many among the country’s majority ethnic Sinhala Buddhists for crushing the Tamil separatist rebels who waged a 26-year-long civil war that ended in 2009.
In the campaign against the now-defunct Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) rebels demanding a separate state in northern Sri Lanka, Mahinda’s younger brother Gotabaya Rajapaksa served as his defence secretary.
According to estimates by the United Nations, nearly 40,000 civilians were killed in the final weeks of the civil war, triggering an international inquiry into the alleged atrocities. After the war, Mahinda was criticised for not doing enough to mend relations with the Tamils, who have been banned from commemorating their war dead.
During Mahinda’s rule, Sri Lanka, a country of 22 million people, also borrowed nearly $7bn from China for infrastructure projects, many of which were mired in corruption.
Despite changing a law that allowed him a third presidential term, Mahinda lost the 2015 election to former political ally, Maithripala Sirisena.
After the deadly 2019 Easter Sunday bombings in churches and hotels blamed on an ISIL (ISIS) offshoot, Gotabaya, who until then was a political novice, used anti-Muslim rhetoric to win the presidential election – the second in the family to hold the post.
Gotabaya appointed Mahinda as the prime minister and gave influential ministerial posts to his other brothers – Chamal and Basil – as well as Mahinda’s son, Namal Rajapaksa.
As the family tightened its control over the island – struck first by the 2019 bombings and later the COVID pandemic – they were also accused of mismanaging the economy and widespread corruption.
The economic crisis ignited historic street protests in mid-2022, forcing Gotabaya to flee the country. A caretaker government ruled the country until elections in 2024 saw Anura Kumara Dissanayake, a 57-year-old Marxist, winning the presidency on an anticorruption platform and promising to act against the Rajapaksa family and previous administrations.
What are the corruption allegations against the family?
The ongoing arrests and legal cases against members of the Rajapaksa family are seen as part of the same promise.
The former First Lady Shiranthi Rajapaksa was arrested last week by the government’s Commission to Investigate Allegations of Bribery or Corruption (CIABOC).
The Siriliya Saviya Foundation, a charity she leads, is accused of misusing donations of nearly 100 million rupees ($303,000) intended to buy equipment for a children’s hospital in the capital, Colombo.
Investigators told a court that an MRI scanner had already been donated by the Chinese government, but the charity allegedly continued to solicit donations for a scanner and misused the funds.
Sagara Kariyawasam, the general secretary of SLPP, the party led by the Rajapaksa family, denies the allegation.
“It is untrue, and the money is safe in the frozen bank account of Siriliya Saviya,” he told Al Jazeera.
But CIABOC told the court its investigations revealed that the money was used to buy a house and that it would initiate steps to freeze the asset.
On Monday, her lawyers approached a court for anticipatory bail on health grounds. But the plea was rejected. On Tuesday, Shiranthi was presented before the court, which extended her custody until Friday.
Meanwhile, Mahinda’s son Namal is being tried in a case involving the alleged payment of a $30,000 bribe in a government deal with Airbus to buy planes for the national airline.
He faces another investigation where he is allegedly linked to a $211,000 bribe paid by a foreign private company to expedite a government land transfer.
Both incidents allegedly happened during his father’s presidency.
Mahinda’s other son Yoshitha, 38, is also being investigated for money laundering, while Shasheendra Rajapaksa, the 50-year-old son of Chamal Rajapaksa, is currently out on bail in connection with a corruption case.
Also, Basil, another Rajapaksa sibling, is facing an arrest warrant for failing to appear before court in a case related to buying properties allegedly using illicit money. He is believed to be in the United States.
Last week, the Financial Crimes Investigation Division seized Basil’s property in Matara, a southern coastal town.
What other charges does the family face?
But it’s not just corruption cases hounding the powerful family.
Gotabaya is barred from travelling abroad over allegations that the 2019 Easter Sunday bombings were staged to boost his popularity before the 2019 presidential election.
Last week, a Sri Lankan court rejected his appeal to prevent his likely arrest in the ongoing investigation into the simultaneous bombings in three churches and three hotels, killing 279 people, 45 of them foreigners, in the worst such attack on the island popular for tourism.
In 2023, a whistleblower told the British network Channel 4 that former Sri Lankan intelligence chief Suresh Salley had met the alleged bombers behind the 2019 attacks, as part of a conspiracy to influence the upcoming election.
Gotabaya declared his candidacy two days after the attacks, and his campaign focused on combating “Islamic extremism”. Salley was arrested in February this year under terror laws and is being investigated over the Easter Sunday bombings.
Ramindu Perera, a researcher in international law at the European University Institute in Italy, says if the allegation that the Rajapaksas were connected to the 2019 attacks is proved, it would have a “devastating effect” on the family.
“Such revelations are likely to further delegitimise the SLPP’s standing in Sri Lankan politics,” he said. The party has been reduced to just three seats in the 225-member national parliament.
Last month, Sri Lanka’s High Court convicted 15 of the 24 Muslim men accused of involvement in the 2019 bombings, but families of many victims said they are still waiting for the “masterminds” to be held accountable.
How have Sri Lankans reacted to the investigations?
Addressing a public rally at Nikaweratiya in northwestern Sri Lanka on Sunday, President Dissanayake said the law will be applied to everyone equally.
“Those who gained social power, political power and positional power used those powers to be above the law. But, under this government, the law is equal for everyone,” he said.
“If anyone believes that the law will not reach them, we are now proving that there is no place where law cannot reach and no one is beyond its reach,” he added.
But SLPP’s Kariyawasam accused the government of misleading the people.
“We don’t have any problem with thieves being punished after proving their wrongdoings,” he told Al Jazeera.
“But the government is taking people to custody without any court trials, and then tells the people that they punish thieves. This is purely a political witch-hunt.”
Researcher Perera said the demand for accountability in corruption cases was the main slogan that brought Dissanayake to power.
“As action against corruption is at the core of the NPP government’s mandate, what is happening now should be seen as an attempt to enforce that mandate,” he told Al Jazeera, referring to Dissanayake’s National People’s Power party.
Political analyst Gamini Viyangoda also rejected Kariyawasam’s claim. “This is not a political witch-hunt, but implementing the rule of law.”

Learning Through Practice: Why Architecture Students Enter Competitions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
07:30:00 UTC
16:30:00 KST

On paper, entering an architecture competition is one of the most challenging things an architecture student can do. What draws students to them is the chance to experiment, approaching a loosely defined program that leaves room to test unconventional ideas and unfamiliar tools outside the rhythm of the semester. That distance from assessment is a relatively recent development, as competitions were once central to architectural education.
At the École des Beaux-Arts, teaching was split between the atelier, where students developed projects under a practising architect, and the competition, where a jury of professors judged the students' work without having followed its development. This model was later brought to schools such as MIT, Penn, and Cornell by French-trained instructors. Over time, most schools held on to the atelier, which became the design studio, and pushed the competition to the edges of the curriculum.

Three more villages and 101 sq km: Ukrainian commander Biletskyi reports new gains in Operation Vivaldi
The 3rd Army Corps and attached units have liberated Zelena Dolyna, Lypove and Kolodiazi on the Lyman front, bringing another 101 sq km of territory back under Ukrainian control during the fourth stage of Operation Vivaldi.
Source: 3rd Army Corps, citing an address by its commander, Brigadier General Andrii Biletskyi; DeepState, a Ukrainian group of military analysts
Details: Biletskyi said the operation had begun with efforts to root out Russian infiltrators but developed into a rapid, large-scale offensive. He said that Russian forces have begun losing control of their units, where "real chaos has broken out".
Quote: "We have prevented the enemy from bypassing the Sloviansk-Kramatorsk urban agglomeration from the flanks and encircling it, while also protecting the Kharkiv-Sloviansk motorway. The enemy has failed to cut the key logistics artery of our grouping in Donbas.
We have disrupted the offensive by Russia's Zapad (West) Group of Forces and forced it to redeploy some units of the 1st Guards Tank Army, easing the pressure on Kupiansk-Vuzlovyi."
Details: The corps reported that Russian forces had suffered about 3,000 casualties during the fourth stage of the operation, bringing their total losses in Operation Vivaldi to 8,000.
Over the four stages of the operation, Ukrainian forces have liberated 277 sq km of territory and restored full Ukrainian control over 16 settlements.
DeepState also reported the liberation of Kolodiazi, Lypove and Zelena Dolyna. The analysts also said the defence forces have regained control of areas near Stavky and Shandryholove.
The corps said the operation involves the 3rd Assault Brigade, the 60th Mechanised Brigade, the 125th Heavy Mechanised Brigade, the 3rd Separate Reconnaissance Battalion, the 25th Anti-Tank Battalion and the 21st Separate Unmanned Systems Regiment, also known as Kraken.
Attached units are also taking part in the operation: the 66th Mechanised Brigade, the 3rd Border Guard Detachment, the 10th Mobile Border Guard Detachment (known as Dozor), tactical groups from the 8th Special Operations Regiment, the Lasar's Group unit of the National Guard, the K-2 unit of the Unmanned Systems Forces and unmanned units from the Security Service of Ukraine's Special Operations Centre A.
Background:
- On 15 September, the 3rd Army Corps reported that it had cleared 75 sq km and liberated another 10 sq km during counteroffensive operations in northern Donetsk Oblast.
- On 20 September, it emerged that the 3rd Army Corps had liberated the villages of Shandryholove and Derylove in Donetsk Oblast as part of Operation Vivaldi and established full control over Drobysheve.
- On 28 September, Biletskyi reported that Russian forces had lost 2,000 military personnel during the third stage of Operation Vivaldi, while more than 250 Russian soldiers had been taken prisoner.
- On 3 October, Zelenskyy told Reuters that 125-140 sq km had been liberated in Operation Vivaldi by that point and that Russian losses had risen significantly over the previous two to three months.

SJM urges Centre to block Starlink’s rollout
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
07:26:27 UTC
16:26:27 KST

Swadeshi Jagran Manch (SJM) urged the Centre to block Starlink’s commercial rollout
NEW DELHI: RSS-affiliated Swadeshi Jagran Manch (SJM) on Tuesday urged the Centre to block Starlink’s commercial rollout, questioning whether Elon Musk’s satellite broadband service could ensure that Indian traffic passes through domestic gateways and comply with orders to restrict connectivity in specified areas.SJM national co-convener Ashwani Mahajan said the concerns involved India’s capacity to monitor communications lawfully and enforce security restrictions. It argued that laser links between satellites could allow traffic to bypass Indian ground infrastructure and travel through foreign networks.“A key regulatory condition is that Starlink must be able to precisely restrict its services at the govt’s behest,” SJM said. It questioned whether the company could meet this requirement, citing terrorism, riots and protests as situations in which authorities may seek local shutdowns.At issue, in SJM’s argument, is whether Indian authorities can enforce security directives on a foreign operator whose network extends beyond the country’s physical borders. SJM contrasted this with incumbent telecom companies which, it said, cooperate with investigators and can suspend services in designated areas.
The group accused Musk of applying public pressure instead of addressing Indian security concerns. Its intervention follows his allegation that “certain oligarchs” were blocking Starlink to protect their businesses and his criticism of Reliance Industries chairman Mukesh Ambani.SJM also flagged potential misuse by insurgents and smugglers. Starlink equipment was recovered during a drug seizure in Andaman and Nicobar Islands and an army search operation in Manipur in 2024. Musk has maintained that Starlink’s satellite beams were never activated over India.Starlink received a telecom licence on June 6, 2025, and authorisation from space regulator IN-SPACe on July 8 that year. Its commercial launch awaits completion of security assessments and spectrum assignment.
On Oct 8, the communications ministry rejected the discrimination allegations as “baseless and misconceived”, saying Starlink, Jio’s satellite venture and Bharti-backed OneWeb were at broadly the same regulatory stage. Each must demonstrate security compliance before seeking spectrum, it said.Starlink has previously said Indian user data would remain within the country and its security controls would meet Indian requirements.Arguing for indigenous alternatives, SJM claimed blocking Starlink would accelerate domestic satellite broadband development and eventually deliver cheaper connectivity to remote areas. It said India’s growing space capabilities and private sector participation could support domestic alternatives, even if their rollout took some more time. It also invoked US trade restrictions, arguing India was entitled to withhold permission on national security grounds.

Pope Leo recovering in Rome hospital after cancer diagnosis

16:25:18 KST

Pope Leo XIV spent a peaceful night in hospital after undergoing surgery for lung cancer, the Vatican said Wednesday, adding that further information about the 71-year-old pontiff's condition would be released later in the day. 
Leo was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer, after doctors removed the lower lobe of his right lung during an operation Tuesday at Rome's Gemelli Hospital. The diagnosis, suspected during preliminary examinations, was confirmed through tissue analysis performed during surgery.
The operation lasted approximately 90 minutes and was completed without complications, according to a statement issued by Stefano Margaritora, the surgeon who led the procedure, and Luigi Carbone, the pope's personal physician. Leo spent about three hours in the operating room before regaining consciousness and returning to his hospital room.
Doctors removed the entire lower lobe of the right lung in an effort to eliminate the cancerous tissue. The human lungs have five lobes, three on the right and two on the left. The Vatican has not disclosed the tumor's precise size or whether cancer cells were found in nearby lymph nodes, factors that could influence the pontiff's prognosis and any need for additional treatment.
Leo was admitted to the hospital Tuesday after a small, localized growth was discovered during routine medical examinations. He had publicly disclosed the finding Sunday, saying doctors believed it was best to remove the nodule because of its early detection.
The Vatican previously said the pope was expected to remain hospitalized for approximately one week. All his public engagements have been canceled through October 20.
Elected in May 2025, Leo is relatively young for a pontiff and has generally maintained an active lifestyle, including playing tennis. He is not known to smoke and had no previously disclosed major health problems during his papacy.

‘Constitution, not convenience’: Harvard-affiliated Indians hit out at anti-EC protests

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
07:23:34 UTC

Harvard-affiliated Indians flag attacks on constitutional institutions and alleged misuse of the university’s name
NEW DELHI: The crackdown on protesters in Delhi has triggered a sharp divide among members of the Harvard University community, with two groups issuing contrasting statements, one condemning alleged police excesses and the other cautioning against what it described as a campaign to undermine India's constitutional institutions.Disapproving the use of terms such as “siege” to describe the police deployment in Delhi and “thieves” or “compromised” to characterise constitutional authorities, a section of Harvard affiliates said such language raised concerns about attempts to undermine public trust in democratic institutions.
"Troubling are reports of the use of Harvard University’s name to lend credibility to a political campaign without appropriate authorisation. The language used to describe India as being under 'siege' and to characterise constitutional authorities as 'thieves' or 'compromised' raises serious concerns about the intent to undermine public trust in democratic institutions," the wider cross-section of the Harvard community, including lawyers, policymakers, civil servants, scientists and academicians, said in a statement.
‘Constitution, not convenience'
The latest statement signed by 44 individuals raised concerns over what it described as a “concerted campaign” against the country's constitutional institutions, including the Election Commission, the Supreme Court, the office of the Chief Justice of India (CJI) and Parliament.
"We are deeply concerned by the negative public discourse and concerted campaign against India’s constitutional institutions, including the Election Commission of India, the Supreme Court, the office of the Hon’ble Chief Justice of India, and Parliament," the statement released on Wednesday said.It also addressed the role of law enforcement agencies in maintaining public order, saying their actions should be subject to fair scrutiny but that allegations must be grounded in evidence and due process.“The actions of law enforcement agencies to uphold public order deserve fair scrutiny, but sweeping accusations and abusive rhetoric cannot substitute for evidence, due process or institutional accountability,” the signatories said.They also stressed the need to respect public officials and the offices they hold, adding that constitutional principles and civil liberties must not be applied selectively.“The Constitution, rule of law, and civil liberties must be respected at all times, not just when it suits our interests,” the statement said.Summing up their appeal, the signatories said: “Our commitment must remain to the Constitution, not convenience; to justice, not selective outrage; and to democratic institutions, not the politics of accusation.”
October 12 statement condemns police action
In a statement dated October 12, around 100 Harvard alumni, students, faculty and staff condemned what they described as the “unprecedented siege of Delhi by police and paramilitary forces” and alleged arbitrary, illegal and unconstitutional action against peaceful protesters across the country on October 10."We, as alumni, students, faculty, and staff of Harvard University, are deeply concerned by the unprecedented siege of Delhi by police and paramilitary forces and arbitrary, illegal, and unconstitutional police actions against peaceful protestors across the country on 10th October 2026. We strongly condemn police brutality, unlawful detention, and violations of constitutional rights of all peaceful protestors," the letter shared by Live Law read.
The signatories condemned alleged police brutality, unlawful detention and violations of protesters' constitutional rights, while expressing solidarity with fellow Harvard affiliates Shadan Farasat, a senior advocate in the Supreme Court and Harvard Law School alumnus from 2009, and Mehr Pasricha, a Harvard Kennedy School graduate from 2025.The signatories called on the government and law enforcement authorities to end alleged violations of constitutional rights, respect the right to peaceful protest and access to legal assistance, and ensure that those responsible for abuses are held accountable under the rule of law.

Finland's new maternity package, often called 'the baby box', was unveiled on Wednesday with more products than last year.
Distribution of the new box has begun, according to the Social Insurance Institution of Finland, Kela. As in the past, it contains a range of clothes, accessories and other essentials for babies.
"This year's box contains 52 products, compared with 38 last year," Kela coordinator for family benefits, Anniina Kuokka told Yle's morning programme.
The package also includes several muslin cloths, a blanket, a sleeping bag, a book, nail scissors and a toothbrush.
Lubricant and a pack of condoms have also returned to the box after being left out of last year’s version.
The box, designed by illustrator Eveliina Muotkavaara, features a peach-coloured space-themed pattern.
Government-promised ball included
The latest maternity package includes a ball, as promised by Prime Minister Petteri Orpo’s (NCP) government.
The plan to include a ball was written into the government programme in 2023 as part of its "Finland on the Move" initiative, which aims to increase physical activity across all age groups.
Kela says the ball is intended to support interaction between parents and babies and encourage families to spend time doing things together.

'This cannot be a coincidence' — Ukraine's Starlink access restricted without warning, Zelensky adviser says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
07:12:58 UTC
16:12:58 KST

'This cannot be a coincidence' — Ukraine's Starlink access restricted without warning, Zelensky adviser says
Key developments:
- SpaceX implemented speed restrictions on Starlink systems for the Ukrainian military on Oct. 14 without warning, limiting speed to 100 miles per hour (160 kilometers per hour)
- The unexpected restriction disrupted active military operations, including the use of mid-range strike drones and interceptors
- Ukrainian officials said they believed the move was tied to the Trump administration's intensifying pressure on Kyiv to stop strikes on Russian oil assets
- Elon Musk said Trump holds ultimate authority over Starlink speed and usage limitations for Ukraine
- Starlink service has stabilized, but the speed cap remains in place, Ukraine's Defense Ministry said
Ukraine's Starlink access has been restricted without warning, severely disrupting "several" military missions, presidential adviser Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov said on Oct. 14.
The speed restrictions were accompanied by signal disruptions and instability, even at lower speeds. Military personnel from mulitple units reported serious issues with Starlink throughout the day.
"I confirm that (Starlink owner) SpaceX implemented speed restrictions on Starlink terminals while in motion last night. Currently, the restriction applies to the Starshield 'military service package' and limits speed to 100 miles per hour (160 kilometers per hour)," Beskrestnov said in a post on social media.
Ukraine's Defense Ministry later told journalists that the actual speeds available during the day were even lower than the 160 kph limit. By the end of the day, service was reportedly stabilized, but the restriction remained in place.
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said only U.S. President Donald Trump had the power to determine the speed restrictions for Starshield systems.
"Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the U.S. military and ultimately (the president). .... Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action," he said.
Ukraine relies on Starlink for several military applications including operating its "middle strike" campaign in Russian-occupied Ukraine, as well as interceptor drones that defend against Russia's new jet-powered attack drones.
This mid-range strike campaign this year has allowed Ukraine to strangle Russian logistics, hampering its ability to fight on the front lines.
Sudden disruption on the front lines
A source in Ukraine's Defense Ministry confirmed to the Kyiv Independent that speed limitations had been discovered and the cause was being investigated.
"This complicates drone missions —specifically those involving interceptors and mid-range strike drones — and hampers capabilities for frontline logistics, reconnaissance, and signal relay," the source added.
A soldier working on mid-range strike drone operations, who requested anonymity, confirmed that "certain issues are being observed" but declined to elaborate, citing operational security.
Two other commanders — both from elite drone units working on the eastern and southern front lines — reported issues with Starlink terminals on "middle strike" drones flying at higher speeds over the last 24 hours.
Both likewise requested to remain anonymous, and declined to describe the problems in more detail, so as to not assist the enemy.
During the day, Ukraine's 7th Air Assault Corps said on social media that it was experiencing a "throttling" of its Starlink connectivity.
"The consequences are already being felt in the field. Since the start of the day alone, a drone unit operating within the 7th Corps' area of responsibility in the Huliaipole sector has had to cancel a number of missions due to these connectivity issues," the corps said.
Service restored — with a speed cap
Later in the evening of Oct. 14, ex-Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov — who famously negotiated with Musk to cut off Russian forces from Starlink while in office — announced that service was being restored, with the speed limit in place.
"Attack drones and interceptor drones should be operational again," he wrote. "Now, the focus should be on completely removing the speed limit for Starshield."
Fedorov, who no longer holds a position in the Ukrainian government after being dismissed by President Volodymyr Zelensky in July, did not provide evidence for his claims or explain where he got his information, though he thanked Musk in his post on X.
The Defense Ministry confirmed that service had been stabilized at a speed of 160 kilometers per hour.
"SpaceX continues to maintain the 161 km/h limit. Throughout the day, the actual limits were significantly lower. However, as of now, we observe that connection quality has improved at speeds up to 160 km/h," the ministry said in a comment to reporters.
The Defense Ministry is currently negotiating with partners and with SpaceX "regarding stable service conditions and the prevention of sudden restrictions."
But Musk's response was not encouraging — particularly for Ukraine's middle-strike campaign.
"Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government," he wrote in response to Fedorov.
"Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the U.S. military and ultimately (the president). .... Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company."
Is Trump to blame? 
Musk comments point to a link between the Starlink disruption and Kyiv's deteriorating relationship with the White House — a fear voiced earlier in the day bey Beskrestnov.
"Obviously, this action cannot be a coincidence and is associated with the current political situation," he said.
As reported by the Kyiv Independent on Oct. 12, U.S. President Donald Trump has threatened Ukraine with the withholding of intelligence and other assistance in a bid to protect Russian oil refineries.
Beskrestnov did not provide evidence that the Starlink restriction was connected to U.S. pressure on Ukraine, and the White House has not commented on the issue.
Serhii Sternenko, an activist and former advisor to Fedorov, also reported the restriction of access, saying "SpaceX likely took these measures at the request of the Trump administration."
The development comes after Ukraine worked with SpaceX earlier this year to deactivate unauthorized Starlink terminals being used by Russian forces. Starlink has played a critical role in Ukrainian military communications throughout the full-scale war.
The threats came after a confusing 48 hours during whichTrump announced a controversial "deal" with Russian President Vladimir Putin to import Russian diesel, followed by repeated demands that Ukraine replace Zelensky as president, followed by Trump announcing a unilateral "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine, which blindsided both Moscow and Kyiv.
Ukraine has since refrained from attacking Russian oil refineries but Russia has continued its blitz on Ukraine's energy infrastructure, most recently overnight on Oct. 14 when "several" power plants in Kyiv were hit. Trump has refused to accuse Russia of breaking the ceasefire.
Consequences of US pivot
The reported Starlink restrictions come as questions have been raised about U.S. intelligence sharing in relation to Russian ballistic missile launches, following two straight nights of attack on Kyiv with little to no warning.
Five Russian S-400 missiles struck the Ukrainian capital shortly after 10 p.m. local time on Oct. 12, causing "massive explosions," Kyiv Independent journalists reported. Air raid sirens and mobile alerts sounded only after the attack.
Zelensky described the strike as "particularly vile," saying Kyiv "received no early warning from our partners about this strike." His remarks raised questions about whether Washington had suspended intelligence assistance to Ukraine.
Despite the failure of Kyiv's early warning system and threats to halt U.S. intelligence sharing with Ukraine, Washington made no such decision, Ukrainian and American sources told the Kyiv Independent on Oct. 13.
But later that day, around 10:30 p.m. another wave of ballistic missiles hit Kyiv, again without the usual warning.
At least three women were killed, and another 24 people, including a 7-year-old girl, were injured as a result of a hit on a residential building in the Desnianskyi District. Three more waves of ballistic missiles struck Kyiv throughout the night.
Air Force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat told Ukrainian TV that Ukraine received no warnings from its partners about the first wave, though it did for the following three.
"Ukraine did not attack Russian oil refineries, yet Trump has already begun imposing sanctions on my country. Meanwhile, sanctions against Russia have been eased," Sternenko said.
