The Trump administration is considering easing sanctions on so-called shadow fleet vessels that have transported oil and petroleum products from countries including Russia, Iran and Venezuela, in an effort to reduce record-high global freight rates, a US official said on Wednesday.
The discussions are happening days after President Donald Trump temporarily lifted sanctions on Russian diesel fuel, a move met with a torrent of criticism from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, European countries and some of Trump's fellow Republicans in the US Senate.
Both Zelenskiy and the US senators called that move a gift to Russian President Vladimir Putin that would provide Russia with revenue to keep funding its war in Ukraine.
The new talks center on the United States potentially allowing "legal oil" to flow on previously sanctioned vessels, the US official said. That means crude or petroleum products not sanctioned by Washington, rather than Russian and Iranian oil, which are under punitive measures.
The goal is to get more refined products and crude out of the Gulf, the official said.
US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said in a video to the World Petroleum Congress in Riyadh this week that the administration was talking about easing the sanctions on shadow fleet vessels in an effort to cut record freight rates that have cut into demand for US crude, according to Energy Aspects, a research group.
Bits of the talk were broadcast on social media, but Reuters was not able to obtain the full video or a transcript. The Department of Energy said it was not available.
Companies seeking to use the sanctioned vessels would have to apply to the US Treasury Department to use the vessels, the official said.
The Department of Energy said any move to relieve sanctions on the shadow fleet would not help Russia to move oil or oil products. The Treasury Department referred questions to the Department of Energy.
But Trump's push to move Russian diesel to global markets quickly could put pressure on the departments to allow shipment via the vessels.
The White House did not respond immediately to a request for comment.
High oil and fuel prices are a risk for Trump in the November 3 midterm elections in which Republicans are hoping to maintain control of both chambers of Congress. He lifted the sanctions on Russian diesel through April 7.
Tanker freight rates soar to record highs
Tanker freight rates have soared to record highs as the wars in Iran and Ukraine have stoked inflation and put US crude oil out of reach for Asian refiners, pushing them to seek alternatives from the Middle East and Latin America.
Energy Aspects said in a note to clients that easing the sanctions on the shadow fleet would not greatly impact freight rates but could allow more movement of oil in the Middle East.
Lifting the sanctions on the tankers that are mostly old and not well maintained is "unlikely to add meaningful mainstream fleet capacity overnight, especially as most tankers sanctioned over Russian or Venezuelan links have been actively trading over the past three months," it said in the note.
Easing the restrictions "could make a small number of additional tankers available for certain (Strait of) Hormuz shuttle runs," in the waterway between Iran and Oman.
Lifting the measures is unlikely to result in a broad easing of freight rates as ship insurers will still be bound by EU and UK regulations, maritime industry sources said.

Israel is blocking construction of a military outpost in the Gaza Strip intended to serve as a base for an international stabilization force operating under U.S. President Donald Trump's Board of Peace, The Guardian reported Wednesday, citing a person with direct knowledge of the project.
According to the British newspaper, the Board of Peace awarded its first Gaza construction contract in early August to Arkel International, a Louisiana-based company tasked with building a fortified compound for approximately 150 international troops.
More than two months later, construction has yet to begin because Israel has not authorized contractors or construction vehicles to enter the territory, the source said.
"Israel won't open the border," the source told The Guardian.
The newspaper said a Board of Peace spokesperson declined to comment, while the Israeli government and IDF did not respond to requests for comment.
A military base holding up Gaza reconstruction
The proposed compound would measure approximately 100 by 100 meters and be built on a site formerly used by the Gaza Humanitarian Foundation (GHF), the now-defunct aid distribution operation that delivered humanitarian supplies through private contractors.
The facility is intended to accommodate rotating deployments of 150 armed international troops, drawn from a larger contingent of approximately 500 personnel dispatched from Morocco and Kosovo, according to the report.
The troops would form part of the International Stabilization Force (ISF), a multinational security mission planned to operate in Gaza under the Board of Peace.
But the source warned that the absence of the military base is preventing the broader reconstruction program from moving forward.
Without the stabilization force on the ground, there would be no security arrangements to enable construction crews to enter, deliver equipment, install utilities or establish basic infrastructure, the source explained.
The delay therefore threatens far more than the construction of a single military facility. It could prevent the launch of the initial reconstruction projects planned for southern Gaza.
Is Israel's election behind the delay?
The source told The Guardian that officials involved in the Board of Peace believe Israel will allow construction to proceed after the country's October 27 election.
That assessment raises questions about whether Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government is reluctant to permit the start of Gaza reconstruction during the election campaign.
However, the report did not establish that electoral considerations were the reason Israeli authorities had withheld the necessary approvals.
The delay comes despite Israel having already approved the Board of Peace's entry into Gaza and the launch of a limited reconstruction initiative.
In July, Israel's security cabinet approved a pilot program to restore basic services in the territory, with the first stage expected to take place in Rafah, in southern Gaza.
The initiative is intended to lay the groundwork for a broader international effort to stabilize the territory and begin rebuilding infrastructure damaged during the war.
Countries expected to contribute troops to the stabilization force include Uganda, Morocco, Kosovo and Kazakhstan. Discussions have also been held with Albania, Vietnam and Georgia about possible participation.
Temporary housing and a Palestinian administration
Beyond the military outpost, the reconstruction initiative calls for temporary housing facilities in Rafah to accommodate Palestinian residents.
Under the reported plans, Palestinians seeking to move into the designated areas would undergo extensive security screening intended to prevent individuals affiliated with Hamas or connected to the terrorist organization from entering.
The pilot area would be the first in Gaza administered by the Palestinian technocratic body known as the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG).
The committee would operate with the backing of the international stabilization force, which is intended to provide security for the reconstruction effort and support the establishment of civilian administration.
The arrangements form part of Trump's broader postwar framework for Gaza, which places the Board of Peace at the center of efforts to stabilize and reconstruct the territory.
For now, however, the plan remains dependent on Israeli authorization to move the first contractors and equipment into Gaza.
According to the source cited by The Guardian, officials involved in the initiative expect that approval may come only after Israelis go to the polls on October 27, leaving the first phase of the reconstruction effort on hold.

Israel's largest Hasidic sect threatens to withhold 30,000 votes in election feud
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
00:18:54 UTC
09:18:54 KST

Less than two weeks before Israel's October 27 election, the country's largest Hasidic movement is threatening to withhold its support from United Torah Judaism (UTJ), potentially costing the ultra-Orthodox alliance some 30,000 votes as an internal power struggle threatens to spill over into the ballot box.
The Gur Hasidic movement, which traditionally holds the most senior position within the Hasidic Agudat Yisrael faction and its representation in the broader UTJ alliance, has yet to begin encouraging its followers to vote. The silence has drawn criticism from within the party, particularly as other ultra-Orthodox communities intensify their election campaigns.
In Hamodia, the newspaper affiliated with Gur, there has been no reference to the election and no public instruction from the movement's spiritual leader, Rabbi Yaakov Aryeh Alter, urging followers to support the party.
The absence is especially unusual so close to election day. In previous campaigns, calls to vote for UTJ were prominently featured in the newspaper weeks before Israelis went to the polls.
Initially, Gur officials dismissed the need for an early campaign, arguing that "the rebbe will tell people on election day whom to vote for, and they will listen."
But the continued silence now appears to reflect a deeper dispute over the balance of power within the ultra-Orthodox political alliance.
The split threatening 30,000 votes
The crisis began just hours before the deadline for submitting candidate lists, when lawmaker Meir Porush, representing the Shlomei Emunim faction, and Elyakim Stark, the representative of the Belz Hasidic movement, broke away from Agudat Yisrael.
The two established a separate party, Homat Torat Yisrael, while remaining within the broader United Torah Judaism electoral alliance.
The move effectively freed them from the authority of Agudat Yisrael's institutions, particularly its Council of Torah Sages, the senior rabbinical body that guides the party's decisions.
Porush and Stark occupy the fourth and sixth positions, respectively, on the joint UTJ candidate list.
In Gur, leaders are now considering withholding an official call for their followers to vote, a move that could reduce the number of seats won by the alliance and prevent Stark from entering the Knesset.
"Goldknopf will get in anyway. Our representative is number two on the list, so his seat is secure," a Gur source said, referring to Yitzhak Goldknopf, the movement's senior political representative.
Gur has approximately 30,000 eligible voters, whose support could translate into roughly one to one-and-a-half Knesset seats.
"If Gur gives its mandate or mandate and a half to the party, it will bring Elyakim Stark into the Knesset, even though he is not loyal to the council and has left Agudat Yisrael," the source added.
The calculation is straightforward: Gur's own representative is placed high enough on the list that his election is considered secure, while Stark, in sixth place, could lose his seat if the alliance wins fewer mandates.
Negotiations before election day
Gur representatives are currently engaged in negotiations aimed at securing an agreement on the distribution of positions within the alliance before the election.
If those negotiations fail, the movement could maintain its current position and refrain from encouraging its followers to vote, potentially depriving UTJ of tens of thousands of ballots.
Agudat Yisrael is seeking understandings with Degel HaTorah, the Lithuanian ultra-Orthodox faction that forms the other major component of UTJ, regarding the standing of Porush and Stark.
It is also demanding that Degel HaTorah refrain from negotiating separately with Homat Torat Yisrael in future elections until the breakaway faction returns to Agudat Yisrael and again accepts its organizational framework.
Agudat Yisrael did not respond to a request for comment.
Another concern within Gur is that a last-minute voting instruction from the rebbe could carry less weight among some followers than the traditional campaign appeals issued well in advance of election day.
Nevertheless, the prevailing expectation within the movement is that its leadership will ultimately instruct followers to vote for UTJ, whose ballot designation is the Hebrew letter gimel, as it has in previous elections.
Before that happens, however, Gur officials want an agreement on the allocation of political positions to prevent the dispute from continuing after the election.
The internal struggle has also been fueled by the leadership change within the Belz Hasidic movement.
The Belz rebbe appointed Stark, a powerful figure within the community, as its new representative on the UTJ list, replacing veteran lawmaker Yisrael Eichler.
Eichler has served in the Knesset almost continuously since 2003 and currently holds the position of deputy communications minister. He previously chaired the Knesset's Labor and Welfare Committee and served as a deputy Knesset speaker.
With election day approaching, the dispute has left one of Israel's most influential ultra-Orthodox voting blocs without its customary campaign instructions, while negotiations continue over whether its 30,000 voters will be mobilized to support the joint list.

To scale up air defense without straining the front, Ukraine enlists business. In under year nearly 100 companies have joined, their crews downing 60-plus targets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
00:17:23 UTC
09:17:23 KST

Ukraine is handing its factories the right to shoot back at the Russian drones hunting them. Nearly 100 companies have joined Ukraine’s experimental program that allows private enterprises to operate their own air defenses, granting them authority to conduct air defense operations and form their own crews, the Defense Ministry says.
Russian drones strike Ukrainian factories, warehouses and power sites so relentlessly that the state cannot shield every one, so the Defense Ministry is enlisting the businesses being hit to defend themselves.
The program has grown quickly, from 24 companies in April to 81 by mid-September and nearly 100 now, and its crews have already destroyed a substantial number of Russian aerial targets.
The companies range from operators of critical infrastructure to state and private firms across the economy. The project is carried out under a Cabinet resolution dated 19 November 2025, which mobilizes enterprise resources to support Ukraine’s defense against air threats.
Civilian crews that answer to the Air Force, not themselves
These teams do not fire into a shared sky on their own. About 50 air-defense groups have been formed and are operating under the relevant Air Force commands, and crews from six enterprises are already carrying out combat missions, the ministry says. The rest are training or finishing preparation before they join.
As of 14 October, the groups have downed more than 60 aerial targets, mostly Russian drones, using interceptor drones and automated turrets with heavy machine guns, according to the ministry. The Air Force command sets each group’s targets based on its weapons and tasks, and, jointly with the company, defines its sector, personnel, and equipment.
Who pays, and who pulls the trigger
The arrangement splits cost and control. Some weapons the enterprises buy with their own money, holding end-user status, while a company can also ask the Air Force to lend arms and ammunition from military stocks.
Private air defense is one layer of a multi-tiered shield, meant to protect industrial capacity, critical infrastructure and civilian staff from systematic drone attacks. The crews began combat work in 2026.

Mexican court closes case against official over 2023 detention centre fire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
00:08:58 UTC
09:08:58 KST

Mexican court closes case against official over 2023 detention centre fire
Victims’ groups, however, have denounced the ruling as ‘selective’ justice that exonerates a former government head.
A Mexican judge has closed the case against Francisco Garduno, former head of the country’s immigration agency, for crimes related to the 2023 fire at a Ciudad Juarez detention centre that killed 40 migrants and injured 30 others.
The incident was the deadliest event ever to occur at a Mexican immigration centre, and critics said it exposed the shortcomings and irregularities in the country’s detention system.
Garduno faced trial for the crimes of abuse of public office and dereliction of duty after footage from the fire showed guards had failed to respond to cries for help.
On Tuesday, Judge Victor Manlio Hernandez Calderon ruled that Garduno had fulfilled the court-mandated measures required to address the damage. But victims rejected that decision and announced they would appeal.
“Yesterday, corruption and the impunity of politicians protected by power won again,” the Foundation for Justice, one of the NGOs representing some of the victims, wrote on social media on Wednesday.
The victims have also compared the judge’s decision to close the criminal case to a de facto exoneration for Garduno.
In their view, the ruling “confirms that justice in Mexico is selective” and denies the victims “full reparations” and concrete guarantees that such an event will not be repeated.
Miguel Zenteno, one of the foundation’s lawyers, noted that the ruling is not yet final because it will be appealed and because another injunction is pending against the court-mandated reparations, which critics say failed to meet the standards for serious events.
On March 27, 2023, some 70 men were crammed into a locked dormitory with no ventilation and barely any water at the Ciudad Juarez immigration detention centre, on the border with El Paso, Texas.
As night fell, a small group set fire to some mattresses in protest, and within seconds, smoke engulfed the entire area.
Security cameras recorded the guards leaving the area despite cries for help. They made no attempt to open the gates of the dormitory. Only the women, held in another cell, were released. Most of the victims were Central Americans and Venezuelans.
Garduno, a former prison guard and current official at the Ministry of Education, led the National Migration Institute (INM) starting in 2019 and continued in the role until 2025 despite the fire.
The judge had previously ordered Garduno to compensate the families, provide them with free specialised medical care, issue a public apology, provide human rights training to migration personnel and guarantee that the events would not be repeated.
Zenteno acknowledged that the measures were implemented only partially because Garduno did not pay the damages as stipulated by the legal process.
Instead, Zenteno pointed out that the funds came from the INM, and the payments did not fully compensate the families. Furthermore, he added, the victims were not even informed how to access free medical services, and the apology “was a mere formality, not substantive”.
In addition to Garduno, prosecutors accused another former director of the institute of the same crimes.
Six immigration agents – including a military officer and a private security guard – and the two migrants accused of starting the fire are charged with homicide and assault. Most of the officials remain free pending trial.

Israeli prison guards have shot Palestinian detainees with rubber bullets in confined spaces, leaving one prisoner requiring surgery and another undergoing an operation for a fractured shin, Israeli daily Haaretz reported, citing medical records and inmate testimonies.
According to Physicians for Human Rights Israel and the Public Committee Against Torture in Israel, at least 21 shooting incidents have been documented across five Israeli prisons since October 2023.
Rights investigators noted that most cases occurred in late 2025 and the first half of 2026, often at point-blank range and without any preceding unrest or security disturbance.
The most severe incident occurred in June at Ketziot Prison in southern Israel.
Hospital records from Soroka Medical Centre confirmed that an inmate's organ was completely destroyed by rubber-coated ammunition, necessitating immediate surgical excision.
In formal legal testimony, the prisoner stated that guards initially kicked him during a strip search a week earlier before members of the prison service's specialised Masada unit discharged rubber rounds directly into his cell, striking his previously injured groin and knee before dragging him roughly 50 metres while bleeding heavily.
Systemic abuse
Further records from Ketziot revealed that another prisoner underwent emergency surgery in July after sustaining a fractured left shin from a rubber bullet.
A former detainee told Haaretz he was shot at close range in April and denied medical care for 15 days, receiving surgery only upon release.
Rights organisations confirmed that shootings occurred inside sleeping cells, exercise yards, and legal consultation waiting areas.
Although rights monitors formally petitioned authorities in August to prohibit the use of rubber and plastic ammunition in confined settings, the Israeli Prison Service rejected a blanket ban.
Meirav Ben Zeev, a lawyer with the Public Committee Against Torture in Israel, emphasised that detainees remain fearful of reporting abuse due to potential retaliation, noting that previous complaints failed to produce prosecutions.
Around 9,350 Palestinians, including 350 children and 90 women, remain incarcerated in Israeli facilities amid widespread reports of torture, starvation, and severe medical neglect.

“Every little boat here, every fisherman… is an act of resistance”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
00:00:00 UTC
09:00:00 KST

Meet Alexandre Anderson – a water defender from Brazil
For Alexandre Anderson de Souza and other artisanal fishers, Guanabara Bay in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, is a source of livelihood, identity and culture.
But pollution from multiple sources, including the oil and gas industry, industrial waste and untreated sewage has turned the bay into a sacrifice zone. Artisanal fishers face contaminated water, declining fish stocks, eroded mangrove, shrinking fishing areas and increasingly dangerous routes, while polluters profit without paying for the environmental degradation they cause.
Alexandre co-founded Associação Homens e Mulheres do Mar (Association of Men and Women of the Sea – AHOMAR), a network of artisanal fishers that has spent nearly two decades defending the bay and their traditional way of life from the impacts of oil and gas infrastructure. Several environmental human rights defenders (EHRDs) told Amnesty International that they feared for their safety, some facing intimidation and harassment.
Among them, Alexandre has been repeatedly threatened and has survived several attempts on his life. Here, he shares his story:
My name is Alexandre Anderson. I am 54 years old; I am a fisherman and I have been living and working in Guanabara Bay since 1997.
Artisanal fishing is not just a means of subsistence. It is our culture, a way of life.
In the 1990s, we felt that something was already changing in Guanabara Bay. Our elders say that when the first refinery started to work, the bay suffered a lot. There was a lot of oil around because it was next to two rivers and these rivers were used to illegally discharge sewage.
I’m not the oldest fisherman in the region, but the elders say that fish used to be abundant here, and they disappeared. It wasn’t a natural phenomenon, it was a phenomenon of man’s influence, an industrial phenomenon. Oil is not synonymous with wealth, it’s not synonymous with growth, it’s synonymous with destruction.
“No one warned us”
I remember that I used to sail, on a rudimentary boat… always built by us. With the disappearance of fish, we had to go further into the sea, and I had to buy an engine for the boat. The fish kept moving away, because the shore was increasingly polluted.
The fishermen were then forced to leave the region or change profession. Some say that this is environmental racism. Some say that this is a ‘sacrifice zone’. There has been no public communication… no consultation in our community. No one warned us. When we came to know about the industry, the infrastructure was already being built in the middle of the sea, or in the middle of a beach. (With growing industry presence) there was violence, physical violence, even personal violence against some leaders. Unfortunately, at dawn on 18 January 2000, there was a big (oil) leak in the water caused by an oil pipeline. This whole area was contaminated, and we were pushed away from artisanal fishing. We were pushed to leave everything that we understand – cultural, religious, traditional – and even leaving the place where we were raised, where we were born.
“We are successful in what we do because we work with the truth”
We revolted against everything that was happening and started to look for actions we could take. In 2003 we started to search for answers as a group, and we founded the Associação Homens e Mulheres do Mar (Association of Men and Women of the Sea – AHOMAR).
Soon after in 2009, through our monitoring efforts, we were able to remove two oil sites which were illegally occupying our space and contaminating our region. We are successful in what we do because we work with the truth and we do not work alone. We’re supported by many well-known organizations, such as Amnesty International and observers have even accompanied us to these sites.
In 2009, we lost a treasurer and our founder was shot. In 2012, we had two more deaths of artisanal fishers monitoring the bay. But we are resilient, history will remember us as a resistance and as heroes, and the oil giants will be remembered as destroyers and polluters.
… History will remember us as a resistance and as heroes,
… and the oil giants will be remembered as destroyers and polluters.
Alexandre Anderson
The killings came after sustained threats against Alexandre Anderson de Souza and other members of AHOMAR. The threats relate to complaints the group have made against the construction of a gas pipeline in the bay, and environmental damage that is threatening artisanal fishers’ livelihoods.
On 22 May 2009, the treasurer of AHOMAR, Paulo César dos Santos Souza, was beaten and shot in the head in front of his wife and children; the following year Márcio Amaro, a founding member of the association, was also shot dead in his house.
Both cases remain unresolved.
“We are resilient, but we didn’t ask for this”
Every little boat here, every artisanal fisher who still bravely wakes up early or arrives late from the sea, is an act of resistance. As long as there are boats like these, they cannot take over Guanabara Bay. Protecting artisanal fishing territories means ensuring that rivers and seas continue to be a source of life and dignity, and not just profit.
Guanabara Bay represents everything. It’s our livelihood and our struggle is against large companies. Sometimes we don’t have any more space to fish, it’s something we always tell them. We are not after money, we only want what is ours, we just want to fish in Guanabara Bay, it’s our right and they are taking away our rights.
We are resilient, but we didn’t ask for this. We must resist or we die. We transformed our tears into struggle. This revolt, this sadness that is part of our history, (but) we transformed it into action.
We transformed our tears into struggle.
This revolt, this sadness that is part of our history, (but) we transformed it into action.
Alexandre Anderson
The struggle in Guanabara Bay reflects a reality observed all over the world: fossil fuel and other extractive projects benefit a few at the expense of nearby individuals and groups. But it also tells the story of community power: artisanal fishers leading the fight for environmental and climate justice.
Their stories cannot be erased.

Florida can enforce state law barring young kids from social media, appeals court rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
00:00:00 UTC
09:00:00 KST

Florida can enforce state law barring young kids from social media, appeals court rules
- Florida can enforce H.B. 3, a law barring under-14s from social media with addictive features, after the 11th Circuit said it does not breach free speech rights.
- Tech groups NetChoice and the CCIA, backed by Meta, TikTok and Snap, sued to block the law. NetChoice said it is “currently evaluating all of our options”.
- The court also sent Florida’s case against Snap back to state court. Florida says the law protects children’s mental health, while critics say it limits teens’ online speech.
AI generated
ATLANTA – A federal appeals court on Oct 14 allowed Florida to enforce a state law barring children under 14 from accessing social media platforms like Instagram, TikTok or Snapchat, rejecting tech industry groups’ claims that the law violates the US Constitution’s free speech protections.
In a unanimous ruling, a three-judge panel on the Atlanta-based 11th US Circuit Court of Appeals vacated a lower court’s preliminary injunction blocking the law, known as H.B. 3.
The court said the law does not regulate the content hosted by social media sites and therefore does not run afoul of the First Amendment.
“HB3 applies to platforms wholly without regard to the topics discussed or the ideas or messages conveyed on them,” wrote Circuit Judge Kevin Newsom, an appointee of President Donald Trump.
“Truth Social is just as likely as Instagram to be affected by HB3.”
Representatives for Florida Attorney-General James Uthmeier, who defended the law, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The law bars social media platforms that have so-called addictive features, which include things like video autoplay and infinite scroll, from allowing children under the age of 14 to create accounts.
Tech industry groups NetChoice and the Computer & Communications Industry Association, which count Meta Platforms, TikTok and Snap as members, had sued in 2024 to block the law.
In a statement after the ruling on Oct 14, Paul Taske, director of the NetChoice Litigation Center, said the group is “currently evaluating all of our options as we continue the fight to ensure Floridians’ rights to free expression online are protected, and parents remain in the driver’s seat when it comes to making decisions for their families”.
Snap sued
Florida was among the first of several states to pass a law regulating social media use for children amid a broader reckoning over the apps’ role in young people’s mental health.
After H.B. 3 took effect, Uthmeier sued Snapchat owner Snap in April 2025, accusing it of illegally employing features that addict children and opening accounts for children aged 13 and younger. S
nap said H.B. 3 and the lawsuit sought to restrict teens’ speech online in violation of the US Constitution.
A few months later, the judge overseeing the industry groups’ lawsuit granted their request for a preliminary injunction blocking the law’s enforcement, saying H.B. 3 was likely unconstitutional.
Uthmeier appealed that ruling to the 11th Circuit, and the court had stayed the injunction while it weighed the case.
Separately, a lower court overseeing Florida’s case against Snap had rejected the state’s request in August 2025 to order Snap to comply with H.B. 3, also finding the law likely violated constitutional rights.
But in a second ruling on Oct 14, the 11th Circuit vacated that decision and said the case should move forward in state court, not federal.
A representative for Snap declined to comment. REUTERS

Lavrov to attend 7th CICA summit in Baku
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
23:14:25 UTC
08:14:25 KST

BAKU, October 15. /TASS/. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov will take part in the 7th Summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence-Building Measures in Asia (CICA) in Baku.
The top Russian diplomat arrives in Baku on Wednesday and has already held a meeting with his Chinese counterpart Wang Yi.
According to the Russian Foreign Ministry, the event will "address the further development of CICA, including its integration into the broader landscape of cross-platform cooperation across the Eurasian space."
"Discussions are expected to cover a wide range of practical cooperation areas on the CICA agenda, including the spheres overseen by Russia: support for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and the assurance of international information security," it said, adding that the participants will also exchange views on pressing international and regional issues.
One of the summit’s expected outcomes is the accession of Laos to the Conference as a full-fledged member, the ministry said.
The summit’s agenda is expected to focus on issues of ensuring the region’s sustainable development, strengthening connectivity across the broader continent, and addressing new challenges and threats, including in the area of international information security.
The summit is expected to yield a general policy declaration and a document on raising the standards of occupational safety.
CICA is a multilateral dialogue platform for addressing pressing regional issues and deepening cooperation among member states to build confidence in the military-political, economic and humanitarian spheres, as well as in addressing new challenges and threats. The initiative to establish this format was put forward by the then Kazakh President Nursultan Nazarbayev in 1992.
CICA has 28 member countries, namely Russia, Afghanistan, Azerbaijan, Bahrain, Bangladesh, Cambodia, China, Egypt, India, Iran, Iraq, Israel, Jordan, Kazakhstan, Kuwait, Kyrgyzstan, Mongolia, Pakistan, Palestine, Qatar, the Republic of Korea, Sri Lanka, Tajikistan, Thailand, Turkey, the United Arab Emirates, Uzbekistan, and Vietnam and 15 observers - Belarus, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, Saudi Arabia, the Philippines, Turkmenistan, the United States, Ukraine, Japan, the Arab League, the International Organization for Migration, the OSCE, and the Parliamentary Assembly of Turkic States.
The CICA Chair is elected for a two-year term, with the possibility of mandate extension. Kazakhstan held presidency in 2020-2024 and was succeeded by Azerbaijan in December 2024. The summits are held every four years.

North Korea test-fires submarine-launched cruise missiles amid rising tensions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
23:12:08 UTC
08:12:08 KST

North Korea test-fires submarine-launched cruise missiles amid rising tensions
North Korea test-fired two types of submarine-launched strategic cruise missiles on Wednesday, state media KCNA reported Thursday, saying the launches posed no threat to neighbouring countries. The tests follow heightened tensions with South Korea after a September 21 landmine explosion in the Demilitarised Zone injured three South Korean soldiers.
North Korea has test-fired two types of submarine-launched strategic cruise missiles, state news agency KCNA said Thursday.
The agency said the missiles were fired Wednesday into the East Sea, also known as the Sea of Japan, without "any adverse impact on the security of neighboring countries".
The reported launch came after weeks of mounting friction over a landmine explosion along the heavily fortified border between North and South Korea.
Three South Korean soldiers were injured in the September 21 blast in the Seoul-controlled area of the Demilitarised Zone (DMZ), with both countries testing upgraded missile technology in the aftermath.
The latest testing "aimed to examine the current mobilized posture of the underwater combat systems" and served as a Navy training exercise, KCNA said.
The tests showed the "high reliability, trustworthiness and ability of the war deterrents of the DPRK," the agency reported, referring to North Korea by the abbreviation of the country's official name.
Photos released by KCNA showed one missile blasting vertically out of the sea trailed by a thick plume of smoke. Another photo appeared to show a projectile erupting from the water at a 45-degree angle.
Read moreNorth Korea launches ballistic missile as tensions with Seoul grow over border mine blasts
Other images showed a missile flying horizontally over the sea, as well as a submarine traveling on the water's surface.
The North's ability to launch missiles from submarines at two different angles carries "tactical significance", Hong Min of the Korea Institute for National Unification told AFP, as the two launch methods serve different purposes.
"Vertical launches allow missiles to climb steeply before descending towards their targets, potentially extending their range," he said.
"Angled launches, on the other hand, allow missiles to fly at lower altitudes from the outset, making them harder for missile defence systems to detect and intercept."
North Korea has carried out several missile launches from submarines in recent years, although its sea-based launch capabilities remain unclear.
Cruise missiles tend to be jet-propelled and fly at a lower altitude than more sophisticated ballistic missiles, making them harder to detect and intercept.
Proven submarine-launched ballistic missile capability would take North Korea's arsenal to a new level, allowing deployment far beyond the Korean peninsula and a second-strike capability in the event of an attack.
North Korea has carried out multiple ballistic missile tests in October, most recently on Monday.
The two Koreas have engaged in a tit-for-tat series of missile tests this month, with both sides test-firing hypersonic weapons.
South Korea test-fired its first homegrown hypersonic missile last week, days after Pyongyang said it had launched an AI-assisted intermediate-range hypersonic missile.
Seoul and Pyongyang remain technically at war as the Korean conflict ended in 1953 with a truce rather than a peace treaty.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

Israel has yet to allow the construction of a military outpost for international troops in the Gaza Strip, The Guardian reported on Wednesday, citing a source familiar with the matter.
The outpost was the subject of the first construction contract issued in Gaza by US President Donald Trump's Board of Peace in August 2026. However, two months later, the source said Israel has yet to allow the project to move forward.
“Israel won’t open the border,” the source said, adding that contractors and trucks have been prevented from entering Gaza to begin construction.
Arkel International, a Louisiana-based company, is expected to build the outpost, which would measure approximately 100 meters by 100 meters, at a site previously used by the Gaza Humanitarian Foundation project, The Guardian reported.
The base would accommodate approximately 150 international troops drawn from a larger group of 500 soldiers already deployed from Morocco and Kosovo, according to the source.
Board of Peace plans can't continue without initial outpost built
However, the source said the Board of Peace's larger plans cannot proceed without the initial construction project.
“You can’t get in without an International Stabilization Force (ISF). You can’t rebuild,” the source said, as quoted by The Guardian. “There’s no security. There’s no deliveries of construction equipment. You can’t even start putting utilities. You can’t start putting in basic life-support facilities, you know, because without the ISF you can’t go in.”
Despite the delays, the source said the Board of Peace believes the Israeli government will allow construction to proceed after the October 27 Israeli elections.

First Israeli ballots cast as diplomats vote abroad from New Zealand to New York
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
23:10:58 UTC
08:10:58 KST

Israeli diplomats have begun casting ballots abroad for the 26th Knesset more than a week before Israel's October 27, 2026 elections, N12 News reported on Thursday.
While Israeli citizens are generally ineligible to vote by absentee ballot, exceptions are made for Israeli diplomats and their family members, with the Foreign Ministry and Central Elections Committee (CEC) operating 101 polling stations at 99 Israeli diplomatic missions around the world.
According to N12, about 4,800 Israelis will use the program to vote abroad, and specific mission employees and government envoys are also eligible.
The first ballots were cast in Wellington, New Zealand, at 11:00 p.m. on Wednesday, Israel time, followed by Israel's newest mission in Suva, Fiji, at 12:00 Thursday.
The voting will continue westward, according to the report, until the final polling stations close in Los Angeles and San Farnciso on the West Coast of the United States at 6:00 a.m. on Friday.
The report noted that the program's largest polling station will be at Israel's New York Consulate, where 700 participants are expected to cast their votes.
Ballots to be transferred to Israel upon completion of program
Once cast and collected, the physical ballots will be transferred to Israel to be counted as a standard part of the upcoming elections, N12 reported.
The N12 report emphasized the logistical coordination required for the program, with the entire voting process lasting around 30 hours.
The physical polling stations and election materials had to be transported to their respective embassies and consulates ahead of time, and the CEC had to train local polling station teams to ensure a uniform and secure procedure in accordance with israeli election law.

moyo shirt jacket weaves korean hanbok silhouette with east african kitenge textile
the moyo shirt jacket brings together two distinct cultural aesthetics, reinterpreting the traditional korean hanbok's silhouette using kitenge, a signature east african textile.
[FEATURED]
HANBOK SILHOUETTES meet EAST AFRICAN KITENGE TEXTILES in MOYO
The MOYO shirt jacket, developed by design-focused social enterprise Jerrybag in collaboration with designer Hyunah Kim of ili studio, combines the structural silhouette of the Korean Hanbok with East African Kitenge textiles. Named after the Swahili word for ‘heart,’ the garment translates the layered construction, wrapping technique, and relaxed proportions of traditional Korean dress into a modern shirt jacket format.
The design pairs the understated geometry of the Hanbok with the high-contrast colors and dynamic patterns of Kitenge fabric, bridging Asian and African design languages. The familiar shirt jacket format serves as an accessible entry point for consumers in both regions to engage with cross-cultural aesthetic elements.
FROM KAMPALA TO SEOUL: SUSTAINABLE PRODUCTION AND DISTRIBUTION
Production of the MOYO jacket takes place in Kampala, Uganda, through a local women’s cooperative trained at Jerrybag’s Sustainable Design Center, an initiative established in 2024 via the KOICA Inclusive Business Program to support skill-building and entrepreneurship. Hyunah Kim, drawing from her experience living in Rwanda, developed the concept to explore shared design possibilities between Korea and East Africa. The shirt jacket is distributed through AFRO LOOM, a lifestyle design retail platform operating in Seoul and Kampala.

What is Starshield, SpaceX’s military version of Starlink?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
23:10:00 UTC
08:10:00 KST

What is Starshield, SpaceX’s military version of Starlink?
- Ukraine says SpaceX limited “military-grade” Starlink, raising concern over battlefield drone and air defence support.
- Starlink is SpaceX’s civilian satellite internet service, with more than 11,000 satellites and about 13 million users worldwide.
- Starshield is the Pentagon’s military version, with secure communications, stronger encryption and separate terminals, but it still uses the Starlink satellite backbone.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – Ukraine said on Oct 14 that Elon Musk’s SpaceX had restricted “military-grade” Starlink services, hampering Ukrainian drone strike missions and air defences.
The complaint has drawn renewed attention to the distinction between Starlink, SpaceX’s commercial satellite internet service, and Starshield, a military version developed for the Pentagon. While Musk has said the two systems are separate, in many cases, they share the same underlying satellite technology.
“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government,” Musk said on Oct 14 in a post on X, adding that any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military or the president.
“Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company.”
What is Starlink?
Starlink, the main profit engine of SpaceX, is a satellite internet network of more than 11,000 satellites that beam broadband service directly to user terminals about the size of a folded newspaper. Its roughly 13 million subscribers range from households and hikers to shipping companies and major airlines.
Since launching its first Starlink satellites in 2019 aboard reusable SpaceX rockets, the company has built a vast low-Earth-orbit constellation that blankets much of the planet, delivering faster connections than traditional communications satellites, which typically operate much farther from Earth and in far smaller numbers.
Starlink gave Ukraine a critical communications advantage early in the war, reshaping how militaries operate on the battlefield. But Musk has restricted Starlink for certain military uses while highlighting Starshield, a more secure network developed for government and military missions.
What is Starshield?
Starshield is a SpaceX business unit that develops military and intelligence satellite systems for the Pentagon.
While its missions are separate from Starlink’s commercial broadband service, the distinction is not always clear-cut: Starshield’s secure communications services use enhanced encryption and dedicated terminals, but rely on the vast Starlink constellation as their backbone.
Starshield leverages the technology, engineering and operational experiences of Starlink, according to SpaceX. In addition to secure communications, the company says the militarised version can also provide users with Earth observation and the ability to integrate sensors or other payloads.
The Pentagon, Starshield’s largest customer, has spent billions of dollars on both Starlink and Starshield services. It has also bought dedicated Starshield satellites, including communications spacecraft for missile-warning missions and a spy constellation for the National Reconnaissance Office, Reuters reported in 2024.
Questions over the relationship between Starlink and Starshield have persisted since Russia threatened Western satellites supporting Ukraine in 2022. SpaceX unveiled Starshield later that year, but the secrecy surrounding national security space programmes has left the precise boundaries between the two systems opaque.
Those distinctions became a point of contention earlier in 2026 when the Pentagon clashed with SpaceX over higher prices for satellite services used by military drones during the Iran conflict, Reuters reported. SpaceX argued that some customers paying roughly US$5,000 (S$6,400) per terminal for Starlink should instead have been using a Starshield service costing about US$25,000 per terminal.
Britain has also adopted Starshield. Under that arrangement, the service uses the same satellite constellation, ground stations and terrestrial infrastructure as Starlink, but operates through dedicated terminals and separate network gateways, Britain’s Defence Ministry has told Reuters.
Other US partners are evaluating the system as well. New Zealand is doing a trial of Starshield to assess its usefulness for military operations, the New Zealand Defence Force previously told Reuters. REUTERS

Colombian Foreign Minister Omar Bula Escobar announced Wednesday that his country was withdrawing from the Hague Group, a coalition of countries seeking diplomatic, legal and economic measures against Israel over the war in Gaza, as he delivered an emotional speech celebrating the restoration of diplomatic relations between the two countries.
Speaking at a reception at Israel's Foreign Ministry following the inauguration of Colombia's embassy in Jerusalem, Bula Escobar described the occasion as a "historic event" and said he was struggling to contain his emotions.
"I'm almost in tears at this event marking the restoration of relations with Israel, which should never have been severed," he said in the presence of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar.
"Today I announce Colombia's withdrawal from the Hague Group, a group of countries that attacked Israel and worked to isolate it. We oppose that approach."
The ceremony marked a dramatic shift in relations between Israel and Colombia following the election of President Abelardo de la Espriella, who took office in August after defeating the political camp of former President Gustavo Petro, whose government severed diplomatic ties with Israel in 2024 over the war in Gaza.
Bula Escobar also delivered an emotional condemnation of the October 7 Hamas massacre.
"The October 7 massacre was a barbaric attack carried out by despicable murderers from a culture of death," he said. "Colombia stands with the truth and with Israel."
The Colombian foreign minister recounted a meeting Tuesday with former Hamas hostage Elkana Bohbot, who survived captivity in Gaza.
"I presented him with a Colombian passport," he said. "The survivors are an inspiration to us all."
The encounter, he added, reminded him of the tragedy Israel had endured and of what he described as the failures of Colombia's previous government.
"The previous government in Colombia behaved disgracefully," he said. "They failed to condemn terrorism and opened the door to an ugly wave of antisemitism."
The reception was also attended by Jerusalem Mayor Moshe Lion, Colombian Ambassador to Israel Tania Gilinski, Israeli Ambassador to Colombia Vivian Aisen and members of the diplomatic corps.
Netanyahu welcomed the restoration of relations, recalling his previous efforts to strengthen Israel's ties with Latin America.
"No Israeli prime minister in 70 years of our history had traveled south of Texas," he said. "I said that couldn't be, and that was indeed the case. We went to Colombia, Argentina and Mexico. Those were very good and friendly visits. Later, we visited Brazil for President Bolsonaro's inauguration. Who knows, perhaps we'll do it again."
"The deep sympathy between our peoples is returning," Netanyahu added. "We want to seize the future together, in agriculture, innovation and artificial intelligence."
Sa'ar noted that Colombia had become the 10th country to establish an embassy in Jerusalem, describing the opening as another milestone in Israel's diplomatic efforts.
"Our diplomatic struggle is also a struggle for historical truth," he said. "The campaign against Israel is based on lies and denial, the denial of our rights to our land and our capital."
"We have no intention of relinquishing our rights in Jerusalem, which will remain Israel's united capital," he added.

Albania protests turn violent as protestors demand PM Rama's resignation
Anti-government protests in Albania’s capital Tirana turned violent for a second consecutive night on Wednesday, leaving several government buildings damaged and at least one ablaze. Thousands demanded Prime Minister Edi Rama’s resignation and improved university conditions. Police fired tear gas and deployed water cannons as protesters smashed windows and attacked buildings.
Anti-government protests in Albania's capital left several official buildings badly damaged and at least one on fire on Wednesday as demonstrations spiralled into violence for a second straight night.
Protesters and riot police clashed in Tirana as thousands of demonstrators rallied for better university conditions and demanded Prime Minister Edi Rama's resignation.
Over several hours, police deployed water cannons and tear gas while demonstrators attacked government offices and shops in the city centre, smashed windows and set fire to multiple buildings.
Riot police repeatedly tried to push them back, even using tear gas, but the crowd showed little sign of dispersing.
As night fell, crowds continued to spread through the city, attacking government buildings.
In one incident, protesters smashed windows before setting a floor of the justice ministry building on fire.
Read moreAlbania's "Flamingo revolution": Trump-linked luxury resort plan triggers mass protests
Police chased protesters away before firefighters brought the blaze under control.
Throughout the day, demonstrators hurled paving stones and petrol bombs, set fire to bins and used street fencing to erect barricades.
Protesters also attacked the finance ministry, using fencing to smash windows and break down doors, with some briefly entering the building.
Pushed back by police, protesters moved towards the prime minister's office, where they threw stones at the building prompting police to use water cannon.
A tree near the building entrance briefly caught fire before firefighters extinguished it.
'Masked mob'
Interior minister Ervin Demo acknowledged the concerns of students but blamed the "malicious hands of outsiders" for the violence.
"To those currently setting fire to and destroying public and private property, I say: pull back before it is too late," he said.
"While individual accountability before the law may be delayed amidst the destructive frenzy of a masked mob, it will never forget."
Earlier, AFP saw two people climb over the education ministry wall and throw flares into the building.
Thick black smoke poured from a window shortly afterwards, before firefighters managed to put out the blaze.
Read moreKushner-backed luxury resort sparks outrage, dividing Albanian population
Local media reported that protesters had also attempted to storm a police station, smashing police cars and damaging the entrance before being chased away.
Several banks were attacked and many shopfronts were smashed in the city centre.
Police said late on Wednesday that 14 officers had been injured and 35 people had been detained. Six officers were injured and 16 people were arrested on Tuesday.
"Police are continuing to identify and detain individuals who have committed acts of violence and worn masks during the protest," a statement said.
Demonstrators originally gathered early on Tuesday to demand Rama's resignation and more support for students in the country, citing poor university conditions and high tuition fees.
For more than four months, anti-government protests have routinely drawn crowds in their thousands.
Originally sparked by a luxury tourism project linked to US President Donald Trump's family in the country's south, the demonstrations have occasionally flared into violence amid ongoing calls for Rama's resignation.
Police said officers had "faced constant violence" on Tuesday and were "pelted with stones, blunt objects, firecrackers and Molotov cocktails by groups of masked demonstrators".
The European Union, which the Balkan nation aspires to join, voiced concern over what it called the "violent escalation at the protest in Tirana".
It also called for a prompt investigation of allegations of excessive force by police and called "all sides to de-escalate the tension".
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

Lawyers for man shot by ICE in New York City say agent did not identify himself
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
22:30:42 UTC
07:30:42 KST

Lawyers for a man wounded by an immigration officer while driving with his young son in New York City said in a court filing Wednesday that the agent who shot him never identified himself before he ran up to the car, smashed one of its windows, then fired several shots into the vehicle.
The account by lawyers for Oscar Belgal contrasted sharply with the version of events outlined by Department of Homeland Security officials. They have said officers opened fire only after Belgal smashed his car into two government vehicles and “accelerated toward other officers”.
The Legal Aid Society, in a petition filed in Brooklyn federal court seeking Belgal’s release, said he had picked up his son from school and was stopped in front of a fire hydrant, looking for a parking spot, when “an anonymous, masked man” stormed up to the vehicle with his gun drawn, followed by other masked men with guns.
“The men did not identify themselves, show any documents or otherwise communicate with Oscar in any substantive way,” Belgal’s lawyers wrote. “Instead, without identifying himself, the first man struck and shattered Oscar’s window and began firing a pistol into Oscar’s car while his son cowered in the back seat. One of those bullets struck Oscar in the neck and he immediately began to bleed.”
New York City police security camera footage released by the department last week shows some of the encounter but doesn’t conclusively resolve the dispute about how the shooting happened.
The video shows a man wearing a sweatshirt and a red hat running up to the car with his gun pointed at Belgal, then immediately using the barrel of his gun to bash the driver’s side window. The window shatters on the second blow.
A second officer comes into view alongside the car and draws his gun. Belgal then pulls into the street, away from the two officers. The car pulls out of view of the camera, with the officer in the red hat in pursuit.
Whatever happened next didn’t appear on the NYPD’s security cameras, but the chase ended just a moment later, with Belgal’s damaged car resting against a concrete barrier with bullet holes in its windshield and a rear window.
Video from bystanders and NYPD body camera footage show that ICE officers handcuffed Belgal and tended to a gunshot wound to his neck as he sat on the pavement outside the car. NYPD officers took Belgal to a nearby hospital.
DHS didn’t comment Wednesday on the claims by Belgal’s lawyers, saying the incident remains under investigation. But DHS officials have maintained that ICE officers fired their weapons because they believed their lives were in danger.
Belgal’s lawyers said he didn’t learn the men were ICE officers until he awoke later in the hospital. They say he remains detained at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn, where he has yet to receive surgery to remove the bullet lodged in his neck. They also say he has lost sensation on the left side of his face and now has impaired hearing.
The Federal Bureau of Prisons, which manages the jail, didn’t immediately comment.

New Delhi: The Enforcement Directorate (ED) Wednesday said it has seized Indian assets worth Rs 2,033 crore belonging to Reliance Power Ltd (RPL), an entity of the Reliance Anil Ambani Group, under Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), for the alleged siphoning of assets worth an equivalent amount to tax havens of British Virgin Islands (BVI) and Cayman Islands.The attached assets include bank balances of RPL and its shareholding in Sasan Power Limited. "The Headquarter Investigation Unit has seized assets worth ₹2,032.81 crore in India belonging to RPL, which are equivalent to the foreign exchange held outside India in contravention of FEMA," ED said. ED has already attached assets worth thousands of crores of the Anil Ambani group, including his residences in Mumbai, in multiple money laundering cases involving over Rs 40,000 crore.ED said its investigation into findings of Sebi, pertaining to write-offs/provisions aggregating ₹2,101.46 crore made by RPL in its books of account, had revealed that "these write-offs were related to overseas investments and advances made to companies in the British Virgin Islands (BVI) and the Cayman Islands".In a statement released to BSE and NSE Tuesday, RPL said the ED order of seizure of assets "relates to foreign currency convertible bonds issued in 2006, i.e.
20 years ago, and the related overseas investment made in 2008, i.e. 18 years ago, in a subsidiary in Singapore with all applicable approvals. The seizure primarily pertains to the shares held by the company in its wholly owned subsidiary Sasan Power Ltd, which are already pledged in favour of Power Finance Corporation Ltd (a govt undertaking) under security arrangements for more than 10 years, as well as certain bank balances of the company".ED had conducted related searches in March and seized "several pieces of incriminating evidence", recording statements of several persons. "Investigation has revealed that Reliance Natural Resources Ltd (since merged with RPL) raised $300 million through foreign currency convertible bonds in 2006. Of this, $275 million was invested in its wholly owned Singapore subsidiary Reliance Natural Resources (Singapore) Pte Ltd (RNRL-S)."RNRL-S placed these funds on deposit with Deutsche Bank (Suisse) SA, Geneva. The deposits were used as collateral for loans extended to entities incorporated in the British Virgin Islands. The investigation found that the BVI entities were controlled and managed from India by the Reliance Anil Ambani Group (RAAG) through front persons, who acted as per the group's directions," ED said.
Further, the loan proceeds were utilised for varied purposes, including temporary round-tripping of funds to India through foreign entities based in Mauritius, the central agency said, adding that this was done to benefit the RAAG."The BVI entities failed to repay the loans extended by Deutsche Bank. As part of cover-up, documents were fabricated to show that RNRL-S and Indonesian subsidiaries of RPL had made advances to these BVI entities for apparently genuine business purposes. During investigation, it was found this documentation was backdated and prepared in order to project these transactions as genuine business transactions," ED said. Further investigation is in progress.

Ebola detected in Kenya for the first time in history: one infected person has died
Kyiv • UNN
Kenya has confirmed its first two cases of Ebola: one patient has died, while the other has been isolated. In neighboring Congo, the outbreak has claimed the lives of nearly half of those infected.
Kenya has confirmed the first two cases of Ebola infection in the country's history. One of the patients died, while the other was placed in quarantine. Meanwhile, a large-scale outbreak of the disease is ongoing in neighboring Democratic Republic of the Congo. Finnish outlet Yle reports this, citing AFP, writes UNN.
Details
The first infected person was a man who lived in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. He died last week in Kenya. Later, doctors detected the virus in his close relative.
The second patient was isolated immediately after symptoms appeared. According to Kenya's Ministry of Health, no new cases of infection have been detected so far; however, specialists continue to identify everyone who may have been in contact with the infected people.
Almost half of those infected have died of Ebola in the Congo
The outbreak, which began in May 2026, has most severely affected the eastern regions of the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
According to local authorities, more than 9,000 cases of Ebola infection have already been confirmed in the country. Approximately half of those infected have died.
Cases of the disease have also been recorded in Uganda, which borders both the Congo and Kenya. At least two deaths are known to have occurred there.

Details

HRW says 31 executed by eastern Libya authorities
The NGO Human Rights Watch said Wednesday that military authorities in eastern Libya executed at least 31 people earlier this year, the first reported death sentences to be carried out in the country since 2010, according to the group.
Forces under the control of military leader Khalifa Haftar and his clan executed the people between late August and September 10 "following grossly unfair military trials", HRW said in a statement, adding another 50 people in detention were "at imminent risk of execution".
Libya has struggled to regain stability since former ruler Muammar Gaddafi was toppled and killed in 2011, and the country remains divided between the Haftars in the east and a UN-recognised government in the west.
Haftar's forces "are putting people to death after secret trials built on confessions allegedly extracted through torture, in courts that Libya's own Supreme Court has said should not be trying civilians", said Bassam Khawaja, HRW's deputy Middle East and North Africa director.
He called on the international community to pressure the military authorities to halt any future executions.
Khawaja said the country had gone more than 15 years without an execution, but the eastern authorities "shattered that moratorium in a matter of weeks".
"The lives of at least 50 more people now depend on whether Haftar's forces, and the governments that back them, choose to stop this," he added.
HRW said the detainees were being held in a prison about 100 kilometres east of Benghazi.
It is largely under military control and outside the jurisdiction of the judicial authorities, and is frequently accused of human rights violations, torture and ill-treatment.
The death penalty is still in force in Libya for the crimes of murder, terrorism and offences against state security, though in recent years sentences have not been carried out.

Maj. Gen. Yoram Halevy, coordinator of government activities in the territories (COGAT), sent an urgent letter Wednesday to senior international officials and Board of Peace Executive Director Nikolay Mladenov, alerting them that private merchants in Gaza had gone on strike over threats from Hamas and the oppressive taxation system it imposes on them. Halevy warned that the flow of goods into the Gaza Strip would drop by 50%, adding: "Hamas will try to blame Israel."
The dramatic move also followed an increase in direct threats against the lives of merchants who refuse to comply with the terrorist organization's demands. The letter was sent to Mladenov, Maj. Gen. Jasper Jeffers, commander of the International Stabilization Force for Gaza, and Ramiz Alakbarov, the U.N. humanitarian coordinator for the region.
According to the statement, the decision to strike came after members of Hamas' security apparatus arrested the son of a merchant whose father had refused to comply with the terrorist organization's demands for extortion payments and taxes.
According to the IDF, reports received from merchants indicate that Hamas demands a cash payment of approximately 10,000 shekels for every truck entering the Gaza Strip. It also requires merchants to sell require merchants to sell about 30% of their merchandise in cash transactions, a measure designed to enable Hamas to seize the proceeds directly and thereby preserving its grip on power. 
Moreover, the practice directly violates the commitment made by merchants authorized to operate in Gaza to conduct payments exclusively through monitored bank transfers. Reports also indicate that the taxation system has recently been expanded to include secondary merchants and that Hamas intends to impose it even on drinking water supplies.
The merchants' strike directly undermines Israel's ability to meet its commitments. Under the ceasefire agreement, Israel is obligated to allow approximately 600 trucks into Gaza each day, divided roughly equally between international organizations and independent Gazan merchants. Because the private sector accounts for about 50% of all trucks entering the Gaza Strip each week, the strike is expected to reduce the daily flow by approximately 300 trucks, a drop of about 50%.
Three years into the war, Hamas remains standing, managing daily life for Gaza's residents and exerting significant influence over the entry of aid trucks. The IDF has acknowledged that it has so far failed to develop a system that would allow aid trucks to enter Gaza and reach residents without passing through Hamas' hands. There are concerns that the consequences of the strike — a de facto reduction in the flow of goods into Gaza — will intensify international criticism of Israel and further delegitimize its operations in the Gaza Strip.
In his letter, Halevy made clear that Hamas bears full responsibility and called on international officials to act immediately to prevent the terrorist organization from interfering with the mechanism for bringing aid and goods into Gaza and exploiting it to strengthen itself economically and militarily. Halevy also warned that Hamas would exploit the merchants' strike to spread false claims about shortages of goods and Israel's alleged failure to comply with the terms of the agreement.
Raids in the West Bank
Meanwhile, the IDF and Shin Bet security agency said they had uncovered cooperation between "charitable organizations" and terrorist groups in Judea and Samaria, the West Bank. During two targeted operations in Ramallah and Yatta, five terrorists who had collaborated with Hamas and the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (PFLP) were arrested. According to the IDF and Shin Bet, the "charitable organizations" served as offices for the terrorist groups.
Earlier this week, IDF and Shin Bet forces raided the offices of the Addameer charitable organization in Ramallah. During the operations, suspects were arrested and computers, documents and checkbooks bearing the logos of organizations designated as Hamas-affiliated funds were confiscated. The IDF said Addameer is financed by terrorist funds and operates to provide legal assistance to imprisoned PFLP terrorists. Some of the terrorists employed by the organization took part in the August 23, 2019, terrorist attack at the Dani Spring, in which Rina Shnerb was murdered.
In another operation targeting centers of incitement and terrorism, IDF forces acting on Shin Bet intelligence raided the offices of the Islamic Association for the Care of Orphans, which has been designated an unlawful association, in the town of Yatta in the IDF's Judea Brigade sector of responsibility in recent weeks.
The detainees and seized materials were transferred to security forces for further investigation. The organization served as an organizational and financial arm of Hamas, including transferring funds to the terrorist group and supporting the families of terrorists and prisoners. The organization's director and other senior officials had also been imprisoned in the past.

Turkey seizes control of opposition TV channel as Erdoğan tightens grip on media
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
21:24:05 UTC
06:24:05 KST

Turkish authorities raided the headquarters of Halk TV on Wednesday, one of the country's most popular television channels and among its last remaining independent media outlets. Citing an ongoing corruption investigation, authorities appointed a state trustee to take control of the channel. The dramatic raid interrupted its live broadcast and is seen as an escalation in President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan's efforts to suppress criticism and silence Turkey's free press.
The raid on Halk TV's headquarters in Istanbul began early Wednesday morning, with large numbers of police officers seen surrounding the building. The channel reported on its website that "hundreds of police officers" entered its offices while its journalists were barred from entering. The live broadcast was cut off at 6:30 a.m., after which the channel began airing prerecorded programs.
The Istanbul prosecutor's office said the raid and takeover of the channel's management were part of an investigation into its owner, Cafer Mahiroğlu, on suspicion of "bribery, bid rigging and laundering assets derived from criminal activity." Arrest warrants were issued for 17 suspects as part of the investigation, 11 of whom were detained. Authorities also announced that several companies linked to Mahiroğlu had been seized and that the Savings Deposit Insurance Fund (TMSF) had been appointed as trustee to manage them.
Mahiroğlu, who lives outside Turkey and was not in the country at the time of the raid, described it as "a dark day for Turkey." In a video he released, he accused authorities of "taking control of the public's access to information for political reasons." He dismissed the allegations against him as baseless and said seven members of his family had been arrested during the raid.
Özgür Özel, leader of the main opposition New Party (Yeni Parti, YEP), also strongly condemned the raid, calling it further evidence of Erdoğan's dictatorial rule.
"A dawn raid on a television channel, the appointment of a trustee — only dictators do such things," he wrote in a post on X. "Those who appointed trustees to take over local governments and trampled on the will of the people are now appointing a trustee to take control of Halk TV, a channel watched by millions. Because they are I-N-C-O-M-P-E-T-E-N-T and C-O-W-A-R-D-S!"
During Erdoğan's more than two decades of increasingly tight control over Turkey, press freedom in the country has been severely undermined. This year, Turkey ranked 163rd out of 180 countries in the World Press Freedom Index compiled by Reporters Without Borders. The organization says 90% of the country's national media outlets are under government control.
Halk TV is the fifth major media outlet in recent years to be placed under the control of a state-appointed trustee by Turkish authorities, in a move aimed at controlling its broadcasts and reporting and preventing criticism of Erdoğan's government.
State-appointed trustees have similarly been installed to run numerous local authorities as part of what is widely seen as a broader crackdown on the opposition. That campaign included the arrest last year of Istanbul Mayor Ekrem İmamoğlu, who was charged with corruption. İmamoğlu is considered Erdoğan's most prominent rival and the opposition's candidate in the next presidential election.
Several other mayors were also arrested, while mounting pressure on the opposition has prompted some opposition mayors to defect to Erdoğan's ruling Justice and Development Party (Adalet ve Kalkınma Partisi, AKP).
Erdoğan's crackdown continued this year when the judiciary, which is under his control, annulled the results of the 2023 internal party leadership election of the Republican People's Party (Cumhuriyet Halk Partisi, CHP) in May. The secular party, founded by modern Turkey's founding father, Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, had until then been the country's main opposition party.
The annulment led to Özel's removal as party leader and the reinstatement of former chairman Kemal Kılıçdaroğlu, who led the CHP to defeat against Erdoğan and his party in the 2023 elections but is now seen as an ally of the president.
The court ruling sparked unrest, and police even stormed the party's headquarters and forcibly removed Özel, around whom the opposition had rallied following Imamoglu's arrest.
Özel subsequently left the CHP and founded the New Party, which was joined by large numbers of lawmakers who defected alongside him. It is now the largest opposition faction in parliament.
Since being reinstated as CHP chairman by court order, Kılıçdaroğlu has expressed positions more closely aligned with Erdoğan's government. The raid on Halk TV came just days after he, too, criticized the channel's coverage and announced that he had filed a complaint against it with the media regulator.
Nevertheless, following the raid, Kılıçdaroğlu also joined the chorus of criticism, describing the move as an example of "systematic pressure" on opposition-affiliated media.
European officials also criticized the raid, although Europe's growing dependence on security cooperation with Turkey, a NATO member, means that, as in previous cases, the criticism is unlikely to be accompanied by concrete action.
Nacho Sánchez Amor, the European Parliament's rapporteur on Turkey, said Turkish authorities were "not happy with controlling 90% of media" and were seeking to extend their control to 100%.
"Amidst detentions of journalists & broad online censorship, freedom of media & expression will soon be just a memory," he warned.
