OpenAI bugging suspect booked one-way ticket to Saudi Arabia with family before arrest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
21:18:13 UTC
06:18:13 KST

Abdulrahman Alfozan, the Saudi national charged with secretly installing a recording device in an executive conference room at OpenAI, had booked a one-way ticket from San Francisco to Saudi Arabia with his wife and a third family member before his arrest, federal prosecutors told a judge in a newly unsealed court filing.
Alfozan "has the means — and will have the incentive — to flee the United States sooner if he learns about this case before he is arrested," the U.S. Attorney's Office in San Francisco said in the Oct. 8 filing, which asked a judge to seal a criminal complaint against him and a warrant for his arrest.
The filing said the tickets were booked for Oct. 12, from San Francisco to Saudi Arabia via Istanbul.
The judge granted the sealing request, and Alfozan was arrested Oct. 9, the Department of Justice has said.
He has been detained since his arrest.
Alfozan, 35, is a venture partner in a Saudi Arabian venture capital firm that lists a prince from that nation's ruling royal family as a fellow partner.
The VC firm, Raed Ventures, says on its website that Alfozan, who lives in the San Francisco area, "is a seasoned technology professional with deep experience in startups, entrepreneurship, and scaling tech companies."
"He currently serves as Engineering Lead at OpenAI, with a focus on AI Agents and the data platform," Alfozan's bio page on Raed's site says.
Raed, which focuses on investments in the Middle East, announced Alfozan had joined the firm on Feb. 8, 2025, two days after Raed said Prince Khalid Bin Bader Al Saud had joined as a venture partner. A venture partner usually is a consulting or project-based role, not an investing partner or director who is responsible for raising funds or leading deals.
Alfozan had worked at OpenAI since July 2025, according to the Department of Justice. The company said it terminated him this month.
The Financial Times reported Wednesday that when Saudi tech influencers visited San Francisco in September, "it was Alfozan who welcomed them to OpenAI offices where he gave them tours."
A former CIA official with extensive experience in the Middle East, who spoke on condition of anonymity because of the nature of their past work, told CNBC that Raed Ventures is "basically a state organ" of the Saudi government. One of Raed's funds in December 2024 received an investment from Saudi Venture Capital, a subsidiary of SME Bank, which is part of Saudi Arabia's National Development Fund.
In addition to being a venture partner in Raed, the prince, Khalid Bin Bader Al Saud, is a member of the ruling Al Saud family, and the managing director and vice chairman of his family's private office, according to his bio on Raed's website.
The former CIA official said that if Alfozan's alleged bugging of OpenAI is part of a state-sponsored espionage effort, it shows that "in the AI and tech boom, even the kingdom of Saudi Arabia has assessed that the risk is worth the gain to engage in economic espionage against a close ally."
The former official also said this incident is "probably the tip of the iceberg."
The criminal complaint against Alfozan does not allege that Raed or its other partners were aware of Alfozan allegedly planting a recording device at OpenAI.
The case is being prosecuted by the National Security, Cyber & Special Prosecutions Section of the United States Attorney's Office for the Northern District of California, according to the Department of Justice.
Alfozan is charged in U.S. District Court in San Francisco with one count of using or attempting to use an electronic, mechanical or other device to intercept oral communications.
He is being detained pending an Oct. 19 detention hearing, where his lawyer could argue for his release on bond. If convicted, he faces up to five years in prison and a $250,000 fine, DOJ said.
Alfozan is not charged with corporate espionage or stealing trade secrets.
OpenAI earlier this year held discussions with Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, the country's sovereign wealth fund, about investing in the AI company.
Raed did not immediately respond to requests for comment. CNBC has also requested comment from the Saudi embassy in Washington.
Alfozan's criminal defense attorney, William Pernik, told CNBC by email, "At this point, the information provided has been extremely limited, as the charging documents have just been unsealed yesterday."
OpenAI declined to comment on Wednesday about whether it knew about Alfozan's position at the Saudi firm. And the company said it can't share more details about the conference room in question due to operational security concerns.
The company said in a post on X on Tuesday, "At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data."
"We take protecting our technology, data and people seriously, and as a matter of national importance,"
the company said. "Our security program is designed to protect against a wide range of threat actors, from insider risks to cybercriminals to nation states, and this case is an example of how AI can help address these sophisticated security threats."
Alfozan, in a recent interview with the podcast Identity Capital about his career, noted that in July 2016, he and other Saudi nationals who were working at various tech companies in Silicon Valley met with their nation's now-de facto ruler, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. The prince was visiting Silicon Valley as part of a U.S. tour to promote his "Vision 2030" economic diversification plan.
"One of the issues we discussed was whether we should move back to [the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia] now and bring our technical skills to improve the economy ... or should we work a few more years before we go back in order to gain more experience," Alfozan said in the interview, which was conducted in Arabic, translated by CNBC and posted online Sept. 24.
Bin Salman replied that "the country was undergoing major development and did not have the talent to train the next generation who would carry on those development plans," Alfozan said.
Alfozan added that the group of young workers "decided it was best to continue to learn and develop our skills before taking our knowledge back to [Saudi Arabia] to improve the tech sector."
Throughout the podcast, Alfozan discusses in detail his trajectory from coding in high school in Dammam, Saudi Arabia, to his career in the U.S. At one point in the interview, he refers to himself as an "introvert," who still pushes himself to help other young professionals find success in Silicon Valley.
Days after the podcast was posted, on Sept. 30, a federal criminal complaint alleges that OpenAI staff discovered "a surreptitious audio recording device inserted into a USB port on the back of a television in" a conference room.
The device, which had a detachable camera sensor, digital microphone, and microSD storage, was concealed in toilet paper, according to the complaint.
Alfozan had no authority to enter the conference room, which is frequently used for "discussions of highly confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information," according to the complaint.
The conference room can be reserved "only by executives and executive assistants," and is typically used "for internal leadership meetings and technical and product sessions, as well as external briefings with government officials and business counterparts," the complaint said.
Closed-circuit TV footage at OpenAI showed Alfozan close to the conference room on multiple days in September at various times, according to the complaint.
The filing also said that in August, and again in September, Alfozan used an AI productivity tool to inquire about OpenAI's building addresses, meeting rooms, meeting-room capacities and calendars, as well as "external partner meetings."
And a chatbot associated with Alfozan's spouse, which the complaint alleges shared several identifying characteristics with his own account, allegedly submitted detailed prompts about building, customizing, installing and remotely accessing a recording device. Alfozan's spouse, who was not identified in the complaint, has not been charged with any wrongdoing.
After the recording device was found hidden in the TV in the conference room, OpenAI placed a camera in that room, the complaint says.
Alfozan was seen on that camera entering the conference room at about 1:20 p.m. on Oct. 5, and "checking behind the television into which Recording Device 1 had been inserted," the complaint alleges.
That same day, the complaint said, Alfozan left a bag unattended in a printer room at OpenAI.
Inside that bag, OpenAI security found his wallet, ID and "another recording device" made by the same Chinese manufacturer, Seeed, which made the device found inserted in the conference room's TV, the complaint says.
The second recording device, like the first one, "had a recording microcontroller," and "had been customized to obfuscate anything stored on the device, such as potentially intercepted audio communications," the complaint said.
Alfozan reported to OpenAI that he had lost the bag, which was returned to him without the second recording device, according to the complaint. He did not inquire about the device, although he asked about certain other items that he said were missing, the complaint said.
"Any attempt to illicitly obtain protected information from U.S. super intelligence and technology companies threatens both American innovation and the national security interests those advancements support," Scott Schelble, special agent in charge of the FBI San Francisco Field Office, said in a statement on Tuesday about Alfozan's arrest, using the Trump administration's preferred term for artificial intelligence.
Before joining OpenAI, Alfozan had a long track record of work experience in the Bay Area.
On his LinkedIn page, Alfozan describes himself as an "Experienced Engineering Lead with 11 years of building scalable and reliable software systems in the data and AI/ML domains."
"Proven track record of leading engineering teams, delivering complex projects and enterprise products. 
Driven by strong project management skills and a passion for cultivating a culture of collaboration and engineering excellence," his bio there says.
Before joining OpenAI, Alfozan was a founding engineer at Nash, an AI firm focused on logistics, according to his LinkedIn page.
And prior to Nash, he worked as a senior systems engineer at Facebook's parent company, Meta, from 2017 through 2022, according to his LinkedIn page. His internships before that included one at Microsoft in 2014, his bio says.
Alfozan studied computer science and engineering at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and data science at the University of California, Berkeley, according to his LinkedIn page.
MIT's media relations office said he was enrolled there from January 2011 through January 2014, and again from February 2016 through May 2016, without receiving a degree.
A UC Berkeley spokesperson said Alfozan attended the school from January 2023 through May 2025, and earned a master's degree.
In 2016, he was a research intern at King Abdullah University of Science and Technology in Saudi Arabia, he said on LinkedIn.
In 2020, he won a $50,000 second prize in the Saudi Covid-19 Challenge, a hackathon event, according to the profile.
Alfozan's home, on a hill in Millbrae, California, overlooks San Francisco Bay with views of Mount Diablo. The small San Mateo County suburb, which is popular with tech workers, is located about 30 minutes south of San Francisco and 25 minutes from Stanford University. No one answered the doorbell of the home Wednesday when a CNBC reporter rang.
The Financial Times reported that Alfozan was "born in the ultraconservative central region of Qassim," but "grew up in Dammam in the kingdom's oil-rich Eastern Province."
The FT also reported that in a documentary about Alfozan that aired on Saudi television, his father said that as a young student in a government-backed program for gifted children to develop skills in mathematics, physics and engineering, Alfozan "would read the encyclopedia cover to cover."
"We are waiting to see what evidence the government has against our client, and look forward to presenting all appropriate defenses in court," Pernik, Alfozan's attorney, said.
"What I can tell you by way of a statement is that, like countless Americans, Mr. Alfozan came to this country years ago as a young person with a dream," the attorney said. "He spent years studying, working and contributing to an American technological sector that leads the world, a sector built in large part by immigrants like him."
"These allegations appear wholly out of character for him, and we will relentlessly investigate all evidence produced by the government in this case to understand what actually happened, who was responsible, and any possible reasons why," Pernik said.
The lawyer noted that Alfozan is "charged with violating a federal recording statute, not stealing trade secrets or working as a foreign agent."
"There is no evidence to suggest otherwise at this time that has been shared with us," Pernik said. "Where someone was born is not evidence of anything and national origins is — and always should be — a protected status under our system of laws."
— Ashley Capoot, Lora Kolodny and Reem Nasr contributed to this report.

Supreme Court sides with Republicans in dispute over cost of campaign ads
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
21:16:49 UTC
06:16:49 KST

Supreme Court sides with Republicans in dispute over cost of campaign ads
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- The Supreme Court gave political parties and their fundraising committees lower rates for broadcast campaign ads.
- Justices Sonia Sotomayor and Ketanji Brown Jackson voted to deny the administration’s appeal.
WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court sided with Republicans on Wednesday and gave political parties and their fundraising committees lower rates for broadcast campaign ads.
Over two dissents, the justices granted a fast-track appeal from the Trump administration and the National Republican Congressional Committee and upheld the use of the GOP-friendly rule in the midterm election.
In a brief order, the court said the issue should be left to the Federal Communications Commission.
The outcome has given Republican candidates an advertising edge in the final weeks of the campaign.
Federal law says a “legally qualified candidate” running for election is entitled to a “lower unit charge” for campaign ads in the 60 days prior to an election.
However, on March 30, the FCC, under Republican control, announced that broadcasters must extend the lower rates to political parties and their joint fundraising committees.
The FCC notice did not explain the basis for this change, and it refused to hold a commission hearing to debate the issue.
But the change was seen as benefiting Republicans.
Democratic candidates have raised more money from direct but limited contributions from individuals, while Republicans have raised far more through party committees that are funded by wealthy donors.
The nonpartisan Campaign Legal Center said the FCC’s rule change was “contrary to the text and purpose of the federal statute and would effectively grant super PACs an advertising discount.”
Anna Gomez, the lone Democrat on the FCC, issued a statement objecting to the change.
“The American public should not have sweeping election-year rule changes forced on them in the dark, on the eve of the election, without a single opportunity for public input,” she said.
Democratic Senate candidates Sherrod Brown of Ohio, Jon Ossoff of Georgia and Roy Cooper from North Carolina objected to the FCC rule change in April and asked for a review.
When no action was taken, they filed suit in federal court. They argued the FCC had no authority to change the law that gave only candidates, not fundraising committees, the benefit of the lower ad rates.
Since then, the two sides have gone back and forth in the courts, with each accusing the other of seeking a late change in the rules.
The U.S. 4th Circuit Court of Appeals in Virginia ruled for the Democrats in a pair of 2-1 decisions.
“Suffice to say that any ‘chaos’ is the FCC’s fault, not ours,” Judge Robert B. King, a Clinton appointee, said on Oct. 7. It “has endeavored to create from whole cloth a new rule entirely outside the purview of judicial review.”
But the Supreme Court stepped in twice to overturn the 4th Circuit and rule for the Republicans.
In an unsigned Sept. 4 order, the court said that the 4th Circuit intervened too soon. The law “makes clear that an aggrieved party must wait for the Commission to resolve its application for review by order before filing a petition for judicial review.”
Only Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson dissented.
In September, the FCC did nothing other than to ask for public comments on its March rule change.
Frustrated with the delay, the 4th Circuit issued a second order requiring the FCC to act by Oct. 9.
Last week, in response to an appeal from Solicitor Gen. D. John Sauer, Chief Justice John G. Roberts put the 4th Circuit order on hold.
On Wednesday, the full court said the 4th Circuit Court should have left the issue to the FCC.
“Our system of separation of powers does not allow the judiciary to meddle in the workings of a coordinate branch of the government in this manner,” the court said an unsigned opinion.
In dissent, Jackson and Justice Sonia Sotomayor voted to deny the administration’s appeal.

AI Is Helping Bring Back the Dodo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
21:00:04 UTC
06:00:04 KST

There are a whole lot of reasons to have a whole lot of concerns about the harm artificial intelligence can cause, which explains why the technology has so many detractors. But even the harshest critics might smile at the news coming out of Dallas-based Colossal Biosciences. There, researchers have just announced that AI may help hasten the return of the extinct dodo, with the flightless bird, which vanished from the world more than 350 years ago, likely walking among us again sometime in the early 2030s. With so few ancient samples of dodo DNA surviving—and that which does exist having degraded over the centuries—the analytic and number-crunching power of AI is just what’s needed to fill in the genetic blanks.
“De-extinction is as much a data problem as a biology problem,” said Colossal CEO and co-founder Ben Lamm in a statement. “[AI] learns how regulatory DNA shapes living birds, then identifies the genetic switches that may have contributed to the dodo’s distinctive anatomy.”
Colossal established its de-extinction bona fides in 2025, when it announced that it had sequenced ancient DNA from the long-extinct dire wolf, used that to rewrite the genome of the extant gray wolf, and brought the Ice Age dire wolf back to life, more than 10,000 years after it vanished. Animals that are also on the company’s de-extinction to-do list include the woolly mammoth, the Tasmanian tiger, the ostrich-like moa, and the antelope-like quagga. The dodo, with its waddling gait, its stubby wings, its goggly eyes, and its preposterous beak, has none of the power, grace, or charisma of those other animals—but that’s part of its charm.
“The dodo never had a chance,” wrote New York Herald Tribune writer Will Cuppy, in his 1941 book How to Become Extinct. “He seems to have been invented for the sole purpose of becoming extinct and that was all he was good for. I’m not blaming the dodo, but he was just a mess. The Portuguese called the birds doudos, or fools, because they would associate with the Portuguese on friendly terms and allow themselves to be hit on the head with clubs.”
But what inspires mockery inspires love too—and it will take plenty of that to bring the dodo back. De-extincting a placental mammal like a dire wolf is a comparatively straightforward process. Colossal researchers first harvested cells from a living gray wolf and made 20 edits to 14 genes, coding for the dire wolf’s white coat, larger size, more powerful jaws, cold weather metabolism, and more. They then extracted the nucleus of that rewritten cell and inserted it into a gray wolf ovum whose own nucleus had been removed. Next, the fertilized egg was allowed to develop into an embryo and was implanted in the womb of a large domestic hound. Just over 60 days later, that mama dog gave birth to a puppy wolf.
De-extincting a bird, which does its gestating outside of any womb, will be harder. For the dodo, the researchers will first harvest primordial germ cells (PGCs)—nascent cells that give rise to eggs and sperm—from the nicobar pigeon, the dodo’s closest living relative. The PGCs will then be rewritten to add dodo traits, in the same way the gray wolf was edited. Those cells will then be injected through the shell of a domestic chicken egg into a microscopic chick embryo. The PGC’s will migrate to the embryonic gonads of the chick-to-be, taking up residence there. When the edited female chick hatches and grows and mates with an edited male, she will lay eggs that will produce not a chicken like her, but a dodo.
“In an ideal world, if we had hundreds of nicobar pigeon [eggs] we would use the pigeon as the surrogate,” says Anna Keyte, Colossal’s avian species director. “But nicobars are seasonal breeders. They only lay for a couple of months out of the year and they usually lay just two eggs in a clutch. Chicken eggs are super easy to get. Some chickens will lay an egg a day. You can just get vastly more surrogate eggs from a chicken than you can from a nicobar.”
But editing the PGCs in the first place will be no small thing, simply because there are so many sites on the dodo genome that code for the species’s traits—especially its ice-cream-scoop-shaped beak. It’s not precisely the genes that the researchers are reading in their work, but the regulatory elements—or the parts of the genome that determine which genes get switched on and off. And for the beak alone, that’s a heavy lift. There are more than 650 regulatory elements associated with beak size and nearly 1,700 with beak thickness and breadth. Worse, the fragmentation of DNA in the ancient samples gives an imperfect record of which of those regulatory switches are to be flipped which way. A new AI platform the company calls GenoMorph can fill in those gaps.
To develop GenoMorph, Colossal scientists built an atlas showing how the genetic switches that control facial development turn on and off as embryos grow in chickens, quail, ducks, and pigeons. They then compared genomes and skull shapes from more than 70 bird species, including the dodo’s closest living relative, the Nicobar pigeon. The result is the list of about 2,350 genetic switches that may help explain the dodo’s unusual beak, which the team is now testing one by one. That work builds on a separate achievement: a remarkably complete dodo genome, assembled from a single well-preserved specimen using software Colossal originally developed for its dire wolf project.
“For an ancient genome, this one is extraordinary,” says Beth Shapiro, Colossal’s chief science officer. “There are a few small holes, but far fewer than we usually see with ancient DNA. We’re really not missing much of the dodo genome.”
The beak might be the most dramatic dodo feature, but there are plenty of others, written in the two billion letters that make up the dodo genome—which is why Colossal scientists urge patience for the five or so years it will take to bring a dodo back into the world.
In the same way that some of the work Colossal did to read and analyze the dire wolf genome helped in the later work developing GenoMorph to read the dodo genome, the dodo work can similarly pay itself forward to reading and editing the genomes of other species to be de-extincted.
“It’s been rewarding to see that an approach developed for the dire wolf is now producing value across another species program,” said Shapiro in a statement. “Every scientific breakthrough becomes part of a scalable technology platform that can accelerate the programs that follow.” For now, the dodo remains biological vaporware—but it’s vaporware that could, before too long, take shape in the 21st century.

Trump Aides Admit the House is a Lost Cause
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
21:00:00 UTC
06:00:00 KST

Trump White House aides see almost no paths to Republicans keeping control of the House in the midterm elections and are more focused on redoubling their efforts to save the Senate majority.
That has been the takeaway for officials in GOP groups who have been discussing the state of play with White House aides in recent weeks, according to three sources familiar with the situation.
It all comes as the White House moves into damage-control mode after contemplating for the first time earlier this month, as Inner Loop previously reported, that Republicans could possibly lose both chambers of Congress.
The general expectation is that the House has become a lost cause. Races that Republican congressional leadership once thought they could flip in order to offset Democratic gains are no longer considered attainable.
The Congressional Leadership Fund, the super PAC aligned with Speaker Mike Johnson, has now pulled ad buys in Democratic districts in Michigan and Ohio they were hoping to flip, as well as in the Republican seat being vacated in Nebraska by the retiring Don Bacon. The fund also started canceling remaining ad reservations in two House races where Republicans are seeking reelection in New Jersey and Iowa.
White House aides have shifted their focus to pushing an all-out defense of the Senate majority, which is also looking problematic but to a lesser degree than the House, the sources say. (Polling models and prediction markets agree.)
The aides see the Senate as still in play in large part because early returns for mail ballots have been relatively strong and comparable to 2024 presidential election levels in key Senate battleground states, sources say.
Trump officials at MAGA Inc. have also privately discussed how if Republicans can win some combination of senate seats in Alaska, Iowa, and Ohio, that would form a firewall that complicates Democrats' path to snatching control of the Senate.
Still, Trump officials appear to have conceded they are unlikely to win in North Carolina. Senate Republicans’ campaign arm has paused ad spending in North Carolina since the start of October, mirroring pullbacks by other outside groups.
“President Trump is committed to maintaining Republican majorities in both the House and Senate,” says White House spokesperson Liz Huston in a statement.
The state of play—retreating from a state like North Carolina, where Michael Whatley, a former Republican National Committee chair is on the ballot—would have been unthinkable just a few months ago.
But it speaks to the torrid political climate for Republicans heading into the last stretch of the midterm cycle, which appears to worsen by the week as high gas and living prices caused by the Iran war remain sticky in voters' minds.
With 20 days until the election, sources say, Trump officials are looking to get maximum turnout from the MAGA base in November, rather than trying to capture swing voters who polls show are not breaking for Republicans.
"Republicans remain laser focused on winning and protecting and expanding President Trump's majorities,” says Republican National Committee spokesperson Natalie Baldassare in a statement. “We're thinking outside the box to fight the typical midterm precedent.”
The effort has manifested in a direct voter outreach play with the president crisscrossing the country to reach out directly to his supporters, showing up at rallies in states that should have been reliably Republican.
Trump started the week by hitting the trail in Ohio, where Democratic candidate Sherrod Brown has been polling consistently ahead of Republican Jon Husted, who has weathered negative ads branding him as "the face of data centers."
On Tuesday, the president flew to Wasilla, Alaska—once the home of former governor and vice presidential nominee Sarah Palin—to help the Republican Senate incumbent Dan Sullivan, who has been trailing Democrat Mary Peltola.
And after stumping in Arizona and Kentucky later this week, Trump is set to host a $1 million-per-plate fundraiser dinner for MAGA Inc. at his Mar-a-Lago club, replenishing a war chest that is being emptied at an increasing rate.
Trump has remained steadfast in his belief that he can drive his supporters to vote in November if he hits the trail, as he did in the 2016 and 2024 presidential elections, a person familiar with his thinking tells Inner Loop.
But Trump, whose polling continues to be among the worst on record for any president, is not always wanted at rallies. To date, the president has not done a rally in Iowa with Republican candidate Ashley Hinson, who recently began to buck the president and called for measures that would help end the Iran war altogether.
This is an edition of Hugo Lowell’s Inner Loop newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

Palantir and London mayor settle lawsuit over UK police contract
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
20:59:59 UTC
05:59:59 KST

Breadcrumb
Palantir and London mayor's office settle lawsuit over UK police contract
US tech firm Palantir and London mayor Sadiq Khan's office have settled Palantir's lawsuit over a decision to block a £50 million ($66 million) contract with London police, both parties said on Wednesday.
Palantir had agreed a two-year contract with the Metropolitan Police to use its artificial intelligence systems to automate certain tasks and for analysing evidence.
But the mayor's office refused to approve the deal, telling the Met Police it had failed to have an open competition for the contract, with reports also quoting a spokesperson for Khan citing concerns Palantir did not align with "London's values".
Palantir's supply of software for the US military and immigration services, plus billionaire co-founder Peter Thiel's political views, have drawn scrutiny as European governments grow increasingly wary about dependency on US tech platforms.
The company was challenging the decision to block the Met contract, but Palantir and the Mayor's Office for Policing and Crime said in a joint statement that they had resolved the case and "withdrawn their allegations against each other".
MOPAC's decision not to enter into the contract "was not based on Palantir's values or ethics or any wider reporting about the company", the statement said.
It added that MOPAC "does not have, and has never had, any policy of not contracting with Palantir" and that it was welcome to participate in any procurement processes.
The settlement comes as Britain is conducting a review of a £330 million National Health Service contract with Palantir, while a parliamentary committee said the company had a "clear mismatch with UK values" and recommended using a break clause, a suggestion Palantir's British CEO Louis Mosley called "irresponsible".

Dimash Qudaibergen featured in GRAMMY’s new “Global Mixtape” series
Dimash Qudaibergen has appeared in the debut episode of “Global Mixtape,” a new series by GRAMMY, discussing his musical journey, Kazakh traditions and plans for an upcoming international tour, Qazinform News Agency cites DimashNews.
In an interview with journalist Valerie Lee, Dimash recalled growing up in a home filled with music. His parents, both classically trained artists, exposed him to a wide range of music, from traditional Kazakh folk songs to recordings of the Three Tenors. He began performing on stage at the age of five and has been performing for nearly three decades.
Describing Kazakh culture, the singer called it “the voice of the steppe,” highlighting traditional instruments such as the dombra and kobyz. He also explained the significance of küi – instrumental compositions that convey history and emotion – and aitys, a traditional poetic contest involving improvised exchanges that he compared in some ways to rap.
Dimash said singing in different languages is his way of expressing gratitude to audiences who embrace him and his culture. During his upcoming tour, he hopes to perform in the languages spoken in the countries he visits.
“My biggest mission isn’t about the commercial side. It’s not about earning money,” he said, adding that he wants his music to remind people of the importance of peace, love and mutual understanding.
The singer said he hopes to visit more than 20 countries on the tour, possibly more than 30 or even 40, although the final number has not been confirmed. He also said that a documentary about his concert at Madison Square Garden in New York would be released on his YouTube channel in a couple of weeks.
Reflecting on his ambitions, Dimash cited a Kazakh saying: “A person without a goal is like a bird without wings.” He added that he sees the journey itself as the true purpose.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that the Brazilian television program Domingo Espetacular highlighted Kazakh singer Dimash Qudaibergen and his influence on a new generation of musicians.

5 arrested in probe into suspected $1.1 million fraud involving NATO vessels
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
20:56:24 UTC
05:56:24 KST

Aysu Bicer
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
Five people have been arrested in Norway, while searches were conducted in Romania and Germany as part of a cross-border investigation into suspected fraud exceeding €1 million ($1.1 million) involving services supplied to NATO military vessels, said the EU justice cooperation agency on Wednesday.
The investigation concerns alleged fraudulent invoices submitted to the NATO Support and Procurement Agency (NSPA) by a company and its subcontractors for husbandry services provided to NATO vessels visiting ports in northwestern Europe.
Eurojust began supporting the investigation in April 2025 after the NSPA identified suspected irregularities in the invoices, according to information provided by the European Union Agency for Criminal Justice Cooperation, or Eurojust.
The suspected fraud also involves allegations that the company bribed foreign public officials through an intermediary in exchange for favorable treatment in its contractual dealings with the NSPA.
The estimated losses to NATO member countries exceed €1 million, although the exact amount remains under investigation.
In July 2025, Eurojust supported the establishment of a joint investigation team, allowing authorities from different countries to cooperate under a common legal framework and exchange information and evidence directly.
Eurojust also hosted coordination meetings to prepare for the joint action day, while the NSPA provided information and support to the investigation team.
During the coordinated operation, five individuals were arrested in Norway, and searches were carried out at residential and business addresses.
In Romania, authorities searched company premises and several homes. In Germany, searches were carried out at two business premises and one residence under a European Investigation Order.
Eurojust said it could not provide further comment because the investigation is ongoing.

The Australian Council of Social Service (ACOSS) is warning that the risks of a "sharp and substantial rise" in unemployment over the next year are "real and growing."
“Since interest rates started to rise in 2022, more than 200,000 additional people have been pushed out of paid work,” said ACOSS CEO Cassandra Goldie.
“Interest rates work with a lag and increases already in the pipeline will push unemployment higher over the coming year.
"Every further rise adds to that risk.
“The biggest threat to a person’s living standards is losing the opportunity for paid work.
"People locked out of the labour market are forced onto JobSeeker, which is just 41% of the minimum wage and leaves them living well below the poverty line.
“The Government must lead on bringing inflation down fairly, so that people on low incomes are protected.
“Governments must step in to slow rent increases and cap out-of-pocket medical costs, including specialist fees, take solar subsidies off energy bills and stop any plans for further tax cuts,” Ms Goldie said.

Auction clearance rate falls in capital cities for the week, lowest figure since June
The auction clearance rate has hit its lowest number since June across all capital cities, falling to 44.1%, according to property data firm Cotality.
The means fewer than half the homes that went to auction actually sold in the past week in yet another sign of the property market's slowdown.
Over in Sydney, 45.6% of homes put on auction sold to a buyer, down from 68.2% in the same week last year.
The number of properties put up for auction over in Melbourne was 43.7% fewer than the year before. 
Only Adelaide and Brisbane held more auctions than in the same week last year.
Although Brisbane is experiencing more homes going to auction, "its clearance rate has fallen the most", the report said.
The clearance rate remained near its 18-year low at 21.8%, down significantly from 66.1% last year in Queensland's capital.

A closer look at small business sectors ahead of jobs results
Following on from my last post, here is a breakdown of key stats from the latest MYOB SME Performance Indicator:
In the 12 months to June, SME employment rose 0.8%. The decline in July (mentioned in the previous post) trimmed that annual growth to 0.6%.
Between April and July, SME headcount was effectively flat (+0.1%), but output per worker fell 2.4% and payroll spend per worker (after inflation) fell 2.3%.
Let's look at the major sectors:
- Coinciding with the Government’s temporary fuel excise relief, the Transport, Postal and Warehousing sector activity was up 10.3% between April and July compared with December to March.
- Trucking, warehousing and freight firms earned more per worker (+3.4%) and spent less (−4.9%), while headcount remained static. Sales jumped in April and held through July.
- Real Estate had the weakest four months, down 12.4%.
- Accommodation and Food Services employment fell 2.3% in July, the sector’s sharpest monthly fall in two years, and was down 1.3% between April and July compared with December to March. Over the same period, revenue per worker held broadly steady (−0.3%) while costs per worker fell 2.8%, lifting output per worker 1.7%.
- Education and Training also reduced staff (−0.9%), as output across the sector fell 8.1%, with revenue per worker down 2.4% and costs per worker up 2.2%.
- Agriculture (−0.5%) also shed jobs.
- Health Care and Social Assistance continued to hire (+1.2%)
- Construction, the largest SME employer, held steady (+0.3%).

Small business hiring and productivity soften ahead of key jobs data
The latest job figures will be released by the Australian Bureau of Statistics at 11:30am AEDT.
Ahead of those numbers, the small business accounting platform MYOB has released its Performance Indicator, which suggests small businesses' across the country had softer hiring processes in July after a steady run of growth through the first half of 2026.
The report is based on anonymised data from more than 200,000 Australian small and medium-sized enterprises (SME).
It shows employment dipped by -0.6% in July, the largest monthly decline since January 2025.
On a three-month average basis, employment eased -0.1%, its first dip since January this year.
MYOB CEO Paul Robson says small businesses are often the first to feel a shift in conditions.
"As the Reserve Bank weighs its next move, small businesses are an important part of the story. The data implies that employees are feeling the effects of economic tightening, and after a stronger first half of the year, they are being more careful with decisions around employment," he says.
"Small businesses are a bellwether for the broader economy. They can turn around quickly, but only if costs stabilise and owners have the confidence to back themselves on the next hire."

Master Builders NSW welcomes the Minns government's announcement that NSW businesses will not be slugged with stamp duty if they are required to restructure out of a trust.
This responds to the federal government's new tax on discretionary trusts.

‘Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government.’ Musk responds to Ukraine’s complaints about restrictions on the military version of Starlink.
SpaceX has restored service in Ukraine for Starlink satellite terminals moving at high speeds, former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov said on the evening of October 14.
“Starlink connectivity at speeds of up to 160 km/h [about 100 mph] is being restored. Removing Starshield’s speed limit entirely is now critical for Ukraine’s defense. Thank you, Elon Musk. We hope for your continued support,” Fedorov said on social media.
In response, Musk said Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government. “Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” Musk said. He said Starlink is a commercial service whose use is “limited to civilian or defensive activities.”
Ukraine’s Defense Ministry told journalists that SpaceX still imposes a speed limit of 161 kilometers per hour (about 100 mph) on the terminals. “However, we’re currently seeing improved connection quality at speeds of up to 160 [km],” officials said.
Ukrainian military personnel and officials said on the morning of October 14 that SpaceX had restricted service without warning for Starlink terminals used by Ukraine’s armed forces on the front lines. The restrictions affected Starshield, the military version of Starlink needed to launch drones. Some even compared the damage the Starlink slowdown caused Ukraine’s armed forces to a nuclear strike on Ukraine.
The restrictions on Starshield came amid a crisis in relations between U.S. President Donald Trump and Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelensky.

World’s oldest shipwreck found off coast of Turkiye
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
20:33:20 UTC
05:33:20 KST

World’s oldest shipwreck found off coast of Turkiye
Culture Minister Ersoy said it sheds light on ancient maritime trade in the eastern Mediterranean.
Turkiye’s Culture Minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy has said the country unearthed ancient treasures from what he called “the world’s oldest shipwreck”.
Underwater excavations near Kekova Island in the southern Antalya province uncovered ceramic storage jars dating back 4,700 years to the Early Bronze Age, Ersoy announced in a post on X on Wednesday.
While the vessel’s wooden hull did not survive, archaeologists recovered the ancient storage jars following an underwater excavation project launched earlier this year.
The jars, believed to have transported olive oil or wine, provide concrete evidence of early maritime trade and cultural exchange across the eastern Mediterranean, according to the ministry.
Clay analysis indicated the containers were manufactured in workshops in the Jordan Valley, matching similar styles previously found in Egypt, Turkiye, and Greece that illustrate extensive Bronze Age sea routes.
One vessel was singled out for its unique design, featuring nine markings and two holes in its body that suggest it may have been used to churn butter or cheese.
Researchers believe the ship was sailing from the Levantine coast towards modern-day Hisarlik in Turkiye or the island of Crete in Greece when it capsized and sank.
The excavation was directed by Hakan Oniz, an associate professor of archaeology at Akdeniz University.
Speaking to the BBC, the professor said when his team first found the wreck four years ago, the jars only appeared to be a century or two old.
“However, we later became excited when we saw the same amphora forms in a publication on Egyptian archaeology and returned to the site,” he said. “Indeed, they were similar to those found at the Giza pyramids in Egypt. We were incredibly excited.”
The discovery has “shed light on the deep-rooted history of maritime trade along the Anatolian coasts,” added Ersoy.

Algeria’s death penalty provisions take effect for forest arson, child kidnapping
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
20:32:50 UTC
05:32:50 KST

Abbas Mimouni and Rania Abushamala
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
New provisions prescribing the death penalty for crimes involving forest arson and child kidnapping have taken effect in Algeria under amendments to the penal code, the Algerian Press Service reported Wednesday.
The amendments, approved by both houses of parliament last week, were published in the Official Gazette, it said.
Under the law, capital punishment applies to anyone who deliberately sets fire to forests, wooded areas, cultivated or uncultivated fields or trees and timber within forests.
The provisions also cover anyone who “deliberately” sets fire to public or private property at the instigation of, or for the benefit of a foreign state or party, or as part of crimes involving treason and collusion with an organized criminal group.
They extend to offenses targeting security and public order, national unity, institutional stability or the national economy, as well as those damaging the environment, ecological balance, and forest, plant, animal and agricultural resources.
The death penalty also applies to anyone who incites, encourages, finances, plans or participates in such acts, or helps prepare or facilitate them by any means, including information and communication technologies and social media.
Arson resulting in the death of one or more people is also punishable by death.
Child kidnapping
The law prescribes capital punishment for anyone who abducts a child by any means, tortures, sexually assaults or subjects the child to brutal treatment, without prejudice to other penalties stipulated in existing legislation.
It bars those convicted of offenses covered by the provisions from benefiting from mitigating circumstances under the penal code.
President Abdelmadjid Tebboune ordered the reactivation of the death penalty for the crimes following widespread fires in late August that caused loss of life and property damage, particularly in the eastern provinces.

Houthis look to build ballistic missiles with Chinese supplies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
20:32:45 UTC
05:32:45 KST

Breadcrumb
Yemen's Houthis look to build ballistic missiles with more Chinese supplies, report says
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels are attempting to build a new advanced medium-range ballistic missile system with the help of Chinese parts, according to a new report released Wednesday by a group that tracks the use of weapons in conflict zones.
The report by the U.K.-based Conflict Armament Research group came as the Houthis, in their ongoing war with Saudi Arabia, are demonstrating remarkable ability to wreak havoc on one of the Middle East’s best equipped militaries.
The weaponry under development could help the group more precisely target the Saudis and Israel. By turning to China, it also appears to be a sign of increasing independence.
The rebels expand their ambition 
The Houthis have tried to acquire key parts from Chinese suppliers that could be used to make a version of Iran’s Kheibar Shekan precision-guided missile, according to the report. The Kheibar Shekan has a range of roughly 1,200 miles (2,000 kilometers).
"The local ambition of the Houthis for manufacturing is beyond what was previously assumed," said Fabian Hinz, a senior analyst at Conflict Armament Research, a research outfit specializing in tracing the flow of arms in war zones around the globe. "These types of parts are very specific, and producing them would have required design information related to the missile."
They're "not goods that can be used for a variety of civilian applications," Hinz said.
The Chinese Embassy in Washington didn't respond to a request for comment.
China is a major purchaser of both Iranian and Saudi oil and leveraged its ties with both countries to broker a rapprochement in 2023. It has condemned a series of attacks on Saudi airports by the Houthis and called for a de-escalation in the fighting.
Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s government launched a military campaign last month aimed at driving back the Houthis from the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a critical Middle East trade route for oil and other goods.
Yemen interdicted key components to building missiles 
The Conflict Armament report was based on information released by Yemeni government authorities in July after officials interdicted two shipments that included suspicious equipment.
The shipments originated from China and were intended to be delivered to Hodeidah, a Yemeni port that Israeli officials say has been commonly used by the Iranians as a weapons transfer point. China accounts for the largest share of seized shipments destined for the Houthis, according to U.N. reports.
Components integral to the functioning of a missile were among the parts found in the cargo. They included stabilizing fin cores, rocket motor aft closures with nozzle attachments, and rocket motor igniters.
The cargo also contained phenolic resin, a material used in creating ablative heat shields. These shields protect ballistic missiles from the intense heat associated with atmospheric flight at high supersonic speeds, the report said.
Hinz said that the combination of materials made clear that the Houthis intended to assemble that specific type of Iranian-designed missile.
"This particular type of system is very difficult to smuggle. And you can’t just disassemble and reassemble them," he said.
Houthi weaponry has grown more sophisticated over time 
The Houthis rose to prominence more than 20 years ago as an insurgent group armed with Soviet-era and North Korean weapons seized from the Yemeni government's military.
But over the years, the group's access to advanced weaponry has expanded and so has its ability to menace neighbors.
In the current weekslong conflict with Saudi Arabia, the Houthis have fired ballistic missiles and utilized maneuverable warheads and long-range drones. They previously have fired scores of drones and missiles at Israel, more than 1,000 miles (1,600 kilometers) away.
Over the past week, they managed to puncture the kingdom’s stout air defense system with strikes on Riyadh’s international airport that killed at least 18 people.
Iran could find value in redundancy 
Iran has been an important supplier of blueprints and components for the Houthis. But procuring parts from beyond Tehran could be crucial for the group.
"Redundancy is an asset, not a liability in military planning," said Benham Ben Taleblu, a senior director of the Iran Program at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a hawkish Washington think tank. "With a blockade of Iran in place, the Houthis are diversifying."
The rebels had long received weapons and materials smuggled from Iran. But the shipments have changed and now more often contain components rather than intact weapons.
The group’s arms program has been "increasingly backstopped by a hybrid, global supply chain serviced by a web of participants — including tribally connected smugglers across Yemen and businessmen working from export hubs in eastern China," according to research published earlier this year by The Century Foundation, a Washington think tank.
Security forces aligned with Yemen’s internationally recognized government have repeatedly intercepted missile components and launch equipment at the port of Aden, according to Yemen’s Aden Counter Terrorism Unit.
Yemen experts believe that the Houthis still rely on Iran for more sophisticated components needed to manufacture guided missiles, including navigation and control systems. But the group has expanded its capacity to manufacture and assemble weapons domestically at facilities deep inside territory under their control.
"The Houthis cannot yet manufacture highly complex weapons systems, and … they still rely heavily on Iran for technology and many critical items," The Century Foundation report said. "The group has reached a capability tipping point and can build a significant proportion of some weapons systems using imported components."
Yehoshua Kalisky, a senior researcher at Israel’s Institute for National Security Studies, said that the Houthis’ supply chain historically mirrored that of other Iranian proxies, including Hamas and Hezbollah.
Iran is among the world’s most advanced in ballistic missile development. And both in Gaza and Lebanon, Iran-backed militant groups have smuggled in raw materials, and relied on Iran for more sophisticated components and assembled weapons themselves, he said.
Kristian Ulrichsen, a Middle East fellow at the Baker Institute, said that the Houthis’ growing reliance on Chinese components could have broader implications for politics in the Gulf.
"Now that the situation has really escalated and seen these attacks on infrastructure and airports, we could see more pressure from the Saudis," he said, noting that China is Saudi Arabia’s largest trading partner.

Meink: Operational Prototypes for MMA Drones Coming in 2028
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
20:32:08 UTC
05:32:08 KST

The Air Force will field operational prototypes for an autonomous drone to replace its MQ-9 Reaper in 2028, Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink said Oct. 14.
“We’re going to be fielding operational prototypes by ’28, and we’re just awarding the contract now,” Meink said during a panel discussion with Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, other service secretaries, and senior Pentagon officials at the annual AUSA conference in Washington. “That’s the speed of what we’re fielding capability, and into production—large-scale production—starting in ’29. That is the goal.”
An Air Force spokesperson confirmed to Air & Space Forces Magazine that Meink was referring to the Massed Modular Aircraft, the planned successor to the Reaper.
“The autonomous fighters are already in production,” Meink said, in reference to the Air Force’s Collaborative Combat Aircraft program. General Atomics’ FQ-42A Vengeance and Anduril Industries’ FQ-44A Fury have been selected for production and are undergoing testing with the Air Force’s Experimental Operations Unit at Creech Air Force Base, Nev.
“Now we’re looking at essentially the autonomous strike platform, the autonomous bomber,” Meink said, referring to MMA. The aircraft is envisioned as a multimission aircraft, like the MQ-9, that can conduct strike missions as well as intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance. In contrast, CCAs are currently focused on an air-to-air role paired with crewed fighters.
Meink previously announced at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference that the Air Force would field 100 MMAs by 2029 and 500 by 2032.
Air & Space Forces Magazine reported Sept. 30 that the Air Force and Pentagon’s Defense Innovation Unit had narrowed the field for MMA down to seven companies. An Air Force spokesperson declined to confirm any selections, but Meink said Oct. 14 that “we just awarded those contracts … in collaboration with DIU.” He did not name the specific companies or say how many finalists there are.
Sources have told Air & Space Force Magazine the seven companies still in contention are Anduril, Chaos Industries, General Atomics, Grid Aero, Otto Aerospace, Shield AI, and Swarm Aero. They will develop their MMA candidates and submit a proposal to build a prototype.
The Air Force and DIU want each MMA drone to cost $10 million for the base aircraft, not counting the sensors, weapons, or other equipment it may carry. That’s half the $20 million target price the Air Force envisions for CCAs. MMAs will also use open architecture so they could be more easily upgraded with new sensor packages or weapons capabilities.
But while MMAs will have some autonomous capabilities, they won’t be built with all the latest cutting-edge technology in a bid to keep their price down below that of CCAs. They will likely be powered by turboprop engines, for example.
MMA drones are intended to be able to fly about 4,000 miles, twice the range of CCAs, and carry a heavier payload than CCAs. But they will be slower than CCAs.
The MMA effort is part of the broader push by the Pentagon and the Air Force to field more autonomous systems at a lower cost than crewed platforms, or even the drones that are in service today. The goal is to build “combat mass” to counter China’s growing military, which Meink said is going through “the largest weapons buildup probably in the history of the world,” and to respond to the proliferation of autonomous systems in conflicts of today, and the Pentagon’s view, tomorrow.
“There’s no question that there’s a shift coming,” Meink said. “It’s adaptability, scalability, and affordability. The only way we’re going to meet the threat is with autonomous systems.”
Meink said the Pentagon will work with Congress to secure the funding needed for MMA. The Trump administration’s $1.5 trillion fiscal 2027 budget request for the Department of Defense is currently stalled on Capitol Hill. With midterm elections approaching next month, Democrats could take control of one or both chambers, which could lead to congressional gridlock, particularly surrounding the Pentagon’s request for a massive budget increase—and plans to continue that—amid the war with Iran. The DOD plans to devote tens of billions to autonomous warfare just this fiscal year.
Meink acknowledged the uncertainty surrounding the Pentagon’s budget, but expressed confidence the Air Force would be able to hit its targets for MMA.
“It is heavily dependent upon the resources we get from the Hill, but I think we are not only going to deliver significant combat capability, but we’re going to deliver quickly and efficiently,” Meink said.
“We’ve got to make sure this stuff is affordable,” Meink added, referring to efforts across the Air Force and Space Force. “We’ve got to make sure we’re buying it efficiently. And depending on how you do the comparisons, we’re talking five to 10 times cheaper to field some combat power with these autonomous systems compared to not. So it’s critically important. The good news is, in my mind, there’s no question that the leadership we have in the Air Force, in the Space Force, both military and civilian, is ready to do that. And you see that with the results already. We are integrating autonomous fighters into experimental ops units out at Creech right now, from a year from when they first flew to when we were integrating them into experimental ops units. That’s unheard of. And it only took two years to build the first one.”
The goal for MMA is similarly ambitious.
“It’s in the scalability and the producibility,” Meink said. “In many ways, cost goes with schedule. If something is super expensive, there’s a reason for it, which means it’s probably going to take a long time to build, so we’re really focusing on rapid production and scalability, which means we have to get the cost down on these systems as well.”
Meink’s comments came during a panel focused on the Pentagon’s Project Agincourt, a drive to accelerate the fielding of autonomous systems and create a new four-star Autonomous Warfare Command, or AUTOWARCOM, which Hegseth announced during a speech late last month.
“The folks who acquire it need to be right there up with the warfighter at the same time who understand how to iterate it and change on and innovate on it,” Hegseth said.
Adversaries such as Russia and Iran have fielded one-way drone attacks to wreak havoc in Ukraine and across the Middle East. Ukraine has used autonomous systems to great effect to defend against Russia’s invasion. Kyiv’s ongoing and thus far successful Operation Vivaldi offensive has relied heavily on the innovative use of drones, including dropping uncrewed ground vehicles behind enemy lines.
“That’s a different battlefield,” Hegseth said. “We’ve learned a lot from Ukraine, but you can’t use everything that’s in Ukraine because of all the Chinese components involved in it. So you’ve got to be able to ensure that we take the best of that and the lessons learned … and then push it through [with] an AUTOWARCOM commander with four stars who has the ability to drive that change. So we’ve done a lot with acquisitions and a lot with industry from day one to modernize, realizing this is the future of warfare.”

Madrid teachers, students protest over public education conditions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
20:31:31 UTC
05:31:31 KST

Aysu Bicer
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
Teachers and students took to the streets of Spain’s capital Madrid as a highly disruptive, indefinite strike sweeps through the region’s public education sector, according to local media reports on Wednesday.
The walkout, which began Wednesday, involves around 65,000 public school teachers, with unions demanding higher salaries, smaller class sizes, reduced teaching hours, and increased investment in school infrastructure.
The strike, backed by several major unions, follows months of unsuccessful negotiations with the regional government.
Clashes, arrests reported
Tensions escalated early Wednesday as students at the Complutense University of Madrid and Rey Juan Carlos University erected barricades, disrupting activities on campus.
Clashes erupted at the Ciudad Universitaria campus after riot police moved to clear the blockades, according to the provided account.
At least five people were arrested and seven injured, including several police officers, regional officials said. Left-wing opposition politicians criticized the police response, accusing officers of using excessive force against student demonstrators.
The disruption also spread to the city center, where early-morning blockades by nursery school educators temporarily halted traffic along Paseo de la Castellana, a major financial and transport corridor.
Unions demand higher pay, smaller classes
Unions say the regional public education system is suffering from chronic underfunding and staff shortages.
Their demands include limiting class sizes to 13 pupils in nurseries, 15 in primary schools, and 20 in secondary schools.
They are also seeking a net monthly salary increase of €600 ($670), arguing that teachers need higher pay to offset inflation and bring salaries closer to those in other Spanish regions.
Other demands include reducing weekly teaching hours to 22 in primary education and 17 in secondary schools, expanding special education resources, and investing in modernizing climate control systems in ageing school buildings.
Regional government rejects demands
Regional Education Minister Mercedes Zarzalejo described the action as politically motivated, while government officials said the unions’ financial demands were unfeasible and unattainable under the current budget framework.
Authorities have imposed minimum service requirements to ensure schools remain open for supervision during the walkout.
Unions, however, have pledged to continue the strike indefinitely until the regional government agrees to establish a formal negotiating framework.
The dispute has intensified pressure on the regional administration as educators call for improvements to working conditions, staffing levels and public education funding.

Musk Says US Government Controls Ukraine’s Starshield Limits as Zelensky Accuses Russia of Exploiting Outage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
20:13:49 UTC
05:13:49 KST

Elon Musk said on Wednesday, Oct. 14, that the US military – including US President Donald Trump himself, not SpaceX – decides speed limits on Ukraine’s military Starshield terminals.
His remarks came after restrictions imposed overnight on Oct. 13-14 disrupted Kyiv’s drone operations, particularly interceptor drones – among Ukraine’s few effective tools against Russian jet-powered Shahed drones, which are significantly harder to intercept due to their speed.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“It is clear that the Russians are trying to exploit problems with Starlink’s operation in Ukraine, as interceptor drones rely significantly on this connection,” President Volodymyr Zelensky said in a statement on Wednesday, after meeting with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham in London.
Speaking during an interview on “Piers Morgan Uncensored,” released on Wednesday, Zelensky said he feels betrayed by Trump and warned that SpaceX’s new Starlink restrictions will cost lives. “I’m sure they knew what they did,” he said regarding the outage.
Meanwhile, Ukraine’s former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov said Starlink’s connectivity at speeds of up to 160 kilometers per hour (100 miles per hour) is being restored. “Removing Starshield’s speed limit entirely is now critical for Ukraine’s defense,” he said in a post on X, thanking Musk for his “continued support.”
EU Disburses Another €2.86B to Cover Ukraine’s ‘Most Urgent Needs’ – Drones and Missiles
According to the latest estimates by Zelensky, Russia launched 124 drones overnight and another 145 during the day, with more than 40 Shaheds still in Ukraine’s airspace as he wrote.
UK fast-tracks missiles against jet-powered drones
Zelensky said he and Burnham agreed to speed up deliveries of British air defense systems to counter the jet-powered drones, which fly faster and higher than older Shahed models.
Earlier on Wednesday, The British government said it would accelerate deliveries of Lightweight Multirole Missiles (LMMs), under a £45 million (approximately $60 million) surface-to-air missile package, bringing forward £10 million (approximately $13 million) to meet Ukraine’s urgent winter needs.
“My message to the Ukrainian people could not be clearer, we are with you for as long as it takes, and we will go further and faster in our support to back your courageous fight for peace in Europe” Burnham said ahead of the meeting.
He has also tasked ministers with preparing new sanctions and further military and financial aid.
According to the BBC, Burnham greeted Zelensky at Downing Street with a military ceremonial guard – the first such honor for a foreign leader.
The visit followed a massive overnight strike in which Russia fired at least 39 missiles and 128 drones, cutting power to at least 600,000 people, according to Zelensky earlier in the day.
Questions over US intelligence sharing
The recent strains with Washington deepened after Ukraine received no early warning from Western partners about incoming Russian ballistic missiles for two nights in a row.
Zelensky said Kyiv’s systems detected the missiles only as they approached the capital.
Although NATO and EU, as well as Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said they had seen no sign that sharing had stopped, recent reports by other senior Ukrainian authorities appeared to suggest otherwise.
The lapse followed reports that Washington had threatened to cut intelligence sharing for Kyiv during roughly eight hours of talks in Miami on Friday, Oct. 9.
Reportedly, senior US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner warned Ukraine’s delegation that it could lose access to US intelligence if it kept striking Russian oil refineries.
Several US media separately reported that Trump’s administration also warned it could suspend the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) – a mechanism that enables European purchases of US weapons for Ukraine, the main channel for buying Patriot interceptors.
US Ambassador to NATO Matthew Whitaker denied the claims, saying that no change has been made.
On Oct. 9, Trump struck a diesel deal with Putin that eased US sanctions on Russian fuel, which 12 senators from both parties called “a betrayal of Ukraine” in a joint letter, urging the US President to rescind the diesel deal and enforce the new Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026.
Around the same time, Trump criticized Zelensky and said it was “time for Ukraine to get a new president.”
The US President then announced an energy truce on Oct. 11 that neither Kyiv nor Moscow confirmed, insisting the two sides agreed “because I said, ‘You agree.’”
Although Ukraine abided by the abrupt ceasefire announcement, Russia continued striking Ukraine nationwide. On Wednesday, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said that Trump’s energy truce was never defined, so Russia cannot be accused of breaking it.

Politico reported on October 13 that US President Donald Trump could cut off US intelligence support for Kiev or pressure Musk to disable SpaceX’s Starlink internet service, on which Ukraine’s military heavily relies. Zelensky said the same day that the US had not warned Ukraine about Russian missile launches the previous night.

NATO sees no threat of an imminent Russian attack but is ready to defend every inch of its territory – Rutte
Kyiv • UNN
Mark Rutte said that NATO has not detected preparations by Russia for an attack, but considers it a long-term threat. The Alliance is ready to respond to aggression.
NATO currently sees no signs that Russia is preparing for a direct attack on NATO countries, although Moscow remains a long-term threat to European security. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said this during a visit to Estonia, The Moscow Times reports, citing the secretary general's press conference, writes UNN.
Details
According to Rutte, Russia is currently not in the best position, and its hybrid attacks against European states indicate weakness rather than strength.
The secretary general stressed that the Alliance is not observing a buildup of Russian forces that could be used to invade NATO territory. At the same time, he assured that the allies would respond immediately if such preparations began.
NATO is ready to respond to any aggression
We will defend every inch of the territory of NATO countries, regardless of whether people live there or not, whether it is located near Paris, Tallinn, Washington, or Ottawa. We have all the necessary plans, and we are ready for this
He recalled that forward-deployed ground forces are already stationed along the Alliance's eastern flank. In addition, Supreme Allied Commander Europe Alexus Grynkewich previously warned that, in the event of an attack on any member state, the Alliance would destroy all forces involved in the aggression.
Rutte separately commented on Russia's hybrid operations in Europe. According to him, NATO has sufficient tools to counter sabotage and other threats, but not all retaliatory measures will be made public.
The secretary general explained that the Alliance's response would not necessarily be reciprocal. In some cases, the allies would respond symmetrically, while in others they would use different methods of counteraction without disclosing their details.

Spanish NGO halts Mediterranean rescue operations, citing fuel prices
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
20:10:15 UTC
05:10:15 KST

Spanish NGO halts Mediterranean rescue operations, citing fuel prices
SMH says it can no longer afford search-and-rescue work in one of the world’ss most dangerous migration routes.
A Spanish charity has postponed its next migrant rescue mission in the Central Mediterranean until next year due to rising fuel costs, underscoring the humanitarian impact of rising energy prices.
Salvamento Maritimo Humanitario (Humanitarian Maritime Rescue, or SMH) said on Wednesday that the doubling of fuel prices forced it to shift its activities to waters around Valencia, southeastern Spain.
The group, which operates a fishing vessel converted into a rescue ship, also launched a crowdfunding campaign to cover the extra costs.
The Central Mediterranean crossing from North Africa to Italy is one of the world’s most dangerous migration routes.
Many of those attempt the crossing on overcrowded, unsuitable boats from Libya’s coast, which has been a main transit point for migrants fleeing war and poverty in Africa and the Middle East.
A report released by the International Office for Migration said migrant sea crossings have dropped sharply since January this year.
The agency said about 60,000 migrants and refugees reached Europe by boat so far in 2026, down 39 percent from roughly 98,000 over the same period last year.
Despite the drop, at least 2,292 died or went missing attempting the crossing this year.
Spanish NGO Open Arms has said it scaled back its Central Mediterranean missions in recent years, also due to rising fuel costs as well as Italy’s policy of assigning rescue vessels ports in Northern Italy.
NGO ships from Spain typically sail for two to three days to reach their operating area, increasing costs and reducing time available for search-and-rescue work.
The Italian prime minister’s right-wing, anti-immigration government says humanitarian rescue attempts encourage migrants to make the crossing.

Slovakia is preparing to resume the work of the joint economic commission with Russia, whose activities were suspended after the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The meeting is scheduled for October 25. Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico announced this during a meeting of the parliamentary Committee on European Affairs, euBrief reports, as cited by UNN.
Details

To avoid any surprises, a joint economic commission with the Russian Federation will also be held on the 25th
Talks with Russia sparked criticism in Slovakia
Slovak Foreign Minister Juraj Blanár first announced the initiative to restore the commission in August. At the time, he reported a preparatory online meeting with Russian Science Minister Valery Falkov, who is under EU sanctions. The opposition criticized these contacts against the backdrop of Russian strikes on Ukraine.

OpenAI employee who left for Apple took files about unreleased device, OpenAI alleges
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
20:04:11 UTC
05:04:11 KST

An OpenAI employee who left the ChatGPT maker for Apple sent more than 100 files about an unreleased product to a personal account and later made a presentation about the unreleased product to senior Apple leadership, a new filing in the lawsuit between OpenAI and Apple alleges.
In a filing in US federal court in San Jose, California, OpenAI alleged that the presentation occurred months ago and that Apple is now developing its own AI products, citing the release of Apple's HomeView product this week.
"OpenAI is very concerned that its trade secret and confidential information is now circulating inside Apple, where Apple engineers can shape Apple’s upcoming products based on OpenAI’s confidential and innovative work," OpenAI said in its filing.
Apple said that it has policies and procedures in place to ensure new employees do not use confidential information from previous employers and that it has found no evidence to support OpenAI's allegations.
The document, filed on Tuesday, is part of an ongoing trade secret dispute that Apple filed earlier this year, in which it alleged that employees of the iPhone maker left and took confidential information to OpenAI's hardware division. OpenAI has denied those allegations.
US district court grants access to digital files from OpenAI
Earlier this week, US District Court Judge Edward Davila granted part of Apple's request to get early access to digital files from OpenAI in the suit.
Davila said Apple could gather data from some of its former employees' devices and sit three of them for depositions on a sped-up schedule, including the two defendants in the case, Chang Liu, a former senior system electrical engineer, and Tang Yew Tan, a former vice president of product design for iPhone and Apple Watch.
The case is likely to go to trial in October 2027, though OpenAI has said in court filings that it could be ready for trial as soon as June 2027.

Donald Trump has sparked outrage after sharing the distressing footage of a 23-year-old man with mental illness being fatally mauled by a tiger at Yorkshire Wildlife Park, captioned "Don't ever mess with nature!" This followed hours later by an AI-generated video of himself taming a tiger. The posts have been condemned as disrespectful to the victim, William Chapman, and his grieving family, who have urged people to stop sharing harrowing content of the attack. Vedika Bahl goes through it.
The 23-second video, posted to Truth Social without a caption, shows Trump wrestling with a tiger before appearing to befriend it, set to the song "The Lion Sleeps Tonight." It begins with Trump pointing his finger at the animal and ends with him playfully hugging it. The pointing gesture bears a resemblance to one made by the victim in the real footage.
Earlier, Trump had reposted the distressing real-life footage of the fatal attack, captioning it: "Don't ever mess with nature! President DJT." This post was also amplified by the White House’s Rapid Response 47 account on X.
Trump also shared other animal-related videos in his posting spree, including a compilation of animal attacks featuring some AI-generated clips, and another portraying him as a lion while comparing Democratic politicians to jackals.
The victim was identified as 23-year-old William Chapman, who died after entering a tiger enclosure at Yorkshire Wildlife Park on Saturday. His family described him as “bright, warm and engaging” and said he had lived with severe mental illness for several years, and was subsequently prescribed strong medication, and that the coroner will decide if this had a role in his death.
The family has also urged people to refrain from sharing photos and videos: "“The family are utterly devastated by their loss and are struggling to come to terms with what has happened. The publication and circulation of deeply offensive media content is causing them severe distress at an exceptionally vulnerable time. We ask people to stop doing this."

British broadcaster Piers Morgan called on Trump to delete the post, describing it as “appallingly tasteless”. Others suggested the president was seeking to distract attention from domestic political issues, although there is no evidence establishing his motive for sharing the videos.
One of the strongest rebukes came from Oliver Coppard, the mayor of South Yorkshire. He said the Chapman family had contacted his office about the distress caused by images and videos circulating online. He accused Trump of using AI to mock the tragedy and the family’s suffering for little more than a “cheap laugh on social media”.

Iran's framework deal with US helped Tehran strengthen military capabilities: Parliament speaker
Unknown
