Sahin Demir
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
The Iran-US framework deal reached this June gave Tehran extra time and resources to strengthen its military capabilities, said the country's parliament speaker on Wednesday.
In a televised address, Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf said Iran’s strategy in the war should combine military action with negotiations to establish what he called “sustainable deterrence.”
“We must be strong enough for the US, the world, and the region to understand that they cannot achieve their objectives,” he said.
Qalibaf argued that neither negotiations and signed agreements alone nor continued fighting would be enough to prevent future attacks on Iran.
He said Tehran should instead pursue a cycle of “war, negotiations, and deterrence,” fighting when necessary while using military gains to secure political advantages at the negotiating table.
“Our goal is to create deterrence by becoming stronger and to establish this strength in the enemy’s mind,” he said.
Qalibaf said Iran should turn military victories into political gains and use negotiations to obtain the resources and time needed to strengthen its capabilities.
Citing the framework deal reached with Washington in Islamabad, Pakistan in June, Qalibaf said Tehran had anticipated that the US would fail to honor its commitments and so structured the deal in two stages.
He claimed Iran had first achieved a “strategic advantage” on the battlefield before compelling Washington to accept the deal, describing the agreement as a “document of defeat” imposed on the US.
Qalibaf said the agreement gave Iran “sufficient time and resources” to strengthen what he called the country’s “components of power.”
He said the agreement helped Iran’s armed forces become stronger and also allowed the Hezbollah group in Lebanon to bolster its capabilities.
‘Resistance front’ and Iran’s deterrence
Qalibaf said Iran’s deterrence capabilities are not limited to its military, citing the strength of its “resistance front,” control over the Strait of Hormuz, national cohesion, social and economic resilience, and the country’s population as other components of deterrence.
On military capabilities, he claimed Iran’s offensive firepower and air defenses had significantly improved between last year’s 12-day war and the current conflict.
He said the cycle of “war, negotiations, and deterrence” would continue until Iran became strong enough that its adversaries no longer considered attacking the country.
Qalibaf also said the US must “change its behavior” and accept what he described as the legitimate demands of the Iranian people.
The framework deal was reached in Islamabad on June 18 following months of fighting that began with US-Israeli attacks on Iran in February, with Pakistan and Qatar acting as mediators.
The deal outlined steps toward ending hostilities, reopening the Strait of Hormuz, and beginning negotiations on outstanding disputes. Its implementation, however, has been complicated by renewed military confrontations and disagreements between Tehran and Washington over their respective commitments.
Iran has accused Washington of violating the deal and insists that fully reopening the strategic waterway depends on the US fulfilling its commitments, including easing its naval blockade and sanctions-related measures.
Tehran and Washington have continued indirect diplomatic contacts through regional mediators amid heightened tensions in and around the Strait of Hormuz.
Iranian officials have said they are reviewing a US proposal for renewed negotiations but insist that Tehran’s preconditions must be met before any talks can begin.
The diplomatic efforts come amid escalating maritime tensions, with commercial vessels targeted in and around the Strait of Hormuz and Tehran imposing restrictions on shipping routes it considers unauthorized.

The latest crisis to hit the party comes at a time when it has been stalling in the polls and faces problems including the fallout from a different undercover investigation which filmed senior officials discussing a potential way to secure foreign donations to the party.

Volodymyr Zelenskyy feels ‘betrayed’ by Donald Trump over Starlink access

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
19:35:55 UTC
04:35:55 KST

Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said he feels personally betrayed by Donald Trump after it emerged that Ukraine’s military has had its access to Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite squeezed, raising doubts about long-term US support for Kyiv.
The Ukrainian president, on a visit to London, accused Trump of picking the other side after more than four years of war, risking a breakdown in relations already strained by the US agreeing to buy diesel from Moscow.
Ahead of a meeting with prime minister Andy Burnham in Downing Street, Zelenskyy appeared in a TV interview where he was asked whether the sudden restriction of Starlink was deliberate and if he felt betrayed by Trump.
“Really, yes … but it’s a little bit more complicated than just my emotions or my feelings,” the Ukrainian president replied, adding: “It’s a pity that we are losing, we are losing a strong partner.”
Overnight, Ukraine’s military reported that, without explanation, the Starlink satellite communications system, produced by Musk’s SpaceX but managed by the US government, was no longer working at speeds greater than 100mph.
That effectively rendered most of the drones used by Ukraine to strike behind the frontlines inoperable – and, it later emerged, affected the most effective air defence system to stop Russian jet-powered attack drones bombing Kyiv.
“I am sure they knew what they did, absolutely. Because it was 1am at night, Starlink was blocked by SpaceX and the United States,” Zelenskyy said in an interview with Piers Morgan. “This decision will bring a lot of human losses … of course, people will die.”
The sudden outage came as Russia launched ballistic missiles at Ukraine without any advance warning from the US for a second night. For years, the US has provided Ukraine with intelligence when strikes were about to take place.
Trump denied that his administration had cut intelligence sharing on Tuesday, but Zelenskyy said in an interview with US broadcaster NPR, aired on Wednesday, that military advisers had received threats from the US that intelligence sharing could be limited in the future.
The US president has demanded that Ukraine stop striking Russian oil refineries, which he has blamed for the high cost of diesel, although most analysts say the closure of the strait of Hormuz after the US-Israel attack on Iran has had a far larger impact on global energy prices.
The two leaders fell out in the spring of 2025 during a disastrous visit by Zelenskyy to the Oval Office, where the US president said: “You don’t have the cards” to win the war. The row was followed by a brief pause in intelligence sharing and a desperate scramble by European allies to calm the row.
Burnham met Zelenskyy in Downing Street on Wednesday, hours after he promised MPs that the Ukrainian president “would not leave empty-handed” and that he had tasked officials with drawing up further sanctions and options for speeding up military aid.
As the pair met at No 10, he promised that Britain’s support for Ukraine would remain constant. “You have seen the solidarity and the support you have got from everybody here in Britain. We are behind you and that will not change,” he said.
Zelenskyy had met King Charles in Buckingham Palace earlier on Wednesday.
In brief remarks to reporters, Zelenskyy said he hoped to raise access to Starlink and intelligence sharing in his meeting with the British prime minister.
Burnham pledged that he would accelerate the supply of British lightweight multi-role missiles to Ukraine, which the country uses to counter Russian drone strikes and said they were looking for “all possible avenues” of further support.
The prime minister also said he was prepared to discuss the ceasefire proposed by Trump on attacks on energy infrastructure but acknowledged that Moscow had not abided by it.
“Sadly, what we have seen from Russia is further attacks on critical national infrastructure in Ukraine,” he said.
Earlier Burnham told MPs at PMQs that he wanted to be “careful” about potential criticism of Trump that might risk exacerbating tensions, saying he was “laying the ground” for a reconciliation: “I will listen to President Zelenskyy carefully, but he won’t be going away from Britain today empty-handed.”
The UK is also set to give £17m in funding towards repairs to the protective roof over the destroyed Chornobyl nuclear power plant which was damaged by Russian drone strike last year.
The meeting, which lasted just over an hour, began as Burnham greeted Zelenskyy with a hug on Downing Street, before the pair walked to the door of No 10 and posed for photographs, flanked by Irish Guards in full ceremonial uniform.
Musk said the decision to curtail Starlink was not one made by him. The communications system is not directly licensed to clients who are using weapons, and the Ukrainian military was linked to a related network called Starshield, which is operated by the US government.
“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” Musk said, referring to Trump.
Terminals travelling at more than 100mph and using a version of Starlink for the military and other national security agencies suddenly lost connectivity, said Serhiy Beskrestnov, an adviser on military technology to Zelenskyy, in what appeared to be a targeted outage meant to disrupt military operations.
“Our armed forces did not receive a warning about these restrictions and this led to the failure of a number of missions,” said Beskrestnov, who is also a popular military blogger. “It’s clear that this action cannot be a coincidence and is connected to the current political situation.”
Limiting Starlink’s access speeds would have a significant effect on Ukraine’s air defences because it is being used, according to Beskrestnov, in “the most current effective solution”: interceptors that target the jet-powered Shahed drones now deployed in large numbers to bomb Ukraine.
“With their actions, our partners are depriving us of one of the few chances we have to defend ourselves,” he added in a follow-up post. Shahed interception rates had already dropped from more than 90% to about 60% when Russia upgraded its engines to jet power in the early summer.
It also complicates Ukraine’s use of medium-range, mid-strike drones for hitting targets in its territories occupied by Russia. But, ironically, it would have no impact on Ukraine’s deep strike bombing of oil refineries because Kyiv is banned from using Starlink to hit targets inside of Russia.
Russia carried out a massive strike against Ukrainian energy infrastructure late on Tuesday evening, Zelenskyy said, launching 39 ballistic missiles and 120 attack drones against Kyiv and Kharkiv. The strikes hit five big power plants, key substations and other infrastructure that sustains major cities including Kyiv.
At least 600,000 people were now without power, he said, adding that outages could become more widespread.
Trump last week announced an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine that has not been confirmed. Zelenskyy said he had not heard of the deal until Trump announced it on his Truth Social site, and the Kremlin on Wednesday claimed it was abiding by the ceasefire because Trump had not specified which energy infrastructure it included.
Dmitry Peskov, the Kremlin’s spokesperson, told reporters: “The energy truce proposed by Trump was not specified in detail, so it cannot be claimed that Russia is failing to observe it.”

In case you needed more proof that leftists have turned feminism into a joke

In case you needed more proof that leftists have turned feminism into a joke
In nanny states, men become state-dependent tradbros whose solution to an inadequate allowance is to pitch a fit, women get infantilized, and kids become insufferable. But what happens when someone dares to step out of line?
Enter Louise Montagnon – a 22-year-old master’s student, right-wing activist, and recent municipal National Rally candidate from Bordeaux, who has been all over French media debating the young left-wing activists indulging in synchronized tantrums across France, some burning their schools down to protest the lack of educational space. When a country is sufficiently infantilized, you may as well send young people to fight each other on ideological front lines over problems ginned up mostly by grey-haired men.
Montagnon is refusing to sing the dominant tune. “You are the useful idiots of this movement,” she told 17-year-old Erwan on television. He made his name by publicly draping himself over left-wing leader Jean-Luc Melenchon and kissing him on the cheek, having already mastered the politician’s mannerisms while explaining why student life sucked at his slum of a Parisian school near Montmartre. The academy boasts a majestic courtyard and a €120 million renovation project. His particular hardship was having to put in full days.
Montagnon’s message was that the kid hadn’t seen much of the working world and might want to compare class timetables with her before declaring himself a victim. Her argument is dangerous to the movement because if one person can manage, then why can’t you? And when that person is a young woman, the reality becomes especially inconvenient for young men.
Which would explain the violent reaction to this young woman’s mere existence. “Last year, I had to leave my classes during the year because it was no longer possible for safety reasons,” she said during a media appearance. “When you arrive at university and there are 80 people waiting to kick you out, you are no longer safe.” She also explained that during student elections, the library staff wanted her to leave despite what she described as about 200 “brainless leftists” waiting for her outside.
It has also emerged that back in February, she was reportedly distributing campaign literature when her young female colleague was pushed to the ground and she was thrown up against a wall.
Women’s groups lament the Taliban’s exclusion of girls from education, yet appear conspicuously absent when a young woman in France says that intimidation has interfered with her university life. Women should be able to study and participate in public life without being threatened into submission – but only subject to ideological approval or an adequate score on the most superficial diversity scale, apparently.
Montagnon’s offence is actively denouncing the left-wing status quo, exercising her democratic right to dissent. The very sort of independent thinking that feminism is supposed to celebrate – until the independent thinker backs the wrong party or causes.
She fails the longstanding litmus test to qualify for sisterly support. Feminism has become entangled with identity politics in much of the movement, to the point where a woman on the right can demonstrate intellectual independence, self-determination, and meritocratic qualities, yet still be treated as a threat to the ideological monoculture that became synonymous with the feminist movement ever since it sprang up around left-wing actions in the civil rights era.
Women should work to get ahead, provided they’re of the right sort, say the right things, and frame their achievements as contributions to the collective. Individual initiative is welcome, as long as it doesn’t become an inconvenient example of what can be done without adhering to a left-wing political script. And the collective must remain a perpetual victim. Otherwise, what’s even the point of its existence?
There’s something ironically paternalistic about a movement that champions women’s freedom while demonstrating – through its action or inaction – that it reserves the right to decide which of them are valid.
Turns out that the system that Montagnon is being told to navigate may not even be capable of delivering the meritocratic returns that her hard work warrants. Not anymore. Just look at France’s finances.
The country’s debt has climbed well above the EU’s 60%-of-GDP reference value. Now the government needs to rummage around in the couch cushions to find savings in the hope that ordinary people won’t notice, by scratching a few bucks here and there from health-care reimbursements and by de-indexing pension spending from inflation. Seems that the best outcome that Montagnon can hope for is a worthy spot in a broken system that won’t parasitize her hard work too much.
The state has failed this young woman. Not because she’s a woman per se, but because she insists on living her life like a full-fledged human being without limitations that the left imposes on one’s possibilities – either through peer pressure or its insistence on victimhood. And no amount of lip service to women’s rights will compensate when the most basic conditions needed for self-sufficiency to thrive have deteriorated to the point where the hardworking middle class gets exploited as a cash cow.
Montagnon also happens to have stumbled upon institutional feminism’s most shameful secret: the sisterhood is universal in its advertising, but highly selective in its customer service. And particularly as the broke nanny state fails in its effort to placate the handout-insistent masses, women’s liberation should mean embracing and championing independent, freedom-minded women on the right actively seeking to break those shackles. Otherwise, we’re just arguing over who gets to hold the leash.

&quot;Roof of Europe&quot; has shrunk — Mont Blanc lost more than a metre in height in a year
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
22:32:56 EEST
04:32:56 KST

"Roof of Europe" has shrunk — Mont Blanc lost more than a metre in height in a year
Kyiv • UNN
Mont Blanc's height has decreased to 4,807.47 metres due to changes in snow and ice. Experts do not associate the annual fluctuations with the loss of glacial mass.
The highest mountain in Western Europe shrank by more than a metre last year. The summit of Mont Blanc in France now stands at 4,807.47 metres above sea level, a team of surveyors said on Wednesday, putting the "roof of Europe" 1.29 metres lower than in 2025, UNN reports, citing The Guardian.
Details
The mountain is approximately 4,792 metres high, but its summit is constantly shifting as heat, wind and precipitation alter the thickness of the snow and ice at the top. The height recorded by scientists during an expedition last month was 1.88 metres greater than in 2023, when it reached its lowest level in recent times.
Certified surveyors from the National Union of Geometry Experts (UNGE) and the Order of Geometry Experts, who have regularly monitored the summit since 2001, used precise satellite technology to measure the mountain and drones to create a detailed model of its snow and ice cap.
The data show that the summit has decreased by 3.43 metres from its height of 4,810.90 metres in 2007.
Experts caution against linking year-to-year fluctuations in elevation with the rapid loss of alpine ice caused by fossil-fuel pollution.
"Regarding the mass of ice, it is important to distinguish between changes in elevation above sea level and changes in the total volume or mass of ice," a UNGE representative said. "An increase in the summit's elevation does not necessarily mean that the mountain has gained glacial mass, and it does not contradict the documented retreat of alpine glaciers."
Climate deterioration contributed to the hottest summer in Western Europe since records began this year, scarring alpine regions and melting ice at a dizzying rate. Earlier this month, Swiss glaciologists warned of an "explosion in the rate of melting" after confirming that one-fifth of the country's ice had been lost over the past five years, while 5.5% of its volume was lost between 2025 and 2026.
Jean de Garet, president of the departmental chamber of surveyors of Haute-Savoie and leader of the expedition to Mont Blanc, said that the warming trend could be seen with the naked eye across the rest of the Alpine massif, but "at the moment, climate change does not appear to have the same impact above 4,000 metres".
"As we climb, we pass the Brigade Blanche hut before the Tête Rousse glacier," he said in comments to French television channel TF1 on Wednesday. "We saw that the glacier had receded. It literally melted before our eyes, and now in some places we cross a stream rather than a glacier."

Trump’s new press secretary faces scrutiny over claims to be a lawyer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
19:12:29 UTC
04:12:29 KST

Donald Trump’s new press secretary, Katie Zacharia, has repeatedly described herself as a lawyer. But when asked after her inaugural press briefing on Tuesday to name the state where she passed the bar exam, she replied curiously: “when I moved to China”.
No public record shows she has ever been licensed to practice law in the US states where she resided, and her answer to reporters’ questions on Tuesday only deepened scrutiny.
Zacharia wasn’t registered in 38 states, as well as DC and the Virgin Islands, where the state’s attorney list was publicly available, according to a review from the Guardian.
After her shaky and widely panned first briefing, a reporter asked Trump which state Zacharia had passed the bar exam in. The president, who had described Zacharia as an attorney when announcing her appointment, turned to her and asked: “Which state?” She replied: “when I moved to China”.
Zacharia’s law degree is real – Pepperdine University confirmed she graduated from its law school in 2011. But a degree is not a license, and no record has surfaced showing she was admitted to practice, according to the report in Popular Information.
In a later statement to the press, Zacharia said she had “practiced international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials”. The White House did not say whether she had passed a bar exam anywhere.
Zacharia’s LinkedIn profile lists her as general counsel of Fix California, a conservative group founded by Ric Grenell, a longtime Trump ally and the special presidential envoy for special missions. Zacharia lived in California, but the state bar of California said it had no record of her being licensed in the state.
“The State Bar of California has no record of Kate Sharon Zacharia or Kate Sharon Black (or Katie in both instances) having been licensed to practice law in California,” a spokesperson for the California state bar said in a statement. Black is her maiden name.
“Due to confidentiality laws, the State Bar can only confirm whether someone passed the bar exam, not whether they took the bar exam,” it added.
No report alleges that Zacharia has been charged with or has committed an offence.
Campaign for Accountability, a non-profit watchdog organization, on Wednesday filed a complaint with the state bar of California, asking it to investigate whether Zacharia misled the public – and potentially violated state law – by describing herself as a lawyer.
“In California, calling yourself a lawyer without a license isn’t puffery; it’s a crime,” said Michelle Kuppersmith, the group’s executive director, in a statement.
California law says anyone “advertising or holding himself or herself out as practicing or entitled to practice law” who is not an active member of the state bar could be punished with a fine of up to $1,000 and up to one year in jail.
“There is a difference between having a JD and being a lawyer, you are licensed as a lawyer by saying that you took the bar,” said Richard Painter, a university of Minnesota law professor and the former chief White House ethics lawyer under the George W Bush administration. “Calling yourself an attorney … it’s a misdemeanor at least.”
Zacharia’s LinkedIn notes that she was remote while at Fix California. But Painter said that was “not relevant – you need to be a member of the bar”.
The profile also says she worked as an associate at the Beijing firm Zhong Lun from 2011 to 2013. Only Chinese citizens can be licensed as lawyers in China, according to Chinese law and legal affairs website China Justice Observer, though foreign staff can work at Chinese firms in other capacities.
The Washington Post, CNN and the independent newsletter Popular Information also found no sign of admission elsewhere, including Texas and Washington DC, where Popular Information said she had worked. The Post found no active or expired admissions under either of her names.
The press office of Gavin Newsom, California’s governor, mocked the exchange on X, asking whether the new press secretary “appears to be a Chinese lawyer”. Steven Cheung, the White House director of communications, in the meantime described her briefing performance as “tremendous” and “commanding”.
Zacharia was relatively unknown when Trump announced her selection to be his next press secretary last week, after the departure of Karoline Leavitt earlier this year. In the days since, several outlets have uncovered a series of since-deleted social media posts that promote debunked or baseless conspiracy.
In a series of now-deleted social media posts on X, reviewed by the Guardian, Zacharia fawned over Tesla and Space X founder, Elon Musk.
On 22 May 2022, the new press secretary described Musk, a tech billionaire and Trump ally, as “based”. She went on to explain the term was applied “when you want to recognize someone for being themselves” and “courageous and unique or not caring what others think”.
In another post from the same year, Zacharia also responded to one user sharing a widely circulated picture of Musk and Ghislaine Maxwell, the co-conspirator of the late sex-offender Jeffrey Epstein, at the Vanity Fair Oscar party in 2014, where Zacharia wrote “oh please, he already responded to this #oldnews”.
Musk has not been charged with any wrongdoing in connection with Epstein, and has denied knowing Maxwell, claiming the photo which pictures her standing close to him is because she “photobombed” him.
In other now-deleted posts, also from the same period, Zacharia directed various complimentary messages at Musk. “#IstandwithElon,” she wrote in one. In another she praised him for renouncing his support for the Democratic party and saying he would now support Republicans. “Smartest and richest man in the world right here is saying out loud what everyone else is thinking,” Zacharia wrote.
However, last year Zacharia questioned whether Musk could have been trusted “from the beginning” while appearing as a guest on conservative commentator Buck Sexton’s podcast.
“He’s heavily invested in China. A lot of people were questioning his allegiance to begin with. Where is his allegiance completely?” she asked on the show. In late 2025, Musk and Trump had a public falling out of the president’s sweeping domestic policy legislation. They have since reconciled and Musk, according to the New York Times, is spending record sums to help Republicans retain control of the midterm elections this cycle.
The Bulwark previously reported on Zacharia’s since-deleted posts where she called on the administration to “suspend habeas corpus” – the constitutional right to challenge detention before a judge.
Meanwhile CNN also found now-deleted social media posts where Zacharia wrote and reshared comments that accused prominent political figures and Hollywood elites of pedophilia. This includes longtime Democratic operative John Podesta – who was the notable target of the debunked Pizzagate conspiracy – which alleged that several prominent Democrats were part of a child sex-trafficking ring.

UN: Lebanon stability as end of peacekeepers' mandate looms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
19:11:41 UTC
04:11:41 KST

Breadcrumb
UN says wants Lebanon stability as end of peacekeepers' mandate looms
A visiting senior United Nations official on Wednesday reaffirmed the body's commitment to stability in Lebanon as the mandate of its peacekeeping force in the country is set to expire this year.
Under-Secretary-General for Peace Operations Jean-Pierre Lacroix met officials as well as representatives of countries contributing to the UN Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL), which counts some 7,500 personnel from nearly 50 countries.
"I thanked them for their critical support to UNIFIL and reiterated the UN's strong commitment to supporting peace and stability in Lebanon," Lacroix said.
UNIFIL has served as a buffer between Israel and Lebanon since 1978, but its presence has been unable to prevent several rounds of conflict.
Under US pressure, the UN Security Council last year voted to end UNIFIL's mandate on December 31, 2026.
Lebanese officials have called for the mandate to be extended.
President Joseph Aoun told Lacroix that Lebanon "is keen on UNIFIL staying, considering the importance of the role that it has played from the start of its mission until today", according to a statement from his office.
"The circumstances resulting from Israel's attacks and occupation of southern villages and towns... make the presence of international forces extremely important," Aoun added.
UNIFIL's "withdrawal will create a vacuum that will have negative repercussions on the security situation in the region", he warned.
'Must be heard'
After meeting Aoun, Lacroix said "we know about Lebanon's positions including the letter which it sent to the United Nations requesting a temporary extension of the UNIFIL mandate".
"The positions of the Lebanese authorities must be heard and taken into consideration," he said.
In July, 86 Lebanese lawmakers signed a letter addressed to the UN Security Council calling for UNIFIL troops to remain with an expanded mandate.
Lebanese militant group Hezbollah drew the country into the broader Middle East war in March by attacking Israel, which responded with massive airstrikes and a ground invasion that Lebanon says have killed more than 4,300 people.
The looming UNIFIL deadline comes as Israeli forces continue to occupy a self-declared "security zone" that runs around 10 kilometres (six miles) inside south Lebanon along the border.
Violence has decreased since a US-Iran understanding in June, and a US-sponsored Lebanon-Israel framework agreed later that month.
The framework deal involves the disarmament of Hezbollah, a gradual withdrawal of Israeli forces from Lebanon's south and the deployment of the Lebanese army to the region, starting in test areas known as "pilot zones", but the process has largely stalled.
Visiting EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas told AFP last week that the bloc was in favour of extending UNIFIL's mandate, also warning against a "security vacuum".
France and Italy have said they want to set up a multinational coalition to succeed UNIFIL.

Jewish teachers cancel Italy trip over ‘antisemitic pressure’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
19:10:19 UTC
04:10:19 KST

Educators from Jewish schools across the US canceled a study trip to Reggio Emilia, Italy, over whether the hosts would require participants to formally distance themselves from Israel’s actions in Gaza and the West Bank.
The controversy has drawn accusations of antisemitism from Jewish educators and from Italian Jewish community leaders. It has also sparked a political dispute in Italy.
In an email sent to participants on October 9, the American organizers, the Paradigm Project, said they canceled the trip because of “antisemitic pressure being placed on the group.” In a Zoom call with the participants, the organizers also cited safety concerns amid the scrutiny of the Jewish school educators’ personal profiles by pro-Palestinian activists who were agitating for the declaration, a participant said.
Reggio Children considered asking for declarations distancing themselves from 'genocide'
In a leaked audio recording broadcast Monday evening by Italy’s Tg3 TV news program, the president of the host organization Reggio Children, Maddalena Tedeschi, discussed asking participants to sign declarations distancing themselves from the “occupation of territories and genocide.” The recording is of an October 6 meeting of the city’s early childhood education council.
In an interview with the Jewish Telegraphic Agency, Reggio Children spokesperson Francesca Severini said the request, intended to appease local pro-Palestinian activists, had never become an official participation requirement, but acknowledged that the additional wording had been discussed.
The Paradigm Project, a professional development network for Jewish early childhood educators, organized the trip for 68 Jewish educators. A separate delegation of 22 educators from Israel arrived in Reggio and was participating in the program this week.
“Now, more than ever, we must bring back the light and keep the bridge between us strong,” the Israeli educators said in opening remarks Monday.
Reggio Children, an educational organization partly owned by the municipality, promotes the city’s internationally influential approach to early childhood education and provides training for educators. Reggio Emilia Mayor Marco Massari and the city’s education official Marwa Mahmoud did not respond to requests for comment.
Pro-Palestinian activists protest ties to Israel
The cancellation, which came in a phone call from Paradigm to Reggio Children on October 7, follows months of tensions in the city, where pro-Palestinian activists had protested the participating schools’ ties to Israel. During the weeks preceding the trip, activist Cosimo Pederzoli had publicly accused some of the schools of supporting the Israeli military.
At the Oct. 6 meeting, Reggio Children presented a charter, titled “For a Democratic and Participatory Education,” asking visiting groups and partners to uphold human rights, oppose discrimination, reject war, and condemn genocide. The charter, which was approved and is now on the organization’s website, also opposes violations of human rights in occupied territories worldwide, without naming Israel or Gaza.
Severini, the spokesperson, said that activists, teachers and parents had pressured Reggio Children and the municipality to take the charter one step further and require participants to agree to the statement: “I … hereby declare that I distance myself from the occupation of Gaza and the violation of children’s and human beings’ rights in occupied territories as well as every place in the world.”
Severini said that the wording was included as “material for discussion” in a private WhatsApp group. The American organizers were not in the chat, she said, and subsequently received the wording without the context that it would not, in the end, be official language.
Her account contradicts Reggio Children’s earlier public statements. On October 7, the organization acknowledged that the educators had been asked to explicitly distance themselves from the policies of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government in response to concerns raised in the city. Mayor Marco Massari also acknowledged the additional commitment in a public statement, which says, “This Charter will be signed by all delegations visiting Reggio Emilia in the coming months and years.”
In an email to parents, leaders of Wilshire Boulevard Temple’s early childhood centers in Los Angeles said seven of their educators had been scheduled to join the trip and expressed support for Paradigm’s decision to cancel.
“Paradigm, on behalf of our educators and dozens of others, rightfully refused and canceled participation in the study tour and conference, due to the refusal to sign and other security considerations,” read the email. “All participants were notified on October 7, 2026.”
Pesha Kletenik, head of Manhattan Day School, had planned to join the trip. “This was one of the most painful experiences I’ve had,” Kletenik told JTA. “I never felt so targeted as a Jew before in my life. I’m an American citizen. I have one passport. I’ve lived here my entire life.”
Kletenik said she had hoped to adapt the Reggio approach to Jewish teaching and practice, including their model Passover seder, because “it aligns so beautifully with Jewish values.”
Steve Freedman, head of Schechter Bergen in New Jersey, said his school withdrew an educator from a separate trip planned for November. In a letter to families, he criticized the demand for a political declaration while affirming the school’s commitment to the Reggio approach.
The council of the Jewish Community of Modena and Reggio Emilia, a single institution based in nearby Modena that serves both cities, condemned efforts to boycott educational and cultural initiatives involving Jews. It described the conflation of diaspora Jews with Israel’s government as antisemitic.
The Reggio Emilia approach, developed after World War II by educator Loris Malaguzzi and local families, places children’s exploration, expression, and participation at the center of early childhood learning. It gained wider international recognition after Newsweek named one of the city’s preschools among the world’s 10 best schools in 1991.
Severini said Reggio Children’s relationships with American Jewish and Israeli educators stretch back roughly three decades. The Israeli liaison first visited in 1996, she said, and educators from Reggio have also traveled to the United States and Israel.
The organization has hosted educators from all over the world, Severini said, including China, Russia, and Iran. She said she knew of no comparable controversy involving other visiting groups, including previous delegations from Jewish schools.
Reggio Children, she said, hoped to continue its dialogue with the American educators. For Manhattan Day School’s Kletenik, the cancellation stood in stark contrast with the educational values that had drawn her to the approach.
“How are we to navigate rejection by the very experts we collectively idealized, the gatekeepers of the sensitive worldviews and teachings we trusted to nurture our most tender children?” she wrote in a message to her school’s board.

Bangladesh arrests two for luring locals to fight for Russia in Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
19:02:51 UTC
04:02:51 KST

Bangladesh arrests two for luring locals to fight for Russia in Ukraine
Twenty Bangladeshi victims have been killed after being used by Russia as ‘bait’ to locate enemy positions, police say.
Police in Bangladesh have arrested two people they say are linked to a trafficking network that deceptively recruited locals to fight for Russia in Ukraine.
The suspects, identified as Mizanur Rahman and Abu Taher, trafficked at least 30 people to Russia with false promises of high-paying jobs, Mohammad Asaduzzaman, commander of the elite police force Special Response Battalion, said on Wednesday.
Once abroad, the victims’ passports and phones were taken, and they were handed over to the Russian military, he said.
Seventeen of the trafficking victims, who arrived in Russia in early May, were killed on the first day of deployment after being given minimal training, Asaduzzaman said. A total of 20 Bangladeshis have been confirmed dead.
“Bangladeshis were used as bait to locate enemy positions,” he said. “Russian forces determined their next course of action after the Bangladeshis fell victim to drone attacks.”
In addition to the 20 Bangladeshis killed, two more are being treated in a Moscow hospital while six others are still on the battlefield, police cited a survivor who was injured and managed to return home as saying.
The victims were from poor backgrounds and had paid around $8,000 for the fake jobs that brought them to Russia, Bangladeshi media reported.
Both Russia and Ukraine have recruited thousands of foreign nationals into their armies since Russia launched its invasion of Ukraine four and a half years ago.
An estimated 28,000 foreigners from 136 countries are said to be fighting in the Russian army, and officials believe Moscow deployed some 14,000 North Korean troops to battle Ukraine’s 2024 incursion into the Kursk region.
Meanwhile, Ukraine says 16,000 foreign nationals from more than 70 countries – including nearly 40 percent from Latin America – are currently serving in its army.
Speaking at the United Nations General Assembly last month, Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned that Russia deceptively recruits people from 47 countries for an “absolutely brutal” campaign and urged countries not to let Moscow “drag” them into the war.
Amnesty International has also accused Russia of using “deceptive, coercive and exploitative practices” to recruit foreigners to fight on the Ukrainian front.
Russia has previously dismissed accusations of coercing foreigners into joining its army.
Amnesty says it cannot conduct inquiries about foreigners in Ukraine’s army as it has no access to prisoners of war held in Russia, which designates the rights group as a “foreign agent”.

Trump’s war on Iran is poised to sink his party in the midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
18:55:56 UTC
03:55:56 KST

The experts love to say that Americans don’t vote based on foreign policy, but it doesn’t take much digging to conclude that isn’t always true.
Sure, U.S. voters are probably thinking primarily about domestic issues when they go to the polls, but there have been a number of big elections in which war has undoubtedly been a major factor.
The Iraq War was the definitive issue of the 2008 Democratic primary, when then-Senator Barack Obama (who opposed the war) beat then-Senator Hillary Clinton, who voted for it. In 2016, Trump generated support by railing against “endless wars” and calling the U.S. invasion of Iraq “a big, fat mistake.” Most recently, Kamala Harris’s refusal to oppose the Gaza genocide helped seal her 2024 loss.
It’s hard to believe that foreign policy won’t be a major factor in November’s midterms, as Trump’s disastrous war on Iran continues to spin out of control with no discernible signs of an exit strategy.
At the beginning of the summer, it seemed that the administration was on the verge of securing an agreement, but its inability to restore the Strait of Hormuz to its pre-war status simply generated a series of botched negotiations and idle threats.
Americans are enduring astronomical gas prices, but they’re also seeing another “Forever War” potentially take shape, and although the Trump team has sought to censor details on the war, news about the scope of the conflict has inevitably trickled out.
A recent Congressional Research Service report reveals that 81 U.S. military aircrafts have been destroyed or damaged in the war. The Intercept’s Nick Turse points out that the Pentagon quietly raised its official count of U.S. casualties to 21, a full six months after Maj. Sorffly Davius died while “conducting operations” at Camp Buehring in Kuwait. According to estimates by Moody’s Analytics’ chief economist Mark Zandi, the war has cost U.S. consumers $265 billion so far, which is roughly $2,000 for every household.
An extensive Drop Site News investigation into the February 28 attack on a Minjab school revealed that at least 156 people were killed, 120 of them children.
“Why is [Trump] saying Iran may have bombed their own people when we can see the wreckage of Raytheon cruise missiles in the photos that we obtained that were taken from under the rubble?,” journalist Jeremy Scahill, who led the report, told NPR. “There were two direct hits on a school filled with children and teachers. It’s not that there hasn’t been reporting on this. It’s that reporting has not been translated into a very robust, aggressive investigation of what I would say is one of the worst single war crimes committed by the United States since Vietnam.”
Polling shows that war was unpopular with the U.S. population from the beginning, but recent surveys show that approval has continued to plummet. According to the Pew Research Center, just 34% of Americans believe that attacking Iran was the right decision, down from 38% in March. That shift has come entirely from Republican voters. 63% of them now believe it was the right call, compared to 69% who believed that in March.
This reality has forced some Republicans, like Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers and Ohio Sen. Jon Husted, to walk a tightrope between calling for an end to the war and remaining loyal to the President.
“The war can no longer be treated solely as a matter of executive decisions and geopolitical calculations,” writes political scientist Brian Hudson. “Responsibility extends beyond the White House to lawmakers who have supported its continuation, remained silent, or used party unity as a substitute for public debate. Accountability is no longer simply an external demand imposed on the party; it has become an internal issue affecting its credibility and cohesion.”
It’s also become an issue that Democrats can pin on the opposition party.
“It’s less Iran in particular than it is this notion of never-ending conflict and war in the Middle East, which Americans are so done with,” declared Rep. Jason Crow, who is demanding answers on a U.S. airstrike that killed at least 5 people attending a wedding in Iran. “It is very salient.”
This week, Democratic challenger Troy Jackson hammered GOP Senator Susan Collins (D-ME) on the issue during a debate, pointing out that the longtime incumbent voted for the war multiple times, despite currently expressing a desire for it to end.
“The reason why our fuel prices is going through the roof, and the way our — the reason why our electricity costs are going through the roof is because the cost of fuel, cost of oil is so high, because she wouldn’t stop President Trump with the Iran war,” he told the crowd.
Conservative W. James Antle III, Executive Editor of The Washington Examiner Magazine, writes that Republicans were always expected to lose some seats as an extension of being in power, but that anger over the war could sustain a massive electoral shellacking.
“Thanks to the Iran war and its fallout, there is a potential for a midterm election more like 2006. Twenty years ago, as Cook Political Report’s Amy Walter pointed out earlier this year, we had an unpopular president waging an unpopular war while Republican congressional incumbents were beset by assorted scandals,” he writes in Responsible Statecraft. “Today, the public has even less patience for the current war than in 2006.”
The reality is that the GOP is headed for a potential disaster in a few weeks, thanks in no small part to Trump’s terrible war.

NIH appears to shut down comments on science peer-review rule change ahead of schedule
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
18:55:23 UTC
03:55:23 KST

Members of the public who tried to submit their views on a proposed change to the National Institutes of Health’s grant funding system say they found themselves locked out after the system shut down ahead of schedule.
The proposed change has been criticized as potentially reducing transparency. It seeks to revise how grant application scores—averaged measures of a research project's predicted outcomes—are communicated to both funding applicants and NIH program officers.
Under the change, applications would be sorted into three broad categories of merit, while their overall score, as determined by a panel of experts, would remain a secret. Some researchers have said this could open up the grant approval process to undue political influence.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Ahead of any rule change, the NIH invited members of the public to have their voices heard by submitting comments through a website portal, which opened in August. On a version of the site soliciting comments stored on the Wayback Machine, the deadline is shown as “11:59:59 P.M. EST [sic]” on October 13. The system for sending in comments appeared to shut down hours early, however, with several scientists posting on social media that when they tried to submit comments ahead of that time, they were unable to do so. Speaking to Scientific American, Joshua Weitz, a biology professor at the University of Maryland, says he attempted to access the site before the midnight deadline and could not.
The proposal marks the latest attempt by the Trump administration to have greater influence over federal science grants. Floated earlier this year, a separate bid to have political appointees—rather than independent expert panels—decide grant recipients garnered significant backlash. That earlier proposal was put on hold until at least December after Congress rejected the change.
The NIH did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Spain’s ruling Socialists widened their lead over the conservative opposition in a state poll released Wednesday, contrasting with other surveys that favor the right ahead of a snap election dominated by the housing crisis.
The Center for Sociological Research (CIS) put Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s party at 34%, nearly 12 percentage points ahead of the Popular Party (PP), compared with a 5.5-point lead last month.

Anomalous poll
However, the CIS findings contrast sharply with other polls suggesting the conservatives and far right could win enough seats to govern together.
A 40db survey for El Pais and Cadena SER conducted after the election announcement gave the PP and Vox a combined lead of about 15 points over the Socialists, Sumar, and Podemos.

The divergence is not new. An El Pais analysis of 44 elections since 2018 found that CIS surveys overestimated support for the left in 43 of them.

In Ukraine, civilian casualties were already rising. Restrictions on Starlink will only worsen the death toll
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
18:54:34 UTC
03:54:34 KST

In Ukraine the situation was already jittery enough. Donald Trump has been inventing ceasefires and buying Russian diesel to shore up his flagging popularity, while a sinister new wave of faster, jet-powered drones are breaking through Kyiv’s stretched air defences. Casualties are rising as the weather turns.
Overnight, Russia bombed three power plants that supply Kyiv, aiming to cut off heating and electricity to the city. According to the president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, for a second night in a row no warning came from Ukraine’s western allies of the incoming ballistic missiles – and so no air raid alert was issued.
Then, on Tuesday night, and without warning, Ukraine’s military found that Elon Musk’s Starlink mobile internet system, on which it heavily relies, had stopped working on its drones flying faster than 160km/h (100mph).
Or at least that was the official limit: in practice, drones flying over 80km/h could no longer communicate.
The immediate assumption in Kyiv is that the White House is once again trying to bully Ukraine into accepting an unattractive deal with Russia.
However, on Tuesday Trump did say that no intelligence-sharing had been paused, and similar comments were made by Mark Rutte, the secretary general of Nato on Wednesday. It is possible the lack of ballistic warning is coincidental.
Even Serhii Beskrestnov, Zelenskyy’s high-profile military technology adviser, has expressed public doubts about whether the US had paused the sharing of missile detection. “Friends, this is not the first time that the launch of an S-400 has not been detected,” he posted on Monday. “We should not jump to conclusions.”
However, there has now been an absence of incoming warnings for two days in a row. The second of these was in tandem with the unexpected throttling of Starlink, a system supplied by Musk with the approval of the US military.
So it is hardly reassuring against the backdrop of White House threats, which have emerged every time a flailing Trump has tried to end the war in Ukraine.
The last time Trump paused intelligence-sharing – which is, in effect, valuable information about Russian positions and movements – was in March 2025, shortly after Zelenskyy’s infamous dusting down in the Oval Office.
“You don’t have the cards,” Trump said, as he took another away. Ukraine rapidly lost a chunk of territory it had occupied in Russia’s Kursk region before sharing was restored.
A confirmed pause this time would mark a serious breach when Ukraine is more than holding off its larger neighbour on the frontline, even as the situation on the home front is worsening.
Russia has bombed two bridges in Kyiv, gas stations, city centre buildings and out-of-town warehouses, showing little restraint as it aims to harm Ukrainian civilians while it struggles to win the conventional war.
The effect of a more permanent halt to Starlink for Ukrainian drones or anything military that moves faster than 50mph is a little more complex. Starlink is how Ukraine directs many of its mid-strike (or mid-range) drones accurately towards their targets into occupied areas behind enemy lines, critical for helping the defenders maintain the rough balance on the front.
Yet, ironically, Starlink is not used for the long-range missions that target the Russian oil refineries about which Trump is so concerned, because it has long been disabled by the company inside Russia’s internationally recognised borders.
“There’s no meaningful effect on deep-strike operations,” one Ukrainian soldier said, while conceding there could be as much as a 30-fold drop in mid-strike operations because the alternatives are 30 times more expensive. Commanders are “replanning everything”, the soldier added, and aiming to find ways to carry on missions using different technologies and techniques.
Starlink is also, more importantly – as Beskrestnov emphasised on Wednesday – used by air-defence interceptors in the most effective system to down Russia’s deadly new jet-powered Shahed drones. These are at least twice as fast as traditional piston-engined Shaheds, and Ukraine’s rate of interception had dropped to 60% in September, before recovering to 75% according to the country’s air force.
The reality, then, is that the Starlink manoeuvre may not have much impact on oil prices, and only a limited effect on Ukraine’s frontline position, while putting the country’s civilians in greater danger.
As the Ukrainian human rights activist Oleksandra Matviichuk put it: “Without that protection, Russian drones will strike residential buildings, hospitals and schools like targets in a shooting gallery.”
Meanwhile, diplomatically, the situation is more finely poised. It was already the case that the Trump White House had proved to be a difficult and unreliable partner. What Zelenskyy, on a visit to London on Wednesday, needs from the likes of the UK prime minster, Andy Burnham, is pressure on the US to ensure the Starlink pause and whatever is happening with intelligence-sharing does not metastasise into a deeper crisis.

A statement said that officers felt "betrayed" by their political leaders because of their "unclear instructions" and what they said were public expressions of "empathy towards the rioters".
French authorities have expressed hope that the student protest movement would ease in coming days because of two weeks of school holidays that start at the weekend.

Education Minister Edouard Geffray told parliament that a third of France's 3,700 lycees, high schools for students aged 15 to 18, had been strongly impacted by the protests, with another third impacted to a limited degree.

Reservists lose municipal-tax discounts after wartime protection expires, petition says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
18:35:20 UTC
03:35:20 KST

Low-income reservists who spent months in IDF reserve service are losing municipal property-tax discounts because their reserve payments push them above income limits, according to a petition Jerusalem’s Hitorerut movement says it submitted to the High Court of Justice on Tuesday.
The movement is seeking to restore a protection that expired at the end of 2025, leaving some students facing full property-tax (arnona) bills after previously receiving discounts of 80%. It argues that the government failed to renew the arrangement despite advance warnings and assurances that it would continue.
One case concerns a Hebrew University medical student who served 425 reserve days from the outbreak of the war through August 6, 2026, including 118 days in 2025. According to the petition, he received an 80% arnona discount in 2025 but was billed the full NIS 5,705.45 for 2026.
His wages from work in October 2025 amounted to just NIS 788, the petition says. Reserve payments and related supplements nevertheless helped bring his recorded annual income to approximately NIS 73,977, averaging NIS 6,165 a month - above the NIS 5,857 ceiling for a single-person household to qualify for an income-based discount in 2026.
Hitorerut argues that the payments did not reflect a lasting improvement in his earnings. After returning to his limited part-time work alongside his medical studies, he faced a full year’s municipal tax without the relief he previously received.
'Reservists should not have to fight twice'
“Reservists should not have to fight twice - once at the front and once against the bureaucracy,” Jerusalem Deputy Mayor and Hitorerut chairman Adir Schwartz said in a statement accompanying the petition.
The dispute concerns income-based discounts, rather than the separate arnona discount available to active reservists. Eligibility depends on household income and size, with national regulations setting the maximum discounts municipalities may grant.
Ordinary reserve compensation counts as income under those rules. For students and other low-paid workers, the minimum payment for military service can substantially exceed their usual wages. Months of service can therefore push them into a lower discount bracket or beyond eligibility altogether.
A temporary regulation allowed municipal councils to exclude those payments when assessing discounts for 2024 and 2025. Jerusalem adopted the arrangement. Hitorerut says its expiration left municipalities without authority to continue excluding the payments in 2026.
The filing describes two further cases. A married reservist and his wife saw their discount fall from 80% in 2025 to 20% in 2026, according to the petition. Another medical student, whose ordinary monthly wages were approximately NIS 2,600-3,000, received a full annual bill of roughly NIS 5,878 after previously receiving an 80% discount.
The movement argues that the result is unequal treatment of students earning comparable wages: those who did not serve can retain their discounts, while reservists lose relief because their previous year’s military compensation is counted against them.
Hitorerut, represented by attorney Matan Gutman, first petitioned over the issue in June 2024. The temporary regulation was published that November.
Extension requested, asks for overpayments to be refunded
In January 2025, the High Court closed that case and awarded the movement NIS 15,000 in costs. Justice Yechiel Kasher found that bringing the petition had been justified from Hitorerut’s perspective and appeared to have contributed to the amendment. He expressly avoided deciding whether the petition would have succeeded had it proceeded to a final ruling.
Schwartz requested an extension in September 2025. Hitorerut says the then-acting interior minister’s office subsequently conveyed approval, but the necessary regulation was never issued. The petition says further demands in August and September 2026 produced only an acknowledgment from the Interior Ministry, with no substantive response from the government offices approached.
A separate change has compounded the problem: An Interior Ministry notice attached to the petition confirms that 2026 eligibility is calculated using average income over 12 months. Applicants can no longer rely on the previous year’s final three months, an option that could help reservists whose service payments fell outside that period.
The movement seeks to restore the exclusion for 2026–2027, retroactive to January 1, 2026, or establish an alternative protecting affected reservists. It also asks for eligibility to be recalculated and overpayments refunded once an arrangement is adopted.
With Jerusalem’s October 31 deadline for discount applications approaching, Hitorerut is also seeking an extension so reservists do not lose the opportunity to apply while the issue remains unresolved. It further asks the government to consider a standing arrangement while emergency reserve call-ups continue.

The new Museum of Moroccan Jewish Culture opened its doors in the city of Fes on Monday, marking the first time in history that an Arab-Muslim country has allocated public funds to establish a museum entirely dedicated to Jewish culture.
According to Morocco's National Foundation of Museums, the 1,700 square meters space invites visitors on a journey into the heart of Moroccan Jewish life and Judaism through a rich and diverse collection of ritual and everyday objects, archaeological, ethnographic and artistic artifacts, archives and rare manuscripts, crafts, traditions, as well as practices and testimonies handed down through the 2500 of Jewish history in the country.
Exhibition galleries display Jewish religious artifacts from Arab World
Local media said the exhibition galleries explore communal institutions, including synagogues, Hebrew schools and rabbinical courts, as well as traditions associated with birth, bar mitzvahs, weddings, funerals and religious holidays. Objects on display include Torah scrolls, prayer shawls, marriage contracts, circumcision chairs, bridal costumes and jewelry.
Traditional crafts also feature prominently, including a reconstructed jeweler’s workshop, tools, silver ornaments, textiles, regional clothing and musical instruments. Audiovisual and digital installations complement the collections, while dedicated spaces will host educational activities for children and school groups.
The front of the building features a brass inscription in four languages: Arabic, Amazigh, Hebrew, and French.
The museum was designed with the involvement of the Moroccan Jewish community, represented in particular by Serge Berdugo, Founding President of the Foundation for Moroccan Jewish Cultural Heritage.
Construction of the museum was initiated by King Mohammed VI during his visit to Fez in April 2019, as part of a program to rehabilitate and showcase the old medina.
The Museums Foundation said the museum "forms part of King Mohammed VI's vision," which places "great importance on preserving and promoting all components of Moroccan identity, in their diversity and complementarity."
The work, completed in March 2023, was carried out by ADER-Fez in consultation with the National Foundation of Museums.
The opening of the Museum of Moroccan Jewish Culture on Monday was attended by Ahmed Toufiq, Minister of Endowments and Islamic Affairs; Khalid Aït Taleb, Wali (regional governor) of the Fez-Meknes region and governor of Fez Prefecture; Serge Berdugo, Founding President of the Foundation for Moroccan Jewish Cultural Heritage; Mehdi Qotbi, President of the National Foundation of Museums; and several other prominent figures, including ambassadors, directors and university presidents.

====================================================================================================

Alleged Chinese spies targeted former premier and AFP commander via LinkedIn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
18:34:59 UTC
03:34:59 KST

Alleged Chinese spies targeted former premier and AFP commander via LinkedIn
In short:
The alleged Chinese spies that targeted businessman Alexander Csergo, the first person to be convicted under Australia's foreign interference laws, also approached dozens of other Australians.
The AFP obtained records from the LinkedIn accounts used by the alleged spies as part of its investigation into Csergo.
What's next?
An expert on Chinese intelligence says the approach signals a "fundamental shift" in China's espionage tradecraft.
Two LinkedIn accounts connected to suspected Chinese spies amassed thousands of connections worldwide and approached dozens of Australians working in government, policing and trade with offers of paid consultancy, an ABC investigation has found.
The alleged spies posed as employees of a think tank, offering their targets competitive pay in return for "valuable advice".
Between 2016 and 2025, the alleged spies targeted more than 100 individuals linked to Australia, including former Queensland premier and now Opposition Leader Steven Miles, an Australian Federal Police commander and several senior federal government officials.
Their LinkedIn profiles appeared in the connection records of two LinkedIn accounts presenting themselves as think tank representatives. The accused foreign agents reached out to 58 of those connections, and some recipients shared their personal contact details.
The ABC can reveal the Australians were targeted by the same alleged Chinese spying network that groomed Australian businessman Alexander Csergo, who has been jailed as the first person convicted of reckless foreign interference.
LinkedIn records obtained by the Australian Federal Police (AFP) during the investigation into Csergo show the accounts approached other Australians, including those who worked at government agencies and state trade and investment bodies.
The AFP alleged the operation was conducted by China's Ministry of State Security (MSS), the country's principal civilian intelligence agency. It said the MSS used fake LinkedIn profiles to contact and cultivate potential foreign sources, before requesting information from them.
The Chinese embassy in Canberra rejected the AFP's claims as "entirely groundless".
"We firmly reject unwarranted accusations and vilification against China and hope that the Australian media will observe professional ethics and report in a fair and objective manner," a spokesperson told the ABC in an email.
In June, the Five Eyes alliance, an intelligence-sharing partnership consisting of the USA, the UK, Australia, Canada and New Zealand, issued a rare joint warning about Chinese intelligence using online job platforms for recruitment "that can provide China with a strategic and tactical advantage over the Five Eyes".
Asked by the ABC if it was aware of or investigating the alleged spying operation, a spokesperson for Australia's domestic spying agency, ASIO, said: "Consistent with long-standing practice, ASIO does not comment on — or confirm — investigations."
Inside the recruitment pitch
In November 2021, while Csergo was living in Shanghai, a LinkedIn account using the name Vera Su offered him part-time work.
The sender introduced herself as being from Nesa Consulting and said the organisation wanted experts to advise on trade between China and Australia.
According to the prosecution case, Csergo subsequently met two people known to him as Ken and Evelyn, prepared reports and received cash payments.
He was convicted in March of reckless foreign interference, an offence introduced under Australia's 2018 national security laws.
The prosecution case was that his conduct involved secrecy or deception and that he was reckless as to whether it supported a foreign principal's intelligence activities.
But an analysis by the ABC of Vera Su's communication records, first obtained by the AFP as part of its investigation into Csergo, revealed how the same LinkedIn accounts sought other people with useful expertise and contacts.
Among those directly approached were people whose profiles listed employment at Austrade — the federal agency that promotes Australian trade and investment — the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade, Investment NSW, Invest Victoria and Tourism Australia.
The accounts' pitches also sought access to people inside government.
"I wonder if you have special source of information… for example: from important people in the government," one message asked.
Some recipients declined.
One Austrade employee said he could not accept money because he worked for the Australian government, although he offered to introduce people in his professional network.
Former Queensland premier Steven Miles was also connected with the same Vera Su account in April 2021 while he was deputy premier.
The ABC has seen no messages between Mr Miles and the account, and the connection alone does not establish that he received a consultancy offer or provided information. The ABC understands that Mr Miles did not respond to any message from Ms Su.
'Honey traps'
Data reviewed by the ABC shows some Australia-linked targets shared contact details or discussed continuing the exchange outside LinkedIn, including through WeChat, phone calls or meetings.
Business consultant Nick Coyle was dealing with the arrest of his former partner, Cheng Lei, in China on espionage charges when he was approached by the alleged Chinese spies.
"During that time, I was getting many strange approaches," he said. Some were "honey traps", people trying to become "friends", both online and in person.
"I just took the approach — if I don't know them from prior — I would steer clear," he said.
Australian life coach Adrian Cahill also exchanged contact with Vera in 2021. He suspects his background as a former soldier made him a more attractive target.
"I would get those a fair bit," he said. "People write to me saying, 'we've got a job, we've got money, we've got a budget.'"
He said his training helped him recognise those tactics, but people without security experience could be gradually drawn into providing "more and more information".
A 'fundamental shift' in tradecraft
Chinese intelligence expert Nicholas Eftimiades described the state-sponsored fishing expedition as a "fundamental shift".
Professor Eftimiades said China's growing AI capabilities may be playing a role, making mass outreach more efficient and safer for Chinese intelligence officers.
"They can reach out to hundreds of thousands at a time, it's a less expensive proposition to try and get people to work for you," he said.
"We can't keep up with that type of onslaught."
Former US federal prosecutor Vikas Didwania, who has run cases involving Chinese intelligence operations for the US government, said LinkedIn was a "goldmine" for intelligence gathering.
"We have seen on LinkedIn, people post information about what kind of classified information they have access to, what kind of clearances that they have."
Didwania said information obtained from LinkedIn recruits may not be classified, or even useful, but could be part of a process of cultivating sources.
"Over the course of that relationship, you can start to push a little more."
Delicate balance for Australians working with China
In recent years, ASIO director-general Mike Burgess has warned the threat of foreign interference in Australia had reached an "extreme level" and was likely to intensify.
Csergo is the first person convicted of reckless foreign interference under the new threat environment.
During Csergo's trial, the court heard he did not disclose any confidential information. His reports were compiled from publicly available material.
At a sentencing hearing last month, District Court Judge Craig Smith described Csergo as "an otherwise decent man" who had committed "a most serious offence".
He sentenced him to three years and six months in jail.
Judge Smith said it was "fundamental and important" to deter people from becoming involved in activities that could harm Australia's national security.
For Australians working with China, however, the verdict has also redrawn the perilous line between legitimate work with a foreign entity and state-sponsored interference.
Some experts have noted a complicating factor is that China has about 2,000 think tanks, with varying and often opaque ties to the Communist Party and the government.
China's 2017 national intelligence law requires organisations and citizens to support national intelligence work. Some experts argue its practical reach can also affect foreign companies operating in China.
Mr Coyle said Australians working in China had to become adept at "walking and chewing gum".
Mr Didwania said efforts to counter China's spying operations needed to be balanced against the risk of creating a chilling effect.
"How do we differentiate between the great kinds of collaboration versus the collaboration that's really part of an MSS recruitment," he asked.
"It becomes a real challenge."

The event was organized by the Ostim Defense and Aviation Cluster (OSSA), with support from the Turkish National Defense Ministry and the Defense Industries Agency (SSB). Anadolu serves as its global communications partner.
Ibrahim Yarsan, chair of OSSA, said at the event’s opening that the event has been rebranded since its 2013 launch to reflect its expanding global mission.
He said the cluster currently includes 359 firms, most of them small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) that form the key supply chain powering major defense firms.
“This event is not just a trade show but a business development gathering,” he said, noting that IDA has facilitated over 8,000 one-on-one business meetings over the years.
“We’re taking it to the next phase, with the first step being IDA Spain,” he added. “We want Turkish firms to work more closely with Spanish firms and we have a key collaboration that began in Valencia, where we will hold the event next year.”
Orhan Aydin, chair of the Ostim Organized Industrial Region, said that Türkiye’s successful domestic defense production model is now being adapted to civilian sectors.
Aydin said that enforcing domestic contribution requirements similar to the SSB’s model enhanced Turkish industries’ capabilities to produce homegrown light rail vehicles, metro cars and high-speed trains with the participation of defense contractors such as Aselsan.
Seyit Ardic, president of the Ankara Chamber of Industry, said that the technological know-how gained through innovations in artificial intelligence (AI), autonomous systems and advanced materials can be brought to the civilian economy to improve efficiency.
“We must look at the success of Turkish defense and benefit from the technological and efficiency gains it brought across the entire industrial sector,” he said.
He suggested establishing a healthcare industries directorate to transfer strategic know-how gained in the defense sector to help accelerate domestic production in healthcare.
He added that efforts are underway to integrate more firms from the machinery, electronics and software sectors into high-value defense projects.
Gursel Baran, president of the Ankara Chamber of Commerce, said that Türkiye’s defense industry reached a domestic content rate of 80% as of this year, while defense and aerospace exports rose from $248 million in 2002 to $11 billion as of August 2026.
He noted that some 4,000 firms active in the sector manage over 1,400 ongoing projects and employ 100,000 workers, while annual research and development (R&D) spending in the sector reached $3.5 billion.
“A technology developed in the defense industry is used in many fields, ranging from automotive to healthcare, from communications to energy, and from transportation to space exploration,” he said. “Defense industry investments are also invested in the country’s scientific knowledge, production capacity, skilled workforce, and economic future.”
The IDA Türkiye 2026 summit will conclude on Friday.

UN peacekeeping chief says talks on future of Lebanon mission must begin soon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14

UN peacekeeping chief says talks on future of Lebanon mission must begin soon
BEIRUT, Oct 14 - UN peacekeeping chief Jean-Pierre Lacroix on Wednesday urged the UN Security Council to begin negotiations on the future of peacekeepers deployed in Lebanon, as Beirut campaigns for an extension to the mandate set to expire at the end of this year.
A UN peacekeeping force known as UNIFIL has been deployed in southern Lebanon since 1978 but the Security Council last year ordered the mission to begin withdrawing at the end of 2026.
Since a new war erupted in March between Israel and Iran-backed Lebanese armed group Hezbollah, the Lebanese government has campaigned for an extension to UNIFIL's mandate, citing its role in monitoring hostilities and facilitating aid deliveries to villages in Israeli-occupied zones.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres earlier this year presented proposals for a continued uniformed UN presence in Lebanon but no action has been taken yet, Lacroix told Reuters in Beirut.
"These proposals are on the table of the Security Council. There has been no movement in the Security Council until now, but I believe that the negotiations will begin ... shortly, in earnest," he said.
"I think it would be better to have a decision soon rather than later, right? Because that would clarify also the horizon for us, certainly from the more limited point of view of our own planning," he said.
FORCES OPERATE HOTLINE TO EASE TENSIONS
Diplomats say the US is not supportive of an extended mandate for UNIFIL, but Lacroix said it was important to focus on Lebanon’s request and that negotiations at the Security Council could yield a constructive outcome.
Some 7,500 UNIFIL peacekeepers are still deployed at about 50 positions in southern Lebanon, which would be expected to be handed over to Lebanese army troops if no new UN force is agreed.
But since most of those posts lie in territory now occupied by the Israeli military, it remains unclear how Lebanese soldiers could deploy to take over the positions.
Lacroix said that clarity on whether a new UN force would deploy to southern Lebanon would help UNIFIL make sure it does not "leave those positions prematurely before we know what could come next".
In addition to facilitating aid deliveries and monitoring hostilities, the force operates a hotline to ease any tensions between the Lebanese and Israeli militaries.
Lacroix said the deconfliction role was particularly crucial given the presence of Israeli troops in a self-declared security zone deep in Lebanese territory.
He said that Israeli and Lebanese troops in the same geographic area presented "the risk of escalation, the risk of incidents getting out of control" and that "there is a need for a third party to de-escalate". REUTERS
