====================================================================================================

Microplastics are linked to inflammation—scientists might have finally worked out why
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
18:02:43 UTC
03:02:43 KST

Microplastics are a source of extreme concern for health: the presence of these tiny pieces of plastic has been linked to heart attacks, stroke, dementia and brain tumors. But what drives these associations is unclear. Now a study published in Nature offers a tantalizing clue: microplastics interact with water, generating highly reactive molecules.
When microplastics come into contact with water, the water near their surface can become chemically active, generating highly reactive species that can modify nearby substances, including biologically important molecules.
As plastics wear down to microscopic sizes, their surface-to-volume ratio increases dramatically. For example, when a credit card is fragmented into particles some 10 microns in diameter, there is a more than 200-fold increase in its surface area, says Wei Min, a chemist at Columbia University and one of the senior authors of the study. As a result, any chemical activity is amplified.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Min and his colleagues examined various microplastics—including polystyrene, polyethylene, polyvinyl chloride, polypropylene and polyethylene terephthalate. Plastic surfaces are hydrophobic, meaning they repel water, Min says. Thus, water molecules cannot form the hydrogen bonds they maintain in liquid form. That changes molecular arrangements, and, in turn, the change influences the local electrical environment and chemical reactivity.
The presumed chemical inertness of bulk plastics overlooks the toxicity of their fragmented microscale forms. “For microplastics, this is especially important because fragmentation creates enormous amounts of new surface area,” Min says.
In past research, microplastics have been shown to cause inflammation, oxidative stress and decreased mitochondrial activity. The new study provides a possible mechanism for this, showing that plastic-water interfaces can perturb proteins, cell membranes, and more.
How this might contribute to damage in living tissues in humans is still unclear, Min says. “Ultimately, we hope to connect fundamental interfacial chemistry with quantitative measurements of biological effects, which would help us better understand potential health risks,” he adds.
Martin Wagner, a toxicologist and a biologist at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology, who was not involved in the new work, says the study’s findings are exciting. The paper gives scientists a new way to look at the effects of plastic pollution, Wagner says. “It implies microplastics themselves are a source of oxidative species ... and oxidative stress is not a secondary effect of exposure.”

Cook last voted to cut rates in December 2025, siding with the majority. The Fed unanimously voted to raise rates after its most recent meeting in September.
"She shouldn't be in an important position," Trump said of Cook in those remarks to reporters after returning from a rally in Tennessee on Saturday.
White House spokesman Matthew Middleton said in response to Lowell's letter that Trump "is performing his constitutional duty in evaluating Lisa Cook's conduct and eligibility to continue serving as a governor on the Federal Reserve."
"The Constitution charges the President with ensuring that the laws are faithfully executed and that the conduct of members of the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System is above reproach," Middleton said in a statement.
An in-person hearing at the White House is currently scheduled for Nov. 5, according to Trump's Oct. 7 presidential memo establishing the "committee of inquiry" into Cook.
Cook's lawyers did not immediately rule out participating in that hearing, and in fact said the Fed governor "welcomes the opportunity to present the facts so she can clear her name," despite their concerns.
But in Tuesday's letter, Lowell said Cook cannot attend a hearing on Nov. 5 because she "will be executing her official duties as Governor at financial and monetary policy meetings in Europe."
After that, Cook will immediately start preparing for the next meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee in early December, Lowell said.
The White House did not immediately respond when asked by CNBC if the scheduled hearing would be moved in light of Cook's alleged scheduling conflicts.
Lowell also said he needs time to speak with Cook about issues raised by the White House's most recent correspondence, as well as to prepare her for any possible hearing, "which, because of her being in Asia on Federal Reserve duties, cannot be done until she returns."
"With all of that (and court hearings I have scheduled in November), the earliest date for any hearing would need to be in December following the FOMC meeting," Lowell wrote Scharf.
Trump established the three-member committee two months after reviving his long-running effort to fire Cook, an appointee of former President Joe Biden, from the central bank's board of governors.
The Supreme Court in late June blocked Trump's first attempt to remove Cook, ruling that she was not given sufficient due process under federal law. But that decision did not stop Trump from trying again.
Middleton said in his statement, "The President is going beyond what the Supreme Court required by offering Lisa Cook an in-person hearing that will be conducted in a fair and open process."
But Lowell wrote Tuesday, "We have significant concerns regarding the objectivity and fitness of the committee," which comprises three executive branch officials, including top Trump economic aide Kevin Hassett.
Hassett "already has publicly insinuated that the President has 'cause' to fire Governor Cook," Lowell noted, citing the economic advisor's comments from August 2025.
Hassett in those remarks also accused Cook of "making a partisan stance contrary to the independence of the Fed" by refusing to step aside while a Justice Department investigation played out into the mortgage fraud allegations, which Cook denies.
The comments suggest Hassett has already prejudged the case, Lowell told Scharf, "surely belying your assertion that the 'hearing' as proposed would be 'substantive and fair.'"
"A hearing with demonstrably biased members, unspecified additional allegations, and an unclear schedule for the disclosure of any additional evidence – with no explanation for why it was not previously produced – is not a process that respects the appearance or history of independence," Lowell wrote.

Israeli Bedouin infiltrated IDF as spy for Gaza terror group linked to Bibas murders
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
17:52:14 UTC
02:52:14 KST

The Beersheba District Court on Wednesday sentenced Shahadeh Abu Alqian, a resident of an unrecognized Bedouin community in the Negev, to 24 1/2 years in prison after he was convicted under a plea agreement of assisting the enemy in wartime, terrorism offenses and weapons violations. Abu Alqian acted on behalf of a terrorist organization based in the Gaza Strip and even enlisted in the Israel Defense Forces on his handlers' instructions to gather intelligence. He also stole a weapon from an IDF soldier and later transferred weapons to the West Bank for the terrorist organization.
According to the amended indictment filed by attorney Hofit Kantrowitz of the Southern District Attorney's Office, Abu Alqian decided in 2019 to take revenge against Israel and harm its security after an administrative demolition order was issued for his father's home. In September of that year, he stole an M4 assault rifle, a magazine and a laser sight from an IDF soldier in the Yatir area, then buried them near his home.
Beginning in 2021, Abu Alqian contacted terrorist operatives in the Gaza Strip through social media and Telegram, expressed support for the struggle against Israel and sought to join Hamas' military wing. He later began operating on behalf of the terrorist organization Kataib al-Mujahideen, providing his handlers with information and photographs of IDF bases, train stations, government-owned companies and shopping centers. He also reported on the movements of soldiers and helicopters near his home.
In March 2022, an operative from the terrorist organization known as "Abu Suleiman" contacted him and asked to purchase weapons. Abu Alqian offered to sell him the rifle he had stolen from the IDF and insisted on delivering the weapons directly to the West Bank. In May 2022, he recruited his cousin to help him, and the two loaded an M4 rifle, thousands of rounds of ammunition and five hand grenades into a vehicle and drove to the West Bank. There, they left the weapons in a hiding place for the terrorist organization.
At the same time, acting on his handler's instructions, Abu Alqian enlisted in the IDF on May 22, 2022, intending to gather information from within the military about Bedouin soldiers, army bases and military positions and pass it to the terrorist organization. About eight days after enlisting, he was arrested by Israeli security forces, thwarting his activities.
In December 2025, Abu Alqian was convicted after admitting to the charges in an amended indictment as part of a plea agreement. The offenses included assisting the enemy in wartime, active membership in a terrorist organization, aggravated theft, weapons offenses involving carrying and transporting firearms and handling weapons for terrorist purposes.
During sentencing arguments, prosecutors sought a lengthy prison term, a suspended sentence and a substantial fine. They also emphasized the severity of Abu Alqian's ties to Mujahideen Brigades, which was involved in the murder of members of the Bibas family during the war that began with Hamas' October 7, 2023, attack on Israel.
A three-judge panel consisting of Daniel Ben Tolila, Tal Lahiani Shoham and Yoav Atar sentenced Abu Alqian to 24 1/2 years in prison, a suspended sentence and a fine of 25,000 shekels.
Kantrowitz, who prosecuted the case, said after the hearing: "This is an exceptionally serious case in which an Israeli citizen chose to act against his country, maintain ties with a terrorist organization and even enlist in the IDF on behalf of a terrorist organization, with the aim of gathering information from within the military and harming national security.
"It is worth noting that, alongside the criminal proceedings, the defendant's details were also forwarded to the interior minister for consideration of revoking his citizenship. The sentence reflects the severity of his actions, the harm to national security and the need for significant deterrence," she added.
"The prosecution will continue to pursue the full extent of the law against those who choose to act on behalf of and assist terrorist organizations, endangering the security of the state, its soldiers and its citizens."

The plane returned to Addis Ababa, where the pilot was replaced, before departing again and landing in Tel Aviv.
Ethiopian Airlines described the incident as a mistake, saying it had been unaware that the pilot was barred from operating flights to Israel, according to the report.

Ukraine's Third Army Corps, together with its attached units, has retaken another 101 square kilometers during the fourth stage of Operation Vivaldi on the Lyman sector in Donetsk Oblast, the corps announced on Oct. 14.
Ukraine liberated the villages of Zelena Dolyna, Lypove, and Kolodiazi, while Russia lost about 3,000 of its soldiers in the fourth stage of the operation, the corps reported on Telegram.
"The enemy was unable to cut the key logistics artery of our group in the Donbas. We thwarted the offensive of the group 'Zapad' and forced it to transfer part of the units of the 1st Tank Army, which weakened the pressure on Kupiansk-Vuzlovyi," corps commander Brig. Gen. Andrii Biletskyi said.

The fight for the heart of the so-called Donbas fortress belt — Sloviansk, Kramatorsk, Druzhkivka, and Kostiantynivka — is crucial going into the winter months, when Russia will look to maximize its foothold in urban areas to prepare for a 2027 offensive campaign.

Of the 45-million-pound package, the U.K. will expedite the delivery of 10 million pounds ($13 million) worth of LMMs to meet the most urgent winter needs.

The U.K. further reiterated that it stands by its plans to ban maritime services for Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG) exports.
London said last year it would implement the phased ban over 2026 "in lockstep with our European partners."
The EU plans to ban Russian LNG imports by January 2027 but has failed to agree on a full ban on maritime services, with Greece securing a carve-out for Russian LNG exports to non-EU countries.

Germany puts Ukrainian on trial over Nord Stream sabotage
Ukrainian citizen Serhii Kuznetsov went to trial in Hamburg on Oct. 14 on suspicion of involvement in the sabotage of the Nord Stream pipelines.
A series of explosions rocked the controversial Nord Stream 1 and 2 pipelines in September 2022, destroying three out of four key gas pipelines linking Russia and Germany via the Baltic Sea.
Kuznetsov, a former soldier, was accused of leading the sabotage group, involving six other people. German investigators claim that he commanded the yacht "Andromeda," from which a team of divers allegedly carried out the attack against the pipelines.
On the first day of the trial, prosecutors accused Kuznetsov of being an accomplice to war crimes by committing an attack against civilian infrastructure.
Kuznetsov and Kyiv have denied any involvement in the sabotage.
The trial — the first held in connection with the Nord Stream sabotage — is expected to run until February.
Kuznietsov was arrested in August 2025 near the Italian town of Rimini under a European arrest warrant before being extradited to Germany.
Another Ukrainian suspect, Volodymyr Zhuravliov, was detained in Croatia in August 2026 and awaits extradition. Zhuravliov was first detained in Poland in September 2025, but a Polish court refused to extradite him to Germany and instead released him a month later.
The Nord Stream 2 pipeline, which never became operational, had long been a flashpoint in European energy politics.
Even before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, critics said it deepened Germany's dependence on Russian gas and undermined European energy security.

Ukraine's Security Service (SBU) has detained an 18-year-old man in Kyiv suspected of working for Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB). According to investigators, he attempted to register 148 Starlink terminals for use by Russian forces.

He was allegedly contacted by an FSB officer who offered him money in exchange for cooperation.
Within days of being recruited, the suspect registered 15 Starlink terminals using the passport details of relatives and acquaintances. He then prepared personal information belonging to other individuals to register another 133 devices.
SBU officers detained the suspect near a post office, where he allegedly planned to activate another batch of terminals.
The 15 previously registered Starlink terminals, whose details had already been sent to his Russian handler via a messaging app, were also blocked.
The suspect remains in custody without the possibility of bail. If convicted, he faces life imprisonment and confiscation of property.
The case adds to a growing number of incidents in which Russia allegedly recruits Ukrainians to carry out assignments on Moscow's behalf, including a recent case on Oct. 12, when Ukrainian authorities detained a 19-year-old suspected of plotting a bomb attack on a bus carrying soldiers in Rivne.

Bank of America, the second-largest US bank, failed to promptly report hundreds of millions of dollars in suspicious transactions bearing signs of Chinese money-laundering networks, US regulators said on Tuesday, announcing more than US$1.21 billion in penalties for broader anti-money-laundering and sanctions failures.

According to data from DownDetector and Sboy.rf, the disruptions affected Sberbank's services, its GigaChat neural network, and Samokat, a grocery delivery service affiliated with the bank. Samokat users were no longer able to place orders.
Complaints also concerned services provided by Rostelecom, MTS, MegaFon, T2, the hosting provider Reg.ru, and Kontur, a digital business services platform.
Tochka Bank's online banking and Business Online services became unavailable. Mail.ru services, including cloud storage, also experienced disruptions, as did services operated by VK, Rosselkhozbank, Alfa-Bank, VTB, the Ozon marketplace, the Avito classifieds platform, and the government services portal Gosuslugi.
Alexander Vedyakhin, Sberbank's first deputy chairman of the management board, confirmed the attack on the data center but claimed that all systems and services were "operating normally" and that no employees had been injured.
Against this backdrop, the bank's shares fell by nearly 0.7%.
Sberbank's data center is still under construction but is already partially operational. It was previously reported that the facility was intended to become one of Russia's largest data centers and would host services for the government's GosTech digital platform. The project is valued at 122.2 billion rubles.
As Ukrinform previously reported, overnight on October 11, drones attacked a data center operated by Russian technology company Yandex in the city of Vladimir. The attack caused disruptions to the company's services.

Iranian Cinema Day to be held during 3rd Toji Somon National Film Festival in Tajikistan

Simultaneously with the 3rd edition of the Toji Somon National Film Festival in Dushanbe, “The Gambler,” a production of the Farabi Cinema Foundation, will be featured in the event’s Iranian Cinema Day, Mehr reported.
In each edition of the festival, the screening of works from one or more specific countries is highlighted. In this edition, Iranian Cinema Day is being held to expand cultural and artistic interactions between the two countries.

The plot centers on a high-stakes cyber-attack targeting one of the country's banks during the 12-day war against Iran. The narrative follows an expert agent who grows suspicious of one of the bank's programmers, sparking a tense race to uncover the truth and safeguard national security.
International distribution for “The Gambler” is handled by the International Affairs Department of the Farabi Cinema Foundation. Previously, the film received the Special Jury Prize at the Across the Lake Film Festival in North Macedonia, and Shabnam Ghorbani won the Golden Crane award for Best Actress for her performance in the film at the Shanghai Cooperation Organization Film Festival in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan.
In the second edition of the Toji Somon National Film Festival last year, the feature film “Knight,” directed by Hossein Namazi, was screened in the festival’s competition section.

The second edition, held October 15 to 20, 2025, screened more than 40 films from 15 countries under the theme "The History of the Development of the Tajik People."
The festival is part of the Cinema Development Program of the Republic of Tajikistan for 2023 to 2027, a state-backed initiative to strengthen the national film industry, support young creative talent, and expand international cooperation in filmmaking.

Tehran puppet theater festival to open with public ceremony
TEHRAN- The 21st Tehran-Mobarak International Puppet Theater Festival will open on Saturday with a ceremony at the open-air grounds of Tehran’s City Theater Complex, bringing together puppetry artists and members of the public in a celebration of the art form.
For the ceremony, festival secretary Poopak Azimpour Tabrizi has invited artists, students, university professors, theater practitioners and other interested participants to attend with their own puppets, the public relations office of the City Theater Complex announced on Wednesday.
The invitation extends to citizens of all ages, highlighting the festival’s effort to encourage public participation and bring puppetry beyond the stage.
The opening event will mark the beginning of the six-day festival, which will run in Tehran from October 17 to 22, featuring puppetry performances and activities dedicated to the art form.
The Tehran-Mobarak International Puppet Theater Festival is one of Iran’s major cultural events dedicated to puppetry, bringing together Iranian and international artists to showcase different traditions, techniques and approaches to puppet theater. Named after Mobarak, a traditional Iranian glove-puppet character known for his humor and lively exchanges with audiences, the festival celebrates the country’s rich heritage of traditional puppetry while providing a platform for contemporary forms of the art. Its programs highlight puppetry as a medium for storytelling, cultural expression and communication across generations.
Over the years, the festival has sought to promote innovation in puppet theater, encourage interaction among artists and introduce younger audiences to the art form. Productions presented at the event range from traditional Iranian performances to experimental works incorporating different puppetry techniques, visual design, music and movement. By bringing together performers, theater practitioners and audiences, the festival also supports professional exchange and helps expand the role of puppetry within Iran’s performing arts scene.

====================================================================================================

'Office' is actually having a scarcity problem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
17:35:44 UTC
02:35:44 KST

A version of this article first appeared in the CNBC Property Play newsletter with Diana Olick. Property Play covers new and evolving opportunities for the real estate investor, from individuals to venture capitalists, private equity funds, family offices, institutional investors and large public companies. Sign up to receive future editions, straight to your inbox.
Barely a few years after what some saw as a pandemic-driven collapse of the U.S. office market, the sector is roaring back to health at an unexpectedly fast clip. That speedy recovery is resulting in a shortage, especially of premium space.
The office market posted its fifth consecutive quarter of positive net absorption, with occupiers adding 6 million square feet in the third quarter of this year, according to a new report from JLL. And employers are expanding, with signed leases now averaging a 13% increase in footprint. Just two years ago, the main theme in office was downsizing.
This all comes at a time when supply is falling — and falling faster than demand is recovering. Just 3.5 million square feet of new office space was delivered in the third quarter, which matches the near-record low supply seen in the second quarter. At the same time, 9.6 million square feet was removed through either conversions or redevelopments. The inventory of office space nationally has lost 45 million square feet since the end of 2023.
There is currently just 23 million square feet of new office space under construction, and with demand for premium office surging, this new space is becoming increasingly scarce. JLL deems it a "flight to scarcity." As a result, rents are finally rising.
Effective rents for first-generation trophy space are now up more than 20% compared with the third quarter of 2025. The lack of available trophy space is now pushing more occupiers to second-generation space. In turn, rents for that sector are up 10% annually.
"Office, which is having a real renaissance right now. … If you own, if you bought that 18, 24 months ago, you've done incredibly well in office in San Francisco and New York," said Willy Walker, CEO of Walker & Dunlop, a commercial real estate finance and advisory firm, on CNBC's "Closing Bell Overtime."
There are, as always, stronger local drivers to different metropolitan markets. Tech is leading the way with the highest net absorption in San Francisco and Austin. Sun Belt markets have also seen strong demand, with gateway area leasing volume up 13% from a year ago. Smaller, tertiary markets have come back to roughly 95% of their 2019 leasing volume.
With supply shrinking and demand rising, construction should be picking up, but it's not.
"Now is the perfect time to be putting a shovel in the ground, except no one's going to do it," said Walker, noting that this year office construction is at about 9% of its normal annual supply. "It's a perfect time to start projects to be delivered in the next two or three years. The problem with it is back to equity capital. You're not finding the equity capital going towards it right now, and as a result of it, we will be in a supply-constrained market, which, what will that do? It'll push rents up."

Kiarostami’s “Where Is the Friend’s House?” selected for Tokyo festival
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
17:35:35 UTC
02:35:35 KST

Kiarostami’s “Where Is the Friend’s House?” selected for Tokyo festival
TEHRAN- The 1987 Iranian film “Where Is the Friend’s House?” by the late acclaimed filmmaker Abbas Kiarostami will be screened at the 39th Tokyo International Film Festival in Japan as part of a special program celebrating films cherished by legendary Japanese director Akira Kurosawa.
Produced by the Institute for the Intellectual Development of Children and Young Adults (Kanoon), the film is scheduled to screen on October 26 at TOHO Cinemas Chanter in Tokyo, according to Kanoon’s public relations and international affairs department.
The film will be presented alongside three other works in the program “Akira Kurosawa’s Favorite Films”: Charlie Chaplin’s “The Circus” (1928), and Kurosawa’s own films “Sanshiro Sugata” (1943) and “Ikiru” (1952).
The special program brings together works associated with Kurosawa’s cinematic legacy, placing Kiarostami’s landmark Iranian film in conversation with major works from the history of world cinema.
“Where Is the Friend’s House?” follows Ahmad, a schoolboy who discovers that he has accidentally taken home his classmate’s notebook. Determined to return it before his friend faces punishment for failing to complete his homework, Ahmad sets out to find the boy’s house in a neighboring village. His search becomes a journey through rural Iranian life, exploring childhood, responsibility, kindness and the challenges children encounter in a world governed by adult rules.
With its understated storytelling, naturalistic performances and close attention to everyday life, the film became one of the defining works of Kiarostami’s career and helped introduce Iranian cinema to wider international audiences. It also established themes that would recur throughout the director’s work, including the moral complexity of ordinary decisions and the relationship between children and adults.
The film has won several awards since its release, including the Bronze Leopard at the Locarno International Film Festival in Switzerland and the Critics' Prize at the Sao Paulo International Film Festival, and the Pasinetti Award at the Venice Film Festival.
“Where Is the Friend’s House?” is one of Kiarostami’s landmark works and the first installment of his Koker trilogy, which also includes “And Life Goes On” (1992) and “Through the Olive Trees” (1994).
The film has been screened at numerous international film festivals and cinematheques over the decades and continues to feature in retrospectives and programs dedicated to world cinema.
Kiarostami was a film director, screenwriter, poet, photographer, and film producer. An active filmmaker from 1970, he was involved in the production of over 40 films, including shorts and documentaries. He attained critical acclaim for directing “Close-Up” (1990), “The Wind Will Carry Us” (1999), and “Taste of Cherry” (1997). In later works, “Certified Copy” (2010) and “Like Someone in Love” (2012), he filmed for the first time outside Iran: in Italy and Japan, respectively.
He was part of a generation of filmmakers in the Iranian New Wave, a Persian cinema movement that started in the late 1960s and emphasized the use of poetic dialogue and allegorical storytelling dealing with philosophical issues. He is known for his use of Persian poetry in the dialogue, titles, and themes of his films. His films also contain a notable degree of ambiguity, an unusual mixture of simplicity and complexity, and often a mix of fictional and documentary elements. The concepts of change and continuity, in addition to the themes of life and death, play a major role in Kiarostami's works.
Kiarostami, the winner of the Palme d’Or at the Cannes Film Festival in 1997 for his “Taste of Cherry”, died of cancer on July 5, 2016 at the age of 76.
The screening in Tokyo offers another opportunity for international audiences, including younger generations of filmgoers, to discover Kiarostami’s work and revisit a film that remains an enduring reference point in Iranian cinema.
The 39th Tokyo International Film Festival will run from October 26 to November 4 under the theme “Connecting — Cinema Connects Us to the World Beyond.” The festival will present more than 200 films across its various sections, with screenings and related events taking place in Tokyo’s Hibiya, Yurakucho, Marunouchi and Ginza areas.

Merck CEO tells CNBC he expects breakthrough cancer vaccine will become faster to make
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
17:33:57 UTC
02:33:57 KST

Merck CEO Rob Davis told CNBC on Wednesday that he expects the company's breakthrough cancer vaccine with Moderna to get faster to manufacture over time.
Shortening the current six-week timeline could potentially help the companies reach more patients.
"We are going to drive for improvement, but right now the focus really is, let's make sure we have the supply ready, we have the market ready to bring this important innovation to the market, and then we'll talk about how do we accelerate," he told CNBC in an exclusive interview. "But I do think over time you're going to see that timeline shortened."
The personalized cancer vaccine turnaround spans from sequencing a patient's tumor to delivering it to the hospital. Merck and Moderna's vaccine is designed to target the specific mutations in each individual patient's tumor rather than using a one-size-fits-all approach, which makes it complicated to produce.
The idea is to train the immune system to recognize and kill those unique cancer markers and then pair that response with Merck's blockbuster immunotherapy Keytruda, which aims to help the body attack the cancer more effectively.
Davis acknowledged that manufacturing the vaccine is a "complex system," but said Merck and Moderna have the process "down to a very tight science."
"I'm actually very confident that we're not going to have complexities in getting this to patients in a very timely fashion," he added. "We're doing it in our clinicals, and I only see improvement going forward."
His comments come after the two companies in August released positive initial data from a late-stage trial on the shot in combination with Keytruda in melanoma patients. Davis said the company is also examining the vaccine in trials across other tumors, including non-small cell lung cancer, types of bladder cancer and renal cell carcinoma.
"You like to talk that maybe you can start moving toward talking about a cure," he said. "We're not there yet, but we're moving in a direction with technology that's really unprecedented."
Merck's new R&D facility
Davis spoke to CNBC after Merck earlier Wednesday officially opened its new 120,000-square-foot research facility, which it has named Advance, in its West Point, Pennsylvania, campus. Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro joined Merck executives and other government officials for a ribbon-cutting ceremony to celebrate the launch of the facility, which features highly automated robotic systems and advanced digital AI capabilities.
Merck says the facility is designed to streamline the analysis of biological samples from the company's ongoing drug programs and improve its research and development.
The opening of the new facility comes as Merck prepares for the upcoming loss of exclusivity of Keytruda, which is one of the world's top-selling drugs and is widely viewed as the backbone of modern cancer treatment. Keytruda's core U.S. compound patent expires in December 2028, while secondary patents extend protection into 2029 and beyond.
Merck has implemented a multi-layered strategy to turn the Keytruda transition into what it views as a manageable "hill" rather than a sharp revenue cliff. That includes accelerating internal research and also funneling $65 billion in external acquisitions and licensing agreements over the five years to build its pipeline of next-generation medicines.
The pharmaceutical giant is also developing new forms of Keytruda and combination regimens that it can transition patients onto and protect the drug's revenue even after key patents expire before 2030.
The Food and Drug Administration in September 2025 approved the subcutaneous form of Keytruda, which is considered a more convenient version because it is administered under the skin in minutes. The standard form of the drug is an intravenous infusion that takes around 30 minutes.
But Merck is facing a legal battle over the newer version in some European markets, raising questions about the market size for the drug.
A Dutch court issued an injunction earlier this month blocking Merck from selling, stocking or manufacturing subcutaneous Keytruda across eight European countries: Belgium, Denmark, France, Ireland, Italy, Sweden, Switzerland and the Netherlands. That followed a patent infringement suit brought by the biotech company Halozyme Therapeutics over its own subcutaneous drug delivery platform.
Merck has said it strongly disagrees with the rulings and plans to appeal. Patients can still receive the original form of Keytruda in Europe while the patent dispute unfolds.
Still, Halozyme has also sued Merck for patent infringement in the U.S., alleging the subcutaneous formulation of Keytruda infringes 15 patents that the biotech has filed since 2011.
Meanwhile, Merck is focused on rolling out a slate of new drugs. That includes Winrevair, a treatment for a rare, life-threatening lung disease that was approved in 2024 and acquired a few years earlier through its $11.5 billion acquisition of Acceleron.
Another closely watched launch is Merck's cholesterol-lowering pill Lipfendra, which was approved by the FDA last month.

Why your cat is the best philosopher
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
17:24:09 UTC
02:24:09 KST

This post was originally published on this site.
A young girl looks out of the classroom window. It’s the end of the day, and she’s bored. She spots a goldfinch land on the ground outside. It hops about and twitches for whatever reasons goldfinches do that, and then takes off. It swoops and dives around the playground, as if doing it all for the girl. Oh, how she would like to fly.
Humans have long looked to the animal kingdom for inspiration. We envy their skills and talents: flight, speed, strength, sociability, and so on. Religions almost always feature animal imagery, and flags will often blazon a lion, an eagle, a wolf — something bold or heroic. And philosophers are in on the game as well.
Even in the earliest historical records, people were exploring the philosophical side of animals. What can this animal teach me? What virtues does it embody? What can I learn about myself by studying this creature?
Joining in an ancient line is John Gray’s book Feline Philosophy. In the book, Gray examines what we can all learn about life from spending more time around cats. His conclusion: We should all be a bit more feline.
Mo the Philosophical Cat
A cat does not do philosophy, and that makes it a better philosopher than anyone else. Gray argues that for humans, philosophy acts as a kind of medicine. We are full of doubt and anxiety about how to live, yes, but most of all we are filled with the existential dread that comes from knowing that we will die.
To combat this, we create systems like religions and ideologies. We try to soothe our death-terror with stories. We become obsessed with “the good life,” “the examined life,” and “time well spent.” We have turned the word “happiness” into a multi-billion-dollar industry, but as a species we are no happier than we ever were. We are sick, craving a cure, but the medicine we have isn’t working.
Cats, though, have no such sickness. Imagine a cat called Mo. Mo does not search for meaning in her life, and she is not trying to become a better cat. She does not experience her life as a project that could fail, and she doesn’t wake up with the imagined burden of a thousand cats’ expectations.
Mo hunts, she sleeps, and she sits in the sunlight. When she suffers, she does not add to her suffering by asking why. She does not need to invent systems or stories because the world is as the world is. Gray’s point is not that Mo is wise; Mo wouldn’t write books even if she could. The point is that Mo is not sick. Humans are.
Be more cat
Gray starts his book by saying that we cannot become a cat. We can try to transfigure if we want, but you’re mostly running up against the immovable wall of cellular biology. Still, we can mimic a cat. We can do more cat things and try to see things like a cat. Gray leans on a point that Blaise Pascal makes about ritual and religion: If you do something enough, it changes you. If you force your mind a certain way, it stays like that.
As the philosopher Mark Vorobej pointed out, it’s not entirely clear why Gray has singled out cats. What’s true here of cats is true of dogs, birds, rats, squirrels, moles, badgers, or mongooses. Should we be more mongoose? It’s a fair critique, but it is somewhat pedantic. I’m sure Gray is not some feline exceptionalist. I take his book to be a lesson in intentionality. We can try to become more like a cat, rat, or badger, and I think he chose cats because they’re both cute and far more present in our lives. We see cats at home or on social media. All over social media. It’s just much easier to talk about something so available. Yes, he could have chosen dogs, but hey — take your pick.
So, how can we be more cat? Well, we need to distance ourselves from this sick and broken human way of seeing things. Stop seeing your lives in terms of some huge, overarching metanarrative. Don’t try to find meaning in your suffering. Stop seeing the world in terms of puzzles to solve. Don’t try to persuade other people to be more reasonable. Recognize that you are who you are, and it is what it is. Sometimes life just happens. So climb trees, play with a ball, sleep a lot more, and lie by the fire when things get cold and dark. Cherish life and think only as much as you want.
Jonny is the creator of the Mini Philosophy social network. He’s an internationally bestselling author of three books and the resident philosopher at Big Think. He’s known all over the world for making philosophy accessible, relatable, and fun.

British Premier Andy Burnham on Wednesday ruled out a partnership between the Labour Party and the Green Party following the Greens' controversial motion declaring that "Zionism is racism."

Tsahkna was responding to Finnish Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen, who called on EU member states to support a letter to the European Commission seeking a complete ban on Russian tourist visas for the duration of Russia’s war.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Russia has also intensified sabotage, espionage, cyberattacks, and other hybrid operations across Europe since the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. In October, Ukraine’s military intelligence warned that Russian intelligence services were preparing further operations across EU and NATO countries aimed at undermining support for Ukraine and weakening allied capabilities.
“Estonia joins Finland’s call to suspend tourist visas for Russian citizens across the European Union,” Tsahkna wrote.
“As Russia continues its relentless assault on Ukraine, bombing cities, destroying civilian infrastructure, and killing innocent people, it is unacceptable that Russian citizens can still enjoy unrestricted leisure travel within the Schengen area,” he added.
Tsahkna argued that EU visa policy should reflect the scale of Russia’s aggression and called for further pressure on the Kremlin.
“Visa policy must reflect the gravity of Russia’s ongoing aggression. The EU should continue to strengthen pressure on the Kremlin through all available means,” he wrote.
The Estonian foreign minister also urged the EU to adopt the measures needed to establish what he described as “a comprehensive entry ban on Russian combatants.”
In her original post, Valtonen called for a complete EU-wide ban on Russian tourist visas, noting that Finland had already stopped issuing visas for non-essential travel to Russian citizens in 2022.
“We must stop issuing tourist visas for Russian citizens across the EU,” Valtonen wrote. “I am calling for a complete EU ban on Russian tourist visas for as long as Russia continues its war of aggression.”
“It is not right that Russians can travel to Europe to enjoy the way of life and freedoms here while their country bombs the homes of Ukrainians,” she added.
Valtonen also called for a Schengen visa ban targeting the Russian leader, Vladimir Putin’s inner circle, tighter restrictions on Russian athletes, and stronger enforcement of existing visa restrictions on Russian combatants.
Finland has maintained stricter visa rules for Russian citizens since 2022, and Valtonen is now seeking to extend that approach across the EU. Her proposal would require coordinated action by member states and the European Commission.
In September, US prosecutors charged five alleged members of a Russian intelligence network accused of recruiting operatives for assassinations, arson attacks, and other violent plots in the US and Europe. Investigators linked the network to planned operations in Lithuania and Prague, while stating that countries supporting Ukraine were among its targets.

Russia’s Newest Drones Are Still Full of Western Tech—Ukraine Just Put the Evidence on Display
Unknown

- Category

Russia’s Newest Drones Are Still Full of Western Tech—Ukraine Just Put the Evidence on Display
Ukraine displayed a captured Russian Geran-2 drone and Western-made components recovered from Russian UAVs at the Warsaw Security Forum, highlighting how foreign technology continues to reach Russia’s weapons industry despite years of sanctions and export controls.
The exhibition was organized by Ukraine’s Independent Anti-Corruption Commission, or NAKO, with support from the Ukrainian Foreign Ministry, the organization told UNITED24 Media on October 14.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The display was intended to show that Russia’s dependence on Western technology has not disappeared as its weapons production expands. Experts continue to identify electronics from the US, Switzerland, Germany, the UK, Japan, and Taiwan inside Russian drones, including newer jet-powered models that Moscow began deploying on a much larger scale in 2026.
According to NAKO, the components cannot simply be explained as old inventories accumulated before Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022. Investigators are finding relatively recent electronics, indicating that Russia continues to acquire restricted technology through sanctions-evasion networks and third countries.
“Why should Western countries reconsider their approach to sanctions policy? This is a matter of Ukraine’s survival and the security of the entire democratic world. And we want to raise it to the political level,” NAKO Executive Director Olena Tregub said.
NAKO also organized a panel at the Warsaw Security Forum focused on sanctions and export controls. Opening the discussion, former US presidential special envoy Gen. Keith Kellogg said Western technology remains one of the factors sustaining Russia’s war effort.
Every foreign component that reaches a Russian defense factory, he argued, represents a failure somewhere in the supply chain and raises questions about enforcement.
EU sanctions envoy David O’Sullivan acknowledged that there is no simple solution.
Russia continues obtaining Western components through third countries that are not required to follow EU sanctions, making cooperation with those governments increasingly important if Europe wants to close the remaining routes into Russia’s defense industry.
Russia’s dependence is also not limited to microelectronics. Its military-industrial complex still relies on imported raw materials, machine tools, and other industrial equipment needed to manufacture advanced weapons.
“Even despite its rich natural resources, Russia still purchases a great deal of raw materials abroad, including rare-earth metals. It also purchases machine tools and other equipment. We have to approach this problem comprehensively,” Ukraine’s Presidential Commissioner for Sanctions Policy Vladyslav Vlasiuk said.
The Warsaw Security Forum brings together government officials, international institutions, and security experts from roughly 90 countries each year.
Previously, Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence Directorate revealed new details about Russia’s Kh-47M2 Kinzhal aeroballistic missile, identifying 58 Russian companies involved in its production, 22 of which remain outside international sanctions.

Iran sets out defense modernization plans as officials stress deterrence and domestic arms productio
TEHRAN — Iran is seeking to accelerate the modernization of its armed forces, expand domestic weapons production and strengthen its defense-industrial infrastructure, according to plans presented by defense minister nominee Mehrdad Akhlaqi, as senior military officials stress the importance of deterrence and preparedness amid continued tensions with the United States and Israel.
Addressing the Iranian Parliament, Akhlaqi outlined six-month and 22-month implementation programs designed to build on existing defense initiatives while adapting them to changing technological and operational requirements. His priorities include expanding the production and supply of military equipment, upgrading advanced weapons systems, developing missile and air defense capabilities, and reinforcing cyber infrastructure.
The proposed agenda places particular emphasis on domestic scientific and industrial capacity, with greater participation by private companies and knowledge-based firms expected to help accelerate research, improve production capabilities and meet the Armed Forces’ requirements.
The plans come as senior commanders of Iran’s Islamic Revolution Guard Corps (IRGC) have reiterated their emphasis on indigenous defense capabilities, describing sustained weapons production and technological development as essential to military preparedness and deterrence.
In a separate meeting with Akhlaqi, IRGC Commander Major General Ahmad Vahidi stressed the strategic importance of maintaining Iran’s defense production chains and expanding cooperation between the Armed Forces’ operational and industrial sectors.
Together, the statements outline a defense agenda centered on technological development, domestic manufacturing, and military readiness, while reflecting Tehran’s stated position that its capabilities are intended to deter aggression and enable a forceful response to any renewed attack.
A timetable for military modernization
Presenting his plans to parliament, Akhlaqi said the Defense Ministry would continue existing programs with appropriate revisions while introducing six-month and 22-month implementation frameworks to advance its objectives.
He identified the production and supply of weapons required by the Armed Forces as a central priority, emphasizing the need to mobilize the country’s industrial, scientific and technological resources.
The nominee also highlighted targeted research projects capable of producing practical results in the near term. He said cooperation with domestic industries, private-sector companies and knowledge-based firms could accelerate technological development, increase production capacity and improve the military’s ability to respond to operational requirements.
Maintaining combat readiness, Akhlaqi said, would require the continuous upgrading of advanced weapons and equipment, the expansion of intelligent systems and investment in emerging fields of warfare.
He called for defense planning and force architecture to evolve alongside technological advances and regular assessments of operational needs. The broader objective, according to his presentation, is to align military requirements with the country’s scientific and industrial capabilities while improving the efficiency of defense-related investment.
Missile capabilities are another priority. Akhlaqi said Iran’s missile capacity should be strengthened in line with the level of regional threats.
His proposed program also includes strengthening air defense, developing ground combat capabilities, pursuing the development of a heavy multirole fighter aircraft and reinforcing cyber infrastructure.
The nominee called for the reconstruction and modernization of defense facilities and infrastructure, stressing that commanders’ assessments should be consolidated to establish priorities and guide the allocation of resources.
IRGC head stresses domestic production and industrial coordination
In a meeting with Akhlaqi, IRGC Commander Major General Ahmad Vahidi emphasized the contribution of specialists and employees in Iran’s defense industries during ‘the US-Israeli wars of aggression.’
Vahidi said domestic knowledge, the determination of technical specialists and the continuity of defense equipment production were essential to maintaining the Armed Forces’ readiness and countering potential threats.
He called for the fuller use of national scientific and industrial capabilities, arguing that closer coordination between operational units and defense manufacturers could strengthen military preparedness and deterrence.
Vahidi also stressed the need to develop strategic technologies, reinforce production infrastructure and mobilize domestic expertise to address both current and future defense requirements.
Akhlaqi, for his part, said the Defense Ministry was prepared to prioritize support for the Armed Forces while ensuring the continuity of production chains and advancing technological development, particularly in strategic weaponry.
He also highlighted the potential for expanded cooperation between the ministry’s industrial sectors and corresponding IRGC divisions in the design, manufacture, supply, and maintenance of military equipment.
IRGC Navy commander issues warning over Strait of Hormuz
IRGC Navy Commander Rear Admiral Ali Ozmaei, in his first televised interview, challenged US forces to approach the waterway if Washington believed the strait was open and secure.
“If the Americans think the Strait of Hormuz is open, let them come closer. We are impatient to sink American warships,” Ozmaei said.
He stated that a US warship worth $13 billion had been rendered ineffective and had moved approximately 700 kilometers away from the strait because it did not dare approach the waterway.
“We are waiting for US warships to approach the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz so we can sink them. We are counting down every moment until this happens,” he added.
Ozmaei also accused the United States and its regional partners of imposing a media blackout to prevent international audiences from learning about vessels penalized for violating rules governing passage through the strait.
He said the IRGC Navy had released footage of two incidents involving vessels that had violated the rules and faced consequences.
IRGC spokesman says Iran has acquired more advanced weapons
IRGC spokesperson Brigadier General Hossein Mohebbi has separately said Iran has acquired substantially more advanced weapons since the 40-day war of aggression imposed by the United States and Israel, arguing that the country’s military capabilities have continued to develop since the conflict.
Mohebbi described a renewed US attack as an illogical course of action but said the possibility could not be ruled out. He suggested that the Trump administration might seek a military or political achievement ahead of the US midterm elections.
He warned that Iran was prepared to respond forcefully to any renewed aggression.
“This time, the consequences for the US will be far more painful,” Mohebbi said.
According to the IRGC spokesperson, Iran relied mainly on older-generation weapons during the 40-day conflict but has since gained access to considerably more advanced weaponry.
Mohebbi also criticized US media coverage of foreign military campaigns, arguing that mainstream outlets were concealing the realities and consequences of military aggression from the American public.
He rejected allegations by US officials that divisions within Iran’s leadership were undermining coordination among the country’s authorities. Describing those allegations as “completely false,” he said they were intended to justify Washington’s failures during the war.
The spokesperson’s remarks reinforce the message conveyed by Akhlaqi’s proposed plans: that military modernization and the development of domestic weapons production remain central priorities following the conflict.
A World War, in the view of the global public
Brigadier General Yadollah Javani, deputy for political affairs of the Islamic Revolution Guards Corps (IRGC), also underscored the full combat readiness of the Iranian Armed Forces to counter potential threats, saying any miscalculation by the enemy will prompt a crushing response.
Speaking at the Administrative Council of the northern province of Golestan on Wednesday, General Javani addressed the regional and global consequences of the US-Israeli aggression, stating that the war imposed on Iran is not labeled a world war, but global public opinion considers it one.
He explained that the US-Israeli war on Iran had the same nature and characteristics as World Wars I and II, which impacted the global order, the geometry of power, and the shifting power equation—creating new realities.
Referring to Iran's evolving capabilities, he said new technologies, weaponry, and equipment have bolstered the country's defense—a reason the US was forced to move its aircraft carriers some 700 to 800 kilometers away. "Today, the Persian Gulf region—which previously hosted over 100 military vessels and warships—is free of foreign military forces."
Iran will dictate terms for ending the war
The advisor to the chief commander of the Islamic Revolution Guards Corps (IRGC), Brigadier General Ramezan Sharif, has also argued that Iran’s geopolitical position and military response would ultimately compel the United States to accept conditions set by the Islamic Republic to end the war.
Speaking in Mashhad on Wednesday in a book unveiling ceremony in Razavi Khorasan Province, Sharif said there was no prospect of a US victory in a war against Iran.
He praised the performance of the Iranian Armed Forces in confronting US-Israeli aggression and said Washington had mobilized its regional and European resources to weaken the Islamic Republic.
According to Sharif, those efforts had failed to achieve their objectives.
He also argued that the United States and Israel had miscalculated the consequences of targeting Iran’s senior leadership and military commanders, believing that such actions could bring about the collapse of the Islamic Republic or overturn the Islamic Revolution, which is approaching its 48th anniversary.
Sharif said the two countries had assumed direct responsibility for the confrontation after their regional allies proved unable to carry out the objectives expected of them. He portrayed Iran’s response as a demonstration of the country’s strategic resilience and its ability to challenge a militarily superior adversary.
The IRGC adviser further stated that Iran’s defense operations had neutralized US capabilities at 17 bases surrounding the country, and the outcome was one that Washington had not anticipated.

He said the restrictions have affected StarShield’s “military package”:

The new limit means the service can no longer be used on jet-powered drones or other high-speed unmanned aircraft.
Georgy Trishkin, a missile-launch analyst and commentator on spaceflight and rocketry, told The Insider that standard Starlink service on drones traveling faster than 160 kph had stopped working in 2025, while StarShield continued to function until Oct. 13.
“Military StarShield is physically a different system and a different service. It is available only to defense and government customers. Starlink stopped working under these conditions last year and never worked on Russian territory in the first place. Drones using it would lose their connection when crossing zones near the border and switch to other methods, including mobile networks using Russian SIM cards.
The decision was not made by SpaceX, but by the customer in the United States [meaning the Pentagon — The Insider]. That does not absolve the company of responsibility, but it is important to understand who made the decision and which service it concerned.”
Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski also commented on the move.
“Hey, Elon Musk, big man, are you playing politics with your products again? As your European customers, we are watching you,” he wrote on Musk’s X platform.

Tens of thousands of students have taken to the streets of Tirana, the Albanian capital, setting alight a government building and two banks and hurling stones at police during a protest over rising education costs and corruption.
Police responded with water cannon and teargas to disperse protesters who started a fire at the ministry of education building, overturned bins and smashed the fronts of local businesses. A branch of Raiffeisen Bank near the education ministry also caught fire.
Authorities said 23 police officers and six other people were being treated for injuries and that 35 people had been detained.
President Bajram Begaj condemned the violence and appealed for calm, adding: “The constitution and the law must remain the boundaries for everyone, without exception.”

The unrest caps a summer of peaceful protests against Rama, triggered by the proposed development of a luxury resort along Albania’s pristine southern coast backed by Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, which has been caught up in legal disputes.
“This is a revolution. We are tired of peaceful protests. We will not stop until Rama resigns,” said Lora, a student who declined to give her last name as she threw rocks at the police.
Others chanted “resignation” and “police of crime”.
Student organisers said the protest was over conditions at universities, higher education costs, a lack of financial support and employment prospects after graduation.
The unrest is part of a broader wave of student activism sweeping Europe over education and living conditions. In France, high school students have staged weeks of protests and school blockades demanding more teachers and better facilities, arguing that deteriorating school buildings and overcrowded classrooms are undermining education.
Albanian media reported that Wednesday’s protests had spread to universities at Elbasan and Shkodër.

I call on students and every honest citizen who believes in the right to protest: distance yourself from violence and vandalism!”
The police issued a statement calling for calm. “Any person who uses violence, burns or destroys property, or attacks police officers, bears individual responsibility and will face the law, in accordance with the offences committed,” they said.
Meanwhile, the EU, which the Balkan nation aspires to join, voiced concern over what it called the “violent escalation at the protest in Tirana”.

Can math stay human in the age of AI?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
17:00:00 UTC
02:00:00 KST

Can math stay human in the age of AI?
When AI companies value competition over collaboration, we may lose out on understanding
“Exponentially exploding,” mathematician Thomas Bloom told me by phone, describing the flood of new results in his field. Little did he know that hours later, OpenAI was going to post 722 mathematical manuscripts an unreleased AI model had produced.
The firehose of new work lends new urgency to the question: How is AI changing mathematical discovery? In their race for headline-grabbing breakthroughs, AI companies typically do not disclose their methods and data. That competition among AI companies threatens to overwhelm human collaboration and understanding.
This tension had been playing out in miniature on a website Bloom runs that tracks progress on more than 1,000 problems originally posed and collected by Paul Erdős, one of the 20th century’s most prolific mathematicians. Here, people used to collaborate to discuss open problems, or ones for which the best solution either hasn’t been found or isn’t known to the greater math community. But increasingly, visitors were competing to close open problems with AI proofs that they often didn’t understand. Bloom, a mathematician at the University of Manchester in England, doesn’t want to spend his days refereeing AI-generated work. So, soon after we spoke, and before he knew that OpenAI would be announcing its latest results, Bloom posted that he’d no longer tag problems as open or solved, and he also closed comments.
It’s definitely exciting that AI can tackle so many open problems so quickly. But can it help mathematicians understand the answers and build on them?
Just two days after OpenAI’s deluge of results, the peer-reviewed edition of a Google DeepMind study became public. First reported in a preprint earlier this year, it offers an inside look at how one AI system tackles open math problems. The system called AlphaProof Nexus solved 9 Erdős problems and made a number of other interesting mathematical advances, researchers report October 8 in Science.
The report includes a detailed description of how the results were obtained. Plus, human mathematicians vetted many of the proofs. That’s “quite different” from how OpenAI and Anthropic are handling their math results, Bloom says.
“The ultimate objective of any AI for math research,” says research scientist and study co-author Swarat Chaudhuri of Google DeepMind in London, should be “to advance mathematics as done by human mathematicians.”
A look inside an AI math machine
In the recently published study Chaudhuri and his colleagues tested different configurations of their system. To tackle a collection of 353 open Erdős problems, they used multiple agents powered by the Gemini language model. These could call on AlphaProof, an AI model specially trained to do math, and the inspiration for the name of the overall system, for difficult steps. The agents also relied on Lean, math software that identifies steps that remain unproven, to check their logic. The agents shared their work, circulating promising proof attempts and discarding ones that weren’t going well.
The team also tested a simpler setup on the nine problems the full system solved. Independent Gemini agents worked through proofs using Lean’s feedback, without sharing attempts or consulting AlphaProof. That setup solved all nine, too. It was cheaper—using fewer computing resources—than the full system on easy problems and more expensive on the two toughest ones. The team did not establish whether the simpler setup would solve any of the problems the full system had missed.
The fact that the simpler setup could solve the same nine problems as the full system surprised Chaudhuri. It suggests that increasingly capable language models can tackle research mathematics with relatively simple checking tools.
But computer-checking comes with a caveat. Lean checks only the statement it’s given, as it is written in its code. And a mathematical statement may be incorrectly translated to or from Lean code. An October 6 preprint shows why this translation matters. In the paper, the researchers pinpoint mismatches between parts of OpenAI’s written Navier–Stokes proof and its Lean counterpart. The mismatches do not mean the written proof is wrong, the team writes, but they note that a valid Lean proof does not automatically validate an AI-generated math paper.
That’s why the vetting human mathematicians did for the DeepMind publication is so important. “The human mathematician has to really think through the problem and set goals for the system,” Chaudhuri says. And even if the system failed to finish a proof, its checked steps helped mathematicians focus on the remaining gaps. “Math is ultimately a human art,” Chaudhuri says. “The system enhances the human user’s insights, and the human user is able to guide the system with new ideas.”
With math ability comes responsibility
The mathematical results that the AlphaProof Nexus system achieved are “not really at the top level of importance,” says Bloom, who wasn’t involved with the work. But that underscores the team’s more measured approach. Google DeepMind, he says, is “trying to be more responsible with the science,” while companies like OpenAI are using math to showcase their software. OpenAI’s papers and accompanying Lean proofs were entirely AI-generated, leaving it up to the math community to work out what’s useful or useless.
OpenAI says they worked with an independent advisory group to develop best practices on how to share their AI math results. But that group has said their advice was to not test unreleased AI models on advanced math, guidance the company clearly ignored.
The company’s fast-moving, competitive approach continues to alienate mathematicians such as Bryna Kra of Northwestern University in Evanston, Ill. She says the company made some improvements in their efforts to cite past literature. And she’s excited about AI’s potential to solve important problems in math. But there is widespread concern, she says, that AI models have accessed people’s unpublished work. “We had a healthy, collaborative, sharing culture that is being destroyed,” she says. “Now, people are wary of sharing their ideas.”
Not all mathematicians feel this way about AI. The technology is “making math more accessible,” says Andrew Turner, who wonders why a small group of mathematicians should get to decide how we solve problems. Turner, who studied math and physics and is Now CTO of the company Plasma AI, based in New York City thinks “math is becoming engineering.” And doing math with machines will allow people to “answer questions previously unfathomable.”
A few days after Bloom shut down the competition on his website, Plasma AI announced a new website to track progress on Erdős problems. They will welcome AI results.
Bloom doesn’t see math as a Silicon Valley–esque move-fast-and-break-things competition. I agree, and hope that curious people will continue to explore problems they care about, with AI helping rather than taking over. At the end of his post announcing the changes to his website, Bloom wrote something that makes me tear up every time I read it. I hope everyone, even the most enthusiastic AI users, can find the time for this type of work: “Be confused, be stuck, be inspired. Find a messy proof, then find a better one,” he wrote. “Get tired, get hungry, get into a flow state. Argue, laugh, give up, drink some coffee and attack it again. Be human. Let your brain be open.”

Israel orders 12 AH-64E Apaches from Boeing for 2030s
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:59:14 UTC
01:59:14 KST

- Israel signed an agreement with the U.S. Department of War to buy 12 Boeing AH-64E Apache helicopters, with deliveries due early next decade.
- The U.S. State Department approved a possible sale of up to 30 AH-64E helicopters to Israel in January for an estimated $3.8 billion.
Israel has signed an agreement with the U.S. Department of War to buy 12 Boeing AH-64E Apache attack helicopters, the newest version of the Apache, with deliveries scheduled to begin early in the next decade, the Israel Ministry of Defense said on Oct. 14.
The ministry’s director general, Maj. Gen. (res.) Amir Baram, instructed Israel’s defense mission in the United States to sign the deal after the Israeli government approved it on Wednesday. The ministry did not disclose the value of the agreement or a specific delivery date, saying only that the helicopters are due at the start of the next decade.
The order is well below the package Washington cleared earlier this year. On Jan. 30, the U.S. State Department approved a possible sale of 30 AH-64E helicopters to Israel, together with 70 engines, Longbow fire-control radars and targeting sights, at an estimated cost of $3.8 billion. A Foreign Military Sales approval sets a ceiling, and buyers often sign for fewer aircraft than the notification covers.
Israeli officials said the agreement was tailored with U.S. counterparts to fit Israel’s needs, and both the defense minister and the ministry’s director general pointed to obstacles that had to be cleared to finish it.
“The execution of the Apache agreement was made possible thanks to creative solutions we developed together with our American partners, without compromising operational needs,” Baram said.
Neither official explained what those challenges were or whether Israel plans to order more of the 30 helicopters approved by Washington. Baram said the ministry will keep working to sign further agreements covering platforms and munitions as well as interceptors.
“The Israeli defense establishment invested considerable effort and acted with determination to overcome the challenges and complete this agreement,” said Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz.
The new helicopters are meant to replace the oldest part of the Israeli Air Force’s Apache force. Israel flies a mix of AH-64A Peten and AH-64D Saraf helicopters, and its 48-strong fleet includes 26 A-models that are up to 39 years old. Israeli Apaches have flown heavily since the war with Hamas began in October 2023, including strikes in Gaza and Lebanon and interceptions of drones.
The AH-64E, also known as the Apache Guardian, has more powerful engines and improved sensors and avionics over earlier models. It can also control drones from the cockpit and receive their video feeds, a feature the U.S. Army uses to pair Apaches with unmanned scouts.
Boeing Israel President Maj. Gen. (res.) Ido Nehushtan said the Apache deal follows Israel’s earlier selection of Boeing’s KC-46A aerial refueling tanker and its decision to buy a second squadron of F-15IA fighters.

Can Trump Strip Ilhan Omar of Her Citizenship? Here's How the Process Works
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:57:47 UTC
01:57:47 KST

In a highly unusual step, federal agents this week aggressively intensified their investigations into Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar of Minnesota, weeks before she stands for reelection in her home district.
The Department of Justice on Tuesday subpoenaed relatives of Omar’s family members, including her sister Sahra Noor, according to The New York Times. The grand jury subpoenas were issued shortly after a raid of the lawmaker’s residence in Washington, D.C. on Monday.
The judicial search warrant, which is under seal, was executed by Homeland Security Investigations, the investigative branch of Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Although the Department of Justice did not provide any more details of the investigation, multiple outlets, citing anonymous sources, reported that the search stemmed from Omar’s immigration paperwork, which was filled out by her late father when she was a child.
Prior to the investigation, multiple Trump Administration officials have accused Omar of immigration fraud without presenting any evidence. In a podcast interview in March, Vice President JD Vance said the White House was exploring “legal remedies” to her alleged immigration fraud. Last month, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the investigation into Omar was “ongoing” and dismissed efforts to frame the case as political retribution.
“If we actually move a case forward, it’s not a political case. It's actually a case because they did things wrong,” Mullin said during the interview with right-wing podcaster Benny Johnson.
Omar, who has long denied the allegations, condemned the raid on her home as “political intimidation” and said she will “not be silenced.”
President Trump, along with many MAGA Republicans, has repeatedly floated the idea of revoking Omar’s citizenship, a process also known as denaturalization, and deporting her.
But legal and immigration experts tell TIME that denaturalizing a U.S. citizen is a rare and difficult process, one that requires federal authorities to clear a high bar in front of a federal judge. Here’s what to know about how the process works.
How does denaturalization work?
Stripping someone of their citizenship is a more arduous legal process than most other immigration efforts that involve the courts. Deportation proceedings, for instance, are initiated by ICE agents under the Department of Homeland Security and are then approved by immigration judges who are hired and work within the Department of Justice. The denaturalization process, on the other hand, must be approved by an independent federal judge, who evaluates the request by a higher standard.
All denaturalization efforts begin at DOJ. In order to revoke a naturalized person’s citizenship, a DOJ lawyer must decide whether to file a civil or a criminal petition in court. Yuripzy Morgan, an attorney and host of Free Range National podcase, said a civil complaint does not have a statute of limitation, whereas a criminal complaint has a statute of limitation of 10 years and must clear a much higher legal bar.
“For civil denaturalization, the government has to show that there is clear, convincing, and unequivocal evidence that the person in question obtained their naturalization either illegally, or they willfully misrepresented a material fact, ” Morgan says. She stressed that simply having an error in an immigration document doesn't mean that a judge is going to approve stripping a person of their citizenship.
For a criminal denaturalization conviction, the federal government must show “proof beyond a reasonable doubt” that the individual knowingly obtained citizenship through fraud, which is the highest legal standard of proof required to secure a criminal conviction. In 2017, the Supreme Court unanimously ruled in Maslenjak v. United States that only an illegal act that played a role in a person’s citizenship application could lead to criminal denaturalization, further narrowing down the scope of such efforts.
Omar’s father filled out and submitted her citizenship application on her behalf when she was 17. It is unclear what evidence, if any, the federal government has to show that anything in the application was fraudulent, or that Omar or her father intentionally misrepresented anything in that application.
Andrew Arthur, a former immigration judge and a resident fellow at the Center for Immigration Studies, pointed out that even after someone gets denaturalized, a deportation is not guaranteed. The person would still be able to retain their previous legal immigration status until a final order of removal is issued to the person by ICE.
“If they had a green card before they naturalized, even after they get denaturalized, they are going to have a green card,” Arthur says.
How did Rep. Omar get naturalized as a U.S. citizen?
According to Omar’s House biography, Omar and her family fled her home country Somalia when she was eight. The family eventually sought asylum in the United States in 1995. She told The New York Times that she became a U.S. citizen in 2000 when she was 17.
At the time Omar went through the process, federal law allowed immigrants under the age of 18 to get naturalized as U.S. citizens if both of their parents had become U.S. citizens. The law was eventually replaced by a new law in 2001, which only requires one parent to become a citizen for the children to be naturalized.
At the center of this investigation is whether Omar’s father, Nur Omar Mohamed, lied about her age in immigration documents so she could be eligible to derive citizenship through him, according to The Washington Post, which cited two unnamed sources.
According to Arthur, the former immigration judge, if Omar was 18 at the time of the naturalization application, she may have been able to apply for her citizenship on her own after having a valid green card for five years.
The allegations regarding Omar’s citizenship gained attention among conservative activists and commentators starting in 2019, when Omar became a member of Congress. Shortly after her election, Omar’s staff sought to change her official birth year in public records from 1981 to 1982, according to multiple outlets.
How often does the U.S. government strip people of their citizenship?
Despite the renewed push from the second Trump administration, denaturalization remains an exceedingly rare legal process. According to the Migration Policy Institute, a Washington, D.C.-based think tank, an average of 11 denaturalization cases were filed per year between 1990 and 2017.
Denaturalization efforts have increased in Trump’s second term. The DOJ has announced efforts to strip at least 108 people of their citizenship in 2026. That is still considerably smaller than the hundreds of thousands of people whom the U.S. government grants citizenship to through naturalization every year.
