US carriers dare not approach Hormuz, we are waiting to sink them
TEHRAN – The commander of the Islamic Revolution Guards Corps Navy says American warships have withdrawn to hundreds of kilometers from the Strait of Hormuz out of vulnerability, warning that Iranian forces are counting the moments for them to come within range.
Rear Admiral Ali Ozmaei said in remarks published Tuesday that the United States Navy, despite its advanced hardware, no longer dares to approach Iranian waters.
"Today, by God's grace and with our naval combatants, we are standing against the vicious enemies," Ozmaei said. "The US Army has turned into a fuel smuggler and its fleet has become useless because it is vulnerable and does not dare to come close to Iran."
The commander said Iran has turned its tactical weaknesses into strengths and challenged Washington to test who really controls the world's most critical energy chokepoint.
"If the Americans want to see whether the Strait of Hormuz is open or closed, let them enter the field to see who controls it," he said.
According to Ozmaei, even the United States' 13-billion-dollar aircraft carrier has been rendered ineffective and is now operating about 700 kilometers away from the Strait because it fears being hit.
"We are waiting for the American warships to approach the entrance of the Strait of Hormuz to sink them; we are counting down moment by moment for this to happen," he said.
Ozmaei said Iran has so far publicized only one or two examples of its punishment of violating vessels, noting that the US and its regional partners of imposing a media blackout to hide the fact that offending ships are being disciplined.
"We showed only two samples of the punishment of offending ships," he said, adding that Iranian forces act without compromise against violators.
The commander stressed that the Strait of Hormuz and the Persian Gulf are under the control of the IRGC Navy, while the Sea of Oman is controlled by the Islamic Republic Army, meaning that any blockade now lies beyond the Sea of Oman, in the Arabian Sea.
"The IRGC Navy conducts smart control of the Strait of Hormuz," Ozmaei explained. Vessels bound to or departing from Iran are issued permits through a hierarchy and transit only through the Iranian waterway, he said.
Addressing the Iranian public, he said naval combatants are in the field alongside the people and deal firmly with offenders.
"We can establish economic, political and military security with our neighbors. We do not need the Americans. They are after plundering the wealth of the people of the region," he said. "Today the American army has been humiliated and reduced to misery."
Ozmaei added that Iran's position is stronger than in the early days of the imposed war, and that its fighters are more prepared today than yesterday.
His remarks coincided with two fresh maritime incidents reported Tuesday in and around the Strait.
In the morning, the IRGC Navy's public relations department announced that a violating container ship carrying more than 2,500 containers, which had attempted to transit the Strait of Hormuz through an unauthorized and dangerous route, struck a naval mine in the southern waters of the Strait, exploded and caught massive fire before sinking.
Local vessels and fishermen were advised to navigate with maximum caution to avoid colliding with floating containers, the statement said.
At noon on the same day, the Islamic Republic Army Navy reported that a violating oil tanker, which had switched off its tracking systems and was trying to pass through a prohibited zone east of the Strait of Hormuz, suffered damage and fire and was detected by Army surveillance teams.
Announcing a new formation and deployment of operational units east of the Strait of Hormuz and in the Arabian Sea and Sea of Oman areas, the Army Navy said it maintains full, round-the-clock surveillance over all enemy activities and vessel traffic.
It advised all vessels to strictly refrain from switching off their electronic equipment in violation of international law and to coordinate with the Armed Forces of the Islamic Republic of Iran for safe passage.

'Unprecedented': Global Palestine movement vows to drive change
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:47:46 UTC
01:47:46 KST

Breadcrumb
'We are driving change': Global Palestine movement hails growing influence worldwide
The global Palestine solidarity movement has reached unprecedented levels of influence, with growing public anger over Israel's genocide in Gaza putting governments under mounting pressure to translate support for Palestinian rights into meaningful political action.
Speaking exclusively to The New Arab, Global Alliance for Palestine (GAFP) secretary-general Anas Altikriti said the movement was gaining momentum worldwide, as hundreds of organisations mobilised across more than 80 countries to mark three years of Israel's war on Gaza.
"This momentum around the world that we've seen build and reach a level was never ever expected – totally unprecedented," he said.
But Altikriti warned that growing international recognition of Palestinian statehood would remain "superficial" unless governments adopted policies to hold Israel accountable for its actions.
"We saw how in late 2025, a catalogue of countries recognised the state of Palestine, how there were Palestinian embassies opened throughout the world – but we insisted then and we insist now that all of this is superficial if not followed with actual policies that first of all hold Israel to account and those who took part in the war crime that we saw and we witnessed."
His comments follow a three-day global solidarity campaign held from 9 to 11 October, which brought together pro-Palestine organisations and campaigners for demonstrations, vigils, cultural events and community gatherings.
The coordinated actions demanded an end to Israel's genocide in Gaza, its decades-long occupation, ongoing settler violence and settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem, as well as accountability for governments accused of enabling Israeli war crimes.
Altikriti said the mobilisation reflected growing frustration not only with Israel's military offensives in Gaza, Lebanon and elsewhere, but also with the international community's failure to stop them.
"People are angry beyond what we've known in terms of the crimes committed incessantly and with impunity by Israel and the Israeli government. But also the silence and the tacit complicity of the entire world and here in the UK," he told TNA.
He also urged Britain's government under Prime Minister Andy Burnham to match its changing rhetoric on Israel and Palestinian rights with concrete policies.
"And whilst this new government under Andy Burnham has adopted a new narrative in regards with Israel and the Palestinian rights, we still need to see actual policies being put in place to reflect that kind of anger and frustration that the streets, not only of the UK, but the entire world, feel."
'Of course, we're vilifying Israel'
The growing international movement has also faced criticism from pro-Israel voices, including Israel's Foreign Ministry, which condemned GAFP's global campaign and highlighted a Fox News report describing the activism as "the protest playbook to vilify Israel".
Asked about the Israeli government's criticism, Altikriti responded defiantly.
"Of course, we're vilifying Israel," he said. “Israel is an occupying terrorist state. We made that proclamation time and time and time again, not just myself, not just the Global Alliance of Palestine, but countless Israelis who have themselves seen the poison that Israel creates, not only in Palestine, but throughout the entire world.”
Altikriti argued that Israel's own policies, rather than the activities of solidarity campaigners, were responsible for the growing international anger towards the country.
“The vilification has actually come from Israeli policies itself. Israel has created this. Israel has created the momentum that we see around the world. The anger that people feel, the questioning of American people as to why their tax dollars are being shipped to Israel for them to then kill Palestinian children.”
His comments come as pro-Palestine campaigners seek to sustain international pressure on governments over their diplomatic, military and economic ties with Israel.
Global solidarity reaches new heights
GAFP hailed its three-day mobilisation as a major success, saying it demonstrated the growing reach and influence of the international Palestine solidarity movement.
“Hundreds of organisations and campaigns in over 80 countries around the world do all sorts of activities, whether there are demos, marches, vigils, stands, flag waving or balloon settings,” Altikriti told TNA.
“We count this as a tremendous success, not only for ourselves, the Global Alliance for Palestine, but also all the activist groups and all the campaigns that took part in this, whether under our umbrella or whether independently, we regard this as being an inspiration from the people of Gaza.”
The campaign culminated in a Global Day of Action on Saturday, 10 October, when tens of thousands of pro-Palestine protesters marched through central London.
GAFP estimates that more than 250,000 people joined coordinated actions organised by established groups, including the Muslim Association of Britain (MAB), Palestinian Forum in Britain (PFB), Palestine Solidarity Campaign (PSC), Stop the War Coalition (STWC), Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament (CND) and Friends of Al-Aqsa (FoA).
The mobilisation came as Palestinians marked three years since Israel launched its devastating military assault on Gaza in October 2023.
More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli attacks since then.
Despite a US-brokered ceasefire agreed in October 2025, which envisaged the eventual reconstruction of the devastated territory, little progress has been made towards implementing the agreement.
At least 1,400 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli fire since the so-called ceasefire took effect.

China’s drone modem pipeline: How mesh technology helps Russian UAVs penetrate deep into Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:45:29 UTC
01:45:29 KST

The Insider's correspondent in Ukraine examined a mesh modem — one made by China’s Xingkai Tech — that was found in a Russian Gerbera drone. Then, posing as a Russian military supplier, they obtained evidence that the Chinese company is knowingly willing to sell its modems to the Russian drone factory in Alabuga. Several banks, including DBS Bank, China Merchants Bank, and Ping An Bank, are actively facilitating these sales. Mesh networks are the most practical technology for controlling Russia’s long-range drones over Ukraine. They allow operators to control drones manually and send commands in flight, exploiting gaps in Ukrainian air defenses. According to The Insider’s estimates, Xingkai Tech accounts for about half the market for high-power mesh modems used in Gerbera and Geran drones, making its supplies critical to Russian military manufacturers.
In February 2026, the Russian military lost access to the Starlink terminals it had previously used to facilitate attacks on Ukraine. As a workaround, it has since turned to the use of Geran and Gerbera drones equipped with Chinese-made mesh modems.
A typical attack involving Geran and Gerbera drones works as follows: some drones flying near the border connect to Russian or Belarusian signal repeaters and relay signals to drones operating deeper inside Ukraine. Each relay node is equipped with a powerful mesh modem.
Gerbera drones are becoming increasingly important. They are significantly cheaper than Gerans and have a similar radar signature, allowing them to serve as decoys for Ukrainian air defenses.
In 2024 Ukraine’s military intelligence agency (HUR) reported finding Xingkai Tech modems in Gerbera drones. Later, the use of these modems and the role of Gerberas in combat operations in 2026 were discussed on a major pro-Russian website. However, there was no evidence that Xingkai Tech was knowingly and openly supplying modems directly to the Russian Alabuga plant where the drones are assembled.
In an earlier investigation, The Insider found that Chinese company Shenzhen Xingkai Technology, also known as Xingkai Tech, had issued an invoice for 30 mesh modems destined for Vladivostok as part of a supply chain supporting Russian drones.
In 2026, The Insider examined a mesh modem obtained privately in Ukraine that had been found in an upgraded Gerbera drone fitted with a vertical stabilizer. This variant first appeared this past summer.
An investigator from the Nordsint project then posed as a Russian military supplier based in Alabuga, where Geran and Gerbera drones are manufactured. Xingkai Tech confirmed that the model was available and that Xingkai Technology was its sole manufacturer. The journalist also obtained an invoice for 500 mesh modems that were identical to the one examined in Ukraine — a shipment worth approximately $2.87 million.
How the modems are sold
Posing as a Russian military supplier, The Insider and Nordsint contacted Xingkai Technology through its official WeChat account to request a quote for modems “similar” to the one shown in a photograph from Ukraine. The undercover investigators made clear that the end user needed exactly the same version, with an identical casing.
A company employee who introduced himself as “Jack Jiang” (his actual name is Jiang Qin (蒋钦), and he is the director and owner of the company) confirmed that Xingkai Technology manufactured the modems; he even provided the investigators with the XK F-359 user manual. Some sources, including the Ukrainian military intelligence agency’s War and Sanctions portal, had previously misidentified the device as a separate but similar model, the XK F-358.
To make sure the end user would receive an identical device, the investigators asked Jiang to take photographs and video of the modem at the production facility. He complied.
The modem examined by The Insider in Ukraine proved identical to the device described in the manual and shown in the warehouse video. It differed only slightly from the models featured in Xingkai Technology’s online catalog. Jiang explained that other versions of the F-359 had different casings but retained the same internal layout.
The Insider and Nordsint then ordered 500 modems for delivery to Alabuga, home to a factory that produces most of Russia’s long-range drones. Jiang responded with an invoice for 19.5 million yuan, offering the “client” two payment options: U.S. dollars to Xingkai Tech’s account at DBS Bank in Hong Kong, or yuan to Jiang’s personal account at Ping An Bank in China.
Jiang also confirmed that identical modems were available through Shenzhen Sinosun Technology (although Xingkai Tech itself manufactured the devices). In their correspondence, Nordsint explicitly stated that the end user was a military production facility. Xingkai Tech’s director raised no objections.
Nordsint explicitly stated that the end user was a military production facility. Xingkai Tech’s director raised no objections
In another message, Jiang asked whether his Russian customer had “won” the “project,” apparently referring to a tender.
After being asked to “update the address,” Xingkai Tech issued a slightly revised invoice. This time, the company spelled “Alabuga” in Latin characters, making it harder to claim later that it had been unaware of the end user’s identity.
The Chinese bank account listed on the revised invoice was in the name of Huang Qiuping, who may also use the name Fanny Huang (she is listed under that name as a contact in the mesh modem’s user manual). According to Tesari records, Huang Qiuping left her management position at Xingkai Tech in 2025.
The revised invoice directed payments to an account at the Hongling branch of the China Merchants Bank in Shenzhen.
The key component of a mesh modem is a field-programmable gate array (FPGA). It enables the modem to make decisions about network topology and optimize communications. This “intelligent” component configures the mesh network linking a swarm of drones.
The Xingkai Tech director who corresponded with an undercover Nordsint investigator said the company uses the XC7Z020-2CLG4001 FPGA made by U.S.-based company AMD. When asked to provide an AMD licensing agreement (ostensibly to meet Russian bureaucratic requirements), Jiang refused, saying Xingkai Tech obtains its FPGAs through an intermediary.
The Insider contacted AMD, which provided the following statement:
“Xingkai Technology is not an AMD customer or authorized partner, and AMD has not sold products to the company. AMD complies with all applicable U.S. export control and sanctions laws and strictly prohibits the export or reexport of AMD products to Russia in violation of those requirements.”
What this little box can do
The XK F-359 modem can maintain line-of-sight communications over distances of 100–300 km. This means that an attack on Kyiv theoretically may require just a couple of Gerbera or Shahed drones acting as relay stations to provide a stable radio link for the entire attacking drone group, allowing the drones to receive updated commands in flight and maneuver to evade air defenses. The technology is also crucial for providing live video feeds from operator-controlled drones equipped with cameras and guidance systems, such as those recently reported by Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov.
Mesh modems can autonomously establish and manage network topology in real time.
The XK F-359 manual states:
“The network operates on a single frequency and uses multi-hop relaying. Each node can move rapidly and freely, while the network topology can change and update rapidly without disrupting data transmission. The network is easy to deploy, flexible to use, and simple to operate and maintain. It provides reliable, timely, efficient and secure integrated IP services, including voice, broadband data, high-definition video, visual command and dispatch, and other multimedia services in challenging conditions, such as rapid movement and the absence of a direct line of sight.”
In other words, the mesh network reconfigures itself automatically, freeing drone operators from having to manage it manually and allowing them to focus on military tasks.
Notably, the manual’s opening line lists military and police operations among the intended applications of mesh technology:
“Broadband self-organizing networks can be widely used in the military, public security agencies, armed police, fire services, civil defense, electric power, the oil industry, mining, transportation, water management, forestry, radio and television, medicine, maritime and aviation communications, and other fields.”
Given these capabilities, the Xingkai Tech XK F-359 is almost ideally suited to Gerbera and Geran drones.
The specific XK F-359 variant documented by The Insider in Ukraine does not appear in Xingkai Technology’s public catalogs. The manual for this version became available only after The Insider established direct contact with the company.
Some online sources, meanwhile, identified Shenzhen Sinosun Technology as the modem’s manufacturer. The company’s website features a photograph of an identical modem, sometimes found among drone wreckage bearing the HX-50 label. When asked about this, Jack Jiang of Xingkai Technology confirmed that his company was the modem’s sole manufacturer.
Who bought them in Russia
The Insider examined Russian customs data and found that Xingkai Technology had shipped its products to Russia, declaring them simply as “antennas” and “remote control equipment.”
One Russian recipient was Atlant-Engineering, a trading company that does not manufacture drones. The company is owned by the family of Rafik Zagrutdinov, a mid-level official in the Moscow city government. Another recipient was LT Global Forwarding.
Both companies filed declarations of conformity, apparently for Xingkai Technology equipment; however, for reasons unknown, Quanzhou Yunzhuo Technology was listed as the manufacturer.
What’s new with the Gerberas
Gerbera drones were initially inexpensive decoys, as their radar signature resembled that of older Geran models without turbojet engines.
Later, Gerberas were fitted with warheads and began carrying out reconnaissance missions. During the summer of 2026, upgraded versions began to appear, distinguished primarily by a vertical stabilizer. Some variants were also equipped with cameras.
Gerberas have been shot down in European countries. Recently, one such drone flew into Lithuanian airspace.
The Insider analyzed a sample of 30 listings for parts from downed Russian drones on Ukraine’s largest online auction site for war trophies. At least nine lots featured easily recognizable Xingkai Tech mesh modems. One listing offered 10 modems at once. Identical Xingkai Tech mesh modems have also been found in Banderol loitering munitions (drone missiles).
Equipping a drone — even one that once served as a decoy — with a modern mesh modem turns it into a weapon capable of threatening Europe. Recently, the Spanish publication El Mundo reported that the CIA had warned European countries that Gerberas could be launched against Europe from vessels belonging to Russia’s “shadow fleet.”
Many of Xingkai Tech’s drone components are available on the popular Russian online marketplace Wildberries.
The Insider contacted the press offices of DBS, Ping An, and China Merchants Bank, and also reached out to DBS by phone. None of the three banks responded.
Another mesh modem
The Insider identified another mesh modem widely used in Shahed drones that had not previously been publicly identified. Comparing listings on Reibert with the manufacturer’s website, it established that the modem is made by China’s Xi'an Sihou Network Technology Co., Ltd.
Xi'an Sihou Network Technology is another major player in the market for captured equipment sold at auction. It accounts for roughly half of the listings for captured mesh modems examined by The Insider. The company’s owner and director is Li Li.
Geran drones, along with Banderol loitering munitions, have become Russia’s main weapons in its campaign of terror against Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, as well as in attacks on railway locomotives. The survival of Ukraine’s civilian population through the coming winter will depend largely on whether the West can use sanctions and diplomacy to quickly halt large-scale sales of mesh modems to Russia.

Israel’s warnings of a PA attack shifts focus from the unresolved Hamas threat - analysis
Netanyahu and Katz warn Palestinian Authority forces could turn their weapons on Israel, but security sources report no concrete threat, raising questions about the timing ahead of elections
As Israel marks three years since the multi-front war launched by Hamas and other Palestinian terror groups on October 7, the various fronts remain open: the IDF continues to conduct near-daily strikes in Lebanon and in the Gaza Strip, where Hamas is still in power; Israeli forces are still deployed in Syria; and the Iranian and Houthi fronts are on pause, but far from resolved.
Last week, the Israeli public was suddenly presented with a new threat. "The IDF is preparing for a scenario in which the Palestinian Authority's security apparatus turns its weapons against Israeli settlers and IDF forces in Judea and Samaria and in communities along the Seam Zone," Defense Minister Israel Katz declared at the weekly cabinet meeting.
"In such an event, we will declare war against the Palestinian Authority, and the IDF will launch a full-scale offensive in accordance with a structured plan formulated and approved by Prime Minister Netanyahu and myself—based on the principles outlined for the IDF."
That's quite a bombshell. Just think about it: tens of thousands of armed Palestinian Authority security personnel deployed throughout the West Bank decide one day to launch an October 7-style attack on dozens of Israeli communities and military bases in Judea and Samaria. The results would be disastrous.
Yesterday, Netanyahu added his own warning. "Our enemies are considering testing us during this period leading up to the elections; we are prepared for any scenario, including a sudden turning of the guns. The IDF has presented a robust plan to me and the Ministry of Defense for such an eventuality; I would advise our enemies not to put us to the test," he said, speaking from the West Bank.
In a post-October 7 reality, Israel's security bodies must be prepared for any scenario, and it's good to know that the country's top leaders are aware of the threat. There is only one problem: there is no indication that such a threat exists. Security sources I've spoken with say the IDF has no intelligence pointing to such an attack, and Shin Bet sources told Israeli media they know of no concrete threat from the PA.
So why the sudden scare, when there is no apparent threat and Israelis have nothing in their power to do about it? There are other possible explanations, from instability within the PA to plain deterrence signaling. But none of them explain the timing. The public first heard of this new threat on October 6, the day before the anniversary of the worst security failure in Israel's history.
Talking about how Hamas is still in power three years after it massacred some 1,200 people and kidnapped 251 more, on their watch, is inconvenient, to say the least, for leaders seeking reelection. So why not shift the conversation to other armed Palestinians, who, apart from a few rogue security personnel, pose no actual threat to Israelis?
Beyond the political cynicism, presenting the PA security forces as an emerging threat is divorced from reality. As you read these words, PA security forces are helping protect Israeli communities in Judea and Samaria. Their contribution to combating Palestinian terror in the West Bank is minimal at best, but their presence and ongoing coordination with the IDF are a net gain for Israel's security.
Could they one day turn on Israel and endanger it? Potentially, yes, and Israel must be prepared for that, especially after October 7. But nothing points to it. The threat posed by Hamas, which is still in power and refuses to disarm, is very real. Talking about that two weeks before the first elections since October 7, however, is politically dangerous. It's far easier to inflate a new threat and divert attention from the failure in Gaza.

Maryam Ashalem de Andres
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
Opposition groups, trade unions, Indigenous organizations and social movements took to the streets in Colombia on Wednesday to protest President Abelardo de la Espriella's government.
“The right to protest is respected, but there is no right to destroy, attack the security forces, assault others or sow chaos,” De la Espriella said in a statement announcing the decree.
The decree allows police to intervene against violent protesters without completing all stages of dialogue and mediation.
The government said the measure protects peaceful demonstrations while enabling authorities to respond to vandalism, assaults and disruptions to essential services.
Protesters oppose the government's economic and social policies and demand labor rights, better public education funding and guarantees for peaceful demonstrations.
Teachers' unions are demanding better working conditions and health care. Student and Indigenous groups want greater protection of their rights.
Authorities monitored demonstrations and traffic conditions in several cities, including Bogota, as the mobilizations unfolded.
The mobilizations mark a major test of opposition groups' capacity to challenge De la Espriella's administration.
Former President Gustavo Petro urged Colombians to join the demonstrations, focusing on the minimum wage and rising food prices.
“If the real minimum wage falls, what we have is a decline in the standard of living of all Colombians,” Petro said in a video on US social media company X.
The decree also establishes a mechanism for addressing social conflicts before they escalate. Under the system, local authorities must convene a dialogue meeting within five working days after an early warning is activated.
The government said the mechanism aims to resolve tensions through dialogue, while critics have questioned whether the new rules adequately protect the right to peaceful protest.

Palestine has said that Colombia’s opening of an embassy in West Jerusalem violates international law and UN resolutions.
The Palestinian foreign ministry said on Wednesday the opening constituted “a flagrant violation of international law and relevant UN resolutions and an assault on the Palestinian people and their just and legitimate national rights.”
It stressed that all measures and decisions to change the legal and historical status of Jerusalem are “null and void and have no legal effect".
It said that “opening an embassy to Israel in occupied Jerusalem violates international legitimacy resolutions, particularly UN Security Council Resolutions 476 and 478.”
The two resolutions that were adopted in 1980 affirm the illegality and invalidity of Israeli measures intended to alter the character and legal status of Jerusalem, amid Israel’s enactment of a law annexing occupied East Jerusalem.
The ministry said Colombia’s move also “undermines the international consensus on the city’s legal status and infringes on the Palestinian people’s inalienable rights.”
It warned that the step encourages Israel to continue its “colonial policies and attempts to impose illegal realities on the ground".
The Palestinian foreign ministry urged Colombia to comply with international law and respect relevant UN resolutions, calling on it to “reverse this step to preserve prospects for achieving a just and comprehensive peace.”
Jordan 
In a statement issued following the embassy’s opening, the Jordanian foreign ministry said the kingdom condemns and rejects the move.
The ministry stressed that any measures or decisions aimed at changing the status or legal standing of Jerusalem are “null and void, illegitimate and without legal effect.”
It said the only way to achieve a just and comprehensive peace is to establish an independent, sovereign Palestinian state along the June 4, 1967, lines, with East Jerusalem as its capital.
Saudi Arabia
Saudi Arabia’s foreign ministry condemned and denounced the move, describing it as a “blatant violation of international law and relevant international resolutions.”
It said the move contradicts the established international position on Jerusalem’s legal and historical status.
Riyadh renewed its demand for the international community, including the UN Security Council and all concerned parties, to fulfil their “legal and moral responsibilities” and act urgently to halt “illegal Israeli policies aimed at imposing a new reality by force and undermining prospects for a just and lasting peace.”
Jerusalem remains at the heart of Israel’s dispossession of Palestinians and subsequent occupation of Palestinian lands and is widely regarded as one of its most sensitive issues.
While Israel claims the entire city as its capital, Palestinians view East Jerusalem, occupied by Israel since 1967, as the capital of a future Palestinian state, in line with longstanding international consensus and UN resolutions.

The UK energy secretary is flirting with a bad idea for bills – the ‘rising block tariff’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:43:15 UTC
01:43:15 KST

‘My mark of failure or success is whether I can get bills down or not. That’s the only thing I’m in this job to do.” So said Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, recently, bracing for the hike in energy bills that looks inevitable in January. Industry projections suggest £400-ish on an annual basis is on the way, with “stubbornly high” levels for the rest of decade even if wholesale gas prices cool down.
So, yes, one can understand why “affordability” is Fahnbulleh’s “top priority”. And, as this newspaper reported last week, there is likely to be an intervention in that direction in chancellor John Healey’s budget this month: £1bn of extra support for poorer households this winter.
But the chat in energy-land is about what comes after that – and what Fahnbulleh’s other remarks about covering the costs of the energy system in a “fairer” way seem to be hinting at.
Will the government finally get round to designing a co-called “social tariff” for energy – a way to get financial support to the most needy on a more targeted basis than the clunky warm homes discount, the mechanism Healey will be obliged to use?
Will Healey, after chopping VAT from electricity for six months, do so permanently and then shift more green levies and other “hidden taxes” of energy transition into general taxation?
And is Fahnbulleh also contemplating something very different? Welcome to the idea of the “rising block tariff” (RBT), the unwieldy name for the proposal to give every household an initial block, or allowance, of cheaper gas and electricity to cover “essential” use and then make subsequent blocks more expensive. In other words, heavier energy consumers would pay higher rates for their extra units.
Fahnbulleh has got officials in her department to explore an RBT model. And, note, the New Economics Foundation, the thinktank she used to lead, is a proponent.
The Joseph Rowntree Foundation is another backer: in its version, the government could fund an RBT with, say, £5bn of public money, allowing bills to fall for most households – but, critically, the biggest savings would flow to light users, who tend to be low-income households. “An RBT would produce greater reductions in bills lower down the income distribution,” it says.
What’s not to like? Plenty. There are at least three reasons why an RBT has few fans elsewhere, not even among charities and thinktanks that focus on fuel poverty.
First, Citizens Advice regards low energy use as a poor proxy for low income in practice. Traditional electric heaters, with high electricity usage, “are more common in social or private rented homes, where people can’t change their heating system”, it argues.
Quite: a progressive-sounding policy could end up being nothing of the sort, especially if second-home owners, by spreading their usage, are winners. If the reply is that an incomes overlay could address tricky cases in both directions, why not just do the data modelling work to design a proper social tariff in the first place?
Second, a rigid RBT would be an awkward fit with a renewables-heavy system where the most interesting innovations are “flex” tariffs to exploit very windy or sunny hours when wholesale power prices are dirt cheap. There is a danger of baffling consumers by making them mix their blocks with their flexes.
Third, a core aim of the energy transition is to drive take-up of electric vehicles, heat pumps and so on. That becomes harder if the message to consumers is that “the more electricity you use, the more you’ll be charged per unit”.
Lobby group Electrify Britain calls block tariffs “hugely counterproductive” for electrification: “You can’t ask families to go electric and then pursue a policy that would charge them more for doing so.”
That feels the killer point: an RBT model cuts across too many other goals. Fahnbulleh should keep things simple: go for a serious social tariff or discount scheme that effectively identifies “vulnerable” energy users. That idea has enjoyed wide support for years. Block tariffs are too complicated and fiddly to administer.

State-run Taiwan Power Co (Taipower, 台電) plans to build 43 substations over the next 15 years to meet growing electricity demand, chairman Tseng Wen-sheng (曾文生) said yesterday.
The expansion also includes about 1,922km of new power lines, Tseng said at a forum during the Energy Taiwan exhibition in Taipei.
Growing demand from semiconductor manufacturing and artificial intelligence (AI) is making the timely delivery of electricity a key challenge for the utility, he said.
Photo: CNA
“We need to build 43 substations in 15 years, averaging about three a year. This is unprecedented,” he said.
Tseng cited the Songhu ultra-high voltage substation project in Taipei’s Neihu District (內湖) as an example of the difficulties facing grid construction.
The project broke ground last month after 26 years of planning and administrative procedures and is scheduled for completion in 2029, Taipower said.
The limited availability of land means shorter transmission distances, but also densely packed infrastructure that makes new lines difficult to build, he said.
Tseng cited growing power demand at the Southern Taiwan Science Park (南部科學園區) as an example of why additional substations were needed.
Grid planning would also need to account for AI equipment spreading beyond large data centers to businesses and potentially homes.
Such equipment could shift evening peak demand between 8pm and 10pm, prompting Taipower to adjust its load forecasts and assess upgrades to older urban grids, he said.
For companies planning new facilities, access to electricity on schedule has become an early investment consideration because power infrastructure could take longer to build than factories, Tseng added.
He urged large data centers to build near power plants, saying shorter dedicated power lines could reduce construction time, engineering difficulties and costs.
Speaking to reporters afterward, Tseng said Taipower is coordinating locations and investment schedules with major users and hopes to work directly with companies committed to investing in computing infrastructure.
Allocating supply capacity to a site developer before an actual investor is secured could leave less capacity available for other projects, he said, adding that Taipower is considering fair rules to address that issue.
The utility’s fastest-growing AI-related electricity demand comes from manufacturing, including chip fabrication, memory production, packaging and server production, rather than computing service providers, Tseng said.
Planning with those industries is beginning earlier, including during industrial park development, to align electricity infrastructure with their expansion schedules, he added.

Fukuyama, Thiel and the revenge of the ‘Last Man’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:42:33 UTC
01:42:33 KST

Stanford University political scientist Francis Fukuyama’s new memoir, In the Realm of the Last Man, is an unmistakable reference to his 1992 bestseller, The End of History and the Last Man.
Fukuyama said the reason he chose it was that people had ignored his book’s warning that “democracy could break down in the future because of some of the intrinsic stresses within a liberal order” — stresses born of the discontent of those whose desire for recognition exceeds what liberal democracy can satisfy.
Yet this claim is an opportunistic twisting of what was only a passing speculation in his celebrated book: that future people facing “no tyranny and oppression worthy of the name” might, out of sheer “boredom” rather than systemic “stresses,” choose to “struggle against the just cause” of liberal democracy. However, liberal democracy has been in retreat for at least two decades. To salvage his career-making thesis that history had ended, then, Fukuyama asserts that we all just misunderstood him.
Illustration: Mountain People
Who is this “Last Man” whom Fukuyama’s readers ignored? Fukuyama borrowed the term from Friedrich Nietzsche, casting the modern version as a political eunuch whose libido has been sapped by the consumer comforts of a “post-historical” world — one in which liberal democracy and capitalism no longer have ideological rivals.
Fukuyama’s Last Man has none of his forebears’ passion for political struggle or new world orders. To be sure, he has aspirations — namely, to make money — but this focus is an unmitigated blessing for his liberal-democratic fellows. Not only does the successful money seeker “create wealth which migrates through the economy,” but he is “kept out of politics and the military,” where his “restlessness” might otherwise lead him “to propose innovations at home or adventures abroad, with potentially disastrous consequences,” Fukuyama said.
SILICON VALLEY MAN
The money seeker who takes Fukuyama most seriously is the storied Silicon Valley venture capitalist Peter Thiel. He is also the money seeker whose thought and behavior make the greatest mockery of Fukuyama’s Last Man thesis.
Thiel — Facebook’s first outside investor, cofounder of PayPal and data-analysis giant Palantir and an early investor in Elon Musk’s SpaceX — has engaged with Fukuyama and his ideas for many years.
In a 2012 interview with Fukuyama, he said that “your ‘end of history’ strikes me as very much true today.” Economic globalization, Thiel believed, was clearly spreading the developed world’s standards of political organization.
However, unlike most self-declared libertarians at the time, Thiel was hardly comforted by this fact. He was instead troubled by the secular decline in developed-world innovation and growth since the late 1960s. In 2009, he had drawn great applause at the Singularity Summit in New York by dismissing Fukuyama’s fears about the human impact of uncontrolled bioscience as “hysterical.”
Restraining technological progress to protect humanity would only impoverish and enslave it, Thiel said.
By 2024, Thiel’s take on the accuracy of the End of History thesis had soured.
“The one that ... got it completely wrong is the Fukuyama book,” he told commentator and current CBS News editor-in-chief Bari Weiss. Authoritarianism was on the march; China’s rise had made that clear.
When Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) effectively became “president for life” in 2017, it was “maybe the year that the end of history comes to an end,” Thiel said.
As for the lobotomized Last Man, he now had every reason to shake off his political indolence and see struggle as meaningful once again.
“We can talk about trends and forces, but it does matter what people do,” Thiel said, adding that in the fractious post-liberal global order, “there’s room for human agency.”
At the Aspen Ideas Festival in June, Thiel again appeared with Fukuyama. No recording or transcript of their discussion was made this time, but a CNN reporter present highlighted the “notable departure” from their last public interaction 14 years earlier.
The pair now “framed the broader fate of Western democracy in more drastic terms,” he said.
Fukuyama, alarmed by US President Donald Trump’s trampling of congressional and judicial prerogatives, stressed the “danger” of “abandoning institutions that have sustained democracy” — still, in his view, humanity’s best political system.
Thiel seemed less sure, observing that US democracy had “gone haywire” over the past few years. To him, the source of democratic failure was not Trump, but the rise of far-left socialists within the Democratic Party. Their ascent had motivated him to finance the political campaigns of Trump, US Vice President J.D. Vance and other Republicans pledging to back tech deregulation.
Although at times accused of promoting “techno-authoritarianism,” Thiel has insisted that tech’s growing influence on US politics is a force for liberty, one that helps disperse entrenched “power centers.”
THE ANTICHRIST
So where do Thiel’s political and economic views come from? An early and enduring intellectual influence is Rene Girard, an eclectic French literary theorist and Christian anthropologist who taught Thiel as a Stanford undergraduate. Girard is best known for his mimetic theory of social life, which holds that people routinely imitate the desires of others, giving rise to rivalries that can engulf entire communities in violence.
Such social crises were traditionally resolved through “scapegoating”: concentrating communal blame and punishment on a single victim, whose expulsion or murder restored peace. Girard held that the New Testament uniquely recounts this process from the perspective of the innocent victim, Jesus, thereby revealing the falsity of the accusation and stripping the ritual of its sacred legitimacy.
Yet Christianity’s vindication of the victim did not eliminate the mimetic rivalries that produced him; it merely deprived societies of their traditional means of containing such rivalries. This loss has left the modern world at once more protective of victims and more vulnerable to violence without end.
Thiel also developed a set of beliefs — sometimes very different from those of the pacifist and anti-individualist Girard — to mitigate the supposedly pernicious political consequences of mimetic pathology. Girard’s reasoning underlies several of Thiel’s distinctly illiberal conclusions.
Since conflict is rooted in mimesis, prosperity cannot eliminate it. To believe, as End of History liberals do, that disagreement can and must be resolved through discussion and debate is to misunderstand the actual, non-rational sources of social dissension. Societies require independent forces — exceptional founders, technological innovators, and alternative jurisdictions — to resist mimetic conformity.
The classical liberal celebration of economic competition is misguided when competition itself becomes a personal ideal, since it induces imitation and therefore conflict. The true entrepreneur serves society by aiming instead to create monopoly — that is, something genuinely new that cannot be imitated.
The nation-state is irreplaceable as a mechanism for keeping conflict geographically contained, Thiel said. Globalization and global institutions erase boundaries and differences, spreading and intensifying mimetic rivalry and ultimately giving some world authority reason to declare an emergency that allegedly only it can contain. This phenomenon is at the root of Thiel’s conception of the modern “Antichrist,” which he sees as a figure or body that promises peace and safety while using that promise to impose total control.
Thiel is clearly no comfort-maximizing Last Man — a figure whose desire for political struggle has been deadened by ample outlets for material ambition. He believes that Western society, whose moral and scientific achievements he celebrates, is threatened by nihilism, neo-socialism, the regulatory state and the rise of what he calls “One-World totalitarian” rule.
THIEL’S CROOKED TIMBER
Thiel’s political vision rests on five elements: individual freedom, untethered by majority rule; jurisdictional competition and easy exit; liberation of “founders” from bureaucratic restraint; informed, decisive and well-armed government; and an embrace of unbounded technological progress.
The tensions among these elements are apparent. More resolute and powerful states are likelier to stifle entrepreneurial heroes than to cultivate them. It is perhaps unsurprising, then, that the thinkers to whom Thiel is most drawn — foremost among them Girard, the political philosopher Leo Strauss and the far-right German jurist Carl Schmitt — were formidable critics of liberalism who proved more adept at exposing its weaknesses than articulating compelling alternatives.
In a short and bracing 2009 article titled “The Education of a Libertarian,” Thiel wrote that he “no longer believe[d] that freedom and democracy are compatible.” The 1920s, under US presidents Warren Harding and Calvin Coolidge, had been “the last decade in American history during which one could be genuinely optimistic about politics.” In contrast to that era of small and mostly non-interventionist government, the 2000s showed “capitalist democracy” to be “an oxymoron.” The government had socialized trillions of US dollars of financial risk, provoking an explosion of debt-fueled speculation.
The coming mass bailout would necessarily mean “way more government” and far less freedom, Thiel said. The great task for libertarians, then, was to “find an escape from politics in all its forms.”
As an investor, Thiel “focused [his] efforts on new technologies that may create a new space for freedom.” He saw three such frontiers. The first was digital businesses, through which “an entrepreneur may create a new world” that would “force change on the existing social and political order.” The second was to “commercialize [outer] space,” which offered a “limitless possibility for escape from world politics.” And the third was the creation of floating communities in international waters, where technology might provide a more immediate means of escaping government control.
These were not merely speculative frontiers for Thiel, who had already made a fortune on the first of them.
PayPal’s founding vision was a “libertarian project” to create “a new world currency, free from all government control and dilution” — nothing less than “the end of monetary sovereignty,” he said. PayPal would eventually become a financial success, but only by speeding the movement of sovereign money. Thiel would later call bitcoin “the centralized currency we [had] fantasized about” when creating PayPal.
Thiel’s US$500,000 investment in Facebook, the company’s first from an outside investor, likewise backed new forms of community and dissent transcending national borders. Yet cyberspace offered only an incomplete escape. Its new worlds remained virtual, and therefore vulnerable to being recaptured by the political orders they were meant to disrupt.
Thiel’s money followed his imagination into the disruption and expansion of physical frontiers. His Founders Fund was an early investor in SpaceX. By 2011, he had committed more than US$30 million to slashing the cost of reaching space, supposedly opening the future to galactic tourism and interplanetary emigration.
Between the virtual and the extraterrestrial frontiers were the oceans. From 2008 to 2014, Thiel contributed about US$1.7 million to Patri Friedman’s Seasteading Institute, which proposed floating “startup countries” whose governments would compete for mobile residents rather than rule over captive ones. Engineering and legal obstacles eventually cooled his enthusiasm for sea cities, but he never gave up on his desire to create alternatives to legacy states.
Through Pronomos Capital, he later backed experimental charter cities, including Prospera in Honduras, which offered regulatory autonomy on land instead of sovereignty at sea. He also leveraged his investments in New Zealand to gain fast-tracked citizenship in 2011, giving himself a form of passport arbitrage should things go awry in the US.
HEAD FOR THE EXITS
Across all three domains, Thiel’s underlying project was the same: to use private capital to escape politics, subject governments to private competition and wrest control of the future from stultifying democratic majorities.
One of his ventures is already reshaping global politics. Starlink, the satellite-based Internet service developed by the Thiel-backed SpaceX, is upending the traditional assumption that states can, and naturally should, control the essential infrastructure through which they govern and defend their territory.
The governments of Iran, South Africa, Cambodia and other countries have tried unsuccessfully to stop the spread of unlicensed portable Starlink terminals across their borders. The company has also become deeply entangled in the Russia-Ukraine war, providing communications and targeting capabilities vital to Ukrainian defenses, initially free of charge. However, Musk exercised his control over Starlink to deny its use for operations to which he personally objects, such as attacks on Russian forces in occupied Crimea. It is no exaggeration to say that the company would play a key role in determining who ultimately controls what territory when the fighting finally stops.
While using his wealth to help entrepreneurs escape government control, Thiel has also invested in ventures that seek to expand the range of government functions outsourced to private companies. The most consequential of these is Palantir, which he cofounded in 2003. Its proprietary software systems now perform critical functions in defense, intelligence, border enforcement and infrastructure protection, significantly altering the traditional relationship between the public and private sectors in areas once handled almost exclusively by the state. Governments that contract Palantir’s services may retain formal sovereignty, but at the cost of becoming dependent on capabilities beyond their control.
The company, for its part, has been unusually forthright about the political ends its capabilities are meant to serve. By proclaiming allegiance to the US and the West more broadly, and openly refusing to work with states outside Western alliances, it rejects neutrality within the existing world order. Instead, it seeks to shape that order according to the political values of its founders, who retain strategic control through an unusual corporate governance structure.
FREEDOM WITHOUT LIBERALISM
At the heart of Thiel’s political vision is an apparent contradiction: He wants to save “the West,” but not liberalism, its most celebrated universal virtue. For Thiel, there is no contradiction. Like Strauss, he draws a sharp distinction between Western civilization and liberal democracy.
In Thiel’s conception, the West encompasses Christian belief and mythology, Greek rational inquiry, Roman institutional capacity, scientific mastery, technological creation and individual distinction. All of these, in his view, are threatened by liberal proceduralism, bureaucracy, conformism, majoritarianism, egalitarianism and universalism.
Like Schmitt, Thiel sees liberal reluctance to confront hostile non-Western civilizations, particularly Islam, as a dangerous denial of “the political,” inhibiting the West from defending its “true” virtues. Yet if political legitimacy rests not on universal principles, but on civilizational identity, technological prowess, military power and elite judgement, then Thiel has merely reduced the West to a peculiar brand of oligarchy with no more claim to legitimacy than authoritarian China.
“The West” is clearly not the same entity for Fukuyama as it is for Thiel. For Fukuyama, the apparent triumph of liberal democracy in the decade before the Sept. 11, 2001 terrorist attacks marked the glorious culmination of political history. Thiel regarded that same moment as a dangerous abandonment of vigilance against the eternal enemies of progress and freedom, at home and abroad.
The irony is that Fukuyama expected money-seeking entrepreneurs to be “kept out of politics and the military.” Thiel has done precisely the opposite. Like some rogue artificial intelligence agent, he has broken out of his capitalist sandbox and hacked into history. The Last Man has taken his revenge.
Benn Steil is director of international economics at the Council on Foreign Relations and the author of The World That Wasn’t: Henry Wallace and the Fate of the American Century.

Unknown

Taiwanese and eligible residents would each receive the universal NT$10,000 (US$311.8) cash handout before the Lunar New Year holiday, if the legislature passes next year’s general budget review before Jan. 5, President William Lai (賴清德) said yesterday.
Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) spokesman Justin Wu (吳崢) quoted Lai as making the statement at the party’s Central Committee meeting in Taipei.
The cash handout is part of next year’s general budget, and its timely passage depends on the legislature, he told the meeting.
Photo: Liu Hsin-de, Taipei Times
Taiwan’s economy is having an exceptional year, with the nation’s exports expected to reach an unprecedented US$900 billion before the year’s end, Lai told the meeting.
The nation’s exports reached US$87.72 billion last month, another record, he said.
The artificial intelligence (AI) sector is largely responsible for the growth, and its benefits should be shared with the rest of Taiwan without affecting the nation’s fiscal health, he said.
The handout dubbed the AI bonus is included in the administration’s proposed budget, which means legislators must collaborate to authorize government spending before Jan. 5 next year, Lai said.
The Executive Yuan has already created a task force to establish mechanisms for distributing the handout, which could be ready before the Lunar New Year holiday, which starts on Feb. 2, he said.
The administration also plans to accelerate the AI-driven transformation of traditional industries and small-and-medium sized enterprises to ensure all sectors of Taiwan’s economy remain competitive, he said.
That would entail funding the administration’s proposed AI infrastructure projects and a NT$100 billion small-business development fund centered on promoting digital technology and developing links between new and traditional industries, he said.
DPP officials and lawmakers are urged to communicate the government’s intent with the public and entrepreneurs, he said.
The administration hopes the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) and the Taiwan People’s Party (TPP) would pass next year’s budget and a bill governing the small-and-medium sized enterprise development fund before the legislative session ends, he said.
Separately, Minister of Finance Chuang Tsui-yun (莊翠雲) yesterday defended the administration’s rejection of the KMT caucus’ counterproposal for a NT$20,000 cash handout at a legislative meeting.
Adopting the KMT proposal would add to the national debt and require passing a supplementary budget act, whereas the government’s NT$10,000 handout is fiscally responsible and more speedily distributed, she said.
Although the government’s revenue increased by NT$700 billion in the first nine months of this year, under the amended Act Governing the Allocation of Government Revenues and Expenditures (財政收支劃分法), the central government and local governments respectively share NT$250 billion and NT$450 billion of the bonus, she said.
The central government would need to borrow more money to fund the KMT’s proposed NT$20,000 handout, contrary to the opposition’s claims that no new debts would be raised, Chuang said.
The tax revenue increase is mostly benefiting local governments, she said.
“I’m not sure if the idea is to take funding from local governments and use them to pay out cash to everyone.”

MODA notifies supermarkets to bolster cybersecurity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:42:33 UTC
01:42:33 KST

The Ministry of Digital Affairs (MODA) yesterday said it had notified the nation’s largest supermarket chains to inspect their Internet of Things (IoT) devices and install firmware updates to address security vulnerabilities, after a cyberattack earlier this week caused about 150 supermarkets in France to incur substantial food losses.
The incident involving Internet-connected refrigeration systems — which resulted in fridges and freezers heating up to 50°C, spoiling food and triggering fires — was one of the main subjects discussed at the legislature’s Transportation Committee meeting yesterday.
Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Legislator Hsu Chih-chieh (許智傑) said Taiwan has an extremely high density of convenience stores and supermarkets, so people’s lives would be hugely disrupted if similar attacks happen in Taiwan.
Photo: Reuters
The ministry should address the issue and prevent hackers from launching cyberattacks on Taiwan’s critical infrastructure using IoT, he added.
Minister of Digital Affairs Lin Yi-ching (林宜敬) said many companies began linking their internal systems to public Internet networks when IoT became a trend about a decade ago, but they overlooked the importance of cybersecurity protection.
“The global trend in the corporate world is disconnecting the internal networks from the Internet unless it is absolutely necessary. They only need to connect to the Intranet and monitor access to internal systems by establishing a whitelist,” Lin said.
Administration for Cybersecurity Director-General Tsai Fu-lung (蔡福隆) said the firmware of the French supermarkets’ refrigeration system was outdated and its vulnerabilities has not been addressed for a long time, so hackers had the opportunity to tamper with the temperature setting.
“After the incident, we quickly notified the supermarket chains around the nation through the Taiwan Computer Emergency Response Team/Coordination Center to examine IoT devices and update firmware,” Tsai said.
Meanwhile, DPP Legislator Lin Chun-hsien (林俊憲) highlighted the national security risks posed by the use of eSIMs, which many Taiwanese travelers purchase when they travel overseas.
A Taiwan’s Consumers’ Foundation survey found that 72 percent of 172 eSIMs purchased from the market have Internet traffic routed through China or Hong Kong, rather than the countries users are traveling in, he said.
This means that the content transmitted through these eSIMs are subject to regulation and surveillance under Hong Kong’s National Security Law or China’s Cybersecurity Law, he added.
The minister said the market is inundated with cheap, but unsafe eSIM cards routed through Chinese telecoms — such as China Mobile — as their massive consumer base gives them greater bargaining power when negotiating profit-sharing arrangements for international roaming services.
The government can regulate eSIMs sold through domestic e-commerce platforms such as momo and PChome, but lacks jurisdiction over those purchased from overseas Web sites, he said.
To reduce the risks associated with cheap foreign SIM cards, the Ministry of Digital Affairs and the National Communications Commission, in collaboration with Taiwan’s three major telecom operators, require customers to purchase domestic eSIMs online using real-name authentication, he added.

Parents on limiting their kids’ social media and AI use
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:42:32 UTC
01:42:32 KST

When it comes to their kids, many parents don’t trust tech companies any more.
Social media companies have spent the better part of the last decade arguing that their platforms are safe for teens, but quite a few parents aren’t convinced. They, along with a growing number of regulators, have increasingly accused companies like Meta of designing products that are addictive to younger users.
AI firm OpenAI, thrust into the public consciousness much more recently than Meta, has had to defend against dozens of lawsuits alleging chatbot ChatGPT lacks safety guardrails. Now, workers at the world’s leading AI firms have warned that their employers prioritize competing with each other over building their models safely.
Photo: AP
Both the AI and social media companies have denied the claims, and introduced additional safety measures such as parent-linked teen accounts.
Still, for many parents, lawsuits and public accusations have been enough to change their minds about whether to allow their children to use both social media and AI.
Parents were asked whether their perspective on their children’s use of social media or AI has changed in the last year and whether they plan to let their kids use either technology. The vast majority of those who responded said they no longer wanted their children to use social media, and many of them said they also try to steer their children away from AI.
“They are the most precious thing in my life,” Caroline Gray Ford, a 42-year-old parent from Cambridge, UK. “So why would I ever turn them over to a bunch of tech companies whose sole motivation is to profit from their time and harvest their data?”
TECH WORKER TORN BETWEEN TWO WORLDS
I work in tech, specifically in the AI sphere, and honestly I worry about the future that’s going to be there for my kids. Not in a doomsayer way, but, being realistic, the world is going to be a very different place when they grow up. I’m torn between two worlds — the world I work in, and that supports their upbringing, and the knowledge that the very work is destroying their future — whether that be on an economic or environmental level.
Do I feel the need to encourage them to use AI? Yes. Do I want to? No. On the flipside, social media is out. They can use WhatsApp to connect and build real-world relationships. But otherwise no good can come of it.
— Andy, 43, London, UK
THE MOM WARY OF SOCIAL MEDIA AND AI
The recent major lawsuits against Meta, along with decisions by non-US governments to limit social media use for under-16s, have enabled me to have meaningful conversations with my daughter about the real risks of social media use for her age group. She still asks to use these products, but I remind her of the decisions we’ve made, together, to wait until she’s older before she can use them.
My 11-year-old is not permitted to use social media on her own. As for AI chatbots, she may occasionally use them if they show up on a Google search when we are looking up a topic, but I encourage her to check the validity of anything AI-generated. She’s very aware of AI hallucinations, and hates AI images. She will actually call me or her older sister out if we accidentally share an AI-generated image.
Our family is very eco-conscious — we’re aware that AI uses massive amounts of water and energy, so we try to avoid AI apps as a family, if there are other options at our disposal to obtain information.
— Kate, 47, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania
TECHNOLOGY IN SCHOOLS
My perspective has become significantly more cautious.
As a parent and someone who works in AI, I’m increasingly concerned about the gap between the way these technologies are marketed and the risks they can pose to children. I want my daughter to grow up understanding and using technology, including AI, but I don’t think children should be treated as unwitting test subjects for products whose effects on their learning, development and wellbeing are not yet fully understood.
What’s particularly concerning is how early these tools are being introduced through schools, often with little meaningful parental involvement or choice. I’m increasingly questioning whether companies are prioritizing children’s interests or engagement and profit, and whether schools and local authorities are doing enough to scrutinize the technology they’re putting in front of children.
I don’t think children are being adequately educated about how to use these tools safely or critically. There’s a huge difference between teaching children how to use technology and simply putting devices and apps in front of them.
But I also think the responsibility shouldn’t fall solely on parents. Schools and local authorities need to ensure that children are being taught digital literacy and critical thinking alongside the introduction of these tools.
— Anonymous, Scottish borders
VIDEO GAME SKEPTIC
I have been skeptical about social media and AI since the beginning. I see in my 12-year-old son the obsessive grip that social media has on him. I include videogaming here, as it comes with YouTube influencers, and interaction with others on Discord servers. It is shaping his childhood and worldview in a way that I don’t like. I’m particularly concerned about digital media crowding out IRL activities that help him grow as a person and understand the world – like reading, exploring, playing with other kids face-to-face ...
My son has been given a Chromebook at school (no choice given to parents), and has a laptop for gaming, with time limits. Managing his screen time is a cat-and-mouse game that everyone hates at home. He has found ways of circumventing restrictions as only a creative child can. He is unable to control his impulse to go on his devices – that’s difficult enough for adults, let alone a child. The lack of guardrails and regulation of children’s access to digital technology means that millions of individual households have to manage and set the rules themselves. It’s stressful and poisons the atmosphere at home.
— Anonymous, Madrid

Cognitive warfare, says the Ministry of National Defense (MND), is the People’s Republic of China’s (PRC) use of “political, economic, cultural, military and legal means, with the intent to divide internal unity and undermine social stability” in Taiwan. Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:42:31 UTC
01:42:31 KST

Rwanda is to host Africa’s first Formula One Grand Prix since 1993 in “the early 2030s” after the circuit on Tuesday announced a decade-long deal with the country.
The East African nation has been chasing a Grand Prix race for years, having already used soccer, basketball and other sports to enhance its image and attract investment.
Rwandan President Paul Kagame had formally announced the bid when the nation hosted a gathering of the FIA, the governing body of the sport, in December 2024.
Photo: AFP
The last time an F1 race was held in Africa was the 33rd South African Grand Prix near Johannesburg in 1993, one year before apartheid formally ended there with democratic, multiracial elections.
The first African Grand Prix in Rwanda would take place “once a new purpose-built circuit in Bugesera, Rwanda, has been completed,” F1 said in a statement.
“Today is a landmark moment for Formula One,” F1 president Stefano Domenicali added. “With Rwanda joining the calendar from the next decade, our sport will race in every inhabited continent, bringing the world championship closer than ever to fans around the globe.”
A landlocked country still widely associated with a horrific genocide in 1994, Rwanda has used sports to revamp its image, attract tourists and impress investors with its organizational efficiency.
It has spent lavishly on soccer sponsorship deals with clubs including Arsenal and Paris Saint-Germain, partnered with the NBA to be the main hub of its African basketball league, and hosted last year’s cycling world championships.
“This partnership is long overdue, but it is a success and a milestone for the entire continent, especially for African fans,” Kagame said.
Seven-time world champion Lewis Hamilton has long called for an African stop on the F1 circuit, backing Rwanda’s plans in 2024 and calling the country “one of my favorite places.”
South Africa had also been bidding to host an F1 race, and its sports minister last week said it should not be ruled out.
“Remember though that one country, Italy, has had two F1s a year, and some react like a continent of 55 countries can only get one,” South African Minister of Sports, Arts and Culture Gayton McKenzie wrote on X on Thursday last week.
He said that “SA will get F1, even before 2030.”

ASML struggles with chip tool demand
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:42:31 UTC
01:42:31 KST

ASML Holding NV yesterday warned that soaring artificial intelligence (AI) spending meant that it faces a potential supply shortfall with its chipmaking machines in the next two years, even as it boosted its own sales forecast for this year.
“We are investigating ways to increase capacity for 2028 beyond the 30 percent increase we previously communicated,” ASML chief executive officer Christophe Fouquet said in a statement on the Dutch company’s results.
“Customers are asking us every single day to get more tools,” he said in a separate video.
Photo: Bloomberg
Robust customer demand prompted ASML to slightly raise its full-year sales forecast, predicting annual sales of between 44 billion euros and 45 billion euros (US$49 billion and US$50 billion). The low end of the range was previously 43 billion euros.
ASML, Europe’s biggest tech firm by market value, said in July that it plans to boost capacity by 30 percent next year for its second-most advanced tool, the low numerical-aperture extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography machine, which would take its annual shipment target to about 85 units.
The chip-gear maker’s customers have boosted their equipment demand forecasts based on the “size and duration of AI-related investments,” Fouquet said.
Some customers “are expressing an interest in placing orders with us for 2029 and even 2030,” he said.
ASML is the only company that makes the cutting-edge lithography machines used to produce semiconductors for the data centers powering the AI boom. Its outlook offers an indication of investment plans by chipmakers such as Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (台積電), Samsung Electronics Co and Intel Corp as spending on AI infrastructure surges.
The company is working to ship tools faster to customers by reducing the cycle time, or the period between starting production in its clean rooms and shipping a completed machine. It began construction on its second industrial campus in the Netherlands, the first phase of which is set to be completed in 2029.
Net sales in the July-to-September quarter rose to 11.66 billion euros, ASML said. That compares with the average analyst estimate of 11.7 billion euros, data compiled by Bloomberg showed.
Net profit came in at 5 billion euros in the quarter, compared with 2.1 billion euros in the same period last year, ASML said.
The company sold 17 EUV machines in the quarter while revenue from the service and upgrades of machines already installed at customers’ sites increased 19 percent as chipmakers looked to be more productive.
“Against the backdrop of an overall 36 percent increase of 2026 in comparison to 2025, you see that that is largely driven by EUV,” ASML chief financial officer Roger Dassen said in a video accompanying the results. “So the EUV business grows over 45 percent this year.”
South Korea remained ASML’s largest market for new system tools in the third quarter, followed by Taiwan and China. China is expected to account for about 20 percent of ASML’s total revenue this year.

His agency, GSI Agency, wrote on Instagram that the trip would give Fairchild an opportunity to experience the enthusiasm of Taiwanese fans in person.
It did not give dates or an itinerary, saying further details would follow.
Photo: Reuters
“From game-changing moments on the diamond to the incredible energy from the stands, STU has always appreciated the unwavering love and support from fans across Taiwan,” the agency wrote.
The 30-year-old, affectionately known to Taiwanese fans as “Feizai,” played for Taiwan at the WBC in March. His mother moved to the US from Taiwan when she was 12.
He hit a grand slam against the Czech Republic and a two-run homer against South Korea, helping Taiwan win both games at the Tokyo Dome.
Fairchild finished the tournament batting .250 with two home runs, six RBIs and three stolen bases, making him one of Taiwan’s leading offensive contributors, although the team were eliminated in the group stage.
Fairchild is also scheduled to receive an Employment Gold Card at a public ceremony next month, under plans announced by the National Development Council in August.
Council Deputy Minister Peng Li-pei at the time said that Fairchild’s application had been approved and that the council and the Ministry of Sports were arranging the presentation.
The card combines an open work permit, resident visa, Alien Resident Certificate and re-entry permit, giving eligible foreign professionals more flexibility to work and live in Taiwan.
A Seattle native, Fairchild made his MLB debut with the Arizona Diamondbacks in 2021. He has since played for the Seattle Mariners, San Francisco Giants, Cincinnati Reds, Atlanta Braves and Cleveland Guardians.
In six major-league seasons, he has played 292 games, batting .221 with 18 home runs, 69 RBIs and 27 stolen bases, according to MLB’s database.
This season, Fairchild appeared in 14 games for Cleveland and one for Seattle, finishing with three hits in 19 at-bats, a .158 batting average, one RBI and two stolen bases.

Advocate urges protection for persecuted activists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:42:29 UTC
01:42:29 KST

Taiwanese democracy advocate Lee Ming-che (李明哲) on Tuesday met with the European Parliament, calling for greater protection for human rights advocates, follow-up action on resolutions concerning Hong Kong and deeper cooperation between Taiwan and Europe in the face of China’s transnational repression.
A delegation led by Lee met with European Parliament members Bernard Guetta and Engin Eroglu, joined by Representative to the EU and Belgium Hsieh Chih-wei (謝志偉), the New School for Democracy said in a statement last week.
Lee thanked the European Parliament for its solidarity when he was detained in China for five years.
Photo courtesy of the New School for Democracy via CNA
Transnational repression not only targets advocates, but also often involves threats against their family members, deterring persecuted people from speaking out, he said.
Lee said that while he was detained, China threatened his wife with concerns about his safety, and demanded that she stop speaking out and cut off contact with the Taiwanese government and civil society groups.
Family members of other people detained in China have reached out to him for help since he returned to Taiwan, he said.
They fear that speaking out or seeking help from the Taiwanese government could impact their loved ones’ safety, Lee said, adding that threats to loved ones’ safety silence people, cover up the truth and leave advocates isolated.
He called on democratic countries to provide state protection and work with non-governmental organizations to ensure that people facing threats can safely seek help and continue participating in public affairs.
Guetta and Eroglu drew parallels between the cross-strait situation and Russia and Ukraine, asking about Taiwan’s assistance to Ukraine and how the nation is resisting Chinese repression and infiltration.
Taiwan’s resistance is visible and invisible, Taiwanese human rights advocate Hsiao I-ming (蕭逸民) said.
For example, China exploits criminal cases and manipulates information to deepen distrust of the government and divide Taiwanese society, Hsiao said.
Supporting and protecting victims, and fostering a society built on mutual assistance and trust are part of the everyday work of defending democracy, he said.
Lee uses the Internet to introduce Chinese to Taiwan’s democratic experience and built a network to support the families of Chinese political prisoners, Hsiao said, citing it as an example of resistance that goes unseen.
This cross-border exchange of democratic ideas and mutual support helps people facing political persecution, he said.
China’s threats against Taiwan do not only involve the military, but also directly impact people’s freedom and democratic rights, he said, adding that judicial reform, protecting victims and advocating for human rights are all part of resisting authoritarianism.
