====================================================================================================

A Pacific pivot ahead for Taiwan?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:42:25 UTC
01:42:25 KST

On Aug. 31 when Minister of Foreign Affairs Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍) joined the Pacific Islands Forum leaders’ meeting in Koror, Palau — invited as a development partner, a status the forum has extended to Taiwan since the early 1990s — Chinese Special Envoy for Pacific Island Countries Affairs Qian Bo (錢波) promised “consequences.” Less than two weeks earlier, China had advised its citizens against travel to Palau, reprising the tourism embargo it imposed in 2017 after Palau reaffirmed ties with Taiwan. Five of the forum’s 18 leaders also stayed home, and Kiribati sent its former ambassador to Beijing to lead its delegation.
The Pacific islands have long occupied an outsized role in Taipei’s foreign policy, and Taiwan continues to be an important part of the region’s fabric. Historically, Taiwan’s engagement has largely been a fight for recognition, but now, as geopolitics descends on the region, stakes are raised for everyone. This is true not only for Taiwan’s place in the Pacific, but also for what sort of diplomatic community the Pacific states want to create for themselves, what sort of partnerships they seek to build, and how they view exercising Pacific sovereignty. When Beijing threatens a host government over its guest list, it claims a veto over Pacific institutions.
While recent history has been grim — in July, Papua New Guinea ordered Taiwan’s office closed without consulting Taipei, which followed the loss of Solomon Islands, Kiribati and Nauru as allies since 2019 — but not all is lost. The partners that Taiwan has kept sit in some of the most strategic waters of the Asia-Pacific region, most importantly Palau, where this year’s drama unfolded, but also the Marshall Islands whose vast exclusive economic zone lies along the routes that connect Hawaii, Guam and Australia.
From Washington’s perspective, Palau is now more important than any time since World War II. A recent US budget request includes US$384.6 million for port improvements, while US Marines are stationed on Peleliu where an imperial Japanese airfield is being overhauled, and Washington has helped Palau establish a Maritime Joint Operations Center. Japan has similarly expanded its own maritime and infrastructure work in Palau, and the Philippines is interested in building closer ties with its neighbor. All this benefits from the physical and social infrastructure Taiwan has built over decades.
Together these countries — Taiwan, the Philippines, Palau, the US and Japan — largely encircle the Philippine Sea, a location of increasing People’s Republic of China (PRC) presence and potentially common geography for these partners to focus cooperation, and the link between the First and Second Island Chains of the Western Pacific.
Taiwan brings expertise this region needs. Every nation around the Philippine Sea faces some version of the same PRC coercion playbook: illegal fishing, research vessels conducting surveys that the law of the sea largely permits, influence operations aimed at local elites and economic punishment calibrated to small economies’ dependence on tourism. Taiwan has faced the full-scale version of this strategy the longest. The National Security Bureau logged more than 2.3 million pieces of disinformation and more than 45,000 inauthentic accounts in a single year. Its Whole-of-Society Defense Resilience Committee, created in 2024, ties civil mobilization, stockpiling, infrastructure protection, medical capacity and communications security into exercises that run across multiple cities. Palau, Guam and the Northern Marianas face the same pressures with a fraction of the analytic and institutional capacity. When the Chinese research icebreaker Ji Di (極地) loitered in Palau’s exclusive economic zone without authorization in May, Palau’s available response was a diplomatic note.
At sea, the region’s smaller states hold purview over vast waters, but they lack the capacity to patrol, while larger states hold means without jurisdiction. Palau has donated patrol craft and too few mariners to crew them. Taiwan, with a capable coast guard and one of the Pacific’s largest distant-water fishing fleets, sits on both sides of the illegal fishing problem, which argues for bringing it inside regional monitoring, where its fleet’s conduct becomes a shared responsibility. Precedent exists in Taiwan’s participation as a fishing entity in the Western and Central Pacific Fisheries Commission, which manages the world’s largest tuna fishery, and the same logic could apply to Palau’s Maritime Joint Operations Center, where partners could post liaison officers to pool data on illegal fishing, research-vessel movements and vessels loitering over undersea cables.
Expanding Taiwan’s space with these neighbors requires no government to change its recognition policy, and Manila has shown how. In April last year, the Philippines lifted most restrictions on officials traveling to Taiwan for trade and economic missions, and in August last year Lin led a trade delegation to Manila in a private capacity. Last month, when Beijing protested Taipei’s plan for a second office in Cebu, the Philippine Department of Foreign Affairs answered that its “one China” policy does not preclude economic, cultural and functional cooperation with Taiwan.
Three steps would move the region forward: The Pacific Islands Forum should convert Palau’s open door into standing practice, so development partners’ attendance stops depending on each host’s tolerance for Beijing’s displeasure. The US, Japan and the Philippines, as they deepen trilateral ties, should bring Palau — as well as Micronesia and the Marshall Islands — into their maritime cooperation initiatives, and build channels on illegal fishing, cable security and disaster response that Taiwan can join from the start. Governments that encourage Pacific states to engage with Taipei should agree in advance on how they would offset the coercion that follows, with tourism promotion, air connectivity and budget support ready before the next coercive tactic or set of “gray zone” activities lands.
The Pacific architecture emerging during today’s geopolitical flux will be built by whoever shows up with something to contribute. For Taiwan, the place to start is close to home: the region surrounding the Philippine Sea, where it can build working channels with Palau, the Philippines, Japan and the US on the waters they share. Taiwan’s story in the broader region is not over — a Pacific that keeps Taiwan at the table will have more with which to build.

UN Security Council renews Haiti sanctions regime for another year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:36:43 UTC
01:36:43 KST

Merve Aydogan
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
The UN Security Council on Wednesday adopted a resolution renewing the sanctions regime on Haiti for one year, including an arms embargo, a travel ban and an assets freeze.
The draft resolution passed with 14 votes, while Russia abstained.
The text also extends the mandate of the Panel of Experts assisting the Haiti sanctions committee for 13 months.
US Deputy Permanent Representative Jennifer Locetta said the decision sent a strong message of support for Haitians.
"Today’s vote is yet another unwavering signal that the international community stands with the people of Haiti," said Locetta.
She said the arms embargo does not apply to the sale, supply or transfer of arms or related materiel, or to related assistance and training, for the Haitian government when intended to further peace and security objectives.
Panama's UN envoy Eloy Alfaro de Alba said the international community’s responsibility does not end with the adoption of the resolution. He stressed that the crisis has many facets and requires sustained attention from the council and member states.
Haiti has been grappling with gang violence and political instability for years, and the sanctions regime is one of the tools the council uses to address the crisis.

Ukraine's Zelenskiy says it is 'painful' for Trump to choose a different side
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:35:51 UTC
01:35:51 KST

Ukraine accuses US of helping Russia as missiles hit Kyiv
LONDON - Ukraine on Oct 14 accused the United States of helping Russia by failing to warn it of incoming missile strikes and hobbling Kyiv’s military response through changes to the Starlink system it uses on the battlefield.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called on US tech billionaire Elon Musk to restore Starlink, which Kyiv says has been slowed down.
“I hope that it’s a mistake, maybe huge technical problem,” Zelensky told UK journalist Piers Morgan. “I don’t know, but we are asking to do it, to switch (it) on.”
Former Ukrainian defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov later said that “Starlink’s operation at speeds up to 160kmh is being restored. Strike drones and interceptor drones should be able to fly again”.
Musk said any disruption was the responsibility of the US government, not his SpaceX company.
He drew a disctinction between the Starshield system, which Ukraine relies on for battlefield communications, and the parallel Starlink civilian satellite system, which Ukraine also deploys but is not allowed to use for offensive operations.
“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” Musk said, referring to US President Donald Trump.
Zelensky replied in the affirmative when asked if he felt “betrayed” after US President Donald Trump announced a diesel-supply deal with heavily sanctioned Moscow.
“It’s painful when President Trump chooses one side, not our side,” he said. “I think his advisors are wrong. I don’t know who is pushing him not to the right side. This is not (the) right side of history,”
Zelensky had framed the lack of warnings from allies about a wave of powerful strikes the night of Oct 13 and early Oct 14 as “completely unjust”, and accused Russia of wilfully flouting a supposed “energy ceasefire” announced unilaterally by Trump.
A senior official in Kyiv confirmed that the United States had in recent days threatened to stop providing intelligence about Russian missile launches that Ukraine uses to thwart attacks. Trump denied doing so on Oct 13.
Defence officials also suggested Washington was behind slower speeds reported on some Starlink internet terminals which help Ukraine’s military hit Russian-occupied territory and operate interceptor drones.
“It’s obvious they (the United States) are helping Russia for some reason,” the senior official told AFP.
Zelensky adviser Sergiy Beskrestnov said the attacks and Starlink restrictions were more than a coincidence.
“Through their actions, our partners are depriving us of one of the few chances we have to defend the country against jet-powered Shahed drones,” he wrote on Telegram.
Close contact
In Moscow, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Russia was watching for any sign that Washington’s backing for Ukraine may have shifted.
“We are carefully noting all this. It is too early to draw any systemic conclusions,” he told reporters.
President Vladimir Putin’s special envoy on economic cooperation, Kirill Dmitriev, meanwhile said the first contracts on providing diesel to the United States would be signed in the coming days.
“We are in close, hourly contact with the American side, and everything is moving very quickly,” he added.
Trump, facing crunch mid-term elections in November, has blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries for the squeeze on fuel supplies and increase in prices at the pump.
But most experts say the real reason is the joint US and Israeli attacks on Iran since late February, which have seen Tehran block off the Strait of Hormuz, a vital route for oil and gas shipments.
‘Disrespect’
Ballistic missiles have now struck the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, for two nights running, before air raid sirens could sound in time to warn people to take cover in basements, bomb shelters or metro stations.
“Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States,” said Zelensky, accusing Moscow of squandering a chance to ease hostilities.
The lack of warning has been reported only rarely during the conflict and Ukrainian officials have previously suggested the Russian military’s use of hard-to-detect missiles or potential technical issues could be to blame.
Fifteen people were killed around the country in the latest round of strikes, while significant damage to energy facilities and equipment knocked out power to swathes of Kyiv.
Power plants came under ballistic-missile attack in the eastern Kharkiv region, while Zhytomyr in the north-west, Sumy in the north-east and Chernigiv in the north were also hit.
Russia has previously targeted Ukraine’s power stations and heating infrastructure, crippling supplies before winter, when temperatures can plummet to as low as minus 20 deg C. AFP

Fossil overlooked for 100 years ID'd as new dinosaur species
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:35:10 UTC
01:35:10 KST

New dinosaur species, a T. rex cousin that "would have chased us," identified from fossil found 100 years ago
London — A previously unknown species of dinosaur — a "long-clawed predator the size of a tiger" and a cousin of the Tyrannosaurus rex — has been identified from a fossil originally found 100 years ago, but which remained hidden away in a British museum until recently.
The species has been named Invictibellatrix amberina, and it belongs to a group of two-legged carnivores known as megaraptorans according to an article published in the Royal Society Open Science research journal.
Megaraptorans were closely related to the group of dinosaurs T. rex originated from, the tyrannosaurs. Unlike T. rex, however, scientists say Invictibellatrix did not attack prey with its mouth, but with its long arms and giant curved claws.
Researchers believe the dinosaur would have been between 10 and 13 feet long and almost 5 feet tall. Its body would have had feathers, and it would have hunted smaller dinosaurs, lizards and mammals.
The fossil that led to the discovery sat in a drawer at the Natural History Museum in London for nearly 100 years, having first been obtained by the vaunted institution in 1924.
Dr. Cassius Morrison of University College London, the lead author of the article that announced the discovery, called it a "real mystery that the fossil was overlooked for so long."
Morrison wrote that while Invictibellatrix "was not the apex predator of its time," it would have been a formidable threat to humans if they had coexisted with the species — even "more dangerous than a T. rex."
"We would have been perfectly sized prey, about a third of their body weight," he said. "They definitely would have chased us. A T. rex would not have bothered, as we would have been too small."
The fossil itself is a chunk of the back of a skull. It was one of 1,000 specimens originally discovered by Reginald Walter Tooley on the Isle of Wight, off the south coast of England, and it was then acquired by the Natural History Museum.
Invictibellatrix lived during the Early Cretaceous period, around 120 million years ago, and is one of the smallest and earliest known members of the megaraptoran group.
To understand Invictibellatrix, researchers first took a CT scan of the fossil to create a 3D model of that part of its skull. The results were compared with the skulls of other two-legged meat-eating dinosaurs, such as tyrannosaurs, spinosaurs and raptors. A number of unique features led researchers to conclude they had discovered a new species.
Invictibellatrix is Latin for "unconquered female warrior" and amberina refers to the amber found in the rocks where the fossil was discovered. The researchers said by naming the dinosaur Invictibellatrix, they wanted to "give hope and strength to all those who are bullied, discriminated, victimized, and oppressed that tomorrow will be theirs and not to give up in the face of such odds."

China records highest trade surplus in nearly 2 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:34:47 UTC
01:34:47 KST

Ali Canberk Ozbugutu, Burhan Sansarlioglu and Emir Yildirim
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
China’s trade surplus hit its highest level since January 2025 at $133.5 billion in September, according to China’s customs authority (GACC).
Chinese exports rose 36.3% year-on-year to $447.1 billion, and imports jumped 31% to $313.6 billion.
Wang Jun, spokesperson and vice president of the Chinese customs authority, said in a recent statement that strong global demand for artificial intelligence (AI) and electrical infrastructure boosted demand for chips and components, driving exports.
Chinese exports to the US surged 39.5%, while exports to the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) jumped 52.2% and those to EU countries rose 25.2%.
Imports have been on the rise since the beginning of the year due to rising global energy and raw material prices.
Having posted a trade surplus of $938.1 billion in the first nine months of the year, China is expected to run a record surplus again this year after reaching a record of $1.19 trillion in 2025.
China’s consumer price index (CPI) rose 0.9% year-on-year last month, moderately accelerating on a monthly basis but falling short of expectations, which signaled that domestic consumption remains weak.
China’s producer price index (PPI) rose 5% year-on-year in September, its fastest rise since June 2022, above the 3.8% estimate.
Chinese economic policymakers may have to implement additional policy support to achieve both short- and long-term growth targets, analysts say.
Lynn Song, chief economist for China at ING Group, told Anadolu that core trade ties are expected to remain stable through the end of the year, ensuring the year’s growth driver continues to operate.
He stated that Chinese exports to the US continued to recover as the trade agreement remains in effect.
“China's exports have evolved significantly over the past decade, both by product breakdown and by destination,” he said. “As China moves up the value-added ladder, its fastest-growing exports increasingly include higher-margin goods, while low-end manufacturing is moving elsewhere in the region.”
Song stated that imports rose 27.5% year-on-year over the first three quarters, reaching $2.43 trillion. “Compared with early-year expectations, imports have been the biggest surprise this year,” he said.
“Technology products remained the main driver of import growth, suggesting China continues to spend in the ongoing tech race,” he noted.
“Yet the subsequent pickup in exports in recent months has set China up to build on last year's record-breaking $1.2 trillion trade surplus this year,” he added.

The Iraqi premier also condemned the attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and other attacks targeting civilians and civilian infrastructure, warning that such actions threaten regional security and stability.

Baghdad pledges stronger security coordination

Mohammed bin Salman reaffirmed Saudi Arabia’s support for the Iraqi government’s efforts to promote dialogue and advance regional stability, according to the INA statement.

Drone launch site raises concerns over Iraqi territory
Security concerns intensified in September when Iraqi authorities announced they had discovered a drone launch site inside the country while investigating attacks on Saudi Arabia’s East-West oil pipeline. The pipeline attacks caused injuries and damage.
In August, Al-Zaidi ordered the formation of a joint security committee tasked with addressing regional threats and developing measures to prevent Iraqi territory from being used to launch attacks against neighbouring countries.
The initiative followed US-Saudi air strikes against Iran-aligned armed groups in Iraq in late July. The US military’s Central Command (CENTCOM) said the joint operation targeted sites linked to attacks on US forces and Saudi energy infrastructure.

In an interview with Le Figaro, Leribault appealed to the government that takes office after France’s presidential election, “whoever it may be,” to support the museum’s transformation.
Without renovation, the Louvre risks losing its standing before ultimately having to “close its doors to the public,” which he described as “a disaster.”

His warning comes nearly a year after the Oct. 19, 2025 burglary in which eight crown jewels were stolen, exposing significant security weaknesses and plunging the museum into crisis.
Leribault is championing the “Louvre New Renaissance” project, arguing that strengthening security requires improvements to the historic building and its infrastructure.
The estimated €1 billion project includes renovating the museum and constructing a new entrance. Completion could take 12 to 15 years.
Leribault did not rule out another increase in admission prices, provided it remained “very reasonable.” Ticket prices for non-European visitors rose this year from €22 to €32.
The museum president aims to raise €360 million from French and international donors to help finance the project, which faces opposition from unions.
No donor commitments have been signed so far, although Leribault told Le Figaro that foreign donors were ready to support the museum.

Why are portions of prepared meals getting smaller in Russia? Rising costs may be only part of the answer.
Portion sizes for prepared food in Russia fell by 10.3% over the past year to 266 grams (about 9.4 ounces), according to calculations by the analytics company Ntec, as cited by Kommersant.
Prepared food remains the fastest-growing category in grocery retail. Retail stores account for about a quarter of the prepared food market, and that share could reach 40% by 2030, according to Stanislav Bogdanov, chairman of the Association of Retail Companies.
Profit margins in the category are very low, however. Retailers have to invest in central kitchens, packaging, and logistics, while 14% of products are written off because of their short shelf life.
Production costs are rising, but producers are finding it harder to pass them on to consumers. Intense competition and weakening demand are forcing them to hold down prices. As a result, producers are choosing to reduce portion sizes, experts said.
Smaller portions may reflect both shrinkflation and changing demand, the experts said. Russians buying prepared food have increasingly been choosing small snacks such as onigiri, sandwiches, and hot dogs. In the first half of 2026, sales of these snacks rose by 48% in value, while sales of main dishes and salads grew more slowly — by 16% and 14%, respectively.

Mariam Ashalem De Andres
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum signed a decree Wednesday to regulate digital platforms and protect children and adolescents from harmful online content, warning that platforms could face legal sanctions if they fail to make progress.
“If no progress is made, it would become a law,” Sheinbaum said at a news conference, adding that legislation would include penalties for the platforms.
She said digital platforms agreed to the measures and requested one month to prepare their systems for implementation.
Presidential legal adviser Maria Luisa Alcalde Lujan said she met representatives of Meta, TikTok, Google, Microsoft and other digital platforms to discuss the decree, and highlighted their willingness to adhere to the measure.
The decree bans platforms from exposing minors to content promoting sexual violence, suicide, self-harm, eating disorders, bullying and other harmful material.
They will be required to immediately identify and remove accounts and content that promote or generate violent behavior, classify content according to age groups and verify the ages of users.
Platforms must alert authorities to content that threatens life, while a 24-hour contact point will support investigations.
The Ministry of Public Education and the Ministry of Health will make the Linea de la Vida, or Lifeline, hotline available to provide psychological support. Authorities will also provide a guide on emotional awareness.
The announcement follows a meeting between government officials and representatives of major technology companies, although additional details on the decree's enforcement mechanisms were not provided.

The veteran British broadcaster Sir Trevor Phillips had some strong words of advice for his CBS News colleagues when facing off against critics who question the editorial integrity of the network: “Why don’t you just fuck off and let us do our jobs?”
Phillips made his blunt suggestion during a contentious meeting of the network’s London bureau on Tuesday, during which the foreign editor, Shayndi Raice, went on a lengthy tirade criticizing unnamed staffers for suggesting that editorial oversight amounted to “interference” and informing colleagues that disobeying editors would be insubordination and “legal grounds for firing”.
Phillips’s decision to join CBS was announced in June. It came after its billionaire owner, David Ellison, installed the opinion journalist and broadcast newcomer Bari Weiss as editor-in-chief in a move that shook staff.
The Guardian, which first reported the Tuesday meeting, reviewed an audio recording of the contentious session that rattled staffers. A CBS News spokesperson and Phillips declined to comment on the meeting.
Phillips spoke up initially to defend Raice, saying that the message she was delivering was common sense. “I’m genuinely surprised that you had to say anything that you just said in the last 15 minutes,” he said during the meeting. “It just seems to be axiomatic in any organization … I did want to say that I’m kind of surprised that in an organization of this vintage and capability, with the clever people I’ve met around here, that any of this actually has to be said.”
He then turned to outside opinion about CBS, telling colleagues that he faced criticism after it was announced he was leaving his perch at Sky News to serve as the network’s senior global affairs correspondent. Phillips is also a contributor to CBS’s flagship news show 60 Minutes, and voiced a short piece on Sunday on protests in Europe. Since CBS parent Paramount Global was acquired by Ellison’s Skydance Media in the summer of 2025, the company’s leadership has faced accusations of tilting the editorial scales in a more conservative-friendly direction.
“I could spend the next hour telling you the number of people when it was announced that I was coming here, the number of people who told me for all of the reasons you just explained, why this is the end of my career and how I was going to destroy everything that I’ve ever created, and all of that bollocks,” Phillips said.
He continued: “I think we’re in a new game now, actually, where we are now players as journalists. And what people are constantly trying to do is to knock us off – to frighten us, essentially, into doing this or doing that. It puts a premium on two things – one is our objectivity, and two: having each other’s backs. I think the worst thing that can happen now is if we start to go about telling people, ‘Well, I would have done this if the higher-ups hadn’t told me to do that.’ That’s exactly what everybody wants us to get into the game of. That’s how we become vulnerable. That’s how we start adjusting our copy according to somebody else’s lines outside of here … I think what you said is really, really important, but it points me in the direction of us having the mentality – forgive my French here – of telling everybody, ‘Why don’t you just fuck off and let us do our jobs?’”

Draft EU summit conclusions reveal what leaders will and will not say on Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:20:40 UTC
01:20:40 KST

Draft EU summit conclusions reveal what leaders will and will not say on Ukraine
A red carpet and European Union (EU) flags in the Europa building ahead of a European Council meeting in Brussels, Belgium, on Thursday, Oct. 23, 2025. (Simon Wohlfahrt/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Editor's Note: Following publication, the Kyiv Independent received the revised draft conclusions, which set out a less ambitious position on Ukraine's bid for EU membership. Read the story here.
BRUSSELS, Belgium — Leaders of the EU's 27 member states have a Ukraine-packed agenda when they meet in Brussels Oct. 15-16, according to the latest draft conclusions of the upcoming meeting seen by the Kyiv Independent.
The 25-page document contains six-and-a-half pages of comments specifically on Ukraine, three-and-a-half pages on defense and security, where Ukraine features prominently, and a page on the future of enlargement.
Those hoping for a long list of decisions from the European Council will be left disappointed, as the document mostly consists of leaders noting developments since they last met in June and issuing calls for what should happen next.
But some of those calls can lead to concrete outcomes further down the line.
For example, the draft conclusions say that the European Council "calls for the swift and effective implementation of the measures concerning Russian ex-combatants, and for further (sanctions) measures."
A visa ban for Russian soldiers was pushed for in the bloc's previous sanctions package, but ultimately fell through after France and Italy railed against it.
Since Russia's drone attack on Leipzig, Germany, the conversation has shifted, and EU diplomats from three countries said France had begun to budge when foreign ministers met in Luxembourg on Oct. 12.
Finland also upped the pressure by issuing a letter arguing against issuing visas to Russians and outlining five key demands.
The draft conclusions signal that concrete action is due to land soon.
In a similar vein, the Council conclusions state that it "underlines the EU's readiness to step up its engagement" on "diplomatic efforts to bring Russia's war of aggression to an end."
The week before, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen's right-hand man discussed peace with the U.S., NATO, and Ukraine.
But those talks were overshadowed by U.S. President Donald Trump's announcement of a likely-illegal diesel deal with Russia — a development that the conclusions note with "regret."
Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha told journalists on Oct. 12 that the U.S.' approach shows that "Europe should take its future in its own hands, speak with one voice, and restore peace," and the conclusions' readiness to do so suggests that the EU agrees.
Shouting into the wind
On other topics, the draft conclusions expose the EU's seeming inability to tackle Ukraine's most pressing issues.
With Kyiv being pummeled by ever more jet-powered drones and ballistic missiles, the call for "further intensified efforts and coordination to strengthen Ukraine's air and missile defense capabilities, the resilience of its critical infrastructure, and its energy system," rings especially hollow.
Similarly, the call for "immediate restoration of safe passage for grain cargo ships in the Black Sea," after weeks of Russian blockade, and the sinking of ships — which has also led to the loss of life — reads as weak in the absence of any accompanying measures.
However, the European Council "stresses the need to prevent grain stolen by Russia from temporarily occupied Ukrainian territories from being exported via the EU," read the conclusions, which suggests support may be gathering for a Russian grain transit ban, as proposed by Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania the week before.
Likewise, support may be brewing for future EU action to prevent Russia's re-entry into international sports and cultural events, which the conclusions say should not be allowed to happen, three days after EU Sports Commissioner Glenn Micallef met with EU foreign ministers for the first time to discuss the issue.
The result of Micallef's meeting was the EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, announcing that her team "will put forward proposals on how to sustain Russia's isolation in global sports."
And in the meantime, some countries take unilateral action, such as the Netherlands, which has denied visas to Russians due to compete at an international gymnastics event in Rotterdam, even as the world body for gymnastics has again allowed Russian and Belarusian athletes to compete under their own flag.
Other mentions in the conclusions can be seen as messages to other allies of Ukraine, in Europe and beyond.
That the EU "strongly condemns the deployment of North Korean military forces in the war against Ukraine" is a useful reminder to South Korea of what is at stake for them, just as relations between Kyiv and Seoul reach a new low.
And the renewed call for "international partners to swiftly step up their support to help meet Ukraine's pressing financing and military needs," likewise points to the fact that since the EU adopted its 90 billion euro loan ($100 billion) for Ukraine in April, third countries appear to have slowed down on their own contributions to Kyiv.
read also
Conspicuously absent: Russia's immobilized assets
One word missing from the draft conclusions: "assets." This is despite a renewed push from various directions to revive discussions about how to use 200 billion euros ($224 billion) of immobilized Russian wealth to directly support Ukraine.
Four EU countries reopened the topic with an open letter in August, and it came up prominently during the Oct. 12 meeting of foreign ministers.
Sybiha spoke about the idea to journalists, published an opinion piece the same day with news website Politico, and had strong support from his Swedish colleague Maria Stenergard, who even brought along visual aids for the discussion.
But the lack of a mention is because the EU is still by no means united on what approach to take.
Belgian newspaper De Morgen reported on Oct. 13 that President Volodymyr Zelensky wants to meet with Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever bilaterally around the EU leaders' summit, which he will also attend on Oct. 16.
De Wever led resistance to the use of Russian assets in December 2025, the last time it was seriously discussed, and as the vast majority of immobilized Russian government assets are in Belgium, a solution that does not work for De Wever will go nowhere.
read also
In response to a question from the Kyiv Independent about the Russian assets, Kallas said "I think this discussion will continue because eventually it is about sharing the risks between member states."
"It is important that it is not off the table. We are thinking about different tools to fill that financing gap," Kallas said.
Alternative options do exist: Russian assets could be invested more profitably to create new funds for Ukraine, as suggested by a plan called the Windfall Optimization Loan Framework, or the EU could simply agree to create new loans.
What is clear is that the topic is not set to disappear just yet, with one senior EU official telling the Kyiv Independent they expect it to dominate EU leaders' December meeting.
read also
Don't forget the future
The October meeting of EU leaders was supposed to have the future of EU enlargement as a main topic, to which end the European Commission issued proposals for consideration on Oct. 6.
Instead, with a new multi-year budget to discuss, energy prices, migration issues, the Middle East, and all the other Ukraine topics on the agenda, enlargement risks being overshadowed, and it only accounts for one page in the 25-page Council conclusions draft.
Even so, that one page contains a potentially big shift, if the conclusions are adopted as written.
"The European Council ... looks forward to the opening of all the other clusters as soon as possible, in line with the merit-based approach," read the draft conclusions.
What looks like an innocuous enough sentence takes on new meaning when one has in mind the last leaders' meeting in July, in which Hungary lobbied hard to remove the words "as soon as possible" because it wanted Ukraine to pass a law bolstering the rights of its Hungarian-speaking minority first.
Ukraine passed that law on Oct. 12, unlocked two further enlargement clusters on Oct. 13, and may have no further obstacles to overcome.
France and Poland were expected in some quarters to make it difficult to unlock the remaining cluster covering agriculture due to fears of Ukrainian competition, but they publicly ruled this out on Oct. 13.
A high-ranking EU official and a European minister told the Kyiv Independent that they expect the last two clusters to open in December 2026, as several EU countries must follow their own political procedures at home to give a formal green light.
For example, Slovenia needs to vote on the decision through its parliament, even if the vote itself is not expected to cause any problems, and has never done so for Ukraine so far.
But that does not mean Ukraine has nothing still to do.
Both for the EU's financial support to be greenlighted, and for Ukraine to join the bloc one day, the Council conclusions "recall the importance of Ukraine continuing its reform efforts and upholding the rule of law."

New York Seeks to Ban Horse-Drawn Carriages

New York Seeks to Ban Horse-Drawn Carriages
Kyiv • UNN
Mayor Zohran Mamdani supported banning horse-drawn carriages in New York starting in June 2028. The Council may vote on the bill on October 22.
Mayor Zoran Mamdani and the speaker of the New York City Council have agreed to ban horse-drawn carriage rides in the city, a popular tourist attraction that has drawn widespread criticism, UNN reports, citing The Guardian.
Details
Mamdani agreed to support a bill backed by Julie Menin, the speaker of the New York City Council, that bans the operation of horse-drawn carriages starting in June 2028, Politico reported on Tuesday. The City Council is expected to vote on the legislation next week.
"The horse-carriage industry is coming to an end in New York City. Our administration will ensure that workers and owners are protected, and that the horses are safe," Mamdani wrote on X on Tuesday.
A person familiar with City Hall confirmed that an agreement had been reached.
Although carriage rides are ubiquitous in Central Park, animal advocates have long raised concerns about the treatment of the horses. Since 2020, several horses have died, at times collapsing during carriage rides.
The push for a ban intensified over the summer after 18-year-old tourist Romanch Mahajan died after being thrown from a carriage.
In a statement, Menin said that horse-drawn carriages had "become a growing public-safety concern."
"We can honor our city's traditions while recognizing that it is time to move forward in the interests of public safety, protecting workers and strengthening the economic vitality of our city," Menin said.
A spokesperson for Menin said that the City Council speaker would bring the bill to a vote on October 22.
In addition
Despite broad support for a ban on horse-drawn carriages, officials have struggled to advance the legislation because the Transport Workers Union of Greater New York, which represents carriage drivers, has raised concerns about the drivers' livelihoods.
Mamdani had previously indicated that he would support a bill banning horse-drawn carriages; however, he expressed concerns about the bill as drafted because it contained insufficient protections for carriage workers.
A copy of the bill sent to The Guardian contains language requiring the city to create a workforce-transition program providing carriage drivers with counseling and referrals to other jobs in the private and public sectors.
The bill also requires the city to "consider" creating a compensation program for carriage owners based on the value of their businesses.
John Samuelsen, the international president of the Transport Workers Union, told Politico that the bill does not provide "significant economic relief for workers."
"This is shameful political opportunism, and Zoran should not simply go along with it, especially when the livelihoods of immigrant families are being destroyed," Samuelsen said. "This entire situation is reprehensible."
It is unclear whether Mamdani plans to sign the bill in its current form or whether additional changes will be made.
Sneha Chowdhury, a spokesperson for City Hall, said in a statement: "We are working closely with the City Council, union partners, carriage drivers, animal-protection advocates and community leaders to ensure a just transition that protects workers while ending the use of horse-drawn carriages in Central Park once and for all."
The bill also requires the city to introduce a program to help drivers humanely relinquish their horses—prohibiting them from selling the horses, transporting them for slaughter or selling them for use in horse-drawn carriage operations elsewhere.

To unlock Britain’s innovation potential, Labour needs to think outside the box | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:19:16 UTC
01:19:16 KST

Gordon Brown wants Britain to invent, invest in and own the future (British households would be £5,000 richer if we were more innovative. Let’s unleash our talents, 9 October). But invent what, and for whom? His hunt for “lost Einsteins” rests on a narrow vision: a lone genius invents, commercialisation scales, the problem is solved.
That may suit a cancer drug, but not the wicked problems of our time – social care, education, climate – which demand not silver bullets but new technologies and practices for collaboration, distributed ownership and collective innovation.
The current struggle to retrofit governance, accountability and benefit on to AI exposes the fiction of genius-engineered “solutions”. Nor do trillion-dollar companies make every household £5,000 richer. They concentrate short-term gain in a narrow founder-investor class; the rest of us carry the work and cost of long-term cleanup.
It’s a vicious cycle: the government worries about big tech yet incentivises more of it, competing with Silicon Valley by doing the same – just not quite as well. My organisation is a community interest company with an asset lock, built for competitive innovation in the public interest.
Labour created this structure in 2005 to enable a new generation of public-good companies, but innovation policy has yet to back it. UK Research and Innovation is closed to us: we aren’t a research organisation. Innovate UK now deems our community interest company ineligible for a knowledge transfer partnership, despite previous success with the University of Edinburgh. The Advanced Research and Invention Agency backs lone inventors. The Seed Enterprise Investment Scheme and the Enterprise Investment Scheme reward only uncapped shareholder returns.
Much is made of Palantir and the NHS, yet current policy doesn’t let a competitive British alternative emerge: one that tackles systemic data problems while letting trusts and communities retain ownership and agency. With funding, that is five years away, not a fantasy. If the government wants innovation that tackles the hardest problems, benefits all citizens, and competes globally, it must look beyond the models it rewards today.
Kate Fleming
Director, IDEMS
Gordon Brown’s analysis of Britain’s innovation ecosystem is largely correct. We do have world-class universities, rigorous research and a track record of discovery, and he’s right to highlight the gap between these strengths and their commercial returns. It’s no doubt a defining challenge of our time.
But there’s one word conspicuously absent from his argument: creativity. In making the case for innovation, Brown has fallen for a common trap, defaulting to a vision of research and development (R&D) that begins and ends with Stem (science, technology, engineering and mathematics). This vision leaves no place for the creative advantage that in many cases makes true innovation possible.
The UK’s creative industries contribute £145bn to the economy annually, growing at four times the national rate. Research by the Creative Industries Policy and Evidence Centre shows that nearly two-thirds of creative micro-firms have engaged in R&D in the past three years, outstripping every other industrial strategy priority sector. Brown might be surprised to learn that the UK university producing the most student startups is actually University of the Arts London (UAL).
UAL startups are using lateral thinking to develop biodegradable alternatives to plastic, building tools that decarbonise supply chains, pioneering food waste fermentation technology, and creating new materials from agricultural byproducts that could transform the construction industry.
They are engaging in real-world R&D to solve major global problems that transcend the creative sector, yet as creative businesses with arts graduates at the helm, they are consistently excluded from the narrative and the wider policy framing.
If we are serious about innovation driving good growth, we cannot afford a definition that excludes one of our most dynamic, inventive and internationally competitive sectors. Unlocking Britain’s full innovation potential means recognising that creativity and science are partners, not opposites.
Jenny Haigh
Head of policy for creative economy, University of the Arts London

India: Release CJP leaders arrested after attempting peaceful protests at Jantar Mantar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:07:00 UTC
01:07:00 KST

The Delhi authorities must immediately release Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, who have been remanded to five days of judicial custody after trying to protest at Jantar Mantar on Tuesday. Their arrests, following the removal of the site’s designation as an authorized protest venue, raise serious concerns about shrinking space for peaceful protest and dissent in India.
According to a post on X by CJP’s legal head, Ratna Singh, Das and Ranka were remanded to judicial custody on Wednesday. Party member Ajinkya Shinde, who was also detained, was released on a personal bond of INR 5,000 (USD 55). A First Information Report (FIR) was registered against Das and Ranka under provisions relating to breach of bond, criminal trespass and disobedience of orders, among other charges. Shinde was also placed under preventive arrest before being released.
“The authorities cannot claim to protect the right to protest while denotifying established protest sites and arresting people who attempt to use them. Peaceful assemblies should not be limited to a few designated sites. Rather, public spaces must remain available for people to peacefully assemble, challenge those in power, demand accountability, and make their grievances heard. Authorities cannot use the criminal justice system to punish people for exercising their right to peaceful assembly. We call for the immediate release of the CJP leaders and an end to the crackdown on peaceful dissent,” said Aakar Patel, Chair of Board, Amnesty International India.
Public spaces must remain available for people to peacefully assemble, challenge those in power, demand accountability, and make their grievances heard
Aakar Patel, Chair of Board, Amnesty International India
Jantar Mantar has long provided people from all walks of life, including workers, students and activists, a platform to bring grievances directly to public attention. Its importance lies not only in its capacity to accommodate gatherings, but in its accessibility and proximity to political institutions like the Parliament house.
On 12 October, Delhi Police officially removed Jantar Mantar from the list of legal, permitted areas for public protests and demonstrations. According to the Delhi police, this was done after a Supreme Court direction concerning alternative protest venues. Authorities identified venues like Ramlila Maidan, Burari Ground and CBD Ground as alternatives. However, naming replacement venues does not adequately guarantee the effective exercise of the right to peaceful assembly. Their accessibility, location, and ability for protesters to assemble within sight and sound of their intended audience are essential considerations. Moreover, as the UN Human Rights Committee has emphasized, “peaceful assemblies may in principle be conducted in all spaces to which the public … should have access.”
Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(b) of the Indian Constitution protects freedom of expression and the right to assemble peacefully and without arms. Although reasonable restrictions are permitted on specified grounds, including public order, authorities do not have unrestricted discretion to exclude peaceful demonstrations from public spaces.
In Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan v. Union of India (2018), the Supreme Court recognized the need to balance protesters’ rights with the interests of residents and other users of public space. Regulation must seek to accommodate competing interests, not impose arbitrary or blanket prohibitions.
International human rights law reinforces these protections. Articles 19 and 21 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR) safeguard the rights to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly.
The prohibition of protests at Jantar Mantar comes amid a broader police crackdown on demonstrations over electoral-roll revisions and demands for accountability from Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
Over the weekend of 10–11 October, police detained thousands of protesters and imposed restrictions affecting access to protest sites, public transport, and mobile internet, according to media reports and human rights organizations. Demonstrations were prevented from proceeding freely, with people detained as they attempted to gather in public spaces, and some detained from their homes even before they left for protest sites. Protesters who were travelling from Gujarat and Maharashtra to Delhi to participate in the protests were also detained by the authorities and prevented from continuing their journey to the capital.
Journalists covering the protests reported detention, physical mistreatment, confiscation of equipment, and obstruction despite displaying press credentials. Women journalists covering the protests have alleged that they were sexually harassed by Delhi Police. Lawyers seeking access to detainees faced also faced restrictions. These incidents raise concerns about journalists’ ability to document police conduct and lawyers’ ability to safeguard detainees’ rights.
“When protesters cannot assemble, journalists are harassed and cannot report freely, and lawyers face obstacles in reaching detainees, the entire system of public accountability suffers. By closing Jantar Mantar and restricting peaceful gatherings, the authorities are making dissent increasingly difficult to exercise. A right that exists only on paper, while people are denied places to assemble and face arrest when they try, is a right hollowed out in practice. These restrictions display strong authoritarian tendencies and risk turning public spaces into places where dissent is unwelcome,” said Aakar Patel.
Background
CJP, a youth-led movement that grew out of online satire, emerged as a protest force in June 2026, mobilizing students and young people against alleged examination irregularities and paper leaks. Its demonstrations at Jantar Mantar demanded the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.
The current crackdown on peaceful protests was not only confined to Delhi. Police detained protesters in Mumbai and Bengaluru.
In Bengaluru, on 12 October, police detained at least 100 people who were marching towards the Karnataka Chief Electoral Officer’s office. In Mumbai, police detained more than 600 people on 10 October as they tried to gather at August Kranti Maidan.

====================================================================================================

The Trump-Xi Summit Exposed the Problems in China-US Crisis Management
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:06:00 UTC
01:06:00 KST

Xi Jinping’s September visit to Washington ended without a major breakthrough on trade or artificial intelligence safety. Most media coverage focused on the ceremony and the limited results. The official accounts, however, raised important questions about crisis management, which has gone largely undiscussed.
China’s readout said the two militaries had “agreed to sign a memorandum of understanding as soon as possible on strengthening crisis communication and prevention.” The White House “fact sheet” did not mention that commitment. A later South China Morning Post report said a U.S. official denied that the discussion had taken place.
Before any MoU can improve crisis management, Washington and Beijing first need a consensus that they agreed to pursue such a mechanism.
China and the United States already have several ways to communicate during military tensions. These include the Defense Telephone Link, direct contact between their leaders, and regular meetings between defense officials. They have also agreed on rules for military encounters at sea and in the air.
Yet having these arrangements in place does not mean they will be used when a crisis occurs. Officials may delay answering a call, and political tensions might lead either government to suspend talks altogether. The proposed memorandum should therefore focus on keeping existing contacts available when they are most needed.
For more than a year after then-U.S. House Speaker Nancy Pelosi’s August 2022 visit to Taiwan, senior U.S. and Chinese military officers had few opportunities to speak directly. Beijing had canceled talks between theater commanders and suspended other defense meetings in protest against the visit. The military contacts themselves were not the source of the disagreement, but they became part of Beijing’s response.
Presidents Xi Jinping and Joe Biden eventually agreed to resume military talks when they met in California in November 2023, and the U.S. Department of Defense welcomed the move. But restoring contact after a leaders’ meeting is one thing; making sure those channels remain open when relations are strained is another.
The current Defense Telephone Link is not designed for situations that require an immediate response. According to the International Crisis Group, arranging a call normally involves giving 48 hours’ notice, and the other side has another 24 hours to respond to the request. Senior officials may be able to work with these rules when arranging meetings in advance. An emergency – say, an aircraft collision in the South China Sea – would leave little time for such procedures. By the time a call was arranged, commanders might already have made decisions without hearing from their counterparts.
The 2001 EP-3 collision offers another example of how difficult communication can be during a military crisis. The U.S. embassy tried to contact Chinese officials after the collision between U.S. and Chinese military aircraft, but received few answers during the first 12 hours. Washington had little information about how Beijing was handling the incident.
The Defense Telephone Link had not yet been established in 2001, making the circumstances different from today. But recent precedent is not encouraging either. In early 2023, after the U.S. military shot down a Chinese surveillance balloon that had overflown the U.S. mainland, the U.S. defense secretary tried to arrange a call with his Chinese counterpart. China reportedly rejected his request for contact.
That episode underscored the limited value of existing crisis management mechanisms. When urgent calls go unanswered, military officers have to make decisions with limited information about the other side’s intentions.
The proposed crisis management MoU needs to handle these two problems. Even if regular military talks break down, both sides should still be able to reach each other in an emergency. It should also require an acknowledgment within 30 minutes of an urgent message being sent. The officer receiving the message would simply confirm that it had arrived and that the information was being checked. Neither side would have to admit fault or agree with the other’s account at this stage. They could leave those disagreements for later, once the immediate risk had been dealt with.
For Beijing, accepting a message is different from deciding how to respond to it. Chinese officers may have to consult their superiors before commenting on an incident, particularly one involving sovereignty or military activity. That process can take time. A simple reply verifying receipt would allow those discussions to continue without leaving Washington unsure whether its warning had been heard. Beijing could still decide what to say after reviewing the incident, while keeping the military line open during the most urgent stage of a crisis.
The International Crisis Group has called for crisis simulations in which Chinese and American officials examine how each side might respond as tensions develop. A hypothetical aircraft collision over the South China Sea would be a useful scenario for a joint exercise before the November Trump-Xi meeting on the sidelines of the APEC summit. The U.S. military could make the initial test call and wait for a response from its Chinese counterpart, following the same procedures that would apply in a real incident. The exercise would give both sides a chance to see how long a message takes to reach the officer responsible for answering it. Any delay caused by the need to seek approval would become apparent.
An emergency channel should focus on what is happening at the time of a crisis. If an incident occurs, both sides need to know where it happened, whether anyone was injured, and whether their forces might come into contact again. They should not have to settle wider disagreements before sharing such information. Questions over Taiwan, technology restrictions, and U.S. military deployments can still be discussed through existing diplomatic and defense channels. Keeping these issues out of emergency communication would allow officers to deal with the immediate situation without waiting for progress in political negotiations.
Xi’s remarks in Washington called for the Chinese and U.S. militaries to “maintain regular dialogue, and improve mechanisms for crisis communication and prevention.” Leader-level diplomacy can authorize this work, but that doesn’t guarantee progress. By the next Trump-Xi summit at APEC, both governments should at least confirm the same commitment and complete a test of the contact route. The MoU itself may take longer if the two sides are still negotiating its terms.
The leader-level summits will matter more if the two governments can agree on how to handle calls during a military crisis. In the past, political disputes have led Beijing to suspend military exchanges with Washington. The same problem could arise again, leaving officers unable to contact their counterparts at a critical moment. One way to prevent this would be to keep emergency hotlines separate from regular defense talks. The first measure of progress is therefore simple: whether both militaries can agree that an urgent message must be acknowledged within 30 minutes.

Pilgrims caught up in Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia
RIYADH - Pilgrims in Saudi Arabia to visit Islam’s holiest sites may not have anticipated being caught up in an air war, but some experienced an attack by Yemen’s Houthis first hand and others have been forced to change their plans.
Footage of the massive blast that killed 13 people and wounded 300 in a Riyadh airport departure terminal struck by a Houthi missile on Oct 10 showed many passengers attired in the simple white clothes of Muslim pilgrims travelling to Mecca.
Saudi media reported that a Bangladeshi imam leading a group of dozens of pilgrims was killed and others wounded in the attack.
While the Houthis have promised not to attack either Mecca or Medina, the two holiest places in Islam that attract millions of pilgrims each year, they are targeting other Saudi airports in what they call retaliation for Saudi attacks on them.
“I feel deeply worried for my family and myself,” said Fadi Anwar, a Jordanian living in Mecca sitting in the courtyard of the main mosque in Mecca who was wearing the pilgrim’s robes. “We constantly receive warnings (phone alerts from the authorities) and it causes us great anxiety.”
Saudi officials have said the kingdom is safe and that the security of visitors is valued above all else, an offer of reassurance even as Western governments have warned against using most Saudi airports.
Pilgrims visit Mecca throughout the year
Although most international pilgrims fly directly into Medina or Jeddah airports, many others travel via Saudi Arabia’s other main air hubs, including the many pilgrims who already live in the kingdom.
Al Amin Hassan Mohammed from Sudan, who was visiting Saudi-based family members before a pilgrimage to Mecca, said he had been in Riyadh during the Oct 10 attack, which sent him and neighbours onto the street.
“We were tired and worried. We went out of the houses and we talked with each other,” he said.
Mohammed, who has a married daughter in Saudi Arabia’s Eastern Province city of Dammam, close to Dhahran where the Houthis targeted a Saudi Aramco building on Oct 13, has made the pilgrimage to Mecca before.
Like Anwar and others visiting the holy city now, outside of the annual hajj that is a requirement for all able-bodied Muslims in their lifetime, he is making a lesser pilgrimage known as umrah that can take place at any time of year.
The vast courtyard of the enormous main mosque in Mecca was a swirl of pilgrims in their white robes on Oct 13, as they circled the black cube of the Kaaba, the point towards which all Muslims face to pray.
Mecca draws millions of people each year, both during hajj and for umrah, from both inside Saudi Arabia and overseas, and the attacks have made some nervous.
“May God keep this away from us and from all Muslims, both in Saudi Arabia and elsewhere,” Anwar said.
Travel disruption hits businesses, embassies and tourism
The strikes between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-allied Houthis, resulting from the reignition of Yemen’s civil war as a spillover from the US-Iran conflict, have caused Saudi Arabia to ground many flights.
Schools in Riyadh have been switched to online learning this week and some offices have told staff to work from home.
The disruption has been particularly acute for those trying to travel, a group that includes pilgrims, business figures attending Saudi Arabia’s many high-profile conferences, Saudi tourists wishing to go on holiday and foreign residents wanting to fly home.
“We’ve had some trips postponed. We had friends who were travelling; it was delayed, they didn’t travel,” said Mohammed. His friends had been planning to fly via Riyadh but in the end they took a boat back to Sudan from Jeddah, he said.
Many people who had planned to fly from Riyadh are reviewing their options, with some making the four-hour trip to Bahrain, the seven-hour drive to Qatar or the 10-hour drive to Dubai.
A senior executive Reuters spoke to on Oct 14 was busy arranging transport for foreign employees, sending them by road to Doha in Qatar for onward flights.
A diplomat in Riyadh said several embassies had also used Doha for trips to and from Saudi Arabia over recent days, including for staff temporarily leaving with their families.
The representative of a company organising transport to Doha and Dubai said fares to those destinations had doubled.
Being prepared to pay is no guarantee of travel - in the early phases of the US-Iran war, Iranian fire grounded many flights around the Gulf and that direct conflict may erupt again with US President Donald Trump threatening to resume strikes. REUTERS

16:05:22 UTC

Palantir and the London mayor, Sadiq Khan, have called off their legal fight over claims the Labour mayor was blocking the US tech company from signing a contract with the Metropolitan police because of its values and ethics.
Palantir and the mayor’s office for policing and crime (Mopac) announced on Wednesday they had withdrawn allegations against each other, heading off a high court trial scheduled for January.
Palantir sued Mopac in June after Khan stepped in to block it from awarding Palantir a two-year, £50m deal for Scotland Yard to use AI to process intelligence in criminal investigations in a system called unified operational analytics (UOA), citing a “clear and serious breach” of procurement rules.
With Palantir also working for the Israeli military and for the Trump administration in its immigration crackdown, Khan has previously said Londoners only wanted to see public money being paid to companies that “share the values of our city”.
Louis Mosley, who heads Palantir in the UK and Europe, responded by accusing Khan of politicising procurement and said he was “putting politics above public safety”. He said: “What Londoners value is not being mugged, not being raped by a serving police officer.”
The agreement to drop the claims against each other comes a month after Palantir hired Tom Watson, the former Labour party deputy leader, as a full-time lobbyist. The firm was concerned that if public authorities were able to block it from winning contracts due to objections over the values of its senior leadership, it would undermine its ability to operate in the UK.
Palantir is facing a battle to retain its £330m NHS medical data contract amid a vociferous campaign from parts of the public and some MPs for it to be replaced by a less controversial company.
Palantir and Mopac said in a joint statement that Mopac’s decision in May to block the contract “was not based on Palantir’s values or ethics or any wider reporting about the company”.
“Mopac recognises Palantir’s concerns that media reporting of a statement from the mayor’s spokesperson before the decision was taken could have incorrectly created the impression that an assessment of the company’s values had been a factor in that decision,” it said.
“Mopac’s consideration was based upon its statutory role of examining spend proposals, against the appropriate legal tests and the relevant guidance on procurement, governance, affordability and ensuring value for money for Londoners.”
Khan said: “London is the technology capital of Europe, and I am proud that leading software firms choose the city as their home. Palantir makes a significant contribution to jobs and investment in the capital, employing a large number of Londoners whose services have been procured legally by organisations across the UK and beyond.”
Watson said: “The mayor and his team have recognised their actions could have created the impression that the decision to block the UOA contract was based on Palantir’s values. I’m very pleased that they have today corrected any such impression, and that even in the face of extreme provocation from highly organised pressure groups, decisions about deploying technology can still be made on their merits and in the public interest.”
A new procurement process for the £50m police tech deal is under way and Mopac has agreed to treat Palantir “fairly and equally” if it bids, as expected. Equally, Mopac is not bound to agree to Palantir’s appointment.
Each side is covering its own legal costs, no admissions of liability are made and no damages have been paid.
