The eyes have it: Reform politician’s ‘smart glasses’ prompt calls for ban in Westminster
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:05:53 UTC
00:05:53 KST

It was a flowing speech packed full of precise statistics – but Jason O’Connell, a Reform UK Senedd member, was not quite the gifted orator he had first appeared. The periodic flashing in his spectacles seemed to give the game away as he spoke for five minutes in the Senedd chamber without a glance at his notes.
“Cardiff reviewed 192 roads, following 933 requests, and only four routes have returned to 30mph,” he said as he led the party’s charge to abolish 20mph traffic zones. “£38.3m wasted to implement this policy and up to £8.9bn in an act of economic self-harm.”
It was probably no feat of memory – rather, the Reform member for Pontypridd Cynon Merthyr was suspected of using smart glasses that turned his lenses into tiny teleprompters.
In the days afterwards, Senedd members said the issue of smart glasses – popularised by Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta – needed to be dealt with at pace, with explicit guidance developed on their use.
There was no suggestion that O’Connell’s glasses were recording. But it has prompted a fresh debate about the increasingly popular technology, with the House of Commons facing calls to ban smart glasses at Westminster.
The Liberal Democrats wrote to Lindsay Hoyle, the Commons speaker, on Wednesday urging him to act amid the “increasing use of smart glasses” on the parliamentary estate. They warned that with Christmas coming, even more people could start using the AI-enabled devices in 2027.
The technology has myriad implications. Anna Sabine, the Liberal Democrat spokesperson for culture, media and sport, said smart glasses could lead to debates becoming increasingly “managed”.
“How much is the quality of what an MP is saying actually down to what they’re getting through the AI glasses?” she said. “It’s a really interesting question.”
She said she had not yet identified anyone wearing smart glasses in parliament but added: “This is the problem: I wouldn’t necessarily know.” A law would help to keep the estate and the work MPs did “private and secure”.
Sabine added: “Smart glasses can record video and take photographs discreetly … creating a particular risk to the existing rules on the parliamentary estate [limiting recording and photography].
“I am regularly in meetings with documents or talking about important, private matters on behalf of my constituents. I am sure you will agree that the details of such cases should never be at risk of being shared because someone is filming or taking pictures discreetly.
“Because smart glasses look like ordinary glasses, and increasingly their recording indicator lights can be covered or disabled, filming could easily go unnoticed by security teams, putting private information at risk.”
A spokesperson for the UK parliament said it was reviewing its policy on the use of camera-equipped smart glasses, as well as other forms of wearable technology, on the parliamentary estate.
The senior deputy speaker of the House of Lords, Lord Ponsonby, told parliament last month that the review “is considering the implications of these emerging technologies and whether additional guidance is required”.
He added: “This work will bring together expertise from those responsible for filming and photography policy, physical and information security, privacy and data protection compliance and accessibility and reasonable-adjustment requirements, ensuring that any future approach appropriately balances security, privacy, operational needs and accessibility considerations.”
O’Connell has been contacted for comment. On Sunday he posted a picture on X of himself wearing a pair of comedy large pink glasses for a breast cancer charity, with the message: “Trialling some new glasses for the chamber this week. Apparently my last ones caused quite a stir.”

Ayhan Simsek
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Wednesday defended his government's financial and military support for Ukraine, rejecting opposition party claims that the aid comes at the expense of social spending at home.
Addressing lawmakers in parliament, Merz said continued support for Ukraine is essential to safeguard peace and security across Europe as Russia’s threats intensify. He argued that military assistance to Kyiv does not reduce funds available for domestic priorities.
“Not a single euro flowing to Ukraine is being diverted from social or educational spending in our country. Not a single euro is missing," Merz said. He added that they had introduced an exception to Germany’s constitutional debt rule to allow defense-related spending to be financed through additional borrowing.
Merz warned that the danger is concrete rather than theoretical. "We see that Russia's readiness to escalate is rising toward Ukraine, toward our Eastern European neighbors, but also toward our own country," he said.
He slammed the right-wing AfD and the socialist Left Party for downplaying threats and fueling division.
"It is incomprehensible to me how those on the far left and far right continue, to this day, to play down the situation,” he said, accusing them of deliberately driving divisions, uncritically spreading disinformation. "One gets the impression you want the chaos because you want to gain party-political advantages from it."
Opposition lawmakers from the AfD and the Left Party have repeatedly argued that billions of euros in support for Ukraine should instead go to domestic priorities such as pensions and infrastructure.
Merz's conservative CDU/CSU alliance is facing pressure as it trails in opinion polls while the right-wing AfD leads. An INSA survey published this week put the AfD at 30%, the CDU/CSU at 18.5%, the environmentalist Greens at 14%, the center-left SPD at 13.5%, and the Left Party at 10%.

An ancient Chinese math puzzle shows how to win at cards, horse races and gerrymandering
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:53:23 UTC
23:53:23 KST

Sun Bin, allegedly descended from The Art of War author Sun Tzu, was a legendary Chinese military strategist who lived more than 2,300 years ago. After one king imprisoned and tortured him, forcing him to use a wheelchair for the rest of his life, he rose to fame as a military advisor for a rival king and lived to record two great victories against his former captor.
One of Sun Bin’s greatest exploits came not on the battlefield but on a racetrack. Like his supposed ancestor, who wrote, “Warfare is a way of deception,” Sun Bin discovered a “way of deception” in horse races that can be boiled down to a simple mathematical puzzle. For reasons that I cannot explain, the most general version of this puzzle remained unsolved and unexamined until 1980, when a college classmate of mine rediscovered it. Thirty years later he told me about the puzzle, and I was hooked. Besides transporting me back to ancient China, solving this problem took me back to my own roots as a mathematician.
I like to approach Master Sun’s problem through several simpler puzzles:
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Puzzle One: Suppose you toss a coin six times. What is the probability of getting exactly three heads and three tails? What if you toss the coin 10, 100 times or any even number of times? How likely are you to get exactly the same number of heads and tails?
Puzzle Two: Now pick an even number, which we’ll call 2N, and a target number, N – k, which is less than N. If you flip a coin 2N times, do you think it is more likely that you will get exactly N heads or that you will get (N – k) or fewer heads? For example, are you more likely to get exactly 10 heads in 20 flips or to get eight or fewer heads in 20 flips? Experiment with different values of k and N and see if you can find a general rule.
The next two puzzles seem, on the surface, to have nothing to do with the first two.
Puzzle Three: Two teams, each with three players, are planning to compete in a match. Each team is supposed to rank its players from best to worst. The number one seed on one team is supposed to play the number one seed on the other, and so on. One coach is honest and ranks their players by true order of ability. The other coach is dishonest and decides to strategically rank their players in a different order. Can the latter coach tilt the odds in their favor? If so, what ranking strategy gives their team the greatest chance of winning the match? What if each team has 10, 100 or N players?
Puzzle Four: The dishonest coach decides to place bets on the individual games rather than the overall team match. For this purpose, they want to know what ranking strategy will give their team the greatest expected number of games won. If there are three players per team, what strategy is optimal, and how many individual games can the coach expect to win? What if there are 10, 100 or N players on each team?
The last two puzzles harken back to a popular legend featuring Sun Bin. According to the story, General Tian Ji and King Wei were planning a friendly series of horse races, and the general asked Master Sun, his trusted retainer, for advice. The wily strategist told Tian Ji to race his best horse against the king’s second best, his second best against the king’s third best and his worst against the king’s best. I call this Master Sun’s strategy. “Just bet heavily, my lord, and I can make you the winner,” Sun Bin said. And indeed, according to the legend, Tian Ji won two out of three races and took home 1,000 gold coins.
That is how the legend goes, but any modern mathematician would be skeptical. Certainly Sun Bin could not guarantee a win. But did the strategy improve Tian Ji’s chances of winning the match? And if so, by how much did it do so? Those questions lead us straight to Puzzles Three and Four.
Before I reveal the answers, we must go back and consider the first two puzzles.
In Puzzle One, the secret to computing the odds of any number of heads lies in the following arrangement of numbers, called Pascal’s triangle:
Each number is generated by adding the two numbers immediately above it; the process can be continued indefinitely. To evaluate the probability of exactly three heads in six tosses of a coin, we look up the third element in the sixth row, which is 20. (Technical note: The top row is traditionally considered to be the zeroth row, and the leftmost element in each row is the zeroth element. So the zeroth element in row six is 1, the first element is 6, and so on.)
We divide 20 by 26, which equals 64, to get the exact probability of three heads in six tosses: 20⁄64 = 0.3125, or 31.25 percent—slightly less than 1⁄3. Are you surprised? More than two thirds of the time, you will not get three heads in six tosses.
As the number of tosses increases, it becomes less and less likely that you will get heads exactly half the time. You can see this visibly from a histogram, in which the height of each bar represents the probability of getting the corresponding number of heads. The peak height of the histogram decreases as the number of tosses, N, gets larger. The appearance of the histogram changes as well: the steps shrink and smooth out into a curve, creating what is known as a normal distribution.
This “view from infinity” provides an approximate—but remarkably good—estimate for the solution to Puzzle One. In 2N flips of a coin, the probability of getting exactly N heads (equal to the peak height of the histogram) is roughly 1⁄√πN. For example, if N = 50, then the probability of 50 heads in 100 tosses is roughly 1⁄√50π ≈ 0.0798, as shown in the figure.
You might wonder at the presence of π, or pi, in the equation, thinking, “What does a ratio between circumference and diameter have to do with flipping coins?” You may also be baffled by the square root. I can’t give you an easy explanation: every proof I have ever seen uses calculus, which is the mathematician’s version of a telescope that gives you a view from infinity.
Puzzle Two is a much more recent variant. It is trickier because we are now comparing the probabilities of two rare events. On one hand, we have an “exceptionally average” result: getting heads on exactly half the tosses. On the other hand, we have exceptionally large deviations from average: the “tail” of the normal distribution. Which one is rarer? It depends on where we start measuring the tail.
For N = 3, we again consult the sixth row of Pascal’s triangle: 1, 6, 15, 20, 15, 6, 1. We add these numbers from the left and ask when the sum first exceeds the central—and largest—number in the row. We notice that 1 + 6 < 20, so the probability of getting zero or one heads is less than the probability of getting three heads. But 1 + 6 + 15 > 20, so the probability of getting zero, one or two heads exceeds the probability of getting three.
To answer the question for N = 10, we need to compute the 20th row of Pascal’s triangle, which is already kind of tedious. It turns out that the crossover happens at eight heads. That is, we are more likely to get 10 heads than seven or fewer but less likely to get 10 heads than eight or fewer.
To solve the puzzle for N = 100, we would have to compute the 200th row of Pascal’s triangle, and I don’t know anyone (aside from computers) with that kind of patience. But the “view from infinity” gives us a shortcut. The area of the central rectangle is roughly 1⁄√πN. The area to the left of the crossover line can be estimated from the normal distribution. By comparing the two, we can show that the crossover happens at 89 heads.
In general, if the crossover happens at (N – k), then k ≈ √Nln(N)⁄2. (Here “ln” means the natural logarithm.) I’ll call k the “crossover number,” so for N = 100, the crossover number is 100 – 89 = 11. This solution is perhaps slightly less remarkable than our solution to Puzzle One, and for small values of N, the approximation is not as good. But I happen to like it better because I discovered it myself! It also turned out to be a key that let me unlock the solution to Puzzle Four.
A few months ago my wife and I ate dinner with a friend who is always interested in mathematical topics. I told her about Puzzles Three and Four and said that I was writing a book about them. “But where is the mathematics?” she asked me. It was an excellent question, and it brings up a little understood point. Math never arises in the real world in pure and unadulterated form, as you see in textbooks. Math is always hiding behind the scenes. To bring it out into the foreground, you must make a mathematical model of a real-world problem.
In Puzzles Three and Four, the clue is that I’m asking about probabilities. So somewhere there must be a source of randomness. I assume that the source of randomness is the assignment of players to the coaches—that is, the coaches drew the players blindly, as if drawing cards from a deck of 2N cards, with each possible draw being equally likely. You may disagree with this assumption; for example, in the story of Tian Ji, the king may have had access to better horses than the general did. But without making some assumptions, you’ll never get anywhere, and it’s best to start with simple ones. The card game model, which I call One-Round War, allows me to create a table that shows the probability that my ith best player beats the other team’s jth best player, for any pair i and j. Using this table, I can evaluate any proposed strategy and figure out which ones work better for me.
It’s important to note that in One-Round War, both players know the seeding of each card within each hand, so we know which card is our ith best and which is our opponent’s jth best, even though the cards are face down. We do not know the actual card values, though. In a fair version of this game, the players would take turns going first, but I am interested in a wildly unfair version in which I go second every time. That gives me the power to react to my opponent’s moves.
For example, suppose I draw cards {1, 3, 5} and my opponent draws {2, 4, 6}. If I play “honestly,” playing my best (5) against my opponent’s best (6), and so on, I will lose all three tricks. But if I use Master Sun’s strategy, playing my best (5) against my opponent’s second-best (4), and so on, then I will win two out of three.
For the case of six cards, we can show that Master Sun’s strategy wins 70 percent (14 out of 20) of the possible hands. As for Puzzle Four, Master Sun’s strategy will win, on average, 55 percent of the tricks. In both puzzles, Master Sun’s scheme is the best possible strategy utilizing only the ranks of the cards. After 2,300 years, Master Sun’s intuition is vindicated!
There is no evidence that Sun Bin ever considered the problem for N > 3. But modern mathematics gives us the tools to answer such questions. It was precisely this question, the basis of Puzzle Four for an arbitrary N, that my college friend Howard Stern, a fellow math major who passed away in 2016, told me about and that quickly turned into an obsession.
We’ve already seen that Master Sun’s strategy is based on the idea of sacrificing some lower-rated cards against your opponent’s stronger cards so that your remaining cards (the ringers) have a better chance of winning. This approach means that your entire hand consists of two types of cards: sacrificial cards and ringers. Stern proved that the sacrificial cards should always be played in reverse order. (Proving this yourself is an excellent challenge.) Your worst card should be paired against your opponent’s best, and so on. The ringers, on the other hand, should be played in direct order of strength.
After determining this, the devil is in the details. Which cards should you select as sacrificial cards? Which cards should they be played against? How many cards should you sacrifice, and how many should you designate as ringers? These were questions Stern could not answer.
The casual math enthusiast will probably find Puzzle Three to be more accessible than Puzzle Four. It requires no more math than we’ve discussed here, just common sense. Puzzle Four, on the other hand, fascinated and entertained me for a full year. My book Master Sun’s Problem, which came out from Princeton University Press on October 13, contains the full answer. It also tells the full historical story, as well as the tales of some other contributors: Stern, who introduced me to Puzzles Three and Four; journalist Gary Antonick, who let me turn his then column Numberplay in the New York Times into a crowdsourcing experiment; retired engineer Bill Courtney, who solved Puzzle Three; and operations research expert Richard Chatwin, who made a vital contribution to solving Puzzle Four.
Though I don’t want to give away too many spoilers, probably the most stunning discovery was that Puzzle Two and Puzzle Four are the same problem. More precisely, the solution to Puzzle Two is embedded within the solution to Puzzle Four. Remember the crossover numbers from Puzzle Two? We saw that the crossover number for 10 tosses of a coin is two and that the crossover number for 100 tosses is 11. These are exactly the same as the optimal number of cards to sacrifice when using Master Sun’s strategy. It’s another example of the amazing propensity of mathematics to unearth connections between things that did not seem to be related.
For example, if you’re playing a game of One-Round War with 100 cards against 100 cards, you should sacrifice 11 cards and designate 89 ringers. On average, none of the sacrificial lambs will win, but 86 of the 89 ringers will, and you will take the match by an astounding margin of 86 to 14.
Any good math problem should leave more questions in its wake. I deliberately did not include the possibility of upsets in my model. In our card game, the higher card always beats the lower one. But in horse races, the faster horse does not always win. How robust is Master Sun’s strategy under those circumstances?
Also, the scheme reminds me very much of gerrymandering, in which you deliberately lose some electoral districts by a large margin in order to win a lot of districts by a small margin. Can you devise an optimal gerrymandering strategy? In a state with 100 districts, would it be smart to draw a map with 11 losing districts and 89 winning ones? I highly doubt that the solution would translate so directly, but the analogy is worth thinking about.
The world is full of asymmetric or unfair contests. While we may wish there was a way to ensure that justice prevails, perhaps we would do well to take a lesson from ancient Chinese sages who understood how to play the asymmetric contests well.

Earth’s ‘life support systems’ are breaking down, climate scientists warn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:53:12 UTC
23:53:12 KST

Earth faces “rapid destabilization” as a result of climate change, an international group of scientists find in the latest edition of an annual checkup of the planet’s “vital signs.”
“This is no longer a warning for the future; it is a diagnosis of the present,” the authors write.
The report, the latest in a series called the “State of the Climate,” measures 16 key markers of Earth’s climate. Seven of these have reached “record extremes,” says report co-author Christopher Wolf, a research scientist at Terrestrial Ecosystems Research Associates. These extremes include soaring greenhouse gas concentrations, melting sea ice and sea-level rise—driven largely by human activities.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
“Global warming appears to be accelerating,” Wolf says.
Carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, a by-product of burning fossil fuels, has reached record-high levels (428 parts per million), as have other greenhouse gases such as methane (1,940 parts per billion) and nitrous oxide (340 parts per billion). The ocean has absorbed a record-breaking jump in heat, which, in turn, has helped fuel unprecedented sea-level rise. At the same time, higher temperatures have meant record losses in the Greenland ice sheet and glaciers.
“Earth’s life-support systems are being pushed beyond stable limits, with changes unfolding faster than our ability to respond,” Wolf and his co-authors write in the report.
Humans are in danger as a result: since September 2025 climate change has fueled myriad natural disasters, including floods in Albania, Bali, Brazil, Columbia, Greece, Indonesia, and Vietnam; heat waves in Europe, India and the U.S.; wildfires in Australia and Florida; and more, the report finds.
The future, the report warns, may be bleak.
“We are increasingly concerned about the risk of crossing climate tipping points that could lead to irreversible changes,” Wolf says.
That could include disruptions to the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC)—the movement of cold and warm water across the Atlantic Ocean, which influences global weather—as well as what the report describes as “irreversible” damage to the Amazon rainforest thanks to the double whammy of global warming and deforestation. Only bold action to reduce fossil fuel use can help halt or reverse this devastation, the authors write.
“The climate emergency is already here, but the future is not yet determined,” Wolf says. “We still have opportunities to avoid some of the worst outcomes through rapid emissions reductions, climate adaptation and broader societal changes. The window for action is narrowing, but it has not closed.”
The report was published in the journal BioScience on Wednesday.

“He was doing a sports course at college, and he had done a work placement at our local leisure centre in Tadley, and the manager there said as soon as he has got his certificate come back to us.”
Brown, who was 17 at the time of the incident, gave evidence at the inquest, saying his father had shown him how to safely use the gun on two occasions.
Talking about what his father told him, he said: “Not to point it at people.”
When asked if he had thought about putting the gun away after shooting in the garden, before his friends came over, he said: “I wanted my friends to use it. I just thought it would be fun.”
The inquest was told that Beechey was arrested by the police after the accidental shooting but no further action was taken.
Giving evidence on Wednesday, Beechey said he had been drinking cider and vodka at the party and he was “a little bit drunk”.
The Hampshire area coroner Jason Pegg ruled that Connor’s cause of death was a gunshot wound to the head and he died from cardiac arrest from a brain injury. He concluded that it was an accident.
Pegg said: “Connor was just 17 years of age at the time of his death. It is quite clear to me, having heard from [Connor’s family], that he was a son, grandson and a friend. He was a young man who had aspirations in the physical fitness field and had a life planned ahead of him. He was full of life and had a cheeky side and had much to live for.”
He added: “This demonstrates the real risk when you have a group of young people drinking alcohol. This is a deeply tragic case.”

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.

Russia’s War Budget Is So Huge It Could Almost Build Another International Space Station
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:50:32 UTC
23:50:32 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia’s War Budget Is So Huge It Could Almost Build Another International Space Station
Russia has allocated roughly $177.4 billion in 2026 to defense and other expenditures connected to its war against Ukraine, while more than $109.5 billion of its so-called defense budget remains classified, according to Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence on October 14.
The official Russian budget line for “national defense” stands at about $144.4 billion this year. When a broader range of war-related expenditures is included, Ukraine’s intelligence service estimates the total rises to approximately $177.4 billion.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Of that defense spending, around $109.5 billion is contained in classified budget items, limiting public visibility into where much of the money is actually going.
Moscow has also earmarked substantial funding to sustain and expand its defense-industrial base. Roughly $189.8 million is allocated to military-industrial development, military-technical cooperation, and scientific and production programs. Those categories receive approximately $73.5 million, $75.2 million, and $41.1 million, respectively.
Additional state support is being directed toward struggling defense companies. Russia has allocated about $24.5 million to reimburse corporate expenses, $5.5 million to prevent bankruptcies, $6 million to offset loan-interest costs, and another $17.9 million for compensation payments to employees.
Ukraine’s intelligence also identified approximately $14.9 million in funding for high-performance computing used in weapons development. Such workloads are carried out at major Russian data centers, including infrastructure operated by Yandex and Sberbank, which Ukraine says links those computing resources directly to Russia’s military-industrial programs.
Another $312 million has been set aside for applied defense research, while approximately $121.9 million is officially allocated to the development and production of various types of drones. Ukrainian intelligence cautioned that this figure does not reflect the true size of Russia’s UAV industry because additional funding comes through private investment, procurement programs, and other channels.
One particularly large allocation is intended for Russia’s National Guard, which is budgeted to receive approximately $8.19 billion for drone purchases.
According to Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence, those UAVs are expected to serve not only in Russia’s war against Ukraine but also inside Russia itself, including the protection of critical infrastructure, urban patrols, surveillance, and possible use by security forces during domestic unrest.
The scale of military spending becomes especially stark when compared with Russia’s civilian priorities. Moscow’s $144.4 billion official defense budget is more than three times the combined funding allocated to education—about $21 billion—and healthcare, at roughly $22.5 billion.
Ukraine’s intelligence noted that $144.4 billion is close to the estimated $150 billion cost of building the International Space Station. The same amount, it argued, could finance more than 150 modern cancer treatment centers instead.
Previously, reports emerged that Russia was preparing a new round of tax increases expected to extract nearly $44 billion from individuals and businesses through 2029 as the government seeks additional revenue to cover rising military spending and a widening budget deficit.

The goal of implementing e-Excise is to create a system that will ensure a level playing field for legal businesses and stable revenue for the state budget.

China's yuan loans increase by 11.52 trln yuan in Jan.-Sept. period
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
22:37:35 CST
23:37:35 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- China's yuan-denominated loans rose by 11.52 trillion yuan (about 1.71 trillion U.S. dollars) in the first three quarters of 2026, central bank data showed Wednesday.
At the end of September, outstanding yuan loans stood at 283.44 trillion yuan, up 4.8 percent year on year, according to the People's Bank of China (PBOC).
M2, a broad measure of money supply that covers cash in circulation and all deposits, stood at 359.63 trillion yuan at the end of September, up 7.2 percent year on year.
M1, which covers currency in circulation, corporate demand deposits, personal demand deposits and provisions received by non-bank payment institutions, reached 116.76 trillion yuan at the end of September, a rise of 3.2 percent from a year earlier.
China's outstanding aggregate financing to the real economy stood at 468.17 trillion yuan at the end of September, up 7.1 percent year on year, according to the central bank.
"China's major financial aggregates have maintained reasonable growth, with M2 and aggregate financing to the real economy growing at appropriate rates," said Tian Xuan, dean of Peking University's Guanghua School of Management. "This has helped create a favorable monetary and financial environment for sustained economic improvement."
Since the beginning of the year, the PBOC has introduced two rounds of structural monetary policy measures to address the needs of China's transition to new growth drivers and help financial institutions better align their services with the needs of the real economy.
The latest round of structural monetary policy measures, announced in September, included cutting the one-year interest rate of the Pledged Supplementary Lending (PSL) facility from 1.75 percent to 1.5 percent, expanding the scope of PSL support, and increasing the quota of the relending facility for sci-tech innovation and technological upgrades by 200 billion yuan.
The policy package will channel more funds to areas such as equipment upgrades, strengthen support for sci-tech enterprises, help ease financing constraints on private businesses and reduce their financing costs, said Dong Qingma, deputy head of the Institute of Chinese Financial Studies of Southwestern University of Finance and Economics.
The effects of the September policy package are expected to emerge gradually, with existing and new monetary policy measures working in tandem to provide continued support for high-quality development of the real economy, experts said. ■

A Zhuque-2E Y4 carrier rocket carrying 10 satellites blasts off from the Dongfeng commercial space innovation pilot zone in northwest China, Oct. 14, 2026. The rocket lifted off at 7:40 p.m. (Beijing Time) and deployed 10 satellites into their preset orbits. The flight test mission was declared a complete success. (Photo by Wang Jiangbo/Xinhua)
JIUQUAN, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- China successfully launched a Zhuque-2E Y4 carrier rocket from the Dongfeng commercial space innovation pilot zone in northwest China on Wednesday.
The rocket lifted off at 7:40 p.m. (Beijing Time) and deployed 10 satellites into their preset orbits.
The flight test mission was declared a complete success.
Eight satellites of the 02 group of a "star compute" plan, developed by Adaspace Technology Co., Ltd. (ADAspace) and designed to operate in dawn-dusk orbits, were included in the launch.
According to ADAspace, a commercial aerospace enterprise, these satellites carry high-performance computing payloads, high-speed inter-satellite and satellite-to-ground laser communication payloads, low-light cameras and other equipment.
They will conduct in-orbit verification of key technologies, such as liquid-cooled fluid loops at the 10,000-watt level, ultra-large deployable radiative cooling wings, full-domain laser communication networks and in-orbit training of foundation models.
ADAspace said it intends to carry out in-orbit tests of the 02 group satellites, advance technological iteration, and promote the space computing technology innovation and industry innovation.
The "star compute" plan is an ambitious project by the company to build AI space infrastructure composed of 2,800 computing satellites. The first group of satellites for the plan was successfully launched in May 2025. The third group is scheduled for orbital deployment in 2026. ■

====================================================================================================

Ukrainian drones are hitting Russia’s biggest data centers. Why are they so vulnerable — and can anything protect them?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:37:10 UTC
23:37:10 KST

Ukrainian drones are hitting Russia’s biggest data centers. Why are they so vulnerable — and can anything protect them?
After strikes on Yandex’s data centers, pro-war channels accused the company of inaction and even sabotage. Elements of critical infrastructure turned out to be completely unprotected against drone attacks. Now similar accusations will likely be directed at Sberbank: the bank’s largest data center in the Saratov region was attacked overnight on October 14. All these facilities were an obvious target for Ukraine’s military, if only because Russian forces are actively striking similar targets in Ukraine. Of course, the inadequate protection of the data centers has nothing to do with malicious intent or negligence on the part of Yandex and Sberbank’s management. It is known that, even before the strikes, authorities and the military discussed measures to defend such facilities with businesses. And judging by video of the attacks, at least in Yandex’s case some defense — probably in the form of mobile fire teams or automatic turrets — did exist: drones were fired at with small arms. This shows that Russia still lacks the resources to build a multilayered anti-drone air defense system anywhere except Moscow. And site-level defenses at individual factories, warehouses, and data centers cannot repel massed strikes.
First, a reminder of which facilities Ukraine’s military struck
Ukrainian strikes hit three of Yandex’s six largest data centers, also known as data processing centers, between October 7 and 11. None were located in the Moscow region, the area most heavily protected by Russian air defenses.
- The data center in Sasovo, in the Ryazan region, which also housed two of Yandex’s three supercomputers, stopped operating entirely. Judging by satellite images from the Planet Labs, the wing of the building housing the data center had burned down completely.
- Data centers in Vladimir, one of two in the city, and in Kaluga sustained significant damage.
A Ukrainian strike hit Sberbank’s Mega Data Center in Balakovo, in the Saratov region, overnight on October 14. Construction began in 2021, when Russian Deputy Prime Minister Dmitry Chernyshenko promised the facility would become the largest in Russia.
When Yandex and Sberbank built these facilities before the full-scale war, they had no reason to design the buildings to withstand drones carrying warheads with dozens of kilograms of explosives. HAKA Moscow, the company that built one of Yandex’s data centers in Vladimir in 2016–2017, said its main objectives were:
- speed of construction;
- the ability to expand the facility;
- and, importantly, reducing the need for active cooling of the equipment, which increased the facility’s energy efficiency.
Reinforced concrete slabs — a material characteristic of Soviet industrial construction — were not used to build the building’s frame.
So what went wrong with the defenses at these data centers?
All buildings of this kind — built with modern technology out of metal structures — are vulnerable to drones carrying relatively small warheads. By contrast, defense and civilian enterprises built during the Soviet era, such as thermal power plants, are difficult targets for these drones.
The full-scale war has confirmed this. When striking targets in Ukraine, Russian forces prefer to hit reinforced concrete buildings with ballistic and cruise missiles, which carry warheads weighing hundreds of kilograms and can penetrate obstacles because of their high kinetic energy.
Likewise, Ukraine’s military, which has not yet received large numbers of missiles with a range of more than 300 kilometers (186 miles), prefers relatively “soft” but economically important targets: oil refineries, warehouses, and now data centers. Ukraine tries to strike Soviet-era industrial facilities with missiles such as the Flamingo cruise missile, but it does not yet have enough of them to achieve an effect of strategic scale.
Ukraine’s army has also used drones to damage facilities that are strategically important to Russia and its military. In most cases, though, foreign companies built the buildings housing these facilities using metal structures.
Optical Fiber Systems JSC in Saransk, Russia’s only major fiber-optic producer, was built turnkey by a Finnish company in the late 2000s. The plant was important to the Russian military because fiber optics are used, among other things, to make fiber-optic-guided drones for the front line. In 2025, Ukrainian drone strikes effectively destroyed the building and its equipment. Rebuilding it will take several years, Russian authorities reported. Other successful attacks on workshops built from metal structures have also been recorded.
Hi, I’m Yulia.
I’m an editor at Meduza, and for almost five years now, I haven’t been sleeping well for one reason: I’m worried about my colleagues in Russia.
I’m often woken up by messages from our freelance reporters inside the country. They sometimes work late at night or early in the morning, and they message me at all hours. I never silence my phone at night in case of an emergency. Every notification jolts me awake. Half-asleep, my first thought is always the same: they’re texting me because the police have come to search their home. In Russia, you can go to prison for working with Meduza. Sometimes I have nightmares about my reporters being interrogated by the FSB. Some of those nightmares have come true.
Meduza’s reporters risk their freedom to tell the world what’s happening inside Russia. They believe their work can help make a better future possible, and they refuse to leave. Please donate so they can keep reporting.
Beyond the vulnerability of the buildings themselves, Yandex and Sberbank also erred in choosing where to build. By the fifth year of the full-scale war, facilities in and around Moscow had gained a major competitive advantage: the military and Russian authorities have clearly chosen to allocate air defense resources to protect the capital, just as Ukraine’s leadership has done for Kyiv.
Traditional short-range air defense systems, the Tor and Pantsir families, remain the backbone of Russia’s drone defenses, and there clearly are not enough of them to protect the country’s entire territory. Concentrating these systems around Moscow, however, has made hitting targets in the capital difficult.
Difficult, but solvable: massing drones in a single wave sometimes lets Ukraine’s military break through the defenses around Moscow and reach particularly important targets, such as the Moscow oil refinery. Many attacks fail, however: videos and photos of drones shot down around Moscow circulate often, with no verified evidence that targets inside the city were struck.
Most of Russia’s key internet infrastructure nodes are located in Moscow and St. Petersburg. M9 (MSK-IX), the most important node, houses the infrastructure for the root DNS servers and sits in the southwest of the capital. During a drone attack on August 18, a fire broke out for unknown reasons at the CHPP-20 power plant, which supplies M9 with electricity, causing problems for thousands of websites. However, the data center itself was not damaged at the time.
How could these fragile targets be defended, in theory?
Methods of protection fall into two categories: passive and active. Passive measures include building physical protective structures around a facility or, where possible, dispersing production.
Building protective structures requires large capital investments with no guarantee the method will work. Russia also used to require government authorization to build these structures, but a 2026 law repealed that rule.
The problem is that not all structures are effective. Expensive protective structures, naturally, have a better chance of working. The same cannot be said for the ordinary anti-drone nets used at the front to counter small drones: they are not very effective against fixed-wing drones carrying warheads of dozens of kilograms.
This fall, Russian oil refineries and oil depots began installing sturdier metal nets of various designs. There is still no data on how much this protection helps. A video showing nets being installed at the Moscow oil refinery was published September 21, while the most recent attack — which again damaged unnamed equipment at the plant — had occurred the day before. The video was probably filmed before that strike, so doubts remain about how effective the netting is. There is also a risk that these barriers could be breached by repeated strikes on the same spot.
Previous experience has also failed to prove the method’s effectiveness. Bashneft, for example, began installing metal nets around its primary oil-refining units in the spring of 2024, yet drone strikes knocked the company’s plants out of operation in 2026.
That doesn’t mean more expensive, complex structures won’t offer protection. These experiments — sturdy metal cages and nets — are being conducted in Gulf states, though they, too, have not yet been tested in combat. Iran and its allies, the Houthis, have not recently used drones for strikes on land, preferring missile attacks instead. Russian companies, however, have already begun building these “fences” at their refineries.
Reliable passive drone defense might force an adversary to use more expensive munitions — missiles above all — to hit targets. Russian enterprises are already trying to build more reliable defenses that could also stop missiles in theory. At some power plants, for instance, construction has begun on structures resembling reinforced concrete sarcophagi.
Ukraine has chosen a second path of passive defense: dispersing potential targets. Fire Point, a manufacturer of drones, cruise missiles, and ballistic missiles, has said more than 20 camouflaged production sites are working on its ballistic missile project. This approach naturally reduces production efficiency, if it doesn’t rule out mass-producing complex products altogether.
Ukraine is helped by its ability to move some production outside the country. In Russia, the equivalent might be relocating sensitive facilities en masse to the Far East, but a shortage of production factors there, labor among them, and complicated logistics stand in the way.
Active defense — air defense and electronic warfare assets — also has its drawbacks. Russia’s model relies on a network of traditional short-range air defense systems backed by mobile fire teams equipped with man-portable air-defense missile systems, small arms, anti-aircraft artillery, interceptor drones, and mobile radars. Covering the entire territory from the Ukrainian border to targets deep inside the country is impossible: Russia’s Aerospace Forces and Ground Forces had 129 Tor-M½ systems and just over 50 Pantsir systems at the start of the year, according to the Military Balance 2026 reference guide. Even mounting them on towers and tall buildings, a widely used practice, does not allow them to detect, track, and hit a low-flying drone at a range of more than 15 kilometers (9 miles).
Saturating the defenses with hundreds or thousands of mobile fire teams, each capable of hitting targets within hundreds of meters or, at most, a few kilometers of itself, is also impossible: the Russian military lacks the personnel for it. The Kremlin has tried to solve the problem by calling up reservists through the Combat Army Reserve of the Country program, created in 2021, under which participants receive small payments and attend annual military training while keeping their regular jobs. Russia, however, appears to have not found enough reservists.
Russia has not yet built a layered system of sensors and interceptor drones similar to Ukraine’s, though individual elements, such as mobile groups with interceptors, have been deployed. Russian Defense Minister Andrei Belousov promised in the spring that the system would be ready by November. Work is underway: new regional structures are being created, and the outlines of a defense are taking shape.
Even so, Ukraine’s layered defense isn’t perfect: Russian forces have managed to temporarily neutralize it by quickly shifting to producing thousands of faster jet-powered drones and miniature cruise missiles. Neither Ukraine’s interceptor drones nor the sensors supporting them are designed for these targets, so Ukraine’s military now has to build a new system and new production lines to counter the Russian drones. Both the jet-powered drones and the tools to counter them have turned out to be far more expensive than the previous generation of equipment.
As a result, Russia’s anti-drone air defense still tends toward protecting individual sites, but there are so many potential targets that protecting all of them is impossible. And where this protection does exist, attackers can overwhelm it by saturating the defenses with a mass of drones.
The Kremlin is trying to get the owners of these facilities to pay for their own drone defenses. A decree now allows the state to temporarily take over management of enterprises that fail to provide their own protection. Beyond passive protection measures, though, enterprises have few tools available for defense. Companies are allowed to “rent” air defense systems from the Defense Ministry, for instance. However, many large companies are trying to build their own radar and interceptor-drone systems. This effort is hindered, among other things, by aviation regulations, which there are now proposals to amend urgently.
A separate problem for private air defense is the inability to use explosive warheads on interceptors. Despite some successes, it is unlikely that fixed-wing drones can be reliably shot down using only the kinetic energy of a small, low-speed interceptor, though manufacturers claim otherwise.

Meanwhile, worries about energy prices, the global economy, exchange rates, and access to credit mounted.

Nevertheless, businesses remain exposed to flood threats across several provinces, where the pace and scope of state assistance, alongside post-disaster rehabilitation efforts, warrant close attention, the FTI said in a statement.
The group called on state authorities to adopt proactive flood risk management, including early warning systems and faster insurance compensation, promote energy efficiency initiatives to counter volatile energy prices, and prioritize Made in Thailand certified goods in public procurement, with tax incentives for private-sector use. ■

What is potash, and why is the US importing it from Belarus?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:36:48 UTC
23:36:48 KST

What is potash, and why is the US importing it from Belarus?
US reliance on Canadian potash, a key fertiliser mineral, adds to farmers’ cost concerns amid trade tensions.
The United States is preparing to receive its first shipment of Belarusian potash in four years, as President Donald Trump seeks cheaper fertiliser for American farmers amid rising costs linked to the Iran war and a trade dispute with Canada.
A 30,000-tonne shipment of potash is expected to arrive at the Port of New Orleans on Wednesday, according to data from Kpler. The shipment follows Washington’s decision to lift sanctions on major Belarusian potash producers in March, opening an avenue for trade to resume.
Although this shipment from Belarus accounts for only a fraction of the 5.6 million tonnes of potash the US imported last year, it signals a tentative opening of relations between Washington and Minsk.
Trump has said the US is working on a larger agreement to buy Belarusian fertiliser at prices substantially below what it pays Canada, its dominant supplier. But analysts have questioned whether Belarus can compete with Canadian producers on price and expand exports enough to significantly change the US market.
What is potash and why does the US need it?
Potash is a potassium-rich mineral that is a primary fertiliser element. Potassium, an essential plant nutrient, has no substitutes, and potash is widely used in agriculture, including in the cultivation of corn and soybeans.
The US depends heavily on imports to meet its potash needs. Canada accounts for almost 80 percent of US potash imports, according to the US Geological Survey’s 2026 Mineral Commodity Summaries. Russia accounts for 12 percent, the second-largest share of US potash imports.
That reliance has made fertiliser supply an economic and political concern, particularly as farmers face rising production costs. In recent months, US farmers have reported higher fuel and fertiliser costs, putting pressure on already tight profit margins.
Trump has reportedly been concerned that financial strain may cost Republicans some of the US farmer vote in this year’s midterms. In 2024, Trump won 78 percent of the vote in farming-dependent counties. At an agriculture roundtable in Wisconsin in June, Trump promised fertiliser prices would “go way down” as the US emerged from the Iran conflict.
Disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz have added to pressure on global fertiliser markets, particularly for nitrogen-based products. Potash, however, is less directly exposed to the crisis, with the US relying heavily on supplies from Canada.
Trump has argued that buying Belarusian potash could reduce those costs. An additional supplier could also give US buyers more options in a market dominated by Canadian imports.
For farmers, the immediate benefits remain uncertain. Fertiliser is one of several major expenses facing agricultural businesses, alongside diesel fuel and machinery. Even a reduction in potash prices would not necessarily offset increases elsewhere.
Can Belarus offer cheaper fertiliser?
In September, Trump boasted on social media about striking a potential potash deal with Belarus.
“The United States is working on a massive Deal with respect to the purchase of Potash from Belarus,” Trump said in the post. “The pricing would be for substantially less than we are currently paying to Canada, very good news for our Farmers and Ranchers.”
Trump promoted Belarusian potash as a less expensive alternative to Canadian supplies, but the economics of delivering it to American buyers complicates that plan.
Belarus is landlocked, and EU restrictions are affecting its export routes, forcing potash shipments to take a more circuitous path through Russia. The incoming cargo was loaded at the Russian port of Bronka near St Petersburg, according to reporting by the Financial Times.
Those logistical challenges could raise transportation costs and make Belarusian supplies less competitive, even if the product itself is cheaper.
The scale of the exports also matters. A single shipment shows that trade between the US and Belarus has resumed, but it does not mean Belarus can replace a substantial share of Canadian potash or drive down prices across the US market.
However, access to an alternative supplier could give Washington greater leverage in negotiations with Canadian producers, potentially helping US buyers secure more competitive potash prices.
Could Belarus replace Canada as the main potash supplier in the US?
Relations between the US and Canada have been strained since Trump’s second term began, when he unleashed a volley of tariffs on most trading partners, including Canada. His administration initially imposed a 25 percent tariff on many Canadian imports in March 2025, including potash, but reduced that to 10 percent following pushback from agricultural groups and lawmakers. Potash that meets the requirements of the USMCA trade agreement – the trade deal between the US, Mexico and Canada – is exempted. Most Canadian potash imports qualify under the USMCA and remain duty-free.
Trump has maintained that Washington would continue buying from Canada, even as Belarus offered to sell potash at a lower price.
But the viability of Belarus as a major supplier remains unlikely. In September, Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko said the country could not supply large volumes of potash fertiliser to the US.
“Even if we wanted to supply [potash] to other, Western markets, we simply do not have those volumes – everything is contracted,” Lukashenko said.
Whether this October shipment becomes part of a much larger deal will depend on the ability to sustain exports and the durability of the diplomatic opening between Washington and Minsk.
Why did the US impose sanctions on Belarus, and why are they being lifted?
The planned shipment marks a significant step in the restoration of trade between Washington and Minsk, which have spent years being at odds over Belarus’s human rights record and its support for Russia’s war against Ukraine.
The US, under former Democratic President Joe Biden, imposed increased sanctions on Belarus in 2021 after Lukashenko’s authoritarian government cracked down on mass protests against its disputed 2020 presidential election. Belarus has also faced Western sanctions for allowing Russian forces to use its territory in the 2022 invasion of Ukraine.
But since Trump returned to the White House in 2025, his administration has pursued direct negotiations with Lukashenko. Those talks have led to the release of political prisoners in exchange for lifting US sanctions, creating a pathway towards renewed economic ties.
In March, Belarus released 250 political prisoners under a US-brokered agreement. Washington subsequently lifted sanctions on major Belarusian potash producers and eased restrictions on several financial institutions. In September, US special envoy John Coale announced a further agreement under which Belarus would release 25 prisoners in exchange for sanctions relief.
The rapprochement has opened the door to proposals for deeper commercial cooperation.
On September 29, Lukashenko said he had agreed with Russian President Vladimir Putin that Russian state-controlled energy company Gazprom would participate in a project to build a nitrogen fertiliser plant in Belarus. He proposed inviting the US to join the project using American technology, according to the Reuters news agency.
Before this agreement, exiled Belarusian opposition leader Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya said that a deal with Lukashenko comes with risks.
“Our position is that it is not time to trade with the regime while all the income from potash goes to repression, goes to support of the Russian war machine,” Tsikhanouskaya told AFP in September.
The proposal has not established that Washington will participate in the project. But alongside Trump’s stated interest in buying Belarusian potash, it illustrates how Minsk is seeking to turn improved political relations into broader commercial opportunities.

EU summit: Leaders tackle energy prices, spar over budget and unite on Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:28:11 UTC
23:28:11 KST

The two-day summit of EU leaders comes with a packed agenda topped by energy prices, the long-term budget and Russia's war on Ukraine. Hybrid warfare, enlargement and migration will also feature prominently.
Spiralling energy prices, the EU's long-term budget and support for Ukraine in the wake of Donald Trump's latest overture to Vladimir Putin will dominate the conversation as the leaders gather for a two-day summit in Brussels.
Enlargement, hybrid warfare, economic stagnation, rising borrowing costs, trade imbalances and irregular migration will also feature in the talks.
The meeting will start early on Thursday with a hotly anticipated discussion on energy prices, which hostilities in the Middle East have sent skyrocketing. Oil remains above $100 per barrel despite a coordinated G7 release, while gas trades at its highest level since winter 2022, with underground storage running below average.
The market shockwaves have rattled EU leaders, who are under mounting pressure to deliver tangible relief for households and industries, especially as temperatures cool down and the heating season begins.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis have led the charge, asking Brussels to relax the bloc's fiscal rules to allow governments to finance "temporary and targeted measures" to cushion the energy crunch.
Other countries, however, worry that excessive flexibility will promote fossil fuel consumption and discourage investments in the green transition.
Meanwhile, six member states (Austria, Germany, Italy, Poland, Portugal and Spain) have proposed an EU-wide windfall tax to capture excess profits from energy companies amid high prices. But the idea remains divisive and has not gained enough traction.
Energy will be followed by another pressing economic challenge: China.
With a €1 billion trade deficit every day, Brussels threw down the gauntlet by imposing a deadline on Beijing to deliver "tangible results" by October at the latest.
Those results emerged last week in Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič's trip to Beijing, where he secured preliminary concessions on hybrid and plug-in hybrid cars, rare earths and permanent magnets, and market access for European companies.
"We're satisfied with the results, but for us, it's only a first step because imbalances are not specific to one sector – there are across the board," a senior diplomat said, cautioning implementation will be key to show whether Beijing is serious.
"Why is China agreeing to something that China has never agreed before? (Because) they're starting to realise they're killing their customers. We're not naïve."
The concessions avert, for now, an all-out trade war. Leaders are expected to call on the Commission to continue "results-oriented dialogue" with China and "urgently enhance" trade tools to retaliate if needed, according to the draft conclusions seen by Euronews.
In a sign of exasperation, Germany and France have pitched a "kill switch" to cut off China's access to the EU market if the deficit remains unsustainable.
Money talks, but does anyone listen?
The summit's most contentious moment will arrive on Thursday afternoon when the next seven-year EU budget is put on the table. The wrangle will take place against the backdrop of steep borrowing costs, particularly alarming in France.
European Council President António Costa has appealed to member states to move away from their red lines and reach an agreement by the end of the year so that the complex legislative work can be fully completed before January 2028.
Ireland, the country holding the rotating presidency, has tabled a proposal that cuts the original draft by €141 billion. But the knife mostly spares agriculture and cohesion funds and falls instead on research, technology, climate action, security and foreign policy.
The Irish "nego-box" has made everyone unhappy.
The so-called "frugals" (Austria, Denmark, Finland, the Netherlands, Sweden and Germany) say the cuts need to go much deeper and across the board. The 17 "Friends of Cohesion" say the opposite, that the cuts have gone far too deep. The European Commission warns its vision of a modernised, flexible budget is in real danger.
On top of that, nobody agrees which EU-wide taxes should be approved to collect additional revenue for the common pot.
The clash of opinions and the unwillingness to compromise bode ill for Costa's ambition to have a unanimous deal in December. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's shock decision to call snap elections adds yet another layer of uncertainty.
"I don't think there will be blood on the wall, but it's important in these sorts of negotiations that leaders feel where the contradictions are," another senior diplomat said. "We are not in a hurry. We need a good deal. We don’t feel any time pressure."
The first day will end with a strategic debate on how to prepare the 27-strong bloc for the admission of new member states and reform its internal decision-making. Montenegro, the frontrunner in the accession race, aims to close all chapters this year.
Backing Zelenskyy, rebuking Trump
Friday will be dedicated to Ukraine in the presence of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
The peace talks took a dramatic turn after US President Donald Trump blindsided Europeans by cutting a deal with his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, to bring tens of thousands of Russian diesel into the US market. Washington issued a sanctions waiver until April 2027 to enable what would until now have been a forbidden sale.
The news jolted Europeans and prompted a scramble to close ranks and rally behind Ukraine to control the fallout from a unilateral, uncoordinated decision that has revived memories from the Trump-Zelenskyy showdown in the White House.
Although the diesel deal is likely to have a limited impact on the prices at the pump, which Trump wants to lower ahead of the midterm elections, there is greater concern over the diplomatic implications of providing relief to Russia at a time when it escalates its attacks to decimate the Ukrainian economy ahead of the winter.
The summit's conclusions have been changed to add a rebuke: "The European Council regrets the United States' decision to temporarily lift sanctions on Russian diesel."
Trump has spent the last few days calling on Zelenskyy to stop attacks on Russia's oil refineries and abide by his energy ceasefire. Zelenskyy says he is ready for the truce as long as Russia complies, but Russia keeps bombing Ukraine's power facilities.
Europeans are reluctant to endorse Trump's petition because the long-range strikes are Kyiv's greatest leverage over Moscow. Giving it up would further tilt the war.
"It's not the first time that we're going through divergences with the US in what the Ukraine war is concerned, but I would disagree with the idea that we're ignored," a senior EU official said.
"We have seen that dialogue with the US doesn't always lead to full agreement in the way the EU and the US see things, but it's always better than not having dialogue," the official added. "This is what needs to continue to be done. It's the normal thing."
The last item on the summit will be a strategic debate on migration poised to pit Sánchez against the Meloni-led majority in the room. In the aftermath of the Ceuta border crisis, Italy introduced border checks with Spain, and Spain retaliated in kind.
The checks, which are conducted randomly at airports, last to this day.

DeepMind co-founder warns AI hacking incidents are ‘early warning shots’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:28:03 UTC
23:28:03 KST

Necva Tastan Sevinc
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
Google DeepMind co-founder Demis Hassabis on Wednesday warned that hacking incidents involving artificial intelligence are “early warning shots,” urging companies and governments to strengthen security as autonomous systems become more powerful.
Speaking at the International AI Summit 2026, Hassabis said AI agents capable of acting on users’ behalf increase both the technology’s usefulness and its risks.
“But also that means that increases also the risks involved with what those systems might do, and we've seen that recently earlier this year with some of these hacking incidents. I think these are early warning shots for us,” he said.
“The systems aren't that powerful yet, so the incidents aren't that major,” he added, warning that incidents could become more serious over the next few years without additional security efforts.
Hassabis said ensuring that systems follow their assigned goals and remain within established safeguards becomes harder as they gain autonomy.
“And that gets increasingly difficult the more automation there is in the systems,” he said.
He also warned that AI “can also be repurposed by bad actors for harmful ends.”
Hassabis called for testing systems in secure environments, initially disconnected from the internet, and drawing on containment practices from biology and nuclear technology.
“I think there's a lot of lessons that can be learned about containment systems, and I think we need to start taking that seriously and bring experts in from those areas,” he said.
He advocated giving trusted defenders, including banks and governments, access to advanced AI tools before wider release to identify and repair software vulnerabilities before attackers could exploit them.
“So we've got to kind of asymmetrically power up our defensive side to keep ahead of the attackers,” he said.
Hassabis also called for an international standards body capable of adapting to technological developments.
“It's going to affect everyone in the world,” he said, urging safeguards that reflect emerging risks while preserving innovation.
“If you legislate for something three years ago, it will be out of date today, and actually probably won't even address what the real problems are,” he said.
He also called for “10 times or more resources” for AI safety and security, including research and computing capacity.

French police hit student protesters with ‘violent charge’ – RT reports (VIDEO)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

French police hit student protesters with ‘violent charge’ – RT reports (VIDEO)
French police have launched violence charges against student protesters in Paris, arresting young demonstrators as security forces crack down on schoolchildren protesting against staff shortages and underfunding in education, RT correspondent Nadege Abderazzak has reported.
The protests began in late September at a high school in Créteil, a Paris suburb, where teachers and students protested severe staff shortages and deteriorating facilities. The movement quickly spread across France, with thousands of students demanding better education funding and an end to cuts in public services. Demonstrators have also challenged government spending priorities, calling for money to be spent on schools rather than weapons.
Reporting from Paris on Wednesday, Abderazzak described police charging at demonstrators and arresting a young protester. “We’re witnessing a very violent charge by the security forces who have just arrested a young individual,” she said, pointing to the detainee lying on the ground.
Abderazzak said that tensions had persisted for two hours, with an estimated 300 to 400 protesters facing three to five times as many police officers and gendarmes. The march had begun at Paris City Hall, she said, noting that two demonstrations had been authorized by the Paris Police Prefecture.
Since the protests erupted last month, the unrest has repeatedly escalated into confrontations, with police deploying tear gas, water cannon, and stun grenades against demonstrators. Thousands have reportedly been detained and hundreds injured nationwide since late September, including minors. A 15-year-old boy reportedly lost a hand after picking up a police grenade.
By early October, protests had disrupted more than 1,000 educational institutions, with over 160,000 demonstrators taking to the streets on Tuesday, according to authorities. Protesters have challenged France’s spending priorities, demanding: “Allocate money to education, not to buying arms,” according to media reports.
The police crackdown has drawn international criticism, including from Iran, which condemned the use of force against students, while French authorities have defended their response and pledged additional school staff.
The protests come as President Emmanuel Macron’s government cuts public spending while pouring billions into militarization and military aid to Ukraine. France has boosted its 2026 defense budget by €6.7 billion to €57.1 billion, with another €36 billion earmarked for military spending through 2030.
Meanwhile, France’s budget deficit is expected to hit 5.4% of GDP this year, with public debt climbing to 119.3%. Despite the mounting financial strain, Paris has pledged to keep supplying Kiev with weapons, including missiles and air defense systems.

Iran's 'soft war': How Tehran turned antisemitism into a weapon against the West
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:23:36 UTC
23:23:36 KST

Antisemitism and anti-Israel rhetoric across the Western political spectrum are being amplified by a decades-long Iranian campaign designed to erode trust in American institutions and forge alliances across ideological divides, according to a report published on Wednesday by the Simon Wiesenthal Center (SWC).
The report, titled “The War on Western Minds: Iran’s 30-Year Campaign to Divide the West,” said that the Islamic Republic has weaponized antisemitism in its ideological “soft war” against the West, exploiting nationalism, religious narratives, and anti-imperialism to spread anti-American and anti-Israel rhetoric.
Unable to match US military power, particularly under decades of sanctions, Iran has instead focused on undermining Western social cohesion and trust in democratic institutions, the report said.
Antisemitism predates the Islamic Revolution, but the SWC said that it provides Iran with a narrative that crosses ideological boundaries. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has exploited this by presenting the regime as an ally against the “Antichrist,” an anti-imperialist force resisting Western hegemony, or a nationalist partner opposing alleged Jewish and Israeli manipulation.
Iran brought conspiratorial claims to the mainstream
The report said Iran has helped accusations of Jewish control over American foreign policy become mainstream, allowing such narratives to spread without continued Iranian involvement. It compared this strategy to methods first developed in the Soviet Union.
Using narrative intelligence (NARINT) to track Iranian influence campaigns, the SWC found that the objective was not simply to spread false information but also to shape how audiences interpret events, assign blame, and identify enemies. Once established, narratives of Zionist conspiracy, Jewish financial control, or Israeli manipulation of US foreign policy can become resistant to conventional fact-checking, the report said.
Iran tailors these narratives to different audiences.
Among religious Christians, it uses apocalyptic language and biblical prophecy to frame geopolitical conflicts as battles against the Antichrist, hoping to manufacture Christian-Muslim religious convergence, weakening the perceived Judeo-Christian affinity that underpins American support for Israel.
The report cited Russian political philosopher Aleksandr Dugin, who consulted Athonite monks before Russia’s 2012 intervention in Syria. According to the report, the monks encouraged Moscow’s participation in the civil war as part of a “final battle” against the Antichrist. Dugin later credited Russia and Iran with saving Syria from destruction allegedly sought by the West and Dajjal, an Islamic term associated with the Antichrist.
Iran has also sought to exploit grievances in other communities.
The report highlighted the January 1996 World Friendship Tour by Nation of Islam leader Louis Farrakhan, a prominent antisemite who visited countries hostile to the United States. The SWC said Iran recognized an opportunity to capitalize on Pan-African grievances while presenting itself as a defender of the mustad’afin, or oppressed and dispossessed.
In February 2001, Tehran hosted a regional preparatory meeting for the United Nations World Conference against Racism, culminating in the Tehran Declaration. The declaration accused Israel of committing “a new kind of apartheid, a crime against humanity, a form of genocide and a serious threat to international peace and security.”
The report said that these forums enabled Iran to combine anti-imperialism, left-wing anti-Americanism, Black internationalist organizing, and antisemitism under the banner of international legitimacy.
Iranian-linked media apparatus amplified 9/11 conspiracies
Iran also used its media apparatus to amplify conspiracy theories. In the weeks following the September 11, 2001, attacks, the Hezbollah-affiliated Lebanese television network al-Manar promoted the false claim that 4,000 Jewish employees had been warned to stay away from the World Trade Center that day.
Although initially confined to fringe circles, such claims helped attract conspiracy theorists and anti-establishment figures who could carry Iranian narratives into Western media, the report said.
It cited former Ku Klux Klan leader David Duke and political writer Michael Collins Piper as examples of Western voices aligned with Tehran’s messaging.
In 2007, Iran launched Press TV to reach Western audiences directly. The report highlighted programming such as Zero Degree Turn, which portrayed Iranians as saviors of Jewish victims of Nazism while comparing Zionism to Nazism and delegitimizing Israel’s founding.
Iranian filmmaker Nader Talebzadeh helped develop programming designed to influence international audiences through polished, emotionally engaging storytelling, the report said.
The SWC also identified MintPress News as an example of an American-facing outlet that presents itself as an independent progressive watchdog but allegedly relays Iranian and Russian narratives.
The outlet’s mix of left- and right-wing contributors, the report said, helps it mimic progressive investigative journalism while promoting positions aligned with Iranian foreign policy. The United Kingdom-based Institute of Contemporary Islamic Thought was cited as another platform promoting Iranian narratives while presenting itself as an intellectual hub for the global Islamic movement.
The report said that this media ecosystem can have real-world consequences. It pointed to the manifesto of Payton Gendron, the perpetrator of the May 2022 Buffalo supermarket massacre, which referenced a 2016 MintPress News article titled “Thousands of Israelis Take to the Streets Calling For Palestinian Genocide.”
By 2026, Iran’s influence operations had expanded to include fake news websites mimicking American media, fabricated online personas posing as American activists, and campaigns designed to simulate grassroots support.
The report said these operations use wire-service material and plagiarized articles to appear credible and embed Iranian narratives within broader coverage. Additionally, they manipulate Wikipedia, which, by extension, manipulates the majority of AI algorithms and allows the network to exploit social media algorithms.
IRGC used cyberattacks to target US institutions
Iran has also conducted hacking operations targeting American institutions. During the 2024 US presidential campaign, an IRGC-linked group sent spear-phishing emails to a senior campaign official using a compromised former adviser’s account, attempting to infiltrate county-level government accounts in swing states, according to Microsoft’s Threat Analysis Center.
OVER THE past year, the SWC identified over 340 influencers, media outlets, organizations, and affiliated entities that it said formed an interconnected influence network with shared amplification channels and consistent information flows.
The report named Dugin, Jackson Hinkle, Max Blumenthal, The Grayzone, and the account GodivaGoddess97 among central figures. It also identified CODEPINK, Jewish Voice for Peace (JVP), and the Party for Socialism and Liberation.
The SWC outlined a six-stage cycle through which these narratives spread.
First, humanitarian organizations publish legitimate reports with appropriate caveats.
Second, academics and credentialed figures provide intellectual frameworks that, according to the report, delegitimize rather than merely criticize Israel.
Third, alternative media outlets such as The Grayzone and MintPress remove caveats, add inflammatory framing, and cite the original organizations as authorities.
Fourth, commentators, such as Andrew Napolitano, Candace Owens, Jackson Hinkle, and Jimmy Dore, repackage the content for left- and right-wing audiences.
Fifth, activist organizations translate online rhetoric into campus organizing and direct action, creating environments hostile to Jewish students.
Finally, conspiracy theorists cite The Grayzone and MintPress as evidence of alleged Jewish conspiracies.
Jewish-affiliated voices and organizations, including JVP and Norman Finkelstein, are also invoked to deflect accusations of antisemitism, the report said.
Several recommendations were offered to combat this threat: mandatory coordinated-threat disclosure for platforms; mandatory AI-generated-content labeling; a congressional review of Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act to remove immunity for content that can be attributed to designated foreign adversaries or their proxies.
“For more than 30 years, Iran has been building an infrastructure designed to exploit the divisions within American society,” said Jim Berk, CEO of the Simon Wiesenthal Center. “What makes this campaign so dangerous is that Iran doesn't need Americans to support its regime to succeed. It only needs Americans to lose trust in their institutions and in one another. Antisemitism has been central to that strategy, giving a hostile foreign government a way to turn existing grievances into deeper divisions. This is a threat not only to Jewish communities, but to the foundations of American democracy itself.”
“This is not about the Jews. It has never been only about the Jews,” said Jim Berk, CEO of the Simon Wiesenthal Center. “Antisemitism is the tool. The real target is Western civilization itself: the Judeo-Christian values, democratic institutions, and shared sense of citizenship that hold free societies together. Jewish communities are simply where the attack shows up first. That is why we called our report The War for Western Minds. Iran’s goal is to break the West’s confidence in its own foundations, and every American, whatever their faith, has a stake in stopping it.”
The full Simon Wiesenthal Center report can be found here: https://wiesenthal.org/iran-report
