Palantir settles dispute with Sadiq Khan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:23:11 UTC
23:23:11 KST

LONDON — The Mayor of London Sadiq Khan and U.S. tech company Palantir have agreed to drop legal proceedings relating to a blocked £50 million police contract.
Palantir brought a claim against the Mayor’s Office for Policing and Crime in the High Court in June after Khan’s deputy mayor refused to sign off on the £50 million contract with the Metropolitan Police for the provision of an AI and data analysis service.
In July, lawyers working on behalf of MOPAC in turn accused the Met Police and Palantir of coordinating to fix the outcome of the procurement process in breach of the rules. Palantir claimed Khan’s office had unlawfully blocked the contract over the company's “values and ethics,” based on media reporting.
Advertisement
A full trial was expected in January but on Wednesday both sides agreed to “settle their differences” and drop the allegations without admitting liability. They will each cover their own legal costs.
In an agreed statement, the two sides said MOPAC’s decision to block the Palantir contract was “not based on Palantir’s values or ethics or any wider reporting about the company,” though MOPAC said it “recognizes Palantir’s concerns that media reporting of a statement from the Mayor's spokesperson before the decision was taken could have incorrectly created the impression that an assessment of the company’s values had been a factor in that decision.”
“MOPAC’s consideration was based upon its statutory role of examining spend proposals, against the appropriate legal tests and the relevant guidance on procurement, governance, affordability and ensuring value for money for Londoners and in doing so it focussed on the available information at the time,” the statement said.
The settlement also notes that MOPAC is working with Metropolitan Police Service to re-run a competitive procurement for the relevant service, which Palantir will be eligible to bid for.
“MOPAC does not have, and has never had, any policy of not contracting with Palantir,” the statement confirms, while noting the mayor’s duty is to ensure “all procurements are lawful, fair, transparent and deliver value for money.”
“London is the technology capital of Europe, and I am proud that leading software firms choose the city as their home. Palantir makes a significant contribution to jobs and investment in the capital, employing a large number of Londoners whose services have been procured legally by organizations across the U.K. and beyond,” Khan said.

America has sided with Russia against Ukraine. Europe should stop pretending and build a coalition against Russia, China, and even the US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:11:59 UTC
23:11:59 KST

On 11 October, Trump declared an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine. It binds only Ukraine. In the two days that followed, Kyiv held its fire while Russia kept hitting Ukrainian energy and critical infrastructure across 19 regions. A Russian strike collapsed an apartment stairwell in Kharkiv and killed three. And before Russia’s latest ballistic missile strike, five missiles and more than 100 drones, Ukraine received no early warning at all. Washington then said both sides were to blame.
This is what one of Trump’s decisions looks like on the ground. There were four of them, in three days, 9 to 11 October.
Three days that further weaken the West and undermine liberal democracies. Three days that encourage Putin to continue his war against Ukraine and his hybrid war against Europe. Like China, the US has sided with Russia against Ukraine and Europe. Whatever the motives in Washington—diesel prices before the midterms, a long feud with the court—the effect is the same.
International law
On 9 October, the Trump administration announced new sanctions against the International Criminal Court (ICC), an institution crucial for holding Putin and the Kremlin responsible for the war of aggression and its atrocities. The sanctions came hours after the Nobel Peace Prize went to Navi Pillay, a former ICC judge.
"We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate," Secretary of State Marco Rubio said. "Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC." He expects allies, many of them ICC members that rely on American servicemembers for their defense, to rein in the court.
The ICC exists to investigate, prosecute, and try individuals accused of the world's gravest international crimes. Washington wants to end it. The court called the measures an assault on the rule of law and the foundations of the international legal order.
What if Russia uses nuclear weapons? Can we say Ukraine brought peace to world? Norwegian professor who nominated Zelenskyy and Ukrainians for 2026 Nobel Peace Prize takes on tough questions
Funding Russia's war
On 9 October, Trump also lifted sanctions on Russian diesel exports. The deal comes less than a month after he signed the sweeping Russia sanctions law dedicated to the memory of Sen. Lindsey Graham, which allows tariffs on buyers of Russian oil. Multiple US lawmakers argue the move violates federal law. Congress banned Russian energy imports in 2022, and a bipartisan group of seven senators, including Republicans Thom Tillis and Lisa Murkowski, stated that the decision "runs directly counter to that law." They also argue that the administration failed to consult Congress or justify its decision as the statute requires.
Western sanctions and Ukraine's strikes on Russian refineries—its own "sanctions"—aim at the same effect: making the war unaffordable for Russia. Trump's decision does the opposite: it helps Russia pay for the war. It also breaks with the principle of unity of effort, further undermining Western cohesion.
Zelenskyy said the deal showed US weakness, as Washington had secured no concessions in return: "What did [Trump] get? That he will have more diesel? For whom? More Russian diesel for Americans? ... It looks like Alaska No. 2. You know, it looks like a happy birthday present for Putin. It looks absolutely terrible."
Stability and sovereignty
On 10 October, Trump said of the elected president of a country fighting off Russia's full-scale invasion: "I think it's time for Ukraine to get a new president... I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal, because he could have made many deals and, for some reason, he never does." He claimed Zelenskyy could have ended the war many times, and insisted that Zelenskyy "wants to make problems for the world" by authorizing strikes on Russian refineries.
The Trump Administration conspicuously ignores the Swiss Summit on Peace in Ukraine, President Zelenskyy’s 10-point peace plan based on international law, and not least, the international effort to establish unity of efforts to enforce a just peace.
Zelenskyy has repeatedly proposed talks and shown willingness to compromise for a peace that guarantees Ukraine's sovereignty. On 18 July, he said: "This year alone, we have reached out to Russia dozens of times with proposals to stop this war—but all we got in return were refusals."
The "deals" Trump alludes to would not have secured peace or guaranteed Ukraine's future existence, nor safeguarded Europe against future Russian aggression. They were not rooted in international law, but in the prospect of great wealth for Trump and his associates—business deals dressed up as "peace plans”. Ukraine and its European partners instead proposed amendments and defined red lines to bring the drafts up to the standards of international law.
The Kremlin itself exposed the absurdity of Trump's claim. In a phone call with Trump, Putin categorically ruled out resuming peace talks, his aide Yuri Ushakov said, and sought to convince Trump that Ukrainian resistance has "no prospects whatsoever."
Supporting Russia
On 11 October, Trump announced: "Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!"
He gave no details. Zelenskyy had no prior knowledge, but said Ukraine would agree if Russia did. He had already offered to stop striking Russian refineries if Russia stopped attacking Ukraine's energy infrastructure.
It was not an energy ceasefire. It was a gift to Putin. A White House official told Axios that, as Trump understands it, the term means only that Russia and Ukraine stop attacking each other's oil refineries—and that this is what Washington expects Ukraine to do. Ukraine has one refinery, while Russia has 38, of which 21 have been targeted by Ukrainian drones.
Three days after Washington announced an energy ceasefire, Russia fires 39 ballistic missiles at Ukraine’s grid
To most of the world, an energy ceasefire covers the whole energy sector: nuclear power, oil refineries, power plants, the grid down to local transformers. But not in Trump's world. The official said a deal on power plants and grids could come next—if Ukraine first stops striking the refineries fueling Russia's war.
Axios wrote that White House officials see Ukraine's refinery strikes as doing more damage to Zelenskyy's relationship with Trump than to Russia. The administration has reportedly threatened to cut Ukraine off from US intelligence if the strikes continue.
Forcing Ukraine to halt its refinery strikes, while Russia keeps hitting not only power plants and the grid but heating and water systems, hospitals, schools, railways, ports and civilians, does not motivate Russia to stop. Within hours of Trump's announcement, Russia struck a power plant in Kharkiv. Trump's one-sided pressure encourages Russia to continue.
Enabling Russian aggression
Moscow paints Ukraine as the intransigent party, though Russia has offered no concessions and rejected numerous compromise proposals from the US and Ukraine. Still, Trump insists that Ukraine, not Russia, is the problem.
In three days, Trump has sanctioned the court that could hold Russia accountable, called on Zelenskyy to step down, secured revenue for the Kremlin's war, and declared an "energy ceasefire" that only asks Ukraine to stop striking Russian refineries, while Russia goes on turning winter into a weapon.
The call for Zelenskyy to step down led Marie-Agnes Strack-Zimmermann, chair of the European Parliament's Committee on Security and Defence, to say: "If Trump calls on Zelenskyy to step down, he is clearly siding with a murderer. Only the Ukrainian people can decide who leads Ukraine in free elections, not the White House, and certainly not the Kremlin." Her conclusion: "By once again attacking allies and democratic institutions, Trump is weakening the West and undermining democracy. [...] Europe must therefore remain firmly on course and support Ukraine, because the US can no longer be relied on."
The US's latest National Security Strategy does not merely shift America's foreign policy priorities. It aligns them with Moscow's on seven separate issues, while explicitly calling for Washington to "cultivate resistance to Europe's current trajectory" by backing nationalist parties against sitting EU-aligned governments.
Europe has 11 ways to choke Russia’s war. It doesn’t need Trump’s permission for any of them
Europe must stand on its own
The last three days demonstrate that the US is no longer an ally, but a strategic adversary. None of Trump's recent decisions helps end the war on Ukrainian or European terms. On the contrary, they encourage Putin and push any realistic hope of peace years away. They undermine international law and support the notion that might makes right.
Worse still, they help explain why war between Russia and Europe by 2029 is becoming more likely. Trump—Putin's close ally—leaves office on 20 January 2029.
Europe must stress its support for continued Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries unless the Kremlin agrees to a comprehensive energy ceasefire in line with Ukraine’s demands.
Europe urgently needs to distance itself from the US and its foreign policy. Heads of state must join Canada's efforts to unite middle and small powers in common defense against increasingly aggressive great powers. As this series has repeatedly argued, Europe must build a Coalition of Like-Minded countries strong enough to confront Russia, China and, sadly, the US.

In Bulgaria, unidentified individuals set fire to 11 of the 17 Starlink antennas providing communications to Ukraine, an MP says
Kyiv • UNN
Near Sofia, unidentified individuals set fire to 11 of the 17 Starlink antennas. The Bulgarian authorities said that an intensive investigation was under way and that security had been tightened.
Near Bulgaria's capital, 11 of the 17 antennas providing connectivity to the Starlink system, which is "actively used" during the war in Ukraine, were apparently set on fire. This was reported on Facebook by Bulgarian MP Ivaylo Mirchev, according to UNN.
Eleven antennas providing connectivity to the Starlink system (the communications network of SpaceX) were deliberately set on fire at a secret facility near Sofia. These antennas serve as the main communications channel with Musk's satellites in orbit, which are also actively used during the war in Ukraine
According to him, two masked unknown individuals set fire to 11 of the 17 SpaceX antennas providing Starlink satellite connectivity.
At the same time, the Bulgarian MP noted that no reports of the incident had come "either from the Ministry of Internal Affairs (of Bulgaria - ed.), or in the media, or from any other sources — as if this event had never happened at all".
Just a few days ago, at a meeting of the Consultative Council for National Security (CCNS), the head of the State Agency for National Security (SANS) assured me that the counterintelligence service was actively working to counter sabotage related to Russia. Obviously, they are not performing their duties properly... My colleague Bozhanov and I sent parliamentary inquiries to SANS and the Ministry of Internal Affairs. We will release additional information tomorrow in parliament
In addition
According to BNR News, Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev refused to disclose details regarding reports of the deliberate arson of antennas used for the Starlink satellite system, citing an ongoing investigation.
"The investigation is ongoing, and it is proceeding very intensively. I urged the head of the State Agency for National Security (SANS) not to disclose details at this stage, despite your great curiosity. However, this is a matter of the near future. We are cooperating with partner agencies to successfully complete this operation. If the head of SANS and the police disclosed the established facts, we would not achieve the desired result; however, I can assure you that the investigation is under control," Radev said.
Meanwhile, Minister of Internal Affairs Ivan Demerdzhiev clarified that security measures concerning such facilities had been strengthened: "I can add — without disrupting the course of the investigation — that although responsibility for the security of these facilities rests with their owners, the structures of the Ministry of Internal Affairs have taken additional measures to protect similar facilities throughout the country."
Recall
Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov, the Adviser to the President of Ukraine on the Development of Defense Technology Areas, confirmed that this night SpaceX introduced speed restrictions on Starlink terminals while they are in motion.
The assumption that Musk's company could restrict the combat capabilities of the Ukrainian military prompted a sharp reaction from Poland, which pays for Starlink services for Ukraine.
"Hey, @elonmusk, big man, are you playing politics with your products again? — Poland's Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski asked Musk on the social network X. — We, your European customers, are watching you."
Reuters notes that Musk is a close political ally of Trump, and the assumption that SpaceX might restrict Ukraine's capabilities has intensified Kyiv's fears that Washington could end its support on the battlefield in order to force its former ally to make concessions.

Nord Stream May Have Been Lawful Target, Argue Lawyers for Ukrainian Accused of Bombing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:09:00 UTC
23:09:00 KST

Lawyers for a Ukrainian ex-military officer accused of leading the bombing of Russia's Nord Stream pipeline in September 2022 argued at the start of his trial in Germany on Wednesday that "an aggressor's infrastructure" may have been a lawful target.
Serhii Kuznetsov is accused of leading a group of Ukrainian agents including divers and an explosives expert that blew up Russia's largest gas pipeline to Europe in one of the biggest infrastructure sabotage operations of modern times.
The case provides the first opportunity for a public hearing of evidence gathered during a years-long investigation, which has been diplomatically and politically awkward for a German government that remains staunchly supportive of Ukraine despite the investigative trail linking Kyiv to the bombing.
Moving to have the case dismissed, Kuznetsov's lawyer Nicola Canestrini argued that the pipeline — which provided half of Germany's imports of natural gas before Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine — was a "Russian weapon."
"Is it unlawful to destroy an aggressor's infrastructure without harming any human beings?" Canestrini asked.
Right to remain silent
Prosecutors have alleged that Kuznetsov, who was arrested under an international warrant in Italy last year, worked with members of the Ukrainian military to plan the clandestine operation on behalf of unidentified Ukrainian state entities.
Kuznetsov, 50, who prior to Wednesday was referred to publicly only as Serhii K. under German legal rules, has denied any involvement in the blasts that ruptured the 1,200-kilometer (750-mile)-long Baltic Sea pipeline.
Wearing a grey suit and with a shaved head, he exercised his right to remain silent in court but did not cover his face. His lawyers said he could not mount a proper defense because he was obliged to withhold Ukrainian state secrets.
The government in Kyiv has also denied any involvement, a sensitive point in its relations with Germany, Ukraine's largest European supplier of military aid. Russia said on Monday it expected a "just verdict" that would reveal the names of the perpetrators and those who ordered the operation.
Kuznetsov's legal team had tried reaching out to Ukraine for information that might assist the defense but heard nothing, according to another defense lawyer, Jes Meyer-Lohkamp.
Attacking civilian targets is considered a war crime
German prosecutors say the actions Kuznetsov is accused of — attacking civilian targets and causing explosions that destroyed infrastructure and damaged public services — would amount to a war crime.
Kuznetsov is the only person on trial, but Croatian authorities have arrested another man, identified as Vladimir Z., who prosecutors believe was one of the divers.
The explosion of Nord Stream sealed the end of Germany's longstanding dependence on Russian natural gas, although Moscow had already cut supplies over Berlin's support for European sanctions following Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
Nord Stream's supply had been due to double with the opening of a twin pipeline, Nord Stream 2, already built, but Berlin canceled approval to open it just prior to Russia's invasion.
Plumes of methane gas
The trial, expected to continue into February next year, could have domestic political implications.
Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), leading in opinion polls for more than a year, has called for an end to military aid for Ukraine and a restoration of energy ties with Moscow.
Although German state parliaments have no role in foreign policy, the AfD filed a motion in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt on Wednesday calling for an end to support for Ukraine, noting the "historical parallel" with the start of the trial.
The Nord Stream system, lying at a depth of 80 to 110 meters under the Baltic and built by Russian gas concern Gazprom to supply up to 110 billion cubic meters of gas to Germany, was formerly at the core of economic ties between the two countries.
The Sept. 26, 2022, blasts that ruptured three of the four concrete-coated steel pipelines created a giant whirlpool at sea as huge plumes of methane gas rose into the atmosphere.
Prosecutors allege that Kuznetsov traveled to Germany through Poland some three weeks before the attack, using a forged Ukrainian passport. He and his group then used a sailboat hired in the northern German city of Rostock to reach an area close to the Danish island of Bornholm, where they rigged specialized military-grade explosives to the sea floor.
The weekly Der Spiegel magazine and ZDF public television have previously reported that five men and one woman were on the rented yacht Andromeda, which left Rostock on Sept. 6 and returned on Sept. 23, 2022.

Colombia inaugurates embassy to Israel in Jerusalem

Colombia inaugurates embassy to Israel in Jerusalem
Palestinian officials condemn move by Colombia’s new government that marked a major shift after former President Petro had severed ties with Israel.
Colombia has opened its embassy to Israel in Jerusalem, joining a small group of countries in taking the controversial step of backing Israel’s claim to sovereignty in the contested city.
Palestinian officials swiftly denounced the inauguration on Wednesday that came as Israel is facing mounting international pressure over the genocidal war on Gaza, where three years of attacks have killed more than 74,000 people.
The move by the administration of new Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella is a major shift from his left-wing predecessor Gustavo Petro, who in 2024 severed ties with Israel over the war on Gaza.
De la Espriella, who was sworn in in August, has also restored a free trade agreement between Israel and Colombia that Petro terminated.
Colombian Minister of Foreign Affairs Omar Bula Escobar said on Wednesday that relations between the two countries “should never have been broken” and that Bogota was taking “taking a concrete step towards restoring diplomatic relations”.
“Israel is a strategic partner. It always has been, and from now on, it will be an even stronger one,” he said during a ceremony that marked the embassy’s opening.
The opening made Colombia the 10th country to establish its embassy in Israel in Jerusalem – most countries keep their formal diplomatic missions in Tel Aviv.
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar welcomed the move during the ceremony. “This is an important date for the State of Israel. It’s also an important date for the city of Jerusalem,” he said while signing the Colombian embassy’s guest book.
Colombian Ambassador Tania Gilinski said Israel had always been a “strategic partner” and that moving forward it “will be so with even greater determination and strength”.
‘Violation of international law’
The Palestinian Authority condemned Colombia’s embassy move, calling it “a violation of international legitimacy resolutions” that undermines “the international consensus on the legal status of the holy city”.
Jordan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs also criticised the move as a “violation of international law and relevant international resolutions”.
United States President Donald Trump moved the US embassy to Israel from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem during his first term in 2018, angering Palestinians and sparking international condemnation. Previous US presidents, as well as nearly every other country, refrained from opening embassies in Jerusalem, arguing that the city’s final status should first be resolved in negotiations between Israelis and Palestinians.
The status of Jerusalem remains one of the core unresolved issues of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, with Israel claiming the undivided city as its capital while Palestinians view occupied East Jerusalem as the capital of a future Palestinian state.
Israel occupied East Jerusalem and annexed it in 1967, in a move not recognised by the vast majority of the international community.
Since Trump relocated the US embassy to Jerusalem, only a handful of small, US-aligned countries have followed suit, namely Fiji, Guatemala, Honduras, Papua New Guinea, Paraguay and Nauru. Kosovo and Somaliland, which are not member-states of the United Nations, have also opened what they consider their embassies in Jerusalem.

The video shows three men accessing the back entrance of a house in Leicestershire accommodating asylum seekers. The men enter via an unlocked back door and move through several rooms of the house, including the kitchen, where they examine the contents of the fridge. They repeatedly claim to be looking for “paperwork”, searching through a pile of letters near the front door and boxes discarded in the back garden. The man filming, who narrates the video, claims he is the first to “document” this property.
When the men filming encounter three men, who are believed to be asylum seekers living at the property, in the kitchen they tell them they are contractors sent to assess the property for repairs. They ask one man living at the property whether the property is run by Serco, a Home Office contractor used for asylum seeker accommodation, which the man confirms, and whether he has “paperwork”, which he says he does not.
When the man living at the property asks the man filming for his ID he briefly shows him a lanyard. It is unclear what information it shows.
In the footage, the man filming specifically names the street and the village where the house is located, and shows the exterior of the property and its surroundings, making it clearly identifiable.
A Serco spokesperson said: “We are aware of this post. We take issues of this nature extremely seriously and are investigating.”

TH101UK entered another asylum seeker property in Norfolk several months ago and posted footage online.

A YouTube spokesperson said: “Harassment and cyberbullying are not allowed on YouTube and as part of this, we do not allow content that reveals someone’s personally identifiable information. Upon review, we have removed the flagged video for violating our harassment and cyberbullying policies.”

The Danish government has presented a proposed budget for 2027 that prioritizes national security, with more money allocated to defence amid an increasingly tense international security situation.

The government wants to ensure that defence spending reaches 3.5 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) by 2030.
Hummelgaard said the proposal reflected the need to make “hard priorities” in response to the current security situation. He also described the Danish economy as being “in top shape”.
“The government’s proposal for the finance bill shows that we take responsibility upon ourselves, and that we lead the way in working for a greener, freer, and more equal Denmark,” Hummelgaard said.
Pia Olsen Dyhr of the Socialist People’s Party (SF), the minister for economic and interior affairs, also highlighted the security situation.
“We do not solve all the challenges we have in Denmark with this finance bill. But we are well on our way,” she said at the press conference.
“I also think everyone must remember that we are in an escalated security policy situation,” Olsen Dyhr said.
Much of the proposed budget had already been announced, either in the government’s policy platform or through statements by ministers in recent weeks.
The proposal allocates 1.2 billion DKK to children’s services and education in 2027, including Denmark’s public primary and lower secondary schools, known as folkeskole.
It also sets aside a total of 10.1 billion DKK in 2030 for tax cuts. These include abolishing the intermediate income tax and the top-top tax, as well as reducing corporation tax.
“We are simplifying the tax system,” said Taxation and Growth Minister Jakob Engel-Schmidt of the Moderates (M).
The tax measures will be negotiated separately as part of a tax reform. While the budget proposal includes tax cuts, the government also plans to freeze several tax thresholds, which would increase the tax burden for some taxpayers as incomes rise.
The liberal think tank Cepos estimates that the government’s various plans will result in a net tax cut of 2.2 billion DKK in 2030.
Business and Competitiveness Minister Martin Lidegaard of the Danish Social Liberal Party (R) highlighted investment in young people and education.
“We are significantly strengthening knowledge, general education, and formal education in Denmark, from ABC to PhD. It is good for the individual young person, but it is also good for Denmark’s future,” Lidegaard said.
Unlike in recent years, when the government’s fiscal room for manoeuvre helped fund much of its budget plans, this proposal includes several measures to find additional savings.
These include cuts to the Danish student grant (SU), savings on senior pension payments, a proposed tax on cruise ships and further reductions in state administration costs.
The government must now negotiate with other parties in the Danish Parliament, the Folketing, to secure a majority for the 2027 budget.
The proposal includes a negotiating reserve of 500 million DKK annually from 2027 to 2030, which other parties can seek to use to fund their own priorities.

Iron Dome architect behind new counter swarm system
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:00:15 BST
23:00:15 KST

A defence technology company founded in Washington and Israel has unveiled what it describes as the world’s first native counter swarm defence system, designed from the outset to engage large numbers of drones at once instead of picking off one target at a time, according to the company.
Skapion said the system has been designed by its founding architect, General (retired) Pini Yungman, who was the architect of Iron Dome and formerly general manager of Rafael’s air and missile defence division. It is built around what the company calls a native many-to-many architecture, allowing multiple interceptors to engage multiple targets at the same time.
The company said the mobile, fully kinetic system is designed to engage more than one hundred targets simultaneously with an interception rate above 97 per cent, at a significantly lower cost per interception than conventional air defence. A vertical launch arrangement gives 360 degree coverage, and the company said it is designed for deployment from ground, airborne and maritime platforms.
Ido Bar-On, co-founder and chief executive, said: “The next generation of threats cannot be defeated by simply stacking yesterday’s air-defense solutions. A swarm is not just a larger number of discrete drones. It changes the dynamics of the engagement, the number of simultaneous decisions, the speed at which they must be made and the economies of every interception. Native Counter-Swarm means designing the entire system from day one for simultaneous mass engagement.”
Most air defence systems were developed to engage single targets or small numbers of them, which creates capacity and cost constraints against simultaneous mass attack. Skapion cited the wars in Ukraine and Iran, where it said legacy air defence is being saturated by swarms built to exhaust the defender’s magazines and budgets.
A Shahed type one-way attack drone costs tens of thousands of dollars. The interceptors fired at it can cost hundreds of thousands or more, and the magazine on any launcher is finite, so an attacker who can generate enough cheap airframes wins on arithmetic even when every shot is defeated. Bringing the cost per interception down, and the number of simultaneous engagements up, is what several companies on both sides of the Atlantic are now chasing.
At the centre of the Skapion system is an AI command and control architecture that fuses data from the company’s own sensors or from third party systems, evaluates and prioritises threats, allocates interceptors and manages engagements in real time. The company said it can run with full end-to-end autonomy or with a single human operator in the loop, depending on customer policy, and that the open, sensor-agnostic design allows integration with existing command and control and other counter-drone systems.

Happiness, not awe, may be the better emotional lever for openness to diversity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:00:14 UTC
23:00:14 KST

Feeling happy might do more to open people’s minds to social diversity than experiencing a sense of awe. New research published in the International Journal of Psychology indicates that a brief burst of joy leads to more positive attitudes toward inclusion, while awe has little effect. The findings challenge the expectation that awe would outperform other positive emotions in fostering acceptance of others.
Awe is an emotional response typically triggered by perceiving something vast and extraordinary that challenges a person’s usual understanding of the world, like a starry night sky or a towering mountain range. This feeling tends to diminish attention to oneself and make people view their surroundings as interconnected and meaningful.
Because awe encourages people to feel part of something larger than themselves, researchers have wondered whether it could help foster more positive attitudes toward diversity. The research, led by Jens Agerström, a professor of psychology at Linnaeus University, set out to test whether experiencing awe could encourage greater openness toward different social groups.
“Previous research has shown that people who are exposed to awe-inducing stimuli (e.g., vast and beautiful landscapes, moon landings) are more likely to act more prosocially (e.g., help another person),” Agerström told PsyPost. “We wanted to extend the research literature by examining whether awe can also make people more diversity oriented by, for instance, expressing more positive attitudes toward ethnic minority groups.”
Prior work provided reason to think awe might bridge social divides. For instance, a 2015 study found that awe shifts attention away from the self and promotes generosity: in one experiment, adults who watched an awe-inducing nature clip gave away more raffle tickets than those who watched a happiness-inducing one. Building on this, an experiment covered by PsyPost in 2023 found that experiencing awe, rather than joy, made children more likely to donate to members of an outgroup.
Happiness served as the comparison. Like awe, it is a positive emotion that tends to broaden people’s outlook and encourage helping and cooperation, which made it a solid benchmark. But the researchers expected awe to come out ahead, because awe is more strongly tied to a sense of a smaller self and a connection to others. Happiness also has a more mixed record: a 1994 study found that happy moods can lead people to rely more heavily on social stereotypes.
To test this, the researchers recruited 3,196 adults through the online research platform Prolific. The participants, who averaged about 40 years old, were randomly assigned to one of three groups, and each group watched a 28-second video designed to evoke a specific emotional response.
The awe group viewed majestic images of the universe, vast landscapes, and the Apollo 11 moon landing accompanied by sweeping music. The happiness group watched cheerful scenes of children playing and birthday parties paired with joyful music. A third, neutral control group saw everyday images of people studying or taking a coffee break with ambient background noise.
Immediately after watching the clips, the participants completed three questionnaires assessing their orientation toward diversity. The first survey measured general attitudes toward diversity, asking respondents if they value getting to know people from different racial or cultural backgrounds. The second survey measured diversity fatigue, which captures feelings of weariness or annoyance toward societal inclusion efforts. The third survey assessed social dominance orientation, which captures how much a person believes some social groups are simply inferior to others and that inequality between groups is acceptable.
The researchers found that the awe video did not measurably change how participants answered the surveys. On all three measures, the awe group’s responses did not differ statistically from those of the neutral control group.
Happiness, on the other hand, consistently shifted responses in a more inclusive direction. The neutral group’s average diversity attitude score was about 4.6 on a 6-point scale, and the happiness group scored about 0.08 points higher. The happiness group also scored 0.10 points lower on diversity fatigue (neutral group average: about 2.1 on a 5-point scale) and 0.15 points lower on preference for group hierarchy (neutral group average: about 2.4 on a 6-point scale).
When the two emotions were compared directly, the happiness group reported more positive attitudes toward diversity than the awe group and showed a slightly lower preference for social hierarchy, a difference that fell just short of statistical significance. The two groups did not differ reliably in diversity fatigue. The results held when the researchers excluded participants who finished unusually quickly or slowly and when they accounted for age and gender.
These shifts are small, but the authors note they emerged after a 28-second video and on measures thought to be fairly stable. The researchers suggest that happiness may promote social bonding, cooperation, and concern for others, which could carry over into more welcoming attitudes, though the study did not test this explanation.
“Brief inductions of awe do not seem to make people more diversity oriented,” Agerström noted. “Somewhat unexpectedly we found that happiness, which we used as a contrasting emotion, resulted in more positive diversity-related attitudes. Perhaps most interestingly, happiness seems to reduce social dominance, an individual difference characteristic capturing preferences for inequality and discrimination.”
The team’s biggest surprise, Agerström said, was “that happiness seems to triumph over awe when it comes to diversity.”
The lack of an effect for awe is in tension with research covered by PsyPost in 2025, which found that evoking awe through science fiction increased people’s identification with all of humanity. However, that earlier study measured a broad sense of global connection rather than specific attitudes toward demographic diversity and social equality.
“The main takeaway is that even a brief experience of happiness can make people more positive toward diversity and reduce diversity fatigue and social dominance orientation. Interestingly, the researchers did not find similar effects for awe,” said Ewa Palikot of the Institute of Psychology at the Polish Academy of Sciences, who was not involved in the study. “Like the authors, I expected awe to have a positive effect on attitudes toward diversity, especially since previous research suggests that awe can make people feel more connected to others and encourage prosocial behavior.”
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. The study relied on a very short video clip to spark emotion. A 28-second video can easily lift a person’s mood, but it might not be intense enough to trigger the profound, transformative sense of awe that comes from standing at the edge of the Grand Canyon. It is possible that a stronger, real-world experience of awe would yield different results.
The researchers note, however, that in a pretest with 125 people, the awe video produced about as much awe as the happiness video produced happiness, so a weaker emotional jolt does not obviously explain the difference. The main study itself did not check how participants felt after watching.
The researchers offer a few possible explanations for why awe fell short. Awe is a complex emotion, and although their awe video produced very little fear, it did produce some surprise, which the authors suggest could prompt a disorienting search for order rather than curiosity and openness. It is also possible the video did not create the “small self” feeling thought to drive awe’s social benefits, something the study did not measure.
“The size of the observed effects of happiness was small and it is important to examine whether happiness has the potential to shape diversity-oriented behavior in real-world settings,” Agerström said. “For example, can a more joyful workplace reduce prejudice?”
Palikot cautioned against generalizing the experimental findings to everyday life. “It is important to remember that these findings do not mean that happier people are necessarily more open to diversity in everyday life,” she told PsyPost. “The researchers looked at how a brief feeling of happiness affected people’s reported attitudes right after watching a video. We still don’t know how long these effects last or whether they influence people’s actual behavior.”
The participants in this study also started out with relatively low preferences for social hierarchy, which left less room for their scores to drop, although the happiness effect still emerged.
“As is always the case, findings need to be replicated before strong conclusions are drawn,” Agerström emphasized. “Also, other awe-inducing methods (than those we tested) may have the potential to increase diversity. Future research needs to look into this.”
Looking ahead, Agerström said the team’s long-term plan is “to unobtrusively study effects of awe and happiness on diversity behavior.” Unobtrusive studies observe what people actually do without making the measured behavior obvious, which can reduce the pull to give socially desirable answers.
“From a cross-cultural perspective, I would be curious to see whether happiness and awe have similar effects across cultures,” Palikot said. “Previous research shows that happiness and positive emotions are not viewed in the same way in different cultural contexts. For example, in some East Asian cultures, emotional balance is more valued, and strong positive emotions like happiness can also be associated with negative consequences. This does not necessarily mean that these emotions have different effects on social attitudes, but I think it would be interesting to explore.”
The study, “Happiness, Not Awe, Makes People More Diversity-Oriented,” was authored by Jens Agerström, Magnus Carlsson, and Towe Nilsson.

Climate Change Is Accelerating Faster Than We Can Respond, Scientists Warn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:00:03 UTC
23:00:03 KST

The climate is warming up faster than we can respond. According to a new report published Oct. 14 in the journal BioScience, “Earth’s climate system is moving deeper into uncharted territory.”
The State of the Climate, an annual report that tracks the Earth’s “vital signs,” monitors several climate related indicators—ranging from greenhouse gas concentrations and temperature changes to tree cover loss due to wildfire. The researchers found that, of the 16 planetary vital signs, seven are currently at record extremes. This includes sea levels and greenhouse gasses in the atmosphere. Meanwhile several others, such as areas burned during wildfires and ocean heat levels, show evidence of acceleration or abrupt shifts.
The researchers warn that the rate of global warming appears to have accelerated, from about 0.05°C per decade between 1880 and 1970 to roughly 0.36°C per decade between 2010 and 2024—and the 2°C threshold meant to limit planetary damage could be reached before 2050 they warn. These accelerating and intensifying changes could raise the risk of reinforcing feedback loops and crossing tipping points—critical thresholds that, when crossed, can lead to accelerating and often irreversible environmental changes. In 2025, the Earth passed its first climate tipping point, as rising ocean temperatures, acidification, overfishing, and pollution are combining to cause coral bleaching and mortality.
"Earth’s life-support systems are being pushed beyond stable limits," the report states, "with changes unfolding faster than our ability to respond."
This year, a number of extreme weather events made the impacts of an acceleratingly warming planet impossible to ignore. July 2026 was the hottest month on record for the contiguous United States, with ocean temperatures also reaching a record high that month. Back-to-back heat waves in Europe lead to an estimated 35,000 excess deaths, preliminary reports show. A number of regions—including Utah in the U.S., Ontario, Canada, along with France, Spain, Britain, and Belgium have either experienced their worst wildfire years in history or are on track to do so. While we don’t yet know enough to link these individual weather events to climate change, research shows that it is supercharging extreme weather events.
Concentrations of greenhouse gases—including carbon dioxide, methane, and nitrous oxide—all reached record levels in 2026, the researchers say. In May 2026, atmospheric carbon dioxide exceeded 428 parts per million, roughly 50% above pre-industrial levels and generally higher than any time in the last 2 million years.
The authors of today’s report also tracked indicators of the human activities driving these planetary changes, like energy use, food production, and economic growth. Fossil fuel consumption remains the dominant driver of these changes. Fossil fuel consumption rose by 0.9% in 2025, the report found, with oil, coal, and gas all reaching record highs, and annual energy-related carbon dioxide emissions surpassed 41 gigatons for the first time—the equivalent of emissions released by over 10,800 coal-fired power plants in one year.
There have, however, been some signs of progress, the report notes. Low-carbon sources provided roughly 43% of global electricity generation in 2025, and solar and wind energy consumption grew by approximately 18%. That was before the war in Iran laid bare the world’s reliance on fossil fuels, and triggered a global green energy boom.
But cutting carbon emissions will no longer be enough on its own, the report states. Adaptation measures—ranging from shifts towards plant-based diets, to restoring mangroves to better protect against storm surges—will be key to adjusting to a changing climate.
The report underscores an unavoidable truth. "We are witnessing the rapid destabilization of the Earth’s climate system,” it states. “This is no longer a warning for the future; it is a diagnosis of the present.”

Russia attacked Ukrainian retailer Epicentr’s warehouse 10 times in one day, destroying about 85% of goods, company says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:53:59 UTC
22:53:59 KST

Russian forces attacked Epicentr’s hub in Khmelnytskyi, a city in western Ukraine, 10 times on 13 October, starting five large fires that destroyed about 85% of the goods stored inside, the company said.
Epicentr is a Ukrainian chain of home-improvement and household-goods stores. The attack adds pressure to Ukraine’s logistics network, already damaged by Russian strikes. On 10 September, Ukrainian entrepreneur Ruslan Shostak, co-owner of the popular retail chains Eva and Varus, said that 2.1 million square meters of Ukraine’s modern warehouse space had been destroyed since Russia’s full-scale invasion began. He put the country’s total modern warehouse space at approximately 5 million square meters. The strike on the hub came the same day Russia opened a barrage of 39 ballistic missiles on Ukraine’s power grid.
About 30 drones in the sky kept the fire from being put out, and the hub burned down completely overnight, Epicentr said. None of its people were hurt, the company said.
“The most important thing is that all our people are alive,” Epicentr wrote.
Russia had earlier completely destroyed Epicentr’s two largest logistics complexes, in Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast, the company said. The Khmelnytskyi hub had remained effectively its only surviving large warehouse complex. Goods were sent from there to the company’s shopping centers, and people worked there every day “so that millions of Ukrainians could buy what they need,” it wrote. Epicentr described every such attack as a blow to Ukrainian businesses’ ability to operate, pay wages, preserve jobs, and support the country’s economy.
Epicentr’s earlier losses
Epicentr said in August that 10 of its shopping centers had been completely destroyed since February 2022. Another 13 retail sites had been damaged, and one in Melitopol remained under Russian occupation, it said. At the time, the company operated 70 shopping centers, down from 80 at the end of 2021.
Earlier, during a Russian missile attack overnight on 5 August, Epicentr’s logistics center in Kyiv burned down completely, Epicentr’s Yulia Chudnovets said. The company’s ceramic tile plant in Kalynivka, one of the largest in Ukraine, was effectively lost, she said. One employee was killed and three were injured, she added.
A fourth Ukrainian pharmaceutical warehouse has burned in a Russian strike since the start of the month
On 25 May 2024, Russian airstrikes on an Epicentr hypermarket in Kharkiv killed 19 people, Interior Minister Ihor Klymenko said.
Attacks across Khmelnytskyi Oblast
Fires broke out at enterprises in Khmelnytskyi and Shepetivka districts on 13 October, Serhii Tiurin, head of the Khmelnytskyi Oblast Military Administration, reported. He did not name the enterprises. On 14 October, Tiurin said one of the fires had been put out, and crews were still fighting the other. Khmelnytskyi Mayor Oleksandr Symchyshyn said six people were injured in Khmelnytskyi district that day, where Russian strikes damaged private enterprises, a gas station, and a medical facility.

Consumer prices rose 3.7% annually in September as gas prices skyrocket
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:53:28 UTC
22:53:28 KST

September brought little relief to the accelerating cost of living, as consumer prices increased again and kept the inflation rate well above the Federal Reserve's goal.
The consumer price index, a broad measure of goods and services costs across the U.S. economy, rose a seasonally adjusted 0.6% for the month, putting the 12-month rate at 3.7%, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Wednesday. Economists surveyed by Dow Jones expected respective gains of 0.6% and 3.6%.
Stripping out volatile food and energy costs, the so-called core CPI rose 0.3% for the month and was up 2.6% on an annual basis, compared with respective estimates for 0.2% and 2.5%.
The annual rate for headline inflation was 3.4% in August while the core rate was 2.4%.
Surging energy costs were again the primary culprit in the inflation picture. The energy index jumped 5.2% as tensions continued between the U.S. and Iran in a war launched in late February that shows no signs of ending anytime soon.
Gasoline prices soared 9.1%, accounting for about half the gain in headline CPI, according to the BLS. Over the past year, gas has posted a 34.2% rise while fuel oil has roared higher by 74.2%.
Food prices were flat on the month and up 2.5% from a year ago. However, shelter prices increased 0.4% and used car and truck prices jumped 0.7%. Apparel prices, which are sensitive to tariffs, increased 0.3% and are up 3.4% on an annual basis.
Stock market futures turned negative following the release while bond yields were sharply higher. Futures traders also raised the odds of a rate hike when the Federal Open Market Committee next meets on Oct. 27-28 to about 54%, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool. Odds for a rate rise before the end of the year increased to better than 96%, with a near 50-50 chance of the Fed boosting rates by half a percentage point by December.
This is the final CPI reading that FOMC officials will get before that meeting. The BLS on Thursday will release the September reading on the producer price index, a measure of wholesale costs.
"CPI came in hot and it wasn't just fuel prices, as core inflation ran at a 3.7% annualized pace in September and 3.2% over three years," said Sonu Varghese, chief macro strategist at Carson Group. "The only surprise is that investors keep getting surprised by broad-based inflation. And we've yet to see the full impact of higher diesel prices and the AI boom."
Inflation as measured by the CPI has surpassed the Fed's 2% benchmark since March 2021. The gauge had been trending lower at the start of 2026, but then spiked following the strikes the U.S. and Israel launched against Iran.
Over the past few months, the year-over-year trend has moderated but still has held well above target.
Fed officials responded in September by approving their first interest rate hike in more than three years, a quarter percentage point move that took the benchmark funds rate to a target range of 3.75%-4%. Markets expect the Fed to skip an October increase but to hike again in December.
The type of supply shocks that have driven the energy surge generally are considered temporary, and policymakers often will look through them when considering where to set rates. However, Fed officials fear that the longer the war drags on, the higher the likelihood that the spike will make its way through the broader economy and become embedded in consumer and business expectations.
Prices also have faced pressure from President Donald Trump's tariffs as well as demand for goods associated with the artificial intelligence build-out.
In recent days, a number of key policymakers have expressed the belief that the Fed doesn't need to rush to implement another hike. However, most say they expect another increase this year. Market pricing implies the Fed could raise rates at least twice more in 2027.
Fed officials follow the CPI and a host of other metrics but use the Commerce Department's personal consumption expenditures price index as their primary forecast and policymaking metric. The PCE numbers for September won't be released until later this month.

Microsoft, OpenAI executives call for AI safety laws, says warnings alone are not enough
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:53:15 UTC
22:53:15 KST

Necva Taştan Sevinç
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
Microsoft Vice Chair and President Brad Smith on Wednesday called for new artificial intelligence safety laws, saying tech companies must prevent harm rather than simply warn of risks.
Speaking at the International AI Summit 2026 in Ireland, Smith said AI capabilities had advanced faster than protections.
“The world here in Europe or anywhere does not expect our industry simply to warn about what could go wrong. They expect us to prevent it. They expect us to take action,” he said.
“And if we need to slow down, then it is up to each company and each leader to slow down.”
Describing 2026 as “a sobering year for AI safety,” Smith cited reports of rogue AI agents hacking networks and AI worms targeting connected homes.
“There are more safety rules for a carton of milk than for AI. There are more safety rules for your oven than for AI,” he said.
He urged the industry to overcome resistance to regulation and to back incident reporting, notification of victims of AI-enabled breaches, and independent evaluations with findings shared with governments and customers.
“But we need law. We need regulation. It needs to be sensible. It needs to be balanced. It needs to take into account innovation,” Smith said.
“We need to recognize that the power of AI has moved faster than the safety for it. Safety needs to catch up.” 
'We need to make sure the defenders have the tools'
Also speaking at the event, OpenAI Chief Financial Officer Sarah Friar supported cooperation among leading AI developers, saying the company had called for global regulation.
Friar said OpenAI is withholding an unreleased model while doing further safety and alignment work, but cautioned against slowing development so sharply that cyber defenders lose ground.
“So the folks with malicious intent have the tools. So we need to make sure the defenders have the tools,” she said.
She said OpenAI had used AI to identify vulnerabilities in its own infrastructure.
“We found the vulnerabilities, we patched them at machine speed,” Friar said.
“Selling fear is not a good way to come to the world. We have to sell solutions and solutions that feel transparent, open, honest, and so on.”

Ukrainian Il-76 spotted leaving Saudi airport near Yemen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:53:03 UTC
22:53:03 KST

- A Ukrainian Air Force Il-76MD flew from Sharurah, near Saudi Arabia’s border with Yemen, toward Istanbul on Oct. 12, flight-tracking data shows.
- Neither Ukraine nor Saudi Arabia has explained the flight, which follows Ukraine’s deployment of counter-drone specialists to Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states.
A Ukrainian Air Force Il-76MD heavy transport aircraft was tracked on Oct. 12 flying out of Sharurah, a Saudi town in Najran Province near the border with Yemen, in a rare appearance of a Ukrainian military cargo plane in the south of the kingdom.
Flight-tracking data shared by the open-source account Egypt’s Intel Observer shows the four-engine jet, registration 76661, heading north over the Red Sea at about 10,350 m (33,975 feet) at 17:28 UTC on its way from Sharurah to Istanbul’s Sabiha Gökçen airport, roughly an hour and 48 minutes after takeoff. The account said the aircraft had earlier flown to Sharurah from Lviv in western Ukraine, a leg not visible in the published screenshot.
Neither Kyiv nor Riyadh has said what the aircraft carried or why it landed at Sharurah. The open-source account speculated that it may have delivered Ukrainian interceptor drones or military specialists, possibly to support Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces, and described Sharurah as their main supply hub, a claim that has not been confirmed by any government.
Sharurah’s airport serves both civilian and military traffic and sits close to the Yemeni frontier. It was one of seven southern airports Saudi Arabia shut to civilian flights in March 2015, when the kingdom began its air campaign against the Iran-aligned Houthi movement in Yemen.
Ukraine already has a documented military footprint in the Gulf. After Iran launched drone and missile strikes on Gulf states during the war that began in March 2026, President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine had sent more than 200 counter-drone specialists to the region, and later put the number at 228 across five partners, including Saudi Arabia, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Kuwait and Jordan. Zelensky signed a defense agreement with Saudi Arabia during a Gulf visit in the spring, and Ukrainian officials have offered partners interceptor drones built to bring down Iranian-designed Shahed attack drones.
According to information obtained by The Defence Blog, Ukrainian specialists are helping Saudi Arabia and other countries in the region defend against hostile drone strikes, and are also training local forces in new tactics for employing attack drones.
That work has drawn threats from Tehran. In March, an Iranian member of parliament said Ukraine’s support to Gulf states made it Iran’s “legitimate war target.”
The Il-76MD is a Soviet-designed strategic airlifter able to carry about 40 tonnes (88,000 pounds) of cargo, and the Ukrainian Air Force operates only a small number of them. Ukrainian military Il-76 flights abroad are usually tied to cargo pickups, equipment deliveries or the movement of personnel.
The routing through Istanbul fits a flight path north over the Red Sea and Turkey back toward Ukraine, though the tracking data does not show the aircraft’s final destination after Sabiha Gökçen or whether it returned empty.
What the aircraft unloaded or picked up at Sharurah, and whether the flight was linked to Ukraine’s counter-drone mission in Saudi Arabia or to the conflict in Yemen, remains unconfirmed.

South African opposition party cancels major rally
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:52:59 UTC
22:52:59 KST

South African opposition party cancels major rally
South Africa’s opposition uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) Party has called off a major rally ahead of next month’s local elections, as party leader and former President Jacob Zuma remains under medical care in the hospital.
The party said the rally, which had been scheduled to be held in Mpumalanga on Sunday and where the party was to launch its election manifesto, had been cancelled to allow it to focus its resources on ward-level campaigning and community engagement. However, there was speculation that the party’s finances were in disarray and it was unable to pay for the function.
The announcement comes amid reports about Zuma’s health, with the Jacob Zuma Foundation responding to speculation about his condition and appealing for his privacy to be respected.
MK Party spokesperson Sifiso Mahlangu said the party would conduct an urgent and independent investigation into reported discrepancies in the final councillor candidate lists published by the Electoral Commission of South Africa (IEC).
The party’s 2026 local government election manifesto, referred to as the People’s Mandate, would be distributed electronically to party structures and members on October 15, Mahlangu said.
Zuma was admitted to Netcare St Anne’s Hospital in Pietermaritzburg last week after reportedly falling ill during an MK Party election campaign in uMsinga, KwaZulu-Natal. The party described his hospital visit as a routine medical check-up. However, speculation about his condition continued after reports suggested he had been discharged and returned to his Nkandla home.
On Tuesday, the Jacob Zuma Foundation dismissed the reports, saying he remained under medical care at the hospital. Foundation spokesperson Mzwanele Manyi said the former president was in good spirits, based on information from someone who had spoken to him and spent time with him. The foundation has appealed for Zuma’s privacy and dignity to be respected while he receives medical care.
The party said candidates whose names had been omitted or inadvertently excluded from the IEC’s final councillor candidate list would be prioritised for the first available positions, subject to its processes and requirements. Its leadership would engage directly with affected ward candidates who had been nominated through community meetings. The party also resolved to establish proportional representation (PR) councillor deployment committees at national, provincial and regional levels to finalise the deployment of councillors from its PR lists.
The MK Party announced the launch of its national Molo Makhelwane campaign, which will run until midnight on November 3, the eve of the elections. The campaign would involve party structures, councillor candidates and volunteers visiting households, engaging churches and listening to residents’ concerns across cities, townships, farms and villages.
The party said its candidates and volunteers must be visible in communities as it seeks to strengthen its relationship with residents. “The streets must now be green!” said Mahlangu.

Russia’s internet shutdowns push state firms back to landline phones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:52:44 UTC
22:52:44 KST

State procurement of landline telephones tripled in the first eight months of 2026 as mobile internet outages hit nearly 80% of the country. Rostelecom’s chief urged Russians to keep one at home “like a fire extinguisher".
Russian state-owned companies spent more than three times as much on landline telephones in the first eight months this year as in the same period in 2025, as mobile internet shutdowns affecting nearly 80% of the country push ministries and businesses to seek alternatives to disrupted networks.
Procurement data cited by the Russian business daily Vedomosti show spending at 118 million roubles (€1.26 million) from January through August, with the number of purchase tenders up 12.5%.
Purchases are concentrated in the country’s largest business and infrastructure hubs.
Market participants told Vedomosti that the surge was driven by the restrictions, a shift by Russian ministries and companies to domestically produced software-based PBX systems after Western vendors withdrew from the Russian market following the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, and demand for secure communications channels.
Russia began systematically shutting down mobile internet access in May 2025, when services went offline in more than 40 regions ahead of Victory Day celebrations. What were initially episodic outages quickly became routine.
An independent monitoring project recorded 655 mobile internet outages in June 2025, rising to 2,099 in July, a figure that exceeded the worldwide total for the entire previous year, according to analysts.
The disruptions have hit banking, taxi services, food delivery and navigation, particularly in rural areas.
The authorities have justified the shutdowns as a defence against Ukrainian drones, which they say are guided via mobile internet signals.
Experts have disputed this, saying drones can fly preset routes without a network connection, and the shutdowns have reached regions far from the front line.
In March, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the presidential administration “uses landline telephones” when asked how restrictions in central Moscow affect the work of the president’s office.
Shortly after, head of state telecoms company Rostelecom Mikhail Oseyevsky urged Russians to return to fixed lines.
“Like a fire extinguisher, there should be one in every home," Oseyevsky said.
Russia has approximately 12.2 landline telephones per 100 residents. In Moscow, around 2 million households use fixed lines provided by MGTS, the city’s main telephone operator.
Across the country, there are about 17.4 million urban household landline connections.
The Ministry of Economic Development forecasts that the number of all landlines will fall to between 8.2 and 8.5 per 100 residents by 2029.

Widespread outages affected banks and other online services across Russia on October 14, following a nighttime Ukrainian drone strike on a Sberbank data center in Russia’s Saratov region.
Russian media outlets The Bell and Important Stories reported the outages, citing data from the service monitoring platforms Sboy.rf and Detector404.
Users across Russia reported problems accessing Sberbank’s app and website, as well as services in its ecosystem, including GigaChat and the Samokat delivery service.
Tochka Bank experienced disruptions to its online banking and Business Online services. Outages were also reported affecting Mail.ru, its cloud storage service, VKontakte, Ozon, Yandex, and other platforms.
Users also reported problems with hosting provider Reg.ru and the business services Kontur and VK WorkSpace.
The problems began to be reported after a nighttime attack on Sberbank’s data center in Balakovo, Saratov region.
Sberbank, however, said that all its services were operating normally despite the drone strike. The extent of the damage to its infrastructure remains unknown.
Construction of the data center, valued at RUB 122.2 billion, is still underway, although the facility is being commissioned in stages.
The project provides for approximately 3,000 server racks and up to 120,000 servers, with a total capacity of up to 82 MW.
The facility is intended to support Sberbank’s IT infrastructure and data processing and storage. It was also planned to host services for the state digital platform GosTech.
This is the second major Russian data center operator whose infrastructure has been hit within the past week.
Militarnyi previously reported that Ukrainian drones attacked a Yandex data center in Vladimir in the early hours of October 11. It was the company’s third facility hit in four days. Reports of widespread service disruptions followed the strikes.

MOSCOW, October 14. /TASS/. Russia’s exports of oil and petroleum products fell by 10,000 barrels per day (bpd) in September 2026 to 6.52 million bpd, according to data from the International Energy Agency (IEA). Meanwhile, monthly export revenues rose by $3.6 billion from August 2026 to reach $17.67 billion, driven by surging oil prices.
Russian crude oil shipments increased by 60,000 bpd in September, while exports of petroleum products decreased by 80,000 bpd.
Revenues from crude oil exports in September totaled $14.5 billion (up $3.15 billion from August), while revenues from petroleum product exports amounted to $3.16 billion (an increase of $440 million compared to August).

Compared to September 2025, Russia's oil export revenues in September 2026 were $4.32 billion higher.

The prosecutor said the woman could not speak through the pain. “She asked him to stop, at first quietly and then louder, a number of times, begging. He did not,” Karmy-Jones said. He then ordered her to “clean up the mess you have made”.
Brand texted the woman the following year after seeing each other in a chance encounter in Scotland. She said she messaged Brand: “Why are you even messaging me?” and he replied: “Because you’re dirty, and I wanna push you further.”
The court heard that she had replied: “I think you pushed me far enough – you treated me like an animal”, and she said Brand had replied: “I’m sorry.”
The woman, the prosecutor said, spent years blaming herself for what had happened, and became extremely anxious and unwell. The final alleged victim was working at Channel 4 in 2009 when she alleges that Brand sexually assaulted her by placing his head in her groin area. She told her manager about the attack but she felt her complaint was not taken seriously.
Karmy-Jones said that Brand had given prepared statements in police interviews, denying all the allegations. He said he had never engaged in nonconsensual sexual activity, and suggested accounts may have been reinvented or imagined after a documentary about his alleged sexual misconduct.
Brand’s wife, Laura Gallacher, sat through the evidence on Wednesday morning. Earlier, the pair arrived at court to a crowd of reporters and photographers. “I feel blessed,” Brand told a journalist. “I feel of course concerned but hopeful that this process will lead to good outcomes for everybody involved. That’s my prayer.”
The trial before judge Mr Justice Bennathan continues.

Entire Swedish reality show season lost weeks before premiere amid disputed AI claims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:46:12 UTC
22:46:12 KST

The project could not be restored, wiping out hundreds of days of work, according to Swedish newspaper Aftonbladet.
An AI agent reportedly deleted an entire edited season of a Swedish reality show just five weeks before its planned premiere, forcing the broadcaster to postpone its release until next year.
Swedish newspaper Aftonbladet, citing unnamed sources, reported that the production company behind a reality show named The Challenge Sverige had given an AI agent access to its server, where it deleted the completed season.
The project could not be restored, wiping out hundreds of days of work, according to the report.
Swedish commercial broadcaster TV4 confirmed to Aftonbladet that a “technical failure” had caused the loss, pushing the planned 22 November premiere back to 2027.
Its news division initially repeated the newspaper’s account of AI involvement, but in an update on Wednesday afternoon, TV4’s head of programmes Mia Lindqvist denied that an AI agent was responsible, saying “that is not true”.
Adapted from the American show The Challenge, the series is billed by TV4 as the world’s toughest reality contest, combining physical challenges, mental endurance and strategic alliances.
How can AI agents go wrong?
Although the Swedish TV channel has rejected the AI explanation in this case, other incidents have exposed the risks of systems that can act on users’ behalf.
AI agents use software tools to carry out tasks, such as drafting and sending emails, rather than simply generating responses. Depending on their permissions, they can make changes to real files, websites and computer systems.
Problems can arise when a system misunderstands instructions, misjudges an action’s consequences or works around an obstacle instead of stopping.
In a report published on Friday, Anthropic said models given impossible tasks could pursue “unintended and sometimes misaligned strategies to achieve their goals”.
In July, its Claude Haiku 4.5 model submitted fabricated information about an unsolved homicide to the US police website while performing example tasks.
TV4 said all the original footage of the show remains available but the season must be edited again from scratch.

The Israel Allies Foundation (IAF) launched two new parliamentary caucuses in Greece and Cyprus this week, seeking to strengthen ties with Israel and expand cooperation on regional security, energy, and technology.
The Greek Parliamentary Israel Allies Caucus was inaugurated at the Hellenic Parliament in Athens on Tuesday, followed by the launch of the Cyprus Israel Allies Caucus at the House of Representatives in Nicosia on Wednesday.
The new caucuses aim to build on the existing trilateral partnership between Israel, Greece, and Cyprus, with a particular focus on security challenges in the Eastern Mediterranean, including tensions with Turkey.
“The new Israel Allies Caucuses in Greece and Cyprus will help translate these commitments into parliamentary action,” said Leo van Doesburg, executive director of IAF Europe.
“Turkish threats must be met with solidarity, not silence. Ankara has no veto over our partnerships or our security,” he added.
Cyprus, Greece, Israel ties 'more vital than ever'

Tsiaras said the initiative comes amid growing regional security challenges and proves the three countries' shared strategic interests and historical ties.
In Cyprus, the new caucus will be chaired by Democratic Party MP Chrysis Pantelides and will include six lawmakers from three political parties.
The launch followed a meeting between the IAF delegation and Cypriot President Nicos Christodoulides at the Presidential Palace. The delegation was also hosted by House of Representatives President Annita Demetriou.
Pantelides emphasized the importance of strengthening relations between Cyprus and Israel in light of regional security threats.
“The strengthening of relations and the development of alliance ties between Cyprus and Israel is more vital than ever,” he said, citing the security challenges facing both countries.
Israeli ambassadors attended the launches in their respective host countries, while the US ambassador to Cyprus also attended the ceremony in Nicosia.
Reinstein welcomed the establishment of the two caucuses, saying they would help strengthen parliamentary cooperation and support for Israel.
“Through faith-based diplomacy, we are building a bridge between parliamentarians who understand that Israel's security, and the security of the free world, depend on strong alliances rooted in shared Judeo-Christian values,” he said.
