Dublin hotel cancels 70 rooms booked for antisemitism conference delegates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:45:57 UTC
22:45:57 KST

The Herbert Park Hotel in Dublin canceled a reservation for 70 rooms intended for delegates attending an international conference on combating antisemitism after learning the purpose of their visit, according to Maurice Cohen, chairman of the Jewish Representative Council of Ireland.
In his speech at the opening event at the Irish Foreign Ministry – sent to The Jerusalem Post – Cohen recalled meeting with hotel management after the booking was completed, and being questioned about whether the gathering was connected to the Israel Defense Forces.
Cohen also remembered the manager’s demeanor changing and becoming tense after he mentioned that the delegates would be Jewish leaders.
“There is an uncomfortable irony in organizing an international conference to discuss antisemitism and finding that, before the conference has even begun, you have already encountered something that forces you to ask exactly the questions the conference was created to address,” he said.
“How quickly does the word ‘Jewish’ change a conversation? How easily does a gathering about antisemitism become associated with the Israeli army?”
He noted that the question about the IDF was not an innocent misunderstanding, as it instead “revealed how quickly Jewish identity can be collapsed into Israel, how quickly Israel can be collapsed into suspicion, and how quickly suspicion can become discrimination because contemporary antisemitism does not always arrive wearing the language of the past.
“It does not always announce itself with a slur, a threat, or a placard. Increasingly, it can present itself as a question, a precaution, a policy, a request for clarification. It begins by treating Jewish identity as evidence of political allegiance,” he said.
Resetting the conversation between Jewish groups and governments
The European Jewish Congress called the incident “deeply disturbing.”
“That a hotel would cancel accommodation for participants in a conference dedicated to combating antisemitism, while raising questions about supposed links to the Israeli military, reflects precisely the kind of prejudice and suspicion that such gatherings seek to confront,” the EJC noted.
“It is profoundly troubling that those working to combat antisemitism should themselves encounter such treatment. Jewish organizations and those standing against hatred must never face exclusion or discrimination because of their work,”
Israel’s Foreign Ministry said. “The Irish government cannot use the fight against antisemitism as a diplomatic PR exercise while failing to confront it at home.”
The conference in question was the 15th meeting of the Special Envoys and Coordinators Combating Antisemitism (SECCA) Forum, organized by the World Jewish Congress in partnership with the European Commission, and convened as an Associated Event under Ireland’s rotating presidency of the Council of the European Union.
Jewish community leaders from across the world joined government envoys, representatives from international organizations, and technology company executives in Dublin from October 12 to 14.
Leaders representing the J7 Large Communities’ Task Force Against Antisemitism – connecting the Delegación de Asociaciones Israelitas Argentinas, Executive Council of Australian Jewry, Canada’s Center for Israel and Jewish Affairs, the Representative Council of French Jewish Institutions, Central Council of Jews in Germany, and Board of Deputies of British Jews, alongside the Anti-Defamation League (ADL) and the Conference of Presidents of Major American Jewish Organizations from the United States – also joined the forum following a series of high-level meetings in London earlier in the week.
Statements, condemnations only go so far
The gathering included a meeting with Ireland’s Taoiseach or government leader, Micheál Martin; visits to the European headquarters of TikTok and Meta; and other discussions.
“Our meeting in Dublin is a much-needed opportunity to reset the conversation between Jewish organizations, governments, and technology companies,” Maram Stern, WJC executive vice president, said. “Statements and condemnation of antisemitism only go so far. Practical solutions must urgently be put in place to protect Jewish life globally.”
The delegates were officially welcomed by Irish ministers despite the current Ireland-Israel tensions.
At the start of Tuesday’s agenda, Colm Brophy, a member of the Irish parliament, said he was “very pleased to welcome Jewish community leaders” and was particularly happy to see that the event has a focus on AI and on the regulation of online platforms, given the “troubling increase in antisemitism and other forms of racism online in recent years.”
The incident comes amid a sharp deterioration in relations between Ireland and Israel, with Jerusalem accusing Dublin of fostering an increasingly hostile environment toward the Jewish state.
Tensions have escalated following Ireland’s recognition of a Palestinian state, its legal and diplomatic moves against Israel, and controversy over Dublin City Council’s proposal to remove the name of former Israeli president Chaim Herzog from Herzog Park in Rathgar and replace it with “Free Palestine Park.”
The attempt was eventually condemned by Irish officials, and the J7 representatives visited the park for a photo-op this week during the conference.

INTERVIEW - ‘You’re not alone, the truth will come out’: Nobel winner Navi Pillay on global support for Palestinians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:45:10 UTC
22:45:10 KST

Nobel Peace Prize laureate Navi Pillay said Palestinians seeking justice are not alone and the truth will emerge, urging the international community to draw lessons from the collective action and economic sanctions that helped end apartheid in her native South Africa.
In an exclusive interview on Wednesday, Pillay, judge at the International Court of Justice and a former UN human rights chief, reflected on her experience fighting apartheid and the importance of international support for Palestinians amid continuing concerns over accountability for violations in the Gaza Strip.
"I imagine I'm correct in saying that even though Palestinians are struggling for their freedom for more than 90 years now, attention by the international community and support by the international community would be of great significance for them," she told Anadolu.
"The message being, you're not alone. That with information and correct information, the truth will come out."
Pillay, 85, who was awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize for her contributions to international justice, chaired a UN commission of inquiry, which concluded last year that Israel committed genocide in Gaza.
Recalling her experience under apartheid, she said South African lawyers fought a lonely struggle with little international attention. "We really had very little relief. And honestly, the rest of the world didn't pay attention to us," she said.
The rights lawyer said a UN commission gathering evidence and presenting its findings internationally would have greatly helped Black South Africans at that time.
Pillay stressed the importance of identifying the root causes of Palestinian suffering, and reiterated her commission's finding that Israel's unlawful occupation was the root cause of the longstanding conflict.
She criticized governments for increasingly prioritizing their political and regional interests over their responsibilities to maintain international peace and justice.
She said the UN Security Council already possessed mechanisms to respond to violations, including peacekeeping operations, investigative commissions, mediation and economic sanctions.
"The principal tool they have is to impose sanctions, economic sanctions against governments that are violating international human rights law, international humanitarian law, they've used this before," she said.
Questioning the international community's response to Gaza, Pillay said: "So, the question that civil society is asking: 'Why are you sitting back and doing nothing in the face of huge violations that we, the people, can see daily? We can see genocide being committed on our television screens'."
"And I am as unhappy as most people that there has been so little action," she added.
Drawing on South Africa's experience, where apartheid ended in 1994, Pillay emphasized the decisive role of international economic pressure.
"Apartheid came to an end mainly because of the economic sanctions imposed by the Security Council, by the United Nations against the apartheid government," she said.
"I never thought apartheid will end in my lifetime, but it's this collective action by governments, by businesses, and civil society all over the world that brought an end to apartheid."
Pillay said she had been hoping for similar international cooperation in response to the situation in Gaza.
"I've been hopefully looking for and calling for that level of cooperation, that level of condemnation of the huge violations and killings of Palestinians," she said.
Asked whether Israel's growing international isolation and sanctions targeting settlers in the occupied West Bank could help end its impunity, Pillay said such developments could contribute to broader collective action.
"The one thing we cannot accept is doing nothing," she said.
Recalling Nelson Mandela's position that South Africans could not fully enjoy freedom while Palestinians remained oppressed and occupied, she said Palestinians were seeking measures similar to those used against apartheid.
"Palestinians are calling for the kind of action that was taken to end apartheid. They see the value of economic boycotts," she said.
She also referred to protests by Israelis against efforts to weaken the country's Supreme Court, urging governments to respect civilians' right to protest and cooperate with international criminal investigations.
She stressed that international legal principles must be applied consistently, without selectivity or bias, particularly when civilians are suffering.
Pillay emphasized that governments, rather than international organizations alone, bear responsibility for preventing genocide.
"The Genocide Convention is very clear. The duty is on every state to prevent genocide," she said. "That's a purpose; it's not to react to genocide and to punish the alleged perpetrators. The main reason is to prevent, because it's an intolerable crime when a whole group is being destroyed in whole or in part."
About the potential legal responsibility of governments supplying weapons, intelligence or political support despite warnings of serious violations, Pillay said the states themselves established international conventions and treaties.
"They set the standards. Now they must implement them without selection," she said, arguing that governments were failing to apply their own commitments because of political interests.
Pillay recalled that her UN commission had urged the General Assembly to seek an advisory opinion from the International Court of Justice (ICJ) concerning Israel's occupation of Palestinian territory.
She welcomed the court's opinion in 2024, which found Israel's continued presence in the occupied Palestinian territory unlawful, and outlined obligations concerning Palestinian rights.
She, however, acknowledged that legal proceedings offered limited immediate relief to people suffering on the ground.
"I agree; they're not very helpful to relieve their immediate dire situation," she said. "Let's use international law to assert and realize the rights of people who are oppressed everywhere in the world."
On shortcomings of the international system and its eroding credibility, Pillay pointed to the dominance of governments within the UN and the shrinking space for civil society.
"Certainly, the system is very skewed. Who controls the United Nations? It's member states, it's governments," she said, urging UN members to conduct their affairs in closer cooperation with civil society organizations.
Turning to Washington's measures against the International Criminal Court (ICC), Pillay called on governments, including those outside the Rome Statute, to oppose the campaign.
"I would like to see states of the world, the member states, whether they're parties to the Rome Statute or not, to condemn the unlawful measures and sanctions that the United States is imposing on this court," she said.
"We should say roundly that it's unacceptable, and then we all have the responsibility to help the court to overcome these obstacles."
The former ICC judge expressed confidence that the court's staff would continue their work despite mounting political pressure.
"They're not going to stop doing what they are doing because they are working out of commitment. They believe that it is possible to realize justice for all," she said.
Reflecting on receiving the Nobel, Pillay described the recognition as unexpected and deeply meaningful. "This award was a huge surprise to me, but a wonderful surprise," she said.
She expressed gratitude that the Nobel Committee had recognized different aspects of her decades-long career, from challenging apartheid to advancing international justice.
"You don't win a case all the time. You win some. You lose many, especially under apartheid South Africa," she said.
Pillay described the committee's recognition of her work as a "memorable moment," saying she appreciated its efforts to examine her contributions to international peace and justice.

France’s Mélenchon sees Spain’s Sánchez as inspiration for fixing public finances
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:44:43 UTC
22:44:43 KST

Jean-Luc Melenchon attends a press conference on the sidelines of the debates on the draft state budget for 2027 at LFI's headquarters in Paris, France on October 14, 2026. | Lou Benoist/AFP via Getty Images
PARIS — Jean-Luc Mélenchon pointed to Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez as proof that greater public spending can boost the French economy and repair its strained public finances.
“Ever since Spain adopted a budget focused on ecological and social growth, it has experienced steady growth and a decline in its debt,” said Mélenchon, the leading left-wing candidate for next year’s presidential election in France.
In a press conference focused on the budget on Wednesday, the 75-year-old radical doubled down on his calls for a positive demand shock driven by billions in new state spending. He also reiterated his proposal to write off billions of euros in French debt held by the European Central Bank, which has drawn strong criticism, including from ECB President Christine Lagarde.
Advertisement
Polls show Mélenchon neck and neck with center-right candidate Édouard Philippe in the race to qualify for a second-round runoff against Marine Le Pen, the far-right frontrunner who presented her own budget plans last week.
Under Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, Spain has significantly reduced its budget deficit, while public debt is projected to fall below 100% of GDP in 2026. His government has raised the minimum wage and supported investment in green energy, alongside other sectors. Although inflation is a major concern and economic growth is expected to moderate in 2027, Spain remains one of Europe’s fastest-growing major economies, with the IMF on Tuesday forecasting 2.5% growth in 2026.
Spanish deficit fell significantly under Sánchez, and became one of the Eurozone’s fastest-growing economies after the pandemic.
Spain’s debt-to-GDP ratio dropped below 100% — while France’s raised to 119% — as the government invested heavily in sectors such as green energy and raised the minimum wage. But the cost of living remains a major concern in the country, particularly housing — one of the issues that led Sánchez to call a snap election earlier this month.
More money, less problems?
Mélenchon wants to boost growth by increasing purchasing power through higher salaries — including a higher minimum wage, a 10% raise for public-sector workers and a nationwide round of collective bargaining — as well as higher benefits for welfare recipients and a monthly payment of €1,337 for every French student intended to lift them above the poverty line.
Together, these measures form what his campaign calls an €82 billion “emergency spending” package.
Advertisement
Eric Coquerel, a Mélenchon ally who heads the French National Assembly’s powerful finance committee, argued in the same press conference that the new spending would drive GDP growth and increase tax revenue.
He also outlined ways to fund it, including a 2% wealth tax on households worth more than €100 million, popularized by French economist Gabriel Zucman, and higher taxes on large inheritances, which would be capped at €12 million under a Mélenchon presidency.
Fiscally conservative think tanks such as Institut Montaigne have argued that Mélenchon significantly underestimated the cost of his proposed spending and the potential tax revenue in previous campaigns. Critics also warn of capital flight if he is elected president, as occurred after his political mentor François Mitterrand was elected in 1981 on a platform of mass nationalizations.
In a statement, Edouard Philippe’s campaign called Mélenchon’s budget proposal “dangerous.”
Mélenchon blamed the current state of France’s finances on President Emmanuel Macron’s decision to cut several taxes early in his presidency, a move Macron said was intended to attract more investment.
“There are no other causes [of the deficit] than the systematic depletion of the state orchestrated by Macronism,” Mélenchon said.
Advertisement
“We are pitting the virtuous cycle of ecological and social recovery … against the vicious cycle of Macronist budgets and the dismantling of the state,” he added.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu’s government has presented a budget with €43 billion in spending cuts, aiming to reduce France’s deficit to 5% of GDP without raising taxes. This year’s deficit is expected to reach 5.4% of GDP, missing the initial 5% target.
The counter-proposal from Mélenchon’s France Unbowed includes €106.4 billion in additional revenue and €81.7 billion in further spending, according to Coquerel, leaving about €25 billion to reduce the deficit.
France’s current center-right government is expected to pass its budget through the country’s hung parliament either by invoking a constitutional mechanism that allows the executive to pass legislation without a vote or by executive order. Mélenchon said his first order of business if elected in May would be to draft a new budget, which he hopes to pass in summer 2027.
France Unbowed advocates for a reduction of France’s contribution to the European Union, which presidential frontrunner Le Pen also wants to cut by €11 billion, though Coquerel clarified that he had not included a potential rebate in his economic forecasts.
Mélenchon intends to use the contribution as leverage to push for revised EU treaties, including scrapping the 3% deficit target for member countries and allowing national governments to adopt protectionist policies.
Critics, including Lagarde, said Mélenchon’s debt proposal was “dangerous” and potentially illegal because it could amount to direct financing of member countries by the ECB, which is prohibited by European treaties.

US judge blocks sanctions against 2 human rights groups engaging with international court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:43:09 UTC
22:43:09 KST

Yasin Gungor
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
A US federal judge blocked the Trump administration from penalizing two human rights organizations communicating with the International Criminal Court (ICC), ruling that the measures unconstitutionally restrict free speech.
US District Judge Jesse Furman granted a preliminary injunction, determining that the federal prohibition against providing services to sanctioned ICC personnel constitutes a content-based regulation of speech that fails strict scrutiny.
The ruling bars federal agencies from enforcing civil fines of up to $377,700 or criminal penalties of up to 20 years in prison under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act against plaintiffs Democracy for the Arab World Now (DAWN) and the Taxpayer Alliance Against Genocide (TAAG). DAWN had routinely submitted war crimes evidence filings under Article 15 of the Rome Statute. TAAG was formed to prepare similar submissions but had withheld filing out of fear of prosecution.
The rights groups welcomed the victory and announced they will immediately resume submitting evidentiary documentation to the tribunal, restart formal coordination with UN Special Rapporteur Francesca Albanese and re-engage with Palestinian human rights bodies Al-Haq, Al Mezan, and the Palestinian Centre for Human Rights.
ICC measures
The litigation challenged Executive Order 14203, issued in February 2025, which directed federal agencies to impose tangible consequences on entities tied to investigations targeting the US or allies such as Israel that have not consented to ICC jurisdiction.
The order targeted former ICC Prosecutor Karim Khan, six judges and UN personnel.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced last Friday that Washington imposed sanctions on the court, warning that the US would dismantle the tribunal if member nations fail to rein in its authority.
US pressure intensified after the court issued arrest warrants in November 2024 for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant for alleged war crimes in the Gaza Strip. The ICC has 125 member states, while neither the US nor Israel is party to the tribunal.

Closer EU trade ties greater prize for UK than making separate deals, minister says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:31:55 UTC
22:31:55 KST

Britain will benefit from much closer trading relations with the EU even if that means giving up its ability to negotiate free trade agreements, the Scotland secretary has said.
Douglas Alexander helped negotiate deals with India and the US when he was a trade minister under Keir Starmer.
But he has told the Guardian he thinks joint trading arrangements with the EU – whether under a customs union or full membership – would be a bigger economic prize, not least because the EU has now negotiated its own similar deal with India.
When Starmer was prime minister, ministers would argue against rejoining the EU because it would mean having to abandon trade agreements with other countries.
Alexander’s comments show how much Starmer’s successor, Andy Burnham, who called this week for a “serious dialogue” on the UK’s relations with the EU, including possible re-entry, has shifted the government’s position.
Speaking to the Guardian from a trade delegation to India, Alexander welcomed the progress made since the Indian agreement came into force earlier this year, since when the price of scotch whisky in India has fallen by 10-15%.
But he said the economic benefits of trading agreements with the EU would be greater.
“In trade policy, geography still matters,” he said. “The Channel is just 21 miles wide. Our largest trading partner is and will remain the European Union in the years to come. We trade almost twice the amount with the European Union that we do with the United States, the largest single-country trading partner.”
He said: “It’s no secret that I was not a supporter of leaving the European Union, and I called out early as trade minister what I described as the ‘post-imperial delusions’ of the Brexiteers. Back in 2016, they promised a world of Britain as a buccaneering free trade nation in a world where barriers were coming down. Sadly, what we’ve witnessed in the year since is a more protectionist, more regionalised world in which barriers have been going up.
“At the time we joined the Pacific trade grouping, the CPTPP [Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership] – which undoubtedly makes a lot of sense geopolitically for the UK – our own analysis made clear that the long-term boost to UK GDP from membership is less than a tenth of 1%. If you compare that with estimates of the structural damage to the UK economy from Brexit, you get a sense of just how important Europe remains to our future trade and prosperity.
“We’re already paying a real economic price for putting up new barriers to our European neighbours who, with almost half of total UK trade, remain easily our largest trading partners.”
Alexander was speaking in Mumbai, where he was joined by the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, and the environment secretary, Angela Eagle, as well as a group of mayors from northern England. He made it clear he did not support any particular method of achieving closer relations with the EU.
The ministers spent much of their time in meetings with Indian officials as they attempt to iron out what they say have been “teething problems” with the early implementation, especially for smaller businesses.
“There are always teething problems,” Alexander said. “We’re also having a conversation at the level of regulation to see how do we overcome non-tariff barriers that can prove to be an inhibitor to the kind of progress we want to see unless they’re addressed.”
Many in the government say a bigger prize will be to reach an agreement at next month’s EU summit, where Burnham hopes to sign new trading deals for emissions, electricity and agricultural products.
One hurdle to delivering that is the UK’s desire to discuss the protectionist “Made in Europe” policy, which British manufacturers fear will shut them out of a key market. EU leaders say they are willing to discuss British entry into that scheme, though they are also pushing for the UK to impose tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles, without which they fear the UK will become a back door into the European market.
Reynolds told the Guardian this week he would not impose tariffs simply because of pressure from Brussels.

Behind the scenes: Kyiv Independent's September digest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:31:04 UTC
22:31:04 KST

Welcome to the Kyiv Independent's monthly digest, where we share company updates, milestones, and the stories behind our work.
In September, we gave our travel series a home of its own, launched a new way to reach readers, saw our community's support translate into practical help for journalists on the front line, and met our community at events in Brazil and the Netherlands.
What's new at the Kyiv Independent
On Sep. 11, the Kyiv Independent War Crimes Investigation Unit presented its latest investigative documentary, Last Seen in Crimea, which investigates a system of secret prisons in Russian-occupied Crimea where Ukrainian civilians have been held without contact with the outside world, often without formal charges, and subjected to torture and other forms of abuse.
Olesia Bida, the film author, shared that the main goal of the investigation was to identify those, who are directly responsible for these unlawful detentions. “Systems like this do not operate on their own — they depend on those who run them and those who carry out their orders,” she says.
The documentary is available to watch on the Kyiv Independent Youtube channel.
Our travel series, Dare to Ukraine, now has its own YouTube channel. The series explores Ukraine beyond the headlines, from its culture and history to its landscapes and, above all, its people. All 11 episodes from both seasons are now available in one place. As our deputy chief editor, Toma Istomina, put it, the series "captures the heart and soul of Ukraine." We hope the new channel will help even more people discover it.
We've also launched a WhatsApp channel, giving readers another way to follow our work. It brings our field reports, investigations, analysis, and long-form stories straight to your phone, alongside a weekly recap of the most important developments in Ukraine.
We also have an update on a project made possible by our community. In May, ahead of World Press Freedom Day, we launched our No News is Bad News collection to help protect journalists reporting near the front line. Through sales of the collection, plus additional donations, our community raised more than $24,000.
The funds enabled the Institute of Mass Information to purchase 26 Vydun 7.5 FPV drone detectors for independent regional journalists working near the front line, exceeding our original goal of funding 20 detectors. The Institute had been seeking funding for the equipment for months, as many potential donors were unable to support purchases of equipment suitable for military use. The detectors provide early warnings of approaching drones, giving journalists crucial time to seek cover.
Thank you to everyone who contributed.
Events
Our editor-in-chief, Olga Rudenko, spent part of September meeting audiences and fellow journalists abroad.
First, she traveled to São Paulo for the Festival piauí de Jornalismo, held under the theme "In the eye of the hurricane: editors-in-chief in times of turmoil." Joining newsroom leaders from eight countries, Olga spoke about what it takes to lead an independent newsroom in a country under attack.
Later in the month, she traveled to Deventer to speak at the Nederlands Journalistiek Festival. In a session titled "The Kyiv Independent: building independent journalism in wartime," she joined Wendelmoet Boersema, the editor-in-chief of Dutch newspaper Trouw and a former correspondent in the post-Soviet countries.
Their conversation explored the challenges of journalism under fire, the importance of holding those in power to account, and why independent reporting is particularly vital when a country is fighting for its future.
In the meantime, Francis Farrell and Olena Zashko travelled to Bucharest, Romania for a screening of Can You Hear Me? The Invisible Battles of Ukrainian Military Medics, the Kyiv Independent documentary co-authored by them. The film follows a group of Ukrainian military medics as they travel from the front-line in Ukraine to the quiet forests of Sweden, for a short mental health retreat.
In other media
September also brought opportunities to share our journalists' experiences and perspectives with international audiences.
Our deputy chief editor, Toma Istomina, spoke to Canadian Affairs about daily life in Kyiv under the threat of Russian aerial attacks. The city is now under round-the-clock air-raid alerts, forcing residents to weigh the risks of carrying on with their lives against the need to seek shelter. Toma also shared her mother's experience of receiving a cancer diagnosis and undergoing treatment during the war, explaining how interrupted sleep and the constant stress of attacks make recovery even harder.
Olga's visit to Brazil also drew interest from local media. In an interview with Marie Claire Brasil, she discussed leading an independent newsroom in wartime. She also spoke to Poder360 about the debate over holding elections in Ukraine during wartime.
For a deeper look at the issue, you can also watch Olga Rudenko and our deputy chief editor, Oleksiy Sorokin, discuss wartime elections on the Kyiv Independent's YouTube channel.
Meanwhile, Helsingin Sanomat, Finland's largest daily newspaper, featured Kyiv in a story exploring how younger Ukrainians view President Volodymyr Zelensky. Its reporters traveled to the Ukrainian capital to hear their perspectives firsthand.
Special recognition
September also brought us two awards that recognized not only our journalism, but also the work that makes it possible to keep that journalism free to read.
Our chief operating officer, Zakhar Protsiuk, was named among INMA's 2026 30 Under 30 honorees. The International News Media Association's awards recognize young professionals making an impact on the news industry. INMA highlighted Zakhar's role in growing the Kyiv Independent's membership from 6,000 to more than 35,000 members, with reader revenue now covering more than 70% of our budget.
We also received the 2026 Online Journalism Award for Innovation in Revenue Strategy from the Online News Association, in the Medium Newsroom category. This marks our second consecutive win in the category. The judges praised our "authentic and transparent membership model" and its central principle: keeping independent journalism freely accessible during wartime.
Neither milestone would have been possible without the people who choose to support us. Consider joining our community of members today.

Archaeologists have discovered a sunken ship off the coast of Turkey that is up to 4,700 years old
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:30:28 EEST
22:30:28 KST

Archaeologists have discovered a sunken ship off the coast of Turkey that is up to 4,700 years old
Kyiv • UNN
Near the island of Kekova, they discovered the remains of an Early Bronze Age vessel with amphorae and anchors. It may be the oldest sunken ship.
Off the coast of Turkey, archaeologists have discovered a sunken Early Bronze Age ship estimated to be 4,400–4,700 years old. The vessel may have transported trade cargo across the Mediterranean Sea. The Independent reports, as cited by UNN.
Details
Although the ship’s wooden structure has not survived, archaeologists dated the storage pottery vessels and stone anchors found near Kekova Island to 2600–2400 BC. This could make the find the oldest known shipwreck in the world.
Previously, this status belonged to a ship that sank near Dokos Island in the Aegean Sea. It is dated to approximately 2200 BC.
Some of the amphorae found—large ceramic vessels with two handles—are similar to Early Bronze Age pottery from the Levant, which includes the territories of modern-day Lebanon, Syria, Israel, and Palestine.
The ceramic vessels were found scattered across the seabed at a depth of about 30 meters. The seabed is partly covered with sand and partly consists of rock.
One of the vessels resembled containers used during the Bronze Age to transport agricultural products, particularly wine and olive oil.
Near the sunken vessel, researchers also found two stone anchors with three holes and one anchor with a single hole. Similar artifacts have been discovered at other Bronze Age archaeological sites.
According to the researchers, anchors with three holes have parallels in Minoan, Cypriot, Anatolian, and Levantine archaeological contexts from the Bronze Age. The single-hole anchor is similar to those found off the coasts of Anatolia and the Levant.
It is not yet known whether these anchors belonged specifically to the discovered ship. At the same time, they may help provide a better understanding of the anchoring technologies used in the region during the Bronze Age.

‘Dune: Part Three’ Cowriter Brian K. Vaughan Has a New Comic on the Way
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:30:00 UTC
22:30:00 KST

Brian K. Vaughan would like to apologize. He knows everyone is dying for details about Dune: Part Three, which he cowrote with director Denis Villeneuve, but his lips are pretty sealed until December 18 when the film finally hits theaters.
“Sorry to be coy,” he says as we’re about to leave the New York coffee shop where we’ve been chatting. “I hope the day will come where I’m able to say much, much more. It was truly so awesome. I can’t believe it happened.”
Vaughan is in the city for New York Comic Con, but not to talk about Dune. Ostensibly, he came to the convention to talk about Paper Girls, the comic he created with Cliff Chiang that was turned into a 2022 Amazon Prime Video series. During the Paper Girls panel, however, the pair announced that they’re working on a new comic, Roam, a superhero sci-fi series set to come out in February of next year.
Roam, Vaughan tells me, came from a deep desire to work with Chiang again. They’d considered doing a short eight-page story or maybe a one-shot, but eventually they said “Fuck it. Let’s do an ongoing series.”
Vaughan has the kind of career writers of a certain ilk would kill for. He started working on comics in the 1990s and has been the pen behind favorites like Saga, Y: The Last Man, and Marvel’s Runaways. (Those last two got turned into TV series; the outlier, Saga, is a story people have wanted to see adapted for years.) He also served as a writer on Lost and created CBS’s adaptation of Stephen King’s Under the Dome.
Still, his heart remains in comics. “I think sometimes people are like, ‘Oh, are you just going to sell out, Vaughan? Are you just going to go to Hollywood full-time?’” he says. “But I’m only able to do work in Hollywood because I have comics.”
Here, he speaks about Roam, his worries about AI, and maybe a little bit about Dune: Part Three as well.
On Roam, his forthcoming comic with Cliff Chiang:
It's completely unlike Paper Girls, completely unlike anything I've ever done. It’s set in the distant, distant future. The logline, as it were, is that in the future, everyone will get to be a superhero, but only while they're young. We're trying not to reveal too much more than that.
I remember seeing The Matrix, and having no idea what the fuck it was gonna be about. That was such a delight. So we're trying to do that here. I've been doing this for 31 years. I started when I was a teenager. I have a Spider-Man story here and there. I did a little Batman, and Ex Machina was my sci-fi political comic that sort of deconstructed the superhero. But this is certainly my first true superhero book.
On his fears about AI impacting comics, film, and TV:
It's terrifying. My friends who work in previsualization and as storyboard artists, these jobs are going away. I've heard about editors going away as well. Show business is a business, first and foremost. I’m lucky to sort of have been grandfathered in. I think there will always be people who are interested in bespoke human-made stories. But the future is terrifying and unknowable, and coming at us very, very quickly.
I’m heartened by the fact I've got two teenagers who are so disgusted by AI and grossed out if they ever hear I used it—and I’ve certainly never used it for anything creative. But I do think we're getting pretty close to the day that someone could be like, “I'm tired of waiting for the next issue. Give me the next issue of Saga.” That's when you get to the point of, do you just want content, something that's a distraction?
In Roam there's an element of this as well; AI is a component in the story. So, it's something I guess I need to write about with my human meat machine to process, but I'm in the middle of thinking about it, as you are, every day.
OK, a little bit about Dune: Part Three, which he has seen:
I can't say very much other than it’s a tremendous, insane, ridiculous honor to be involved with it, and my contributions are modest. Denis’ true cowriter on this is Frank Herbert. The novel is the star. And it's obviously the greatest cast and crew ever assembled. It's a fucking beautiful movie. It's my favorite of the three. which I can say with genuine humility. I can't say anything other than it's just as wonderful as you can imagine.
I got special thanks in the first movie. I was doing a tiny amount of consulting. I was working at Legendary [the media company that owns the rights to Dune] at the time, and they just invited me in to see an early cut, which was as fantastic as the finished product. But I just ended up talking to Denis, honestly. Never before has a director been that talented, also that decent and warm as a human being. I wasn't anticipating getting this call at the beginning of three, but it's obviously a call I could not refuse.
I should probably just be discreet at this point. The movie doesn't need me to promote it. I'm reluctant to do anything that makes me sound more important to this process.
On the future of Hollywood:
I am a small worker in the world of Hollywood. It is changing so rapidly that who knows what it's gonna be like tomorrow, six months from now.
But again, I've got teenagers and I see how delighted they were by Backrooms, by Obsession. It feels like Gen X has been force-feeding them a lot of my childhood stories that we have gussied up, and they are clearly hungry for something new.
On why he doesn’t write adaptations of his own comics:
I've taken stabs at it in the past. Richard Price, the novelist, I once heard him say in response to “Why don't you adapt your own stuff more?” that adapting your own work is like being a dentist and giving yourself a root canal. Just because you can do it, doesn't mean you should. Let some other motherfucker handle that. I believe those were Mr. Price's words.
It's been constructive and a thrill to adapt other people, and I like getting to watch other people adapt me, but I've also been doing a lot of it for the last decade, where it feels like I've either been adapting or being adapted. I think that was part of the siren song of Roam. It’s time to break some new ground.
Denis says that to adapt something you love is to do violence to it. When I've been adapted, that has always been what I've told people. It is much more important for this to be good than to be faithful. He's a master of cinema, and cinema is rarely about people sitting in a room having dialog. How do you transliterate this to cinema? That's an alchemy that I don't understand. He's just unparalleled at that.
On Lost and why writing for commercial breaks was a challenge:
I love my prestige drama without commercials, but there was a degree of difficulty working on Lost and having a cliff-hanger five times an episode. To have that was such a challenge and so rewarding when you were able to pull it off. Can you write something where people are like, “OK, I'll just wet my pants. I cannot risk not coming back [before the break is over].”

Deputy Prime Minister Radosław Sikorski takes part in Warsaw Security Forum 2026

On 13 October, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs Radosław Sikorski attended a ministerial panel during the Warsaw Security Forum. Together with his counterparts from Norway, Germany, and the UK, he discussed the future of Europe in the context of ongoing changes in the global security architecture.
Minister Radosław Sikorski’s interlocutors during the panel were: Norway’s Minister of Foreign Affairs Espen Barth Eide, UK’s Secretary of State for Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Affairs Ed Miliband, and Germany’s Federal Minister for Foreign Affairs Johann Wadephul.

In his remarks, Sikorski also highlighted Europe’s enormous economic potential, which Poland is currently seeking to translate into specific defence capabilities to ensure security by deterring potential aggressors. The head of Polish diplomacy also recalled that the EU remains attractive in terms of culture and investment.
We don't just need to have culture and to be in the right in facing evil. The side that is right has to have the power to defend it. And, you know, we had all the right in the world in 1939. We didn't have the power. We had to create it
said Minister Radosław Sikorski.
He also noted the region’s constant determination in its responsibility for the security of Europe. As its example, Minister Sikorski pointed to, among other things, the growing Baltic–Nordic cooperation, which illustrates these countries’ commitment to building a strong regional wing of NATO. This was a particularly important issue, as Norway is the Partner Nation of this year’s Warsaw Security Forum.
Livestream: WSF2026 (DAY2) 13.10: The Return of Power Politics: Europe Between War and Rivalry
The ministerial panel provided an opportunity to exchange views between representatives of countries of key importance to European security. Such meetings also serve to improve the coordination of efforts aimed at strengthening European defence and Europe’s position in the world.

They also reaffirmed support for Syria's unity and sovereignty and Lebanon's efforts to strengthen state authority, as well as condemned Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia.
In opening remarks at Parliament House, Albanese said "it's never been more important for countries to work together in the interests of international security," highlighting cooperation on defense and security, humanitarian efforts, resources, and energy.
Abdullah also pointed to military and intelligence affairs as areas for enhanced bilateral cooperation.
Bilateral goods and services trade totaled Australian $348.7 million ($242 million) in 2024-25, including A$217.2 million in Australian exports and A$131.5 million in imports, according to the Australian Embassy in Amman. Major traded products include meat and fertilizers.

Finnish cities pushing for mandatory school attendance law
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:18:17 EEST
22:18:17 KST

Helsinki and five other Finnish cities are calling for stricter laws on homeschooling.
According to Helsinki Mayor Daniel Sazonov (NCP), homeschooling should only be allowed in exceptional cases, for example for health reasons.
In practice, the cities are proposing that in-school attendance should be compulsory.
"Going to school is much more than just learning defined academic content, it is also a social process," Sazonov said.
Attending school is also a tool for integration, according to the mayor.
"In Helsinki, many pupils speak a language other than Finnish or Swedish as their mother tongue; it is also essential from an integration perspective that they are at school and part of the school community," he said.
Homeschooling is not a widespread phenomenon in the capital. Just over 200 children in Helsinki were being home-schooled this year, accounting for about 0.4 percent of all pupils. The number has increased in recent years, however.
A total of around 1,000 children in Finland are home-schooled, with many choosing the option for health or wellbeing reasons.
Last week, the Helsinki City Council decided to tighten supervision of homeschooled pupils.
Supervision abilities limited
But according to Sazonov, the jurisdiction of municipalities regarding homeschooling is limited.
Not all home-school instructors have accepted more active supervision, Sazonov said.
He noted that there have been no major problems with homeschooling in Helsinki. However, he did point to concerns raised by the Finnish Security and Intelligence Service (Supo) that homeschooling can carry the risk of promoting radicalisation.
Supo's national security review suggested that homeschooling could, over time, heighten security risks linked to social fragmentation. Its report warns that isolated educational settings may enable the spread of extremist ideologies, including radical Islamist or far-right teachings.
Helsinki University terrorism researcher Leena Malkki noted that Finland should not close its eyes to these concerns.
"Finland is a society built on trust. Supervision, and even support, is not always the strictest when it comes to home schooling," she said.
Tampere is among the cities calling for educational law change. But according to Tampere Deputy Mayor for cultural services, Anne-Mari Jussila, radicalisation risks are not the reason.
"I would prefer to see children among their peers at school, learning together with other children," she said.
Tampere currently has about 50 home-school pupils.
Jussila emphasised that radicalisation is not a problem in Tampere, even though it may be a problem elsewhere.
Newspaper Helsingin Sanomat on Tuesday queried parliamentary groups regarding homeschooling.
Left Alliance leader Minja Koskela told HS that Finland needs to introduce mandatory school attendance, arguing every child has the right to education.
Some Swedes have moved to the Åland Islands, attracted by the option of homeschooling.

Iran targets Starlink as ‘tool of war’ with hints of more internet curbs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:17:34 UTC
22:17:34 KST

Iran targets Starlink as ‘tool of war’ with hints of more internet curbs
One official claims satellite internet could erode online governance in Iran amid war with the US and Israel.
Tehran, Iran – Iranian authorities have pledged to continue a crackdown against satellite internet service Starlink, along with further restrictions on the global internet as the US-Israel war on Iran continues.
Elon Musk’s Starlink, which is free of the heavy filtering and restrictions imposed by Tehran, is outlawed in Iran on national security grounds. The use of satellite-based internet services and the distribution of Starlink terminals are subject to fines and imprisonment.
It is one of the many measures imposed by Iranian authorities since the United States and Israel launched strikes on the country on February 28, leading to a prolonged and economically punishing war between the countries.
Iran’s 90 million people have undergone two lengthy state-imposed global internet shutdowns in 2026 – for three weeks during nationwide protests in January and for 88 days at the start of the ongoing war.
Mohammad Amin Aghamiri, secretary of the Supreme National Cyberspace Council, described Starlink as a “tool of war” for enemies.
“It is a tool used for command and control by the enemy, for espionage and information gathering,” he said. “We have several systems for cutting off Starlink satellite terminals.”
He did not elaborate on what measures or devices were being used to block Starlink, but one was deployed during the January protests and authorities were prepared to share the technology with aligned countries.
Iran is among several countries that have banned or restricted Starlink due to national security concerns.
It has set baseline sentences of between six months and two years for using or possessing Starlink. Importing and distributing the devices carry jail terms of up to five years. If paired with national security or espionage charges, individuals can even face the death penalty.
Aghamiri has called on Iranians to use domestic platforms, supported by what the authorities call the National Information Network. He also backed a tiered-access model, which envisages protected international access for selected groups – such as traders, researchers and journalists – during periods of internet restrictions.
A Tehran-based internet and telecommunications expert, speaking on condition of anonymity, told Al Jazeera that Iranian authorities use a combination of measures to block Starlink connections.
This includes the use of multiple jammers with different configurations to disrupt services, along with spoofed GPS locations to slow new devices being set up. They can also identify Starlink-associated internet protocols if they connect to local applications and services.
Authorities also try to physically intercept terminals using patrols and drone searches, or raid locations selling the terminals.
In June, Israeli politician Naftali Bennett claimed that Israel had smuggled tens of thousands of Starlink devices into Iran when he was prime minister, between 2021 and 2022, to aid antigovernment protesters.
Since 2023, Iran has also pursued the matter at the International Telecommunication Union’s Radio Regulations Board, trying to pressure the US and Norway, which plays a role in the satellite network’s regulatory filings, to halt transmissions.
On October 4, Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs summoned the Norwegian ambassador in Tehran to protest against what it described as a failure to act over unauthorised Starlink operations.
During a governance meeting at the end of September, Deputy Technology Minister Mohammad Hafez Hakami had warned authorities that Starlink could signify “the last nail in the coffin of the [cyberspace] governance” of Iran if it becomes prevalent, due to the unfettered internet access it provides.
He pointed out that the government blocked the messaging app Telegram after the cost-of-living protests in 2017-18, but had to resort to a weeklong internet shutdown for the first time during the nationwide protests in 2019. WhatsApp and Instagram were blocked after the 2022-23 protests, which preceded the near-total shutdown during the January 2026 protests.
“If this trend continues, in the next crisis we will have to cut electricity, because Starlink, as a new tool of evading state governance, is fundamentally not even dependent on our network,” Hakami said.
Starlink has allowed Iranians to send out videos of the protests abroad since 2022 despite state restrictions. Tens of thousands of terminals are believed to have been smuggled into the country since, but exact figures are unknown.
Due to the risk of a state crackdown, limited availability and financial costs, most people still have no access to Starlink and must rely on Iran’s domestic internet, which blocks most international services and thousands of websites. US sanctions and banking restrictions further impede Iranians’ access to global services.
To circumvent the many roadblocks, most Iranians use virtual private networks (VPNs) and other methods that grant access to the free internet. But those tools can reduce connection speeds, prove costly or provide unsafe connections that jeopardise user data, and become harder to come by during periods of state-imposed internet blackout.
According to the authorities, more restrictions were possible in the future if the war intensifies, after a relative decrease in violence since the June memorandum of understanding, which eventually lapsed without a permanent ceasefire, between the US and Iran.
Government spokesperson Fatemeh Mohajerani told a news conference on Tuesday that state bodies were deliberately disrupting the internet ostensibly to protect people and national assets from cyberattacks.
“It is obvious that due to the importance of our databases and internet-based services, decision-making bodies are sometimes forced to bring down internet speeds,” she said. “We don’t deny this issue.”
The authorities claim that they have considered removing restrictions on some platforms, although no action has been taken yet.
State-linked media late on Tuesday released a policy and governance framework document that the cyberspace council’s Aghamiri said has been under consideration for nearly two years but remained confidential due to security concerns.
The document offered no timeline for reopening any platform, and media reports said implementation had been halted by wars and protests.
The document says Google Play and WhatsApp could potentially be unblocked, while YouTube and Telegram would have to negotiate with Iran and accept certain conditions determined by the authorities to be unblocked. Such steps by the social media giants are considered extremely unlikely.

In Confronting China, The West Needs Partners in Southeast Asia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:17:00 UTC
22:17:00 KST

Leaders from across Southeast Asia will be meeting in Manila on November 10 for the upcoming ASEAN summit. This is the same date on which the China-U.S. trade truce was set to expire. While the September 24 summit between Presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump has widely been characterized as “heavy on pomp and light on substance,” it did deliver one tangible benefit: more time. The extension of the trade truce offers Washington a modicum of breathing room. With that extra time, engaging leaders at the ASEAN summit should be top of the U.S. priority list.
Meanwhile, Europe is signaling a greater willingness to confront China’s unsustainable trading practices. The limits of this relationship must be managed, so that Western countries can reindustrialize and regain market share. However, that effort should not come at the cost of compromising economic partnerships with countries in Asia.
Since 2020, ASEAN and China have been each other’s largest trading partner. Furthermore, Southeast Asian countries have come to rely heavily on China as a provider of intermediate goods. Economic partners in Asia are restrained in their options; for them, some form of relationship with Beijing remains unavoidable. Thus, as the West seeks to shift its relationship with Beijing, it must not do so at the cost of Southeast Asian countries who are willing to cooperate toward a fairer global trade picture.
The U.S. and European position is valid. China is fully integrated into the global economy, and continues to be a manufacturing powerhouse. Problematically, however, Beijing seems to have abandoned its attempts at fixing its domestic consumption issues, as it also looks ahead to an impending demographic crisis. While the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) may outwardly project that it can sustain a globally competitive manufacturing sector, analysis of its economic outlook reflects that Beijing is far more restrained in the kind of development it can pursue. Crucially, however, China’s massive trade imbalance is likely a symptom of internal factors, and not a concerted policy objective.
The CCP’s legitimacy continues to be derived, in large part, from its ability to guarantee domestic economic prosperity. As such, the regime’s targeted growth rates can be observed as a political goal, with overarching implications for the economy. In past years, to achieve a consistent 5 percent growth rate, Beijing has leveraged subsidies and targeted sectoral investments, while growing its exports. The net effect of these policies has resulted in a competition crisis marked by diminishing returns amongst different industries, which is further compounded by the problem of weak domestic consumption. A less ambitious growth target this year, coupled with Xi’s call for “high-quality growth,” signals that there is pressure to restructure aspects of the economy.
Further, in the context of both global and regional trade, Beijing itself has shown an unwillingness to keep trade relationships entirely separate from its political ambitions. A study of China’s relationship with trading partners, published in 2020, has revealed a trend of politicization over time. Researchers considered the case of China-U.S. trade, and their findings were intriguing: “A positive shock to America’s exports to China leads to persistently worse relations with China… It stands to reason that Chinese officials genuinely do feel that China’s relations with the U.S. worsen when the U.S. increases its exports to China.”
Trade activities themselves are not necessarily immune from political effect, and Chinese officials are sensitive to greater market penetration by foreign countries. In effect, this also demonstrates Beijing’s unwillingness to work toward a balanced trading relationship, and its preference for exporting more than it consumes, unless it is importing energy and commodities.
Southeast Asian countries have no choice but to confront this reality. Despite Beijing’s territorial claims in the South China Sea, China’s neighboring states continue to seek agreement on economic issues where it is possible. Interdependence runs deep, as evidenced by China’s $296 billion trade surplus with ASEAN in 2025. There is simply no other option for Southeast Asian countries seeking to move up the global value chain.
This does not mean that these countries are unaware of Beijing’s coercion, or that they are not responding. Yet, with few international options, they are exposed to Beijing’s attempts at intertwining foreign aid with its regional ambitions. To that end, while simultaneously increasing its trade surpluses, China has also created parallel institutions such as the Belt and Road Initiative, the Silk Road Fund, and the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, which have been used as leverage to reward countries that support its political objectives.
It is a fundamentally positive development that the West is looking to take a stronger stance against China’s global trading practices, in pursuit of a more balanced relationship. This position opens the door to Western reindustrialization and stimulates a push for innovation, while harboring high domestic political support within democracies. However, both Washington and Brussels must not lose sight of the constrained position of Southeast Asian countries, which rely on Chinese intermediate goods to develop and rise within the global value chain. A plan to confront Beijing without subsequent outreach toward these same countries will sacrifice national imperatives for willing partners; and those are hard to come by.
For Brussels, an alternative would be its accession to the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP), with the goal of stimulating market access between the West and its Southeast Asian partners. For Washington, the fact that it has become ASEAN’s largest export market is a positive step, but subsequent policies should seek to displace China as the supplier of intermediate goods without punishing Southeast Asian countries seeking to develop away from Beijing.

The complaints come as US President Donald Trump has ramped up pressure on Vladimir Zelensky to stop strikes on Russian oil refineries and hold a long-overdue presidential election.
The development was reported on Wednesday by Sergey Beskrestnov, Zelensky’s technology adviser, who claimed that SpaceX had imposed a speed limit of 100 miles per hour (160 km/h) on Starshield, its military-grade satellite communications service, without informing Kiev in advance. 
“Our defense forces were not notified of this restriction, and it has resulted in the disruption of several missions,” he wrote, adding that the move was clearly connected to the “current political situation.”
Later, he added that the curbs imposed on long-range missions are only part of the problem, as the restrictions also impact Ukraine’s interceptor drones, rendering them less potent in tackling Russia’s own strike UAVs.
The disruption was corroborated by four Ukrainian frontline sources cited by Ukrainskaya Pravda. According to the article, one commander provided footage showing two drones losing connectivity above cloud cover and becoming unable to complete their mission.
Ukraine’s 7th Air Assault Corps also confirmed serious operational problems, noting that satellite connections were dropping for 10–20 seconds at speeds of just 110–120 km/h, well below the reported 160 km/h limit. It also warned that slower-flying drones become more vulnerable to Russian air defenses, while aircraft used in mid-range strikes against Russian logistics could become impossible to launch or operate effectively.
Sergey Sternenko, a Ukrainian activist and former Defense Ministry adviser, suggested that SpaceX had acted at the request of the Trump administration. Neither Washington nor Musk has commented on the reports.
Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski also weighed in, addressing Musk directly. “Hey, Elon Musk, big man, are you playing politics with your products again?” he wrote on X. Poland spends approximately $50 million annually on Starlink services supporting Ukraine, and Sikorski had previously threatened to reconsider those payments after SpaceX announced roaming restrictions affecting Polish customers, a decision which was later rolled back.
Meanwhile, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Russia had no independent information about the reported restrictions but argued that “it would be better if remarkable technologies such as Starlink were not used for military purposes at all.”
Starlink has become a cornerstone of Ukraine’s military communications since the escalation of its conflict with Russia in 2022, with Kiev’s forces relying on the network for reconnaissance, logistics, and drone control. However, SpaceX has refused to enable the service for strikes deep inside Russia, with Musk reportedly believing that doing so would escalate the conflict.
The reported disruption comes as Trump has ramped up pressure on Kiev to stop attacking Russian oil refineries – something Zelensky said he was ready to agree to on the condition that Moscow stops targeting Ukraine’s energy infrastructure. The US president has also eased restrictions on Russian diesel exports following talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin, triggering Zelensky’s pushback.
Musk echoed Trump’s criticism of the strikes, writing on X that “Zelensky has gone too far.”
The Trump-Zelensky feud also turned personal, with the US president suggesting that Ukraine needs “a new president.” The Ukrainian leader’s presidential term ended in 2024, and he has refused to call a new election, citing martial law. Russia has since declared him “illegitimate,” arguing that his dubious status is a major obstacle to signing a binding peace deal.

US inflation rises to 3.7% as fuel costs climb ahead of midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:07:23 UTC
22:07:23 KST

Higher petrol prices and airfares pushed US inflation to 3.7% in September, adding pressure on households and the Federal Reserve weeks before the midterm elections.
US inflation accelerated last month as petrol, clothing and airfares became more expensive, adding pressure on households just a few weeks before the midterm elections.
The consumer price index rose 3.7% in September compared with a year earlier, the US Department of Labor said on Wednesday, up from 3.4% in August. On a monthly basis, prices jumped 0.6%, up from 0.4% the previous month.
The annual figure was above the 3.6% forecast by economists surveyed by data provider FactSet.
The figures underscore the lingering impact of the Iran war on petrol prices and the persistence of inflation, which fell sharply from a 9.1% peak in 2022 but has risen since the war began in late February.
Excluding the volatile food and energy categories, core prices rose 2.6% from a year earlier, up from 2.4% in August. Monthly core inflation held at 0.3%.
“CPI came in at 3.7%, slightly above expectations, and similarly core inflation was above predictions, suggesting that prices are feeding into the wider economy,” said Richard Carter, head of fixed interest research at Quilter Cheviot.
Elevated inflation has posed political problems for Republicans in Congress and complicated the Federal Reserve’s efforts to bring price rises under control.
A poll by The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research found that just 17% of US adults approve of President Donald Trump’s handling of the cost of living. Only 26% approve of his handling of the economy overall, a new low.
Markets react: Will the Fed raise rates again?
Following the higher-than-expected inflation figures, major US stock indices turned negative. Gold fell more than 1.7% to $4,105.50 an ounce, while silver was down more than 4% at $56.91 an ounce.
Oil prices were mixed, with international benchmark Brent trading just above $105.70 a barrel, close to its opening level. US benchmark WTI rose 1.4% to $95.50 a barrel.
Bond yields jumped following the news. The policy-sensitive two-year US Treasury yield rose 13 basis points to 4.93%, as traders increased bets on further Fed rate rises. The benchmark 10-year yield climbed about eight basis points to around 5.3%.
Inflation moving further away from the Federal Reserve’s 2% target was the “last thing” global bond markets needed, according to Robin Brooks, a former Goldman Sachs economist and a senior fellow in economic studies at the Brookings Institution.
Carter warned that persistent inflation could push US government borrowing costs higher. “It is not inconceivable that ten-year Treasury yields continue to march higher,” he said.
The figures add pressure on the Fed as it weighs whether to raise rates again at its next meeting on 27–28 October.
Last month, the central bank raised rates for the first time in three years, to a range of 3.75%–4%. Fed chair Kevin Warsh said inflation was not falling quickly enough towards its target.
“The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long,” Warsh said at a news conference last month. He added that summer inflation reports “do not tell me that underlying trends have meaningfully improved”.
Some Fed officials have since suggested they can wait before raising rates again, although their latest projections point to one more increase this year.
Higher borrowing costs can slow spending and growth, helping to ease inflation. But they cannot resolve supply disruptions such as those caused by the Iran war, leaving the Fed trying to prevent higher energy costs from feeding into broader price rises.
Higher fuel costs feed through to other prices
Warsh has said his goal is to keep the petrol price spike from spreading to other areas of the economy. Higher fuel costs have already helped push airfares up by about 23% from a year ago.
Petrol prices jumped about 9% from August to September, driving much of the overall increase in inflation.
Prices at the pump have eased in recent weeks, though they remain higher than a month ago. Petrol averaged $4.34 a gallon nationwide on Tuesday, up a few cents from a month earlier.
Higher fuel prices also raise shipping costs for businesses, some of which pass those costs on to consumers. Last week, PepsiCo said it would raise prices for some snacks and soft drinks to offset higher costs for fuel, aluminium and food ingredients.
The expansion of artificial intelligence infrastructure has also sharply increased the cost of semiconductors, computer equipment and electrical components, feeding through to prices for consumer electronics such as gaming devices, laptops and smartphones.

Sally Rooney says she can no longer sell books in UK due to Palestine Action support
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:06:08 UTC
22:06:08 KST

Sally Rooney has said she is being forced to withdraw her books from sale in the UK because of her support for the banned organisation Palestine Action.
The Irish novelist, whose books include Normal People and Conversations With Friends, said her public support for the direct action group meant she could no longer receive royalties from UK sales.
After Palestine Action was banned last year, Rooney said she would use proceeds from her sales to support Palestine Action. Supporting organisations banned under the Terrorism Act is an offence and she subsequently cancelled a trip to the UK to pick up an award, for fear of arrest.
In a statement provided to the Guardian, the bestselling author said: “‘In July 2025, the direct-action protest group Palestine Action was proscribed as a terrorist organisation in the UK. The following month, I wrote an opinion piece expressing my intention to go on supporting Palestine Action, which is not a proscribed or otherwise prohibited group here in the Republic of Ireland.
“As a result, the fulfilment of contracts to publish my work in the UK could now constitute a serious criminal offence. After a process of consultation and deliberation, and with my full agreement, my publisher Faber has therefore determined that it can no longer supply my work within the UK. I have made every effort to be honest with the public about my beliefs and intentions, and I am wholly prepared to accept the consequences.”
In a high court statement in support of the legal challenge to proscription, warning against its impact on freedom of expression, Rooney said her books could disappear from UK stores and the publication of new works in the UK could be prevented.
Her books have been critically acclaimed – she has been described as the voice of a generation – and hugely commercially successful in the UK. Normal People has sold more than 1m copies, while Conversations With Friends and Beautiful World, Where Are You have each sold more than 500,000. Normal People and Conversations With Friends were adapted by the BBC, and the former racked up 62.7m views, becoming the broadcaster’s most-streamed series of 2020.
Rooney said last year that she had been advised by the independent producer of the TV dramatisations that any payment to her for those series, both broadcast before the ban, would be a breach of terrorism laws if it knew or suspected that she was using the royalties to fund Palestine Action.
Section 15 of the Terrorism Act makes it an offence if a person “provides money or other property, and knows or has reasonable cause to suspect that it will or may be used for the purposes of terrorism”. It carries a maximum sentence of 14 years in prison.
Her UK and Ireland publisher, Faber, said: “Current legislation in the UK has led to circumstances where Faber cannot pass on UK earnings to Sally Rooney for her work. To sell a writer’s work and not be able to pass on earnings is an unconscionable situation for a publisher.
“As such, and in full agreement with Sally, we have taken the decision that we can no longer supply her works in the UK in any format. We remain the proud publisher of her remarkable body of work, which we will continue to sell in other territories.”
More than 3,700 people are believed to have been arrested in the UK for alleged support of Palestine Action since it was banned in July last year, most for holding placards saying: “I oppose genocide, I support Palestine Action.”
About 2,500 people have been charged, although none have been tried as a legal challenge to the ban is continuing and will be heard by the supreme court next month. Most arrests and charges have related to section 13 of the Terrorism Act, which carries a maximum jail term of six months.
Huda Ammori, a co-founder of Palestine Action who has brought the legal challenge against the ban, said: “Sally Rooney being unable to publish her work in the UK marks a new low in the escalating assault on free speech caused by the proscription of Palestine Action …
“[She] took a brave and principled stand from the moment plans to ban Palestine Action were announced. She has refused to compromise her convictions, even at considerable personal and professional cost. Her work should be celebrated and widely available, not driven off the shelves of British bookshops because she refuses to be complicit in the suppression of solidarity with the Palestinian people. No author should have to choose between their principles and their freedom to publish.”
Kerry Moscogiuri, the chief executive of Amnesty International UK, said: “Whatever one’s views on Palestine Action, we should all be concerned when laws intended to combat terrorism end up silencing artistic freedom and the ability to engage in peaceful political dissent.
“Writers should not find their books disappearing from shelves because of their political beliefs. Nor should people have to choose between expressing their conscience and pursuing their livelihoods.
“Sally Rooney’s willingness to accept the personal consequences of her convictions deserves recognition. There is a real danger that others, seeing the price she has paid, will decide they cannot afford to speak out.”
Rooney’s books were still on sale in central London on Wednesday afternoon, and Waterstones said that existing stock could still be sold.
Gian Carlo, a bookseller at Henry Pordes Books, said the same, adding: “Nothing goes to Sally Rooney in this case. We sell books of all types, they’re not connected to the author. I can’t say I don’t agree with her.
John Clegg, a bookseller at London Review Bookshop, said: “I ordered more as soon as I saw the news. I saw the number go down to zero, so I hope they go through. People are going to want them and we’re not going to be able to get them through Faber.
“Good on her for taking a stand, it seems a ridiculous law. If this thing convinces the Home Office to move faster to get rid of it, I’m all for it.”
