AI worms, ‘major’ incident fears spur safety calls at industry summit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:05:00 UTC
22:05:00 KST

AI worms, ‘major’ incident fears spur safety calls at industry summit
- AI safety dominated the Dublin summit, as experts warned of “major” incidents and possible AI worms. Demis Hassabis said current problems are “early warning shots”.
- Brad Smith urged urgent regulation, saying there are more safety rules for milk and ovens than AI. He backed “safety brakes” and mandatory incident reporting.
- The EU said firms must test models more and keep control, while OpenAI warned rules must not slow innovation too much. The AI Act now gives the Commission new powers.
AI generated
DUBLIN – From the spectre of refrigerator-infecting AI worms to warnings of “major” security incidents at the horizon, calls to prioritise safety in the development of artificial intelligence dominated an industry summit on Oct 14.
Concerns about AI guardrails have soared after models developed by OpenAI and Anthropic were involved in security incidents during testing, piling on pressure to regulate the technology.
Google DeepMind chair Demis Hassabis warned AI capabilities were growing fast, telling the conference in Dublin such instances were “early warning shots” fired by systems that “aren’t that powerful yet”.
“So the incidents aren’t that major,” he said.
“But they could be, looking into next year and the next couple of years, if we don’t do more work as an industry and individually as companies and governments on securing these systems,” Hassabis warned.
New AI models should likely first be tested in offline “sandboxes”, after other companies’ models escaped the closed environments used to assess their capabilities, he added.
Milk and worms
Microsoft president Brad Smith called for regulation saying industry and governments must “act with urgency” to create “real and effective safety standards” to contain the risks linked to artificial intelligence.
“There are more safety rules for a carton of milk than for AI. There are more safety rules for your oven than for AI,” he told the conference.
“We need to recognise that the power of AI has moved faster than the safety for it. Safety needs to catch up. And we’re going to need some new AI safety laws and rules.”
AI agents should be equipped with “safety brakes” that users could activate in the event of an incident and AI providers should face mandatory incident-reporting obligations, he said.
Highlighting worries about the technology, Smith pointed to a recent Anthropic report suggesting small AI models may be only months away from behaving like computer worms, copying themselves from one internet-connected device to the next.
As tech companies race to build ever more powerful AI directly into phones, laptops, cars and household devices rather than running it in distant data centres, Anthropic said such AI might eventually autonomously hop from device to device.
“I mean, seriously? I don’t want AI worms in my refrigerator.” Smith told the Dublin conference. “I just don’t want any worms of any kind in my refrigerator. And I think most of the public feels that way too.”
Speed and control
A self-replicating AI worm would be hard to stamp out, because there would be no central switch to turn off, Anthropic said.
The European Union’s tech chief, Henna Virkkunen, told the conference AI firms needed to invest more time into testing their systems to retain control over them.
“The competition is so hard globally that it seems that all the companies, they are not investing enough time and resources really to test their models,” Virkkunen told reporters upon arrival.
“They have to be able to control... these systems,” she said, noting that the European Union has sent information requests to all major AI companies asking what safety and security measures they have in place.
The European Commission gained new regulatory powers in August under the AI Act, the world’s most far-reaching rules to curb potentially dangerous uses of the technology.
But OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar warned a “balance” needed to be struck so that safety rules did not pull the brakes on innovation.
“We want to be open, we want to make sure the right people can review models, but again we need to make sure that doesn’t slow us down to the extent that we then end up behind the folks who are on the malicious side of deployments,” she said. AFP

Lebanon united on keeping UN peacekeeping mission in south: Official
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:04:29 UTC
22:04:29 KST

Wassim Seifeddine and Ikram Kouachi
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
Lebanese Parliament Speaker Nabih Berri said Wednesday that there is an official consensus in Lebanon on keeping the UN Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL) and continuing its mission in the south in accordance with UN Security Council Resolution 1701.
During a meeting in Beirut with Jean-Pierre Lacroix, the UN under-secretary-general for peace operations, Berri said Lebanon would continue its efforts at all levels “to safeguard its sovereign rights, protect its borders and liberate every last inch of its land from Israeli occupation.”
In a statement, Berri said Resolution 1701 tasks UNIFIL with monitoring the international border along the Blue Line, helping identify disputed points over which Lebanon has reservations, and monitoring and documenting daily Israeli violations of Lebanese sovereignty.
Adopted by the UN Security Council in August 2006, the resolution established the international framework for ending hostilities between Israel and Hezbollah at the time.
Berri said UNIFIL’s role “extended beyond security and military matters to include humanitarian, social, cultural and economic activities.”
He said there was an official Lebanese consensus on “maintaining the presence of the international forces and their mission,” pointing to parliamentary efforts to engage the international community and the UN on the issue. 
According to the statement, Berri and Lacroix also discussed the general situation in Lebanon, particularly developments on the ground in UNIFIL’s area of operations in the south, amid continued Israeli attacks and violations of Resolution 1701.
They also discussed Lebanon’s unified position calling for an extension of the international force’s mandate in southern Lebanon in a way that serves the interests of Lebanon and the region.
UNIFIL was established in 1978 following Israel’s invasion of southern Lebanon. Its mandate was significantly expanded after the July 2006 war under Security Council Resolution 1701.
In August 2025, the UN Security Council decided to end UNIFIL’s mandate on Dec. 31, 2026, after which a gradual, safe and coordinated drawdown and withdrawal is to begin over the course of a year.

Thales quadruples Belfast missile output
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher

14:03:55 BST
22:03:55 KST

Thales is now building Lightweight Multirole Missiles at its Belfast site at four times the rate it managed in 2022, and has committed £100 million to expanding that capacity further, the company told the UK Defence Journal after the Prime Minister announced accelerated deliveries of the weapon to Ukraine.
Phil Siveter, chief executive of Thales in the UK, said: “We are proud that the Prime Minister continues to see Thales in the UK as a trusted partner of the UK Government. Our Lightweight Multirole Missiles are designed and built at our site in Belfast, which has been supplying complex weapons to the UK for more than 70 years. With the support from Government, we have been able to quadruple our production to meet the global demand, and we are committed to investing £100m to expand this capacity further.
“The work carried out in Northern Ireland helps to sustain 1,100 direct jobs and supports around 700 more across our UK supply chain, giving the UK a sovereign capability it can rely on when it matters.”
Andy Burnham hosted Volodymyr Zelensky in Downing Street on Wednesday, pledging faster deliveries of air defence missiles alongside further military aid and tighter sanctions on Russia, with Britain pressing international partners to restrict Russian liquefied natural gas exports and to lean harder on Moscow over its attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
The Prime Minister said: “Our rock-solid support to Ukraine is vital for keeping us safe here in the UK and ensuring those on the frontlines have the equipment they need to push back Russia.”
All of that rests on a single production line in Belfast, a site that has built complex weapons for Britain for more than seventy years, through Shorts and then Thales, and it is the home of the Starstreak family from which LMM descends. Starstreak and LMM share the launcher and much of the surrounding equipment, which is part of why the line has been able to grow quickly.
LMM is a laser beam riding missile weighing around thirteen kilograms, with a range of about six kilometres. It is fired from shoulder launchers, from lightweight multiple launchers on vehicles, and from the Royal Navy’s Wildcat helicopters, where it carries the name Martlet. Against drones it is substantially cheaper than the surface to air missiles that would otherwise be expended on them, which is the characteristic that has driven demand since 2022.
The Belfast expansion is the kind of industrial response the Strategic Defence Review and the Defence Investment Plan have both called for, with onshore capacity that can be surged when a war consumes stock faster than peacetime contracts replace it.

Russian air attacks on Kyiv have intensified since late August. Air attacks occur both day and night, and Russian drones target not only military facilities but also civilian buildings, including apartments. Russian attacks on Kyiv have become more frequent
Russia attacked Kyiv with drones throughout the day, Suspilne Kyiv reported on 27 August. Air raid alerts were issued 12 times in the capital, drone debris was found in five districts, and at least four people were injured, the report said. Russian forces used about 140 attack drones against Ukraine throughout the day, more than 100 of them jet-powered, the Ukrainian Air Force reported at the time.

On 1 October, a Russian drone struck a school in Kyiv’s Solomianskyi district while 104 children were inside, Suspilne reported. Students and school staff took shelter, so no one was injured, the report said.
Russian attacks continue after Trump’s announcement of an energy ceasefire
Following US President Donald Trump’s announcement of an energy ceasefire, Russia continued striking Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, including in Kyiv. Russia attacked energy and critical infrastructure in Kyiv, Kyiv Oblast, and Kharkiv with 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 attack drones, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on 14 October. At least 600,000 people were left without electricity, he said. Later that day, an accident on the grid cut power to part of Kyiv’s right bank, energy company DTEK said.

Colombia opens embassy in Jerusalem
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
20:57:32 CST
21:57:32 KST

This photo taken on Oct. 14, 2026 shows the newly inaugurated Colombia's embassy in Jerusalem. Colombia inaugurated its embassy in Jerusalem on Wednesday as its new president Abelardo de la Espriella moved to restore full diplomatic relations with Israel, reversing his predecessor's decision to sever ties over Israel's military operations in Gaza. (Photo by Jamal Awad/Xinhua)
JERUSALEM, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- Colombia inaugurated its embassy in Jerusalem on Wednesday as its new president Abelardo de la Espriella moved to restore full diplomatic relations with Israel, reversing his predecessor's decision to sever ties over Israel's military operations in Gaza.
The ceremony was attended by Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar and his Colombian counterpart, Omar Bula Escobar.
Under de la Espriella, the two countries reached an agreement on July 15 to restore full diplomatic and economic relations, which took effect after the new Colombian president took office in August. On Tuesday, Colombia and Israel formally reinstated their free trade agreement.
In May 2024, then-Colombian President Gustavo Petro announced that Colombia would sever its ties with Israel, accusing its government of committing genocide in Gaza, an allegation Israel rejects.
In October 2025, after Israel intercepted a Gaza-bound flotilla and detained two Colombian nationals, Petro expelled Israel's remaining diplomats and terminated the free trade agreement between the two countries.
Colombia's embassy, previously located in Tel Aviv, is the tenth foreign embassy in Jerusalem.
The Palestinians see East Jerusalem as the capital of their future state. Israel annexed East Jerusalem after the 1967 Middle East war and declared the whole city as its "eternal and indivisible capital" in 1980.
The United Nations Security Council declared the move "null and void" in Resolution 478 in 1980, stating that it violates international law and does not alter the status of East Jerusalem as occupied territory under the Fourth Geneva Convention.
The United States recognized Jerusalem as the capital of Israel in December 2017 and relocated the U.S. embassy in Israel to the city in May 2018.
As the city's status remains disputed, most countries maintain diplomatic relations with Israel but keep their embassies in Tel Aviv or elsewhere. ■

WINDHOEK, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- Namibia has launched a compulsory vaccination drive in the Karasburg State Veterinary District, the epicenter of an ongoing foot and mouth disease (FMD) outbreak, a government official announced Wednesday.
In an update, Romeo Muyunda, deputy director for public relations at the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries, Water and Land Reform, said the exercise will begin on Wednesday and run in three rounds over three months.
"Animal owners must present their animals as instructed by the District State Veterinary Office, at the time and place to be communicated by the Office," he said, noting that the campaign covers all farms south of the B3 and C10 roads up to the Orange River, plus a band of two farms north of those roads.
Veterinary officials will conduct the campaign and livestock owners are not allowed to vaccinate their animals.
To further contain the virus, Muyunda said that authorities will construct a new animal disease control fence stretching from Klein Manasse to Naute Dam and onward to the Fish River Canyon. Construction will commence after the official notification to affected landowners, in accordance with the Animal Health Act.
Surveillance figures indicate that a total of 63,011 animals have been inspected, with 131 testing positive for FMD across 18 confirmed infected farms. The outbreak in the Kharas Region remains confined to the Karasburg State Veterinary District, he highlighted.
Addressing the recent detection of FMD in the northern Zambezi Region on Oct. 11, Muyunda stressed that there is no epidemiological link between the southern outbreak in Kharas and the northern cases.
As of Oct. 13, active surveillance had detected no new clinical cases or additional lesions in the Zambezi Region since the 12 positive cases reported on Oct. 7.
"The Zambezi Region remains at high risk of FMD introduction due to the presence of resident buffalo populations in protected areas, which are known carriers of the FMD virus, as well as ongoing FMD outbreaks in neighboring countries," Muyunda said.
He said the ministry is monitoring the situation closely and urged the public and the livestock industry to report any suspected unauthorized movements of meat and meat products violating containment measures. ■

EU proposes one-year delay to methane import rules
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
20:57:18 CST
21:57:18 KST

BRUSSELS, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- The European Commission on Wednesday proposed postponing certain obligations for fossil fuel importers to ease pressure on them due to high energy prices and supply concerns.
The obligations under the European Union (EU) Methane Regulation would be postponed for one year, it was announced.
The proposal came as the conflict in the Middle East has put further strain on global energy markets, driving up prices and raising the risk of reduced availability of oil and gas, the Commission said.
The proposed amendment to the regulation would delay monitoring, reporting and verification obligations for importers of natural gas, oil and coal, as well as methane-intensity reporting requirements for both importers and EU producers.
The Commission said the postponement would give importers additional time to comply with the rules, while helping avoid further pressure on security of supply of imported fossil fuels.
Nevertheless, it added that the amendment would not change the overall ambition, integrity or scope of the regulation, reaffirming the bloc's commitment to reducing methane emissions.
The proposal will now be submitted to the European Parliament and the Council of the EU for adoption.
Adopted in 2024, the EU Methane Regulation introduced phased requirements to increase transparency on methane emissions. It covers domestic energy production, transportation and processing, as well as imports of oil, gas and coal.
According to the Commission, methane is the second-largest source of greenhouse gas emissions after carbon dioxide. ■

Maldives tightens foreign investment rules

Unknown Publisher

MALE, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- The Maldives has tightened foreign investment rules in several sectors, requiring at least 25 percent Maldivian ownership for certain construction, real estate, auditing and information technology investments, while reserving some activities entirely for Maldivians, state media PSM News reported on Wednesday, quoting a minister.
Minister of Economic Development, Transport and Trade Mohamed Saeed said that, under the revised framework, foreign investors may participate in construction projects valued below 15 million U.S. dollars and real estate projects valued below 100 million dollars only if Maldivians hold at least a 25 percent stake.
The same local ownership requirement applies to auditing and information technology services, he said. Residential real estate projects valued below 100 million dollars and general sea transport services have been reserved for Maldivians.
Saeed said 150 foreign investments are required to comply with the new conditions introduced under a policy developed in line with the Foreign Investment Act, which came into effect in 2024.
Saeed said 29 foreign investments operating in sectors now reserved for Maldivians had already been discontinued, while 17 foreign investors had submitted applications to comply with the revised requirements.
The policy also covers wholesale and retail trade, logistics, general sales, and passenger and cargo sales agencies representing airlines operating in the Maldives.
Saeed said 17 businesses previously operating in wholesale and retail trade had expressed interest in bringing Maldivian shareholders into their operations.
Existing foreign investors operating in newly reserved sectors will be given time to restructure their businesses or withdraw from those activities, while joint ventures and partnerships with Maldivian shareholders will remain possible in certain sectors.
The Economic Ministry said the revised framework is intended to expand opportunities for Maldivian businesses while retaining foreign investment in areas where international expertise can contribute to economic development. ■

Language legislation in administrative matters

This legislation stipulates that a local authority in the Dutch-speaking region may only communicate in Dutch.

A strange country
The whole affair is a storm in a teacup, says Draye. “I assume that far worse offences are committed, and that any penalty will therefore be proportionate to the offence,” he explains. “In some respects, we are quite a strange country. In the meantime, surely we shouldn’t need to be afraid of dispatching a message in a language that is not our mother tongue?”
The Flemish nationalist party N-VA, on the opposition benches on Herent council, takes a slightly different view. “At first glance, this might seem like a minor issue, but in Brussels and the Vlaamse Rand, the Flemish borderlands, we can see where this leads when language legislation is relaxed,” says councillor Esther Deroo. “Think of medical procedures where patients are not assisted in their own language, or citizens who cannot file a police report in Dutch. Economic Watch: China's foreign trade maintains sound momentum as new drivers power exports
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
20:56:58 CST
21:56:58 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- China's foreign trade maintained sound momentum in the first three quarters of 2026, with both exports and imports growing rapidly and the overall growth rate reaching its highest level for the same period in five years, official data showed Wednesday.
The country's total imports and exports rose 18.8 percent year on year to 39.94 trillion yuan (about 5.94 trillion U.S. dollars) in the January-September period, according to the General Administration of Customs (GAC).
Growth accelerated through the year, with the expansion rate rising from 15.3 percent in the first quarter to 18.3 percent in the second quarter and 22.3 percent in the third quarter.
Foreign trade growth in the first three quarters was the fastest for the same period in the past five years, with both quarterly and monthly growth rates generally accelerating, said Wang Jun, GAC's deputy head.
"Latest international data show that such a growth rate ranks among the top among major economies, and China remains the world's largest trader of goods," the official told a press conference on Wednesday.
Wang said the performance could be summed up in four words: "fast, new, quality and open." Describing the "new," he noted that trade in industrial robots, electronic components, computer parts and electrical equipment exceeded 10 trillion yuan in the first three quarters, up 58.9 percent and driving overall import and export growth by 11.3 percentage points.
Exports increased 16.4 percent year on year to 23.2 trillion yuan, while imports expanded by 22.3 percent to 16.74 trillion yuan, GAC data showed.
In September alone, China's total imports and exports reached 5.16 trillion yuan, up 27.5 percent from a year earlier and crossing the 5-trillion-yuan mark for the first time. This figure also marked the sixth consecutive month of double-digit monthly growth.
Exports rose 29.6 percent year on year to 3.03 trillion yuan, while imports grew 24.6 percent to 2.13 trillion yuan for the month.
Exports continued to shift toward smarter and greener products. Integrated circuit exports surged 99.1 percent year on year in the first three quarters, while exports of electric vehicles, lithium batteries, and wind power generating sets and their parts rose 72.3 percent, 36.4 percent and 22.4 percent, respectively.
In east China's Anhui Province, robotics manufacturer EFORT Intelligent Robot Co., Ltd. has continued to see growth in overseas orders this year. After completing simulated spray-painting tests on vehicle bodies, a batch of its spraying robots will be exported to Italy.
The company's overseas revenue increased by more than 50 percent year on year in the first half of 2026. "We provide well-known automakers like Maserati and Volkswagen with integrated robotics solutions for smart production, covering painting, welding, precision assembly and the handling of materials," said You Wei, EFORT's chairman and CEO, adding that EFORT's overseas robot business has grown at a compound annual growth rate of nearly 100 percent over the past three years.
Foreign-invested enterprises in China remained active players in the trade expansion. Their total imports and exports rose 19 percent to 11.69 trillion yuan, a record high for the same period, with intermediate goods trade up 27.4 percent to 7.9 trillion yuan and high-tech product exports up 42.1 percent. Wang said more foreign firms are embracing "China Opportunity 2.0," deepening their integration into China's industrial and innovation chains.
"The global AI investment boom has kept overseas demand firm, and rising prices will continue to drive rapid growth in chip exports, which is currently the main driver of China's export expansion," said Wang Qing, chief macro analyst at Golden Credit Rating. He added that China's manufacturing upgrading has continued to boost exports of new energy vehicles and high-tech products.
The country's trade with more than 180 countries and regions expanded during the first three quarters. Trade with free trade partners reached 19.55 trillion yuan, up 30 percent and contributing over 70 percent of the total trade increment. Meanwhile, trade with other APEC economies rose 23.9 percent to 24.07 trillion yuan.
Trade with ASEAN grew 22.7 percent to 6.84 trillion yuan, that with the European Union rose 8.4 percent to 4.78 trillion yuan, and trade with the United States increased 4.1 percent to 3.18 trillion yuan.
Exports continued to shift toward new and higher-quality growth drivers. The equipment manufacturing sector contributed nearly 90 percent of the export increment, while intermediate goods accounted for more than half of total exports, underpinning global industrial and supply chains, according to the GAC. ■

Failure to activate Hormuz fertilizer plan could trigger food crisis, UN official says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:51:09 UTC
21:51:09 KST

Failure to activate Hormuz fertilizer plan could trigger food crisis, UN official says
BANGKOK, Oct 14 - A failure by the United States and Iran to agree within weeks on a UN-backed plan for moving fertilizer through the Strait of Hormuz could cause a food security crisis in parts of Asia and Africa, an official overseeing the proposed scheme said on Wednesday.
The United Nations set up a taskforce in March to facilitate passage of fertilizers through the strait. It is yet to implement the mechanism it drew up, but United Nations Under-Secretary-General Jorge Moreira da Silva said this could be activated within 7-10 days of an agreement between Washington and Tehran.
"It's absolutely crucial to get the deal in the next few weeks. Otherwise, we will miss the planting season," he said in an interview in Bangkok, on the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank annual meetings.
The White House, US State Department and Iran's Embassy in Bangkok did not immediately reply to a request for comment.
Iran has sought to tighten its grip on the Strait of Hormuz since US and Israeli strikes on February 28, using the chokepoint to pressure Washington, which has been pressing its own naval blockade of Iranian ports.
Before the war, the waterway handled roughly a third of globally traded urea — the world's most widely used fertilizer — and nearly half of seaborne sulphur, a key input. It is also a major conduit for global oil supplies.
Fertilizer shipments out of the Gulf region remained largely halted more than six months after the start of the conflict, the Washington-based International Food Policy Research Institute said in a note last month. Fertilizer products accounted for a "very negligible" share of the resumption of some shipping during a ceasefire between mid-June and mid-July, it said.
FIVE VESSELS A DAY
If the Hormuz disruption continues, commodity prices could rise by up to 81% for cereals, 66% for oil crops and 30% for animal products, according to an August report by the International Chamber of Commerce.
"If we miss that planting season, the productivity of agriculture would significantly drop and the impact on prices will significantly increase," Moreira da Silva said.
The proposed operation would use a coordination centre in Oman to register vessels and coordinate safe passage, with UN monitors working alongside local authorities at Gulf ports to verify cargo loading.
The passage of only five vessels per day through Hormuz could keep fertilizer supplies flowing to countries in critical need, Moreira da Silva said.
Ships would be tracked during transit, and additional inspections could be carried out if countries raised concerns about a vessel or its cargo, he added.
MULTIPLE SHIPPING CHOKEPOINTS
Iran and the United States have exchanged proposals through intermediaries since a June interim ceasefire collapsed, but efforts to reopen the Strait of Hormuz have stalled over Tehran's conditions and Washington's insistence on addressing Iran's nuclear programme from the outset.
The proposed UN mechanism could operate alongside negotiations on a comprehensive deal aimed at securing lasting peace and freedom of navigation, Moreira da Silva said.
"What we are telling them is, while you continue your discussions towards a comprehensive deal, let us work, let us do our job," he said, declining to specify the exact bottlenecks to a deal as discussions continue with both sides.
Beyond the Hormuz crisis, a deteriorating situation in the Black Sea region, where cargo vessels have come under attack, and an offensive by Iran-backed Houthi militants along a key Red Sea shipping route are compounding the threat to global food security.
"What we are witnessing now is a concentration of factors," Moreira da Silva said. "Climate crisis, simultaneous disruption of maritime chokepoints on the Black Sea, on the Red Sea and on Hormuz." REUTERS

Mücahithan Avcıoğlu
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
US annual consumer inflation accelerated to 3.7% in September, exceeding market expectations of 3.6%, as surging gasoline prices drove a sharper monthly increase, official data showed Wednesday.
The annual inflation rate rose from 3.4% in August, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
On a monthly basis, the Consumer Price Index (CPI) increased 0.6% in September, up from 0.4% in August.
Gasoline prices jumped 9.1% over the month, accounting for more than half of the overall monthly increase. Energy prices rose 5.2%, accelerating from a 2.1% gain in August.
Shelter costs also contributed to price pressures, increasing 0.4% after rising 0.3% the previous month.
Food prices were unchanged overall, as a 0.1% decline in grocery prices offset a 0.2% increase in the cost of eating out. 
Core inflation also accelerates
Core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, rose to 2.6% annually in September from 2.4% in August.
Monthly core inflation remained at 0.3%.
Prices increased across several categories, including recreation, used cars and trucks, education, airline fares, and apparel.
Used vehicle prices rose 0.7% over the month, while airline fares increased 1.2% and recreation costs climbed 0.5%. Communication prices fell 0.2%.
On an annual basis, energy prices surged 20.4%, with gasoline up 34.2% and fuel oil rising 74.2%.
Electricity prices increased 4.4% from a year earlier, while natural gas prices rose 5%.
Food prices climbed 2.5% annually, and shelter costs increased 3.2%.

Rising oil prices are not saving russia’s budget from falling revenues - intelligence
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:42:41 EEST
21:42:41 KST

Rising oil prices are not saving russia’s budget from falling revenues - intelligence
Kyiv • UNN
In September, russia’s budget received only $5.28 billion in oil and gas revenues, down 22.3% year-on-year. Compensation payments to oil companies reached $25.7 billion.
The sharp rise in oil prices in September did not bring a corresponding increase in revenues for the Russian budget. The Kremlin is forced to return a significant portion of the taxes collected to oil companies, compensating them for the costs of supporting the domestic fuel market. This was reported by the Foreign Intelligence Service, UNN writes.
In September, gross receipts from oil and gas taxes amounted to about $10.16 billion. After compensation payments and tax deductions, only $5.28 billion reached the budget—22.3% less than in the same month of 2025. The state effectively returned nearly half of the funds collected to the sector
The largest increase was in fuel damper payments, from $2.30 billion in August to $3.56 billion in September. This was 55% more than the previous month and the largest amount since April 2022.
As the intelligence service notes, high oil prices only increase the amount of such compensation payments. The more profitable it is to sell oil on foreign markets, the greater the difference from domestic prices, which the state compensates fuel producers for.
The situation is worsened by declining refined-products production. Due to the fuel shortage, the Kremlin is restricting fuel exports and increasing imports. In August–September, seaborne deliveries of oil products to the Russian Federation amounted to about 350,000–370,000 tonnes per month. Compensation was also extended to imported fuel, shifting additional costs onto the federal budget.
From January through September, the Russian Federation’s oil and gas revenues fell by 17.2% year-on-year, to $63.82 billion. At the same time, oil companies received about $25.7 billion in compensation.
Against this backdrop, Russia’s Finance Ministry lowered its forecast for oil and gas revenues in 2026 to $88.4 billion—14.5% below its previous estimate. In the first nine months, the budget received about 72% of the new annual plan.
For the Russian budget, the problem is no longer only the price of oil. Declining refining and fuel shortages are forcing the Kremlin to spend increasingly more money on maintaining the domestic market. If disruptions at oil refineries continue, high oil prices will not offset these costs, and the oil and gas sector will remain a source of increasingly weaker budget revenues

Kremlin comments on restrictions on Ukraine’s access to Starlink, settlement process

MOSCOW, October 14. /TASS/. Reports about restrictions on Ukraine’s access to Starlink, the settlement process and the potential weaponization of artificial intelligence were among the main topics of the October 14 briefing by Kremlin Spokesman Dmitry Peskov.
TASS has compiled the Kremlin spokesman’s key statements.
On Ukrainian settlement
- Moscow has taken note of the risk that Europe could sabotage agreements on resolving the Ukraine conflict: "The risk of sabotage by European countries does exist."
- Unlike European countries, the US is working to steer the Ukrainian crisis toward a peaceful settlement: "The US, specifically its negotiators and President [Donald] Trump, is making efforts to help steer the settlement of the Ukrainian crisis toward peace."
- European countries, unlike the United States, which is seeking a peaceful solution, are doing everything they can to prolong the hostilities in Ukraine: "Europeans are taking a different approach: they are doing everything they can to ensure that this war continues."
- There is currently a lot of "media hype" around proposals for a settlement in Ukraine, and much of this hype does not correspond to reality: "There’s a lot of media hype around all of this right now, and much of it doesn’t correspond to reality; it’s pure fiction."
- Work on the possibility of an "energy ceasefire" is continuing.
- No international meetings on the Ukraine issue have been agreed upon at present: "There are no agreed-upon meetings on the agenda."
- Efforts to resolve the Ukraine conflict continue discreetly and will remain so: "This work is ongoing discreetly and it will continue discreetly."
On restrictions on Ukrainian army’s access to Starlink
- The Kremlin has seen media reports about restrictions on the Ukrainian army’s access to the Starlink satellite internet service but has no further information: "No, we know nothing beyond the media reports that we have read about it."
- Brilliant technologies such as Starlink would be better off not being used for military purposes at all: "In general, of course, it would be better if brilliant technologies such as Starlink were not used for military purposes at all."
- It is too early to conclude that Washington has changed its approach to military support for Kiev: "It is too early to draw any systemic conclusions. We proceed from the information available from the statements that are being made."
- "We have seen numerous media reports on the matter. On the one hand, there are statements that assistance continues to be provided, while on the other, there are reports of various technical restrictions and disruptions in information supplies to Ukraine. We have been carefully recording it all."
On Russian assets
- Russia sees difficulties in recovering assets frozen by the European Union but will fight to get them back: "In any case, the Russian side will make every possible effort on all fronts, including legal work, court proceedings and litigation, to fight for the return of its stolen assets."
On detention of Japanese journalist in Russia
- The detention of a Japanese journalist on Sakhalin is evidence that Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) is carrying out its duties to identify and detain spies: "The FSB has made relevant statements [on this matter]. The Federal Security Service is carrying out its duties: if there are spies, they are caught."
On AI
- Some countries are weaponizing artificial intelligence: "Attempts by a number of countries to turn these new technologies into weapons, the so-called weaponization of artificial intelligence, pose threats to entire sectors of any country’s economy, and, of course, we are no exception."
- The technology itself remains necessary, as it brings many benefits: "Artificial intelligence technologies bring many benefits, improve efficiency and do a lot of good."
- Russia must be prepared for its use as a weapon: "We must be prepared for these challenges."

South Korea, US, Japan seek nuclear alliance against regional countries — Russia’s MFA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:29:04 UTC
21:29:04 KST

MOSCOW, October 14. /TASS/. South Korea, the United States and Japan are essentially working to create a nuclear alliance directed against other countries in the region, Konstantin Vorontsov, deputy head of the Russian Foreign Ministry’s Department for Nonproliferation and Arms Control, said.
"South Korea has decided to bring ‘peace and stability’ to the Korean Peninsula by brandishing the US nuclear bludgeon at North Korea," he pointed out at a meeting of the First Committee of the United Nations General Assembly.
"First, it deployed nuclear weapons to its territory in 1958-1991. In 1976, it started to engage in joint drills with the US that practice nuclear strikes and carpet bombings of North Korea, an activity that continues to this day. Now, building on this years-long aggressive policy, Seoul has teamed up with Washington and Tokyo, effectively seeking to form a nuclear alliance directed against the countries of the region," Vorontsov added.
The Russian diplomat highlighted "Seoul’s regular attempts to blame Russia for its own years-long deliberate escalatory moves, which are the root cause of the current crisis facing the Korean Peninsula."
"In Resolution 3390B, adopted at the 30th session of the UN General Assembly, the First Committee already outlined specific steps required to provide strong guarantees of peace on the Korean Peninsula, which include withdrawing all foreign troops stationed in South Korea and replacing the Armistice Agreement with a peace treaty," Vorontsov emphasized. "Since none of the above features in the long-term plans of Washington and Seoul, no comprehensive solution to the nuclear issue on the Korean Peninsula should be expected in the near future," he concluded.

Delivering the integrated force at DSEI UK in London
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:28:51 BST
21:28:51 KST

DSEI UK will run under the theme of delivering the integrated force in 2027, with four sub-themes covering innovation, industrial capacity, international collaboration and digital technology, the show’s senior defence adviser has told the UK Defence Journal.
Organisers are forecasting around 2,000 exhibitors and up to 60,000 visitors at ExCeL in September next year.
Air Vice-Marshal (Retired) Gary Waterfall CBE is senior defence adviser to Clarion Defence and Security, the company that runs the show. He left the Royal Air Force at the end of 2019, retiring from the Permanent Joint Headquarters as a two-star, and joined Clarion the following year. His job, he said, is to stand with his back to Clarion and look at the Ministry of Defence.
Themes have to be set at least a year ahead of the doors opening, “If you can tell me what’s going to happen in September 27, right here, right now, on the world stage, then please fire away,” he said.
The 2025 theme had to survive a defence review landing part-way through the cycle, and Waterfall said it did.
Sub-themes are built from research among the people who come to the show, Clarion’s own view of the market and talks with the department. “We don’t set the theme in isolation,” he said. “We confer with the Ministry of Defence.”
Defence and security exports used to sit in the Department for Business and Trade, and have now moved into the Ministry of Defence under the National Armaments Director. Waterfall said that gives the show one door to knock on in Whitehall, and he expects it to change what the department puts on its stand. “When it’s the MOD capability showcase, that’s going to be a much broader aspect,” he said.
Waterfall said the theme follows from the same reform drive, and that it is broad enough to mean something to everyone on the floor. “Everyone talks about integration and being that integrated force,” he said. “Therefore the theme for next year is delivering the integrated force. There’s a lot in those four words, but you can hang your hat on that.”
He said it applies to an SME with reservists on the books as much as to a prime, to CSOC or to a frontline command, and that it does not stop at the UK border. The four sub-themes are innovation and emerging technologies, supply chain and industrial capacity, deepening global defence collaboration and partnerships, and digital transformation, AI and cyber. Waterfall said the digital strand runs through all of them.
Choosing the wording for the collaboration sub-theme took some arguing inside the company. “We agonised, would you believe, over the global defence collaboration. Is that NATO?” he said. “It’s not just NATO.”
He cited Royal Navy, Royal Air Force and British Army units working with regional partners around Iran, and British activity in the High North through the Joint Expeditionary Force, both outside the alliance. Waterfall also made a case for the show itself as a form of deterrence. “Those that would wish harm to us will be sat there watching the power of DSEI, seeing it as that convening authority across the global allied defence sector,” he said.
Asked what rising British and European budgets will mean for the conversations on the floor, he spoke about procurement speed. Three years of war in Ukraine have made a 10, 15 or 20 year acquisition cycle impossible to defend, he said, and smaller firms have gained most from that.
“The winners are the small and medium enterprises that can work at a pace that outstrips the routine of a big prime,” he said. The primes have noticed, he added, and are buying into them while trying to leave them alone to work.
Waterfall said buyers now arrive wanting the part of a system that lets it keep changing. “I want it yesterday, please.”
James Samuel took over this year as managing director for live events at Clarion Defence and Security. The job covers DSEI UK, the company’s Japanese business and a conference portfolio that includes UDT in Europe and a UDT Australia launching in December. He has been at Clarion for seven years and has worked in exhibitions for 26.
Around 1,750 companies exhibited at the 2025 show, and Samuel is forecasting 2,000 to 2,100 next year, with the floor growing in square metres as well. The last edition drew 45,000 attendees and he expects 55,000 to 60,000 next time, “if there’s no tube strikes or DLR strikes during our week”.
Samuel said he judges the show on connections made instead off floor space sold. “We can’t just rely on the industry to meet itself,” he said.
Registration answers and what visitors then do on the show platform are used to push suggested sessions, events and contacts at them before they arrive. Samuel said the size of the venue makes that necessary. “It’s a kilometre from one end to the other. You could walk there three or four times and you’ve done that before you’ve even met anyone.”
The 2025 show hosted 114 official delegations from 66 nations, and Samuel said the list is drawn up with government. “This isn’t just us picking out who would like to come to the show,” he said, describing a test of whether there is real business for a delegation to do with British government and British industry.
Clarion is launching DSEI Germany in Hannover in March 2027, six months before London, and DSEI Japan follows in April. Samuel said its offices in Berlin and Tokyo let exhibitors and national pavilions carry one pitch across all three. “Their narrative continues, whether it be from Germany to London to Tokyo,” he said. Between shows the company runs smaller events of 150 to 200 people under the name DSEI Gateway, on the basis that four days every two years leaves a long gap.
Asked what he looks forward to most, Waterfall picked the first morning, telling me that he envisions, “There’s a Nigerian delegation talking to a Polish delegation. The interaction is just unbelievable,” he said. “We are facilitating this show for His Majesty’s government to stand on a stage and project soft power around the world, and that’s a real humbling factor.”
DSEI UK 2027 runs from 7 to 10 September at ExCeL London.

EU-China trade progress welcomed, yet trust issues linger
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:27:27 UTC
21:27:27 KST

Linlin Liang, Holger Weintritt and Kathleen Van Brempt during POLITICO’s European Resilience Summit on Oct. 14, 2026. | Davis Baatzsch/Dejaview via POLITICO
BRUSSELS — The EU and China are in a good place to talk after last week’s trade deal on hybrid cars, but challenges remain, panelists at POLITICO’s European Resilience Summit on Wednesday agreed.
“From the Chinese business perspective this is very welcome,” said Linlin Liang of the China Chamber of Commerce to the EU, calling the understanding reached in Beijing “quite balanced from our perspective.”
An agreement to halve China's exports hybrid vehicles to Europe was the main deliverable brought home by Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič.
Advertisement
The two sides said in a joint statement that they would keep talking about issues such as market access for medical devices and the Foreign Subsidies Regulation, an EU measure that scrutinizes foreign subsidies that distort competition in public procurement and corporate acquisitions.
Šefčovič will hold further talks with Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao in January, and they will meet again in March, as he pushes to rein in a €1 billion-a-day bilateral trade deficit.
Liang said Beijing stands ready to act if further talks go off track.
“I would like to remind all what MOFCOM mentioned: that they reserve the right to retaliate in case that things ... don’t go around as agreed,” she told the panel on Europe in global trade, referring to the Chinese Ministry of Commerce.
Kathleen Van Brempt, a Belgian MEP for the Socialists & Democrats, said the most important outcome of last week’s Beijing talks was that there was “some sort of trade deal or result.”
Yet Beijing’s aggressive subsidy policies remain a hurdle, the senior trade lawmaker said, referring to a widely cited OECD study which found that Beijing’s subsidies to industry are up to eight times higher than in other countries: “It’s not normal,” she said.
Advertisement
Liang said that China’s export success should not be attributed solely to subsidies, and was the result of “decades of investment in innovation.”
She also said there was “a super appetite” among Chinese businesses to invest in Europe, but that they needed to assess the profitability of the EU market just like European companies.
The discussion also revealed differences between policymakers and businesses over the EU’s proposed Industrial Accelerator Act, a flagship measure aimed at steering public procurement spending toward European companies in sectors ranging from renewable energy to steel and the automotive industry.
Van Brempt, the S&D group’s lead lawmaker on the file in the trade committee, said the parliament’s three co-leads are aligned on the bill. While the center-right European People’s Party was “very divided” over the measure, she said lawmakers should be able to come to a common position.
The bill’s “Made in Europe” provision is a cause for concern for industry, meanwhile, as it risks isolating the EU from global supply chains.
“I would be careful always saying, okay, localize, put fences up,” said Holger Weintritt of German pharmaceutical company Bayer. “Let’s make sure that we still remain globally connected and look for reliable partnerships instead of isolating ourselves .”

‘From liabilities to goldmines’: refineries eye record profits from diesel shortage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:26:27 UTC
21:26:27 KST

Days after Donald Trump announced a deal to import Russian diesel into the US in an effort to lower soaring pump prices, the world’s energy watchdog has warned that the global fuel shortage will drag into 2027.
Trump’s temporary sanctions reprieve was criticised for offering “too little, too late” to temper the sky high pump prices triggered by the shutdown of war-damaged refineries in the Middle East and Russia – once the world’s second-largest diesel exporter behind the US.
The International Energy Agency said on Wednesday that the shortage would stretch into the new year despite plans to ease trade sanctions or release emergency stockpiles, in a blow to the global economy.
“Record diesel prices are already having broad economic consequences by raising the cost of goods and impacting real incomes, economic activity, and inflation,” the IEA added.
Yet amid this gathering economic gloom some of the western refineries that turn crude oil into fuels are preparing to have their day. The global shortage that has led to high prices on UK forecourts is poised to hand them record profits.
“I prefer the world of disruption to the peaceful world,” the boss of the French energy company TotalEnergies, Patrick Pouyanné, mused last week. He said the energy crisis ignited by almost eight months of war in the Middle East had provided “plenty of opportunities if you’re able to capture them”.
For Pouyanné, the key to reaping the benefits of a global fuel crisis lies in owning a string of refineries across Europe that stand ready to cash in by selling diesel into a starved market.
Diesel accounts for 10% of the world’s energy consumption, and is known as a “workhorse” fuel for its role powering the equipment vital for sectors ranging from agriculture, mining and manufacturing to shipping and logistics. But by last month supplies into the global market had fallen by about 1m barrels a day from their 2025 level, owing to a combination of damage to refineries in the Gulf and Russia, and export restrictions from China.
The soaring costs for businesses and consumers have economists worried. They are already piling pressure on areas of the global economy from US farmers in the midwest corn belt to local bus operators in England. Many fear a broader impact, as fuel prices raise the cost of food, goods and transport across the economy.
However, for some of the companies that turn crude into diesel this is a very lucrative crisis.
Refinery ‘goldmines’
“We’re doing really well by being integrated,” Pouyanné explained. “Integration means your refineries in Europe, which you thought were liabilities, are suddenly becoming goldmines.”
These goldmines helped TotalEnergies to its strongest quarterly profits in three years this summer, after income from its refining and chemicals business more than quadrupled to $1.8bn (£1.35bn) between April and June.
TotalEnergies is far from alone in its good fortune. The biggest windfalls are likely to come from refiners in the US, where exports of fuel products have climbed by more than 50% in the past year from about 1.25m barrels a day to an all-time high of 1.9m barrels a day over the summer, effectively offsetting the losses from Gulf refineries.
The market value of three of the largest US oil refiners – Marathon Petroleum, Valero Energy and Phillips 66 – have more than doubled since the start of the crisis. The US listed stocks have climbed by a combined $215bn this year as their shares rose steadily to reach successive record highs. In the coming weeks these refineries are expected to reveal their largest-ever profits.
Europe’s largest oil and gas company, Shell, told investors last week it expects to make record profits from each barrel of fuel produced over the last three months after it reported its second highest quarterly profit ever over the summer. Shell’s refining margins are forecast to nearly double to $42 for each barrel of refined product sold in the July to September period, up sharply from $24 a barrel in the second quarter.
The companies are benefiting from the price difference between a barrel of crude oil and the barrel of refined fuel. The Brent crude benchmark price has eased back to oscillate around the $100 a barrel level in recent weeks, helped by an uptick in cargoes leaving the Gulf region, although given recent fears about the Middle East conflict escalating it is back above the $106 mark. . Meanwhile, fuel exports have remained constrained and global stockpiles of diesel, gasoline and jet fuel have continued to shrink. The supply squeeze means that while oil prices are lower than feared at this point, the cost of diesel is far higher.
Fuel flex
Refiners that produce diesel and jet fuel have fared best in the crisis. Some have been able to flex their capacity to produce more of the fuels in high demand; a strategy that has helped to ease the supply crunch and capture high revenues.
“Think about the early days of the crisis,” the BP chief executive, Meg O’Neill, said last week. “If you go back to March and April, the first front of shortage risks was in Australia, where they were very worried about diesel and diesel availability; and you might have seen news coverage of petrol stations being out of diesel. Our team responded very quickly.”
O’Neill, who officially stepped into the top job in April this year, told an industry conference in London that BP was able to ship diesel to its customers in Australia from its Rotterdam refinery in the Netherlands and its Cherry Point refinery on the US west coast.
“Roll forward, the next wave of the crisis was jet fuel in Europe, and everybody was saying, ‘Can people go on their holidays? Maybe we shouldn’t travel.’ Our refineries were able to adapt their runs to produce 30% more jet [fuel] in May than they did before the conflict, again to make sure that the customer need was met,” she said.
“Roll forward to even more recently, the diesel price pressures that we’re seeing around the world, and our refineries have adjusted back to try to max diesel.”
However, not all refiners have been as able to adapt to benefit from the fuel supply squeeze. Many are shouldering the “crippling” cost of crude and fast-rising costs of hiring a supertanker while manufacturing products such as naphtha and gasoline (petrol) where prices are well below the highs seen for diesel and jet fuel, the IEA said.
In north-west Europe, the profit margins for refineries – known as the “crack spread” – have fallen from $54 a barrel at the start of September to as low as -$11 a barrel earlier this month.
Ultimately, the shift to diesel could lead to a surplus of the fuel by early next year, according to the IEA, while creating the conditions for the next fuel squeeze: gasoline. If refineries that produce the fuel were forced to lower their run rates to avoid spiralling losses, then petrol pumps could become the next frontier of the crisis.

U.S. Marine Corps orders SAFE MULE loaders
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:15:00 UTC
21:15:00 KST

- The U.S. Marine Corps awarded SAFE Structure Designs a contract worth more than $10 million for an initial, low-quantity order of SAFE MULE loaders.
- The tracked loader lifts a loaded 10,000-pound 463L pallet from the ground and is light enough to fly inside a V-22 Osprey.
The U.S. Marine Corps is buying a small tracked cargo loader that can pick a fully loaded 4,500 kg (10,000-pound) air cargo pallet off the ground and still fit inside an MV-22 Osprey, under a contract worth more than $10 million to Las Vegas-based S.A.F.E. Structure Designs.
The company announced the award for its SAFE MULE expeditionary logistics platform on Oct. 13 in a press release, describing it as an initial, low-quantity order that includes operator training and ongoing technical support. SAFE did not say how many vehicles the U.S. Marine Corps is buying, which command placed the order, or when deliveries will begin, and it said talks are underway on a larger purchase expected in 2027, subject to final requirements, funding and procurement decisions.
The machine is built around the 463L pallet, the standard aluminum cargo pallet U.S. military aircraft use to move supplies. A loaded 463L tops out at about 10,000 pounds, and the SAFE MULE is designed to lift one from the ground onto its own deck and drive away with it, a job that at most forward sites would otherwise call for a forklift and a separate truck or a large aircraft loader that may not be available.
“The engineering challenge was to deliver substantial lifting capability without creating a machine too heavy to travel with the force it supports,” said Johnny Buscema, president and CEO of SAFE Structure Designs.
According to the company, the loader is light enough to ride inside a V-22 and can also be carried in the aft ramp position of a U.S. Air Force C-17 transport. Its adjustable cargo deck has built-in rollers so pallets can slide straight across to an aircraft floor or a truck bed, while rubber tracks let it move loads across unimproved ground where wheeled forklifts struggle.
A 2024 company technical sheet described an earlier configuration that weighed roughly 2,950 to 3,080 kg (6,500 to 6,800 pounds), was operated remotely by a single person and could work in mud, water or snow up to 61 cm (24 inches) deep. The same document listed a scissor deck able to raise more than 10,000 pounds to 165 cm (65 inches) and a towing capacity of over 10,000 pounds.
The version going to the U.S. Marine Corps uses non-radio-frequency controls, so it can be operated without a wireless control link. SAFE said that matters around ammunition and ordnance, where units limit radio emissions near explosives, though handling specific loads still depends on military safety rules and approvals.
SAFE announced in March 2026 that it had finished research and development on the SAFE MULE and moved it into production, presenting it as a platform for U.S. Navy, U.S. Marine Corps and U.S. Air Force logistics. The company’s other work includes aircraft maintenance stands and specialized military support equipment.

Iranian delegation attending WHO RC73
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:14:28 UTC

Iranian delegation attending WHO RC73
TEHRAN – An Iranian delegation led by Ali Jafarian, a senior advisor to the health minister, is participating in the 73rd session of the WHO Regional Committee for Eastern Mediterranean (RC73), being held from October 13 to 15 in Cairo, Egypt.
The event has brought together health ministers and high-level delegates from the 22 countries and territories to set regional health priorities and guide WHO work with member states.
The Iranian official is scheduled to deliver a speech focusing on different health issues such as the impacts of sanctions and wars on the health system, the supply chain of medical items and equipment, the health ministry’s website reported.
Strengthening preparedness and response to public health emergencies, expanding technical and regional cooperation, and benefiting from the capacity of WHO to support the priorities of national health systems are among the issues to be discussed by the Iranian delegation. Jafarian is also planned to hold meetings with health officials from the Eastern Mediterranean office and the region.
The opening ceremony celebrated outstanding contributions to health in the Region. The State of Kuwait Prize for the Control of Cancer, Cardiovascular Diseases and Diabetes in the Eastern Mediterranean Region was presented to three laureates from Iran, Egypt, and the United Arab Emirates.
Amir-Ali Hamidieh, an Iranian professor at Tehran University of Medical Sciences, grabbed the prize for his pioneering work in paediatric haematology, oncology and stem cell transplantation.
A distinguished physician, academic and pioneer in paediatric haematology, oncology and stem cell transplantation, Hamidieh earned his M.D. from Islamic Azad University, Tehran, and pursued postgraduate training in paediatrics and paediatric haematology/ oncology at Shahid Beheshti University of Medical Sciences. He later completed advanced fellowships in haematopoietic stem cell transplantation at The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center and Baylor College of Medicine in Texas, United States of America.
Hamidieh currently serves as Professor of Pediatric Hematology/ Oncology and Stem Cell Transplantation at Tehran University of Medical Sciences, where he also directs the Pediatric Cell and Gene Therapy Research Center.
He is the founder of the Iranian paediatric stem cell transplantation programme and the national stem cell donor network, which established the country’s first human leukocyte antigen (HLA) registry.
He chairs the National Council for Development of Stem Cell Sciences and Technologies under the Vice-Presidency for Science and Technology and is a member of the executive boards of the Asia-Pacific Blood and Marrow Transplantation Group and the Iranian Food and Drug Administration.
His leadership has enabled the development of seven paediatric transplant centres across the Islamic Republic of Iran and the successful completion of more than 2100 paediatric stem cell transplants.
 
Hamidieh has authored more than 100 peer-reviewed articles on research spanning regenerative medicine, gene therapy, immunodeficiencies and paediatric cancers.
He has also led clinical innovations in CAR-T cell therapy and photopheresis across many countries. Through his academic leadership, clinical excellence and commitment to equitable care, Hamidieh has significantly advanced the field of paediatric stem cell transplantation in Iran and the broader Eastern Mediterranean Region.
RC73 at a critical time for health
The opening of RC73 comes at a critical time for health in the Region. Protracted and escalating emergencies continue to disrupt health systems, putting millions of lives at risk, at a time when countries are contending with disease outbreaks, persistent inequities, a growing burden of noncommunicable diseases and mounting financial pressures.
In his opening remarks, Adham Rashad Ismail, Officer-in-Charge of the WHO Regional Office for the Eastern Mediterranean, highlighted the immense humanitarian and financial pressures facing the Region.
The official reaffirmed WHO’s commitment to sustaining essential health services and supporting countries through ongoing crises: “WHO must continue to support populations affected by conflict and crisis, protect essential health services and advocate for uninterrupted humanitarian access and funding. The people relying on health services in Afghanistan, the Gaza Strip, Sudan, Yemen and elsewhere cannot bear the consequences of shrinking resources.”
With the opening ceremony concluded, member states will discuss the Annual Report of the Regional Director 2025/2026, which provides a regional stock take of health progress, persistent challenges and WHO’s work with countries over the past year, helping to identify areas where progress needs to be sustained or accelerated.
The Committee will discuss two technical papers, “Advancing health financing for stronger financial protection in the Eastern Mediterranean Region: pathways to equity and resilience” which focuses on ways to build equity and resilience in health care funding and enhance financial protection for populations across the Region, and “A multi-disease elimination architecture for communicable diseases in the Eastern Mediterranean Region” which outlines joint strategies to tackle and eliminate multiple communicable diseases simultaneously.
Discussions will also cover health emergencies and polio eradication, and a panel on artificial intelligence for health will explore the opportunities presented by rapidly evolving technologies.
Member States will hold a regional consultation on the draft Program Budget 2028–2029 and review governance matters and resolutions and decisions of regional interest adopted by the World Health Assembly and WHO Executive Board.
The discussions and decisions taken at RC73 will guide collective action across the Eastern Mediterranean Region, from protecting health amid emergencies and completing the last mile of polio eradication to strengthening health financing, accelerating disease elimination and preparing health systems for the future.

Laser vision correction: can the surgery be performed before pregnancy, and what is important to know about the procedure
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:12:57 EEST
21:12:57 KST

Laser vision correction: can the surgery be performed before pregnancy, and what is important to know about the procedure
Kyiv • UNN
Planning a pregnancy is not a contraindication to laser vision correction, but the surgery is postponed during pregnancy and breastfeeding. A comprehensive examination is required before the procedure.
Laser vision correction is surrounded by a number of myths; however, in reality, the possibility of performing a safe and effective procedure depends on several important factors. An ophthalmologist, medical director and scientific consultant at the German Eye Clinic, Professor Oksana Vitovska, told UNN journalist more about who laser vision correction is actually suitable for, whether it can be performed before pregnancy, and what examinations are necessary before the procedure.
Laser Vision Correction and Pregnancy
One of the most common myths is that women who have not yet given birth or are planning a pregnancy cannot undergo laser vision correction. According to the doctor, planning to have children in itself is not a contraindication to the procedure.
The fact that a woman has not yet given birth or is planning a pregnancy in the future is not a contraindication to laser vision correction. The operation does not affect reproductive function, does not prevent a future pregnancy, and in itself is not a reason to change the method of delivery
According to the ophthalmologist, this myth may have arisen from another recommendation—not to perform laser vision correction directly during pregnancy, because of the changes that occur in a woman’s body during this period.
During pregnancy, hormonal levels, water balance, and the condition of the tear film change. Refraction, curvature, thickness, and other characteristics of the cornea may temporarily change. This matters for refractive surgery, where highly accurate measurements are important. That is why the operation is postponed during pregnancy. A cautious approach is also used during lactation. It is advisable to wait until hormonal levels, refraction, and the condition of the ocular surface have stabilized. But this is a temporary restriction, not a ban on correction for women planning to have children
At the same time, according to the doctor, temporary changes in vision during pregnancy are possible; however, they may be related not to a previous operation but to natural changes in the body.
In most cases, pregnancy after successful laser vision correction does not “cancel” its result. During pregnancy, some women may experience temporary changes in refraction. This can happen regardless of whether laser vision correction was performed previously. After childbirth and the completion of hormonal changes, refraction often returns to its previous state. At the same time, laser vision correction does not stop natural processes in the eye. Therefore, it is important to undergo surgery when refraction is stable
That is why, before surgery, doctors consider not only the current prescription but also whether vision has remained stable over a certain period; if vision is still changing, they may suggest waiting before proceeding with the intervention.
Does Age Matter?
Another common question is whether there is an age after which laser vision correction is no longer performed. Oksana Vitovska explained that there is no universal upper age limit; however, age does affect the choice of treatment method.
The usual lower age limit is considered to be 18, but what matters more than the number in one’s passport is the stability of refraction. If myopia continues to progress in a young person, it is advisable to postpone the operation
At the same time, another factor may emerge with age, to which doctors will pay attention.
After the age of 40–45, it is not so much the possibility of performing laser vision correction that changes as its strategy. At this age, presbyopia develops—the natural decline in accommodation. A laser can provide good distance vision, but it does not stop age-related changes in the lens and accommodative apparatus. For example, a person with mild myopia may be able to read up close without glasses. After full correction of myopia, they may see well at a distance but require reading glasses. This is not a complication of the operation, but a manifestation of presbyopia, which myopia had previously partially compensated for
Therefore, if there are already age-related changes in the lens or an incipient cataract, laser corneal correction may be technically possible, but it is not always strategically optimal.
In such cases, a doctor may suggest another refractive approach. Therefore, it is more appropriate to ask not “Am I too old to undergo laser surgery?” but “Which vision-correction method would be optimal for my eye at my age?”
Thus, age alone does not determine whether the procedure can be performed. Instead, a comprehensive evaluation enables the doctor to determine which correction option is appropriate in a particular case.
What examinations are needed before laser vision correction
According to Oksana Vitovska, preoperative diagnostics largely determine the safety, predictability, and quality of the outcome, so determining visual acuity and the number of diopters alone is not enough.
The doctor must answer three main questions: Is the cornea healthy, can its shape be safely changed, and which correction method best corresponds to the specific characteristics of the eye
And in order for the doctor to determine this accurately, the patient must undergo the following procedures:
"- Refraction and visual acuity. The current optical error and its stability are assessed; examinations are performed under cycloplegia.
- Corneal topography and tomography. The shape of the anterior and posterior surfaces, symmetry, and other parameters important for detecting keratoconus and other ectasias are examined.
- Pachymetry. The thickness of the cornea and its distribution are determined, and the future biomechanical reserve after the planned correction is also assessed.
- Ocular surface. The tear film, the presence of dry eye, and meibomian gland dysfunction are assessed. If necessary, these conditions are treated first.
- Anterior and posterior segments of the eye. The cornea, anterior chamber, lens, intraocular pressure, retina, and optic nerve are assessed.
- Additional examinations. Where indicated, OCT, a detailed examination of the retinal periphery, aberrometry, and other tests are performed," explained Oksana Vitovska.
In addition, the doctor says, a personalized approach plays a special role in modern refractive surgery. This means that when planning the procedure, not only standard vision parameters but also as many individual characteristics of the specific eye as possible are taken into account. Modern AI-based technologies assess all the parameters of the eye, rather than just the cornea; they make it possible to create a digital model of the patient’s eye, select the optimal correction plan, and predict its outcome.
Modern refractive surgery is increasingly moving from the simple principle of "removing diopters" toward personalized modeling of the optical system of a specific eye. That is why the quality of preoperative diagnostics is of fundamental importance. At our clinic, before surgery, the InnovEyes Sightmap platform conducts a comprehensive examination of the eye and creates its individual three-dimensional digital model — a kind of digital optical twin. Based on these data, a personalized laser-correction profile is automatically created
What else is important to know about laser vision correction
The doctor also draws attention to myths directly related to how the laser works.
Myth 1: "The laser burns the cornea".
"Modern laser systems model the shape of the cornea with high precision. This involves a controlled change in a microscopic volume of tissue, not "burning" the eye," the expert says.
Myth 2: "It will be impossible to operate on cataracts after laser vision correction"
"Cataract surgery can be performed. It is important to inform the ophthalmologist about the previous refractive surgery, as this is taken into account when calculating the intraocular lens," the professor noted
Myth 3: "A high prescription automatically means that laser correction is impossible"
"The degree of myopia is only one of the parameters. The shape and thickness of the cornea, the extent of the required correction, biomechanical risk, and other characteristics of the eye are important. For some patients, another technology may be more suitable," Oksana Vitovska emphasized.
