Scientists reveal why some workout recovery tricks can backfire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:04:20 UTC
21:04:20 KST

Scientists reveal why some workout recovery tricks can backfire
- Date:
- October 14, 2026
- Source:
- The Conversation
- Summary:
- Ice baths, massages, compression garments, and recovery supplements promise faster muscle recovery, but research suggests their benefits are often overstated, and some techniques may even undermine long-term gains. Scientists say the most effective recovery methods are far simpler and cheaper: getting enough sleep, eating well, and giving muscles time to rebuild.
- Share:
Finishing a tough workout always feels good. That is, until a few hours later when those uncomfortable muscle aches start setting in. This discomfort can linger for days – making easy, everyday tasks a challenge.
In search of relief, some recreational gym-goers are adopting the kind of recovery techniques once reserved for elite athletes. Social media and professional sport have helped popularize everything from ice baths and compression garments to massage and recovery supplements.
While many of these products promise faster recovery, reduced soreness and improved performance, the science is often more nuanced.
Ice baths
Few recovery strategies have received as much attention as ice baths. This involves immersing oneself in water that is below 15°C to boost recovery. But the evidence for this benefit is mixed.
Ice baths help ease inflammation, which research suggests can reduce muscle soreness and help athletes recover muscle function more effectively in a 24-hour period.
But there’s a catch. While inflammation causes soreness, it also triggers adaptations that build muscle. Dampening this response with ice baths may limit some of the long-term benefits of training – particularly if they’re used regularly.
When it comes to ice baths, side-stepping short-term pain may sacrifice long-term gains. It’s best to only use them when rapid recovery is vital.
Compression garments
Compression garments are commonly worn after exercise to speed recovery. The idea is that the external pressure they apply supports circulation, enhances blood flow to the muscles, and reduces swelling.
But while compression garments might make you think they’re helping as they reduce soreness, evidence showing they actually improve muscle recovery is generally less convincing.
A study from 2022 put them to the test. One group was given compression garments; the other group was given a placebo tablet that they were told was equally as effective as compression.
The compression garments were shown to improve circulation and muscle blood flow, while the placebo had no effect on these measures. This suggests the effects of compression garments on recovery are physiological and aren’t simply due to expectation or perception.
However, whether these changes meaningfully improve performance is less clear. Although emerging evidence suggests compression garments genuinely affect some markers of recovery, this is unlikely to directly restore muscle function.
So, compression garments may mainly help because they make you feel better recovered.
Massage
Massage is one of the few recovery interventions with relatively consistent scientific support. It can reduce soreness and improve perceived recovery after exercise.
It’s not currently clear what mechanisms actually trigger the recovery benefits of massage. But it could be due to the fact that massage reduces muscle stiffness, improves circulation and boosts relaxation.
But although athletes feel less sore and perceptions of recovery are improved after a massage, objective measures of performance and muscle function are modest and inconsistent.
Massage might ease the discomfort of training, but don’t expect miraculous performance restoration.
Recovery supplements
The nutrition supplement market is a big business, with hundreds of brightly coloured recovery drinks and capsules promising reduced soreness and faster recovery. But not all supplements are created equal. Some appear to confer small benefits, while some come with hype that science doesn’t back up.
Whey protein, for instance, is a well-researched supplement. Rich in amino acids (the building blocks of protein), it stimulates muscle protein synthesis – the process which helps your muscles grow. Whey protein is shown to have small-to-moderate benefits for muscle recovery – but evidence that it can alleviate soreness is inconsistent.
Branch chain amino acids (BCAAs) are widely-used supplements that typically contain a mixture of the amino acids leucine, isoleucine and valine. BCAAs are popular because it’s believed the leucine they contain switches on protein synthesis.
Yet despite their popularity, BCAAs appear less effective than complete protein sources for muscle recovery. This is because muscle repair requires all essential amino acids – not just the ones found in BCAAs. Food sources such as chicken, beef, salmon and tofu contain all the essential amino acids.
Tart cherry juice is a relatively new supplement in the fitness world. It’s rich in polyphenols – plant compounds that are said to have anti-inflammatory and antioxidant (reducing or preventing cell damage) effects. It’s for these reasons that tart cherry juice is thought to help reduce muscle damage and soreness.
Although this is still an emerging area of research, evidence suggests these compounds have small-to-moderate effects on reducing soreness after workouts, and may also help restore muscular strength and power.
Omega-3 (fish oil) supplements are often championed as a way to reduce inflammation and accelerate recovery after exercise. While some research suggests they can modestly reduce muscle soreness and help preserve muscle function after strenuous exercise, results are far from consistent. As such, omega-3 supplements are unlikely to vastly improve recovery.
Importantly, all of these nutrients can be obtained from a healthy, balanced diet. Science also shows that it’s better to get these nutrients from whole foods over expensive supplements, as whole foods provide other important nutrients that may interact synergistically to support health.
What actually works?
Popular recovery techniques might have small benefits for reducing feelings of soreness, but they don’t actually tend to restore muscle function all that much. Instead, the strongest evidence for good recovery comes from the basics:
- Prioritize sleep: Get 7-9 hours of sleep per night so the body can conduct vital recovery and adaptive processes.
- Fuel properly: Consume 20-40g of protein after exercise for muscle repair and adequate carbohydrate intake to replenish energy stores.
- Train smart: Pair good sleep and nutrition with a sensible, well-structured training plan. This includes allowing rest days between sessions, challenging yourself a bit more each time, and scheduling easier sessions when needed to allow recovery.
So, perhaps the biggest lesson here is that recovery cannot be bottled and sold.
Story Source:
Materials provided by The Conversation. Original written by Max Davis, Postgraduate Research Student, Centre for Nutrition, Exercise and Metabolism, University of Bath. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

What is dengue virus?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:02:47 UTC
21:02:47 KST

More than 2.2 million dengue cases and nearly 1,200 deaths were reported across 97 countries and territories in the first eight months of 2026, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).
In October, Bangladesh's reported total surpassed 103,000 cases and 300 deaths, while Cuba has recorded 11,235 cases so far in 2026. Florida is also experiencing the largest dengue outbreak in any US state in decades, with nearly 300 locally acquired cases reported this year.
One of the world's fastest-growing mosquito-borne viral diseases, dengue has expanded its geographic reach in recent decades. Climate crisis-linked rising temperatures and rapid urbanisation are among the factors contributing to its spread.
About half the world's population is now at risk, with an estimated 100–400 million infections occurring annually, according to WHO.

The operation was designed to reach dealers behind the drug supply chains operating in Jerusalem. According to police, the reputation the agent had built in the criminal underworld allowed him to gain the trust of dealers and carry out dozens of controlled drug transactions under the direction of YAMAR's undercover agents division.
During the operation, the agent purchased commercial quantities of cocaine, ecstasy, and other drugs, with a total value of hundreds of thousands of shekels. The transactions were conducted under the supervision of the Jerusalem District Attorney's Office, and the evidence gathered was used to build cases against the suspects.
When the investigation entered its overt phase, officers from the Jerusalem District and other police districts, along with Border Police officers, National Guard personnel, and the canine unit, launched the arrest operation.
During searches, police seized more than NIS 100,000 in cash, drugs, and 12 vehicles suspected of having been used to transport drugs and carry out transactions. Police intend to seek the forfeiture of the vehicles as part of the subsequent legal proceedings.
Operation aimed to undermine trust among criminals, police say
At a ceremony on Wednesday marking the agent's public unveiling, Jerusalem District Police Commander Maj.-Gen. Avshalom Peled said the operation was intended not only to target drug suppliers but also to undermine trust among criminals.
"We can certainly say this morning that we achieved the two main objectives we set for this operation. The first was to strike at the criminals operating the supply chains and bringing drugs into the capital, targeting those in their closest circles. The second was to undermine the trust between criminals and their ability to rely on one another, thereby making it harder for them to operate," Peled said.
He added, "No criminal involved in this field knows this morning whether the next deal will be the one that ends his criminal career and puts him behind bars."
The suspects are expected to be brought before a court later Wednesday for hearings on extending their detention. The investigation remains ongoing.

First ever Israeli fashion museum anticipated to open in Tel Aviv in early 2027

2026-10-14

21:01:41 KST

Israel's first museum dedicated entirely to fashion as a cultural field is expected to open in Tel Aviv in early 2027, marking a new chapter for fashion exhibitions in the country.
The Tel Aviv Fashion Museum, a joint initiative by Azrieli Group and fashion historian and curator Dr. Ya'ara Keydar, will be housed at Azrieli Sarona.
In Paris, London, and New York, fashion museums have long been part of the cultural landscape, while fashion exhibitions at the Metropolitan Museum of Art attract blockbuster crowds. In Israel, by contrast, fashion has entered exhibition spaces only through a handful of shows. The opening of the new museum is expected to change that.
The museum is a joint venture between Azrieli Group, led by CEO Dana Azrieli, and Keydar, and the project has been underway for about three years. Located at Azrieli Sarona, it will cover approximately 1,150 square meters across three floors and include exhibition spaces for rotating shows, an auditorium for lectures and events, and a museum shop.
Alongside the exhibitions, the museum plans to offer educational activities, guided tours, and themed evenings. Its founders aim to attract more than 250,000 visitors annually.
Azrieli malls intertwined with fashion industry
The choice of location is no coincidence. Azrieli operates some of Israel's largest shopping malls, and the museum continues the group's ties to the fashion industry.
"The group's malls are spaces where the public encounters brands, designers, and trends from Israel and around the world, and the museum expands on that encounter," Dana Azrieli said.
She also described a personal connection to the world of fashion: Her grandfather, Rafael Hirsch Azrilovich, was a tailor and workshop owner in Poland.
Keydar is perhaps the figure most closely associated with bringing fashion into Israeli museums. Over the past decade, she has curated 12 exhibitions in Israel and abroad, including four presented at the Design Museum Holon: an exhibition dedicated to Ronit Elkabetz, The Ball, an exhibition on Alber Elbaz, and Heroines. Together, the four exhibitions attracted more than half a million visitors.
A graduate of the fashion design department at Shenkar College of Engineering, Design and Art, Keydar holds a master's degree from New York University and a doctorate from the Hebrew University of Jerusalem. She also trained at the Metropolitan Museum of Art's Costume Institute.
Museum will promote Israeli designers, build relationships with institutions abroad
According to Keydar, the museum will present original exhibitions, promote Israeli designers, and develop relationships with institutions abroad.
"Especially in a complex reality, we need spaces of beauty," she said.
Ilan Jarbi, the group's director of strategic content initiatives and a partner in establishing the museum, added that the opportunity to build a museum from scratch makes it possible to rethink both exhibitions and the visitor experience.
The theme of the museum's inaugural exhibition will be revealed at a later date.

Elections delayed: A generation of Palestinians is being denied its right to choose - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:01:40 UTC
21:01:40 KST

What pains me most about the postponement of the Palestinian elections is that I know the faces of those who were waiting for them. I spoke with them, heard their dreams, and saw how the prospect of voting restored some of their confidence in themselves and their country. They were not expecting a miracle. They wanted a simple right: to choose their representatives and have a say in their future. Then the door was closed.
Based on my close observation of the political process leading up to the decision, I hold Vice President Hussein al-Sheikh and Jamil Mezher primarily politically responsible for pushing for this postponement. This does not absolve others of responsibility. But it prevents those who drove the decision from hiding behind vague phrases about “national consensus” and “creating the right conditions.” Palestinians have the right to know who closed the door, and why. Those responsible have a duty to answer.
In my assessment, Sheikh worked persistently to prevent the election decree from being issued last July. Once it was issued, he continued his efforts to cancel the date it had set. He succeeded in securing the postponement. The painful irony is that his success in closing the path to elections followed a series of failures in areas that should have opened a way out of the crisis.
Postponement of the elections
Internal dialogue within Fatah and national dialogue were used to justify the postponement. Yet these are two processes the vice president helped lead over many years. Numerous capitals hosted lengthy meetings without achieving reconciliation or ending the division.
How does the failure of dialogue become a reason to deny people elections? Why should citizens pay the price for their leadership’s failures and then be denied the democratic means to hold it accountable?
As for Palestinian-American relations, where is the breakthrough ordinary citizens can see? And as for civilian coordination with Israel, ask the worker cut off from his job, the student arriving late to university, or the employee who leaves home before dawn without knowing when he will arrive.
The occupation bears direct responsibility for the checkpoints, restrictions, and humiliation. But the Palestinian official entrusted with coordination must also be held accountable for the results he has achieved in protecting people’s interests. It is not enough for the office to remain in place while citizens’ lives become harder every day.
Holding leadership accountable
I have known Sheikh since his release from prison in the early 1990s, after many years of detention. At the time, I headed Fatah’s youth movement in Jerusalem and served in its leadership across the West Bank and Gaza Strip. He was a member of Fatah’s Higher Movement Committee: well liked, cheerful, and close to ordinary people and the youth movement’s activists. We had a strong relationship, as he did with many leaders of our generation.
I do not know what these long years have done to the leader we once knew. But I know that the young man who once defended his generation’s right to participate has now become, in my assessment, one of the leading figures denying that same right to a new generation.
These young people are present within Fatah, too. In recent weeks, I saw its members and activists eager to stand as candidates and participate. According to the information I followed, more than 430 people in Hebron alone applied for a place on the movement’s electoral list, including many young grassroots leaders. This was a clear expression of a desire to take part in political life, and of talent waiting for an opportunity, even within the organization to which the vice president belongs.
As for Mezher, deputy secretary-general of the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine, who holds a leading role while Secretary-General Ahmad Sa’adat remains imprisoned, his responsibility raises a question no less painful: How can an organization with such a substantial political history and popular following accept a role in closing the path to political renewal?
For me, that question has a face and a name: Nidal al-Rabadi.
He was my friend and schoolmate, and a supporter of the Popular Front. During a demonstration in Jerusalem in 1988, a bullet struck him and he fell beside me. We were 15. Lying on the ground, he looked at me and spoke his last words: “Don’t leave me.”
I have never left him behind in my memory. To this day, I keep his photograph in my home beside those of my children, and I cannot hold back my tears whenever his name is mentioned.
When I think about Mezher’s position on the elections, I remember Rabadi and ask: How do we honor that generation by denying its children the right to choose? What future do we preserve for their sacrifices if young people remain outside our institutions, waiting for permission to participate from those who have held their positions for decades? I invoke Rabadi because politics, to me, means responsibility toward people’s lives and toward those who died believing their sacrifices would open a better path for future generations.
The Popular Front was once the second-largest force in the Palestine Liberation Organization, with a clear grassroots presence during the First Intifada. In my assessment, that presence has diminished considerably over the years. Recently, I have witnessed young people and activists moving from its ranks to other political groups and electoral lists, including Masar Jadid.
This phenomenon extends beyond any single organization. Many of my colleagues in Masar Jadid and I came from other political movements. We brought our history and convictions with us, but we sought a space where we could work, make a difference, and participate. When organizations fail to make room for their members’ abilities, people look for other doors. Postponing elections will not resolve this alienation. It will deepen it.
The cost of delay
The cost of waiting is visible in almost every Palestinian household. Employees receive delayed portions of their salaries, workers have lost their incomes since October 2023, and families borrow money to pay rent and buy food. I have met people overwhelmed by loans, checks, and obligations they can no longer meet. Fear of creditors and the courts has become part of their daily lives.
In education, the financial crisis affects both regular schooling and teachers’ lives. When a teacher must seek additional work or sell goods on the street to support a family and afford the journey to school, the future of all our children is at risk.
In Gaza, families – many displaced into tents – are approaching a third winter since the war began. Mothers and fathers spend their days searching for the bare minimum of food, water, and medicine for their children.
Amid these conditions, I spoke for hours every day with young men and women from Gaza by phone, Zoom, and social media. Their education, knowledge, and capacity to think and act impressed me. I was moved by the hope in their voices simply because a political organization existed that allowed them to express their views and participate.
For them, elections offered a chance to become decision-makers in a society accustomed to treating them as recipients of aid. How painful it is to see these abilities buried once again beneath a closed bureaucracy and leaders who refuse to make room for them.
There are Palestinians approaching 40 who have never once voted in a national election. There are leaders who have held their positions for most of these young people’s lives. This imbalance cannot be corrected through more waiting or through dialogue that continues for years without restoring people’s rights – especially when the cost of postponement extends beyond our internal affairs.
French President Emmanuel Macron invested significant political effort in supporting recognition of Palestinian statehood and advancing an international path toward a two-state solution. Those efforts were linked to Palestinian commitments to reform, renew democratic legitimacy, and hold elections.
When we postpone this vote again, we confront our partners with a difficult question: How can they defend support for Palestinian institutions that deny their own people the opportunity to choose their representatives?
I cannot say with certainty that donor countries will freeze their assistance. But I fear this decision will weaken their willingness to honor their commitments and make it harder to defend support for us before their parliaments and taxpayers.
When our institutions and public services depend on that support, international trust becomes a direct Palestinian interest. Squandering it places an additional burden on citizens who are already suffering. Even so, I still see an opportunity to correct course, and I place cautious hope in it.
President Mahmoud Abbas has the authority on the Palestinian side to bring the date forward. Macron can use his diplomatic influence to support that correction and link the reform process to a clear electoral timetable in the near future.
We may have missed the opportunity to hold elections on November 28, 2026, but that does not justify waiting until September 11, 2027. I call for presidential and legislative elections to be brought forward to no later than March 2027, with preparations beginning immediately and conditions created that allow all Palestinian lists and political forces wishing to stand to carry out their preparatory work and activities on the ground.
Elections alone will not solve all our crises. But they give people a peaceful means of demanding accountability, open institutions to new talent, and rebuild trust between citizens and their leadership. Every day we postpone this opportunity makes it harder to recover.
At Masar Jadid, we will continue reaching out to everyone who can help. We will use the political, administrative, and legal means available to advocate for an earlier date. We will participate in every serious national dialogue that leads to a clear outcome: returning the decision to the people.
I hold Sheikh and Mezher politically responsible for pushing for the postponement. I call on Abbas to correct the decision he signed, and I urge Macron to help protect the opportunity that remains.
Thirty-eight years ago, Rabadi told me: “Don’t leave me.”
Today, in those words, I hear the voice of an entire Palestinian generation waiting for someone to open the door.
We have a duty not to leave them behind.
Samer Sinijlawi is a Palestinian political figure from Jerusalem and the founder and president of Masar Jadid (New Path), a Palestinian political movement advocating democracy, nonviolence, reform, and regional peace.

Iran's stock market climbs despite US blockade, energy shortages, collapsing currency
Unknown

2026-10-14
12:01:40 UTC
21:01:40 KST

Iran’s stock market has recently rallied despite its plummeting economy.
Iran International reported on Tuesday that the Iranian stock market has seen an influx of Investments, despite increasing power outages, a shortage of foreign currency, and the rate of the rial tanking.
The report noted that this could mean one of two things: either investors believe Tehran and Washington will reach a peace deal soon, or they have no other way to stop their savings from losing value.
Iran International points to a few competing analyses of the situation to better explain investors’ choices.
One analysis from Farau indicates that a lack of foreign exchange currency in the country, energy shortages, and uncertainty over the war are the primary stressors for Tehran’s economy.
Why is Iran's stock market rallying?
Iranian oil exports have effectively stopped under the US blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, leaving Iran with a dwindling supply of foreign currency.
The report noted that Khabar Online cited a 35,000-toman rise ($.003495) in the free-dollar market in the last month alone.
Additionally, energy shortages in Iran are exacerbating the problems. Iran's energy sector was already underfunded before the war began, and strikes on Iranian energy infrastructure have further strained production.
On top of that, Iranian investors are unsure what comes next. The economic effects of a third round of war would be disastrous, but diplomatic efforts continue.
Businesses that rely on imported goods are feeling these effects, as they face higher operating costs with less access to foreign currency, Iran International added.
These factors significantly complicate long-term investment and leave Iranians seeking assets that will preserve their value.
Some analyses indicated that investors are optimistic about a deal.
Rouydad24 argued that investors expect a deal and believe more access to international markets is on the horizon.
However, Iran International noted that other analyses show a different picture.
Just because the market is rising does not mean that investors in Iran are optimistic about the country’s economic prospects. Instead, it might indicate that Iranian’s lack alternatives for preserving their wealth.
The rial’s value has tanked, property is losing value, and bank deposits are losing purchasing power, making domestic equities more attractive to investors, the report noted.
This could offer a more stable assessment than the first: investors may be buying domestic stocks out of fear that cash will lose value in the country.
This comes as the International Monetary Fund forecasted that Iran’s economy would contract by 7.6% in 2026, as compared to the rate of 5.4% projected in July.
Notably, Iran International noted that the Middle East and Central Asia were expected to contract by 0.3%.

Even more borrowers choose riskier mortgages, as higher interest rates crush affordability
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:01:31 UTC
21:01:31 KST

Mortgage rates moved to the highest level in nearly three years last week, causing overall demand to drop. Riskier mortgages, however, continue to gain a growing share of what demand there is.
Total mortgage application volume dropped 2.7% last week compared with the previous week, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association's seasonally adjusted index. It is also 37.5% lower than the same week one year ago.
The average contract interest rate for 30-year fixed-rate mortgages with conforming loan balances, $832,750 or less, increased to 7.50% from 7.49%, with points decreasing to 0.83 from 0.84, including the origination fee, for loans with a 20% down payment. The rate was more than a full percentage point higher than it was a year ago.
"As a result, borrowers continue to rely more on ARM [adjustable-rate mortgage] loans to help lower their monthly payments," said Joel Kan, an MBA economist, in a release. "The ARM share at 10.5 percent was at its highest level since October 2025."
ARMs offer lower interest rates and can be fixed for up to 10 years, but then they adjust depending on future interest rates. That is why they are considered riskier.
Applications to refinance a home loan have been hit hardest by higher rates, as a shrinking pool of borrowers can now find much relief. These applications declined 0.4% for the week and were 56% lower year over year.
Applications for a mortgage to purchase a home fell 4% for the week and were 16% lower than the same week one year ago. There are more homes available for sale now, but mostly on the higher end of the market. Supply is also rising not because of new listings, but because of slower sales. Home prices also continue to rise.
While closed home sales increased very slightly in September from August, according to a report Tuesday from the National Association of Realtors, those sales were based on market conditions over the summer, when rates were lower.
"Despite the small monthly gain on a seasonally adjusted basis, August and September marked the two slowest months for home sales this year," said Lawrence Yun, NAR's chief economist, in a release. "Further increases in mortgage rates in recent weeks mean fewer buyers can qualify to purchase a home."
Correction: Total mortgage application volume dropped 2.7% last week compared with the previous week. An earlier version misstated the figure. Closed home sales increased very slightly in September from August. An earlier version misstated the timeline.

Foreign workers underpaid at Helsinki school project linked to organised crime
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:56:25 EEST
20:56:25 KST

A state-funded school renovation project in Helsinki has become the centre of a labour exploitation scandal involving unpaid wages, false employment records and a subcontractor allegedly managed from an Estonian prison by a man convicted of involvement in organised crime.
Finland's Construction Union (Rakennusliitto) identified the suspected violations at the Valteri Ruskis school in Ruskeasuo, which serves children and young people requiring special educational support.
Add Helsinki Times as a preferred source on Google (opens Google in a new tab)
The union said its investigation uncovered 30 workers classified as self-employed despite working under conditions resembling regular employment. Several foreign workers received wages below collective agreement rates, while the authorities had not properly verified the right of some workers to work in Finland.
State property agency Senaatti Properties commissioned the renovation, with Mirlux Oy acting as the main contractor. The allegations concern subcontractors Varatek Oy and Kore Metal Oy.
According to the union, Varatek registered 36 people to work at the site, although only three were its direct employees. Others worked through an invoicing service, raising concerns that the company had disguised employment relationships to avoid labour obligations.
The union also identified unpaid overtime and Sunday work allowances. Some workers received trainee-level wages despite working extended hours.
Finnish newspaper Helsingin Sanomat reported that three employees worked 122 hours across 13 days within a two-week period. Union calculations indicated that each had lost nearly €1,500 in wages.
The investigation also found that up to 12 workers had not undergone proper checks of their right to work in Finland. Most workers came from outside the European Union, particularly Ukraine. Some Ukrainian nationals had been incorrectly registered as Finnish citizens.
Rakennusliitto placed Varatek under a union boycott on Tuesday after the company allegedly failed to resolve the wage disputes.
Toni Malmström, senior expert at the union, criticised the oversight failures, warning that companies violating labour agreements gain an unfair advantage over employers following the rules.
The union said such practices also threaten Finnish construction workers amid continued unemployment in the sector.

Cornell scientists identify rare human genetic disorder in two unusually long-legged cats
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:56:22 UTC
20:56:22 KST

Cornell scientists identify rare human genetic disorder in two unusually long-legged cats
- Date:
- October 14, 2026
- Source:
- Cornell University
- Summary:
- Two unusually long-legged cats have helped scientists uncover the first genetically confirmed cases of Marfan syndrome in domestic felines. Researchers at Cornell University discovered that the brothers carried two altered copies of a gene linked to the rare connective tissue disorder, which can affect the eyes, heart, and blood vessels. Surprisingly, the cats survived into adulthood because their genetic mutation still allowed some normal function.
- Share:
Two brothers named Gary and Shaggy have helped Cornell University researchers make a rare genetic discovery. In a study published in Scientific Reports, scientists reported the first molecular characterization of Marfan syndrome in domestic cats, a condition primarily recognized in humans.
Gary and Shaggy first stood out as kittens because of their unusually long limbs. As they grew older, veterinarians also identified abnormalities in their eye structures and an enlarged aorta, the body's main artery. Together, these symptoms suggested Marfan syndrome, an inherited condition that weakens connective tissues throughout the body. The disorder affects approximately 1 in 4,000 people, but these brothers represented the first known documented feline cases.
"The findings provide a foundation for improved veterinary diagnostics," said senior author Dr. Jacquelyn Evans, assistant professor in the College of Veterinary Medicine and at the Baker Institute for Animal Health. "It can help veterinarians recognize similar cases in the future and may help develop genetic tests."
Scientists Uncover a Surprising Genetic Twist
To determine what caused the brothers' unusual symptoms, researchers from multiple disciplines conducted thorough medical examinations and analyzed their DNA. Their investigation identified changes in a gene called FBN1, which provides instructions for producing fibrillin-1. This protein is essential for healthy connective tissue, helping support structures throughout the body, including blood vessels, bones, ligaments, skin, and eyes.
Genetic testing revealed that Gary and Shaggy each had two altered copies of FBN1, having inherited one from each parent. This was especially notable because, in humans, a mutation in just one copy of the gene can be enough to cause Marfan syndrome. Having two altered copies is exceptionally uncommon and can severely disrupt the production of normal fibrillin-1.
Yet the brothers' genetic changes had an unexpected effect. Further analysis showed that their particular variant did not completely disable the gene. Instead, it interfered with how the gene's instructions were processed while still allowing some normal activity to continue. That remaining function helps explain why Gary and Shaggy were able to survive into adulthood, even though carrying two copies of such a mutation could otherwise have resulted in a much more severe form of the disorder.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Cornell University. Original written by Teresa Griffin. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Shawna R. Cook, Jessica J. Hayward, Soon Hon Cheong, Linda Impe, Ian R. Porter, Brian Lamendola, Gavin R. Hitchener, Urs Giger, Philip R. Fox, Jacquelyn M. Evans, Bart J. G. Broeckx. A homozygous hypomorphic FBN1 splice region variant in domestic cats with Marfan syndrome. Scientific Reports, 2026; DOI: 10.1038/s41598-026-70702-3

Wie Maroš Šefčovič der Durchbruch im Handel mit China gelang
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:56:11 UTC
20:56:11 KST

Wie Maroš Šefčovič der Durchbruch im Handel mit China gelang
Europas Handelskommissar hat ein erstes Zugeständnis aus Peking errungen. Nun muss er die EU-Spitzenpolitiker davon überzeugen, dass der Dialog noch mehr bewirken kann.
Als Maroš Šefčovič im Juli den EU-Botschaftern seine Strategie für den Umgang mit China vorstellte, richtete er eine Warnung an die Regierungen, die auf strengere Handelsmaßnahmen gegen Peking drängten.
„Manchmal ist es sogar populär, einen Handelskrieg zu beginnen, aber es ist sehr schwierig, ihn zu beenden“, erinnerte sich der EU-Handelskommissar später in einem Interview mit POLITICO.
Drei Monate später ist Šefčovič ein erster Durchbruch gelungen: Letzte Woche wurde in Peking eine Vereinbarung erzielt, die Importe chinesischer Hybridautos drastisch zu reduzieren. Dieser symbolische Erfolg ist ein kleiner Schritt zur Stabilisierung der Handelsbeziehungen, die nach Ansicht Brüssels einen gefährlichen Wendepunkt erreicht haben.
Für Šefčovič, der im vergangenen Jahr mit Donald Trump einen Zollwaffenstillstand ausgehandelt hatte, deutet die Vereinbarung darauf hin, dass sich seine Strategie des Engagements, gestützt durch die Androhung härterer Handelsmaßnahmen, allmählich auszuzahlen beginnt.
Šefčovič hatte sich bei einem Treffen mit dem chinesischen Handelsminister Wang Wentao Ende Juni in Brüssel darauf geeinigt, den Handelsdialog aufzunehmen.
Der slowakische Kommissar hoffte, wenn er sich zuerst auf den Automobilsektor konzentrieren würde – einem Bereich, in dem die EU als einer der wenigen großen Märkte, die chinesischen Herstellern noch offenstehen, über Einfluss verfügt – einen vertrauensbildenden Erfolg zu erzielen. Erst später will er sich den schwierigeren Fragen zuwenden: den kritischen Rohstoffen bis hin zu Chinas enormen industriellen Überkapazitäten.
Gleichzeitig bemühte er sich darum, die europäischen Regierungen parallel hinter einer Initiative zur Stärkung der Handelsschutzmaßnahmen der EU zu vereinen. Šefčovič untermauerte seine Verhandlungsposition mit der Androhung härterer Maßnahmen, um das Handelsdefizit der EU gegenüber China in Höhe von einer Milliarde Euro pro Tag zu senken.
Der Hybrid-Deal ist jedoch nur der erste Schritt in einem weitaus größeren Wettstreit.
Advertisement
Die Staats- und Regierungschefs der EU treffen sich am Donnerstag in Brüssel, um Bilanz zu ziehen. Sie müssen abwägen, ob sie die Forderungen nach aggressiveren Maßnahmen zum Schutz der europäischen Industrie durchziehen.
Das Treffen wird zeigen, ob ein Kommissar, der seine Karriere darauf aufgebaut hat, Kompromisse mit schwierigen Partnern zu finden, die Unterstützung Europas für eine Strategie aufrechterhalten kann, deren Erfolg alles andere als sicher ist.
„Man hat es mit demselben Partner am Verhandlungstisch zu tun“, sagte Šefčovič im August in einem Interview mit POLITICO über die Risiken eines Handelskriegs. „Wenn man das also vermeiden kann, wäre das viel besser.“
Marktmacht
Šefčovičs erster Schritt bestand darin, sich auf einen Bereich zu konzentrieren, in dem Europa noch Einfluss hat: den Zugang zu seinem Markt mit 450 Millionen Menschen.
Chinas Hersteller haben sich zu globalen Kraftzentren entwickelt, kämpfen jedoch mit einer schwachen Nachfrage im Inland. Ein anhaltender Einbruch auf dem Immobilienmarkt belastet den Privatkonsum, während der gnadenlose Wettbewerb Preiskämpfe ausgelöst hat. Die Inlandsverkäufe von Pkw gingen im September gegenüber dem Vorjahr um 28 Prozent zurück.
Dadurch gewinnen die Märkte in Übersee zunehmend an Bedeutung. Da die USA chinesische Importe ausschließen, bleibt Europa einer der lukrativsten Märkte, der chinesischen Herstellern noch offensteht.
Advertisement
Šefčovič setzte darauf, dass Peking lieber Exportbeschränkungen akzeptieren würde, als den Zugang zum europäischen Markt gänzlich zu riskieren.
Er richtete sein Augenmerk auf den Automobilsektor, in dem chinesische Hersteller sehr schnell Fuß gefasst haben. Im Jahr 2024 hatten chinesische Autohersteller einen Anteil von lediglich 2 Prozent sowohl am europäischen Hybrid- als auch am Plug-in-Hybrid-Markt; bis zur ersten Hälfte des Jahres 2026 waren die jeweiligen Anteile laut Branchenzahlen auf 14 Prozent beziehungsweise 25 Prozent gestiegen.
Die Kommission bereitete sich darauf vor, die Einfuhr von Hybridfahrzeugen auch ohne ein Abkommen zu beschränken. Eine Verhandlungslösung bot Šefčovič jedoch auch einen politischen Mehrwert: den Beweis, dass der Dialog mit Peking zu greifbaren Ergebnissen führen kann.
Die Verhandlungen verliefen intensiv, wie eine mit den Gesprächen vertraute Person auf chinesischer Seite berichtete.
„Es war sehr, sehr hart“, sagte die Person, die anonym bleiben wollte, um offen über die hinter verschlossenen Türen stattfindenden Verhandlungen zu sprechen. „Beide Seiten hatten seit langem keine solche Intensität mehr erlebt. Keine Sommerpause, keine Feiertage. Sie arbeiteten rund um die Uhr, sogar noch ein oder zwei Tage vor Šefčovičs Reise nach Peking.“
Während Brüssel den Dialog suchte, wollte es Peking gleichzeitig davon überzeugen, dass es bereit sei, härtere Maßnahmen zu ergreifen, sollten die Verhandlungen scheitern.
Advertisement
Šefčovič hatte zuvor Pläne für ein neues „Diversifizierungsinstrument“ angekündigt, das Unternehmen in kritischen Sektoren dazu verpflichten würde, wesentliche Vorleistungen von mindestens drei Lieferanten zu beziehen – ein Schritt, um Chinas Fähigkeit einzuschränken, Europas Abhängigkeit von seinen kritischen Rohstoffen auszunutzen.
Dann, nur drei Tage vor Šefčovičs Reise nach Peking, erhöhten Frankreich und Deutschland den Druck.
Präsident Emmanuel Macron und Bundeskanzler Friedrich Merz forderten eine wirkungsvolle neue Handelswaffe, die es Brüssel ermöglichen würde, Ländern, denen unlautere Wettbewerbsvorteile vorgeworfen werden, innerhalb weniger Tage den Zugang zum europäischen Markt zu beschränken – oder sogar ganz zu sperren.
Der Vorschlag nannte China zwar nicht ausdrücklich, doch Peking war das offensichtliche Ziel.
Den Zusammenhalt wahren
Mehreren Diplomaten zufolge werden die EU-Staats- und Regierungschefs die Einigung voraussichtlich begrüßen, die Kommission jedoch gleichzeitig dazu drängen, rasch zu handeln, um die Handelsschutzmaßnahmen der Union zu stärken. Die in Peking erzielte Einigung hat Zeit gewonnen, aber noch nicht geklärt, wie weit Brüssel gehen sollte, falls die chinesischen Exporte weiter steigen oder die Verhandlungen ins Stocken geraten.
„Wir verlieren Tausende von Arbeitsplätzen in der Industrie; Olivenöl und Eiscreme werden das Kernproblem nicht lösen“, sagte ein EU-Diplomat, nachdem Šefčovič die Botschafter am Sonntag informiert hatte, und bezog sich dabei auf die gemeldeten Ergebnisse der Gespräche.
Advertisement
Ein hochrangiger deutscher Beamter begrüßte das Abkommen von Peking als einen ersten Schritt in die richtige Richtung. „Es ist ein positives Zeichen – das natürlich das Problem des Handelsdefizits mit China nicht vollständig löst“, sagte der Beamte.
Doch Berlins Unterstützung für eine härtere Linie könnte sich als kurzlebig erweisen.
Alicia García-Herrero, Senior Fellow beim Thinktank Bruegel, argumentierte, dass Pekings Zugeständnisse darauf ausgelegt gewesen seien, Berlin zu beschwichtigen, angesichts der Bedeutung der Automobilindustrie für die deutsche Wirtschaft.
„Ich hoffe nur, dass Merz nicht von dem Brief abrückt, den er an die Kommission geschickt hat“, sagte sie. Da der deutsche Bundeskanzler im eigenen Land politisch geschwächt ist, befürchtet García-Herrero, dass er zögern könnte, eine langwierige Konfrontation zu riskieren: „Ich mache mir Sorgen, dass Merz diesen schnellen Erfolg nutzen und sich aus dem Staub machen wird.“
Damit steht Šefčovič vor einem Balanceakt: Er muss die EU-Regierungen bei der Fortsetzung des Engagements mit China an Bord halten und gleichzeitig die glaubwürdige Drohung mit härteren Maßnahmen aufrechterhalten, falls die Gespräche scheitern sollten.
„Ich gehe davon aus, dass [die Staats- und Regierungschefs] der Kommission grünes Licht geben werden, weitere handelspolitische Schutzmaßnahmen voranzutreiben. China könnte dies als Verrat auffassen. Sollte das der Fall sein, könnten wir sehr schnell wieder in einen Konflikt geraten“, sagte Noah Barkin, Senior Advisor im China-Team der Rhodium Group.
Advertisement
Der bevorstehende Kampf
Für Šefčovič besteht die Herausforderung nun darin, einen begrenzten Durchbruch bei den Autos in eine umfassendere Neuausrichtung des Handels mit China umzumünzen – und Europa gleichzeitig Zeit zu verschaffen, seine Abwehrmaßnahmen zu stärken, falls die Verhandlungen scheitern sollten.
„Es spricht einiges dafür, China das anzutun, was China Europa jahrelang angetan hat – Peking in Dialogen und Verfahren zu verzetteln, während Europa seine Instrumente bereitstellt. Aber die EU muss die Zeit, die diese Gespräche bieten, voll ausschöpfen“, sagte Barkin von Rhodium.
Der Handelskommissar wird voraussichtlich im Januar ein Videogespräch mit Wang führen, bevor sich die beiden im kommenden März erneut treffen. Diese Gespräche werden zeigen, ob Peking bereit ist, weitere Zugeständnisse in Sektoren zu machen, in denen die europäische Industrie zunehmend in die Defensive gerät, darunter die Chemieindustrie.
Eine weitere Priorität sind kritische Rohstoffe, bei denen China zugestimmt hat, weiterhin Ausfuhrlizenzen für Seltene Erden zu erteilen. Pekings Kontrolle über deren Versorgung verschafft dem Land erheblichen Einfluss auf europäische Hersteller, was die Grenzen von Šefčovičs Verhandlungsposition deutlich macht.
Die Kommission bereitet zudem zwei Vorschläge für Dezember vor: das Diversifizierungsinstrument, das darauf abzielt, die Abhängigkeit von chinesischen Lieferungen zu verringern, und einen Mechanismus zum Schutz europäischer Industrien und Regionen vor Vergeltungsmaßnahmen.
Das Ausmaß der Herausforderung ist gewaltig: Chinesische Importe von Hybridautos beliefen sich im ersten Halbjahr 2026 auf 6,7 Milliarden Euro, während das Handelsdefizit zwischen der EU und China im vergangenen Jahr bei 360 Milliarden Euro lag. Das Abkommen verschafft den europäischen Automobilherstellern zwar eine gewisse Erleichterung, trägt aber kaum dazu bei, das zugrunde liegende Ungleichgewicht zu beheben.
Advertisement
Brüssel hofft, dass die Schutzmaßnahmen für Hybridfahrzeuge als Blaupause für den Schutz anderer Branchen dienen können, die mit einem Anstieg chinesischer Importe konfrontiert sind.
„Wir hören auf unsere Industrie. Dazu gehören die chemische Industrie, die Windkraftbranche und die Möbelindustrie. Wir wissen, wo es zu einem Anstieg kommt, und wir wissen, was uns im Hinblick auf unsere Deindustrialisierung am härtesten trifft“, sagte ein hochrangiger Kommissionsbeamter am Montag.
Šefčovič räumte in seinem Interview im August die Grenzen des Dialogs ein und warnte, dass Verhandlungen ohne greifbare Fortschritte immer schwieriger aufrechtzuerhalten seien.
„Es wäre sehr wichtig, zurückzukommen und zu sagen, dass das Problem anerkannt wird und es bereits einige Pilotprojekte gibt, die wir testen wollen, um zu sehen, ob sie funktionieren“, sagte er.
„Aber wenn einfach nichts geschieht, dann wird es für uns natürlich viel schwieriger sein, nur über diese Themen zu sprechen.“
Jordyn Dahl in Brüssel und Hans von der Burchard in Berlin haben zu diesem Artikel beigetragen.

Uvision shows remote kamikaze drone launcher at AUSA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:54:37 UTC
20:54:37 KST

- Uvision is showing an eight-canister HERO 120 launcher at AUSA 2026, designed for remote operation in mobile, fixed and containerized configurations.
- The HERO 120 is already on contract with the U.S. Army under a Lethal Unmanned Systems deal worth up to $982 million.
Israeli loitering munition maker Uvision is showing an eight-canister launcher for its HERO 120 at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting in Washington, pitching the remotely operated system as a way to spread strike capacity across land and maritime platforms and tie it to the company’s AI-enabled CORTEX mission management software.
The Multi-Canister Launcher holds up to eight HERO 120 loitering munitions and is designed for remote operation, according to the company’s Oct. 13 announcement. Uvision says it can be fielded in mobile, fixed and containerized configurations, and that CORTEX, which the company describes as an AI-enabled battle intelligence and mission management system, links the launcher with sensors and decision-makers in what it calls a sensor-to-effect network.
Loitering munitions, often called kamikaze drones, can circle over an area while an operator searches for a target and then dive onto it with a warhead. The HERO 120 is a mid-range design aimed at armored vehicles and other high-value targets, combining reconnaissance and strike in one airframe with a built-in camera that lets the operator abort an attack and re-engage.
Uvision singled out border defense as one use for the multi-canister setup, with launch nodes spread across long stretches of border in mobile and fixed positions and connected through CORTEX to surveillance assets, so that a threat spotted in one sector can be answered from the nearest launcher. The company did not name any customer that has ordered the launcher or say whether it is being offered to the U.S. Army.
At the same show, Uvision is demonstrating Wayland Autonomy’s IRIS airborne surveillance payload running with Tactical CORTEX, a version of the software for forward units. The company says the pairing adds wide-area surveillance and onboard target generation, including in areas where GPS signals are jammed or unavailable.
“It’s not just about having more effects in the field. It’s about having them where you need them, when you need them, and giving forces the flexibility to use the right capability for the mission,” said Dr. Ran Gozali, CEO of Uvision.
The HERO 120 already has a foothold in the U.S. Army, and in October 2025 the service awarded Mistral Inc. and Uvision a multi-year contract worth up to $982 million under the Lethal Unmanned Systems program to buy, field, train on and sustain the weapon, with Mistral as prime contractor and Uvision as design authority. Production systems passed their first lot acceptance tests in August 2026, and the companies then received an additional order worth more than $50 million to increase the number of HERO 120 systems and support equipment going to soldiers.
The smaller HERO 90 supports the U.S. Army’s Low Altitude Stalking and Strike Ordnance effort, known as LASSO, which tests soldier-portable, tube-launched loitering munitions for infantry units. The U.S. Marine Corps fitted HERO 120 munitions on one of its Long-Range Unmanned Surface Vessels in 2023, an early example of the maritime launch role Uvision now advertises for the multi-canister launcher.
Beyond the HERO line, Uvision markets the VIPER encapsulated multi-mission systems and the PEREGRINE tactical kinetic systems, and says CORTEX is meant to manage effectors across all three families.

US dollar’s rally pauses as markets brace for inflation report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:52:53 UTC
20:52:53 KST

Ali Canberk Ozbugutu, Burhan Sansarlioglu, and Emir Yildirim
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
The US Dollar Index paused its upward rally and traded flat on Wednesday, ahead of the key US inflation data expected to shape the Federal Reserve’s future policy roadmap.
The US dollar closed Tuesday after a 0.4% decline to 102.2, while retreating slightly from a recent peak of 102.6 that was its highest since April 2025.
The index stood relatively flat at 102.2 as of 1100GMT, as currency markets are bracing for the inflation report.
The US headline inflation is expected to rise 3.4% on an annual basis to a range between 3.6-3.7%, while core consumer inflation is expected to rise from 2.4% to 2.5%.
The Fed’s hawkish expectations could rise with higher-than-expected inflation, while money markets expect the bank to maintain rates this month with an 80% probability and to hike rates in December with a 92% likelihood.
New York Fed President John Williams’ remarks cooled the dollar’s immediate momentum after he said further tightening after a singular rate hike this year will likely be unwarranted, noting that the disinflationary factors remain and that the US inflation will decline next year.
The US dollar is expected to sustain its broader dominance over other currencies due to deep structural weaknesses and political turmoil pressuring the euro, analysts say.
Jane Foley, senior foreign exchange strategist at Rabobank, told Anadolu that the US’ strong economic growth allowed markets to overlook the country’s fiscal deficit but similar fiscal indiscipline is currently pressuring the euro.
“The same is not true for France — in both late 2024 and 2025, tough budget negotiations in France led to government instability and an underperformance of French government debt. By the end of last year, the 10-year Oat-Bund yield spread was trading at levels significantly wider than those in early 2024, before President Macron called a snap election,” she said.
Foley stated that the European economy showed some resilience but other factors continue to weaken the currency.
“Factors such as the region’s energy importer status, concerns about hybrid Russian warfare and political worries concerning growing far-right support in both Germany and France are likely undermining the EUR,” she said.
“These worries are reflecting kindly on the USD, given its safe haven status. We expect the dollar index to remain well supported in the coming months,” she added.
Kit Juckes, head of foreign exchange strategy at Societe Generale, told Anadolu that the Middle East conflict beginning in late February drove the US dollar’s rise from its lowest levels since 2022.
“The US is a major energy producer now and higher oil prices, as well increased global uncertainty, are dollar supportive,” he said.
He noted that the developments in artificial intelligence (AI) supported the American economy’s growth than other countries, which was evident when growth forecasts for the US were upwardly revised in the first quarter.
He mentioned that the reshaping of monetary policy expectations after the Fed’s Jackson Hole summit also supported the dollar, as Fed chair Kevin Warsh emerged “not afraid” to raise rates.
“The shift in market pricing of Fed Funds since then, has taken the dollar to current levels,” he said. “The fourth (factor driving up the US dollar) has been the rise in global bond yields, which has caused concern about the European bond market and underpinned the dollar.”
“Now, the question is, with a peak level of rates at 4.7% priced into the market, whether that will prove excessive — the key to expectations about where rates will peak, will be sensitive to tomorrow’s US CPI data, where the market expects core CPI inflation to rise from 2.4%, and headline inflation to increase from 3.4% to 3.6%. Further near-term dollar strength may be predicated on a higher-than-expected inflation print, or increased strain in global bond markets,” he added.

Saudi-led coalition intercepts Houthi missile launched towards Riyadh
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:39:06 UTC
20:39:06 KST

Saudi-led coalition intercepts Houthi missile launched towards Riyadh
Saudi civil defence says danger passed after it issued two warnings through its national early warning platform.
The Saudi-led coalition says it intercepted and destroyed a Houthi ballistic missile launched towards Saudi Arabia’s capital, Riyadh, as the Yemeni armed group said it carried out more attacks on the kingdom.
Coalition spokesman Major-General Turki al-Maliki on Wednesday announced the thwarted attack on X, days after two separate strikes hit Riyadh’s King Khalid international airport, killing 14 people and injuring hundreds.
The General Directorate of Saudi Civil Defence also issued two alerts through its national early warning platform, later saying the danger had passed. One alert was for the Al-Kharj governorate in Riyadh province, and the other for the capital.
The Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for supporters of God), issued a statement saying they targeted facilities of Saudi Arabia’s national oil company Aramco in Dhahran, an Aramco refinery in Riyadh, and the capital’s King Khalid international airport.
Overnight, the Saudi Ministry of Energy confirmed that the administrative building belonging to Aramco in Dhahran was hit.
Al Jazeera’s Zein Basravi, reporting from the Qatari capital Doha, said any notion that the Saudi-led coalition could contain the conflict to Yemen had been shattered over the last 10 days, which saw the targeting of several sites in Saudi Arabia.
Houthi attacks on Riyadh’s King Khalid international airport over the weekend killed 14 people and wounded more than 300 others. Houthi attacks have also been reported on other airports, including the Abha international airport, where two people were killed, and on Aramco facilities.
Meanwhile, Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces have launched a counteroffensive in Yemen to retake coastal territory from the Houthis near the Bab al-Mandeb strait at the entrance to the Red Sea, a vital maritime trade chokepoint.
Fighting in Yemen between the Iran-aligned Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces escalated sharply last month, shattering a United Nations-brokered ceasefire that had largely held since 2022.
The Houthis have controlled Yemen’s most populous areas, including the capital Sanaa, since seizing the city in 2014, forcing the internationally recognised government to flee to southern Yemen.
The Muslim World League on Wednesday condemned the continued Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, saying they deliberately target civilians and civilian sites. The league’s secretary-general, Sheikh Mohammad bin Abdulkarim Al-Issa, said their nature confirms “the criminal approach of this terrorist militia in deliberately targeting civilians and civilian infrastructure”.
Meanwhile, Yemen’s Houthi-affiliated Al-Masirah television reported that four air strikes hit the Harib district in the country’s Marib governorate. The results of the attacks were not immediately clear.
Nawaf Obaid, a security and intelligence analyst and senior research fellow at King’s College London, told Al Jazeera that while air strikes are intensifying, the “actual ground war hasn’t really begun” for the Saudi-led coalition.
Obaid broke down the phases in which such an operation could unfold, saying the first phase would be “to hit at basically the power and the energy source that’s allowing the Houthis to operate … tanks, armoured vehicles, trucks”.
Phase two would be to look at the “systematic increase of Houthi control in the region, which is critical,” he said.
Phase three would involve a discussion on how “to start taking back these territories that the Houthis have gained since the beginning of the war”.
Obaid said these “multipronged phases” would include “extra-specialised” troops, especially in mountain warfare, because the Houthis are taking the battlefield into difficult terrain.

EU allocates $188.2M to boost defense production under new program
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:38:45 UTC
20:38:45 KST

Melike Pala
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
The European Commission allocated Wednesday €168.2 million ($188.2 million) to eight projects aimed at boosting Europe's defense production capacity under the European Defense Industry Program.
The projects are expected to mobilize €1.26 billion in industrial investments to accelerate and expand the production of energetic components used in missiles, drones, and ammunition, according to a statement.
The projects, which will become operational from 2027, are expected to reduce manufacturing times by up to 90% and enable annual production of more than 20,000 tons of energetic materials, 3,500 drone and missile propulsion systems, 200,000 loitering munition warheads, and 60 million rounds of ammunition.
The investments will cover 17 production sites across 14 member states and Norway, while also strengthening their protection against growing physical and cyber threats.
The initiative builds on the EU's Act in Support of Ammunition Production, an emergency instrument introduced to address production bottlenecks and increase ammunition manufacturing capacity following the start of the war in Ukraine.

IEA warns diesel prices in Europe could rise as global crunch lasts into 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:37:32 UTC
20:37:32 KST

Europe could face renewed wholesale diesel price rises in the coming weeks, the International Energy Agency warned on Wednesday, as disrupted supplies leave markets tight well into 2027 despite recovering Gulf oil output.
Diesel markets will remain tight well into 2027, and wholesale diesel prices in Europe could rise again in the coming weeks, the International Energy Agency (IEA) warned on Wednesday.
In its monthly report, the Paris-based energy watchdog said recovering Gulf oil supplies had failed to resolve the fuel squeeze, with global output still falling short of consumption.
Supply rose by 2.5 million barrels a day (mb/d) to 102.3 mb/d in September on a Saudi-led jump in Gulf crude exports to more than three-quarters of pre-war levels, but remains slightly below global demand of around 103.5 mb/d, the IEA estimated.
The war that began with US-Israeli strikes on Iran on 28 February is far from over.
Iran has choked the Strait of Hormuz, the route for about a fifth of the world’s oil, and recently stepped up attacks on ships there, while Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels are striking Saudi oil sites.
"Renewed attacks in the Gulf leave the recovery fragile," the IEA stated.
On Tuesday, Britain’s maritime security agency UKMTO said projectiles of unknown origin had hit a tanker and a container ship in the strait.
Early on Wednesday, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said a container ship carrying more than 2,500 containers sank south of the strait after hitting a naval mine and catching fire, claiming it took an unauthorised route and warning others of continued dangers in the maritime chokepoint.
Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil prices, rose around 1%, spiking above $107 per barrel in early trading on Wednesday, but it later pared gains and is hovering around $106 at the time of writing.
Meanwhile, the US benchmark, West Texas Intermediate, has traded flat at roughly $94.75 per barrel.
Diesel crunch
Diesel prices have retreated from September’s records above $200 a barrel, but benchmarks "remain nearly double the price of crude oil and their pre-crisis levels", the IEA stated.
With Middle Eastern fuel exports below half of their pre-war levels and Russian refineries hit by Ukrainian drones, diesel supplies remain under pressure.
Rising shipping costs could add to that pressure.
"As tensions in the crude freight market have spread to other tanker categories, delivered diesel prices in the dominant gasoil importing markets – Europe, Africa and Latin America – could rise again in the coming weeks," the IEA said.
The IEA said lost diesel stocks were unlikely to be replenished beyond normal seasonal changes before the second half of 2027.
The G7 pledged on 2 October to release up to 100 million barrels of emergency stocks through the IEA, diesel first.
However, an internal document seen by Euronews shows this would cover barrels still owed under March’s 400 million pledge, 326 million of which have been released, rather than add to it.
Diverging demand views
The IEA now expects high prices and weaker growth to cut global oil demand by 2.6 mb/d this year to 102.4 mb/d, slightly more than the 2.5 mb/d drop it forecast last month.
It also trimmed next year’s rebound to 2 mb/d from 2.6 mb/d, meaning 2027 demand would stay 0.6% below 2025 levels instead of edging above them.
On the other hand, OPEC, the oil exporters’ group, is more upbeat.
It lowered its forecast for 2026 demand growth for a sixth month running on Tuesday, to 180,000 barrels a day from 380,000, but raised its 2027 estimate to 2.55 mb/d from 2.36 mb/d, expecting stocks drained by the war to be rebuilt.
Crude output from OPEC+, which includes Russia, rose by about 900,000 barrels a day to 39.07 mb/d in September, OPEC said.
Seven core members kept November targets unchanged on 4 October, with most pumping below quota due to the war, and will meet again on 1 November. The UAE quit both groups in May.
Unless the conflicts in the region are resolved, "oil markets may experience more turmoil in the months ahead before any eventual surplus emerges in 2027", the IEA warned as its board meets on Thursday.

European players are joining forces to curb the dominance of the American giant in the satellite communications industry. Politico reported on how "Europe plans to push Starlink out," writes UNN.
Details
"Taking the stage at the International Space Summit in Paris, French President Emmanuel Macron called on leading European players to create a new 'alliance' to strengthen collective satellite capabilities. The real target of the 'let's unite' message? Elon Musk's Starlink," the publication says.

On Tuesday, communications ministers from EU national governments gathered in Ireland to discuss a legislative proposal that could make it easier for leading European operators to access satellites.
According to the publication, the initiative "envisages Deutsche Telekom, Orange, Vodafone and Telefónica joining forces to secure critical and desirable frequencies that will become available next year, as the European Commission considers a new allocation procedure that would reserve frequencies for European players." The plan, reported by Bloomberg before Macron's September 10 speech, was confirmed by two sources familiar with the negotiations.
"We are looking at this issue," said Mikael Trabbia, a senior executive at French telecommunications group Orange, in an interview, declining to comment further on the plans. "As a leading, innovative telecommunications group, we want to be able to offer this service to our customers. We do not want to have one dominant player."
Vodafone declined to comment, while Deutsche Telekom and Telefónica did not respond to requests for comment.
The future of space, the publication writes, is attracting attention in Europe as geopolitical conflicts increase its strategic importance, while security requirements and technological advances create business opportunities.
Musk has made it clear that Starlink seeks to deepen its dominance in low Earth orbit, where satellites fly close to Earth to provide faster connectivity. The company hopes to obtain these valuable frequencies in order to offer mobile services without having to cooperate with local telecommunications providers.
SpaceX, Starlink's parent company, did not respond to a request for comment, it was reported.
The question of control
As noted, amid the EU's need to reallocate the 2 GHz satellite communications band in 2027, the proposal under discussion envisages a licensing process that would favor European operators.
A group of members of the European Parliament submitted amendments to the European Commission's May proposal aimed at raising the barrier to non-European players' access to strategic radio frequencies.
"Starlink is not sitting idle. Musk's company has stepped up its lobbying in Brussels over the past two years, holding more meetings with the European Commission and lawmakers ahead of policy initiatives that could delay its expansion," the publication notes.
Earlier this year, the American company warned that the EU plan would leave Europeans without reliable direct-to-device connectivity services. "Starlink Broadband and Starlink Mobile [SpaceX subsidiaries focused on consumers] have done more to achieve the European Commission's connectivity objectives than any other satellite operator," the company's four-page submission obtained by the publication says.
It also warned that the plan could create "global interference problems, particularly for emergency services, such as those in Ukraine."
"Starlink may not be trying to make countries dependent on it, but it is trying to make itself indispensable," said Célestine Rabouam, a researcher at the French Institute of Geopolitics (GEODE). "Right now, they are the only ones that can deploy so quickly and adapt so easily."
What was said at the EU meeting
"We must also have our own technological sovereignty when it comes to satellites," EU Perspectives quotes Henna Virkkunen, Executive Vice-President of the European Commission, as saying at a meeting of ministers responsible for telecommunications on Tuesday, October 13.
She wants the Digital Networks Act to simplify the rules and strengthen the European telecommunications market.
Against the backdrop of Europe's desire for reliable satellite communications and faster broadband access, governments, as reported, put forward different priorities: Germany sought reliable satellite services and competition, while the Czech Republic emphasized opportunities for European companies. Finland warned against giving Brussels greater control.
Thomas Jarzombek, Parliamentary State Secretary at Germany's Federal Ministry for Digital Affairs, advocated satellite services that Europe could rely on even under difficult circumstances. He also called for competition between at least two providers, arguing that this would foster innovation.
Asked about allocating frequencies to Starlink, Thomas Jarzombek "pointed to Ukraine as evidence of the dependence that such technology can create," the publication writes. Access to frequencies should be accompanied by obligations to provide a reliable service, particularly at critical moments, he argued. Satellite connections will complement terrestrial networks, not replace them. "They need a partner on the ground," he said.
Opening the roundtable, Ireland's Minister for Communications Patrick O'Donovan emphasized protection against extreme weather, cyberattacks and hybrid threats, including the protection of undersea cables. "Greater security, diversity and redundancy can help reduce strategic vulnerabilities," he said. However, the talks in Limerick were interrupted when chair Patrick O'Donovan was taken to hospital by ambulance.
Ireland, which holds the presidency of the EU Council, wants the discussions to produce a first compromise on the legislation by December, when the EU Telecommunications Council will meet in Brussels, the publication writes.

The secret to easier exercise as an adult may start in childhood
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:36:23 UTC
20:36:23 KST

The secret to easier exercise as an adult may start in childhood
A surprising new study suggests that staying active while growing up could make exercise easier and less exhausting for the rest of your life.
- Date:
- October 14, 2026
- Source:
- Penn State
- Summary:
- Exercise during childhood could have a surprising lifelong benefit, potentially making physical activity less exhausting in adulthood. In a study involving guinea fowl, researchers discovered that birds accustomed to carrying weights while growing up could carry those weights as adults without using extra energy, while untrained birds burned 23% more.
- Share:
How much energy your body needs to move as an adult could be influenced by how active you were during childhood. A new study led by researchers at Penn State suggests that physical activity early in life may have lasting effects on movement efficiency. Using birds as a model, the scientists provided the first direct evidence that experiences during development can change how much energy animals expend when moving as adults.
According to Jonas Rubenson, a professor of kinesiology at Penn State, the ability to move efficiently could play an important role in animal evolution. Animals that spend less energy getting around may have more resources available for essential activities such as finding food, hunting, and reproducing. The findings, published in Proceedings of the Royal Society B, Biological Sciences, suggest that the energy demands of movement are more adaptable than scientists previously believed.
To investigate, the researchers attached small weights to one leg of young guinea fowl, birds closely related to chickens that walk on two legs like humans. They wanted to determine whether carrying extra weight during development would change how efficiently the birds moved once they matured.
The results revealed a striking difference. Birds that grew up carrying the weights could walk with the added load without expending additional energy. By comparison, birds raised without weights required 23% more energy when the same load was attached to their legs.
"This study showed how limb loading -- the application of mechanical stress on arms or legs, typically through weights or exercise -- during development can help an animal save energy during movement throughout its lifespan," said Rubenson, senior author of the study. "This is one of the first studies to indicate that animals' behaviors and environments in youth can affect how effortful moving is as adults."
Why Childhood Exercise Could Matter for Lifelong Health
Although the experiment involved birds, the findings raise important questions about human physical activity. One widely accepted scientific hypothesis proposes that people tend to avoid movement when it feels physically demanding or requires substantial energy.
If early activity influences movement efficiency in humans as it does in these birds, people who were less active during childhood might need to expend more energy to perform the same movements as adults. That additional effort could make them less inclined to exercise, potentially reinforcing a pattern of inactivity.
Rubenson believes the discovery could have broad implications for public health, particularly as children today are generally less physically active than those in earlier generations.
"Overall, children in the U.S. today are much less active than previous generations," Rubenson said. "This study suggests that more exercise through play and exercise during childhood could make it easier for people to remain or become more active as adults. If people do not need to exert as much energy to move as adults, then exercise -- and all its health benefits -- will be more accessible to them. This could have implications for many aspects of our nation's well-being, from heart health to mental health."
How Researchers Tested the Effects of Early Exercise
The experiment followed 12 guinea fowl from two weeks of age until they reached 16 weeks, when the birds were approaching their full adult size.
Half of the birds wore lead bands on one leg, with each band weighing 4% of the bird's body weight. The remaining six birds developed without any added weight. Apart from this difference, all 12 animals experienced the same living conditions and exercise routines.
When the birds reached nine weeks of age, the researchers began training them to walk on a treadmill.
At 16 weeks, the team assessed their energy expenditure using a flow-through metabolic chamber fitted to the treadmill. This equipment measured the oxygen each bird consumed, along with the carbon dioxide and water vapor it released. According to the researchers, this approach is considered the gold standard for determining how much energy an animal uses during a particular activity.
Each bird was tested under three conditions: standing still, walking on the treadmill without added weight, and walking while wearing a weight band on one leg. By comparing oxygen consumption and carbon dioxide production across these conditions, the scientists could determine how the additional load affected energy use.
Early Training Produced a Surprising Energy-Saving Effect
The researchers found no differences in energy consumption when the birds were standing still. However, their responses changed considerably once they began walking with weights.
Birds that had not carried weights while growing up experienced a 23% increase in energy expenditure when walking with the added load compared with walking without it.
The birds that had worn weights throughout development showed a remarkably different response. Their bodies had adapted so effectively that walking with the extra load required slightly less energy than walking without it. This unexpected result surprised the research team.
"The birds became so efficient that they were not using any more energy to carry the weight than they needed to walk without the weight," Rubenson said.
Another unexpected finding emerged when the researchers compared the two groups. On average, birds accustomed to carrying weights throughout development used no more energy while walking with their bands than ordinary birds used when walking without any added weight.
Together, these observations suggest that experiences early in life can substantially influence how efficiently animals move as adults.
"This shows that animals -- and this probably includes humans -- can become more efficient based on their life experiences. So, when humans exercise regularly throughout our childhood and adolescence, it could build our capacity for exercise throughout our lives."
The findings provide new evidence that physical activity during development can have lasting effects on the energy required for movement. Whether the same adaptations occur in humans remains to be established, but the research suggests a potential mechanism through which childhood exercise could help support physical activity later in life.
Research Team and Funding
Stephen Piazza, a professor of kinesiology at Penn State, also participated in the research, along with several current and former graduate students working with Piazza and Rubenson.
The study's two co-first authors were Talayah Johnson and Kavya Katugam-Dechene. Johnson completed her master's degree at Penn State and is now pursuing a doctorate at the University of Pennsylvania. Katugam-Dechene received her doctorate from Penn State and currently serves as a research assistant professor of biomedical and rehabilitation engineering at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill.
Other contributors included Ian Dechene, who worked as research staff on the project and is now a software engineer, and Roberto Castro, a Penn State doctoral student jointly advised by Piazza and Rubenson.
Funding was provided by the National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases, part of the National Institutes of Health, through awards R21AR071588 and R01AR080711. The researchers are solely responsible for the study's content, which does not necessarily reflect the official positions of the National Institutes of Health.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Penn State. Original written by Aaron Wagner. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Talayah A. Johnson, Kavya Katugam-Dechene, Ian Dechene, Roberto Castro Jr., Stephen J. Piazza, Jonas Rubenson. Chronic limb loading results in remarkable load carriage economy in growing fowl. Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences, 2026; 293 (2074) DOI: 10.1098/rspb.2026.0199
