British troops training to ‘recapture’ Falklands – Times
British troops have practiced retaking the disputed Falkland Islands in the event of another Argentine attempt to take over the territory, The Times has reported.
The exercise comes as tensions rise between Britain and Argentina over a British-Israeli oil project near the islands, known in Argentina as the Malvinas. Buenos Aires claims sovereignty over the territory and surrounding waters.
The drills, held from September 27 to October 2, included amphibious landings for the first time in years, according to the newspaper. During the exercise, Argentina announced international arbitration proceedings against Britain in an effort to block the $2.2 billion oil project.
British forces regularly hold exercises with local troops on the islands. The latest Cape Upholder drills involved around 150 British paratroopers from the 2nd Battalion, Parachute Regiment (2 PARA), and 100 members of the Falkland Islands Defense Force.
The exercise took place in several locations on East Falkland, including near San Carlos where British troops landed during the 1982 war with Argentina. According to The Times, the drills included amphibious operations to retake the islands, rather than the usual focus on defending them.
Argentine President Javier Milei, an ally of US President Donald Trump, has renewed his country’s claim to the islands and opposed the Sea Lion oil project. British firm Rockhopper and Israeli company Navitas plan to begin oil production about 220 km (137 miles) north of the islands in early 2028.
Britain has also urged Interpol to reject Argentine requests to arrest people involved in the Sea Lion project, including British nationals, The Guardian reported. London argues that the requests are politically motivated.
In early September, Milei announced plans to revive a naval base project in Ushuaia, southern Argentina. He called British plans to extract oil claimed by Argentina a threat to its sovereignty and reaffirmed Buenos Aires’ goal of regaining control over the Falklands.
Trump has also questioned whether Britain retains the military capabilities it had under Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher during the 1982 Falklands War, while declining to give a clear commitment of US support in the event of another conflict.
“You went there and you just took it back very quickly,” Trump said in a September interview with GB News. “I just don’t know if you have the capacity to do it.”
The Times quoted the commanding officer of the 2 PARA contingent as saying the exercise “gave us the opportunity to walk in the footsteps of our forefathers” while also exploring “how the cyber and space domains could affect missions like this in the modern era.”
The islands had no permanent indigenous population before European settlement. France, Britain, Spain, and Argentina subsequently established settlements or asserted authority over the archipelago before Britain took control in 1833.
The Russian government supports neither side’s territorial claim, advocates for peaceful resolution of the dispute, and opposes possible militarization of the South Atlantic.

The attacks have increased pressure on US President Donald Trump, who has said he is considering whether American forces should join Saudi strikes against the Houthis.
Saudi officials have reported repeated attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh over the past week, with strikes killing at least 18 people and injuring more than 300.
The Houthis described the latest attacks as retaliation for what they called Saudi aggression against Sanaa, Yemen's rebel-held capital, and other areas under their control.
Russia and China involved in ceasefire efforts
Despite the escalation, diplomatic efforts to halt the fighting are underway.
Mohamed al-Bukhaiti, a senior member of the Houthis' political bureau, told AP that Oman had attempted to bring the warring sides back to negotiations, while Russia and China had also pursued contacts through Iran.
"We're welcoming any mediation that leads to an end of the war and the blockade between Sanaa and Riyadh," al-Bukhaiti said.
"We're ready for a comprehensive end of the war and the blockade from both sides, not just a temporary ceasefire."
The Houthis nevertheless continued threatening Saudi airports and oil installations.
The attacks have severely disrupted air travel across the kingdom. More than 3,000 flights scheduled to depart from Saudi airports over the past week were canceled or listed as not operating, according to aviation analytics firm Cirium.
The campaign has also highlighted the Houthis' ability to inflict significant disruption despite Saudi Arabia's advanced Western-supplied air defenses.
Saudi air defenses under growing pressure
Saudi Arabia, one of the world's largest purchasers of American weapons, has sought additional military support from allies as it confronts daily missile and drone attacks across a vast territory.
Regional officials have warned that the kingdom is running low on missile interceptors, while military analysts say completely preventing Houthi strikes is virtually impossible.
Saudi Arabia covers an area approximately three times the size of Texas, and Houthi weapons are capable of reaching targets more than 1,600 kilometers, or 1,000 miles, away. Some missiles can also change course during flight, complicating interception efforts.
Even successful interceptions can cause casualties and damage on the ground.
Saudi Arabia's Civil Defense said debris from two intercepted Houthi ballistic missiles fell on residential neighborhoods in Riyadh overnight, injuring four people, including a child, and damaging 15 homes.
The escalating attacks have revived concerns about the vulnerability of Saudi Arabia's oil infrastructure and transportation networks, with repeated strikes threatening facilities central to the kingdom's economy.
Saudi strikes intensify inside Yemen
Saudi Arabia has responded with its own military operations against Houthi-controlled areas of Yemen, supporting the country's internationally recognized government.
The latest confrontation erupted after the Houthis accused Saudi Arabia of attacking an airport in Sanaa, reigniting tensions over the longstanding Saudi blockade of rebel-held territory.
The Houthis subsequently announced their own blockade against Saudi Arabia, while the Saudi-led coalition launched a major military offensive approximately a week and a half ago.
On Wednesday, the Houthi-run Health Ministry said two people had been killed and two wounded in a Saudi airstrike Tuesday on an oil facility in the Ras Isa port area of Hodeida province.
The Saudi-led coalition also struck an oil facility in Sanaa.
Ahmed Nagi, a senior Yemen analyst at the International Crisis Group, said the attacks on fuel storage facilities in Houthi-held areas represented a new phase in the conflict.
He warned that a prolonged war of attrition could significantly weaken the Houthis' military capabilities.
"The Houthis are betting on pressure, while the Saudis are betting on time," Nagi said.
"The Houthis are trying to strike critical infrastructure in Saudi Arabia to raise the cost of continued military intervention and support for the Yemeni government."
Humanitarian crisis deepens
The renewed fighting has also threatened to plunge Yemen deeper into the civil war that devastated the country before four years of relative calm.
The International Committee of the Red Cross reported an unprecedented increase in people suffering weapons-related injuries along Yemen's front lines, particularly in Marib, Taiz and areas near the Red Sea.
Hospitals are struggling to cope with the surge in casualties, with increasingly frequent incidents involving large numbers of wounded patients.
The World Food Program also warned that it could no longer reach more than 600,000 people dependent on humanitarian assistance in the besieged city of Taiz.
With Saudi Arabia and the Houthis continuing to exchange strikes, the diplomatic efforts involving Oman, Russia and China have yet to produce a breakthrough, leaving both the kingdom's critical infrastructure and Yemen's civilian population exposed to further escalation.

“As Russia stalls on the frontlines, it continues to escalate its aerial attacks - cruelly targeting Ukrainian civilians and infrastructure. With today's €2.86 billion disbursement, we keep addressing Ukraine's most urgent operational needs, including drones and missiles vital to its defence,” Ursula von der Leyen, President of the European Commission, said.
The Ukraine Support Loan totals €90 billion for 2026–2027, including €60 billion for defence needs and development of Ukraine’s defence‑industrial base, and €30 billion for budget support.
During 2026, €28.3 billion is expected to be directed to support Ukraine’s defence industrial capacity. The Commission said further disbursements under the 2026 defence leg of the instrument will continue in the coming weeks.
By the end of 2026, Ukraine will still have access to €29.64 billion available in EU financial assistance. This includes €25.24 billion under the Ukraine Support Loan (with €12.54 billion for defence‑industry support and €12.7 billion for budget financing) and €4.4 billion in remaining budget support under the initial Ukraine Facility.
In total, more than €17 billion is earmarked to ensure the stability of Ukraine’s budget for the remaining months of 2026. Disbursement depends on meeting conditions set out in the Ukraine Plan and the Memorandum of Understanding.
As reported, since 2022 the European Union and its Member States have provided €231.5 billion in assistance to Ukraine, including €3.8 billion from the proceeds of immobilised Russian assets.
In February 2026, the European Parliament and the Council adopted Regulation (EU) 2026/467, establishing the Ukraine Support Loan. The Regulation provides for up to €90 billion in support to Ukraine. The support is designed to strengthen Ukraine’s defence capabilities and ensure the uninterrupted functioning of the state, delivery of essential public services and economic resilience amid Russia’s aggression.

China-EU consensus on vehicle trade to stabilize industry expectations: CAAM
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
19:23:12 CST
20:23:12 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- The consensus reached between China and the European Union (EU) on hybrid and electric vehicle trade will help stabilize industry expectations on both sides and ensure the smooth operation of automotive industrial and supply chains, the China Association of Automobile Manufacturers (CAAM) said on Wednesday.
The consensus follows intensive bilateral talks under the China-EU trade and investment consultation mechanism, guided by the principles of mutual respect and equal consultation, the CAAM said in a statement.
As major global economies and automotive markets, China and the EU have strong industrial complementarity and broad scope for cooperation, the association said.
Managing differences and properly addressing trade frictions through institutionalized consultations, replacing confrontation with dialogue and resolving disputes through cooperation, are a rational choice that serves the fundamental interests of both sides, the CAAM noted.
Escalating trade tensions would raise business costs, disrupt normal market order and harm consumers, while hindering the automotive industry's transformation and upgrading, the CAAM said.
Regarding hybrid vehicles, the two sides emphasized and confirmed three basic principles: respect for facts, non-discrimination and compliance with World Trade Organization rules.
On electric vehicles, China and the EU achieved a "soft landing" in the EU's anti-subsidy case in January this year, with the bloc issuing a general guidance document on price undertakings. The EU will continue to advance relevant procedures concerning price undertakings by companies involved in the case, as well as other review procedures.
The consensus will provide a more predictable environment for automotive companies to pursue trade and investment cooperation and help safeguard the shared interests of industry players and consumers on both sides, the CAAM said.
The association said it would continue to promote industry dialogue and coordination, support China and the EU in working together under their trade and investment consultation mechanism to implement the consensus and properly resolve differences, and jointly uphold a fair, open and non-discriminatory international trading environment. ■

Scandal surrounding the Director of the NABU: witness reveals details of the 2008 case involving Kryvonos’s vote-buying and deception of contractors
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:19:38 EEST
20:19:38 KST

Scandal surrounding the Director of the NABU: witness reveals details of the 2008 case involving Kryvonos’s vote-buying and deception of contractors
Kyiv • UNN
Serhii Kutsenko accused Semen Kryvonos of organizing voter bribery and failing to pay contractors in 2008. The court found Kryvonos guilty, but he was amnestied.
The current head of the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU), Semen Kryvonos, has found himself at the center of a public scandal over testimony concerning his activities in 2008. Serhii Kutsenko, the owner of an advertising agency, spoke about the current official’s involvement in organizing a voter-bribery system, nonpayment to partners, and manipulation of court proceedings. This is reported by "Fakty".
According to the witness, in the spring of 2008 he worked with Kryvonos, who acted as a client on behalf of the Yulia Tymoshenko Bloc (BYuT). The task was to recruit up to 8,000 people from leading universities in the capital (Kyiv Polytechnic Institute, Kyiv National Economic University, National Aviation University, and National University of Life and Environmental Sciences of Ukraine) to create a campaign network.
The scheme involved three stages of funding:
First tranche (30%): collection of voters’ personal data (full name, telephone number, address).
Second tranche: payment before voting.
Third tranche: financial remuneration for confirmed voting.
Kutsenko said that, fearing wiretapping, coordination meetings were held exclusively in parks near the universities. When it became clear that the campaigning was turning into direct vote-buying, Kutsenko’s agency refused to participate any further.
The witness says that his agency refused to become involved in black vote-buying schemes and left Kryvonos’s operation after the first legal stage. Because of this withdrawal, Semen Kryvonos, who personally handed out money to contractors, underpaid the company by about 6,000 US dollars. According to Kutsenko’s testimony, after the project was shut down, Kryvonos’s team disappeared, leaving about 10 other contractors unpaid as well.
The witness alleged that Kryvonos manipulated the registration of paternity over a child in order to avoid a prison sentence in a criminal case, which he later renounced after a DNA test.
"That is neither humane nor manly. If you declared yourself the father, then keep your word. But as it turned out, you used a small child solely to cover your own backside," Serhii Kutsenko remarked.
The witness expressed surprise at Kryvonos’s appointment to a leadership position at NABU, given his past background. He noted that Kryvonos’s pathologically condescending attitude toward people, failure to fulfill obligations, and readiness to break the law for his own benefit were personally obvious to him as far back as 2008.
For reference The Holosiivskyi District Court of Kyiv found Semen Kryvonos guilty of committing a crime under Part 3 of Article 157 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine (voter bribery). However, in 2009 the official avoided actual punishment by registering paternity and submitting to the court a document confirming that he had a minor child dependent on him. Just eight days later, the court applied an amnesty to Kryvonos. Subsequently, in 2018–2019, the same Holosiivskyi court, following a lawsuit filed by Kryvonos and based on the results of a DNA examination, officially annulled the record of his paternity with respect to that child.

Estonian defence minister: "Russia could attack NATO. I'm not sure if we can deter the mad person"
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:19:00 EEST
20:19:00 KST

Estonian defence minister: "Russia could attack NATO. I'm not sure if we can deter the mad person"
Martin Herem is Estonia’s new minister of defence, having taken office less than a month ago. His predecessor, Hanno Pevkur, was forced to resign amid a scandal over arms procurement for Ukraine.
Herem is not a politician, but a career officer in the military.
And the new minister isn’t just any officer.
He is a full general, holding the highest military rank. Herem served as Commander of the Estonian Defence Forces from 2018 to 2022, and in that capacity he witnessed the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. In this interview, he also acknowledges that he has been on the front line in Ukraine.
While in Kyiv, General Herem met with the editor of European Pravda to discuss this, as well as his expectations regarding Russia’s next attack, including whether Russia might attack NATO.
European Pravda is the first non-Estonian media outlet to interview Martin Herem since his appointment as defence minister.
"Prevent a Russian attack? I'm not sure if we can deter the mad person"
Ukrainians are used to saying that Ukraine will definitely not be the last country that is attacked by Russia. Do you believe that as well?
If I take into account the attitude of the Russian state [towards its neighbours], and if I look at what they are producing right now for military purposes, then I think when they stop here [in Ukraine] – it doesn't matter how, whether you kick them out beyond the border, or the war is frozen – then every day they will start collecting military fat. And given their attitude, they will definitely test somebody.
Whether their first attack will be against Estonia, I'm not sure. It could be Latvia or somewhere else.
What they want to achieve is influence. They need power.
For that they don't need to occupy us, for example, Estonia.
They need to harm us and make us distrust each other, both in Estonia and among the Allies.
And if we have any nasty, ugly aggression, and Russians are gathering along the border, then we don’t want to see it again. And then we may choose the Russia-proposed solution.
That's exactly what they want: influence and instability.
You referred to Estonia and Latvia as examples, I believe, because both are in NATO. Does that mean that you expect an attack on NATO?
They may do it against NATO just to break NATO.
Acting below [the threshold of] Article Five, you mean?
Below Article Five, or under Article Five.
Because when Article Five is invoked, and we win this conflict but the victory is too ugly, then many will start blaming NATO and each other. And that’s the moment when the Russians will offer their solution: "Let's talk, let's do business as usual," and so on. And once we are under Russian influence, we go down.
I grew up in the Soviet Union, I have some understanding about this.
And Estonia has a history which teaches that Russia always attacks.
For the last thousand years, yes.
Can you see any way of preventing those attacks from happening?
I'm not sure if we can deter the mad person. But what we have to do is to prepare. And that's the only thing.
We have to prepare very seriously [for an attack] and if we do that, we may prevent it.
We have to be ready.
What are some practical ways in which small countries can prepare to contain the aggression?
First, our own self-defence capability must be very, very strong.
We must be ready to fight like Ukraine – on the front line and in the rear. And also to be able to eliminate all the threats coming from the enemy's depth, which means we need to develop our own deep strike [long-range] capability as well.
And we cannot do it on our own. We need our allies. Usually Estonia is seen as a country without strategic depth. I say we have a strategic depth. All of Europe is our rear.
That’s why we have to pay special attention to the sea. And again, it's not aggressive, it's not blocking the Baltic Sea or anything. It's ensuring the sea lines of communication at any given time. And that's what we’re doing right now together with our allies.
"In July 2022, I was in Estonian uniform on the front line in Ukraine"
Estonia is one of the countries active in the JEF (Joint Expeditionary Force).
JEF is a tool within NATO – it's not additional to NATO. JEF could make us faster to provide some support, but it still must follow the NATO plan. So it's nothing additional. It’s not an alternative – it's a small NATO inside NATO.
Does Ukraine have a place in the JEF?
I'm too young a minister to have any experience of discussions about Ukraine joining JEF, but I would say, if Ukraine has aspirations or a plan to join JEF, Estonia will definitely support it.
Let’s talk about Ukraine’s role in helping Estonia and NATO to deter threats and defend itself. You've just signed a drone deal. What are some practical ways to implement it?
The drone deal brings us not just technology, but experience.
And it's not just about how to operate an interceptor drone. It's about how to build our system of air defence or our system of fortifications, our counter-drone system. You have a lot of knowledge, a lot of data which we must adapt and bring to Estonia.
So it's not just the technology, and not even just the experience – it's about the knowledge.
How does it work in practical terms?
It could work in many ways. One of them is that we must come here to Ukraine and learn on the ground. Also, we must bring Ukrainian experts to Estonia to get advice on how we are building our defence line. That includes not just the fortifications or positions, but also sensors, energy, communications, all the necessary counter-drone assets and so on.
To be honest, it’s also about how we prepare our rear area – hospitals, local municipalities, police stations, energy, everything – against whatever air threat, be it an Iskander ballistic missile, a cruise missile, or hundreds of Shahed-type drones.
You mentioned that you could come here. Do you expect Estonian, i.e. NATO, military personnel in Ukraine during the war?
To be honest, we have been visiting since 2022.
I was here for the first time in July 2022 – I came here to learn. At that time, I was Commander of the Estonian Defence Forces.
How does that fit with statements that NATO military personnel are not in Ukraine?
In July 2022, I was in Estonian uniform on the front line, and the front line then was a few kilometres from Kharkiv. I was there in uniform.
The difference is that we do not operate here. We learn. So we don't take up weapons, we don't operate the radar or whatever. But we visit.
And this is not a threat to Russia at all.
But it is, because you bring what you’ve learned back to Estonia.
Estonia will never use this knowledge unless Russia crosses our border.
We have no plan to cross the border and attack Russia. We have no such plan and never have had. But if they come, then we will use everything we have learned from Ukraine.
"Russian hybrid attacks aim to keep conflicts warm"
Russia is not that active in conventional attacks against Estonia, but in the hybrid domain they are. Would you agree?
In the conventional domain, I don't think we should expect anything active from Russia as long as they are tied down here in Ukraine. But actually, with conventional power, sometimes you don't have to use it.
It's enough to show it.
It’s like my fist. (The general shows his fist.) Threatening with a fist is also something. Because if you show it, then one day you may use it. And since Russia is showing it, like they do today against us, that’s also part of conventional power.
How are they showing it?
They're building the Leningrad Military Region, for example. They're building new units. They are producing tanks, artillery, ammunition, aircraft, everything, behind our border.
Why are they doing this? They know NATO has no plan to cross the border. We have no plan to attack.
Then why are they building fortifications and new military bases behind the border of Finland? Why did they create this Leningrad Military Region and so on?
They’re doing it to threaten us, and maybe to prepare.
And what about hybrid threats?
Referring to hybrid operations, we used to talk about sabotage, cyber operations, information operations, whatever.
But in general, hybrid actions serve to prepare the conditions and the environment, keeping the conflict warm.
Because if you want to use conventional power, you need to explain to your own nation and to third countries that you had a problem with Estonia, or with the West. You need a kind of justification for your actions.
And no one will know later that it was you who caused the sabotage. The people in Russia only see that "we had a problem with them and we had to solve it". Now, [Russian] Foreign Minister [Sergei] Lavrov has said very clearly: everybody supporting Ukraine will be punished by us. He said it one or two months ago, and now we see their actions.
But all these hybrid actions just cause harm – it hurts – but it's not a threat to our being, our existence.
Isn’t it? People in Estonia expect NATO to protect them against hybrid threats, and it doesn’t. This could also diminish public trust in the Alliance.
There are no good solutions, no good response, to this problem.
However, if you look at what the Russians have done during the last few months, for example – that armed drone in Germany [that attacked the airport], or when they set fire [to a military production base] in Estonia – what was our response? The Germans increased their support to Ukraine. Estonia decided to support Ukraine through PURL with another €10 million.
Next week we will have a meeting in Tallinn to discuss what kind of support we will send to Ukraine next year – and that will be more than €100 million just from Estonia.
These are actually the responses to all these acts, sabotage and so on. We say to Russia: you can try, but we will not stop.
And one more element of our response is the public disclosure of Russian actions.
If there is something burning, blowing up or falling down, and the Russian special services are behind it, then we must say that openly and attribute it to them as fast as possible. If Russia is not the cause and it's just criminal activity, then okay. But if the Russians are behind it, we must attribute it to them immediately.
"I would like to see Ukraine win this war"
How do you see Ukraine’s role in the future security architecture of Europe?
First, Ukraine has experience. And not just experience in fighting. You’ve learned how to stop this aggressor which is a threat to us as well. And your experience can contribute to European security.
Secondly, I think Ukraine must be an equal member of this security system. It doesn't matter whether we talk about the EU or NATO or whatever. Whether it would be full membership or some kind of association – that's up to Ukrainians and NATO. But if you asked me, I would say: why not full membership?
Is NATO ready to accept Ukraine as a full member?
I don’t know how we [Estonia] joined NATO – whether it was our success, or a miracle, or just a lucky moment.
I can tell you why. It’s because Russia was weak.
Russia was weak. And maybe not everyone realised what they were doing when they agreed to take us into NATO. I don't know.
But if we are in NATO, my question is:
Why wouldn't Ukraine join NATO then? What is the difference?
The only difference is that you have an active war going on right now. But when the war is over, frozen, whatever – why not?
For example, Estonia doesn't even have an official border with Russia. We are not at war, but still, we don't have an agreed border, and that’s also a little bit shaky.
So, it's up to the politicians, but first of all it’s up to the Ukrainian nation and then the other 32 Allied nations to decide.
As you mentioned, because Russia is stuck in Ukraine, they cannot attack you. They don’t dare to cross the border of Estonia, Latvia, Finland – anywhere. Doesn't that mean that to some degree, some Western allies may have an interest in keeping Russia stuck in Ukraine as long as possible?
I've been asked this many, many times. We may say yes, that's possible. But I say honestly: even if stopping the war here is risky for us because then the threat against us will grow, thinking like that goes against our values.
If we forget our values – freedom, democracy, whatever we want to achieve – then we will very soon lose everything.
That's why we should not abandon Ukraine. That's why we have to support Ukraine as much as possible – not to keep the war here, but to support Ukraine to win the war.
If somebody says "Maybe we should just keep the war boiling here, so it doesn’t come to us," that’s definitely not my aim or objective. I would like to see Ukraine win this war. That's my understanding.
Do you believe this is how other allies see it as well?
Maybe I'm too naive, but it's hard to believe that Latvians, Finns, Lithuanians or Poles have this kind of plan to keep Russia fighting here and to let Ukraine suffer. Maybe I'm too naive, but I say: I don't believe that. Because all of us – Finns, Latvians, Lithuanians – see Ukraine as our alter ego. And we don't want Ukraine to suffer. Definitely not.
Otherwise we would not spend so much money and resources or pay that much attention to this.
Sergiy Sydorenko
European Pravda

The Kremlin said on Wednesday that there is a “great deal of noise” present in the media concerning peace proposals to end the ongoing Russia-Ukraine war, calling much of it “fabrication.” 
Speaking at a press briefing, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov commented on a story by The Washington Post published on Monday, which, citing an unnamed US official, reported on a joint peace proposal under development by the US and Europe. 
“There is a great deal of noise in the press about all this right now, and much of that noise does not correspond to reality – it is pure fabrication,” Peskov said.

Earlier Wednesday, Serhii Beskrestnov said on Telegram that SpaceX implemented speed restrictions for Starlink terminals without notification, limiting speed to 100 miles per hour. 
Neither US officials nor SpaceX have commented on the statement.

"And what was announced? What are the parameters of the energy truce, and what does it entail? Were any specific details provided?" Peskov said. 
The spokesman also spoke about artificial intelligence, arguing that some countries were weaponizing it and that it is necessary to be prepared for the challenges brought by these technologies.

Powerful explosions meanwhile rattled the Saudi capital, as the coalition fighting the Houthis said it had intercepted a missile fired by the Iran-backed group towards Riyadh.
Saudi Arabia, the world’s top crude oil exporter, has in recent days come under sustained attack in a dramatic escalation in the war with the Houthis.
It has hit back with strikes against the group’s stronghold in the Yemeni capital Sanaa, which for years has been under their grip.
Yahya Saree, Houthi military spokesman, said their forces had conducted “a high-quality military operation targeting Aramco in Dhahran” as well as strikes targeting Riyadh airport and a refinery in the capital.
“This was carried out using a large number of ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and drones,” he said, adding that “operations toward Saudi depths will continue in the coming days, targeting Saudi enemy airports and oil facilities.”
Earlier, a Saudi Energy Ministry official said a building belonging to Aramco in Dhahran was struck, resulting in a “limited fire” but “no casualties or fatalities.”
Dhahran is home to Aramco’s headquarters, a vast complex comprising numerous buildings and residential compounds.
According to two company employees who spoke to AFP on condition of anonymity, a tower in the headquarters was hit overnight.
“Top three floors have gone,” said one of the employees.

Lawyers at Start of Nord Stream Trial Argue Bombing May Not Have Been a Crime
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:17:00 UTC
20:17:00 KST

Lawyers for a Ukrainian ex-military officer accused of leading the bombing of Russia's Nord Stream pipeline in September 2022 argued at the start of his trial in Germany on Wednesday that "an aggressor's infrastructure" may have been a lawful target.
Serhii Kuznetsov is accused of leading a group of Ukrainian agents including divers and an explosives expert that blew up Russia's largest gas pipeline to Europe in one of the biggest infrastructure sabotage operations of modern times.
The case provides the first opportunity for a public hearing of evidence gathered during a years-long investigation, which has been diplomatically and politically awkward for a German government that remains staunchly supportive of Ukraine despite the investigative trail linking Kyiv to the bombing.
Moving to have the case dismissed, Kuznetsov's lawyer Nicola Canestrini argued that the pipeline — which provided half of Germany's imports of natural gas before Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine — was a "Russian weapon."
"Is it unlawful to destroy an aggressor's infrastructure without harming any human beings?" Canestrini asked.
Right to remain silent
Prosecutors have alleged that Kuznetsov, who was arrested under an international warrant in Italy last year, worked with members of the Ukrainian military to plan the clandestine operation on behalf of unidentified Ukrainian state entities.
Kuznetsov, 50, who prior to Wednesday was referred to publicly only as Serhii K. under German legal rules, has denied any involvement in the blasts that ruptured the 1,200-kilometer (750-mile)-long Baltic Sea pipeline.
Wearing a grey suit and with a shaved head, he exercised his right to remain silent in court but did not cover his face. His lawyers said he could not mount a proper defense because he was obliged to withhold Ukrainian state secrets.
The government in Kyiv has also denied any involvement, a sensitive point in its relations with Germany, Ukraine's largest European supplier of military aid. Russia said on Monday it expected a "just verdict" that would reveal the names of the perpetrators and those who ordered the operation.
Kuznetsov's legal team had tried reaching out to Ukraine for information that might assist the defense but heard nothing, according to another defense lawyer, Jes Meyer-Lohkamp.
Attacking civilian targets is considered a war crime
German prosecutors say the actions Kuznetsov is accused of — attacking civilian targets and causing explosions that destroyed infrastructure and damaged public services — would amount to a war crime.
Kuznetsov is the only person on trial, but Croatian authorities have arrested another man, identified as Vladimir Z., who prosecutors believe was one of the divers.
The explosion of Nord Stream sealed the end of Germany's longstanding dependence on Russian natural gas, although Moscow had already cut supplies over Berlin's support for European sanctions following Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
Nord Stream's supply had been due to double with the opening of a twin pipeline, Nord Stream 2, already built, but Berlin canceled approval to open it just prior to Russia's invasion.
Plumes of methane gas
The trial, expected to continue into February next year, could have domestic political implications.
Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), leading in opinion polls for more than a year, has called for an end to military aid for Ukraine and a restoration of energy ties with Moscow.
Although German state parliaments have no role in foreign policy, the AfD filed a motion in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt on Wednesday calling for an end to support for Ukraine, noting the "historical parallel" with the start of the trial.
The Nord Stream system, lying at a depth of 80 to 110 meters under the Baltic and built by Russian gas concern Gazprom to supply up to 110 billion cubic meters of gas to Germany, was formerly at the core of economic ties between the two countries.
The Sept. 26, 2022, blasts that ruptured three of the four concrete-coated steel pipelines created a giant whirlpool at sea as huge plumes of methane gas rose into the atmosphere.
Prosecutors allege that Kuznetsov traveled to Germany through Poland some three weeks before the attack, using a forged Ukrainian passport. He and his group then used a sailboat hired in the northern German city of Rostock to reach an area close to the Danish island of Bornholm, where they rigged specialized military-grade explosives to the sea floor.
The weekly Der Spiegel magazine and ZDF public television have previously reported that five men and one woman were on the rented yacht Andromeda, which left Rostock on Sept. 6 and returned on Sept. 23, 2022.

Iran steps up Hormuz surveillance: Attacks soar, oil flows crash again
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:16:21 UTC
20:16:21 KST

Iran steps up Hormuz surveillance: Attacks soar, oil flows crash again
Ships in the Strait of Hormuz have been experiencing the worst spate of attacks since the start of the US-Israel war on Iran.
Iran’s military said it has expanded its surveillance of the Strait of Hormuz by deploying new units to target ships, amid a desperate tussle between Tehran and Washington to control the waterway, among the world’s most important passages for energy transport.
With the United States naval blockade of Iran’s southern ports in place and sanctions tightening, Tehran has repeatedly said it will pursue military and diplomatic efforts to put pressure on Washington to submit to its demands regarding reopening the strait.
Tehran’s latest announcement coincides with a surge in attacks in the waterway and a fall in oil transit after crude flows had risen back to pre-war levels in September.
Chris Featherstone, a political scientist at the University of York in the United Kingdom, told Al Jazeera the increased attacks and their impact on energy flows demonstrate the fragility of the strait as a key pathway for oil exports.
So, what’s going on and who controls the Strait of Hormuz now?
Here’s what we know:
What has Iran said about expanding its presence in Hormuz?
The navy said these units would maintain “real time surveillance of enemy activities and maritime traffic in the region”.
It also warned vessels not to switch off their transponders and urged them to coordinate with Iranian armed forces for safe passage through the area.
Separately, an Iranian official told the Reuters news agency that Tehran had started using different offensive tactics against vessels it considered in violation of its restrictions about 10 days ago, adding that this had led to an increase in attacks on such ships.
The strategy includes a change in the type as well as the pace of attacks, with one goal being to influence the outcome of the November midterm elections in the US, according to the official.
Attacks in Hormuz rise to record levels
Ships in the Strait of Hormuz have been experiencing the worst spate of attacks since the start of the US and Israel’s war on Iran in late February.
According to maritime tracking firm Kpler, 10 tankers were struck in the strait between September 28 and October 4, followed by another strike on October 5.
The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) centre has separately recorded 15 other attacks between October 6 and October 14, with 11 of them occurring in just the past four days. They include a container ship and a tanker hit by unknown projectiles in the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday, UKMTO said.
Iran maintains that its attacks and restrictions in the waterway are a matter of national security and self-defence in response to the US-Israel war. Iranian authorities have also signalled they intend to disrupt a US-assisted shuttle system that has enabled more energy exports through the strait during the war.
In its latest report on Sunday, the US Navy-led Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC) noted that the threat to merchant shipping in the Strait of Hormuz remained “severe”, the second-highest level.
Attacks by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), “attempted attacks, and/or harassment activity persisted including UAV overflight, targeted surveillance of merchant shipping, and occasional VHF hailing,” JMIC said.
UAV stands for unmanned aerial vehicle, or drone, while VHF hailing refers to Iranian forces using standard marine radio to verbally contact, track, and intimidate passing merchant ships on international communication channels.
How have attacks affected oil flows?
Before the US-Israel war on Iran began on February 28, the Strait of Hormuz typically handled about 125 large commercial vessels a day and shipments through it accounted for about 20 percent of global crude and liquefied natural gas supplies.
In retaliation for the US-Israeli attacks, Iran effectively closed the strait and has stepped up attacks on vessels trying to break its regulations. Meanwhile, Washington has also maintained a blockade on Iranian ports.
In September, however, Gulf oil flows through Hormuz, excluding Iran, recovered to more than 81 percent of pre-war levels, while crude exports from the wider Middle East exceeded pre-war levels on 14 days during the month, Kpler reported. Shepherded by the US Navy, more and more oil tankers had started passing through.
The Iranian threat meant ship crew were being paid hefty bonuses, insurance rates remained very high, and some analysts suspect that Gulf nations may also have been paying off Iran to allow tankers to transit. This means that while more oil was being exported from the region, crude prices remained high.
But the surge in Iranian attacks in recent days has changed the equation. According to Kpler, only 2.9 million barrels of oil were carried through the waterway on October 11, the lowest level this month. As recently as October 8, nearly 20.8 million barrels of oil passed through the strait. The pre-war average was 17.1 million barrels a day.
Oil prices continued to climb on Wednesday morning, with Brent crude futures gaining 89 cents, or 0.8 percent, to $106.58 a barrel as of 00:30 GMT. Brent futures had closed at $105.69 a barrel on Tuesday, while West Texas Intermediate settled at $94.14.
What is the US saying?
On Wednesday, a US military official confirmed to Reuters that Iran had changed tactics in the Strait of Hormuz in one significant way.
The official noted that after Washington destroyed much of Iran’s radar capabilities, the IRGC had started using unarmed spotters in small boats to identify potential targets, including US naval vessels.
The US military determined that Iranian spotters were operating from dhows, calling in targets to the IRGC, the official said, adding that US forces confronted one such vessel, told its occupants to abandon ship and then destroyed it.
US Central Command (CENTCOM) has also rejected assertions by the commander of the IRGC that Tehran controls the Strait of Hormuz and would sink approaching US warships.
“IRGC’s navy commander has no navy. American forces and regional partners clearly control the Strait of Hormuz,” CENTCOM said on X.
The military command added that US forces assisted Gulf partners to ship more than 19 million barrels of crude oil through the strategic chokepoint on Monday.
So, who controls Hormuz?
Since Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz after the war began, the US Navy has reportedly opened up a route so Gulf states can export oil and other commodities amid the energy crisis caused by Iran’s attacks on ships.
On Sunday night, Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, claimed that US Central Command, with the assistance of the United Arab Emirates military, was using smaller vessels to transfer oil to larger tankers.
He said this US shuttle system was an explicit target for Tehran, and that Iran has been striking five or six participating vessels nightly for weeks.
“You are smuggling, but the strait is under Iran’s control, and we manage it,” he asserted.
This appeared to be a taunt aimed at US President Donald Trump, who has hailed energy exports at times reaching pre-war levels over recent weeks.
Iran has claimed that the US accepted some of its seven conditions for the full reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and for ending the war, but that Washington’s response was “insufficient”. Tehran insists that a deal will only materialise when all its demands are met.
“The Trump administration has not moved to engage with continued negotiations, and hasn’t sought further help from potential interlocutors, such as Qatar and Pakistan,” Chris Featherstone, the University of York political scientist, said.
“For Iran, they may be seeing this as a point to increase pressure on the Trump administration.”
But he noted that the strait is not under Iranian control, and that Tehran’s attacks only attempt to show that Washington does not control the waterway either.
“As such, US allies will increase pressure for the Trump administration to bring more stability to the region, or show a path towards achieving greater stability,” he added.

Scarborough soldier buried in Belgium more than a century after his death
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:03:00 BST
20:03:00 KST

Scarborough soldier buried in Belgium more than a century after his death
Scarborough soldier, Lance Corporal (LCpl) Claude Stanley Dell, has been laid to rest more than a century after his death in World War 1.
A young Scarborough soldier of World War 1, killed just a week after his arrival in France, has finally been laid to rest with full military honours. LCpl Claude Stanley Dell of the 5th Battalion Yorkshire Regiment was laid to rest today (13 October 2026) at Commonwealth War Graves Commission’s (CWGC) Poelcapelle British Cemetery in Belgium.
In 2021, workmen digging a rainwater cistern in Hazeweidestraat, St Juliaan, Belgium spotted human remains in their trench. A few days later an archaeological excavation was undertaken by the Flanders Heritage Agency. Artefacts recovered alongside the remains showed them to be those of a soldier who had served in the 5th Battalion Yorkshire Regiment.
The Ministry of Defence’s Joint Casualty and Compassionate Centre (JCCC), known as the ‘MOD War Detectives’, launched an investigation to name him. Research identified twenty men from the regiment missing in the area, all of whom died in the Spring of 1915. Following genealogical investigation, living descendants of the missing men were traced one by one until eventually DNA testing proved that the remains were those of LCpl Claude Stanley Dell.
LCpl Dell joined up alongside his brothers Charles and Guy at the outbreak of war. All three joined the 5th Battalion Yorkshire Regiment, whilst their older brother Leighton was in the Royal Field Artillery, and another brother - Frederick - served with the Yorkshire Hussars.
5th Battalion left the UK on 17 April 1915 and arrived in Boulogne the following day. On 23 April they arrived on the Ypres Salient, and just two days later on 25 April 1915 LCpl Dell was killed in action. Claude’s brothers wrote home to tell their parents, ‘poor Claude met his end…whilst doing his duty’.
Today, LCpl Dell was buried with full military honours in the presence of both his military family, and his great-niece Judith.
The service, organised by JCCC, was supported by serving soldiers of the Royal Yorkshire Regiment, as well as staff from the CWGC.
Alexia Clark, MOD War Detective, said:
  It has been a privilege to research this case, to have been able to identify LCpl Dell, and to have been able to lay him to rest today. I am extremely grateful to 2nd Battalion the Royal Yorkshire Regiment who have provided the bearer party for the funeral, and to the members of Claude’s family who have been involved in his commemoration.
Claude’s grave will now be cared for in perpetuity by the Commonwealth War Graves Commission, ensuring his sacrifice is never forgotten. Dr Daniel Seaton, Commemorations Case Officer at CWGC, said:
  Lance Corporal Dell lay in an unmarked grave on the former battlefields for well over 100 years. It is a great privilege to have worked alongside the JCCC and our Belgian partners in the effort to restore his identity. He is now laid to rest in a Commission cemetery not far from where he fell, ensuring that his grave can be visited in perpetuity and his sacrifice remembered.

As Yemen-Saudi tensions rise, Palestinians question Iran's goals

As Yemen-Saudi tensions rise, Gaza's Palestinians question Iran's endgame
The recent round of fighting between Yemen's Houthis and Saudi Arabia has sparked debate among Palestinians over the role of Iran and its allies in the region.
While some Palestinians supported Houthi attacks in the Red Sea during the Israeli genocidal war, others question their impact, especially as the latest round of fighting in Yemen that erupted since mid-September, and spread to Saudi airports and other civilian facilities.
On Monday, the Palestinian Authority's Presidency condemned the Houthi attacks, denouncing strikes on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and expressing solidarity with Saudi Arabia.
In a press statement, it backed measures taken by the Kingdom to protect its security and facilities and warned against threats to the Two Holy Mosques in Mecca and Medina.
Hamas, meanwhile, had not issued a public comment despite repeated attempts by The New Arab to obtain its position.
Other Palestinian factions, particularly those with ties to Iran, had also not publicly stated their positions.
Palestinian factions' calculations
Mohammed Hijazi, a Jordan-based Palestinian researcher specialising in Islamist groups, told TNA that Palestinian factions maintained alliances with Iran and its regional allies, including the Houthis.
Hijazi said these ties were largely political and did not necessarily involve participation in the war or material support.
He added that the factions were reluctant to openly support the Houthis against Saudi Arabia, fearing this could damage relations with Riyadh, a key regional supporter of the Palestinian cause and an important ally of the Palestinian Authority.
He further elaborated that the factions' regional influence had diminished significantly since Israel's genocidal war in Gaza, while their political activities had done little to improve Palestinians' lives.
So, their position on Yemen, he believed, reflected political alignment with Iran and its allies, tempered by the need to avoid alienating Saudi Arabia or exposing the Palestinian cause to further political risks.
Regional rivalries and Gaza's suffering
Palestinian political analyst Akram Atallah told TNA that the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia reflect wider regional rivalries and Iran's efforts to expand its influence across the Middle East.
He argued that the Houthis' actions served Tehran's regional ambitions, while the group's ties to Hamas further complicated the political dynamics surrounding the Palestinian cause.
The increased violence has also raised questions about Washington's willingness to support Saudi Arabia against the Houthis, given its broader regional interests and relations with the parties involved.
Atallah said the United States might be reluctant to side directly with Saudi Arabia against the Houthis because of its wider regional calculations and its understandings with the group.
He added that Saudi Arabia's position on normalising relations with Israel could also influence Washington's response.
Atallah noted that Israel was seeking to capitalise on regional tensions to advance its own political and strategic interests, while Riyadh appeared unwilling to make normalisation a condition for securing support against regional threats.
For some Palestinians, the confrontation has also prompted questions about whether Iran and its allies have done enough to support their cause.
Abdul Majeed Zaqout, a 42-year-old father of three from Gaza City, told TNA that his view of the Houthis had changed over time.
Initially, he regarded their Red Sea attacks as an attempt to support Palestinians and pressure Israel to end its genocidal war on Gaza.
"At first, I believed the Houthi attacks were intended to support Gaza, but I have increasingly come to see them as linked to political and regional calculations, particularly Iran's interests," Zaqout said.
"What increased my doubts was the expansion of the confrontation to include attacks on Saudi Arabia, the largest Muslim-majority country with a Sunni majority, putting civilians, including Muslim pilgrims performing Umrah, at risk," he added.
Zaqout noted that Saudi Arabia had linked normalising relations with Israel to resolving the Palestinian issue, while he believed Iran had failed to do enough to alleviate Gaza's suffering despite supporting Hamas and Hezbollah in Lebanon.
"It is difficult to understand how Iran raises the slogan of supporting Palestine while the people of Gaza continue to suffer without seeing tangible results from that support," he said.
"The Israeli army destroyed our homes, and forced us to live in tents, while regional alliances and conflicts continue to be shaped by the calculations of different powers," he added.
Iran's regional influence
Zaqout's frustration is shared by other Gaza residents who argue that Iran's regional ambitions have come at the expense of ordinary people across the region.
Fadi Al-Assar, a resident of the al-Nuseirat refugee camp in central Gaza, also condemned the Houthi attacks, accusing Iran of using its regional allies to expand its influence at the expense of Arab countries, particularly Saudi Arabia.
"I believe Iran is using its regional allies to exert pressure on Arab countries, particularly Saudi Arabia," he told TNA.
Al-Assar said Tehran's support for groups involved in confrontations with Arab states had intensified regional tensions without helping to end the war on Gaza or stop Israel's attacks.
"Saudi Arabia is a pivotal state in the Arab and Islamic worlds, and I believe Iran is attempting to weaken it through its regional allies," he said.
"Meanwhile, Tehran champions hostility towards Israel, yet we have not seen its actions halt the war on Gaza or prevent its destruction. The problem is not limited to Gaza; it extends across the entire Middle East, where civilians pay the price for conflicts they had no say in initiating," he added.
While Zaqout and Al-Assar focused on the regional consequences of Iran's alliances, Rahaf Abu Hajar, a university student from Gaza's al-Maghazi refugee camp, described their impact through the disruption of her own life and future.
Abu Hajar said she opposed the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and Hamas's political and military approach, criticising Iran's support for both groups.
She argued that they had devastated Palestinian families and disrupted an entire generation's education.
For her, the consequences extend beyond the destruction of homes to the loss of opportunities that young Palestinians had once taken for granted.
After graduating from high school during the war, Abu Hajar had hoped to begin university and plan for her future. Although she enrolled, she said she could attend classes only one day a week.
"I used to dream of finishing high school, going to university, and living like other young women -- studying, meeting friends, and planning my future," she said.
"But I graduated during the war, and even after enrolling, I couldn't experience university life the way I had hoped. I feel as though years of our lives and our dreams have been stolen from us," she added.
Abu Hajar held Hamas responsible for its role in bringing war to Gaza and criticised Iran's support for the movement, arguing that Palestinians should not have to bear the consequences of regional alliances.
"I do not want to remain a prisoner of war and regional conflicts. I want to learn and build my future, just like any young woman dreaming of a normal life," she said
Ultimately in Gaza, where the Israeli genocidal war has and continues to devastate lives and futures, frustration is growing over the gap between political rhetoric and tangible support from all sides.

Iran, Kenya chambers of commerce chart strategic trade path
TEHRAN- The head of the Iran Chamber of Commerce, in a meeting with the head of the Kenya Chamber of Commerce, described Kenya—due to its strong financial infrastructure and the strategic port of Mombasa—as the most important gateway for Iran and other countries to the African market, and stated: Iran sees Kenya as a strategic and reciprocal partner and can play a role as a gateway for Kenya to Central Asia and Eurasia.
Samad Hassanzadeh, Head of the Iran Chamber of Commerce Industries, Mines and Agriculture (ICCIMA), during a trip to Nairobi, in a meeting with Eric Ruto, President of the Kenya National Chamber of Commerce and Industry (KNCCI), congratulated the 60th anniversary of the founding of the Kenya Chamber.
He described Dr. Ruto’s membership in the General Council of the World Federation of Chambers as a foundation for cooperation between the two chambers in international chamber forums, and said: The statistics of trade exchanges between Iran and Kenya, despite the very good capacities of the Islamic Republic of Iran and Kenya’s capacities, are not at an appropriate level, and the chambers of commerce of the two countries can provide very good opportunities together.
Referring to the restrictions caused by economic sanctions on our country’s economic relations, the head of the Iran Chamber noted: In the private sector and chambers of commerce, we have a heavy responsibility toward our nations, and we must help properly and fulfill these duties.
He described Kenya—due to its powerful financial infrastructure and the strategic port of Mombasa—as the most important gateway for Iran and other countries to the African market, and stated: Iran sees Kenya as a strategic and reciprocal partner and can play a role as a gateway for Kenya to Central Asia and Eurasia.
Hassanzadeh enumerated Iran’s capacities, emphasizing the fields of health and medicine, agriculture, energy, petrochemicals and fertilizer, infrastructure, housing, and technology, and considered these capacities aligned with Kenya’s development needs. He emphasized: Although the Islamic Republic of Iran has been under sanctions for several decades, despite the sanctions it has achieved very large capacities, and we are interested and consider it a duty to share these capacities with African countries.
He announced the readiness of Iran’s private sector to participate in supplying medicine and medical equipment, and also in joint production in Kenya in line with the policy of domestic production of medicine, and said: In the field of agriculture and food security, we are ready to transfer technical knowledge in mechanization, modern irrigation, processing and conversion industries, and reducing post-harvest waste, and for joint investment with Kenyan partners in the agricultural value chain.
Hassanzadeh, stating that Iran has a competitive advantage in bitumen, petrochemical products, and chemical fertilizer and is ready to participate beyond the supply of goods in energy development projects and renewable energies, also said regarding Iran’s capacities in infrastructure, housing, and technology: We are ready to share the capabilities of Iranian companies in construction, dam building, power plants, mass housing, and information technology in order to participate in Kenya’s development projects.
The head of the Iran Chamber named joint investment by Iranian and Kenyan economic actors in overseas cultivation, road construction, and the establishment of petrochemical and refinery industry facilities as other areas of interest for developing economic cooperation between Iran and Kenya.
The Head of the Iran Chamber of Commerce, Industries, Mines and Agriculture, expressing interest in sustainable trade between Iran and Kenya and the import of tea, coffee, and other agricultural products from Kenya, emphasized: With most countries, we develop trade through barter for greater cooperation.
In explaining ways to facilitate trade between the two countries, he emphasized establishing direct flights between Tehran and Nairobi to ease the movement of traders from the two countries, and invited Dr. Ruto to travel to Tehran at the head of a trade delegation and stressed expanding the dispatch and reception of trade delegations between the two countries.
Seyed Mehdi Tabibzadeh, President of the Kerman Chamber of Commerce, Industries, Mines and Agriculture, also in this meeting, referring to the diverse capacities of different Iranian provinces, called for the formation of a joint business committee and the removal of trade obstacles, including customs and tariff barriers, and emphasized facilitating trade communications.
The head of the Kerman Chamber noted that the establishment of a permanent center for displaying Iranian products in Nairobi can be examined.
Eric Ruto, President of the Kenya National Chamber of Commerce and Industry, also welcoming the presence of the head of the Iran Chamber and the accompanying delegation in Nairobi, emphasized that attracting the participation of economic actors from other countries in dam construction, road construction, mining, and health services is important for Kenya.
Mostafa Ramadan, Vice President of the Kenya Chamber, also considered the current figures for trade between the two countries insufficient given the population and capacities of Iran and Kenya, and said: Iran cn gain access to Africa’s market worth over one billion dollars through Kenya.
He said: Energy, logistics, and technical and engineering services are among the areas where Iran has high advantages and can increase its presence in these fields in the Kenyan market, and the Kenya Chamber should take the necessary measures to remove obstacles to Iran’s presence in this field.

Germany has joined the Ukraine Transport Support Fund with a contribution of EUR 1 million, bringing the total announced funding to EUR 4.1 million, including contributions from Sweden, Norway, Lithuania and Estonia, Ukrainian Minister for Recovery, Infrastructure and Transport Mykola Kalashnyk said.
"These are the first contributions that will make it possible to test the Fund's operating mechanism in practice, from Ukraine identifying its immediate needs to the procurement and delivery of equipment," he wrote on Telegram.

He also said that the initial projects would serve as the basis for further expanding the Fund and attracting new partners.
"I thank Germany and all the countries that have supported the launch of this mechanism," the minister said in the statement.
In turn, Ukraine's Ministry for Recovery, Infrastructure and Transport specified in a press release that Germany had previously announced its readiness to join the Fund during the International Transport Forum in Leipzig in May 2026.
In particular, the parties discussed the restoration of Ukraine's transport infrastructure, logistics development, renewal of Ukrzaliznytsia's rolling stock, and continued support for the railway, road and maritime sectors.
The ministry recalled that the Ukraine Transport Support Fund was established in 2025 by Ukraine, Lithuania, Sweden and Canada under the framework of the International Transport Forum (ITF). The Fund's activities cover all modes of transport: rail, road, urban, aviation, maritime and inland waterway transport.
"Its task is to promptly meet the urgent needs of the transport sector that are difficult or time-consuming to address through large-scale international funding programs," the ministry added.

Türkiye has launched a new effort to draft its personal data protection legislation to better align with European standards, taking a tangible step toward meeting the remaining criteria for visa-free travel to the European Union (EU), daily Hürriyet reported on Oct. 14.
The move follows an interministerial initiative launched in August to remove the outstanding obstacles to visa liberalization, with Ankara now preparing to enter technical talks with the European Commission on one of the six remaining benchmarks.
A revised draft of the legislation has been prepared, and the process has reached the stage of technical consultations with the European Commission.
Officials from relevant Turkish ministries and the EU executive body are expected to meet in the near future, the report said.
The initiative is part of a new strategic approach announced in August by Vice President Cevdet Yılmaz, aimed at overcoming the obstacles preventing Türkiye from securing visa-free access to the bloc.
The upcoming talks are expected to mark one of the first steps toward fulfilling the relevant benchmark and help shape the subsequent stages of the process.
The European Commission’s assessment of whether the proposed changes have the potential to meet EU expectations will be crucial in determining how the process moves forward.
The six outstanding benchmarks include amending counterterrorism legislation, concluding an agreement with Europol, taking further steps to combat corruption, establishing judicial cooperation with all EU member states, fully implementing all provisions of the Readmission Agreement, and aligning personal data protection legislation with European standards.
The Visa Liberalization Dialogue between Türkiye and the EU was launched on Dec. 16, 2013. Türkiye met 65 of the 72 benchmarks within the first three years of the process. The number of outstanding criteria fell to six in 2018, when Ankara fulfilled one additional requirement.

does the paris of the impressionists still exist? alix urien finds it through her lens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:55:04 UTC
19:55:04 KST

does the paris of the impressionists still exist? alix urien finds it through her lens
french photographer alix urien revisits impressionism in circa 2020s, using movement, light and color to capture the fleeting beauty of contemporary paris and normandy.
[FEATURED]
FINDING IMPRESSIONISM IN CONTEMPORARY PARIS
Does the Paris of the great Impressionist painters still exist? French photographer and videographer Alix Urien believes the answer may lie in the way we look rather than in what we see. In her series Circa 2020s, created between Paris and Normandy, she transforms ordinary contemporary scenes into photographs and videos shaped by the light, color and fleeting sensations of nineteenth-century Impressionism. Rather than reproducing famous paintings through a camera lens, Urien explores the emotions that connect different generations, suggesting that while cities and societies evolve, certain human experiences remain remarkably unchanged.
‘Impressionism was an answer to a changing world,’ Urien tells designboom, recalling the industrialization, urban transformation and accelerating pace of life that accompanied the movement’s emergence. ‘They looked for the poetry in their everyday lives,’ she explains, finding inspiration in nature, intimate circles and familiar surroundings. A century after Claude Monet’s death in 1926, the photographer sees striking parallels between the nineteenth century and today, when technological change and an increasingly restless world make the simple act of observing feel almost radical.
PAINTING WITH MOVEMENT, LIGHT AND COLOR
Urien’s photographic process begins with reality: an ordinary moment unfolding before her lens. From there, she experiments with movement, captured directly through the camera, introducing a degree of unpredictability that recalls the spontaneity of an Impressionist brushstroke. ‘I’m drawn to the physicality and randomness of it, to the fact that I can never fully control the outcome,’ she explains. Rather than pursuing the precision usually associated with photography, she embraces uncertainty, allowing the image to move beyond documentation and toward something more sensory. The result occupies a space somewhere between a photograph and the memory of a scene.
Color plays an equally important role in her compositions. Drawing on color theory, Urien works with fragmented touches of light and color to emphasize the emotional atmosphere of an image. Yet her interest in Impressionism goes beyond aesthetics. Just as the arrival of photography challenged painters to reconsider their medium in the nineteenth century, she sees a parallel in the questions raised by artificial intelligence today. In response, she observes a renewed interest in experimental approaches to image-making, where personality and creative intuition matter more than technical perfection. For Urien, the camera becomes less a tool for reproducing reality than a means of interpreting how it feels.
SEVEN YEARS OF REDISCOVERING THE SAME CITY
Paris itself has become an ongoing subject of this exploration. After returning from London in 2019, Urien began discovering the French capital through a photographer’s eyes, finding a city that, despite its extraordinary density of history, could still feel like a small village. Hidden museums, overlooked corners and art shops revealed themselves alongside the changing character of its neighborhoods. Over seven years, she has returned to familiar places through different seasons and everyday encounters, observing how the same setting can take on an entirely different atmosphere from one moment to the next. Photography and video have become her ways of tracing these subtle transformations.
This fascination with the city’s evolving identity also informs Paris is for the Dreamers, her forthcoming photography book project, conceived somewhere between an artistic collection and a personal guide to the capital. ‘We all have our own idea of a Paris shaped by paintings or movies,’ Urien reflects, while emphasizing that the real city continues to evolve with its seasons, stories and inhabitants. Her work offers neither an exercise in nostalgia nor an attempt to preserve Paris as an open-air museum. Instead, it suggests that the world of the Impressionists has never entirely disappeared. It simply requires a different way of looking.

Ukraine National Bank eases lending rules for defense and energy sectors
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:53:02 EEST
19:53:02 KST

The National Bank of Ukraine (NBU) has adopted a third package of regulatory measures to support lending to the economy, focusing on the defense-industrial complex (DIC), the energy sector and businesses affected by the war, the regulator said.
In particular, the collateral liquidity coefficient for property rights to revenue under contracts with entities in the security and defense sector, guaranteed by the electricity buyer and the transmission system operator, has been raised from 0.3 to 0.75.
The National Bank expects this measure to increase financing for defense-industrial and energy companies that hold state contracts but have limited ability to provide banks with traditional collateral.
Banks have also been authorized to take into account the value of goods held in inventory or undergoing processing and pledged as collateral for loans with terms of up to 18 months, based on their actual balance on the valuation date. This relaxation will remain in effect until September 1, 2027.
In addition, the central bank has expanded the ability to assess whether legal entities generate sufficient operating financial results to service their debt using projected figures if their property has been significantly damaged, destroyed or mined. Previously, this option was available to businesses operating in territories adjacent to the front line.
For loans under the 5-7-9% program, banks will be allowed to continue applying collective credit risk assessments or a simplified approach and will not be required to initiate nonperforming asset management procedures if the overdue payments arose solely because of delays in partial compensation for interest rates by the National Development Institution.
The amendments were approved by NBU Board Resolution No. 118 dated October 11, which entered into force on October 14.
As reported, in August and September, the NBU adopted the first two packages of regulatory measures to support lending amid intensified Russian shelling. They concerned, in particular, lending to the agricultural sector, manufacturers and companies implementing projects to restore critical infrastructure.

Türkiye and the European Union are making progress on updating their Customs Union agreement, with technical discussions covering e-commerce, public procurement, investment and agricultural products, Turkish trade minister Omer Bolat has said.
Speaking to reporters during a visit to Brussels, Bolat said negotiations were advancing on a “case-by-case basis”, despite the EU Council not yet formally authorising the European Commission to launch modernisation talks.

Industrial and digital trade
Bolat said Türkiye had spent the past year working to address concerns over restrictive provisions in the EU’s proposed Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA).
He warned that some measures in the draft legislation could affect future investment and disrupt integrated supply chains, particularly in the electric vehicle and automotive sectors.
Ankara is maintaining communications with EU officials to convey its expectations and reduce the potential economic impact of the proposed rules, he added.
Bolat also said the EU was coordinating with Türkiye on preparations for digital trade legislation. Türkiye remains exempt from a newly implemented EU regulation imposing a €3 fee per package, he said.
He cautioned that political intervention by the European Parliament could have adverse consequences, adding that many European officials also supported including Türkiye in the “Made in EU” origin framework.
However, he noted that the EU comprises countries with differing economic interests, urging a “calm and level-headed” approach.
Bolat said he had made three official visits to Brussels over the past three months, following five visits last year, and expressed hope for positive developments in the talks.

The student movement in Albania has aligned with the broader "Flamingo Revolution" protests, which began as an opposition movement against a luxury real estate development on the Adriatic coast involving Jared Kushner, son-in-law of U.S. President Donald Trump.
The project, backed by Socialist Prime Minister Edi Rama, transformed local flamingos into an anti-corruption symbol against the political establishment. Protesters are demanding the resignation of Rama, who has governed since 2013, amid allegations of systemic corruption shared by both the ruling Socialists and opposition Democrats.
Meanwhile, in neighboring Greece, scores of university students pitched tents in central Athens' Syntagma Square facing Parliament Tuesday, defying heavy rain to demand emergency relief from soaring accommodation costs.
Greek students organized a overnight camp-out and concert to press the conservative government for rent caps, increased housing subsidies, and the construction of new state-run dormitories.
Rent for small apartments has surged across Greece, where flat-sharing is uncommon, putting students in direct competition for limited housing with young couples, single-parent households and digital nomads.
The unrest mirrors recent student demonstrations in France, where high school students organized nationwide strikes and blockades over educational underfunding and living costs.

MEPs urge EU to shield International Criminal Court from US sanctions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:44:11 UTC
19:44:11 KST

Lawmakers from across the political spectrum say the EU should activate the Blocking Statute to prevent European companies from complying with measures imposed by the US administration, defined as an "attack by a foreign power."
Fifty-eight members of the European Parliament have urged the European Commission to shield the International Criminal Court (ICC) from US sanctions that threaten to disrupt its operations.
In a letter sent on Tuesday and seen by Euronews, the MEPs called on Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to defend the Netherlands-based court against what they described as “an attack by a foreign power on an entity on EU territory”, warning of "devastating" consequences.
US President Donald Trump’s administration announced sanctions against the ICC last Friday, following repeated criticism of the court over its arrest warrant for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and its investigation into the conduct of US troops in Afghanistan.
After an initial six-month grace period, the sanctions could severely hamper the court's operations by barring US banks and companies from doing business with it, although exemptions are envisaged for some telecommunications, software and payment services.
Given the dominance of US firms in global finance and technology, the restrictions could leave the ICC struggling to pay its bills and conduct financial transactions.
European banks, insurance companies and other intermediary firms with business interests in the US could also be affected, potentially facing secondary penalties if they continue working with the ICC.
The MEPs called for the use of “all instruments at our disposal” to shield the ICC from the sanctions. In particular, they urged the Commission to activate the EU's Blocking Statute, a mechanism designed to protect European companies and individuals from the extraterritorial effects of foreign sanctions.
The statute can prevent foreign court rulings based on specified laws from being enforced in the EU and allows European companies to seek compensation for losses caused by their extraterritorial application.
The Commission can add foreign laws to those covered by the statute, subject to scrutiny by the European Parliament and EU member states.
The letter was drafted by European People’s Party (EPP) MEP Dirk Gotink and Socialists and Democrats (S&D) MEP Aurore Lalucq, and signed by lawmakers from the EPP, S&D, Renew Europe and the Greens/EFA groups.
The signatories warned that the sanctions threatened Europe's ability to protect its own citizens and institutions.
In a statement last Saturday, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas described the threat of sanctions against the ICC as “not acceptable”, reaffirming the bloc's commitment to international law. However, the EU has yet to take concrete action.
The ICC has 125 member states. The United States signed the Rome Statute, which established the court, but never ratified it.
