EXPLAINER – Arctic’s new trade routes come with climate cost
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:40:54 UTC
19:40:54 KST

What happens when a region transformed by climate change begins to attract an industry associated with global emissions?
As rising temperatures accelerate the loss of Arctic sea ice, the region is becoming more accessible to commercial shipping, creating new opportunities for trade while raising concerns about the environmental costs.
Chinese container shipping company Sea Legend announced in mid-August the launching of the first regular container shipping service through the Arctic.
The route connects Ningbo on China's eastern coast with Felixstowe in the UK along Russia's Northern Sea Route (NSR) and is expected to cut the usual 40-day sailing time roughly in half.
The company has branded the weekly service the "Ice Silk Road," in reference to the historic trading routes that connected China and Europe.
The development follows a rise in commercial activity along the route, with 23 transits recorded last summer compared with 15 in 2024, according to Financial Times.
South Korea is also testing the route.
The 2,800-TEU PanStar Acro departed Busan in late August for the country's first trial voyage along the Arctic shipping route, passing through the Bering Strait and Arctic Ocean toward European ports.
Meanwhile, experts warn that growing commercial shipping along the route could intensify climate impacts, pollution and biodiversity loss in the fragile Arctic.
The growing interest in the route thus highlights a climate paradox: can a region becoming increasingly navigable because of climate change absorb the environmental consequences of becoming a new artery of global trade?
Sian Prior, lead adviser to the Clean Arctic Alliance, told Anadolu that the increase in Arctic shipping has coincided with the loss of sea ice.
“The Arctic Council’s Protection of the Arctic Marine Environment indicates a 40% increase in the number of ships and an almost doubling of the amount of the distances being sailed in the Arctic in the 12 years to 2025,” she said.
Arild Moe, a research professor at Norway-based Fridtjof Nansen Institute, said shorter transit times are a major attraction for companies, although the route remains constrained by vessel size and its limited operating season.
“When it comes to transit to Europe, the advantage is speed, the drawback is relatively small ships, compared to the regular container lines,” Moe told Anadolu.
He said the route can only be used for about three to four months a year, meaning companies are currently testing whether it can work commercially.
A study published in Nature Reviews Earth and Environment found that September Arctic sea ice area decreased by 35.8% between 1980 and 2024.
During 2013-2023, meanwhile, the number of ships entering the Polar Code Arctic area increased by 37.3%, while shipping-related CO2 emissions rose 6.3%.
“The loss of sea ice is allowing ships to access Arctic waters previously covered by sea ice and leading to access at times of the year when there was previously little opportunity,” Prior further said.
She cautioned, however, that melting ice is not the only factor driving increased activity.
“It is however the desire to control the Arctic and the demand for access to Arctic resources - oil and gas, minerals, and fish - that are creating new opportunities - not the reduction in sea ice,” Prior said.
Elizabeth Wishnick, senior research scientist at the Center for Naval Analyses, pointed to disruptions on traditional maritime routes as another factor making the Northern Sea Route more attractive.
“The war in Iran has disrupted shipping via the Red Sea as well as the Persian Gulf,” Wishnick, who is also a distinguished fellow at Columbia University's Weatherhead East Asian Institute, told Anadolu.
The emergence of regular container services also adds a commercial dimension to growing interest in a route largely controlled and regulated by Russia.
“The dominant cargo traffic on the NSR has since 2018 been exports of LNG from Yamal, mainly westwards to Europe and also oil in that direction,” Moe said.
He noted that private Chinese companies have increasingly used the route to transport consumer and industrial goods to Russia.
“I see these activities as commercially driven, although Chinese authorities take an interest in the NSR over the longer term,” Moe said.
He added that Russia has become more accommodating toward Chinese involvement as it seeks Chinese investment in Arctic infrastructure, although future cooperation will depend on the broader Russia-China relationship.
Wishnick also said the new container services should be viewed in the context of wider China-Russia cooperation in the Arctic.
“China is seeking to normalize its presence in the Arctic and reduce the skepticism among the Nordic countries about China's role in the region,” she said.
She also linked South Korea's trial voyage to Seoul's longstanding interest in Arctic cooperation with Russia.
“Although the same feasibility/profitability drivers we see in China are likely at work here, too, I think Korea may be viewing this NSR container service as a more discreet means of engaging with Russia while still maintaining sanctions,” Wishnick added.
As the Arctic becomes more accessible, greater shipping activity could add pressure to the environment that made the route possible.
One of the main concerns is black carbon, a short-lived climate pollutant produced by burning fossil fuels. When it settles on snow and ice, it reduces their ability to reflect sunlight, increasing heat absorption and accelerating melting.
“Shipping is already contributing to the loss of ice, through greenhouse gas emissions, and emissions of the short-lived climate pollutant black carbon from the burning of fossil fuels,” Prior said.
She explained that black carbon can travel hundreds or thousands of kilometers, but its impact is particularly significant when released near the Arctic because it is more likely to settle on snow and ice.
“Local warming and snow and ice melt from air pollutants such as black carbon have a disproportionate impact when they are released in and near the Arctic, up to five times higher than when released in temperate or tropical regions some studies have shown,” Prior underscored.
Prior also highlighted the wider climate feedback triggered by the loss of Arctic ice.
"The loss of ice results in greater absorption of heat as underlying dark land and water are exposed creating a self-sustaining cycle of melting ice and increasing heat," she said
A Clean Arctic Alliance assessment found that black carbon emissions increased across all of its Arctic geographic scopes between 2019 and 2024, rising from 259 to 759 metric tons in the Polar Code area.
“Shipping is a primary source of black carbon emitted north of 70N latitude,” Prior further recalled.
Environmental risks also extend beyond emissions.
Prior said greater vessel traffic can increase underwater noise, disturb marine wildlife and raise the risk of oil and chemical spills, with consequences for communities that depend on Arctic marine resources.
“These impacts and risks aren’t theoretical for the daily lives of people in the North,” Prior underscored.
The region's remoteness also creates difficulties in responding to accidents.
"Spills of oils and chemicals are a threat with major consequences for Indigenous communities, particularly since the equipment required to respond to spills is very limited in the Arctic," Prior said.
"If a shipping accident happens and people need to be rescued, search and rescue response will be very limited."
For now, the experts say the Northern Sea Route is unlikely to replace traditional routes, despite its potential to significantly shorten voyages.
“In the foreseeable future, only as a seasonal addition. It cannot replace Suez,” Moe said.
Wishnick similarly cautioned that unpredictable ice conditions could undermine the reliability required by container shipping.
"The receding ice is unpredictable and the on-time deliveries needed for container shipment may not work as planned," she said.
"The route is no panacea for shipping problems elsewhere," Wishnick added.
For Prior, reducing the environmental footprint of vessels that do operate in the Arctic is a priority.
"A switch to cleaner distillate fuels immediately could result in a 50-80% reduction in black carbon emissions," she said, calling for monitoring and reporting of black carbon emissions.
Prior warned that long-term environmental costs of expanding Arctic shipping will outweigh the economic and logistical benefits, saying that Arctic ice acs as a thermoregulator and reflects the sun’s heat.
“Disturbances and changes in the Arctic will not be experienced only in the Arctic,” she cautioned.
“What happens in the Arctic does not stay in the Arctic.”

Russia arrests Japanese journalist on espionage charges (VIDEO)

Russia arrests Japanese journalist on espionage charges (VIDEO)
Russian security officers have detained a Japanese journalist accused of collecting defense-related information for one of Tokyo’s intelligence services, the Federal Security Service (FSB) has announced.
The suspect, identified by Russia’s Foreign Ministry as Yuki Imai, worked for the Japanese newspaper Hokkaido Shimbun’s bureau in the Far Eastern Russian city of Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk and held ministry accreditation. He was detained in Sakhalin Region ahead of a planned departure from Russia and transferred to Moscow, the FSB said.
According to the agency, the correspondent gathered and stored restricted information about the number of Kuril Islands residents mobilized or volunteering to serve in the Ukraine conflict, intending to pass it to Japanese intelligence.
An FSB officer said the journalist repeatedly tasked local residents with obtaining the data despite knowing it was restricted and could not be published. The agency also said he had privately admitted to having contacts with Japanese intelligence.
The FSB released footage of the detention and documents found in the journalist’s hotel room bearing the label “For official use only.” The remaining text on the pages was blurred.
The journalist is currently being held in custody while the investigation continues.
Commenting on the arrest, Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova accused Tokyo of using accredited journalists to gather information aimed at undermining Russian security, saying this was not an isolated incident.
She warned that the case would further damage bilateral relations, lamenting Japan’s “anti-Russian course” and its refusal to address Moscow’s concerns about Japanese “remilitarization.” Zakharova urged Tokyo to abandon hostile actions against Russia.
Tokyo said on Wednesday that it had requested more information about the arrest and has demanded “fair and impartial treatment” for the journalist. The Hokkaido Shimbun said it was still confirming the details, stating that ensuring the journalist’s safety was its top priority.
Relations between Moscow and Tokyo have deteriorated since Japan joined Western sanctions over the Ukraine conflict in 2022, prompting Russia to suspend peace treaty negotiations. Last month, Russia also demanded the removal of US Typhon missile systems deployed in Japan, describing them as a threat to regional security.
The countries have never signed a post-World War II peace treaty, although a 1956 declaration ended the state of war and restored diplomatic ties. A longstanding obstacle remains Japan’s claim to the four southernmost Kuril island groups, which came under Soviet control in 1945. Tokyo calls them the Northern Territories, while Moscow regards them as an integral part of Russia.

JackRabbit MG Cargo Bike Review (2026): Compact and Powerful
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

Petite, lightweight, and kind of kicky for a cargo bike. Can fit in a car’s back seat. Fat tires provide stability. Cushy bike seat is comfortable for long rides. So many accessories. Surprising 500-pound payload.
TIRED
Fast braking requires a firm hand. Range is middling. Battery indicator sneaks up on you. Not as petite as other JackRabbits. Technically a scooter, not an ebike.
I am not an obvious target customer for a cargo ebike, as I neither have kids to tote nor a large space for bike parking. But the new JackRabbit MG Cargo is so tiny, it doesn't conjure the dully utilitarian, heedlessly bulky nature that's common to other cargo ebike models. In fact, when I tested the wee, plucky ebike, I found its fat tires and tiny wheelbase make it feel more like a speedy urban dirt bike than anything else.
But despite being a relative lightweight (55 pounds) and petite enough to fit in the back seat of my old Montero, the MG sports a 750-watt motor that can haul nine times the bike's weight uphill. I even threw a grill onto a bike trailer to test this claim, which held up.
Note that likeall JackRabbits WIRED testers have reviewed, the MG is less an ebike than a scooter that looks and acts like an ebike: Instead of pedals, you get pedal-like footrests, plus a throttle. This means when the battery runs out, the bike stops moving. Also, the listed 48-mile range drops considerably when you ride at top speed or haul a large load. Nonetheless, the MG may have converted me to the pannier class.
After testing this MG for a couple of months, I no longer use my car when I need groceries, even when I'm taking a longer trek to the Grocery Outlet for discount steaks or salmon. The same is true when I want to haul a slushie machine across Portland’s steep mid-city ridge to a friend's house for cheeky weekday margaritas. By not acting like a cargo bike, the MG has convinced me to haul cargo on a bike.
Zippy Little Devil
Photograph: Matthew Korfhage
“How exactly is this a cargo bike?” my editor asked when I showed her a photo of the MG Cargo after it arrived. She wasn't asking out of wonderment. As mentioned, the MG flat-out looks less like a bike you'd use to haul stuff and more like a dirt bike.
JackRabbit is known for making lightweight, zippy, fun little scooter hybrids that physically resemble BMX trick bikes. I loved the easy mobility and high-speed capability of JackRabbit's equally powerful XG Pro (8/10, WIRED Recommends) when I tested that model last year. I'd worried that the MG Cargo—18 pounds heavier and nearly a foot longer than the XG—would compromise too much on these virtues. I needn't have worried. As I quickly learned, the pleasantly peppy MG rides like an off-road bike when you're not hauling a big load.
Its three throttle speeds max out at about 20 mph, 15 mph, and 7 mph, respectively. The lowest speed is manageable for a sidewalk, while the fastest hits top speed within about 50 feet on flat ground, unless you've got some weight behind (or on) you. The MG advertises a range of 48 miles, though I'll assume this requires being a lighter rider who is gentle on the throttle. As a man north of 200 pounds with an admittedly heavy throttle thumb, I only made it to about 25 miles, even with minimal cargo. Because the bike's battery indicator shows up as at least half-full for the vast majority of this range, you'll need to test and learn your personal range when doing so is not mission-critical.
Note that because JackRabbits don't have working pedals, the bikes exist in an interesting technical gray area in some states in terms of their classification. Specifically, one could debate whether they're really a Class 2 ebike that can ride on bike lanes and trails. Given the MG's maximum speed of 20 mph—aside from an honor-system 24-mph jailbreak speed you can unlock for off-road riding—it mostly looks and quacks like a Class 2 ebike. In my experience, it's also treated as such.
The MG also offers nice customization options for accessorizing. It's easy to add a couple of rear pannier bags to the rear mounting rack or side racks ($75) on each side, offering enough capacity for most small grocery trips or beach excursions without adding much bulk. You could also opt for a rear basket.
Photograph: Matthew Korfhage
While I can't quite stow the MG as easily as other JackRabbit models, it's still small enough that I can slide it into my back seat—as long as I uncork the front handlebars and turn its front wheel backward. (Some sources refer to the MG as “foldable,” but this isn't strictly true: it just has a quick-release wheel and an easily removed handlebar.)
Which is to say, even without the cargo component, I could like the MG just as a fun little commuter, especially with the welcome addition of a cushy Kinekt active-suspension seat post that provides some added give for longer rides.
The Little Cargo Ebike That Could
Despite its petite size, the MG performs well as a true cargo hauler that you could use to move trailers full of groceries or the more precious cargo of your own children. I didn't borrow any kids to test rear child trailers or JackRabbit's mini-me rear seat and handlebar set ($175). But I did use the MG's preinstalled Burley trailer hitch to haul a box containing a 150-pound grill up a hill with a 7 percent grade. While the MG didn't get to full speed on the ascent, it pulled the grill and my 200-plus-pound self surprisingly well.
The MG's stability and cornering capabilities also fared better than I expected, given its short base. Cargo bikes tend to lengthen their frame to add stability and make room for riders to pedal comfortably while carrying loads on the front or the back. The MG Cargo's stability mostly comes from its cushy fat tires, largely thanks to the clever design of the larger front tire, which both adds stability up front on rugged terrain and lowers the center of gravity where cargo hangs. The lack of pedaling also naturally removes some wobble.
You will make compromises, though: Cornering can be jumpy, leading to the occasional overcorrection. The range also drops considerably with heavy carries, given that you can't add your own pedal power. Braking is fast but does require a good grip, especially with larger loads downhill.
For the Occasional Hauler
The MG Cargo lives in an interesting middle ground between commuter and cargo ebike. If I were primarily using it to transport children or work gear, I'd probably opt for a bulkier hauler or the Specialized Global Haul ST, WIRED's top-pick electric cargo bike that offers a more reliable long range.
The best use cases for the MG Cargo are as a fun recreational ebike that stows easily into your back seat or as a multipurpose commuter with built-in storage that saves its rider from needing to wear a backpack. In either case, the cargo capabilities function as bonus features as opposed to being the main draw.
It's less a workhorse than a hobby pony: I've slipped books and a blanket into a pannier so I can read at the park, and I've spontaneously brought home six-packs from the brewery a couple of miles down the road. When I grocery shop using the MG Cargo, I'm spared the bother of tightly packed parking lots that make me angry before I reach the aisles. I zip in, I unlock the panniers, pop in my groceries, and zip right back out. In this way, the MG Cargo also doubles as the cheapest therapist I know.

He also covered food, drink, business, technology, and culture for more than a decade at USA Today Network, The Virginian-Pilot, and his hometown newspaper in Portland, Oregon. His reporting has ... The Politics of Solar Energy Are Getting Weird, Mean, and a Little MAGA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

A mysteriously named political action committee has started running ads reminding voters in Colorado about that time GOP representative Lauren Boebert of Colorado and her date were caught on camera in 2023 getting handsy during a performance of the musical Beetlejuice.
That same PAC is producing a spot hitting Anthony Constantino, a Trumpist congressional candidate in upstate New York, because someone used his sticker-printing company to briefly make stickers that read, “Kill the Police.”
Attack ads are everywhere in the last month ahead of November’s election. But these spots are a little different. The semi-anonymous PAC that’s funding and making the ads, the Invest in Tomorrow Coalition, is a pro-solar-energy outfit. It’s funded in part by crypto billionaire Chris Larsen and run by a team of New York City political operatives.
“Playing hardball politics, that's what our opponents do, right, in oil and gas? And I just think the solar industry has been—I don't know how to describe it—a little too nice,” says Larsen, the cofounder of the blockchain finance firm Ripple and a major backer of the Invest in Tomorrow Coalition.
Green groups don’t usually act like this, with knives out, ready to stab opponents between the ribs. They tend to make appeals based on scientific consensus, or fears of what will happen to a warming planet without collective action. They’re also traditionally Democratic, but a few high-profile members of the MAGA movement are now speaking up for solar too. Texas, the home of the fossil fuel business, has quickly become a solar powerhouse. There are some signs that the Trump administration’s across-the-board opposition to solar may be starting to crack, at least a little, after years of slashing greentech subsidies and throwing up one roadblock after another to clean power projects.
Some of Larsen’s natural allies in the renewables field aren’t too happy about the PAC’s efforts, arguing that they’re alienating the decisionmakers they need most. But the politics of energy, especially solar energy, are changing.
Larsen’s PAC is devoting $15 million to go after seven of the more prominent opponents of renewable energy in this year’s congressional elections. That’s on top of roughly $5 million they’ve already spent in the primaries, cutting ads against Republican representatives Ralph Norman of South Carolina (whom the PAC called a “MAGA traitor”), Andy Ogles of Tennessee (“He doesn’t even bother going to work”), and Chip Roy (“chosen the side of powerful pedophiles”) of Texas. A PAC that received funding from Invest in Tomorrow has also gone after one Democrat, Rhode Island governor Dan McKee. All four lost their primary races.
In Roy’s case, the Invest in Tomorrow Coalition spent almost $1.5 million to stop his run for Texas attorney general. Most of the money went to ads on right-wing platforms like Truth Social and Rumble. The word “solar” was never mentioned.
“Don't talk about renewables. Don't talk about climate,” says Chris Coffey, the chief executive of the consultancy Tusk Strategies, which is running the PAC. “Pick the best issue that we can pick. And in a Republican primary, we should savage this guy for not being MAGA enough.”
Roy received a 100 percent rating from Heritage Action, the political arm of the Trumpist think tank. Coffey said he got some pushback from a few Democratic operatives, who were concerned that replacements for Roy and other PAC targets might not be any less extreme—on climate or any other issue. Without their far-right track record, the argument went, those replacements might even be stronger candidates in the general election.
“Who fucking cares? Who cares? Like, it can't be worse,” Coffey, a veteran of New York City mayor Michael Bloomberg’s City Hall, says in response. “At least we'll have extracted some payback.”
The PAC is currently putting $2 million into ads blasting GOP representative Victoria Spartz of Indiana as allegedly corrupt; it’s aiming to target Texas Republican Brandon Herrera for his “abolish old people” jokes and his plan to get rid of Social Security. Then there is the $1.5 million ad campaign about Boebert and the Beetlejuice incident. “If Lauren Boebert can’t be trusted in a room full of kids, then she can’t be trusted in the halls of Congress,” the commercial’s narrator says.
Other special-interest organizations have been running this playbook for decades. Groups supporting labor and opposing gun regulations regularly try to make examples of politicians who oppose their agenda. Green groups haven’t been as aggressive historically. That’s a problem, says Steph Bosh, the board chair of the Community Clean Energy Coalition. While her group has raised nearly $2 million to promote their favored hyperlocal candidates this cycle—and the League of Conservation Voters’ affiliated super PAC is spending another $50 million—Bosh says she appreciates that someone else is taking a less friendly approach.
“As a broad renewable energy industry, we need to be loved, respected, and feared,” Bosh adds. “We need to have a carrot, and we need to have a stick.”
James Carville, the Democratic pundit and former campaign manager, doubts the stick is big enough. “Twenty million—what the fuck do you think the carbon industry spends in a year?” he recently said to the Washington Monthly.
Roy, for his part, insisted that the PAC’s spending had played “zero role” in his race (while his campaign staff put out statements denouncing the “radical California Marxists trying to buy Texas elections”). Ralph Norman, his fellow solar target, warned about the “elite” taking out “the $1 million attack ad against me,” while Ogles complained, “they literally are trying to make an example out of me.”
“They were the difference maker,” Chris Burger, a Republican political consultant in Tennessee, says of the pro-solar group. “I don't think Charlie [Hatcher, Ogles’ primary opponent] wins if the PAC doesn't come in with $2 million.”
The Trump White House and its allies in Congress have been beyond hostile to renewables, which they believe to be intermittent sources of energy, and dominated by China. The administration has done everything it can to promote the production of oil, gas, and coal, while kneecapping renewable alternatives, from tying green projects in bureaucratic knots to pulling billions of dollars’ worth of solar subsidies and paying companies billions more to stop offshore wind farm construction. Then the Trump team tried to get other countries to adopt similar attitudes. “If you don’t get away from the green energy scam, your country is going to fail,” the president told the United Nations General Assembly last year.
But the Trumpists have been slightly less hostile to solar than to offshore wind farms, which, according to the president, cause cancer, “kill all your birds,” and drive whales “crazy.”
“While wind is dead, solar is merely in the ICU,” Richard Goldberg, a former member of the administration's National Energy Dominance Council, tells WIRED.
That has provided a small but real opening to promote solar to the America First set, especially with energy prices spiking at home, the war in Iran pushing up oil prices around the world, and the spread of AI data centers creating a borderline-insatiable need for more power.
In February, the American Clean Power Association launched a campaign to do just that, releasing a poll from former Trump campaign manager Kellyanne Conway’s consulting company showing that 75 percent of MAGA voters in key states supported the idea of adding more solar energy to the national mix. According to an internal memo reviewed by Politico, soon to follow were “paid media partnerships with podcasts like the Katie Miller Pod” (hosted by the former DOGE spokesperson, who is married to White House deputy chief of staff for policy Stephen Miller) as well as “advertorials and sponsorships with right-of-center publications.”
Katie Miller, once a consultant for Elon Musk, a renewable energy advocate, has repeatedly pushed for solar on social media since then. “Over 70 percent of the new utility-scale capacity went into states won by President Trump,” reads one of her posts. “Electricity generation is a national security issue—not a partisan one.” (Miller, who did not respond to requests to comment for this story, has previously denied receiving any funding from the clean power group.)
There’s also the data center issue. China hasn’t had problems powering its data centers, thanks in part to its widespread deployment of renewables—315 gigawatts of solar added to the grid last year, about six times more than the United States added from all sources combined. The US is in an entirely different situation. MAGA-minded promoters of solar are trying to leverage that gap to make a Trumpy argument for renewable energy. Concerns about the climate are out; fears about losing the AI race to China are in.
T1 Energy, which bills itself as one of the few truly all-American solar manufacturing companies, has hired Checkmate Government Relations, a lobbying firm led by Donald Trump Jr.’s old hunting buddy, and Tower Strategy, helmed by a former CIA operations officer, Rick De La Torre, to press its case in the administration. These lobbyists have tried to make the case that the administration’s beef isn’t with solar in general; it’s with Chinese solar. They’ve done it in the kind of pec-flexing language that’s become MAGA’s stock-in-trade.
“American-made, utility-scale solar is one of the few technologies that can be deployed at the speed and scale required” for data centers, De La Torre posted on LinkedIn. “China knows this. That is why it continues to flood markets, compress margins, and keep U.S. manufacturers on the defensive. Undercut. Outscale. Outlast.”
“Washington has a choice. Treat solar manufacturing as a strategic industry, the way we now treat semiconductors and critical minerals,” he added. Or only claim “to compete with Beijing.”
There are some indications that the argument may be gaining traction. In August, the Trump administration added a new 15 percent tariff and price floors on foreign-made solar components. T1’s CEO hailed it as a victory for domestic supply chains and manufacturing. More recently, negotiations in Congress are continuing on a bipartisan permitting reform bill that would, among many other things, make it easier for solar providers to plug into the electric grid.
Which led some solar executives to question whether it’s smart for the group to beat up on Republicans, right as a few of them seem to be creeping in solar’s direction.
“We’ve been hard at work speaking to Republicans about why supporting solar and batteries helps with energy abundance and affordability. And we’ve been successful. If this [Invest in Tomorrow Coalition] becomes about going after Republicans and turns solar back into a partisan issue, that would be an epic blunder,” says Russell Gold, T1’s executive vice president for strategic communications.
Tom Matzzie, the chief executive of solar company CleanChoice Energy, is serving as executive chair of the Invest in Tomorrow Coalition PAC. Cofounders include Peter Davidson, CEO of the investment firm Aligned Climate Capital, and Michael Brune, former executive director of the Sierra Club. But it’s Larsen who supplied the lion’s share of the early money for the PAC—$6 million of the initial $7 million or so it had raised through August 31, according to federal election commission records.
He’s had an uneven record of political giving, of late. Earlier this year, Larsen spent $3.5 million to support congressional candidate Alex Bores, who was targeted by the AI industry and lost his race. Larsen’s company, Ripple Labs, has donated nearly $100 million to Fairshake, the pro-crypto PAC, which racked up electoral successes in 2024 but just lost a major fight when its preferred bill to regulate cryptocurrencies died in the Senate.
The willingness to go on the attack isn’t the only way that Larsen’s PAC differs from others in the green movement. Not that long ago, renewable advocates talked about an “energy transition” away from old, dirty fossil fuels and toward newer, cleaner ones. Larsen is suggesting instead to red-district politicians that they embrace the idea of fossil and renewable energy sources existing side-by-side, even as the PAC he funds throws haymakers at solar’s enemies.
“You could be pro oil and gas and pro solar,” he says.

Ministry urges next government to tackle transport tax reform without delay
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:29:25 EEST
19:29:25 KST

The Ministry of Transport and Communications is urging the incoming government to implement a reform of transport taxation, warning in a new statement that further delay is no longer an option.
Transport tax revenues are set to fall sharply over the next decade as vehicles become increasingly battery-powered. The ministry also points to mounting pressure to raise transport taxation given the state of public finances.
Olli-Pekka Rantala, Head of Department at the Ministry of Transport and Communications, says current emission-based taxation is working as intended, but that very success is eroding the funding base.
The ministry’s statement follows a similar one issued by the Ministry of Finance last week.
1. Vehicle tax overhaul likely as electric car numbers grow
To secure sufficient funding for basic road maintenance, the ministry proposes linking vehicle tax to road maintenance costs. Currently, a significant portion of vehicle tax is based on a car's carbon dioxide emissions, while the state also levies a seperate fuel tax on vehicles that do not run on petrol.
"It is likely that taxation of electric vehicles would become stricter as a result. In that case, it will be essential to ensure through other means that road traffic emissions are reduced in line with Finland's international commitments," Rantala says.
Under the ministry's policy, tax revenue collected from transport should continue to cover at least the costs and nuisances caused by it.
The finer details of any tax changes, Rantala notes, will need to be worked out together with the Ministry of Finance.
2. Emission targets remain non-negotiable
Even if the focus of vehicle taxation shifts, the ministry stresses that emission targets must still be met through a broad set of tools — including transport emissions trading, energy taxation, distribution obligations and other EU legislation.
The EU's new road transport emissions trading system (ETS2), takes effect in 2028 and will impact fuel prices, according to Rantala.
The ministry also ties the shift away from fossil fuels directly to national security.
"It is also a security measure. Giving up fossil fuels strengthens Finland's strategic independence, since we won't be dependent on oil imports," Rantala says.
3. Congestion charges and even road tolls could be introduced
With public finances under strain, the ministry has also been exploring new ways to fund major road and rail projects — including new user fees and cost-sharing arrangements among those who benefit from them.
This approach, they argue, would help guide the selection of economically efficient projects. In practice, this could mean collecting separate user fees from those who use a major new road or railway line.
The ministry also wants regional congestion charges introduced in large urban areas, with revenue from such charges planned and agreed jointly with the cities concerned.
4. Maintaining existing infrastructure remains top priority
The ministry's statement also flags the poor condition of Finland's road and rail network. With funding already insufficient to repair anything beyond the busiest routes, the backlog of repairs — now at 4.3 billion euros including railways — is set to keep growing.
Sabina Lindström, Head of Department at the Ministry of Transport and Communications, says maintaining existing infrastructure — basic road upkeep in particular — remains the top priority.
Without confirmed funding, the current savings trajectory will have to tighten further, with direct consequences for provisional and lower-tier roads.
"In practice, this means that we can maintain these busiest routes, but unfortunately, all those that fall into a lower category will continue to receive too little maintenance," Lindström says.
Some in the public debate have occasionally floated the idea of stripping asphalt from roads in poor condition and converting them to gravel. Lindström says this offers little relief.
"Removing the surface is already part of the solution, and it's done every year. Unfortunately, it doesn't solve the problem. It's costly in itself, and maintaining a gravel road isn't cheap either. It's done on an appropriate scale," Lindström says.

At least 10 vessels have been attacked in or near the Strait of Hormuz since Sunday, a high since war broke out between the United States, Israel and Iran, security data showed Wednesday.
Four vessels were struck on Tuesday and six on Sunday — the highest number of attacks in a single day since the start of the conflict — according to data from security firm Vanguard, the International Maritime Organization and the British maritime agency UKMTO.

The attacks have disrupted shipping through the strait, which is normally one of the busiest routes for exporting oil and other commodities from Gulf countries.

Khulbey called for healthier eating, regular physical activity and routine medical examinations, saying early identification of risk factors could help prevent serious complications, ease pressure on health services and save lives across the Pacific. ■

English and Welsh water firms could be forced to return £107m via lower bills
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:21:05 UTC
19:21:05 KST

Thames Water, Yorkshire Water and other providers could be forced to cut tens of millions of pounds from household bills after the regulator said they had missed performance targets.
Customer bills at Yorkshire Water could fall by £27 on average, while those at Thames could decrease by £7, according to estimates by Ofwat, the regulator of the privatised industry in England and Wales.
The water industry has faced growing criticism in recent years amid rising bills, scrutiny over sewage pollution, high levels of debt and underinvestment in ageing infrastructure.
As water customers cannot switch away from their provider if it underperforms, Ofwat instead has an “outcome delivery incentive” (ODI) system of automatic payments or penalties based on agreed targets.
Yorkshire and Thames will have to return £75.1m and £45.8m, respectively, after missing targets in 2025-26, Ofwat said. The payments will add to the financial pressures on the companies, although Thames has been allowed to delay some of the penalties by a year.
Yorkshire is among the companies subject to enhanced monitoring by Ofwat over its financial resilience, while the government is considering whether to bring Thames Water under public control after years-long negotiations to reduce its crippling debts.
The other companies that must return money to customers include: Dŵr Cymru (or Welsh Water), at £16.7m; South West Water, at £16m; and United Utilities in north-west England, at £13.4m.
However, some companies will receive a reward payment because they met their targets – covered by higher bills.
Severn Trent, which serves the Midlands, south-west England and parts of Wales, and Northumbrian Water are in line to receive an extra £41.8m and £35.9m respectively, Ofwat said.
Northumbrian customers’ bills could rise by an average of £21, the regulator said. Severn Trent customers could pay £8 more per year.
Overall, the industry is expected to cut its bills by a net £240m for failures during 2025-26. Of this, £107m is expected to be returned to customers via lower bills in 2027-28.
Ofwat said at this stage the figures were still at the draft stage and not every household would receive the same change. Bills are “affected by a range of factors and the effect will vary by company and customer type”, the regulator said.
It will make its final decision on the payments by 15 December, which will take effect on bills from 1 April 2027.
Ofwat recently announced that water companies could increase annual tariffs by an extra £3.4bn, on top of the 36% average rise agreed over five years to 2030. Customer bills are rising to pay for long-overdue investments to fix leaking pipes and treatment works, as well as to pay for new assets such as reservoirs.
Andy Burnham last month said the government would pave the way for public ownership of water firms and promised a 10-year path to a “very different water system in the UK”.
The comments suggested the prime minister might opt for a temporary nationalisation of debt-laden Thames Water as the government seeks to make a decision on a £10bn rescue takeover put forward by lenders for the UK’s biggest water supplier.
Ofwat’s announcement came after Burnham said customers must not be “treated as a blank cheque” and after the regulator said in August it planned to allow yet more bill increases on top of those already agreed.
A government spokesperson said: “This government won’t allow customers to be treated as a blank cheque, and we are committed to protecting households from cost-of-living pressures. We will always challenge water companies where they seek to pass unnecessary costs on to households.
“We will deliver a strengthened water bill that puts people first, ensuring affordable access to clean water, driving down pollution, and strengthening public control.”
A Yorkshire Water spokesperson said: “We recognise that our performance last year fell short of the standards we and our customers expect in some areas, and we remain focused on improving.
“We are already delivering Yorkshire’s largest ever environmental investment programme and with the help of over 1,000 new colleagues, we’ve completed improvements at almost 300 locations across the county.”
A Thames Water spokesperson said: “To help smooth customer bills, Ofwat has agreed to defer the timing of some ODI penalties by one year. This does not remove or reduce the penalties. Customers still receive the full benefit, and Thames Water does not gain financially. We recognise these penalties reflect areas where our performance fell short. The deferral will prevent sharp year-on-year bill movements, which research shows our customers want us to avoid.”

EU's methane rules face two-year delay, sparking environmental backlash
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:18:58 UTC
19:18:58 KST

Environmentalists warn that delaying EU methane rules will do little to lower energy prices, accusing Brussels of using energy security and competitiveness to justify weakening the Green Deal.
The European Commission proposed on Wednesday a one-year delay for importers to show compliance with EU methane rules, giving companies until May 2029 to prove that their supplies meet equivalent EU standards.
The proposal follows pressure from industry and governments concerned about compliance costs and energy security, but falls short of calls from some EU countries for a three-year delay.
Environmental groups condemned the move, arguing that the methane rules pose no threat to Europe's energy security and that the current supply crisis stems instead from the US-Israeli war against Iran, which has disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
Under the Commission proposal, importers of oil, gas and coal from outside the EU have more time to comply with the bloc’s methane rules. Originally, importers were expected to demonstrate by January 2027 that their suppliers had systems in place to monitor and report methane emissions equivalent to those required under EU law.
Under the proposed changes, the requirement would start applying in 2028, with the first report and proof of compliance due by 31 May 2029, covering supplies from the previous year.
EU governments and industry have pushed for a delay amid turmoil in energy markets, while climate campaigners accuse Brussels of weakening a recently adopted law without tackling the underlying causes of the crisis.
EU countries adopted methane rules in May 2024, introducing requirements to measure, report and verify emissions from the energy sector as part of efforts to curb one of the most potent greenhouse gases.
But the latest energy crisis, which has driven up prices and threatened diesel and gas supplies, has fuelled concerns that the rules could aggravate shortages.
French President Emmanuel Macron recently joined industry calls to delay the requirements, which were due to take effect in early 2027.
"It is also important not to weaken European production capacities while preparing for long-term supply difficulties," Macron said in a letter to the Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.
The United States, the EU's largest supplier of liquefied natural gas (LNG), has also repeatedly complained about the impact of the rules on American energy companies.
Suspending penalties
The Commission had already offered significant flexibility, including a three-year suspension of certain penalties, in a concession to industry. But it had stopped short of formally postponing the compliance deadline.
The EU methane law requires fossil fuel importers to provide information on emissions associated with production.
In practice, importers may need to collect reliable data from producers operating thousands of kilometres away, at the other end of a complex supply chain.
Importers argue that they still face legal uncertainty despite the proposed suspension of penalties, and have called for more time and clearer obligations.
Environmental groups, however, warn that even a limited delay could pave the way for further concessions, while doing little to improve Europe's energy security.
They also argue that reopening the legislation risks penalising companies and producing countries that have already invested in monitoring and reporting systems, while undermining confidence in EU rules.
Jack Corscadden, senior Campaigner at Environmental Investigation Agency, said there was no demonstrable link between the implementation of the EU methane rules and the current energy supply challenges.
“After a summer of record-breaking heatwaves and wildfires, the Commission is failing European citizens by delaying this vital piece of climate legislation to appease fossil fuel producers and exporters," Corscadden said.
Esther Bollendorff, fossil free program manager at the NGO Climate Action Network Europe, said that delaying the EU methane rules made no economic or strategic sense.
"At a time of yet another energy price crisis and tensions on the gas market, methane mitigation could unlock over 40 billion cubic meters of gas from the EU’s main fossil fuel suppliers - more than half the volume of US LNG imported by the EU in 2025," Bollendorff said.
The Commission's proposal still requires approval from the European Parliament and EU governments. It is set to be discussed by EU leaders at a summit in Brussels on Thursday, alongside broader concerns about European competitiveness and soaring energy prices.

Scientists discover how harmful “zombie cells” hide from the immune system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:17:58 UTC
19:17:58 KST

Scientists discover how harmful “zombie cells” hide from the immune system
Cedars-Sinai identified a protein that may allow harmful “zombie cells” to evade the immune system and accumulate as we age.
- Date:
- October 14, 2026
- Source:
- Cedars-Sinai Medical Center
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered a protein that may help harmful aging cells hide from the immune system, allowing them to accumulate and fuel age-related health problems. Blocking the protein in mice reduced these cells and inflammation while improving blood sugar regulation and strength, offering a promising new direction for anti-aging research.
- Share:
Researchers led by Cedars-Sinai Health Sciences University have discovered a protein that may allow harmful aging cells to escape detection by the immune system. By helping these cells remain in the body instead of being cleared away, the protein could contribute to their accumulation and the development of health problems associated with aging.
The discovery, published in Cell Metabolism, identifies PD-L2 as a potential target for therapies aimed at eliminating harmful aging cells. Scientists also believe the protein could serve as a blood marker, providing a way to detect and monitor these cells.
"Our findings suggest that PD-L2 may help aging cells stay in the body when they would normally be removed by the immune system," said Selim Chaib, PhD, research assistant professor of Medicine at Cedars-Sinai and first and co-corresponding author of the study.
How Harmful Aging Cells Escape the Immune System
As cells age or become damaged, some enter a state known as senescence. These cells stop dividing but remain alive, lingering in tissues rather than disappearing. Over time, they can accumulate and release substances that trigger inflammation and disrupt the normal activity of surrounding cells.
The buildup of these senescent cells has been associated with a range of health problems that become more common with age. Understanding why they persist, particularly when the immune system would normally remove them, could help scientists develop new ways to reduce their harmful effects.
The researchers found that PD-L2 may play an important role in this process by helping aging cells avoid immune clearance.
Blocking PD-L2 Reduces Aging Cells in Mice
To investigate the protein's role, scientists conducted experiments in laboratory mice in which PD-L2 was either removed or blocked. Both approaches reduced the accumulation of senescent cells and lowered levels of the inflammatory substances they release.
The benefits extended beyond changes at the cellular level. Mice with reduced PD-L2 activity also showed improvements in their ability to process sugar and demonstrated greater grip strength, suggesting that targeting the protein could influence physical functions affected by aging.
The team also examined human cells and tissues. They discovered that senescent human cells produced more PD-L2 than younger cells and that levels of the protein rose with age in certain human tissues. These findings suggest the mechanism observed in mice may also be relevant to human aging.
A Potential New Target for Age-Related Diseases
The results raise the possibility that blocking PD-L2 could help the immune system recognize and eliminate harmful aging cells, potentially reducing some of the health problems associated with their buildup.
"If we can find a way to block this protein, we may be able to help the immune system get rid of these cells and potentially improve health problems linked with aging," said James Kirkland, MD, PhD, director of the Center for Advanced Gerotherapeutics and senior author of the study.
Although the findings are promising, more research is needed before the approach can be considered for treating people. Future studies will investigate whether blocking PD-L2 is safe and can deliver meaningful health benefits in humans. Researchers also hope to clarify how the protein contributes to diseases associated with aging.
Additional Cedars-Sinai researchers who contributed to the study include Larissa Langhi Prata, Masayoshi Suda, Andres Sola, Jia Nie, Hyungsoo Kim, Tamar Pirtskhalava, Nino Giorgadze, Nicolas Musi, Ze'ev Ronai, and Tamara Tchkonia.

Ukrainian Citizen Accused of Organizing NordStream Pipeline Blasts to Stand Trial in Germany
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:17:45 UTC
19:17:45 KST

The trial of a Ukrainian citizen accused of organizing the sabotage of the Nord Stream gas pipelines in September 2022 is set to begin in Germany on October 14.
Reuters reports this.
According to German prosecutors, Serhii K. (Serhii Kuznetsov) led a group of Ukrainians that included divers and an explosives expert.
Investigators believe the group planned and carried out the sabotage operation on the orders of unidentified Ukrainian state agencies, planting explosive devices on the pipelines near the Danish island of Bornholm in the Baltic Sea.
Kuznetsov was arrested in Italy last year under an international warrant and extradited to Germany. He denies any involvement in the explosions. Ukrainian authorities have also denied Kyiv’s involvement in the pipeline sabotage.
While in custody, Kuznetsov repeatedly tried to prevent his extradition, including by going on hunger strike.
The trial is expected to be the first opportunity to examine the evidence gathered during the years-long investigation publicly.
German prosecutors classify the alleged actions of Kuznetsov as a war crime. They believe the likely aim of the operation was to destroy one of Russia’s main sources of revenue following its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Meanwhile, Croatian authorities have arrested another man, Volodymyr Zhuravliov. German prosecutors believe he was one of the divers involved in the operation to sabotage the Nord Stream gas pipelines.
On September 18, the County Court in the Croatian city of Pula approved extraditing the Ukrainian national to Germany.
Germany submitted two requests to Croatia to extradite Zhuravliov under European arrest warrants issued in June 2024 and August 2026.
Zhuravliov and his defense team argued that the requests should be rejected, citing a ruling by the Warsaw District Court, which refused Germany’s extradition request in October 2025. At the time, the Polish court questioned whether German law applied to the explosions in international waters and stated that the case should be considered in the context of Russian aggression.

Taiwan's EVA Air workers protest court rulings on disputed union

2026-10-14
10:17:34 UTC
19:17:34 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — EVA Air workers protested outside Taoyuan District Court on Wednesday after judges rejected requests to dissolve a union they say is controlled by company managers.
CNA reported that the dispute involves the Evergreen Airline Services Corporation Enterprise Union, which workers accuse management of controlling. Labor groups said managers have prevented ordinary employees from joining the union and challenging its leadership.
Taoyuan's labor department said the union had failed to hold valid membership meetings since 2024 because too few members attended. This prevented it from operating normally under labor laws and its own rules.
The department asked the court to dissolve the union on April 18, 2025, but the court rejected the request on March 24. The department appealed on April 10, but the court rejected the appeal on Aug. 21, prompting another appeal on Aug. 27.
The court ruled that the union could still operate because it continued to issue meeting notices, organize meetings, and hold leadership elections. Labor groups disagreed, arguing that the rulings allowed managers to retain control while denying ordinary workers a voice, per CTS News.
The groups also raised concerns about disputed union elections and the suspension of numerous members last year. They said these actions had made it harder for workers to take part in union affairs and seek changes to its leadership.
Labor groups said the labor ministry had previously found that company managers improperly interfered in union affairs, including leadership elections. The ministry determined that their actions constituted unfair labor practices, per Liberty Times.
Protesters questioned whether the court's rulings upheld workers' right to organize or allowed management to maintain control of the union. They urged the court to reconsider its decisions and protect workers' rights.

Ukrainian Ex-Officer Stands Trial in Germany Over Nord Stream Bombing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:17:05 UTC
19:17:05 KST

Lawyers for a Ukrainian ex-military officer accused of leading the bombing of Russia's Nord Stream pipeline in September 2022 argued at the start of his trial in Germany on Wednesday that "an aggressor's infrastructure" may have been a lawful target.
Serhii Kuznetsov is accused of leading a group of Ukrainian agents including divers and an explosives expert that blew up Russia's largest gas pipeline to Europe in one of the biggest infrastructure sabotage operations of modern times.
The case provides the first opportunity for a public hearing of evidence gathered during a years-long investigation, which has been diplomatically and politically awkward for a German government that remains staunchly supportive of Ukraine despite the investigative trail linking Kyiv to the bombing.
Moving to have the case dismissed, Kuznetsov's lawyer Nicola Canestrini argued that the pipeline — which provided half of Germany's imports of natural gas before Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine — was a "Russian weapon."
"Is it unlawful to destroy an aggressor's infrastructure without harming any human beings?" Canestrini asked.
Right to remain silent
Prosecutors have alleged that Kuznetsov, who was arrested under an international warrant in Italy last year, worked with members of the Ukrainian military to plan the clandestine operation on behalf of unidentified Ukrainian state entities.
Kuznetsov, 50, who prior to Wednesday was referred to publicly only as Serhii K. under German legal rules, has denied any involvement in the blasts that ruptured the 1,200-kilometer (750-mile)-long Baltic Sea pipeline.
Wearing a grey suit and with a shaved head, he exercised his right to remain silent in court but did not cover his face. His lawyers said he could not mount a proper defense because he was obliged to withhold Ukrainian state secrets.
The government in Kyiv has also denied any involvement, a sensitive point in its relations with Germany, Ukraine's largest European supplier of military aid. Russia said on Monday it expected a "just verdict" that would reveal the names of the perpetrators and those who ordered the operation.
Kuznetsov's legal team had tried reaching out to Ukraine for information that might assist the defense but heard nothing, according to another defense lawyer, Jes Meyer-Lohkamp.
Attacking civilian targets is considered a war crime
German prosecutors say the actions Kuznetsov is accused of — attacking civilian targets and causing explosions that destroyed infrastructure and damaged public services — would amount to a war crime.
Kuznetsov is the only person on trial, but Croatian authorities have arrested another man, identified as Vladimir Z., who prosecutors believe was one of the divers.
The explosion of Nord Stream sealed the end of Germany's longstanding dependence on Russian natural gas, although Moscow had already cut supplies over Berlin's support for European sanctions following Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
Nord Stream's supply had been due to double with the opening of a twin pipeline, Nord Stream 2, already built, but Berlin canceled approval to open it just prior to Russia's invasion.
Plumes of methane gas
The trial, expected to continue into February next year, could have domestic political implications.
Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), leading in opinion polls for more than a year, has called for an end to military aid for Ukraine and a restoration of energy ties with Moscow.
Although German state parliaments have no role in foreign policy, the AfD filed a motion in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt on Wednesday calling for an end to support for Ukraine, noting the "historical parallel" with the start of the trial.
The Nord Stream system, lying at a depth of 80 to 110 meters under the Baltic and built by Russian gas concern Gazprom to supply up to 110 billion cubic meters of gas to Germany, was formerly at the core of economic ties between the two countries.
The Sept. 26, 2022, blasts that ruptured three of the four concrete-coated steel pipelines created a giant whirlpool at sea as huge plumes of methane gas rose into the atmosphere.
Prosecutors allege that Kuznetsov traveled to Germany through Poland some three weeks before the attack, using a forged Ukrainian passport. He and his group then used a sailboat hired in the northern German city of Rostock to reach an area close to the Danish island of Bornholm, where they rigged specialized military-grade explosives to the sea floor.
The weekly Der Spiegel magazine and ZDF public television have previously reported that five men and one woman were on the rented yacht Andromeda, which left Rostock on Sept. 6 and returned on Sept. 23, 2022.

Indonesia wildfires choke Singapore, force East Timor schools shut
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:16:00 UTC
19:16:00 KST

Air pollution in parts of Singapore reached "very high" levels Wednesday while East Timor closed schools, as haze from Indonesian forest fires triggered a regional crisis.
The blazes in Indonesia have burned through hundreds of thousands of hectares of forest and plantations on Borneo and Sumatra islands, sickened local residents and sent thick haze across the region.
Air pollution in western Singapore on Wednesday hit "very high" – the country's top level – the National Environment Agency said.
It recorded levels of tiny particulates capable of penetrating the bloodstream and lungs, known as PM2.5, at 288 micrograms per cubic meter, vastly exceeding the World Health Organization's recommended average annual exposure of 5 micrograms.
Indonesia regularly battles wildfires during the dry season, but has seen stronger-than-usual blazes this year as a powerful El Nino cycle brings drought.
Experts also point to slash-and-burn land-clearing practices that have changed the naturally fire-resistant landscape of Sumatra and Borneo.
The haze has drifted into neighboring Singapore, Malaysia and East Timor, which said it would shut schools nationwide for three days from Thursday, and as far afield as the Philippines.
The closures in East Timor were necessary "as a preventive measure to protect the health of students, teachers and other members of the educational community, given current air quality conditions", the government said.
It urged families to keep children indoors and to use "respiratory protection" if going outside.
Singapore rolled out subsidies for haze-related medical treatment from Monday, a measure last activated in 2015 when similar blazes in Indonesia cloaked Southeast Asia in toxic smoke for weeks.
The city-state has also begun distributing N95 masks to eligible residents when pollution reaches very unhealthy levels.
Singapore's National Trades Union Congress said Monday that public transport workers and delivery riders could receive free N95 masks, but AFP found uptake was slow.
"It's a little bit uncomfortable to wear a mask, and some orders we have to walk around blocks, or park outside," a delivery rider, who gave his name only as Daniel, told AFP.
"With the mask, I will have to breathe heavier," the 27-year-old said.
Ong Kwang Wei, 57, who has asthma, said he wore an N95 mask outdoors and carried his inhaler and medication with him at all times.
He was accompanying his 88-year-old mother – also masked – for a health check-up after a recent bout of flu.
"Once the flu kicks in my asthma is exacerbated ... I get breathless, I cough, I get phlegm, so I need to use my inhaler," Ong said.
In Indonesia, tens of thousands of people have sought treatment for respiratory illness linked to haze from fires burning in Borneo, South Sumatra and Papua regions.
On Sumatra island, a fire razed nearly 300 homes, forcing hundreds of people to evacuate, an official said Tuesday.
Residents first spotted the fire approaching their village in Bangka Belitung province Saturday and tried to put it out themselves with portable water pumps.
But the fire continued to smoulder underground in peatland and when the wind shifted, the flames moved toward their homes.
The local disaster agency said nearly 1,000 people fled the village.
"My house is gone," Leni, a 55-year-old villager now staying at a shelter with her family, told AFP.
"There's nothing left. I could only save myself and take my kids with me ... I panicked and didn't have the time to grab anything," said Leni, who like many Indonesians has one name.
President Prabowo Subianto on Monday ordered the government to mobilize maximum efforts, with officials saying more than 60,000 personnel had been deployed to combat fires on the ground.
But efforts so far, including cloud seeding and water-bombing, have had limited success.
The haze has prompted Malaysia to request a meeting of regional body ASEAN and on Tuesday Malaysian parliamentarian Syed Saddiq Rahman urged a "diplomatic protest."
"We must send a diplomatic protest note, not just on behalf of Malaysia, but ASEAN. You need to treat them as an outcast in the region," he said.

EU proposes delaying methane obligations amid pressure on energy importers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:15:59 UTC
19:15:59 KST

Melike Pala
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
The European Commission proposed Wednesday postponing by one year the implementation of certain provisions of the EU Methane Regulation concerning fossil fuel importers, aiming to ease cost pressures on European industry amid rising energy prices.
The proposed amendment would delay monitoring, reporting, and verification obligations for importers of natural gas, oil, and coal, as well as reporting requirements related to methane intensity for both importers and EU producers, according to a statement.
The bloc said the move comes as the conflict in the Middle East puts additional pressure on global energy markets, driving up energy prices and potentially reducing the availability of gas and oil.
"This is driving up energy prices and may cause reduced availability of gas and oil, hampering the EU's competitiveness and security of supply," the statement said.
The proposed one-year postponement is intended to prevent additional pressure on the security of imported fossil fuel supplies while giving companies and national administrations more time to prepare for compliance with the regulation.
The proposal will now be submitted to the European Parliament and the European Council for consideration and adoption.
The EU Methane Regulation, adopted in 2024, is the world's first comprehensive legislation addressing methane emissions associated with imports of oil, natural gas, and coal.
The regulation covers domestic production, transportation, and processing, as well as imports, and introduces progressively stricter requirements to improve transparency and reduce methane emissions.
The commission stressed that the proposed amendment would not affect the regulation's overall ambition, integrity, or scope, reaffirming the bloc's commitment to reducing methane emissions.

From black soldier flies to mealworms: farming insects for food, fodder and fertiliser in Uganda
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:00:01 UTC
19:00:01 KST

A few minutes’ walk from his home in the Kyaka II refugee settlement, Kanane Bikanyale feeds black soldier fly larvae to chickens in a coop above a fishpond. The larvae disappear in a scrum of chickens. Nearby, more larvae grow in modified jerrycans, while adult flies are kept in netted boxes.
Bikanyale kept chickens before he fled to Uganda from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). But the cost of conventional feed and shortages of ingredients made them increasingly difficult to raise – a widespread pressure for millions of smallholder farmers whose margins are tight.
In 2019, he began farming black soldier flies in the settlement, giving the larvae to his chickens and tilapia fish, and using the insects’ debris and excrement, known as frass, as fertiliser. The insects themselves feed on organic material, from household food scraps to crop residues.
Kavira Musabingo, also from DRC, arrived at the settlement in 2018 with her husband, daughter and five grandchildren. The family had almost no possessions and struggled to find enough food.
She joined a women’s group learning to raise black soldier flies. She initially sold her share of the larvae for urgent household expenses. Later, she began rearing insects at home.
Today, she provides chicken, eggs and vegetables for her family and earns an income from selling what they do not need.
Uganda harbours one of the world’s largest refugee populations; Kyaka II alone, in the west of the country, is home to nearly 140,000 people, most of them, like Bikanyale and Musabingo, displaced by years of conflict and instability in neighbouring DRC. Women and children make up 78% of people in the camp. As the settlement expanded, land allocations got smaller: by 2018, new arrivals received plots of about 30 by 30 metres. Split between a home and crops, and with humanitarian support declining, families had to secure enough food from less and less space.
About 500 people in the camp now work in 32 insect-farming groups. Insect rearing requires less space and water than conventional livestock farming, and trays of insects can be stacked vertically.
Alongside black soldier flies, they raise crickets and mealworms, both consumed as food in many parts of the world. Traditionally, including in Uganda, insects have been gathered from the wild, making supply seasonal and uncertain. Urbanisation and western food habits have also changed perceptions: dismissed as rural or backward, insects disappeared from diets.
“Their nutritional potential is particularly relevant for vulnerable groups such as women of reproductive age and children under five, since some species are particularly rich in proteins and micronutrients such as iron and zinc,” says Dorothy Nakimbugwe, an associate professor in the food technology and nutrition department at Makerere University in the capital, Kampala.
Nakimbugwe has also led Refugee Insect Production for Food and Feed (RefIPro), a project organised by the Danish non-profit organisation Raise, which has worked with local groups to train and support farmers in Kyaka II and neighbouring communities since 2018.
Rearing insects has also been introduced to more than 10 schools through RefIPro. Among them are Bukere primary school and Kako primary school, which now run their own insect farms and were involved in a randomised trial involving 342 children testing the effects of mealworm-enriched porridge. The University of Copenhagen, another partner in the project, reports that children grew taller and showed improved body composition.
But before insects can become feed or food, the rearing system has to work. Edward Ssebbombo, working on RefIPro in Kyaka II, has trained farmers and provided technical support over the years, while also designing equipment for their farms, including a pedal-powered sieve, sorters made of recycled motorcycle-wheel spokes and Bikanyale’s rail-mounted shelter, which protects the breeding unit from rain and excessive sun, and covers it overnight.
However, making it work in practice remains challenging. “In a food-insecure setting such as a refugee settlement, households produce very little food waste,” Ssebbombo says.
“Farming black soldier flies therefore often requires collecting organic material from markets or other sources,” he says, noting that even when the waste itself is free, “sorting, collecting and transporting it can still be costly for small-scale producers.”
Mealworm production faces similar constraints: larvae are fed organic residues and dry feed such as maize and wheat bran. At Bukere, families contribute banana and sweet-potato peels, but the dry feed remains costly.
Violet Gwokyalya leads Mothers Against Malnutrition and Hunger (Mamah), which coordinates RefIPro’s work on the ground.
She hopes to involve families through a model in which “parents can rear mealworms at household or community level and supply them to schools, helping sustain school feeding while creating an income opportunity for themselves”.
Where organic residues instead accumulate beyond what local systems can handle, black soldier fly farming takes on a different role.
Outside Kampala, the Kollekt Village, a recycling centre run by a local environmental organisation, works with food markets and waste pickers to separate organic material before it reaches dumpsites, integrating insect farming into a zero-waste system.
In Jinja, Bioconvision turns organic waste from food processors and markets into black soldier fly larvae for animal feed and frass-based fertiliser for farmers, including those farming fish on Lake Victoria. In 2025, the company processed nearly 1,000 tonnes of organic waste, producing about 60 tonnes of fresh larvae and 83 tonnes of fertiliser. Both are connected to Bugs-Africa, a project that promotes black soldier fly waste processing in Uganda and elsewhere in Africa.
Uganda is also Africa’s second-largest coffee producer, after Ethiopia, and processing the crop results in large amounts of organic residues. In Kasese in western Uganda, Proteen, a Ugandan social enterprise, turns coffee pulp into feed protein and frass-based fertiliser used by coffee farmers, which returns nutrients to the soil.
Insect farming is a rapidly growing industry – the market for insects as food and animal feed is estimated to be worth up to $8bn (£6bn) by 2030. Increased investment has led to industrial-scale ventures in wealthier countries in Europe, Asia and North America but the practice is also spreading across rural tropical regions, where the climate favours insect growth, helping keep the practice affordable and accessible.
According to the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), feed can account for up to 70% of the cost of keeping livestock, leaving small-scale farmers particularly exposed to rising feed and fertiliser costs. At the same time, as populations increase and concentrate in megacities, the organic waste they generate can outgrow the systems built to manage it.
Insect farming ranges in scale from a single cut-open jerrycan to automated industrial facilities. Wider adoption could reduce the use of soya meal and fishmeal in animal feed, lowering agricultural demand for land and reducing pressure on marine ecosystems. Frass can return nutrients to the soil. But to become a lasting part of agricultural systems, insect farming needs more than individual projects.
In Uganda, a recent conference on insect farming brought together Ssebbombo, Gwokyalya, researchers such as Nakimbugwe and members of refugee communities, alongside representatives from Bugs-Africa, FAO Uganda and public institutions.
Speaking at the conference, Ronald Kaggwa, of Uganda’s National Planning Authority called for insect farming to be seen not as an isolated farming practice but as part of a broader system linking waste management, livestock, aquaculture, income generation and food security, and to be integrated into the country’s agricultural system.
“For this sector to contribute meaningfully to Uganda’s development, we must understand the entire value chain,” he said. “It’s about transforming innovation into productive enterprises, turning research into practical solutions, creating opportunities for communities and contributing to more nutritious, resilient, circular and competitive food systems.”
- Umberto Diecinove’s INSCTS project documents the growing role of insect farming around the world
