Ukraine Says SpaceX Limits Starlink Operations, Disrupting Military
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:17:29 UTC
18:17:29 KST

Ukraine accused Elon Musk's SpaceX on Wednesday of limiting Starlink services, crippling its drones, as Russian missiles knocked out power stations in attacks President Volodymyr Zelensky called "ostentatious disrespect" to Donald Trump.
Kyiv's relationship with Washington has taken a sharp turn for the worse since U.S. President Trump abruptly lifted sanctions on Russian diesel last week and publicly turned on Zelensky.
Trump, under political pressure to lower fuel prices that have soared since he launched a war against Iran, has called on Kyiv to halt attacks on Russian refineries, and said Ukrainians should replace their wartime leader.
The U.S. president also announced that Ukraine and Russia had both agreed to halt attacks on energy targets, although neither side confirmed this and the past two days have seen intensive Russian bombing, including of Ukrainian power stations.
No warning before Starlink cuts
Ukrainian military officials said Musk's SpaceX had without warning interrupted functioning of military-grade Starlink terminals moving at high speed, effectively preventing Kyiv from using them as onboard guides for drones.
"Our defense forces did not receive a warning about this limitation, and this led to the disruption of several missions," presidential adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov wrote on Telegram.
The apparent suggestion that Musk's company might limit Ukrainian military capabilities drew a sharp response from Poland, which pays for Ukrainian Starlink subscriptions on Kyiv's behalf.
"Hey, @elonmusk, big man, are you playing politics with your products again?" Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski asked Musk on X. "As your European customers, we are watching you."
There was no immediate response from Musk, who in the past has called Sikorski a "small man." SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment outside of U.S. business hours.
Musk is a close political ally of Trump, and the suggestion that SpaceX might limit Ukrainian capabilities reinforced wider Ukrainian concerns that Washington could withhold battlefield support to compel its onetime ally to make concessions.
Sources have told Reuters and other news organizations that the U.S. has threatened to cut off intelligence for early warning of missile strikes on Ukraine, to press Kyiv to suspend attacks on Russian oil refineries.
No warning ahead of missiles
Rescue workers in Kyiv were stretchering the injured from the wreckage of a blasted-out residential building overnight, while firefighters battled a huge blaze in the darkness. Officials said 2 people were killed and 21 wounded at the site.
Some 600,000 people were left without power as Russian missiles careened into power stations during hours of attacks that primarily targeted Kyiv and Kharkiv, Ukraine's second-largest city. Russia's Defense Ministry confirmed it had struck four power plants in and around Kyiv and two in Kharkiv, among other targets. Zelenskiy said more than 30 power stations were damaged.
Ukrainian officials said late on Tuesday they had received no warnings from Western partners for a second day before the massive Russian attacks on the capital. Trump had insisted on Tuesday that Washington was still sharing intelligence.
Zelensky cast the latest attacks as a deliberate snub to Trump's declaration of a ceasefire on energy targets.
"Russia does not consider the American President's statements strong," Zelensky wrote on X. "The strike was entirely deliberate and demonstrative in its scale – Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States."
Zelensky has said Ukraine is willing to observe an energy ceasefire and has not targeted Russian refineries since Trump announced it, but will not continue to hold back if Russia ignores the purported truce. The Kremlin said on Tuesday that contacts were continuing about an energy truce.
Ukraine reported downing just four out of 39 Russian missiles, reflecting Kyiv's weakened air defenses against fast-moving ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones amid a shortage of weapons.
Starlink does not work inside Russia, and Ukrainian drones hitting Russia's oil industry use other means of communication, but Ukraine uses Musk's system to guide drones over its own territory, including parts of Ukraine occupied by Russia.
"According to our observations, during flights, the connection could drop for 10-20 seconds at speeds of just 110-120 km/h [68-75 mph]. The drones kept moving, but these interruptions made them harder to control," Ukraine's 7th Rapid Reaction Corps, deployed in the southeast, said in a statement to Reuters.
A source in Ukraine's Defense Ministry said the limitations significantly complicate logistics and some drone operations.
Since being turned on over Ukraine in the early days of Russia's invasion in 2022, Starlink has been the lifeblood of Ukrainian battlefield communications.
Its resistance to electronic signal jamming has made it a crucial tool for flying long-range attack drones and drones used to drop supplies to frontline troops.

Italian premier says Trump's Russian diesel deal 'very risky'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:17:02 UTC
18:17:02 KST

Melike Pala
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni on Wednesday described US President Donald Trump's agreement on Russian diesel as a "very risky" decision, ANSA news agency reported.
Speaking in the Senate ahead of the European Council summit, Meloni, who was considered a "Trump whisperer" before they fell out, said the surge in fuel prices was primarily driven by the war in Iran rather than Ukraine, questioning the rationale behind the US decision.
"Therefore, the outcome of this decision is uncertain, while the risks are clear: legitimization for Moscow," Meloni said, highlighting the potential risks of "additional revenues to finance its war and a weakening of Western sanctions leverage."
She said the agreement could send "contradictory" signals at a time when Western countries, including the US, have been seeking to pressure Russian President Vladimir Putin to negotiate an end to the war in Ukraine, which continues since 2022.
The Italian premier also called for a stronger European role in efforts to end the war, urging EU member states to appoint an authoritative representative with a mandate from all 27 countries to ensure Europe has a unified voice in negotiations.
"We must ensure that Europe does not stand idly by," Meloni stressed.
She criticized the possibility of France, Germany and the UK pursuing diplomatic initiatives through the so-called E3 format without a collective EU mandate, saying any such efforts should be conducted on behalf of all member states.
Trump has urged Russia and Ukraine not to strike each other's energy sites, and last week announced that Moscow will supply diesel to global markets in an effort to lower fuel prices. His administration also temporarily lifted US sanctions on Russian fuel.
 
- EU budget priorities
Meloni identified high energy prices as the main challenge facing the Italian economy and business competitiveness, calling for a coordinated and rapid European response.
She reiterated Rome's position on the next EU budget, saying Italy would not accept an agreement that comes at the expense of the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), fisheries or cohesion funding.
Acknowledging the objective set by the bloc to reach an agreement by the end of the year, she said Italy would not support a deal simply to meet a deadline.
"We will only sign an agreement when it is right for Italy," Meloni said.

Ukrainian Defence Forces strike Russian drone storage and launch site near Donetsk

Ukrainian Defence Forces strike Russian drone storage and launch site near Donetsk
Ukrinform reports this, citing the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine in a Telegram post.
On October 13 and during the night of October 14, Ukraine's Defence Forces struck several Russian military targets.
In the Donetsk area, they hit a site used to store, prepare, and launch attack drones.
Systematic strikes against such facilities are intended to reduce Russia's ability to attack civilian infrastructure across Ukraine.
In addition, Russian military logistics depots were struck near Popova Balka and Hirnyk in the Donetsk region.
As Ukrinform previously reported, Ukraine's Defence Forces struck a maintenance base in Russia's Kursk region for self-propelled launchers and transport-loading vehicles belonging to the Iskander-M tactical ballistic missile system.

Ukraine Accuses SpaceX of Crippling Drone Missions as Ties With U.S. Worsen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Some 600,000 people were left without power as Russian missiles careened into power stations during hours of attacks that primarily targeted Kyiv and Kharkiv, Ukraine's second-largest city. Russia's Defense Ministry confirmed it had struck four power plants in and around Kyiv and two in Kharkiv, among other targets. Zelenskiy said more than 30 power stations were damaged.
Ukrainian officials said late on Tuesday they had received no warnings from Western partners for a second day before the massive Russian attacks on the capital. Trump had insisted on Tuesday that Washington was still sharing intelligence.
Zelensky cast the latest attacks as a deliberate snub to Trump's declaration of a ceasefire on energy targets.
"Russia does not consider the American President's statements strong," Zelensky wrote on X. "The strike was entirely deliberate and demonstrative in its scale – Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States."
Zelensky has said Ukraine is willing to observe an energy ceasefire and has not targeted Russian refineries since Trump announced it, but will not continue to hold back if Russia ignores the purported truce. The Kremlin said on Tuesday that contacts were continuing about an energy truce.
Ukraine reported downing just four out of 39 Russian missiles, reflecting Kyiv's weakened air defenses against fast-moving ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones amid a shortage of weapons.
Starlink does not work inside Russia, and Ukrainian drones hitting Russia's oil industry use other means of communication, but Ukraine uses Musk's system to guide drones over its own territory, including parts of Ukraine occupied by Russia.
"According to our observations, during flights, the connection could drop for 10-20 seconds at speeds of just 110-120 km/h [68-75 mph]. The drones kept moving, but these interruptions made them harder to control," Ukraine's 7th Rapid Reaction Corps, deployed in the southeast, said in a statement to Reuters.
A source in Ukraine's Defense Ministry said the limitations significantly complicate logistics and some drone operations.
Since being turned on over Ukraine in the early days of Russia's invasion in 2022, Starlink has been the lifeblood of Ukrainian battlefield communications.
Its resistance to electronic signal jamming has made it a crucial tool for flying long-range attack drones and drones used to drop supplies to frontline troops.

Kazakhstan’s camel milk may hit shelves in China and Middle East stores
Kazakhstan approved a new national standard for pasteurized camel milk to help domestic producers expand exports to China, the Middle East, and Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) countries, Qazinform News Agency reports.
Deputy director general of the Kazakh Institute of Standardization and Metrology Alexander Razzarenov told a briefing at the Central Communications Service.
According to him, Kazakhstan has long had a standard for saumal (fresh mare's milk). This year, a separate standard for pasteurized camel milk was developed based on scientific research.
He noted that laboratory tests showed Kazakh camel milk products outperform comparable products from trading partners in terms of quality. As a result, the new standard introduces stricter quality requirements, which are expected to strengthen the competitiveness of Kazakh producers in international markets.
Camel milk is widely used in Kazakhstan to produce the traditional fermented beverage shubat. Pasteurized camel milk is also used in the production of ice cream, jams, and coffee-based drinks, including the popular “camelccino,” a camel-milk version of cappuccino.
The Ministry of Trade and Integration said that the national pasteurized camel milk standard was approved on September 11, 2026, and will come into effect on November 1. The document establishes unified requirements for the quality, safety, labeling, packaging, transportation, and storage of pasteurized camel milk.

As Ebola spreads in eastern DR Congo, mothers and children shun vital care

As Ebola spreads in eastern DR Congo, mothers and children shun vital care
- Fear of Ebola in eastern DR Congo is stopping women and children from using healthcare, leading to more home births, delayed treatment and rising maternal deaths.
- UN figures show maternal deaths in Ituri rose nearly 70% from May to July, while hospital deliveries and obstetric care have fallen sharply.
- Misinformation and fear of Ebola treatment centres are also cutting childhood vaccinations and paediatric visits, risking bigger health problems for years.
AI generated
BUTEMBO, Democratic Republic of Congo – The fear of Ebola is keeping women and children from seeking healthcare in eastern Congo, health workers and aid agencies say, contributing to soaring maternal deaths and falling childhood immunisation rates that could strain the system for years to come.
Health workers say that misplaced anxiety about contact with Ebola is the primary reason women are forgoing crucial prenatal care and opting to give birth at home, and dying more often in the event of complications.
There is still limited data available but figures for Ituri province are raising alarm. United Nations figures show that maternal deaths in Ituri province soared nearly 70% between May and July compared with a year earlier, a troubling indicator of the impact of the Ebola outbreak – currently Congo’s worst on record – on the primary healthcare system.
Steep international aid cuts have also led to shortages of some life-saving medications.
In eastern Butembo city, nurses at the Masiki healthcare centre told Reuters that births have fallen sharply at their maternity ward since the Ebola outbreak was declared in May. Just one mother was resting with her newborn during a recent visit, among rows of empty beds.
“They think the medicines we give them contain the Ebola virus,” head nurse Liliane Adronga told Reuters – highlighting just one of many unfounded suspicions circulating about the virus and healthcare.
She described how women often avoided seeking care until it was too late, recalling a recent case where a woman was believed to have lost her baby while suffering from untreated malaria.
The UN Population Fund has reported a more than 30% drop in hospital deliveries and 50% drop in treatment for obstetric complications for the May to July period since the outbreak began.
Children missing routine vaccines
The Ebola outbreak has spread across seven provinces, infecting more than 8,000 people and killing over 4,000. Officials say it is far from being contained, although infections have slowed in parts of the country.
Routine data collection is a growing challenge but aid agencies say data for the first three months of the outbreak shows a sharp fall in routine childhood vaccinations and paediatric visits.
The United Nations Children’s Fund warned in August that routine vaccinations fell by more than half across Ebola hot spots in Ituri between April and June. In Mongbwalu, first-dose measles vaccinations declined by 69%. “We should be concerned not only about the direct impact of Ebola, but also its indirect effects on health, nutrition, child protection and insecurity,” said Raoul Kamadjeu, a public health emergencies expert at UNICEF. “The longer an epidemic persists, the greater the risks.”
Congo has long struggled with recurring measles outbreaks, for example, with tens of thousands of cases recorded every year, and 126,000 cases so far in 2026, according to data by its health ministry. UNICEF says that health facilities administered 23,000 fewer routine vaccine doses in May and June than in April.
Misinformation, superstition adding to concerns
For some parents, concerns about Ebola overshadowed the benefits of vaccination. “We didn’t want to bring our children to health facilities for fear of being referred to an Ebola treatment centre. Because once you end up there, you can die,” said Masika Furaha, a mother of three in Butembo. She did in the end have her youngest child vaccinated after seeing that children who received the shots remained healthy.
Mupenzi Mumbere, a paediatrician in Butembo, said misinformation is contributing to the fears among parents with sometimes tragic consequences. He described an episode in which a mother burst into tears when he referred her son to the main hospital for an X-ray because she believed staff would take him and kill him with Ebola. Many parents first try self-medication or seek help from traditional healers before eventually turning to hospitals, he said, often with devastating consequences.
“That’s when I realised how great the misunderstanding was,” said Mumbere. “In the worst cases, children arrive in such poor condition that there is little left to do but watch them die.” REUTERS

Business association Delovaya Rossiya proposes partially scrapping simplified tax system, taxing Russians’ passive income
The business association Delovaya Rossiya has drafted proposals to overhaul the Russian economy, the Russian business news outlet RBC reported. Some of the proposed measures would significantly tighten conditions for small and medium-sized businesses, while others target citizens’ passive income.
The draft document, which RBC reviewed, includes 52 proposals covering a wide range of topics. Among other things, the organization proposes the following:
- Eliminate the tax regime known as the “Income” version of the simplified tax system (USN), which carries a 6% rate. The Bell explains that this would mean “primarily an increase in the tax base for entrepreneurs who earn income through their own skilled labor.”
- Lower the threshold for applying VAT under the auto-USN regime from 60 million to 20 million rubles (matching the current threshold for the “standard” USN).
- Eliminate the patent-based tax system, which The Bell says is widely used by microbusinesses.
- Introduce social security contributions for citizens whose income mainly comes from interest or dividends.
- Introduce an inheritance and gift tax on amounts exceeding 50 million rubles.
- Restrict imports of “strategic innovative products.”
The Bell calls the proposal “a blow to small business” and says it “looks very bad” for medium-sized businesses too.

Davis, 63, was sentenced Tuesday to two consecutive terms of 20 years to life, one for first-degree murder and another for the use of a deadly weapon.
Tupac’s sister Sekyiwa Shakur and brother Maurice “Mopreme” Shakur delivered victim-impact statements during the hearing, recalling the rapper as a generous brother and an artist committed to social change.
“The loss of Tupac crippled my family emotionally,” Sekyiwa told the court.
“He dedicated his career to the advancement of his people, he was gently kind to women and children, he fed anyone he knew that didn’t have, he was truly my shining star,” she added.
Mopreme focused on the future his brother was denied.
“Pac didn’t have a chance to have kids, he didn’t have a chance to see his nieces and nephews grow up,” he said. “All Pac got was a death sentence.”
Clark County District Attorney Steve Wolfson said the sentence represented a long-delayed measure of accountability.
“Today, justice has been served for Tupac Shakur and his loved ones,” Wolfson said in a statement.
“While no amount of time in prison can bring Tupac back, we hope this sentencing brings some measure of closure and peace to his family after nearly 30 years. This case is a reminder that no matter how much time passes, our commitment to seeking justice never wavers.”
District Judge Carli Kierny also addressed the consequences of the killing before imposing the sentence.

She said the world had never forgotten the rapper or his death.

A jury convicted Davis on Aug. 31 of first-degree murder with the use of a deadly weapon. Prosecutors did not accuse him of firing the fatal shots but argued that he organized the retaliatory attack under Nevada’s accomplice-liability law.
Tupac was shot on Sept. 7, 1996, while riding in a car near the Las Vegas Strip and died six days later at the age of 25.

Rostec claims its 30mm anti-drone gun beats Western rivals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:06:18 UTC
18:06:18 KST

- Rostec says its 30 mm ZAK-30 Tsitadel anti-drone gun competes with Rheinmetall’s Skynex and the U.S. Phalanx and C-RAM on the world market.
- The system fires programmable shrapnel shells guided by radar and electro-optical sensors and has been used in the war in Ukraine, Rostec says.
Russian state defense conglomerate Rostec is pitching its new 30 mm ZAK-30 “Tsitadel” anti-drone gun as a direct competitor to Western systems such as Germany’s Skynex and the U.S.-made Phalanx, saying its combat use has shown advantages in automation, cost per shot, and effectiveness on the world market.
Rostec made the claim in a statement this week, arguing that each of the Western systems has drawbacks Tsitadel avoids. The company said Germany’s Skynex, which fires 35 mm AHEAD programmable rounds, produces a powerful cloud of fragments but is heavier and more expensive because of its larger caliber. It said the American Phalanx and its land-based version, the Counter-Rocket, Artillery and Mortar system known as C-RAM, fire at very high rates from 20 mm Vulcan Gatling guns but do not use programmable “smart” rounds, so they burn through more ammunition for each target.
Tsitadel fires 30 mm shells packed with shrapnel and fitted with a remotely set fuze. The system’s computer works out the best point on the drone’s flight path to detonate each shell, so the round bursts just ahead of the target and showers it with fragments, which Rostec says means fewer shells are needed per kill than with ordinary rounds. The gun finds and tracks targets with both radar and an electro-optical sensor that works in visible light and infrared, and Rostec says the process from detection to engagement is highly automated.
“The Russian programmable 30 mm shrapnel round creates a deadly cloud of fragments right in front of the drone. When fighting drones, economics are extremely important,” Russian military commentator Dmitry Kornev told the newspaper Izvestia.
Kornev also said Tsitadel’s accuracy and effectiveness put it far ahead of older systems such as Germany’s Gepard. Ukraine has used Gepard self-propelled anti-aircraft guns, supplied by Germany since 2022, as one of its main weapons against Russian Shahed-type attack drones.
Rostec first unveiled Tsitadel in May at a security forum near Moscow, describing it as a system for protecting fixed sites such as plants, depots and energy facilities from both multicopter and fixed-wing drones around the clock. Russian media have reported that the gun module appears to be based on the BM-30-D Spitsa weapon station with the 2A42 cannon used on Russian infantry fighting vehicles, and that the system can hit fixed-wing drones at up to about 1 km (0.6 miles) and small multicopters at up to about 800 meters (2,600 feet). Russian industry sources have also said a mobile version mounted on Ural trucks is planned. At the time of the unveiling, Rostec said the system had already been tested in real combat conditions during the war in Ukraine.
The Western systems Tsitadel is being compared with have their own combat records. Germany has supplied Skynex to Ukraine to protect key sites from Russian drones and cruise missiles, while the U.S. Navy has used Phalanx aboard warships and C-RAM has defended U.S. bases in Iraq and Afghanistan against rockets and mortars.

China’s exports surge amid AI-driven demand
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:05:17 UTC
18:05:17 KST

China’s exports surge amid AI-driven demand
Exports grew by 36.3 percent in September, the biggest leap since the COVID-19 pandemic.
China’s exports surged by more than one-third in September, a boost to the world’s second-largest economy as it faces slowing growth.
Exports grew by 36.3 percent last month year-on-year to reach $447.18bn, accelerating from a 25 percent gain in August, government figures released on Wednesday show.
The leap marked the biggest monthly rise in exports since 2021, when China’s trade figures were skewed by the effects of the COVID-19 pandemic and stringent lockdowns.
Tech-related trade led the growth, with semiconductor exports surging more than 108 percent and shipments of automatic data processing machines jumping nearly 55 percent.
Imports increased 31 percent year-on-year, up from 28.2 percent in August, according to the figures from the General Administration of Customs.
“High-tech demand, supported by the global and domestic AI upcycle, remained the key driver, while China’s pricing and supply-chain competitiveness in other major export categories also helped sustain the momentum,” Taylor Wang, an economist at HSBC in Hong Kong, said in a note to clients.
China’s total exports in the first nine months of the year rose 21.3 percent to $3.37 trillion, while imports gained 27.5 percent to $2.43 trillion.
The gap between exports and imports in the first three quarters gave China a trade surplus of $938.1bn.
The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) was China’s biggest export market by a wide margin, with exports rising more than 52 percent in September to $81.7bn.
Exports to the European Union rose 25.3 percent in September to $60.15bn, while shipments to the United States jumped 39.6 percent to $47.88bn.
After decades of relying on state-led investment and exports to power its economy, China is striving to find new avenues for growth amid a falling population, deflating property market, and weak domestic consumption, which contributes far less to gross domestic product (GDP) than in advanced economies.
China’s economy is expected to grow 4.5 percent in 2026, according to the International Monetary Fund’s latest growth outlook, which would be the slowest expansion since 1990, excluding the outlier years of the COVID pandemic.
“The strong export growth should keep China’s growth on track to achieve its growth target of 4.5-5 percent for 2026,” Lynn Song, chief economist for Greater China at ING, told Al Jazeera.
“Nonetheless, growth remains quite unbalanced, with domestic data quite soft in comparison,” Song said.
“It will be important to rebalance growth over the medium term if China is to achieve its longterm growth targets.”

The Maldives Plans to Offer Residency to the World’s Ultra Rich – And Create Islands From Scratch to Do It
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:05:00 UTC
18:05:00 KST

Nearly half of its population of just over half a million people are packed into the capital city of Malé, a small island that is only two square kilometers in size.
The government has spent recent years expanding existing islands and building brand new ones to ease overcrowding. There are plans to connect one future artificial island city, Ras Malé, to the capital via an undersea tunnel featuring what the president’s office has called a “railway on which tourists can observe the underwater beauty.”
Tourism has followed the same path. Since 2019, developers have begun opening up artificial island complexes that host a mix of hotels, shops, and entertainment at a scale impossible on smaller, naturally occurring islands. 
But with the exception of a handful of leasehold villas built on some resorts, existing developments have left little room for foreigners to call the Maldives home – until now. 
Some Maldivian politicians are trying to push back. In July, opposition lawmaker Ahmed Shamheed filed a resolution calling for the Maldives Pearl Residence program to be immediately suspended and to disclose all related agreements. (His resolution was rejected by parliament in August.) 
The lawmaker also fears SEZs like Project Ayla could effectively become miniature states within a state.
“Money laundering, terrorism financing, and what they do with banks set up there, we don’t know any of this. We have very few resources in the Maldives. We’re talking about billionaires, and we wouldn’t know if the world’s big mafia gangs come and operate there,” Shamheed told reporters.
“And this is just one city — apparently many such cities are to come.”
Azza Mohamed, a governance manager at Transparency International’s Maldives chapter, said the SEZ push is raising fears authorities could recreate the same sort of permissive conditions that led to a massive corruption scandal a dozen years ago. 
That scandal, investigated by OCCRP, saw senior politicians improperly lease islands to tourism developers in 2014 and 2015, while pocketing tens of millions of dollars in proceeds.
Avoiding a similar fate “would require full transparency over beneficial ownership, genuinely independent oversight of procurement and approvals, and enforcement systems that can trace, freeze, and recover illicit funds, including across borders,” Mohamed said.
Meanwhile, precisely who is financing Project Ayla is unknown. 
The project is being developed by the local entity Crystal Holdings Private Limited, which holds the SEZ permit, and the Dubai-based BluRock Group, both of whose underlying investors, equity partners, and ultimate beneficial owners are not made available to the public. 
Crystal Holdings and BluRock did not respond to reporters’ requests for comment.
‘Sovereign Portfolios’
The new residency by investment program will be developed and implemented by the Maldives government and Henley & Partners — a passport brokerage firm that has left behind a string of scandals in other island states.

Explosions reported in Saudi capital after Houthi attack near Aramco HQ
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:04:43 UTC
18:04:43 KST

Powerful explosions rattled the Saudi capital on Wednesday, hours after a strike by the Houthi militia hit a building in the area housing energy giant Aramco's operations centre, in a fresh escalation of the war between the kingdom and the Yemeni group.
Regional powerhouse Saudi Arabia unleashed salvos against the Houthi stronghold in the Yemeni capital Sanaa, while the Iran-aligned militia fired back at sites across the kingdom, which is the world's top crude oil exporter.
Most strikes on Saudi Arabia have targeted infrastructure on the outskirts of the capital, but the barrages appear to be getting closer to the city centre.
On Wednesday the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said it had intercepted a missile fired by the militia towards Riyadh.
In the city's downtown, residents have been seen parking their cars to stop and look up at the sky, an AFP journalist said.
On Tuesday night, the white plumes of air defence missiles could be seen streaking across the sky followed by explosions.
While walking down a major avenue, a witness told AFP he "saw a projectile cutting across the sky" above a mall, saying it left "a yellowish trail of light followed by a trail of smoke. Then, we heard an explosion".
"People were calm; no one was speaking. We were scared and all looking up at the sky," he added, requesting anonymity.
More blasts were heard on Wednesday, AFP journalists in Riyadh reported, as messages were received on phones warning of an "aerial threat" and urging people to take shelter.
The alert was lifted a few minutes later.
A Saudi energy ministry official said a building belonging to Aramco in Dhahran was struck on Tuesday, resulting in a "limited fire" but "no casualties or fatalities".
Dhahran is home to Aramco's headquarters, a vast complex comprising several buildings and residential compounds.
Strikes on Yemen
In Riyadh, the civil defence agency said four people — two women, a man and a child — were wounded by debris from two intercepted Houthi cruise missiles and that 15 homes were damaged.
The Saudi-led coalition meanwhile struck oil sites across western Yemen, with spokesperson Turki Al-Malki saying the attacks targeted facilities used to supply the Houthis' effort to "threaten the kingdom, Yemen, the southern Red Sea and waterways".
An AFP correspondent in Sanaa reported an explosion, while a breaking news alert on the Houthi-affiliated Al-Masirah TV channel said "Saudi aggression" targeted an oil firm.
The coalition has supported Yemen's government militarily against the Houthis since 2015 in a long-running civil war that has created a humanitarian crisis.
Many civilians in the Houthi-controlled Yemeni capital, fearing shortages, have rushed to queue in front of fuel stations, an AFP journalist said.
Renewed threats
The escalation in violence follows a strike on Riyadh's international airport on Saturday that left 13 people dead and operations suspended in the worst attack on the kingdom since 2015.
The Saudi cabinet vowed in a meeting led by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman that it "will not allow its security or freedom of navigation in the Red Sea and Bab al Mandab Strait to be threatened".
Many countries have issued travel warnings to their citizens in Saudi Arabia, with France telling its nationals on Tuesday to avoid Riyadh, Jeddah and Dammam airports.
Traffic in perennially gridlocked Riyadh was noticeably lighter this week as remote learning for all schools and work-from-home orders for some companies took effect, according to AFP journalists.
Saudi Arabia faces a major economic contraction this year, with GDP expected to shrink 3.3 percent, the International Monetary Fund said on Tuesday, predicting a regional drop over Iran's blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.
The kingdom was already facing headwinds from Iran's chokehold on Hormuz since the start of the Middle East war in February, when the US and Israel attacked Iran.
But the restart in July of Yemen's frozen war has further roiled the kingdom and brought the fight to its own soil.
Houthi attacks have also targeted oil tankers in the Red Sea — Saudi Arabia's alternative export route.
'Behaving very badly'
The Riyadh airport attack had prompted US President Donald Trump to say he was considering joining Saudi strikes against the Houthis.
He wrote on his Truth Social platform that "the Houthis are behaving very badly", accusing them of acting "probably at the behest of Iran".
"I'll be there after the elections, and I will never forget!" he wrote, referring to next month's midterms.
The Houthi militia warned the US against intervention, with political bureau member Mohammed Al Bukhaiti telling AFP they would target American interests in the region.
Bukhaiti said the purpose of the campaign against Saudi targets was to send a message to the crown prince "that he can no longer wage aggression against Yemen from a safe position".

inside ‘la voile’, norman foster’s former waterfront home on the french riviera
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

inside ‘la voile’, norman foster’s former waterfront home on the french riviera
the architect's former waterfront villa in saint-jean-cap-ferrat, france, is now on the market for €29.5 million, featuring a sail-inspired canopy, sweeping steel arches, and expansive views of the mediterranean.
[FEATURED]
Norman Foster’s villa on the French Riviera lists for €29.5 million
Originally built in the 1950s and transformed between 1998 and 2002 under the direction of its former owner, architect Norman Foster, Villa La Voile occupies a waterfront hillside in Saint-Jean-Cap-Ferrat, France. The residence brings together sweeping steel arches, extensive glazing, and a retractable sail-like canopy, using its steep site to organize a series of interconnected living spaces around views of the Mediterranean. Now offered for sale, the 480-square-meter property provides a glimpse into Foster’s approach to residential architecture.
La Voile is arranged across seven levels, with reception rooms and terraces following the slope. Double-height spaces and a four-level atrium bring natural light into the interiors, while floor-to-ceiling windows frame views of the coastline. Suspended walkways connect the different levels, creating a sense of openness throughout the residence. Steel arches and glass facades define the architectural language of the villa, while a retractable canopy gives the house its maritime character. The canopy resembles a sail, a reference to the Mediterranean setting that also informs the name of the project, La Voile, which translates from French as ‘the sail’.
Architecture between interior and landscape
Saint-Jean-Cap-Ferrat, between Nice and Monaco, is known for its waterfront villas and steep coastal landscape. La Voile takes advantage of this setting, with its different levels, terraces, and glazed facades opening the house to views of the Mediterranean. Originally built in the 1950s, the residence was extended and redesigned between 1998 and 2002. The renovation changed the layout and orientation of the house to make better use of the hillside and its waterfront position, transforming the existing building into the residence seen today. With its steel arches, retractable canopy, and multi-level interiors, La Voile reflects Foster’s interest in structure and light. Terraces at different levels extend the living spaces outdoors, offering changing views of the Mediterranean. A rooftop pool overlooks the coastline, while the landscaped grounds follow the hillside, giving the property a sense of privacy despite its open waterfront setting.
The two-story library and four-level atrium are among the defining features of the house. The atrium draws natural light into the interior, while the library creates a more intimate space within the otherwise open layout. A MudWork fresco by British land artist Richard Long brings an artistic element to the interiors, complementing the connection of the villa to the natural landscape. Alongside its main living spaces, the residence includes five bedrooms, a separate apartment, and garage facilities.

Ukraine’s Air Force: partners warned of later missile waves
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
08:55:28 UTC
17:55:28 KST

- Ukraine received no partner warning before the first Russian ballistic missile wave overnight into Oct. 14, but did for the next three, Col. Yurii Ihnat said.
- The first wave hit Kyiv at about 22:40 after a similar gap in warnings the previous night, the Ukrainian Air Force said.
Ukraine’s partners warned it about three of the four waves of Russian ballistic missiles launched overnight into Oct. 14, but sent no alert before the first wave hit Kyiv, Ukrainian Air Force spokesman Col. Yurii Ihnat said on national television.
Ihnat said he wanted to clarify the issue because many people had asked whether Ukraine was still receiving launch warnings from its partners. The Air Force had said late on Oct. 13 that, for a second night in a row, no information about ballistic missile launches from Russian territory had come from partners before an attack on Kyiv at about 10:40 p.m., and that the reasons were being investigated.
“Indeed, we first issued a notice at around 22:40 that there had been no notification from partners about ballistic missiles, but in the next three waves of attacks, notifications from partners about the use of ballistic missiles did come through,” said Col. Yurii Ihnat.
The early warnings come from partner satellites and monitoring systems that can detect the heat of a missile launch deep inside Russia within moments, and Ukraine has relied heavily on data from the United States for this. With a warning, air defense crews have time to prepare and cities can sound air raid sirens earlier. Without one, Ukrainian forces only spot the incoming ballistic missiles once they come within range of ground radars, a few minutes before impact, which leaves interceptor crews less time to react and civilians less time to reach shelters and metro stations.
The first wave struck Kyiv without that warning, and the attack grew through the night. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia fired 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 attack drones and loitering munitions at energy and critical infrastructure in Kyiv, the Kyiv region and Kharkiv, damaging 26 facilities in the power system and four in the oil and gas sector and leaving at least 600,000 people without electricity. Zelenskyy said the strike hit energy infrastructure covered by the ceasefire President Donald Trump announced on Oct. 11, and asked Washington for more Patriot interceptors, the main U.S.-made system Ukraine uses to shoot down ballistic missiles.
During the same night, Starlink terminals used by Ukraine’s military stopped working at speeds above 160 km/h (100 mph), disrupting combat missions, according to Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to Zelenskyy who has tracked Russian efforts to jam Starlink along the front. Starlink is not used for Ukraine’s strikes inside Russia, where SpaceX already blocks the service, so the restriction falls on tactical strike and interceptor drones operating over Ukrainian and occupied territory.
Ihnat did not say why the warning for the first wave did not come, or why no alert arrived before the previous night’s attack. The Air Force said earlier that it was looking into the reasons, and neither the White House nor the U.S. Department of War has commented on the missed warnings.

Spain plans to buy 15 more Turkish Hurjet trainer aircraft: TAI chief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
08:52:27 UTC
17:52:27 KST

Spain is planning to purchase 15 additional Hurjet trainer aircraft from Türkiye after signing an agreement for 30 jets, Turkish Aerospace Industries (TAI) CEO Mehmet Demiroglu has said.
Speaking at an event in Türkiye’s northern province of Kastamonu, Demiroglu said deliveries to Spain were expected to begin in 2028.
“Before we even started deliveries to our Air Force, Spain said, ‘We like it, we want to buy 30,’ and bought them. We signed the agreement,” he said. “We are working towards deliveries in 2028. They are planning to buy another 15.”
Demiroglu also highlighted TAI’s production capabilities, saying its campus brings together work on the Kaan combat aircraft, Hurjet and Hurkus aircraft, helicopters, unmanned aerial vehicles, satellites and aircraft components.
The facility conducts testing and production across six fields, he said, describing it as a source of national pride.
Demiroglu said deliveries of the Hurkus aircraft had begun and would continue in the coming years. He identified Azerbaijan as an export destination and said the company aimed to secure further overseas sales.
Demiroglu said Türkiye’s defence industry had strengthened the country’s international standing and generated growing global interest in its technology.
“In the 2020s, particularly with the successes in the defence industry, tremendous admiration for Türkiye has emerged around the world,” he said. “They admire our products, what we do and our achievements.”
‘We are building it so we don’t have to use it’
He described deterrence as a central objective of Türkiye’s defence programmes, including the Kaan combat aircraft.
“We are not working to wage war. We need to work to avoid war,” Demiroglu said, stressing the need to prepare Türkiye’s armed forces and the country for security threats.
“We do not want to use Kaan,” he added. “We are building it so that we do not have to use it.”
Addressing students at the event, Demiroglu encouraged younger generations to develop their skills and learn technologies that would prepare them for the future. He pointed to the expansion of the TEKNOFEST aerospace and technology festivals as helping foster technological ambition.

Agricultural producer prices fall further in September
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
08:52:00 UTC
17:52:00 KST

Türkiye’s agricultural producer prices fell 1.99 percent in September from the previous month, while annual price growth slowed to 12.93 percent, official data showed on Oct. 14.
The monthly decline deepened from 0.93 percent in August, when the annual increase stood at 21.91 percent, according to the Turkish Statistical Institute (TÜİK).
The annual rate was 46.83 percent in September last year.
The agricultural producer price index was 7.03 percent higher than at the end of 2025. The increase based on 12-month averages stood at 30.64 percent.
The index measures prices received by producers at the first point of sale in the agriculture, forestry and fishing sectors, excluding value-added tax and other taxes.
Prices for agricultural and hunting products and related services fell 1.66 percent month-on-month, while forestry products and related services declined 2.75 percent.
Fish, fisheries and aquaculture products and related services recorded a larger monthly decline of 9.93 percent.
Among the main product groups, perennial crop prices dropped 8.37 percent. Prices for non-perennial crops edged up 0.03 percent, while live animals and animal products rose 1 percent.
Vegetables, melons, roots and tubers recorded the strongest annual price increase among subgroups, at 61.07 percent.
Tropical and subtropical fruits posted the steepest monthly decline, with prices falling 14.69 percent.

Air India flight diverted after pilot sends hijack code amid bomb threat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
08:51:00 UTC
17:51:00 KST

An Air India flight from Frankfurt to New Delhi was diverted to Jaipur Wednesday after the pilot reportedly activated a hijack emergency code following an alleged bomb threat, according to local media reports.
India Today reported that the mid-air scare occurred when pilots of the Air India flight broadcast a “squawk 7500” emergency signal, the international code for a hijacking.
The alert, first received by Ahmedabad Air Traffic Control, prompted immediate security protocols. The aircraft was rerouted to Jaipur International Airport, where it landed safely. All passengers were deboarded without incident.
Aviation authorities conducted a thorough inspection of the plane after landing. India's Directorate General of Civil Aviation has launched an investigation to determine the circumstances that led the crew to activate the hijack alert.
No explosives were found aboard the aircraft, and authorities have not reported any injuries or further threats. The incident remains under official review.

Global markets seek direction as oil rises ahead of US inflation release
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
08:50:57 UTC
17:50:57 KST

Global markets are searching for direction with tech stock volatility, surging oil prices, and mixed signals from American bank earnings, while all eyes turned to the US inflation data to be released on Wednesday.
The US inflation, which is expected to accelerate due to rising energy costs, will give insight into the Federal Reserve’s potential monetary policy pathway moving forward.
The Fed is 78% likely to maintain its rates this month, money market estimates show.
Ongoing geopolitical tensions in the Middle East continue to dampen risk appetite.
December-delivery Brent crude is up 0.6% at $106.3 a barrel on Wednesday following a Yemeni Houthi militias’ attack on Saudi Arabia.
Meanwhile, New York Fed President John Williams said he still thinks the bank should hike rates once more this year but no further rate hikes will be necessary, expecting inflation to decline significantly next year.
The US 10-Year Treasury bond yield dropped by one basis point to 5.21% following Williams’ statements.
The US dollar declined 0.1% in value to 102.2, while gold dropped 0.1% to $4,158 per ounce.
The daily crude oil production by the OPEC group rose 920,000 barrels month-on-month in September, totaling nearly 20.1 million barrels, leading to a downward revision of global oil demand growth for this year and an upward revision for next year.
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) said rising borrowing costs in a period of high debt burdens exert mounting pressure on public finances, urging fiscal consolidation measures to be implemented.
The New York Stock Exchange traded negatively due to a broader selloff in chipmaker stocks.
Micron Technology shares dropped 3.6%, SK Hynix fell 3.2%, AMD declined 1.9%, and Western Digital’s shares were down 1.6%.
Separately, major US banks reported their financial results.
JPMorgan Chase’s profit and revenue fell short of expectations, while its shares dropped by nearly 1%.
Citigroup shares contracted 5.6% despite profit and revenue exceeding estimates, while Goldman Sachs shares fell 0.2%.
Wells Fargo posted better-than-expected profits but its revenue did not meet expectations, losing the bank 3.1% in stock value.
At the same time, US existing-home sales grew 1.5% in September, beating expectations of a 0.8% decline.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.35% and the Nasdaq Composite declined 0.15%, while the S&P 500 traded flat on Tuesday. American indexes started Wednesday on a positive trend.
European stock markets also saw selloffs amid tech stock declines.
Dutch chipmaker ASML’s shares dropped 4.1%, German tech firm Infineon’s shares declined 2.6%, Aixtron shares fell 3.4%, and Suss Microtec shares contracted 3.5%.
Germany’s BMW posted a 6.3% drop in global sales in the third quarter to 551,072 units as sales in China declined, but the carmaker’s shares closed Tuesday up 2.4%, led by the European electric vehicle (EV) demand.
Germany’s consumer price index (CPI) rose 0.6% on a monthly basis and 3.3% year-on-year, within estimates.
The UK’s FTSE 100 fell 0.06%, while Germany’s DAX 40 and France’s CAC 40 declined 0.07%. Italy’s FTSE MIB 30 traded flat.
European indexes started Wednesday on a mixed trend.
Near the close, however, Asian equity markets traded mostly higher.
China’s producer price index (PPI) rose 5% on an annual basis, marking its fastest rise since June 2022, and rising above the 3.8% estimate. Rising energy prices contributed to the rise, while signaling that the country’s economy is gradually moving away from deflationary pressures.
China’s CPI rose 0.9% on an annual basis this month, accelerating moderately compared to August but coming in below estimates, revealing that domestic demand remained sluggish.
At the same time, China’s exports and imports surged above expectations by 36.3% and 31%, respectively, gaining momentum compared to August.
Chinese economic policymakers may have to implement further policy support to reach short- and long-term growth targets, analysts say.
The People’s Bank of China cut the one-year lending rates of three policy banks by 25 basis points on Sept. 29.
Near the close of trading on Wednesday, South Korea’s Kospi rose 1.2%, Japan’s Nikkei 225 gained 0.9%, and Hong Kong’s Hang Seng was up 0.2%, while China’s Shanghai Composite traded flat.

Ukrainian Drones Hit Sberbank Data Center After Yandex Attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
08:30:36 UTC
17:30:36 KST

Ukrainian drones targeted a major data center under construction for Russian state lender Sberbank in the Saratov region overnight, First Deputy CEO Alexander Vedyakhin said Wednesday, as attacks on Moscow disrupted more than 500 flights.
Vedyakhin said all banking systems and online services continued to operate normally and no employees were injured in the attack in the Volga River city of Balakovo, according to the state-run news agency TASS.
Users across Russia nevertheless reported disruptions to Sberbank and its GigaChat artificial intelligence service, as well as several other major online platforms, according to outage tracker Detector404. The reports did not establish a link between the disruptions and the drone attacks.
NASA’s satellite fire-monitoring system showed multiple fires in Balakovo.
Saratov region Governor Roman Busargin said “all infrastructure facilities” were operating normally, without identifying Sberbank’s data center as a target. He said one woman was killed and several homes were damaged in the drone strikes.
The attack on Sberbank follows three consecutive Ukrainian drone strikes that disabled half of tech giant Yandex’s data centers. Ukraine says it is responding to Russian attacks on its own data sites.
“You didn’t think it would stop with just Yandex, did you?” Ukraine’s Fire Point arms company said in a social media post Wednesday morning.
Sberbank began construction of the 55,000-square-meter (592,000-square-foot) facility in 2021, promoting the 122.2 billion ruble ($1.4 billion) project as one of Europe’s largest data centers, with completion expected in 2030.
Sberbank and its main domestic rival, Yandex, are leading Russian developers of artificial intelligence, with their respective GigaChat and YandexGPT models. State media reported in 2024 that Sberbank’s Balakovo center would host Russia’s biggest supercomputer, which was scheduled to go into operation in 2027.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said its air defense systems destroyed 902 Ukrainian drones over 19 Russian regions and annexed Crimea between Tuesday evening and Wednesday morning.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said “most” of the 493 Ukrainian drones flying toward the region were neutralized, 180 of them on direct approach to the capital.
The attacks on Moscow prompted civil aviation authority Rosaviatsia to restrict arrivals and departures at all four Moscow airports after 10 p.m. Tuesday, in the second prolonged shutdown of Moscow’s airports in less than a week.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said its forces struck seven Ukrainian energy infrastructure facilities and a data center with ground-launched missiles and long-range strike drones overnight.
Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak later accused Ukraine of attacking two oil refineries in the Saratov and Ryazan regions Wednesday, saying Kyiv was showing no signs of moving toward an energy ceasefire announced by U.S. President Donald Trump.
Ukrainian presidential adviser Dmytro Lytvyn denied those statements, telling reporters that Ukraine struck a data center and another unnamed target but not refineries.
Reuters contributed reporting.

China chip exports jump 136% to US$45b as AI frenzy jacks up prices

China chip exports jump 136% to US$45b as AI frenzy jacks up prices
ICs among the fastest-growing categories in September, underlining country’s growing influence in semiconductor supply chain
China’s integrated circuit (IC) exports surged 136 per cent year on year in September to US$45 billion, exceeding the 108 per cent growth rate in the first nine months of the year in a sign of the country’s rising influence in the global semiconductor supply chain.
In September, China exported 32.7 billion units of ICs, according to customs data released on Wednesday, a 1 per cent year-on-year increase in volume. But higher prices fuelled the 136 per cent jump in value amid a memory chip shortage stemming from the global building spree in artificial intelligence infrastructure.
The first three quarters as a whole saw exports of 275.2 billion IC units worth nearly US$302 billion, according to the General Administration of Customs.

Redress of individual grievances: service complaints (JSP 831)
A guide for Ministry of Defence (MOD) service and civilian personnel on the application of policy for service complaints.
Documents
Details
The aim of this Joint Service Publication (JSP) is to provide guidance on the procedures to follow in order that statutory complaints (service complaints) raised by service personnel and former service personnel are handled and resolved in accordance with legislation, using a process that is efficient, fair and transparent.

In Hong Kong, accountability must be more than a slogan

Opinion
In Hong Kong, accountability must be more than a slogan
The Anderson Road, One Stanley and Queen Mary Hospital cases suggest that the city remains better at talking about accountability than ensuring it
3-MIN READ3-MIN
4
 Listen
Mike Rowse is an independent commentator. 
When news broke last week that three newly completed housing blocks were to be demolished without ever having been occupied, I suffered an immediate attack of deja vu. In early 1974, I was in the first wave of recruits to the Operations Department of the newly established Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC).
As luck would have it, my first posting was to the team dealing with the old Public Works Department. That was my introduction to the wide world of corruption and shoddy work in the local construction industry. The terrible thing is that some practices seem to have hardly changed at all despite half a century of efforts to eradicate them.
Common problems we found in those days were foundations not dug deeply enough or concrete not up to strength. There seemed to be a particular issue with steel reinforcement bars: there were not enough of them, or they were too short, too thin or in the wrong place. Sometimes they were deficient in all four aspects.
The Anderson Road project is a classic example of the genre. A CK Asset subsidiary was successful in the tender for a residential site in Kwun Tong. There were to be six blocks comprising 2,930 flats for starter homes, at least 1,000 of which were to be sold at a significant discount to eligible buyers as required by the Housing Bureau.

Police hold 11 in raid on Turkey pro-opposition Halk TV
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
08:30:00 UTC

Breadcrumb
Police hold 11 in raid on Turkey pro-opposition Halk TV
Turkish police raided the headquarters of the pro-opposition Halk TV, halting its live broadcasts and arresting 11 people, the channel and prosecutors said early Wednesday.
"Police raid at Halk TV headquarters! A trustee (manager) has been appointed, broadcasts have been halted," the channel wrote on X shortly before 7:00 am (0400 GMT).
Halk's news channel and the live broadcasts on its YouTube site were both offline.
It was the latest crackdown on the pro-opposition media and came just two weeks after the authorities shut down the website and social media accounts of T24, a leading digital news website, citing its "LGBT propaganda".
In a statement to Turkish media, prosecutors said they had issued a warrant for 17 people, 11 of whom had been detained as part of an investigation into Halk's chairman Cafer Mahiroglu on suspicion of "bribery", "rigging tenders," and "money laundering."
It said companies co-owned or managed by Mahiroglu had been seized and that the authorities put a government-appointed trustee in charge of them.
Of the remaining six people named in the warrant, four were abroad, one was in a correctional facility, and the last was still being sought for, it said.
Mahiroglu was not among those detained as he lives abroad.
'We're under a blockade'
In several posts as dawn was breaking, Halk journalists said they were unable to get into the building.
"The police have sealed off the entrance to our building. That's the situation... There's nothing left to say," wrote Onur Dalar on X, his words echoed by a colleague.
"At Halk TV, the management is now under a trustee. Broadcasting systems have been seized. Our channel is literally under blockade. I still can't get into the institution where I've worked for 5 years—none of us can. The police haven't left the building," wrote Gamze Altunay.
The move came just hours before the start of the defence's arguments in the sprawling corruption trial of jailed Istanbul mayor Ekrem Imamoglu and some 400 other defendants.
The move drew a furious reaction from the main opposition Yeni Parti and the Turkish Journalists' Union (TGS)
"In recent years, the lawlessness used by the political authorities to overcome every problem has once again struck freedom of the press today... We do not accept this tyranny!" wrote TGS on X.
And opposition leader Ozgur Ozel also lashed out against a TV channel "watched by millions" describing the government's action as "weak and cowardly".
"Storming a TV channel with a police raid at dawn and appointing a trustee is something only dictators do. Unfortunately, they have brought our country to this state," he wrote.
He said it was no coincidence the raids came just hours before the start of the defence arguments in Imamoglu's trial.
"They did this on the very day the defence was to begin in Turkey's biggest political trial. Those who appoint trustees to municipalities and usurp the will of the people have now appointed a trustee to Halk TV, watched by millions. Because they are WEAK and COWARDLY!"
Last year, Halk TV—which has faced repeated sanctions from Turkey's broadcasting regulator—was threatened with possible closure over its critical tone towards the government of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

Bank and fintech: How partnership is transforming the auto lending market
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
08:29:41 UTC
17:29:41 KST

Bank and fintech: How partnership is transforming the auto lending market
Today, creating a financial product that meets market demand requires more than simply issuing a loan. It is important to make the entire customer journey fast, convenient and digital. That is why banks are increasingly combining their financial expertise with the technologies of fintech companies. Bank RBK and Sapa Digital Finance demonstrate how this approach works in practice, Qazinform News Agency reports.
Stronger together
The global financial market is gradually changing its traditional development model: instead of building all the infrastructure themselves, banks are engaging technology partners. This allows them to launch products faster, automate processes and scale their businesses without unnecessary operating costs.
For Kazakhstan, this approach is particularly relevant in auto lending. According to the First Credit Bureau, the market grew by almost 44% over two years, from 2023 to 2025, reaching 2.39 trillion tenge. Amid growing demand, competitive advantage is determined not only by loan terms but also by how quickly and easily customers can obtain financing.
From application to car purchase — a digital process
Bank RBK and Sapa Digital Finance (SDF) have been cooperating since 2023. The partners have combined their competencies: the bank provides the financial component and sets lending parameters, while SDF is responsible for technological support, process automation and interaction with customers and partners.
“Today, a bank’s competitiveness is determined, among other things, by its ability to quickly turn technology into tangible benefits for customers. Our partnership with Sapa Digital Finance allows us to leverage an established technological infrastructure, scale our auto lending business and make the financing process more convenient. This is an example of how combining expertise helps create products that meet market demand and develop business,” says Natalya Akentyeva, Chairwoman of the Management Board of Bank RBK.
Since the partnership began, 65,000 Kazakhstanis have received auto loans. SDF’s technological platform brings together all participants in the process within a single digital environment, providing access to financing through a partner network across different regions of the country.
Loan applications are assessed in real time using artificial intelligence, while the loan application process, including collateral registration, can be completed on the same day. This is particularly important for those who need a vehicle not only for personal use but also for work: more than 10,000 auto loans have been issued to individual entrepreneurs over the course of the partnership.
At the same time, lending speed should not come at the expense of loan portfolio quality. Amid increased market attention to the quality of auto loans, modern credit scoring models play a particularly important role, allowing lenders to comprehensively assess borrowers’ creditworthiness and determine credit risk levels more accurately. Their application helps make well-informed lending decisions, combining access to financing with a responsible approach to loan portfolio management. Technology therefore not only speeds up processes but also enhances the quality of lending decisions.
Another area of cooperation is subsidizing the purchase of domestically manufactured vehicles, which helps make them more affordable for buyers and supports demand for cars assembled in Kazakhstan.
Technology at the service of customers
“For us, the importance of technology lies primarily in how it helps people. Today, customers want not only to obtain an auto loan on favorable terms but also to complete the process quickly, conveniently and without unnecessary complications. Together with Bank RBK, we have combined the bank’s reliability, our AI-based technologies and an extensive network of car dealerships to make the car-buying process simpler and more accessible. The use of AI helps us accelerate processes, reduce waiting times and offer customers more convenient services. Behind the 65,000 auto loans issued are real people, their needs and their plans. For us, this is the main result of the partnership and confirmation that modern technology should, above all, serve the interests of people,” says Yeldar Tenizbayev, Chairman of the Supervisory Board of Sapa Digital Finance.
The partnership between Bank RBK and SDF reflects a key trend in the financial market: technology delivers the greatest impact when combined with banking expertise. The bank gains opportunities to scale its lending operations, the fintech partner provides the technological foundation, and customers benefit from simpler and faster access to financing.
This is precisely the new logic of the financial business: rather than building everything independently, partners combine their strengths to offer customers higher-quality and more accessible solutions.
Bank RBK is one of Kazakhstan’s largest commercial banks, ranking 5th in terms of corporate loan portfolio size, 7th in total assets and 10th in equity.
Sapa Group is a Kazakhstan-based technology group of companies developing solutions in fintech, artificial intelligence and business process automation.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that Bank RBK led Kazakhstan’s banks in term deposit growth, recording a 47.8% year-on-year increase.
License No. 1.1.821.135, issued by the Agency for Regulation and Development of the Financial Market of the Republic of Kazakhstan on July 15, 2026.

Kazakhstan’s vice minister calls for labeling AI-generated content

Kazakhstan’s vice minister calls for labeling AI-generated content
Kazakhstan’s First Vice Minister of Culture and Information Kanat Iskakov has called for labeling content created using artificial intelligence. He made the remarks during a panel session at Astana Media Week 2026, Qazinform News Agency correspondent reports.
According to Iskakov, viewers, readers and online users should be aware when AI technologies have been used to produce news and other media content. He described this as one of the key principles for building a transparent media environment and strengthening public trust.
Iskakov also stressed the need to develop professional and ethical standards for the use of artificial intelligence. At the same time, journalists and editorial teams must remain responsible for the content they publish.
“We greatly overestimate the capabilities of AI. It is a tool, a way to speed up the preparation and delivery of documents and materials. But the most important thing is responsibility, and that responsibility lies with the journalist,” the vice minister said.
Speaking about the future of the media industry, he also suggested that digital technologies would gradually erase the traditional boundaries between different types of media.
“In the near future, there will be no distinction between websites, television and news agencies. Information will be delivered through multiple channels and in multiple formats. We will have an entire information ecosystem,” Iskakov said.
Astana Media Week, which is celebrating its 10th anniversary this year, is taking place in the Kazakh capital from October 14 to 16. The forum focuses on the transformation of the media industry, the impact of artificial intelligence on journalism and new approaches to building trust in information.
Earlier,Qazinform News Agency reported that new AI transparency requirements came into effect in the European Union on August 2. The rules require the labelling of deepfakes and certain other categories of AI-generated content, including text on matters of public interest published without human editorial oversight or review.

====================================================================================================

Moscow, Washington vs. Kyiv: Can Trump Force Ukraine to Capitulate?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
08:29:26 UTC
17:29:26 KST

US President Donald Trump’s recent statements have by now fully aligned with those coming from the Kremlin.
Meanwhile, on the front line, the Russian army has had no advantage for almost a year. Indeed, the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) is counterattacking and liberating settlements in the Donbas itself – the region Putin has identified as a key objective for the Russian military.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Against this backdrop, Trump has partially lifted energy sanctions on Russia and announced an agreement to import several hundred thousand tons of diesel fuel from Russia to the US.
Then, under the guise of a peace plan, Trump began issuing ultimatums to Ukraine, demanding that it stop striking Russian oil refineries, and calling for “no strikes on oil refining facilities.” The plan is supposedly bilateral but is, in practice, one-sided in Ukraine’s case, since Ukraine has only one oil refinery, which Russia has already destroyed.
After the ultimatum, Trump went further, declaring that Ukraine “should get” a new president because he was dissatisfied with Zelensky’s refusal to sign a “peace agreement.”
Predictably, this was followed by threats to stop supplying Ukraine with intelligence about Russian ballistic missile strikes against Ukrainian civilian targets.
By Oct. 13, after the initial emotions and passions had subsided, new US proposals for a peace agreement were revealed by Washington Post columnist David Ignatius. There has been some progress: the Russian demands for territorial concessions are no longer repeated.
US-Russia Diesel Deal: What’s The Big Idea?
Ukrainian reaction
The reaction of most Ukrainians to the latest developments is extremely sharp.
“Trump’s energy truce means that Ukraine does not strike Russian oil refineries that are operating, while Russia does not strike the Ukrainian refinery that is not operating. The next step in Trump’s incredible plan will be to announce a ceasefire. Ukraine will have to promise not to strike the Russian army, and Russia will give its word not to strike the Russian army. And peace will immediately follow,” investment banker Serhiy Fursa wrote.
“The overall strategy has long been clear: blame Ukraine for your own miscalculations and use Russian oil refineries as an example, while shielding a target that is genuinely painful for the Russians. The figures for Russian diesel supplies to the US are not what matters here. What matters is the violation of laws passed by Congress, as well as the creation of new precedents for cooperation and business with the Russian war machine,” said Olha Aivazovska, head of the OPORA civil society analytical group.
“By refusing to provide us with intelligence on the trajectories of missile attacks against Ukraine, America is, in effect, becoming complicit in Russia’s murder of Ukrainian civilians,” said Oleksandr Shvets, editor-in-chief of the Fakty newspaper.
A member of the Cabinet of Ministers told Kyiv Post that Trump’s move had come as a complete surprise to Ukrainians.
“This is simply unthinkable. It is a betrayal of every allied position. It is worse than the Russians,” he said.
Why do Trump and Putin need the diesel deal?
The US president’s motives are clearly an attempt to forestall an Election Day disaster for Republicans on Nov. 3. He hopes, at the very least, to convince Americans that he is doing something about sky-high fuel prices.
Putin’s motives, however, are more perhaps more complex. Despite the negligible export volumes, Russian experts believe he can present the deal to a war-weary Russian population as a victory –signaling renewed warming of relations and rapprochement with the US.
“What does Putin need this for? To damage Trump’s relations with Zelensky and Europe, which, like Zelensky, has condemned the deal. And to try to use it as leverage, so that Trump pressures Zelensky to restrict Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries,” wrote Russian economist Kirill Rogov.
Zelensky is presented as the problem… again
Among other things, Trump said that Ukraine should “have a new president” because, supposedly, Zelensky did not want to sign a peace agreement – a capitulation in a war that Ukraine is not losing.
Numerous analyses have been published in Ukraine and elsewhere showing that the various peace-plan proposals put forward by Russia through US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were effectively one-sided. They took into account only the aggressor’s demands, in a form that was absolutely unacceptable to Ukraine. In particular, Russia wanted to obtain, without a fight, territories where its army had made no progress over the preceding four years despite suffering heavy losses.
Trump’s statements about the need to replace Ukraine’s president are fundamentally at odds with the principles of a democratic country – the kind of country Trump represents.
First, elections cannot be held in Ukraine during wartime because most people living near the front line, in occupied territories, or as refugees, as well as those currently fighting on the front line, would be unable to vote.
Second, holding elections during the war without the participation of Zelensky’s main competitors – who are senior officers or generals and therefore cannot leave their posts while martial law remains in force – could produce a result Trump would not expect: Zelensky would have a strong chance of winning.
Third, the issue goes far beyond the president. According to opinion polls, the overwhelming majority of Ukrainians do not want to make concessions to Moscow. Nor is there any evidence of declining morale in the army or of soldiers wanting to hand over anything to Russia.
The main reason is that everyone understands that as soon as Putin gets one territory, he will use it as a base to attack others and demand those as well – endlessly.
“The issue is not Zelensky. It is the Ukrainian army and Ukrainian civil society that do not want to capitulate to Moscow. To think that changing the president will change Ukrainians’ approach to the war is nonsense. But Donald Trump has demonstrated a complete lack of understanding of the nature of Russian aggression against Ukraine since the very beginning of his presidency. He likewise fails to understand the essence of Ukrainian resistance,” said writer and journalist Radomyr Mokryk.
Not even the ‘peace party’ can accept capitulation
Ukraine’s political discourse includes not only the determination to continue resisting Russia but also a willingness to hold peace talks with Russia and make some concessions to the aggressor as a compromise for peace.
This tendency is represented by various politicians. Some are trying to establish themselves among the military “heavyweights,” while others are seeking to appeal to Trump. Still others are simply trying to capitalize on the war fatigue felt by part of society, along with constant power outages and the fear of being killed by shelling far from the front line.
These politicans from different parties are not taking part in one initiative, but informally known among journalists as the “peace party” (with ironic sense of this term).
Among them - many politicians associated with this tendency are figures of varying stature.
They include popular lawmakers Oleksiy Honcharenko and Danylo Hetmantsev, Kharkiv Mayor Ihor Terekhov, etc.
It is important to note, however, that none of them supports capitulation exclusively on Russia’s terms, let alone handing over territories that the Ukrainian army firmly controls.
For example, Honcharenko, who has faced a wave of public condemnation and accusations of “capitulationism” (in commentsaries on his pages in social media), explained his position as follows:
“Peace cannot be achieved with a single decision. Yes, we will have to discuss compromises, but compromise is not capitulation. It means finding terms under which Ukraine can end the war, obtain real security guarantees, and preserve its national interests. We must not give Russia anything. Every agreement must take Ukrainian interests into account,” Honcharenko said.
Even with such wording, however, he faced criticism on social media.
The issues of existential survival and capitulation lie largely outside the political sphere and do not depend on the identity of the president or members of parliament.
Attempts to change or dismiss this reality are naturally perceived as a form of coercion into capitulation, and anyone engaged in such efforts is seen as Putin’s accomplice and complicit in Russian aggression.
This is the dividing line between “peace” and “capitulation.”
