Ukraine says SpaceX limits Starlink operations, disrupting military
- SpaceX has limited some Starlink services in Ukraine, and officials say this disrupted military drone missions and key battlefield communications.
- Ukraine’s forces said the limits caused 10–20 second dropouts and forced some missions to be cancelled, making drones harder to control and logistics more difficult.
- The change comes as Starlink remains vital to Ukraine’s war effort, but the reason for the throttling is unclear amid US pressure to stop strikes on Russian oil refineries.
AI generated
KYIV - SpaceX has introduced a limit on some Starlink services in Ukraine, disrupting combat drone missions for which the technology is crucial, officials said on Oct 14.
The satellite internet terminals from Elon Musk’s company are vital for guiding Ukraine’s longer-range drone strikes in occupied southern and eastern Ukraine, which have wreaked havoc on Russian logistics.
“Our defence forces did not receive a warning about this limitation, and this led to the disruption of several missions,” presidential adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov wrote on Telegram.
Beskrestnov said SpaceX had stopped the operation of its military-grade version above 160kmh.
Ukraine’s 7th Rapid Reaction Corps, deployed in the south-east, added that units had been forced to cancel some missions.
“According to our observations, during flights, the connection could drop for 10–20 seconds at speeds of just 110–120kmh. The drones kept moving, but these interruptions made them harder to control,” it said in a statement to Reuters.
A source in Ukraine’s defence ministry added that the limitations significantly complicate logistics and some drone operations.
SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment outside regular US business hours.
Although it was not immediately clear why the Starlink service was throttled, the move comes as Washington pressures Kyiv to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries.
Starlink does not work inside Russia and the Ukrainian drones hitting Russia’s oil industry use other means of communication.
Ukraine has already said that it did not receive the usual advance warning from its allies about some recent missile strikes on the capital.
Since being turned on over Ukraine in the early days of Russia’s invasion in 2022, Starlink has been the lifeblood of Ukrainian battlefield communications, with units using its satellite internet to talk to each other.
Over time, its resistance to electronic signal jamming also made it a crucial tool for flying long-range attack drones as well as large hexacopters which drop supplies to Ukraine’s frontline. REUTERS

Dastyar: we aim to make a strong start against Iraq
TEHRAN - Iran’s national wheelchair basketball team are determined to begin their campaign at the Nagoya Asian Para Games with a strong performance against Iraq, according to team coach Mohammadreza Dastyar.
Iran have been drawn in Group B alongside Iraq, South Korea and the Philippines. The Iranian team will face Iraq in its opening match on Friday at Aichi International Arena in Nagoya, Japan. Iran will then take on South Korea on Saturday before meeting the Philippines on Monday.
Dastyar highlighted the challenges the team faced during their journey to Japan, explaining that the lengthy trip had affected the players’ physical condition.
“We held our first training session in Nagoya on Wednesday. However, we had a 60-hour journey to Japan, which had a considerable negative impact on the players’ physical readiness,” he said.
The team travelled from Tehran to Istanbul, then continued to Manila before finally arriving in Nagoya. The demanding itinerary kept the players on the road for approximately three days, leaving some of them experiencing muscle stiffness and fatigue.
Despite these difficulties, Dastyar stressed that the team were focused on preparing for their opening match against Iraq.
“Fortunately, despite the problems we experienced during the journey, we held an energetic training session. We reviewed our tactical plans and worked on preparing the players for the first game. Our aim is to make a strong start to the competition,” he told Tehran Times correspondent’s Masoud Hossein.
The coach also referred to Iran’s absence from the recent Wheelchair Basketball World Championships in Ottawa, Canada. The Iranian team missed the tournament after visas were not issued to some members of its coaching staff.
According to Dastyar, missing the World Championships had a negative psychological impact on the players. However, a period of rest helped them recover mentally and move forward.
“That experience affected the players’ morale, but fortunately, they were able to recover mentally during their break and put the disappointment behind them. We now have a new challenge ahead, and our entire focus is on achieving the best possible results in Nagoya,” he said.
Iran will need to perform consistently throughout the group stage before facing a playoff match, with the ultimate objective of reaching the semifinals.
Dastyar expressed hope that his team would successfully navigate the demanding schedule and defend Iran’s reputation in wheelchair basketball.
Iran have an impressive record at previous editions of the Asian Para Games, having won one silver medal and secured two third-place finishes across the last four editions. The team now hopes to build on that record in Nagoya, overcome the challenges of their long journey and launch their campaign with a victory over Iraq.

Biletsky cited the primary strategic achievement of the four stages of Operation Vivaldi as disrupting the enemy's plans to capture the Sloviansk-Kramatorsk agglomeration in northern Donetsk region from the flanks and encircle it. Ukrainian forces also secured the Kharkiv-Sloviansk highway, preventing the enemy from severing the key logistical artery for the Donbas grouping. Furthermore, the corps' offensive forced the Russian military command to withdraw units of the 1st Tank Army from the Kupiansk direction in Kharkiv region and redeploy them to the Lyman direction, easing Russian pressure on Kupiansk-Vuzlovy.

The move came just hours before the start of the defence's arguments in the sprawling corruption trial of jailed Istanbul mayor Ekrem İmamoğlu and some 400 other defendants.
Turkish police raided the headquarters of the pro-opposition Halk TV news channel, halting its live broadcasts and arresting 11 people, the channel and prosecutors said early on Wednesday.
"Police raid at Halk TV headquarters! A trustee (manager) has been appointed, broadcasts have been halted," the channel wrote in a post on X shortly before 7:00 am (0600 CET).
Halk's news channel and the live broadcasts on its YouTube site were both offline.
It was the latest crackdown on the pro-opposition media and came just two weeks after authorities shut down the website and social media accounts of T24, a leading digital news website, citing its "LGBT propaganda."
In a statement to Turkish media, prosecutors said they had issued a warrant for 17 people, 11 of whom had been detained as part of an investigation into Halk's chairman Cafer Mahiroğlu on suspicion of "bribery", "rigging tenders," and "money laundering."
It said companies co-owned or managed by Mahiroğlu had been seized and that the authorities put a government-appointed trustee in charge of them.
Of the remaining six people named in the warrant, four were abroad, one was in a correctional facility and the last was still being sought, it said.
Mahiroğlu was not among those detained as he lives abroad.
'We're under a blockade'
In several posts as dawn was breaking, Halk journalists said they were unable to get into the building.
"The police have sealed off the entrance to our building. That’s the situation...There’s nothing left to say," wrote Onur Dalar on X, his words echoed by a colleague.
"At Halk TV, the management is now under a trustee. Broadcasting systems have been seized. Our channel is literally under blockade. I still can’t get into the institution where I’ve worked for 5 years, none of us can. The police haven’t left the building," wrote Gamze Altunay.
The move came just hours before the start of the defence's arguments in the sprawling corruption trial of jailed Istanbul mayor Ekrem İmamoğlu and some 400 other defendants.
The move drew a furious reaction from the main opposition Yeni Parti and the Turkish Journalists' Union (TGS)
"In recent years, the lawlessness used by the political authorities to overcome every problem has once again struck freedom of the press today...We do not accept this tyranny!" wrote TGS on X.
And opposition leader Özgür Özel also lashed out against a TV channel "watched by millions" describing the government's action as "weak and cowardly."
"Storming a TV channel with a police raid at dawn and appointing a trustee is something only dictators do. Unfortunately, they have brought our country to this state," he wrote.
He said it was no coincidence the raids came just hours before the start of the defence arguments in İmamoğlu's trial.
"They did this on the very day the defence was to begin in Turkey’s biggest political trial. Those who appoint trustees to municipalities and usurp the will of the people have now appointed a trustee to Halk TV, watched by millions. Because they are WEAK and COWARDLY!"
Last year, Halk TV, which has faced repeated sanctions from Turkey's broadcasting regulator, was threatened with possible closure over its critical tone towards the government of President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan.

U.S.-Russia deal on diesel is "very risky choice," Italy PM Meloni says

U.S.-Russia deal on diesel is 'very risky choice,' Italy PM Meloni says
ROME, Oct 14 - The deal between the United States and Russia over diesel supply is a "very risky choice" that runs counter to efforts to force Vladimir Putin to sit at a negotiating table with Ukraine, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said on Wednesday.
The United States and Russia agreed last week that Moscow would initially supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel to U.S. and global markets.
"The outcome of this decision is uncertain, while the risks are clear," Meloni told the Italian parliament ahead of an EU summit this week.
"It provides Moscow with legitimacy as its bombs continue to fall on Ukrainian cities, generates new revenue to finance the war, and implicitly weakens the effectiveness of sanctions," she added.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy criticised the accord, calling it "an investment in a war that must be ended."
U.S. President Donald Trump said it would lower energy prices in the United States, a major political headache for his Republican Party ahead of pivotal midterm elections that determine control of Congress.
Meloni told parliament the 27 EU countries should appoint "an authoritative figure" to negotiate for Europe over the Russia-Ukraine war, without ruling out a formal mandate for the E3 Group comprising Germany, France and Great Britain.
"If France, Germany, and Great Britain believe they can do better on their own than we could all do together, and so far that is the choice they have made, then at least let them do so on behalf of everyone and with an official mandate," Meloni said.
In other remarks, she said the EU summit would discuss what she said had been an escalation in Russian hybrid attacks, referring to drone incursions, cyber attacks, sabotage and other covert operations aimed at weakening backing for Kyiv.
"We need to protect our critical infrastructure: energy grids, undersea cables, ports, airports, and the underwater domain, where Italy possesses outstanding expertise," she said. REUTERS

Denmark’s biggest retailer is training robots for supermarket night shifts. When will they be ready?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
08:10:33 UTC
17:10:33 KST

For now, they are slower than supermarket workers, though the start-up says advances in AI will help improve their speed and precision.
In the Danish town of Lyngby, just north of Copenhagen, the supermarket night shift is getting some unusual trainees.
Humanoid robots are learning to restock shelves after closing time, part of a multi-year trial to take on routine tasks and free employees to help customers.
With their arms, legs and fingers, the robots can operate in spaces built for people without stores having to change their layouts, according to the Danish start-up, Hive Robots.
For now, they are slower than supermarket workers, though the start-up says advances in AI will help improve their speed and precision.
How do robots learn?
Getting robots to work in real-world settings takes training and data collected on the job.
In a corner of the store, a human operator uses virtual reality glasses and handheld controllers to guide a robot as it picks up pasta bags and places them on shelves.
His demonstrations provide data to teach the machines to perform the tasks independently.
“There are a lot of small things that we as humans don’t think about that basically we need to teach the robot,” said Roger Sala, a robot pilot at Hive Robots.
Training began in June at grocery chain Føtex, owned by Denmark’s largest retailer, Salling Group, which operates more than 2,100 stores across Denmark, Germany, Poland, Latvia, Estonia and Lithuania.
Hive Robots develops the software and trains the machines, which are manufactured by Chinese robotics company Unitree.
The Danish start-up hopes they can independently restock some products at night by early 2027, with stores paying by the hour for the service.
What could it mean for workers?
The deployment of humanoid robots in workplaces adds to the debate over whether AI will ease labour shortages or reduce demand for workers.
AI could change how around 60% of jobs across the EU are done, according to a 2024 report from the International Monetary Fund, helping workers perform some tasks while potentially taking over others.
The technology offers opportunities to improve productivity as well as risks of job displacement, the report said.
Salling Group says the purpose of its trial is to support employees rather than replace them.
The grocery store Føtex estimates that restocking accounts for 40% to 50% of staff time.
Hive Robots says the chain also struggles to recruit young workers for the task.
Føtex operations director Simon Kudsk says it could take up to five years to have robots in every store. Further tasks could include identifying missing or misplaced products, removing empty cardboard boxes and checking best-before dates.
“Our vision or the dream right now is that we eventually could have one or two humanoids in every Føtex store that could support our colleagues to make it more efficient and create more time for value-adding activities focused on customers,” Kudsk said.

If we had a government that came in, if it was a Reform government, and the first thing they did was sack the cabinet secretary, and got rid of the career officials who came in under the Northcote-Trevelyan merit, not partisanship rubric of selection, and had a go at the judges, too – it would be very easy if they had a big enough majority for them to take away the fundamentals … as the first act that they were doing week one.

Government says 900,000 people could get stronger rights under crackdown on bogus self-employment loopholes
Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, has told published a consultation paper on employment status reform. This sets out how the government proposes to implement plans he announced at Labour conference to close the “bogus self-employment loopholes” that deny workers basic rights.
Explaining the plans, the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade says:
Bogus self-employment is a practice whereby some businesses mislabel staff as self-employed to avoid statutory obligations.
However, the day-to-day reality is that many of these people are treated as workers, not self-employed. External estimates suggest that as many as 900,000 people may currently be affected by this and could be missing out on core employment rights.
The proposals to be consulted on could provide greater clarity to businesses and workers, levelling the playing field for those businesses who are already doing the right thing and clamping down on abuses. This could help workers such as parcel couriers, delivery drivers, hairdressers and gig economy workers.
But, in a good article on this topic for LabourList, Tom Berger points out that the plans don’t include a firm commitment to create a single status of worker in employment law – something that in opposition the party did commit to.
Meri Ahlberg, a senior policy adviser at the Joseph Rowntree Foundation, a thinktank that has argued for employment status reform, said:
The measures in the government’s consultation are a step forward for making sure people have the rights and protections everyone deserves. But without putting single worker status and tax reform on the table for the near future, it will still be cheaper to employ people in less secure jobs and millions of workers will be left without sick pay and parental pay. It’s time basic protections were in place for everyone, however they work, and that existing protections are enforced properly.

India remains a ‘natural partner’ for Russia – Jaishankar
India remains a natural partner for Russia as Moscow turns increasingly toward Asia amid its deteriorating relations with European nations, Indian Foreign Minister S. Jaishankar has said. Maintaining strong ties with Moscow serves the interests of both countries and the wider world, he added. 
Russia’s relationship with Europe has become “pretty much a broken, embittered relationship,” pushing Moscow to strengthen its ties with Asia, particularly China, Jaishankar told the Bloomberg New Economy Forum in New Delhi on Tuesday. 
He noted that Russia had historically considered itself a European country and valued its relationships with both Europe and the US, but that sanctions following the escalation of the conflict in Ukraine had pushed it toward Asia. 
The European Union on Monday adopted new sanctions targeting 826 Russian companies and 743 executives, saying the restrictions were intended to increase pressure on Moscow over the Ukraine conflict.

The Indian foreign minister said it is in New Delhi’s interest, and that of the wider world, for Russia to have multiple choices and maintain substantial partnerships with other Asian powers. “We are a natural option in that regard,” Jaishankar said, pointing to nearly eight decades of steady relations between New Delhi and Moscow. 
India has continued to assure Russia that despite changes in the international order and Moscow’s strategic calculations, the longstanding bilateral partnership remains intact, he said. 
The relationship has served both countries and contributed to the balance of power in Asia, Jaishankar added.
India and Russia have maintained close ties for decades, particularly in defense, energy, and space cooperation. The two countries formalized a strategic partnership in 2000 and elevated it to a Special and Privileged Strategic Partnership in 2010.
They are also targeting $100 billion in bilateral trade by 2030, compared with $68.7 billion in the 2024-25 financial year. Russian oil remains a major component of India’s imports, despite pressure from Washington to scale back purchases.
New Delhi has also stepped up its involvement in efforts to end the Ukraine conflict, which it has maintained should be resolved through dialogue and diplomacy.

China's foreign trade maintains sound momentum in first three quarters
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:00:06 CST
17:00:06 KST

The State Council Information Office (SCIO) holds a press conference on China's import and export of the first three quarters of 2026 in Beijing, capital of China, Oct. 14, 2026. (Xinhua/Jin Liangkuai)
BEIJING, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- China's foreign trade maintained sound momentum in the first three quarters of 2026, with both exports and imports growing rapidly and the overall growth rate reaching its highest level for the same period in five years, official data showed Wednesday.
The country's total imports and exports rose 18.8 percent year on year to 39.94 trillion yuan (about 5.94 trillion U.S. dollars) in the January-September period, according to the General Administration of Customs (GAC).
Growth accelerated through the year, with the expansion rate rising from 15.3 percent in the first quarter to 18.3 percent in the second quarter and 22.3 percent in the third quarter.
Foreign trade growth in the first three quarters was the fastest for the same period in the past five years, with both quarterly and monthly growth rates generally accelerating, said Wang Jun, GAC's deputy head.
"Latest international data show that such a growth rate ranks among the top among major economies, and China remains the world's largest trader of goods," the official told a press conference on Wednesday.
Exports increased 16.4 percent year on year to 23.2 trillion yuan, while imports expanded by 22.3 percent to 16.74 trillion yuan, GAC data showed.
In September alone, China's total imports and exports reached 5.16 trillion yuan, up 27.5 percent from a year earlier and crossing the 5-trillion-yuan mark for the first time. This figure also marked the sixth consecutive month of double-digit monthly growth.
Exports rose 29.6 percent year on year to 3.03 trillion yuan, while imports grew 24.6 percent to 2.13 trillion yuan for the month.
The country's trade with more than 180 countries and regions expanded during the first three quarters. Trade with free trade partners reached 19.55 trillion yuan, up 30 percent and contributing over 70 percent of the total trade increment. Meanwhile, trade with other APEC economies rose 23.9 percent to 24.07 trillion yuan.
Trade with ASEAN grew 22.7 percent to 6.84 trillion yuan, that with the European Union rose 8.4 percent to 4.78 trillion yuan, and trade with the United States increased 4.1 percent to 3.18 trillion yuan.
Exports continued to shift toward new and higher-quality growth drivers. The equipment manufacturing sector contributed nearly 90 percent of the export increment, while intermediate goods accounted for more than half of total exports, underpinning global industrial and supply chains, according to the GAC. ■

An Australian court has overturned a government order protecting an Aboriginal heritage site that halted a billion-dollar gold mine project in New South Wales, ruling that the decision was legally invalid.
The Federal Court ruled in favor of mining company Regis Resources, which challenged a 2024 protection order covering 400 hectares of its McPhillamys Gold Project near Blayney, the Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC) reported Wednesday.
The order, issued by then-Environment Minister Tanya Plibersek, prevented construction of a tailings dam intended to store mining waste, rendering the project financially unviable, according to the company.
Justice James Stellios ruled that procedural requirements had not been followed when considering an Aboriginal heritage protection application involving a culturally significant area associated with the Wiradyuri people.
The original application, lodged in 2020 by Wiradyuri elder Aunty Nyree Reynolds, sought protection for an area linked to the Blue Banded Bee Dreaming story.
Stellios stressed that the ruling concerned procedural errors rather than the merits of the Aboriginal heritage claims.
The matter will return to Environment Minister Murray Watt for reconsideration.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the government was examining the judgment, while Watt pledged continued engagement with Indigenous communities and industry.
Regis Resources welcomed the ruling, describing it as a significant step toward reviving one of Australia’s largest undeveloped gold projects.

How Israel’s ‘Yellow Line’ is reshaping southern Lebanon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
07:38:09 UTC
16:38:09 KST

How Israel’s ‘Yellow Line’ is reshaping southern Lebanon
Demolished homes, shifting military lines, stalled withdrawals leave Lebanese uncertain if they can return.
Beirut, Lebanon – Ali is from Khiam, a Lebanese village on the southern border with Israel, but for the last few months he has rented a house in Hasbaiyya, about a half-hour drive away to the northeast. He is one of tens of thousands of Lebanese who have been displaced from their homes in villages throughout the south of the country.
“Southerners are living a tragedy,” Ali, who did not wish to give his full name, told Al Jazeera. “This is all from flawed tragedies and failed politics.”
Despite a framework agreement between Lebanon and Israel signed in June – with the objective of securing Israel’s phased withdrawal from Lebanon – Israel has continued to occupy large parts of its neighbour’s south, where it has systematically demolished homes and infrastructure in dozens of villages.
Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz has previously said that his country’s troops will not be withdrawn from Lebanon, suggesting an extended occupation similar to the last Israeli occupation, which lasted 22 years.
‘Hard boundary’
The Lebanese Shia group Hezbollah fired rockets at Israel on March 2, for the first time in more than a year. The Iranian-backed group said the attack was a response to daily Israeli violations of the November 2024 ceasefire and the assassination two days prior of Iran’s Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, at the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran.
Israel responded by intensifying its war on Lebanon for a second time in under two years. Israeli attacks, as well as its reinvasion of southern Lebanon, displaced more than 1.2 million people. Since then, Beirut has entered into US-brokered direct negotiations with the Israeli government, despite the objections of Hezbollah, which has fought Israel since October 2023. The group traces its origins in the 1980s to resistance against Israeli occupation of Lebanese territory.
Yet the Lebanese government continued with the discussions, which eventually resulted in the framework agreement. One element of the agreement was the establishment of “pilot zones”, from which Israel would withdraw and be replaced by the Lebanese Armed Forces, who would then disarm any Hezbollah forces in the area.
Israel currently occupies a zone stretching up to 10 kilometres (6.2 miles) deep into southern Lebanon. Behind the “Yellow Line” that marks the end of that occupation zone, Israel continues to detonate homes. Israel uses the same “Yellow Line” term to refer to the areas it controls in Gaza.
“Israel’s primary goals were to empty, depopulate, and make those dozens of frontline villages and towns uninhabitable, and we’ve seen that now with the satellite imagery,” Mohamad Bazzi, a New York-based political analyst originally from Bint Jbeil in southern Lebanon, told Al Jazeera. “It was a way of applying that Gaza model to Lebanon.”
Around 50 frontline villages, including places like Khiam and Bint Jbeil, have been destroyed.
“Unlike previous occupations, the Israeli goal this time has been to empty those towns and villages of their residents, push them out, destroy as much of the housing and infrastructure as possible, and to make it extremely difficult if not impossible for people to return to their homes,” he said, adding that most of the destruction of the towns had occurred since April, despite several announcements of ceasefires.
“[The Yellow Line] is treated as a hard boundary, both in terms of troop presence and the controlled demolition of villages, which continues unabated despite the ceasefire,” Ahmad Baydoun, a Lebanese architect and open-source researcher based in the Netherlands, told Al Jazeera. “It is as if the ceasefire applies to the rest of Lebanon but not to this territory.”
On the northern side of the Yellow Line, residents have returned to devastated villages, including a couple of towns included in the “pilot zone” programme.
One of those towns is Froun, which the Israeli military destroyed via air and drone strikes, but which its troops did not enter.
“We were surprised that it was [included as a] pilot zone,” Hasan Bazzi, the president of Froun’s municipal office, told Al Jazeera.
Lines of all colours
The Yellow Line is not the only coloured line used in Lebanon to reference military demarcations. The Blue Line was established in 2000 in the wake of the end of Israel’s years-long occupation of southern Lebanon, with Israeli forces withdrawing behind it.
And there are now discussions in Israel about creating a “Grey Line”. Reports indicate that this line could extend 4 kilometres (2.5 miles) into Lebanese territory. The area behind the Grey Line would remain uninhabited, effectively serving as a buffer zone for Israel, which would not allow Lebanese civilians to rebuild their homes in the area.
“Part of the Israeli strategy here with the Grey Line, Blue Line, Yellow Line is to sow confusion and to hide or obfuscate the reality of what Israel has done on the ground [which is] to depopulate this vast Lebanese territory and to make it uninhabitable,” Bazzi, the analyst, said. “In the end, it doesn’t really matter what the definitions of these lines are because they are often shifting. We’ve seen that play out in Gaza, and the bottom line is Israel is illegally occupying and has illegally destroyed and ethnically cleansed a huge part of southern Lebanon, and the world sat silent while that happened for the most part.”
But even within the area on the Israeli-controlled side of the Yellow Line, some villagers remain, reflecting Israeli attempts to play on Lebanon’s sectarian divides. The majority of the population of southern Lebanon is Shia Muslim, but officials from non-Shia areas have said that they have received warnings not to host displaced people in their towns. Even those allowed to stay do not live in total freedom.
“The villages Israel has allowed to remain inhabited inside the Yellow Line are largely Christian and Sunni,” Baydoun explained. “But being allowed to stay is not the same as being free to live. In Kfarchouba, municipal workers were abducted while pumping the village’s water, and the mayor himself was detained. Even in Deir Mimas, a village outside the Yellow Line, the Lebanese army set up a post so farmers could reach their olive groves, and Israeli tanks came to the entrance of the village to confront it.”
Baydoun described the new reality of southern Lebanon as the “West Bankification of those who remained”, referring to Israel’s occupation of the West Bank.
“Residents are permitted to exist on their land but not to use it freely,” he said. “Access to fields depends on checkpoints, coordination and the mood of a patrol. Municipal officials are detained and questioned at will. It is a model of control that does not need to empty a village to govern it.”
Permanence of displacement
Analysts believe the occupation of southern Lebanon could extend into the foreseeable future. The Lebanese government has promised to erect prefabricated homes in some areas, but it may struggle to provide state services like water, electricity and sewage disposal to areas where infrastructure has been widely damaged or destroyed.
Even if the Israelis were to withdraw, much of the border area lies in complete ruin, collections of dust, rubble and ash lying where homes and agricultural lands once prospered.
“There are some towns where it might be possible to return with significant work, but in the 50 or so frontline towns or villages, I don’t think it will be possible in the short or medium term,” Bazzi said.
The subject is an open wound for many southerners, forced to continue their lives elsewhere while their homes and lands lie in ruins and under occupation. For them, Israel’s military occupation is reshaping southern Lebanon for the next generation.
“Khiam is destroyed, there’s nothing, it’s uninhabitable for the next 10, 15, 20 years,” Ali, the displaced man from Khiam, said. “They returned us to the Stone Age.”

Pope's AI adviser warns Australia's copyright changes risk 'new form of colonialism'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
07:36:56 UTC
16:36:56 KST

Pope's AI adviser warns Australia's copyright changes risk 'new form of colonialism'
In short:
The AI adviser to Pope Leo has praised Australia for taking a considered approach to tech companies.
Father Paolo Benanti warned Australia that changes to copyright laws to allow AI training would be risky.
He says tech companies openly court religious leaders to protect their business interests.
Australia risks reviving a "new form of colonialism" if it allows AI companies to train on copyrighted work without permission and send profits offshore, an influential AI adviser to the Vatican has warned.
Asked about Australia's consideration of copyright changes to attract AI training, Father Paolo Benanti compared the risk with Europe's history of taking resources from other countries and profiting from them elsewhere.
"You go, you take resources, and you monetise it outside the place where the resources [were]," he said.
He said Australian writing could become another resource used by foreign companies, with the money and tax revenue ending up overseas.
"Is it … a new form of colonialism from foreign power that could … exploit from the resources and monetise it outside of the place where they are taken?" he asked.
"So is this fair? Is this something that will produce real richness or pay back to Australia? I don't know."
Those were questions he said he would ask before voting on such a change.
Last month, the ABC reported that the attorney-general's department was quietly consulting on changes that would mean AI companies could train on copyrighted content unless its owner had opted out.
In June Attorney-General Michelle Rowland told 7.30: "This government has repeatedly said that there are no plans to weaken copyright protections when it comes to AI."
Earlier this week, the federal parliament's AI committee took the unusual step of pre-empting its own process to write a letter that urged reforms to pave the way for AI training.
Father Benanti praised Australia's efforts to regulate social media and AI when he met Prime Minister Anthony Albanese last week, and told 7.30 other countries should follow Australia's lead in reining in tech companies with policies like the teen social media ban.
On his visit to Australia as a guest of the Italian embassy, he described the country as being at the "foremost frontier" and defended it against aspersions about the effectiveness of laws like the social media minimum age.
He said the essential democratic principle was that "no-one should be above the law".
That included overseas social media companies, which he said could rely on protections in their home countries to avoid other governments' rules.
He said Australia's first steps were important, and hoped other countries would follow.
Working together would give governments more power to make technology companies comply with the rules in countries where they wanted to do business, he said.
'We need a brain helmet'
Father Benanti studied engineering before becoming a Franciscan friar and a professor specialising in the ethics of technology. He advised Pope Francis on artificial intelligence and now advises his successor, Pope Leo.
In May, Pope Leo presented his first encyclical, Magnifica Humanitas, a major papal letter sharing his teachings about humanity in the age of AI.
The landmark document made global headlines for criticising autonomous weapons as well as algorithms that could deny people access to health care, employment or security.
Father Benanti said the encyclical resonated beyond the Catholic Church's followers because it addressed moral questions they were already asking about how technology could change their lives.
"Human dignity is the core,"
he said.
He said its appeal came from keeping those questions open for public debate and allowing society to shape how AI was governed.
Father Benanti's concerns about AI extend to the emotional attachments people can form with the technology.
He is concerned that companies exploit loneliness and romantic attachment to their products to make money from people's emotions.
"Those are not neutral things, but are things that are designed by someone," he said.
The question, he said, was whether these products could operate without laws to protect the most vulnerable people.
Asked about protecting children, he compared minors' adoption of AI and smartphones to his experience with riding motorised scooters as a child.
When he was old enough he was given a small vehicle rather than a powerful model that could kill him.
He said smartphones put the same device in the hands of children and adults, without being tailored to children's capabilities.
"Probably we need a brain helmet," he said.
Business vs faith
Father Benanti said he believed tech companies had been courting religious leaders to attempt to protect their business interests.
He has been part of meetings with leaders of top tech companies held at company locations, rather than at the Vatican.
Their purpose, he said, "was not because they would like to talk about faith".
"There are politicians, there are religious leaders, there are scientists and things like that," he said.
"They don't want to have leaders against them that can move the people.
"So it's a matter of business-oriented interest."
Father Benanti said these leaders tried to persuade them of their own beliefs; that their work was bringing humanity close to an extraordinary moment in history, and even raising the possibility AI could be conscious.
Asked whether he found the pitch compelling, his answer was blunt.
"Not at all."

- Russia fired 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 drones at Ukrainian energy sites overnight, leaving at least 600,000 people without power, Zelenskyy said.
- Zelenskyy asked Trump for strong sanctions under the Graham law and more Patriot interceptors after the strike hit infrastructure covered by Trump’s ceasefire.
Russia fired 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 attack drones and loitering munitions at Ukraine’s energy and critical infrastructure overnight into Oct. 14, knocking out power to at least 600,000 people days after President Donald Trump announced a halt to strikes on energy facilities, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
Zelenskyy said that the attack targeted Kyiv, the surrounding Kyiv region and Kharkiv, and damaged equipment at 26 facilities in Ukraine’s power system and four in the oil and gas sector. He warned that outages could spread further and said there were dead and injured, without giving numbers. Repair crews, power company staff and the State Emergency Service were working to restore supply on Wednesday morning.
Zelenskyy described the ballistic missile salvo as aimed specifically at the energy infrastructure covered by the ceasefire Trump announced on Truth Social on Oct. 11, and called the scale of the strike deliberate and demonstrative.
“Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States,” said Zelenskyy.
Moscow never confirmed accepting Trump’s energy ceasefire, and its scope remained disputed after the announcement, with a White House official telling Axios that the proposal initially covered oil refineries, while power plants and electricity grids might follow later. Zelenskyy told Fox News on Oct. 12 that Ukraine had held off on striking Russian energy facilities after the announcement, while Russia kept hitting Ukrainian gas and power sites. Ukraine’s charge d’affaires in Washington, Denys Sienik, said Russia had struck electricity generation and transmission facilities more than 200 times in the week before the announcement.
“Russia has squandered the opportunity for de-escalation and has clearly chosen to continue its insane war of annihilation,” said Zelenskyy.
Ballistic missiles are the hardest part of a Russian strike package for Ukraine to stop, because they fly too fast and too high for most of the country’s air defenses, and Ukraine relies mainly on U.S.-made Patriot systems to intercept them. Zelenskyy asked Washington and other partners for additional packages of Patriot interceptors, saying no country should be left alone against Russia.
He also called on Trump to impose strong sanctions on Russia under the sanctions law sponsored by Sen. Lindsey Graham, which Trump signed on Sept. 18 and which gives the president authority to raise tariffs and restrict Russian energy trade, with key measures due to take effect by Oct. 18.
“We ask President Trump to impose STRONG sanctions on Russia, especially since the Lindsey Graham bill, which was recently passed and signed into law, authorizes and regulates such measures,” said Zelenskyy.
The strike followed Trump’s Oct. 9 announcement of a deal to release Russian diesel onto U.S. and world markets, starting with 300,000 tons immediately and 500,000 tons in November, after the Treasury waived diesel sanctions until April 2027. Critics in Congress have said the arrangement gives Moscow additional revenue for the war. The White House had not responded publicly to the overnight strike by Wednesday morning, and Russia’s Defense Ministry had not commented on its targets.

As US pursues mine deals, Xi warns African resources are not tools for ‘rivalry’

"Troubling are reports of the use of Harvard University’s name to lend credibility to a political campaign without appropriate authorisation. The language used to describe India as being under 'siege' and to characterise constitutional authorities as 'thieves' or 'compromised' raises serious concerns about the intent to undermine public trust in democratic institutions," the wider cross-section of the Harvard community, including lawyers, policymakers, civil servants, scientists and academicians, said in a statement.
‘Constitution, not convenience'
The latest statement signed by 44 individuals raised concerns over what it described as a “concerted campaign” against the country's constitutional institutions, including the Election Commission, the Supreme Court, the office of the Chief Justice of India (CJI) and Parliament.
"We are deeply concerned by the negative public discourse and concerted campaign against India’s constitutional institutions, including the Election Commission of India, the Supreme Court, the office of the Hon’ble Chief Justice of India, and Parliament," the statement released on Wednesday said.It also addressed the role of law enforcement agencies in maintaining public order, saying their actions should be subject to fair scrutiny but that allegations must be grounded in evidence and due process.“The actions of law enforcement agencies to uphold public order deserve fair scrutiny, but sweeping accusations and abusive rhetoric cannot substitute for evidence, due process or institutional accountability,” the signatories said.They also stressed the need to respect public officials and the offices they hold, adding that constitutional principles and civil liberties must not be applied selectively.“The Constitution, rule of law, and civil liberties must be respected at all times, not just when it suits our interests,” the statement said.Summing up their appeal, the signatories said: “Our commitment must remain to the Constitution, not convenience; to justice, not selective outrage; and to democratic institutions, not the politics of accusation.”
October 12 statement condemns police action
In a statement dated October 12, around 100 Harvard alumni, students, faculty and staff condemned what they described as the “unprecedented siege of Delhi by police and paramilitary forces” and alleged arbitrary, illegal and unconstitutional action against peaceful protesters across the country on October 10."We, as alumni, students, faculty, and staff of Harvard University, are deeply concerned by the unprecedented siege of Delhi by police and paramilitary forces and arbitrary, illegal, and unconstitutional police actions against peaceful protestors across the country on 10th October 2026. We strongly condemn police brutality, unlawful detention, and violations of constitutional rights of all peaceful protestors," the letter shared by Live Law read.
The signatories condemned alleged police brutality, unlawful detention and violations of protesters' constitutional rights, while expressing solidarity with fellow Harvard affiliates Shadan Farasat, a senior advocate in the Supreme Court and Harvard Law School alumnus from 2009, and Mehr Pasricha, a Harvard Kennedy School graduate from 2025.The signatories called on the government and law enforcement authorities to end alleged violations of constitutional rights, respect the right to peaceful protest and access to legal assistance, and ensure that those responsible for abuses are held accountable under the rule of law.

AI generated
VATICAN CITY – Pope Leo spent a peaceful night in hospital after undergoing surgery for lung cancer, the Vatican said on Oct 14, adding that further information about his condition would be released later in the day.
The Pope was diagnosed on Oct 13 with lung adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer, after doctors removed the lower lobe of his right lung during an operation.
The 71-year-old pontiff had been admitted to Rome’s Gemelli hospital after doctors discovered a growth during a recent routine health check.
The operation lasted about 90 minutes and was completed without complications, the Pope’s lead surgeon, Stefano Margaritora, and his personal physician, Luigi Carbone, said late on Oct 13.
The doctors said in a joint statement that the entire lower lobe of the right lung was removed in an effort to eliminate all cancerous tissue.
Human lungs have five lobes – three in the right lung and two in the left.
The Vatican has not disclosed the size of the tumour or whether the disease had spread to nearby lymph nodes, key factors in determining prognosis.
The Vatican said earlier this week that the pope was expected to remain in hospital for about a week and that all his public engagements had been cancelled until Oct 20.
Elected by the world’s cardinals in May 2025, Leo is relatively young for a Church leader.
He enjoys sports, including tennis, and is not known to be a smoker or to have had recent health issues.
Messages of sympathy
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he and his wife Jeanette were praying for the Pope, an American who was born in Chicago. “May the Lord give him strength and the Holy Spirit guide the medical professionals taking care of the Holy Father,” he said on X.
German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, whose role is largely ceremonial, wished Leo a speedy and full recovery, German Catholic news agency KNA reported. “The Pope’s voice on the current issues and challenges of our time is of particular importance and of value to many people worldwide, including in Germany, beyond denominational boundaries,” he was quoted as saying.
Leo normally follows a very busy schedule. He is due to make an 11-day tour of Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from Nov 6 to Nov 17, but it was not clear if this trip would still go ahead.
The Pope is the ultimate earthly authority for the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics and does not have a deputy who steps in when he is sick.
When a pope is incapacitated, the business of the Vatican’s vast bureaucracy carries on as usual, holding off on any decisions that require papal approval.
A mass in St Peter’s Square on Oct 14 was led by Filipino Cardinal Luis Tagle in place of Leo.

IMF warns rising borrowing costs intensify global debt pressures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
06:56:46 UTC
15:56:46 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
Rising government borrowing costs are intensifying fiscal pressures worldwide, the International Monetary Fund warned on Wednesday, urging credible measures to contain deficits as global public debt heads above 100% of economic output by 2030.
In a blog post, the IMF said average 10-year government bond yields across the Group of Seven economies rose by more than 1 percentage point between February and September, reaching their highest level in nearly two decades.
The fund cited the oil price shock, persistent inflation, stronger investment demand and expectations of growth linked to artificial intelligence among the drivers.
High debt, spending pressures and expectations of large government bond issuance are also pushing yields higher, with borrowing costs in major economies potentially worsening debt dynamics elsewhere.
The effective average interest cost of government financing is projected to rise from 2.3% in 2021 to 3.7% by 2031.
US interest payments are forecast to increase from about 2.8% of GDP before the pandemic to 5.7% in 2031, roughly matching projected Social Security spending.
In low-income countries, interest payments already consume more than 15% of tax revenues.
Rising debt-servicing costs leave less room for investment and social spending while limiting governments' ability to respond to downturns.
The global primary deficit, which excludes interest payments, is expected to reach about 3.3% of GDP in 2026. Stabilizing the debt ratio would require reducing it to around 2.6%.
Shorter debt maturities are accelerating the transmission of higher policy rates to government financing costs.
The IMF urged advanced economies to adopt credible fiscal plans and emerging markets to strengthen debt management, warning that delayed action would require larger adjustments.

Kazakhstan forecasts inflation at 7.5-9.5% in 2027

Kazakhstan forecasts inflation at 7.5-9.5% in 2027
Kazakh Deputy Prime Minister - National Economy Minister Serik Zhumangarin presented the country’s socio-economic development forecast for 2027-2029 during a plenary session of the Qurultay, Qazinform News Agency reports.
According to Zhumangarin, the forecast was prepared taking into account current economic conditions, projections by international financial institutions for global economic growth, and external market trends.
He said that the IMF projects the global economy to grow by 3% this year and 3.4% in 2027.
Despite the improved global outlook, economic growth is expected to slow in Kazakhstan’s key trading partner countries.
He added international organizations and major investment banks have also revised down their oil price forecasts for 2027, with the consensus forecast lowered to 70.3 US dollars per barrel. The analysis considered three development scenarios based on external conditions.
The optimistic scenario expects oil prices to reach 85 US dollars per barrel, with average annual economic growth projected at 5.9%.
The pessimistic scenario assumes oil prices of 50 US dollars per barrel, with GDP growth averaging 3.2%.
The baseline scenario assumes an oil price of 70 US dollars per barrel. Under this scenario, Kazakhstan’s average annual real GDP growth is projected to exceed 5% between 2027 and 2029. Nominal GDP is forecast to increase from 199.3 trillion tenge in 2027 to 245 trillion tenge in 2029.
The Government forecasts inflation at 7.5-9.5% in 2027 and 6-8% in 2028-2029.
Primarily, non-oil sectors are expected to fuel economic growth. Manufacturing is projected to outpace mining, with metallurgy, machinery manufacturing, building materials, chemicals, and food production making the largest contributions.
Agriculture is also expected to remain a key growth driver, with annual growth averaging at least 5%.
In construction, growth is forecast to increase from 16% in 2027 to 17.3% in 2029, supported by infrastructure projects in transport, logistics, energy, water systems, housing, utilities, and social services.
The services sector is expected to maintain strong momentum, with trade growing by an average of 5.7% annually, transportation and warehousing by 10.4%, and information and communications by 9.2%.
Goods exports are projected to rise from 82.8 billion US dollars in 2027 to 88.5 billion US dpollars in 2029, while imports are expected to increase from 80.5 billion US dollars to 88.4 billion US dollars over the same period.
Earlier, he said Kazakhstan’s economy grew by 4.2% in the first nine months of 2026, driven largely by the non-resource sector.

Despite Trump’s reference to “our new” Greenland, the island remains a self-governing territory within the Kingdom of Denmark. The agreement recognises Danish sovereignty and Greenlanders’ right to self-determination.
Greenland stopped issuing new oil and gas exploration licences in 2021 over environmental and climate concerns, although licences granted before the decision remain valid.

Read moreUS, Denmark and Greenland sign security deal to bolster Arctic security
Greenland, which lies on the shortest route for missiles between Russia and the United States, represents a highly strategic location for Trump's desired "Golden Dome" defense shield.
It also has untapped rare earth deposits and could be a critical player as melting polar ice opens up new shipping routes.

Trump on Wednesday hailed Greenland as "second to none" for US and European security, saying any future attack on America would have to pass through the Arctic island.

Yemen's Houthis use Chinese parts to build Iranian ballistic missile, boost attack range - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
06:40:39 UTC
15:40:39 KST

Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis are developing their own version of Iran's Kheibar Shekan precision-guided missile using parts imported from Chinese companies, according to a Tuesday Wall Street Journal report citing new data from UK-based independent monitor Conflict Armament Research.
The missile would have a maximum range of approximately 1,200 miles, according to the WSJ. This would put all of Saudi Arabia and Israel in range.
The Houthis, a US-designated terrorist organization under a United Nations arms embargo that controls large parts of Yemen, have been fighting the Saudi-backed Yemeni government in a civil war since 2014.
The Yemen conflict has resumed as a spillover from the wider US-Iran war that began with the US-Israeli attack on the Islamic Republic on February 28. Iran, Saudi Arabia's longtime regional rival, has offered to mediate between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, its foreign minister Abbas Araghchi said on Sunday in statements reiterated by the ministry on Monday.
The Conflict Armament Research report was based on information from Yemeni authorities in July after officials interdicted two shipments in 2025, which included the missile equipment hidden among a range of other goods, according to the WSJ.
“When you have imports like that, there is a possibility that they are already manufacturing or that they are trying and it doesn’t really work out,” Fabian Hinz, a senior analyst at Conflict Armament, told the Wall Street Journal, adding that because the Houthis weapons facilities are well camouflaged, it is unclear how far along missile production has proceeded.
China says it is respecting arms sales ban
China claims to be adhering to the UN arms embargo on the Houthis, per the WSJ. However, the report noted that while some of the Houthi-imported materials could have civilian uses, some were parts specifically designed for missile production.
The imported parts include custom-made metal missile components, including parts of the motor and of the airframe, the missile’s basic structure, the Wall Street Journal noted, adding that Yemeni authorities also found fins which stabilize the missile in flight and parts of a solid-propellant rocket motor of a Kheibar Shekan-series missile.
Yemeni authorities also seized tools, testing equipment, and raw materials, including the ablative material which protects sections of the missile from the intense heat produced by a ballistic missile, the WSJ added.
Why are Iranian Kheibar Shekan missiles particularly advantageous?
Iran has been using Kheibar Shekan missiles, cheap, mobile, and accurate missiles, which have a range of at least 1,400 kilometers in their strikes against US assets across the Middle East, the Wall Street Journal cited US officials as saying in July.
The solid-fuel, medium-range Kheibar Shekan missiles differ from older Iranian missiles that require prelaunch fueling, a lengthy process which the Kheibar Shekan can bypass by being kept fueled and are capable of being loaded quickly into trucks or other vehicles for launching, making it easier to evade US and Israeli warplanes seeking to knock out Iranian missile launch sites, military experts told WSJ at the time.
Danya Saperstein and Reuters contributed to this report.

IDF establishing new corps for countering low-altitude drones amid growing UAV threat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
06:40:26 UTC
15:40:26 KST

IDF Ground Forces Commander Maj.-Gen. Nadav Lotan is working to establish a new corps dedicated to countering low-altitude drone threats, as part of an effort to strengthen Israel's defenses against the growing threat posed by unmanned aerial vehicles, Walla learned on Tuesday.
For more than a decade, the IDF has been trying to address the threat posed by drones operating in the airspace close to the ground, using a variety of methods. However, these efforts have accelerated since the October 7 massacre, alongside a worldwide push to develop solutions.
The threat became evident during Hamas's attacks along the Gaza border at the beginning of the war and during the initial stages of the IDF's ground maneuver deep into the Gaza Strip. Hezbollah subsequently employed drones against IDF troops in southern Lebanon and civilians in Israel's home front.
The drone threat has also manifested itself in the smuggling of weapons and drugs across the Egyptian and Jordanian borders. Smugglers have used particularly heavy drones capable of carrying payloads weighing dozens of kilograms. There are also growing concerns that drones could become a significant threat in the IDF's Judea and Samaria Division and along the Syrian border.
The Defense Ministry and the IDF have accelerated projects to improve drone protection within the defense establishment. Some of these projects involve Israeli companies, while others entail purchasing technology from abroad.
Accordingly, the IDF has begun deploying various defense systems in the field to improve and refine protection against different types of drones, including fiber-optic drones. These pose a considerable challenge for conventional militaries because they are difficult to detect. As a result, armies generally counter them using nets, interceptor drones, and ground-based gunfire.
Five border defense battalions to form the foundation of new corps
The IDF recently decided to establish the new low-altitude airspace defense corps using the existing border infantry battalions as its foundation.
The corps will initially be based on five battalions that routinely protect the borders with Jordan and Egypt, as well as the security barrier area in the West Bank.
Under the plan, these battalions will assume an additional mission alongside their existing responsibility for defending Israel's land borders: protecting against mobile threats operating in the airspace close to the ground.
According to assessments, the corps' sixth battalion will be the tactical air defense battalion established during the war in response to threats from Gaza and Lebanon that emerged on an unprecedented scale.
IDF transferring Ground Forces resources to support new anti-drone corps
To support the new corps' establishment, the IDF will transfer significant resources from the Ground Forces to supplement the capabilities already available within the Border Defense Corps.
These resources will include additional training personnel to develop a drone school focused on defensive missions.
The IDF's Ground Forces already operate significant defensive drone capabilities, including intelligence-gathering operations conducted using drones by Unit 9900 of the Military Intelligence Directorate.
It can therefore be assessed that Military Intelligence will play a role in developing the emerging combat doctrine, operational methods, and the type and scale of procurement involving drones and associated technologies, as well as training.

Attacks on Saudi could have negative spillover 'everywhere', IMF chief says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
06:38:12 UTC
15:38:12 KST

International Monetary Fund head Kristalina Georgieva said on Wednesday that recent attacks on Saudi Arabia could impact people "everywhere", as conflict in the energy-rich region adds to wide-ranging economic concerns.
A violent battle between a Saudi-led coalition and Houthi militia has erupted in recent days, with missile strikes on airports and energy facilities across the kingdom.
The latest round of fighting was triggered by Houthi militia strikes on Riyadh's international airport at the weekend that left 13 people dead and operations suspended in the worst attack since 2015.
The escalation compounds fears about the impact of the Middle East crisis on global growth, with crude prices sent soaring since Iran effectively shut the crucial Strait of Hormuz after it was attacked by the US and Israel in February.
"The Saudi economy is important for the region and the world," IMF managing director Georgieva said at a news conference during the Annual Meetings of the Fund and World Bank in Bangkok.
"In that sense, these developments have potentially negative spillovers for everybody, everywhere," she said.
The warning comes as officials and experts gather in the Thai capital to discuss challenges facing the global economy, including higher energy costs and concerns about the sustainability of an artificial intelligence boom.
Other hurdles include ballooning debt in advanced economies, with bond yields at multi-decade highs as pressure grows on central banks to hike interest rates to cool inflation.
"What is our loudest call to policymakers right now? Make urgent repairs to the fiscal house before the cracks widen," Georgieva said.
"Now is the time to enhance revenues, to rationalise spending and improve public financial management."
'Reaching limits'
In its closely watched World Economic Outlook released on Tuesday, the IMF raised its 2026 global growth forecast by 0.1 percentage points to 3.1 percent.
However, it warned that while new economic activity has been sparked by rising investment in AI, poorer countries are not benefiting as they deal with soaring energy costs.
The global economy "remains resilient in the face of very frequent repetitive shocks and in the face of uncertainty", Georgieva said. "But this resilience is reaching its limits."
The IMF chief called for greater support for low-income countries to "strengthen their fundamentals so they can withstand shocks".
She noted that a global rise in interest rates had also caused debt servicing costs to increase from around six percent of government revenues a decade ago to 14 percent today.
And in its Global Policy Agenda released on Wednesday, the Fund warned that debt servicing challenges had become particularly acute for "low-income and vulnerable economies".
Georgieva said the IMF had been "ringing the alarm bell on excessive global economic imbalances growing".
"To put it very simply, China needs to spend more, the US has to save more and Europe has to invest more," she added.
Advanced economies have seen their debt-to-GDP ratios skyrocket since the COVID-19 pandemic and wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, with governments forced to increase spending to cushion the impact of those shocks.
Addressing the issue of how to tackle spiking bond yields, Georgieva admitted "there is no magic".
"You have to go in a direction of tightening debt (and) bringing it down," she said.
"(The) message that we are sending to our members: fundamentals matter. Get your house in order; otherwise, your people, your businesses will pay a price."

Portuguese hospitality has once again won over international travellers. Porto was voted Europe's friendliest city, with Lisbon second in Condé Nast Traveller readers' ranking.
Portugal is often considered one of the most welcoming and hospitable countries in the world, with international studies and surveys repeatedly placing the Portuguese people at the top of tourists’ favourites. It is therefore no surprise that Porto has been awarded the title of "Europe's friendliest city".
The distinction comes from readers of Condé Nast Traveller in the Readers’ Choice Awards 2026, which also place the city of Lisbon in second position in this category.
The vote aims to identify cities where "hospitality is at its warmest" and "you find locals eager to help, whether you’re trying to make sense of a neighbourhood restaurant’s menu or looking confused on the metro".
The recognition now given to the Invicta, as Porto is known, "reflects the significant rise in Porto’s popularity as the ideal city-break refuge, both for lovers of good food and for culture enthusiasts", the magazine explains, also highlighting the city’s authenticity and relaxed atmosphere.
"Unwind in a stunning square lined with azulejo tiles or share petiscos – small portions of local delicacies – with residents in a neighbourhood restaurant," Condé Nast encourages, "and you will quickly realise how generous hospitality has made Porto a destination many of us end up returning to time and time again".
Lisbon appears in the next spot. In the European ranking, the top five is completed by mentions of Amsterdam in the Netherlands, Stockholm in Sweden and Valletta in Malta.

North America’s largest alpine lake offers skiing in the winter and kayaking or paddleboarding come summer, making it a perfect year-round destination.
The 10 destinations chosen by the group in its Unpack ’27 trends report span North America, South America, Asia and Australasia – with only two in Europe.
Hyogo in Japan claimed second place, with searches up 95%. The prefecture, which is “one of Japan’s most unsung destinations with coastline, mountains and castles in one stretch”, was also identified as deserving of Expedia’s Smart Travel Health Check.
Introduced last year, the check identifies places managing tourism responsibly while offering rich experiences.
Third place went to Punta del Este, Uruguay’s glamorous coastal city which saw a 65% surge in searches, while fourth place went to Sedona in Arizona, which was praised for its yoga retreats, hiking opportunities and world-class spas.
Rounding out the top five was Busan, the port city on South Korea’s southeast coast, best known for its beaches and film festival (and, of course, the zombie movie Train to Busan).
Trending destinations in Europe
Perugia in Italy came out seventh overall, with searches up 35% compared to last year.
The capital of Umbria, visitors flock here year-round for its 14th-century hilltop city centre filled with historic sights, but the jazz and chocolate festivals are also a big draw.
The only other European destination to make the cut was Chichester in the UK, with searches up 30%.
Located on the West Sussex coast, Chichester is known for its Roman ruins, with a city walls trail looping the historic city.
From here, you can take a stroll through South Downs National Park, feel the sand between your toes at West Wittering Beach or take a trip to Arundel Castle.

Sudan cannot afford to dismiss a chance for dialogue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
05:51:09 UTC
14:51:09 KST

Sudan cannot afford to dismiss a chance for dialogue
A new initiative faces serious questions about military influence, but its critics should not write it off prematurely.
More than three years into the war between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), Sudan is desperately in need of a political settlement. The fighting has caused immense suffering, and a military solution alone cannot rebuild the state or reunify its fractured society. Under such circumstances, any effort aimed at encouraging Sudanese-Sudanese dialogue deserves serious consideration rather than outright rejection.
In August, a self-appointed committee of 19 Sudanese public figures, chaired by Ahfad University President Qasim Badri, launched an initiative to prepare the ground for national dialogue inside Sudan. Its members had earlier met SAF chief General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and called for legal restrictions on opposition politicians to be lifted. The authorities subsequently issued a decree to drop certain politically motivated charges against Sudanese abroad returning for dialogue and grant participants temporary legal protections. These are limited but important confidence-building measures.
The initiative has nevertheless faced strong opposition. The civilian coalition Sumoud, led by former Prime Minister Abdalla Hamdok, and Ta’sis, an alliance that includes the RSF, have opposed the proposed internal dialogue. They question its independence and warn that holding talks in army-controlled areas could legitimise al-Burhan’s authority and entrench the country’s divisions. These concerns are legitimate and deserve serious attention. But the committee says it is not seeking to negotiate Sudan’s future or determine the agenda of a national dialogue. Its role is to help create the conditions for Sudanese political actors to engage one another directly. The question is whether it can fulfil that role without allowing one side of the conflict to dominate the process. Dismissing the initiative before it has had an opportunity to demonstrate its value would be premature.
The country’s political actors and civil society organisations remain deeply divided, previous mediation efforts have faltered, and the war continues to make comprehensive political engagement increasingly difficult. The committee’s initiative is an attempt to break the deadlock. Efforts to prepare for political dialogue should not be postponed until the fighting stops. Securing a ceasefire and ensuring humanitarian access are urgent priorities, but preparations for political dialogue can proceed alongside efforts to achieve them.
The committee’s members were not elected, and they do not represent every political constituency. Yet the committee’s legitimacy cannot be judged solely by how it was created. It must also be judged by whether it can help bring a broader range of political actors into a national dialogue.
Good intentions alone cannot resolve concerns about credibility. Political dialogue can succeed only if participants believe the process is fair and independent. The legitimacy required to facilitate a political opening is not necessarily the same as that required to negotiate a national settlement. But even a preparatory initiative must earn the trust of those it seeks to bring together.
The committee’s meeting with al-Burhan was a practical necessity. As army chief and head of the Sovereignty Council, he was in a position to respond to the committee’s demands for legal protections. Engaging with al-Burhan does not in itself amount to an endorsement of his authority. But if the initiative becomes too closely associated with the army, other political actors may view it as an extension of al-Burhan’s political agenda rather than an independent facilitator. The committee must therefore demonstrate that its engagement extends beyond the military authorities and that it is prepared to work with political forces that oppose them.
The initiative was launched in Khartoum, which is under army control. This raises a genuine concern about whether a process beginning in territory controlled by one side of the war can attract the confidence of political forces across the country. A national dialogue cannot be confined to one geographical or political constituency. Entire regions have experienced different realities of war, governance, displacement and insecurity. The committee must find ways to reach those living outside army-controlled areas, including Sudanese displaced by the fighting, and ensure they can participate freely and without intimidation.
Sumoud and Ta’sis’s decision to reject the initiative does not automatically invalidate the process. Their concerns deserve consideration, but outright rejection at this early stage risks closing off an opportunity for political engagement. At the same time, their absence matters. Sudan’s crisis is too deep and complex to be addressed by any single political current. The committee cannot expect every stakeholder to endorse its initiative immediately, but it must create conditions that persuade reluctant actors to participate. If it fails to do so, the initiative itself will have failed.
The African Union Commission and the Arab League have also welcomed the initiative, providing an important measure of regional support. Their endorsement lends weight to the effort to revive Sudanese-led political dialogue, although external backing cannot substitute for the confidence of Sudan’s own political forces.
The committee’s initiative should therefore be judged without excessive optimism or automatic suspicion. The legal measures announced following its engagement with al-Burhan are an encouraging first step, but the real test lies ahead. Does it help remove legal and political obstacles facing opposition actors in practice, not just on paper? Can it win the confidence of those who have rejected it? Can it ensure that Sudanese across the country’s political and geographical divides have an opportunity to participate freely?
What is clear, however, is that Sudan’s crisis will ultimately require Sudanese actors with profoundly different visions of the country’s future to sit together and engage one another politically. No committee can do that on their behalf. No external actor can do it for them. At best, a preparatory initiative can help create the conditions under which such engagement becomes possible. The concerns raised by its critics should not be dismissed, but neither should they be grounds for rejecting the initiative before it has had an opportunity to address them. Those who have rejected it should remain open to reconsidering their position if the committee demonstrates that it can build an independent and inclusive process. If it succeeds, it will have rendered an important national service.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

Israel returns 22 artifacts to Greece in first antiquities repatriation between Jerusalem, Athens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
05:49:11 UTC
14:49:11 KST

Israel on Tuesday returned a collection of 22 artifacts illegally removed from Greece, in the first repatriation of its kind between the two countries, as Athens renews its push to recover illegally taken and stolen antiquities from around the world.
Among the artifacts returned are fifteen ancient Attic vessels, six vases from Corinthian workshops, and one bronze statue of a female figure, all dating to between the 8th and 4th centuries BCE.
Of the Attic vessels, 11 are black-and-white, three are red-and-white, and one is ambergris, dating to the ancient and classical periods. The six Corinthian vases date to the ancient period, while the authenticity of the bronze female statuette requires further investigation.
The antiquities were seized in 2020 during a joint investigation into illegal antiquities trafficking conducted by the IAA’s Theft Prevention Unit, Israel Police, and the Israel Tax Authority. As part of the operation, the forces raided a gallery, warehouses, and apartments in the Gush Dan area, where thousands of illegally acquired archaeological items from Israel and around the world were found.
They were officially returned in a Tuesday handover ceremony at the National Archaeological Museum in Athens, attended by Greek Culture Minister Lina Mendoni, Israeli Ambassador to Greece Pninat Yanay, and Israel Antiquities Authority’s (IAA) Theft Prevention Unit Director Amir Ganor.
“This celebration is not only about returning antiquities to their rightful home. It is also a celebration of something much greater and deeper: the special, strong, and profound friendship between the State of Israel and Greece,” she wrote.
Combating illegal antiquities trade
“Two modern states, two ancient nations, and two great civilizations that deeply understand the meaning of history, the importance of heritage, and the responsibility to preserve it for future generations. These antiquities belong to Greece’s past. Today, through their return, they also become part of the shared future of Israel and Greece.”
“Let us try to imagine a child looking at one of these ancient vessels today and feeling a spark of wonder,” Yanay added. “They see what another child might have seen and felt 2,000 years ago, and thus become another link in the chain of generations that had been broken.”
“For me, there is also something deeply moving in the thought that I have the privilege, as Ambassador of Israel, of placing this ancient object into your capable hands, and that my country had the honor of contributing to this significant moment and mission.”
“The illegal trade in antiquities knows no borders, neither the boundaries of the law nor the borders between countries,” Ganor said. “Antiquities that are looted in one country find their way to another, causing irreversible damage to the cultural heritage of the country of origin.”
“The illegal trade in antiquities serves as a cover for the financing of terrorism and organized crime, and it serves as a means of money laundering. Cutting off smuggling chains and preventing continued illegal profiting on the back of antiquities helps to thwart and prevent various types of criminal activity, and certainly helps to protect cultural heritage assets.”
Becoming links in the chains between generations
Heritage Minister Amichai Eliyahu added that “The State of Israel is well aware of the deep connection between a people and its heritage, and the importance of preserving the historical evidence that tells its story.”
“The return of these antiquities to Greece expresses our commitment to protect cultural heritage assets, and to act resolutely against the illegal trade in antiquities, wherever it takes place.”
He continued, congratulating the IAA and both Greek and Israeli law enforcement agencies for their actions that led to the return of the artifacts.
“The strengthening cooperation between the countries expresses a shared responsibility to preserve the treasures of the past, for the sake of future generations,” he said.
Israel, Greece expected to sign a heritage MoU
As a result of cooperation between the IAA’s Theft Prevention Unit and the Greek Antiquities Police in this case, a joint international enforcement workshop was held for representatives of the two units last month.
During the workshop, the two units discussed the possibility of expanding information sharing, identifying items suspected of being looted, and tracing antiquities trade routes.
In her remarks at the handover ceremony, Mendoni noted that during her visit to Jerusalem in March 2025, she discussed the expansion of cultural cooperation between Israel and Greece with Culture and Sports Minister Miki Zohar.
According to Mendoni, the return of these antiquities is a practical expression of the commitment that the two ministers discussed at their meeting. A memorandum of understanding is expected to be signed between the countries, which will anchor their cooperation in the field of protecting cultural heritage assets.

Defense officials warn of possibility Houthis may conduct land or sea attack against Israel
Unknown
