2026-10-14
05:48:52 UTC
14:48:52 KST

The threat posed by the Houthis in Yemen has intensified amid fighting with Saudi Arabia, Israeli defense officials assess, prompting heightened preparations for a possible surprise attack against Israel by land or sea.
Israel is on heightened alert over the possibility of such an attack, given the Houthis' efforts to improve their ability to carry out attacks from both directions.
As part of these preparations, the IDF is expected to establish a fire coordination center within the Edom Division.
Over the past two years, the Houthis have released numerous videos documenting training exercises simulating ground raids against Israel, including scenarios involving mock military outposts and fortified guard towers.
According to defense officials, the Houthis have increasingly warned in recent weeks and months that they could carry out ground attacks, including against Israel.
Defense officials say the Houthis are unpredictable and have posed significant challenges to Saudi Arabia through their methods of warfare, as well as their extremist and uncompromising culture and ideology.
As a result, Israel is taking no chances and is preparing for unexpected developments through several parallel measures.
These include maintaining reserve and rapid-response troops in the Eilat area, conducting training exercises, deploying weapons systems, and improving coordination and connectivity among ground, naval, and air units.
The preparations also involve shortening response times and conducting joint exercises with the Israel Police and Border Police operating in the area.
In addition, Israeli defense officials are not ruling out the possibility of a chain reaction in which the Houthis significantly increase their attacks on the Saudi home front, causing additional casualties and substantial damage.
Such a development could force Saudi Arabia to intensify its military response, potentially drawing the US military into a more forceful confrontation.
Houthis could target US interests in Israel
Under such circumstances, the Houthis could target American interests on Israeli territory, potentially requiring the IDF to respond.
"The Houthis have long since ceased to be regarded as proxies of the Iranians, and they are demonstrating operational independence with an inexplicable determination against the Saudis," one defense official said.
The threat from Yemen features prominently in Israeli security assessments, alongside extensive intelligence-gathering efforts aimed at monitoring Houthi intentions and capabilities.
At the same time, operational and intelligence coordination between the IDF and the US military's Central Command (CENTCOM) is aimed at refining early-warning mechanisms against attempts to catch Israel by surprise and reducing the likelihood of unexpected attacks as much as possible.

FIFA plans to distribute more than $3.5 billion (€3 billion) from reserves boosted by the success of the 48-team World Cup, according to two officials who spoke anonymously as the proposal has yet to be announced.
FIFA expects around $15 billion (€12.9 billion) in revenue for the 2022–2026 cycle, including the men's World Cup hosted by the US, Canada and Mexico, significantly exceeding projections, the officials told AP.
Infantino under scrutiny

UEFA's 55 member associations represent more than a quarter of FIFA's 211 voting members ahead of the presidential election on 18 March in Rabat, Morocco.

Asia must guard against repeat of 1997 financial crisis: Philippine central bank chief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
05:46:12 UTC
14:46:12 KST

Advertisement
Asia must guard against repeat of 1997 financial crisis: Philippine central bank chief
The pre-crash boom of the 1990s ‘wasn’t really a miracle’, Eli Remolona says, urging Asean to prepare for fresh shocks
2-MIN READ2-MIN
 Listen
Asian countries must remind themselves about what happened during the region’s financial crisis in the late 1990s and guard against a recurrence of such shocks, the head of the Philippine central bank said on Wednesday.
Before the Asian financial crisis started in 1997, regional economies saw huge capital inflows that prompted the World Bank to describe it as the “East Asian miracle”, Eli Remolona, governor of the central bank, said in an International Monetary Fund panel on the outlook for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations.
“Investment poured into Asia and then you had the crisis because it wasn’t really a miracle. I think we have to remind ourselves about that. We have to guard against that kind of crisis,” he said. “We have not really been making a lot of effort looking at that kind of crisis.”
The remarks came at the annual meetings of the IMF and World Bank being held in Bangkok, Thailand, which was an epicentre of the Asian financial crisis.
Krishna Srinivasan, director of the IMF’s Asia and Pacific Department, pushed back against the view, arguing in the panel discussion that the IMF had made progress assessing financial vulnerabilities and potential spillovers among each economy.

Gigantic prehistoric snake discovered in India may have been one of the largest ever
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14

Gigantic prehistoric snake discovered in India may have been one of the largest ever
- Date:
- October 14, 2026
- Source:
- Scientific Reports
- Summary:
- A massive prehistoric snake discovered in India may have rivaled the largest snake ever known. Called Vasuki indicus, the 47-million-year-old giant could have reached up to 50 feet long, making it comparable to the legendary Titanoboa. Scientists believe its enormous body made it a slow-moving ambush predator, similar to a modern anaconda.
- Share:
A colossal prehistoric snake that lived in India about 47 million years ago may have been one of the largest snakes ever to exist. Known as Vasuki indicus, the ancient reptile could have reached an extraordinary 15.2 meters (50 feet) in length, putting it in the same league as Titanoboa, the enormous extinct snake long regarded as the largest ever discovered.
The remarkable discovery, described in 2024 in the journal Scientific Reports, came from fossils unearthed in Gujarat, western India. Researchers estimate that Vasuki measured between 10.9 and 15.2 meters (36 and 50 feet) long, although its exact size remains uncertain. Its enormous body and unusual evolutionary history offer a glimpse into a time when giant snakes inhabited the warm, tropical landscapes of ancient India.
Giant Snake Fossils Unearthed in India
Paleontologists Debajit Datta and Sunil Bajpai of the Indian Institute of Technology Roorkee identified the species from fossils recovered at the Panandhro Lignite Mine in Kutch, Gujarat. The remains date to the Middle Eocene, a period roughly 47 million years ago when Earth's climate was considerably warmer than it is today.
The researchers examined 27 fossilized vertebrae, the individual bones that make up a snake's backbone. Many were remarkably well preserved, and some remained connected in their original arrangement. The bones appear to have belonged to a fully grown animal.
The species was named Vasuki indicus in honor of Vasuki, the mythical serpent associated with the Hindu deity Shiva, who is traditionally depicted with the snake wrapped around his neck. The second part of the name refers to India, where the fossils were discovered.
How Big Was This Prehistoric Snake?
Although the scientists did not recover a complete skeleton, the preserved backbone provides important clues about the snake's enormous proportions.
Individual vertebrae measured between 37.5 and 62.7 millimeters (1.48 and 2.47 inches) long and between 62.4 and 111.4 millimeters (2.46 and 4.39 inches) wide. Their unusually broad shape suggests that Vasuki possessed a thick, cylindrical body capable of supporting tremendous weight.
To estimate its total length, the researchers compared the fossilized bones with vertebrae from living snakes whose body lengths are known. Two different methods produced estimates ranging from 10.9 to 12.2 meters (36 to 40 feet) and 14.5 to 15.2 meters (48 to 50 feet).
Those measurements place Vasuki among the largest snakes ever identified. Its estimated length rivals that of Titanoboa, the giant snake that inhabited what is now Colombia approximately 60 million years ago and is thought to have reached around 13 meters (43 feet).
However, the researchers caution that their calculations involve considerable uncertainty. Different methods can produce substantially different estimates, particularly when scientists must reconstruct an extinct animal using an incomplete backbone. It remains unclear whether Vasuki actually exceeded Titanoboa in length.
A Massive Predator That Likely Hunted by Ambush
Despite its intimidating size, Vasuki probably was not a particularly fast or agile hunter.
The researchers suggest that its enormous body and distinctive vertebral structure would have favored relatively slow movement. Rather than actively chasing prey, the snake may have relied on ambush tactics, remaining concealed until another animal came within striking distance.
Its hunting behavior could have resembled that of modern anacondas and large pythons, which can overpower prey through constriction. These snakes use their muscular bodies to tighten around captured animals, interfering with circulation until the prey dies.
Scientists suspect Vasuki may have hunted in a similar way, although its precise diet and hunting behavior cannot be determined from the surviving fossils.
Its anatomy also suggests that the snake may have spent much of its time on land or in shallow, swampy environments, rather than living exclusively in water. The ancient landscape surrounding the fossil site contained wetlands and marshes that could have provided suitable habitat for an enormous ambush predator.
Ancient India's Warm Climate May Have Helped Snakes Grow Enormous
The discovery also raises questions about why some prehistoric snakes reached sizes far beyond those of most species alive today.
During the Middle Eocene, the region where Vasuki lived experienced tropical conditions, with average temperatures estimated at approximately 28 degrees Celsius (82 degrees Fahrenheit).
Snakes are ectothermic animals, meaning they depend heavily on external sources of heat to regulate their body temperature. Warm environments can support the activity, digestion, and growth of large reptiles, potentially helping explain why exceptionally large snakes appeared during some of Earth's warmer periods.
However, temperature alone does not determine how large a snake can become. Food availability, suitable habitat, evolutionary history, and other environmental factors also influence body size.
A Lost Lineage of Giant Snakes That Spread Across Continents
Beyond its extraordinary size, Vasuki provides evidence of an ancient branch of snake evolution.
The species belonged to Madtsoiidae, an extinct family of snakes that survived for roughly 100 million years, from the Late Cretaceous to the Late Pleistocene. Members of this group occupied regions including India, Africa, Europe, South America, and Australia.
Unlike modern anacondas and pythons, Vasuki represented a separate evolutionary lineage within this long-extinct family.
The researchers found that its closest relatives included Madtsoia pisdurensis, a fossil snake from ancient India, and Gigantophis garstini, another large prehistoric snake known from North Africa.
These relationships suggest that a lineage of giant madtsoiid snakes originated on the Indian subcontinent before spreading into other parts of the world.
As India moved northward and collided with Asia around 50 million years ago, changing geographic connections may have allowed these snakes to disperse through southern Eurasia, including southern Europe, and eventually into Africa during the Eocene, approximately 56 to 34 million years ago.
Later Fossil Discoveries Reveal an Ancient World Filled With Snakes
Research published in 2025 has added important context to the discovery of Vasuki.
In a study published in the Journal of Paleontology, Datta and Bajpai described additional fossil snakes from Eocene deposits in western India. Their findings revealed a surprisingly diverse community of ancient reptiles, including aquatic snakes, another large member of the madtsoiid family, and other extinct snake groups.
Among the discoveries was Pterosphenus rannensis, an ancient aquatic snake species that adds to scientists' understanding of how these reptiles evolved and spread.
The researchers also identified another madtsoiid snake that appears to have shared a marshy environment with Vasuki. This suggests that the giant predator was part of a broader community of snakes occupying different ecological roles, rather than an isolated evolutionary oddity.
Evidence from the fossil deposits indicates that some of these snakes inhabited tidal environments, while others occupied swamps and marshes. Together, the discoveries paint a more detailed picture of the complex ecosystems that existed in India tens of millions of years ago.
What Modern Anacondas Reveal About Giant Snakes
Additional evidence about snake gigantism emerged from a separate 2025 study published in the Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology.
Researchers examining fossilized anaconda vertebrae from Venezuela found that these enormous snakes had already evolved large bodies by approximately 12.4 million years ago. Ancient anacondas reached estimated lengths of around 5.2 meters (17 feet), comparable to the size of many living anacondas.
The findings suggest that anacondas maintained their impressive size for millions of years, even as climates and ecosystems changed. They also show that prehistoric snakes did not necessarily grow larger simply because the planet was warmer.
Although anacondas are evolutionarily distinct from Vasuki, the research offers a useful comparison for understanding how different snake lineages became giants and adapted to their environments.
For Vasuki indicus, the full story remains incomplete. Its precise size, appearance, and behavior are still uncertain, but the fossil evidence establishes it as an extraordinary example of prehistoric gigantism.
Together with later discoveries from the same region, the ancient snake is helping scientists reconstruct a largely forgotten world in which massive serpents occupied the tropical landscapes of India.

Journal References:

- Debajit Datta, Sunil Bajpai. Fossil snakes from the Eocene of India: new material with comments on phylogenetic relations and biogeographic and paleoecological implications. Journal of Paleontology, 2025; 99 (2): 403 DOI: 10.1017/jpa.2025.10101
- Andrés F. Alfonso-Rojas, Jorge D. Carrillo-Briceño, Rodolfo Sánchez, Marcelo R. Sánchez-Villagra, Jason J. Head. An early origin of gigantism in anacondas (Serpentes: Eunectes ) revealed by the fossil record. Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology, 2025; 45 (4) DOI: 10.1080/02724634.2025.2572967

Cheese tart, corn salad, squash with ’nduja, radicchio salad: Joe Otway’s recipes for early autumn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
05:00:46 UTC
14:00:46 KST

Early autumn is one of the most generous and comforting times of year to cook with British produce: sweetcorn is at its peak, squash begins to sweeten as the weather cools and bitter leaves such as radicchio provide balance to the season’s abundance. Today’s recipes are simple celebrations of British ingredients, using just a handful of carefully chosen components to let each vegetable shine. Whether it’s a buttery cheese tart for sharing; a fresh, herby corn salad; sweet roast squash with warm, spicy ’nduja; or bitter leaves lifted with a floral dressing, they all rely on cooking with ingredients at their seasonal peak and allowing nature to guide the menu.
Cheese tart
Prep 10 min
Chill 30 min+
Cook 1 hr
Makes 4 individual tarts
90g unsalted butter, plus extra for greasing
120g plain flour, plus extra for dusting
110g mature cheddar, finely grated
70g whole eggs
25ml whole milk
10g ready-made English mustard, or to taste
110ml double cream
Sea salt and black pepper
First, make the pastry. Rub the butter into the flour until the mix resembles coarse breadcrumbs, then add 60g of the grated cheddar and knead gently until the mix comes together into a dough. Divide into four, wrap and chill for at least 30 minutes.
Meanwhile, make the custard. Blend the eggs, milk, remaining 50g grated cheddar and mustard until smooth, then stir in the cream by hand and season to taste.
Heat the oven to 180C (160C fan)/350F/gas 4, and grease and line four individual 8-10cm tart tins. Lightly flour a work surface, roll out each piece of pastry, then use to line the tins. Line each pastry base with baking paper, fill with baking beans or similar, then blind bake for 15 minutes, until lightly golden. Lift out the paper and beans, then return the tarts to the oven for a further five minutes, until the bases are crisp and golden.
Carefully pour the custard into each tart case until they’re almost full, then bake for another 15-25 minutes, depending on your oven (the actual temperature of domestic ovens varies a fair bit, after all), until the custard is lightly browned and just set with a slight wobble in the centre.
Leave to cool to room temperature, then serve, either with a bitter leaf salad or with one of the following two sides.
Corn salad with soured cream and oregano
Prep 5 min
Cook 15 min
Serves 4
Sea salt and black pepper
4 fresh sweetcorn cobs, or 1 400g tin good-quality sweetcorn
150g soured cream
100ml extra-virgin olive oil
Juice of ½ lemon
Sea salt
20g fresh oregano leaves, plus extra to garnish
30g parmesan, shaved
Bring a large pan of salted water to a boil, drop in the corn cobs, cook for four or five minutes, until tender, then drain and refresh. Once the cobs are cool enough to handle, cut off the kernels and put in a bowl (if you’re using tinned corn, skip the blanching stage and simply drain the water from the can).
Mix the soured cream with 20ml of the olive oil, the lemon juice and a pinch of salt. Blend the oregano with the remaining olive oil until fragrant. Dress the sweetcorn with the oregano oil, then season generously with salt and a little more lemon juice, if needed.
Spread the soured cream mix over a platter, spoon the dressed corn on top, scatter over a few more oregano leaves and finish with generous shavings of parmesan and a final twist of black pepper.
Roast winter squash with ’nduja
Prep 10 min
Cook 45 min
Serves 4
1kg winter squash (uchiki kuri is ideal, although butternut works well too), halved, deseeded and cut into skin-on wedges
5 tbsp olive oil
Sea salt
20g pumpkin seeds
120g ’nduja
2 tbsp good-quality honey
150g Greek yoghurt
1 tbsp lemon juice
1 small handful flat-leaf parsley, leaves picked and roughly chopped
Heat the oven to 220C (200C fan)/425F/gas 7. Toss the squash wedges with two tablespoons of the olive oil and a generous pinch of salt, then arrange on an oven tray and roast for 30-40 minutes, turning every 10 minutes, until tender and caramelised. Add the pumpkin seeds to the tray for the final 10 minutes of cooking.
Meanwhile, in a small saucepan gently warm the ’nduja, honey and the remaining olive oil until the mix comes together into a loose dressing. In a small bowl, mix the yoghurt with the lemon juice and a pinch of salt.
Spread the yoghurt on a platter, arrange the squash wedges and toasted pumpkin seeds on top, then spoon over the warm ’nduja dressing. Finish with the parsley and serve.
Radicchio with elderflower vinaigrette
Yes, elderflower is an early-summer flavour, but that’s why they invented cordial, so we can enjoy that gentle fragrance all year round.
Prep 10 min
Serves 4
3 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil
2 tbsp elderflower cordial
2 tbsp white-wine vinegar
1 tsp dijon mustard
Sea salt and black pepper
2 heads bitter leaves – radicchio, treviso, chicory or endive will all work well here
40g hard sheep’s cheese, or pecorino
In a small bowl, whisk the oil, cordial, vinegar, mustard, and salt and pepper to taste, until lightly emulsified.
Trim the bases off the radicchio heads, then separate the leaves and put them in a medium bowl. Dress the leaves generously with the vinaigrette, then season with a little more salt and pepper if needed. Leave to marinate for five to 10 minutes, so the leaves soften slightly and absorb the dressing, then arrange on a serving plate and finish with generous shavings of the cheese.
- Joe Otway is chef/co-owner of Higher Ground, Bar Shrimp and Flawd, all in Manchester.

UK will not put tariffs on Chinese vehicles, says Jonathan Reynolds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
05:00:45 UTC
14:00:45 KST

The business secretary has hit back at European demands for British tariffs on Chinese imports, saying the government will not change its trade rules because of pressure from Brussels.
Jonathan Reynolds warned that the government would not bow to calls from other countries for the UK to hit Chinese vehicles with import taxes, despite political pressure to align with the EU in exchange for deeper future economic ties.
The EU imposed tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles in 2024 and last Friday agreed a 350,000 a year quota on Chinese hybrid cars amid fears cheaper alternatives are causing deindustrialisation and job losses.
Reynolds conceded that levying sanctions on Chinese goods was an option in the future, but he dismissed concerns from Brussels that the UK could provide a back door to the European market.
His comments highlight the divisions that remain between the UK and EU on trade and industrial policy, which could derail the prime minister’s attempts to move closer to Brussels.
“I just want to be clear: when we make any trade decision in terms of trade defence tariffs in relation to the EU, that’s based on the UK interest – it’s not based on any other country asking for that,” said Reynolds during a trade trip to India.
“In 2024, [we] looked at this issue carefully, and we keep it under review depending on what the needs of industry are … But it comes down to what is the fundamental nature of the UK automotive sector. It’s an export-led sector, so that’s what I’ve got to take into account.”
With Europe having imposed tariffs of up to 45% on Chinese electric cars, some believe that the UK has opened an alternative route into the EU for Chinese companies setting up in the UK to sell into the bloc.
Nissan, for instance, has agreed to look at building cars in northern England for the Chinese manufacturer Chery.
Reynolds rebutted those accusations, however, saying: “The UK currently has no major Chinese manufacturer based in its automotive sector, so we’re not making vehicles here and sending them to the single market through some sort of back door.”
His comments raise the stakes ahead of intense final weeks of negotiations before the long-awaited UK-EU summit, which Andy Burnham confirmed this week would be held in Brussels on 20 November.
The prime minister told the Commons on Monday he wanted a “serious dialogue” over the UK’s place in Europe, as he framed the summit as a possible first step to EU membership.
The new Made in Europe trade rules aim to protect European companies from subsidised Chinese imports, but British manufacturers worry they will also be shut out of supply chains.
The issue will not formally be on the agenda at the November summit, but British officials are hoping to use those talks to shape the European legislation.
Diplomats on both sides of the Channel say the summit will now be an early test of whether Burnham’s desire for a “real reset” in UK-EU relations is likely to bear fruit.
One EU official said this week that the UK’s negotiating position would determine whether it was worth pursuing more fundamental changes such as British access to the single market, a new customs union or re-accession.
Some in Brussels have been pushing for Britain to levy tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles in return for getting access to the European market under the new trade rules.
Reynolds has previously dismissed such an option in part because of the risk that Beijing could hit the UK with reciprocal tariffs, damaging British companies such as Jaguar Land Rover.
He said it would be to Europe’s detriment if it did not admit the UK into the scheme. “If you look at the impact analysis of such a policy, the consequences for the EU [of] excluding the UK are much more difficult,” he said.
“This is not just in the UK’s interest; it’s not in the EU’s interest because obviously we have integrated supply chains.”
Reynolds said the summit was an important milestone in EU-UK relations but also insisted that new trading terms for electricity, emissions and food and drink products would be a major achievement in themselves.
Speaking from a two-day trade delegation to Delhi and Mumbai, he acknowledged that the landmark free trade agreement he helped strike last year with India would become defunct if Britain does rejoin the EU.
“Obviously, if you enter those arrangements, you are doing things collectively. So there would be trade relationships with the UK that were based on Europe, the EU as a whole – that is how the European Union works in terms of its relationship.
“That’s why obviously when we were part of it, we didn’t have these separate bespoke arrangements.”
But he insisted that it remained worth continuing to push to broaden the scope of the agreement, as he unveiled a series of UK-India investments which officials say are worth over £1bn to the UK over the next 15 years.
The deal has already begun to reduce the price of Scotch whisky in Indian shops, after tariffs were reduced from 150% to 75%. Now British officials are keen to free up trade in services as well as goods, for example, pushing for both countries to recognise each other’s legal qualifications.
“There are some specific things regarding who can practice law and in which area,” Reynolds said. “I am confident over the medium to long term that this will improve over time.”
He added: “We’ve got to be cognisant of this long-term position with the EU. But frankly, there’s a job to be done here and now, which we’re doing.”

Global financial system is failing developing countries, says Ed Miliband
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
05:00:45 UTC
14:00:45 KST

The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, will claim the global financial system is failing developing countries, as he calls for a “new deal” for governments struggling under the burden of debt.
Promising to throw the UK’s diplomatic weight behind urgent reform, he will evoke the example of the Gleneagles summit under the last Labour government in 2005 – the culmination of the Make Poverty History campaign.
“The global financial system and indeed the global order is failing to serve developing countries on debt, on resilience and on climate. This is not just against our values but against our national interest,” Miliband is expected to say.
“In the interconnected world we live in, more than ever, the opportunities and challenges we confront are collective.”
Speaking in Bangkok on Wednesday, he will call for the World Bank and other multilateral development banks (MDBs) to use the resources they have available to lighten the load for governments trapped by hefty borrowing costs.
“We need action on developing country debt through the MDBs,” he is expected to say. “Action that leverages the balance sheets of the international financial institutions to support these countries to repay over longer time horizons, and crucially, refinancing, with better rates, to give them precious fiscal space.”
The foreign secretary will be in Bangkok to attend the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank annual meetings.
He opted to take up the UK’s seat on the bank’s board himself instead of leaving it to the development minister, Kirsty McNeill.
Labour’s manifesto in 2024 promised to restore the UK’s international reputation on development issues – but Keir Starmer subsequently slashed the aid budget to pay for defence.
Campaigners have long claimed the high interest rates paid by many developing countries mean the repayments crowd out vital public spending – including on tackling the climate emergency. In sub-Saharan Africa, more than three times as much is spent on debt servicing as on education.
Miliband will argue that making the global financial system work better for emerging economies will also help to attract more private investment – a key aim of the World Bank under the current president, Ajay Banga.
The UK is due to take up the presidency of the G20 group of nations next year – a key global forum for discussing global financial issues, including sovereign debt, which includes emerging economies such as China, India, South Africa and Brazil.
The chancellor, John Healey, will set out his own G20 priorities in Bangkok later this week, including mobilising more resources from the balance sheets of the IMF and the World Bank.
When the UK held the chair of the narrower G8 group in 2005, at the leaders’ summit at the Gleneagles hotel the UK secured agreements that eventually resulted in more than 30 countries receiving large-scale debt write-downs.
Miliband will say resources are now more constrained – but as well as debt refinancing for a large number of countries, he will demand an overhaul of the “common framework” for restructuring the debts of countries unable to pay.
The framework is widely criticised as too slow and cumbersome. Among other reforms, the UK wants to see changes to ensure private creditors cannot hold up negotiations – as has happened in recent cases including that of Ethiopia.
The foreign secretary will also call for overhauls to allow help to be made available more rapidly to countries in trouble. “We need finance teed up in advance of crises, so that governments get support in days, not months,” he will say.
Miliband will be speaking at the launch of a report by the Rockefeller Foundation that calls for a “surge” in affordable financing from the IMF and the World Bank to debt-burdened countries.
Tim Jones, the policy director of the campaign group Debt Justice, welcomed Miliband’s focus on the issue but said a litmus test of any plan would be whether private sector creditors bear some of the costs. “Action on debt relief is urgently needed. That must include private lenders sharing in the cost. Otherwise public money will just bail out private lenders rather than be used for investment.”

Palantir is worming its way into the British state – it’s time to curb this controversial US company’s influence | George Monbiot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
05:00:44 UTC
14:00:44 KST

What a world we live in. Imagine: gangs dragging civil servants off commuter trains and beating them up because they handed government data jobs to the wrong contractor – and the government is changing its procurement decisions as a result. Well, OK, it might not have happened yet, but it’s only a matter of time. As the former Labour deputy leader Tom Watson asks: “Do you want to let the rule of law lead procurement practice, or do you want mob rule to lead procurement practices?” No, I absolutely don’t want the latter, and it’s always good to get ahead of trouble.
But then I remember there are two common meanings of mob rule. One is intimidation by crowds of thugs. The other is a pejorative term for democracy. And while I’ve yet to see government procurement practices in the UK determined by pitchforks and flaming torches, democratic transparency could be a genuine threat to certain contractors. One might have hoped that Watson, who once took on the Murdoch empire, would have recognised the distinction. But then again, one might have hoped that Watson would not have taken a job as a senior vice-president at Palantir.
Over the past few years, this US company has been worming its way into the British state. It has landed contracts worth hundreds of millions with the Ministry of Defence, several police forces, the Financial Conduct Authority, the atomic weapons establishment and the NHS. Its superpower, according to a deep investigation by Peter Geoghegan and Lucas Amin in the London Review of Books, is that it is “willing to spend more on securing political access than almost all of its British and continental competitors”. It made abundant use of Peter Mandelson’s company Global Counsel, which seems, in turn, to have made abundant use of the UK’s remarkably flimsy lobbying laws. Watson is one of more than 30 former UK ministers and officials Palantir now employs.
Palantir’s contracts might have been awarded lawfully, but some of us might question the ways in which doors were opened for it. These include an unrecorded meeting between Boris Johnson, Dominic Cummings and the co-founder of Palantir, Peter Thiel, in Downing Street in 2019. It was invited back to Downing Street when the Covid-19 pandemic began a few months later, and was working in the NHS within days, on a contract for which it charged only £1. The mayor of London, Sadiq Khan, has criticised such loss-leaders, which can quickly lead to reliance on a company, at which point it can name its price.
Another controversial meeting was brokered by Mandelson in 2025, when he was UK ambassador to the US. Keir Starmer visited Palantir’s showroom in Washington, where he met the company’s global and UK chief executives, Alex Karp and Louis Mosley. They talked about defence spending. No 10, Geoghegan and Amin tell us, “refused to say whether Starmer knew that Palantir was a client of Global Counsel, in which Mandelson still held a stake of around a fifth at the time. The meeting was never declared on transparency registers.” A few months later, Palantir secured a £241m contract with the Ministry of Defence, without an open tender.
Now we learn that Martha Dalton, a key player in Andy Burnham’s campaign to win the Makerfield byelection, enabling him to become prime minister, was on unpaid leave from the lobbying company she co-founded, Lodestone. Lodestone had done extensive work for Palantir. And the Financial Times reports that Samantha Jones, then the lead non-executive director on the board of the health department, was an adviser to one of Palantir’s partners when the company was bidding for its huge and controversial NHS contract. Now she is permanent secretary in the same department.
There have been repeated allegations that some of Palantir’s products are rubbish. But, as the House of Commons science, innovation and technology committee warns, government agencies can quickly succumb to “vendor lock-in”: once you start using them, it can be very hard to stop.
Thiel, has claimed that “the NHS makes people sick”, and that we should “just rip the whole thing from the ground and start over”. The company is deeply embedded in the Trump administration, where it supplies software that helps ICE find undocumented people. It also works for the Israeli government on identifying targets in Gaza. When Karp was confronted by a protester who told him that “Palantir kills Palestinians”, he replied: “Mostly terrorists, that’s true.”
This is the company handling our critical information. After official denials, it turns out that NHS England has granted Palantir “unlimited access” to patient data. This is a huge issue. Identifiable patient data is supposed to be visible only to people directly involved in a patient’s care, or who have received the patient’s informed consent. There are widespread concerns about how this and other datasets might be used.
So, as Palantir runs into ever-greater controversy, it’s not hard to see why it might have hired Watson, who, with Burnham, was a minister in Gordon Brown’s government. I wouldn’t presume to speculate about what attracted Watson to the multibillion-dollar company.
In July, the government’s ethics and integrity commission recommended a major shake-up, enabling us to see all the encounters between lobbyists and ministers, aides and senior officials. I’ve heard this call many times before. The pattern is always the same: a scandal, followed by a call to action, followed by … little or nothing.
Before he became prime minister, David Cameron noted that lobbying “has tainted our politics for too long”. He would shine “the light of transparency” on it. Instead, he oversaw an act that was “more loophole than law”. It did nothing to protect us from lobbying by people such as Cameron – pulling strings, once out of office, among his old colleagues, to try to drum up government business for the bank Greensill .
You could almost believe that the real purpose of government was to do the bidding of corporations, foreign states and the ultra-rich. You could almost believe that some government ministers may have an eye on future opportunities when they resist effective reform.
So this is another key test for Burnham. Will he allow the mob rule of private business to keep dominating our lives, or will he ensure that government is for the people?
- George Monbiot is a Guardian columnist

World's oldest shipwreck found off coast of Turkey
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
06:00:35 BST
14:00:35 KST

World's oldest shipwreck found off coast of Turkey
- Published
The world's oldest shipwreck has been discovered off the coast of Turkey, archaeologists say.
They have dated it to between 4,400 and 4,700 years old, which is the Early Bronze Age, and is around the same time that the Great Pyramid was being built.
The ship's wooden structure has not survived, but the ceramic storage pots it was carrying were lying on the sea floor and, remarkably, some still contain traces of what they held inside.
The archaeologists who found the ship say it was about 10m in length and was a trade vessel carrying cargo across the Mediterranean Sea.
"The shipwreck is a time capsule at the bottom of the sea," said Prof Hakan Öniz, from Akdeniz University in Turkey, who led the Mediterranean Archaeology Association expedition.
The wreck is close to the shore of Kekova Island in Antalya, Turkey. The artefacts lie scattered across an underwater slope, just 30m beneath the waves.
Three large stone anchors were found, as well as more than 30 ceramic storage pots, called amphorae.
The fact that none of the ship's wood remained meant techniques like radiocarbon dating - which measures a form of carbon in organic materials - could not be used to determine its age.
Instead, archaeologists analysed the shape of the amphorae. Because pottery styles have changed over time, different styles are linked to particular periods.
The Kekova ceramics are distinctive, with two handles, a ridge in the middle and a flat base.
Öniz said this design matched other amphorae unearthed in Egypt and the Middle East that were known to be 4,400-4,700 years old.
"Comparing the decoration techniques… we can definitely say our wreck is Early Bronze Age. This is 100%."
Divers from the expedition brought the pots up to the surface, where they are now being carefully conserved after so many thousands of years underwater.
Dr Karin Sowada, an archaeologist from Macquarie University, Australia, examined the amphorae after they were recovered. Some were intact and she was surprised to see they still contained a viscous, glossy residue.
"I looked inside and nearly fainted. I could not believe how much [residue] was visible. It wasn't just like spots…. a lot of this material was still remaining," she said.
The team is now working to find out exactly what was being carried in the amphorae.
"It could be olive oil, it could be wine, it could be tree resins," Sowada said.
"It's possible that [the residue] could actually be the result of reuse of the jars. I mean, these jars are huge - they're not things that you just ship away and then never see again. People would have emptied these jars on arrival and potentially used them for many, many, many years."
The wreck and its cargo are also shedding light on trade in the ancient world.
The archaeologists say the ship started its voyage from somewhere along the eastern coast of the Mediterranean.
They believe it was taking goods to either the ancient city of Troy, in what is now north-western Turkey, or to the Minoan people in Crete.
Travelling by sea was fraught with danger, particularly around Kekova Island, where the strong currents and winds have claimed many ships.
There are hundreds of wrecks in the area, and the Mediterranean Archaeology Association specialises in finding and studying them.
Öniz says that when he is diving on the wreck his first thoughts are about the lives of the people who were connected to this vessel.
"We are the first humans who [have] touched these objects after 5,000 years.
"We are always thinking of the sailors... the producers of the amphora and the person who carried the amphora on their shoulders to the ship, and the women who were waiting for their husbands, and they unfortunately couldn't go back."
The shipwreck is owned by the Turkish Ministry of Culture. Its minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy said the artefacts that have been recovered would be put on display in the new Mediterranean Underwater Archaeology Museum in Antalya when it opens in the coming months.
The Kekova discovery now tops the list of the world's oldest shipwrecks.
Previously, the record holder was a wreck off the coast of Dokos, an island in southern Greece, which dates to about 4,200 years ago.
The oldest known intact shipwreck, where the wood is still preserved, was found in the Black Sea off the coast of Bulgaria. It dates to about 2,400 years ago.

Missile alert interrupts Saudi minister mid-speech (VIDEO)

The incident occurred at the Riyadh International Convention and Exhibition Centre, when warning notifications sounded simultaneously on the minister’s phone and those of audience members.
Al Rajhi, the human resources and social development minister, briefly acknowledged the alerts before calmly continuing his speech.
“We are under the protection of the Lord of the Worlds. God willing, may God turn their plot back upon them,” he told the audience.
The interruption came after two consecutive Houthi attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh over the weekend, which killed more than a dozen people, including several foreign nationals.
Residents reported hearing several powerful explosions in the Saudi capital on Monday night, according to Al Jazeera. The Saudi military said its air defenses had intercepted at least one Houthi ballistic missile targeting Riyadh, along with two additional projectiles launched toward the southwestern city of Khamis Mushait.
Saudi Arabia’s aviation authority announced on Monday that Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport would remain closed until October 17 following the deadly strikes.
The Houthis claimed responsibility for Saturday’s attack. In an exclusive interview with RT, Mohammed al-Bukhaiti, a spokesperson for the group, described the strike as retaliation for years of Saudi bombardment of Yemen’s civilian infrastructure.
He warned that the Houthis would continue targeting Saudi military facilities and critical infrastructure until Riyadh ended its involvement in Yemen, lifted its blockade and agreed to a “comprehensive and permanent peace.”
Saudi Arabia intervened in Yemen’s civil war in 2015, leading a military coalition supporting the internationally recognized government against the Houthis.
Large-scale fighting largely subsided following a UN-brokered truce in 2022 but flared up again in July after Saudi-backed Yemeni forces struck the Houthi-held Sanaa Airport.
Last month, the Houthis seized large stretches of Yemen’s Red Sea coast and territory around the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait, including the port of Mocha.
Saudi-backed government forces have since launched a counteroffensive, claiming to have recaptured key positions near the vital shipping route connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.
Riyadh has stepped up its air support for the offensive, intensifying strikes on Houthi-held territory in recent days. According to the group, Saudi bombardments have killed nearly 400 people since early September, many of them civilians.

Beyond the Box: What Shipping Container Architecture Gets Right and Where It Falls Short
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

Using shipping containers as the basis for a structure—also known as "cargotecture"—seems like a simple approach to building. Perhaps deceptively so. While it's true that containers are a quick, cost-effective, and often low-effort building material, and that they're durable and customizable, container conversions also bring their challenges. Without careful planning, the build process can be painful and the results underwhelming.
To understand whether containers are the right choice for a construction project, it's important to look past their industrial allure to the realities and constraints of steel boxes as a building material.
"Cargotecture" Challenges and Limitations
The use of shipping containers for architectural projects is an exercise in creating a beautiful and functional structure while overcoming an array of rigid constraints.
The most obvious is the width: at 2.44m, intermodal containers are only slightly wider than a caravan or motorhome. Side-opening containers can mitigate this constraint, or you can remove entire walls and connect two or more containers, though this brings engineering challenges, as will any alteration to the container's structure.
Another key hurdle is thermal conductivity. Containers are made from weathering steel, which gets cold in winter and hot in summer. Insulation and ventilation are critical, particularly for living and working spaces, but installing thick batts eats into the already limited space within the container.
There are a wealth of other challenges to navigate, from foundations to utility connections to the long-term mitigation of rust. Each, however, can be addressed through careful design and planning.
Overcoming Confines: Scandinavian-Inspired Tiny Home With Terrace
Despite a footprint of less than 14m², this tiny home uses a smart design to feel far larger. A clever internal layout creates distinct bed, kitchen, and bathroom spaces, while French doors open onto an outdoor terrace, extending usable space and bringing more natural light into the interior.
From Cramped to Open Plan: District 10 Container Building
Need more space than a container offers? Joining two or more containers can create a larger footprint, as demonstrated by this Dundee development, which uses more than 30 containers. Carefully removing internal walls and reinforcing the structure allows the individual units to function as a larger, more open-plan space.
Easy Access: Private Garage for Vehicle Preservation
Traditional containers feature doors at their ends, which can make access awkward, not just for home and workspace conversions, but for storage too. A car enthusiast faced this issue and solved it by converting a side-opening container that protects the vehicle while providing direct access.
Comfort in Extreme Temperatures: Dual-Layer Insulation
The thermal conductivity of steel means insulation is a must for any living or working space conversion. But extreme temperatures demand thick insulation, which can quickly eat into the limited space within a container. One approach is to combine internal insulation with external cladding, adding another layer of protection without taking up too much internal room.
Where Conventional Construction Still Wins
While shipping containers offer a range of advantages as a building material, for certain projects the cost-benefit analysis will still lean toward a traditional build. It's important to recognize the point at which extensive container modifications negate the financial and time advantages of modular steel.
This typically occurs when a build features complex geometries, wide-span clear spaces, or local zoning constraints that govern aesthetics. Container conversions can also have multi-decade lifespans, but they typically won't last as long as a traditional build.
Ultimately, containers shine in architecture when their intrinsic benefits—prefabrication, modularity, rapid assembly, the industrial look—are preserved, rather than modified beyond recognition.

Taiwan cites progress on Alaska LNG after Trump says it will buy 30% of output

- Trump said Taiwan would buy 30% of output, but Taiwan did not confirm a binding deal. The project still needs more agreements and financing.
- Alaska LNG could help Taiwan raise US gas imports to about one third by 2026. Developers aim for a final investment decision in 2026 and first exports in 2031.
AI generated
WASILLA, Alaska/TAIPEI – Taiwan said on Oct 14 it was making progress in talks to buy LNG from Alaska and would invest US$4.4 billion (S$5.64 billion) in the project after US President Donald Trump told a rally in the state that Taipei would buy 30% of its output.
Taiwan’s economy ministry said state-owned energy firm CPC Corp has made significant progress with the project developer after nearly a year and a half of negotiations and evaluation.
Alaska LNG, which would produce 20 million tonnes annually, has been discussed for decades, but many in the industry are sceptical about its commercial viability given that it requires a lengthy pipeline and capital that mean it would cost more than double a comparable US Gulf Coast plant, analysts have said.
Under the plan, CPC would purchase 6 million tonnes of Alaska LNG per year once production begins, in line with a letter of intent signed in 2025, and participate in the project’s development with an estimated investment of up to US$4.4 billion, the ministry said.
“Specific investment arrangements, equity stakes and related terms will be determined through subsequent negotiations and commercial contract procedures,” it said.
The ministry did not say whether a binding sale-and-purchase agreement had been signed.
Trump was in Alaska campaigning for Republican Senator Dan Sullivan, who is in a tight race against Democratic candidate Mary Peltola ahead of the Nov 3 congressional elections.
Taiwan officials said in February they would ramp up purchases of US natural gas to constitute about a third of the island’s imported supply in 2026, and reduce purchases from other countries.
Push to supply Asia
In 2025, Taiwan Presidential Office secretary-general Pan Men-an visited the site of the proposed LNG project in Alaska that the Trump administration has been pushing hard to allies in Asia as a supply option.
So far, Alaska LNG it has lined up agreements covering 13 million tonnes a year from buyers in Asia and French major TotalEnergies. It needs agreements for another 3 million tonnes and must turn them into binding deals in order to line up financing for the project.
It would open direct access for US-made LNG to Asian markets including Taiwan without having to go through the Panama Canal or around the Horn of Africa, reducing transit time and costs.
The project’s developers aim to take a final investment decision on the 1,287km pipeline in 2026, followed by the export facility in 2027, with first LNG exports targeted for 2031.
Trump said last month that South Korea had agreed to invest in the US$54 billion pipeline for the Alaska LNG project, but Seoul said it was not yet set in stone.
Taiwan was the No. 5 LNG importer in 2025 behind China, Japan, South Korea and India, shipping in 23.8 million tons of the super-chilled fuel, mostly from Australia and Qatar, according to Kpler data.
Taiwan’s economy ministry said on Oct 14 that if the project proceeded on schedule, it could begin supplying additional natural gas to Taiwan as early as 2032. REUTERS

Fair Friend Group has order visibility through the first quarter of 2027, with domestic orders mainly coming from the semiconductor and AI sectors. Its energy-sector customers are primarily involved in the US shale oil industry.
Quaser Machine Tools Inc. has an order backlog worth at least NT$2 billion, mainly from the aerospace and defense industries. Orders extend beyond the second quarter of 2027.
The company has also secured an order from a customer in the solid oxide fuel cell (SOFC) industry. Certification is expected to be completed in November, and the first set of equipment is scheduled to ship from the company’s UK plant by the end of the year.
At Shieh Yih Machinery Industry Co., orders related to AI server manufacturing have surpassed those for high-end household appliances this year. The company expects its order visibility to extend through the end of 2027.
Taiwan Takisawa Technology Co. has received orders mainly from manufacturers of AI server cooling systems, hydraulic pipe fittings, and drone components. Its order visibility extends through the second quarter of 2027.

As demand for AI servers and robots grows, manufacturers are investing in the equipment needed to produce their components, according to Gugu Fund and UDN Money.

Bipartisan US senators urge Trump to scrap Russian diesel deal
- Bipartisan US senators urged Trump to cancel his Russian diesel deal, calling it a “betrayal” that would help Moscow’s war in Ukraine.
- They said the diesel would do little to cut fuel prices, but would give the Kremlin more money and hurt US and allied security interests.
- The letter, led by Richard Blumenthal and backed by six Republicans, pressed Trump to revoke the licence and use tougher sanctions on Russia and its supporters.
AI generated
WASHINGTON - Republican and Democratic US senators joined forces on Oct 13 to urge President Donald Trump to scrap his diesel deal with Russia, calling it a “betrayal” that would bankroll Moscow’s war in Ukraine while doing little to ease soaring fuel prices.
The 12 lawmakers – including six members of Trump’s Republican Party – called on the president to reverse his agreement with Russian leader Vladimir Putin to allow the country’s diesel onto global markets.
“Granting Moscow the ability to sell Russian diesel freely in global markets damages American security interests and is a betrayal of the people of Ukraine, who continue to defend themselves from Putin’s murderous, illegal war,” they wrote in a letter spearheaded by Democrat Richard Blumenthal.
“This deal is a gift to our adversary and a betrayal of our Allies; it should be rescinded.”
The senators acknowledged the urgent need to reduce energy costs, which have surged amid the US war with Iran, but argued that the Russian supplies would have a negligible effect on prices.
Instead, they said, the deal would provide the Kremlin with additional revenue to finance its invasion of Ukraine, now in its fifth year.
The Republican signatories included former Senate majority leader Mitch McConnell and other senators with decades of experience, putting prominent members of Trump’s own party at odds with the president ahead of November’s midterm elections.
Trump announced on Oct 9 that Putin had agreed to release more than 300,000 tons of diesel immediately, with another 500,000 tons to follow in November, in an effort to curb fuel prices.
The US Treasury Department subsequently issued a temporary license allowing transactions involving Russian-origin diesel, including its sale and import.
The senators urged Trump to revoke the license and use new sanctions powers approved by Congress in September to increase economic pressure on Moscow and countries helping sustain its war, particularly China.
“Putin is a tyrant,” they wrote, demanding that Trump instead pursue a settlement that protects Ukraine’s sovereignty and security.
The senators’ scepticism over the economic benefits of the deal was echoed on Oct 13 by European Union economy chief Valdis Dombrovskis.
The proposed Russian diesel supplies were “not of any macroeconomic significance,” he told AFP, also questioning whether Moscow could deliver the promised volumes.
The agreement has added to tensions over Trump’s approach to the Ukraine war, with the US president repeatedly criticising Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries.
On Oct 10, Trump warned Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky that he “better damn well stop” the attacks.
Blumenthal accused Putin of exploiting the diplomatic impasse while seeking to inflict further hardship on Ukraine as winter approaches.
“Once again, he’s playing Trump for a fool,” he wrote on X. AFP

What is celebrated on October 14 in Ukraine and around the world
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
05:23:26 EEST
11:23:26 KST

What is celebrated on October 14 in Ukraine and around the world
Kyiv • UNN
October 14 marks World Standards Day, Environmental Education Day, World Spine Day, and Occupational Safety Day. According to church calendars, saints and the Intercession are commemorated.
On October 14, the world observes World Standards Day and World Environmental Education Day. According to the church calendar in the new style, the holy martyrs Nazarius, Gervasius, Protasius and Celsus, the venerable Paraskeva of Serbia and the venerable Nicholas Sviatosha are commemorated, while according to the old style, the great feast of the Protection of the Most Holy Theotokos is celebrated, UNN writes.
World Standards Day
The official date was established in 1970 to commemorate October 14, 1946, when the first conference of national standards organizations opened in London, laying the foundation for the creation of the International Organization for Standardization.
The event unites the efforts of ISO, IEC, that is, the International Electrotechnical Commission, and ITU, the International Telecommunication Union, to highlight the role of unified technical standards, protocols and quality requirements in global trade and consumer safety.
World Environmental Education Day
The date was established in 1972 during the United Nations Conference on the Human Environment in Stockholm and formalized at the UNESCO and UNEP conference in Tbilisi in 1977.
The main goal of the day is to raise public environmental awareness, implement sustainable development programs in educational institutions, preserve biodiversity, and foster a caring attitude in society toward natural resources and the planet's climate.
World Spine Day / World Back Day
A medical initiative under the auspices of the World Federation of Chiropractic, supported by international orthopedic organizations. The event draws attention to the widespread prevalence of spinal diseases, musculoskeletal disorders and chronic back pain.
The day emphasizes the importance of physical activity, correct posture in the workplace, ergonomics and the prevention of a sedentary lifestyle.
International Safety Officer Day
A professional observance dedicated to specialists who ensure compliance with safety regulations, protect workers' health and prevent occupational injuries at enterprises and construction sites around the world.
Remembrance Day of the Holy Martyrs Nazarius, Gervasius, Protasius and Celsus
According to the new calendar, Orthodox and Greek Catholic believers commemorate the holy martyrs Nazarius, Gervasius, Protasius and Celsus, who suffered for the Christian faith in Milan in the 1st century during the reign of Emperor Nero.
This day also commemorates the venerable Paraskeva of Serbia — an ascetic who practiced her spiritual life in the Jordan Valley, known for her prayerful silence and miracles, and the venerable Nicholas Sviatosha, who renounced the princely throne and wealth and took monastic vows at the Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra.
According to the old calendar, believers celebrate the great great feast of the Protection of the Most Holy Theotokos. The feast was established to commemorate the apparition of the Mother of God in the Blachernae Church in Constantinople in the 10th century, when She spread her omophorion over the praying people and protected the city from an enemy siege.
According to the old style, the venerable Romanos the Melodist is also commemorated — a prominent Byzantine church hymnographer and author of many kontakia.

Demonstrations backing France’s protesting students gather strength
- Tens of thousands marched across France to back protesting students demanding better school conditions, putting more pressure on President Emmanuel Macron as his term ends.
- The interior ministry said 161,500 joined rallies, while unions claimed 480,000. Most protests were peaceful, but clashes in Paris and Lyon led to tear gas, fires and injuries.
- Students and unions rejected the government’s offer of 3,000 substitute teachers, saying they want real action and dialogue, not repression, as more protests are planned on Oct 17.
AI generated
PARIS - Tens of thousands of people joined rallies across France on Oct 13 to support protesting high school students demanding better conditions in a major challenge to President Emmanuel Macron as his term winds down.
Some 161,500 people turned out in the rallies, according to the interior ministry – more than double the 71,500 estimate it gave for demonstrations on Oct 8.
Although most of the demonstrations were peaceful, violence erupted on the sidelines of one of two Paris marches that the interior ministry said drew 41,500 people.
AFP journalists saw some cars set on fire and police fired tear gas in the Invalides square as masked youths tried to erect barricades across roads and threw objects.
Tear gas was also fired during a demonstration in Lyon.
Swedish activist Greta Thunberg took part in one demonstration in the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis.
She said she had joined the protests because “our future is being robbed”.
French unions said 480,000 people took part in the rallies and the numbers suggested increased street opposition to the government just six months before a vote for a successor to Macron, who is completing his maximum second mandate.
The latest agitation came as the centrist government launched a debate in Parliament on a cost-cutting budget, facing fierce opposition from the left and right, while France’s worsening debt has spooked the bond market.
Pressure will increase as on Oct 17 national demonstrations against the cost of living are to take place, and unions and student groups see the two protest currents merging.
The students have been given strong backing by the far-left opposition France Unbowed (LFI) party whose leader and presidential hopeful Jean-Luc Melenchon was seen among crowds in Paris.
Dialogue, ‘not repression’
Thousands also marched in the cities of Nantes, Lyon, Lens, Strasbourg, Toulouse, Bordeaux and Marseille, according to police and AFP reporters.
“We stand in solidarity with the high schools that are worse off. We need real measures and proper dialogue, not repression,” said 16-year-old Emeline, outside a Marseille school.
“We’re here because we really feel we’re not being heard by the government,” said Nina, 17.
The student movement sprang up in September at lycees – high schools for those aged 15 to 18 – with students blocking the entrances to many schools to demand better classroom conditions.
Perceived heavy-handed police action against the students drove many to join Oct 13’s demonstrations.
One teen lost his hand when he picked up a police stun grenade during the protests, while another lost an eye, and another teeth when an officer fired a tear gas canister in his face.
Police have opened internal investigations into 36 allegations of violence against demonstrators, according to Interior Minister Laurent Nunez who said nearly 900 police had suffered injuries during the protests.
Some 147 teaching staff have been injured, the education ministry said.
‘Not budging’
“We’re not giving up the fight, whether it’s for the high school students who were hit with a harsh crackdown, or for denouncing police violence,” said Patricia, a 20-year-old university student in Paris who did not give her last name.
Some Indian tourists who wandered into the Paris demonstration said they were unnerved.
“Initially we were terrified,” said Snehil Jain, a 45-year-old visiting Paris for a week with his wife.
“We had seen the media images of violence around these protests. But then we saw it was a peaceful protest, so we were OK then.”
France’s education ministry said 214 schools, mostly high schools, were closed on Oct 13.
University student union l’Union Etudiante reported 90% of universities had closed nationwide to show support.
French students say they are determined to press their demands over absent teachers, dilapidated buildings, overcrowded schedules and other grievances.
They have dismissed a government pledge – made after last week’s demonstrations – to send 3,000 substitute teachers to the 114 worst-affected schools.
“We are continuing the blockades. We are not budging,” said Naouel, a high school student in Brest. She said she hoped the protests would continue after the half-term holidays, in late October.
On Oct 12, Macron had urged restraint from protesters, saying the issues “deserve time, consultations, discussion and respect”. AFP

US deploys hundreds of troops to Latin America amid anti-drug campaign — report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
00:59:35 UTC
09:59:35 KST

The United States has deployed several hundred soldiers to Latin America to conduct training with regional armed forces, as the Pentagon significantly expands its military campaign against narcotics trafficking networks, The New York Times reported.
Citing unnamed US military officials, the report stated that initial elements of a 600-soldier battalion from the 10th Mountain Division, based at Fort Drum, New York, have begun occupying a newly established jungle training facility in Panama.
The personnel are scheduled to train alongside armed forces in Colombia and Honduras, with potential missions supporting US Special Operations troops advising partner units on direct counter-cartel raids.
Other division personnel will help staff a newly formed Western Hemisphere operations command in Miami.
The troop movements follow the redeployment of multiple MQ-9 Reaper drones from Africa to Colombia and Ecuador, alongside the establishment of a dedicated counter-cartel oversight office by Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth.
Southern Vanguard
The deployed soldiers will participate later this month in the Southern Vanguard joint military exercises in Colombia.
While US officials described the deployments as rotational, they acknowledged the mission could evolve into an enduring regional military presence.
Washington continues to lobby regional governments to authorise combined operations and escalate offensives against cartels, though only a few countries—including Colombia and Honduras—have formally agreed.
To date, the US military has executed 71 boat strikes across the Caribbean and eastern Pacific, killing at least 239 individuals it claimed, without making evidence public, were narcotics traffickers.
